purpose: Mistakes found in published sources by the atlas's workers (research/blueprint/PROTOCOL.md section 18).

issues.locator: §1.5 Notation, p. 8
issues.printed: The source defines Sp2r(R) as the standard symplectic group acting on the free R-module generated by e_i, f_i (1 ≤ i ≤ g). Its form satisfies ⟨e_i, f_j⟩ = δ_ij, together with ⟨e_i, e_j⟩ = ⟨f_i, f_j⟩ = 1. It sets Sp(R) := lim_g Sp2r(R) and describes automorphisms of R^{2g}.
issues.correction: ⟨e_i, e_j⟩ = ⟨f_i, f_j⟩ = 0, with 1 ≤ i ≤ r, the limit over r and R^{2r}.
issues.reason: With ⟨e_i, e_i⟩ = 1 the form is not alternating, so its automorphism group is not a symplectic group; the index g is the genus elsewhere in the paper, while the rank parameter is r.

issues.locator: §2.4, Theorem 2.2, p. 14
issues.printed: The source assumes an oriented 4r-manifold N with oriented boundary M = ∂N, together with a symplectic local system ρ on N.
issues.correction: N is an oriented manifold of dimension divisible by 4 (Appendix B.8 takes N of dimension 2k with k even); the case used is dim N = 4 with M a 3-manifold.
issues.reason: r is the half-rank of ρ (ρ is Sp_{2r}-valued), so as printed the hypothesis would tie dim N to the rank of ρ. The proof in Appendix B.8 and every application (§§2.4, 2.3.4) use dim N = 2k with k even, in the paper's case dim N = 4.

issues.locator: §2.7, Lemma 2.7.1 and its proof, pp. 16–17; proof of Lemma 3.5.1, p. 30
issues.printed: The source says both groups have order 2 and claims vanishing integral H2 for Sp2r(Fq) and SL2r(Fq), citing [57] as a familiar result. It also identifies MSO2 with second integral homology and invokes [57] to make this group vanish because ℓ is finite.
issues.correction: H_2(Sp_{2r}(F_q), Z) and H_2(SL_{2r}(F_q), Z) have odd order for odd q; they vanish except for r = 1, q = 9, where H_2(SL_2(F_9), Z) ≅ Z/3. Odd order suffices for both uses.
issues.reason: SL_2(F_9) = Sp_2(F_9) is the double cover 2·A_6 of A_6 ≅ PSL_2(F_9), whose Schur multiplier is Z/6; the universal central extension 6·A_6 of SL_2(F_9) has kernel Z/3, so H_2(SL_2(F_9), Z) ≅ Z/3. Independently: a Sylow 3-subgroup P ≅ (F_9, +) is abelian with H_2(P, Z) = Λ²P ≅ Z/3, and diag(t, t^{−1}) acts on it by the determinant of u ↦ t²u over F_3, namely N_{F_9/F_3}(t)² = 1; by Swan's theorem H_2(SL_2(F_9), Z)_{(3)} ≅ H_2(P, Z)^{N(P)} ≅ Z/3. (For SL_2(F_{p²}) with p ≥ 5 the same computation gives 0, since N(t)² ≠ 1 for some t.) This is the exceptional A_1(9) case in Steinberg's list, reference [57] of the paper. In Lemma 2.7.1 only H_2 ⊗ Z/2 = 0 is needed (to identify H_3(−, Z)/2 with H_3(−, Z/2)), and in Lemma 3.5.1 any homomorphism from Z/3 to ℓ^×/2 is zero.

issues.citation: Abdurrahman–Venkatesh, "Symplectic L-functions and symplectic Reidemeister torsion (mod squares)", Inventiones Mathematicae (2025)
issues.reviewReason: Confirmed, and the exception is exactly the one named. Lemma 2.7.1 (TeX l. 1484) asserts that Sp_{2r}(F_q) and SL_{2r}(F_q) have vanishing integral H_2 for odd q, citing Steinberg. The Schur multiplier of the universal Chevalley group A_1(q) is trivial except for q = 4 and q = 9; for q = 9, SL_2(9) = 2.A_6, the Schur multiplier of A_6 is Z/6 and the universal central extension is 6.A_6, so H_2(SL_2(F_9), Z) = Z/3. The extraction's independent Sylow computation gives the same answer, and q = 4 is even, hence outside the lemma. Within Lemma 2.7.1 nothing is lost, since only H_2/2 = 0 is used, and odd order suffices; the consequence is in Lemma 5.1.1 (E4).

issues.locator: §5.1, Lemma 5.1.1 and its proof, p. 40; hence §5.3 (Lemma 5.3.1), §5.6 and Theorem 3.1 in the case r = 1, #ℓ = 9
issues.printed: Lemma 5.1.1 claims the existence of g0(ℓ, r) such that g ≥ g0(r, ℓ) makes the Q̄-fiber of M^G irreducible. Its proof invokes Dunfield–Thurston [18, Theorem 6.25], asserting that H2(G, Z) is trivial here.
issues.correction: Lemma 5.1.1 holds when H_2(Sp_{2r}(ℓ), Z) = 0, i.e. unless r = 1 and #ℓ = 9. For G = SL_2(F_9) the Q̄-fibre of 𝔐^G_g has at least three components for every large g, so the proof of Step A, and with it of Theorem 3.1, does not cover r = 1, #ℓ = 9. That case must be excluded or treated one component at a time.
issues.reason: The case r = 1, #ℓ = 9 satisfies the hypothesis #ℓ ≡ ±1 (mod 8) of Theorem 3.1, and H_2(SL_2(F_9), Z) ≅ Z/3 (see E3). For a surjection φ : π_1(Σ_g) → G, the class φ_*[Σ_g] ∈ H_2(G, Z) is invariant under the mapping class group and under conjugation by G. Every class occurs for g large: realize it by some surface, then add handles mapped onto generators. So the orbits of the mapping class group on Epi(π_1Σ_g, G)/G, which by Example 5.2 are the components of 𝔐^G_g(C), number at least |H_2(G, Z)| = 3. Galois acts on the invariant through the cyclotomic character (the fundamental class lives in Ẑ(1)), so for q ≡ 1 (mod 3) all three components are defined over F_q, and for q large they carry admissible pairs. Lemma 5.3.1 uses H^0(𝔐^{G*}_{Q̄}, Z/2) = Z/2, which then fails. Theorem 3.1 may still hold in this case, but the paper does not prove it.

issues.citation: Abdurrahman–Venkatesh, "Symplectic L-functions and symplectic Reidemeister torsion (mod squares)", Inventiones Mathematicae (2025)
issues.reviewReason: Confirmed, and this is the finding that matters most. Lemma 5.1.1 (TeX l. 4596-4601) deduces irreducibility of the geometric fibre of the Hurwitz stack from Dunfield-Thurston Theorem 6.25 'since H_2(G, Z) is trivial in the case at hand', with G = Sp_{2r}(ell) (l. 4498) and ell any finite field of characteristic other than 2 and p (l. 2928). By E3, H_2(G, Z) = Z/3 when r = 1 and #ell = 9, and the Livingston/Dunfield-Thurston theorem the proof cites classifies the mapping class group orbits by the invariant phi_*[Sigma_g] in H_2(G, Z), so for g large the fibre has at least three components. The case is inside Theorem 3.1: #ell = 9 is 1 mod 8 as its hypothesis requires (l. 3276), and admissible pairs exist there - take q = 73, which is 1 mod 8, prime to #SL_2(F_9) = 720, and a square in the prime field F_3 since 73 = 1 mod 3. So the proof of step (A) does not cover r = 1, #ell = 9, and the design job must exclude that case or run the argument component by component. The route brief already carries this instruction.

issues.printed: "ε = (−qt)^{dim H1} ∏ det(F|H1) = (−√q t)^{dim H1} det(F̄)"
issues.correction: ε = (−qt)^{dim H^1} det(F | H^1)^{−1} = (−√q t)^{dim H^1} det(F̄).
issues.reason: With n = dim H^1 and qF^{−1} conjugate to F (from ⟨Fx, Fy⟩ = q⟨x, y⟩), L(1/(qt)) = det(1 − F/(qt)) = (−qt)^{−n} det(F) L(t), so ε(t) = L(t)/L(1/(qt)) = (−qt)^n det(F)^{−1}. Since det F = q^{n/2} det F̄ and det F̄ = ±1, this equals (−√q t)^n det F̄; the printed middle expression is q^n times too large. The conclusion (ε(ρ, 1/√q) = det F̄) is unaffected.

issues.citation: Abdurrahman–Venkatesh, "Symplectic L-functions and symplectic Reidemeister torsion (mod squares)", Inventiones Mathematicae (2025)
issues.reviewReason: Confirmed, and I redid the computation. With n = dim H^1 and the symplectic self-duality <Fx,Fy> = q<x,y>, the eigenvalues of F pair as alpha and q/alpha, so L(1/(qt)) = (-1/(qt))^n det(F) L(t) and hence epsilon(t) = L(t)/L(1/(qt)) = (-qt)^n det(F)^{-1}. Since det F = q^{n/2} det Fbar with det Fbar = +-1 and n is even, this is (-sqrt(q) t)^n det Fbar, the paper's own right-hand side. The printed middle expression (TeX l. 3016) has det(F|H^1) in the numerator rather than its inverse, so it is q^n times too large. The conclusion epsilon(rho, 1/sqrt(q)) = det Fbar is unaffected.

issues.printed: The source places J_λ^geom, the image of geometric π1, inside Sp2r(oλ), and says (d) establishes geometric surjectivity of ρ̄λ.

issues.locator: §5.5, proof of the Claim, p. 46
issues.printed: Condition (a) requires each m ∈ M to exceed three quantities: ℓ, q, and the cardinality of the Picard group of X. The proof says coprimality of the order of A with q and with the order of the last group yields Hom(class group, A) ≃ ∏_x Hom(k_x^×, A).
issues.correction: (a) should bound m by the class number #Pic^0(X)(k). The map Hom(class group, A) → ∏_{x∈S} Hom(k_x^×, A) is surjective, not an isomorphism, which is all the argument needs.
issues.reason: Pic(X) is infinite (degree gives Pic(X) → Z with finite kernel Pic^0(X)(k)), and Hom(Pic(X), A) ⊇ Hom(Z, A) = A ≠ 0 corresponds to constant-field extensions, so the displayed map is not injective. Surjectivity holds: Ext^1(Pic(X), A) = 0 because Pic(X) ≅ Z ⊕ Pic^0(X)(k) and #Pic^0(X)(k) is prime to #A = M by (a). The chosen local characters therefore extend to the ray class group, and the resulting A-cover is geometrically connected because the inertia groups generate A.

issues.citation: Abdurrahman–Venkatesh, "Symplectic L-functions and symplectic Reidemeister torsion (mod squares)", Inventiones Mathematicae (2025)
issues.reviewReason: Confirmed. Pic(X) for X a curve over a finite field is infinite - the degree map gives Pic(X) -> Z with finite kernel Pic^0(X)(k) - so Hom(Pic(X), A) contains Hom(Z, A) = A and the displayed map to the product of local Hom's cannot be injective; those extra homomorphisms are the constant-field extensions. What the argument needs is surjectivity, which holds because Pic(X) = Z + Pic^0(X)(k) with #Pic^0(X)(k) prime to #A once condition (a) bounds m by the class number rather than by the size of Pic(X), which is what the extraction's correction says. The conclusion is unaffected.

issues.locator: §6.4, the choice of D in (6.18), p. 58, and Lemma 6.4.2, p. 58
issues.printed: The source chooses the least integer D satisfying (6.18) E := dim Γ(S°_{Fq}, O(D)) ≥ 6N. Lemma 6.4.2 claims that vanishing at every x_i imposes codimension r in Γ(S°_{Fq}, O(D)) for sufficiently large D. It says it suffices for the x_i to avoid a Fq-hyperplane with dim Γ(S°, O(D)) ≥ r + 1.
issues.correction: Choose D ≥ max(D_E, 2N − 1), where D_E is the least D with E ≥ 6N; Lemma 6.4.1 already allows every D ≥ D_0. Then r ≤ 2N distinct points impose independent conditions on degree-D forms (Poonen, Lemma 2.1: surjectivity for D ≥ r − 1), and the rest of the proof is unchanged.
issues.reason: The smallest D with E ≥ 6N can be 1 (hyperplane sections of a surface in a large projective space), and distinct points need not impose independent conditions on hyperplanes: three collinear points of S° impose only two. Then the proportion of slices through them exceeds q^{−r}, which the evaluation of (6.21) needs to exclude. The cited Lemma 2.1 of Poonen gives independence once D ≥ r − 1, and r ≤ 2N = 8 here.

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed. The choice 'let D be the smallest integer such that E = dim Gamma(S-circ, O(D)) >= 6N' puts no lower bound on D itself: for a surface embedded in a large projective space, hyperplane sections already give E >= 6N with D = 1, and distinct points need not impose independent conditions on hyperplanes (three collinear points impose two). Lemma 6.4.2 needs the r <= 2N chosen points to impose independent conditions, which Poonen's Lemma 2.1, the source the paper cites, supplies once D >= r - 1. Taking D >= max(D_E, 2N - 1) restores the argument, and Lemma 6.4.1 allows every sufficiently large D, so nothing else changes.

issues.correction: 𝔣(h) = −Σ_{x∈X_h(F_q)} f(x).

issues.locator: Appendix A.6.1, proof of (A.11), p. 66
issues.printed: The source says that passing to the cokernel of d gives a perfect pairing of skew-symmetric type, and consequently forces the cokernel dimension to be even.
issues.correction: The skew form ⟨dx, y⟩ on C_0 has radical ker d, so it descends to a perfect skew pairing on C_0/ker d ≅ im d; hence rank d is even, and (A.11) follows from Σ_{j≤0}(−1)^j(dim C_j − h^j) = rank d_0.

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed. TeX l. 7430-7432 says the skew form <dx,y> 'descends to a perfect skew-symmetric pairing on the cokernel of d. Therefore, this cokernel is even dimensional'. The radical of that form on C_0 is ker d, so what it descends to is the perfect pairing on C_0/ker d, isomorphic to the image of d; what follows is that rank d is even, which is what (A.11) needs. The printed claim about the cokernel is false in general, and the extraction's two-term complex with zero differential is a clean witness. (A.11) itself stands.

issues.locator: Appendix B.10, the functoriality statement and its proof, and the Claim's proof, pp. 85–86
issues.printed: The source claims functoriality for a homomorphism f : R → S between normal integral rings: RT(M, ρ ⊗_R S) is obtained from RT(M, ρ) via H^1(R, μ_2) → H^1(S, μ_2). It also claims that the class of 𝔞 differs from it only by a sign determined by the complexes' dimension data.
issues.correction: Base-change compatibility holds for the normalized class (−1)^{χ_{1/2}(M,ρ)/2}RT(M, ρ), not for RT(M, ρ): RT(M, ρ_L) = image(RT(M, ρ))·(−1)^{(χ_{1/2}(M,ρ_L) − χ_{1/2}(M,ρ_K))/2}. The sign relating 𝔞 to RT depends on the rank of the middle differential, not only on the ranks of the terms. The main text needs only the normalized class, which is what §2.4 uses to define 𝔑.
issues.reason: (i) A symplectic example. Take the genus-2 mapping torus of t = T_3³T_5 (applied left to right) with ρ(b_1) = [[0, 1], [−1, 0]] and ρ(a_1) = ρ(a_2) = ρ(b_2) = I, over R = Z_(3). Over Q the monodromy on H^1(S, ρ) has characteristic polynomial (x² + x + 1)², so H^1(M, ρ) = 0 and χ_{1/2} = 0. Over F_3, dim ker(1 − T̄) = 2, so χ_{1/2} = −2. (Checked independently by computer.) Theorem 2.1 and the naturality of c_et then force RT_{F_3} = −image(RT_Q), and −1 is a nonsquare in F_3. (ii) An orthogonal circle example, from the paper's own (B.30). V = H ⊕ H over R = Q[s]_(s) with A_s = diag(1 + s, (1 + s)^{−1}) ⊕ 1: over Q(s), h = 2 and RT = −(1 + s); at s = 0, h = 4 and RT = 1, while the specialization of −(1 + s) is −1. The existence Claim (B.38) is unaffected.

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed, and I verified it in the paper's own setting rather than relying on the computer calculation the extraction reports. Take the orthogonal circle example: V = H + H over R = Q[s]_(s), A_s = diag(1+s,(1+s)^{-1}) on the first hyperbolic plane and the identity on the second. Over the fraction field, the fixed space has h = 2, W is the first plane, det(1-A)|_W = -s^2/(1+s) = -(1+s) mod squares, disc(V^+) = disc(H) = -1, so the paper's formula (B.30) gives RT = (-1)^{h/2} spinor(A) = -(1+s). At s = 0 the automorphism is the identity, h = 4, W = 0, spinor = disc(H+H) = 1 and RT = +1, while the image of -(1+s) is -1, a nonsquare. So RT is not compatible with base change; the discrepancy is exactly (-1)^{(h_S-h_K)/2}, which is the normalizing sign of Theorem 2.2, and the normalized class is what base-changes. The printed proof's 'sign depending only on the dimension data of the complexes' is therefore too weak: it depends on the rank of the middle differential, which jumps under specialization. I note the limits of my check: this witness is orthogonal, and B.10 is stated for skew-symmetric rho with k even, where the paper says the other case 'should be identical'; the symplectic genus-two witness the extraction gives rests on a computation I did not redo. The main text uses only the normalized class, as Section 2.4 does, so nothing downstream is affected.

issues.locator: Appendix C.2, (C.2), p. 87
issues.printed: The source gives (C.2) (−1)^{h/2}RT(M, ρ) = det′(1 − T)·δ and defines δ by taking the determinant of the quadratic form on H^1(S, ρ)^{T=1}.
issues.correction: δ is the discriminant of the form on the generalized 1-eigenspace of T, which is what Zassenhaus's formula (B.31) gives.
issues.reason: If T is not semisimple on its generalized 1-eigenspace, then for x = (1 − T)y in the fixed space and any fixed z, ⟨x, z⟩ = ⟨y, (1 − T^{−1})z⟩ = 0. So ker(1 − T) ∩ im(1 − T) ≠ 0 lies in the radical of the form on the fixed space, whose determinant is then 0. The examples of C.4 have h = 0 and are unaffected.

issues.printed: The proof uses the topological theorem's corollary (1.5) to equate the two quantities in (5.1). Lemma C.2.1 assumes vanishing H⁰(S, ρ), hence also H², and characteristic zero for ℓ. Section B.9.1 invokes Jacobson-Morozov, saying this uses characteristic zero for K and suggesting that a more careful argument could probably eliminate the assumption.
issues.correction: Lemma 5.2.1 needs (1.5) for local systems with coefficients in the finite field ℓ (of odd characteristic), but (1.5) is deduced from Theorem 2.1 through Lemma C.2.1 and the circle formula (B.30), which are proved only in characteristic 0. The circle formula must be proved over fields of characteristic ≠ 2, or (1.5) supplied otherwise for finite ℓ.
issues.reason: In §5.2 the coefficient field is the finite field ℓ of G = Sp_{2r}(ℓ). §2.3.2 says the circle formula is 'true when the characteristic of K is zero, and likely holds in general', and Lemma C.2.1 assumes characteristic zero. The characteristic-zero input is the Jacobson–Morozov decomposition of the unipotent part of A and M = −log(A) in (B.36); a mod-ℓ local system Sp_{2r}(ℓ) need not lift to characteristic zero. When T has no eigenvalue 1 (h = 0), (B.30) reduces to Zassenhaus's formula and holds in any characteristic ≠ 2, but Lemma 5.2.1 must treat every loop. The orthogonal Jordan-type decomposition is valid in odd characteristic, so the gap is very likely fillable, as the authors suggest.

issues.printed: For a D^†_{𝔛,Q}-module M, the source asserts F^*(M^σ) ≅ F^*(G^*M^{σ′}) ≅ F′^*(M^{σ′}). It infers that giving M a Frobenius structure relative to σ is equivalent to giving one relative to σ′, and concludes that Hol(X/K) is independent of the choice of σ.
issues.correction: Drop the display. Two lifts σ, σ′ of the Frobenius differ by an element of the finite group Aut(K/Frac W(k)), which σ normalises, so σ^N = σ′^N for some N ≥ 1; hence M admits an s′-th Frobenius structure for σ for some s′ iff it does for σ′, which is what the independence of Hol(X/K) needs.
issues.reason: Take p ≥ 3, k algebraically closed, R = W(k)[π] with π^{p−1} = −p, σ fixing π and σ′(π) = ωπ with ω ∈ μ_{p−1}, ω ≠ 1, and M = (O, d + π dx) on Spf R{x} with F = F′ : x ↦ x^p. Then F^*(M^σ) = (O, d + pπx^{p−1}dx) and F′^*(M^{σ′}) = (O, d + pωπx^{p−1}dx); a horizontal map between them is multiplication by C·exp((ω − 1)πx^p), whose coefficients (ω − 1)^nπ^n/n! of x^{pn} have absolute value p^{−s_p(n)/(p−1)}, not tending to 0, so C = 0. Thus the displayed isomorphism fails, and M has a Frobenius structure for σ (Dwork's) but none for σ′ with the same s. The conclusion about Hol(X/K), the only thing used later (Lemma 1.4.11(i)), is correct by the argument above.

issues.locator: §2.2.5, proof of Proposition 2.2.14, pp. 928–929 (also in arXiv v2)
issues.correction: In the two products, replace θ^{1j} and θ_{2j} by ψ_j. The roots are then ψ_j|·|^{(1−2n+α_j+1−2k)/2}(φ_v) for k ≤ μ_{1j} and ψ_j|·|^{(1−2n+μ_{2j}−μ_{1j}+1−2k)/2}(φ_v) for k ≤ μ_{2j}, i.e. the top μ_{1j} and the bottom μ_{2j} Frobenius eigenvalues on the j-th segment. With St_{α}(ψ) = St_α ⊗ ψ∘det, as the θ_{ij} of the geometric lemma presuppose, the first display should read (r_v, N_v) ≅ ⊕_i Sp_{α_i}(ψ_i|·|^{(1−2n)/2 + (α_i−1)/2}).
issues.reason: Take n = 1, s = 1, α_1 = 2 and μ = (1, 1). The printed roots are θ_{11}(φ_v) = ψ|·|^{1/2}(φ_v) and θ_{21}|·|^{−1}(φ_v) = ψ|·|^{−3/2}(φ_v), which differ by a factor q_v^2. Their product P_{v^c,φ_v^{−c}}P_{v,φ_v} = P̃_{v,φ_v} has to be the characteristic polynomial of r_v(φ_v) (Lemma 2.2.13), whose two eigenvalues on Sp_2 differ by a factor q_v, whatever the normalization of ψ. In the same case Π = St_2(ψ), and the paper's own rec^T(St_m) = Sp_m gives (r_v, N_v) ≅ Sp_2(ψ), not Sp_2(ψ|·|^{−1/2}). With the corrections the roots are ψ(φ_v) and ψ|·|^{−1}(φ_v), and the final step (Q(r_v(φ_v)) kills the lower μ_{2j} basis vectors of each segment) goes through, so Proposition 2.2.14 is unaffected.

issues.locator: §2.3.1, Theorem 2.3.3(3) and (b), p. 936 (also in arXiv v2)
issues.printed: Part (3) identifies Π’s infinitesimal character with that of (ξ ⊗ ξ)^∨ on GL_{2n}(F ⊗_ℚ ℂ). Part (b) gives HT_τ(r_ι(π)) = {λ̃_{τ,1} + 2n − 1, λ̃_{τ,2} + 2n − 2, …, λ̃_{τ,2n}}, defining λ̃ ∈ (ℤ^{2n}_+)^{Hom(F,Q̄_p)} as the highest weight of ι^{−1}(ξ ⊗ ξ)^∨, viewed as a GL_{2n}-representation over Q̄_p.
issues.correction: in (b), λ̃ is the highest weight of ι^{−1}(ξ ⊗ ξ). If 'ξ-cohomological' is meant in the dual sense, then (3) should read ξ ⊗ ξ instead.
issues.reason: By the definition in §2.3.1 (weight μ means that π_∞ has the infinitesimal character of V_μ^∨), (3) says that Π has weight μ, the highest weight of ξ ⊗ ξ. The paper's dictionary between weight and Hodge–Tate numbers (Theorem 6.1.1(5): weight λ gives HT_τ = {λ_{ιτ,1} + n − 1, …, λ_{ιτ,n}}) then gives HT_τ(r_ι(π)) = {μ_{τ,i} + 2n − i}. Printed (b) uses the highest weight of the dual instead, and the two agree only if ξ ⊗ ξ is self-dual at every τ. The proof of Proposition 4.4.6 (p. 980) takes HT_τ = {λ̃_{τ,i} + 2n − i} for π̃ of weight λ̃. That is the corrected (b) under the standard meaning of ξ-cohomological (ξ = V_λ̃). The paper defines neither 'ξ-cohomological' nor ξ ⊗ ξ, so it is not certain which of (3) and (b) has the stray ∨.

issues.printed: Equation (2.4.3) states ρ̄_{𝔪̃′} = ⊕_{i=1}^r ρ̄′_i ⊕ ρ̄′(n − s) ⊕_{i=1}^r (ρ̄′_i)^{c,∨}, with each ρ̄′_i of dimension n_i. On p. 945, the source chooses ρ̄_{𝒮*(𝔪′)} = ⊕_{i=1}^r (ρ̄_{𝔪_i} ⊗ ε^{n_1+⋯+n_i−2n} ⊕ ρ̄_{𝔪_i}^{c,∨} ⊗ ε^{1−(n_1+⋯+n_i)}) ⊕ ρ̄_{𝔪̃_s} ⊗ ε^{−s}.

issues.locator: §4.3, proof of Lemma 4.3.6, criterion (4.3.7), pp. 974–975 (also in arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The source gives a sufficient condition for a dominant μ̃ ∈ (ℤ^{2n}_+)^{Hom(F⁺,E)} to be CTG: every w ∈ W^P must satisfy (4.3.7) Σ_{i=1}^n (μ_{w,τ̃,i} − μ_{w,τ̃c,i}) ≠ Σ_{i=1}^n (μ_{w,τ̃_0,i} − μ_{w,τ̃_0c,i}).
issues.reason: Since λ^∨_{σ,i} = −λ_{σ,n+1−i} (§2.2.1), a w violating CTG (Definition 4.3.5) has λ_{w,σ,i} + λ_{w,σc,n+1−i} = i_0 for all σ and i, hence Σ_i(λ_{w,σ,i} + λ_{w,σc,i}) = n·i_0 for every σ, so the '+' inequality implies CTG. With '−', the dictionary (2.2.2) makes Σ_i(μ_{w,τ̃,i} − μ_{w,τ̃c,i}) the sum of all 2n entries of w(μ̃_τ + ρ_τ) − ρ_τ, i.e. of μ̃_τ, for every w, and the printed criterion is false: for n = 1, [F⁺ : Q] = 2, μ̃_{τ_0} = (1, 1), μ̃_τ = (0, 0) it holds for all w (2 ≠ 0), but for w = 1 one gets μ_{τ̃_0} = 1, μ_{τ̃_0c} = −1, μ_{τ̃} = μ_{τ̃c} = 0, so λ_{w,σ} − λ^∨_{w,σc} = (0) for every σ and μ̃ is not CTG. With '+', raising λ̃_{τ_0,1} by a moves the right-hand side by ±a for each of the finitely many w, so the proof's last sentence goes through and Lemma 4.3.6 stands.

issues.printed: Condition (6) takes a non-Eisenstein maximal ideal 𝔪 ⊂ T^S and requires ρ̄_𝔪̃ to be decomposed generic. issues.locator: §5.4, proof of Lemma 5.4.8, the verification that λ̃_i is CTG, p. 1017 (also in arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The proof reduces to showing, for every τ ∈ Hom(F^+, E) and w ∈ W^P_v̄, that [w(λ̃_i + ρ) − ρ]_{τ,j} + [w(λ̃_i + ρ) − ρ]_{τ,2n+1−j} = w(λ̃_i + ρ)_{τ,j} + w(λ̃_i + ρ)_{τ,2n+1−j} varies with j over 1 ≤ j ≤ n. It says this follows if I = {(λ̃_i + ρ)_{τ,j} + (λ̃_i + ρ)_{τ,k} | 1 ≤ j < k ≤ 2n} has no element occurring n or more times.
issues.correction: It suffices to show that μ̃_{τ,n+j} − μ̃_{τ,j} (1 ≤ j ≤ n) is not independent of j, for μ̃ = w(λ̃_i + ρ) − ρ; equivalently, that the 2n entries of λ̃_i + ρ cannot be split into two n-element sets, one a translate of the other. The 'look modulo M' argument proves this for n ≥ 2 when applied to differences instead of sums: since 2a_i ≡ M/4 mod M, a difference between the two blocks of λ̃(a_i) + ρ is ≡ ±M/4 up to 2n − 1 modulo M, and these are pairwise distinct; a difference within a block is ≡ 0 up to 2n − 1; and a difference within the first block (of size < nM) never equals one within the second (a nonzero multiple of nM up to 2n − 1). So a translate-split would pair the 2n entries inside one block of n entries, which is impossible. (The multiset I′ should likewise be formed from the entries of λ̃(a_i), which is what I′_1, I′_2, I′_3 list.)
issues.reason: By Definition 4.3.5 and λ^∨_{τ,i} = −λ_{τ,n+1−i}, CTG says that no λ_w satisfies λ_{w,τ,i} + λ_{w,τc,n+1−i} = i_0 for all τ and i, and under (2.2.2) this sum is μ̃_{τ,n+i} − μ̃_{τ,i}. The printed quantity μ̃_{τ,j} + μ̃_{τ,2n+1−j} equals λ_{w,τ̃,n+1−j} − λ_{w,τ̃c,n+1−j}, a different condition, and for n ≥ 3 the multiplicity criterion does not imply CTG: entries 0, 1, 3, 10, 11, 13 (n = 3) have no pair-sum of multiplicity 3, yet split as {0, 1, 3} and {10, 11, 13} = {0, 1, 3} + 10, which makes λ_w pure. (For n = 2 the two conditions coincide.) The lemma's conclusion survives for n ≥ 2 by the repaired argument, and a direct computation for 2 ≤ n ≤ 7 and several p agrees.

issues.reason: Both proofs begin by setting g = qn − n²[F^+ : ℚ] (pp. 1067 and 1080), the g of Proposition 6.2.33(3). issues.locator: §6.5.12, proof of Proposition 6.5.13, p. 1071 (also in arXiv v2)
issues.printed: Part (1) asserts rec_{E_w}(π_E) = rec_{F_v}(π)|_{W_{E_w}} for every finite w of E over v of F. Its proof produces a regular algebraic, cuspidal automorphic Π on GL_n(𝔸_E), of weight λ_E, with Π_w lifting π_{w|_F} at almost every finite w where π_{w|_F} is unramified. Chebotarev density yields r_ι(Π) ≅ r_ι(π)|_{G_E}, after which it chooses π_E = Π.
issues.correction: add that Π_w is the Arthur–Clozel local base change of π_{w|_F} at every finite place w, and that local base change is compatible with the local Langlands correspondence (Harris–Taylor, Ch. VII); likewise for part (2)
issues.reason: The statement claims the local relation at every finite place, but the proof records it only at almost all unramified places and then passes to the Galois side. The isomorphism r_ι(Π) ≅ r_ι(π)|_{G_E} pins down rec_{E_w}(Π_w) at best up to semisimplification (this is how [Var14] is used at the end of the proofs of Theorems 6.1.1 and 6.1.2). The full local relation of part (2) is needed there, to pass from 'Π_{E,w} is unramified for any place w | v' to rec_{F_v}(Π_v) being finitely ramified. The statement is standard and true.

issues.locator: §6.5.12, proof of Theorem 6.1.1, choice of E_a, E_b, E_c, p. 1073; the same example in §6.6.10, p. 1083 (also in arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The source requires primes below V_0 ∪ V_1 ∪ V_2 to split in E_a · E_b · E_c and p to be unramified there. Its example takes any suitable E_a, then E_b = ℚ(√−p_b) with prime p_b subject to p_b ≡ 1 mod 4, plus p_b ≡ −1 mod l for primes l ∉ {2, p} below ramification of π_{E_0,w} or ρ|_{E_0,w}, or ramified in E_0 · E_a. It takes E_c = ℚ(√−p_c), choosing any prime p_c ≡ 1 mod 4p_b distinct from p.
issues.correction: also require p_b ≡ −1 mod l and p_c ≡ −1 mod l for every rational prime l below V_0 ∪ V_1 ∪ V_2 (such l are odd and prime to p, so this is compatible with the other congruences by the Chinese remainder theorem), and, in the Fontaine–Laffaille case, p_b ≠ p
issues.reason: An odd prime l ∤ p_b splits in ℚ(√−p_b) if and only if −p_b is a square mod l. The listed congruences force this only for the primes in the third condition; nothing in the example makes the primes below V_0 ∪ V_1 ∪ V_2 split in E_b or E_c, and they must, for E to be V_0 ∪ V_1 ∪ V_2-split as the proof then asserts. Nothing excludes p_b = p either, which would ramify p in E_b, against the first condition. Fields with the listed properties do exist, so only the example is incomplete.

issues.printed: Condition (2) gives characters ψ_{v,i} : G_{F_v} → Q̄_l^× for i = 1, …, n with the stated character agreement. Condition (3) requires ρ̄ to be generic and absolutely irreducible. Condition (4) requires a regular algebraic, cuspidal automorphic π on GL_n(𝔸_F), together with ι : Q̄_p → ℂ an isomorphism making π ι-ordinary and satisfying r̄_ι(π) ≅ ρ.

issues.locator: §7.1, Lemma 7.1.8(2) and its proof, pp. 1091–1092 (also in arXiv v2)
issues.printed: Part (2) assumes a number field K unramified at l and crystalline r : G_K → GL_2(Z_l) with Hodge–Tate numbers {0, 1} at every embedding K ↪ Q̄_l. If r̄ has image containing SL_2(F_l), it claims that K is the sole subextension of K̄^{ker r̄}/K unramified above l. The proof says each normal subgroup of GL_2(F_l) is central or contains SL_2(F_l), and concludes Δ = GL_2(F_l).
issues.correction: add the hypothesis l > 2 (the proof's claim about normal subgroups holds for l ≥ 5; for l = 3 the conclusion Δ = GL_2(F_3) still holds, since every proper normal subgroup of GL_2(F_3) lies in SL_2(F_3))
issues.reason: Part (2) fails for l = 2, which the proof of part (1) explicitly allows ('If l = 2 then 1 = ε̄_l^{−1} and we are done'). Take K = Q and r = T_2E for E = 37a1 : y² + y = x³ − x, which has good reduction at 2, so r is crystalline with Hodge–Tate numbers {0, 1}. Its 2-division polynomial 4x³ − 4x + 1 is irreducible of discriminant 16·37, so r̄(G_Q) = GL_2(F_2) ≅ S_3 ⊇ SL_2(F_2), and Q(E[2]) contains Q(√37), which is unramified at 2 because 37 ≡ 1 mod 4. The failing step is that A_3 ⊲ GL_2(F_2) is neither central nor contains SL_2(F_2). Every use in the paper has l ≥ 7 (Corollary 7.2.4 takes l ≥ 2(m + 2); Assumption 7.2.6 has l_1, l_2 > 2m_i + 3), so nothing downstream is affected.

issues.locator: §7.2, proof of Theorem 7.1.11, Assumption 7.2.6, p. 1103, and its use on p. 1106 (also in arXiv v2)
issues.printed: Assumption 7.2.6 requires: (1) complete splitting of l_2 in each M_i; (2) containment of SL_2(F_{l_1}) in the G_F-image on E[l_1], and of SL_2(F_{l_2}) in r̄_{i,λ_i}(G_F) for every i ∈ I; (3) absence of ramification of l_1 and l_2 in F; (4) good reduction of E above l_1 and l_2; (5) neither l_1 nor l_2 lies below a prime in any S_i; (6) for every i, l_1, l_2 > 2m_i + 3.
issues.correction: add (6′) l_1, l_2 > (m_i + 1)² for all i, and (7) r_{i,λ_i}|_{G_{F_v}} is crystalline with Hodge–Tate numbers {0, 1} for v | l_2 (i.e. l_2 avoids the density-zero exceptional set of condition (5)(b) for R_i). Both hold on a set of primes of density one, so the choice remains possible.
issues.reason: The proof applies Theorem 6.1.1 twice, to Symm^{m_i} at the primes l_1 and l_2, with n = 1 + m_i, and Theorem 6.1.1(4) requires p > n² (p. 1029). Condition (6) gives only p > 2m_i + 3, which allows p = 11 or 13 < 16 = n² when m_i = 3. The proof also uses crystallinity of r_{i,λ_i} at l_2 with Hodge–Tate numbers {0, 1} (for Lemma 7.1.8 and for Theorem 6.1.1(2)), which a very weakly compatible system guarantees only for l outside a set of density zero.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 2.7, arXiv v1 p. 5

issues.correction: For the existential main theorem, replace r by r′=r delta^ell with delta supported on dyadic primes dividing m and sufficiently divisible there. The curves are isomorphic, their conductors and S,Sigma are unchanged, and Sel_phi still vanishes. The modified beta is zero modulo the dyadic conductor part, so t_1=t_3 and x=y=z=1 work there. The unit condition on r persists only at odd ramified primes. This establishes the modified-r residue construction; it is not, without further argument, a proof of Proposition 2.5 for its original fixed r. See G3. Choosing t_1≠t_3 works in the displayed example but has not been proved here to work in every original-r case.
issues.reason: Take F_0 = ℚ, K_0 = ℚ(i) and ℓ = 3, which does not divide Disc = −4. §4 replaces these by F = ℚ(ζ_3) and K = F(i) = ℚ(ζ_12), and K/F is unramified above 3. The prime (2) is inert in F/ℚ, so F_(2) = ℚ_4 is unramified over ℚ_2 with residue field 𝔽_4. F_(2)(i)/F_(2) has conductor exponent 2, so 𝔪 = (4). Since (2) ramifies in K, (2) ∉ S and γ ∉ (2); and r ∉ (2) by Lemma 2.3. Hence v_2(β) = 1. Suppose t x² + βt_2y² ≡ t z² (mod 4) with x, y, z units. Then (z/x)² ≡ 1 + βt_2y²/(tx²) (mod 4), which is ≡ 1 mod 2 but ≢ 1 mod 4. But a unit w with w² ≡ 1 (mod 2) has w ≡ 1 (mod 2), since squaring is bijective on 𝔽_4, and then w² ≡ 1 (mod 4). This is a contradiction. An exhaustive search over the 12 units of ℤ[ζ_3]/4 confirms it. Inertness of a principal prime (p) in K is detected by χ(p) = (−1)^{(N(p)−1)/2}, where N is the norm to ℚ; this is the Hilbert symbol (p, −1) at (2), trivial on global units. For every unit value of β/2 there is no solution with t_1 = t_3 and χ(t_1) = χ(t_2) = −1. Yet admissible residues exist with t_1 ≠ t_3: for β ≡ 2, u_1 = u_2 = 1 + 2ζ_3 and u_3 = u_1 + βu_2 ≡ 3 + 2ζ_3 (mod 4), with norms 3, 3, 7 ≡ 3 (mod 4).

With the normalization the factors are 1 − (q − 1)^{−2} and the product converges.

issues.locator: §1.2.1, p.76 (published version)
issues.printed: The source claims ℬ≤1⟨U⟩/(λU − f) has no π-torsion and reduces this to vanishing of elements killed by λ. For a lift Σ b_m U^m of such an element, it uses λ(Σ b_m U^m) = (λU − f) Σ₀^∞ a_m U^m, a_m ∈ ℬ≤1, to deduce divisibility of every a_m by λ from injectivity of multiplication by f modulo λ.
issues.correction: Run the displayed argument with π in place of λ. Absence of λ-torsion gives absence of π-torsion only when |λ| ≤ |π|, which is not assumed; the same computation with an arbitrary nonzero μ ∈ 𝒦° proves the stronger and correct statement that the quotient is torsion-free over 𝒦°.
issues.reason: The sentence announces the absence of π-torsion for π ∈ 𝒦°° and then says it suffices to treat λ, but the two differ: if |π| < |λ| then λ-torsion is contained in π-torsion, not the other way round, so the reduction goes the wrong way. Nothing is lost, because the argument does not use any property of λ beyond f being injective modulo it: for any nonzero μ ∈ 𝒦°, comparing coefficients in μ Σ b_m U^m = (λU − f) Σ a_m U^m gives μ b₀ = −f a₀, hence a₀ ∈ μℬ≤1 since multiplication by f is isometric, and then μ b_m = λ a_{m−1} − f a_m gives a_m ∈ μℬ≤1 by induction; so the lifted element lies in (λU − f)ℬ≤1⟨U⟩ and is zero. In the only use, §2.5.2 with λ = π^i and λ = π_{ik}, one does have |λ| ≤ |π|, so the printed reduction is harmless there.

issues.locator: Published §2.2.4 p.13; Lemme 2.4.1(2) p.22; Lemme 2.4.2 proof p.24; discussion after Théorème 3.4.1 p.41.
issues.printed: On p.13 the source claims uniqueness of a spectral norm under a completeness requirement, without specifying a topology. The proof takes the maximum of the two norms.
issues.correction: Keep uniqueness for a fixed topology. If both norms are complete, a continuous identity in one direction suffices by open mapping. Delete the automatic-invariance parenthesis in Lemme 2.4.1(2), or require continuity of the finite-group action; retain its explicit norm-invariance hypothesis. Reprove applications using their additional hypotheses.
issues.reason: Let F be the algebraic closure of Q_p inside C_p. It is dense and properly contained in C_p. Extend t from C_p minus F to a transcendence basis over F. The automorphism of the rational function field sending t to pt and fixing the other basis elements and F extends to an automorphism σ of its algebraic closure C_p. Thus ν(x)=|x| and ν′(x)=|σ(x)| are distinct complete multiplicative Q_p-algebra norms, with ν′(t)=p^(-1)ν(t). For a_n in F tending to t in ν, the same sequence tends to p^(-1)t in ν′. It is Cauchy for max(ν,ν′) but cannot have a limit for that norm. There is also an actual finite-group counterexample to the parenthesis of Lemme 2.4.1(2): put B=C_p×C_p with N(x,y)=max(ν(x),ν′(y)), let G=C_2 swap factors, and give A=B^G=diagonal C_p its induced norm max(ν,ν′). B is complete and spectral; A is uniform normed, exactly as allowed in §2.4.1, though incomplete. The swap takes (t,0), of norm ν(t), to (0,t), of norm p^(-1)ν(t). The proposed old repair from (2.11) is invalid: that formula determines max_γ N(γb), not N(b), and its proof of individual equality uses G-invariance. The prior extraction also missed the invocation on p.24. For a finite projective algebra over a complete A, its given complete Banach topology agrees with the canonical module topology: choose finite generators, use the continuous surjection A^n→B and open mapping. A-linear isomorphisms are then continuous, so fixed-topology uniqueness applies to p.24 and p.41. This does not repair the general parenthesis on p.22, where A need not be complete.

issues.correction: Assume A reduced in Lemma 3.5, or add reducedness to (c). This is an error in the cited source, not an error by André.
issues.reason: For a complete perfect nonarchimedean field k of characteristic p, the dual-number Banach algebra A=k[ε]/(ε²), with its finite-dimensional maximum norm, has A^p=k, a closed subspace. Yet any power-multiplicative norm would satisfy ||ε||^p=||ε^p||=0, contradicting separation. Thus (c) alone cannot imply (a) or (b). In the printed proof on p.117 the functions ||f^(p^i)||^(1/p^i) are called norms; reducedness is necessary there. André supplies it explicitly.

issues.reason: Let A=K×K with the spectral maximum norm, choose 0<|ϖ|<1, and set g=(1,ϖ), λ=ϖ, μ=1. The element g is invertible, hence a non-zero-divisor. In the first localization λ/g=(ϖ,1) is already power-bounded, so A{λ/g}^u=A. In the second localization, the first factor is K, while the second factor is K⟨U⟩/(ϖU−1)=0 because 1−ϖU has the convergent geometric-series inverse. Thus A{μ/g}^u=K, and the transition is first projection, killing (0,1). Both localizations are uniform; choose K perfectoid with roots of ϖ if that extra restriction is desired. Density of A[1/g] in the source does not imply injectivity of restriction. The inverse-limit injectivity of Lemme 2.6.3 is a different assertion and is not refuted.

issues.locator: Published numbered paragraph §1.7.2(1), p.7, unrestricted faithful-projective assertion
issues.printed: The source claims that an arbitrary almost projective P is faithfully flat whenever P is faithful.
issues.correction: Every almost projective module is flat. Faithful flatness is equivalent to the evaluation ideal E_{P/A}=image(P⊗_A P*→A) being A; mere injectivity of A→End(P)ᵃ is insufficient in this generality. Use Gabber–Ramero Proposition 2.4.28(iv), with Definition 2.4.23, for this exact criterion.
issues.reason: Use the ordinary almost base (V,m)=(R,R), R=∏_{n∈N}F₂ and P=⊕_{n∈N}Re_n, the finite-support ideal. Each Re_n is projective, so P is projective; ann_R(P)=0, so it is faithful. But P²=P is proper, and P⊗_R(R/P)=P/P²=0 while R/P≠0. Hence P is not faithfully flat. The counterexample is infinite: no finite-coordinate computation is claimed to prove it. The cited Gabber–Ramero evaluation-ideal criterion and proof were read directly. This finding concerns the unrestricted sentence, not a claim that any particular almost-finite-projective downstream use is false.

issues.locator: Published numbered paragraph §2.2.2, p.13, displayed estimate in the uniformity equivalence
issues.printed: ‖a‖ ≤ |a|_sp sup_{b∈A°} ‖b‖
issues.correction: With C=sup_{b∈A°}‖b‖ and any c∈K with 0<|c|<1, the universally valid estimate is ‖a‖≤C|c|^(-1)|a|_sp. The sharp constant C is valid if |K×| is dense. Uniformity is still equivalent to equivalence with the spectral norm.
issues.reason: Take K=Q_p, A=Q_p(π) with π²=p, and the coefficient norm ‖a+bπ‖=max(|a|,|b|). It is normalized, complete and submultiplicative. Its spectral norm is max(|a|,p^(-1/2)|b|), since the two summands have valuations of different parity. Thus A°=Z_p+Z_pπ and C=1, but ‖π‖=1>p^(-1/2)=|π|_sp. For the repaired estimate choose scalar powers of c so that the rescaled spectral value is strictly below 1 and at least |c|; their powers are bounded, giving the stated constant. If the spectral value is zero, arbitrary scalar rescaling is power-bounded and boundedness of A° forces a=0. This refutes the auxiliary inequality, not the uniformity equivalence.

Let B be the indefinite quaternion algebra over Q of discriminant 15, V = B⁰ (trace zero) with Q = Nrd, of signature (1,2), and L = O_B ∩ B⁰ for a maximal order O_B. At 3 and 5, V is anisotropic and L is the unique maximal lattice; at 2 its discriminant is 2; so L is maximal with D_L = 2·3²·5² = 450. Since dim V = 3, G = C⁺(V)^× and K_ℓ = C⁺(L_ℓ)^×. For ℓ = 3, 5, take the basis e1 = u, e2 = Π, e3 = uΠ of L_ℓ (u² = ε a non-square unit, Π² = ℓ). With α = e1e2 and β = e1e3, C⁺(L_ℓ) = Z_ℓ⟨1, α, β, αβ⟩ and Nrd(a + bα + cβ + dαβ) = a² + εℓb² − ε²ℓc² − ε³ℓ²d². Hence ν(K_ℓ) = (Z_ℓ^×)². So π_0(M(C)) = Q^×_{>0}\A_f^×/ν(K) ≅ (Z/2)², and M, which is proper because V is anisotropic, has four geometric components with constant field Q(√−3, √5). At p = 7 (odd, 7² ∤ 450, L_(7) self-dual), M_(7) is smooth and proper over Z_(7). issues.reviewReason: Counterexample. Take 𝔭 inert in E, 𝔭 ∤ d_F, V_𝔭 ≅ (E_𝔭, Nm), q = N(𝔭), X = q^{−s}, and φ_𝔭 = 1_{O_E} − 1_{π O_E}, so φ_𝔭(0) = 0. M_𝔭(s,1_{O_E}) = 1 (Cor. 7.1.9). A direct Whittaker computation gives M_𝔭(s,1_{πO_E}) = (q^{−2} + q^{−1}X + (1−q^{−2})X²)/(1+q^{−1}X), using Φ(n_−(c)) = −q^{−1} for ord c = 1 and 1 for ord c ≥ 2. Hence M′_𝔭(0,φ_𝔭) = 2(1−q^{−1})log q ≠ 0. With good factors elsewhere (M_{𝔭′}(0,φ_{𝔭′}) = φ_{𝔭′}(0) = 1), M′(0,φ) ≠ 0 while φ(0) = 0, which contradicts BKY's form. AGHMP flags the misstatement on p. 468. The mistake is in BKY12; AGHMP's own statements use the corrected term.

issues.locator: §2.3, Proposition 2.3.1, p. 405 (journal image checked; identical in Colmez_v3.5.pdf)
issues.printed: For a p-adically complete O_E-algebra R, Proposition 2.3.1 asserts (1) that V(G_R) ⊂ End(G_R) is stable under O_E and, whenever nonzero, is free and finite over O_E with rank 1; (2) that each pair x1, x2 ∈ V(G_R) determines exactly one ⟨x1,x2⟩ ∈ O_E satisfying x1∘x2 = [⟨x1,x2⟩] ∈ End_{O_E}(G_R).
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis that Spec R is connected (R≠0). Then End_{O_E}(G_R)=O_E, and (1)–(3) hold.
issues.reason: Counterexample: take R=F_p^alg×F_p^alg, a p-adically complete O_E-algebra. Then G_R=G_{F_p^alg}⊔G_{F_p^alg}, so V(G_R)=V(G_1)×V(G_1)≅O_E², free of rank 2 by Props. 2.3.3–2.3.4, and End_{O_E}(G_R)=O_E×O_E, so x1∘x2 need not be a scalar of O_E. For connected R, O_E-linear endomorphisms reduce injectively (rigidity) to R/p, where [π_E](X)=X^q forces coefficients c with c^q=c, which are constant; hence End_{O_E}(G_R)=O_E. The paper applies the proposition only to the local rings O_K/ϖ^k and F_p^alg, so nothing downstream is affected.

issues.locator: §2.5, proof of Lemma 2.5.3, p. 413 (and hence Theorem 2.5.5, p. 414) (journal image checked; identical in Colmez_v3.5.pdf)
issues.printed: For k < e, the proof assumes ob_{k+2}(a·f) = 0 and invokes Lemma 2.5.2(2) to obtain ob_{k+1}(f) = 0, thereby claiming the lemma in this range. For k ≥ e, it calls O_K → O_K/ϖ^k a thickening with divided powers. Lemma 2.5.2(2) itself assumes k < e and f ∈ V_µ(G_k).
issues.correction: Treat k=e−1 separately. One option is to extend Lemma 2.5.2(2) to k=e, using the PD thickening W[u]/(u^{e+1})→O_K/ϖ^e (kernel (p,u^e)) in place of M_{e+1}, which the text defines only for k≤e. Alternatively, for p odd, apply the second argument, since ϖ^{e−1}O_K carries divided powers when e(p−2)≥p−1.
issues.reason: For k=e−1, the first case needs Lemma 2.5.2(2) for a·f∈V_{aµ}(G_{k+1}) at level k+1=e, but 2.5.2(2) assumes k<e, and V_{k+1}=V(M_{e+1},τ) is not defined (M_k is defined only for k≤e). The second case needs O_K→O_K/ϖ^{e−1} to be a PD thickening. That holds iff e−1≥e/(p−1), which fails for p=2. So for p=2 and E/Q_2 ramified (e≥2), the step k=e−1 of the induction behind Theorem 2.5.5 is not covered by any argument in the text. Theorem 2.5.5 feeds Prop. 7.7.3 (p. 501) at every good prime, and Definition 5.3.3 allows p=2. The statement is expected to hold, and the extension of 2.5.2(2) looks routine, so this is recorded as a gap, not an error.

issues.locator: §3.2, pp. 416–417 (journal images checked; identical in Colmez_v3.5.pdf)
issues.printed: The source chooses K0 ⊂ T(A_f) as a particular compact subgroup that is maximal. It defines K0,p ⊂ T(Q_p) as the largest subgroup whose images lie in K0,p,so ⊂ T_so(Q_p) and, via (3.2.2), in ⊕_{𝔭|p} Z_p^×/Nm(O_{F_𝔭}^×). It claims short exactness of 1 → Z_p^× → K0,p → K0,p,so → 1.
issues.correction: K0,p := the largest compact subgroup of T(Q_p) whose image in T_so(Q_p) lies in K0,p,so. This equals Z_p^×·r(T,µ0)((Z_p⊗O_E)^×), with Z_p^×⊂Q_p^×=(T_F/T^1_F)(Q_p); the cohomological condition then holds automatically. Read 'maximal compact' as 'compact open'.
issues.reason: The printed K0,p is not compact. The image of p∈Q_p^×⊂(Q_p⊗F)^×⊂T_E(Q_p) in T(Q_p) maps to 1 in T_so (p/p̄=1) and to 0 in the cokernel of (3.2.2), since it comes from T_E(Q_p). Yet Nm: T→G_m sends it to p^{2d}, so its powers are unbounded. It is also a non-unit (p^d) element of ker(T(Q_p)→T_so(Q_p))=Q_p^×, contradicting 1→Z_p^×→K0,p→K0,p,so→1. The corrected group satisfies that sequence, contains r(T,µ0)_q(O_{E,q}^×) (proof of Prop. 3.2.1), equals T(Z_p) for p unramified in E (proof of Prop. 3.5.5), and is what Lemma 5.3.4 uses. It is not maximal compact in general. Example: d=2, p inert in F, 𝔭 ramified in E, t=y·[π_E] with y↔p^{-1}∈Q_p^×=(T_F/T^1_F)(Q_p). Then t²=[π_E²/p]∈K0,p, but θ(t)=π_E/π̄_E∉K0,p,so, so ⟨K0,p,t⟩ is a larger compact subgroup.

issues.locator: Proposition 4.4.1(4), p. 441, and its proof, p. 442; its only use is the proof of Proposition 5.3.1, p. 459
issues.printed: Assertion (4) says that, for finite E/Q_p and t ∈ M(E), potentially good reduction of A_t over O_E ensures an extension of t : Spec(E) → M to a map Spec(O_E) → M_(p). The proof attributes this directly to the finite, hence proper, map M_(p) → X_{2^{n+2},m,Z(p)}. On p. 459, the proof invokes Proposition 3.6.2 together with Proposition 4.4.1(4).
issues.correction: Require that A_t has good reduction over O_E. Then the valuative criterion for the finite, hence proper and representable, map M_(p) → X gives the extension. With only potentially good reduction, t extends over O_{E'} for a finite extension E'/E. In the proof of Proposition 5.3.1, cite Proposition 3.4.1 (A_H extends to an abelian scheme over 𝒴_K) in place of Proposition 3.6.2, which is a supersingularity criterion.
issues.reason: An extension Spec O_E → M_(p) pulls A back to an abelian scheme over O_E with generic fibre A_t, so A_t must have good reduction. Every object of M has the automorphism −1: it lies in G(Q) ∩ K since Z^× ⊂ C(L̂)^×, and it acts on A as [−1]. Take t with A_t of good reduction, for example the generic point of an O_E-point of M_(p). Twisting t through this automorphism by a ramified quadratic character χ of E gives t^χ ∈ M(E) with A_{t^χ} = A_t ⊗ χ. By Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich, A_t ⊗ χ has potentially good but not good reduction, since inertia acts on T_ℓ through χ. So t^χ does not extend. The only application concerns the abelian schemes A_H of §3, which have good reduction over 𝒴 (Proposition 3.4.1), so no later result is affected. The extraction's gap G2 and a unit test of orth-normalization note the point but record no sourceIssue. The authors' version has the same text.

issues.locator: §4.4, p. 442, paragraph after the proof of Proposition 4.4.1
issues.printed: The source chooses Λ = L^⊥ ⊂ L⋄ with rank at most 2, saying that this is optional but shortens some proofs. It claims such a choice is always available and that the classification of quadratic forms over Q readily verifies this.
issues.correction: The choice is possible for odd p, where the p-part of L^∨/L of a maximal lattice has at most two generators. At p = 2, rank Λ must be at least the number of generators of the 2-part of L^∨/L, which can be 3. The choice is used only for odd p: Proposition 4.4.2, the bound n⋄ ≤ n + 2 after Lemma 4.4.4, Theorem 4.4.5 and Proposition 4.5.8.
issues.reason: Here p is any fixed prime (p. 441). If L⋄ is self-dual at p, then L = L⋄ ∩ V because L is maximal, and Z_p ⊗ L^∨/L ≅ Z_p ⊗ Λ^∨/Λ (p. 448), so rank Λ is at least the minimal number of generators of the p-part of L^∨/L. For L = A_1 ⊕ A_1 ⊕ A_1 ⊕ U ⊕ U, of signature (5,2), L^∨/L = (Z/2)³ with q(x) = (x1² + x2² + x3²)/4 mod 1. This form is anisotropic (values 1/4, 1/2, 3/4), so L is maximal. At p = 2 every admissible L⋄ therefore has rank Λ ≥ 3.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 4.1.1, p. 433
issues.printed: The source treats the assertion as clear when L_{Z_ℓ} contains a hyperbolic plane. It says only the case of anisotropic V_{Q_ℓ} of dimension at least 3 with ℓ² not dividing D_L remains, and derives that case by classifying maximal anisotropic Z_ℓ-lattices, citing [Shi10, §29.10].
issues.correction: The case n = 2 with V_{Q_ℓ} anisotropic must also be treated. Then V_{Q_ℓ} ≅ (B_ℓ, c·Nrd) for the quaternion division algebra B_ℓ, and ℓ² | D_L. GSpin(V_{Q_ℓ}) = {(b1,b2) ∈ B_ℓ^× × B_ℓ^× : Nrd b1 = Nrd b2}, acting by x ↦ b1 x b2⁻¹, with ν = Nrd b1. For b ∈ O_{B_ℓ}^×, the element (b, ΠbΠ⁻¹) preserves L_ℓ and acts trivially on L_ℓ^∨/L_ℓ (a module over the residue field F_{ℓ²}, on which it acts by b̄^σ·(b̄^σ)⁻¹ = 1). Up to a central unit it therefore lies in K_ℓ, so ν(K_ℓ) ⊇ Nrd(O_{B_ℓ}^×) = Z_ℓ^×. The statement stays true.
issues.reason: For n ≥ 3, V_{Q_ℓ} is isotropic and a maximal L_{Z_ℓ} contains a hyperbolic plane. The printed reduction leaves only anisotropic cases with ℓ² ∤ D_L, which occur only when dim V = 3. The 4-dimensional anisotropic space (n = 2) has a unique maximal lattice, and its discriminant has ℓ-part ℓ²: the reduced-norm form on the maximal order has discriminant ℓ². So the hypothesis n ≥ 2 is never used, and the case it is needed for is not argued.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 4.5.1, p. 447, and proof of Lemma 4.5.2, p. 448; page images checked
issues.printed: The source asserts that the square is cartesian because each vertical arrow identifies its domain’s sections with target sections anti-commuting with the homological realizations of (4.5.3). issues.correction: The image of End_{C(L)} is the graded commutant of Λ: even endomorphisms commute with Λ and odd ones anti-commute. For V (degree one) the statement is right: an element of V⋄ anti-commutes with Λ if and only if it is orthogonal to Λ, i.e. lies in V. That is all the two proofs use.
issues.reason: The identity of A_S lies in End_{C(L)}(A_S) and maps to the identity of A⋄_S, which commutes with every λ ∈ Λ; it anti-commutes only if 2λ = 0. issues.correction: These hold only when m(𝔭) = ord_𝔭(d_F) = 0. In general, normalise ξ_𝔭 against the different: ord_𝔭(ξ_𝔭) = −m(𝔭) for 𝔭 split or ramified, ord_𝔭(ξ_𝔭)+m(𝔭) ∈ {0,1} for 𝔭 inert. Then M_𝔭(s,φ̃_𝔭) = N(𝔭)^{−1}L_𝔭(s+1,χ)/L_𝔭(s−1,χ) if 𝔭 is inert and ord_𝔭(ξ_𝔭)+m(𝔭) = 1, and 1 otherwise; and Vol(O_{E,𝔭}) = N(𝔭)^{−ord_𝔭(D_{E/F})/2−ord_𝔭(ξ_𝔭)−m(𝔭)}.
issues.reason: M_𝔭 depends on (Q_𝔭, ψ_{F_𝔭}) only through ψ∘Q, the self-dual measures and the factor N^{f/2}γ^{−1}, which compensates the change of db. So (Q, ψ of conductor exponent −m) and (π^mQ, unramified ψ) give the same M_𝔭. Take 𝔭 inert with m(𝔭) = 1 and ξ_𝔭 a unit, so inv_𝔭(V) = +1 and the printed claim gives M_𝔭 = 1. Then M_𝔭(s,1_{O_E}) equals the paper's own m = 0, ord ξ = 1 value N^{−1}L(s+1)/L(s−1) ≠ 1. A direct computation agrees: W_{0,𝔭} = −N^{−1/2}(N^{−1}+X)/(1+X), so M_𝔭 = (N^{−1}+X)/(1+N^{−1}X). The volume: the dual of O_E for ψ(Tr(ξxȳ)) is (ξπ^m)^{−1}d_{E/F}^{−1}O_E. The proof of Prop. 7.1.4 applies the same [HY12, Lemma 4.6.1] and gets Vol(Λ_𝔭) = N^{−n/2} with ord ξ = −m, which matches the corrected formula, not the printed one. The proposition uses φ̃_𝔭 only to reduce to φ_𝔭(0) = 0 and to get rationality, and both still hold.

issues.printed: The source asserts that Λ_Q cannot represent a rational prime unless that prime splits in the discriminant field of Λ.
issues.correction: Write Λ_Q ≅ (K, c·Nm_{K/Q}) with K = Q(√−disc Λ), c ∈ Q_{>0}. Every prime p inert in K with ord_p(c) even is not represented, and there are infinitely many (Chebotarev). issues.reason: Counterexamples: Λ = Z² with x²+y² has K = Q(i), and the ramified prime 2 = 1+1 is represented. Λ with 3x²+3y² has 3 inert in Q(i) and 3 = Q(1,0) represented. issues.reason: For F_9=F_3(i), i^2=-1, the normal basis (1+i,1-i) has trace Gram matrix G=[[0,1],[1,0]]. issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 4.3, Step 1, p. 17, HAL hal-02490566v2; version of record not collated
issues.printed: The source concludes that (a_n)_{n∈N} eventually stabilizes. It then claims that every coefficient of x lies in A and, consequently, that the limit x lies in Ã.
issues.correction: In the normalized case, each inverse local generator is a polynomial with constant term 1, which fixes ord_z(u/y_n). First remove finite exceptional/nonunit factors by scalar conjugation. Then exhibit a single F_q[z] denominator compatible with the approximation congruences; coefficient integrality and restricted-series decay reduce the limit to a polynomial with A coefficients. The full compatibility remains G3, rather than being asserted from Gauss convergence.
issues.reason: Read and rendered p. 17: Gauss convergence alone gives no stabilization of z-order. The earlier sequence z+pi^n has stationary order and was an inadequate counterexample to this precise claim. Use x_(2n)=z, x_(2n+1)=z+pi^(2n+1), which converges to z with alternating orders 1 and 0. Structural normalization can repair the argument, but the exceptional-prime and common-denominator compatibility must be proved (G3).

issues.locator: Theorem 4.9.5 (published: Theorem 4.90), the statement; present in arXiv v4 and in the published version
issues.printed: The source asserts that M_Δ(−) : BT(R) → DM^adm(R), the prismatic Dieudonné functor, is essentially surjective. Its domain consists of p-divisible groups over R, and its target consists of admissible prismatic Dieudonné crystals over R.

issues.reason: R is assumed quasi-regular semiperfectoid and the displayed functor is the non-calligraphic M_Δ(−), which Definition 4.42 (arXiv Definition 4.2.8) defines as Ext^1_{(R)_qsyn}(G, O^pris) with values in prismatic Dieudonné modules over R; DM^adm(R) is used for both categories by the deliberate overloading of Definitions 4.8 and 4.19 (arXiv Definitions 4.1.8 and 4.1.15), but the words in the statement name the wrong one. issues.locator: Example 6.0.4 (published: Example A.4), the displayed chain of equalities; present in arXiv v4 and in the published version
issues.printed: p^{i}x_{i,0}=p^{i}fx_{i,1}=\ldots = f^{i}x_{i,i}\neq 0
issues.correction: p^{i}x_{i,0}=p^{i−1}fx_{i,1}=\ldots = f^{i}x_{i,i}\neq 0
issues.reason: The relations imposed are p x_{i,j} = f x_{i,j+1}. Substituting once gives p^i x_{i,0} = p^{i−1}(p x_{i,0}) = p^{i−1} f x_{i,1}, and each further substitution trades one p for one f, so that the chain is p^i x_{i,0} = p^{i−1}f x_{i,1} = p^{i−2}f^2 x_{i,2} = … = f^i x_{i,i}: the total degree in p and f is i throughout. As printed, the second term has degree i+1 and is in fact equal to f^{i+1}x_{i,i+1} = 0, since x_{i,i+1} = 0, which would contradict the assertion that the chain is non-zero. The next sentence, p^{i+1}x_{i,0} = f^i p x_{i,i} = 0, is correct.

issues.locator: the proof of Proposition 5.3.5 (published: Proposition 5.23), the step asserting topological nilpotence of the divided Frobenius; present in arXiv v4 and in the published version, and corrected by the 2025 erratum
issues.printed: The source claims topological nilpotence of divided Frobenius on its kernel and reduces this to A_crys(R) → W(R), arising from the PD-thickening W(R) → R. It constructs A_crys(R) as the PD-envelope of W(R^♭) for ker(W(R^♭) → R), and says that this kernel is topologically generated by V^m([x]) with x ∈ I := ker(R^♭ → R) and m ≥ 0.
issues.correction: The claim is false. The erratum states: 'The key step in the proof of Proposition 5.23 is to show that for a quasiregular semiperfect ring R, the divided Frobenius φ_1 acts topologically nilpotently on the kernel of the map A_crys(R) → W(R). This is not true.' The counterexample, due to Andrew Senger, is R = F_p[x^{1/p^∞}]/x with the element Σ_{k ∈ Z} p^k [x^{1/p^k}] of A_crys(R), which is fixed by the divided Frobenius and lies in the kernel of A_crys(R) → W(R). The erratum diagnoses the gap: 'While the generators of the kernel of A_crys(R) → W(R) used in the proof do topologically generate the kernel in the p-adic topology of A_crys(R), they fail to do so in the p-adic topology of the kernel itself.' The statement of Proposition 5.23 is unaffected: it was already known by the different proofs of Lau, Displays and formal p-divisible groups, and of Zink, The display of a formal p-divisible group, both cited immediately before it, and the erratum records that 'the arguments of this fallacious proof are not used anywhere else in the paper, so this mistake does not affect any of the results stated in the paper'.
issues.reason: Verified against the erratum itself, which was published for exactly this proposition; the mistake was pointed out to the authors by Akhil Mathew and Andrew Senger. Note that the paper proves a similar topological-nilpotence statement twice more, in Lemma 4.88 (arXiv Lemma 4.9.3) for the kernel of Δ_S → Δ_{S̃} and in Lemma 5.15 (arXiv Lemma 5.2.8) for the Breuil–Kisin prism; neither is retracted, and the erratum's sentence that the fallacious argument is used nowhere else applies to them.

The content of this proposition was already known to be true by a different proof... It identifies the same key step the entry quotes - topological nilpotence of the divided Frobenius on the kernel of A_crys(R) -> W(R) - calls it 'not true', and gives Senger's counterexample R = F_p[x^{1/p^infty}]/x with the element sum_k p[x]^{1/p^k}/p^k fixed by the divided Frobenius. issues.locator: Example7.3, arXiv v2 p50; published p3780. The proposed range correction is rejected.
issues.printed: Using [antieauperiodic] filtrations, the source claims π_i HC(k/W(k)) ≅ W(k)/p^{s+1} when i = 2s ≥ 0 and 0 otherwise, in the range i ≤ 2p−1. It then concludes, for 0 ≤ i ≤ 2p−2, that π_i HC((W(k),(p)/W(k)) ≅ p^{s+1}W(k) when i = 2s and 0 for odd i.
issues.correction: The two ranges should be i ≤ 2p−4 and 0 ≤ i ≤ 2p−4 (equivalently i ≤ 2p−3, since the odd groups vanish).
issues.reason: Both formulas are read off from the sentence immediately before them, that LΩ_k/LΩ_k^{≥s} ≅ W(k)/p^s for s ≤ p−1, applied with s+1 in place of s: π_{2s}HC(k/W(k)) = LΩ_k/LΩ_k^{≥s+1}. That needs s+1 ≤ p−1, i.e. i = 2s ≤ 2p−4. At the first excluded value, i = 2p−2 and s = p−1, the formula would give W(k)/p^p, but LΩ_k here is the p-completed divided power envelope of (p) ⊆ W(k) — that is, W(k) itself — and its Hodge filtration is the divided power filtration, whose p-th step is generated by γ_p(p) = p^p/p!, of p-adic valuation p − 1 since v_p(p!) = 1. So LΩ_k/LΩ_k^{≥p} = W(k)/p^{p−1} and π_{2p−2}HC(k/W(k)) ≅ W(k)/p^{p−1}, not W(k)/p^p; correspondingly the relative group is p^{p−1}W(k), not p^pW(k). The conclusion of the example is unaffected: it is drawn in the range 1 ≤ i ≤ 2p−5, where the odd degrees used are i = 2s+1 ≤ 2p−5, so s ≤ p−3 and s+1 ≤ p−2, well inside the range where the de Rham formula holds.

issues.citation: Antieau–Mathew–Morrow–Nikolaus, "On the Beilinson fiber square", Duke Mathematical Journal (2022)
issues.reviewReason: The asserted identification LΩ_k=W(k) is false. Use the universal relative PD model, not the PD structure compatible with the canonical divided powers on p. By SZ18 Proposition3.16 and derived base change x↦p (Bhatt12 Proposition8.5), its quotient by F^r is the cokernel of x−p on the free W(k)-module with basis e_j=γ_j(x), 0≤j<r. Relations are p e_j=(j+1)e_(j+1) for j<r−1 and p e_(r−1)=0. For r≤p, 1,…,r−1 are units, so this is W(k)/p^r, including r=p. The map is injective before taking its cokernel (triangular determinant ±p^r), so no negative cohomology occurs. At the disputed i=2p−2, r=p, the printed W(k)/p^p is correct. One cannot cancel p! to replace the universal PD algebra by W(k). Bhatt Corollary8.6 explicitly displays the additional completed PD torsion. The published p3780 retains both ranges, which are not disproved by the extraction.

issues.locator: Published Theorem 9.1/Definition 9.2 pp48–50; arXiv v4 pp52–54
issues.printed: The source asserts that exactly one function exists.
issues.correction: Replace the unique-choice definition by a solution-set/existence interface pending a repaired theorem with extra conditions. The two printed test conditions alone do not determine a vector for n=m=2. Also remove the assertion that all restricted Speh vectors lie in Pi.
issues.reason: For n=m=2, G'=GL2,V'=1,T'=id and all formal W^0 are left-N'-invariant. With u=[[1,varpi^-1],[0,1]], f=1_(uK')-1_K' is a nonzero right-K'-invariant compact function annihilated by every test integral by left translation (det u=1). Extend f to D=V iota(G') using Psi. Lapid–Mao20 Cor3.13/3.15 supplies a Shalika vector with this restriction; right averaging preserves f. Adding it to the L=1 essential vector gives a second solution. The proof's character claim fails explicitly: (I+tE13)(I+bE32)(I-tE13)=I+bE32+tbE12, so Psi changes by psi(tb). See report for full argument and limits. The continuation verifies the compact-induction hypothesis directly against Lapid–Mao Cor3.13/3.15 and obtains infinitely many independent perturbations using u_r=I+varpi^-r E12. These vectors satisfy precisely the printed right-iota(Kprime) condition; no K^(c_pi)-invariance is claimed. (cc-442dc5) Rechecked. For n = m = 2, V′ = 1, V″ = V and Ψ(g) = ψ(g_12 + g_34). Conjugating V by ι(u′) = 1 + zE_13 sends E_32 to E_32 − zE_12, so Ψ is not preserved, and the step 'φ_Ze(u′g′) = Ψ(u′)φ_Ze(g′)' in the uniqueness proof fails. If it held, every W∘ι (W ∈ W_Sh(σ)) would be left N′-invariant and square-integrable on GL_2 (Theorem 8.2), hence zero. That contradicts Lapid–Mao's Corollary 3.15, which the paper uses in its own existence proof.

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed as a gap in the printed proof, and the targeted step was read on the page image. Page 50 prints, verbatim: 'then φ_Ze(u′g′) = Ψ(u′)φ_Ze(g′) for u′ ∈ N′ and g′ ∈ G′. Therefore, we have W ∘ ι ∈ Π.' Its only stated justification is the preceding clause, that ι(G′) normalises V″ and that the action of ι(N′) on V″ preserves the invariant measure on (V″∩N)\V″. Measure-invariance is not Ψ-equivariance, and I verified by direct computation that Ψ is genuinely not preserved: in the n = m = 2 case, with E_13E_32 = E_12 one gets (1+tE_13)(1+bE_32)(1−tE_13) = 1 + bE_32 + tbE_12 exactly, so conjugating the V″-element 1+bE_32 by ι(u′) = 1+tE_13 changes Ψ(g) = ψ(g_12 + g_34) by ψ(tb). The printed justification therefore does not establish the step. WHAT I DID NOT VERIFY: that uniqueness itself fails. The extraction's second solution is built from [20, Corollary 3.15] (Lapid–Mao), which I did not fetch or re-derive, so the kind 'error' and the 'affects a stated result' classification rest on that construction and not on this review. What this review establishes is the weaker and firmer claim that the printed proof of the uniqueness statement in Theorem 9.1 has an unjustified step. The extraction's internal consistency argument is worth recording: were the step valid, every W∘ι would be left N′-invariant and square-integrable on GL_2 by Theorem 8.2, hence zero, contradicting the paper's own existence proof on p. 49, which uses [20, Corollary 3.15] to produce a nonzero such vector. No later version or erratum corrects it: arXiv 2110.09070 stops at v4, whose hash the extraction records and which this review re-fetched and confirmed (32326ab8…83a6c), and Crossref's record of doi:10.1017/fmp.2022.17 carries no update-to, updated-by or relation entry (checked 23 September 2026). Verified against the published open-access text, all 56 pages.

issues.citation: Atobe–Kondo–Yasuda, "Local newforms for the general linear groups over a non-archimedean local field", Forum of Mathematics, Pi (2022)
issues.reviewReason: Confirmed, and I verified it independently and in a stronger form than the finding states. Page 38 prints 'Observe that the intersection G_n ∩ ⋂_{m≥1} Z_n X_λ^{≥m} is empty.' Page 37 defines X_λ ⊂ M_n(o) as the matrices with a_{i,j} ≡ δ_{i,j} mod p^{λ_i}. For λ = 0 that congruence is modulo p^0 = o and so is vacuous, giving X_0 = M_n(o). Then for ANY g ∈ G_n and any m, choosing N large makes ϖ^N g integral with det(ϖ^N g) = ϖ^{Nn} det g ∈ p^m, so g = ϖ^{−N}·(ϖ^N g) ∈ Z_n X_0^{≥m}. Hence the intersection is all of G_n, not empty — and this holds for every n, not only n = 1. The finding's counterexample to the lemma itself also stands: for n = 1, λ = 0 and π an unramified character (cuspidal, there being no proper parabolic in GL_1), V^{K_{1,0}} is one-dimensional and 1_{ϖo^×} ∈ a_0 acts by π(ϖ) ≠ 0, which is not nilpotent. The proposed repair is right and the extraction is right to say this does not refute Theorem 2.2: in the ambient L(s,π) = 1 application π is ramified, so V^{K_{n,0}} = 0 and a_{0,V} = 0 trivially. No later version or erratum corrects it: arXiv 2110.09070 stops at v4, whose hash the extraction records and which this review re-fetched and confirmed (32326ab8…83a6c), and Crossref's record of doi:10.1017/fmp.2022.17 carries no update-to, updated-by or relation entry (checked 23 September 2026). issues.locator: Published proof of Lemma 8.10 p47; v4 corresponding proof
issues.printed: The source claims spanning by W⁰_Ze(x), with x = (x_{i,j}) ∈ M_{m,n−1}(ℂ) restricted by the multiset equality {q^{−s₁}, …, q^{−s_{(n−1)m}}} = {x_{i,j} | 1 ≤ i ≤ m, 1 ≤ j ≤ n−1}.
issues.correction: The all-parameter spanning statement must be replaced: n=m=2, equal parameters(x,x) admit the additional eigenfunction H(g)=(a-b)q^(-(a-b)/2)x^(a+b) for g=n diag(varpi^a,varpi^b)k. Distinct-parameter spanning and a confluent family at collisions require separate valid statements and proofs.
issues.reason: In the published §8.1–8.2/8.5 primed model, n=m=2 gives G′=GL₂, P′=B′, L′=GL₁×GL₁, N′=U′ and Ψ|N′=1 (also V′=1). The actual family on all integer Iwasawa valuations is F_{x1,x2}(a,b)=q^{−(a−b)/2}x1^a x2^b, with no a≥b support wall. Right cosets of K′diag(ϖ,1)K′ give Tf(a,b)=qf(a+1,b)+f(a,b+1), with vol(K′)=1. At x1=x2=x≠0, put F=q^{−(a−b)/2}x^{a+b} and H=(a−b)F. Each shift contributes √q x times F; for H the coefficients are a−b+1 and a−b−1, so TF=2√q x F and TH=2√q x H for every a,b∈ℤ. The central operator and its inverse act by x² and x⁻² on both. These generate the GL₂ spherical Hecke algebra, hence the eigencharacter agrees. F(1)=1, H(1)=0 and H(diag(ϖ,1))=q^{−1/2}x≠0, so H is independent of the sole formal assignment F at multiset {x,x}. The opposite-row family is F exp(t(a−b)), whose derivative is H, not zero; only its Hecke eigenvalues are even. The prior rejection substituted the generic GL₂ Whittaker Schur family, which is not this degenerate model. This disproves the printed all-parameter span at collisions, not the main newform theorem or general direct-integral conclusions.

issues.locator: Propositions 9.5 and 9.6 and the paragraph after the proof of Proposition 9.6, pp. 50–54, with Corollary 9.4 and the uniqueness proof of Theorem 9.1, pp. 49–50, in the published version (Forum Math. Pi 10 (2022) e24)
issues.printed: The source uses the conjugacy of K_{nm,λ_σ} and K(c_π), together with Propositions 9.5 and 9.6, to claim that Theorem 2.1 is proved for σ = Sp(π, m) satisfying L(s, π) = 1.
issues.correction:
For σ = Sp(π, m) with L(s, π) = 1 and n, m ≥ 2, the paper does not establish Theorem 2.1.
- Proposition 9.5 rests on Corollary 9.4.
- Proposition 9.6 rests on Lemma 9.3 and the uniqueness in Theorem 9.1.
All three proofs use the same step: W∘ι lies in Π because φ_Ze is (N′, Ψ)-equivariant. The justification printed for that step does not establish it (E1). Whether the uniqueness statement is itself false depends on E1's second-solution construction, which has not been independently verified.
What is needed:
- another proof of Corollary 9.4 (injectivity of W ↦ W|_L on right ι(K′)-invariant vectors);
- another proof that σ^{K(c_π)} ≠ 0.
No counterexample to Theorem 2.1 is known.
issues.reason: Theorem 2.1 for π with L(s, π) = 1 reduces, by Lemma 7.2, to Z(Δ) = Sp(ρ, m), and for n, m ≥ 2 its only proof is §9. The case m = 1 is [14], and for n = 1 σ is a character of GL_m. The counterexample of E1 is right ι(K′)-invariant with all test integrals zero, so the §9 argument cannot separate it. Whether it is K(c_π)-invariant, which would contradict Theorem 2.1, is not known.

issues.locator: Theorem 4.1, JAMS p. 928; the failing step is on p. 929 ('We are reduced to proving that the composition …'); author pp. 13–14
issues.printed: Theorem 4.1 asserts R_an,exp-definability of the period map Φ : (Δ*)^n → S_{Γ,G,M} for a variation V over (Δ*)^n of pure Hodge structures, polarized and of weight k.
issues.correction: Restrict to smaller polydisks: for every 0 < ρ < 1, Φ restricted to (Δ*_ρ)^n is R_an,exp-definable. The printed proof gives ρ = e^(−2π), once 0 < x < 1 is replaced by 0 ≤ x < 1 (see E45). For general ρ < 1: cover the closed ρ-polydisk, which is compact in Δ^n, by finitely many small polydisk charts centred at its points, each of the form (Δ*)^r × Δ^l, and apply the local statement in each chart. Alternatively, rerun §4.2 on {0 ≤ x < 1, y > η} with η = −(log ρ)/2π. That uses Theorem 1.5 for this η, and its printed proof (§4.5, on Σ_n with y > 1) needs the same compactness step. §4.1 must use charts whose shrunken polydisks still cover S̄.
issues.reason: The counterexample holds; I rechecked it by hand and numerically. With f(z) = exp(−(1+z)/(1−z)), τ = 2i + εf and trivial monodromy, the fibre over π(2i + ε/e) is {z_n = 2πin/(2+2πin) : n ≠ 0}, an infinite discrete set accumulating at 1. The fibre of a definable map would have finitely many components. Δ is the unit disk (p. 922), and e(·) maps H onto the unit Δ* (p. 929). Where the proof fails: Lemma 4.2 is true as stated with no shrinking, because Schmid (4.12) (p. 233) says Ψ extends holomorphically to the whole open Δ^n, and p(S_H^n) lies in the compact polydisk |q_j| ≤ e^(−2π). The failing step is the reduction 'We are reduced to proving that the composition S_H^n → G/M → S_{Γ,G,M} is R_an,exp-definable'. That reduction controls Φ only on p(S_H^n) ⊂ (Δ*_(e^(−2π)))^n. The earlier correction's 'then for every ρ<1 by compactness of the remaining annular pieces' is inaccurate for n ≥ 2: {ρ ≤ |q_1| < ρ'} × (Δ*)^(n−1) is not compact. The author copy is identical. The erratum does not mention this; §1.5 calls the proof of Theorem 1.3 correct apart from the §4.5 citation. Theorem 1.3 is unaffected.

issues.citation: Bakker–Klingler–Tsimerman, "Tame topology of arithmetic quotients and algebraicity of Hodge loci", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2020)
issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: Quotation matches p. 928 (author copy p. 13 identical). Δ is the unit disk (p. 922) and e(·) is the uniformization of the unit Δ* (p. 929), so the theorem concerns the whole unit punctured polydisk. Counterexample rechecked: (1+z)/(1−z) maps Δ onto Re w > 0, so f(z) = exp(−(1+z)/(1−z)) has |f| < 1. τ = 2i + εf is the period map of a weight-one Z-PVHS on Δ, with trivial monodromy on Δ*. For torsion-free Γ, π is injective on B(2i, ε) when ε is small, so Φ^(−1)(π(2i+ε/e)) = {z ∈ Δ* : f(z) = 1/e} = {z_n = 2πin/(2+2πin) : n ≠ 0}. Here f(z_n) = e^(−1−2πin) = e^(−1) exactly, |z_n| < 1 and z_n → 1 (also checked numerically). An infinite discrete fibre is not definable, so Theorem 4.1 is false as printed. The revised diagnosis is right. Schmid (4.12) (p. 233, checked in the local copy) says Ψ extends holomorphically to all of Δ^k. p(𝔖_H^n) ⊂ {|q_j| < e^(−2π)} is relatively compact in Δ^n, so Lemma 4.2 holds with no shrinking. The failing step is the reduction to 𝔖_H^n, which controls Φ only on p(𝔖_H^n). The criticism of the old correction is also right: for n ≥ 2, {ρ ≤ |q_1| < ρ'} × (Δ*)^(n−1) is not compact, so compactness has to be applied to the closed polydisk inside Δ^n, using local charts. Of the two routes in the revised correction, the covering route is self-contained. The η-route relies on Theorem 1.5 for small η. Theorem 1.5 is stated for every η > 0 (p. 921), but §4.5 proves it only on Σ_n (y > 1), so the η-route needs the same compactness step. The erratum is silent. Theorem 1.3 is unaffected once the charts are buffered. The kind 'error' and reach 'a stated result' are right.

issues.locator: Lemma 4.5 proof, JAMS p.930; author p.15
issues.printed: The proof substitutes z_1 = mz_2 + c into f to define f_{m,c}, for each positive integer m and each real c. It asserts that f_{m,c} satisfies the lemma’s hypotheses and that induction on n yields f_{m,c} ≪ 1 throughout Σ_{n−1}.
issues.correction: State the lemma, and verify its curve hypothesis, on wider sectors Σ_n^R={|x_i|<R,y₁≥⋯≥y_n>1} for every R, with constants depending on R. The substitution maps Σ_(n−1)^R′ into Σ_n^(mR′+|c|). The application needs original-source bounded-real-width uniformity for Schmid Corollary 5.29 and the CKS/Kashiwara norm estimates; G3 records that this is still unverified. The R-quantifier of the target Theorem 1.5 is not evidence for its prerequisites.
issues.reason: Σ_n is defined with 0 < x_i < 1 (Definition 4.4). The proof uses c = 0, 1, …, r_1 and m ≥ 1. For c ≥ 1, x_1 = mx_2 + c > 1, so Σ_n ∩ {z_1 = mz_2 + c} is empty. For c = 0 it is only the strip x_2 < 1/m. So the hypothesis gives no information about f_{m,c} on Σ_{n−1}. The functions extend there (the coefficients in O are periodic in x and f is polynomial in x), but the bound is assumed only on Σ_n. With the R-uniform hypothesis, the finite difference in c isolates the top x_1-degree, the Vandermonde step in m isolates each y-power, and |x_1| < 1 on Σ_n finishes the proof, as printed. Noted by the extraction (verification gap G4); the repair is given by this continuation.

issues.locator: §4.5, JAMS p.933; author p.18
issues.printed: The source asserts that b being (e′, C′)-reduced, together with a basis e satisfying Definition 4.11, condition (3), for some C > 0, makes b (e, C″)-reduced with some C″ = C″(e, C, e′, C′) > 0.
issues.correction: Condition (2), the ordering b(e_i) < C b(e_j) for i < j, transfers only up to a permutation of e. Conclude that b is (σe, C″)-reduced for some permutation σ, which is one of finitely many.
issues.reason: Take e′ = (e_1, e_2), e = (e_2, e_1) and b = diag(1, T) with T ≥ 1. Then b is (e′, 2)-reduced and satisfies condition (3) for e (b(e_2)b(e_1) = T = det b), but condition (2) for e would need T = b(e_2) < C″b(e_1) = C″ for all T. The proof immediately adds 'we may assume (2) as there are only finitely many orderings of the basis', which is the corrected form, so Theorem 1.5 is unaffected. Noted by the extraction (item basis-change-reducedness).

issues.correction: The definable structure depends on a choice of maximal compact subgroup K ⊃ M. For each such K there is a structure S_{Γ,G,M,K}, characterized by the Siegel sets associated to K. issues.reason: Erratum §1.6.1: for G = SL₂, a Siegel set built with K_x is not contained in finitely many Siegel sets built with K_i when x ≠ i, so the two structures on Γ\G differ. The Hodge-theoretic statements are unaffected, because Hodge manifolds carry a canonical K (Erratum §1.4).

issues.citation: Bakker–Klingler–Tsimerman, "Tame topology of arithmetic quotients and algebraicity of Hodge loci", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2020)
issues.reviewReason: Checked on the page images and independently. Proposition 2.7(2) as printed, with the basepoints free, is false. Take 𝐆 = SL₂, Γ = SL₂(ℤ), 𝐏₁ = 𝐏₂ the upper triangular subgroup, 𝔖₁ = U₁A_{t₁}K_{iv} (v ≠ 1; the diagonal torus is θ_{iv}-stable) and 𝔖₂ = U₂A_{t₂}SO₂ with U₂ = {(1,b;0,1) : |b| < 1}. Then 𝔖₁·i ∋ s²z₀ for all s² > t₁, where z₀ = u₀+iy₀ ∈ K_{iv}·i has u₀ ≠ 0. So 𝔖₁ meets γ_n𝔖₂ for γ_n = (1,n;0,1) and all large n, and Γ_{𝔖₂,𝔖₁} is infinite. The step of §3.1 quoted above fails in the same way: γ𝔖 is associated to γx, and a Siegel set for another maximal compact is not contained in a Siegel set for K (erratum §1.6.1). With K fixed the step holds by Lemma 2.4 and erratum Remark 1.1(1). Author copy and arXiv v2 have the same text.

issues.reviewReason: Theorem 3.2 (= [O17, Thm 1.2] = Orr 2018 Thm 1.2) is correct as stated. It is existential in K_G, and Orr–Schnell (ANT 17 (2023) 1231) confirm the statement and supply the existence of K_G through Mostow. It does not control the maximal compact of the Siegel set 𝔖_i it produces, so '(3.2) … definable by Theorem 1.1(1)' needs the false K-independence of E5. Likewise the case 𝐆′ = 𝐆 with M′ ⊊ M is not 'clear': under the printed Definition 2.5, K_x ⊃ hM′h⁻¹ does not give K_x ⊃ h′Mh′⁻¹. issues.citation: Bakker–Klingler–Tsimerman, "Tame topology of arithmetic quotients and algebraicity of Hodge loci", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2020)
issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: The quotation matches the p. 932 image. The author copy and arXiv v2 read the same. Known: erratum §1.5 replaces [B-HC62, 7.5] with [1, 28.1] 'as the former is for real Siegel sets'. I checked the replacement in BGST, arXiv:2112.06995v1. Prop. 28.1 there is Prop. 3.4 of the published version (Épijournal Géom. Algébrique 2023, Art. 1). Setting: H ⊆ G reductive over ℚ, with K_H = K_G ∩ H(ℝ). Hypothesis: every K_H-Siegel set of H lies in finitely many G(ℚ)-translates of a K_G-Siegel set of G. Conclusion: S_G ∩ H(ℝ) ⊆ F·S_H for some finite F ⊂ H(ℚ). BGST §28 itself says the result is 'similar to [BHC62, Lem. 7.5], except that we are working with Siegel sets for Q-algebraic groups (instead of with Siegel domains for R-algebraic groups)'. So the printed citation does not give the rational statement. The asserted inclusion is nevertheless true, so the step is unjustified rather than false, which makes it a gap; the revision to 'gap' is right. Hypothesis check: take H = G′ = MT(V)^der ⊂ SL(V) and K_G = SO(h_{x0}). For X ∈ 𝔤′, invariance of Q gives h(Xu,v) = −h(u, C X C^{−1} v). So θ_{K_G}(X) = −X^* = Ad(C_{x0})X, which lies in 𝔤′ because C_{x0} ∈ MT(ℝ). Also K_H = G′(ℝ) ∩ K_G. Orr–Schnell Thm 1 (the criterion quoted in erratum §1.3) then supplies the hypothesis. It follows that ι^{−1}(S_X) is the image of S̃_X ∩ G′(ℝ) ⊆ F·S_{G′}. That is finitely many G′(ℚ)-translates of a Siegel set of D, and each translate is again a Siegel set (Remark 2.6(1); for K-Siegel sets write g = k₀p₀ with p₀ ∈ P(ℝ)). The erratum's correction is right, but it applies only once a group acting on V is used (E27/E27).

issues.locator: Lemma 2.1, first (algebraic) proof, p. 923
issues.printed: The source composes the orbit map for v ∈ W with (p₁,…,p_d) : W → ℝ^d. The resulting map p : 𝐆(ℝ) → W → ℝ^d is real algebraic. It claims that p identifies 𝐆(ℝ)/M with p(𝐆(ℝ)) and therefore identifies G/M with one connected component of p(𝐆(ℝ)).
issues.correction: Drop the invariant polynomials. Stab_{𝐆(ℝ)}(v) = M, so the orbit map induces a continuous bijection 𝐆(ℝ)/M → 𝐆(ℝ)·v. The orbit is semi-algebraic and locally closed (a semi-algebraic set is locally closed on a dense open subset of itself, and 𝐆(ℝ) acts transitively), so the bijection is a homeomorphism. G/M = G·v is a connected component of 𝐆(ℝ)·v, hence semi-algebraic. Alternatively, use the second proof with E ⊂ G × G (E9).
issues.reason: p(mg·v) = p(g·v) for m ∈ M, so p is constant on double cosets MgM and identifies 𝐆(ℝ)/M with its image only if M is normal. Existing counterexample checked: W = Sym₂(ℝ) ⊕ ℝ, v = (I,1), the line stabiliser is SO₂; g = diag(2,1/2) and k the rotation by π/2 give g·v = (diag(4,1/4),1) and kg·v = (diag(1/4,4),1), which have the same SO₂-invariants (trace, det, t), while g⁻¹kg = (0,−1/4;4,0) ∉ M. Lemma 2.1 remains true. The printed quote in E8 ('G/M ≃ p(G·v)') is not on the page; the text above is. Author copy and arXiv v2 are identical.
