issues.citation: Bakker–Klingler–Tsimerman, "Tame topology of arithmetic quotients and algebraicity of Hodge loci", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2020)
issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: Revision accepted. The revised quote matches the p. 923 image word for word. The ledger's 'G/M ≃ p(G·v)' is a paraphrase and does not appear on the page. The author copy and arXiv v2 have the same text. Independent check: p(g) = (p_1(g·v),…,p_d(g·v)). For m ∈ M, p(gm) = p(g) because M fixes v, and p(mg) = p(g) because the p_j are M-invariant. So p factors through the double-coset space M\𝐆(ℝ)/M. It is injective on 𝐆(ℝ)/M only if mgM = gM for all m and g, that is, only if M is normal. This holds for every Chevalley module W, not just a special one. For SL₂ ⊃ SO₂ the double-coset space is 1-dimensional and G/M is 2-dimensional, so no W can work. The ledger's explicit example is correct: g·v = (diag(4,1/4),1) and kg·v = (diag(1/4,4),1) have the same SO₂-invariants (tr, det, t), while g⁻¹kg = (0,−1/4;4,0) ∉ SO₂. The lemma itself survives, and the proposed repair is sound. Stab_{𝐆(ℝ)}(v) ⊂ Stab(l) = M and M fixes v, so Stab(v) = M. The orbit 𝐆(ℝ)·v is semi-algebraic (Tarski–Seidenberg). It is locally closed: a semi-algebraic set is locally closed on a dense open subset of itself, and 𝐆(ℝ) acts transitively on the orbit by homeomorphisms of W. So the orbit is locally compact, and the continuous bijection 𝐆(ℝ)/M → 𝐆(ℝ)·v is a homeomorphism (Baire, 𝐆(ℝ) σ-compact). G/M is then an open and closed connected piece, i.e. a connected component. The second proof (with E9) also works. The first proof's key step is false as written, so kind error and affects the proof are right.

issues.citation: Bakker–Klingler–Tsimerman, "Tame topology of arithmetic quotients and algebraicity of Hodge loci", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2020)
issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: Revision accepted. I checked the p. 923 image at 400 dpi: 'We recall (see [BJ06a, Lemma 2.3] that the right action of P on itself under the horospherical decomposition is given by (2.3) (n₀a₀m_o)(n,a,m) = (n₀·(a₀m₀)n(a₀m₀)⁻¹, a₀a, m₀m)'. The font data confirm that the first subscript is an italic letter o (CMMI7 'o'), while every other subscript is a roman zero. The parenthesis opened before 'see' is never closed. Computation: n₀a₀m₀·nam = n₀[(a₀m₀)n(a₀m₀)⁻¹](a₀m₀)am = [n₀(a₀m₀)n(a₀m₀)⁻¹](a₀a)(m₀m), because P normalises N_P and A_P commutes with M_P. So (2.3) is left multiplication by p₀ = n₀a₀m₀. The right action would be nam·n₀a₀m₀, which is a different formula. The same computation holds on G with m ∈ M_PK, as used later (Siegel sets in G). Changing 'on itself' to 'on G' is optional: with m ∈ M_P, i.e. with (2.1), the formula is also correct on P. The same text is in the author copy and arXiv v2.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition A.2, pp. 935–936: the compatibility step (p. 935), the independence claim and the definability of i_X (p. 936)
issues.printed: The source assumes the subset U_x ⊂ R^n_k is semi-analytic and relatively compact, making it R_an-definable. It claims real analytic compatibility of (U_x, φ_x) and (U_y, φ_y) immediately gives R_an-compatibility. On p. 936 it asserts independence from the choices, including the relatively compact semi-analytic U_x, and infers R_an-definability of i_X : ∂X → X directly from its weak real analyticity.
issues.correction: Take each U_x to be a relatively compact semianalytic subset, open in R^n_k (e.g. a corner box), whose closure is compact inside the domain of a larger analytic chart φ'_x. Then {(u,v) ∈ cl U_x × cl U_y : φ'_x(u) = φ'_y(v)} is compact, and near each of its points it is the graph of an analytic extension of the transition. So the graph of the transition over U_x × U_y is bounded and semianalytic at every point of R^{2n}, hence globally subanalytic, i.e. R_an-definable. The same buffered argument proves the independence of choices (mixed transitions between two buffered atlases) and the R_an-definability of i_X (its local expressions in buffered charts of ∂X and X).
issues.reason: I checked the counterexample: F(x) = x + (x²/4) sin(1/x) on (0,1) has F' ≥ 1 − 1/2 − 1/4 = 1/4, so it is an analytic diffeomorphism onto a bounded interval. Then (0,1) → S¹ and its reparametrisation by F^{-1} are analytically compatible charts with bounded semialgebraic domains, but {F(x) = x} = {1/(nπ)} is infinite and discrete, so F is not definable in any o-minimal structure. So the 'immediate' inference fails for charts that are merely relatively compact in R^n_k. It works only if 'relatively compact' is read as relatively compact in the domain of a larger chart; that reading is the case for the defence, but it is not stated. The same unbuffered inference recurs twice on p. 936 (independence of choices; i_X definable), so the record is widened to cover them. Proposition A.2 itself is true. The author copy is the same, and the erratum does not mention it.

issues.citation: Bakker–Klingler–Tsimerman, "Tame topology of arithmetic quotients and algebraicity of Hodge loci", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2020)
issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: I checked the quotations on the images of pp. 935–936. The author copy is word for word the same, and the erratum is silent here. I re-derived the counterexample. F(x) = x + (x²/4)sin(1/x) on (0,1) has F'(x) = 1 + (x/2)sin(1/x) − (1/4)cos(1/x) ≥ 1/4, so F is an analytic diffeomorphism onto the bounded interval (0, 1 + sin(1)/4). F(x) = x exactly at x = 1/(nπ), n ≥ 1, an infinite discrete set, so F is not definable in any o-minimal structure. Take φ(t) = e^{iπt} on (0,1) and ψ = φ∘F^{-1}. Both are real analytic charts of S¹ with bounded semialgebraic domains. They are real analytically compatible in the paper's sense (p. 934: the transition ψ^{-1}∘φ = F extends analytically to an open neighbourhood of its domain), but they are not R_an-compatible. So the printed hypotheses (U_x relatively compact in R^n_k and semianalytic) do not give the 'immediate' implication. For the defence: a WLOG shrinking naturally stays inside the original chart domain, and with that buffer the implication holds (see the correction). So Proposition A.2 is true and the proof is repairable. But the buffer is neither stated nor implied by 'relatively compact in R^n_k': in the example above no shrinking is triggered. The two p. 936 claims rest on the same unbuffered inference. Mixed transitions between two such atlases, and the local expressions of the weakly real analytic i_X, are only known to be analytic on open neighbourhoods of their domains. Definability needs analyticity up to the closure. So widening the locator is justified, and the classification (gap, affects the proof) is right.

issues.locator: §1.3 (p. 920: 'let G be its associated adjoint semi-simple Q-group') against §4.2 (p. 928) and §4.4 (p. 931); also §4.5, second paragraph, p. 932
issues.printed: The source places T_i, the monodromy transformation, in G(Z) ⊂ GL(V_Z). It also says the natural embedding G(ℚ) ⊂ SL(V_ℚ) induces ι : D → X with ι(x) := h_x.
issues.correction: Take G = MT(V)^der ⊂ SL(V_Q), which is semisimple and acts on V, throughout §4. Unipotent T_i lie in the identity component of the monodromy group, which is contained in MT^der, so T_i ∈ MT^der(Q) and N_i ∈ Lie(MT^der) = g_Q. Γ is torsion-free, so it meets the finite centre trivially. D, the Siegel sets and the definable structure of S_(Γ,G,M) correspond under the isogeny MT^der → MT^ad (a surjective morphism of arithmetic quotients as in §3.2). Erratum §1.4 likewise uses a group inside GL(V_Q). Also: Merge into E27 as an additional locator (§4.5, second paragraph, p. 932). Read G′ = MT(V)^der ⊂ SL(V) in place of G, and note that the Siegel sets of D = G/M are the same whether defined through G′ or through G.
issues.reason: §4 treats G as acting on V: T_i ∈ G(Z) ⊂ GL(V_Z), γ(z) ∈ G(C) applied to u ∈ V_C (p. 931), and G(Q) ⊂ SL(V_Q) (p. 932). An adjoint group does not act on V in general (−I ∈ SL_2 acts nontrivially). The fix is routine and changes no statement, so I downgrade 'affects' from 'the proof' to 'nothing'.

issues.citation: Bakker–Klingler–Tsimerman, "Tame topology of arithmetic quotients and algebraicity of Hodge loci", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2020)
issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: Quotations confirmed on the images. p. 920: 'let G be its associated adjoint semi-simple Q-group'. p. 928: 'T_i ∈ G(Z) ⊂ GL(V_Z)'. p. 931: γ(z) ∈ G(C) is applied to u ∈ V_C. p. 932: 'G(Q) ⊂ SL(V_Q)'. An adjoint group need not act on V. For a non-isotrivial family of elliptic curves, MT = GL_2 and G = PGL_2, and V = Q^2 is not a PGL_2-representation because −I ∈ SL_2 acts nontrivially. So §4 silently uses a different group. The revised fix works. A unipotent T_i lies in the identity component of the algebraic monodromy group, since the Zariski closure of the group a unipotent element generates is connected. That identity component lies in MT^der (Deligne/André). If one wants T_i ∈ MT(Q) first: the tensors defining the generic MT group become flat after a finite étale cover, and then the torus argument of the revision applies. MT^der ⊂ SL(V) is semisimple. A torsion-free Γ' ⊂ MT^der(Q) meets the finite centre trivially, so it maps isomorphically onto an arithmetic subgroup of G(Q). D and the rational parabolics and Siegel sets correspond under the central isogeny. The identification S_(Γ',G',M') ≅ S_(Γ,G,M) is a surjective morphism of arithmetic quotients, handled as in §3.2 (compatible with the Hodge-theoretic maximal compacts of erratum §1.4), so it is definable. Erratum §1.4 does take G to be the Q-Zariski closure of t(S¹) in GL(V_Q). The adapter is routine, uses only results in the paper and changes no statement. So the downgrade to 'nothing' is acceptable and consistent with the other routine gaps of this range. The kind 'gap' stands. The same place also has: The quotation matches the p. 932 image, and arXiv v2 reads the same. On p. 920, G is 'its associated adjoint semi-simple ℚ-group', the adjoint group of MT(V). An adjoint group need not act on V at all. Example: PGL_2 ≅ SO(3) has only odd-dimensional irreducible representations, so it has no faithful 2-dimensional representation and does not act on the standard weight-one V. There is therefore no 'natural embedding G(ℚ) ⊂ SL(V_ℚ)'. The map ι(x) = h_x itself is well defined without a group, but the comparison of Siegel sets through BGST 28.1 (E-E7) needs a subgroup of SL(V). The repair is routine. G′ = MT(V)^der ⊂ SL(V) is semisimple, and G′(ℝ)^+ → G(ℝ)^+ is surjective, so G′(ℝ)^+ acts transitively on D. ℚ-parabolics correspond under the central isogeny, N_P and A_P^0 map isomorphically, and the kernel is finite, so the Siegel sets of D defined by G′ and by G agree. The erratum's §1.4 reformulation uses G = ℚ-Zariski closure of t(S^1) ⊂ GL(V), consistent with this fix, but it does not amend §4.5. This is the same issue as E27 (T_i ∈ G(ℤ) ⊂ GL(V_ℤ), p. 928) at a further locator.

issues.printed: The source defines HL(S_{Γ,G,M}) by taking the countable union of the special subvarieties in S_{Γ,G,M}, and asserts HL(S, V) equals Φ_S^{−1}(HL(S_{Γ,G,M})).
issues.correction: Read 'the (countable) union of strict special subvarieties of S_{Γ,G,M}' (Y ≠ S_{Γ,G,M}). Then HL(S,V) = Φ_S^{-1}(HL(S_{Γ,G,M})) holds because Φ_S(S) is Hodge generic. The same slip is in [K17, Def. 3.13 and Prop. 3.20].
issues.reason: With the definition on p. 933, the identity Hodge morphism makes S_{Γ,G,M} itself special. Read literally, HL(S_{Γ,G,M}) = S_{Γ,G,M} and the next sentence would give HL(S,V) = S. The intended meaning (strict special subvarieties, the convention of [K17] and the only one consistent with the §1.4 definition via exceptional Hodge tensors) is clear. The proof then shows that Φ_S^{-1}(Y) is algebraic for every special Y, strict or not, so nothing downstream changes. I therefore classify it as a misprint (an omitted word) rather than an error. The identification HL(S,V) = ⋃_{Y strict} Φ_S^{-1}(Y) is asserted without proof but is standard.

issues.citation: Bakker–Klingler–Tsimerman, "Tame topology of arithmetic quotients and algebraicity of Hodge loci", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2020)
issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: I checked the text on the images of pp. 933–934. By the definition on p. 933 the identity is a Hodge morphism, so S_{Γ,G,M} is itself special. Read literally, HL(S_{Γ,G,M}) = S_{Γ,G,M}, and the next sentence then gives HL(S,V) = S. That contradicts §1.4 (p. 921), where HL(S,V) is the set of points with exceptional Hodge tensors. The intended object is the union of the strict special subvarieties. Hod^0(S,V) is built from the generic Mumford–Tate group (§1.3), so Φ_S(S) is Hodge generic and HL(S,V) = Φ_S^{-1}(⋃_{Y strict} Y). The proof then shows that Φ_S^{-1}(Y) is algebraic for every special Y, strict or not, so nothing downstream changes. I endorse the revision from error to misprint: the qualifier is missing but the meaning is clear. One correction to the proposed reason: [K17] is not a source of the 'strict' convention. arXiv:1711.09387v1, the version cited, Definition 3.13 reads 'The Hodge locus HL(Y) of the connected mixed Hodge variety Y is the union of all special subvarieties of Y'. Its Proposition 3.20 states HL(S,V) = Φ_S^{-1}(Φ_S(S) ∩ HL(Hod^0(S,V))). So the paper inherits the same slip from [K17], while K17's own HL(S,V) (§§1.1, 2.6: the non-Hodge-generic points) matches the strict reading. The author copy has the same text, and the erratum is silent.

issues.locator: Theorem 4.12 and proof, JAMS p.933

issues.correction: Either restrict this proof to smooth S or supply algebraicity descent through a resolution/stratification and the necessary singular-source analytic comparison.

issues.locator: Erratum §1.2, p. 1
issues.printed: The source says K specifies a real Levi L ⊂ G with decomposition L = AQ, where A is its center and Q is semi-simple.
issues.correction: L = A_P M_P as in [2, §2.2]: A = A_P is the identity component of the real points of the maximal ℚ-split torus in the centre of 𝐋, and Q = M_P = ⋂_{χ∈X*(𝐋)} ker χ², which is reductive (not semisimple) in general.
issues.reason: For 𝐆 = R_{F/ℚ}SL₂ (F real quadratic) and 𝐏 = R_{F/ℚ}𝐁, L ≅ (ℝ^×)² is its own centre, A_P ≅ ℝ_{>0} is one-dimensional, and M_P = {(x₁,x₂) : (x₁x₂)² = 1} is a non-compact torus, not semisimple. The erratum refers to [2, §3.1] for the actual definition.
searched: Crossref record of doi:10.1090/jams/952, checked 2026-09-23: no update relation; the only correction is the authors' erratum, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 36 (2023), doi:10.1090/jams/1025, which was read in full
issues.citation: Bakker–Klingler–Tsimerman, "Tame topology of arithmetic quotients and algebraicity of Hodge loci", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2020)
issues.reviewReason: The quote matches erratum p. 1. Counterexample checked: 𝐆 = R_{F/ℚ}SL₂ with F real quadratic, and 𝐏 = R_{F/ℚ}𝐁. The real Levi is L ≅ (ℝ^×)², which is abelian and equal to its own centre. X*(𝐋) is generated by the norm, so A_P = {(t,t) : t > 0} and M_P = {(x₁,x₂) : (x₁x₂)² = 1}, a non-compact torus that is not semisimple. With 'A = the centre' read literally, the cone A_{>0} = {x₁² > c₁, x₂² > c₂} is 2-dimensional. The resulting sets UaA_{>0}W meet their translates under the units diag(ε^k, ε^{-k}) for unboundedly many k. So π restricted to them would not be definable, and the erratum's Theorem 1.2(1) would fail. The intended objects are those of [2, §2.2], which the erratum points to ('Briefly', 'as in [2, §3.1]', and 'as in Definition 2.3' in §1.1): A = A_P, the identity component of the real points of the ℚ-split centre, and Q = M_P, which is reductive in general. With these, everything is correct. The description is exact when the centre of 𝐋 is ℚ-split up to finite groups (e.g. 𝐆 ℚ-split), so this is a misprint with clear meaning, affecting nothing.

issues.correction: 'to be a real analytic map (φ, g) …' as in [2, §1.1].

issues.reviewReason: The quote matches erratum p. 2 ('to be a real semialgebraic map (φ, g)'). For maps between the ℝ_alg-definable manifolds S_{Γ,G,M,K}, 'semialgebraic' can only mean ℝ_alg-definable. So Theorem 1.2(2) ('Any morphism … is ℝ_alg-definable') would be true by definition, and so would Corollary 1.3, whose morphisms are defined through this notion. The proof instead derives definability from the group data (φ, g, K′ ⊂ gKg⁻¹, θ-compatibility) via Orr–Schnell. The original definition ([2, §1.1], p. 917) says 'real analytic map'. The slip is clear from context.

issues.reason: For g = n₀a₀m₀ ∈ P, g(U × A_{P,t} × W) = U′ × a₀A_{P,t} × m₀W with a₀A_{P,t} = {a : a^α > t·a₀^α for all α}. This is not of the form A_{P,t′} when rank 𝐏 ≥ 2 and the a₀^α differ. The two definitions are cofinal, so containment suffices wherever the remark is used.

issues.citation: Bakker–Klingler–Tsimerman, "Tame topology of arithmetic quotients and algebraicity of Hodge loci", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2020)
issues.reviewReason: The quote matches erratum p. 2. Defence: Remark 1.1(1) is exact for the definition stated just before it in §1.2 (𝔖 = UaA_{>0}W with a ∈ A). Take g = n₀a₀m₀ ∈ P(ℝ). By (2.3), g·ua′w = [n₀(a₀m₀)u(a₀m₀)⁻¹](a₀a′)(m₀w), so g𝔖 = U′(a₀a)A_{>0}(m₀W), again of that form. And 𝔖g = p⁻¹(p(𝔖k))p for g = kp. However, the erratum's §1.1 rewrites Definition 2.5 with Siegel sets 'as in Definition 2.3', where A_{P,t} has one threshold for all simple roots. For those sets a₀A_{P,t} = {a : a^α > t·a₀^α} is not an A_{P,t′} when rank 𝐏 ≥ 2 and the a₀^α differ. So under the definition §1.1 points to, the remark is literally false. The two definitions are cofinal: A_{P,t} = a_tA_{>0} with a_t^α = t, and aA_{>0} ⊂ A_{P,min a^α}. Containment suffices in Remark 1.1(2) and wherever else the remark is used. The mistake is really the inconsistency between §1.1 and §1.2, not the remark alone. It is a misprint that affects nothing.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 917 image: 'For S_{Γ,G,K} a connected Shimura variety, ... the uniformization map π : G/M → S_{Γ,G,K}'. The author copy has the same text. The uniformization of the Shimura variety Γ\G/K is the quotient map from the Hermitian symmetric domain G/K, which is the map studied in the works cited ([P11], [PT14], [KUY16], ...). The composite G/M → G/K → S_{Γ,G,K} exists when M ⊂ K, but it is not 'the uniformization map', and M is not specified in the sentence. The general G/M → S_{Γ,G,M} only appears in the next sentence, which announces it as the paper's generalisation. So this is a slip with clear meaning.

issues.locator: §1.2, p. 918, before (1.1); same in author copy p. 2
issues.printed: The source says every g ∈ G(Q) commensurates Γ and hence gives Hecke correspondence (1.1). It identifies the middle map as left multiplication by g, represented by the arithmetic-quotient morphism (Int(g), g).
issues.correction: any element g ∈ G(Q)^+ = G(Q) ∩ G (as in Theorem 1.1(2)) defines the Hecke correspondence (1.1). Commensuration of Γ holds for all g ∈ G(Q).
issues.reason: The definition of morphism on p. 917 requires g ∈ G = G(R)^+. For g ∈ G(Q) outside G(R)^+, left multiplication by g does not preserve G(R)^+, so (Int(g), g) is not a morphism in the paper's sense. Commensuration itself holds for all g ∈ G(Q). The diagram (1.1) is otherwise correct: x ↦ gx maps (g^{-1}Γg ∩ Γ)x to (Γ ∩ gΓg^{-1})gx.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 918 image. The quote is exact, and the author copy is the same. The claim holds up under the paper's own definitions. The p. 917 definition of a morphism (φ, g) requires g ∈ G = G(R)^+. For (Int(g), g), the formula Γ'h'M ↦ Γ g h' g^{-1} g M = Γ g h' M is left multiplication by g. It satisfies φ(g^{-1}Γg ∩ Γ) = Γ ∩ gΓg^{-1} and φ(M) = gMg^{-1}, and it lands in G/M only if g ∈ G. For g ∈ G(Q) outside G(R)^+, which can happen when G(R) is disconnected (e.g. PGL_2, SO(p,q), and adjoint groups in general), left multiplication moves G(R)^+ to another component. So (Int(g), g) is then not a morphism. Theorem 1.1(2) on p. 919 correctly writes 'c_g, g ∈ G(Q)^+'. The commensuration part holds for all g ∈ G(Q), and the diagram (1.1) is correct for g ∈ G(Q)^+. Nuance: for some M a correspondence still exists for g ∉ G(Q)^+, e.g. (Int(g), 1) when M = {1}, or (Int(g), g·k) with k in the maximal compact of G(R) when M = K. It is just not 'left multiplication by g, i.e. (Int(g), g)'. Hence the fix is G(Q)^+, not a failure of the Hecke-correspondence idea.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 918 image. The quote is exact, and the author copy has 'riemannian'. Read literally, the statement is false. A torsion-free, infinitely generated Fuchsian group Γ gives a complete hyperbolic surface Γ\H with infinitely generated π_1. Such a surface is not homotopy equivalent to a finite CW complex, so it is not the interior of a compact manifold with boundary. [Rag68], 'A note on quotients of real algebraic groups by arithmetic subgroups', proves compactifiability for Γ\G/K with Γ arithmetic and torsion-free. On p. 917 the paper itself calls the S_{Γ,G,K} 'the arithmetic Riemannian locally symmetric spaces', with Γ neat. The surrounding paragraph is about arithmetic quotients, so the omitted qualifier 'arithmetic' is clear from context. The text is motivational and never used. So this is a misprint, not an error: a dropped qualifier that makes a cited theorem read as false. The 'Hence ... non-singular semi-algebraic set' sentence inherits the same qualifier. Akbulut–King even gives a non-singular real algebraic set.

issues.reviewReason: All five quotes match the images (pp. 924, 925, 927), and the author copy and arXiv read the same. The paper defines 𝐆(ℚ)⁺ := 𝐆(ℚ) ∩ G (p. 917) and requires g ∈ G for a morphism (φ,g) (p. 917). Left multiplication by g ∈ 𝐆(ℚ) \ 𝐆(ℝ)⁺ maps G to the other coset gG, and G/M to gG/M. Such components exist, e.g. for 𝐆 = PGL₂, where diag(−1,1) ∈ 𝐆(ℚ). So Remark 2.6(1) ('g𝔖 is a Siegel set of G/M'), 'the left 𝐆(ℚ)-multiplication on G' (p. 925, against 'the left 𝐆(ℚ)⁺-action' earlier on the same page) and the morphism (Int(g),g) with Int(g)(h)g = gh (p. 927) all need g ∈ 𝐆(ℚ)⁺. For g ∈ 𝐆(ℚ)⁺ they hold: g·π(S) = π(gSg⁻¹), which is a Siegel set for (g𝐏g⁻¹, gx) with K_{gx} ⊃ (gh)M(gh)⁻¹. Lemma 2.4 leaves g unquantified. It holds for every g ∈ 𝐆(ℚ), since conjugation preserves G = 𝐆(ℝ)⁺ (a normal subgroup) and g𝐏g⁻¹ is rational. For a general real g it fails (g𝐏g⁻¹ need not be rational). Definition 2.5 is a slip only if one reads the identification G/gMg⁻¹ ≃ G/M as right translation (hgMg⁻¹ ↦ hgM, the reading that makes 'some g' meaningful). The identification induced by conjugation needs no restriction. The erratum rewrites Definition 2.5 with a fixed K ⊃ M and no g, so that part is superseded. The meaning is clear throughout, so kind misprint and affects nothing are right.

issues.locator: Remark 3.1, p. 927
issues.printed: The source says the semi-algebraicity of \bar{𝔖_i}, 1 ≤ i ≤ k, does not generally give S̄^BS_{Γ,G,M} a natural ℝ_alg-definable manifold structure with corners. For parabolics 𝐏 ⊂ 𝐐 of 𝐆, it cites [BJ06a, Prop. 6.2] to describe the corner inclusion G(Q) ⊂ G(P) as real analytic but generally not semi-algebraic.
issues.correction: Delete the remark. In the corner coordinates of Proposition 2.8 the inclusion G(Q) ⊂ G(P) is (n_Q, u, y) ↦ (n_Qn′(y), (u·a′(y)^{-α}) on Δ_P^Q and a′(y)^{-α} on Δ_{P′}, m′(y)), which is semi-algebraic. The Γ-action is semi-algebraic as well, so S̄^BS_{Γ,G,M,K} carries an ℝ_alg-definable manifold-with-corners structure (for fixed K), compatible with Theorem 1.1(1).
issues.reason: The paper's own charts are the corner coordinates (n, e_P(a), m) (Proposition 2.8 and p. 925; §3.1 uses U × \bar{A_{P,t}} × W as analytic charts). On the dense open subset G of G(Q) the transition to P-coordinates is: invert the Q-horospherical map, then take P-horospherical coordinates. Both horospherical maps are semi-algebraic bijections given by multiplication, and e_P, e_Q are algebraic characters. Explicitly, if m_Q = n′a′m′ in the P ∩ L_Q decomposition of M_QK, then (n_Q,a_Q,m_Q) ↦ (n_Qn′, a_Qa′, m′). A continuous extension of a semi-algebraic map from a dense subset has as graph the closure of that graph cut to domain × target, so it is semi-algebraic. The Γ- and M-actions are semi-algebraic in these coordinates as well. Defence: I could not consult [BJ06a, Prop. 6.2]; if it uses other corner coordinates the remark may concern those, but then the p. 925 description would be inaccurate instead.

issues.reviewReason: The quote matches the p. 927 image, and the author copy and arXiv have the same remark ('real-analytic'). The remark is false for the structure the paper itself describes. On p. 925 (citing [BJ06a, Prop. 6.3]) the analytic structure of Ḡ^BS is given by the corner coordinates N_P × Ā_P × M_PK, with Ā_P = [0,∞)^r through e_P(a) = (a^{-α})_{α∈Δ_P} (2.4). §3.1 uses the charts U × \bar{A_{P,t}} × W. Take P ⊂ Q and let P′ be the parabolic of M_Q determined by P. Then N_P = N_QN_{P′}, A_P = A_Q × A_{P′} and M_P = M_{P′}. Also M_QK = N_{P′}A_{P′}(M_PK) uniquely, and the multiplication map N_{P′} × A_{P′} × M_PK → M_QK is a semi-algebraic bijection. So its inverse y ↦ (n′(y), a′(y), m′(y)) is semi-algebraic. Since A_Q is central in L_Q, g = n_Qa_Qy = (n_Qn′)(a_Qa′)m′. The simple roots split as Δ_P = Δ_{P′} ⊔ Δ_P^Q, where the roots in Δ_{P′} are trivial on A_Q and restriction to A_Q maps Δ_P^Q bijectively onto Δ_Q. The corner inclusion G(Q) ⊂ G(P) is therefore (n_Q, u, y) ↦ (n_Qn′(y), (u_{α|A_Q}·a′(y)^{-α})_{α∈Δ_P^Q} ∪ (a′(y)^{-α})_{α∈Δ_{P′}}, m′(y)). This formula is polynomial in u = e_Q(a_Q) and semi-algebraic in y, and it extends to u ∈ [0,∞)^{r_Q}. So the map is semi-algebraic (indeed Nash). For example, in SL₃ the A-components are square roots of sums of squares of minors of g. The Γ-action (more generally the 𝐆(ℚ)-action) in corner coordinates is semi-algebraic on the dense interior, being a composite of multiplications and inverse horospherical maps. A continuous map whose restriction to a dense semi-algebraic subset is semi-algebraic has as graph the closure of that restricted graph inside domain × target, so it is semi-algebraic too. Hence the finite atlas \bar{V_i} of §3.1 (after the chart refinement of E23) has semi-algebraic transitions. This gives S̄^BS_{Γ,G,M,K} an ℝ_alg-definable manifold-with-corners structure extending the one of Theorem 1.1(1). Defence: I could not consult [BJ06a, Prop. 6.2] (the paper is paywalled). But whatever coordinates it uses, the atlas above is the one the paper attributes to [BJ06a, Prop. 6.3], so the remark's conclusion fails. The remark is not used anywhere, so affects nothing is right. It is a false assertion, not a slip, so kind error is right.

issues.locator: Definition 4.4, JAMS pp. 929–930 (author p. 14)
issues.printed: The source calls f ∈ O(x, y) roughly polynomial when f = g/h with g ∈ O[x, y, y^{−1}] and roughly monomial h. It asserts that these functions constitute a ring denoted T_n.
issues.correction: Require the denominator h to be a roughly monomial element of O[x,y,y^(−1)] (complex coefficients allowed for complex-valued functions). Then g/h + g'/h' = (gh' + g'h)/(hh') stays in the class, so T_n is a ring. In the proof of Lemma 4.7(3), write (4.4) over the denominator B(γ w_det K^(i−1))·B(γ w_det K^i), which lies in O_C[y] and is roughly monomial up to a constant phase by part (2), instead of dividing by the ratio (4.2).
issues.reason: As printed, h may be any roughly monomial element of O(x,y), and the sum of two roughly polynomial functions need not be roughly polynomial. Counterexample on Σ_1: let c = (x−1/2)² + y^(−2) ∈ O[x,y,y^(−1)] and k = (c + y^(−1))/(c + 2y^(−1)) ∈ (1/2, 1), so k ∼ 1. Then 1/k (g = 1, h = k) and −1 are roughly polynomial, but 1/k − 1 = y^(−1)/(c + y^(−1)) is not. Suppose it equals g/h with h ∼ y^s. Then g = h/(yc + 1). Write g = P(x,y) + O(y^A e^(−2πy)) with P ∈ R[x,y,y^(−1)], since the coefficients in O are analytic in q with |q| = e^(−2πy). For fixed x ≠ 1/2, |g| ≪ y^(s−1), so every y^j-coefficient of P with j ≥ s vanishes at every x ≠ 1/2, hence identically. But at x = 1/2, g ≫ y^s, a contradiction. The ring property is used in 'Proposition 4.6 follows immediately from Lemma 4.7' (sums over I-components) and in h(u,v) = Σ_i h(ũ_i,ṽ_i). Both hold with the repaired definition. The author copy is identical, and the erratum is silent.

issues.reviewReason: Quotation confirmed (pp. 929–930; author p. 14 identical). As defined, h may be any element of O(x,y) that is ∼ a monomial on Σ_n. Products stay in the class, but sums need not. I rederived the counterexample on Σ_1 = {0 < x < 1, y > 1}. Take c = (x−1/2)² + y^(−2) and k = (c + y^(−1))/(c + 2y^(−1)) ∈ O(x,y). Since c > 0, 1/2 < k < 1, so k ∼ y^0 and 1/k = 1/k is roughly polynomial; −1 is too. Their sum is 1/k − 1 = y^(−1)/(c + y^(−1)). Suppose it equals g/h with g ∈ O[x,y,y^(−1)] and h ∼ y^s. Then g = h/(yc+1). Each coefficient a ∈ O is analytic at q = 0 with |q| = e^(−2πy), so g = P + O(y^A e^(−2πy)) uniformly, with P ∈ R[x,y,y^(−1)]. For fixed x ≠ 1/2, yc + 1 ≥ y(x−1/2)², so |P(x,y)| ≪_x y^(s−1). Hence every y^j-coefficient of P with j ≥ s vanishes on (0,1)∖{1/2}; these coefficients are polynomials in x, so they vanish identically, and P(1/2,y) = O(y^(s−1)). But at x = 1/2, yc + 1 = 1 + 1/y ≤ 2, so g ≥ y^s/(2C): a contradiction. (Numerically, 1/k − 1 → 1 at x = 1/2 and ≈ 1/(0.04y) at x = 0.3.) So the stated claim 'roughly polynomial functions form a ring' is false. The ring property is used when Proposition 4.6 is said to follow 'immediately' from Lemma 4.7 (sum over I-components; §4.5 applies Proposition 4.6 to rational basis vectors e_i, not I-vectors). It is used again when h(u,v) = Σ_i h(ũ_i,ṽ_i) is summed after each term is shown roughly polynomial with the non-polynomial denominator (4.2). The repair covers both uses. B(γa,γb) = Q(g(q)a, e^(−2iy·N) ḡ(q) b̄) lies in O_C[y], and B(γ w_det K^i) has constant phase ±1 or ±i on the connected Σ_n. So (4.4) can be written with the denominator B(γ w_det K^(i−1))·B(γ w_det K^i), which is polynomial and, up to that phase, roughly monomial by Lemma 4.7(2). No numbered result becomes false: Lemma 4.5, Proposition 4.6, Lemma 4.7 and Theorem 1.5 hold with the narrower class. The false stated claim is the unnumbered ring assertion; T_n is not used again. The erratum is silent.

issues.reviewReason: The quotation matches the p. 932 image. The proof writes γu − e^{zN}u = Σ_i t_i e^{zN}g_i(t)u and bounds the ratio |t_i|² h(e^{zN}g_i u)/h(e^{zN}u) by |t_i|² times a monomial in y_i,…,y_n. On Σ_n that monomial is at most y_i^A, and e^{−4πy_i}y_i^A is bounded for y_i>1. By the triangle inequality, the upper bound h(γu) ≪ h(e^{zN}u) therefore holds on all of Σ_n. The lower bound needs the perturbation to be small, which the proof obtains only for y_n ≥ Y_0(ε). For n = 1 the remainder {0<x<1, 1<y≤Y_0} has compact closure in 𝔥, so continuity and positivity (u ≠ 0) finish the argument. For n ≥ 2, Σ_n ∩ {y_n ≤ Y_0} contains points with y_1 → ∞. There |t_n| ≥ e^{−2πY_0}, and the t_n-term is of the same order as h(e^{zN}u). The printed 'whence the claim' gives no lower bound there. The lemma is very likely true on all of Σ_n: one route is parametric norm estimates, another is uniform bounds on A_z = γe^{−zN} and its inverse via asymptotic orthogonality. Neither argument is in the paper. Defence: the paper says the lemma is 'also proven in [CKS86, Theorem 5.21]'. As later authors quote it (e.g. arXiv:2302.10200, Thm 2.1), that theorem holds on regions {log|s_1|/log|s_2| > ε, …, −log|s_n| > ε}, which include bounded y_n. I did not check that it covers h(γu), which is not the norm of a flat section. §4 also allows shrinking the polydisk (Lemma 4.2), and shrinking repairs everything needed for Theorem 1.3. This gap is the local cause of part of E56; cross-reference the two.

issues.reviewReason: I checked the quote on the image of p. 933. The author copy is the same. By §1.1, a morphism of arithmetic quotients comes from a morphism φ of semisimple Q-groups. The connected Hodge varieties of [K17, §3.3] are Γ\D^+ for a reductive P, and Hodge morphisms come from ρ : P' → P, which need not map Z(P') into Z(P). With the adjoint presentation that §1.3 uses, the claim is false in simple cases. Take the Hodge morphism from a product of modular curves to A_2, with P' = GL2 ×_{G_m} GL2 ⊂ GSp4. Any φ : PGL2 × PGL2 → PGSp4 inducing it would have to agree with SL2 × SL2 → PSp4, since the difference is a continuous map into the finite pointwise stabiliser of the image of H×H. But the latter does not kill (1,−1). The claim becomes true only after re-presenting the source through the image of the derived group, which here is (SL2×SL2)/±1, not the adjoint group. It may also need a finite-index subgroup, i.e. a finite cover of the source. So the 'in particular' needs an argument. The images Y, and hence the definability of special subvarieties, are unchanged. Erratum Cor. 1.3 treats morphisms of Hodge manifolds directly, which makes this remark unnecessary for §5.

issues.correction: (a) Pull back along f the weight-0 polarized Z-VHS on D = G/K given by the adjoint representation on g with a Γ-stable lattice, polarized by minus the Killing form. Griffiths transversality is automatic because D is Hermitian symmetric. Use the adjoint representation rather than an arbitrary faithful one, which need not carry a VHS when G is not adjoint. Since Γ is torsion free, Γ ∩ Z(G) = 1 and S_{Γ,G,K} = S_{Γ^ad,G^ad,K^ad}. Alternatively, note that the proof of Theorem 1.3 applies verbatim to the period map of f^*V into Γ\D. (c) If a finite étale cover of S is used, descend algebraicity: the graph of f is the image of the graph of the lifted map under a finite map.

issues.reviewReason: I checked the quote on the image of p. 933. The author copy is the same. Theorem 1.3 (p. 920) concerns Φ_S : S → Hod^0(S,V), after a possible finite étale cover. Its target is built from the adjoint group of the generic Mumford–Tate group of V and a suitable Γ. An arbitrary holomorphic f : S → S_{Γ,G,K} is the period map of the pulled-back VHS: transversality is automatic because D is Hermitian symmetric. But Hod^0(S, f^*V) is built from MT(f^*V), which can be strictly smaller than G, e.g. when f(S) lies in a proper special subvariety such as a Hecke translate of a modular curve in A_2. So f = ι∘Φ_S with ι a Hodge morphism. The definability of ι is not automatic. It is exactly the functoriality that erratum §1.1 says fails for general morphisms of arithmetic quotients, and that erratum Cor. 1.3 restores for Hodge morphisms. Another route is to observe that the proof in §§4.1–4.5 works for period maps into Γ\D whenever D is an orbit of a group containing the Mumford–Tate group. The paper says neither. So 'f is a period map, hence definable by Theorem 1.3' skips a real step. Borel's theorem is true and the repair is standard, hence 'the proof'. This is distinct from E14 (the heading) and E29 (smoothness of S).

Theorem 1.3 makes the graph of f definable for the R_an,exp-structure on S_{Γ,G,K} that extends the Theorem 1.1 structure (p. 920). Theorem 4.13 needs definability for the structure induced by the algebraic structure of S × S_{Γ,G,K}. On p. 919 the paper says the R_an-structures from Borel–Serre and Baily–Borel differ. It asserts without proof that the map BS → BB is R_an,exp-definable, and adds 'As we won't need this result in this paper'. Yet §4.6 needs exactly its consequence on the interior: the two R_an,exp-structures on S_{Γ,G,K} coincide. §4.6 never invokes this, so the printed proof has a missing step. §5 is unaffected: there only the source S carries its algebraic structure, and Y and Φ_S are definable for the Theorem 1.1 structure. Both proposed repairs work. With KUY16's fundamental set F covered by finitely many Siegel sets, the graph of the identity is the image of F under (π_{1.1}, π_{BB}), which is definable. Alternatively, S_{Γ,G,K} is smooth quasi-projective by [BB66], and Theorem 1.3 applied to the identity (the period map of the adjoint VHS) makes the identity definable from the algebraic structure to the Theorem 1.1 structure. The inverse of a definable bijection is definable. The second route avoids [KUY16]. This is the same gap as E59 (§1.2 p. 919 / §4.6), so the two should be recorded once. The same place also has: Both quotes are exact on the images (p. 919 and Remarks 1.4(2) on p. 921), and the author copy is the same. Proof of Theorem 4.12 (p. 933): 'f ... is R_an,exp-definable by Theorem 1.3. The graph of f is thus a ... R_an,exp-definable subset of the smooth complex algebraic manifold S × S_{Γ,G,K}.' The step fails as written. The structure on the target in Theorem 1.3 is explicitly the one 'extending the R_alg-definable manifold structure defined in Theorem 1.1' (p. 920), which is induced by Borel–Serre. Theorem 4.13 needs definability for the canonical structure of the algebraic manifold S × S_{Γ,G,K}, which is induced by Baily–Borel. On p. 919 the paper says these differ at the R_an level. It asserts, without proof ('As we won't need this result'), that the map BS → BB is R_an,exp-definable, and that is exactly the comparison §4.6 silently uses. So a needed step is missing and its only statement in the paper is unproved. The gap is easily filled, so Theorem 4.12 (Borel's theorem) stands. (a) Internally: S_{Γ,G,K} is smooth quasi-projective (§1.1, Baily–Borel). Put the tautological integral variation on it, for instance a Γ-stable lattice in g with Hodge structure Ad∘h_x. Up to a finite étale cover, its period map is the identity. So Theorem 1.3 makes id: S^alg → S^Thm1.1 R_an,exp-definable, and its inverse has the same graph. For M = K the Theorem 1.1 structure is canonical (erratum Remark 1.1(2)). Conditions (1) and (3) do not depend on the ordering, so h_z is (σ_z e, C′)-reduced for any C′ > max(C,1), where σ_z sorts the values h_z(e_i). Hence ι∘Φ̃(Σ_n) ⊂ ∪_{σ∈S_m} T_{σe,C′}, a union of m! reduced sets with m = dim V. The curve statement should read: along each curve τ, h_z satisfies (1) (and (3)) for e with a constant C_τ.
issues.reason: Counterexample showing the Claim fails for every basis. Take V = V_a ⊗ V_b over (Δ*)^2, where V_a is H^1 of a Tate-curve family in t_1 and V_b is Sym^2 H^1 of one in t_2. On Σ_2, h_z is uniformly comparable to diag(y_1^s y_2^b) in the integral basis e_{s,b}, s ∈ {±1}, b ∈ {−2,0,2}. If h_z were (f,C)-reduced on Σ_2 for one basis f, then h_z(f_i) ≍ λ_i(h_z)² by (2), (3) and Minkowski's second theorem. At (y_1,y_2) = (Y,Y) and at (Y³,Y) the third minimum is ≍ Y^{-1}. This forces f_1, f_2, f_3 into span(e_{−1,−2}, e_{−1,0}), which is impossible. The same example shows that no fixed ordering satisfies (2) along both the curve z_1 = z_2 and the curve z_2 = ζ. So the printed Claim and the curve statement are false. The following sentence ('we may assume (2) as there are only finitely many orderings') shows the intended Claim′. Claim′ is what the argument proves, and it gives Theorem 1.5, which asserts finitely many Siegel sets, consistent with GGLR's |I| = 1 counterexample. Same root as E3, but a different statement. issues.reviewReason: Quotations confirmed on the p. 933 image; the author copy and arXiv v2 are identical. I checked the counterexample and it holds. Take V = V_a ⊗ V_b over (Δ*)², with V_a = H^1 of the Tate family in t_1 (τ = z_1) and V_b = Sym²H^1 of the Tate family in t_2. The Hodge norm on H^1 in the integral basis is (m+nx)²/y + n²y, which is ≍ diag(y^{−1},y) uniformly for 0<x<1, y>1. Comparability passes to Sym² and to tensor products, so h_z ≍ diag(y_1^s y_2^b) in the integral basis e_{s,b}, s ∈ {±1}, b ∈ {−2,0,2}. This agrees with the monomials of Theorem 4.8 (s_1 = s, s_2 = s+b). Suppose h_z were (f,C)-reduced on Σ_2 for a ℚ-basis f. Condition (2) gives λ_i² ≪ h(f_i). Condition (3) together with Minkowski's second theorem gives Π h(f_i) ≪ det ≍ Π λ_i². Hence h(f_i) ≍ λ_i², and the successive minima for ⟨f⟩ and V_ℤ agree up to constants. At (Y,Y) and at (Y³,Y), both in Σ_2, the sorted exponents are (−3,−1,−1,1,1,3) and (−5,−3,−1,1,3,5), so λ_3² ≍ Y^{−1} at both points (checked numerically). Then f_1, f_2, f_3 have zero coefficient on every e_{s,b} with s+b ≥ 1 or 3s+b ≥ 1. That leaves only span(e_{−1,−2}, e_{−1,0}), which is 2-dimensional: a contradiction. So the Claim fails for every basis. For the J-adapted basis e, h(e_{1,−2}) ≍ Y^{−1} and h(e_{−1,2}) ≍ Y along z_1 = z_2, while the order is reversed along z_2 = ζ. No fixed ordering satisfies (2) on both curves, so the curve statement is false as printed. Conditions (1) and (3) do not depend on the ordering. The printed argument therefore proves Claim′, and sorting gives finitely many reduced sets, which suffices for Theorem 1.5. The finding has the same root as E3, which the ledger records with affects 'nothing'; the two reaches should be harmonized or the entries cross-referenced. Correction to the proposed text: the number of orderings is (dim V)!, not n!.

issues.locator: Published Lemma 4.7 and its proof, pp.913–914; arXiv v1 Lemma 4.5, p.20
issues.printed: Lemma 4.7 asserts that a class Z satisfying (a)–(d), under ρ(J) = ρ(J_{Q_p}), comes from a nice element of Pic(X × X). The proof invokes Berthelot–Ogus [BO83, §3.8], the p-adic Lefschetz (1,1)-theorem, to infer from (b) a lift to NS(J_{Q_p}) ⊗ Q_p.
issues.correction: Only the forward direction holds: classes of nice correspondences satisfy (a)–(d). The converse is not established. The space of Rosati-symmetric correspondences can have smaller dimension than ∧²H^1_dR(X_{Q_p})^{φ=p} ∩ Fil¹.
issues.reason: Property (a) and the Tate conjecture put Z in NS(J_{F_p}) ⊗ Q_p, a Q_p-linear combination of divisor classes. Berthelot–Ogus lifts a divisor class over F_p whose crystalline class lies in Fil¹. A Q_p-combination lying in Fil¹ need not be a combination of such classes: a Z-lattice can meet a Q_p-subspace in smaller rank than the dimension of its intersection with the lattice's Q_p-span. The conclusion 'an element of Pic(X × X)', rather than of Pic(X × X) ⊗ Q, also only holds up to a rational multiple.

issues.locator: Published proof of Lemma 3.7, p.907, and the sketch of Theorem 2.3, p.899
issues.printed: The source uses the assumption r = g to assert H^1_f(G_T, V) ≃ H^1_f(G_p, V) ≃ H^0(X_{Q_p}, Ω¹)*.
issues.correction: Under the assumptions of §1.4 (r = g and J(Q) of finite index in J(Q_p)), what is available is κ(J(Q)) ⊗ Q_p ≃ H^1_f(G_p, V). The equality with H^1_f(G_T, V) needs Sha(J/Q)[p^∞] to be finite. The proof only needs h on κ(J(Q)) ⊗ Q_p. There π_1(A_Z(b,x)) = κ(x − b) lies for x ∈ X(Q), and π_2 = E_Z κ(x − b) + [IA_Z(b)] does too, [IA_Z(b)] being the class of a Chow–Heegner point (Remark 3.11).
issues.reason: dim H^1_f(G_T, V) = r + corank Sha(J/Q)[p^∞], so the stated isomorphism is an extra hypothesis. The sketch of Theorem 2.3 likewise bounds the global side by r; that holds for the Selmer variety, which §2.1 cuts down by the image of J(Q) ⊗ Q_p. For X_s(13), Sha is finite by Kolyvagin–Logachev, since each conjugate of f has analytic rank one; this is the theorem already used for Proposition 6.2.

E₁ (Lemma 12.2, p. 59) constrains only pairs of parts that are both ⩽ n/4: 'there are no integers k, ℓ ⩽ n/4 with gcd(k, ℓ) ⩾ n^{κα} such that {k, ℓ} ⊂ ρ'. In Case 2b and in Case 3 on p. 63 the companion cycle L₃ lies in the union of the r′ blocks met by L_i, a set that can be as large as the whole of [n], so its length mk, and with it the part k ∈ ρ, is not bounded by n/4, and the concluding 'contradicts our assumption that ρ ∈ E₁' is unlicensed. The long part ℓ_i is fine, being ⩽ n/log n. The repair stands up: (i) a cycle meeting r′ blocks of a single block orbit has length divisible by r′, so two long parts sharing a block orbit would have gcd ⩾ r′ > n^α with both ⩽ n/4, against E₁ - hence the orbits X_ℓ are pairwise disjoint; at most three cycles exceed n/4, and at most one ℓ falls in Case 2a (two would give s | ℓ, s | ℓ′ with s = n/r > n^α), so five long parts in Case 2 and four in Case 3 leave one whose companion cycles are all ⩽ n/4, where the printed argument applies verbatim; (ii) the strengthened E₅ is free, because the proof of Lemma 12.6 (p. 61) bounds P(B₅(r)) by P(Σ_{k∈ρ} f_r(k) ⩽ t L_r) with L_r = 2α(1 - 1/r) log n + O(log log n) → ∞, so replacing the threshold 1 by 4 is swallowed by tL_r for large n and the bound ≪ (log n)^κ n^{-2κα(1-1/r)} is unchanged. The statement of Lemma 12.9 is untouched. The published Inventiones text is paywalled and was not compared, as the extraction states; the verdict is for arXiv v3, whose SHA-256 this review re-fetched and matched.

issues.locator: Remark 3.2, p. 23 (arXiv v3; the author version of 24 May 2023 has the same text and pages; the published pagination was not seen)
issues.printed: The source takes µ uniform on N := {f(n) : n ∈ {1, 2, …, N} ∩ ℤ} and asserts Σ_{a≡b (mod Q)} µ(a) = Σ_{k∈ℤ/Qℤ, f(k)≡b (mod Q)} #{1 ⩽ n ⩽ N : n ≡ k (mod Q)}/N. For square-free Q, it invokes the Chinese Remainder Theorem for #{k ∈ ℤ/Qℤ : f(k) ≡ b (mod Q)} ⩽ d^{ω(Q)}. With N ⩾ Q and every prime factor of Q ⩾ d^{4/ε}, it bounds the right-hand side by ⩽ Q^ε/2.
issues.correction: (i) The identity holds for the push-forward of the uniform measure on {1, …, N} under f, which is the uniform measure on 𝒩 when f is injective there. (ii) The root count needs f mod p non-constant for every p | Q. (iii) The final bound needs d ≥ 2. /122 states the corrected estimate.
issues.reason: (i) f(x) = x(x − 3) on {1, 2, 3} takes the values −2, −2, 0: the uniform measure on 𝒩 gives −2 mass 1/2, the formula 2/3. (ii) f(x) = 5x and Q = 5: all five residues satisfy f(k) ≡ 0. (iii) For d = 1 the bound 2d^{ω(Q)} ≤ Q^ε/2 would need Q^ε ≥ 4, false for Q = 2 when ε < 2. The remark is not used elsewhere.

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed in all three parts, each by an explicit counterexample I checked. Remark 3.2 on p. 23 is printed as recorded. (i) The displayed identity computes the push-forward of the uniform measure on {1, ..., N} under f, not the uniform measure on the set 𝒩 = f({1,...,N}) that the remark defines: for f(x) = x(x - 3) on {1, 2, 3} the values are -2, -2, 0, so μ(-2) = 1/2 while the formula returns 2/3. The two agree exactly when f is injective there. (ii) #{k ∈ ℤ/Qℤ : f(k) ≡ b (mod Q)} ⩽ d^{ω(Q)} needs f - b non-constant modulo every p | Q: for f(x) = 5x, Q = 5, b = 0 all five residues are roots, against d^{ω(Q)} = 1. (iii) The final step bounds 2d^{ω(Q)} ⩽ Q^ε/2, which needs Q^ε ⩾ 4; with d = 1 the hypothesis 'all prime factors of Q are ⩾ d^{4/ε}' is empty and Q = 2 defeats it for every ε < 2. For d ⩾ 2 the hypothesis forces Q ⩾ 2^{4/ε} and the bound holds. The remark states results but is used nowhere else in the paper. The published Inventiones text is paywalled and was not compared, as the extraction states; the verdict is for arXiv v3, whose SHA-256 this review re-fetched and matched.

issues.printed: The source asserts Σ_{k∈ℤ/Qℤ} |µ̂_j(k/Q + ℓ/R)|^s ⩽ (Σ|µ̂_j(k/Q + ℓ/R)|^{us})^{1/u} (Σ|µ̂_j(k/Q + ℓ/R)|^{vs})^{1/v} ⩽ Q^{1−γ(us)/u−γ(vs)/v}. It infers γ(s) ⩾ γ(us)/u + γ(vs)/v and describes θ as decreasing with θ(s) ⩾ 2θ(2s).

The comparisons γ(s) ≥ γ(us)/u + γ(vs)/v and θ(s) ≥ 2θ(2s) are false. /125 states the correct properties.
issues.reason: The displayed Hölder step bounds Σ|µ̂|^{2s}, not Σ|µ̂|^s. Counterexample: P = 210 and μ uniform on 1, …, 210 with weight 3/4 spread over the even and 1/4 over the odd integers. issues.citation: Bary-Soroker–Koukoulopoulos–Kozma, "Irreducibility of random polynomials: general measures", Inventiones Mathematicae (2023)
issues.reviewReason: Confirmed decisively, and I rebuilt the counterexample from scratch. Remark 2.2(b) on p. 14 is printed as recorded. The displayed Hölder step is the interpolation Σ|x|^{2s} ⩽ (Σ|x|^{us})^{1/u}(Σ|x|^{vs})^{1/v}, whose left side is Σ|x|^{2s} and not Σ|x|^s - taking f = g = |x|^s in Hölder, or λ = 1/u in Lyapunov, both give exponent u^{-1}·us + v^{-1}·vs = 2s - and since |μ̂| ⩽ 1 the printed inequality is the stronger one, so it does not follow. It is also false, with its consequences: take P = 210 and μ uniform on {1, ..., 210} weighted 3/4 on the even and 1/4 on the odd residues, so that |μ̂(j/210)| = 1 at j = 0, 1/2 at j = 105 and 0 otherwise; the binding pair is Q = 2, giving γ(s) = 1 - log₂(1 + 2^{-s}). Then γ(1) = 0.41504 and γ(2) = 0.67807, so γ(s) ⩾ γ(us)/u + γ(vs)/v fails at s = 1, u = v = 2, and θ(1) = 0.41504 < 2θ(2) = 0.67807. The extraction's replacements are correct: γ is non-decreasing because |μ̂| ⩽ 1; θ = γ/s is non-increasing, from Σ|x|^s ⩽ Q^{1-s/t}(Σ|x|^t)^{s/t} for s ⩽ t, which is the 'θ is a decreasing function' the paper wanted; and γ is concave, being a minimum of the concave functions 1 - log(Σ|x|^s)/log Q. The published Inventiones text is paywalled and was not compared, as the extraction states; the verdict is for arXiv v3, whose SHA-256 this review re-fetched and matched.

issues.locator: proof of Lemma 3.7, p. 27 (arXiv v3; the author version of 24 May 2023 has the same text and pages; the published pagination was not seen)
issues.printed: The proof gives S ≪ … × (ΣΣ_{Q₁⩽x^{i₁}, R₁⩽x^{j₁}, (Q₁,R₁)=1} Σ_{ℓ₁∈(ℤ/R₁ℤ)*} Σ_{k₁∈(ℤ/Q₁ℤ)*} |µ̂(k₁/Q₁ + ℓ₁/R₁)|²)^{1/2}. It substitutes q = Q₁R₁ and invokes the Chinese Remainder Theorem to conclude S ≪ … (Σ_{q⩽x^{i₁+j₁}} Σ_{a∈(ℤ/qℤ)*} |µ̂(a/q)|²)^{1/2}.
issues.correction: Keep Q₁ ∈ 𝒩_{i₁}(x) and R₁ ∈ 𝒩_{j₁}(x) (products of distinct primes from [x/2, x]) instead of enlarging to all Q₁ ≤ x^{i₁}, R₁ ≤ x^{j₁}. Then q = Q₁R₁ ∈ 𝒩_{i₁+j₁}(x) has at most C(i₁+j₁, i₁) ≤ 6 such factorizations, and the bound holds with an extra factor √6.
issues.reason: Over all coprime Q₁ ≤ x^{i₁}, R₁ ≤ x^{j₁} the same q arises from every factorization into coprime parts in range, for instance q = 6 from (1, 6), (2, 3), (3, 2), (6, 1), and each time k₁/Q₁ + ℓ₁/R₁ runs over all a/q with a ∈ (ℤ/qℤ)*. The change of variables therefore loses a factor up to 2^{ω(q)}, which is unbounded. The Cauchy–Schwarz step before it only needs the restricted range.

issues.locator: Inventiones mathematicae 222 (2020), Theorem 3.16 (ii), p. 55, and its introduction form Theorem A (ii), p. 4
issues.printed: dim(X) > 0
issues.correction: Part (ii) needs dim(X) ≥ 2 whenever X(R) ≠ ∅. The hypothesis dim(X) > 0 of Theorem 3.16, and the hypothesis d ≥ 1 of Theorem A, are too weak: the case dim(X) = 1 with X(R) ≠ ∅ must be excluded. Part (i) is not affected by this counterexample.
issues.reason: Take X = E the elliptic curve y^2 = x^3 - x over R = ℝ, with its rational point at infinity. All the printed hypotheses hold: dim(X) = 1 > 0; H^2(X,O_X) = 0 because X is a curve; and the real integral Hodge conjecture for 1-cycles is the codimension-0 case, which holds trivially, since X is geometrically irreducible, so H^0_G(X(ℂ),ℤ(0)) = ℤ and the class of the codimension-0 cycle [X] generates it. The left-hand side of (ii) fails: the only integral closed subscheme of dimension 1 in a curve is the curve itself, and E has geometric genus 1, which is odd, so X contains no geometrically irreducible curve of even geometric genus. The right-hand side holds: by Hochschild–Serre, Pic(X) → Pic(X_ℂ)^G is injective with cokernel embedding in Br(ℝ), and that obstruction is killed by the real point, so the map is an isomorphism and is in particular onto on 2-primary torsion. Hence (ii) is false as printed. The proof combines Theorems3.3 and3.6 with Proposition3.9, whose real-point argument assumes dimension at least2. Prior worker checked the published and arXiv statements; retained here without an independent-review verdict. (cc-442dc5) Rechecked against Theorem A (p.4) and Theorem 3.16 (p.55): for a curve the only integral curve is X itself, so the genus-one real curve makes the left side of (ii) false and the right side true.

issues.reason: Set T(Q)(x)=conjugate(Q(f(x))). The weight4 space Λ_2 has basis a=x0x4,b=x1x5,c=x2²,d=x3². Direct substitution gives T(a)=−b,T(b)=a,T(c)=−d,T(d)=c, so T²=−id. A stable complex line would give TQ=uQ and −Q=|u|²Q, impossible. For a smooth four-quadric complete intersection in P⁶, its quadratic ideal is exactly the span of Q0,...,Q3, by the twisted Koszul resolution and projective-space cohomology. Its weight4 intersection is the line C Q2. Stability under f forces T-stability of that line, a contradiction. Thus the asserted dense set cannot intersect the asserted nonempty smooth locus. The original surface consequence is not disproved for other constructions. (cc-442dc5) Rechecked: f² = diag(ζ, ζ^{-1}, ζ², ζ^{-2}, ζ³, ζ^{-3}, 1), so Λ_2 is spanned by x0x4, x1x5, x2², x3², and the antilinear T maps Λ_2 to itself with T² = −1 (rescaling T by a constant does not change the sign). issues.locator: Author-hosted published Inventiones222(2020), §1.1.4, equation(1.16), p14
issues.printed: The source describes the groups as abelian, with finite exponent.
issues.correction: For the algebraic perfect-pairing statement use a locally constant sheaf of finite abelian groups (finite stalks). A broader continuous-dual or one-sided contract needs its own precise topology and proof.
issues.reason: Take V a point and M=⊕_N F2. Its algebraic dual is ∏_N F2. The quotient of this product by the finite-support subspace is nonzero, so a nonzero F2-linear functional on the quotient pulls back to a nonzero functional vanishing on every coordinate vector. Such a functional cannot be evaluation by a finite-support element of M. Hence M→M^{∨∨} is not onto. The cited SGA4 XVIII §3.2.6 explicitly assumes constructible locally constant Z/n coefficients. The paper’s finite-coefficient consumers remain valid.

issues.locator: arXiv v1 Proposition 6.7(c) and its proof, pp.46–47; Proposition 1.8(c), p.6
issues.printed: Condition c) requires the count of ψ ∈ Σ with [G_v : G_{w_ψ}] < 4 to be ≥ (1/(d+1)) dim_{Q_p}(A). The source then claims that #Σ ≤ dim_{Q_p}(A) ensures that A satisfies (c) too.
issues.correction: Replace dim_{Q_p}(A) by #Σ_A in (c), or assume A split (A ≅ Q_p^n as a Q_p-algebra), where #Σ_A = dim_{Q_p}(A). Reduced or étale is not enough: A = Q_{p²} gives Σ_A = ∅. This is what the proof shows, and every application has A|G_v ≅ H^0_ét(X_{y_v,K̄_v}, Q_p) = ∏ Q_p, which is split.
issues.reason: The reduction step needs #Σ ≥ dim A, the opposite of what it cites. A counterexample to (c) as printed: K = Q (every place self-conjugate), E/Q an elliptic curve, A = Q_p[ε]/(ε³) with trivial Galois action, V = A ⊗_{Q_p} H^1_ét(E_Q̄, Q_p), L = A(−1), and ω the A-linear extension of the Weil pairing. This is a symplectic pair with V of rank 2 (d = 1), de Rham with Hodge–Tate weights {0, 1} and pure of weight 1 outside a finite set. Σ_A has one point, fixed by G_v, so (a) and (b) fail, and (c) asks 1 ≥ 3/2. The pair is also S-good, so Proposition 1.8 fails in the same way. A reduced (étale) but non-split A fails too, since Σ_A = Hom_{Q_p-alg}(A, Q_p) consists of Q_p-points: take the same K, E and d = 1, but A = Q_{p²} with trivial action, V = A ⊗_{Q_p} H^1_ét(E_Q̄, Q_p), L = A(−1) and ω the A-linear Weil pairing. The pair is S-good, but Σ_A = ∅, so (a) and (b) fail and (c) as printed asks 0 ≥ 2/2 = 1. (Correction (30 September 2026, FIX-RT-PAPER-BETTS-STIX-25), after RT-PAPER-BETTS-STIX-25/3; the earlier alternative 'A reduced (hence étale)' was wrong.)

issues.locator: arXiv v1 proof of Proposition 2.16(1), p.12
issues.printed: The source uses G_v-equivariance of each ψ_i on D to obtain Σ_i σ(αλ_i)ψ_i = 0 for every α ∈ Q_p^nr and σ ∈ G_v. It then claims that an appropriate linear combination yields Σ_i tr_{Q_p^nr/Q_p}(αλ_i)ψ_i = 0.

issues.correction: State Lemma A.2 for filtrations with F^pA^n = 0 for p ≫ 0 in each degree (a finite filtration is a special case). Then the printed proof is valid: replace A by F^pA filtered by F^{max(k,p)}A, which is finite, and apply [Del71, Proposition 1.3.2]. In the proof of Theorem 3.12(2), apply Lemma A.2 to Rπ_dR*E, whose filtration is finite and whose Hodge–de Rham spectral sequence degenerates at the first page by [Sch13, Theorem 8.8(ii)]; so its cohomology sheaves R^iπ_dR*E are filtered, with locally free graded pieces (Theorem 3.12(1)). Then compute the cohomology of OB_dR,U ⊗_{O_U} Rπ_dR*E as OB_dR,U ⊗_{O_U} R^iπ_dR*E with the tensor filtration. This step needs every quotient Fil^a/Fil^b OB_dR,U (a < b) to be flat over O_U, not only OB_dR,U. [Sch13] does not state that flatness, and it is the missing ingredient. Its Proposition 6.10 and Corollary 6.15 describe gr^i OB_dR locally as ξ^i Ô_X[X_1/ξ, …, X_n/ξ], a free Ô_X-module, so the flatness follows from flatness of Ô_X over O_X on the pro-étale site.
issues.reason: Lemma A.2 does not define 'bounded below'. Read as F^pA^n = A^n for p ≪ 0, it is false: take A^0 = A^1 = K with d = id, F^pA^0 = K for p ≤ 0 and 0 for p ≥ 1, and F^pA^1 = K for all p. Every gr^pA^1 is 0, so the only non-zero E_1 term is E_1^{0,0} = gr^0A^0 = K and the spectral sequence degenerates at E_1, but H^1(F^1A) = K → H^1(F^0A) = 0 is not injective. Read as F^pA^n = 0 for p ≫ 0, it is true and the printed proof works. The one application, on p.22, fits neither reading. The filtration of OB_dR,U ⊗_{O_U} Rπ_dR*E is never 0 and never everything in any degree, because Fil^a OB_dR,U is neither (Remark 3.13), and it is not complete. Applied instead to Rπ_dR*E, which fits, the lemma says nothing about the tensor product, and the passage to it is not argued. So the claim that OB_dR,U ⊗_{O_U} Rπ_dR*E has filtered cohomology objects, which the proof of Theorem 3.12(2) (η_E^∧ an isomorphism) needs, is not justified as printed. Take it from Beuzart-Plessis–Liu–Zhang–Zhu Theorem 4.14(4) (the Annals numbering) with its Proposition 4.13(1) repaired: suppose 𝔇(G′, 1)^♥_{χ′} = ∅ and isolate with Theorem 3.19 instead of Theorem 3.6 (PAPER-BEUZARTPLESSIS-LIU-ZHANG-ETAL-21/E1). issues.reason: The cited result is BPLZZ Theorem 4.14(4): if the weak base change of π exists and is hermitian, the base change of χ_{π_∞} is χ_{BC(π)_∞}. Its proof reduces to BPLZZ Proposition 4.13(1), whose argument by contradiction only rules out 'weak base change does not exist'. When the weak base change exists but is not cuspidal, the T-character χ′ is CAP, Theorem 3.6 does not apply, and nothing in the printed argument reaches the archimedean component. This paper applies the theorem to σ whose weak base change is a Hermitian Arthur parameter Π. In the endoscopic case, the one the paper is about, Π is not cuspidal. The common infinitesimal character is needed to choose the multipliers μ^h with μ^h(σ) = 1 for all (U_h, σ) ∈ 𝔛^h_0, compatible with μ(Π) = 1 under base change, which (10.1.6.6) uses. issues.correction: Suppose instead that 𝔇(G′,1)^♡_{χ′} = ∅, and take μ′ from Theorem 3.19 (for G′, ω = 1 and χ′) instead of Theorem 3.6. Then R(μ′⋆g) = 0 for every g ∈ S(G′(A_F))_{K′}. This survives Lemma 4.12, since μ̃′ = μ′·ν′ for a T-multiplier ν′, so μ̃′⋆f′ = μ′⋆(ν′⋆f′). Hence μ̃′⋆f′ is trivially quasi-cuspidal and every I_Π̃(μ̃′⋆f′) vanishes. Propositions 4.8, 4.2, 4.7 and 4.1 then give a contradiction. Hence 𝔇(G′,1)^♡_{χ′} ≠ ∅, which gives existence together with (1). The argument for (2) stands as written. Locator: pp. 38–39.
issues.reason: Checked on the p. 39 image; the symbol is ♡ (\heartsuit), not ♥ as in the ledger quotation. Read literally, the argument derives a contradiction from 'χ′ not (G′,T)-CAP and L²_cusp[χ′] = 0'. So it proves: χ′ is CAP, or L²_cusp[χ′] ≠ 0. In the second case a cuspidal Π̃ realises χ′ including χ′_∞ = bc(χ_{π^V_∞}), and then (1) follows by uniqueness. This covers every case in which BC(π^V) is cuspidal, and all of case (b). When BC(π^V) exists but is a non-trivial isobaric sum, χ′ is (G′,T)-CAP and the written argument yields nothing: 'weak base change exists' (Definition 1.6, split places only) does not give 𝔇(G′,1)^♡_{χ′} ≠ ∅, which also requires the archimedean infinitesimal character to match. This happens, e.g., for endoscopic π^V, which are not CAP. Exactly this case is used in Theorem 4.14(4) for hermitian non-cuspidal BC(π), and through it in the last assertion of Lemma 4.16 for non-cuspidal Π. Theorems 1.8–1.10 need only cuspidal Π_m, and there the written argument suffices; the archimedean T-character in the proof of Theorem 1.8 also exists directly by conjugate self-duality. issues.citation: Beuzart-Plessis–Liu–Zhang–Zhu, "Isolation of cuspidal spectrum, with application to the Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture", Annals of Mathematics 194 (2021), no. 2
issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: I checked the quotation on the p. 38–39 images and in main.tex ll. 2532–2566. The quoted passage starts on p. 38 ('Suppose that … does not exists' is at the foot of p. 38), so the locator should read pp. 38–39. The symbol is \heartsuit, printed as ♡, so the first reading's symbol fix is right. The first reading's revised wording is more precise than the ledger and correct. By Definitions 3.3 and 3.4, T = S ∪ T_0 contains every nonsplit prime, so χ′ and CAP only involve split primes outside S. The written argument assumes only that χ′ is not (G′,T)-CAP and that L²_cusp[χ′] = 0, and it contradicts that conjunction. So it proves that χ′ is CAP or L²_cusp(G′(F)∖G′(A_F)/K′,1)[χ′] ≠ 0. In case (b) the not-CAP hypothesis is never used (Theorem 3.7 plus the supercuspidal f′_{v_0}), so L²_cusp[χ′] ≠ 0 always. Then a cuspidal Π̃ realises χ′ at ∞ and at every v ∉ T, so (G′,Π̃) ∈ 𝔇(G′,1)^♡_{χ′}, and (1) follows by [Ram, Thm A]. The same holds whenever BC(π^V) is cuspidal. Otherwise χ′ would be CAP, and uniqueness of weak base change would make BC(π^V) a non-trivial isobaric sum. Suppose BC(π^V) is a non-trivial isobaric sum and π^V is not CAP. This case occurs; by the paper's own Theorem 4.14(3), for example, it covers every π^V whose base change is hermitian and non-cuspidal. Then χ′ is CAP and the written argument proves only existence. The step 'Therefore 𝔇(G′,1)^♡_{χ′} ≠ ∅, that is, weak automorphic base change exists' confuses two statements. 𝔇^♡_{χ′} ≠ ∅ (Definition 3.16: matching at every v ∉ T and of the archimedean infinitesimal character) is strictly stronger than weak base change (Definition 1.6: almost all split places). Reading the proof as 'suppose 𝔇^♡_{χ′} = ∅' does not help either, because 𝔇^♡_{χ′} = ∅ does not imply that χ′ is not CAP, so Theorem 3.6 cannot be used. As the first reading says, this is the case that Theorem 4.14(4) needs for hermitian non-cuspidal BC(π), and through it the last assertion of Lemma 4.16. Theorems 1.8–1.10 use only cuspidal Π_m: Π_{n+1} directly, and Π_n is cuspidal by the Burger–Sarnak partner and 4.14(2). There the written argument is enough. I checked the repair. Theorem 3.19 for (G′, ω = 1, χ′) gives μ′ with R(μ′⋆g) = 0 for all g ∈ S(G′(A_F))_{K′} when 𝔇^♡_{χ′} = ∅. Lemma 4.12(1) makes μ̃′ = μ′·ν′ with ν′ a T-multiplier, so R(μ̃′⋆f′) = R(μ′⋆(ν′⋆f′)) = 0. Then μ̃′⋆f′ is trivially quasi-cuspidal and every I_Π̃ vanishes. The unitary side is unchanged: Theorem 3.6 in case (a), Theorem 3.7 plus the supercuspidal f^V_{v_0} in case (b), then Propositions 4.8, 4.2, 4.7 and 4.1. This is a contradiction. Conversely, 𝔇^♡_{χ′} ≠ ∅ gives existence and (1). If (M,σ) ∈ 𝔇^♡_{χ′} with parameter s, then the isobaric sum of the σ_s is a weak base change, and its archimedean infinitesimal character is χ^{G′}_{σ_s,∞} = χ′_∞ = bc(χ_{π^V_∞}). Proposition 4.13(1) is true, so the gap affects the proof, not a stated result. The first reading's side remark is correct in outline. For conjugate self-dual Π_∞ the infinitesimal character lies in the image of bc_∞. So the archimedean part of χ^V in the proof of Theorem 1.8 can also be chosen directly.

issues.printed: The source says its theorem allows multipliers to modify f ∈ S(G(A_F))_K with the same effect as composition with projection onto any selected factor L²_cusp(G(F)\G(A_F)/K, ω)_π.
issues.correction: In the anisotropic case, Theorem 3.6 (with T = S, χ = χ_{π^S}) gives μ with R(μ⋆f) = R(f)∘P_[χ], where P_[χ] is the projection onto L²_cusp(…)[χ_{π^S}] ⊆ L²_cusp(…)_π. The stated 'composition with the projection onto the whole factor L²_cusp(…)_π' follows if the K-invariant members of the near-equivalence class of π have only finitely many S-characters: sum the Theorem 3.6 multipliers over them. This is expected in general and known in many cases, but it is not proved in the paper. The remark should either be restricted to L²_cusp(…)[χ_{π^S}] or state this extra input.
issues.reason: Checked on the p. 2 image and in main.tex l. 718. For G anisotropic modulo centre, the remark says 'our theorem implies' that multipliers can make R(μ⋆f) equal to R(f) composed with the projection P_π onto the whole near-equivalence factor L²_cusp(…)_π. That factor is the K-invariants of all π̃ with π̃_v ≃ π_v for almost all v. Theorem 1.1 gives only (1) R(μ⋆f) = P_π∘R(μ⋆f), so the other factors are killed, and (2) π(μ⋆f) = π(f). It says nothing about π̃(μ⋆f) for π̃ ≇ π in the class, so the implication does not follow from the theorem as stated. Theorem 3.6 (p. 23) does more, with T = S and χ = χ_{π^S}; every χ is non-CAP here, since G has no proper F-parabolic. Because a T-multiplier acts on each irreducible π̃ by the scalar μ(χ_{π̃^S}), it gives R(μ⋆f) = R(f)∘P_[χ], where L²_cusp[χ] ⊆ L²_cusp(…)_π. It also forces μ(χ̃) = 0 for every member of the class with a different S-character χ̃. So the claim needs one further fact: the K-invariant members of the class have only finitely many S-characters, in fact only χ_{π^S}. That is, nearly equivalent π̃ with π̃^K ≠ 0 have the same infinitesimal character and the same unramified components at all v ∉ S. Given finitely many such χ̃, summing the Theorem 3.6 multipliers gives the claim, since each one is 1 at its own χ̃ and 0 at the others. This fact is expected (it follows from Arthur's conjectures and strong multiplicity one for GL_N). It is known in some cases, for example through strong multiplicity one or the endoscopic classification [Mok15, KMSW] for unitary groups. The paper neither proves nor cites it for general G. Note that the first reading's wording 'can have a different infinitesimal character' overstates this: no such π̃ is known, and the point is only that nothing in the paper rules one out. The case for the defence is that this is an expository remark, and it is correct when the K-invariant part of the factor lies in L²_cusp[χ_{π^S}] (conjecturally always). So it is a gap in justification, not a false result.

issues.locator: §1.2, Remark 1.7, bullet, p. 4
issues.printed: The source asserts existence of weak automorphic base change for π, as defined in Definition 1.6, whenever infinitely many places v of F are split in E and have generic π_v.
issues.correction: If π is cuspidal automorphic, its weak automorphic base change (in the sense of Definition 1.6) exists as long as there exist infinitely many places v of F split in E such that π_v is generic (Theorem 4.14(1)).
issues.reason: In Remark 1.7, π is the irreducible admissible representation of Definition 1.6, and for such π the claim is false. There are uncountably many restricted tensor products of generic unramified π_v at the split places, but only countably many isobaric automorphic Π, so most such π have no weak base change. Theorem 4.14(1), which the remark announces (see Remark 4.15), assumes that π is cuspidal automorphic. The omitted hypothesis is clear from context ('as a byproduct of the Jacquet–Rallis relative trace formulae'), so this is a misprint rather than an error.

issues.citation: Beuzart-Plessis–Liu–Zhang–Zhu, "Isolation of cuspidal spectrum, with application to the Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture", Annals of Mathematics 194 (2021), no. 2
issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 4 image and in main.tex l. 781. The bullet says the weak automorphic base change 'of π exists as long as there exist infinitely many places v of F split in E such that π_v is generic'. In this remark π is the π of Definition 1.6, an arbitrary irreducible admissible representation of G(A_F). For such π the statement is false. The tail classes of (π_v)_{v split}, with π_v generic and unramified and taken modulo finitely many changes, are uncountable, while isobaric automorphic Π are countable. A weak base change Π determines π_v at almost all split v, since split local base change is injective. So most such π have no weak base change. The result being announced, Theorem 4.14(1) (p. 39, referred to via Remark 4.15), assumes that π is cuspidal automorphic, and its proof needs this. The context ('as a byproduct of the Jacquet–Rallis relative trace formulae', 'See Remark 4.15') makes the intended hypothesis clear, so this is an omitted hypothesis, i.e. a misprint. 'Places' versus 'primes' is harmless, since only finitely many places are archimedean.

issues.locator: §1.3, first step of the Section 3 strategy, p. 6
issues.printed: The source claims this step leaves only finitely many components L²_(M,σ)(G(Q)\G(A)/K) for M ∈ {M_(1,...,1), M_(n)}, while infinitely many survive for other M. It then selects M = M_(1,...,1,2) as the simplest nontrivial example and infers n ⩾ 3.
issues.correction: 'This will exclude all but finitely many components L²_(M,σ)(G(Q)∖G(A)/K) with M = M_(1,…,1). However, for other M (including M = M_(n) = G), there are still infinitely many components remaining.' In the next paragraph, drop '(hence n ⩾ 3)' or replace it by '(for n = 2 this is M = G)'.
issues.reason: For M = G = PGL_n, the components L²_(G,σ) are the cuspidal σ with nonzero K-invariants, and the first step only asks that σ_∞ contain a K_∞-type in 𝔗. 𝔗 is nonempty, because π itself survives. Take n = 2 and K = PGL_2(Ẑ). Every K_∞-type of PO(2) occurs in the spherical or the sign-twisted principal series of PGL_2(R), and each of these is the archimedean component of infinitely many level-one Hecke–Maass cusp forms (Selberg; Weyl law). So infinitely many components with M = G survive the first step. The torus case is fine: over Q, characters of T(Q)∖T(A)^1 = (Ẑ^×)^{n-1} with a fixed level are finite in number. The actual proof in §3.3 treats M = G like every other standard Levi subgroup. Lemma 3.14 is stated 'for every standard Levi subgroup M of G', Proposition 3.15 takes the product over all of them, and the proof of Lemma 3.13 uses [Don82, Theorem 9.1] for M_der. So only the heuristic sketch is wrong. Case for the defence: this is an informal overview. But the sentence is a definite claim, and '(hence n ⩾ 3)' shows that the authors meant it.

issues.citation: Beuzart-Plessis–Liu–Zhang–Zhu, "Isolation of cuspidal spectrum, with application to the Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture", Annals of Mathematics 194 (2021), no. 2
issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 6 image and in main.tex l. 854. The first step only gives μ^0_∞ with μ^0_∞(χ_{π_∞}) = 1 and a finite set 𝔗 of K_∞-types. A component with no K_∞-type in 𝔗 is killed. The text then says: 'This will exclude all but finitely many components … with M ∈ {M_(1,…,1), M_(n)}'. For M_(n) = G (the paper itself writes 'M = M_(n) = G' in the third step), this is false. 𝔗 must contain a K_∞-type of π_∞, since otherwise π would be killed. Take n = 2, K = PGL_2(Ẑ), and π with spherical π_∞, for example a level-one even Maass form. For K_∞ = PO(2), the types trivial and ρ_m (m ≥ 2 even) occur in every spherical principal series of PGL_2(R), and det and ρ_m occur in every sign-twisted one. So whatever 𝔗 is, the infinitely many level-one even (or, if 𝔗 = {det}, odd) Hecke–Maass cusp forms (Selberg's Weyl law) keep a K_∞-type in 𝔗 and nonzero K-invariants. So infinitely many components with M = G survive. The K_∞-type condition does not bound the continuous spectral parameter. The 𝓜^♯ condition (Definition 2.8(3)) only restricts the discrete parameters ϖ ∈ Y*_ϑ, not the principal-series parameters. The torus part is correct over Q: T(Q)∖T(A)^1 ≅ (Ẑ^×)^{n−1} has only finitely many characters of fixed level. It is a definite claim, not a loose summary: for n = 2 it would make the second step unnecessary, and the following '(hence n ⩾ 3)' is consistent with this reading. The actual proof is unaffected. Lemma 3.14 (p. 26) is stated 'for every standard Levi subgroup M of G', and p. 25 sets '𝔗_M = 𝔗' and 'K_{M,S} = K_S' 'when M = G'. So M = G gets the Casimir/[Don82] treatment (Lemmas 3.12–3.13), and Proposition 3.15 takes the product over all standard Levis.

issues.correction: μ^0_∞ ⋆ f annihilates the component L²_(M,σ)(G(Q)∖G(A)/K) if it has no K_∞-types in 𝔗

issues.locator: §1.4, definition of lattice, p. 8; §2.1, Corollary 2.6 and proof, pp. 9–10
issues.printed: The source defines a lattice L in U as a subgroup for which L ⊗_Z C → U is injective, and a full lattice by bijectivity. Corollary 2.6 asserts that for a lattice L in U_C and finite A ⊆ U_C, there is a holomorphic ν on U_C with moderate vertical growth, zero on L ∖ A and nonzero throughout A. Its proof chooses λ_1, …, λ_r : U_C → C as linearly independent complex linear maps and satisfy L ⊆ ∩_{i=1}^r λ_i^{−1}Z.
issues.correction: A lattice (resp. full lattice) of U is a finitely generated subgroup L of U such that L ⊗_Z C → U is injective (resp. bijective).
issues.reason: As printed, the definition also admits groups that are not finitely generated. For example Z[1/2] ⊆ C: Z[1/2] ⊗_Z C → C, a ⊗ c ↦ ac, is an isomorphism, so Z[1/2] is even a 'full lattice' of C. For U = R, L = Z[1/2] and A = {1/3}, a holomorphic ν vanishing on L ∖ A = Z[1/2], which has accumulation points, is identically 0, so Corollary 2.6 fails. The first step of its proof also needs L finitely generated. The intended meaning is clear, and the only use (Lemma 2.10, on a lattice of h*^−_{ϑ,C} containing Y*_ϑ, which lies in (1/4)(1−ϑ)X*) is finitely generated.

issues.citation: Beuzart-Plessis–Liu–Zhang–Zhu, "Isolation of cuspidal spectrum, with application to the Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture", Annals of Mathematics 194 (2021), no. 2
issues.reviewReason: Confirmed on the images of pp. 8–10. As printed, a 'lattice' is any subgroup L with L ⊗_Z C → U injective, and this does not force L to be finitely generated or discrete. For Z[1/2] ⊆ C, Z[1/2] ⊗_Z C ≅ C and the map is a ↦ ac, an isomorphism, so Z[1/2] is even a 'full lattice'. With U = R, L = Z[1/2] and A = {1/3}, any holomorphic ν vanishing on L ∖ A, a set dense in R, is ≡ 0, so Corollary 2.6 fails. Its proof's first step (L ⊆ ∩ λ_i^{-1}Z) also needs L finitely generated. The intended standard meaning, a finitely generated subgroup generated by C-linearly independent vectors, is clear. Correction to the first reading: Corollary 2.6 has three uses, not one. They are Lemma 2.10 (a lattice in h*^−_{ϑ,C} containing Y*_ϑ ⊆ ¼(1−ϑ)X*), the proof of Lemma 3.14 on p. 26 (L_M, differentials of characters of a compact abelian Lie group), and the proof of Proposition 4.11 on p. 37 (compact G^V). All three involve finitely generated groups, so nothing is affected.

issues.locator: §2.2, list before Definition 2.8, p. 10; proof of Lemma 2.10, p. 11
issues.printed: The source defines Aut(X*, Φ, X_*, Φ^∨)^♡ as the automorphisms of (X*, Φ, X_*, Φ^∨) whose order is at most 2, calling this set finite and invariant under W-conjugation. Lemma 2.10 uses the finiteness of θ to form ν := ∏_{ϑ∈θ} ν_ϑ ∈ M^♯_θ(h*_C).
issues.correction: Delete 'which is finite'. Assume in §2.2 (or in Lemma 2.10) that the W-stable subset θ is finite. Note that the θ of §2.3 lies in a single W-coset, hence is finite. (Aut^♡ itself is finite when the connected centre of G has dimension ≤ 1, but not in general, e.g. for G_m² or GL_n × GL_{n+1}.)
issues.reason: Both quotations are confirmed on the images of pp. 10–11. 'Aut(X*,Φ,X_*,Φ^∨)^♡ … which is finite' is false in general. For the split torus G_m² (Φ = ∅), Aut = GL_2(Z), and it contains the pairwise distinct involutions [[1,n],[0,−1]], n ∈ Z. This is x ↦ x + ⟨x,c⟩z with c = e_2^*, z = (n,−2), ⟨z,c⟩ = −2. More generally, x ↦ x + ⟨x,c⟩z with z ∈ (Φ^∨)^⊥ ∩ X*, c ∈ Φ^⊥ ∩ X_* and ⟨z,c⟩ = −2 is an involutive automorphism of the root datum: it fixes Φ, and its dual y ↦ y + ⟨z,y⟩c fixes Φ^∨. For GL_n × GL_{n+1} (the U(n) × U(n+1) of §4 at a real place), take z = a·det_n + b·det_{n+1} and c the sum of the two central cocharacters. Then ⟨z,c⟩ = an + b(n+1) = −2 has infinitely many integer solutions, so Aut^♡ is infinite there too. (the first reading's claim that this works whenever (Φ^∨)^⊥ has rank ≥ 2 is overstated: for GL_3 × GL_3 the pairing takes values in 3Z, although Aut^♡ is still infinite there via other involutions.) Aut^♡ is finite when the connected centre has dimension ≤ 1. Over Q, X* = QΦ ⊕ (Φ^∨)^⊥_Q and an automorphism preserves both summands. On QΦ it lies in the finite group Aut(Φ), and on the line (Φ^∨)^⊥_Q it is ±1. In §2.2 θ is an arbitrary W-stable subset of Aut^♡. issues.printed: Citing Harish-Chandra, the source identifies ∪_{ϑ∈θ_G} h*_{ϑ,C} ⊕ Y*_ϑ with the entire set in h*_C of infinitesimal characters arising from irreducible admissible G-representations. It consequently describes the preceding homomorphism’s kernel as precisely the μ vanishing on ∪_{ϑ∈θ_G} h*_{ϑ,C} ⊕ Y*_ϑ.
issues.correction: The infinitesimal characters of irreducible admissible representations of G lie in ⋃_{ϑ∈θ_G} h*_{ϑ,C} ⊕ Y*_ϑ; the inclusion can be strict (e.g. G = SU(2), at 0). The kernel of the conjectural homomorphism consists of the μ that vanish at every infinitesimal character of an irreducible admissible representation of G. The conjecture's growth condition should be imposed on the set of actual infinitesimal characters (or the 'only if' read modulo that kernel); as stated it fails for SU(3).
issues.reason: Confirmed on the p. 12 image. Take G = SU(2). Then X* = Z, Φ = {±2}, ρ = 1, θ_G = {−1} (Remark 2.14), h*_{−1} = 0 and Y*_{−1} = ρ + X* = Z, so the union is Z. The irreducible representations Sym^n have infinitesimal characters ±(n+1), n ≥ 0, so 0 ∈ Z is not an infinitesimal character, and only the inclusion holds. The kernel claim fails as well. μ(z) = sin(πz)/(πz) is even, entire and bounded on Z, so it lies in M_{{−1}}(h*_C)^W (Example 2.15(2)). It vanishes at every infinitesimal character, so μ⋆ = 0, but μ(0) = 1. Correction to the first reading: this does not happen for every compact G. For SO(3), ρ + X* = (1/2 + Z)α has no singular points and equality holds. The failure happens whenever ρ + X* contains singular elements (SU(2), U(2), SU(3), …). Correction to the first reading's defence: the conjecture in the same remark is not unaffected in general. For SU(3), ρ + X* = P contains the infinitely many singular weights kω_1. Let ν(λ) = 1 − ∏_{β>0}(1 − s(⟨λ,β^∨⟩)) with s(w) = sin(πw)/(πw). It is entire and W-invariant, equals 0 on regular weights and 1 on singular ones. Then μ = ν·exp(q(λ)), with q the W-invariant quadratic form, vanishes at every infinitesimal character, so it 'gives a multiplier' (μ⋆ = 0). But μ(kω_1) = exp(k²q(ω_1)) is not polynomially bounded on Y*_{−1}, so μ ∉ M_{θ_G}(h*_C)^W. So the 'only if' half of the conjecture as stated, and the claim that it 'can be easily checked when G is anisotropic', fail for SU(3) (and for SU(2) × U(1)). They hold for SU(2), where there is only one singular point. Nothing later in the paper uses Remark 2.16. The analogous 'exactly' in the proof of Proposition 2.24 uses only the inclusion.
