issues.locator: §2.3, proof of Lemma 2.18, p. 13
issues.printed: The source claims finiteness, modulo conjugation and unramified twists, of pairs (M, σ) with M Levi and σ irreducible discrete series on M, for which μ does not vanish at the infinitesimal character of the induction of (M, σ). It uses Langlands classification and the inheritance of minimal K-types by Langlands quotients of standard modules [Kna01, Theorem 15.10] to choose 𝔗(μ) as the minimal K-types occurring in these finitely many inductions.
issues.correction: Let σ run over discrete series and (nondegenerate) limits of discrete series of Levi subgroups M; there are still finitely many such pairs up to conjugation and twist with μ nonzero on their infinitesimal characters, and take 𝔗(μ) to be the minimal K-types of their inductions. Alternatively, keep discrete series and add that every summand of a representation unitarily induced from a discrete series contains a minimal K-type of that induced representation.
issues.reason: The pairs (M, σ) in the proof use discrete series σ only. The standard modules of the Langlands classification are induced from tempered representations or from limits of discrete series, for example the limits of discrete series of SL_2(R). So the minimal K-types of π's standard module are not directly among the minimal K-types of the inductions of the listed pairs. Passing to an induction from discrete series needs a further step that the proof does not state. In defence: the missing facts are standard (Harish-Chandra, Knapp–Zuckerman, Vogan's minimal K-type theory), and Lemma 2.18 is true with a finite 𝔗(μ) either way.

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed on the p. 13 image. The proof takes the finitely many pairs (M, σ) with σ a discrete series of M, and sets 𝔗(μ) to be the minimal K-types of their inductions. But the Langlands classification writes π as the Langlands quotient of I_P(σ ⊗ ν) with σ tempered (Knapp–Zuckerman: σ a discrete series or nondegenerate limit of discrete series). For example, the limits of discrete series D_0^± of SL_2(R) are their own standard modules and are not induced from discrete series. The cited [Kna01, Thm 15.10] gives that π contains the minimal K-types of its own standard module. To land in the stated 𝔗(μ), one also needs this: a tempered σ is a summand of I_{P'∩M}^M(δ ⊗ iν') with δ a discrete series of M' ⊆ M, and each summand of a representation unitarily induced from a discrete series contains a minimal K-type of the whole (Vogan). Being a summand alone does not give this. The proof does not state it. Defence: these facts are standard, the finiteness argument is unchanged (limit-of-discrete-series parameters also lie in h*_{ϑ,C} ⊕ Y*_ϑ), and Lemma 2.18 is true as stated. For SL_2(R), for instance, D_0^+ contains the K-type 1, which is a minimal K-type of the odd principal series.

The proof then says 'Take a function μ ∈ N_{θ∪{1}}(h*_C) that vanishes on H_s'. The restriction matters in principle: for μ ∉ N, a particular seminorm p_{ϑ,M+M_s,r}(μ) can still be finite, so the inequality is not vacuous. But the argument (the Cauchy estimate (2.2), the discreteness bound (2.3), and the passage to ϑ′) never uses μ ∈ N. It proves the stated generality word for word, and that generality is what Lemma 2.20 uses.

issues.locator: §2.4, proof of Lemma 2.22, p. 16 (with the definition of t_w on p. 14)
issues.printed: The source writes Λ(τ) ⊂ X* for τ’s weights and, for each z ∈ Z(g), defines P_z(X) := ∏_{λ∈Λ(τ)} (X − t_λ z). It cites [Kos75, Theorem 4.9] for P_z(δ(z)) = 0. On p. 14 it defines the action by (t_wP)(α) = P(w^{-1}α).
issues.correction: P_z(X) := ∏_{λ∈Λ(τ)} (X − t_{−λ}z), i.e. the roots are α ↦ z(α + λ). Equivalently, take the product over −Λ(τ) (the weights of τ^∨) and take λ_1, …, λ_r ∈ −Λ(τ) in the diagonalisation that follows. Alternatively, declare that λ ∈ X* acts on h*_C by α ↦ α − λ.
issues.reason: Under the usual action of W̃ = X* ⋊ W on h*_C (λ acts by α ↦ α + λ) and the paper's definition of t_w, t_λ z is α ↦ z(α − λ). But δ(z) acts on π ⊗ τ with eigenvalues z(χ_π + λ), λ ∈ Λ(τ). Test case: G = GL_1, g = C·X_0, Z(g) = U(g) = C[X_0] = C[h*_C] (W and ρ trivial), τ(g) = g^k with weight k ≠ 0. Then End(W_τ) = C, R_τ = C[X_0] with basis v_1 = 1, and δ(z)(X_0) = z(X_0 + k), so δ(z) = t_{−k}z. The printed P_z(X) = X − t_k z gives P_z(δ(z)) = z(X_0 + k) − z(X_0 − k), which is 2k ≠ 0 for z = X_0. Case for the defence: the paper never says how X* acts on h*_C, and with translation by −λ the printed formula is right. The rest of the proof uses only that the roots are the pairwise distinct characters z ↦ t_λ z for λ in a finite W-stable subset of X*, and that the t_λ lie in R; −Λ(τ) has these properties, so Lemma 2.22 is unaffected.
searched: Crossref record of doi:10.4007/annals.2021.194.2.5, checked 2026-09-23: no update, correction or erratum relation
issues.citation: Beuzart-Plessis–Liu–Zhang–Zhu, "Isolation of cuspidal spectrum, with application to the Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture", Annals of Mathematics 194 (2021), no. 2
issues.reviewReason: Quotation checked on the images of p. 16 (P_z(X) := ∏_{λ∈Λ(τ)} (X − t_λ z), [Kos75, Thm 4.9] gives P_z(δ(z)) = 0) and p. 14 ((t_wP)(α) = P(w^{-1}α), W̃ := X* ⋊ W acting on h*_C). The paper never says how X* acts on h*_C, and it gives no normalisation of the Harish-Chandra isomorphism beyond citing [HC51]. So the defence that 'the sign is a convention' was checked. Take the standard conventions: λ ∈ X* acts on h* = X* ⊗ ℝ by α ↦ α + λ, and the Harish-Chandra isomorphism is the usual ρ-shifted one, which is the identity S(h) = C[h*] for a torus. Then t_λz(α) = z(α − λ). But on V ⊗ W_τ, with V of infinitesimal character α, δ(z) has generalised eigenvalues z(α + λ), λ ∈ Λ(τ) (Kostant). I rechecked the first reading's test independently. For G = GL_1, W_τ = ℂ with τ(t) = t^k, k ≠ 0: U(g) = Z(g) = ℂ[X_0] = C[h*_C], End(W_τ) = ℂ, R_τ = ℂ[X_0] with v_1 = 1, and δ(z) = z(X_0 + k), so S(z) = t_{−k}z. The printed P_z gives P_z(δ(z)) = z(X_0 + k) − z(X_0 − k), which equals 2k ≠ 0 for z = X_0. The sign matters only when Λ(τ) ≠ −Λ(τ): it does not matter for SL_2, but it does for GL_1, SL_3 and unitary groups, all within the paper's generality. With the printed t_w, the formula is right only if X* acts by α ↦ α − λ. That convention is nonstandard and the paper does not state it, so the sign is a slip, not a declared convention. It is harmless. The rest of the proof uses only three facts: the roots are pairwise distinct ring homomorphisms z ↦ t_ν z; ν runs over a finite W-stable subset of X*; and the t_ν lie in R. All three hold for ν ∈ −Λ(τ). Lemma 2.22 and everything after it are unaffected.

issues.locator: §2.4, proof of Proposition 2.24, p. 17 (and its use on p. 19)
issues.printed: The source describes ℂ[G] ⊗ U(g) ≃ D(G) as canonical, via P ⊗ X ↦ P · L(X), and calls L(X) the left invariant operator associated with X on G. On p. 19 it claims that pre-composition with (π ⊗ τ)(f), followed by a limit, yields (π ⊗ τ)(μ ⋆ f) = Σ_{i,j} S_i(μ)(χ_π) · (1_{V_π} ⊗ A_ij) ∘ (π ⊗ τ)(L(u_ij)f).
issues.correction: … where L(X) stands for the differential operator on G obtained by differentiating the left regular representation, (L(X)f)(g) = d/dt|_{t=0} f(exp(−tX)g) (a right-invariant operator), extended to U(g); then ρ(L(u)f) = ρ(u)ρ(f) for every representation ρ of moderate growth.
issues.reason: The last step on p. 19 identifies (π⊗τ)(u_ij) ∘ (π⊗τ)(f) with (π⊗τ)(L(u_ij)f). With ρ(f) = ∫ f(g)ρ(g) dg (p. 12), that holds for the derivative of the left regular action, which is what 'L' denotes in the appendix ('L denotes the left regular action'). It fails for left-invariant operators: for the left-invariant vector field (X̃f)(g) = d/dt f(g exp tX) one gets ρ(X̃f) = −ρ(f)ρ(X), a right composition. The other two uses on p. 17 (the decomposition D(G) ≅ ℂ[G] ⊗ U(g) and L(X)(μ⋆f) = μ⋆L(X)f) hold for either choice. So 'left invariant' is a slip for 'right invariant' (or 'coming from the left regular representation').

issues.citation: Beuzart-Plessis–Liu–Zhang–Zhu, "Isolation of cuspidal spectrum, with application to the Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture", Annals of Mathematics 194 (2021), no. 2
issues.reviewReason: Quotations checked on the images of p. 17 ('L(X) stands for the left invariant differential operator on G associated to X') and p. 19 ('Pre-composing (π⊗τ)(f) … (1_{V_π} ⊗ A_ij)∘(π⊗τ)(L(u_ij)f)'). The p. 19 step needs (π⊗τ)(u)∘(π⊗τ)(f) = (π⊗τ)(L(u)f). The paper defines ρ(f) = ∫ f(g)ρ(g) dg (p. 12), and Haar measure is left-invariant. With these, ρ(X)ρ(f) = ρ(L(X)f) holds exactly when (L(X)f)(g) = d/dt|_0 f(exp(−tX)g), the derivative of the left regular representation. That operator commutes with right translations, so it is right-invariant. For the left-invariant field (X̃f)(g) = d/dt|_0 f(g exp tX), unimodularity gives ρ(X̃f) = −ρ(f)ρ(X): the composition is on the other side and has the opposite sign, so (∗) would fail as written. The other two uses on p. 17 hold for either reading: C[G] ⊗ U(g) ≅ D(G), and L(X)(μ⋆f) = μ⋆L(X)f (check this one by applying π). The appendix (proof of Prop. A.1) itself says 'L denotes the left regular action'. So the phrase 'left invariant' is a wording slip; the intended operator is clear.

issues.locator: §2.4, proof of Proposition 2.24, p. 18
issues.printed: Invoking Harish-Chandra [HC75], the source identifies the union of χ_π over π ∈ Temp(G) with precisely ⋃_{ϑ∈θ_G} ih*_ϑ ⊕ Y*_ϑ, a W-stable subset of h*_ℂ.
issues.correction: … the infinitesimal character χ_π of every π ∈ Temp(G) is contained in (meets) the W-stable subset ⋃_{ϑ∈θ_G} i h*_ϑ ⊕ Y*_ϑ of h*_ℂ. (The same correction, 'is contained in the union', applies to the corresponding sentence of Remark 2.16, p. 12.)
issues.reason: Equality fails. Take G = SU(2), the anisotropic form of SL_2: X* = ℤ, Φ = {±2}, ρ = 1 (Example 2.15), and θ_G = {−1} (Remark 2.14, G anisotropic). Then h*_{−1} = 0 and Y*_{−1} = ρ + X* = ℤ, so the right side is ℤ. The irreducible representations of SU(2) (all tempered) are Sym^n, n ≥ 0, with infinitesimal characters ±(n + 1), so their union is ℤ ∖ {0}. The point 0 ∈ Y*_{−1} is a singular parameter that no tempered representation (indeed no irreducible admissible representation) has. The same happens for any G with a compact factor whose ρ + X* contains singular points. The inclusion does hold (discrete-series and limit parameters of the Levi of a θ-stable Cartan lie in Y*_ϑ, since the projection of ρ onto h*^−_ϑ is ρ_M for a suitable positive system), and it is all the next display uses, where |μ(χ_π)| is bounded by the sup over this set.

issues.citation: Beuzart-Plessis–Liu–Zhang–Zhu, "Isolation of cuspidal spectrum, with application to the Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture", Annals of Mathematics 194 (2021), no. 2
issues.reviewReason: Quotation checked on the image of p. 18. Counterexample, checked independently. G = SU(2): G_C = SL_2, X* = ℤ, Φ = {±2}, ρ = 1. The only maximal tori are compact, so a_T = 0, and Lemma 2.19 gives θ_G = {−1}, as Remark 2.14 says for anisotropic groups. Then h*_{−1} = 0, h*^−_{−1} = h*, and Y*_{−1} = ρ + X* = ℤ, so the right-hand side is ℤ. Every irreducible representation of the compact group SU(2) is tempered: these are Sym^n, n ≥ 0, with infinitesimal character the W-orbit ±(n + 1), under either sign normalisation of the Harish-Chandra isomorphism. The union is ℤ ∖ {0} ≠ ℤ. 0 lies in the right-hand side, but no irreducible representation of SU(2) has infinitesimal character 0. So 'exactly' is false. This is not a one-word slip: Remark 2.16 (p. 12) makes the same equality claim for all irreducible admissible representations ('is the union ⋃_{ϑ∈θ_G} h*_{ϑ,ℂ} ⊕ Y*_ϑ'), and that is also false for SU(2). The inclusion is true. A tempered π is a constituent of an induced representation from a (limit of) discrete series σ of M, twisted by iν on a θ-stable Cartan t_c ⊕ a. The Harish-Chandra parameter of σ lies in ρ_M + (characters of T_c). Take an ordering that puts the a-part first. Then non-imaginary roots pair as β, ϑβ, so the projection of ρ onto h*^−_ϑ is ρ_M. The parameter therefore lies in Y*_ϑ, and χ_π ∈ i h*_ϑ ⊕ Y*_ϑ. The next two displays use only this inclusion: the bound on |μ(χ_π)|, and the choice of z_1, …, z_N. So the proof and Proposition 2.24 are unaffected.

issues.locator: §2.4, proof of Theorem 2.13, statements (1)–(2), p. 20, and their use, p. 21
issues.printed: Statement (2) asserts that for sufficiently small ϵ > 0 and any M > 0 one can choose C_{ϵ,M} > 0 with |exp(−P(α+ϖ)) − 1| ⩽ C_{ϵ,M}‖α+ϖ‖^ϵ for all ϑ ∈ θ ∪ {1}, α ∈ h*_{ϑ,ℂ} satisfying ‖Re α‖ < M, and ϖ ∈ Y*_ϑ. On p. 21, (2) is used to deduce lim_{n→∞} p_{ϑ,M,r}(μ_n − μ) = 0.
issues.correction: In (1) and (2), let ϖ range over h*^−_ϑ, not only over Y*_ϑ, and rename the exponent in (2) (say ϵ′, 0 < ϵ′ ≤ d) so that it does not clash with the ϵ in Re P(α+ϖ) ≥ ϵ‖α+ϖ‖^d. Then apply (1) and (2) at (α + ϖ)/n.
issues.reason: μ_n − μ = (exp(−P(x/n)) − 1)μ(x) with x = α + ϖ, so (2) has to be applied at x/n = α/n + ϖ/n, where ϖ/n ∈ h*^−_ϑ is in general not in Y*_ϑ. As stated, (2) says nothing about exp(−n^{−d}P(x)) − 1. With the h*^−_ϑ version one gets p_{ϑ,M,r}(μ_n − μ) ≤ C_{ϵ′,M} n^{−ϵ′} p_{ϑ,M,r_M}(μ) → 0 for 0 < ϵ′ ≤ r_M − r. For (1) there is a way out even as stated: by homogeneity |exp(−P(x/n))| = |exp(−P(x))|^{n^{−d}}, so (1) at x with exponent n^d(r_M − r) suffices. The conclusion of Theorem 2.13 is unaffected.

issues.citation: Beuzart-Plessis–Liu–Zhang–Zhu, "Isolation of cuspidal spectrum, with application to the Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture", Annals of Mathematics 194 (2021), no. 2
issues.reviewReason: Quotations checked on the images of pp. 20–21. Statements (1) and (2) are stated only for ϖ ∈ Y*_ϑ. Set x = α + ϖ. Then (μ_n − μ)(x) = (exp(−P(x/n)) − 1)μ(x), so (2) is needed at x/n = α/n + ϖ/n. Here ‖Re(α/n)‖ < M, but ϖ/n ∈ h*^−_ϑ is not in Y*_ϑ in general (for SL_2(ℝ), ϑ = −1, Y* = ℤ). As stated, (2) says nothing about exp(−n^{−d}P(x)) − 1, so the step 'From (2), we obtain lim p_{ϑ,M,r}(μ_n − μ) = 0' does not follow literally. The fix is the first reading's. The estimate just before, Re P(α+ϖ) ≥ ϵ‖α+ϖ‖^d, is stated for all ϖ ∈ h*^−_ϑ, and (2) follows from it on that larger set for 0 < ϵ′ ≤ d. Near 0, |e^{−P} − 1| ≲ |P| ≲ ‖x‖^d; on the bounded middle region it is bounded; for ‖x‖ ≥ δ^{−1}M it is ≤ 2. This gives p_{ϑ,M,r}(μ_n − μ) ≤ C n^{−ϵ′} p_{ϑ,M,r+ϵ′}(μ) → 0 for 0 < ϵ′ ≤ min(d, r_M − r). The first use can be rescued as stated, as the first reading notes: |exp(−P(x/n))| = |exp(−P(x))|^{n^{−d}}, and (1) at x with exponent n^d(r_M − r) < 0 gives the bound. The ϵ in (2) also clashes with the ϵ fixed just before; this is cosmetic. The derivation 'This implies the following statements' already gives the stronger version, so the restricted range in (1)–(2) is a slip whose intended meaning is clear, not a missing argument. Theorem 2.13 is unaffected.

issues.printed: The source attributes to the proof of Theorem 2.13 the continuity of μ⋆ for each μ ∈ M_{θ∪{1}}(h*_ℂ), and says that each element of M(h*_ℂ) supplies a multiplier on S(G)_{(K)}.

issues.locator: §3.2, footnote 6, p. 23
issues.printed: The source says [Art05, Art13] use a_M^G for a_M, and identifies it with the real Lie algebra attached to the maximal Q-split torus in Res_{F/Q} Z∖M.
issues.correction: … it is the real Lie algebra of the maximal Q-split torus contained in the centre of Res_{F/Q}(Z∖M).
issues.reason: a_M = Z(A_F)M(A_F)^1∖M(A_F) ≅ a_M^G has dimension dim A_M − dim Z (A_M the maximal F-split central torus of M), which is the dimension of the maximal Q-split central torus of Res_{F/Q}(Z∖M). A maximal Q-split torus of Res_{F/Q}(Z∖M) that need not be central is larger in general. Example: M = G = GL_2, Z its centre: a_G = 0, but Res_{F/Q}PGL_2 contains a 1-dimensional Q-split torus. The word 'central' was dropped from a footnote that is otherwise standard.

issues.citation: Beuzart-Plessis–Liu–Zhang–Zhu, "Isolation of cuspidal spectrum, with application to the Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture", Annals of Mathematics 194 (2021), no. 2
issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 23 image (footnote 6). a_M := Z(A_F)M(A_F)^1∖M(A_F) has dimension dim A_M − dim Z, where A_M is the maximal F-split torus in Z_M. This is the dimension of the maximal Q-split torus in the centre Z_M/Z of Z∖M, after restriction of scalars. It is Arthur's a_M^G, as the footnote says. As printed ('maximal Q-split torus contained in Res_{F/Q} Z∖M'), the statement is false. For M = G = GL_2 over Q with Z the centre, Z(A)G(A)^1 = G(A) because |det z| = |z|^2 covers R_{>0}, so a_G = 0. But PGL_2 contains a 1-dimensional split torus. Also, a maximal split torus of a non-commutative group is not unique, so 'the' only makes sense for the central one. The word 'centre' was dropped. The meaning is clear from the reference to a_M^G in [Art05, Art13], and the footnote is never used.

issues.locator: §3.2, construction of the cuspidal components, p. 24
issues.printed: The source defines Φ̃(g) := ∫_{i a*_M} Φ_s(g)·ξ_s(m(g)) ds on g ∈ P(F)∖G(A_F), then introduces the pseudo-Eisenstein series by E(g, Φ) := Σ_{γ∈P(F)∖G(F)} Φ̃(γg).

The parabolic in play is P_M: 𝒜^G_{(M,σ)} consists of functions on N_{P_M}(A_F)∖G(A_F) whose restrictions φ_x are automorphic on M, hence left M(F)-invariant. issues.printed: The source asserts the equivalence of c*_M = a*_M with the two conditions Z = 1 and discreteness of Z_M(A_F)^1.
issues.correction: Thus, c*_M = a*_M holds if and only if Z = 1 and Z_M(A_F)^1 is totally disconnected (equivalently, Z_M(A_F)^1 ∩ Z_M(F_∞) is discrete);
issues.reason: The cotangent space of Z_M(A_F)^1 Z(A_F) at the identity only sees its archimedean part, so its vanishing means Z = 1 and Z_M(A_F)^1 ∩ Z_M(F_∞) is discrete. Taken literally, 'Z_M(A_F)^1 is discrete' almost never holds, because Z_M(A_F)^1 contains an open compact subgroup of Z_M(A_F^∞), which is infinite. Counterexample to the printed equivalence: G = SL_2 over Q and M = T the diagonal torus. Then Z = 1, c*_T = h* and a*_T are both 1-dimensional, so c*_T = a*_T, yet T(A)^1 = A^1 ⊇ Ẑ^× is not discrete. The intended meaning is clear from the first sentence of the remark.

issues.citation: Beuzart-Plessis–Liu–Zhang–Zhu, "Isolation of cuspidal spectrum, with application to the Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture", Annals of Mathematics 194 (2021), no. 2
issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 25 image and main.tex l. 1864. The first sentence is right. dim c*_M = [F:Q]·dim Z_M, because c*_M = X*(T/(T∩M_der)) ⊗ R. dim a*_M = dim A_M − dim Z. The Lie algebra of Z_M(A_F)^1Z(A_F) has dimension [F:Q]dim Z_M − dim A_M + dim Z, which is the difference. So c*_M = a*_M iff that group has trivial Lie algebra, i.e. iff Z = 1 and Z_M(A_F)^1 ∩ Z_M(F_∞) is discrete. The printed 'Z_M(A_F)^1 is discrete' is literally much stronger. Z_M(A_F)^1 contains the compact open subgroup Z_M(Ô_F) of Z_M(A_F^∞), which is infinite as soon as dim Z_M > 0. So the literal condition forces M to be semisimple. Counterexample to the literal 'only if': G = SL_2 over Q, M = T diagonal. Then Z = 1, b*_T = 0, so c*_T = h* is 1-dimensional, and a_T = T(A)^1∖T(A) ≅ R. So c*_T = a*_T, yet T(A)^1 = A^1 ⊇ Ẑ^× is not discrete. The literal 'if' direction holds. The intended meaning (no archimedean continuous part) is clear from the preceding 'cotangent space at the identity'. Only that first sentence is used (proof of Lemma 3.14).

issues.printed: The source asserts that c*_M = a*_M for all standard Levi subgroups M precisely when G is both semisimple and split over Q.
issues.correction: … and c*_M = a*_M holds for every standard Levi subgroup M if and only if G is semisimple and the identity component of the centre of Res_{F/Q}M_0 is Q-split (i.e. either F = Q and G is split, or G is semisimple and anisotropic over F).
issues.reason: The 'only if' direction is false. Take G = SL_1(D) for a quaternion division algebra D over Q. The only standard Levi subgroup is M = G. Since M_der = G, b*_G = h* and c*_G = 0, and a_G = 0 because G has no rational characters. So c*_M = a*_M for every standard M, but G is not split (the same holds for SL_2 × SL_1(D)). In general dim c*_M = [F:Q]·dim Z_M^0 and dim a*_M = dim A_M − dim Z, so c*_M = a*_M iff Z = 1 and Res_{F/Q}Z_M^0 is Q-split. Since Z_M ⊆ Z_{M_0} for M ⊇ M_0, this holds for all M iff it holds for M_0, and for M = G it forces G to be semisimple. The 'if' direction as printed is right. The sentence is never used: only the first sentence of Remark 3.10 enters the proof of Lemma 3.14.

issues.citation: Beuzart-Plessis–Liu–Zhang–Zhu, "Isolation of cuspidal spectrum, with application to the Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture", Annals of Mathematics 194 (2021), no. 2
issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 25 image. Counterexample to 'only if', verified independently. Let D be a definite quaternion division algebra over Q and G = SL_1(D). G is Q-anisotropic, so M_0 = P_0 = G and G is the only standard Levi. M_der = G gives b*_G = h* and c*_G = 0. Z = 1 (the centre is μ_2), and G has no rational characters, so G(A)^1 = G(A) and a_G = 0. Thus c*_M = a*_M for every standard M. But G is not split over Q, nor even over R. In general, c*_M = a*_M iff [F:Q]·dim Z_M = dim A_M − dim Z, iff Z = 1 and Res_{F/Q}Z_M^0 is Q-split. Since Z_M ⊆ Z_{M_0} for standard M, this holds for all M iff it holds for M_0 and G. For M = G it forces Z_G^0 = 1. So the right condition is: G semisimple and Res_{F/Q}Z_{M_0}^0 Q-split, i.e. F = Q and G split, or G semisimple and F-anisotropic. The printed 'if' direction is correct. The sentence is a false claim in a remark and is never used.

issues.locator: §3.3, proof of Lemma 3.12, p. 26
issues.printed: The source reduces the proof to finite rank of the set of Casimir eigenvalues arising from 𝔆(M_der; K_{M_der}, 𝔗_{M_der}), claiming that finiteness of 𝔗_{M_der} makes this follow immediately from [Don82, Theorem 9.1].
issues.correction: Add: the finite abelian group M(A_F)/M(F)N, N := Z_M(A_F)M_der(A_F)K_M M_∞ (open, normal, of finite index since M(F)∖M(A_F)^1 has finite volume and A_M^∞ ⊆ N), has representatives m_1, …, m_r ∈ M(A_F^∞). For σ ∈ 𝔆(M, ω; K_M, 𝔗_M) take a nonzero K_M-invariant φ ∈ σ of K^M_{0,∞}-type τ ∈ 𝔗_M. Some ψ = R(m_i)R(κ)φ (κ ∈ K^M_{0,∞}) has nonzero restriction to M_der(A_F). This restriction is a cusp form invariant under M_der(A_F^∞) ∩ m_i^{−1}K_M m_i, with K^{M_der}_{0,∞}-types in 𝔗_{M_der}, on which the Casimir of M_der acts by λ_M(γ_M^−(χ_{σ_∞})). So it suffices to apply [Don82, Theorem 9.1] with K_{M_der} replaced by K′ := ⋂_i (M_der(A_F^∞) ∩ m_i^{−1}K_M m_i).
issues.reason: Checked on the p. 26 image. The proof reduces Lemma 3.12 to the set 𝔆(M_der; K_{M_der}, 𝔗_{M_der}) with the specific level K_{M_der} := K_M ∩ M_der(A_F^∞), and gives no argument. The reduction needs, for every σ ∈ 𝔆(M, ω; K_M, 𝔗_M), some ς at that level whose Casimir eigenvalue is λ_M(γ_M^−(χ_{σ_∞})). The eigenvalue and type parts are routine: restriction to M_der(A_F) preserves cuspidality, and M_∞ = K^M_{0,∞}·Z_M(F_∞)·M_der,∞. The level part is not. A K_M-invariant φ ∈ σ has a K_{M_der}-invariant restriction to M_der(A_F), but that restriction can only be nonzero if φ is nonzero on the normal subgroup M(F)N, N := Z_M(A_F)M_der(A_F)K_M M_∞. This subgroup has finite but in general nontrivial index in M(A_F). For GL_2 ⊃ SL_2 the quotient is Cl_F/Cl_F^2. If φ lives on another coset M(F)N·m, one must restrict R(m)φ, which is invariant only under M_der(A_F^∞) ∩ m^{−1}K_M m. That is an M(A_F^∞)-conjugate of K_{M_der}, not in general an M_der(A_F^∞)-conjugate. For example, diag(ϖ_v, 1) swaps the two classes of hyperspecial subgroups of SL_2(F_v). Nothing in the paper, including the sketch in §1.3, addresses this. So the step is unjustified as written. The repair is standard: use finitely many conjugate levels, or one smaller level. Lemma 3.12 is true, and nothing downstream changes. The gap is minor but real.

issues.locator: §3.3, proof of Lemma 3.13, p. 26
issues.printed: The source invokes [Don82, Theorem 9.1] to claim that only finitely many members of 𝔆(M_der; K_{M_der}, 𝔗_{M_der}) have Casimir eigenvalue in λ_M(γ_M^−(χ_∞)). It concludes finiteness of the χ_∞-typical members of 𝔆(M, ω; K_M, 𝔗_M)^♡.
issues.correction: Add: (a) ω_σ := (central character of σ)|_{Z_M(A_F)^1Z(A_F)} is a character of the compact abelian Lie group Z_M(F)∖Z_M(A_F)^1/(K_M ∩ Z_M(A_F^∞)) (extended by ω on Z(A_F)), with differential γ_M^+(χ_{σ_∞}) (Remark 3.10). The first typicality condition puts this differential in the finite set γ_M^+(χ_∞), so ω_σ takes finitely many values, and up to ∼ so does the central character of σ. (b) By Donnelly (at a suitable level, cf. Lemma 3.12) only finitely many ς satisfy the Casimir condition, so γ_M^−(χ_{σ_∞}) takes finitely many values. Hence χ_{σ_∞} lies in a finite set modulo a*_{M,C}, and Harish-Chandra's finiteness theorem (fixed level K_M, types in 𝔗_M, central and infinitesimal character) leaves finitely many σ up to ∼.
issues.reason: The printed argument uses only the Casimir condition, together with an unexplained passage from M_der back to M. The first condition of Definition 3.11 is never mentioned, and without it the conclusion is false. If M is a torus, then M_der = 1 and λ_M ≡ 0, so the Casimir condition is vacuous. Example: G = GL_2 over a real quadratic field F, ω = 1, K = GL_2(Ô_F) (S = ∅), χ_∞ the infinitesimal character of the (irreducible) spherical unitary principal series 1 ⊞ 1 at both real places, and M = T the diagonal torus. By Lemma 2.18 that principal series contains a member of 𝔗, so 𝔗_T contains the trivial type. Then 𝔆(T, 1; K_T, 𝔗_T)^♡ contains the classes of (η, η^{−1}) for all unitary characters η of F^×∖A_F^× trivial on Ô_F^× and on the archimedean sign groups, taken modulo |·|^{it}. There are infinitely many of these, since F^×∖A_F^1/Ô_F^× has a circle as identity component. Only the γ_T^+ condition, which fixes the archimedean parameter of η on that circle up to finitely many choices, cuts this down to a finite set. Lemma 3.13 is true (the γ_M^+ half is the lattice argument the authors give in Lemma 3.14), but its proof is incomplete.

issues.locator: §3.4, after Theorem 3.19, p. 29
issues.printed: The source derives Theorem 1.3 by choosing χ = χ_{π^T} together with T = S, then invoking strong multiplicity one for G = Res_{F′/F} GL_n [PS79].
issues.correction: … and the classification of automorphic representations of Res_{F′/F}GL_n [JS81, Theorem 4.4] (strong multiplicity one for isobaric representations).
issues.reason: To deduce Theorem 1.3 when M ≠ G, one needs χ_{π^S} to occur in no cuspidal datum other than (M, σ). That is, two cuspidal data whose induced representations agree at almost all places must be conjugate. This is Jacquet–Shalika's theorem [JS81, Theorem 4.4], which the paper cites for exactly this purpose before Theorem 1.3 (p. 3). Piatetski-Shapiro's 'Multiplicity one theorems' [PS79] treats multiplicity one and strong multiplicity one for cuspidal representations only, which covers only M = G. This is a wrong reference; the right one is in the paper.

So no other cuspidal datum (M′, σ′), twisted by any s ∈ a*_{M′,C}, may have almost all local components equal to those of Ind(σ). This is the Jacquet–Shalika classification theorem [JS81, Theorem 4.4] for isobaric representations. It is needed even when M = G, to rule out M′ ≠ G. The paper itself names [JS81, Theorem 4.4] as the relevant input just before Theorem 1.3 (p. 3, main.tex l. 727). So this is a wrong reference with the right one given elsewhere in the paper. issues.locator: §4.2, proof of Proposition 4.7, p. 34
issues.printed: The source says [CZ21] proves the assertion for pure tensor Schwartz functions, but extends the proof to arbitrary Schwartz functions through [AG10, Corollary 2.6.3]: ⊗_{v|∞} S(G′(F_v)) is dense in S(G′_∞), and ⊗_{v|∞} S(G^V(F_v)) is dense in S(G^V_∞).
issues.correction: Supply the argument that the Chaudouard–Zydor identity holds for complete smooth transfers whose archimedean components lie in the completed space S(G′_∞) (resp. S(G^V_∞)), not only in ⊗_{v|∞}S(G′(F_v)). One route is to rerun CZ's density and transfer theorems with F_∞ = ∏_{v|∞}F_v treated as one place. Another is to keep all test functions in the algebraic tensor product, e.g. by choosing the archimedean multipliers in Propositions 4.8, 4.13 and Theorem 1.8 as products over the archimedean places. Otherwise cite a reference that does this.
issues.reason: Quotation checked on the p. 34 image. Definition 4.4 (p. 33) allows f′_□ ∈ S(G′(F_□)) = S(G′_∞) ⊗ (algebraic tensor product over the finite places of □). Here S(G′_∞) is the Schwartz space of ∏_{v|∞}G′(F_v), i.e. the completed tensor product, and matching is imposed on f′_□ and f^V_□ as wholes. In CZ (arXiv:1611.09656 v1, §16.1–16.2), Théorème 16.2.4.1 is stated for corresponding elements of I(η) = lim_S ⊗_{v∈S} I(η_v), with correspondence Orb_Ω(f) = Orb(f′) taken as a whole. Algebraic sums of pure tensors, including the Hecke-algebra sums, are therefore not the problem. What is not covered is a matching pair whose archimedean component lies in the completion S(G′_∞) but outside ⊗_{v|∞} S(G′(F_v)). That case only arises when F has at least two archimedean places, the typical case (F totally real, E CM). Density of the algebraic tensor product plus continuity of I_γ, J_δ would settle it only if every matching pair in the completion were a limit of matching pairs in the algebraic tensor product, with both sides converging simultaneously. Approximating f′ and f^V separately does not keep the matching condition. At nonsplit archimedean places, transfer is only known on a dense subspace ([Xue19]) and nothing about its continuity is known. The alternative is to rerun CZ's argument with F_∞ = ∏_{v|∞}F_v as a single 'place', which would need CZ's density theorem and the Fourier-transform compatibility of matching for S(G′_∞). This is plausible but is not checked; the paper gives one sentence. The general case is used. On p. 39 (Proposition 4.13) and p. 42 (Theorem 1.8), Proposition 4.7 is applied to μ′⋆f′ and μ^V⋆f^V. The archimedean part of a T-multiplier (Definition 3.5) is a general element of M^♯_{θ′}(h′*_C)^{W′}, where h′* = ⊕_{v|∞} h′_v*, so μ′⋆f′ generally lies outside ⊗_{v|∞}S(G′(F_v)). The two sides match only as wholes, through Proposition 4.8 and Lemma 4.9. So Theorem 4.14 and Theorems 1.8–1.10 rest on this unproved extension. Case for the defence: the extension is very plausible and the stated results are not in doubt. The same framework is used in later work (BPCZ, arXiv:2007.05601, §10.1, which takes transfers in the sense of BLZZ Definition 4.4 and cites [CZ] for them). A different write-up might avoid the issue by choosing archimedean multipliers as products over the archimedean places. For these reasons this is a gap in the proof, not an error in a stated result.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 37 image. Here G^V(F) = U(n) × U(n+1) is compact. Its irreducible representations have infinitesimal characters W^V·(λ+ρ), with λ dominant in X^{V*}. As a subset of h^{V*}_C these form the set of regular elements of the coset ρ + X^{V*}. That set is not closed under addition, does not contain 0 when ρ ∉ X^{V*}, and omits the walls. For example, the U(2) factor gives {(x, y) ∈ (½+ℤ)^2 : x ≠ y}. So it is not a lattice. Corollary 2.6 only uses that L ⊆ ∩_i λ_i^{-1}ℤ, and a function vanishing on L′∖A for a lattice L′ ⊇ L also vanishes on L∖A. It is therefore enough that the set is contained in a lattice, for instance ½X^{V*}. That lattice is W^V-stable, and base change maps it into the W′-stable lattice ½X′*. The intended argument goes through.

issues.reason: Proposition 4.13 is stated for the S fixed in §4.2 and an arbitrary π^V ∈ ℭ(G^V, 1). But χ_{(π^V)^T} is defined only when π^V_v has K_{0,v}-fixed vectors for every v ∉ T (§3.1, p. 22). If π^V_v has no K^V_v-fixed vector at some prime v ∉ S, then π^V(1_{K^V_v}) = 0 and J_{π^V}(f^V) = 0. In (b), f^V_{v_0} would have to be both 1_{K^V_{v_0}} and a supercuspidal matrix coefficient unless v_0 ∈ S; v_0 is split, so v_0 ∈ T only if v_0 ∈ S. The same condition is needed for f′_{v_0} to kill the non-cuspidal spectrum. The applications (Theorem 4.14, Theorem 1.8 (2) ⇒ (1)) never specify S. Defence: the missing step is a routine enlargement of S. The authors choose S to contain the ramification explicitly in the proof of Theorem 1.8 (1) ⇒ (2).

issues.citation: Beuzart-Plessis–Liu–Zhang–Zhu, "Isolation of cuspidal spectrum, with application to the Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture", Annals of Mathematics 194 (2021), no. 2
issues.reviewReason: I checked the quotations on the p. 38 image and in main.tex ll. 2532–2542. S, K′ and K^V are fixed in §4.2 (main.tex ll. 2339–2349): S is any finite set containing the primes ramified in E, K^V_v is relative hyperspecial for v ∉ S, and T = S ∪ T_0. Proposition 4.13 allows any π^V ∈ ℭ(G^V,1), and ℭ has no level condition (Definition 3.9, main.tex l. 1811). The proof uses S in three ways. (i) It sets χ^V = χ_{(π^V)^T}. By Definition 3.3 (p. 22), this is defined only when π^V_v has K_{0,v}-fixed vectors (here K^V_v) for every v ∉ T; the (G^V,T)-CAP hypothesis in (a) is only meaningful under the same condition. (ii) It takes f^V_v = 1_{K^V_v} at every prime v ∉ S, split or inert, and claims J_{π^V}(f^V) > 0. If π^V_v has no K^V_v-fixed vector for some v ∉ S, then π^V(f^V) = 0 and J_{π^V}(f^V) = 0. (iii) In case (b) it needs f^V_{v_0} and f′_{v_0} to be supercuspidal matrix coefficients, which clashes with f_{v_0} = 1_{K_{v_0}} unless v_0 ∈ S; a supercuspidal π^V_{v_0} has no hyperspecial fixed vectors anyway. The applications in the proof of Theorem 4.14 and in Theorem 1.8 (2)⇒(1) never choose S. The fix is a routine enlargement of S. π^V is K^V_v-spherical for almost all v, and V ∈ 𝔙_(S) is preserved. CAP is insensitive to finitely many primes, and K′, K^V can be extended by hyperspecials. So the stated result is unaffected. The step is omitted, not wrong, which makes this a minor gap. The authors do choose S to contain the ramification of Π explicitly in the proof of Theorem 1.8 (1)⇒(2).

issues.locator: §4.3, Theorem 4.14(4), p. 39 (proof p. 40)
issues.printed: For a hermitian V° over E, G° := U(V°), and irreducible admissible π = ⊗_vπ_v on G°(A_F), statement (4) claims that existing hermitian weak automorphic base change sends χ_{π_∞} to χ_{BC(π)_∞}. The source calls all statements trivial in rank 1. Its proof uses (3) to exclude (G°, T_0)-CAP for π, induction to exclude (G^V, T_0)-CAP for π^V, and Proposition 4.13(1) to conclude (4).
issues.correction: (4) If π is cuspidal automorphic and weak automorphic base change of π exists and is hermitian, then the base change of χ_{π_∞} is χ_{BC(π)_∞}.
issues.reason: As printed, (4) is about an arbitrary irreducible admissible π. Parts (1) and (2) say 'If π is cuspidal automorphic'; (3) and (4) do not. Weak base change (Definition 1.6) sees only almost all split finite places, while (4) concerns π_∞, so (4) is false in general. Counterexample in rank 1: G° = U(1), π = ⊗_{v≠v_1} 1 ⊗ ξ with ξ a character of U(1)(F_{v_1}) with nonzero differential at an archimedean place v_1 (e.g. z ↦ z^k, k ≠ 0, on U(1)(R) = S¹). Then π is irreducible admissible and BC(π) = 1 is hermitian (L(s, 1, As^−) = L(s, η_{E/F}) is regular at s = 1). But χ_{π_∞} is nonzero at v_1 and its base change is not χ_{1_∞} = 0, because the base-change map h^{V*}_C → h′*_C is injective on W-orbits. Modifying the archimedean component of any cuspidal π with hermitian base change gives such examples in every rank. This also contradicts 'trivial when the rank of V° is 1'. The proof of (4) uses π^V = π^V_n ⊠ π^V_{n+1} with π^V_{n+1} = π ∈ ℭ(G^V_{n+1}, 1) and a Burger–Sarnak partner, which needs π cuspidal automorphic. (3) is fine for arbitrary π: its proof uses only split components and (1) for the cuspidal σ•. Defence: the only use of (4), in Lemma 4.16, is for cuspidal automorphic π. With the hypothesis added, (4) holds (given E1's repair of Proposition 4.13(1) when BC(π) is not cuspidal). Nothing downstream is affected. The analogous omission in the bullet of Remark 1.7, which announces (1), is recorded as a misprint (E11). Here a reader cannot tell from the text that (4), unlike (3), is meant only for automorphic π, so 'error' seems apt.

issues.citation: Beuzart-Plessis–Liu–Zhang–Zhu, "Isolation of cuspidal spectrum, with application to the Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture", Annals of Mathematics 194 (2021), no. 2
issues.reviewReason: I checked this on the p. 39 image and in main.tex ll. 2578–2590. The theorem is set up for 'π … an irreducible admissible representation of G°(A_F)'. Parts (1) and (2) begin 'If π is cuspidal automorphic'; parts (3) and (4) do not. By Definition 1.6 (main.tex l. 773), weak automorphic base change depends only on π_v at almost all split primes and does not require π to be automorphic, while (4) is a statement about π_∞. So (4) is false as printed. Take π cuspidal with hermitian BC(π) and replace π_∞ by an irreducible admissible π′_∞ with a different infinitesimal character. The result π′ is irreducible admissible, BC(π′) = BC(π) is hermitian, and bc(χ_{π′_∞}) ≠ bc(χ_{π_∞}) = χ_{BC(π)_∞}. Here bc_∞ is injective on W-orbits: h^{V*} ⊆ h′* (main.tex l. 2352), and the W′-orbit to W^V-orbit splitting ℓ_V of Lemma 4.12 shows that W′λ ∩ h^{V*} = W^Vλ. I checked the first reading's rank-1 example. Take U(1), trivial components away from an archimedean v_1 and z ↦ z^k (k ≠ 0) at v_1. Then BC(π) = 1, which is hermitian by Definition 1.5 with n = 1, since L(s,1,As^−) = L(s,η_{E/F}) is regular at s = 1. But bc(χ_{π_∞}) = (k,−k) ≠ 0 = χ_{1_∞}. So 'trivial when the rank of V° is 1' also fails as printed. The proof of (4) uses π^V = π^V_n ⊠ π^V_{n+1}, with π^V_{n+1} coming from 'Since π is cuspidal automorphic', and Proposition 4.13, which needs π^V cuspidal. Part (3) is correct for arbitrary π, since its proof uses only split components and (1) for the cuspidal σ^•. So the omission in (4) cannot be read off from the statement, where the hypotheses are set item by item. This is why it is an error, and not a misprint like E11 (Remark 1.7, which only announces the correctly stated 4.14(1)). The only use of (4), in Lemma 4.16, is for a cuspidal automorphic π from [GRS11], so nothing downstream is affected. With the hypothesis added, (4) holds, using the repair in E1 when BC(π) is not cuspidal.

issues.locator: Appendix A, proof of Proposition A.1, before (A.4), p. 44
issues.printed: The source makes the definitions K^0_Z := K ∩ Z^0; K^0_der := K ∩ G^0_der; Z^0_der := Z^0 ∩ G_der = K^0_Z ∩ K^0_der. It calls Z^0_der finite and claims inclusion induces (K^0_Z × K^0_der)/Z^0_der ≅ K^0, as well as (A.4) (Z^0 × G^0_der)/Z^0_der ≅ G^0.
issues.correction: Z^0_der := Z^0 ∩ G^0_der = K^0_Z ∩ K^0_der.
issues.reason: Checked on the image; G_der := G_der(R) is the full group of real points, defined in the same paragraph. Z^0 ∩ G_der can be larger than Z^0 ∩ G^0_der. Example: G = (SO(2) × SO(3,1))/μ_2, with μ_2 generated by (−1, −1). The centre is the image of SO(2), so Z^0 ≅ SO(2), and G_der = SO(3,1). The element −1 of SO(3,1) equals the image of (−1, 1), so it lies in Z^0 ∩ G_der, but it reverses time orientation, so it is not in G^0_der = SO^+(3,1). Then Z^0 ∩ G_der = {±1}, while K^0_Z ∩ K^0_der ⊆ Z^0 ∩ G^0_der = {1}, so the printed equality fails. The quotient in (A.4) makes sense (the kernel of Z^0 × G^0_der → G^0 is the antidiagonal copy of Z^0 ∩ G^0_der) and is an isomorphism only with Z^0 ∩ G^0_der. The printed '= K^0_Z ∩ K^0_der' and the use in (A.4)–(A.5) show the intended group.

issues.citation: Beuzart-Plessis–Liu–Zhang–Zhu, "Isolation of cuspidal spectrum, with application to the Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture", Annals of Mathematics 194 (2021), no. 2
issues.reviewReason: I checked this on the p. 44 image and in main.tex l. 2777: '$Z^0_\der\coloneqq Z^0\cap G_\der=K^0_Z\cap K^0_\der$'. Here G_der := G_der(R), the full real points, which can be disconnected. I checked the first reading's example: G = (SO(2) × SO(3,1))/μ_2 with μ_2 = ⟨(−1,−1)⟩, a connected reductive group over R. The centre is (SO(2) × μ_2)/μ_2 ≅ SO(2), so Z = Z^0 ≅ S¹. The derived group SO(3,1) maps isomorphically into G, since (1 × SO(3,1)) ∩ μ_2 = 1, so G_der = SO(3,1) and G^0_der = SO^+(3,1). The class [(−1,1)] = [(1,−1)] lies in Z^0 ∩ G_der. As an element of SO(3,1) it is −1, which reverses time orientation and so is not in SO^+(3,1). Hence Z^0 ∩ G_der has order 2, while K^0_Z ∩ K^0_der ⊆ Z^0 ∩ G^0_der = {1}, so the printed equality fails. With Z^0 ∩ G^0_der, which is contained in K^0 because it is a finite central subgroup of G^0, the equality holds, and (A.4) holds: S¹ × SO^+(3,1) → G^0 is bijective. The printed group does not even embed in Z^0 × G^0_der. The printed '= K^0_Z ∩ K^0_der' and the use in (A.4)–(A.5) make the intended group clear, so this is a misprint.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 16, inequality (6), pp. 10–11 (arXiv v3)
issues.printed: The source treats even m and k with y = m/2 separately, writing f(m, k, y) = …. In every other case it claims σ fixes some element of {1, …, m}, labelled m, and uses f(m, k, y) = f(m − 1, k − 1, y) + f(m − 1, k, y) to invoke induction.
issues.correction: Treat the fixed-point-free case with k odd separately (then no k-subset is σ-invariant, so f = C(m, k) ≥ (4/5)C(m, k)), and run the induction over 1 ≤ k ≤ m/2 with (m, k) = (4, 2) excluded: at m = 2k, f(2k, k, y) = 2f(2k − 1, k − 1, y) by complementation when σ has a fixed point, and C(2k, k) − C(k, k/2) ≥ (4/5)C(2k, k) for even k ≥ 4 when it has none.
issues.reason: 'Otherwise' also covers m even, y = m/2, k odd, where σ has no fixed point. And for m = 2k + 1 the step invokes (6) at (m − 1, k) = (2k, k), outside the stated range 1 ≤ k < m/2; (6) fails at (4, 2, 2) (f = 4 < 4.8), though the step only reaches (2k, k) for k ≥ 3, where the complementation argument proves it. (6) itself was checked by enumeration for all m ≤ 14, and Theorem 16 is unaffected.

issues.locator: Corollary 6, p. 4, and its justification, p. 5 (arXiv v3)
issues.printed: Corollary 6 asserts N_n(G, H) = O(H^{3n/11 + 1.164}) for regular permutation G with |G| = n. The source derives it from Theorem 2 using a(G) = 3/8 + ε and ind(G) = (p−1)n/p, with p the least prime divisor of n.

Ellenberg–Venkatesh's 3/8 needs |G| > 4 ([18, Prop. 2.8]; Prop. 1.3 of the published version says n > 4). For n = 2, G = C_2 is regular and every irreducible monic quadratic has it, so N_2(C_2, H) ≍ H², above H^{1.709}.

issues.correction: Restrict to k≤8, or k=9 with G≠S_9. Retain the M_11 bound separately.
issues.reason: Take G=S_9. Fix one monic integral degree-11 polynomial h with Galois group M_11 (existence follows from König, arXiv:1503.06686v2, Lemma 2, followed by Hilbert specialization and an integral primitive element). There are ≫T^9 monic S_9 polynomials g of height≤T. issues.locator: Theorem 44, pp.34–35 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The source assumes a large congruence family F and primes p, q each a quadratic nonresidue modulo the other. It requires F to contain f, pf, qf, pqf and the associated hyperelliptic curves to admit Q_p and Q_q points. A further condition gives J split semistable reduction at p with toric dimension 1, and good reduction at q.
issues.correction: Add the conditions at 2 whenever 2 has a unique prime above it in Q(√p, √q). That happens exactly when one of p, q is ≡ 3 mod 4 and the other ≡ 5 mod 8, e.g. (p, q) = (5, 3). The condition needed is that J has good reduction at 2 and the four twists have Q_2-points. Alternatively, restrict to p ≡ q ≡ 1 mod 4, or to the prime ≡ 1 mod 4 being ≡ 1 mod 8.
issues.reason: The natural proof (none is written) applies Theorem A.3 with F = Q(√p, √q) and p_0 = p. Theorem A.3 requires good reduction and local points of all four twists at every prime with a unique prime above it in F. The primes p and q have this property, as the hypothesis makes each inert in the other's quadratic field. So does 2 when it ramifies in one quadratic subfield and is inert in another. For p = 5, q = 3: 2 is inert in Q(√5) and ramified in Q(√3). The hypotheses of Theorem 44 say nothing at 2.

issues.citation: Bhargava–Gross–Wang, "A positive proportion of locally soluble hyperelliptic curves over Q have no point over any odd degree extension", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2017)
issues.reviewReason: Confirmed. Theorem 44 on pp.34–35 imposes local conditions only at p and q, while the only proof available is Theorem A.3 (p.36), which requires C(K_p) ≠ ∅ and good reduction at every p ≠ p_0 with a unique prime above it in F, and, for the 2-Selmer conclusion, points on all four twists at every such p. For F = Q(√p, √q) the primes with a unique prime above them are p and q — which is what the non-residue hypothesis buys — and 2 exactly when 2 ramifies in one quadratic subfield and is inert in another, that is when one of p, q is ≡ 3 mod 4 and the other ≡ 5 mod 8; (p,q) = (5,3) satisfies both that and the non-residue hypothesis, since (5/3) = (3/5) = −1. No other prime can have a unique prime above it, because an unramified decomposition group in a Klein four extension is cyclic of order at most 2. Both stated alternatives also work: for p ≡ q ≡ 1 mod 4 the prime 2 is unramified in F and so has at least two primes above it, and if the prime that is ≡ 1 mod 4 is ≡ 1 mod 8 then 2 splits in that quadratic subfield and the decomposition group again has order at most 2. Theorem 44 carries no proof of its own in the paper, so the missing hypothesis is a gap in a stated result, as recorded.

issues.locator: §1, p.4 (arXiv v3)
issues.printed: The source characterizes strong divisibility p² of ∆(f) by either two distinct multiple roots of f modulo p in F̄_p or an F_p-root of multiplicity at least 3. It characterizes weak divisibility by p² | ∆(f) together with exactly one multiple root modulo p, lying in F_p and being a simple double root.
issues.correction: This holds for odd p. For p = 2, 4 always divides Δ(f) strongly when 2 | Δ(f), so W^{(2)}_m is empty for even m.
issues.reason: By Stickelberger's congruence, the discriminant of a monic integer polynomial is ≡ 0 or 1 mod 4, so 2 | Δ(f + 2g) implies 4 | Δ(f + 2g) for every g. For example f = x² + 1 ≡ (x + 1)² mod 2 has a single simple double root, yet Δ(x² + a_1x + a_2) = a_1² − 4a_2 ≡ 0 mod 4 whenever a_1 is even. A brute-force check over all f mod p confirms the criterion for p = 3 (n ≤ 5) and p = 5 (n ≤ 4), and finds failures at p = 2 for every n = 2, …, 5. The proofs only use the implication "two multiple roots or a triple root ⇒ strong", which holds at p = 2 as well (in Proposition 2.2), and the tail estimates concern large primes, so nothing else changes.

Example: x⁴ − 2 = (x² − √2)(x² + √2) over Q(√2) has Galois group D_4 of order 8 > 2·2! = 4. Every use of Proposition 4.3 (§§2.4, 3.4, (4)) needs only O(X^{n(n+1)/2−1/5}), which X^{10−8/3+ε} satisfies. This index correction alone is compatible with the error term needed downstream; it does not resolve the other proof gaps recorded here.

issues.citation: Bhargava–Shankar–Wang, "Squarefree values of polynomial discriminants I", Inventiones Mathematicae (2022)
issues.reviewReason: Independently checked against the arXiv-v3 locator and the explicit argument below. For f=x²+x+q, q>=2, the complex-embedding norm is ||u+vθ||²=u²-uv+qv²=(u-v/2)²+(q-1/4)v². The unique shortest vectors are ±1, and both θ and θ+1 are shortest extending vectors of squared length q. The bases (1,θ) and (1,θ+1) are not related by independent signs. More generally take odd 0<a_1<X/2 and X²/2<a_2<X². Their discriminants are negative, hence these quadratics are irreducible, and translating θ by (a_1-1)/2 gives x²+x+q with q>=2. There are X³/8+O(X²) such polynomials of height<X, out of 4X³+O(X²) total: a positive proportion (at least asymptotically 1/32) are not strongly quasi-reduced. A measure-zero argument in continuous Gram space cannot remove this arithmetic tie family. No readable version-of-record comparison was obtained; the finding is not asserted for the published text.

issues.locator: Lemma 7.2 and proof, pp.52–53; proof of Theorem 3, p.53; published 2025 version
issues.printed: Lemma 7.2 claims that isomorphic rank-n rings R_f and R_{f*} imply SL_2(Z)-equivalence of f(x, y) and f*(x, y). The proof invokes unique Minkowski-reduced bases to say that φ sends R_f's basis 1, ζ_1, …, ζ_{n−1} respectively to R_{f*}'s basis 1, ζ*_1, …, ζ*_{n−1}.
issues.correction: Interpret strong uniqueness up to independent vector signs; literal uniqueness is impossible for any nonzero lattice. For reduced representatives, comparing signed basis images gives f*(x,y)=ε s^n f(sx,y), ε,s∈{±1}. Thus retain an overall sign as well as x-reflection (at most four alternatives). Odd degree absorbs the overall sign through −I; the former universal ordinary-GL2 repair was not established in even degree. A separate uniform family/multiplicity argument is still needed for Theorem 3.
issues.reason: The proposed cubic f=x³−x²y+xy²+y³ is indeed strongly reduced under the UNWEIGHTED real-plus-one-complex-place norm specified on p.52. Its unique real root r lies in [−5437/10000,−5436/10000]. Exact rational interval arithmetic for the basis 1,θ,θ²−θ proves Gram–Schmidt squares λ_2>2.1087, λ_3>2.6073, while ||θ||²<2.1352 and ||1||²=2; strict diagonal-dominance inequalities prove that the unique successive extending vectors are ±1,±θ,±(θ²−θ) over all integers, not a finite search. Reflection f(−x,y) has the same lattice and signed basis. The cubic is irreducible (no rational root) with nonsquare discriminant −44, hence S_3. A rational projective stabilizer would centralize the full S_3 on its roots and is therefore trivial; a scalar stabilizer of the cubic has scalar 1. There is no determinant −1 stabilizer, so the two forms are not SL2(Z)-equivalent. The full certificate and sign derivation are in the review.

issues.printed: The source attributes the n = 2 case to classical sieve methods. It gives Theorems 1 and 2 the range n ≥ 2, while Theorem 5 and Corollary 6.27 have the range n ≥ 3.
issues.correction: Add the n = 2 tail estimate. For N ≠ 0, #{(a_0, a_1, a_2) ∈ [−X, X]³ : a_1² − 4a_0a_2 = N} ≪_ε X^{1+ε}, since for each a_1 with a_1² ≠ N the product a_0a_2 = (a_1² − N)/4 has ≪ X^ε factorizations, and at most two a_1 have a_1² = N. Summing over N = m²k with m > M and 0 < |k| ≪ X²/m² gives O_ε(X^{3+ε}/M), which is what Theorem 7.1 needs. Exclude Δ=0 from this weighted tail first; its box count is O(X²), by choosing a_0,a_1 and solving for a_2 when a_0≠0, and treating a_0=0 separately. issues.printed: The source sums over f ∈ W_m : H(f)<X, including cases with Δ(f)=0.

issues.locator: Bhatt arXiv:1608.08882v2 (11 Nov 2017), proof of Theorem 5.4, p. 10. Published full text not collated.
issues.printed: The proof reduces to a noetherian A0 that is regular, local, and of mixed characteristic (0, p). It selects g ∈ A0 coprime to p so that inverting pg makes A0 → B0 finite étale.
issues.correction: Before choosing g, replace B0 by B0/𝔮 for a prime 𝔮 of B0 with 𝔮 ∩ A0 = 0 (it exists since A0 → B0 is injective and integral); a splitting of A0 → B0/𝔮 composed with B0 → B0/𝔮 splits A0 → B0. issues.locator: Bhatt arXiv:1608.08882v2, proof of Theorem 5.4, p. 10 (first sentence, and 'as A0 is p-adically complete'); the proof of Theorem 6.1, p. 11, repeats the argument. Published full text not collated (G1).
issues.printed: The proof reduces to noetherian regular local A0 of mixed characteristic (0, p). It asserts Hom_{A0}(Q0, A0[1]) ≃ lim_m Hom_{A0}(Q0, A0/p^m[1]), citing p-adic completeness of A0.
issues.correction: Reduce also to a complete A0: completion is faithfully flat and preserves regularity, and the finite A0 → B0 has an A0-linear retraction iff it has one after completion, since Hom_{A0}(B0,A0) → A0 is surjective iff it is so after a faithfully flat base change. Complete before the domain reduction of E9. Alternatively keep A0 and use only injectivity: by Lemma 5.3 the target is the p-adic completion of the finite module Hom_{A0}(Q0,A0[1]), into which it injects by Krull's intersection theorem, and injectivity is all the argument uses.
issues.reason: The reduction does not make A0 complete; Proposition 5.2's 'we may assume that A0 is complete' is internal to its own proof. For A0 = Z_(p)[x]_(p,x), regular local of mixed characteristic but not p-adically complete, and B0 = A0 × A0/(x), one has Q0 ≅ A0/(x), Hom_{A0}(Q0,A0[1]) = Ext¹(A0/(x),A0) ≅ Z_(p), and Ext¹(A0/(x),A0/p^m) ≅ Z/p^m with limit Z_p, so the displayed map is Z_(p) → Z_p, injective but not an isomorphism. The order matters: for p ≡ 1 mod 4, Z_(p) ⊂ Z_(p)[i] is a finite domain extension whose completion Z_p[i] ≅ Z_p × Z_p is not a domain. In v1 the sentence was right, because A0 was p-adically formally smooth; v2's new reduction dropped completeness. The theorem is unaffected.

issues.locator: Lemma 2.56, second assertion, p.101 of the published version; the same wording is arXiv v1 Lemma 2.37 (p.20), v2 Lemma 2.50 (p.26) and v3 Lemma 2.56 (p.29)
issues.printed: The source fixes D and takes a semiample Q-Cartier Q-divisor A with A ∼_Q M + Λ. Here M is effective Cartier and its support contains no exceptional curve of Y → X; −δD ≤ Λ ≤ δD with δ > 0. For x ∈ F ∩ M having multiplicity k ∈ Z_{>0} in M, it claims ε_sa(A; x) tends to k as δ → 0.
issues.correction: Only a lower bound holds. For every rational γ with 0 < γ < k there is δ₀ > 0, depending only on f, D and γ, such that ε_sa(A; x) = ε(A; x) ≥ k − γ for all δ < δ₀ and all such A, M, Λ and x. Equivalently, liminf_{δ→0} ε_sa(A; x) ≥ k, uniformly. This is exactly what the printed proof establishes; there is no upper bound.
issues.reason: Counterexample with Λ = 0. Let k be a field of characteristic p > 0, X = A²_k, and f: Y → X the blow-up of the origin with exceptional curve E = F. Let M be the sum of the strict transforms of the two axes. Then M ∼ −2E, so M is effective, Cartier, globally generated over X (O_Y(−E) = m·O_Y) and has no exceptional component. Let x = E ∩ (strict transform of the y-axis), so mult_x M = 1 = k. Blow up x, with exceptional curve G and strict transform E′. Then E′² = −2, G² = −1, E′·G = 1 and π*M − tG ∼ −2E′ − (2+t)G, which has degree 2 − t on E′ and t on G. Hence ε(M; x) = 2. At t = 2 the ideal (x, y²) pulls back to O(−E′ − 2G) (charts x = ab, y = b, then a = c, b = cd, giving c²d, and a = ef, b = f, giving f²). So π*M − 2G ∼ −2E′ − 4G is globally generated and ε_sa(M; x) = 2. Taking A = M and Λ = 0 (any D), ε_sa(A; x) = 2 for every δ, not converging to k = 1. The proof only shows that π*A − (k − γ)E is nef. The consumers need only the lower bound: Proposition 8.15 (p.173) uses the first assertion ε_sa(M; x) ≥ 1, which is correct, and Claim 8.21 (p.178) needs ε_sa > 2 for k = 3. So the paper's results are unaffected. Checked on the page image and by exact arithmetic. Noted by the extraction (diagnostic A, gap-seshadri-limit); verified and proved in the corrected form by this continuation.

issues.locator: Proposition 6.28, p.154 of the published version (and arXiv v3 Proposition 6.28, p.71)
issues.printed: Proposition 6.28 assumes a Q-divisor Δ ≥ 0 on X with (X, Δ) globally +-regular, or completely purely globally +-regular over R, respectively. If Δ_Y ≥ 0 and K_Y + Δ_Y = f*(K_X + Δ), it claims (Y, Δ_Y) is globally +-regular in both respective cases.
issues.correction: The conclusion in the resp. case is "completely purely globally +-regular over R", with the pure boundary S_Y the strict transform of S and B_Y = Δ_Y − S_Y. This is what arXiv v2 (Proposition 6.28, p.64) prints, and arXiv v1 (Proposition 6.22, p.48) prints "purely ... purely".
issues.reason: The printed resp. conclusion is false. Take R = k[[t]] with k of characteristic p, X = Y = Spec R, f = id and Δ = S = V(t). Then (X, S) is purely globally +-regular. For a finite normal R′ ⊇ R with uniformizer s and ramification e, the map R → s^{1−e}R′ splits because R′ is R-free and 1 ∉ t·s^{1−e}R′ = sR′. But (X, S) is not globally +-regular: already for the identity cover, a splitting of O_X → O_X(S) = t^{−1}R would send 1 = t·t^{−1} into tR. The cited proof (Proposition 6.26, which applies because R is complete, together with Lemma 4.27 with B′ = B_Y) proves the pure conclusion. The consumer in Theorem 7.14 (p.165) uses the pure conclusion. In arXiv v3 the qualifier is visibly garbled as "( ly globally +-regular, resp.)", so the published wording is a typesetting slip. Checked on the page images of v3 p.71 and published p.154. Noted by the extraction (diagnostic B, gap-pure-birational); the version history was established by this continuation.

issues.locator: Theorem 1.19 of the introduction (= Theorem 7.3), and Remark 7.4(2) (arXiv v4, the version read)
issues.printed: The source takes K nonarchimedean, complete, and algebraically closed; a classical affinoid K-algebra A of dimension d; a prime ℓ; and an étale sheaf F on Spec(A) with ℓ-power torsion. Assuming A smooth or ℓ different from K's residue characteristic, it asserts H^i(Spec(A)_ét, F) = 0 for i > d.
issues.correction: The disjunct 'if A is smooth' is not proved in the paper at this generality. Theorem 7.3, which Theorem 1.19 is labelled as, proves the vanishing above degree d only for ℓ prime to the residue characteristic; the smooth case is claimed only in Remark 7.4(2), only for constant coefficients, and only as an adaptation: 'The algebraization method used to prove Lemma 7.8 below can be adapted to prove this statement when A is smooth (in the sense of rigid spaces) and F is constant, thanks to [Elkik, Theorem 7 and Remark 2 on page 587].' Either the introduction should restrict the smooth case to constant coefficients and point at Remark 7.4(2), or the adaptation should be written out for arbitrary ℓ-power torsion sheaves.
issues.reason: Theorem 7.3 as printed has two parts: (1) H^i = 0 for i > d + 1 for every torsion sheaf, and (2) H^i = 0 for i > d when F is ℓ-power torsion with ℓ prime to the residue characteristic. Neither mentions smoothness of A, and Remark 7.4 opens 'We would expect that part (2) of Theorem 7.3 holds for arbitrary torsion sheaves', listing the smooth constant-coefficient case as one of two special cases that are 'within reach'. issues.citation: Bhatt–Mathew, "The arc-topology", Duke Mathematical Journal (2021)
issues.reviewReason: Confirmed, and it is the one finding that reaches a stated result. Theorem 1.19 of the introduction (p. 7), labelled ‘Theorem 7.3’, reads ‘Fix a prime ℓ and let F be an ℓ-power torsion étale sheaf on Spec(A). If A is smooth or if ℓ is not the residue characteristic of K, then H^i(Spec(A)_ét, F) = 0 for i > d.’ Theorem 7.3 itself (p. 56) has no smoothness clause at all: its part (2) assumes ‘ℓ prime to the characteristic of the residue field of K’, and part (1) gives only i > d + 1 in general. What the paper says about the smooth case is in Remark 7.4, which opens ‘We would expect that part (2) of Theorem 7.3 holds for arbitrary torsion sheaves’ and lists two special cases ‘within reach’, the second being ‘The algebraization method used to prove Lemma 7.8 below can be adapted to prove this statement when A is smooth (in the sense of rigid spaces) and F is constant’. So the introduction asserts for arbitrary ℓ-power torsion sheaves what the body offers for constant sheaves only, and offers as an adaptation rather than a proof. The same remark closes by saying that over p-adic fields ‘the general case remains out of reach by our methods’, which is the opposite of a claim. The extraction’s two proposed remedies — restrict the introduction’s smooth disjunct to constant coefficients and point at Remark 7.4(2), or write the adaptation out — are both right, and it is careful to record this as a gap in what is claimed rather than as a false statement. Checked in arXiv v4, re-fetched by this review and hashed to 4cdf5593…6620, matching the recorded PDF hash byte for byte. The published Duke version remains unavailable: Unpaywall reports is_oa false for doi:10.1215/00127094-2020-0088 and lists no open location, which independently confirms the extraction’s account, and arXiv’s submission history ends at v4 (14 December 2020).

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 5.8, p. 24 (arXiv v2 §5.4)
issues.printed: The proof uses regular local R's UFD property to assert R[1/p]^× = π^Z ⊕ R^×. It takes (1 + πa) ⊗ b_1 ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ b_{i−1} with b_1, …, b_{i−1} ∈ R[1/p]^× and claims that unique factorization, together with the vanishing of the image of π ⊗ (−π), reduces matters to i = 2.
issues.correction: R[1/p]^× = R^× × t_1^Z × ⋯ × t_r^Z, where t_1, …, t_r are the local equations of the components of the special fibre through x (π = u·t_1⋯t_r with u ∈ R^×). The argument as written proves the claim only when r = 1, for example when X is smooth over A. For r ≥ 2, the symbols (1 + πa) ⊗ b_1 ⊗ ⋯ with several b_j among the t_k need a separate argument.
issues.reason: Take X = Spec Z_p[x, y]/(xy − p), regular and semistable over Z_p, at the point x = y = p = 0. Then x ∈ R[1/p]^× because xy = p, but x ∉ p^Z·R^×, since v_x(x) = 1 ≠ 0 = v_y(x). For i = 2, the same bilinearity trick applied to each t_k repairs the case: 1 + πa is a product of elements 1 + t_k w with w ∈ R^×, and {1 + t_k w, −t_k w} = 0. For i ≥ 3 and r ≥ 3, symbols such as (1 + πa) ⊗ t_1 ⊗ t_2 are not reduced to i = 2 by {π, −π} = 0, and the proof does not treat them.

issues.locator: Lemma 3.20, p. 255, and the last sentence of its proof, p. 256 (arXiv v3, lemma_Tate_perfectoid)
issues.printed: The source claims that perfectoid R^+, bounded in R, makes R perfectoid in Fontaine's sense. The proof concludes by claiming π = θ([π^{♭1/p^n}]) has the required property once n is sufficiently large.
issues.correction: Conversely, if R^+ is perfectoid and bounded in R and p is topologically nilpotent in R, then R is perfectoid in Fontaine's sense. The hypothesis holds, for example, in any Tate ring whose structure map from Q_p (or K) is continuous, such as a Banach Q_p-algebra; an abstract Q_p-algebra structure is not enough (Q_p((T)) with ring of definition Q_p[[T]]).
issues.reason: In a ring that is perfectoid in Fontaine's sense p is topologically nilpotent: p = π^p w with w ∈ R° gives p^n = π^{pn}w^n → 0. Counterexample to the printed converse: let A be the (p,T)-adic completion of O_C[T^{1/p^∞}], R = A[1/T] with the T-adic topology on A, and R^+ = A. Then R is a complete Tate ring and A is open and bounded. The Gauss valuations v_r(Σ c_e T^e) = min_e(v_p(c_e) + re), r > 0, are multiplicative, and if g/T^k is integral over A then v_r(g) ≥ rk for all r > 0, which forces c_e = 0 for e < k; so A is integrally closed in R, and the same argument gives R° = A. A is perfectoid: it is p-adically complete, p^{1/p} is a non-zero-divisor with (p^{1/p})^p = p, and Frobenius A/p^{1/p} → A/p is bijective (Lemma 3.10(ii)). But the continuous map A → O_C, Σ c_e T^e ↦ c_0, kills TA and sends p^n to p^n, so no power of p lies in TA and p is not topologically nilpotent in R. The proof fails at its last sentence: with π_0 = T one gets π ≈ T^{1/p^n}, and p/π^p has negative v_r for large r. With the added hypothesis the proof goes through: choose M with p^M ∈ π_0R^+; then (p/π^p)^{p^{n−1}} = p^{p^{n−1}}/(uπ_0) lies in R^+ once p^{n−1} ≥ M, so p/π^p ∈ R^+ because R^+ is integrally closed. The paragraph after the lemma concerns rings that are already Fontaine-perfectoid and topological K- and Q_p-algebras, and is unaffected.

Since [ζ_{p^r}] − 1 is a non-zero-divisor of W_r(O) (Proposition 3.17(i)), U_i is not invariant, so U_i ∉ 𝒲_r^0(D). The proof's own identification U_i^{1/p^s} ↦ [T_i^{1/p^{r+s}}] sends U_i^{p^r} to [T_i]. issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: Checked on the page images. v3 p. 5, the last sentence of Example 2.3, reads verbatim: 'Any valuation on Y that specializes from the generic point to (0,0) in the direction corresponding to the missing point of X does not admit a lift to X̃.' The ledger's 'printed' ('does not lift to X-tilde') is a paraphrase, and the revision rightly replaces it with the verbatim text. The mathematics: X̃ → Y is the blow-up, which is proper and surjective. So by the paragraph's own Example 2.3(ii) it is a v-cover, and the valuative criterion lifts every such valuation to X̃. The printed sentence is therefore false as written, and it would not show that X → Y fails to be a v-cover. With X it is correct. Take Spec V → Y with the generic point going into Y∖{0}, where X → Y is an isomorphism, and the closed point going to (0,0) along the removed direction x ∈ E. Its unique lift to X̃ (Y is separated, so the lift is unique) sends the closed point to x. Any lift to X after an extension V ⊂ W would give a lift to X̃ that misses x, contradicting uniqueness. So X → Y is surjective but not a v-cover, which is the point of the example. The meaning is clear from context and nothing depends on it, so this is a misprint that affects nothing. The revision's correction and reason are accurate.

issues.citation: Bhatt–Scholze, "Projectivity of the Witt vector affine Grassmannian", Inventiones Mathematicae (2017)
issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: The quotation checks out verbatim on v3 p. 5. The text is identical in v1 p. 5 and v2 p. 5. In the lemma, n is bound by the statement ('of inductive level ≤ n, for some n ≥ 0'). The proof then says it will show 'the more precise result that f : X → Y is of inductive level ≤ dim Y, by induction on dim Y'. It never sets n = dim Y, yet the induction step writes 'dim Z ≤ n − 1' and 'inductive level ≤ n − 1'. Here n can only mean dim Y. The ledger's current reason ('n denotes an eventual inductive-level bound, not the dimension parameter') is therefore wrong, because the level bound being proved is dim Y itself. The revision fixes this. With n read as dim Y, the step is sound. Take Y reduced and of finite type over Z. Generic flatness gives a dense open U over which f is flat. Raynaud–Gruson 5.2.2 gives a U-admissible blow-up X_0 → Y whose strict transform X' → X_0 is flat and proper, and surjective, because U is scheme-theoretically dense in X_0. Z = Y∖U is nowhere dense, so each irreducible component of Z is a proper closed subset of a component of Y, and dim Z ≤ dim Y − 1. X_0 → Y has closed image containing the dense set U, so it is surjective. Hence X_0 ×_Y Z → Z is proper, surjective and of finite presentation. By induction it has level ≤ dim Z. Levels are monotone: level ≤ m implies level ≤ m + 1, by the trivial factorization with Z = ∅. So the bound ≤ dim Y − 1 follows. Case for the defence: a reader can take 'the more precise result' as fixing n := dim Y, so this is the mildest kind of slip. Still, the symbol is formally unbound in the proof, and the recorded correction is the right one. It is a misprint that affects nothing.

issues.printed: The source assigns Perf^{[a,b]}(−) a presheaf on Perf with (b − a)-truncated values. Given X ∈ Perf and K, L ∈ Perf^{[a,b]}(X), it writes Map(K, L) := τ^{≤0}RHom(K, L) ≃ τ^{≤0}RΓ(X, K^∨ ⊗ L). It claims (b − a)-truncation of this space from K^∨ ⊗ L ∈ D_qc^{≥−b+a}(X).
issues.correction: Observation (1): 'Perf^{[a,b]}(−) gives a presheaf of (b−a+1)-truncated spaces on Perf (the core of Perf^{[a,b]}(X)): the mapping spaces Map(K,L) ≃ τ^{≤0}RΓ(X, K^∨ ⊗ L) are (b−a)-truncated, since K^∨ ⊗ L ∈ D_qc^{≥a−b}(X), and so the space of objects is (b−a+1)-truncated.' The rest of the proof is unchanged, since only finiteness of the bound is used.
issues.reason: The quotation is now exact. The mapping-space computation is right, but π_1 of the core at K is π_0 Aut(K), one degree higher. For a = b = 0 and X = Spec F_3, the core of Perf^{[0,0]} is the groupoid of finite-dimensional F_3-vector spaces, which has π_1 = F_3^× ≠ 0 at O_X, so it is not 0-truncated. The core reading is the paper's: 'spaces' in Theorem 11.2, and the next paragraph obtains full faithfulness of Perf(S) → lim Perf(X^•) separately by 'calculating Map(O_S, O_S) using this equivalence', which only makes sense if the equivalence is one of cores. The rest of the proof only needs some finite truncation bound (totalizations of truncated cosimplicial spaces commute with filtered colimits; truncated sheaves are hypercomplete), so it goes through with b − a + 1. issues.citation: Bhatt–Scholze, "Projectivity of the Witt vector affine Grassmannian", Inventiones Mathematicae (2017)
issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: Quotation checked on the v3 p. 47 image, observation (1) in the proof of Theorem 11.2(2). The mapping-space computation is correct. For K, L of Tor-amplitude in [a,b], K^∨ ⊗ L has amplitude in [a−b, b−a], so τ^{≤0}RΓ(X, K^∨ ⊗ L) is (b−a)-truncated. But the paper then calls Perf^{[a,b]}(−) 'a presheaf of (b−a)-truncated spaces'. Theorem 11.2 (p. 40) says to 'regard … Perf(−) … as presheaves of spaces', and the space of objects (the core) has π_{k+1} at K equal to π_k Aut(K) ⊂ π_k Map(K,K). That is one degree higher, so the core is only (b−a+1)-truncated. Counterexample: a = b = 0 and X = Spec F_3. The core of Perf^{[0,0]}(X) is the groupoid of finite-dimensional F_3-vector spaces, with π_1 = F_3^× ≠ 0 at O_X. So it is not 0-truncated. The core reading is confirmed a few lines later: full faithfulness of Perf(S) → lim Perf(X^•) is deduced separately, 'by … calculating Map(O_S,O_S) using this equivalence'. If 'truncated space' instead meant an ∞-category with (b−a)-truncated mapping spaces, the phrase would still be wrong, because Corollary 2.14 and Lemma 2.12 concern presheaves of n-truncated spaces. What the proof uses is only that the bound is finite: totalizations of cosimplicial n-truncated spaces commute with filtered colimits, and n-truncated sheaves are hypercomplete. Both hold with n = b−a+1. So a false intermediate claim sits inside the proof, and Theorem 11.2(2) is unaffected.

issues.locator: arXiv v1 p. 16 and arXiv v2 p. 16 (same text in both), proof of Lemma 4.6(ii); replaced in arXiv v3 pp. 16–17 by a reduction to blowups; acknowledged in v3 p. 4
issues.printed: The source justifies n using formal functions, citing [GD61, Corollaire 3.3.2] for H^i(X, I^m) ≃ I^{m−c} · H^i(X, I^c), with fixed c and conditions m ≫ 0, i ≥ 0. Because f is an isomorphism away from I, coherence allegedly makes a power of I annihilate higher cohomology. It concludes vanishing H^i(X, I^m) = 0 whenever i ≥ 1, m ≫ 0.
issues.correction: arXiv v1 p. 16 and v2 pp. 16–17: the vanishing H^i(X, I^k/I^{k+1}) = 0 for i > 0 and k ≫ 0 fails for a general proper f that is an isomorphism outside Z. v3 (pp. 16–17) first reduces, by Raynaud–Gruson, the 2-out-of-3 property and full faithfulness, to X = Bl_Z Y. There I·O_X is invertible and relatively ample, so Serre vanishing on E gives H^i(X, I^k/I^{k+1}) = 0 for i > 0 and k ≥ n. Then the Frobenius-twist and formal-existence argument proceeds as before.
issues.reason: The claimed vanishing is false for a general proper map that is an isomorphism outside Z. Example: take Y = Spec A with A = k[x,y,z]/(F), the cone over a smooth plane cubic C over a perfect field k of characteristic p (or its x-adic completion), I = (x), Z = V(x), and X → Y the blowup of the vertex. X is integral and x is a nonzerodivisor, so I^m O_X ≅ O_X. Hence H^1(X, I^m O_X) ≅ H^1(X, O_X) ≅ H^1(C, O_C) = k ≠ 0 for every m. Also H^1(X, I^m/I^{m+1}) ≅ H^1(E, O_E) ≠ 0, because x acts by 0 on H^1(X, O_X). The displayed isomorphism fails for the A-module structure: x^{m−c} kills H^1(X, I^c O_X). The graded module ⊕_m H^i(X, I^m O_X) is finitely generated only over the Rees algebra, and 'killed by a power of I' in H^i(X, I^c) does not propagate to H^i(X, I^m). The same text appears in v2, not only in 'the first version' as the v3 acknowledgement says. The statement of Lemma 4.6 survives, as the v3 proof shows. The original EGA III 3.3.2 passage was not re-read here.
issues.known: Known: arXivv3 acknowledgments p4 explain the earlier Lemma4.6 error and its origin in [GD61, Corollary3.3.2]; revised proof pp16–17. Both earlier and revised BS passages read.

issues.citation: Bhatt–Scholze, "Projectivity of the Witt vector affine Grassmannian", Inventiones Mathematicae (2017)
issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: The revision is right; one locator detail is refined. Quotation checked on the page images. In v1 the passage is all on p. 16. In v2 it runs across pp. 16–17: the words 'for i ≥ 1 and m ≫ 0. In particular …' open v2 p. 17. The wording is identical in v1 and v2. v3 pp. 16–17 replaces the passage by the Raynaud–Gruson reduction to a blowup. The v3 acknowledgement (p. 4) speaks only of 'the first version', but the flawed text is also in v2. Counterexample re-derived independently. Let k be a perfect field of characteristic p and C = V(F) ⊂ P^2 a smooth cubic. Let A = k[x,y,z]/(F) = ⊕_d H^0(C, O(d)), which holds because plane curves are projectively normal. Let f : X → Y = Spec A be the blowup of the vertex, so X = Spec_C ⊕_{d≥0} O_C(d), the total space of O_C(−1). Then f is proper and an isomorphism outside the vertex, which lies in V(x). So (f, Z = V(x), I = (x)) satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma 4.6. Since X → C is affine, H^1(X, O_X) = ⊕_{d≥0} H^1(C, O_C(d)) = H^1(C, O_C) = k, because deg O_C(d) = 3d > 0 = 2g − 2 for d ≥ 1. X is integral and f is birational, so x is a nonzerodivisor on O_X and I^m O_X = x^m O_X ≅ O_X. Hence H^1(X, I^m O_X) ≅ k for every m, contradicting the printed 'H^i(X, I^m) = 0 for i ≥ 1 and m ≫ 0'. The quantity the proof actually needs also fails. Multiplication by x^m gives I^m/I^{m+1} ≅ O_E with E = div(x). The sequence 0 → O_X → O_X → O_E → 0 (first map x), together with H^2(X, O_X) = 0, gives H^1(E, O_E) = coker(x on H^1(X, O_X)). Multiplication by x sends the degree-0 piece H^1(C, O_C) into H^1(C, O_C(1)) = 0, so H^1(X, I^m/I^{m+1}) ≅ k ≠ 0 for every m. No n as required exists, and the obstruction argument collapses. Everything survives the flat base change to the x-adic completion, which is the situation the proof reduces to: H^1 = k is killed by x, hence unchanged. Diagnosis: EGA III 3.3.1 gives finite generation of ⊕_m H^i(X, I^m O_X) over the Rees algebra ⊕ I^m, i.e. surjectivity of I^{m−c} ⊗ H^i(X, I^c O_X) → H^i(X, I^m O_X) for m ≥ c. That I^N kills H^i(X, I^c O_X) as an A-module does not make these Rees multiplication maps zero, because H^i(X, I^m O_X) → H^i(X, I^c O_X) need not be injective. Here x : H^1(X, O_X) → H^1(X, xO_X) is an isomorphism while its composite back to H^1(X, O_X) is 0. If I^{m−c}·H^i(X, I^c) is instead read as an A-submodule of H^i(X, I^c), the displayed isomorphism is itself false (k versus 0). Classification: a false assertion used in the proof, so an error affecting the proof. The statement of Lemma 4.6 is true, as the v3 proof shows (modulo the routine gap E29). The EGA passage itself was not re-read; the verdict does not depend on it.

issues.printed: In v2, the source claims one may take N = d := dim(R). Induction allegedly bounds the Tor-dimension of M/JM and Tor_1^R(R/J, M) by ≤ d − 1 because each is an R/J-module, using R/J ⊗^L_R R/J ≃ R/J from Lemma 5.10. It says the second assertion gives M Tor-dimension ≤ d.
issues.correction: (v2 Remark 5.33, as corrected in v3 Remark 11.33) For a perfectly finitely presented k-algebra R, where k is the perfection of a regular F_p-algebra of finite Krull dimension (e.g. a perfect field), and d = dim R, every R-module has Tor-dimension ≤ 2d. The bound d is false already for R = (k[x,y]/(xy))_perf. Gabber's bound 2d+1 for the global dimension (v3 footnote 24) is announced without proof.
issues.reason: The printed text is now quoted from the v2 images of pp. 26–27. The failing step is the one quoted: the induction bounds the Tor-dimension of M/JM and Tor_1^R(R/J, M) over R/J, but the step then uses that bound over R. Idempotence R/J ⊗^L_R R/J ≃ R/J does not justify this, because R/J has Tor-dimension 1 over R (J is flat). Passing to R costs one degree per step, which gives 2d (the v3 proof). For R = (k[x,y]/(xy))_perf, d = 1: Ann(x) = J_y := (y^b : b > 0) is flat, and 0 → J_y → R →x R → R/(x) → 0 gives Tor_2^R(R/(x), R/(y)) = Tor_1^R(R/J_y, R/(y)) = ker(J_y/yJ_y → R/yR), which contains the class of y ≠ 0. R/(x) and R/(y) are not perfect, so Lemma 3.16 does not apply. The corrected v3 argument (Noether normalization, almost étaleness, J = IR, Lazard, the two short exact sequences) was re-checked and is sound. v3 also changed Remark 11.34 so that it no longer calls [AH97, Theorem 3.1] a special case of Remark 11.33. issues.citation: Bhatt–Scholze, "Projectivity of the Witt vector affine Grassmannian", Inventiones Mathematicae (2017)
issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: Quotations checked on the v2 images of pp. 26–27 (Remark 5.33): 'We will show that, in fact, one can choose N = d := dim(R).' The text continues: 'By induction, both M/JM and Tor_1^R(R/J, M) have Tor-dimension ≤ d − 1 since they both admit R/J-module structures; here we use that R/J ⊗^L_R R/J ≃ R/J by Lemma 5.10' … 'the second one then implies that M has Tor-dimension ≤ d.' The failing step is the transfer from R/J to R. Idempotence gives Tor^R(N,Q) = Tor^{R/J}(N,Q) only for R/J-modules Q, but Tor-dimension over R must be tested against all R-modules. Since J is flat, R/J has Tor-dimension 1 over R, so passing from R/J to R costs one degree. I recomputed Gabber's counterexample. R = (k[x,y]/(xy))_perf has basis x^a (a ≥ 0) and y^b (b > 0) with a, b in Z[1/p], and d = 1. Here Ann(x) = J_y = (y^b : b > 0), which gives exact sequences 0 → J_y → R →(x) R → R/(x) → 0. Hence Tor_2^R(R/(x), R/(y)) = Tor_1^R(R/J_y, R/(y)) = ker(J_y/yJ_y → R/yR), and this kernel contains the nonzero class of y. So Tor-dimension ≥ 2 > d. R/(x) is not reduced, hence not perfect, so Lemma 3.16 does not apply. The v3 proof on p. 49 checks out step by step. By induction, M/JM and Tor_1 have Tor-dimension ≤ 2d−2 over R/J = (R_0/f)_perf. Flat R/J-modules have Tor-dimension ≤ 1 over R (flat J, then Lazard), so these are ≤ 2d−1 over R. Then JM ≤ 2d and M ≤ 2d. The bound 2d is sharp at d = 1. The authors corrected the remark in v3 (Remark 11.33, footnote 24, crediting Gabber). They also changed Remark 11.34, which in v2 called [AH97, Thm 3.1] 'a special case of Remark 5.33', to 'can be deduced from Lemma 3.16'. Gabber's global-dimension bound 2d+1 is explicitly not proved ('we do not prove that here'). The mistake is the false bound stated in v2, so the reach is a stated result, already corrected by the authors.
