issues.locator: Theorem 1.3, p. 3 (with its pointer '(see Theorem 6.8, Remark 6.12)')
issues.printed: Theorem 1.3 considers f : X → Y, the perfection of a proper surjection of F_p-schemes, with every geometric fibre connected. It claims that a vector bundle E on X has a necessarily unique descent to Y precisely when its restriction to each geometric fibre of f is trivial.
issues.correction: Theorem 1.3. Let f : X → Y be the perfection of a proper surjective map of F_p-schemes that is of finite presentation (for Y qcqs, equivalently: f is a proper surjective perfectly finitely presented map in Perf) … (see Theorem 6.13, Remark 6.12). Finite presentation is automatic when the unperfected base is locally noetherian.
issues.reason: The body proves the statement only as Theorem 6.13 (p. 25), for f proper surjective and perfectly finitely presented in Perf; 'proper' in Perf is defined only for pfp maps (Definition 3.14). The proof chooses 'a model f_0 : X_0 → Spec(V) of f, so f_0 is a finitely presented proper map', and the uniqueness uses Proposition 6.1, which is also stated for pfp maps. A proper map of F_p-schemes need only be of finite type, and over a non-noetherian base its perfection need not be pfp. Example: Y = Spec F_p[t_1,t_2,…]_perf and X ⊂ P^1_Y the closed subscheme t_i s_0 = 0 for all i. X → Y is proper and surjective, with geometric fibres a point or P^1, hence connected. But the locus of 1-dimensional fibres, V(t_1,t_2,…), is not constructible, so X_perf → Y is not pfp. For such maps the paper gives no argument. Case for the defence: this is the introduction's summary with an explicit pointer to §6. For noetherian Y, which covers all applications (e.g. Demazure resolutions over a field), proper maps are finitely presented and Theorem 6.13 applies. Non-qcqs Y reduces to qcqs Y by gluing and uniqueness. Remark 6.12 says the result is not used elsewhere. I have no counterexample to the literal statement; in the example above the conclusion does hold, via the section s_0 = 0. So this is unproved extra generality, not an error. The pointer to Theorem 6.8 is also slightly stale: Theorem 6.8 is the R f_*O_X = O_Y version (Remark 1.4), while the stated result is Theorem 6.13, which Remark 6.12 announces.

issues.citation: Bhatt–Scholze, "Projectivity of the Witt vector affine Grassmannian", Inventiones Mathematicae (2017)
issues.reviewReason: The quotations check out on the images: Theorem 1.3 (p. 3), Definition 3.14 (p. 13; 'proper' is defined only for perfectly finitely presented maps in Perf), Proposition 6.1 (p. 20; pfp assumed), Theorem 6.8 (p. 23; pfp with Rf_*O_X = O_Y), and Remark 6.12 with Theorem 6.13 (p. 25; 'proper surjective perfectly finitely presented map in Perf'). Theorem 1.3 assumes only that f is 'the perfection of a proper surjective map of F_p-schemes'. The paper sets no convention making 'proper' include finite presentation (compare §3, pp. 10–13). With the standard definition (finite type), the perfection need not be pfp. I re-derived the first reading's example. Let Y = Spec F_p[t_1,t_2,…]_perf and let X ⊂ P^1_Y be cut out by t_i s_0 = 0 for all i. Then X → Y is proper and surjective. Its fibres are P^1 over the single closed point V(t_1,t_2,…) and the reduced point s_0 = 0 elsewhere, so they are geometrically connected. If X_perf → Y were pfp, its locus of 1-dimensional fibres would be constructible (Chevalley applied to an fp model, which is a homeomorphic model). But V(t_1,t_2,…) has complement ∪D(t_i), which is not quasi-compact. So Theorem 6.13 does not apply to such maps, and the paper offers nothing else for them. The pfp hypothesis is used in the valuation-ring step: the limit argument that reduces to finite rank (Lemma 6.4, first paragraph), and the finitely presented model f_0 in the proof of Theorem 6.13. (The page prints 'Choose a model f_0 : X_0 → Spec(V) of f_0', which is itself a slip for 'of f'.) The gap is not a routine remark: over a valuation ring of infinite rank, finite-type proper models still need not be pfp. The same mismatch between the introduction and the body is in v1 and v2: Theorem 1.3 there reads 'proper map of F_p-schemes', while Theorems 6.7 and 7.7 there assume pfp in Perf. Case for the defence: Theorem 1.3 is an introductory summary that points to §6. When the unperfected base is locally noetherian, proper implies finite presentation and Theorem 6.13 applies. This covers every use in the paper, and Remark 6.12 says the result is not used elsewhere. Non-qcqs Y reduces to qcqs Y by gluing, using the uniqueness from Proposition 6.1. No counterexample to the literal statement is known; in the example above the conclusion holds via the section s_0 = 0. So this is unproved extra generality in a stated theorem (a gap), not a false statement (an error), and it reaches the stated result, not only a proof step. The pointer 'Theorem 6.8' names the older Rf_*O_X = O_Y version (Remark 1.4). The result as stated is Theorem 6.13, which Remark 6.12 introduces.

issues.locator: Proposition 3.12, p. 12, read with Remark 3.3, p. 10
issues.printed: Remark 3.3 replaces Perf by perfect qcqs schemes admitting covers by Spec(A) with |A| < κ, calls this version essentially small, and says the arguments remain valid. Proposition 3.12 asserts that any cofiltered system X_i in Perf with affine transition morphisms has X = lim X_i in Perf, equal to its limit in schemes.
issues.correction: In the truncated Perf, Proposition 3.12 should read: 'Let X_i be a cofiltered inverse system in Perf with affine transition maps, whose limit X in schemes lies in Perf. Then X is the limit in Perf, and the pullback functor 2-colim_i Perf^fp_{/X_i} → Perf^fp_{/X} is an equivalence.' The hypothesis X ∈ Perf holds in each of the following cases. (a) The index category has size < cf(κ). Then each affine piece of X has as ring a colimit of fewer than cf(κ) rings of size < κ, because every affine open of an object of the truncated Perf has ring of size < κ. (b) The index category has size < κ and the rings of the affine opens of the X_i are bounded by one λ < κ. (c) Every use in the paper, where X is given in advance. Taking κ regular instead would require an inaccessible cardinal. Choosing κ with cf(κ) > ω, for example κ = ℶ_{ω_1}, handles all countable systems.
issues.reason: Counterexample under the paper's own convention. Let |S| = κ. For finite F ⊂ S put X_F = Spec F_p[x_s^{1/p^∞} : s ∈ F]. These are countable perfect rings, so X_F ∈ Perf, and the X_F form a cofiltered system with affine transition maps. The scheme limit is Spec A with A = F_p[x_s^{1/p^∞} : s ∈ S], a perfect domain of cardinality κ. Take any nonempty open affine Spec A′ of it and some D(g) ⊂ Spec A′. The composite A → A′ → A_g is injective, so |A′| ≥ κ. Hence the limit is not 'covered by Spec(A) with |A| < κ', so it is not in the truncated Perf, and 'agrees with the limit taken in schemes' fails. Remark 3.3 allows singular κ (e.g. ℶ_ω). Then even an ℕ-indexed chain Spec F_p[x_s^{1/p^∞} : s ∈ S_n] with |S_n| = ℶ_n has a limit of cardinality κ. Case for the defence: in the untruncated (large) category the statement is true and the GD66 argument is fine. In every use in the paper the limit is already known to lie in Perf: the proof of Proposition 3.11 (iii)⇒(ii) (Z = Spec A ∈ Perf), the proof of Proposition 3.13 (Y ∈ Perf given), and Definition 11.1 on p. 40. So no later result depends on the false instance. It is a set-theoretic slip in the blanket claim of Remark 3.3, but Proposition 3.12 as literally stated in the truncated category is false.

issues.reviewReason: Both quotations checked on the page images: Remark 3.3 (p. 10) and Proposition 3.12 (p. 12, with footnote 7). The same wording is in v1 and v2, and no erratum is known. Remark 3.3 lets κ be any uncountable strong limit cardinal and says to 'replace Perf by' the truncated category, adding that 'all arguments will go through'. Proposition 3.12 puts no size bound on the index category. Counterexample: let |S| = κ and, for finite F ⊂ S, let X_F = Spec F_p[x_s^{1/p^∞} : s ∈ F]. These are countable and perfect, so they lie in Perf, and the transition maps are affine. The scheme limit is Spec A with A = F_p[x_s^{1/p^∞} : s ∈ S], a perfect domain with |A| = κ. Every nonempty open affine U ⊂ Spec A has |O(U)| ≥ κ, because restriction is injective on an integral scheme. So the limit is not in the truncated Perf. In fact the limit does not exist in the truncated Perf at all, which is stronger than the first reading's claim. Test it with Y = Spec K, K = the algebraic closure of F_p. A cone from Y is a ring map A → K, and these form a set of size |K^S| = 2^κ > κ. But any L in the truncated Perf is covered by finitely many Spec C_j with |C_j| < κ, so Hom(Spec K, L) ⊂ ∪_j Hom(C_j, K) has fewer than κ elements, since each |K|^{|C_j|} ≤ 2^{|C_j|+ℵ0} < κ because κ is a strong limit. So both 'exists in Perf' and 'agrees with the limit taken in schemes' fail, and the 2-colimit assertion then has no meaning. The singular case is also correct. κ = ℶ_ω is allowed, and an ℕ-indexed chain with |S_n| = ℶ_n already fails by the same argument. In ZFC, every uncountable strong limit cardinal is singular unless an inaccessible cardinal exists. Case for the defence: under Definition 3.2 (no size bound), Proposition 3.12 is true by the GD66 §8.8 argument. So the false assertion can equally be placed in Remark 3.3's blanket claim 'all arguments will go through'. Reach: I checked every use of Proposition 3.12 and of 'by approximation'. These are the proof of Proposition 3.13 (p. 13), Definition 11.1 (p. 40, which cites it as 'Lemma 3.12'), and the approximation steps on p. 17, in Lemma 6.9 (p. 24) and in Theorem 11.27 (p. 46). Each applies it to a limit that is already a given object of Perf. Proposition 3.11(iii) states Z ∈ Perf_{/Y} explicitly. Lemma 6.2 uses products, not Proposition 3.12. Proposition 9.2 gives L^+G an affine ring of size at most |k| + ℵ0. So no later result is affected. Still, the first sentence of Proposition 3.12, read in the paper's operative category, is false, so the entry is an error that affects a stated result.

issues.locator: arXiv v3 pp. 16–17, proof of Lemma 4.6(ii)
issues.printed: Using faithfully flat completion and Zariski descent, the proof reduces to Y = Spec(A), Z = Spec(A/I), with A noetherian and I-adically complete. It then replaces Z and E by Z′ and E′ to make X the blowup along Z. Affineness and deformation theory are invoked to make Vect(Y) → Vect(Z) bijective at the level of isomorphism classes; formal existence is invoked for Vect(X) ≃ lim Vect(mE).
issues.correction: After passing to Z′ (with X = Bl_{Z′} Y), re-apply the opening reduction to (Y, Z′). Base-change along the flat map A → Â, the I′-adic completion, and descend along the fpqc cover {Spec Â, Y − Z′} of Y, over whose second member f is an isomorphism. Blowing up commutes with flat base change, so X ×_Y Spec Â = Bl_{Z′Â}(Spec Â), and the rest of the proof applies verbatim. Equivalently, do the Zariski reduction, then the Raynaud–Gruson reduction and the passage to Z′, and complete along I′ only afterwards.
issues.reason: Completeness is imposed for the original ideal I of Z. Raynaud–Gruson gives Z′ only set-theoretically inside Z, possibly smaller, and the proof then renames Z′ as Z. A ring complete for I need not be complete for a larger ideal I′ ⊇ I (e.g. A = k[s][[t]], I = (t), I′ = (s, t)). Two later steps need completeness along the new ideal: lifting bundles from Z to Y, and Grothendieck's existence theorem Vect(X) ≃ lim Vect(mE). For X = Bl_{(s,t)} Spec k[s][[t]], lim_m Hom over mE computes sections over the (s,t)-adic completion k[[s,t]], not over A. So the step fails as written. Case for the defence: the completion reduction is a general 'we may assume' and can be re-applied at this point, since all constructions commute with flat base change. The repair is routine and Lemma 4.6 is unaffected.

issues.reviewReason: Quotations checked on v3 pp. 16–17. The proof first assumes that A is I-adically complete for the ideal I of Z. Raynaud–Gruson then gives a centre Z′ = V(I′) that 'does not meet Y − Z', so Z′ lies inside Z only set-theoretically. After thickening Z, I ⊆ I′, and the proof then replaces Z by Z′. Completeness transfers only when V(I′) = V(I). Otherwise it can fail. Take A = k[s][[t]], Z = V(t) and f = Bl_{(s,t)} Spec A, so that Z′ = V(s,t). A is t-adically complete but not (s,t)-adically complete. Two later steps then fail as written. (a) Formal existence: by the formal functions theorem, lim_m H^0(mE′, O) = Â_{(s,t)} = k[[s,t]], whereas H^0(X, O_X) = A. So Vect(X) → lim Vect(mE′) is not fully faithful, and compatible isomorphisms ψ_m do not algebraize. (b) 'Vect(Y) → Vect(Z) is bijective on isomorphism classes' needs a henselian pair (A, I′). For A = R[[t]] with R a Dedekind F_p-algebra with nontrivial Pic, Z = V(t) and Z′ = V(m, t), a nontrivial L ∈ Pic(A) = Pic(R) becomes trivial on Z′. Starting from the triple of G = L, the proof would lift ℱ_0|_{Z′} to G_0 = O_Y. But ψ_0 then cannot extend to X, since f_*O_X = O_Y forces f^*L ≇ O_X. So the argument really does need completeness along I′. Case for the defence: the opening reduction ('faithful flatness of completions and Zariski descent') works for any instance of the lemma, and the reductions to a blowup do not use completeness. So the fix is routine, and Lemma 4.6 is unaffected. Still, the written order of reductions leaves the step unjustified: a minor gap in the proof.

issues.locator: arXiv v3 p. 19, proof of Corollary 5.6
issues.printed: The source chooses a flat, p-adically complete Z_p-algebra A_0 deforming R_0 and φ : A_0 → A_0 lifting its Frobenius. It claims these choices exist because the obstructions belong to coherent cohomology in positive degrees on Spec(R_0), where they vanish.
issues.correction: Justify the lift as written only when Ω_{R_0/F_p} is finite projective, e.g. R_0 smooth, essentially of finite type, or F-finite. For general regular R_0, reduce to the smooth case: write R_0 = colim R_λ with R_λ smooth (Popescu), and use that both K(R) and K(W(R) on R) commute with this filtered colimit. For the latter, use the p-completion argument of the proof applied to colim W(R_{λ,perf}), together with TT90 Prop. 3.20.
issues.reason: The obstructions to lifting R_0 over Z/p^{n+1} and to lifting Frobenius lie in Ext^2_{R_0}(L_{R_0/F_p}, R_0) and Ext^1_{R_0}(L_{R_0/F_p}, Frob_*R_0). F_p → R_0 is a regular morphism, so by André L_{R_0/F_p} ≃ Ω_{R_0/F_p}[0] with Ω flat. These Ext groups are coherent cohomology groups of an affine scheme only when Ω is finitely generated, hence finite projective. For a general (non-F-finite) regular noetherian F_p-algebra, Ω_{R_0/F_p} is flat but not finitely generated, and its Ext groups need not vanish in positive degrees. The paper gives no other argument. Corollary 5.6 is stated for every regular F_p-algebra. Case for the defence: the proof is correct in the case used later, and the general statement can be recovered as above. So only the proof, not a result, is affected.

issues.reviewReason: Quotation checked on v3 p. 19; the text is identical in v1 (p. 19) and in v2 (p. 31, where the result is numbered Corollary 6.6). Corollary 5.6 is stated for the perfection of any regular (noetherian) F_p-algebra R_0. The obstruction to lifting a flat Z/p^n-deformation of R_0 to Z/p^{n+1} lies in Ext^2_{R_0}(L_{R_0/F_p}, R_0). The obstruction to lifting the Frobenius lift lies in Ext^1_{R_0}(L_{R_0/F_p}, Frob_*R_0). Since F_p is perfect, F_p → R_0 is a regular morphism. By Popescu and André, L_{R_0/F_p} ≃ Ω_{R_0/F_p}[0] with Ω flat. These Ext groups are positive-degree coherent (quasi-coherent) cohomology of the affine Spec R_0, and hence zero, when Ω is finite projective. That covers R_0 smooth, essentially of finite type, or F-finite, since then Ω_{R_0/F_p} = Ω_{R_0/R_0^p} is finite. For a non-F-finite regular R_0, Ω is flat but in general not finitely generated. The groups Ext^i(Ω, −) are then not coherent cohomology groups, and a flat non-projective module can have nonzero Ext^1. The paper's stated reason therefore does not apply, and it gives no other argument. The first reading's phrase 'need not vanish' is stronger than what is established: no explicit R_0 with a nonvanishing obstruction is known here. The gap is the missing justification. The corollary itself holds. By Popescu, R_0 = colim R_λ with R_λ smooth over F_p, so R = colim R_{λ,perf}. K(R) commutes with filtered colimits. Let B = colim W(R_{λ,perf}); it is p-torsion-free with p-completion W(R). By the paper's own p-completion argument, Perf(W(R) on R) ≃ Perf(B on V(p)) = colim Perf(W(R_{λ,perf}) on V(p)), and K-theory with supports commutes with this colimit (TT90 Prop. 3.20). The only use, Theorem 5.7 via de Jong's alterations, needs just smooth affine R_0. So only the proof is affected.

issues.reviewReason: The p. 23 image reads 'K ≃ 0 if and only if K ⊗^L_R k for any residue field k of R.' The right-hand side has no predicate: '≃ 0' is missing. The intended statement is true for unbounded K ∈ D(R) with R noetherian: residue fields detect vanishing (Neeman, 'The chromatic tower for D(R)', 1992, and Foxby for bounded complexes). It needs the residue fields κ(p) at all primes, not only at maximal ideals. For example, K = Q over R = Z has K ⊗^L F_p = 0 for every p, but K ⊗ κ((0)) ≠ 0. 'Residue field of R' normally means κ(p) for p ∈ Spec R, so the only slip is the missing '≃ 0'. The remark is not used anywhere. The same sentence is in v1 (Remark 6.6) and v2 (Remark 7.6).

issues.locator: arXiv v3, proof of Theorem 6.13, first paragraph, p. 25
issues.printed: The source claims that g_0 : X′_0 → Spec(V) is flat and proper, with geometrically connected fibres, because g_{0,*}O_{X′_0} is a finite torsionfree V-algebra having rank 1 and therefore equals V.
issues.correction: Replace X'_0 by (X'_0)_red, or take the closure with its reduced structure. It is still V-torsion-free, hence flat, and flat of finite type over the valuation ring V, hence finitely presented, and it has the same perfection over the generic fibre. Its generic fibre is reduced, proper and geometrically connected over the perfect field K, so H^0(X'_{0,η}, O) = K. Therefore g_{0*}O ⊂ K is a finite V-algebra, hence integral over V, and so equals V. The geometric connectedness of the fibres of g_0 and the rest of the argument are unchanged.
issues.reason: Proposition 3.13 allows any finitely presented model, and for a non-reduced one the rank claim is false. For f = id : Spec V → Spec V, the model X_0 = Spec V[ε]/(ε^2) has X′_0 = X_0 and g_{0*}O = V[ε]/(ε^2) of rank 2. Nothing in the paragraph forces reducedness. In defence, the next paragraph explicitly takes 'a proper flat and reduced model', and the needed conclusion survives passing to reductions. So this is a small, immediately repairable gap. New in v3.

issues.reviewReason: The quotation matches the p. 25 image. Proposition 3.13 (p. 12) calls *any* finitely presented f_0 with (f_0)_perf = f a model, so non-reduced models are allowed. Counterexample: take f = id : Spec V → Spec V. It is proper, surjective and perfectly finitely presented, and its geometric fibres are points. X_0 = Spec V[ε]/(ε²) is a model, because Frobenius kills ε and so the perfection of V[ε]/(ε²) is V. V[ε]/(ε²) is V-torsion-free, so the scheme-theoretic closure of the generic fibre is all of X_0. Then g_{0*}O = V[ε]/(ε²) is free of rank 2, not of rank 1, and it is not equal to V. Rank 1 needs H^0(X'_{0,η}, O) = K. That holds when X'_{0,η} is reduced: H^0 is then a finite reduced connected K-algebra, hence a field L, separable over K because K is perfect. The fibre X_η is geometrically connected, and X_η ⊗ K̄ surjects onto Spec(L ⊗_K K̄), which has [L:K] points, so L = K. It fails with nilpotents. The case for the defence: (a) if 'closure' means the reduced induced structure on the topological closure, then X'_0 is reduced and still V-flat. Indeed, if va = 0 with v ≠ 0, then V(a) is closed and contains the dense generic fibre, so a is nilpotent, hence 0. In that case the rank-1 claim holds. But then the next sentence, 'X'_0 → X_0 is an isomorphism away from the special fibre', holds only after perfection. So under either reading the paragraph ignores nilpotents. (b) The next paragraph explicitly takes 'a proper flat and reduced model of f', which shows that reducedness is a condition the authors add when they need it. (c) The repair is immediate, and what the proof really uses is only topological (geometric connectedness of the fibres of X'_0, and constancy of global functions on the perfect X'_s), which does not change on passing to the reduction. So this is a small, easily repaired gap in the proof, not an error in Theorem 6.13.

issues.locator: arXiv v3, proof of Lemma 7.7 ('only if' direction), p. 29
issues.printed: The source calls the kernel N projective. It claims that checking the dense characteristic 0 points in Spec(W(R)) gives rank n for N, hence makes it finite projective.
issues.correction: p^mQ = 0, so p^mM ⊂ N ⊂ M. For every prime q, N_q is free (Kaplansky), receives an injection from p^mM_q ≅ W(R)_q^n, and injects into M_q = W(R)_q^n, so its rank is exactly n. A projective module of constant finite rank n is finitely generated. To see this, write N ⊕ N' = F with F free. Lift a basis of N_q to x_1,…,x_n ∈ N. Some n×n minor d of their coordinates in F is nonzero in κ(q). Over W(R)_d, L = ⟨x_i⟩ is free and a direct summand of F_d, so N_d = L ⊕ (N_d ∩ ker π). The second summand is projective of rank 0 everywhere, hence 0. So N is locally free of rank n on a finite cover by D(d), hence finite projective.
issues.reason: At this point N is only known to be projective, not finitely generated. For such modules the rank need not be locally constant. For example, the projective ideal ⊕_i e_iR of R = ∏_N F_p has rank 1 on the dense set of principal ultrafilters and rank 0 elsewhere. So density of the characteristic-0 locus only bounds the rank on V(p) from above (by lower semicontinuity), and 'rank n ⇒ finite projective' needs its own argument. Finiteness of N matters: it is the finite presentation of Q, and Lemma 7.8's proof ('N is a finite projective W(R)-module (as Q is of projective dimension 1)') and Proposition 7.11 rely on it. The statement is true; the repair above fixes the proof. Present in v1 and v2.

issues.reviewReason: The quotation matches the p. 29 image. At this point N is only known to be projective. Projective modules that are not finitely generated can have a rank function that is not locally constant. In R = ∏_N F_p, the ideal I = ⊕ e_iR has rank 1 at the principal ultrafilters, which are dense in Spec R = βN, and rank 0 at every non-principal one, because there e_i = e_i² ∈ m_U I. For a projective N, {rank ≥ r} is open (lower semicontinuity: the minors in an ambient free module). So density of the characteristic-0 locus, where N[1/p] = M[1/p] has rank n, gives only rank ≤ n on V(p). The lower bound, and hence finiteness, needs a different input, and the step 'rank n, and thus finite projective' also needs proof when N is not finitely generated. The statement is true: Q is finitely generated and p-power torsion, so p^mQ = 0, and p^mM ⊂ N ⊂ M. p is a nonzerodivisor in W(R), so at each prime q the free module N_q (Kaplansky) contains an injective image of W(R)_q^n and injects into W(R)_q^n, so it has rank exactly n. Finiteness matters: it is equivalent to finite presentation of Q, and the proof of Lemma 7.8 ('N is a finite projective W(R)-module (as Q is of projective dimension 1)') and the Quot-scheme constructions in Proposition 7.11 use it. A caution on the first reading's correction: the n×n minor must be taken in a free module F of which N is a direct summand, not in M = W(R)^n. N is not a direct summand of M, and in M the relevant determinant can lie in q, for example when N = pM. Present in v1 (Lemma 7.7) and v2 (Lemma 8.7).

issues.locator: p. 35, proof of Theorem 8.3, second paragraph
issues.printed: The source invokes induction for ampleness of L|Gr≤μ when μ < λ. Citing [Kee99, Lemma 1.8], it deduces ampleness of L|∪μ<λGr≤μ and then semiampleness of L̃|ψ−1(∪μ<λGr≤μ).
issues.correction: Before invoking Keel, show that Y = ∪_{μ<λ}Gr_{≤μ} is the perfection of a proper algebraic space. Here Y is the image sheaf of ⊔_{μ<λ}Gr_{≤μ}, equivalently the closed complement of Gr_λ. The map ⊔Gr_{≤μ} → Y is a v-cover. Its equivalence relation is given by the closed intersections Gr_{≤μ} ×_{Gr_{≤λ}} Gr_{≤μ'}. So Y is the iterated pushout of the Gr_{≤μ} along these intersections. Affine-locally this pushout is A1 ×_{A12} A2, which is perfect and satisfies A1 ⊗_A A2 = A12. On finite-type models the pushout is a proper algebraic space by [Ar70, 6.1]. Next, every subvariety of Y lies in some Gr_{≤μ}, where L is ample, so E(L|_Y) = ∅. Keel's Lemma 1.8, applied inductively over the pieces, then makes L|_Y semiample. Its morphism contracts no curve, hence is finite, so L|_Y is ample. Alternatively, cite Zhu's Theorem 8.2, which makes Y a closed subspace of a proper perfect algebraic space; but then the proof is no longer independent of Zhu as claimed (p. 32).
issues.reason: Keel's Lemma 1.8 is a gluing statement for semiampleness on a proper algebraic space X = X_1 ∪ X_2 with E(L) ⊂ X_1. To obtain ampleness it has to be combined with E(L) = ∅ and Nakai. Applying it requires Y = ∪_{μ<λ} Gr_{≤μ} to be (the perfection of) a proper algebraic space. The induction hypothesis makes each Gr_{≤μ} a projective perfect scheme, but not their union inside the v-sheaf Gr_{≤λ}, whose representability is what is being proved. The union is not a single Gr_{≤μ} in general: for n = 3, λ = (4,2,0), both (3,3,0) and (4,1,1) are maximal below λ and are incomparable. Applying Keel's lemma on the scheme ψ^{-1}(Y) instead does not work, since the exceptional locus there does not lie in one piece. Defence: the missing step is standard and fillable (pinching of perfect schemes along closed subschemes, or gluing sections as above). Theorem 8.3 itself is not in doubt.

issues.reviewReason: Quotation checked on p. 35. Keel's Lemma 1.8 (Ann. Math. 149 (1999), p. 262; arXiv math/9901149) reads: 'Let X be an algebraic space, proper over a field of positive characteristic, and let L be a nef line bundle on X. Suppose X is union of closed subspaces X = X1 ∪ X2. If L|Xi is semi-ample … and E(L) ⊂ X1 then L is semi-ample.' Applying it to Y = ∪_{μ<λ} Gr_{≤μ} has two requirements. First, Y must be (the perfection of) a proper algebraic space. Second, ampleness needs an extra step: E(L|_Y) = ∅, so the semiample morphism contracts no curve and is finite. The paper states neither. The induction hypothesis makes each Gr_{≤μ} a projective perfect scheme. But Y is a sub-v-sheaf of Gr_{≤λ}, whose representability is exactly what is being proved, and Y is generally not a single Gr_{≤μ}. Under the dominance order of Definition 7.1 with n = 3 and λ = (4,2,0), both (4,1,1) and (3,3,0) are maximal below λ, and they are incomparable. Applying Keel's lemma on the scheme ψ^{-1}(Y) instead does not work. Its exceptional locus contains positive-dimensional ψ-fibres over every stratum, so it lies in no single piece. The step is standard and fillable, and Theorem 8.3 itself is not in doubt.

issues.locator: p. 37, the sentence introducing Kottwitz' map and Proposition 9.7 ([Zhu14, Proposition 1.21])
issues.printed: The source uses Kottwitz’ map κ : LG(k̄) → π1(G)_{Gal_K} for each algebraically closed k̄ containing k. Proposition 9.7, attributed to [Zhu14, Proposition 1.21], gives κ : π0(LG) ≅ π0(Gr_𝒢) ≅→ π1(G)_{Gal_K} as canonical bijections for parahoric 𝒢, with Gal_K denoting K’s absolute Galois group.
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis 'k algebraically closed' (as in [Zhu14, §1.5.2]); then Gal_K is the inertia group. For a general perfect k: Kottwitz's map is κ: LG(k̄) = G(W_{O_K}(k̄)[1/p]) → π1(G)_{I_K}, where I_K ⊂ Gal_K is the inertia subgroup. It induces Gal(k̄/k)-equivariant bijections π0(LG_{k̄}) ≅ π0(Gr_{𝒢,k̄}) ≅ π1(G)_{I_K}. The connected components over k are the Gal(k̄/k)-orbits on π1(G)_{I_K}.
issues.reason: §9 fixes only a perfect residue field k, but Zhu states Prop. 1.21 in a subsection (§1.5.2 of arXiv v1/v2, §1.4.2 of v3) that opens 'We assume that k is algebraically closed'. Kottwitz's map for the field W_{O_K}(k̄)[1/p] = K̆ lands in the inertia coinvariants π1(G)_{I_K}, not in π1(G)_{Gal_K}. Counterexample for finite k: let K'/K be unramified quadratic with residue field k', T = Res_{K'/K} G_m, and 𝒢 = Res_{O_K'/O_K} G_m its connected Néron model (parahoric). Then Gr_𝒢 = Res_{k'/k}(Z), whose geometric components form Z² with Frobenius swapping the factors, while π1(T)_{Gal_K} = Z²/(e1−e2) = Z. Neither the k-components (Frobenius orbits, e.g. {(0,0)} and {(1,−1),(−1,1)} both lying over 0) nor the geometric components (Z²) are in bijection with Z. Defence: for k algebraically closed, the case of Zhu's source, the statement is correct. The only later use, in the proof of Proposition 10.3 for SL_n where π1 = 0, is unaffected. The same text appears in v1 and v2.

issues.reviewReason: Quotation checked on p. 37. §9 (p. 36) fixes only a perfect residue field k, and Proposition 9.7 is stated in that generality with Gal_K 'the absolute Galois group of K'. The cited source is Zhu arXiv:1407.8519, Prop. 1.21. It sits in §1.5.2 of v1 (§1.4.2 of v3), which opens 'We assume that k is algebraically closed'. Zhu's target is π1(G)_{Gal(F̄/F)}, and under that assumption this Galois group is the inertia group. For k̄ ⊇ k algebraically closed, L̆ = W_{O_K}(k̄)[1/p] has absolute Galois group I_K. So Kottwitz's map G(L̆) → π1(G)_{I_K} lands in the inertia coinvariants, and the displayed κ to π1(G)_{Gal_K} is only its composite with a projection. Counterexample, checked independently. Let K'/K be unramified quadratic with residue field k'. Take T = Res_{K'/K}G_m and 𝒢 = Res_{O_{K'}/O_K}G_m, which is parahoric: it is the connected Néron model, with connected special fibre Res_{k'/k}G_m. Then W_{O_K}(R) ⊗_{O_K} O_{K'} = W_{O_{K'}}(R ⊗_k k'), so Gr_𝒢 = Res_{k'/k}(Z). Its geometric components are Z², with Frobenius swapping the two coordinates. Its k-components are the classes {(n,n)} and {(a,b),(b,a)} with a ≠ b. Meanwhile π1(T)_{Gal_K} = Z²/(e1−e2) ≅ Z, and κ is (a,b) ↦ a+b. This fails to be injective under either reading of π0: (0,0) and (1,−1) both map to 0. So no canonical bijection exists. The statement is correct when k is algebraically closed. It also holds whenever Frobenius acts trivially on π1(G)_{I_K}. The only later use is the proof of Proposition 10.3 (p. 38) for SL_n, where π1 = 0, so that proof is unaffected. The same text is in v1 (Prop. 9.7) and v2 (Prop. 10.7).

issues.locator: p. 37, Proposition 10.1 (second assertion) and its proof
issues.printed: The source defines a natural ample bundle on Gr_SLn by L = det̃_R(p^a W_OK(R)^n/M), for a ≪ 0. It claims that composing det̃_R : K(W(R) on R) → Pic^Z(R) with K(W_OK(R) on R) → K(W(R) on R) gives an analogous determinant map, and that the choice of a ≪ 0 does not affect L.
issues.correction: Add the argument. Choose a W(k)-basis of O_K, so that W_{O_K}(R)^n = W(R)^{ne}. On a bounded piece X ⊂ Gr_{SL_n} (proper by Corollary 9.6), for a ≪ 0 the map M ↦ p^{-a}M ⊂ W(R)^{ne} sends X into some Gr_{≤λ} for GL_{ne}. The cokernel is Q = W(R)^{ne}/p^{-a}M ≅ p^aW_{O_K}(R)^n/M, killed by a bounded power of p, of constant length −ane. This map is proper and injective on points, hence finite (pass to finite-type models). By definition of det̃ on K(W_{O_K}(R) on R), L|_X is the pullback of the Theorem 8.3 bundle det̃(Q). So L|_X is ample by Theorem 8.3.
issues.reason: The proof constructs L and notes independence of a, but never addresses the asserted ampleness. For ramified O_K the lattices are W_{O_K}(R)-lattices, and Theorem 8.3 (stated for W(R)-lattices in W(R)^n) does not apply without the restriction-of-scalars comparison. Proposition 10.5 (Serre vanishing, infinite-dimensionality) depends on this ampleness. The missing argument is short and the statement is true.

issues.locator: arXiv v3, proof of Proposition 11.6, p. 41
issues.printed: The source proposes induction via A_{i+1} = F_p ⊗^L_{A_i} F_p, claiming π_{i+1}(A_{i+1}) ≃ π_{i+1}(F_p ×_{A_i} F_p) ≃ π_i(A_i) as an identification compatible with Frobenius.
issues.correction: '…to get an isomorphism π_{i+1}(A_{i+1}) ≃ π_{i+1}(F_p ⊔^h_{A_i} F_p) ≃ π_i(A_i) (pushout of simplicial modules; equivalently, the suspension map π_i(A_i) → π_i(F_p ×^h_{A_{i+1}} F_p) ≅ π_{i+1}(A_{i+1}) induced by the pushout square), which sends the fundamental class to the fundamental class and is compatible with Frobenius.'
issues.reason: As printed, the middle term is wrong. For P = F_p ×^h_{A_i} F_p, the long exact sequence of the fibre square gives π_j(P) ≅ π_{j+1}(A_i) for j ≥ 1, so π_{i+1}(P) ≅ π_{i+2}(A_i), not π_i(A_i). For i = 1, A_1 = F_p ⊗^L_{F_p[x]} F_p has homotopy F_p in degrees 0 and 1 only, so the printed chain reads F_p ≃ 0 ≃ F_p. The intended step is the suspension of the fundamental class. It is natural in Frobenius (Frobenius is additive on F_p-algebras, so it commutes with boundary maps), and π_i(A_i) is spanned by the fundamental class (the higher symmetric powers are more highly connected). So the induction, and Proposition 11.6, stand. The same sentence is in v2 (Proposition 5.6, p. 18).

issues.reviewReason: Checked at 300 dpi on the v3 p. 41 image; the same sentence is in v2, Proposition 5.6, p. 18. The printed chain is 'π_{i+1}(A_{i+1}) ≃ π_{i+1}(F_p ×_{A_i} F_p) ≃ π_i(A_i)'. For the homotopy fibre product P = F_p ×^h_{A_i} F_p, the long exact sequence gives π_j(P) ≅ π_{j+1}(A_i) for j ≥ 1 (a loop, not a suspension). So π_{i+1}(P) ≅ π_{i+2}(A_i). For i = 1, A_1 = F_p ⊗^L_{F_p[x]} F_p = F_p ⊕ F_p[1], so the chain reads F_p ≃ 0 ≃ F_p. Nor can '×' be read as the derived fibre product of spectra, i.e. the tensor product: then the first ≃ would just restate the formula and the second would be left unargued. The intended identification is true. Since Sym preserves colimits, F_p[i+1] = 0 ⊔_{F_p[i]} 0 gives A_{i+1} = F_p ⊗^L_{A_i} F_p. The resulting square yields a suspension map π_i(A_i) → π_{i+1}(A_{i+1}) sending the fundamental class to the fundamental class. Both groups are F_p on that class, because LSym^n(F_p[i]) is more highly connected for n ≥ 2 (by décalage). The map commutes with Frobenius, since Frobenius is a natural additive endomorphism of simplicial commutative F_p-algebras, so the square is Frobenius-equivariant. The one-symbol slip (fibre product for pushout, or a misplaced index) has an evident intended meaning, and the induction and Proposition 11.6 stand.

issues.locator: arXiv v3, Remark 11.13 and footnote 22, p. 42
issues.printed: The source claims that, for noetherian schemes, pulling back through an h-cover detects perfection or pseudo-coherence. Footnote 22 directs the reader to the argument of Lemma 11.30 for detection of pseudo-coherence.
issues.correction: Replace footnote 22 by: 'For detection of pseudo-coherence along an h-cover f : X → S of noetherian schemes, reduce to f proper surjective. By Proposition 11.25, O_S is a retract of Tot_{≤n}((Rf_*O_X)^{⊗•+1}) for some n. Hence K is a retract of the finite limit Tot_{≤n}(Rf^{(•)}_*f^{(•)*}K), whose terms are pseudo-coherent by proper pushforward on the derived schemes X^{(•+1)/S}.' Alternatively, follow Lemma 11.30, but with f a blowup along I and Z = V(I^N) for N ≫ 0, so that the square O_Y → Rf_*O_X, O_Z → Rf_*O_E is a pullback.
issues.reason: Lemma 11.30's devissage rests on the pullback square O_Y → Rf_*O_X, O_Z → Rf_*O_E for abstract blowups. That square is available for perfect schemes but fails for noetherian ones: for the normalization of the cusp, k[t^2,t^3] ≠ k[t] ×_k k. So the referenced argument does not carry over as written. The claim itself is true by the argument above. Remark 11.13 is not used later. v2 footnote 8 (p. 20) has the same pointer.

issues.reviewReason: The gap is real, but the first reading's example needs fixing, and the reach should be 'the proof', not 'nothing'. Checked on the v3 p. 42 image: Remark 11.13 says that 'being perfect or pseudo-coherent can be detected after pullback along an h-cover for noetherian schemes', with footnote 22: 'one argues as in Lemma 11.30 below'. v2 footnote 8 (p. 20) points the same way, to Lemma 5.30. Lemma 11.30 (p. 48) is a devissage in Perf whose key input is the unproved 'pullback diagram' O_Y → Rf_*O_X over O_Z → Rf_*O_E. In Perf, that square follows from h-descent (Corollary 11.28). For noetherian schemes it fails for general choices of Z and E, so the argument does not carry over as written. The first reading's example, cusp normalization with reduced E, uses the reduced preimage. With the scheme-theoretic preimage, E = Spec k[t]/(t^2), the cusp square is a pullback: k[t] ×_{k[t]/(t^2)} k = k[t^2,t^3]. A correct example: Y = Spec k[t^2,t^5], X = Spec k[t], Z = V(t^2,t^5) and E = f^{-1}(Z) = Spec k[t]/(t^2). The maps to k[t]/(t^2) are jointly surjective, so the derived and classical pullbacks agree, and k[t] ×_{k[t]/(t^2)} k = k + t^2k[t] contains t^3 ∉ k[t^2,t^5]. The square can be restored, but only by an argument the pointer does not give: thicken Z (for f finite, until I^N O_X lies in the conductor), or refine f to a blowup along I and take Z = V(I^N), N ≫ 0, using Serre vanishing and Γ_* = Rees algebra in high degrees. The claim itself is true. The first reading's descendability argument works: reduce to f proper surjective (h-covers of noetherian schemes are refined by a Zariski cover of a proper surjection, and pseudo-coherence is Zariski-local). Proposition 11.25 then makes O_S a retract of a finite partial totalization Tot_{≤n}((Rf_*O_X)^{⊗•+1}), so K is a retract of a finite limit of the complexes Rf^{(i)}_*f^{(i)*}K. These are pseudo-coherent by proper pushforward on the noetherian derived schemes X^{(i+1)/S}. Since the offered justification fails as written but the claim stands (and Remark 11.13 is not used later), this is a gap in the proof sketch, reach 'the proof'. 'Nothing' would understate an inadequate justification.

issues.locator: arXiv v3, Remark 11.24, p. 45
issues.printed: The source attributes to Mathew descendability of a faithfully flat map A → B between discrete rings whenever B is countably generated over A. It says the necessity of countable generation is unknown.
issues.correction: 'Mathew shows that if A → B is a faithfully flat map of discrete rings, and B is countably presented as an A-algebra (more generally, has a presentation with at most ℵ_k generators and relations), then A → B is descendable [Mat14, Corollary 3.31] (Mathew's arXiv v2, Corollary 3.33). We do not know if the countability assumption is necessary.'
issues.reason: Mathew's proof applies Proposition 3.30 (π_*(A) countable) after descending A → B to a countable base, which needs countably many relations. Countably generated faithfully flat algebras need not be countably presented. Take A = ∏_{R} F_2, which is von Neumann regular, so every module is flat, and I = ⊕_{R} F_2, which is not countably generated. Then B = A × A/I = A[e] is faithfully flat and generated by one element, but setting x ↦ 0 maps the kernel of A[x] → B onto I, so B is not countably presented. (This B is trivially descendable, having a retraction; the point is that Mathew's result does not cover the hypothesis the paper attributes to him.) The claim is not used elsewhere; Lemma 11.23(2) needs only finitely presented fppf maps. v2 (Remark 5.24, p. 22) has the same wording.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on the v3 p. 45 image (Remark 11.24); v2 Remark 5.24, p. 22, has the same wording. Mathew never states the countably generated case. v1 (the cited version) has Corollary 3.31, 'π_0(B) is countably presented as a π_0(A)-algebra', and the text on its p. 25 also says 'faithfully flat and countably presented'. v2 has Corollary 3.33: at most ℵ_k generators and relations. His argument applies Proposition 3.30 (π_*(A) countable) after base change from a countable subring, and that base change needs countably many relations. The two hypotheses differ. I re-derived the first reading's example. A = ∏_ℝ F_2 is von Neumann regular, so every module is flat. I = ⊕_ℝ F_2 is not countably generated: countably many generators have countable total support. B = A × A/I ≅ A ⊕ A/I as an A-module, with A a direct summand, so B is faithfully flat. B is generated by e = (1,0), since (x, ȳ) = y + (x−y)e. The kernel of A[t] → B, t ↦ e, is {q : q(1) = 0, q(0) ∈ I}, and t ↦ 0 maps it onto I (take i(1−t)). So B is not countably presented. (This B is itself descendable, being split, so the example shows only that the citation does not cover the hypothesis.) Thus the remark asserts, as a known result, a statement that the cited source does not prove, and the paper gives no proof of its own. In the defence: over a noetherian A the two notions agree, since every ideal of A[x_1, x_2, …] is countably generated. Mathew's v2 also covers |A| ≤ ℵ_k. So the unsupported case concerns only very large non-noetherian rings. The remark is not used later; Lemma 11.23(2) needs only finitely presented fppf maps. The claim is unproved (not known to be false), so gap is the right kind, and its reach is the remark's stated claim.

issues.reason: In Higher Topos Theory (checked in arXiv math/0608040v4 and in the current version on Lurie's website, which agree here), Proposition 6.5.1.18 says a morphism is n-connective iff its diagonal is (n−1)-connective and it is an effective epimorphism. Proposition 6.5.1.19 says a morphism of X is n-connective iff the corresponding morphism of the slice X_{/X} is n-connective, which is the fact used, applied for all n. The printed book was not collated, but its numbering is expected to match arXiv v4. The other citation in the proof, Lemma 6.5.2.9 (truncated objects are hypercomplete), is correct. v2 (p. 28) has the same citation.

issues.locator: arXiv v3, proof of Proposition 11.41, p. 53
issues.printed: The source constructs Y′ = X ⊔_E Z by pushing out E ↪ X through E → Z. It claims the resulting square […] is Cartesian modulo universal homeomorphisms and describes the induced Y′ → Y as a finite universal homeomorphism.
issues.correction: Define Y′ := Spec_Y(f_*O_X ×_{f_*O_E} O_Z) = Spec B′, with B′ = H^0(X,O_X) ×_{H^0(E,O_E)} A/J (Y = Spec A, J the thickened ideal of Z, JO_X = O_X(−E)). Then: (i) B′ is finite over A; (ii) B′ → A/J is surjective with kernel K = H^0(X, JO_X) ⊆ √(JB′), because s^m ∈ H^0(X,J^mO_X) = image of J^m for m ≫ 0 (X = Bl_J Y); (iii) B′_j = A_j for j ∈ J. Hence Y′ → Y is a finite universal homeomorphism. KO_X = JO_X, so E = X ×_{Y′} Z. Y′ is the ringed-space pushout X ⊔_E Z, and the rest of the proof applies to X → Y′.
issues.reason: E → Z is proper but not finite (E is the exceptional divisor of a blowup), so Ferrand's pinching theorem does not give the pushout in schemes. The paper gives no argument that it exists, that it is finite and a universal homeomorphism over Y, or how the square relates to the cartesian square Lemma 11.45 requires. The rest of the argument is fine once the gap is filled as above. H^0 is left exact by construction and right exact since H^1(X, O_X(−E)) = 0; H^i(X,O_X) ≅ H^i(E,O_E) for i > 0; and Y′ and Z are affine. The same passage also uses Y affine (Serre vanishing, 'as Y is affine', Lemma 11.45) without stating the reduction, which is harmless because F is a Zariski sheaf. This argument is new in v3: v2 (Proposition 5.41, p. 29) used the pushout only for finite f, where it exists by pinching, and then argued with the formal functions theorem.

issues.citation: Bhatt–Scholze, "Projectivity of the Witt vector affine Grassmannian", Inventiones Mathematicae (2017)
issues.reviewReason: Checked on the v3 p. 53 image. After arranging that X is the blowup of Y along Z and thickening E and Z so that H^i(X, O_X(−E)) = 0 for i > 0, the proof says: 'Now set Y′ = X ⊔_E Z be the pushout of E ↪ X along E → Z … which is a Cartesian square up to universal homeomorphisms, and the induced map Y′ → Y is a finite universal homeomorphism.' Here E → Z is the exceptional divisor over the centre. It is proper but in general not finite, so Ferrand's pinching theorem (which requires E → Z finite) does not apply. The paper gives no argument that the pushout exists as a scheme, nor that it is finite and a universal homeomorphism over Y, and Lemma 11.45 needs these. The v2 proof (Proposition 5.41, p. 29) used the pushout only 'Assume first that f : X → Y is finite', where pinching applies, and otherwise used formal functions. So the unjustified step is new in v3. I checked the first reading's repair; it is correct. Take Y = Spec A (noetherian; the affine reduction is implicit, via Serre vanishing and 'as Y is affine', and harmless because 𝓕 is a Zariski sheaf), J the thickened ideal with JO_X = O_X(−E), and B′ = H^0(X,O_X) ×_{H^0(E,O_E)} A/J. B′ is a finite A-algebra, being a submodule of H^0(X,O_X) × A/J with f proper. B′ → A/J is onto, with kernel K = H^0(X, JO_X), and JB′ ⊆ K. For s ∈ K, s^m ∈ H^0(X, J^mO_X), which is the image of J^m for m ≫ 0, since X = Bl_J Y and Γ_* agrees with the Rees algebra in high degrees. Hence K ⊆ √(JB′). Over D(j) with j ∈ J, B′_j = H^0(f^{-1}D(j), O) = A_j. So Spec B′ → Y is finite, bijective and has trivial residue field extensions, hence is a universal homeomorphism. Moreover KO_X = JO_X, so the square is exactly Cartesian, stronger than the paper's 'up to universal homeomorphisms'. Localizing at b ∈ B′ shows Spec B′ is the ringed-space pushout. The rest then goes through as written: H^0 left exact by construction and right exact as H^1(X, O_X(−E)) = 0, H^i(X,O_X) ≅ H^i(E,O_E) for i > 0, and Y′ and Z affine. Proposition 11.41 stands, but the proof asserts a nontrivial construction without justification.

issues.locator: Construction 12.5, pp. 56–57
issues.printed: The source sets N(C)(S) = N({(X_T)_{T⊂S∖{s}}, X_{T⊔T′} ≅ X_T ⊗ X_{T′}}). This is described as the nerve of a groupoid consisting of X_T ∈ C indexed by T ⊂ S ∖ {s}. Its objects carry isomorphisms X_{T⊔T′} ≅ X_T ⊗ X_{T′}, required to be compatible, whenever T, T′ ⊂ S ∖ {s} are disjoint.
issues.correction: Add the nullary case: require an isomorphism X_∅ ≅ 1 such that X_{∅⊔T} ≅ X_∅⊗X_T ≅ 1⊗X_T is the unit constraint. Equivalently, index the family by nonempty T and set X_∅ = 1, as in the naive model of Remark 12.6, where an empty tensor product is 1. A property-only fix also works: require X_∅ to be isomorphic to 1. The groupoid of pairs (X_∅ ≅ 1, φ) satisfying the associativity condition is then contractible, and associativity for (∅,∅,T) forces unit compatibility. With either fix, N(C)([0]) ≃ * and N(C)([1]) ≃ N(C).
issues.reason: Take S∖{s} = ∅. The data are then an object X_∅ with an isomorphism X_∅ ≅ X_∅ ⊗ X_∅ (from T = T′ = ∅), and nothing forces X_∅ ≅ 1. Counterexample: let C be the discrete symmetric monoidal groupoid of the commutative monoid {1, e}, e² = e, with all constraints identities. Both (1, id) and (e, id) satisfy every associativity and commutativity compatibility. So N(C)([0]) has two points, and the Segal condition for n = 0 (X([0]) contractible, which the paper uses on p. 56) fails. Likewise N(C)([1]) = {(1,1), (1,e), (e,e)}, which is not ≃ C. An associativity or commutativity condition on the given isomorphisms cannot repair this: stating unit compatibility needs a map X_∅ → 1, which is extra data. Segal's original version avoids the problem, because there families are functors on subsets that take disjoint unions to sums, and that forces X_∅ to be initial ([Seg74, §2, p. 299]). The case for the defence: the authors explicitly leave the compatibility to the first reading, and they present §12 as conveying meaning, not proofs. In both cases the paper uses, the literal definition already gives the right answer. For Vect(R) under ⊕, X ≅ X ⊕ X forces X = 0, uniquely. For a Picard groupoid, X_∅ is invertible, hence ≅ 1, and the groupoid of pairs (X_∅, φ) is contractible (φ corresponds to u ∈ Aut(1), and v acts by u ↦ vu). So it is an incomplete definition with a standard fix, and no result is affected.

issues.citation: Bhatt–Scholze, "Projectivity of the Witt vector affine Grassmannian", Inventiones Mathematicae (2017)
issues.reviewReason: Quotation checked on the images of pp. 56-57. The data are objects X_T for all T ⊂ S∖{s}, including T = ∅, with isomorphisms X_{T⊔T'} ≅ X_T ⊗ X_{T'} for disjoint T, T'. Only the binary isomorphisms are listed. There is no nullary one (X_∅ ≅ empty tensor product = 1), and the first reading is told to spell out only the 'compatibility' of the listed isomorphisms (p. 57). I re-derived the counterexample. Take C discrete on the commutative monoid {1, e}, e² = e, with identity constraints; it is a symmetric monoidal groupoid, and every coherence diagram commutes because hom-sets have at most one element. For S∖{s} = ∅, both X_∅ = 1 and X_∅ = e carry the (identity) iso X_∅ ≅ X_∅⊗X_∅, and there is no isomorphism between them. So N(C)([0]) has two points. That violates the n = 0 case of Definition 12.4, which the paper uses on p. 56 ('X([0]) is weakly contractible'). For S∖{s} = {1}, the condition from T = ∅, T' = {1} is X_1 = X_∅·X_1, which leaves exactly (1,1), (1,e), (e,e). So π_0 N(C)([1]) has 3 elements, not C/≃ as the proof of Prop. 12.15 asserts. A more natural example is one the paper itself names: Vect(R) under ⊗ (Example 12.2(i), second paragraph). There X_∅ = 0 (with 0⊗0 = 0, all maps unique) is a second, non-unit solution alongside X_∅ = R. No associativity or commutativity condition on the binary isomorphisms rules out such idempotents: in the discrete example, every such condition holds automatically. So spelling out 'compatibility' cannot repair the definition; a nullary structure (or the property X_∅ ≅ 1) must be added. Segal's formulation [Seg74, §2, pp. 298-299], which uses functors P(S) → C taking disjoint unions to sums, and his Definition 2.1(i), requiring C(0) ≃ point, do not have this problem. For the defence: §12 is an expository appendix ('we only try to convey the meaning', p. 56), and the construction is used only for C = Vect(A) under ⊕ (Def. 12.16, Cor. 12.17, Prop. 12.18, Prop. 5.3) and for Picard groupoids such as Pic^Z. In both cases the literal definition already gives the right answer. For finite projective modules, X ≅ X⊕X forces rank 0, so X_∅ = 0 uniquely. For a Picard groupoid, X_∅ ≅ X_∅⊗X_∅ with X_∅ invertible gives X_∅ ≅ 1. I checked the claim's contractibility computation: writing φ = λ⁻¹∘u with u ∈ Aut(1), an automorphism v acts by u ↦ vu, freely and transitively. The associativity condition for the triple (∅,∅,T) then forces the isomorphisms X_T ≅ X_∅⊗X_T to be the unitor twisted by the same u, so no spurious data remain. It is an incomplete definition with a standard fix, not a false stated result, and nothing downstream is affected. The classification and reach in the claim are right.

issues.printed: Corollary 15.4 claims that a bounded prism (A, I) and smooth formal A/I-scheme X admit a canonical E_∞-algebra isomorphism in D(X_ét, A/I): ∆_{X/A} ⊗̂^L_{A,φ} A/I ≅ Ω^*_{R/(A/I)}.

issues.reason: The statement quantifies over a smooth formal A/I-scheme X and produces an isomorphism of algebras in D(X_ét, A/I); no ring R is introduced anywhere in the statement or in the two-line proof. Theorem 6.4 on p. 53, of which Corollary 15.4 is the version without the technical hypothesis that W(A/I) be p-torsionfree, states the same isomorphism correctly as ∆_{X/A} ⊗̂^L_{A,φ} A/I ≅ Ω^*_{X/(A/I)}, and Theorem 1.8 (3) on p. 4 states it as RΓ_dR(X/(A/I)) ≅ RΓ_∆(X/A) ⊗̂^L_{A,φ_A} A/I. The likely origin is that the proof of Theorem 6.4 reduces to the affine case R.

issues.printed: The source assumes an oriented prism (A,(d)) whose Frobenius on A/p is flat and whose A/(d) has no p-torsion. It claims the universal oriented prism of Example 3.4 meets these assumptions.
issues.correction: Weaken the hypothesis to d-complete flatness of the Frobenius on A/p, which is what Example 3.4 proves and what the construction uses.
issues.reason: Example 3.4 records only that 'the Frobenius map φ: A/p → A/p is d-completely flat'. For the universal oriented prism A/p is a d-adic completion of a polynomial ring over F_p in infinitely many variables, which is not noetherian, and flatness of its Frobenius is not proved. The construction uses only the flatness of A/(p,d) → A/(p,d^p), x ↦ x^p, which the checker verified makes the target free.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 1011 image and against §1.1. Type (C) needs only F = F0 and B ⊗_{F,τ} R ≅ M_n(R) with the transpose involution (p. 979), so an indefinite quaternion division algebra over Q with p ∤ disc(B) satisfies Hypothesis 1.1.1 and gives compact Shimura curves. Type (A) with d = 2 and signatures (1, 1) and (0, 2) above the two primes of F0 over a split p is allowed by Lemma 1.1.4 and gives compact unitary curves; definite signatures give zero-dimensional varieties, where 'donc a le demi-plan de Poincaré' is itself false. [Col96] and [Kas06] treat only modular curves, and [Joh13], cited in the introduction, gives for quaternionic curves over Q only the classicality of the Hecke eigenvalues (Theorem 33(b)), so it does not close the gap. The repair holds, and the correction is amended to cover the zero-dimensional cases, which are proper too. Gap, affects the proof.

issues.locator: §4.5, pp. 1005–1006, and the proof of Proposition 4.5.8, p. 1009 (published version)
issues.printed: At p. 1005 the source fixes an integer i between 1 and h, choosing an interval I_j in [0, d_ja_j] for each j ≠ i. At p. 1006 it says f is defined on δ_i^{−1}([d_ia_i − 1 + β_0, d_ia_i]) ∩ W_0 and bounded there by M because that space is quasi-compact. At p. 1009 it claims extension of f to δ^{−1}([0, d_1a_1] × ]d_2a_2 − 1, d_2a_2] × ⋯ × ]d_ha_h − 1, d_ha_h]).
issues.correction: Run §4.5 only for closed intervals I_j; then U_γ and δ_i^{−1}([d_ia_i − 1 + β_0, d_ia_i]) ∩ W_0 are quasi-compact and f is bounded there. In the proof of Proposition 4.5.8, extend f over each box whose sides are [d_ja_j − 1 + η, d_ja_j] for j > i, for every rational η > 0, and glue: at each point both extensions are limits of the Kassaei series computed from f on the U_i^N-images of that point, so they agree on overlaps, and these boxes form an admissible covering of the box with half-open sides, since each δ_j is −log_p of the absolute value of a section (item 11).
issues.reason: With I_j = ]d_ja_j − 1, d_ja_j] for some j, as in every step of the proof of Proposition 4.5.8 but the last, δ_i^{−1}([d_ia_i − 1 + β_0, d_ia_i]) ∩ W_0 is the increasing union of the quasi-compact opens where δ_j ≥ d_ja_j − 1 + η, and is not quasi-compact. So f, known only on W, need not be bounded there, and M need not exist. Likewise U_γ is then not quasi-compact, which Definition 4.3.2 (good sequences of a quasi-compact open) and Proposition 4.1.2 need. The repair is routine, but the paper does not state it.

issues.locator: §1.3, p. 984 (published version, Annals 183 (2016), exact PDF in sourceVersions)
issues.printed: The source asserts formal étaleness for the morphism P without restricting the test bases to those on which p is nilpotent.
issues.correction: Restrict formal étaleness to p-locally-nilpotent test schemes; equivalently use the p-adic formal completions with fixed height/dimension/signature components. Keep the unrestricted algebraic morphism and Iwahori fibre product.
issues.reason: Katz Theorem 1.2.1 assumes p nilpotent. Over algebraically closed K of characteristic zero the étale p-divisible group lifts uniquely across K[ε]/ε², while the Legendre elliptic curve t=3+ε has nonzero j-derivative 31360/27 and a nontrivial deformation. Thus unrestricted P is not formally unramified. The restricted deformation assertion suffices for the formal use.

issues.locator: Proposition 17, p.12, under the §3 setup of a pure m-dimensional analytic set (published version)
issues.printed: The source asserts the existence of a ball B′⊂B avoiding S¹·X, with α:=2n−2m−1.
issues.correction: Require m<n for this complementary-ball assertion. Treat m=n separately when proving Corollary 18. Use 1+vol(X) in the quantitative bound unless a positive volume lower bound is assumed.
issues.reason: The setup allows X=B with m=n. Then S¹·X=B, so no positive-radius ball B′⊂B is disjoint. The comparison of packing exponents in the proof also requires 2n>2m+1. The extraction recorded that it 'could not be consulted'; that is not so, and every finding has now been re-checked against the published text. Confirmed, and present in print. Lemma 8.15's hypothesis names M and N without introducing them, while its proof begins 'We therefore need show that for each proper standard parabolic P = M N of G' — which I located in the published text — and Lemma 8.16 supplies the vanishing for every proper P. So the statement must quantify over all proper standard parabolics, as the correction says; as printed the hypothesis concerns one unspecified parabolic and the conclusion does not follow. This is the only one of the sixteen the extraction classes as affecting the proof, and that is the right classification.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 8.16, p. 44 (arXiv v2); published Acta Math. 223 (2019), p. 65 (located by review REV-PAPER-BOCKLE-HARRIS-KHARE-ETAL-19)
issues.printed: For a standard parabolic P = MN of G, the source defines I_P by collecting the irreducible constituents of A_0(N(A_K)M(K)\G(A_K))_χ that have nonzero U-invariants, with χ ranging over X_P.
issues.correction: irreducible constituents of A_0(M(K)\M(A_K))_χ, i.e. cuspidal automorphic representations of M(A_K).
issues.reason: Proposition 8.12, which this paragraph invokes ("We are now in the situation of Proposition 8.12"), requires I_P to consist of irreducible admissible C[M(A_K)]-modules π_i with (i^G_Pπ_i)^U ≠ 0; the next sentence induces them, i^{G(A_K)}_{P(A_K)}(π ⊗ ψ) for π ∈ I_P, which is meaningless for constituents of a space of functions on G(A_K). A_0(N(A_K)M(K)\G(A_K)) is a G(A_K)-module, and by [MW95, I.2.17] it is already the induction of A_0(M(K)\M(A_K)).

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 5.19, p. 23 (arXiv v2); published Acta Math. 223 (2019), p. 34 (located by review REV-PAPER-BOCKLE-HARRIS-KHARE-ETAL-19)
issues.printed: The source derives h^1(Γ_{K,S∪Q}, ĝ_k) = r#Q = h^1(Γ_{K,S∪Q}, ĝ_k) + (r − 1)#Q and says this proves the proposition's third assertion.
issues.correction: the second occurrence should be h^1(Γ_{K,S}, ĝ_k).
issues.reason: As printed the identity forces (r − 1)#Q = 0, which is false for r > 1. The intended chain uses the equalities just established, h^1(Γ_{K,S}, ĝ_k) = h^1(Γ_{K,S}, ĝ^∨_k(1)) = #Q, and it is what produces the generator count g = h^1(Γ_{K,S}, ĝ_k) + (r − 1)#Q of part (iii) — the number that makes dim R_∞ = dim S_∞ in the patching argument.

issues.locator: §§5–6, pp. 21, 25, 26, 32 (arXiv v2): four hat- and index-slips; published Acta Math. 223 (2019), p. 31 (located by review REV-PAPER-BOCKLE-HARRIS-KHARE-ETAL-19)
issues.printed: On p. 21 the source reuses the argument for G = SL_n from Theorem 5.13. On p. 25 it takes W as G's Weyl group and Λ = ZΦ(H,T) ⊂ X^*(T). On p. 26 it calls j_0 : Ĝ_{Q̄_λ} ≅ G_{λ_0} tautological. On p. 32 it conjugates ρ_{U_0} by an element of Ĝ(R_U) reducing to the identity in Ĝ(k), obtaining ρ_{U_0}|_{W_K} = ιχ^∨ for a character χ^∨ : W_K → T̂(R_U).
issues.correction: (a) Ĝ = SL_n, the hypothesis of Theorem 5.13; (b) the Weyl group of H; (c) j_0 : Ĝ_{Q̄_{λ_0}} ≅ G_{λ_0}; (d) Ĝ(R_{U_0}) and T̂(R_{U_0}).
issues.reason: (a) G is the automorphic group over F_q and plays no role in §5. (b) The whole paragraph works with the reductive group H over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero — Φ(H,T), H⫽H ≅ T/W, the Dynkin diagram of H. (c) G_{λ_0} is the Zariski closure of the image of α_{λ_0} = R∘ρ inside GL(V)(Q̄_{λ_0}), and φ_{λ_0}∘j_0 is formed three lines later, so the source must be Ĝ over Q̄_{λ_0}. (d) ρ_{U_0} is valued in Ĝ(R_{U_0}), of which R_U is a quotient; the parallel statement in Proposition 7.9 correctly writes Ĝ(R_{U_1}) and T(K) → R^×_{U_1}.

issues.locator: §§2–4, pp. 15, 16, 17 (arXiv v2): four hat- and index-slips in the proofs of Theorems 4.5, 4.8 and Proposition 4.7
issues.printed: The source calls QN_P parabolic in G and deduces n(δ) = N ≤ dim QN_P. It claims g, g′ ∈ G(k) make (g_1, …, g_n, g, g′) Ĝ(k)-conjugate to T(δ_1, …, δ_n, γ, γ′). For m ≥ 1, γ = (γ_1, …, γ_m) ∈ Γ^m and f ∈ Z[Ĝ^n]^Ĝ, it gives f(ρ(γ_1), …, ρ(γ_m)) = Θ_m(f)(γ). It characterizes ρ(γ) as the unique g ∈ Ĝ(k) making (g_1, …, g_n, g) have a closed orbit in Ĝ(k), and defines Ĝ(E)^0 using g ∈ G(E) with χ(g) ∈ O_E^× for all χ ∈ X^*(Ĝ).
issues.correction: (a) a parabolic subgroup of Ĝ_k; (b) g, g′ ∈ Ĝ(k); (c) f ∈ Z[Ĝ^m]^Ĝ; (d) a closed orbit in Ĝ^{n+1}_k; (e) g ∈ Ĝ(E).
issues.reason: Throughout §4 the ambient group is Ĝ over Z and no group G is in play, so the unhatted G of (a), (b) and (e) is undefined; in (b) the elements are conjugated inside Ĝ(k) in the very same sentence, and in (e) Ĝ(E)^0 is being defined as a subgroup of Ĝ(E). In (c) the tuple and Θ_m are indexed by m, so f must be an invariant function of m variables for both sides to be defined; n is an unrelated integer fixed earlier in the proof. In (d) the tuple has n + 1 entries and the relevant orbit, throughout §§3–4, is the diagonal conjugation orbit in Ĝ^{n+1}.

issues.locator: §§2–3, pp. 5, 10, 11, 12, 13 (arXiv v2): five slips with mathematical content; published Acta Math. 223 (2019), p. 7 (located by review REV-PAPER-BOCKLE-HARRIS-KHARE-ETAL-19)
issues.printed: The source defines Art_{K_v} : K^× → Γ^{ab}_{K_v} as the local Artin map. It justifies self-duality by a nondegenerate symmetric G-invariant form on G, citing [SS70, Lemma I.5.3]. It places f(T) = T^n + a_1T^{n−1} + ⋯ + a_n ∈ K[X], the characteristic polynomial of multiplication by a. It takes S integral, locally closed in X and smooth over O, with O_{S,x}/(λ) = O_{S_0,x}. Closedness of G_k·φ(x) in X and finiteness of η are used to declare η^{-1}(G_k·φ(x)) closed in X′_k.
issues.correction: (a) Art_{K_v} : K_v^× → Γ^{ab}_{K_v}; (b) a symmetric bilinear form on 𝔤; (c) ∈ K[T]; (d) O_{S,x}/(̟) = O_{S_0,x}; (e) G_k·x, twice.
issues.reason: (a) The local Artin map has the local multiplicative group as its source; K^× is the global one. (b) The assertion being justified is that the **Lie algebra** 𝔤 is self-dual as a G-representation, which needs an invariant form on 𝔤; [SS70, Lemma I.5.3] is about the Lie algebra. (c) The polynomial is in the variable T over K, whereas K[X] would be functions on the scheme X being acted on. (d) One divides by the uniformizer ̟ of O fixed in §2 to pass to the special fibre; λ is never introduced as an element of O and denotes a cocharacter in Proposition 3.6. (e) Here φ : G × S → X and x ∈ X(k), so φ(x) is not defined; the hypothesis of Proposition 3.13 is that G_k·x is closed, and the point of G × S in play is (1, x), as the last line of the same proof writes.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 10.2, p. 54 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The source uses t̂^{ẇ}_k = 0 and dim_k ĝ_k ≥ r to conclude dim_k ĝ^{ẇ}_k = #R = r.
issues.correction: dim_k ĝ^{ẇ}_k ≥ r.
issues.reason: As printed the middle clause is vacuous, since dim ĝ_k ≥ r holds for any reductive group of rank r and gives no information about the ẇ-invariants. The fact being used is that the invariants of a lift of a Coxeter element have dimension at least the rank, which with the free action of ẇ on the roots forces equality and hence regularity of ẇ.

issues.locator: Appendix A (by D. Gaitsgory), step 3, p. 68 (arXiv v2); published pp. 100–101
issues.printed: The source claims it may assume strong regularity of Ē_Ť: for every w′ ∈ W, the objects Ē_Ť^{w′} and Ē_Ť are non-isomorphic. It also asserts automatic strong regularity for Ē_Ť1 on the grounds that G_1 has simply connected derived group.
issues.correction: Strong regularity must exclude w′ = 1: Ē_Ť^{w′} ≇ Ē_Ť for every w′ ≠ 1. The claim that Ē_Ť1 is automatically strongly regular is false; assume instead that Ē_Ť is strongly regular. This holds for the Ť-local systems attached to Coxeter parameters, where the geometric monodromy contains v ∈ T̂[t]^{w=q} with Stab_W(v) = 1 (proof of Proposition 10.2(iv)), which is the only case Theorem 10.11 needs.
issues.reason: Counterexample. G = G_2 is simply connected and adjoint, so G_1 = G_2 × T′ and strong regularity of Ē_Ť1 is equivalent to that of Ē_Ť. Take an elliptic curve X over F_q whose Frobenius acts on X[2] with order 3 (for example y² = x³ − x + 1 over F_3), and let Ē_Ť be the Ť[2]-torsor given by [2] : X → X and an identification X[2] ≅ Ť[2] carrying Frobenius to a Coxeter element w (both have order 3 in GL_2(F_2)), so that Fr^*Ē_Ť ≅ Ē_Ť^w. No root of G_2 is trivial on Ť[2], so Ē_Ť is regular; the induced Weil Ǧ-local system has finite image ⟨Ť[2], w̃⟩, and a torus centralizing it lies in Ť^w = 1, so it is irreducible. But −1 = w³ ∈ W acts trivially on Ť[2], so Ē_Ť^{−1} ≅ Ē_Ť and strong regularity fails. The orthogonality [BG08, Prop. 10.6] behind (11.14) of v2, (A.5) in print, needs strong regularity, so the general argument of Appendix A has a gap. Whether the general cuspidality statement holds is left open. The application is safe: for a Coxeter parameter, Stab_W(v) = 1 as above.

issues.locator: §4.2, Lemma 4.2.4 and its proof, p. 37
issues.printed: The source asserts that Ψ is defined over M and satisfies Ψc(Ψ) = |·|^{N−n}. It gives V_{c(λ)} ≅ V_λ^∨(1 − N) and, separately, E_{c(λ)} ≅ E_λ^∨(1 − n) as c-linear isomorphisms, attributing the last assertion to Schur's lemma.
issues.correction: V_{c(λ)} ≅ V_λ^∨(2 − N), and hence Ψ·c(Ψ) corresponds to ε^{n+1−N} (so Ψ has weight N − n − 1; the printed |·|^{N−n} is off by one, and its sign depends on the normalisation of Art).
issues.reason: V_λ is an eigenpiece of the middle cohomology H^{N−2} of the fibres of Z, smooth hypersurfaces of dimension N − 2 (§4.1; Proposition 4.2.5 uses H^{N−2}), so it is pure of weight N − 2 and Poincaré duality pairs it into O(2 − N). Weights confirm it: V^∨(1 − N) has weight N, not N − 2. Since E_λ is pure of weight n − 1, (4.2.3) gives Ψ weight N − n − 1; comparing V^c ≅ V^∨(2 − N) with E^c ≅ E^∨(1 − n) through (4.2.3) gives Ψ·c(Ψ) ↔ ε^{n+1−N}, one less in absolute value than the printed exponent. Nothing later uses the exponent: W_λ = V_λ(Ψ_λ^{−1}) and its pairing into k(λ)(1 − n) are stated directly and are consistent with either value.

issues.locator: Corollary 6.4.3, its statement and the spectral sequence in the first line of its proof (published version pp. 338–339; §6.4 of arXiv:1812.09269v3)
issues.printed: The corollary asserts that e(U^I)H^i(𝓧_{K(I,p^n)}(ε), ω^κ(−D)) → e(U^I)H^i(𝓧_{K(I,p^n)}(ε), 𝓕^{κ,w} ⊗ (det ω_𝓖)^2(−D)) is bijective when i = 0 and injective when i = 1. Its proof attributes to Proposition 6.4.2 the spectral sequence E_1^{p,q} = ⊕_{s∈W^{(p)}} H^q(𝓧_{K(I,p^n)}(ε), 𝓕^{s•κ,w} ⊗ (det ω_𝓖)^2(−D)).
issues.correction: both occurrences of 𝓕^{κ,w} and 𝓕^{s•κ,w} should read 𝓕^{κ,w^-} and 𝓕^{s•κ,w^-}
issues.reason: The sheaf 𝓕^{κ,w^-} = colim_{w'<w}𝓕^{κ,w'} is defined immediately before Proposition 6.4.2, which resolves ω^κ(−D) by the 𝓕^{s•κ,w^-} and not by the 𝓕^{s•κ,w}; the sentence between Proposition 6.4.2 and Corollary 6.4.3 says that the Hecke operators act on 𝓕^{κ,w^-} ⊗ (det ω_𝓖)^2(−D); and within the proof of Corollary 6.4.3 itself the differentials θ_{s,s'} are written between the 𝓕^{s•κ,w^-}. So the spectral sequence of that proof is the one attached to a resolution by the w^- sheaves, and the map in the statement of the corollary is the first map of that resolution. The slip is exactly the one the authors correct in the source they are citing: the proof of Proposition 6.4.2 says in parentheses that in Andreatta–Iovita–Pilloni §7.2 "one needs to replace 𝓕^{κ,w} with 𝓕^{κ,w^-} as defined above". The distinction is visible in both PDFs, where the minus is typeset in the exponent of Proposition 6.4.2 and of the sentence after it, and is absent in the statement and the spectral sequence of Corollary 6.4.3.

issues.locator: Remark 5.8.5, the sentence announcing the proof of the strengthened vanishing (published version p. 315; §5.8 of arXiv:1812.09269v3), against Proposition 5.9.1 and Remark 5.9.2 on p. 316
issues.printed: The remark promises a Fourier–Jacobi expansion proof sketch in §5.9 for p>3. For p=3, it omits the details because a full argument would require a more extensive treatment of toroidal compactifications than the paper otherwise needs.
issues.correction: the hypothesis should read "in the case p > 3 and [F:Q] > 1"
issues.reason: What §5.9 actually proves is Proposition 5.9.1, which assumes both p > 3 and [F:Q] > 1, and Remark 5.9.2 immediately afterwards says in as many words that for F = Q, as for p = 3, the authors have only a sketch: "We also have a sketch of an argument for F = Q." So the case F = Q is in exactly the same position as the case p = 3, and Remark 5.8.5 names only the latter. Nothing depends on this: §5.9 opens by saying that the result "partially strengthens Corollary 5.4.5 but is not needed in this paper", and the doubling theorem actually used, Theorem 5.8.4, is proved for all p ≥ 3 and all totally real F from Corollary 5.4.5 alone.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 2.4.20, the sentence that appeals to Proposition 2.4.17 (arXiv v3 p. 24; published p. 180, with the statement and the start of the proof on p. 179)
issues.printed: The proof compares with Proposition 2.4.17 and claims that reordering the Hecke parameters of π entails no loss of generality and yields α′_v + β′_v = α_v + β_v,  α′_v β′_v = α_v β_v.
issues.correction: Replace "Comparing to Proposition 2.4.17," with the following. The computation cited for Proposition 2.4.17, [GT05, Prop. 3.2.1, Cor. 3.2.2], needs no genericity. For every unramified character χ′, the operators U^naive_{Kli(v),i} act on the 4-dimensional space π(χ′)^{Kli(v)} by upper-triangular matrices in the basis (e_w), w ∈ W_{M_1}\W. Their diagonal entries are the four systems (q_v^{-2}, a+b, q_v^{-1}ab), one for each edge {a,b} of the square [α′_v, β′_v, q_v(β′_v)^{-1}, q_v(α′_v)^{-1}]. Taking Kli(v)-invariants is exact in characteristic 0, so π^{Kli(v)} is a Hecke-stable subquotient of π(χ′)^{Kli(v)}. Hence the given eigenvector has one of these four systems. Then continue with "hence, without loss of generality, we may rearrange ... α′_v + β′_v = α_v + β_v, α′_v β′_v = α_v β_v" as printed.
issues.reason:
Proposition 2.4.17 is stated only for a general unramified principal series. By Definition 2.4.11, "general" means that the four Hecke parameters are pairwise distinct and that no ratio of two of them is q_v. In the proof of Proposition 2.4.20, π is known only to be a constituent of some unramified principal series π(χ′) with parameters [α′_v, β′_v, q_v(β′_v)^{-1}, q_v(α′_v)^{-1}], and nothing forces π(χ′) to be general. It may be reducible. Then Proposition 2.4.17 says nothing about the constituent π, and the proof never addresses the passage from π(χ′) to π. It may also be irreducible, satisfy every hypothesis of 2.4.20, and still have repeated parameters. For example, q_v = 5 and α_v = β_v = 2 give the square {2, 2, 5/2, 5/2}. No ratio in it is 5, so the principal series is irreducible and satisfies 2.4.20, but it is not general, and there two different edges {2, 5/2} give the same eigensystem. So the step invokes Proposition 2.4.17 outside its hypotheses: it is asserted without adequate proof.

The step is true and fills in directly. The computation that the paper itself cites for 2.4.17, [GT05, Prop. 3.2.1, Cor. 3.2.2], is carried out for an arbitrary unramified character. In the basis (e_w) of π(χ′)^{Kli(v)} the Klingen operators are upper-triangular, with the four edge systems (q_v^{-2}, a+b, q_v^{-1}ab) on the diagonal. Kli(v)-invariants are exact on smooth representations in characteristic 0, so π^{Kli(v)} is a Hecke-stable subquotient of π(χ′)^{Kli(v)}. The invariant flag induces a flag on it whose graded pieces are subquotients of the one-dimensional diagonal pieces. So any simultaneous eigenvector in π^{Kli(v)} has one of the four edge systems. Matching u_{v,1} and u_{v,2} gives a+b = α_v+β_v and ab = α_vβ_v, so {a,b} = {α_v, β_v}. Since D_8 acts transitively on the edges of the square, the parameters can be rearranged so that {a,b} = {α′_v, β′_v}, which gives exactly the two equations the proof uses. The rest goes through unchanged: α′_v = α_v and β′_v = β_v up to reordering, so no ratio of the parameters of π(χ′) is q_v, and π(χ′) is irreducible by Proposition 2.4.6 and equals π. Proposition 2.4.20 is therefore true as stated, and only the justification of this one step is missing.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 3.5.2 (arXiv v3 p. 52; publ. p. 214)
issues.printed: The proof argues that normality makes X_{K,Σ} the normalization, in X_{K,Σ} × Spec C, of Y_K. It therefore regards extension of the action over C as sufficient.

issues.locator: Lemma 4.2.20, second ("Similarly") clause on T̃_w, and the proof sentence that leaves it to the reader; the printed proof of the T̃_w assertion of Corollary 4.2.21 relies on it (arXiv v3 p. 86; published p. 255)
issues.printed: For k_w ≥ 2p+3, the source states T̃_w = T''_{w,et} ∘ T'_{w,et} ∈ End(RΓ(X^{I'_{a,b},J,=_w1}_{K'',1}, ω^κ)). It asserts T̃_w Ha'(G_w) = Ha'(G_w) T̃_w ∈ Hom(RΓ(X^{I'_{a,b},J,=_w1}_{K'',1}, ω^κ), RΓ(X^{I'_{a,b},J,=_w1}_{K'',1}, ω^κ ⊗ det ω_{G_w}^{(p²−1)})). The proof handles T_w and leaves the analogous T̃_w argument to the reader.
issues.correction: In Lemma 4.2.20 read "Similarly, if l_w ≥ p+2 and k_w ≥ 2p+3, then we have T̃_w = T''_{w,et} ∘ T'_{w,et} …". Only the T̃_w clause changes; the T_w clause keeps l_w ≥ p+1. With the new bound, T̃_w = T''_{w,et} ∘ T'_{w,et} follows from T'_{w,m} = T'_{w,00} = T''_{w,m} = T''_{w,00} = 0 (Lemma 4.2.19). Corollary 4.2.21 can stay as printed, but its T̃_w assertion should be deduced from its first assertion. Put S = T^{I'_b,J}, which commutes with T'_w and T''_w. For n ≥ 1, (S T̃_w)^n = T''_w (T^{I_b,J})^{n−1} T'_w S, so local finiteness of T^{I_b,J} on H^*(X^{G_1,I'_{a,b},J,=_w1}_{K,1}, ω^κ) gives local finiteness of S T̃_w on H^*(X^{G_1,I'_{a,b},J,=_w1}_{K'',1}, ω^κ).
issues.reason:
The paragraph before (4.2.17) defines T'_w and T''_w on the ≤_w1 locus for l_w ≥ p+1. The T̃_w clause adds no bound on l_w, so it also claims both identities at l_w = p+1.

Lemma 4.2.19 gives T'_{w,m} = T'_{w,00} = 0 and T''_{w,m} = 0. Expanding the composite therefore gives T̃_w = T''_{w,et}∘T'_{w,et} + T''_{w,00}∘T'_{w,et}. However, Lemma 4.2.19 gives T''_{w,00} = 0 only for l_w ≥ p+2. [Pil20, Rem. 7.4.2.1(1)] records that at l_w = p+1 this piece (Pilloni's T_2^{oo}) does not vanish.

The printed argument for T_w does not carry over:
- For T_w = T'_w∘T''_w, the composite passes through X_{K'',1}^{=_w1}. That space splits into its 00 and m-et parts compatibly with p_2 by (4.2.17)–(4.2.18), so the cross terms vanish, and T'_{w,00} = 0 removes the rest.
- For T̃_w = T''_w∘T'_w, the composite passes through X_{K,1}^{=_w1}, which has no such splitting. At a point of p-rank 1, G_w[p] ≅ μ_p ⊕ E[p] ⊕ Z/p (E supersingular) has exactly one étale, one multiplicative and one α_p subgroup of order p. So all three components of X_{K',1}^{=_w1} lie over every point, and the term T''_{w,00}∘T'_{w,et} has nonempty support.

At l_w = p+1, then, the first identity holds exactly when T''_{w,00}∘T'_{w,et} = 0. The second identity needs the same vanishing. At the shifted weight l_w + p² − 1 ≥ p+2 we have T''_{w,00} = 0, and T'_{w,et}, T''_{w,et} commute with Ha' by Lemma 4.2.19. Since Ha'(G_w) is invertible on the =_w1 locus, T̃_w Ha' − Ha' T̃_w = −Ha'∘T''_{w,00}∘T'_{w,et}. The paper gives no argument for this vanishing, and its truth is not settled, so this is a gap and not an error.

The reach is a stated result: Lemma 4.2.20 is unproved as printed at l_w = p+1, and the printed "essentially identical" proof of the T̃_w part of Corollary 4.2.21 rests on it. Nothing further is lost:
- The T̃_w part of Corollary 4.2.21 still holds for l_w ≥ p+1 by the identity (S T̃_w)^n = T''_w (T^{I_b,J})^{n−1} T'_w S.
- The second diagram of Lemma 4.2.22, and Lemma 4.2.24, assume l_w ≥ p+2.
- Lemma 4.2.25 (l_w = p+1) cites Lemma 4.2.20 only for T_w. It uses T̃_w only at weight l_w + p² − 1 on the ≤_w1 locus.
- Corollary 4.2.26 uses only the T^{I_b,J} part of Corollary 4.2.21.

So Theorem 4.2.12 and the main theorems stand. The new bound must go on the T̃_w clause alone, because Lemma 4.2.25 applies the T_w clause at l_w = p+1.
