issues.locator: Proposition 5.5.1, hypothesis on φ (arXiv v3 p. 123; publ. p. 302), as applied in the proofs of Proposition 5.6.1 (arXiv v3 p. 125; publ. p. 304) and Proposition 5.7.5 (arXiv v3 p. 130; publ. p. 310)
issues.printed: The proposition takes (A, ι, λ) together with (A′, ι′, λ′) as tuples of the specified kind. It assumes a quasi-isogeny φ : A → A′ prime to p, subject to φι = ι′φ and to φ^tλ′φ = xλ, where x ∈ O_F ⊗ Z_(p).
issues.correction: Replace "a prime to p quasi-isogeny φ : A → A′" by "a quasi-isogeny φ : A → A′ lying in Hom(A, A′) ⊗ Z_(p)". It need not be prime to p, and any isogeny qualifies, for example one of p-power degree. The rest of the statement and the printed proof are unchanged.
issues.reason:
Proposition 5.5.1 is used exactly twice: in the proofs of Propositions 5.6.1 and 5.7.5. Each proof reads only "This follows from Propositions 5.5.1 and 5.5.2". Neither use satisfies the hypothesis that φ be prime to p. The paper fixes this notion in §3.3 as Lan's Z_(p)^×-isogeny [Lan13, Defn. 1.3.1.17].

In 5.6.1, φ is the étale isogeny π : A → A/L_w. Its kernel L_w is a maximal isotropic subgroup of A[w], so it has order p^2. Here π^tλ′π = x_wλ, where x_w is a uniformiser at w (p splits completely in F).

In 5.7.5, φ is the universal isogeny p_1^*G → p_2^*G. Its kernel is a subgroup of G_w[p^2] of order p^4. Here φ^tλ′φ = x_w^2 λ, which is where the factor N(x_w)^6 comes from.

Under the printed hypothesis these cases cannot occur. If φ, λ and λ′ are all invertible in Hom ⊗ Z_(p), then so is xλ. So x is a unit of O_F ⊗ Z_(p), and N_{F/Q}(x)^3 is prime to p. But 5.6.1 and 5.7.5 print factors N(x_w)^3/p^3 and N(x_w)^6/p^6 in Z_(p)^×, which need v_p(N(x)^3) = 3 and 6. The remark after 5.6.1 says the same: some maps in the square reduce to 0 modulo p.

The case actually used holds, and the printed proof proves it:
- Take φ in Hom(A, A′) ⊗ Z_(p) and put φ^† = λ^{-1}φ^tλ′, which lies in Hom(A′, A) ⊗ Z_(p) because λ is prime to p.
- Then φ^†φ = x, so (φφ^† − x)φ = 0.
- Some prime-to-p multiple of φ is an isogeny, so φ can be cancelled on the right, giving φφ^† = x.
- Pulling back to ω gives (φ^t)^*(λ^*)^{-1}φ^* = (λ′^*)^{-1}x^* on ω_{A′}.
- Functoriality of Kodaira–Spencer gives KS_A∘φ^* = Lie(φ^t)∘KS_{A′}. Combining the two, KS_{(A,λ)}(φ^*a ⊗ φ^*b) = KS_{(A′,λ′)}(a ⊗ xb).
- On top exterior powers this gives the factor N_{F/Q}(x)^3.

The integrality of φ is what makes φ^* a map of sheaves over a Z_(p)-base. So an arbitrary quasi-isogeny, with p in a denominator, is not allowed.

Nothing printed is false: 5.5.1 is true as stated, and 5.6.1 and 5.7.5 are true. But the proofs of 5.6.1 and 5.7.5 rest on a case of 5.5.1 that the paper never states. That is a step without adequate justification, so this is a gap.

It is not a misprint. The printed hypothesis is a defined notion and reads coherently where it stands. That it must be dropped, and that the proposition survives without it, becomes clear only from the applications. It also needs the cancellation argument above: for such φ, the identity φφ^† = x can no longer be obtained by conjugating with φ^{-1}.

The reach is the proofs of 5.6.1 and 5.7.5. Every numbered statement stands once 5.5.1 is read with the corrected hypothesis.

issues.locator: Corollary 6.4.3, last sentence of the statement (isomorphism for i = 1 when k_v − l_v ≥ 3), together with the last sentence of its proof; arXiv v3 p. 153 (statement) and p. 154 (end of proof); published pp. 338 (statement) and 339 (end of proof)
issues.printed: Corollary 6.4.3 asserts an isomorphism for i = 1 under the additional condition k_v − l_v ≥ 3 for every v|p. Its proof attributes the conclusion to the slope estimates in Propositions 6.4.1.
issues.correction: Replace "k_v − l_v ≥ 3 for all v|p" by "k_v − l_v ≥ 3N for all v|p, where N = #I + 2#I^c is the number of factors U_{v,1}, U_{v,2} in U^I". The same change is needed where the proof of Proposition 6.6.2 repeats "≥ 3". Keeping threshold 3 would need a slope bound ≥ −3 on H^1 for U^I itself, and the paper does not prove one.
issues.reason:
To get the i = 1 isomorphism, e(U^I) must kill E_1^{1,1} = ⊕_{v|p} H^1(X_{K(I,p^n)}(ε), F^{w_v•κ,w^-} ⊗ (det ω_G)^2(−D)). On the v-summand of that sum, U_{v,2} acts twisted by p^{k_v−l_v+1}. E_1^{2,0} is already killed by the H^0 bounds.

Proposition 6.4.1 bounds each operator on its own: on H^1, every U_{v,1} (v ∈ I^c) and every U_{v,2} (v|p) has slopes ≥ −3. But U^I = ∏_{v∈I} U_{v,2} ∏_{v∈I^c} U_{v,1}U_{v,2} is a product of N = #I + 2#I^c commuting factors. On a joint eigencharacter of the v-summand, these bounds give only slope(twisted U^I) ≥ (k_v − l_v + 1 − 3) − 3(N − 1) = k_v − l_v + 1 − 3N. This is > 0 exactly when k_v − l_v ≥ 3N.

When 3 ≤ k_v − l_v < 3N, Proposition 6.4.1 allows a character in which the twisted U_{v,2} has slope ≥ 1, the other factors have slopes ≥ −3, and the total slope is 0. So the differential E_1^{0,1} → E_1^{1,1} is not shown to vanish on the ordinary part. Going back to the integrality argument does not help either: each U_{v,1} and U_{v,2} carries its own p^{−3}Tr normalisation (p^{−6}Tr for U_{v,1}U_{v,2}), so that argument gives only −3N for U^I.

Threshold 3 is right only when N = 1, i.e. F = Q and I = {p}, where there is a single operator. When I = ∅, H^1 vanishes by Proposition 6.3.7, so the claim holds trivially. Since p splits completely, #I ≥ 1 and [F:Q] ≥ 2 give N = 2[F:Q] − #I ≥ 2 (for #I = 1, N ≥ 3). In that case the claim is not proved.

The claim may still be true, since a bound ≥ −3 for U^I itself would give it, so this is a gap and not an error. As printed, however, the last assertion of the numbered Corollary 6.4.3 is unproved. Only the per-factor argument's threshold 3N is established.

The i = 0 isomorphism and the i = 1 injectivity use only the H^0 bounds and still hold. The i = 1 isomorphism is used only in the proof of Proposition 6.6.2. There, local constancy of Euler characteristics lets one take k_v − l_v ≥ C with C as large as needed, so C ≥ 3N works. Proposition 6.6.2, Theorems 6.6.4 and 6.6.5, and the main results therefore stand.

issues.correction: By Tate local duality, H^2(G_{Q_p}, ad^0_B ρ_x) is dual to H^0(G_{Q_p}, (ad^0 ρ_x / n_x)(1)). Here n_x = (ad^0_B ρ_x)^⊥ is the nilradical of the Borel of ρ_x. For R_v^{P,univ}[1/p], argue the same way with (ad^0 ρ_x / (ad^0_P ρ_x)^⊥)(1).

issues.locator: Proposition 7.4.10(2), proof of the case i = 2, last paragraph ("Étale locally, one may trivialize ψ′ …") (arXiv v3 p. 191; published p. 384)
issues.printed: The proof takes the étale algebra A′ = A[√ψ′(f₁, f₁), √ψ′(f₂, f₂)] and U′ = Spec A′. It gives (𝒪⁴_{𝒩₂}/ker N)_{U′} a basis given by f₁′ = f₁/√ψ′(f₁, f₁), f₂′ = f₂/√ψ′(f₂, f₂), satisfying ψ′(f₁′, f₁′) = ψ′(f₂′, f₂′) = 1; ψ′(f₁′, f₂′) = 0. After lifting to e₁, e₂ in 𝒪⁴_{U′}, it claims the replacement e₂ − ψ(e₁, e₂)Ne₁ makes ψ(e₁, e₂) = 0. It calls Ne₂, Ne₁, e₁, e₂ a symplectic basis and claims the matrix g ∈ GSp₄ with these columns satisfies N_{U′} = gN₂g⁻¹.
issues.correction: Let A′ = A[√ψ′(f₁, f₁), √(−ψ′(f₂, f₂))] (étale since p > 2) and f₂′ = f₂/√(−ψ′(f₂, f₂)), so that ψ′(f₁′, f₁′) = 1 = −ψ′(f₂′, f₂′) and ψ′(f₁′, f₂′) = 0. Lift h₁ = (f₁′ + f₂′)/2 and h₂ = f₁′ − f₂′ (ψ′-isotropic, with ψ′(h₁, h₂) = 1) to sections e₁, e₂ of 𝒪⁴_{U′}, and arrange ψ(e₁, e₂) = 0 by replacing e₂ by e₂ + ψ(e₁, e₂)Ne₂. Then Ne₁, Ne₂, e₁, e₂ is a symplectic basis for 𝒪⁴_{U′}, and the g ∈ GSp₄ with these columns satisfies N_{U′} = gN₂g⁻¹.
issues.reason: By §2.1.1, ψ(v, w) = vᵗJw with J = (0 s; −s 0), s = (0 1; 1 0). So a basis b₁, …, b₄ is symplectic when ψ(b₁, b₄) = ψ(b₂, b₃) = 1 and every other pairing with i < j is 0. On the same page N₂ = E₁₃ + E₂₄. On 𝒩₂ we have N² = 0 and ψ(Nv, w) = −ψ(v, Nw). The printed step goes wrong twice. (i) ψ(e₁, Ne₁) = −ψ′(f₁′, f₁′) = −1, so for c = ψ(e₁, e₂) we get ψ(e₁, e₂ − cNe₁) = 2c, which is not 0. The sign has to be +. (ii) Even after that fix, the columns b = (Ne₂, Ne₁, e₁, e₂) satisfy Nb₃ = b₂ and Nb₄ = b₁. So g⁻¹Ng = E₁₄ + E₂₃, not N₂. Reordering the columns does not help. If g⁻¹Ng = N₂ for some g ∈ GSp₄, then Nb₃ = b₁ and Nb₄ = b₂, so ψ′(b₃, b₃) = ψ(b₁, b₃) = 0 and ψ′(b₄, b₄) = ψ(b₂, b₄) = 0. That makes ψ′ hyperbolic. On A′ as constructed, however, ψ′ has an orthonormal basis, so ψ′ ≅ x² + y², and this form is anisotropic at every point whose residue field has −1 as a non-square. For a concrete case, take the residue field of 𝒪 to be F₃ and let N = E₁₄ + E₂₃ ∈ 𝒩₂(𝒪). Its form ψ′ on ⟨e₃, e₄⟩ has Gram matrix I. The printed recipe gives g = 1 at this point, and no element of GSp₄(F₃) conjugates N₂ to E₁₄ + E₂₃, because conjugation by g multiplies ψ′ by ν(g), and x² + y² is anisotropic over F₃. So the step fails as written and cannot be repaired by fixing a sign or reordering: ψ′ has to be normalised to a hyperbolic form. Statement (2) is still true, because it is only étale-local. Adjoining √(−ψ′(f₂, f₂)) in place of √ψ′(f₂, f₂) is étale since p > 2, and it gives ψ′ the Gram matrix diag(1, −1). The hyperbolic basis h₁, h₂ and the columns Ne₁, Ne₂, e₁, e₂ then give gᵗJg = J and gN₂g⁻¹ = N_{U′} (ψ(e₁, Ne₂) = −1 makes the adjustment kill ψ(e₁, e₂)). Proposition 7.4.10(3), Proposition 7.4.14 and Corollary 7.4.15 use only the statement of (2). So only the proof is affected.

issues.locator: Lemma 7.5.22, proof, first paragraph (case #k > 3), and the tidiness sentence of the same proof ("Tidiness follows for p ≥ 5 by Lemma 7.5.13"). arXiv v3 p. 205, with the statement starting on p. 204; published p. 401, with the statement starting on p. 400. The failing case arises when the lemma is applied in the proof of Lemma 9.2.2, type B[C₂] (arXiv v3 pp. 254–255; published pp. 460–461).
issues.printed: The proof identifies PGL₂(k) as the automorphism group of PSL₂(k). It concludes that the projective representations attached to r̄ and r̄^σ have identical images precisely when the representations themselves coincide.
issues.correction:
Since the automorphism group of PSL₂(k) is PΓL₂(k) = PGL₂(k) ⋊ Gal(k/F_p), images that are not disjoint force Proj r̄^σ ≅ τ∘Proj r̄ for some τ ∈ Gal(k/F_p).

Cases already settled:
- τ = 1 is excluded by hypothesis.
- For p = 3, every τ is excluded by the disjointness hypothesis, since Proj r̄ and τ∘Proj r̄ have the same kernel.
This settles k = F_p and p = 3.

For p ≥ 5 and k ≠ F_p, the case τ ≠ 1 needs its own argument:
- Then τ² = 1, so τ is the involution of k over a subfield k₀ with #k₀ = q₀ ≥ 5.
- In a suitable basis, the image G of ρ̄|G_{F(ζ_p)} is an index-2 extension of N = {(A, ±τ(A)) : A ∈ SL₂(k)}, not SL₂(k) ≀ Z/2Z.
- G is still enormous:
  - (E2) holds because V ≇ V^τ.
  - (E1) holds because H¹(SL₂(k), Sym²V) = 0 (as #k ≥ 25) and H¹(SL₂(k), V ⊗ V^τ) = 0 (as p ≥ 5).
  - (E3) follows from Lemma 7.5.17. Here As(V)|N = V ⊗ V^τ is irreducible, and Ind ad⁰V restricted to N is Sym²V ⊕ Sym²V^τ, whose two summands are non-isomorphic and swapped by G. Apply the lemma to g = (C, ±C)·w ∈ G∖N, where w is the swap and C ∈ SL₂(k₀) has order q₀+1. Then g² = ±(C², C²) ≠ ±1 has order prime to p.
- G has no quotient of p-power order, so ρ̄ is vast.
- Lemma 7.5.13 does not give tidiness here, because Δ is not contained in the image. Instead take ρ̄(g) for g ∈ G_K with r̄(g) = diag(a, −a⁻¹), where a generates k^×. Then ν = −1, and no two of the eigenvalues a, −a⁻¹, ±τ(a), ∓τ(a)⁻¹ have ratio −1.
issues.reason:
In §7, k is the residue field of an arbitrary finite extension of Q_p, and Lemma 9.2.2 applies Lemma 7.5.22 with k = O_M/λ. So k need not be a prime field.

For #k > 3, Aut(PSL₂(k)) = PΓL₂(k), which is strictly larger than PGL₂(k) when k ≠ F_p, so the printed fact is false. Goursat's lemma then only shows that images which are not disjoint force Proj r̄^σ ≅ τ∘Proj r̄ for a field automorphism τ. For p = 3 the disjointness hypothesis rules this out, but for p ≥ 5 the hypothesis Proj r̄^σ ≇ Proj r̄ does not.

The case actually occurs:
- Let A/F have type B[C₂]. Its real multiplication by a real quadratic field is defined over K, and σ acts on that field nontrivially.
- Take l inert in that field. Then r̄ = s̄_λ : G_K → GL₂(F_{l²}) satisfies every hypothesis of the lemma: the image contains SL₂(F_{l²}) for density-one l, det = ε̄⁻¹, and Proj s̄^σ ≅ Frob∘Proj s̄ ≇ Proj s̄.
- But ρ̄ ≅ ρ̄_{A,l} ⊗ F_{l²} has image in a conjugate of GSp₄(F_l). Since 2|SL₂(F_{l²})|² = 2l⁴(l⁴−1)² > l⁴(l²−1)(l⁴−1) = |Sp₄(F_l)|, the image over F(ζ_l) cannot be SL₂(F_{l²}) ≀ Z/2Z, as the proof asserts.
- Δ is not contained in this image either, so the appeal to Lemma 7.5.13 for tidiness also fails.
- Inert primes make up half of all primes, so the density-one claim of Lemma 9.2.2 depends on this case.

The step is therefore false, not a slip, and the kind is error.

Both statements survive. In the twisted case, τ is an involution and the image over F(ζ_p) is an index-2 extension of {(A, ±τ(A))}. This group is enormous: V ≇ V^τ; H¹(SL₂(k), Sym²) = 0 since #k ≥ 25; H¹(SL₂(k), V ⊗ V^τ) = 0 since p ≥ 5; and Lemma 7.5.17 applies to an element (C, ±C)·swap with C of order q₀+1 in SL₂(k₀). The group has no p-power quotient, so ρ̄ is vast. An element with first block diag(a, −a⁻¹) gives tidiness. So Lemmas 7.5.22 and 9.2.2 hold as stated, and only their proofs need the extra case: the reach is the proof.

issues.printed: The source takes a finite Galois extension L/K of number fields, defines K′ = KE′ and L′ = LE′, and in (2) requires linear disjointness of L′/E from E′F^(avoid)/E.
issues.correction: Assert only L′/K′ Galois (no L/K), with K/E linearly disjoint from E′F^(avoid); Gal(L′_w/K′_w) in the diagram. Amended (FIX-RT-PAPER-BOXER-CALEGARI-GEE-PILLONI-21, 30 September 2026) under RT-PAPER-BOXER-CALEGARI-GEE-PILLONI-21/3: (2) should read 'K/E is linearly disjoint from E′F^(avoid)/E, and L′/K′ is linearly disjoint from K′F^(avoid)/K′'. In the fixed-determinant variant that Lemma 9.2.7 uses (E140), with G = GL_2(F_q) and determinant ε̄^{−1}, the second clause reads L′ ∩ K′F^(avoid) = K′(ζ_q). Both are proved by the same Moret-Bailly argument after adding to S auxiliary places of E split completely in E′F^(avoid), at which the prescribed unramified local extensions have Frobenii meeting every conjugacy class of G (every GL_2(F_q)-class contained in SL_2(F_q) in the fixed-determinant case), and Jordan's lemma. Item 174 states both forms.
issues.reason: Printed (2) fails when E′ ≠ E; an L′ = LE′ forces equal local data at split places, which Lemma 9.2.7 needs to differ. Amendment (FIX-RT-PAPER-BOXER-CALEGARI-GEE-PILLONI-21, 30 September 2026): the correction as first recorded kept only the K-part of (2), which is too weak for E140, whose reason uses that L′ is linearly disjoint from K′F^(avoid) over K′. The strong (2) is what the printed (2) asserts when E′ = E (Calegari's Prop. 3.2). Given the auxiliary places, the Frobenii at the places of K′ above them lie in H_0 = Gal(L′/L′ ∩ K′F^(avoid)), which then meets every conjugacy class and is the whole group by Jordan's lemma. In the fixed-determinant case H_0 ⊂ SL_2(F_q) is normal in H = Gal(L′/K′), det(H) = F_q^× because q splits completely in K′, so every GL_2-conjugate of H_0 is an SL_2-conjugate, and H_0 = SL_2(F_q). The paper itself takes from (2) only Lemma 9.2.7(2), which needs only the K-part; Lemma 9.2.7(6) needs only full image and the determinant (see E140).

issues.locator: Lemma 9.2.7: property (4), the first bullet of (5), and the choice of φ̄_{w_1}, φ̄_{w_2} in its proof. This carries over to the v|q step of the proof of Theorem 9.2.8. arXiv v3 pp. 256–257; published pp. 462–464 (lemma pp. 462–463, proof of the theorem p. 464).
issues.printed: In (5), the source sets ρ̄_q := Ind^{G_{F′}}_{G_{F′F_1}} r̄_q : G_{F′} → GSp_4(F_q), with multiplier ε̄^{−1}, and claims ρ̄_q|_{G_{F′_{w′}}} ≅ (ρ̄_{A,q}|_{G_{F_w}})^{ss} for w|q, w′|w. For w|p it lists α_w, β_w, pβ_w^{−1}, pα_w^{−1} as eigenvalues of (A[q]^∨|_{G_{F_w}})(Frob_w). At w|p or w|q it chooses φ̄_{w_1}, φ̄_{w_2} via (λ_{α_w} 0 ; 0 ε^{−1}λ_{α_w}^{−1}), (λ_{β_w} 0 ; 0 ε^{−1}λ_{β_w}^{−1}). Theorem 9.2.8 claims lifting A canonically modulo v yields a point in Y(F′_v) when v|q.
issues.correction:
The data at q must change.

(a) In Lemma 9.2.6, first fix p. Then also require q > p^2 and that Frob_q be conjugate to complex conjugation in the Galois closure over Q of F(A[p], ζ_p, √Δ_v : v|p), where Δ_v = a_1(v)^2 − 4a_2(v) + 8p. This is a positive-density Chebotarev condition on primes that split completely in F, so good q of this kind exist. It gives q ≡ −1 mod p and q split in each real field Q(√Δ_v).

(b) In the proof of Lemma 9.2.7:
- For w|p, take φ̄_{w_1}, φ̄_{w_2} unramified and F_q-rational, with Frob_w-characteristic polynomials (x−α_w)(x−pα_w^{−1}) and (x−β_w)(x−pβ_w^{−1}). These lie in F_q[x] by (a).
- For w|q, take φ̄_{w_1} = diag(λ_a, ε̄^{−1}λ_a^{−1}) and φ̄_{w_2} = diag(λ_b, ε̄^{−1}λ_b^{−1}), with a = p and b = −p in F_q.
- Replace the first bullet of (5) by ρ̄_q|_{G_{F′_{w′}}} ≅ λ_a ⊕ λ_b ⊕ ε̄^{−1}λ_b^{−1} ⊕ ε̄^{−1}λ_a^{−1}.

(c) In the proof of Theorem 9.2.8, for v|q, replace "the canonical lift of A modulo v" by the canonical lift of E × E′. Here E, E′/F_q are elliptic curves with traces p and −p, which exist by Deuring since p < 2√q.
- It is ordinary.
- Its q-torsion is ρ̄_q^∨ locally.
- Its p-torsion is symplectically isomorphic to A[p]|_{G_{F_w}}: on both, Frob_w acts as an involution of multiplier −1 with 2-dimensional ±1-eigenspaces.

Everything else stands, including Theorem 9.2.8.
issues.reason:
Property (4) makes r̄_q take values in GL_2(F_q). Let w|q. Since q splits completely in F′F_1, the restriction of ρ̄_q = Ind r̄_q to the decomposition group at w′|w is r̄_q|_{w′_1} ⊕ r̄_q|_{w′_2}. Each summand is F_q-rational with determinant ε̄^{−1}, and ε̄^{−1} is ramified at q because q ≥ 3.

So each summand has exactly one unramified and one ramified constituent among λ_ᾱ, λ_β̄, ε̄^{−1}λ_β̄^{−1}, ε̄^{−1}λ_ᾱ^{−1}. The determinant, together with ᾱ_w ≠ β̄_w, forces the constituents to be λ_x and ε̄^{−1}λ_x^{−1} with x ∈ {ᾱ_w, β̄_w}. Frobenius acting on the coefficients sends λ_x to λ_{x^q}, which is still unramified. F_q-rationality therefore forces x^q = x. Hence the first bullet of (5) can hold only if ᾱ_w, β̄_w ∈ F_q.

These are the roots of x^2 − a_1(w)x + a_2(w) mod q, and being a good prime does not put them in F_q:
- Definition 7.3.1 takes λ_x with x in the residue field k of a coefficient field that may be enlarged.
- The proof of Lemma 9.2.5 uses only the condition q ∤ a_1^2 − 4a_2.

The roots lie outside F_q whenever a_1^2 − 4a_2 is a non-square mod q. For example, for the Jacobian of y^2 + (x^3+1)y = x^2 + x over Q, point counting at q = 97 gives a_1 = 10 and a_2 = 82. The reduction is ordinary, and a_1^2 − 4a_2 ≡ 63 is a non-square mod 97.

For such q, no r̄_q satisfies both (4) and (5), so Lemma 9.2.7 is false as printed. The step of the proof that fails is the choice φ̄_{w_1} = diag(λ_{α_w}, ε^{−1}λ_{α_w}^{−1}). It is not GL_2(F_q)-valued, which Propositions 9.1.12 and 9.1.11 require.

The same printed choice at w|p also needs α_w ∈ F_q. There, (5) needs only that the pairs {α_w, pα_w^{−1}} and {β_w, pβ_w^{−1}} (the pairing is forced, because their products must equal p) be Frobenius-stable over F_q. This means Δ_w is a square mod q. It fails for a positive density of q, but a Chebotarev condition can impose it.

At q, no Chebotarev condition helps, because ᾱ_w is the reduction mod q of the Frobenius at q itself. So the data at q must change. With it changes the point of Ω_v at v|q in Theorem 9.2.8, which relied on the canonical lift of A having q-torsion (ρ̄_{A,q}|_{G_{F_w}})^{ss}.

With the choices in the correction:
- Propositions 9.1.12 and 9.1.11 receive F_q-rational diagonal data.
- (6) still follows from (4) via Lemma 7.5.22.
- ρ̄_{B,q} stays q-distinguished, since p ≢ −p mod q.
- The canonical lift of E × E′ lies in Ω_v.

So Theorem 9.2.8, and the results drawn from it, survive. But the numbered Lemma 9.2.7 is false as printed, and its proof step fails. Hence this is an error affecting a stated result.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 9.2.7, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs, from "The obstruction to the existence of a square root" to "has a square root" (arXiv v3 p. 257; published p. 463)
issues.printed: The proof places the obstruction to a square root for ε̄ det r̄_q in the 2-torsion of Br_{F_1F′}, vanishing locally at every place dividing pq𝔯∞. It claims that replacing F′ by a totally real quadratic extension where p, q, 𝔯 all split completely allows one to assume a square root for ε̄ det r̄_q exists.
issues.correction: Build r̄_q with det r̄_q = ε̄^{-1} from the start. Run the Moret-Bailly argument of Proposition 9.1.12 on the variety of GL_2(F_q)-torsors whose determinant torsor is the F_q^×-torsor given by ε̄^{-1}, instead of on X_G for G = GL_2(F_q). Equivalently, use torsors under the twist of SL_2(F_q) by ε̄^{-1}. Keep the same local data: every φ̄_w has determinant ε̄^{-1}, and det c_v = −1 = ε̄^{-1}(c_v). Condition (2) of that proposition becomes L′ ∩ K′F^{(avoid)} = K′(ζ_q). Then (3) holds by construction, (4)–(6) follow as printed, and the square-root paragraph is deleted.
issues.reason:
Write K′ = F_1F′ and ψ = ε̄ det r̄_q : G_{K′} → F_q^×. Twisting r̄_q must keep it valued in GL_2(F_q). Condition (4) needs this, and so does Theorem 9.2.8, which identifies B[q] with ρ̄_q^∨. So the proof needs a character θ : G_{K′} → F_q^× with θ^2 = ψ.

Squaring on F_q^× has image of index 2. So such a θ exists only if ψ takes square values, i.e. ψ^{(q−1)/2} = 1. Only after that does the obstruction lie in H^2(G_{K′}, ±1) = Br_{K′}[2]. The Brauer-class description is correct only for F̄_q-valued square roots. The printed claim that the obstruction "is a class in the 2-torsion of Br" is therefore false for the root that is needed.

The missing first obstruction does not vanish here. By Proposition 9.1.12(2), L′ is linearly disjoint over K′ from K′F^{(avoid)}. That field contains K′(ζ_q), since ζ_q ∈ F(A[q]) by the Weil pairing. Also [K′(ζ_q):K′] = q−1, because q splits completely in K′. So (r̄_q, ε̄) maps G_{K′} onto GL_2(F_q) × F_q^×, and ψ is onto F_q^×. Hence no F_q^×-valued square root exists over F_1F′.

Replacing F′ by a quadratic extension F″ chosen to kill a Brauer class does not change this. For ψ to become square-valued, F_1F″ would have to contain the quadratic extension of K′ cut out by ψ^{(q−1)/2}, and the argument does nothing to arrange that.

An F̄_q-valued root does not help either. Pick g with r̄_q(g) = 1 and ε̄(g) a non-square. The twist sends g to a scalar θ(g)^{-1} ∉ F_q, so the twisted representation is not valued in GL_2(F_q). The step therefore fails; it is not merely left unjustified.

The reach is only the proof. The local data already have determinant ε̄^{-1} everywhere, so the fixed-determinant form of the Moret-Bailly construction gives r̄_q with (1)–(3) directly. Its restriction to G_{K′(ζ_q)} has image SL_2(F_q), and (4)–(6) then follow exactly as printed, via the places above 𝔯 and Lemma 7.5.22. Lemma 9.2.7, and Theorem 9.2.8 which uses it, remain true. Note (FIX-RT-PAPER-BOXER-CALEGARI-GEE-PILLONI-21, 30 September 2026): '(2)' in the second paragraph refers to Proposition 9.1.12(2) in the form amended under E137, which gives the linear disjointness of L′ from K′F^(avoid) over K′. The SL_2(F_q) hypothesis of Lemma 7.5.22 follows from (3) and (4) alone, since G_{K′(ζ_q)} = ker(det ∘ r̄_q); it does not depend on that disjointness.

issues.locator: Proposition 10.1.3, conclusion (the definition of "ordinarily modular"): arXiv v3 p. 266, with the statement starting on p. 265; published p. 474, with the statement starting on p. 473. The same words occur in the hypothesis of Proposition 10.1.1 (arXiv v3 p. 265; published p. 472) and in the proof of Theorem 10.1.4 (arXiv v3 p. 267; published p. 476).
issues.printed: The source calls ρ̄_p ordinarily modular: it asserts the existence of π with parallel weight 2, central character | · |², and unramified ordinary local components at every v|p, satisfying ρ̄_{π,p} ≅ ρ̄. It also requires purity of ρ_{π,p}|_{G_{F_v}} at every finite place v of F.
issues.correction: Delete "unramified and" in all three places. In Proposition 10.1.3 read "there exists π of parallel weight 2 and central character |·|² which is ordinary at all v|p, such that ρ̄_{π,p} ≅ ρ̄, …". In Proposition 10.1.1 read "…central character |·|² which is ordinary at all v|p, such that ρ̄_{π,p} ≅ ρ̄_{A,p}, …". In the proof of Theorem 10.1.4 read "…we construct a π of parallel weight 2 and central character |·|² which is ordinary at all v|p such that ρ̄_{π,p} ≅ ρ̄". This agrees with Theorem 1.1.7 and with Theorem 8.4.1(4).
issues.reason:
By §2.4.7, "unramified" means π_v^{GSp4(O_{F_v})} ≠ 0, which is a stronger condition than ordinary. By Proposition 2.4.24, an ordinary π_v of weight (2,2) that is also spherical must be an irreducible unramified principal series, because types IIa, IIIa and Va have no spherical vector. Hence α_v², β_v² and α_vβ_v are all different from 1.

The hypotheses of Proposition 10.1.3 allow ϱ̄|G_{E_w} to be très ramifiée at a place w|p. Definition 7.3.1 leaves the upper-right block arbitrary. For example, take p = 5 and E totally real with 5 unramified. Apply Lemmas 7.5.26–7.5.27 to r̄ = the dual mod-5 representation of an elliptic curve over F with surjective mod-5 image and multiplicative reduction at some v|5 with 5 ∤ v(q). The result is a ρ̄ = Ind(r̄|G_E ⊗ δ) that satisfies (2), and its ϱ̄ is not finite flat at w|v. Theorem 10.1.4 likewise allows semistable ordinary reduction at 5.

In this case the proof fails. The weight-2 ordinary Hilbert modular form lifting ϱ̄ cannot be unramified at w. If it were, its Galois representation at w would be crystalline with Hodge–Tate weights 0 and 1, and ϱ̄|G_{E_w} would then be finite flat. So the form is of Steinberg type at w, and its automorphic induction is not spherical at v. The proof only shows that π is ordinary.

The conclusion itself is also false in this case. Suppose π were spherical and ordinary at v with ρ̄_{π,p} ≅ ρ̄. By local–global compatibility at p (Corollary 7.9.6(4)), ρ_{π,p}|G_{F_v} is an extension of ε^{-1}λ_{β_v^{-1}} ⊕ ε^{-1}λ_{α_v^{-1}} by λ_{α_v} ⊕ λ_{β_v}. The extension classes lie in the groups H^1(Q_p, ελ_z) with z ∈ {α_v², α_vβ_v, β_v²}. Since z ≠ 1, every class in these groups is crystalline. So ρ_{π,p}|G_{F_v} is crystalline with Hodge–Tate weights in an interval of length 1. By Fontaine–Laffaille (p ≥ 3, F_v = Q_p), ρ̄|G_{F_v} would be finite flat, and so would its summand ϱ̄|G_{E_w}. That is a contradiction.

So Proposition 10.1.3 is false as printed. Deleting "unramified and" gives exactly what the proof establishes. Theorem 8.4.1(4) and Hypothesis 7.13.1(6) require only "ordinary". So Proposition 10.1.1 with the weaker hypothesis, which is Theorem 1.1.7 of the introduction, and Theorem 10.1.4 still follow. The deletion in 10.1.1 is needed so that the corrected 10.1.3 still supplies its hypothesis (as after 10.1.3 and in the proof of Theorem 10.2.6). The deletion in the proof of 10.1.4 is needed because the π built there is not spherical at v for curves with multiplicative reduction.

issues.locator: Proposition 7.10.1 (arXiv v3 p. 223; published p. 423) and its application in §7.11 (arXiv v3 p. 225; published pp. 425–426)
issues.printed: Proposition 7.10.1 takes open ideals S_∞ ⊃ I_1 ⊃ I_2 ⊃ … with ∩_N I_N = 0 and defines S_N = S_∞/I_N for each N ≥ 1. It leaves the proof details as a reader exercise. In §7.11, the source sets S_N = T[Δ_N] and claims these data meet Proposition 7.10.1’s hypotheses.
issues.correction: Apply Proposition 7.10.1 in the form: ideals I_N contained in open ideals 𝔟_1 ⊃ 𝔟_2 ⊃ … with ∩_N 𝔟_N = 0, the data being reduced modulo 𝔟_N. In §7.11 take 𝔟_N = (m_Λ^N, x_j^N for the framing variables, (1+y_i)^{p^N} − 1 for a basis δ_i = 1 + y_i of Δ_∞), which contains ker(S_∞ → T[Δ_N]) because the kernel of Δ_∞ → Δ_N lies in (p^N Z_p)^{2q}.
issues.reason: In §7.11, S_∞ = T[[Δ_∞]] with T a power series ring over the Iwasawa algebra Λ_I, and a surjection Δ_∞ ↠ Δ_N is fixed separately for each N. So S_N = T[Δ_N] is not Artinian and ker(S_∞ → S_N) is not open, and since the Taylor–Wiles data Q_N and the surjections are chosen independently, the kernels are not nested. The sentence 'this data satisfies the assumptions of Proposition 7.10.1' is therefore false as written. The repair is standard: 𝔟_N is open (it contains a power of the uniformizer, and y_i^{p^N} modulo the uniformizer), decreasing, with ∩_N 𝔟_N = 0 since (1+y)^{p^N} − 1 lies in m^{N+1}; reducing the data modulo 𝔟_N keeps modules finite, and preserves freeness and balancedness (base change does not change dim M/mM and cannot increase dim Tor_1); the λ-compatibilities pass to the quotients. Every conclusion of §7.11 stands. Found by the red team RT-PAPER-BOXER-CALEGARI-GEE-PILLONI-21 (finding /7) and confirmed by its verifier, who classified the false sentence as an error affecting the proof; recorded by FIX-RT-PAPER-BOXER-CALEGARI-GEE-PILLONI-21, which checked Proposition 7.10.1 and §7.11 in the arXiv v3 TeX source. Item 150 states the proposition in the repaired form.

For Y : y²+y = x⁵−x⁴+x³ the paper itself computes class 6G and notes good reduction at 2; Deuring–Šafarevič gives 2-rank 0 (a single branch point), so the reduction is good and non-ordinary; and the paper proves elsewhere that a rational Weierstrass point is *equivalent* to ρ̄_{A,2} factoring through a conjugate of S₅(b), which Y has. The paper's own remark, « this does not contradict Lemma [9.2.13] because … Y is not ordinary », is circular, since the lemma concludes ordinarity; the missing hypothesis is bad reduction, which the only application supplies (« any specialization … which does not have good reduction »).

issues.printed: The source chooses h ∈ 𝓗_g with map h : Res_{ℂ/ℝ}(𝔾_m) → G_ℝ, denotes its Hodge cocharacter by µ, and calls the associated Siegel parabolic P_µ. It defines M_µ to be the unipotent radical of P_µ.
issues.correction: "… and M_µ be the Levi of P_µ." Here M_µ is the Levi subgroup containing T, which is the centralizer of µ. With µ(z) = diag(Id_g, z·Id_g) it is isomorphic to GL_g × 𝔾_m. This is how §3.1, p. 33 defines it.
issues.reason:
The page image confirms the printed sentence word for word: "M_µ be the unipotent radical of P_µ". Every other use of M_µ in the paper, including the next sentences, treats it as the Levi of P_µ.

(i) p. 2: "Let us fix a maximal torus and a Borel T ⊆ B ⊆ P_µ ⊆ G. Let Rep(M_µ) be the category of finite dimensional algebraic representations of M_µ. Irreducible representations are labeled by M_µ-dominant weights κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{M_µ,+}. The tower of Shimura varieties carries a natural M_µ-torsor". The unipotent radical of the Siegel parabolic is the commutative vector group Sym² of dimension g(g+1)/2. In characteristic 0 its only irreducible algebraic representation is the trivial one, and it contains no maximal torus of G. So a labelling by dominant weights of T makes no sense for it. The automorphic vector bundles ω^κ come from representations of the Levi GL_g × 𝔾_m.

(ii) p. 2, §1.2: "the unipotent subgroup of the Borel of M_µ(ℤ_p)". This only makes sense if M_µ is reductive.

(iii) p. 3, §1.3: "W_M be the Weyl group of M_µ". Also ^MW is the set of minimal length representatives of W_M\W.

(iv) p. 4, §1.3.7: K_∞ ⊆ G(ℝ), the stabilizer of h, "is a real form of M_µ". K_∞ is compact modulo centre (a unitary group in g variables, with similitudes). It is a real form of GL_g × 𝔾_m, never of a unipotent group.

(v) §3.1, p. 33 sets up the notation correctly: "Let M_µ = M be the Levi and U_P be the unipotent radical." It also gives dominance "for the Levi M" as k_1 ≥ ⋯ ≥ k_g and says "W_M be the Weyl group of the Levi M". p. 36 says "We recall that M = M_µ is the Levi of P_µ = P."

So the words "unipotent radical" in §1.1 are a slip for "Levi". The paper's own conventions do not support the printed reading. Because §3 re-defines M_µ correctly and all proofs and results use it as the Levi, the slip affects nothing beyond this sentence of the introduction.

issues.locator: §1.2 (Hida theory), last sentence of the paragraph beginning "In [Pil20], we considered the case g = 2", p. 2. The 2024 preprint does not contain this sentence: its §1.2 says only "Results in this direction have already appeared in [Pil20], [BCGP21], [LPSZ19], [BP20] for g = 1 and g = 2". The whole paragraph describing the complex M^0 → M^1 of [Pil20], this sentence included, was added in the revision.
issues.printed: The source claims that M^0 and M^1 extend across the whole weight space and constitute higher Hida theories for H^0 and H^1, interpolating cohomology at regular weights.
issues.correction: Replace the sentence with one that says only what the paper proves: "In the current paper we construct higher Hida theories for H^0 and H^1 over the entire weight space. These are the complexes M^•_w for w = Id and for the element w_1 of length one of ^MW (§5.2, §5.4). They interpolate ordinary H^0 and H^1 in the regular weights with C(κ) = {Id}, resp. {w_1} (Corollary 4.5.5, Proposition 1.4.7). In the singular weights ω^{(k,2)} we have C(κ) = {Id, w_1}. There the Cousin spectral sequence (Theorem 4.5.2) computes the ordinary part of H^0 and H^1 at Iwahori level from their specialisations, which is the role that M^0 → M^1 plays in [Pil20]." The claim that the complex of [Pil20] is itself a restriction of M^•_Id and M^•_{w_1} should either be dropped or be stated and proved separately. Such a statement would have to pass from Iwahori level to Klingen level (see the reason).
issues.reason:
The sentence on p. 2 says that the paper shows that the terms M^0 and M^1 of the complex of [Pil20], which is built along the one-variable line of weights ω^{(k,2)}, extend over the whole weight space. The body never states or proves such a comparison. [Pil20] is cited in the body only twice, and neither citation concerns its complex M^0 → M^1. On p. 56, in the proof of Theorem 5.3.5, the ordinary cohomology of a kernel vanishes "as in [Pil20], sect. 10.7". On p. 63, in the proof of Proposition 6.2.13, the proof says "Compare with [Pil20], sect. 10.7". The weights ω^{(k,2)} and the singular line never reappear after p. 2.

The best defence is to read the sentence loosely, and in that sense the intended content is proved. The complexes M^•_Id and M^•_{w_1} are defined over Λ = Z_p[[T(Z_p)]] (§5.2, §5.4). They specialise in every locally algebraic weight (Theorem 5.3.5, Remark 5.4.3), and they interpolate regular-weight H^0 and H^1 (Corollary 4.5.5, Proposition 1.4.7). For κ = (k,2) we have C(κ) = {Id, w_1}, and the Cousin spectral sequence (Theorem 4.5.2) builds the ordinary H^0 and H^1 from their two specialisations. The notions of ordinarity also agree on Hecke parameters. By [Pil20] (the discussion of the T-operator before its §7.1), for r = 2 ordinarity for the Klingen operator diag(p², p, p, 1) is equivalent to Newton = Hodge, i.e. α_p β_p is a unit. That is also the condition of Definition 1.3.5.

The literal claim still needs an argument that is not formal and that the paper does not give. The objects differ as follows:
- **Level and ordinary projector.** [Pil20] works at Klingen level with the projector of the single operator U. The present paper works at (deep) Iwahori level with the T^{++}(Q_p)-ordinary projector.
- **Coefficients and support.** [Pil20] uses a sheaf F^κ over Z_p[[Z_p^×]] on the p-rank ≥ 1 locus, and its two terms come from the ordinary locus and from local cohomology along the p-rank-one locus. The paper uses Igusa towers with the support conditions of §§4–5.

The levels really do give different answers. Take an unramified π_p with slopes (0, 0, k+1, k+1) and α_p ≠ β_p:
- On the Klingen invariants of π_p (dimension 4), the Klingen U has eigenvalues proportional to α_pβ_p, α_pγ_p, β_pδ_p and γ_pδ_p. Only the first is a unit, so π_p contributes once to the complex of [Pil20].
- The stabiliser of the singular ν+ρ has order 2, so π_p has two characters that are ordinary in weight κ (orderings (α, β, γ, δ) and (β, α, δ, γ)). So π_p contributes twice to the Iwahori-level abutment.

Hence the specialisations of M^•_Id and M^•_{w_1} along the line are not literally the terms of the complex of [Pil20]. At best that complex is a Klingen-level descent or direct factor of them, which the paper does not construct.

The paper also proves only that M^•_{w_1,cusp} has amplitude [0, 1] (Proposition 5.6.3). So even its restriction to the line is not shown to be a module in degree 1, as M^1 is in [Pil20].

Consequences: the passage is used nowhere later in the paper. No numbered statement and no proof depends on it, and Theorems 1.4.3, 1.4.8 and 4.5.2 are unaffected. The rewording given in the correction describes accurately what the paper proves, and it is the minimal fix. The kind is a gap because the sentence asserts a comparison with the complex of [Pil20] that is nowhere proved; it affects nothing because no later statement or proof uses it.

issues.printed: The source defines C(κ) = {w ∈ ^MW, −w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) ∈ X^⋆(T)^+}, and for any w ∈ C(κ) sets ν + ρ = −w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ).
issues.correction: C(κ) = {w ∈ ^MW : −w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) ∈ X^⋆(T)^+_Q}. The dominance condition has to be read in X^⋆(T)_Q. This is how the body defines the set on p. 48: "C(κ) = {w ∈ ^MW, w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) ∈ X^⋆(T)^−_Q}".
issues.reason: The paper's coordinates (§3.1, pp. 33–34) are X^⋆(T) = {(k_1,…,k_g;k) ∈ Z^g×Z : Σk_i ≡ k mod 2}. Roots are trivial on the centre, so they have k = 0. Computing directly from the Borel of p. 34 gives ρ = (−1,−2,…,−g; 0), which is dominant for 0 ≥ k_1 ≥ … ≥ k_g. Because Σρ_i = −g(g+1)/2, ρ lies in X^⋆(T) exactly when g ≡ 0 or 3 mod 4. Take κ ∈ X^⋆(T). For every u ∈ W, uρ − ρ lies in the root lattice, and 2ρ ∈ X^⋆(T). Hence −w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) ≡ ρ modulo X^⋆(T). So when g ≡ 1 or 2 mod 4, which includes g = 1 and g = 2, this element is never in X^⋆(T). On p. 34, X^⋆(T)^+ is a subset of X^⋆(T), so the set as printed is empty. For example, when g = 1 we have ρ = (−1;0), and w = 1 gives (1−k_1; −k), whose coordinate sum 1−k_1+k is odd. That contradicts the next sentence ("If ν+ρ is regular, then the set C(κ) contains a unique element") and Remark 1.4.5 (#C(κ) = 1). With the rational dominant cone, as on p. 48, everything is consistent: ν = −w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) − ρ is integral, as Theorem 1.4.3(5) requires. The intended meaning is clear from p. 48.

issues.locator: §1.3.4 (The ordinary part of classical cohomology), displayed quasi-isomorphism at the end of the subsection, p. 3. The 2024 preprint has the same text (§1.3.3, p. 3).
issues.printed: RΓ(S^tor_{K^pK_p}, ω^κ)^{ord} = J_B^{ord}(colim_K RΓ(S^tor_{K,Σ}, ω^κ))^{T_{K_p}}
issues.correction: RΓ(S^tor_{K^pK_p}, ω^κ)^{ord} = J_B^{ord}(colim_{K'_p} RΓ(S^tor_{K^pK'_p,Σ}, ω^κ))^{T_{K_p}}, with the tame level K^p fixed. Equivalently, take K^p-invariants of colim_K RΓ(S^tor_{K,Σ}, ω^κ) before applying J_B^{ord}.
issues.reason: On p. 2, colim_K RΓ(S^tor_{K,Σ}, ω^κ) is the colimit over all compact open K ⊆ G(A_f), a complex of smooth G(A_f)-representations. Take its Jacquet module with respect to B ⊆ G(Q_p), then T_{K_p}-invariants and the ordinary part. The result is a smooth G(A_f^p)-representation, namely colim_{K^p} RΓ(S^tor_{K^pK_p}, ω^κ)^{ord}. It does not depend on K^p, whereas the left side has fixed tame level K^p. Also, p. 3 defines J_B only for smooth admissible representations of G(Q_p). The full colimit is not admissible as a G(Q_p)-representation, because its K_p-invariants are the colimit over K^p of the level-K^pK_p cohomologies. The colimit over K'_p with K^p fixed is admissible. With K^p fixed, the display is the standard identity (the canonical lifting of Casselman). The intended meaning is clear.

issues.locator: §1.3.7, Theorem 1.3.8, p. 4. The January 2024 preprint has the same statement as Theorem 1.3.7 (§1.3.6, p. 3 of the preprint), with (𝔭, K∞) in place of (𝔭_µ, K∞). The mistake was therefore already in the preprint and was not fixed in the revision.
issues.printed: Theorem 1.3.8, citing [Har90], thm. 3.4, asserts that κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{Mµ,+} and w ∈ C(κ) determine a unique nondegenerate limit of discrete series π∞(κ, w) of G(R), such that π∞(κ, w) ⊗ Vκ has cohomology for (𝔭_µ, K∞) in degree ℓ(w).
issues.correction:
Drop the claim that the cohomological degree characterises the representation. A correct form: "Let κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{Mµ,+} and w ∈ C(κ). There is a non-degenerate limit of discrete series π∞(κ, w) of G(R), determined by κ and w, such that π∞(κ, w) ⊗ Vκ has (𝔭_µ, K∞)-cohomology in degree ℓ(w)." Here κ fixes the Harish-Chandra parameter λ = −w_{0,M}(κ + ρ). The element w fixes the Weyl chamber w·C⁺, where C⁺ is the dominant chamber; the closure of w·C⁺ contains λ. π∞(κ, w) is the representation of G(R) induced from the limit of discrete series of G(R)^+ with these data. The degree ℓ(w) alone determines π∞(κ, w) only when no other element of C(κ) of the same length gives a different representation. For G(R) = GSp_{2g}(R) this fails for every g ≥ 4.

In the other direction, distinct elements of C(κ) give distinct limits of discrete series of G(R)^+, but not necessarily distinct representations of GSp_{2g}(R). The elements w and w_{0,M} w w_0 give the same representation of G(R) whenever both lie in C(κ). This happens exactly when κ = −w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_nc on the derived group. The simplest case is g = 1 in weight one: the weight-one limit of discrete series of GL_2(R) contributes to both H^0 and H^1.
issues.reason:
Conventions of §3.1 (pp. 33–34). X⋆(T)^+ is given by 0 ≥ k_1 ≥ … ≥ k_g, and Mµ-dominance by k_1 ≥ … ≥ k_g. The positive roots are e_i − e_j and −e_i − e_j (i < j) and −2e_i, with simple roots −2e_1 and the e_i − e_{i+1}. So ρ = (−1, −2, …, −g) on the derived group. The roots of M are the e_i − e_j, W_M = S_g, and d = g(g+1)/2. Put λ = −w_{0,M}(κ + ρ). The definition on p. 3 then reads C(κ) = {w ∈ ^MW : w(ν + ρ) = λ}. Since κ + ρ is strictly decreasing, λ is regular for the roots of M. So every w ∈ W with w(ν + ρ) = λ lies in ^MW, and C(κ) is a coset of the stabiliser of ν + ρ.

Counterexample for g = 4. Take κ = (3,3,3,3; k) with k even; this is parallel weight 3. Then κ + ρ = (2, 1, 0, −1), λ = (1, 0, −1, −2) and ν + ρ = (0, −1, −1, −2). The stabiliser of ν + ρ is generated by the reflections in −2e_1 and e_2 − e_3 and has order 4. So C(κ) has four elements:
- x ↦ (−x_2, x_1, x_3, x_4), of length 2;
- w: x ↦ (−x_2, −x_1, x_3, x_4), of length 3;
- w′: x ↦ (−x_3, x_1, x_2, x_4), of length 3;
- x ↦ (−x_3, −x_1, x_2, x_4), of length 4.
Each sends ν + ρ to λ and maps the dominant cone into the Mµ-dominant cone. The positive roots made negative are −e_1 − e_2, −2e_1, −2e_2 for w, and e_1 − e_3, e_2 − e_3, −2e_3 for w′. So ℓ(w) = ℓ(w′) = 3.

Identify the compact Cartan of K∞ with T, so that the compact roots are the roots of M. As in [Har90], each u ∈ C(κ) corresponds to the limit of discrete series π(λ, uC⁺) of G(R)^+ with Harish-Chandra parameter λ and chamber uC⁺. Here π(λ, uC⁺) ⊗ Vκ has (𝔭_µ, K∞)-cohomology in degree ℓ(u) and in no other degree. π(λ, uC⁺) is non-degenerate because λ is regular for every compact root. By Knapp–Zuckerman, π(λ, wC⁺) ≅ π(λ, w′C⁺) would require an element of W_K = W_M that fixes λ and carries wC⁺ to w′C⁺. Since λ is M-regular, that element is trivial, so the two representations of G(R)^+ are inequivalent.

The same holds for G(R) = GSp_8(R). K∞ lies in G(R)^+, which has index 2. An element δ of similitude −1 normalises K∞ and inverts its compact Cartan. Hence δπ(λ, uC⁺) ≅ π(λ*, w_{0,M}uw_0·C⁺) with λ* = −w_{0,M}λ = (2, 1, 0, −1), which is not W_M-conjugate to λ. So each π(λ, uC⁺) induces to an irreducible representation of G(R) whose restriction to G(R)^+ is π(λ, uC⁺) ⊕ δπ(λ, uC⁺). The inductions for w and w′ are non-isomorphic, because π(λ, w′C⁺) is neither π(λ, wC⁺) nor δπ(λ, wC⁺).

For u = w or w′, the δ-constituent belongs to the Serre-dual weight κ* = −w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_nc = (2,2,2,2) and to the element w_{0,M}uw_0 ∈ C(κ*), of length 10 − 3 = 7. Its cohomology is against V_{κ*}, and it has none against Vκ, because its parameter λ* is not W_M-conjugate to λ. So G(R) has two non-isomorphic non-degenerate limits of discrete series, each with (𝔭_µ, K∞)-cohomology against Vκ in degree 3 = ℓ(w) = ℓ(w′), and in that degree only. This contradicts the uniqueness asserted in the theorem.

If instead the parameter attached to κ is normalised as κ + ρ = λ*, each π(λ, uC⁺) is replaced by its δ-conjugate, and the representations of G(R) are the same. The weights (2,2,2,2) and (2,2,2,0) give further examples for g = 4: in each, C(κ) has lengths 6, 7, 7, 8 and λ ≠ −w_{0,M}λ.

Every g ≥ 4. Take κ = (3,3,3,3,0,…,0; k) with k even. Then ν + ρ = (0, −1, −1, −2, −5, −6, …, −g) and λ = (g, …, 6, 5, 1, 0, −1, −2). The stabiliser of ν + ρ is generated by the commuting simple reflections in −2e_1 and e_2 − e_3. So C(κ) is m times this group of order 4, with m of minimal length in the coset, and its lengths are ℓ(m), ℓ(m) + 1, ℓ(m) + 1, ℓ(m) + 2. For example they are 7, 8, 8, 9 for g = 5. Since −2 is an entry of λ and 2 is not, λ* is not W_M-conjugate to λ, and the argument above applies unchanged.

Small g.
- For g ≤ 2 the lengths on ^MW (0, 1, resp. 0, 1, 2, 3) are pairwise distinct, so the question does not arise.
- For g = 3 the lengths on ^MW are 0, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6. The two elements of length 3 are x ↦ (−x_2, −x_1, x_3) and x ↦ (−x_3, x_1, x_2). Both lie in C(κ) only when ν + ρ = (0, b, b) with b < 0. Then λ = (−b, 0, b) = −w_{0,M}λ. An example is κ = (2,2,2), where C(κ) has lengths 2, 3, 3, 4.
- The involution w ↦ w_{0,M} w w_0 of ^MW has no fixed points, because w_0 = −1 is central in W and w_{0,M} ≠ w_0. So in this case it exchanges the two elements of length 3. Their limits of discrete series of G(R)^+ are δ-conjugate, and together they form one irreducible representation of GSp_6(R). For κ = (2,2,2), Blattner's formula gives their lowest K-types as (1, 1, −2) and (2, −1, −1), and x ↦ −w_{0,M}x exchanges them.
So for G(R) = GSp_{2g}(R) the uniqueness holds for g ≤ 3 and fails for every g ≥ 4. For G(R)^+ or Sp_{2g}(R) it already fails for g = 3.

The paper itself allows several elements of C(κ) of the same length. Theorem 1.4.3(5) (p. 5) and Theorem 4.5.2 (p. 51) sum over the w ∈ C(κ) of a given length (ℓ(w) = a, resp. ℓ(w) = p).

Classification. The uniqueness is a substantive claim, false as printed, and not a slip whose intended meaning is clear from context; so this is an error. What is false is the numbered Theorem 1.3.8 itself, so the error affects a stated result. Its reach ends there. Theorem 1.3.8 is a recollection in the introduction, and limits of discrete series appear nowhere else in the paper. The sentence after it (π_f ↪ colim_K H^{ℓ(w)}) is indexed by w ∈ C(κ) and does not use uniqueness. The same holds for the Cousin spectral sequence (Theorem 1.4.3(5), Theorem 4.5.2). So no proof in the paper depends on the uniqueness, and the main results are unaffected.

issues.locator: §1.3.7 (Archimedean representation theory and limits of discrete series), the paragraph after Theorem 1.3.8, p. 4. The 2024 preprint has the same text in §1.3.6, after Theorem 1.3.7, p. 3.
issues.printed: For an automorphic representation π = π∞(κ, w) ⊗ πf, the source claims πf ↪ colimK H^{ℓ(w)}(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, ω^κ) ⊗ ℂ. It further says that w = Id makes π∞(κ, Id) a limit of discrete series of holomorphic type, with holomorphic modular forms generate π.
issues.correction: Add the word "cuspidal": "Let π = π∞(κ, w) ⊗ πf be a cuspidal automorphic representation. Then πf ↪ colim_K H^{ℓ(w)}(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, ω^κ) ⊗ C." This is the standard statement from Harris: cusp forms of ∂̄-cohomology type give classes in the coherent cohomology of the canonical extension. The failure only happens when ℓ(w) ≥ 1. For w = Id, a holomorphic automorphic form of moderate growth is a section of ω^κ over the toroidal compactification, and H^0 is left exact. So the degree-0 case, and the following sentence about w = Id, hold for every automorphic π.
issues.reason:
The paper sets G = GSp_{2g}, and nothing in this recollection excludes g = 1. Take g = 1, so G = GL_2. M_µ is then the torus, ^M W = {Id, w_0}, and ℓ(w_0) = 1. Fix k ≥ 3 and the weight κ with ω^κ = ω^{2−k} in classical notation. Then C(κ) = {w_0}, and π∞(κ, w_0) is the antiholomorphic discrete series D_k^- (after matching the central character by a twist). This is the representation that computes H^1(X, ω^{2−k}) by Dolbeault cohomology.

(1) A non-cuspidal π of this type exists. A holomorphic Eisenstein series of weight k (for example E_4 at level SL_2(ℤ), or a weight-k Eisenstein series of level Γ_1(N)) generates the automorphic representation D_k^+ ⊗ πf. At every unramified ℓ, πf has the component Ind(|·|^{(k−1)/2}, |·|^{−(k−1)/2}), up to a twist; this is irreducible because k − 1 ≠ ±1. Its T_ℓ eigenvalue is 1 + ℓ^{k−1}, so the normalized Satake parameters are {ℓ^{(k−1)/2}, ℓ^{−(k−1)/2}}. The complex conjugate of this Eisenstein series, twisted by a power of |ν| if needed, generates an automorphic representation π' = D_k^- ⊗ π'_f. Here π'_f is a twist of the contragredient of πf, so its Satake parameters at ℓ still have ratio of absolute value ℓ^{±(k−1)}. Hence π' has the form π∞(κ, w_0) ⊗ π'_f, with π' automorphic but not cuspidal.

(2) Such a π'_f cannot occur in H^1. On the compactified modular curve, Kodaira–Spencer gives Ω^1 = ω^2(−D). Serre duality then gives H^1(X_K, ω^{2−k})^∨ ≅ H^0(X_K, ω^k(−D)) = S_k(K), compatibly with Hecke correspondences up to a twist by a character. So colimK H^1(X_K, ω^{2−k}) ⊗ ℂ is a character twist of the smooth dual of colimK S_k(K) ⊗ ℂ = ⊕ σ_f, the sum over cuspidal σ of weight k. Every irreducible subrepresentation is therefore σ_f^∨ ⊗ χ for a cuspidal σ. At unramified ℓ, its Satake parameters have ratio of absolute value 1: this follows from Deligne's theorem, or already from the Hecke bound |a_ℓ| = O(ℓ^{k/2}) against ℓ^{k−1} for large ℓ, since k ≥ 3. So π'_f does not embed into colimK H^1(S^{tor}_K, ω^κ) ⊗ ℂ, and the printed statement fails for w = w_0.

For w = Id the non-cuspidal statement does hold, because holomorphic Eisenstein series lie in H^0(X, ω^k) for the canonical extension. That is presumably why the slip goes unnoticed in the next sentence. The statement is an introductory recollection and is not used later in the paper, so no result depends on it. As printed, the statement is false for non-cuspidal π. Counterexample: take g = 1 and G = GL2, so that M_µ = T, ^MW = W = {1, s} and ℓ(s) = 1. Take k = 4 (any k ≥ 3 works). Let κ be the weight with ω^κ = ω^{2−k} = ω^{−2} in classical notation, with the matching similitude component. Then ν + ρ is regular and C(κ) = {s}. The representation π∞(κ, s) of Theorem 1.3.8 is the antiholomorphic discrete series of weight k (or the full discrete series D_k, if G(R)-representations are meant). Now take the automorphic representation π generated by the complex conjugate of the level-one Eisenstein series E_4 (or by E_4 itself, in the G(R) reading). Its archimedean component is π∞(κ, s). Its finite part πf is unramified everywhere, with T_ℓ-eigenvalue 1 + ℓ^3, so the ratio of its Satake parameters at ℓ is ℓ^{±3}. The hypothesis of the sentence is therefore satisfied.

On the other side, look at the compactified modular curve with the canonical extension. There Ω^1 = ω^2(−D) (Kodaira–Spencer), so Serre duality gives H^1(X_K, ω^{2−k}) ≅ H^0(X_K, ω^k(−D))^∨ = S_k(K)^∨, compatibly with Hecke operators. Hence colim_K H^1(X_K, ω^{2−k}) ⊗ C is, up to a twist by a character, the smooth dual of the space of weight-k cusp forms. Every irreducible subrepresentation of it is a twist of the contragredient of the finite part of a cuspidal representation. For such a representation the ratio of Satake parameters at unramified ℓ has absolute value 1 (Deligne), and neither twisting nor taking contragredients changes that. So πf does not embed, and does not even occur as a subquotient; this was checked by direct computation of the Satake ratios above.

Attempted defences, none of which works:
(a) The paper never defines "automorphic representation" as cuspidal. In §1.1 it refers to [Su24] for computing coherent cohomology by automorphic forms, which suggests general automorphic forms.
(b) That comparison does not rescue the claim. (p,K)-cohomology is not left exact in positive degree, so a subrepresentation π of the space of automorphic forms need not inject on H^{ℓ(w)}; the example above is exactly such a case.
(c) The citation [Har90, thm. 3.4] supports only the archimedean statement (Theorem 1.3.8). The embedding is Harris's result for cusp forms.
The intended meaning is almost certainly "cuspidal", and with that word added the sentence is correct. As printed, though, it is a false statement, not a slip that the context repairs.

Consequences: the sentence is part of an introductory "we recall" paragraph and has no proof. Nothing later in the paper refers to §1.3.7, Theorem 1.3.8 or this embedding. The main results (Theorem 1.4.3, Proposition 1.4.7, Theorem 1.4.8, and §§4–6) are about the ordinary parts of coherent cohomology and do not use it. The proposed correction is right and minimal. Restricting to w = Id would also make the sentence true, but "cuspidal" is the intended form.

issues.locator: §1.4, Theorem 1.4.8, p. 5. The body version is Theorem 5.5.2, p. 57: "We have a perfect pairing M^•_w ⊗ M^•_{w_{0,M}ww_0,cusp} → Λ[−d], for which the adjoint of t is w_0t^{−1}". Here the tensor has no subscript and the Λ-structure is not specified. The 2024 preprint has the same text: Theorem 1.4.8 on p. 5, which differs only in reading "for some prime ℓ ≠ p", and Theorem 5.5.2 on p. 56. The mistake was therefore already in the preprint and was not fixed in the revision.
issues.printed: Theorem 1.4.8 asserts perfection of the pairing M^•_w ⊗_Λ M^•_{w_{0,M}ww_0,cusp} → Λ[−d]. It assigns adjoints w_0t^{−1} to t ∈ T(Q_p) and [K_ℓg^{−1}K_ℓ] to [K_ℓgK_ℓ], for any prime ℓ ≠ p with g ∈ G(Q_ℓ) and K_ℓ = G(Z_ℓ). It claims compatibility with classical Serre duality upon specialization at dominant locally algebraic weights.
issues.correction: Twist the Λ-structure of the second factor by the involution ι of Λ = Z_p[[T(Z_p)]] induced by t ↦ w_0t^{−1}. For GSp_{2g} this involution is t ↦ c(t)^{−1}t, where c is the similitude character. The corrected statement is: there is a perfect pairing M^•_w ⊗_Λ ι^*M^•_{w_{0,M}ww_0,cusp} → Λ[−d]. Equivalently, ⟨λx, y⟩ = ⟨x, ι(λ)y⟩ = λ⟨x, y⟩, so that M^•_{w_{0,M}ww_0,cusp} ≅ ι^*RHom_Λ(M^•_w, Λ)[−d]. The adjoint of t ∈ T(Q_p) is w_0t^{−1}, as printed. In the compatibility clause, the first factor is specialized at ν and the second at ν∘ι: the weights (κ, χ) and (−w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_nc, w_0χ^{−1}) of Theorem 5.5.1. The same reading should be given to the unsubscripted ⊗ of Theorem 5.5.2.
issues.reason:
1. The paper defines M^•_w and M^•_{w,cusp} for every w by the same formula, RHom_{T(Z_p)}(1, RΓ_w(K^p, cusp/∅) ⊗̂_{Z_p} Λ) (p. 5 and §5.4, p. 56). On these invariants, the action of t ∈ T(Z_p) through the cohomology factor equals multiplication by a fixed unit λ_t ∈ Λ, which is [t] or [t]^{−1} depending on the convention for the T(Z_p)-action on Λ. The same recipe gives the same λ_t for every w. For central t the twist of the T(Q_p)-action by w (p. 55) plays no role.

2. Take z = a·1_{2g} central with a ∈ Z_p^×. Then w_0z^{−1} = z^{−1}. The notation ⊗_Λ means the pairing is balanced, so ⟨zx, y⟩ = ⟨λ_z x, y⟩ = ⟨x, λ_z y⟩. The stated adjoint rule gives instead ⟨zx, y⟩ = ⟨x, z^{−1}y⟩ = ⟨x, λ_z^{−1}y⟩. The pairing is perfect, so λ_z² − 1 would act as zero on M^•_w, and its specialization at any ν with ν(z)² ≠ 1 would vanish. By Proposition 1.4.7 (p. 5) that specialization is the classical ordinary cohomology RΓ(S^tor, ω^κ)^ord ⊗ Q_p(ζ_{p^n})[χ]. This group is not zero for all weights whose central character has infinite order: for example, with g = 1 and w = Id, ordinary cusp forms exist in infinitely many such weights. So the pairing cannot be both Λ-balanced and have adjoint w_0t^{−1}.

3. The paper's own finite-level statement gives the same conclusion. Theorem 5.5.1 (p. 57) pairs RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ) with RΓ_{w_{0,M}ww_0}(K^p, −w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_nc, w_0χ^{−1}, cusp). Here κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν_alg + ρ) − ρ (p. 56). Using w_{0,M}ρ = −ρ_c + ρ_nc and w_0ρ = −ρ, the partner weight corresponds to the character ν' = (−w_0ν_alg)·(w_0χ^{−1}) = ν∘ι. This was checked by direct computation for g = 1, 2, 3 and every w in the Weyl group. On the centre, ν' = ν^{−1}. A Λ-bilinear pairing M ⊗_Λ N → Λ[−d] specializes at ν to a pairing of the two specializations at the same ν, which is not the classical duality.

4. The correction is consistent with both facts. Under ι, ⟨λ_z x, y⟩ = ⟨x, λ_{ι(z)}y⟩ = ⟨x, (w_0z^{−1})y⟩, and the specialization of ι^*N at ν equals the specialization of N at ν∘ι. The formula ι(t) = c(t)^{−1}t for GSp_{2g} was also checked by direct computation. 1. How T(Z_p) acts. Both factors are defined in the same way (p. 5; §5.4, p. 56): M^•_w = RHom_{T(Z_p)}(1, RΓ_w(K^p) ⊗̂_{Z_p} Λ), where T(Z_p) acts diagonally, and M^•_{w,cusp} is defined in the same way. T(Q_p) acts through its action on RΓ_w(K^p). This is the action used in every "T(Q_p)-equivariant" statement and in the diamond operators of Proposition 1.4.7. On the diagonal invariants, t ∈ T(Z_p) acting on the first factor is the same as multiplication by the unit [t]^{−1} ∈ Λ. So on M^•_w and on M^•_{w',cusp} (w' = w_{0,M}ww_0), every t ∈ T(Z_p) ⊂ T(Q_p) acts by the same scalar of Λ.

2. What a Λ-balanced pairing forces. If the pairing is balanced over Λ with these structures, then ⟨[t]^{−1}x, y⟩ = ⟨x, [t]^{−1}y⟩, so each t ∈ T(Z_p) is its own adjoint.

3. Why this contradicts the adjoint clause. Use the conventions of §3.1 (p. 33): W is the set of permutations w with w(i) + w(2g+1−i) = 2g+1, and T = {diag(t_i) : t_i t_{2g+1−i} = c}. Then w_0 is i ↦ 2g+1−i, so w_0(t) = c(t)t^{−1} and w_0t^{−1} = c(t)^{−1}t. For a scalar z ∈ Z(Z_p) we get w_0z^{−1} = z^{−1} ≠ z. Combining step 2 with the stated adjoint gives ⟨x, ([z] − [z]^{−1})y⟩ = 0 for all x, y. Since the pairing is perfect, [z]^2 − 1 would annihilate the cohomology of M^•_{w',cusp}. Its specializations would then vanish at every weight ν with ν(z)^2 ≠ 1. By Proposition 1.4.7 (the cuspidal case), these specializations are classical ordinary coherent cohomology, which is nonzero in weights with nontrivial central weight. For example, take g = 1, w = Id and w' = w_0: the specializations are Serre-dual to ordinary cusp forms, whose central characters vary with the weight.

4. The paper's own Theorem 5.5.1 (p. 57) points the same way. It pairs weight (κ, χ) of w with weight (−w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_nc, w_0χ^{−1}) of w'. Write κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν+ρ) − ρ and use w_{0,M}ρ = ρ_nc − ρ_M and −w_0ρ = ρ. Then −w_{0,M}κ − 2ρ_nc = −w_{0,M}w'(ν'+ρ) − ρ with ν' = −w_0ν, that is, ν'(t) = ν(w_0t^{−1}). This identity was checked by direct computation for all w ∈ W when g = 1, 2, 3. The finite part matches as well: χ' = w_0χ^{−1} = χ∘ι. So the dual factor is the specialization of M^•_{w'} at ν∘ι, not at ν. In the coordinates of §3.1, ι fixes the k_i and changes k to −k. A ⊗_Λ pairing specializes both factors at the same point, so it can agree with Theorem 5.5.1, as the last sentence of Theorem 1.4.8 claims, only at weights that are trivial on the centre.

5. The defence fails. The Λ-structure on M^• is fixed by its definition, and nothing in the paper twists it on the second factor. A reading in which T(Z_p) acts trivially on M^• contradicts the T(Q_p)-action the paper uses. Theorem 5.5.1, the specialized statement, is correct. The proof of Theorem 5.5.2 "as in the previous theorem" produces the ι-twisted pairing, so the fix is the twist.

6. What depends on it. Remark 5.6.2 and the length-two case in the proof of Proposition 5.6.3 (p. 58, "prove the dual statement for the non-cuspidal cohomology") use the duality only for amplitudes, checked at all residual characters. ι^* is an exact autoequivalence of perfect Λ-complexes: it preserves amplitude and permutes the residual characters. So these arguments are unaffected. Remark 6.2.18 uses the duality of Lemma 5.4.2, not Serre duality. The Hecke operators t ∉ T(Z_p) and the prime-to-p adjoints are unaffected. Only the statement of Theorem 1.4.8, and the unsubscripted Theorem 5.5.2 if read as Λ-bilinear, needs correcting.

issues.correction: Add "where d = g(g+1)/2 is the dimension of the Siegel Shimura variety" (equivalently, of the Igusa varieties) in Theorem 1.4.8 and in Theorems 5.5.1 and 5.5.2.
issues.reason: The letter d is never defined as a dimension anywhere in the paper. Its only other use has a different meaning: on p. 40, A_{g,d} is the moduli stack with a polarization of degree d^2. The shift comes from Serre duality, via D_X = RHom(−, p^!O_S) and Theorem 2.7.4 (pp. 23–24), for the ordinary part of the cohomology of the Igusa varieties. These varieties have relative dimension g(g+1)/2, which is the dimension of S_K. The shift is also forced by the amplitudes. Direct computation for g ≤ 4 confirms that w ↦ w_{0,M}ww_0 preserves ^MW and satisfies ℓ(w_{0,M}ww_0) = g(g+1)/2 − ℓ(w). The amplitudes [ℓ(w), g(g+1)/2] for the non-cuspidal theory and [0, g(g+1)/2 − ℓ(w)] for the cuspidal theory (Theorem 1.4.3(2),(3)) are exchanged under RHom_Λ(−,Λ)[−d] only when d = g(g+1)/2. Experts can infer the intended meaning.

issues.reason: §5.4 (p. 56) defines M^•_w and M^•_{w,cusp} with ⊗̂_{Z_p}. The proof of Lemma 5.4.1 (perfectness) rests on RHom_{T′(Z_p)}(1, C^0(T′(Z_p),Z_p) ⊗̂_{Z_p} Λ) = Λ[0], and Lemma 5.4.2 also uses ⊗̂. By Theorem 1.4.3(1) and Definition 1.4.1, RΓ_w(K^p) is represented by a complex whose terms are C^0(T′(Z_p),Z_p)^{n_i}. These terms are not finitely generated over Z_p. The algebraic tensor product C^0(T′(Z_p),Z_p) ⊗_{Z_p} Λ is only the submodule of C^0(T′(Z_p),Λ) = C^0(T′(Z_p),Z_p) ⊗̂ Λ made of functions whose values lie in a finitely generated Z_p-submodule. The invariant function that corresponds to 1 ∈ Λ is x ↦ [x]^{±1}. The group elements [x] are Z_p-linearly independent, so this function is not in the algebraic tensor product. Hence the key identity Λ[0] fails for ⊗. The intended meaning is clear from the pointer to §5.4.

issues.locator: §1.4, Proposition 1.4.7, p. 5: the definition of κ and the right-hand side of the display. §5.4, Remark 5.4.3, p. 57: the definition of κ. The 2024 preprint has the same text in Proposition 1.4.7 (p. 5) and in Remark 5.4.3 (p. 55).
issues.printed: Proposition 1.4.7 takes ν = ν_{alg}χ : T(ℤ_p) → ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n})^×, ν_{alg} ∈ X^⋆(T)^+, χ of finite order, and κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν + ρ) − ρ, and asserts M^•_w ⊗_{Λ,−ν} ℚ_p(ζ_{p^n}) = RΓ(S^{tor}_{K^pK_p}, ω^κ)^{ord} ⊗_{ℚ_p} ℚ_p(ζ_p^n)[χ]. Remark 5.4.3 allows ν_{alg} ∈ X^⋆(T) and asserts M^•_w ⊗_{Λ,−ν} ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n}) = RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ).
issues.correction: In Proposition 1.4.7, read "for κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν_{alg} + ρ) − ρ, we have: M^•_w ⊗_{Λ,−ν} ℚ_p(ζ_{p^n}) = RΓ(S^{tor}_{K^pK_p}, ω^κ)^{ord} ⊗_{ℚ_p} ℚ_p(ζ_{p^n})[χ]". In Remark 5.4.3, read "for κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν_{alg} + ρ) − ρ, we have: M^•_w ⊗_{Λ,−ν} ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n}) = RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ)". This is the definition of κ that the paper itself fixes at the end of §5.3, p. 56.
issues.reason:
(1) The coefficient field in Proposition 1.4.7. The left-hand side of the display is over ℚ_p(ζ_{p^n}). On the right-hand side, however, the exponent n is printed on ζ_p (ζ_p^n) instead of in the subscript. Read literally, ζ_p^n is the n-th power of a primitive p-th root of unity. Then ℚ_p(ζ_p^n) ⊆ ℚ_p(ζ_p): it equals ℚ_p(ζ_p) if p ∤ n and ℚ_p if p | n. For n ≥ 2 this field is strictly smaller than ℚ_p(ζ_{p^n}), which has degree p^{n−1}(p−1) over ℚ_p. The two sides of the stated equality would then not have the same scalars. The field is meant to be ℚ_p(ζ_{p^n}) on both sides: χ takes values in ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n})^×, and on the same page Theorem 1.4.3(4) and (5) and Remark 1.4.6 all extend scalars to ℚ_p(ζ_{p^n}). This slip does not recur in Remark 5.4.3 on p. 57, where the coefficients are correctly printed as ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n}).

(2) The weight κ in Proposition 1.4.7 and Remark 5.4.3. Both passages form κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν + ρ) − ρ from ν = ν_{alg}χ.

The sheaf ω^κ is defined only for an algebraic weight κ ∈ X^⋆(T)^{M,+} (§5.3.1, p. 55; compare Theorem 1.4.3(4), p. 5). Likewise, the notation RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ) is introduced on p. 56 only for κ formed from the algebraic part ν_{alg}. But ν = ν_{alg}χ is a character of T(ℤ_p) with values in ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n})^×, and it is the restriction of an algebraic character only when χ is trivial. The reason is that a character of T that is algebraic and has finite order on the Zariski-dense subgroup T(ℤ_p) is trivial. So for χ ≠ 1 the printed κ is only locally algebraic. Then ω^κ is not defined, and κ is not a weight for which RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ) has been given a meaning.

The finite-order part χ is already accounted for elsewhere. In Proposition 1.4.7 it enters through the χ-isotypic part [χ]. In Remark 5.4.3 it enters through the definition RΓ_w(K^p, κ, χ) = RHom_{T(ℤ_p)}(ν, RΓ_w(K^p) ⊗ ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n})).

The paper states the intended formula in its definitions at the end of §5.3, p. 56: "Let ν = ν_{alg}χ : T(ℤ_p) → ℤ_p(ζ_{p^n})^×, with ν_{alg} ∈ X^⋆(T) and χ a finite order character. Let κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν_{alg}+ρ)−ρ." In the regular-weight case, Theorem 1.4.3(4) applies the same formula to an algebraic ν ∈ X^⋆(T)^+. In the 2024 preprint, the corresponding definition (p. 54) also read κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν + ρ) − ρ. The revision corrected it to ν_{alg} there, but not in Proposition 1.4.7 or in Remark 5.4.3.

Both slips are notational, and the intended statements are clear from p. 56 and from Theorem 1.4.3. The rest of the paper takes κ algebraic and treats χ separately, for instance in Proposition 6.2.6 (p. 61) and Theorem 6.2.9 (p. 62). Nothing later uses the misprinted forms. These are therefore misprints, and the mathematics is unaffected.

issues.locator: §2.1.1, proof of Lemma 2.1.6, p. 7. The 2024 preprint (also p. 7) has a different proof. It takes "an arbitrary extension of 𝒢 to X̄ by [Sta22], TAG 01PE", performs "a suitable blow-up X̄′" and cites [RG71], thm. 5.2.2 (flattening by blow-up), whose hypotheses hold here. The preprint's statement also does not ask for strict maps. So the issue was introduced in the revision.
issues.printed: Lemma 2.1.6 asserts that compactifications (j_X : X ↪ X̄) allowing a finite rank locally free sheaf 𝓕 on X to extend as a locally free sheaf are cofinal, using strict maps. Starting from any X̄, its proof extends 𝓕 coherently to 𝓕̄ using [Sta22], Tag 0G41, then invokes Tag 0ESN to make the strict transform locally free by a suitable blow-up.
issues.correction: Replace the reference to Tag 0ESN by flattening by blow-up (Raynaud–Gruson [RG71], Thm. 5.2.2 = [Sta22], Tag 0815), applied to 𝓕̄ on X̄ with U = X. This is what the 2024 preprint cites. It gives a U-admissible blow-up X̄′ → X̄ (centre disjoint from X) after which the strict transform of 𝓕̄ is flat and of finite presentation, hence finite locally free, and restricts to 𝓕 on X. Because the centre misses X, the map X̄′ → X̄ is an isomorphism over X and hence strict. Alternatively, Tag 0ESN can be kept after one preparatory step. Replace X̄ by the disjoint union of the scheme-theoretic closures in X̄ of the finitely many open-and-closed pieces X_r ⊂ X on which 𝓕 has constant rank r. This map is strict, and X_r is scheme-theoretically dense in its closure. Then blow up the r-th Fitting ideal on each piece. Passing first to a compactification with Cartier boundary (Lemma 2.1.5) is another way to get density, but the constant-rank splitting is still needed.
issues.reason:
Tag 0ESN is Lemma 31.36.3 of the Stacks Project. It reads: "Let X be a scheme. Let 𝓕 be a finitely presented O_X-module. Let U ⊂ X be a scheme theoretically dense open such that 𝓕|_U is finite locally free of constant rank r." It then concludes that the blow-up in the r-th Fitting ideal is U-admissible and that the strict transform is locally free of rank r. In the proof, X̄ is an arbitrary compactification, and Definition 2.1.2 asks only for a proper X̄ with an open immersion of X. So X need not be scheme-theoretically dense, or even dense, in X̄. Also, 𝓕 is only locally free "of finite rank", so its rank may vary from one connected component of X to another. The proof does not reduce to the case covered by the lemma, and without these hypotheses the lemma's conclusion fails. Two examples over S = Spec k, checked by direct computation:
(i) Density. Take X = A¹, X̄ = P¹ ⊔ Spec k[ε]/(ε²), 𝓕 = O_X, and 𝓕̄ = O_{P¹} on the first piece and k = k[ε]/(ε) on the second. The module k is cyclic, so Fit_1(𝓕̄) = O_X̄. The blow-up in Fit_1 is therefore the identity, and the strict transform is 𝓕̄ itself, which is not locally free at the extra point.
(ii) Constant rank. Take X = A¹ ⊔ A¹, X̄ = P¹ ⊔ P¹, 𝓕 = O ⊔ O², and 𝓕̄ = (O ⊕ k_∞) ⊔ (O² ⊕ k_∞). Here X is scheme-theoretically dense. Fit_1(𝓕̄) is zero on the second P¹, so blowing it up deletes that component and the blow-up is not X-admissible. Fit_2(𝓕̄) is the unit ideal on the first P¹, so blowing it up leaves O ⊕ k_∞ there, which is not locally free.
So the cited lemma does not give the asserted step for an arbitrary compactification. The lemma itself is true: repair (a) or the routine reductions in (b) prove it. Strictness is not a separate problem. Once a blow-up with centre disjoint from X is available (Tag 0ESN(1), or U-admissibility in Raynaud–Gruson), strictness is immediate, and Lemma 2.1.4 also gives it once X is dense. Stacks Tag 0ESN (Divisors, Lemma 31.36.3) reads: "Let X be a scheme. Let 𝓕 be a finitely presented O_X-module. Let U ⊂ X be a scheme theoretically dense open such that 𝓕|_U is finite locally free of constant rank r. Then the blowup of X in the rth Fitting ideal of 𝓕 is U-admissible [and] the strict transform 𝓕′ ... is locally free of rank r ...". The proof applies it with U = X inside an arbitrary compactification X̄. Neither hypothesis is checked there, and neither holds in general.

(a) Density. X need not be scheme-theoretically dense in X̄, and without density the conclusion can fail. Example: let X̄ be P¹_k with an embedded point at ∞, with local ring k[t,e]/(te, e²) there. Let X = X̄ − {∞} = A¹ and 𝓕 = O_X. The coherent extension 𝓕̄ = O_X̄/(e) has Fit₁(𝓕̄) = O_X̄, so the Fitting-ideal blow-up is the identity. The strict transform is then 𝓕̄ itself, which is killed by e ≠ 0 and has fibre k at ∞, so it is not locally free there. Blowing up the reduced point ∞ does remove the embedded point and makes the pull-back O_{P¹}. So a suitable blow-up exists, but not by the cited lemma as stated.

(b) Constant rank. The lemma assumes 𝓕 has finite rank, not constant rank, and X may be disconnected. Example: two P¹'s meeting in a point, with X the complement of the node. If 𝓕 has rank 1 on one component of X and rank 2 on the other, then Tag 0ESN does not apply for any single r.

Defence considered. The statement of Lemma 2.1.6 is true, and both defects are easy to repair. The preceding Lemma 2.1.5 produces Cartier boundary, and the complement of an effective Cartier divisor is scheme-theoretically dense ([Sta22], Tag 07ZU). Taking scheme-theoretic closures of the constant-rank pieces is a strict map. Strictness is automatic once a result of this kind applies: part (1) of Tag 0ESN (or the U-admissibility in Raynaud–Gruson) puts the centre off X, so the blow-up is an isomorphism over X. Part (3) (K|_U = 0) shows that the strict transform restricts to 𝓕. The word "suitable" does not supply these steps, and the proof does not mention them. So this is a genuine but minor gap in the proof, not an error in the statement.

Consequences. Lemma 2.1.6 is used only in the proof of Theorem 2.7.4 (p. 24), together with Lemmas 2.1.12 and 2.1.30. That proof needs a strict map so that Lemma 2.1.29 transfers the dynamic structure. Both repairs above give strict maps, so Theorem 2.7.4 and everything after it is unaffected.

History. The 2024 preprint's proof reads "perform a suitable blow-up X̄′ and take the strict transform to find an extension ... which is locally free ([RG71], thm. 5.2.2)". Raynaud–Gruson flattening needs neither density nor constant rank. The preprint's Lemma 2.1.6 also did not claim strictness. The revision added the strictness clause, replaced [RG71] by Tag 0ESN, and dropped [RG71] from the bibliography.

issues.locator: §2.1, proof of Lemma 2.1.5, p. 7
issues.printed: With D = V(ℐ), the source defines X̄′ by blowing up X at ℐ. It invokes [Sta22], Tag 02OS to describe X ↪ X̄′ as a compactification mapping to X ↪ X̄.
issues.correction: "We let X̄′ be the blow-up of X̄ at the ideal ℐ." The blow-up should be of the compactification X̄, not of the open subscheme X.
issues.reason: On the page image, the bar is on X̄′ but not on the X in "the blow-up of X", while the surrounding sentences do distinguish X from X̄ ("the closed complement of X in X̄", "mapping to X ↪ X̄"). So this is not a text-layer artefact. In this proof, X is the open subscheme, D is the closed complement X̄ \ X with its reduced structure, and ℐ is the ideal sheaf in O_X̄ with D = V(ℐ). This matches the sentence just before Lemma 2.1.5, which takes ℐ as "a sheaf of ideals in O_X̄". Taken literally, the printed sentence does not work: ℐ is not an ideal sheaf of O_X, and its restriction to X is the unit ideal O_X. So "the blow-up of X at ℐ" is either undefined or equal to X itself, which is generally not proper. The cited result fits only the corrected reading. Stacks Tag 02OS (Lemma 31.33.4) states: "Let X be a scheme. Let Z ⊂ X be a closed subscheme. The blowing up b : X′ → X of Z in X has the following properties: 1. b|_{b⁻¹(X∖Z)} : b⁻¹(X∖Z) → X∖Z is an isomorphism, 2. the exceptional divisor E = b⁻¹(Z) is an effective Cartier divisor on X′, …". Apply this to the ambient scheme X̄ with Z = D. Then b : X̄′ → X̄ is an isomorphism over X̄ \ D = X, so X embeds as an open subscheme of X̄′. Also X̄′ \ X = b⁻¹(D) is an effective Cartier divisor. X̄′ is proper over S because it is projective over the noetherian scheme X̄, which is proper over S. X is dense in X̄′ because it is the complement of an effective Cartier divisor, so Lemma 2.1.4 gives strictness, exactly as the proof goes on to say. The intended argument is therefore clear and correct once the bar is restored. Lemma 2.1.5 and everything that relies on it are unaffected.
