The printed text is confirmed on the page image of p. 42. Here S^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n}} is a normal scheme over Spec Z_p whose generic fibre is non-empty (§4.1.1, p. 41, following §3.4.23, p. 40). S̃^{tor} is a blow-up of it. The proposition calls S̃_{=j_1,…,=j_k} an open subset of S̃^{tor} and says it maps to S^{tor} by an open immersion. Corollary 4.1.14 takes "× Spec F_p" as a separate step. So the paper has no convention under which "empty" refers only to the special fibre.

(a) Every Z lies in the special fibre. Section 4.1.8 (p. 41) gives D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^n) with both divisors effective. So supp D_i ⊆ V(p), and the same holds for every Z_i = Σ_{l≤i} D_{g+l}. On the generic fibre, V(p^{nj}) is also empty. By (1), Z_{i,>j} and Z_{i,<j} have disjoint supports and Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj}). This difference restricts to 0 on the generic fibre. If two effective divisors are equal and have disjoint supports, both are 0. So every Z_{i,>j} and Z_{i,<j} is supported in the special fibre. The blow-up also changes nothing over the generic fibre, because the ideals (O(−Z_{k+1}), O(−V(p^{nj}))) are the unit ideal there. Hence every S̃_{=j_1,…,=j_k} contains the preimage of the generic fibre, which is isomorphic to S^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n},Q_p} and so non-empty.

(b) A counterexample. Take g ≥ 2, k = 2 and (j_1, j_2) = (0, 2). This sequence is admissible (j_i ≤ i as (1) requires) and has j_2 − j_1 = 2. By (a) the open set is non-empty, so the printed claim is false. For g = 1 the claim is vacuous.

(c) The special-fibre version holds (checked by direct computation). On the open set, Z_{i,>j_i} and Z_{i,<j_i} are both absent, so Z_i = V(p^{nj_i}) there for i ≤ k (with Z_0 = 0 and j_0 = 0). Hence D_{g+i} = V(p^{n(j_i−j_{i−1})}) and D_{g+1−i} = V(p^n) − D_{g+i} = V(p^{n(1−(j_i−j_{i−1}))}). If j_i − j_{i−1} ≥ 2, this effective divisor would have local equation p^{−n(d−1)} with d − 1 ≥ 1. That is impossible at any point where p is not a unit. So the special fibre of the open set is empty. The inductive step of the proof needs only that the blow-up is an isomorphism over S̃_{k,=j_1,…,=j_k}. That holds, because there Z_{k+1} − V(p^{nj}) is effective for j ≤ j_k and anti-effective for j ≥ j_k+1.

(d) Nothing downstream uses the literal claim. Corollary 4.1.14 (p. 42) base-changes to F_p. The filtration F_i of §4.1.16 and Lemma 4.1.18 (p. 43) live inside S^{tor}_{F_p}. Lemma 4.2.11 (p. 44) uses only the disjoint supports in (1). So the stated result is wrong as printed, but the proof and later results are unaffected. A separate index slip appears in the same proof: "−D_{g−k−1} = −Z_{k+1,<j_k+1}" should read −D_{g−k}, as in statement (3), since D_{g+k+1} + D_{g−k} = V(p^n). No convention in the paper saves the printed claim. Section 4.1.1 (p. 41) defines S^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n}} as a scheme over Spec Z_p: a normalization of an object that lives over Q_p. Its p-adic formal completion is introduced separately in §4.1.5. The proposition speaks of a blow-up of this scheme, of an "open subset", of an open immersion and of an "open sub-scheme". Corollary 4.1.14 (p. 42) takes "× Spec F_p" as a separate step, which shows that S̃_{=w_1,…,=w_g} is not itself inside the special fibre.

(a) Every divisor involved lies in the special fibre. Section 4.1.8 (p. 41) gives D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^n) with both divisors effective, so supp D_i ⊆ V(p). The 2024 preprint says it outright on p. 40: D_i is "supported on the special fiber". Hence every Z_i and every V(p^{nj}) is supported in V(p). By (1), Z_{i,>j} and Z_{i,<j} are effective with disjoint supports, and Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj}). This difference restricts to 0 on the generic fibre. Two equal effective divisors with disjoint supports are both 0, so Z_{i,>j} and Z_{i,<j} are also supported in V(p). The ideals blown up are generated by O(−Z_{k+1}) and O(−V(p^{nj})), and these are the unit ideal on the generic fibre. So the blow-up is an isomorphism there. Therefore every S̃_{=j_1,…,=j_k} contains the preimage of S^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n},Q_p}, which is non-empty.

(b) A counterexample. Take g ≥ 2, k = 2 and (j_1, j_2) = (0, 2). This sequence is allowed, because (1) only requires 0 ≤ j_i ≤ i. It has j_2 − j_1 = 2, yet by (a) the open subset is non-empty. For g = 1 the claim is vacuous.

(c) The special-fibre version is true (checked by direct computation). On U = S̃_{=j_1,…,=j_k}, the divisors Z_{i,>j_i} and Z_{i,<j_i} restrict to 0. Hence Z_i|_U = V(p^{nj_i}) for i ≤ k (with Z_0 = 0 and j_0 = 0). Therefore D_{g+i}|_U = V(p^{nd}) with d = j_i − j_{i−1}, and D_{g+1−i}|_U = V(p^n) − V(p^{nd}). So p is invertible on U, and U lies over the generic fibre. The proof's intended mechanism gives the same result. On S̃_{k,=j_1,…,=j_k}, the divisor Z_{k+1,>j} (for j < j_k), respectively Z_{k+1,<j} (for j > j_k+1), has support equal to the whole special fibre of that open set, so the next open set misses the special fibre. The rest of the proposition is correct on the whole scheme. The filtration F_i of §4.1.16, Lemma 4.1.17 and Lemma 4.1.18 (p. 43) live in S^{tor}_{F_p}, where the corrected statement holds. A separate slip sits in the same proof: "Z_{k+1} − V(p^{n(j_k+1)}) = −D_{g−k−1}" should read −D_{g−k}, as statement (3) has it, since D_{g+k+1} + D_{g−k} = V(p^n).

Proposition 4.1.13(1) defines the effective Cartier divisors Z_{i,>j} and Z_{i,<j} only for 0 ≤ i ≤ g and 0 ≤ j ≤ i, with disjoint supports and Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj}).
issues.correction: Prop. 4.1.13(1) should also cover j = −1, with Z_{i,>−1} = Z_i + V(p^n) and Z_{i,<−1} = 0. These two divisors satisfy Z_{i,>−1} − Z_{i,<−1} = Z_i − V(p^{n·(−1)}) and have disjoint supports, so no further blow-up is needed. As a closed subset, Z_{i,>−1} is then the whole special fibre S^tor_{F_p}. With this convention Z_{>w−1} is defined for every w ∈ ᴹW. Lemma 4.1.17, the equality F_{g(g+1)/2} = S^tor_{F_p} and the inclusion S^tor_{F_p,w} ⊆ ∩_i (Z_{i,>w_i−1} ∩ Z^c_{i,>w_i}) on p. 43 then hold as stated.

The symbol is undefined. At the end of §3.1 (p. 34), the sequence attached to w ∈ ᴹW satisfies w_0 = 0 and w_i − w_{i−1} ∈ {0,1}. So 0 ≤ w_i ≤ i, and w_i = 0 does occur. For example, w_1 = 0 exactly when g+1 ∉ w^{−1}{g+1,…,2g}. Whenever w_i = 0, the index w_i − 1 in Z_{i,>w_i−1} is −1. But Prop. 4.1.13(1) defines Z_{i,>j} only for 0 ≤ j ≤ i, and the paper gives no convention for j = −1.

This case matters. Let w_max be the longest element of ᴹW (the open cell). Then w_max^{−1}{g+1,…,2g} = {1,…,g}, so every w_i = 0 and every factor of Z_{>w_max−1} is undefined. Every w satisfies w ≤ w_max. Lemma 4.1.17(2) is stated for all w, so it gives F_{g(g+1)/2} = Z_{>w_max−1} = ∩_i Z_{i,>−1}. Hence, given Lemma 4.1.17(2), the stated equality F_{g(g+1)/2} = S^tor_{F_p} holds exactly when each Z_{i,>−1} contains the special fibre.

Example, g = 1. Here ᴹW = {1, s}, with ℓ(1) = 0 and ℓ(s) = 1. For the identity w_1 = 1, and for s, w_1 = 0. We have Z_1 = D_2, and D_1 + D_2 = V(p^n) by §4.1.8 (p. 41). The proof of Prop. 4.1.13 gives Z_{1,>0} = D_2. Also Z_{1,>1} = 0: we have Z_{1,>1} − Z_{1,<1} = Z_1 − V(p^n) = −D_1 ≤ 0, and the two divisors have disjoint supports. So F_0 = D_2 and F_1 = D_2 ∪ Z_{1,>−1}. Thus F_1 = S^tor_{F_p} requires Z_{1,>−1} to contain S^tor_{F_p} \ D_2. By Cor. 4.1.14, this set is the stratum S^tor_{F_p,s}.

The paper's own formula forces the value. Put j = −1 in Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj}). This gives Z_{i,>−1} − Z_{i,<−1} = Z_i + V(p^n), which is effective. Now let A and B be effective Cartier divisors with disjoint supports such that A − B is effective. Near any point of the support of B, A is trivial, so −B ≥ 0 there. Hence B = 0. So Z_{i,<−1} = 0 and Z_{i,>−1} = Z_i + V(p^n). By §4.1.8 (p. 41), D_{g+k} + D_{g+1−k} = V(p^n), so each D_{g+k} ≤ V(p^n). Hence Z_i is supported in the special fibre, and Z_i + V(p^n) has support exactly S^tor_{F_p}.

The paper uses the same formula at negative indices elsewhere. Prop. 6.2.2(2), p. 61, asserts divisors with Z_{i,>w_j+η} − Z_{i,<w_j+η} = Z_i − V(p^{n(w_j+η)}) for η ∈ {±ε, ±ε′}, and w_j − ε < 0 when w_j = 0. The paper also identifies such a divisor with the whole special fibre around it. The proof of Prop. 4.1.13 (p. 42) writes "Z_{k+1,>j} = S̃^tor_{k,=j_1,…,=j_k} for j < j_k". On that open Z_k = V(p^{nj_k}), so Z_{k+1,>j} = V(p^{n(j_k−j)}) + D_{g+k+1}, whose support is the whole special fibre there.

With this convention, the surrounding statements hold:
- The formula at j = 0 gives Z_{i,>0} = Z_i and Z_{i,<0} = 0. So Lemma 4.1.17(1) extends to the index −1: for 0 ≤ j ≤ i we have Z_{i,>j} ≤ Z_{i,>0} = Z_i ≤ Z_i + V(p^n), and Z_{i,<−1} = 0. Hence Lemma 4.1.17(2) holds for all w and w′, and F_{g(g+1)/2} = ∩_i Z_{i,>−1} = S^tor_{F_p}.
- Consider the open S̃^tor_{=w_1,…,=w_g}, whose special fibre is S^tor_{F_p,w} (Cor. 4.1.14). On it, Z_{i,>w_i} and Z_{i,<w_i} are trivial, so Z_i = V(p^{nw_i}). For w_i ≥ 1 this gives Z_{i,>w_i−1} − Z_{i,<w_i−1} = V(p^n), so Z_{i,>w_i−1} = V(p^n) there by the disjoint-support argument. For w_i = 0 the convention gives Z_i + V(p^n) = V(p^n) as well. So on this open every Z_{i,>w_i−1} equals V(p^n). This proves the inclusion S^tor_{F_p,w} ⊆ ∩_i (Z_{i,>w_i−1} ∩ Z^c_{i,>w_i}) stated on p. 43.
- The same computation shows two more things over 𝔖^tor_w. First, the closed set Z_{>w−1} is the whole special fibre there. Second, the ideal of Z_{>w−1} obtained from these divisors is (p^n) there, with n the level, and this ideal has the same radical as (p). This is all that the last step of the proof of Prop. 4.5.8 (p. 53) needs: "the inclusion (p) ⊆ 𝓘_{Z,>w−1} is an equality over 𝔖^tor_w". The reason is that the completion lim_m 𝒪/𝓘^m of §2.9.1 depends on 𝓘 only up to radical, since on a noetherian scheme two ideals with the same radical have cofinal powers.
- Lemma 4.1.18 gives the expected strata. For g = 1 it gives F_1 \ F_0 = Z_{1,>−1} ∩ Z^c_{1,>0} = S^tor_{F_p} \ D_2 = S^tor_{F_p,s}. In general its top piece is S^tor_{F_p} \ Z_g, which is S^tor_{F_p,w_max} by Cor. 4.1.14.

So the text uses a symbol it never defines. The paper's own formula allows only one value for it, and that is the value the stated equality F_{g(g+1)/2} = S^tor_{F_p} needs. With that value filled in, the statements above follow from the paper's own arguments with no new step. Nothing false is stated and no argument is missing; the definition simply omits the case j = −1. The filtration and its top step feed the spectral sequence of Theorem 2.9.7 in §4.5.6 (p. 52). Lemma 4.5.7 and Prop. 4.5.8 involve Z_{>w−1} for every w, including those with w_1 = 0. The omission does not affect any of these results, nor Theorem 4.5.2.

issues.locator: §4.2.9: proof of Corollary 4.2.10 (p. 45) and proof of Proposition 4.2.15 (p. 46), in both places the step that invokes Proposition 4.2.8 to conclude that p⋆1 H is a BT_n. The 2024 preprint has the same text (pp. 43–44).
issues.printed: Corollary 4.2.10's proof infers deg(p⋆2 H_{g+i,x}) ≥ deg(p⋆1 H_{g+i,x}) from Proposition 4.2.8. For equality and t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p), it calls p⋆1 H_{g+i,x} and p⋆1 H_{g+i,x} BT_n's with degree divisible by n. Proposition 4.2.15 assumes deg(p⋆2 H_{k′,x}) = deg(p⋆1 H_{k′,x}) for g+1 ≤ k′ ≤ k, invokes the same proposition for p⋆1 H_{k′,x}, and concludes p⋆1 Gr_{k′,x} ≃ p⋆2 Gr_{k′,x} is a multiplicative or étale BT_n for every k′.
issues.correction: Prove only the degree statement; it is all that is needed. Corollary 4.2.10: write the transports of H = p1*H_{g+i,x} along the factorization of §4.2.5 as H = H^(0), H^(1), …, H^(k) = p2*H_{g+i,x}. By Prop. 4.2.8, deg H^(0) ≤ … ≤ deg H^(k). If the two ends have equal degree, every step is an equality. Let j0 be the first step with kernel rank p^s where s = 2g − i; such a step exists by Remark 4.2.6. There Prop. 4.2.8(2) applies to H^(j0) and shows that H^(j0) is a BT_n. Every later step has i + s ≤ 2g, so it is a generic isomorphism, and it has equal degrees, so it is an isomorphism ([Far10], sect. 3, cor. 3, as in the proof of Prop. 4.2.8). Hence p2*H_{g+i,x} ≅ H^(j0) is a BT_n. Its degree is then n times its dimension, so deg p1*H_{g+i,x} = deg p2*H_{g+i,x} ∈ nZ. The claim that p1*H_{g+i,x} is a BT_n should be dropped or given a separate proof. Proposition 4.2.15: apply this for every 1 ≤ k′ ≤ k. By additivity of the degree, deg p1*Gr_{g+k′,x} = deg p2*Gr_{g+k′,x} lies in nZ ∩ [0, n] = {0, n}. So on both sides Gr_{g+k′,x} is étale (degree 0) or multiplicative (degree n), and of the same type. The same passage also contains three small misprints: the second "p⋆1H_{g+i,x}" on p. 45 should be p⋆2H_{g+i,x}; "section 4.2.1" should be 4.2.5; and "for all g+1 ≤ k′ ≤ k, deg(p⋆2H_{k′,x}) = deg(p⋆1H_{k′,x})" should read "for all 1 ≤ k′ ≤ k, deg(p⋆2H_{g+k′,x}) = deg(p⋆1H_{g+k′,x})".
issues.reason:
In §4.2.5 the isogeny p⋆1 A → p⋆2 A is factored as G_0 → G_1 → … → G_k, with kernels L[p^{j+1}]/L[p^j] of rank p^{s_j}. Multiplication by p embeds L[p^{j+2}]/L[p^{j+1}] into L[p^{j+1}]/L[p^j], so s_j does not increase with j. For t ∈ T^{++} the s_j take every value 1, …, 2g−1 (Remark 4.2.6).

The second assertion of Prop. 4.2.8 is about one step: if i + s = h and deg H = deg H′, then the source H of that step is a BT_n. For the flag member of rank p^{in}, this is the step with s = 2g − i.

For i = 1 the proof works. Every step before that one has s = 2g, where H′ = φ(p^{-1}H) is identified with H through G/G[p] ≅ G, so the source really is p⋆1 H.

For g ≥ 2 and 2 ≤ i ≤ g it does not work. The step with s = 2g − i comes after a step with s = 2g − 1, and there i + s > 2g. At that earlier step case (2) applies: the transported group is φ(p^{-1}H ∩ p^{-n}L), and §4.2.5 identifies only its graded piece Gr′ with Gr, not the group with H. At such a step Prop. 4.2.8 gives only deg H′ ≥ deg H. So Prop. 4.2.8 makes an intermediate group a BT_n, not p⋆1 H_{g+i,x}. The step "We deduce from proposition 4.2.8 that p⋆1 H_{k′,x} is a BT_n" (k′ ≥ g+2) is asserted without proof, and Cor. 4.2.10 makes the same claim for p⋆1 H_{g+i,x}.

The conclusions survive. The BT_n statement does transfer forward to p⋆2 H, and the degree argument in the correction gives everything the two results use. A direct computation at ordinary points, where degrees are read off the multiplicative part of the Tate module, found no failure of the p⋆1 claim itself. It used g = 2, t with elementary divisors (1, p^{-1}, p^{-2}, p^{-3}), p = 2, 3 and n = 2, 3, over randomly sampled flags and multiplicative parts. The degrees never decreased along the chain. In every sampled case with equality for i = 2, p⋆1 H_{g+2} was a BT_n, and a degree-preserving case-(2) step never changed the type of the multiplicative part. So what is missing is a proof, not a true statement. Section 4.2.5 factors p1*A → p2*A as G_0 → G_1 → … → G_k. The step G_j → G_{j+1} has kernel L[p^{j+1}]/L[p^j], of rank p^s with s non-increasing in j. The flag is carried step by step: H' = φ(H) if i + s ≤ 2g, and H' = φ(p^{-1}H ∩ p^{-n}L) if i + s > 2g. Proposition 4.2.8 gives deg H' ≥ deg H at every step. So deg p1*H ≤ deg p2*H, and when the two are equal, every step is an equality.

The second part of Prop. 4.2.8 (L is a BT_1 and H is a BT_n) needs i + s = h = 2g. So it applies only at a step whose kernel has rank p^{2g−i}, and only to the group carried to that G_j, not to p1*H_{g+i,x}. For t ∈ T^{++}, every rank p, …, p^{2g−1} occurs (Remark 4.2.6). Hence for i ≥ 2 (so g ≥ 2), a step with 2g − i < s < 2g, for example s = 2g − 1, comes before it. At such a step, φ gives only one relation between H' and H. Multiplication by p maps H' onto H'' = H ∩ p^{-(n-1)}L. That map has kernel G[p]/L, of order p^{2g−s}, and H'' has order p^{ni − (2g−s)} < p^{ni}. The construction of §4.2.5 identifies only the graded pieces Gr_{g+i} and Gr'_{g+i}. Example: g = 2, i = 2, s = 3 with p = 2, n = 2. There H' has order 16, but its image H'' in H has order 8, checked by direct computation. So no statement about H' being a BT_n carries back to H.

Defence attempts:
- The case i = 1 is fine. Every earlier step then has s = 2g and L = G[p], and H' is H under G/G[p] ≅ G.
- The p2 side is fine as well. After the first step with i + s = 2g, every step is a generic isomorphism, and equal degrees make it an isomorphism. So p2*H_{g+i,x} is a BT_n.
- Running the isogeny backwards does not help. At a step with i + s > 2g, H' contains φ(G[p]), which is the kernel of the reverse isogeny. So the hypotheses of Prop. 4.2.8 fail for the reverse step.
- No other statement in the paper supplies the p1 claim. In the setting of Prop. 4.2.15 the claim does hold, but only a posteriori. Once every Gr_{g+k′} is known to be étale or multiplicative, H_{g+k′} is an extension of étale by multiplicative groups of this type, killed by p^n, hence a BT_n. That knowledge comes from the degree argument. In Cor. 4.2.10, where equality is assumed for a single i, the paper does not settle the claim.

So the step "p1*H is a BT_n, by Prop. 4.2.8" is asserted without proof. The consequences it is used for still hold by the degree argument given in the correction.

Later uses need only the degree and support conclusions:
- Prop. 4.2.15(3) in the proof of Prop. 4.3.13 (p. 48);
- Cor. 4.2.10 in the proof of Lemma 4.4.2 (p. 50) and for the action of t on the spectral sequence (p. 52);
- Prop. 4.2.15 in the proof of Prop. 6.1.9 (p. 60), in the form "deg H_{g+i}(p1(x)) ≤ deg H_{g+i}(p2(x)) and if equality holds they are multiples of n".

No stated result changes.

Notation: p^{−1}H = [p]^{−1}(H) and p^{−n}L = [p^n]^{−1}(L). Both are finite flat subgroups of G[p^{n+1}] over V. Write X for the schematic closure of p^{−1}H_K ∩ p^{−n}L_K in G. This is the group the paper calls p^{−1}H ∩ p^{−n}L. Since p^{−1}H and p^{−n}L are finite flat, each is the schematic closure of its generic fibre, so X lies in both.

(1) The degree is defined in §4.2.7 (p. 44), following Fargues, only for finite flat group schemes over Spec V. The generic fibre L_K lives over K, where the degree is not defined. Every other term in the inequality is integral: p^{−1}H, X and G[p^{n+1}]. The inequality comes from the displayed generic sequence. Embed X in p^{−1}H × p^{−n}L by x ↦ (x, −x), and map the product to G[p^{n+1}] by (a, b) ↦ a + b. Over K this is the displayed sequence. So the quotient (p^{−1}H × p^{−n}L)/X maps to G[p^{n+1}] by a generic isomorphism, and its degree is at most deg G[p^{n+1}] ([Far10], sect. 3, cor. 3). Additivity of the degree then bounds the degree of the integral product p^{−1}H × p^{−n}L by deg X + deg G[p^{n+1}]. The next sentence computes deg p^{−n}L = deg L + deg G[p^n] from 0 → G[p^n] → p^{−n}L → L → 0. So the term meant is the integral group p^{−n}L.

(2) Multiplication by p on G is finite flat and surjective with kernel G[p]. So p^{−1}H → H is surjective with kernel G[p], not H[p]. Ranks confirm this. Étale locally H_K ≃ (Z/p^n)^i, so the generic fibre of H[p] has rank p^i. The kernel G[p] has rank p^h, where h is the height of G. These differ unless i = h. The formula in the same sentence, deg p^{−1}H = deg H + deg G[p], uses the correct kernel G[p].

With both corrections the argument closes. Since v(p) = 1, deg G[p^m] = m·dim G. Hence deg p^{−1}H + deg p^{−n}L − deg G[p^{n+1}] = (deg H + dim G) + (deg L + n·dim G) − (n+1)·dim G = deg H + deg L. So deg X ≥ deg H + deg L.

The final equality deg H′ = deg X − deg L holds exactly, not only as an inequality. L ⊂ G[p] ⊂ p^{−1}H and L ⊂ p^{−n}L, so L_K ⊂ X_K. Since L is finite flat, it is the closure of L_K, so L ⊂ X. The quotient X/L is finite flat. The kernel of X → G′ is X ∩ L = L, so the induced map X/L → G/L = G′ has trivial kernel. It lands in G′[p^{n+1}], so it is a monomorphism of finite V-schemes and hence a closed immersion. Its generic fibre is φ(p^{−1}H_K ∩ p^{−n}L_K). A closed subscheme that is flat over V is the schematic closure of its generic fibre, so H′ = X/L. Additivity of the degree then gives deg H′ = deg X − deg L. Therefore deg H′ ≥ deg H, as the paper states, and the printed "=" does not need to be weakened to "≥". Only in the case i + s ≤ h is the map H → H′ merely a generic isomorphism, and there the proof correctly uses [Far10], sect. 3, cor. 3.

In each slip the intended meaning is fixed by the degree formulas that follow it in the proof, deg p^{−1}H = deg H + deg G[p] and deg p^{−n}L = deg L + deg G[p^n]. These formulas use the kernel G[p] and the integral group p^{−n}L. Neither slip affects the statement of Proposition 4.2.8, or the results that use it: Corollary 4.2.10 and Propositions 4.2.14 and 4.2.15.

issues.locator: §4.2.9, Corollary 4.2.10 and its proof, p. 45
issues.printed: Corollary 4.2.10 states p⋆₂Z_i ≥ p⋆₁Z_i on C_t^{tor}, 1 ≤ i ≤ g. For t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p), it claims that the support associated to p⋆₂Z_i − p⋆₁Z_i includes p⋆₁ ∩_{j=0}^{i} (Z_{i<j} ∪ Z_{i>j}); also p⋆₂ ∩_{j=0}^{i} (Z_{i<j} ∪ Z_{i>j}). The proof says normality permits checking codimension 1 alone, taking V = 𝒪_{C_t^{tor},x} at a generic special-fiber point, since both divisors have special-fiber support. It invokes Proposition 4.2.8 after factoring the isogeny into maps with finite flat kernels killed by p.
issues.correction:
The reduction to codimension 1 proves the inequality p⋆_2 Z_i ≥ p⋆_1 Z_i. On a normal scheme, a rational function is regular once it is regular at every codimension-one point. At a generic point x of the special fibre, 𝒪_{C_t^{tor},x} is a DVR to which Proposition 4.2.8 applies. The reduction does not prove the 'Moreover'. That is a containment of closed sets whose left-hand side need not be a union of codimension-one pieces, so it has to be proved at every point.

Repair, with the same tools. Let y ∈ C_t^{tor} with p_1(y) ∈ ∩_{j=0}^{i}(Z_{i,<j} ∪ Z_{i,>j}). Take a complete rank-one valuation ring V (normalised by v(p) = 1) and a map Spec V → C_t^{tor} sending the closed point to y and the generic point into the generic fibre, as in the proofs of Propositions 4.2.14–4.2.15.

For each 0 ≤ j ≤ i, the point p_1(y) lies in exactly one of Z_{i,>j} and Z_{i,<j}, because their supports are disjoint (Proposition 4.1.13(1)). Hence v(p⋆_1 Z_i) − nj = v(p⋆_1 Z_{i,>j}) − v(p⋆_1 Z_{i,<j}) ≠ 0. Since deg p⋆_1 H_{g+i} = v(p⋆_1 Z_i) lies in [0, ni], this degree is not a multiple of n.

Factor the isogeny p⋆_1 A → p⋆_2 A into isogenies with kernel killed by p, as in §4.2.5. By Proposition 4.2.8, the degrees of the successive images of H_{g+i} do not decrease. Since t ∈ T^{++}, Remark 4.2.6 gives a step whose kernel has rank p^{2g−i}, that is, a step with i + s = 2g. If deg p⋆_2 H_{g+i} = deg p⋆_1 H_{g+i}, all the degrees in the chain are equal. Proposition 4.2.8 then makes the group at that step a BT_n, so its degree deg p⋆_1 H_{g+i} is a multiple of n, which is a contradiction.

So the local equation f of the Cartier divisor p⋆_2 Z_i − p⋆_1 Z_i at y satisfies v(f) = deg p⋆_2 H_{g+i} − deg p⋆_1 H_{g+i} > 0. Hence f is not a unit at y, and y lies in the support. The same argument applied to p_2(y) gives the second containment.

The same proof also has two misprints: 'see section 4.2.1' should read 'see section 4.2.5', where the factorisation is constructed; and the second 'p⋆_1 H_{g+i,x}' should read 'p⋆_2 H_{g+i,x}'.
issues.reason:
This was checked on the rendered p. 45.

The proof takes V = 𝒪_{C_t^{tor},x} with x a generic point of the special fibre and argues only there. For the inequality that is enough. The 'Moreover' is a containment of closed sets. The support of an effective Cartier divisor on a normal scheme has pure codimension 1, so a point y lies in supp(p⋆₂Z_i − p⋆₁Z_i) exactly when some codimension-one point specialising to y does. The printed argument shows only that generic points x of the special fibre with p₁(x) (or p₂(x)) in ∩_j(Z_{i,<j} ∪ Z_{i,>j}) lie in the support. It says nothing about points of the preimage that are not specialisations of such x.

Such points occur. For g = 1, n = 1, i = 1, Proposition 4.1.13 and its proof give Z_{1,>0} = D_2, Z_{1,<0} = 0, Z_{1,>1} = 0 and Z_{1,<1} = D_1, so the set is D_1 ∩ D_2. By Lemma 4.1.9 and Remark 4.1.4 this is the non-ordinary (supersingular) locus of the Iwahori-level model, a finite set of closed points of the two-dimensional S^{tor}; no blow-up is needed when g = 1. The fibres of p₁ and p₂ over these points are finite: over F̄_p a supersingular elliptic curve has a unique subgroup scheme of each p-power order, namely ker F^j. So the preimage in C_t^{tor} has codimension 2, and no generic point of the special fibre maps into it.

The statement is still true. It follows from the valuation argument above, which was checked step by step. For g = 1 it was also checked by direct computation with the Katz–Lubin degrees. For a supersingular E with Hasse valuation h < p/(p+1), the canonical subgroup has degree 1−h and the other subgroups have degree h/p. For h ≥ p/(p+1), every subgroup has degree 1/(p+1). The new subgroup E[p]/L has degree 1 − deg L, which is strictly larger than deg H in every case with 0 < deg H < 1.

Dependence: the 'Moreover' is used in the proof of Lemma 4.4.2 (p. 50). There it shows that, on C_{t,F_p,(w−1,w+1)}, the support of p⋆₂(Z_{i,>w_i}−Z_{i,<w_i}) − p⋆₁(Z_{i,>w_i}−Z_{i,<w_i}) contains p⋆₁Z_{i,>w_i} and p⋆₂Z_{i,<w_i}. For g = 1 and w the identity (w_1 = 1), S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} is D_2 and D_{w,+} = Z_{1,<1} = D_1. So the needed containment is at points lying over D_1 ∩ D_2, exactly the codimension-two case. Lemma 4.4.2 feeds Proposition 4.4.4 (strict dynamic compactifications), on which the complexes RΓ_w and Theorem 4.5.2 rest.

The citation of Corollary 4.2.10 on p. 52, for the action of t on the spectral sequence, needs only the inclusion p₁^{-1}(F_l) ⊆ p₂^{-1}(F_l) that Proposition 2.9.9 requires. That inclusion follows from Lemma 4.2.11, which uses only the first (inequality) part. So the gap does not touch the p. 52 citation.

The statement is true and the repair is short, so only the proof is affected. The proof works only at the local rings 𝒪_{C_t^{tor},x} of generic points x of the special fibre. That shows only this: a generic point x with p_1(x) (or p_2(x)) in T := ∩_{j=0}^{i}(Z_{i,<j} ∪ Z_{i,>j}) lies in the support, and so do its specialisations. A point of p_1^{-1}(T) that is not a specialisation of such an x is not covered.

Such points exist. Take g = 1, n = 1, i = 1. By Proposition 4.1.13 and its proof (the blow-up is trivial for g = 1), Z_{1,>0} = D_2, Z_{1,<0} = 0, Z_{1,<1} = D_1 and Z_{1,>1} = 0. So T = D_1 ∩ D_2, the supersingular points of the special fibre of the Iwahori-level model, which are closed points of a two-dimensional scheme. The quasi-isogeny extends over C_t^{tor} (Lemma 4.2.2). Over F̄_p a supersingular elliptic curve has only finitely many finite subgroup schemes of each order (one of each p-power order). So p_1 and p_2 have finite fibres over these points. The preimage therefore has codimension 2, and no generic point of the special fibre maps into it. So the codimension-one argument proves nothing about this set.

A charitable reading does not save the argument. One could read ∩ and ∪ as gcd and lcm of divisors, which would make the codimension-one reduction valid. But then the claim is empty in this example (gcd(D_1, D_2) = 0), and the paper itself uses ∩ of the Z's as intersections of closed sets (§4.1.16, Lemma 4.1.18, §4.4.1). Lemma 4.4.2 needs the set-theoretic claim. Proposition 4.2.15 concerns Σ_{l≤k} Z_l, not a single Z_i, so it does not supply the step. Only its technique does: a valuation ring through an arbitrary point.

The statement itself is true, by the repair above. In the example it was also checked by direct computation with the Katz–Lubin degrees. Let h be the valuation of the Hasse invariant.
- If 0 < h < p/(p+1), the canonical subgroup has degree 1 − h and the other subgroups have degree h/p.
- If h ≥ p/(p+1), every subgroup of order p has degree 1/(p+1).
For H ∩ L = 0 the new level subgroup E[p]/L has degree 1 − deg L. In every supersingular case this is strictly larger than deg H: 1 − h/p > 1 − h, h > h/p, 1 − h/p > h/p, and p/(p+1) > 1/(p+1).

What uses the passage: the proof of Lemma 4.4.2 (p. 50) applies the 'Moreover' on C_{t,F_p,(w−1,w+1)}. It concludes that the support contains p⋆_1 Z_{i,>w_i} and p⋆_2 Z_{i,<w_i}. For g = 1, n = 1 and w = 1 (so w_1 = 1), S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = D_2, D_{w,+} = D_1 and D_{w,−} = 0. The needed containment is then exactly at points over D_1 ∩ D_2, the codimension-two case above. Lemma 4.4.2 feeds Proposition 4.4.4, the complexes RΓ_w, Proposition 4.4.5 and Theorem 4.5.2, and it is also invoked in §6 (pp. 58, 61).

The citation on p. 52 (the action of t on the Cousin spectral sequence) needs only p_1^{-1}(F_l) ⊆ p_2^{-1}(F_l) for Proposition 2.9.9. That follows from Lemma 4.2.11, which uses only the inequality, so that citation is unaffected.

Since the statement is true and the repair is short and uses only Proposition 4.2.8 and Remark 4.2.6, no stated result is affected. Only the proof of Corollary 4.2.10 is incomplete, and with it the justification of the step in Lemma 4.4.2. The text is identical in the 2024 preprint.

issues.printed: The proof assumes D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = (p^n) and says the assertion restates p_2^⋆ Σ_{i=1}^k D_{g+i} ≥ p_1^⋆ Σ_{i=1}^k D_{g+i}.
issues.correction: Replace k by g: the inequality p_2^⋆ Σ_{i=1}^g D_{g+i} ≥ p_1^⋆ Σ_{i=1}^g D_{g+i}, i.e. p_2^⋆Z_g ≥ p_1^⋆Z_g (Corollary 4.2.10 with i = g). Also, 'identity' should read 'inequality'.
issues.reason: The letter k is not defined in Lemma 4.2.12 or its proof. The lemma's left side minus its right side is (p_2^⋆ − p_1^⋆)(Σ_{i∈I_{w,2}} D_{w^{-1}(i)} − Σ_{i∈I_{w,1}} D_{w^{-1}(i)}). As i runs over I_{w,1} ∪ I_{w,2} = {1,…,g}, the indices w^{-1}(i) run over w^{-1}{1,…,g}. Because w lies in the Weyl group of GSp_{2g}, this set contains exactly one element of each pair {c, 2g+1−c}. The elements lying in {1,…,g} come from I_{w,1}, and those lying in {g+1,…,2g} come from I_{w,2}. Substitute D_c = (p^n) − D_{2g+1−c} for c ≤ g and use p_1^⋆(p^n) = p_2^⋆(p^n). The difference then becomes p_2^⋆Z_g − p_1^⋆Z_g, where Z_g = Σ_{i=1}^g D_{g+i}. This was checked by direct computation for every w and g ≤ 4. So the proof needs exactly the case k = g, which is Corollary 4.2.10 for i = g. The argument is otherwise correct.

issues.locator: §4.2, proof of Proposition 4.2.15, p. 46
issues.printed: The proof takes a mixed-characteristic valuation ring V and x : Spec V → C_t^{tor} landing in the specified open. It assumes deg(p⋆_2 H_{k′,x}) = deg(p⋆_1 H_{k′,x}) for every g+1 ≤ k′ ≤ k, and uses Proposition 4.2.8 to conclude that p⋆_1 H_{k′,x} is a BT_n.
issues.correction: "for all g+1 ≤ k′ ≤ g+k, deg(p⋆_2 H_{k′,x}) = deg(p⋆_1 H_{k′,x})". Equivalently: deg(p⋆_2 H_{g+k′,x}) = deg(p⋆_1 H_{g+k′,x}) for 1 ≤ k′ ≤ k.
issues.reason:
The page image confirms the printed range "g+1 ≤ k′ ≤ k". Proposition 4.2.15 begins "Let t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p) and let 1 ≤ k ≤ g", so k ≤ g < g+1 and the printed range is empty. Read literally, the sentence assumes nothing.

The range the argument needs follows from the paper's conventions. On p. 41 the Iwahori flag is 0 ⊆ H_{g+1} ⊆ H_{g+2} ⊆ … ⊆ H_{2g} ⊆ H_1 ⊆ … ⊆ H_g = A[p^n], with Gr_i = H_i/H_{i−1}. Also on p. 41 (§4.1.8), D_i is the Fargues divisor of Gr_i, and Z_i = Σ_{j=1}^{i} D_{g+j}. Fargues' degree is additive in short exact sequences. Pulling back along x therefore gives deg(x^* Σ_{i=1}^{k′} D_{g+i}) = Σ_{i=1}^{k′} deg Gr_{g+i,x} = deg H_{g+k′,x}.

The same proof, a few lines earlier, restricts to the open subscheme where p⋆_2 Σ_{i=1}^{k′} D_{g+i} = p⋆_1 Σ_{i=1}^{k′} D_{g+i} for all k′ ≤ k. This follows because Σ_{i=1}^{k} Z_i = Σ_{i=1}^{k}(k+1−i)D_{g+i} and p⋆_2 Z_i ≥ p⋆_1 Z_i by Corollary 4.2.10. That condition is exactly deg p⋆_2 H_{g+k′,x} = deg p⋆_1 H_{g+k′,x} for 1 ≤ k′ ≤ k, i.e. for the groups H_{g+1}, …, H_{g+k}. So the upper bound should be g+k, not k.

The rest of the proof agrees. It then concludes that p⋆_1 Gr_{k′,x} ≃ p⋆_2 Gr_{k′,x} is multiplicative or étale "for all k′", which is point (1) for the graded pieces Gr_{g+1}, …, Gr_{g+k}. This only works if k′ runs over g+1, …, g+k.

issues.locator: §4.3.1 (Automorphic sheaves), definition of V_κ, p. 46. The 2024 preprint has the same text (p. 45).
issues.printed: The source defines V_κ as functions f : M → A^1 satisfying f(mb) = w_{0,M}κ(b^{−1})f(m), ∀(m, b) ∈ M × B ∩ M, and specifies the action m′.f(m) = f(m^{−1}m′).
issues.reason: The equivariance condition f(mb) = w_{0,M}κ(b^{−1})f(m) concerns right translation by B ∩ M, so M has to act by left translation. - Remark 3.4.18 (p. 39) warns: "In general this map doesn't descend to a map IG_{K^pK_{p,P}} → S_{K^pK_p} because the level structure on both sides are formulated in a different way. One uses isomorphisms with μ_{p^∞}^g ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)^g on the left, and isomorphisms with (Q_p/Z_p)^{2g} on the right." It then points to Section 4.1, which handles only K_{p,n}.
Level K_{p,1,n} over Z_p(ζ_{p^n}) is exactly a case where this descent must be argued: one has to match trivialisations by Z/p^nZ on the Shimura side with trivialisations by μ_{p^n} on the Igusa side.

The assertion itself is correct. Both sides are finite étale T(Z/p^nZ)-covers of a smooth formal scheme, hence normal, and they agree on the generic fibre once ζ_{p^n} is fixed. Checked directly for g = 1. There K_{p,1,n} = {(a b; c d) : a ≡ d ≡ 1, c ≡ 0 mod p^n}, so a K_{p,1,n}-level structure is a point P of exact order p^n (generating the flag subgroup H) together with a generator of A[p^n]/H. On the locus where H is multiplicative (resp. étale), it becomes a trivialisation μ_{p^n} ≅ H and Z/p^n ≅ A[p^n]/H (resp. Z/p^n ≅ H and μ_{p^n} ≅ A[p^n]/H) once ζ_{p^n} is fixed. That is the Igusa level structure for K_{p,P,1,w}.

So the lemma is true, but its second half is asserted without any argument. It is not idle: the nebentypus comparison RΓ_w(K^pK_{w,p,P},κ,χ) = RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ) stated on p. 56 compares the sheaf ω^κ(χ), defined through this normalised cover, with the Igusa tower. That comparison needs this identification. The lemma makes two claims. The printed proof establishes only the first. After extending the Gr_i as finite flat groups, it shows étale-locally on U that the normalisation is T(Z/p^nZ) ×_{Spec Z_p(ζ_{p^n})} U, and it ends there. The Igusa variety 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P,1,w}K^p} does not appear anywhere in the proof, so the second claim ("Moreover, ...") is asserted without argument. Showing that a torsor is trivial étale-locally does not identify it with a particular global torsor.

Defence attempts:
(a) Lemma 3.4.24 (p. 40) gives an open immersion 𝔍𝔊_{K^pK_{p,P}} ↪ S_{K^pK_p} for K_{p,P} = P(Q_p) ∩ xK_p x^{-1}, but only over Z_p^cycl, after fixing Z_p(1) = Z_p. Remarks 3.4.18 and 3.4.25 say explicitly that in general this map does not descend, because the Igusa level structure uses μ_{p^∞}^g ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)^g and the Shimura level structure uses (Q_p/Z_p)^{2g}. Remark 1.4.6 (p. 5) says scalars must be extended to Q_p(ζ_{p^n}) for exactly this reason.
(b) Lemma 4.1.7 (p. 41) is the analogue at level K_{p,n}, where the authors do give a justification ("follows from lemma 3.4.24 ... here the embedding is defined over Z_p"). Nothing comparable is given at level K_{p,1,n}, where the descent to Z_p(ζ_{p^n}) is the only non-formal point.
So no nearby statement supplies the step as written.

The claim is nevertheless true, and the missing argument is routine (see the correction). Checked directly: K_{p,1,n} = ker(K_{p,n} → T(Z/p^nZ)), so K_{p,P,1,w} is normal in K_{p,P,w}. That identification compares the Shimura-side complexes with Nebentypus (built from O(χ) on p. 47) with the Igusa-side complexes. I rendered pp. 48–49 at high resolution, and the subscript clearly reads "2g+i−1". The printed index cannot be right, for three reasons.

1. **Undefined divisors.** In §4.1.8 (p. 41), D_i is defined only for 1 ≤ i ≤ 2g ("For all 1 ≤ i ≤ 2g, we let D_i be the effective Cartier divisor … associated to … Gr_i"). For g ≥ 2 and 2 ≤ i ≤ g, the index 2g+i−1 is between 2g+1 and 3g−1, so D_{2g+i−1} is not defined. For i = 1 the two indices agree (both equal 2g), so for g = 1 the printed formula happens to be correct.

2. **Inconsistency with the rest of the paper.** Everywhere else the relevant locus pairs D_i with D_{2g+1−i}:
   - §4.1.8 states D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^n).
   - Lemma 4.1.9 (p. 41) gives ∪_{w∈^MW} S^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n},𝔽_p,w} = S^{tor}_{K^pK_{p,n},𝔽_p} ∖ ∑_{i=1}^g D_i∩D_{2g+1−i}.

   - On the same page, the source of p_1 in the proof of Proposition 4.3.11 is printed correctly as C_t^{tor}∖∑ p_1^⋆D_i∩p_2^⋆D_{2g+1−i}, while its target, written in the same line, has 2g+i−1.

   The slip is the transposition "+i−1" for "+1−i".

3. **The corrected set is the right target.** By Lemma 4.2.13, C^{tor}_{t,w} lies in the complement of ∑_{i=1}^g p_1^⋆D_{w^{-1}(i)}. So p_1 maps C^{tor}_{t,w} into the complement of ∑_i D_{w^{-1}(i)}, which by Lemma 4.1.9 is the w-stratum of the special fibre. Hence p_1 maps the stated source into S^{tor}∖∑ D_i∩D_{2g+1−i}.

Proposition 4.3.17 defines t_w : p_2^⋆ω^κ(χ) → p_1^!ω^κ(χ) over ℭ^{tor}_{t,w,Z_p(ζ_{p^n})} by ⟨−w^{−1}(w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ, t⟩t_w^{naive}, with t_w^{naive} a rational tensor-product map.
issues.correction:
In all three pairings, delete the unmatched "(" after (w′)^{−1} or w^{−1}. Equivalently, close it right after (κ + ρ).
- Remark 4.3.12 should read n_{w′} = ⟨(w′)^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) + ρ, t⟩ − ⟨w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) + ρ, t⟩. Here the pairing is used additively, as the pairing with v(t). The ρ terms cancel, so n_{w′} = ⟨(w′)^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ), v(t)⟩.
- Proposition 4.3.17 should read ⟨−w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ, t⟩t_w^{naive}. This is the normalisation of Proposition 4.3.9, and the one used to define t right after Proposition 4.3.17.
issues.reason:
The parentheses are unbalanced as printed on pp. 48–49, and the 2024 preprint has the same text. Each pairing can be balanced in two ways: close the parenthesis after (κ + ρ), or after the trailing ±ρ. The paper's own normalisations settle which is meant. The second reading makes the Remark's positivity claim false and gives the wrong normalisation in Proposition 4.3.17.

Notation. Write λ = w_{0,M}(κ + ρ). Characters are written (k_1, …, k_g; k) as on p. 33. In these coordinates W acts by signed permutations of (k_1, …, k_g) and fixes k. The conventions on p. 34 are:
- X^⋆(T)^+ is the cone 0 ≥ k_1 ≥ ⋯ ≥ k_g.
- T^+(Q_p) is the set of t with v(t) dominant; T^{++}(Q_p) is the set with v(t) dominant regular. So ⟨α, v(t)⟩ ≥ 0 for every α ∈ Φ^+, strictly for t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p).
- ^MW is defined by the condition wX^⋆(T)^+ ⊆ X^⋆(T)^{+,M}.
C(κ) is defined on p. 48: w ∈ ^MW lies in C(κ) exactly when w^{−1}λ ∈ X^⋆(T)^−_Q. This is the antidominant cone −X^⋆(T)^+_Q; compare the definition of C(κ) on p. 3.

Remark 4.3.12. The intended formula follows from the normalisations:
- By Proposition 4.3.9, t_{w′} = ⟨−(w′)^{−1}λ − ρ, t⟩t_{w′}^{naive}.
- By Proposition 4.3.11, t = ⟨−w^{−1}λ − ρ, t⟩t^{naive} for any w ∈ C(κ).
- On ℭ^{tor}_{t,w′}, the rational map t^{naive} restricts to t_{w′}^{naive}.
So t restricts there to ⟨(w′)^{−1}λ − w^{−1}λ, t⟩t_{w′}. The p-adic valuation of this factor is ⟨(w′)^{−1}λ + ρ, v(t)⟩ − ⟨w^{−1}λ + ρ, v(t)⟩ = ⟨(w′)^{−1}λ − w^{−1}λ, v(t)⟩. That is the printed formula with ")" inserted after (κ + ρ).

Closing the parenthesis after "+ ρ" instead gives ⟨(w′)^{−1}(λ + ρ) − w^{−1}(λ + ρ), v(t)⟩. This adds the term ⟨(w′)^{−1}ρ − w^{−1}ρ, v(t)⟩, which is nonzero in general, and with it the Remark's positivity claim fails.

Example: GSp_4 (g = 2) with κ = (2, −6; k), where k is even (the parity condition of p. 33). Then ρ = (−1, −2; 0) and λ = (−8, 1; k). C(κ) = {w}, where w^{−1}λ = (1, 8; k). Take the w′ ∈ ^MW with (w′)^{−1}λ = (−1, 8; k); it does not lie in C(κ). Then:
- (w′)^{−1}λ − w^{−1}λ = (−2, 0; 0). This is the positive root t ↦ t_4/t_1. The intended value is n_{w′} = v(t_4) − v(t_1), which is > 0 for every t = diag(t_1, …, t_4) ∈ T^{++}(Q_p).
- (w′)^{−1}ρ − w^{−1}ρ = (4, 0; 0), which is −2 times that root. So the other reading gives v(t_1) − v(t_4), which is < 0 for every such t.
For instance, take (v(t_1), …, v(t_4)) = (−1, −2, 2, 1). This t lies in T^{++}(Q_p), since v(t_3) > v(t_4) > v(t_1) > v(t_2). The intended value is 2 and the other reading gives −2.

The positivity claim holds with the intended formula. For w ∈ C(κ), μ = w^{−1}λ is the unique antidominant element of Wλ. Hence σμ − μ is a non-negative rational combination of positive roots for every σ ∈ W, and it is nonzero when σμ ≠ μ. Take σ = (w′)^{−1}w. Then n_{w′} = ⟨σμ − μ, v(t)⟩ ≥ 0 for t ∈ T^+(Q_p). If w′ ∉ C(κ), then (w′)^{−1}λ is not antidominant, so it differs from μ, and n_{w′} > 0 for t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p).

Proposition 4.3.17. The other balancing, ⟨−w^{−1}(w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ), t⟩, gives the weight −w^{−1}λ + w^{−1}ρ instead of −w^{−1}λ − ρ. This is a different normalisation: the valuations differ by ⟨w^{−1}ρ + ρ, v(t)⟩. In the GSp_4 example above, with (v(t_1), …, v(t_4)) = (−1, −2, 2, 1), the intended factor has valuation 12 and the other reading gives 17. The paper excludes that reading in four ways:
- The proof says only "This is analogue to proposition 4.3.9", and Proposition 4.3.9 (p. 48) has ⟨−w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ, t⟩t_w^{naive}.
- The Nebentypus adds no normalisation, since p_2^⋆O(χ) → p_1^⋆O(χ) is an isomorphism (Lemma 4.3.16).
- The definition of t immediately after the proposition (p. 49) uses the balanced factor ⟨−w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ, t⟩. So does Proposition 6.2.6 (p. 61), the correspondence with Nebentypus used in §6.
- Proposition 4.4.5 (p. 51) and Corollary 4.5.5 (p. 52) give the algebraic part of the resulting action as ν = −w^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ. Remark 4.4.6 (p. 51) says that T(Z_p) acts on the Nebentypus complexes by νχ.

Consequences. Neither Remark 4.3.12 nor Proposition 4.3.17 is cited by number later in the paper. Proposition 4.3.17 supplies the correspondence t_w behind the Nebentypus complexes RΓ_w(K^pK_{w,p,P}, κ, χ) of p. 51, and their weight νχ matches the intended normalisation. The Remark's positivity statement is the fact that makes the summands with w′ ∉ C(κ) vanish in the Cousin spectral sequence of Theorem 4.5.2, and it holds for the intended formula. The intended meaning is clear in all three places, so this is a typographical slip that changes no result or argument.

issues.correction: We let S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i (Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i−1}). The second index should be w_i − 1, not w_i + 1. issues.reason:
p. 50 reads: "We let S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i+1}." Notation:
- D_1, …, D_{2g} are the Cartier divisors of §4.1.8, with D_k + D_{2g+1−k} = V(p^n), and Z_i = D_{g+1} + … + D_{g+i} (§4.1.12).
- For 0 ≤ j ≤ i, Z_{i,>j} and Z_{i,<j} are the Cartier divisors of Proposition 4.1.13 (p. 42). They have disjoint supports, and Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj}).
- (w_1, …, w_g) is the sequence attached to w at the end of §3.1. The identity has w_i = i.
- All intersections are taken of supports, inside the special fibre.

1. The printed set cannot be what is meant.
- Lemma 4.1.17(1) gives Z_{i,>w_i+1} ⊆ Z_{i,>w_i}.
- By p. 43, S_{F_p,w} ⊆ ∩_i (Z_{i,>w_i−1} ∩ Z^c_{i,>w_i}).
- So the printed set never meets the non-empty stratum S_{F_p,w}.
- In fact the printed set is empty for every w, because each factor Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i+1} is empty. If w_i < i, then j = w_i + 1 ≤ i, and Z_{i,<j} and Z_{i,>j} have disjoint supports. If w_i = i, the extension in the correction gives Z_{i,>i+1} = 0, since Z_i − V(p^{n(i+1)}) = −V(p^n) − (D_{g+1−i} + … + D_g) is anti-effective.

Lemma 4.4.2, however, says that this set compactifies S_{F_p,w}. By Definitions 2.1.9 and 2.1.26 (pp. 7 and 10), S_{F_p,w} must be open in it, with complement D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−}. So Lemma 4.4.2 is false as printed.

Example, g = 1. The proof of Proposition 4.1.13 gives Z_{1,>0} = D_2 and Z_{1,<1} = D_1, and §4.1.8 gives D_1 + D_2 = V(p^n). Hence Z_{1,>1} − Z_{1,<1} = −D_1, so Z_{1,>1} = 0. For w ≠ Id, §3.1 gives w_1 = 0. The printed set is then Z_{1,<1} ∩ Z_{1,>1} = ∅. But S_{F_p,w} = S_{F_p} ∖ D_2 (Lemma 4.1.9) is not empty: it is the locus where H_2 is étale.

2. The corrected set works.
- Let S̃_{=w} = ∩_i (Z^c_{i,>w_i} ∩ Z^c_{i,<w_i}) be the open set of Proposition 4.1.13(2). It is the complement of D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−}.
- On S̃_{=w}, Z_i = V(p^{nw_i}) (proof of Proposition 4.1.13). So there Z_{i,<w_i+1} − Z_{i,>w_i+1} = V(p^n) and Z_{i,>w_i−1} − Z_{i,<w_i−1} = V(p^n).
- In each pair the two divisors have disjoint supports. So Z_{i,<w_i+1} and Z_{i,>w_i−1} both contain the whole special fibre of S̃_{=w}, which is S_{F_p,w} (Corollary 4.1.14).
- Hence the corrected set is closed in the proper S^{tor}_{F_p} and contains S_{F_p,w}. Removing D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−} from it leaves exactly S_{F_p,w}.
- For g = 1 and w ≠ Id: the corrected set is Z_{1,<1} = D_1, D_{w,+} = Z_{1,<0} = ∅ and D_{w,−} = Z_{1,>0} = D_2. So D_1 ∖ D_2 = S_{F_p} ∖ D_2 = S_{F_p,w}.

The proof of Lemma 4.4.2 uses exactly these two bounds. Inside the set, it needs Z_{i,>w_i} and Z_{i,<w_i} to lie in ∩_{j=0}^{i}(Z_{i,<j} ∪ Z_{i,>j}). This follows from Lemma 4.1.17(1):
- for j ≤ w_i, Z_{i,>w_i} ⊆ Z_{i,>j};
- for j ≥ w_i + 1, the set lies in Z_{i,<w_i+1} ⊆ Z_{i,<j};
- the case of Z_{i,<w_i} is symmetric, using Z_{i,>w_i−1}.

- The notation "(w−1, w+1)" and Z_{>w−1} = ∩_i Z_{i,>w_i−1} (§4.1.16, p. 43) both point to the lower bound w_i − 1.
- On p. 58 (proof of Proposition 5.6.3, g = 2, w of length one) the paper writes "Concretely, S^{tor}_{(w−1,w+1)} = Z_{2,<2} ∩ Z_{1,>0}". Here (w_1, w_2) = (1, 1), which matches D_{w,+} = Z_{1,<1} and D_{w,−} = Z_{2,>1} on the same page.
- The corrected definition gives Z_{1,<2} ∩ Z_{1,>0} ∩ Z_{2,<2} ∩ Z_{2,>0}. Here Z_{1,<2} is the whole special fibre and Z_{1,>0} = Z_1 ⊆ Z_2 = Z_{2,>0}. So it equals Z_{2,<2} ∩ Z_{1,>0}, exactly as on p. 58. The printed definition would give ∅, since it includes Z_{2,<2} ∩ Z_{2,>2}.
- The proof of Corollary 4.4.3 uses (∪_{w'} C^{tor}_{t,F_p,w'}) ∩ p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = C^{tor}_{t,F_p,w}. Here p_i maps C^{tor}_{t,F_p,w'} into S_{F_p,w'}. On S̃_{=w'} we have Z_i = V(p^{nw'_i}). So there Z_{i,<w_i+1} − Z_{i,>w_i+1} = V(p^{n(w_i+1−w'_i)}) and Z_{i,>w_i−1} − Z_{i,<w_i−1} = V(p^{n(w'_i−w_i+1)}). Hence the first factor misses S_{F_p,w'} when w'_i > w_i, and the second misses it when w'_i < w_i. So S_{F_p,w'} meets the corrected set only if w'_i = w_i for all i. Since the sequence determines w (§3.1), this means w' = w, so the equality holds for the corrected set. With the printed set the left-hand side is empty.

So the slip is a single index, and the notation and p. 58 fix the intended set. With that set, Lemma 4.4.2 holds as intended. The later uses of the set and of the lemma (Corollary 4.4.3, Proposition 4.4.4 and Proposition 5.6.3) all refer to the corrected set.

Also, F is the divisor of the function h = p_1^⋆f_+ p_2^⋆f_− / p_2^⋆f_+ that the proof's identity p_1^⋆f_+ p_2^⋆f_− = h p_2^⋆f_+ defines.

(1) The first sentence. As printed, the second inequality compares a divisor with itself, so it says nothing. The inequality that Lemma 4.2.11 gives, and that the proof uses, is p_1^⋆Z_< ≥ p_2^⋆Z_<. This inequality makes F effective, so h is regular. Without it, h is not known to be regular. The end of the proof states the same inequality in strict form: "there exists 0 < s < 1 such that s p_1^⋆Z_{i,<w_i} ≥ p_2^⋆Z_{i,<w_i}". So the subscript 1 on the right-hand side is a slip for 2.

(2) The "In particular" sentence. The printed claim is that the support of F contains p_1^⋆Z_>. This is trivially true, because F = E + p_1^⋆Z_> with E effective. It is also not what the argument uses. The next sentence says that h vanishes on p_1^⋆Z_<, and this is the property the argument needs. Since Z_> and Z_< have disjoint supports, there are local functions a and b with af_+ + bf_− = 1. Together with p_1^⋆f_+ p_2^⋆f_− = h p_2^⋆f_+, this gives p_1^⋆f_+ = (p_1^⋆f_+ p_2^⋆a + h p_2^⋆b) p_2^⋆f_+. Because h vanishes on p_1^⋆Z_<, so does the factor p_1^⋆f_+ p_2^⋆a + h p_2^⋆b. That gives s p_1^⋆Z_< ≥ p_2^⋆Z_< for some 0 < s < 1. This is the condition of Definition 2.1.19(2) (p. 9) for Z_{i,<w_i}. Summing over i, as the proof does at the end, gives the same condition for D_{w,+}. So the sentence should end with p_1^⋆Z_<.

(3) The sentence just before the "In particular" sentence is true, and it is enough. It says that, on C^{tor}_{t,F_p,(w−1,w+1)}, the support of E contains p_1^⋆Z_> and p_2^⋆Z_<. We have p_1^⋆Z_< − p_2^⋆Z_< ≤ E. So the support of p_1^⋆Z_< = (p_1^⋆Z_< − p_2^⋆Z_<) + p_2^⋆Z_< lies in supp E ∪ supp p_2^⋆Z_<. By that sentence, this union is supp E, and supp E ⊆ supp F. This proves the corrected sentence (2). In the same way, p_2^⋆Z_> ≤ E + p_1^⋆Z_>, and supp E ⊇ p_1^⋆Z_>, so supp E ⊇ p_2^⋆Z_>. This is the input needed for "One argues similarly with Z_{i,>w_i}". There, h' = p_2^⋆f_− p_1^⋆f_+ / p_1^⋆f_− has divisor E + p_2^⋆Z_<, and h' must vanish on p_2^⋆Z_>.

That sentence follows from Corollary 4.2.10 as follows. The definition just before the lemma on p. 50 prints S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i+1}. As printed, this set is empty, because Z_{i,<j} and Z_{i,>j} have disjoint supports. So the second term should read Z_{i,>w_i−1}. By Lemma 4.1.17(1) (p. 43), Z_{i,>j} decreases and Z_{i,<j} increases as j grows. Hence Z_{i,>w_i} ∩ Z_{i,<w_i+1} ⊆ ∩_{j=0}^{i} (Z_{i,<j} ∪ Z_{i,>j}) and Z_{i,<w_i} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i−1} ⊆ ∩_{j=0}^{i} (Z_{i,<j} ∪ Z_{i,>j}). So on C^{tor}_{t,F_p,(w−1,w+1)}, the support of E contains p_1^⋆ and p_2^⋆ of both Z_{i,<w_i} and Z_{i,>w_i}. In particular it contains the printed pair, and also the alternative pair.

Why this is a misprint that affects nothing. Each slip is a wrong subscript, and the intended form is clear. Lemma 4.2.11 and the proof's own final inequality fix the first slip. The sentence that follows fixes the second. With these two corrections, the paragraph's argument goes through. The statement of Lemma 4.4.2 is unaffected, and so is Proposition 4.4.4 (p. 51), which rests on it.

issues.locator: §4.4.1, proof of Corollary 4.4.3, p. 50
issues.printed: The proof says p_2^⋆Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i − p_1^⋆Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i and p_1^⋆D_{w,+} + p_2^⋆D_{w,+} have equal supports over p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}. It obtains f_i^n = h_ig_i, X_i = b_{i,j}X_j, Y_i^n = a_{i,j}Y_j^n, f_i = a_{i,j}f_j, g_i = b_{i,j}g_j and g_j(h_j − b_{i,j}a_{i,j}^{-1}h_i) = 0. Setting m = 2n, it claims Y_i^m ↦ g_ih_i^2X_i glues into O_{p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}}(−2m(p_2^⋆Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i − p_1^⋆Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i)) → O_{p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}}(−p_1^⋆D_{w,+} − p_2^⋆D_{w,+}).
issues.correction:
Replace the first two sentences with: "Over p_i^{-1}S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}, the support of p_1^⋆D_{w,+} + p_2^⋆D_{w,+} is contained in the support of p_2^⋆Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i − p_1^⋆Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i. Indeed, the complement of p_1^⋆D_{w,+} + p_2^⋆D_{w,+} contains C_{t,F_p,w}, since S_{F_p,w} ∩ D_{w,+} = ∅." The third sentence then gives the inclusion, and the rest of the proof uses nothing more. That sentence needs S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i−1}; the definition on p. 50 prints Z_{i,>w_i+1}.

Equality of supports would hold only with D_{w,+} replaced by D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−}, but the corollary needs D_{w,+}.

The same proof has two more slips, both harmless:
- 'f_i = a_{i,j}f_j' should read f_i^n = a_{i,j}f_j^n.
- The glued map is O(−m(p_2^⋆ΣZ_i − p_1^⋆ΣZ_i)) → O(−p_1^⋆D_{w,+} − p_2^⋆D_{w,+}) with m = 2n, not O(−2m(…)).
issues.reason:
Setting. By Proposition 4.1.13 (p. 42), Z_i = Σ_{k≤i} D_{g+k}, and Z_{i,>j}, Z_{i,<j} are effective with disjoint support, with Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj}). On S_{F_p,w′}, the reduction of S̃_{=w′_1,…,w′_g} (Corollary 4.1.14), we have Z_k = V(p^{nw′_k}) locally. In §4.4.1 (p. 50), D_{w,+} = ∪_i Z_{i,<w_i}, D_{w,−} = ∪_i Z_{i,>w_i}, and S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} is printed as ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i+1}. As printed, this set misses S_{F_p,w}: it would need w′_k ≤ w_k and w′_k ≥ w_k+2. So it must be read as ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i−1}. This reading agrees with the GSp4 case on p. 58, where S_{(w−1,w+1)} = Z_{2,<2} ∩ Z_{1,>0}, D_{w,+} = Z_{1,<1} and D_{w,−} = Z_{2,>1} for (w_1,w_2) = (1,1).

Counterexample to the printed sentences. Take g = 1, n = 1 and w the non-identity element. By §3.1, w_1 = 1 exactly when 2 ∈ w^{-1}{2}, so here w_1 = 0. Then:
- Z_1 = D_2, so Z_{1,>0} = D_2 and Z_{1,<0} = ∅.
- D_2 − V(p) = −D_1, so Z_{1,<1} = D_1 (as also stated on p. 42).
Hence D_{w,+} = ∅, D_{w,−} = D_2, S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = D_1 and S_{F_p,w} = D_1 \ D_2. So p_1^⋆D_{w,+} + p_2^⋆D_{w,+} = 0, and its complement is all of p_i^{-1}(D_1). This set contains points x with p_1(x) and p_2(x) supersingular, and such points are not in C_{t,F_p,w}.

By Proposition 4.2.15(3) with k = g = 1, supp(p_2^⋆Z_1 − p_1^⋆Z_1) = p_1^⋆D_1 ∩ p_2^⋆D_2. This contains those supersingular points, for i = 1 and for i = 2. For i = 1 it also contains a component on which p_1^⋆H is étale and p_2^⋆H is multiplicative. That component comes from triples (E, H, L) with E ordinary, H ≠ L both non-canonical, and φ(H) = E[p]/L the canonical subgroup of E/L. So the two supports differ, and both 'have the same support' and 'the complement … is C_{t,F_p,w}' are false. The claims also fail for general w, since the complement of p_j^⋆D_{w,+} includes points over D_{w,−} \ D_{w,+}.

The corollary still holds. To get f_i^n ∈ (g_i) one only needs V(g_i) ⊆ V(f_i), that is, the inclusion of supports. This inclusion holds:
- The divisors in Propositions 4.2.14(1) and 4.2.15(3) coincide after reindexing: both are Σ_j p_1^⋆D_j ∩ p_2^⋆D_{2g+1−j}. So the complement of supp(p_2^⋆ΣZ_i − p_1^⋆ΣZ_i) in C_{t,F_p} is ∪_{w′} C_{t,F_p,w′}.
- At a point y ∈ S_{F_p,w′}, locally Z_k − V(p^{nj}) = V(p^{n(w′_k−j)}). Hence y ∈ Z_{k,<w_k+1} if and only if w′_k ≤ w_k, and y ∈ Z_{k,>w_k−1} if and only if w′_k ≥ w_k. So S_{F_p,w′} meets S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} only when w′ = w.
- S_{F_p,w} is disjoint from D_{w,+}.
So the paper's own third sentence already gives the inclusion. The corrected statement about complements was checked the same way, using S_{F_p} \ (D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−}) = S_{F_p,w} (Proposition 4.1.13(2)).

The two slips:
- Since Y_i^n ↦ f_i^n, the relation Y_i^n = a_{i,j}Y_j^n gives f_i^n = a_{i,j}f_j^n. The printed relation g_j(h_j − b_{i,j}a_{i,j}^{-1}h_i) = 0 follows from exactly this, via h_ig_i = f_i^n = a_{i,j}h_jg_j and g_i = b_{i,j}g_j. With f_i = a_{i,j}f_j it would read a_{i,j}^{-n}.
- Gluing Y_i^{2n} ↦ g_ih_i^2X_i requires g_j(a_{i,j}^2h_j^2 − b_{i,j}^2h_i^2) = 0, which is the printed identity. The composite sends Y_i^{2n} to g_i^2h_i^2 = f_i^{2n}, which is the canonical map. So the source is O(−m(…)) with m = 2n, and the printed −2m is inconsistent, though harmless because m is only asserted to exist.
All of this was checked by direct computation.

Downstream. Corollary 4.4.3 is used only through its statement, in the proof of Proposition 4.5.8 (p. 53). That statement is correct, so only the proof is affected. Setting (pp. 41–42, 50):
- Z_k = Σ_{l≤k} D_{g+l}.
- Z_{k,>j} and Z_{k,<j} are effective, have disjoint support, and satisfy Z_{k,>j} − Z_{k,<j} = Z_k − V(p^{nj}) (Prop. 4.1.13).
- D_{w,+} = ∪_k Z_{k,<w_k} and D_{w,−} = ∪_k Z_{k,>w_k}.
- S_{F_p,w} is the special fibre of S̃_{=w_1,…,w_g} = ∩_k Z^c_{k,>w_k} ∩ Z^c_{k,<w_k} (Prop. 4.1.13(2), Cor. 4.1.14). So S_{F_p,w} is disjoint from D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−}.
- Write E = p_2^⋆ΣZ_k − p_1^⋆ΣZ_k, which is effective by Cor. 4.2.10.

Counterexample. Take g = 1 and w = s, the non-trivial element of ^MW = W. By §3.1, w_1 = 0, since 2 ∉ s^{-1}{2}.
- Z_{1,>0} − Z_{1,<0} = Z_1 = D_2 is effective and the two parts have disjoint support, so Z_{1,<0} = 0. Hence D_{w,+} = ∅ and p_1^⋆D_{w,+} + p_2^⋆D_{w,+} = 0 has empty support.
- S_{F_p,w} = S_{F_p} \ D_2 is the locus where H = Gr_2 is étale. With the corrected definition, S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = Z_{1,<1} = D_1 (p. 42 gives Z_{1,<1} = D_g).

(a) Supersingular points. Cor. 4.2.10 with i = 1 shows that supp E contains p_1^{-1}(D_1 ∩ D_2) and p_2^{-1}(D_1 ∩ D_2). This set is non-empty: over a supersingular curve A[p^n] is connected, so neither Gr_1 nor Gr_2 is étale. It lies in p_i^{-1}(D_1) for i = 1 and for i = 2.

(b) Points over S_{F_p,w} itself. These do not depend on the misprinted definition, because Lemma 4.4.2 requires S_{F_p,w} ⊆ S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}.
- In the correspondence of §4.2.5, L has order p and meets H trivially, and H′ = φ(H).
- Take E ordinary with H non-canonical, and L ≠ H non-canonical.
- Then φ(H) = E[p]/L is the kernel of the dual isogeny, which is the multiplicative (canonical) subgroup of E/L.
- At the resulting point y, p_1(y) ∈ S_{F_p,w} while p_2^⋆D_2 > 0 = p_1^⋆D_2. So y ∈ supp E.
So over p_1^{-1}S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} the support of E is non-empty, while that of p_1^⋆D_{w,+} + p_2^⋆D_{w,+} is empty. This refutes the first sentence. The point y lies in the complement of p_1^⋆D_{w,+} + p_2^⋆D_{w,+}, but not in C_{t,F_p,w} = p_1^{-1}S_{F_p,w} ∩ p_2^{-1}S_{F_p,w}. This refutes the second sentence.

The failure is general. For i = 1, any y with p_1(y) ∈ S_{F_p,w} and p_2(y) ∈ S_{F_p,w′}, where w′ ≠ w, gives a counterexample:
- y ∈ supp E by Props. 4.2.14(1) and 4.2.15(3).
- p_2^⋆Z_k ≥ p_1^⋆Z_k forces w′_k ≥ w_k, so p_2(y) ∉ D_{w,+}.
Equality holds only in special cases, such as w = Id, where D_{w,−} = ∅.

Defence. No faithful reading saves the equality. The claim uses D_{w,+} alone, and the point in (b) does not involve D_{w,−}. What is true is this: since S_{F_p} \ (D_{w,+} ∪ D_{w,−}) = S_{F_p,w}, the complement of p_1^⋆(D_{w,+}+D_{w,−}) + p_2^⋆(D_{w,+}+D_{w,−}) inside p_i^{-1}S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} is C_{t,F_p,w}.

Why the corollary survives. The step "f_i^n = h_ig_i" needs only V(g_i) ⊆ V(f_i), that is, the inclusion of supports. The paper's third sentence supplies it:
- The complement of supp E in C_{t,F_p} is ∪_{w′}C_{t,F_p,w′}. After reindexing, the divisors in Props. 4.2.14(1) and 4.2.15(3) agree.
- At a point of S_{F_p,w′}, locally Z_k − V(p^{nj}) = V(p^{n(w′_k−j)}). So the point lies in Z_{k,<w_k+1} if and only if w′_k ≤ w_k, and in Z_{k,>w_k−1} if and only if w′_k ≥ w_k. Hence S_{F_p,w′} meets S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} only when w′ = w.
- This needs the reading Z_{k,>w_k−1}. With the printed Z_{i,>w_i+1}, S_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} would miss S_{F_p,w}. The GSp_4 case on p. 58 uses Z_{1,>0} for (w_1,w_2) = (1,1), which agrees with the corrected reading.
- C_{t,F_p,w} avoids p_1^{-1}D_{w,+} ∪ p_2^{-1}D_{w,+}.
Then f_i^n ∈ (g_i), because O(U_i) is Noetherian. The squares h_i^2 make g_ih_i^2 independent of the choice of h_i, so the gluing goes through.

The two slips:
- Only f_i^n = a_{i,j}f_j^n yields the printed g_j(h_j − b_{i,j}a_{i,j}^{-1}h_i) = 0. The printed f_i = a_{i,j}f_j would give a_{i,j}^{-n} instead.
- Y_i^m generates O(−mE). The composite with O(−p_1^⋆D_{w,+} − p_2^⋆D_{w,+}) → O sends Y_i^m to g_i^2h_i^2 = f_i^m, which is the canonical map. So the source is O(−mE), not O(−2mE).
The identities were checked by direct computation.

Downstream. Cor. 4.4.3 is cited once, in the proof of Prop. 4.5.8 (p. 53), and only through its statement. That statement is correct, so only the proof of Cor. 4.4.3 is affected.

issues.reason: Y_i generates O(−(p_2^⋆ΣZ_i − p_1^⋆ΣZ_i)) on U_i, so Y_i^m generates O(−m(p_2^⋆ΣZ_i − p_1^⋆ΣZ_i)). The source of the map is therefore the −m twist, not the −2m twist. This twist also matches the statement of the corollary and the dual maps displayed at the start of the proof. The map is compatible with the inclusions into O: Y_i^m has image f_i^{2n} = h_i^2g_i^2, which is the image of g_ih_i^2X_i. The gluing check (Y_i^{2n} = a_{i,j}^2Y_j^{2n}, X_i = b_{i,j}X_j, g_j(h_j^2 − b_{i,j}^2a_{i,j}^{-2}h_i^2) = 0) also applies to this map. Read literally, the −2m twist would need a generator Y_i^{2m}, which the construction does not provide. Only the existence of some exponent matters, so nothing downstream is affected.

issues.correction: For s = 1, cite Lemma 4.4.2 together with Lemma 2.1.29 (p. 10). S̄^tor_{w,F_p} is closed in S^tor_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} and contains S^tor_{F_p,w} as an open subscheme. So the closed immersions S̄^tor_{w,F_p} ⊂ S^tor_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} and C̄^tor_{t,w,F_p} ⊂ C^tor_{t,F_p,(w−1,w+1)} form a strict map of compactifications of (C^tor_{t,w,F_p}, S^tor_{w,F_p}). Lemma 2.1.29 then makes (C̄^tor_{t,w,F_p}, S̄^tor_{w,F_p}), with the pull-backs of D_{w,+} and D_{w,−}, a strict dynamic compactification. For general s, add one more step before citing Lemma 2.1.35. The reductions of C̄^tor_{t,w,Z/p^sZ} and S̄^tor_{w,Z/p^sZ} are the reductions of C̄^tor_{t,w,F_p} and S̄^tor_{w,F_p}. They inherit the strict dynamic structure because inclusions of powers of ideals are preserved under pull-back, which is the same argument as in the proof of Lemma 2.1.34. issues.reason:
The two compactifications differ. Lemma 4.4.2 (p. 50) is about X̄ = S^tor_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} with C̄ = p_1^{-1}X̄ ∩ p_2^{-1}X̄. The proof of Proposition 4.4.4 uses a different space: the closure S̄^tor_{w,F_p} of S^tor_{F_p,w}, with C̄^tor_{t,w,F_p} = p_1^⋆S̄ ∩ p_2^⋆S̄.

A side remark on the definition on p. 50. It is printed as ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i+1}, and must be read with Z_{i,>w_i−1}. The worked case on p. 58, "S^tor_{(w−1,w+1)} = Z_{2,<2} ∩ Z_{1,>0}", uses that reading, and Z_{i,>w_i+1} does not meet S^tor_{F_p,w}. With the intended definition, S^tor_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} is closed and contains S^tor_{F_p,w}, so it contains the closure.

In general the closure is strictly smaller. Example: g = 1, n ≥ 2, where no blow-up is made and Z_{1,<1} = D_1. For w with w_1 = 0, S^tor_{F_p,w} is the ordinary part of the component on which H_2 is étale. S^tor_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = D_1 ∩ S_{F_p} contains every component on which A[p^n]/H_2 is not étale. That includes the components on whose ordinary locus H_2 is an extension of Z/p^b by μ_{p^a} with a, b ≥ 1 (compare Remark 4.1.4), and these are not in the closure. So the sentence "lemma 4.4.2 proves that this is a strict dynamical compactification" leaves out a step: restricting to a closed subscheme.

Defence: the missing step is routine, and the paper itself supplies it in Lemma 2.1.29 (p. 10; Lemma 2.1.28 in the preprint). The pair (C̄^tor_{t,w,F_p}, S̄^tor_{w,F_p}) is a compactification in the sense of Definition 2.1.9. Both spaces are proper, being closed in proper schemes. Also C̄ ×_{S̄×S̄} (S_w × S_w) = p_1^{-1}S^tor_{F_p,w} ∩ p_2^{-1}S^tor_{F_p,w} = C^tor_{t,w,F_p}. The inclusion into Lemma 4.4.2's compactification is a map of compactifications, and it is strict because S̄ ∩ S^tor_{F_p,w} = S^tor_{F_p,w}. Lemma 2.1.29 then gives the s = 1 case.

Lemma 2.1.35 has a hypothesis on the reduced pair (C̄^red, X̄^red). Here these are the reductions of the s = 1 pair, which inherit the strict inequalities by pull-back, as in the proof of Lemma 2.1.34.

The mistake is a missing citation and a missing one-line remark. No statement is false.

What uses the passage: the definition of RΓ_w (p. 51), which needs only existence; the proof of Proposition 4.4.5 (p. 51), which needs S̄^tor_{w,Z/p^sZ} and D = D_+ ∪ D_− to be independent of t (true of the closure); and Theorem 5.1.4 (p. 53), which needs only existence. The compactification named in the proof really is a strict dynamic compactification, so none of these is affected.

issues.locator: §4.4, proof of Proposition 4.4.5, p. 51 (the sentences "We deduce that T^+(Q_p) acts on RΓ_{D_+,D_−}(…)" and "Since there exists n and u, u′ … it is easy to deduce …"). The 2024 preprint has the same text on its p. 49; the only difference is that the ordinary parts there are indexed C^{tor}_{t,Z/p^sZ} rather than C^{tor}_{t,w,Z/p^sZ}.
issues.printed: The proof says Proposition 4.4.4 constructs S̄^{tor}_{w,Z/p^sZ}, with D = D_+∪D_−, independently of t ∈ T^+(Q_p), hence T^+(Q_p) acts on RΓ_{D_+,D_−}(S̄^{tor}_{w,Z/p^sZ}, ω^κ). For t,t′ ∈ T^{++}(Q_p), their ordinary cohomology summands RΓ(S^{tor}_{Z/p^s,w}, ω^κ)^{C^{tor}_{t,w,Z/p^sZ}−ord} and RΓ(S^{tor}_{Z_p/p^s,w}, ω^κ)^{C^{tor}_{t′,w,Z/p^sZ}−ord} are said to be quasi-isomorphic because some n and u,u′ ∈ T^+(Q_p) satisfy t^n = t′u′ together with (t′)^n = tu.
issues.correction:
The sentence "We deduce that T^+(Q_p) acts on RΓ_{D_+,D_−}(S̄^{tor}_{w,Z/p^sZ}, ω^κ)" needs two ingredients that the paper does not supply.
(a) For each t ∈ T^+(Q_p), the operator T_t is defined on that complex. This part is easy. By Lemma 4.2.11, the tuple (C̄_{t,w}, S̄_w, D_+, D_−) is a dynamic compactification for every t ∈ T^+(Q_p), not only for t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p). Proposition 2.2.10 applied to t_w of Proposition 4.3.9 then gives T_t.
(b) A composition law: T_t T_{t′} ≃ T_{tt′} ≃ T_{t′} T_t for all t, t′ ∈ T^+(Q_p). This is the missing step. Proving it requires:
- an identification C_{t,w} ×_{S_w} C_{t′,w} ≅ C_{tt′,w}, which is the integral, Igusa-level analogue, via Proposition 4.2.4, of the double-coset identity [K t K][K t′ K] = [K tt′ K] from [Cas], lem. 4.1.5, cited on p. 43;
- multiplicativity of the normalizing factors ⟨−w^{-1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ)−ρ, t⟩;
- a proper-base-change argument, as in the proof of Proposition 2.8.2, showing that composing the operators on cohomology with partial support gives the operator of the composite correspondence.
Once (b) is available, the deduction is indeed easy.
issues.reason:
Checked against the paper's constructions. The operators on RΓ_{D_+,D_−} come from these results:
- Proposition 4.3.9 (p. 48): for each t separately, the normalized cohomological correspondence t_w = ⟨−w^{-1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ)−ρ, t⟩ t_w^{naive} on C^{tor}_{t,w}.
- §§2.2–2.3 (Proposition 2.3.13, p. 17): its extension to a dynamic compactification.
- Proposition 4.4.4: the compactification p_1^⋆S̄ ∩ p_2^⋆S̄.

The only justification offered for "T^+(Q_p) acts" is that the compactification S̄^{tor}_{w,Z/p^sZ} does not depend on t. That gives one endomorphism T_x for each x on a common complex. It says nothing about how these endomorphisms relate to one another.

The relations t^n = t′u′ and (t′)^n = tu hold in the group. They carry information about the operators only through T_{t^n} = T_t^n = T_{t′}T_{u′} (and symmetrically) with commuting operators. Without this, the t- and t′-ordinary projectors on RΓ_{D_+,D_−} are unrelated.

The paper proves no such composition law in this setting:
- §2.8 (Proposition 2.8.2, pp. 25–27) handles only the iterates C^{(n)} of a single correspondence. It does not compare C_t ×_S C_{t′} (or C_t^{(n)}) with C_{tt′} (or C_{t^n}), and it says nothing about the normalizations.
- Casselman's lemma, cited on p. 48, gives the algebra map Z[T^+(Q_p)/T(Z_p)] → C_c(K_{p,n}\G(Q_p)/K_{p,n}, Z). That is multiplicativity in the abstract Hecke algebra, i.e. on cohomology of the generic fibre. It does not cover the mod p^s cohomology with partial support over the strata S^{tor}_w, defined via integral models and integrally normalized maps.

That §2.8 is needed even for iterates of one correspondence shows that such compatibilities are not formal in this framework. The step is therefore asserted without adequate proof.

The result itself is not in doubt, and the gap looks fillable:
- For t, t′ ∈ T^+ the double cosets multiply at level K_{p,n}, so the composite correspondence is C_{tt′} on the generic fibre.
- The normalizing factors are multiplicative in t.
- Maps p_2^⋆ω^κ → p_1^!ω^κ on the normal Z_p-flat integral models are determined by their generic fibre.
- The remaining bookkeeping is of the kind done in Proposition 2.8.2.

As printed, however, "it is easy to deduce" rests on the unproved sentence "We deduce that T^+(Q_p) acts". The multiplicativity is also needed for the asserted T(Q_p)-action, since T(Q_p) is generated by T^{++}(Q_p) acting invertibly on the ordinary part. 1. What the paper actually shows. Independence of the compactification from t gives, for each t, an endomorphism T_t of the one complex M = RΓ_{D_+,D_−}(S̄^{tor}_{w,Z/p^sZ}, ω^κ). It does not give a monoid action, meaning T_{tt′} = T_t T_{t′} with the operators commuting.

2. Why the argument needs such an action. The relation t^n = t′u′ is useful only if T_t^n = T_{t′}T_{u′} and T_t commutes with T_{t′}.

3. Nothing nearby supplies the composition law. I searched the paper for it and found the following.
- Section 2 constructs the operator of a single dynamic correspondence (Proposition 2.2.10) and checks that it does not depend on the compactification (Proposition 2.2.11).
- Section 2.8 treats only the iterates of one fixed correspondence C, not products C_t ∘ C_{t′} of different Hecke correspondences.
- Section 4.2 cites [Cas] only for the abstract Hecke algebra map Z[T^+(Q_p)/T(Z_p)] → C_c(K_{p,n}\G(Q_p)/K_{p,n}, Z). That map does not transfer to the integral, normalized cohomological correspondences restricted to S_w with partial supports. Transferring it requires checking that the fibre product of the finite flat formal schemes C_{t,w} and C_{t′,w} over S_w matches C_{tt′,w} integrally, and that the fundamental classes and normalizations compose.
- Proposition 4.2.4 and Lemma 4.3.8 contain the right ingredients: the Igusa description, and trace factors additive on T^+ because the sign of α(w(v(t))) is constant there. They are never assembled into a composition statement.
The step is standard and very likely true, so the defence fails only as a matter of written proof.

4. The final deduction does go through once (b) holds, even with commutativity only up to homotopy. By Proposition 2.5.4, H^i(M^{t-ord}) is a finite Z/p^s-module on which T_t is invertible. Then T_{t′} is invertible on it, because T_t^n = T_{t′}T_{u′} with commuting operators. The t′-non-ordinary factor is a Z/p^s[[T]]-module, so T_{t′} acts nilpotently on any finite-length piece of it. Hence the projection of H^i(M^{t-ord}) to the t′-non-ordinary factor vanishes. Symmetrically, the composite of inclusion and projection between the two direct factors is a quasi-isomorphism.

5. The proposed correction is right and essentially minimal. I add only (a), which follows from Lemma 4.2.11, and the note that (b) is exactly what the sentence "T^+(Q_p) acts" presupposes.

6. What depends on this passage.
- The T(Q_p)-action asserted in the statement of Proposition 4.4.5. Its only justification is this sentence, together with inverting T^{++}(Q_p) on ordinary parts, which also needs commutativity.
- Corollary 4.5.5 (an isomorphism of T(Q_p)-modules).
- The definition of RΓ_w(K^pK_{p,P}) on p. 54 ("the argument of proposition 4.4.5 shows that the ordinary part does not depend on the choice of t") and Proposition 5.2.3 (these complexes lie in D(Z_p[T(Q_p)])).
- Through these, the T(Q_p)-equivariance claims in Theorem 1.4.3 and the adjoint statement in Theorem 5.5.1.
No stated result is shown to be false, so the gap affects the proof only.

The January 2024 preprint has the same text (its §4.5.6, "proof of the main result", pp. 50–51).
issues.printed: Theorem 4.5.2(1) states ⊕_{w∈C(κ), ℓ(w)=p} H^{p+q}_w(K^pK_{w,p,P}, κ) ⇒ H^{p+q}(S^{tor}, ω̃^κ)^{t−ord}, with analogous other versions. Its proof cites Lemmas 2.9.3 and 4.5.7 for RΓ_c(F̂_p \ F̂_{p−1}, ω̃^κ) = ⊕_{w,ℓ(w)=p} RΓ(S^{tor}, lim_m lim_n ω̃^κ(−mD_{−,w})/𝓘^n_{Z,>w−1}). It says the subsequent proposition proves the theorem because Corollary 2.3.11 identifies the right side's ordinary part as RΓ_w(K_pK_{w,p,P}, κ).
issues.correction:
Replace the parenthetical with the following argument, applied to each w with ℓ(w) = p. Also, "K_p" printed as a subscript should be the superscript K^p. Below, s indexes the truncations mod p^s (this index is written n in Proposition 4.5.8), and n is the level of K_{p,n}, as in Proposition 4.1.13.

(a) Comparison. By Corollary 2.3.11, the right-hand side of Proposition 4.5.8 is lim_s RΓ_{D_{−,w},D_{+,w}}(S^tor_{Z/p^s}, ω̃^κ/p^s). Modulo p^s, the complement of D_{+,w} ∪ D_{−,w} in S^tor is the stratum 𝔖^tor_w (Proposition 4.1.13(2), Corollary 4.1.14). By Lemma 4.2.11, (C_t^tor, S^tor, p_1, p_2, D_{+,w}, D_{−,w}) mod p^s is a dynamic compactification of (ℭ^tor_{t,w}, 𝔖^tor_w) mod p^s, though not necessarily a strict one. The strict dynamic compactification of Proposition 4.4.4 is made of the closures of the stratum, and it maps to this one by a strict map made of closed immersions. So Proposition 2.2.11 (through Lemma 2.2.8) identifies the two cohomologies with partial support, compatibly with the Hecke operators. Theorem 2.5.1(1) then lets one pass between the two orders of support. On 𝔖^tor_w the divisors Z_{i,>w_i} and Z_{i,<w_i} are empty, so Proposition 4.1.13(1) gives Z_i = V(p^{n w_i}) there. So ω̃^κ = p^{n k' Σ_i w_i} ω^κ on 𝔖^tor_w, and this is the same scalar on both sides of the correspondence. Under the resulting identification of ω̃^κ with ω^κ, t̃ therefore corresponds over ℭ^tor_{t,w} to the restriction of t. By Remark 4.3.12 (with w' = w), this restriction is p^{n_w} t_w, and n_w = 0 for w ∈ C(κ).

(b) Case w ∈ C(κ). The operator is t_w. With Lemma 2.4.4(1), the ordinary part of the right-hand side of Proposition 4.5.8 is RΓ_w(K^pK_{w,p,P}, κ) as defined in §4.4 (p. 51). By that proposition, it is also the ordinary part of the w-summand of the E_1 term.

(c) Case w ∉ C(κ). The ordinary part of the w-summand is 0. Since t ∈ T^{++}(Q_p), Remark 4.3.12 gives n_w > 0. Modulo p^s the operator is therefore p^{n_w} t_w, and its s-th power p^{s n_w} t_w^s vanishes. So each level is a module over the polynomial ring Z/p^s[t_w], and in that ring the image p^{n_w} t_w of t is nilpotent. Inverting it gives the zero ring, so the level has zero ordinary part by Definition 2.4.2 (as in case (1) of the proof of Lemma 2.4.3). The limit then has zero ordinary part by Lemma 2.4.4(1). The relation t = p^{n_w} t_w holds only over ℭ^tor_{t,w}, where t_w is defined. So the vanishing has to be read off on the right-hand side of Proposition 4.5.8 and carried over to the E_1-summand by that proposition. This works because Proposition 4.5.8 holds for every w. Its proof (pp. 52–53) uses only Lemma 4.3.14, Corollary 4.4.3, Lemma 2.4.4 and the equality (p) = 𝓘_{Z,>w−1} over 𝔖^tor_w, and it never uses w ∈ C(κ).

Case (c) is what cuts the E_1 term down from all w with ℓ(w) = p to w ∈ C(κ), as Theorem 4.5.2 states. The same argument applies to the cuspidal and Nebentypus variants.

issues.locator: §4.5, Corollaries 4.5.4 and 4.5.5, p. 52
issues.printed: Corollaries 4.5.4 and 4.5.5 assume κ ∈ X⋆(T)⁺ with C(κ) = {w}. They assert canonical isomorphisms RΓ_w(K^p K_{w,p,P}, κ) ≃ RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ)^{t−ord} and RΓ_w(K^p K_{w,p,P}, κ) ⊗ Q_p(−ν) ≃ RΓ(S^tor_{Q_p}, ω^κ)^{ord}, respectively, with ν = −w⁻¹w_{0,M}(κ + ρ) − ρ.
issues.correction: In both corollaries, read "Let κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{M,+} be such that C(κ) = {w}". This is the M-dominant cone k_1 ≥ ··· ≥ k_g. It is written X⋆(T)^{+,M} on p. 34, and κ ranges over it from p. 48 onward ("Let κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{M,+}", just before Proposition 4.3.9).
issues.reason:
The page image confirms the printed hypothesis: the superscript in both corollaries is a bare "+", with no M.

Conventions (p. 34). X⋆(T)⁺ is the dominant cone "0 ≥ k_1 ≥ ··· ≥ k_g". X⋆(T)^{+,M} is the M-dominant cone "k_1 ≥ ··· ≥ k_g". Also ρ = ½Σ_{α∈Φ⁺} α. P is the stabiliser of ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩, so the positive roots are e_i − e_j (i < j), −(e_i + e_j) and −2e_i. Summing them gives ρ = (−1, −2, …, −g), which is dominant and regular, as it should be.

On p. 48, C(κ) = {w ∈ ^M W : w⁻¹w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) ∈ X⋆(T)⁻_Q}; the introduction (p. 3) gives the equivalent form −w⁻¹w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) ∈ X⋆(T)⁺.

Take κ ∈ X⋆(T)⁺. Then κ + ρ = (k_1 − 1, …, k_g − g) is strictly decreasing and negative, so it is dominant regular. Since W acts simply transitively on regular chambers, w⁻¹w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) is antidominant only when w⁻¹w_{0,M} = w_0, that is, when w = w_{0,M}w_0. This element lies in ^M W: it is its longest element, of length g² − g(g−1)/2 = g(g+1)/2. So for every κ ∈ X⋆(T)⁺ we have C(κ) = {w_{0,M}w_0} automatically. As printed, the hypothesis "C(κ) = {w}" is therefore empty, and the corollaries only cover the top-degree theory w = w_{0,M}w_0.

Example, g = 1 (checked by direct computation). Here ρ = −1 and ^M W = {1, s}. Every κ ∈ X⋆(T)⁺ (k_1 ≤ 0) has C(κ) = {s}. The weights with C(κ) = {1} are exactly k_1 ≥ 2, which are M-dominant but not in X⋆(T)⁺. So the printed statement does not even contain the degree-0 (classical Hida) control theorem.

The intended hypothesis is clear from the rest of the paper:
- On p. 48, κ is fixed in X⋆(T)^{M,+} before Proposition 4.3.9. The ω̃^κ of Theorem 4.5.2 is defined in that setting.
- Theorem 4.5.2 is the spectral sequence ⊕_{w∈C(κ), ℓ(w)=p} H^{p+q}_w ⇒ H^{p+q}(S^tor, ω̃^κ)^{t-ord}. When C(κ) = {w}, it has a single column and degenerates, for any κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{M,+}. So the proof of the corollaries needs no G-dominance.
- Theorem 1.4.3(4) on p. 5 is labelled "(Classicality in regular weight 4.5.5)". It takes ν ∈ X⋆(T)⁺ and κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν+ρ) − ρ ∈ X⋆(T)^{M_µ,+} for arbitrary w ∈ ^M W. One checks −w⁻¹w_{0,M}(κ+ρ) = ν + ρ, which is dominant regular, so C(κ) = {w}.
- Remark 1.4.5 says point 4) is the case #C(κ) = 1 of point 5), where 5) is stated for κ ∈ X⋆(T)^{M,+}.

The corrected statement follows from Theorem 4.5.2 by the same one-line degeneration argument.

Consequences. As printed, the two corollaries are true but much weaker than intended. They do not support the uses made of them:
- Theorem 1.4.3(4), classicality for every w.
- The interpolation Proposition 1.4.7 (p. 5), which combines the specialisation formula of §5.4 (p. 57) with κ = −w_{0,M}w(ν_alg+ρ) − ρ for arbitrary w.
With the M-dominant hypothesis these results are fine.
