issues.locator: §4.5.6 (proof of Theorem 4.5.2), p. 52: the first display after Lemma 4.5.7. It cites Theorem 2.9.7 (p. 28), whose setup is in §2.9.5 (p. 28). The January 2024 preprint has the same text: §4.5.6 ("proof of the main result") is on p. 50, §2.9.5 on p. 26 and Theorem 2.9.7 on p. 27.
issues.printed: §4.5.6 recalls F_{−1} = ∅ ⊆ F_0 ⊆ ··· ⊆ F_{g(g+1)/2} = S^tor_{F_p}, F_i = ∪_{w,ℓ(w)≤i} Z_{>w−1}, and invokes Theorem 2.9.7 for H_c^{p+q}(F̂_p \ F̂_{p−1}, ω̃^κ) ⇒ H^{p+q}(S^tor, ω̃^κ). That theorem assumes a filtration Z_{−1} = ∅ ⊆ Z_0 ⊆ Z_1 ⊆ Z_2 ⊆ ··· ⊆ X = Z_d by closed subschemes and F ∈ D^−(O_{X,■}), and gives E_1^{p,q} = H_c^{p+q}(Ẑ_p \ Ẑ_{p−1}, F) ⇒ H^{p+q}(X, F).
issues.correction:
Here the X of Theorem 2.9.7 is the Z_p-scheme S^tor = S̃^tor_{K^pK_{p,n}} (p. 42). The filtration ends at F_{g(g+1)/2} = S^tor_{F_p}, which is not X, so Theorem 2.9.7 does not apply as stated. The missing step is to append F_{g(g+1)/2+1} = S^tor. The extended filtration satisfies the setup of §2.9.5. It also satisfies the hypothesis of Proposition 2.9.9, because for the added step the condition p_1^*(S^tor) ⊆ p_2^*(S^tor) holds trivially. Theorem 2.9.7 then gives a spectral sequence, equivariant for t, that converges to H^*(S^tor, ω̃^κ).

Its E_1 page has one extra column: RΓ_c(S^tor_{Q_p}, ω̃^κ) = RΓ(S^tor, j_! j^* ω̃^κ), where j : S^tor_{Q_p} → S^tor. Apply Corollary 2.3.4 with X̄ = S^tor. Let the special fibre S^tor_{F_p} = V(p) play the role of the divisor of §2.3.1, and let multiplication by p : O_{S^tor} → O_{S^tor} play the role of O(−D) → O. Corollary 2.3.4 then gives this column as the derived limit of the tower ··· → RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ) → RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ), in which every map is multiplication by p. S^tor is proper over Z_p and ω̃^κ is coherent, so RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ) is a perfect complex of Z_p-modules, and this derived limit is 0. The extra column vanishes, and the spectral sequence is the one printed.

Equivalently, the printed E_1 terms give a spectral sequence that converges to H^*(F̂_{g(g+1)/2}, ω̃^κ) (first triangle of Lemma 2.9.6, for l = 0, …, g(g+1)/2). By Lemma 2.9.3, with the special fibre defined by the ideal (p), RΓ(F̂_{g(g+1)/2}, ω̃^κ) = lim_n RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ/p^n). By the same perfectness this equals RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ). The same argument applies to ω̃^κ(−D) on S^tor, and to ω̃^κ(χ) and ω̃^κ(χ)(−D) on S^tor_{Z_p(ζ_{p^n})}, which is proper over Z_p(ζ_{p^n}). Here D is the boundary.
issues.reason:
The proof of Theorem 2.9.7 needs Z_d = X. With U_l = X \ Z_l, it filters RΓ(X, F) = RΓ_c(U_{−1}, F) by the subcomplexes RΓ_c(U_l, F) for l = −1, …, d−1. The second triangle of Lemma 2.9.6 identifies the graded pieces with the RΓ_c(Ẑ_l \ Ẑ_{l−1}, F). The last piece, RΓ_c(U_{d−1}, F), equals RΓ_c(Ẑ_d \ Ẑ_{d−1}, F) only because U_d = ∅.

In §4.5.6, X = S^tor is a scheme over Z_p, and the filtration of §4.1.16 stops at the special fibre, so U_{g(g+1)/2} = S^tor_{Q_p} is not empty. So the printed E_1 terms are the graded pieces of RΓ(F̂_{g(g+1)/2}, ω̃^κ) = lim_n RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ/p^n). This is the cohomology of the p-adic completion. It is not, a priori, RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ).

The two can differ, and here it is properness that makes them agree. Take X = A^1_{Z_p}, F = O and the filtration ∅ ⊆ X_{F_p}. The same construction gives H^0 = lim_n (Z/p^n)[T] = Z_p⟨T⟩, but H^0(X, O) = Z_p[T].

In the paper's setting the two do agree. S^tor is proper over Z_p: it is a blow-up (Proposition 4.1.13) of the proper integral toroidal model of §4.1.1. The sheaf ω̃^κ = ω^κ(−k′ Σ_{i=1}^g Z_i) (p. 49) is coherent. So RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ) is a perfect complex of Z_p-modules. Now let M be a finitely generated Z_p-module and consider the tower M ← M ← ⋯ in which each map is multiplication by p. Every term of a compatible sequence lies in ∩_n p^n M = 0, so the limit of the tower is 0. Its lim^1 is also 0: for any sequence (a_n), the series m_n = Σ_{k≥0} p^k a_{n+k} converges and satisfies m_n − p m_{n+1} = a_n. By the Milnor sequence, the derived limit of the corresponding tower of perfect complexes vanishes. This is the vanishing of the extra column. Equivalently, RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ) → lim_n RΓ(S^tor, ω̃^κ/p^n) is an isomorphism.

One could read X as the formal completion 𝔖^tor of §4.1.5, whose underlying space is the special fibre, but that does not avoid the problem. Theorem 2.9.7 is stated for schemes. Theorem 4.5.2 and Corollary 4.5.4 state the abutment for the scheme S^tor. Corollary 4.5.5 inverts p to reach RΓ(S^tor_{Q_p}, ω^κ), which requires the algebraic cohomology. So on either reading the two cohomologies must be compared. The paper has the tools for this (Lemma 2.9.3, Remark 2.9.4, Corollary 2.3.4), but it never makes the comparison. §4.5.6 does not address the abutment. Neither does the proof of Proposition 4.5.8, which ends on p. 53 and treats only the E_1 terms.

The spectral sequence as stated is true, and the missing argument is short. So this is a gap in the proof, not an error. The step cites a theorem whose hypotheses the filtration does not meet. It also never uses the fact that makes the conclusion hold, namely that S^tor is proper over Z_p. Once the step is added, the proof of Theorem 4.5.2 is complete. The results deduced from it are then also proved: Corollaries 4.5.4 and 4.5.5 and Theorem 1.4.3 (4) and (5) (p. 5). The 2024 preprint has the same text.

issues.locator: §4.5.6, proof of Proposition 4.5.8, pp. 52–53 (the sentence at the top of p. 53 that justifies the triangle at the foot of p. 52), citing Corollary 4.4.3 on p. 50. The 2024 preprint has the same text.
issues.printed: The proof invokes Lemma 4.3.14's factorization through O_{C_t^{tor}}((k′ − k) Σ_{i=1}^g p⋆_2 Z_i − Σ_{i=1}^g p⋆_1 Z_i) ⊗ p⋆_2 ω̃^κ and applies Corollary 4.4.3 with sufficiently large k′. The corollary supplies m ∈ Z≥0 depending on w and i ∈ {1, 2}, factoring the canonical map through the twist p⋆_1 D_{w,+} + p⋆_2 D_{w,+} over p_i^{−1} S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}. The stated locus is S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i+1}.
issues.correction: Corollary 4.4.3 should be stated over p_i^{-1}(Z_{>w−1}), for any closed-subscheme structure on that set, and in particular over V(p_2^{-1}I_{Z,>w−1}·O_{C_t^{tor}}). This set contains p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}. The proof is unchanged except for the support comparison. It only needs supp(p_1^⋆D_{w,+}+p_2^⋆D_{w,+}) ⊆ supp(p_2^⋆ΣZ_i − p_1^⋆ΣZ_i), and this inclusion holds on all of p_i^{-1}(Z_{>w−1}) (see the argument below). Then take k′ ≥ k + m, with m the constant for V(p_2^{-1}I_{Z,>w−1}). This m does not depend on n or on the twist m in D_{−,w}, because every I^{n−1}_{Z,>w−1}/I^n_{Z,>w−1} is killed by I_{Z,>w−1}. No restriction to the complement of p_2^⋆D_{−,w} is needed, and no argument through the limit over m.
issues.reason:
Checked from the definitions of §4.1, using Z_{i,>j} − Z_{i,<j} = Z_i − V(p^{nj}) and D_i + D_{2g+1−i} = V(p^n), where n is the level. On the open stratum S̃_{=w′} we have Z_i = V(p^{n w′_i}). Hence Z_{>w−1} = ∩_i Z_{i,>w_i−1} contains every stratum S_{F_p,w′} with w′_i ≥ w_i for all i. By contrast, S_{(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i(Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i−1}) meets only the stratum S_{F_p,w}.

Explicit case, g = 2 and w = (1,1), i.e. Gr_3 multiplicative and Gr_4 étale:
- Z_{1,>0} = D_3 and Z_{2,>0} = D_3 + D_4. So Z_{>w−1} = supp D_3, which contains S_{F_p,(1,2)}, the locus where Gr_3 and Gr_4 are multiplicative.
- Z_2 − V(p^{2n}) = −(D_1 + D_2). So Z_{2,<2} = D_1 + D_2, and this vanishes on S_{F_p,(1,2)}. Hence S_{F_p,(1,2)} ∩ S_{(w−1,w+1)} = ∅.
- D_{+,w} ⊇ Z_{1,<1} = D_2 ≠ 0. So the required factorization is not vacuous.

The sheaves ω̃^κ(−mD_{−,w}) ⊗ I^{n−1}_{Z,>w−1}/I^n_{Z,>w−1} are supported on all of Z_{>w−1}. So "an application of corollary 4.4.3" does not, as stated, give the factorization on the whole support of p⋆_2 of these sheaves. The missing extension is short: either the support argument in (a), or the extension-by-zero argument in (b). For (b) one uses that Z_{>w−1} ∖ D_{−,w} ⊆ S_{(w−1,w+1)}. Here is why. At a special-fibre point x off Z_{i,>w_i}, we have Z_{i,>w_i+1} − Z_{i,<w_i+1} = −Z_{i,<w_i} − V(p^n) near x. If x were not in Z_{i,<w_i+1}, an effective divisor would equal an anti-effective one containing V(p^n), which is impossible at a point where p is not a unit.

This is an omitted argument, not a false statement. The factorization in the proof of Proposition 4.5.8 is applied to p_2^⋆(ω̃^κ(−mD_{−,w}) ⊗ I^{n−1}_{Z,>w−1}/I^n_{Z,>w−1}). This is a module over O/p_2^{-1}I_{Z,>w−1}, so it lives on p_2^{-1}(Z_{>w−1}), where Z_{>w−1} = ∩_i Z_{i,>w_i−1} (§4.1.16). The divisor D_{+,w} of p. 52 is the D_{w,+} of p. 50.

Corollary 4.4.3 only gives the factorization over p_i^{-1}S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}. Here S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)} = ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1} ∩ Z_{i,>w_i−1}. Page 50 prints Z_{i,>w_i+1}, which is a slip: with it the set would not contain S^{tor}_{F_p,w}, which the proof of 4.4.3 requires. So S_{(w−1,w+1)} = Z_{>w−1} ∩ ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+1}, and this is in general strictly smaller than Z_{>w−1}.

- On S̃_{=w′} one has Z_i = V(p^{nw′_i}). Together with Lemma 4.1.17(1), this shows that S^{tor}_{F_p,w′} ⊆ Z_{>w−1} exactly when w′_i ≥ w_i for all i.
- S^{tor}_{F_p,w′} misses Z_{i,<w_i+1} whenever w′_i > w_i.
- Example: for g = 2 and w = (0,1), the strata w′ = (1,1) and (1,2) lie in Z_{>w−1} but not in S_{(w−1,w+1)}.
- The excess Z_{>w−1} \ S_{(w−1,w+1)} lies in D_{−,w}.

So the sheaves in question are not covered by Corollary 4.4.3 as stated, and no other statement in the paper covers them. For g = 1 the problem does not arise (either D_{w,+} = ∅ or the two sets coincide).

Why this is only a gap. The proof of Corollary 4.4.3 uses two things:
- the scheme is quasi-compact;
- supp(p_1^⋆D_{w,+}+p_2^⋆D_{w,+}) ⊆ supp(E), where E = p_2^⋆ΣZ_i − p_1^⋆ΣZ_i.

The inclusion is what gives f_i^n = h_i g_i; the reverse inclusion is never used. This inclusion holds on all of p_i^{-1}(Z_{>w−1}):
1. By Propositions 4.2.14(1) and 4.2.15(3), the complement of supp E is ∪_{w′} C^{tor}_{t,w′}, where C_{t,w′} = p_1^{-1}S_{w′} ∩ p_2^{-1}S_{w′}.
2. If such a point lies over Z_{>w−1}, then S_{w′} meets every Z_{i,>w_i−1}. This forces w′_i ≥ w_i for all i: otherwise Z_{i,>w_i−1} ≤ Z_{i,>w′_i} by Lemma 4.1.17(1), and Z_{i,>w′_i} misses S_{w′} by definition.
3. Then Z_{i,<w_i} ≤ Z_{i,<w′_i} also misses S_{w′}, so the point lies on neither p_1^⋆D_{w,+} nor p_2^⋆D_{w,+}.

Hence the proof of Corollary 4.4.3 goes through verbatim over the fixed closed subscheme V(p_2^{-1}I_{Z,>w−1}), with a single m that serves all n. Proposition 4.5.8, Theorem 4.5.2 (item (5) of the introduction) and Corollaries 4.5.4–4.5.5 are unaffected.

On the scheme structure: the paper takes (p) ⊆ I_{Z,>w−1} (last sentence of the proof, p. 53), so these graded pieces are killed by p. The argument does not depend on this in any case.

issues.printed: Remark 5.1.2 takes t_0 = diag(1_g, p1_g) and a decomposable compact K_{p,P}, claiming t_0^{−n} K_{p,P} t_0^{n} ⊆ P′(Z_p) for sufficiently large n. issues.reason:
Conventions (§3.1, pp. 33–34). Matrices act on column vectors. P is the stabiliser of ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩, and x^{−1}Px is described as the stabiliser of x^{−1}⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩. So P is block lower triangular and U_P is the lower-left g×g block. The Borel B ⊆ P is upper triangular on the diagonal blocks, and its unipotent radical is N = N_M·U_P.

The definition of T^+(Q_p) on p. 34 is v(t_{g+1}) ≥ … ≥ v(t_{2g}) ≥ v(t_1) ≥ … ≥ v(t_g). This is exactly the condition that v(t_i) ≥ v(t_j) for every entry (i, j) of N, that is, that n ↦ tnt^{−1} maps N(Z_p) into itself. The dominant cone 0 ≥ k_1 ≥ … ≥ k_g on the same page gives the same picture. With row vectors, B would be upper triangular, and for g ≥ 2 neither condition would cut out the chamber of B or of its opposite.

By Lemma 3.4.3 and the paragraph after it (p. 36), P′(Q_p) has the group structure of P(Q_p), with M(Q_p) acting on U_P(Q_p)(1) by the usual conjugation. Also P′(Z_p) = M(Z_p) ⋉ U_P(Z_p)(1) (Remark 3.4.6).

Computation. t_0 = diag(1_g, p1_g) is a similitude with factor p. It is central in M and lies in T^+(Q_p). For u ∈ U_P and an entry (i, j) with i > g ≥ j, (t_0^{a} u t_0^{−a})_{ij} = p^{a} u_{ij}. So conjugation by t_0^{a} fixes M and scales U_P by p^{a}. Hence t_0^{−n}(·)t_0^{n} enlarges the unipotent part.

The printed inclusions are false. Let K = K_{p,P}. Since K is open in P′(Q_p), U_K = K ∩ U_P(Q_p)(1) is a nonzero compact open subgroup. Then t_0^{−n}Kt_0^{n} ∩ U_P(Q_p)(1) = p^{−n}U_K, and this is not contained in U_P(Z_p)(1) once n is large. So Remark 5.1.2 fails for every K and all large n. The group K′_{p,P} = wK″_pw^{−1} ∩ P(Q_p) is compact, so t_0^{−r}Kt_0^{r} ⊆ K′_{p,P} also fails for all large r.

Example: take g = 1 and w = 1. Then M = T and B = P. K = P′(Z_p) = T(Z_p) ⋉ U_P(Z_p)(1) is decomposable, and K′_{p,P} = P(Z_p). But t_0^{−n}Kt_0^{n} contains the unipotent element with lower-left entry p^{−n}. So both inclusions fail for every n, r ≥ 1.

The corrected inclusions hold. By condition (1), t_0^{r}Kt_0^{−r} = M_K ⋉ p^{r}U_K. By condition (3), M_K lies in the Iwahori subgroup of M(Q_p) with respect to B ∩ M = B_w ∩ M. That subgroup is contained in M(Z_p) and equals wK″_pw^{−1} ∩ M. For r large, p^{r}U_K ⊆ pU_P(Z_p) ⊆ wK″_pw^{−1} ∩ U_P, since elements of pU_P(Z_p) reduce to 1 mod p. Hence t_0^{r}Kt_0^{−r} ⊆ P′(Z_p) and t_0^{r}Kt_0^{−r} ⊆ K′_{p,P}. Conjugation by t_0 also preserves decomposability.

Why this is a misprint and not an error. As printed, both inclusions are false in every case, not only in an edge case. But the intended statement is unambiguous. "For n large enough" can hold only for the conjugation that contracts U_P. The proof of Lemma 3.4.8 (p. 37) conjugates by the same central element diag(1,…,1,p,…,p) of M(Q_p) for exactly this purpose ("to have K_{p,U_P} ⊆ U_P(Z_p)(1)"), without stating a direction. For t_0 ∈ T^+, the map x ↦ t_0xt_0^{−1} fixes M and shrinks U_P ⊆ N (Remark 5.1.3: N_{K_{p,P}} = N_{M_{K_{p,P}}} × U_{K_{p,P}}). The fix is the same change of sign in both places.

Consequences: none. In the proof of Theorem 5.1.4, the theorem holds for t_0^{r}Kt_0^{−r} ⊆ K′_{p,P} by Proposition 4.4.4 and Lemma 2.1.34. It then holds for K, which is the conjugate of t_0^{r}Kt_0^{−r} by t_0^{−r}. The proof invokes invariance under conjugation by t_0, and this applies equally to t_0^{−1}: both lie in T(Q_p) ⊆ M(Q_p), so both commute with t ∈ T_w(Q_p)^{++} ⊆ T(Q_p). The later appeal in the proof of Proposition 5.2.5 (p. 54), "by conjugating by t_0, we may assume that K_{p,P} ⊆ P′(Z_p)", states no direction and is correct in the corrected one.

The only use of the proposition is Proposition 5.2.7, whose construction does not depend on K_{p,P}; that independence is proved as in Proposition 5.2.5, without Proposition 5.2.3. Base change along θ: Λ → R gives RHom_T(ψ^{−1}, RΓ_w(K^p)⊗R), where ψ(t) = θ([t]). Along −ν this is the ν-isotypic part RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ), which is what the last display of the remark states. Proposition 1.4.7 combines this identity with the classicality theorem, Theorem 1.4.3(4). In sheaf form, the definition has T acting on Λ through t ↦ c(t)[t].

The sheaf formula of the remark. Here T acts on Λ through w^{−1}w_{0,M}κ^{univ} = −ν^{univ} + c, i.e. through t ↦ c(t)ν^{univ}(t)^{−1}. Base change along θ commutes with the invariants and with the ordinary part. It gives the complex in the proof of Theorem 5.3.5 for the character θ∘ν^{univ}, i.e. the θ∘ν^{univ}-isotypic part of RΓ_w(K^p). This is RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ) when θ∘ν^{univ} = ν.

With the usual universal character ν^{univ}(t) = [t], the two displays of the remark contradict each other.
- The sheaf formula has T acting on Λ through c(t)[t]^{−1}, not c(t)[t]. So it is M_w^• with its Λ-structure twisted by ι: [t] ↦ [t^{−1}].
- Specialised along −ν, it gives the ν^{−1}-isotypic part RΓ_w(K^p, −w_{0,M}w(−ν_{alg}+ρ)−ρ, χ^{−1}), not RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ).
- A toy case shows this. Take T = Z/5, replace Λ by F_11[T] (F_11 contains the 5th roots of unity), take c trivial and let ν be a nontrivial character. Let V = ν⊕ν. Its ν-isotypic part has dimension 2 and its ν^{−1}-isotypic part is 0. Along −ν, the definition gives (V⊗ν^{−1})^T, of dimension 2. The remark's formula gives (V⊗ν)^T = 0. Along +ν, the remark's formula gives (V⊗ν^{−1})^T, of dimension 2.

Resolution. The pair (Λ, t ↦ [t^{−1}]) also represents continuous characters of T, so ν^{univ}(t) = [t^{−1}] is a legitimate universal character.
- With this choice the sheaf formula has T acting on Λ through c(t)[t], as the definition does.
- ⊗_{Λ,−ν} then sends ν^{univ} to ν. Both displays of the remark hold, and they agree with the definition.
- §6.2.11 (p. 63) takes ν_A to be the restriction of the universal character, with κ_A = −w_{0,M}w(ν_A+ρ)−ρ and F^{ν_A} = (π_⋆O⊗̂A)^{B_{K_{p,n}} = −w_{0,M}κ_A}. The (−w_{0,M}κ_A)-eigenspace of π_⋆O⊗̂A is the torus invariants of π_⋆O⊗A, where the torus acts on A through w_{0,M}κ_A. So on the torus this is the remark's sheaf formula base-changed to A. Under the same normalisation, Proposition 6.2.13 ("follows from the definition. See remark 5.4.3") and Theorem 6.2.15(1) need no change of sign.
- The sign matters in only one other place, the phrase "a continuous character inducing a map ν: A → O_C" (p. 64). It must mean the map sending ν_A to ν. The phrase only names the sheaf F̃^{ν,n}. Theorem 6.2.15(2) and Corollary 6.2.16 are asserted for every A and every ν. As A runs over all quasi-compact opens, they do not depend on this sign.

If instead ν^{univ}(t) = [t] is kept, the last display of the remark and Proposition 1.4.7 still follow from the definition. Proposition 6.2.13 and Theorem 6.2.15(1) then hold once M_w^• ⊗ A is formed along Λ → A composed with ι.

Either way, the context fixes the intended meaning: the definition of M_w^•, and the "−ν" in Proposition 1.4.7 and in the remark itself. The slip is a sign, namely an unstated, non-standard normalisation of the universal character, or equivalently of the character through which T_w(Z_p) acts on Λ. So this is a misprint.

Consequences. Remark 5.4.3 is cited by number only in the proof of Proposition 6.2.13. Proposition 1.4.7 refers to section 5.4 as a whole. Through Proposition 6.2.13 the remark feeds Theorem 6.2.15(1), and from there Corollary 6.2.17 and Theorem 1.4.3(3). Those amplitude bounds do not depend on the sign: ι is an automorphism of Λ, and the opens Spa(A[1/p],A) and their images under ι both cover weight space. With the normalisation above, no stated result needs a change of sign. The January 2024 preprint has the same text (Remark 5.4.3, p. 55; Proposition 6.2.13, p. 61; Proposition 1.4.7, p. 5).

For F = ω^κ we have F^∨ = ω^{−w_{0,M}κ}, because the dual of the irreducible M-representation of highest weight κ has highest weight −w_{0,M}κ. By Remark 4.3.3 (p. 47), ω_A has weights (e_i; −1), Lie(A) has weights (−e_i; 1), and ω_{A^t} has weights (e_i; 1). By Kodaira–Spencer, Ω^1(log D) is the symmetric part of ω_A ⊗ ω_{A^t}, with weights (e_a+e_b; 0) for a ≤ b. Its determinant has weight (g+1,…,g+1; 0).

P is the stabiliser of ⟨e_{g+1},…,e_{2g}⟩, so the root of the entry (g+a, b) of u_P is t_{g+1−a}^{−1}t_b^{−1}. Hence Φ^{+,M} = {(−e_a−e_b; 0) : a ≤ b}. Checked by direct computation, this is consistent with the dominant cone 0 ≥ k_1 ≥ … ≥ k_g on p. 35. It gives 2ρ_{nc} = (−(g+1),…,−(g+1); 0), so the canonical bundle Ω^d(log D)(−D) is ω^{−2ρ_{nc}}(−D). The Serre dual of ω^κ is therefore ω^{−w_{0,M}κ−2ρ_{nc}}(−D), which is exactly what the statement asserts. The cuspidal complexes are defined with O(−D) on p. 54.

Checks:
- For g = 1 the statement gives the classical pairing of ω^k with ω^{2−k}(−D). The printed proof would give ω^{k+2}.
- The statement is internally consistent. Take w′ = w_{0,M}ww_0 and κ′ = −w_{0,M}κ−2ρ_{nc}. Since −w_{0,M}ρ = ρ−2ρ_{nc}, we get κ′+ρ = −w_{0,M}(κ+ρ). Then ν′ = −w′^{−1}w_{0,M}(κ′+ρ)−ρ = −w_0ν, using w_0ρ = −ρ. This agrees with the adjoint t ↦ w_0t^{−1} and the character w_0χ^{−1}.
- The printed κ−2ρ_{nc} agrees with the correct weight only when −w_{0,M}κ = κ.
- Conjugation by w_{0,M} ∈ M(Z_p) preserves the weight of the equivariant sheaf, so the corrected sheaf belongs on both sides of the final isomorphism.

issues.locator: §5.6, proof of Proposition 5.6.3, case g = 2, w of length one, p. 58

It says S^{tor}_{(w−1,w+1)} \ D_{w,+} lies in the locus of p-rank at least one, whose minimal-compactification cohomological dimension is 1 because two affines cover it. The paragraph specifies D_{w,+} = Z_{1,<1}, D_{w,−} = Z_{2,>1} and invokes Lemma 4.4.2 for a strict dynamic compactification.
issues.correction:
The sheaf should be twisted along D_{w,−}. The sentence should read: "... is a direct summand of RΓ(S^{tor}_{(w−1,w+1)} \ D_{w,+}, ω^κ(−cusp)(−kD_{w,−})) for suitable k ≫ 0."

Justification. Write S̄ = S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}. By the definitions in §4.4 and Proposition 2.6.2, RΓ_w(K^pK_{w,p,P}, κ, cusp)⊗Z/pZ is the ordinary part of RΓ_{D_{w,+},D_{w,−}}(S̄, ω^κ(−cusp)).
- The divisors D_{w,±} are locally principal. So Proposition 2.5.4, applied after replacing D_{w,±} by a common multiple (Lemma 2.5.3), identifies this ordinary part with RΓ(S̄, ω^κ(−cusp)(k_+D_{w,+} − k_−D_{w,−}))^{ord} for all k_± ≥ m. The operator acts compatibly on all these complexes.
- Fix k_− ≥ m and take the colimit over k_+ (Corollary 2.3.9, Lemma 2.4.4(1)). On ordinary parts all transition maps are quasi-isomorphisms, so the ordinary part is also RΓ(S̄ \ D_{w,+}, ω^κ(−cusp)(−k_−D_{w,−}))^{ord}.
- By Lemma 2.4.4(3) this is a direct summand of RΓ(S̄ \ D_{w,+}, ω^κ(−cusp)(−k_−D_{w,−})).

The cohomological-dimension step must then be applied to this twisted sheaf.
issues.reason:
The page image confirms the printed text. For w = Id the passage from support conditions to ordinary sheaf cohomology is correct, because D_− = ∅. In the length-one case D_{w,−} = Z_{2,>1} is non-empty, and the printed sentence silently drops the support condition along it, which amounts to taking k_− = 0.

The paper's own formalism does not allow this. The Hecke operator extends over the compactified correspondence only after a twist by −nD_− (Proposition 2.3.13). The ordinary parts of the twisted cohomologies are only shown to agree with the ordinary part with support for k_± ≥ m (Lemma 2.5.3, Proposition 2.5.4; also Theorem 2.11.4(4)). This is also why §4.3 works with ω̃^κ = ω^κ(−k′ΣZ_i), k′ large (Proposition 4.3.13, Lemma 4.3.14). So with k_− = 0 the operator need not act on RΓ(S̄ \ D_{w,+}, ω^κ(−cusp)), and even when it does, nothing shows that its ordinary part equals RΓ_w⊗Z/pZ.

The support condition also cannot be dropped as harmless. RΓ_{D_+,D_−} is a limit over k of twisted cohomologies, and such a limit can acquire lim^1 terms even on an affine scheme. For example, on A^1 over a field k, R lim_m t^m k[t] = (k[[t]]/k[t])[−1], checked by direct computation from 0 → t^m k[t] → k[t] → k[t]/t^m → 0.

The fix is the twisted statement above, which the paper's Proposition 2.5.4 supplies directly (Theorem 2.11.4 is not needed). The amplitude [0,1] = [0, ℓ(w)] then follows, provided the paper's cohomological-dimension step (itself only sketched) is applied to the twisted sheaf. So Proposition 5.6.3, and item (2) of Theorem 1.4.3 (p. 5), which quotes it, are unaffected. The only defect is in the proof. The page image confirms the printed text.

By §4.4 and Proposition 2.6.2, RΓ_w(K^pK_{w,p,P}, κ, cusp)⊗Z/pZ is the ordinary part of RΓ_{D_{w,+},D_{w,−}}(S̄, ω^κ(−cusp)), where S̄ = S^{tor}_{F_p,(w−1,w+1)}. By Definition 2.2.4 and Corollary 2.3.11 this complex is RΓ(S̄ \ D_{w,+}, (j_−)_!ω^κ(−cusp)) = R lim_n RΓ(S̄ \ D_{w,+}, ω^κ(−cusp)(−nD_{w,−})). So it has compact support towards D_{w,−}. For w = Id the paper notes that D_− = ∅, so usual cohomology is correct there. In the length-one case D_{w,−} = Z_{2,>1} is non-empty, and the printed sentence silently drops the support condition, which amounts to taking n = 0.

Possible defences, and why they fail:
(a) The notation does not hide a support condition. The parenthesis in the w = Id case explicitly contrasts D_− = ∅ ("so we consider usual cohomology") with the general case.
(b) The paper's own formalism does not allow n = 0.
- The Hecke operator extends over the compactified correspondence only after a twist by −nD_− (Proposition 2.3.13). For the Siegel correspondence, Proposition 4.3.13 and Lemma 4.3.14 likewise twist by −k∑Z_i.
- The ordinary parts of the twisted cohomologies are identified with the ordinary part with support only for k_± ≥ m (Lemma 2.5.3, Proposition 2.5.4, Theorem 2.11.4(4)).
- Theorem 2.11.4(3) would allow no twist, but only if T factors through p̄_1^!F(−D_−) with no pole along D_−. This is not verified for this correspondence.
- So nothing in the paper shows that the operator acts on RΓ(S̄ \ D_{w,+}, ω^κ(−cusp)) at all, or that its ordinary part there equals RΓ_w⊗Z/pZ.
(c) The support condition cannot be dropped as harmless, because an R lim of complexes in degrees [0,1] can have cohomology in degree 2 (lim^1). Already on an affine scheme a lim^1 appears. For example, on A^1 over a field k, the sequences 0 → t^m k[t] → k[t] → k[t]/t^m → 0 give R lim_m t^m k[t] = (k[[t]]/k[t])[−1], which is non-zero in degree 1 (checked by direct computation). So a degree bound for the limit does not follow from cohomological dimension 1.

With the twisted statement in the correction, which the paper's own Proposition 2.5.4 and Lemma 2.4.4 supply, the complex is a direct summand of the cohomology of a single coherent sheaf on S̄ \ D_{w,+}. The amplitude [0,1] = [0, ℓ(w)] then follows, provided the cohomological-dimension step is applied to the twisted sheaf. That step is only sketched in the paper (it concerns the map from S̄ \ D_{w,+}, inside the blown-up toroidal model, to the p-rank ≥ 1 locus of the minimal compactification). If it is read as a property of the scheme S̄ \ D_{w,+}, it covers the twisted sheaf automatically. If it is read as sheaf-specific, as in the w = Id case, where it rests on [Lan17] thm. 8.6, then it is unproved for both the untwisted and the twisted sheaf. So this correction introduces no new difficulty.

Consequences. The passage is used only in this proof: the cuspidal length-one case for g = 2, and through the duality of Theorem 5.5.2 the non-cuspidal case paired with it. Proposition 5.6.3 is quoted as Theorem 1.4.3(2) on p. 5. With the correction these statements stand, so only the proof is affected.

The 2024 preprint has the same text (p. 56), with the same Definition 2.2.4, Corollary 2.3.11 and Proposition 2.5.4. The gap is therefore present in both versions and was not fixed in the revision.

issues.locator: §6.1, proof of Proposition 6.1.7, p. 59
issues.printed: The proof uses Lemma 6.1.5 to assume quasi-compact support conditions. It claims (U ∪ U′, Z ∪ Z′) is again a support condition whenever (U, Z) and (U′, Z′) are, and hence reduces to U ⊆ U′, Z ⊆ Z′. It handles U ⊆ U′ with Z = Z′, saying the case U = U′ with Z ⊆ Z′ is analogous.
issues.correction:
Compare both pairs with the intersection pair (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵 ∩ 𝒵′), not with the union.

The intersection pair is again a quasi-compact support condition:
- T(closure of 𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′) ⊆ T(𝒰̄) ∩ T(𝒰̄′) ⊆ 𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′;
- T^t(𝒵 ∩ 𝒵′) ⊆ 𝒵° ∩ 𝒵′° = (𝒵 ∩ 𝒵′)°.

Write L for the common limit set. The nested case treated in the proof uses the hypothesis only through one fact: the limit set of the larger pair lies in the smaller pair. That fact is what gives ∩_{m,n} 𝒰′_m ∩ 𝒵_n ∩ 𝒰^c = ∅. Now go in two steps:
- From (𝒰, 𝒵) to (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵): L ⊆ 𝒰, and L = L′ ⊆ 𝒰′.
- From (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵) to (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵 ∩ 𝒵′): the limit set of (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵) is contained in L, and L ⊆ 𝒵 ∩ 𝒵′.

The same two steps work for (𝒰′, 𝒵′). So both finite slope parts are canonically quasi-isomorphic to that of (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵 ∩ 𝒵′). In fact every pair in these chains has limit set exactly L, so the nested case applies even in its printed form, with equal limit sets.

The union pair can be used only when the mixed sets 𝒰_∞ ∩ 𝒵′_∞ and 𝒰′_∞ ∩ 𝒵_∞ lie in L, and in general they do not. Here 𝒰_∞ = ∩_m 𝒰_m and 𝒵_∞ = ∩_n 𝒵_n. With this change the statement of Proposition 6.1.7 stands.
issues.reason:
The printed text on p. 59 is as quoted: the pair is (U ∪ U′, Z ∪ Z′), with ∪ in both places.

Why the union reduction fails. The proof must compare (U, Z) and (U′, Z′) with the union pair. Its own special case U ⊆ U′, Z = Z′ uses equality of the limit sets: the step "∩_{m,n} U′_m ∩ Z_n ∩ U^c = ∅" needs L′ = L ⊆ U. So the union pair would need limit set L, and nothing guarantees that.
- Since T(Ū) ⊆ U and T^t(Z) ⊆ Z°, the sets U_m and Z_n decrease.
- T commutes with unions.
- For decreasing sequences, ∩_m (A_m ∪ B_m) = (∩A_m) ∪ (∩B_m).
So the union pair has limit set (U_∞ ∪ U′_∞) ∩ (Z_∞ ∪ Z′_∞) = L ∪ (U_∞ ∩ Z′_∞) ∪ (U′_∞ ∩ Z_∞). The hypothesis L = L′ says nothing about the two mixed terms.

Counterexample, checked by direct computation:
- Setup: X̄ = three points {a, b, c}, C̄ = X̄, p̄_1 = p̄_2 = id, so T = T^t = id and every pair of subsets is a quasi-compact support condition. Let (U, Z) = ({a,b}, {a,c}) and (U′, Z′) = ({a,c}, {a,b}).
- Limit sets: both pairs have limit set {a}, but the union pair (X̄, X̄) has limit set X̄.
- Cohomology: for F = O, the finite slope parts are one-dimensional for the two pairs and three-dimensional for the union pair. So neither pair can be compared with the union pair.

In finite discrete models (directed graphs, with U closed under successors and Z under predecessors), the union pair changed the limit set in 1349 of 12662 random instances with L = L′. The intersection pair never did.

The statement itself survives. The intersection pair (U ∩ U′, Z ∩ Z′) always has limit set L, by the compactness argument in the correction, which is the same argument the proof already uses. So this is a gap in the proof, not an error in the result.

Downstream use: Proposition 6.1.7 is not cited by number later. Implicitly, it is what identifies the degree-defined support conditions of Proposition 6.1.10 (used in Theorems 6.2.9 and 6.2.15) with the Hodge–Tate ones of Proposition 6.1.11. Both have limit set S_w^tor. The deductions of Corollaries 6.2.10, 6.2.16 and 6.2.17 from [BP21] go through that identification. Since the proposition holds with the repaired proof, none of these results is affected. The page image of p. 59 shows the text as quoted, with ∪ in both entries of the pair. The 2024 preprint (p. 57) has the same words.

**What the reduction needs.** To pass to nested pairs, the proof must compare (𝒰, 𝒵) and (𝒰′, 𝒵′) with (𝒰 ∪ 𝒰′, 𝒵 ∪ 𝒵′), using the two nested special cases. The nested case (p. 59) needs the limit set of the larger pair to lie in the smaller pair: "we know that ∩_{m,n} 𝒰′_m ∩ 𝒵_n ⋂ 𝒰^c = ∅", which follows from L′ = L ⊆ 𝒰. So the union pair would need limit set L.

**Why that fails.** Since T(𝒰̄) ⊆ 𝒰 and T^t(𝒵) ⊆ 𝒵°, the sequences 𝒰_m and 𝒵_n decrease. T and T^t commute with unions, and for decreasing sequences ∩_m(A_m ∪ B_m) = (∩A_m) ∪ (∩B_m). Hence the limit set of the union pair is L ∪ (𝒰_∞ ∩ 𝒵′_∞) ∪ (𝒰′_∞ ∩ 𝒵_∞). The hypothesis says nothing about the two mixed terms. Replacing 𝒰 by 𝒰_m or 𝒵 by 𝒵_n (Proposition 6.1.4) does not change any limit set, so shrinking first does not help.

**Counterexamples** (checked by direct computation). In both, the conclusion of the proposition holds for the two given pairs, but the union pair has different finite slope cohomology. So neither given pair can be compared with the union pair: the route through the union fails, it is not merely left unproved.
- (a) Take 𝒳̄ = 𝒞̄ = three points {a, b, c}, p̄_1 = p̄_2 = id, so T = T^t = id, and F = O with the identity correspondence. Let (𝒰, 𝒵) = ({a,b}, {a,c}) and (𝒰′, 𝒵′) = ({a,c}, {a,b}). Both are quasi-compact support conditions with limit set {a}, and each finite slope part is 1-dimensional. The union pair (𝒳̄, 𝒳̄) has limit set 𝒳̄ and a 3-dimensional finite slope part.
- (b) Take 𝒳̄ = 𝒞̄ = P^1 over Q_p, p̄_1 = id, p̄_2(z) = z^2, and F = O, so T acts by f ↦ f(z^2). Let (𝒰, 𝒵) = ({|z| < p^{-1}}, {|z| ≥ p^{-1}}) and (𝒰′, 𝒵′) = ({|z| > p}, {|z| ≤ p}). Both pairs have empty support 𝒰 ∩ 𝒵, hence zero cohomology. The union pair has 𝒵 ∪ 𝒵′ = P^1, and on its cohomology the functions constant on each of the two discs are eigenvectors of T with eigenvalue 1. So its finite slope part is non-zero.

In random finite models (a relation on a finite set, with 𝒰 stable under T and 𝒵 stable under T^t) whose two pairs have equal limit sets, the union pair changed the limit set in about 6% of cases. The intersection pair, and the intermediate pair (𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′, 𝒵), never did.

**Defence tried.** No convention in §6.1 makes the union step valid. Nor do the cited [BP21] results. Theorem 5.3.7 of [BP21] concerns one fixed pair. Corollary 5.3.8 is a sandwich criterion (T^{m+s}(𝒰) ∩ (T^t)^n(𝒵) ⊆ 𝒰′ ⊆ T^m(𝒰), and similarly for the supports). It cannot apply to the union pair, because in (a) and (b) the cohomologies really differ.

**The statement survives.** The repair in the correction is sound. That the intersection pair has limit set exactly L follows from the compactness argument already in the proof. That argument gives m0, n0 with 𝒰_{m0} ∩ 𝒵_{n0} ⊆ 𝒰′ ∩ 𝒵′. Now take x ∈ L:
- For each m, write x as the end of a T-chain of length m + m0 that starts in 𝒰. The chain's point at step m0 lies in 𝒰_{m0} ∩ 𝒵_{n0} ⊆ 𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′. So x ∈ T^m(𝒰 ∩ 𝒰′).
- Symmetrically, x ∈ (T^t)^n(𝒵 ∩ 𝒵′) for each n.

So this is a gap, not a false result. The claimed reduction to nested pairs is achievable, but not by the route given.

**Consequences.** Proposition 6.1.7 is not cited by number later. It is the implicit link between two kinds of support conditions:
- the degree-defined ones of §6.1.8 and Proposition 6.1.10, used in Theorems 6.2.9 and 6.2.15;
- the Hodge–Tate-defined ones of Proposition 6.1.11, which are those of [BP21].

Both kinds have limit set the closure of S_w^tor. This identification is what transfers the results to the cohomology of [BP21]: Corollaries 6.2.10, 6.2.16 and 6.2.17, and the remark after Corollary 6.2.10 that yields Theorem 1.5.1. The proposition holds with the repaired proof, so none of these stated results is affected.

issues.reason: In §6.1.8 the letter n is already fixed as the level: the Shimura variety 𝒮^{tor} has level K_{p,n}, where K_{p,n} consists of the elements of G(Z_p) that reduce to B(Z/p^nZ) (p. 41). This n enters the definition of 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ} and 𝒰_{≤w+ϵ} through the bounds deg H_{g+i}(x) ≥ n(w_i − ϵ) and deg H_{g+i}(x) ≤ n(w_i + ϵ). Items (3)–(4) nevertheless rebind n as an existentially quantified number of iterations of T or T^t, inside sets that themselves depend on the level n. The number of iterations depends on ϵ − ϵ′ and must be allowed to vary with the level held fixed. issues.locator: §6.2.1, Proposition 6.2.2(2) and its one-line proof, p. 61. The earlier preprint (build of 15 Jan 2024) has the same text.
issues.printed: Proposition 6.2.2 claims a blow-up π : S̃^{tor} → S^{tor} such that for 0 ≤ i ≤ g and η ∈ {ϵ, −ϵ, ϵ′, −ϵ′}, effective divisors Z_{i,>w_j+η} and Z_{i,<w_j+η} have disjoint supports and satisfy Z_{i,>w_j+η} − Z_{i,<w_j+η} = Z_i − V(p^{n(w_j+η)}). Its proof says the argument is identical to that for Proposition 4.1.13.
issues.correction: Choose an integer q ≥ 1 with q·n(w_i+η) ∈ Z for all i and all η ∈ {±ϵ, ±ϵ′}. Read V(p^{n(w_i+η)}) as the Q-Cartier divisor n(w_i+η)·V(p), and read Z_{i,>w_i+η} and Z_{i,<w_i+η} as effective Q-Cartier divisors. When n(w_i+η) ≤ 0, which happens only if w_i = 0 and η < 0, take Z_{i,<w_i+η} = 0, because the difference is already effective. Otherwise, apply Proposition-construction 4.1.11 to the Cartier divisors qZ_i and V(p^{q n(w_i+η)}). Locally this is the blow-up along (f^q, p^{qn(w_i+η)}), where f is a local equation of Z_i. Divide the two resulting divisors by q. Equivalently, keep the two Cartier divisors themselves: they have the same supports, and the identity holds after multiplying by q. The subscripts w_j in (1), (2) and in the definitions of D_±, D_{±,ϵ}, D_{±,ϵ′} should read w_i. This is a separate index slip. The reported correction is right and essentially minimal. The one addition needed is the case n(w_i+η) ≤ 0, where the "apply 4.1.11" form would involve a negative power of p.
issues.reason:
The model S^{tor} is a scheme over Spec Z_p: in 4.1.1, p. 41, it is defined as a normalisation of a product of the A_{g,d_i} × Spec Z_p. In §6.2.1 the numbers ϵ ∈ ]0,1[∩Q and ϵ′ ∈ ]0,ϵ[∩Q are arbitrary, and the level n is any element of Z_{≥0} (p. 41). Take n = 1. Then for every η ∈ {±ϵ, ±ϵ′} the exponent n(w_i+η) = w_i + η is not an integer, because the w_i are integers and 0 < |η| < 1. So p^{n(w_i+η)} is not a function on S^{tor}, and V(p^{n(w_i+η)}) is not an effective Cartier divisor in the sense of p. 7 (a closed subscheme V(I) with I invertible). Therefore no pair of effective Cartier divisors can satisfy the printed identity. The same happens for any n whenever nη is not an integer. Passing to Z_p(ζ_{p^n}), the ring used for the Nebentypus, does not help: its value group is (1/(p^{n−1}(p−1)))Z, and ϵ is an arbitrary rational.

The proof says it is "identical to the proof of proposition 4.1.13". That proof (p. 42) applies Proposition-construction 4.1.11, which is stated for effective Cartier divisors, to Z_{k+1} and V(p^{nj}) with j an integer. It does not cover a rational exponent. The missing step is to scale by a common denominator q as in the correction. On the blow-up of the ideal locally generated by (f^q, p^{qn(w_i+η)}), where f is a local equation of Z_i, one of the two generators divides the other, and the quotients generate the unit ideal. This gives E_>, E_< with disjoint support, and dividing by q gives the Q-divisors.

This intended reading fits the rest of the paper. The adic definition on p. 60 already uses rational exponents: U_{≥w−ϵ} is defined by |f_{g+i}|_x ≤ |p^{n(w_i−ϵ)}|_x. Rational multiples of divisors also appear without comment in Lemma 4.4.2 ("there exists 0 < s < 1 such that s p_1^⋆Z_{i,<w_i} ≥ p_2^⋆Z_{i,<w_i}") and in Proposition 6.2.3(4) (s ∈ ]0,1[∩Q). Later the divisors D_{±,ϵ} and D_{±,ϵ′} are used only through their supports (U_{≥w−ϵ} = S^{tor} \ D_{+,ϵ}, and cohomology with supports) and through the inequalities of Proposition 6.2.3. Both make sense for Q-divisors, or after replacing each divisor by q times itself. So the statement as printed is not meaningful, and its cited proof does not apply literally, but the repair is routine and no result changes. Why the statement is not meaningful as printed:
- The w_i are integers (bottom of §3.1, recalled before Corollary 4.1.14).
- ϵ is an arbitrary rational in ]0,1[. Theorem 6.2.9 is stated for every such ϵ.
- ϵ′ is not free either. By Proposition 6.1.9(1) the admissible ϵ′ fill an interval ending at ϵ, but that interval need not contain a point of (1/n)Z. For n = 1, no ϵ in ]0,1[ has nϵ ∈ Z at all.
- So n(w_i+η) is in general not an integer.
- S^tor is a scheme over Z_p: it is the normalisation in §4.1, and with a nebentypus the base is Z_p(ζ_{p^n}). A rational power of p is not a function on it, so V(p^{n(w_i+η)}) is not a closed subscheme.
- In the paper, "divisor" always means a closed subscheme, Cartier or locally principal (§2.1.14). The only rational coefficients the paper allows are in the relation D ≤ sD′ of Definition 2.1.15(2). It never defines Q-divisors.
- Every other occurrence of V(p^·) in the paper has integer exponent nj with 0 ≤ j ≤ i: Proposition 4.1.13, its proof, and Lemma 4.2.11.

Why the cited proof does not literally cover it: the proof of Proposition 4.1.13 applies Proposition-construction 4.1.11 "to the divisors Z_{k+1} and V(p^{nj})". Proposition-construction 4.1.11 is stated only for effective Cartier divisors D_1, D_2. So "identical to the proof of proposition 4.1.13" does not apply as written.

The defence, and why it succeeds only as a repair. The intended meaning is clear from §6.1.8, where U_{≥w−ϵ} is defined by |f_{g+i}|_x ≤ |p^{n(w_i−ϵ)}|_x. That is a meaningful condition on rank-one points. The repair described in the correction works:
- Blowing up (f^q, p^m) with m = qn(w_i+η) gives disjoint-support Cartier divisors whose difference is qZ_i − V(p^m).
- Point (3) survives. By the proof of Proposition 4.1.13, Z_i = V(p^{nw_i}) on the open S̃_{=w_1,…,w_g}. There the ideal (f^q, p^m) is generated by a power of p times a unit, so the extra blow-up is an isomorphism over it.

What later uses the passage:
- The divisors D_{±,ϵ} and D_{±,ϵ′} defined just below it on p. 61.
- Proposition 6.2.3(1)–(3). These inequalities follow as in Lemma 4.2.11, either with Q-coefficients or after multiplying by q, which is compatible with Definition 2.1.15(2).
- The open C_t^tor \ (p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} ∪ p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ}) in Proposition 6.2.7.
- Z_{<w+ϵ} and U_{≥w−ϵ} = S^tor \ D_{+,ϵ} in §6.2.8.
- The support conditions RΓ_{D_{+,ϵ},D_{−,ϵ′}} in the proof of Theorem 6.2.9.

All of these use only the supports of the divisors, or inequalities that are unchanged by rescaling. Lemma 2.10.2 and Proposition 2.10.4 need only closed subschemes and containments of supports. The integral model ω̃^κ(χ) = ω^κ(χ)(m(D_+ − D_−)) and Proposition 6.2.3(4) use only D_±, which are built from the integers w_i. So Theorem 6.2.9 and Corollary 6.2.10 are unaffected.

Classification: this is an unjustified step with a routine repair, and no result changes. Hence a gap that affects nothing.

issues.printed: Theorem 1.4.10 claims the slope lower bounds of [BP21], conjectures 5.9.2 and 6.8.1. Corollaries 6.2.10 and 6.2.16 claim these conjectures in the Siegel case. The former equates the specified lower bound for t ∈ T^+(Q_p) on finite slope cohomology with lattice preservation by its normalized action, reducing to T^{++}(Q_p) because it generates T(Q_p) as a group and citing Theorem 6.2.9. The latter similarly reduces nonnegative locally analytic slopes to T^{++}(Q_p), citing 6.2.15(2).
issues.correction:
(1) Reduction to T^{++}. Replace "as they generate T(Q_p) as a group" with a cone argument. Let λ be a character of T^+ on the finite slope cohomology. For Conjecture 5.9.2 put β = w^{-1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ)+ρ, and for Conjecture 6.8.1 put β = 0. Let f(t) = v(λ(t)) − ⟨v(t), β⟩. Then f is additive on T^+. Take t ∈ T^+ and t_0 ∈ T^{++}. For every m ≥ 1, v(t^m t_0) = m·v(t) + v(t_0) is regular dominant, so t^m t_0 ∈ T^{++}. Theorem 6.2.9 (resp. 6.2.15(2)), applied with t^m t_0 as the element of T^{++} fixed in §6.2, gives m·f(t) + f(t_0) ≥ 0 for all m, and hence f(t) ≥ 0. Put differently, f(t) = ⟨v(t), v(λ) − β⟩ is a linear form in v(t) that is ≥ 0 on v(T^{++}). The positive multiples of v(T^{++}) are dense in the closed dominant cone, which contains v(T^+), so the form is ≥ 0 on v(T^+).

(2) The cuspidal '+' theories. Before the two corollaries, state the cuspidal analogues of Theorems 6.2.9 and 6.2.15. These are the same statements for ω̃^κ(χ)(−D) and F̃^{ν_A,n}(−D), with the cuspidal higher Hida theory as ordinary part, and they are proved in the same way. Here D is the boundary divisor of the toroidal compactification, as in the definition of cuspidal higher Hida theory in §4.4; it is not one of the divisors D_± of §6.2. Together with the theorems as printed, these analogues give part (1) of [BP21] Conjectures 5.9.2 and 6.8.1 (the bound for characters of T^+ on the '+' theories), for both the non-cuspidal and the cuspidal theories.

(3) Part (2). Add the deduction of part (2) of both conjectures (the bound for characters of T^− on the '−' theories) from part (1), using the Serre duality of [BP21]: Theorems 5.7.1–5.7.2 in the coherent case, and 6.7.1–6.7.2 in the locally analytic case. Put κ^∨ = −2ρ_nc − w_{0,M}κ. The pairing H^i_w(K^p,κ,χ,cusp)^{±,fs} × H^{d−i}_w(K^p,κ^∨,χ^{-1})^{∓,fs} → F is perfect on generalized eigenspaces, and t is adjoint to t^{-1}. So a character λ of T^+ on one side corresponds to a character λ' = λ∘inv of T^− on the other, and v(λ') = −v(λ). Since w_{0,M}ρ = 2ρ_nc − ρ, we have κ^∨ + ρ = −w_{0,M}(κ+ρ). Hence the part (1) bound at κ is exactly the part (2) bound at κ^∨, and conversely ([BP21] Remark 5.9.5). For Conjecture 6.8.1 both bounds are 0, and duality turns v ≥ 0 on T^+ into v ≤ 0 on T^−. Duality pairs cuspidal with non-cuspidal theories, so (2) is needed here. Without it, the printed theorems give part (2) only for the cuspidal '−' theories.

(4) The proof of Corollary 6.2.10 and the sentence before Corollary 6.2.16 should stop describing each conjecture as a statement about T^+ alone.

[BP21] is cited as arXiv:2110.10251. Version v1 (19 October 2021) is used here, and its numbering matches every [BP21] reference in §6.2.

What is conjectured. Conjecture 5.9.2 of [BP21] has two parts, and each is asserted for both the non-cuspidal and the cuspidal theory:
(1) every character λ of T^+ on RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ)^{+,fs} or RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ,cusp)^{+,fs} satisfies v(λ) ≥ w^{-1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ)+ρ;
(2) every character λ of T^− on RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ)^{−,fs} or RΓ_w(K^p,κ,χ,cusp)^{−,fs} satisfies v(λ) ≤ w^{-1}(κ+ρ)−ρ.
Conjecture 6.8.1 makes the same four assertions for RΓ_{w,an}(K^p,ν)^{±,fs} and its cuspidal version, with bounds v(λ) ≥ 0 and v(λ) ≤ 0. By [BP21] Remark 5.9.3, both parts are lower bounds on slopes: part (2) means v(λ(t)) ≥ ⟨v(t), w^{-1}(κ+ρ)−ρ⟩ for all t ∈ T^−. So Theorem 1.4.10 ("The lower bounds on slopes of conjectures 5.9.2 and 6.8.1") claims both parts in full. It is not a narrower statement.

What the proofs cover. The proof on p. 62 describes the conjecture as a statement about t ∈ T^+ only, and so does the sentence before Corollary 6.2.16 on p. 64. Both proofs appeal only to Theorems 6.2.9(3) and 6.2.15(2). Those give a lattice in the cohomology of ω^κ(χ), resp. F̃^{ν,n}, with the '+' support condition (U_{≥w−ε}, Z_{<w+ε}) and with t ∈ T^{++} acting. Propositions 6.1.7, 6.1.10 and 6.1.11 compare this cohomology with the '+' theory of [BP21]. There is no (−D) twist, so this is the non-cuspidal '+' theory. Section 6 contains no '−' support condition, no T^− and no cuspidal sheaf. Remark 6.2.18 uses duality, but only for vanishing. So as written, each proof establishes one of the four assertions of its conjecture: part (1) for the non-cuspidal theory. In the same way, the proof of Corollary 6.2.17 (p. 64) derives the amplitude of M^•_{w,cusp} ⊗ Q_p "from 6.2.15", although 6.2.15 is stated only for the non-cuspidal sheaf. There too the cuspidal case is left implicit.

Duality supplies only some of part (2). The locally analytic pairing of [BP21] Theorems 6.7.1–6.7.2 behaves in the same way as the coherent one. In the coherent case, w_{0,M}ρ_M = −ρ_M and w_{0,M}ρ_nc = ρ_nc, so w_{0,M}ρ = 2ρ_nc − ρ. Hence (−2ρ_nc − w_{0,M}κ) + ρ = −w_{0,M}(κ+ρ). Now take κ^∨ = −2ρ_nc − w_{0,M}κ and s = t^{-1} ∈ T^−. In the form of Remark 5.9.3, the part (2) bound at κ^∨ is v(λ'(s)) ≥ ⟨v(s), w^{-1}(κ^∨+ρ)−ρ⟩. This reads v(λ(t)) ≥ ⟨v(t), w^{-1}w_{0,M}(κ+ρ)+ρ⟩, which is part (1) at κ. Since ρ_nc is W_M-invariant, κ ↦ κ^∨ is an involution of X^*(T^c)^{M_μ,+}, so every weight is covered. However, the pairing matches cuspidal '±' with non-cuspidal '∓'. From the printed theorems it therefore yields part (2) only for the cuspidal '−' theories. Theorems 6.2.9 and 6.2.15 as stated do not cover the cuspidal '+' case of part (1), nor therefore, through duality, the non-cuspidal '−' case of part (2). Both need the cuspidal analogues of those theorems. The paper never states these analogues. They follow by the same argument, because the integral models and the higher Hida theory of §4.4–§5 are also set up for cuspidal cohomology.

The reduction to T^{++}. The stated reason does not justify the reduction. Suppose a lower bound on slopes holds for t_1 and t_2. That says nothing about t_1 t_2^{-1}. And every t ∈ T^+ with v(t) on a wall of the dominant cone has this form with t_1, t_2 ∈ T^{++}: take any t_2 ∈ T^{++} and t_1 = t·t_2. [BP21] §5.9 defines the slope v(λ) of a T^±-character by extending λ to T(Q_p) ("recall that T(Q_p) is generated by the monoids T^±"). So group generation does show that v(λ) is a linear form determined by its values on T^{++}. But the inequality needs one more fact: the positive multiples of v(T^{++}) are dense in the closed dominant cone. The bound then passes to T^+ by linearity and continuity, as in (1) of the correction. The sentence on p. 62 does not say this, and the proof of Corollary 6.2.16 gives no reason at all. The reduction itself cannot be skipped, since §6.2 fixes t ∈ T^{++} (p. 61) and builds its integral models from that choice. So Theorems 6.2.9 and 6.2.15 say nothing directly about t on a wall.

Why only the proof is affected. Later statements use the corollaries at full strength:
- Theorem 1.4.10 (p. 6), and the paragraph after it. That paragraph replaces "strongly small slope" by "small slope" in [BP21] 5.12.3, 6.8.4 and 5.12.20.
- The remark after Corollary 6.2.10 (p. 62). It replaces "strongly small slope" by "small slope" in [BP21] Theorems 5.12.3, 5.12.5 and 5.12.11. All three are stated for both signs ±. Theorems 5.12.3 and 5.12.5 cover cuspidal and non-cuspidal coherent cohomology, and 5.12.11 covers ordinary, compactly supported and interior Betti cohomology. Theorem 1.5.1 is deduced from these on p. 62.
- The remark after Corollary 6.2.16 (p. 64). It improves [BP21] Corollary 6.8.4 and Theorem 6.9.3(2). Corollary 6.8.4 includes a '−' morphism and the cuspidal versions (see [BP21] Remark 6.8.5).
All the missing steps are routine: the cone argument, the cuspidal analogues, and then duality. With them, the two corollaries and all of these consequences hold, so no stated result is lost. Only the written proofs are incomplete.

The proof's last sentence names a different space from the one in the statement. Theorem 6.2.9(3), as printed on p. 62, is about the slope ≤ h part, and the statement itself notes that this part is a finite-dimensional ℚ_p-vector space. The 2024 preprint stated (3) for the finite slope part (superscript fs) instead. The statement was later changed, but this sentence of the proof was not.

The two spaces differ. Proposition 6.1.4 takes the finite slope part from [BP21], sect. 5.1.1, where it is the projective limit of the slope ≤ h parts over all h. This space is in general infinite-dimensional: already for g = 1 it contains the finite slope overconvergent modular forms of a given weight. So there cannot be a ℤ_p-lattice there in the sense of (3), meaning a finitely generated submodule that spans the space.

The best defence of the wording is that [BP21] Lemma 5.9.10 is itself stated for the finite slope part. It says that the image there is an "open and bounded submodule". On that reading, "a lattice in the finite slope part" can only mean that the projection of the integral cohomology to every slope ≤ h part is a lattice, which is (3) for every h. This is also the order of the argument in the cited proof. It first shows, for each h, that the image in the slope ≤ h part is open and bounded (a lattice, since that part is finite-dimensional), and only then "passes to the limit over h".

So the intended meaning is clear and the mathematics is unaffected. The slope ≤ h form for every h is also all that Corollary 6.2.10 uses, since every eigenvalue of t on the finite slope cohomology occurs in some slope ≤ h part. Theorem 6.2.15(2), whose proof is "similar to the proof of theorem 6.2.9", was changed from the finite slope part to the slope ≤ h part in the same way, and the corrected sentence covers it too. The citation still supplies what the statement needs: the proof of [BP21] Lemma 5.9.10 first shows, for every h, that the image in the slope ≤ h part is open and bounded, and only then passes to the finite slope part. So the intended meaning is clear, and nothing depends on the wording.

issues.locator: §6.2.11 (Big sheaves), p. 63: the definition of π′, the displays defining 𝔉^{ν_A} and 𝔉^{ν_A,n}, the sentence just before Proposition 6.2.12, and Proposition 6.2.14. Also the proof of Proposition 6.2.14, p. 64. The January 2024 preprint has the same text (p. 61).
issues.printed: The source pushes π to π′ : 𝔍𝔊_{U_{K_p}} ×^{M_{K_{p,n}}} 𝔍𝔚_n → 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,n}}, and defines 𝔉^{ν_A} = (π_⋆𝒪_{𝔍𝔊_{U_{K_{p,P}}}} ⊗̂ A)^{B_{K_{p,n}} = −w_{0,M}κ_A} and 𝔉^{ν_A,n} = (π′_⋆𝒪_{𝔍𝔊_{U_{K_p}} ×^{M_{K_{p,n}}} 𝔍𝔚_n} ⊗̂ A)^{𝔅𝔍𝔚_n = −w_{0,M}κ_A}. Reduction modulo p^r yields ℱ_r^{κ_A,n} and ℱ_r^{ν_A}. For small ε, Proposition 6.2.14 extends 𝔉^{ν_A,n} over 𝔘̃_{[w−ϵ,w+ϵ]}, a further blow-up 𝔘̃_{[w−ϵ,w+ϵ]} → 𝔘_{[w−ϵ,w+ϵ]} away from 𝔖^{tor}_w; the proof cites [BP21], lem. 6.6.2.
issues.correction:
(a) The torsor π′. Read π′ : 𝔍𝔊_{U_{K_{p,P}}} ×^{M_{K_{p,P}}} 𝔍𝔚_n → 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P}} = 𝔖^{tor}_w, and make the same change in the subscript of 𝒪 in the display defining 𝔉^{ν_A,n}. That is, replace U_{K_p}, M_{K_{p,n}} and 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,n}} by U_{K_{p,P}}, M_{K_{p,P}} and 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P}}.
(b) The invariance group. In the display defining 𝔉^{ν_A}, the invariance condition is for the Borel subgroup B_M(Z_p) = B ∩ M_{K_{p,P}} of M_{K_{p,P}}, not for B_{K_{p,n}}. This group is the image in M of the group written B_{K_{p,P}} in §5.
(c) The reduced sheaves. Read "We let ℱ_r^{ν_A,n} and ℱ_r^{ν_A} be the sheaves obtained by reduction modulo p^r."
(d) The formal open. Add a definition before Proposition 6.2.14. Use the notation of §6.2.1: S^{tor} now denotes the blow-up S̃^{tor} of Proposition 6.2.2, and 𝔖^{tor} is its p-adic completion. Let 𝔘_{[w−ϵ,w+ϵ]} = 𝔖^{tor} ∖ (D_{+,ϵ} ∪ D_{−,ϵ}). This is the formal open whose generic fibre is 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ} ∩ 𝒰_{≤w+ϵ}.
Also state that the ϵ fixed in §6.2.1 is from now on taken small enough for Proposition 6.2.14, and write ϵ for ε in the first line of that proposition. The smallness is already tacit in the definition before Theorem 6.2.15 and in that theorem.
With this definition, the correspondences live on the modification, lying over 𝔘̃_{[w−ϵ,w+ϵ]}, of the open C_t^{tor} ∖ (p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} ∪ p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ}) of Proposition 6.2.7. No separate statement about this is needed.
issues.reason:
(1) The base and total space of π′. By §4.1 (p. 40), K_{p,n} is the Iwahori subgroup of G(Z_p) of matrices that reduce modulo p^n into B(Z/p^nZ). It is not contained in P(Q_p). Igusa varieties 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P}} are defined only for compact open subgroups K_{p,P} of P′(Q_p) (§3.4.5, pp. 36–37), so 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,n}} has no meaning.
Nor can K_{p,n} be read as K_{p,n} ∩ P(Q_p). By Lemma 4.1.7 (p. 41), 𝔖^{tor}_w = 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P,w}} with K_{p,P,w} = wK_{p,n}w^{−1} ∩ P(Q_p). This is the group K_{p,P} of §6.2.11. Since w is a minimal length representative of W_M\W, w^{−1} sends the positive roots of M to positive roots. So for w ≠ 1 there is a root α of U_P with w^{−1}α < 0. Then K_{p,P} meets U_α in U_α(p^nZ_p), whereas K_{p,n} ∩ P(Q_p) contains U_α(Z_p). Here n ≥ 1, since n is large in §6.2.11.
The symbol U_{K_p} is not defined in §6 either. In §1 (pp. 3, 5) it denotes the unipotent factor of an Iwahori decomposition K_p = U_{K_p} × T_{K_p} × Ū_{K_p} of a subgroup of G(Q_p), which is a different object.
π′ is the push-out of the M_{K_{p,P}}-torsor π along M_{K_{p,P}} → 𝔍𝔚_n, and a push-out keeps its base. So the base is 𝔍𝔊_{K_{p,P}} = 𝔖^{tor}_w and the total space is 𝔍𝔊_{U_{K_{p,P}}} ×^{M_{K_{p,P}}} 𝔍𝔚_n. The text confirms this in three places:
- the "canonical restriction map 𝔉^{ν_A,n} → 𝔉^{ν_A}" needs both sheaves on one base;
- Proposition 6.2.13 takes cohomology of ℱ_r^{ν_A,n} on S^{tor}_{w,Z/p^rZ};
- the proof of Proposition 6.2.14 (p. 64) speaks of "the 𝔍𝔚_n-torsor on 𝔖^{tor}_w".
The subscript in M_{K_{p,n}} does no mathematical harm. With the convention M_K = K ∩ M(Q_p) of p. 37, M_{K_{p,n}} is the depth-n Iwahori subgroup of M(Z_p), that is, the set of m with m mod p^n ∈ B_M. This is the same group as M_{K_{p,P}} = wK_{p,n}w^{−1} ∩ M(Q_p). Indeed, m ∈ M(Z_p) lies in wK_{p,n}w^{−1} if and only if m mod p^n ∈ wBw^{−1} ∩ M, and wBw^{−1} ∩ M = B_M because w^{−1} sends the positive roots of M to positive roots. The notation is still inconsistent with that of π.

(2) The group B_{K_{p,n}} in the definition of 𝔉^{ν_A}. The symbol is defined, but it names the wrong group. The Iwahori decomposition K_{p,n} = B_{K_{p,n}} × U^{op}_{K_{p,n}} on p. 61 gives B_{K_{p,n}} = B(Z_p). The group that acts on the sheaf π_⋆𝒪_{𝔍𝔊_{U_{K_{p,P}}}} over 𝔖^{tor}_w is the structure group M_{K_{p,P}} of π (Proposition 3.4.9(5), p. 37). So the invariance condition must be for a subgroup of M_{K_{p,P}}. B(Z_p) is not one. It is not contained in M(Q_p), and for w ≠ 1 it is not even contained in K_{p,P}. Indeed, for the root α of (1), U_α(Z_p) ⊂ B(Z_p) but w^{−1}U_α(Z_p)w = U_{w^{−1}α}(Z_p) ⊄ K_{p,n}. The intended group is B_M(Z_p) = B ∩ M_{K_{p,P}}, the image in M of B ∩ K_{p,P}. In §5 the corresponding group is written B_{K_{p,P}} and acts through this image: Remark 5.4.3 (p. 57) calls T_w(Z_p) "the diagonal torus of B_{K_{p,P}}". As with the subscripts in (1), K_{p,n} is written where K_{p,P} is meant.

(3) ℱ_r^{κ_A,n}. The sheaves reduced modulo p^r are the two just defined, 𝔉^{ν_A,n} and 𝔉^{ν_A}. The notation ℱ_r^{ν_A,n} is used from then on:
- in both diagrams of Proposition 6.2.12 and its proof;
- in Proposition 6.2.13 and its proof (the map ℱ_r^{ν_A,n} → ℱ_r^{ν_A});
- in Proposition 6.2.14.
The superscript κ_A is a slip, presumably prompted by the weight κ_A = −w_{0,M}w(ν_A+ρ)−ρ that appears in the invariance conditions.

(4) 𝔘_{[w−ϵ,w+ϵ]}. This symbol and its blow-up 𝔘̃_{[w−ϵ,w+ϵ]} occur only in Proposition 6.2.14 and the first line of its proof. They are defined nowhere, and the paper uses no other interval subscript 𝒰_{[·,·]}, U_{[·,·]} or 𝔘_{[·,·]}. The only sets defined by degree conditions are:
- the opens 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ} and 𝒰_{≤w+ϵ} and the closed sets 𝒵_{<w+ϵ} and 𝒵_{>w−ϵ} (§6.1.8, p. 60);
- integrally, U_{≥w−ϵ} = S^{tor} ∖ D_{+,ϵ} and Ẑ_{<w+ϵ} (§6.2.8, p. 62).
The proof cites [BP21] (Higher Coleman theory), Lemma 6.6.2, which does not supply the notation. Its proof builds formal models of π_{HT}^{−1}(U) for affinoid opens U ⊆ ]C_{w,k}[_{n,n}K_p of the flag variety, not for opens cut out by degree conditions.
The statement does not say over which part of C_t^{tor} the correspondences and their factorisation through D_± live.
The phrase "For ε sufficiently small" puts a new condition on the ϵ already fixed in §6.2.1 (p. 61, "Let ϵ ∈ ]0,1[∩Q"). It is also printed with a different glyph (ε, against ϵ in the subscripts). Theorem 6.2.15 uses the same ϵ with no smallness condition. Yet its complex RΓ_{𝒵_{<w+ϵ}∩𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}}(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}, 𝔉̃^{ν_A,n})^{int} makes sense only when 𝔉̃^{ν_A,n} exists, that is, only for such ϵ.
The intended meaning can be recovered. The reading 𝔘 = 𝔖^{tor} ∖ (D_{+,ϵ} ∪ D_{−,ϵ}) is the one the notation and its uses require. Here D_{+,ϵ} = Σ_i Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ} and D_{−,ϵ} = Σ_i Z_{i,>w_i+ϵ} (p. 61), with Z_i as in §4.1.12 (p. 42). The following checks use Proposition 4.1.13 and Corollary 4.1.14 (p. 42) and the definitions and results on pp. 59–62.
- Generic fibre. Proposition 6.2.2(2) gives Z_{i,>w_i+η} − Z_{i,<w_i+η} = Z_i − V(p^{n(w_i+η)}), with disjoint supports. So off Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ} we have Z_i ≥ V(p^{n(w_i−ϵ)}), and off Z_{i,>w_i+ϵ} we have Z_i ≤ V(p^{n(w_i+ϵ)}). These are the conditions deg H_{g+i} ≥ n(w_i−ϵ) and deg H_{g+i} ≤ n(w_i+ϵ) of §6.1.8. So the generic fibre of 𝔘 is 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ} ∩ 𝒰_{≤w+ϵ}, matching U_{≥w−ϵ} = S^{tor} ∖ D_{+,ϵ} in §6.2.8.
- 𝔘 contains 𝔖^{tor}_w. By Proposition 4.1.13(2) and Corollary 4.1.14 (p. 42), 𝔖^{tor}_w is the open where all Z_{i,>w_i} and Z_{i,<w_i} vanish, so the degrees there are exactly nw_i, that is, Z_i = V(p^{nw_i}). Hence Z_{i,>w_i−ϵ} − Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ} = V(p^{nϵ}) there. Since the two divisors have disjoint supports, Z_{i,<w_i−ϵ} vanishes on 𝔖^{tor}_w, and likewise Z_{i,>w_i+ϵ}. So D_{+,ϵ} and D_{−,ϵ} vanish there, and "extends" makes sense.
- The support in the definition before Theorem 6.2.15 lies in 𝔘. The supports of Z_{i,<w_i+ϵ} and Z_{i,>w_i+ϵ} are disjoint, so Ẑ_{<w+ϵ} = ∩_i Z_{i,<w_i+ϵ} misses D_{−,ϵ}. Hence Ẑ_{<w+ϵ} ∩ U_{≥w−ϵ} is a closed subset of U_{≥w−ϵ} that lies inside 𝔘. By excision, RΓ_{Ẑ_{<w+ϵ}∩U_{≥w−ϵ,Z/p^rZ}}(U_{≥w−ϵ,Z/p^rZ}, ℱ̃_r^{ν_A,n}) is meaningful even though its sheaf lives only on 𝔘̃: it is cohomology on 𝔘̃ with support in the preimage.
- The domain of the correspondences. Only supports matter here. By Proposition 6.2.3(1), supp D_{+,ϵ} ⊆ supp D_{+,ϵ′} and supp D_{−,ϵ} ⊆ supp D_{−,ϵ′}. The choice of ϵ′ in §6.2.1 gives T(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}) ⊆ 𝒰_{≥w−ϵ′} and T^t(𝒰_{≤w+ϵ}) ⊆ 𝒰_{≤w+ϵ′}. So supp p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ′} ⊆ supp p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} and supp p_1^⋆D_{−,ϵ′} ⊆ supp p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ}. These are the second statements of Proposition 6.2.3(2) and (3), read as inclusions of supports. Hence supp p_2^⋆D_{+,ϵ} ⊆ supp p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} and supp p_1^⋆D_{−,ϵ} ⊆ supp p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ}. So p_1^{−1}(𝔘) ∩ p_2^{−1}(𝔘) = C_t^{tor} ∖ (p_1^⋆D_{+,ϵ} ∪ p_2^⋆D_{−,ϵ}), which is exactly the open of Proposition 6.2.7. The domain therefore follows from the definition and fits the rest of §6.2.
Shrinking ϵ does no harm. By Proposition 6.1.10 (p. 60), ∩_{m,n} T^m(𝒰_{≥w−ϵ}) ∩ (T^t)^n(𝒵_{<w+ϵ}) is the closure of 𝒮^{tor}_w for every ϵ ∈ ]0,1[∩Q. So by Proposition 6.1.7 (p. 59) the finite-slope parts do not depend on ϵ. The ordinary part is M_w^• ⊗_Λ A for every such ϵ, by Theorem 6.2.15(1), whose input Proposition 6.2.13 does not involve ϵ.

Kind and reach. Each item is a slip of notation, an omitted definition or an omitted standing assumption, and in each case the surrounding text fixes the intended meaning. None is a false statement or a missing argument. The passage is used by the definition before Theorem 6.2.15 and by Theorem 6.2.15 (p. 64). Through these it is used by Corollaries 6.2.16 and 6.2.17, Remark 6.2.18, and Theorems 1.4.3(3), 1.4.9 and 1.4.10 of the introduction (pp. 5–6). None of these involves the misprinted symbols, and each is correct as intended.

issues.locator: Published §4 p.141, paragraph after Corollary 15, and its uses: proof of Lemma 16 p.142 ('We may assume that X is non-parabolic'), the remark after Definition 18 p.144 ('it is immediate to check that t-b.l. sections are quasi-t-b.l.') and the proof of Theorem A p.146; arXiv v3 §4 the same
issues.printed: The source claims that every Galois section of parabolic affine X is cuspidal, referring to [18, Theorem A] for the sole nontrivial case. It therefore treats the assumption that X is non-parabolic as always available.
issues.correction: The sentence holds when the boundary is split (every section of A^1 or G_m lies in each cuspidal packet), and for proper genus-zero curves Schmidt's theorem gives X ≅ P^1 once the section is b.l. It is false for X ≅ P^1_k minus a closed point of degree 2, which has geometric sections but no cuspidal ones. That case of Theorem A needs its own proof, and so does the remark after Definition 18, whose identity-map argument needs X non-parabolic. Over number fields the extraction records a proposed repair (items /169–/177, not in the paper, unreviewed). Over fields of positive transcendence degree no argument is known: Proposition 22 takes quasi-t-b.l. sections as input. Theorem A for non-parabolic curves, and Theorems B and C, which only use hyperbolic curves, are unaffected. Items /96 and /112 state what is proved.
issues.reason: X = P^1_Q minus V(T²−2) is affine and parabolic, 0 ∈ X(Q) gives a geometric section, and the boundary has no Q-point, so X has no cuspidal section. Schmidt's theorem concerns the splitting of the completion, not rationality of the boundary. The reductions in Lemma 16 and in the proof of Theorem A therefore leave unhandled the t-b.l. sections of such X that are not geometric. Reclassified by cc-442dc5 from 'the proof' to 'a stated result', because the missing case of Theorem A has no proof in the paper or elsewhere over fields of positive transcendence degree. This is not a claim that Theorem A fails there.

issues.correction: π = (α − 1)/β is a uniformiser for F′₋₃.
issues.reason: In §6.4, α is a root of X³ − 4, so α is a unit, and β² = −√−3 gives v(β) = 1/4 (v(3) = 1); hence v(α/β) = −1/4 and α/β is not integral. The data recorded afterwards fit (α − 1)/β: π¹² = (α − 1)¹²/β¹² = −3(1 − x − x²)⁴, so G(0) = −1 and c_π ≡ 1 mod (3, u) as printed; and γ₃(π)/π = ζ + (ζ − 1)/(α − 1) (ζ = (−1 − √−3)/2) is ≡ 1 + unit·π² mod π⁴, whereas γ₃(α/β)/(α/β) = ζ. issues.locator: Lemma 2.3.2, printed p. 315
issues.printed: The lemma asserts flatness of f : Y → Z for noetherian schemes when Z is regular, Y is Cohen-Macaulay, and every fibre is equidimensional with dimension dim Y − dim Z.
issues.correction: Assume instead that dim O_{Y,y} = dim O_{Z,f(y)} + dim O_{f⁻¹(f(y)),y} for every y ∈ Y (Matsumura, Commutative Ring Theory, Theorem 23.1; EGA IV 6.1.5). issues.reason: The printed statement is false. Take Y = Spec k ⊔ A¹_k → Z = A¹_k, the isolated point mapping to 0 and A¹ by the identity. Z is regular, Y is Cohen–Macaulay of dimension 1, and every fibre is equidimensional of dimension 0 = dim Y − dim Z, but f is not flat at the isolated point, since k[t]_(t) → k, t ↦ 0, is not flat. The proof uses the local equality 'dim S/(f_1, …, f_d)S = dim S − d', which the global hypothesis does not give. Every use satisfies the local equality: κ_{i,w} on the irreducible X_w (p. 316), f₁ on V_w (p. 317), and on p. 408 the spectra of local rings, where the hypothesis at the closed fibre is exactly the local equality.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 10.9, p. 886 (Invent. Math.); same text in arXiv v5
issues.printed: The source takes any wildly ramified degree p extension L/K and repeats the earlier calculation to obtain rsw_{e′_L}(res_{L/K} A) = [c̄_L ω, 0]_{π_L, e′_L}. Here L has uniformiser π_L, with e′_L = pe′ and non-zero c̄_L in F.

For such L, e′_L = e′, not pe′. Concretely, take L = K(x̃^{1/p}), where x̃ lifts the x in ω = dx/x ∧ dy/y. This is wildly ramified of degree p, and x̃ is a p-th power in L, so res_{L/K}A = (x̃, ỹ)_p = 0 and the claimed rsw_{e′_L}(res A) = [c̄_L ω, 0] with c̄_L ≠ 0 fails (ω also dies in Ω²_{F_L}, since dx = 0 there). issues.locator: Introduction, paragraph before Theorem C, p. 823 (Invent. Math.); same text in arXiv v5
issues.printed: The source credits Wittenberg’s suggestion to apply these methods to Question 1.4. It says the next result answers that question positively and gives a negative answer to Question 1.3 in general.
issues.correction: Theorem C gives a positive answer to Question 1.4 for every V that has good ordinary reduction at some prime of L, for example abelian surfaces and K3 surfaces. In general the positive answer is conditional on the existence of such a prime, conjectured by Serre and recorded by the authors right after Theorem C. The negative answer to Question 1.3 is unconditional, e.g. via K3 surfaces. Update as of this review: the general vanishing follows from Ambrosi–Newton–Pagano Corollary 1.1.2, independently of an ordinary prime; retain Theorem C's actual hypothesis when extracting the 2023 paper.
issues.reason: Theorem C assumes a prime 𝔭 of good ordinary reduction, and its proof uses ordinarity through [BK, Theorem 0.7(iii)] to get gr⁰ H²(V̄_𝔭, Q_p) ≠ 0. For a smooth projective V with H²(V, O_V) ≠ 0 (so H⁰(Ω²) ≠ 0 by Hodge symmetry), nothing in the paper supplies such a prime. Ordinarity is geometric and does not change under finite extension of L. The paper itself says, after Theorem C, that ordinary reduction at a positive density of primes is only conjectured in general (Joshi, attributing it to Serre), and known for abelian surfaces and K3 surfaces. So the claim holds only for varieties with an ordinary prime.

The compact-family chart argument shows that the normal coordinate x0/x1 at a large radius R defines a homomorphism endWind: π1(Hco,g) → Z with endWind([F]) = −1. Meanwhile X ≃ ∨ S^{39} (Pham join), so Ω²X is connected and simply connected. The printed proof fails at 'this convex combination will not introduce any new zeroes in a neighbourhood', which is not uniform in families (w = −1 at s = 3r(R)/2). The failure is already visible on H^1(−;Q), the input Theorem 7.7 uses. The reviewer adds a corollary: in this reading Conjecture 7.1 itself fails at j = 1, because H^1(Hco;Q) ≠ 0 while H_c^{2D−1}(Mor) = 0 by Corollary 1.2 at i = −1, inside even the conservative range. So the authors must have intended a finer topology. The source specifies none, so 'gap' is the right kind; under the natural compact-open reading the statement is false. No correction is known. Searched: Annals article page and PDF (no linked correction), arXiv 1711.10451 versions v1–v3 (no v4), as listed in the result; no further search by this reviewer.

issues.locator: Corollary 1.4, p. 696, and Corollary 7.18, p. 767 (also Theorem 6.1, p. 732)
issues.printed: The source takes arbitrary CM points z_1 of discriminant d_1 and z_2 of discriminant d_2 < 0, allowing a nonfundamental d_2 and requiring, when d_1 = d_2, that z_1 ≠ z_2. It asserts the existence of α ∈ H_{d_1}·H_{d_2} and r ∈ Z_{>0} satisfying (d_1d_2)^{j/2}G_{j+1,f}(z_1, z_2) = (1/r)log|α|.
issues.correction: For the unregularized Green function require avoidance of every contributing Hecke correspondence T_m with c_f(-m) nonzero. This is a sufficient precise off-divisor hypothesis; do not identify it with support of a signed sum without handling cancellation. Alternatively define and separately prove a finite regularized extension. Distinct CM points alone do not suffice.
issues.reason: Take j=1, z_1=i, z_2=2i, discriminants -4 and -16, and f=(j_modular-504)E_10/Delta=q^-2-2160+O(q). Its Fourier coefficients are integral. The determinant-two matrix diag(1,2) sends 2i to i (equivalently diag(2,1) sends i to 2i); the relevant Q_1(1) term diverges. Thus the unregularized value is not a finite logarithm. The extraction’s q^-2+O(q) witness was inaccurate and is corrected to q^-2+O(1). Remark 7.14’s noncontinuous finite extension is a different object, and the square case after Corollary 7.15 explicitly excludes these translates.

issues.locator: arXiv:1802.02637v5, Propositions 3.17 and 3.19 and Corollary 3.21 (§3.6), pp.24–31
issues.printed: Proposition 3.17 assumes σ ∈ Irr(GL_l), τ ∈ Irr_gen,u(GL_k). Proposition 3.19 and Corollary 3.21 assume π ∈ Irr_rel(G), τ ∈ Irr_gen,u(GL_k), the latter retaining (3.16). In proving 3.17, the source invokes Lemma 3.16 for χ_π W_ψ(ρ_c(τ)) = W_ψ(ρ_c(χ_π τ)), the (k, c) model; χ_π τ is also the input for Theorems A.6 and A.11.
issues.correction: Either assume χ_π unitary (π ∈ Irr_rel,a.u.(G), as in Theorem 3.12), or reduce to that case: write χ_π = |·|^r χ_0 with r real and χ_0 unitary. Then W_ψ(ρ_c(χ_π τ)) = |det|^r W_ψ(ρ_c(χ_0 τ)), the factor |det a|^r pulls out of Z^2 because r_z is unipotent, and L(s, σ^∨ × χ_π τ) = L(s + r, σ^∨ × χ_0 τ).
issues.reason: Lemma 3.16 (through [CFGK23, §3.2]) and Theorem A.11 are stated for unitary τ, but in Propositions 3.17, 3.19 and Corollary 3.21 the relevant representation is χ_π τ, and χ_π need not be unitary for π ∈ Irr_rel(G) when G = GSpin_c (for Sp_c and SO_c, χ_π = 1). The twist above repairs the argument, and the only use, Theorem 3.12, assumes χ_π unitary, so the main results are unaffected.
searched: arXiv v5 (SHA-256 dd49d944…), the latest version, read in full by cc-442dc5 on 23 September 2026; Crossref lists no correction or update for 10.4007/annals.2024.200.3.2.
issues.citation: Cai–Friedberg–Kaplan, "Doubling constructions: Global functoriality for non-generic cuspidal representations", Annals of Mathematics 200 (2024), no. 3
issues.reviewReason: (1) Is the gap real? Yes. Irr_rel(G) imposes nothing on χ_π, and for G = GSpin_c, χ_π can be non-unitary: since ⟨Υ_c, e_0^∨⟩ = 2, π = |Υ_c|^t π_0 has χ_π = |·|^{2t} χ_{π_0}. (For Sp_c and SO_c, χ_π = 1 by convention, p. 11.) The proof of Proposition 3.17 needs χ_π τ ∈ Irr_gen,u(GL_k) in three places, all outside their stated hypotheses when χ_π is not unitary. First, Lemma 3.16 assumes τ ∈ Irr_gen,u(GL_k), and its proof uses the realisation of [CFGK23, §3.2] 'which is applicable when τ ∈ Irr_gen,u(GL_k)' (p. 21). Second, Theorem A.11 assumes 'τ ∈ Irr_gen(GL_k) be unitary' (p. 55). Third, Theorem A.6 lies under the standing assumptions 'Henceforth also assume τ is unitary' (p. 44) and 'Recall that … τ is also unitary and k > 1 … until the end of the appendix' (p. 50); Proposition A.10 also uses unitarity to separate the poles of L(s + a_1, σ_{1,0} × τ) from those of L(1 − s − a_1, …) (p. 54). Propositions 3.19 and 3.21 apply Proposition 3.17 with the χ_π of an arbitrary π ∈ Irr_rel(G), so the written proofs do not cover non-unitary χ_π. (2) Is the twist correct? Yes; I checked each step. ρ_c(χτ) = χρ_c(τ) follows from the definition through Langlands data (§3.1). The (k, c) functionals are unchanged by the twist, since det is trivial on U_(c^k). det r_z = 1, since r_z ∈ diag(U_(l,c−2l,l) ∩ U_(l,c−n−l,n), I) (p. 21). The exponents match: with c replaced by l, (3.32) reduces to the appendix exponent s − (kl − 2l + 1)/2. The Rankin–Selberg L-factor satisfies L(s, σ^∨ × |·|^r τ′) = L(s + r, σ^∨ × τ′). The appendix itself records this twist (Theorem A.6(4)). Lemma 3.16 likewise extends to χτ_0, since T(|det|^r W_0 ⊗ μ) = T(W_0 ⊗ μ) and a ↦ |det a|^r W_{0,l}(m′_a) lies in |det|^{(kc−kl−c+l)/2} W_ψ(ρ_l(χτ_0)). The remaining steps of Proposition 3.19 and Corollary 3.21 are Proposition 3.18 (π ∈ Irr(G)), Lemma 3.20 (π ∈ Irr(G); its bound already carries |χ_π(det a)^i χ_π(det t)^j|, p. 30), Lemma 3.13 (any generic τ) and the Fubini arguments. None needs χ_π unitary. They do need the Langlands data in the form a_d > r; the printed a_d > r/2 is a separate misprint, recorded below. (3) Is Theorem 3.12, with χ_π unitary, the only downstream use? Yes. Proposition 3.17 is used only in the proof of Proposition 3.19 (p. 28), and Proposition 3.19 only in the proof of Corollary 3.21 (p. 31). Corollary 3.21 is used in the proof of Theorem 3.12 (p. 31), which assumes π ∈ Irr_rel,a.u.(G). The other references are the Fubini justification on p. 26 and 'as in the proof of Corollary 3.21' in Appendix A (p. 52), which reuses a technique for GL. Theorem 3.12 is applied in Theorem 4.8 (p. 39) to local components of a unitary cuspidal π, whose χ_{π_ν} are unitary. So Theorems 0.1, 4.8, 4.10 and Corollary 4.11 are unaffected. One small inaccuracy in E1's printed field: Corollary 3.21 begins 'Assume that…', not 'Suppose that…'. The locator pp. 24–31 is right.

issues.locator: arXiv:1802.02637v5, Introduction, p. 3
issues.printed: The source claims that the result for special orthogonal groups follows from the general spin case of Theorem 0.1, identifying special orthogonal representations with general spin representations having trivial central character.
issues.correction: '… are simply the representations of general spin groups that are trivial on C°_G = e_0^∨(GL_1) (the kernel of GSpin_c → SO_c), i.e. those with χ_π = 1.'

issues.printed: The source takes σ ∈ Irr(GL_l), l > 0, as the unique irreducible quotient of ×_{i=1}^d σ_i. It writes σ_i = |·|^{a_i} σ_{i,0}, with σ_{i,0} tempered, and takes π′ ∈ Irr(G_{c−2l}) essentially tempered. It requires a_1 > … > a_d > r/2, choosing r so that |Υ_{c−2l}|^{−r} π′ is tempered, with r = 0 if G ≠ GSpin_c.
issues.reason: With the paper's normalisation ⟨Υ_l, e_0^∨⟩ = 2 (p. 7), Υ_{c−2l} = 2e_0 + e_{l+1} + ⋯ + e_n. Pairing the real exponent ν = a_d·det(last block) + r·Υ_{c−2l} with the coroot of the simple root that separates GL_l from G_{c−2l} gives a_d − r (for e_l^∨ − e_{l+1}^∨ when l < n; 2a_d − 2r for 2e_n^∨ − e_0^∨ in GSpin_{2n+1}). So Langlands data need a_d > r. A counterexample to the printed condition: take GSpin_3 ≅ GL_2 (Υ_3 = det, Υ_1(g) = g², i_M^{−1}(a, g) = diag(ag, g)), σ = |·|^{3/2} and π′ = |Υ_1|^2, so r = 2 and a_1 = 3/2 > r/2. Then σ ⋊ π′ = Ind(|·|^{3/2} ⊗ |·|^{5/2}), whose unique irreducible quotient is π = |det|^2 St, with χ_π = |·|^4. For a character τ, (3.17) gives L(s, π × τ) = L(s + 3/2, τ) L(s + 5/2, τ), while the essentially tempered clause (π = |Υ_3|^2 St) gives L(s + 5/2, τ), the correct factor. So the printed condition makes the definition inconsistent. With a_d > r the data are the standard ones, and the operator I of §3.6 (p. 25) converges, which Proposition 3.19 and Corollary 3.21 need when χ_π is not unitary. Every use on the path to the main theorems has χ_π unitary, so r = 0 and the two conditions agree. The r/2 is probably left over from [CFK22]'s normalisation of Υ, which Remark 3.6 says differs. Checked on the page image.

issues.locator: Lemma 4.3, proof, p. 36, in arXiv v5 (the published version was not available)
issues.printed: The source claims holomorphy of L(2s+c′,τ×θ^{−1}τ)/L(2s,τ×θ^{−1}τ) M_2(s) when Re(s−1/2) > Re(−s−c′/2). Citing [JS81a, JS81b, Sha81], it says L(2s+c′,τ×θ^{−1}τ) is holomorphic for Re(2s+c′) > 1, hence Re(s) > 0, and L(2s,τ×θ^{−1}τ) has no zeros for Re(2s) ≥ 1, equivalently Re(s) ≥ 1/2. It concludes that M_2(s) is holomorphic throughout Re(s) ≥ 1/2.
issues.correction: Since [L(2s+c′)/L(2s)]·M_2(s) = N_2(s) is holomorphic, M_2(s) = [L(2s, τ×θ^{−1}τ)/L(2s+c′, τ×θ^{−1}τ)]·N_2(s). Holomorphy in Re(s) ≥ 1/2 therefore needs two facts. First, L(2s+c′, τ×θ^{−1}τ) is nonvanishing there, which holds because Re(2s+c′) ≥ 1+c′ ≥ 2. Second, L(2s, τ×θ^{−1}τ) is holomorphic there. It converges absolutely for Re(2s) > 1. On Re(2s) = 1 it could only have a pole at 2s = 1 − it with θ^{−1}τ ≅ τ^∨|det|^{it}, i.e. |det|^{−it}τ ≅ θτ^∨ ([JS81a, JS81b]), which the hypothesis of Theorem 4.1 excludes. So Lemma 4.3 remains true, but the M_2 part uses the hypothesis |det|^{it}τ ≇ θτ^∨ as well.
issues.reason: The printed argument gives holomorphy to the wrong L-function and nonvanishing to the wrong one. Poles of M_2 can come only from poles of L(2s) or zeros of L(2s+c′), so holomorphy of L(2s+c′) and nonvanishing of L(2s) say nothing about M_2. The displayed normalization is itself right: the Gindikin–Karpelevich factors L(x_j − y)/L(1 + x_j − y), with x_j − y = 2s + c′ − 1 − j for j = 0, ..., c′−1, telescope to L(2s)/L(2s+c′). Check with k = c′ = 1 and τ = χ: M_2(s) acts on the spherical vector by L(2s, χ²)/L(2s+1, χ²). This is holomorphic in Re(s) ≥ 1/2 exactly when L(2s, χ²) has no pole on Re(2s) = 1, i.e. when χ² ≠ |·|^{it}, which is the hypothesis.

issues.locator: Lemma 4.5.11, second line, p.663 (published version; the same in arXiv v3–v4)
issues.printed: The source states dim H¹(Γ(5), F₃)^{SL₂(F₅)} = 0 and asserts that, for N = 3, 4, 5, the result persists when these modules are replaced by their semisimplifications.
issues.correction: dim H¹(Γ(5), 𝔽₅)^{SL₂(𝔽₅)} = 0 (coefficients 𝔽₅), and likewise for its semisimplification.
issues.reason: Diagram (4.5.10) requires ℓ | N, and the proof of Theorem 4.5.2 takes N = ℓ ∈ {3, 5}, so ℓ = 5 is the case used. As printed the statement is false: SL₂(𝔽₅) is perfect, so inflation–restriction for Γ(5) ⊴ SL₂(ℤ) makes restriction H¹(SL₂(ℤ), 𝔽₃) = Hom(ℤ/12, 𝔽₃) ≅ 𝔽₃ → H¹(Γ(5), 𝔽₃)^{SL₂(𝔽₅)} injective (the character SL₂(ℤ) → SL₂(𝔽₃) → ℤ/3 stays nontrivial on Γ(5), which maps onto SL₂(𝔽₃)). Over 𝔽₃ the semisimplification claim also fails: H¹(Γ(5), ℚ) = 3 + 3′ + 5 as an A₅-module, and the 5-dimensional character, with Brauer character (5, 1, 0, 0) on the 3-regular classes, reduces mod 3 to 1 + 4. Over 𝔽₅ the lemma holds: H¹(SL₂(ℤ), 𝔽₅) = 0 and H²(SL₂(𝔽₅), 𝔽₅) = 0 (Lemma 4.5.5) give vanishing invariants, and 3, 3′, 5 reduce to the Brauer irreducibles 3, 3, 5 of PSL₂(𝔽₅), none trivial.
