issues.locator: §4.4, the sentence before Lemma 4.4.4, p.659, and its use in (4.4.9)–(4.4.10), p.660 (published version; the same since arXiv v3)
issues.printed: The source asserts that π : ⟨E, Γ(N)⟩ ∩ Γ0(p) → B is a natural surjective map and identifies Γ(Np) as its kernel.
issues.correction: For N > 2 the kernel of reduction mod p on ⟨E, Γ(N)⟩ ∩ Γ₀(p) is ⟨E, Γ(N)⟩ ∩ Γ(p), which contains Γ(Np) with index 2. Restrict to Γ(N) ∩ Γ₀(p), where the kernel is Γ(Np): Lemma 4.4.4 holds there, and it gives ⟨G ∩ Γ(Np), A⁻¹GA ∩ Γ₀(p) ∩ Γ(N)⟩ = Γ(N) ∩ Γ₀(p); adjoining E gives (4.4.9) as printed. Twisting π by the sign x ≡ ±I mod N works equally.
issues.reason: Some x ∈ SL₂(ℤ) has x ≡ −I mod N and x ≡ I mod p (SL₂(ℤ) → SL₂(ℤ/Np) is onto). It lies in ⟨E, Γ(N)⟩ ∩ Γ₀(p) and in ker π, but not in Γ(Np). So, as written, ker(f₁, π) = G ∩ Γ(p), and the deduction yields (4.4.9) only with G ∩ Γ(p). That is weaker than the (4.4.10) used in the proof of Theorem 4.3.1, where f(pτ) is known to be invariant only under G ∩ Γ(2Np). The proof of Lemma 4.4.4 already works on Γ(N) ∩ Γ₀(p): (f₁, f₂) stays surjective there, and π(γ) still generates the unipotent radical. So the corrected deduction goes through, and Theorems 4.3.1–4.3.2 stand.

issues.locator: Abstract (p. 298) and §1 Introduction (p. 305), compared with the §4.1 set-up for Theorem 4.8 (p. 361) and Lemma 4.11 (pp. 364–365). arXiv v2 has the same text ("completely solved", l. 316; same parenthetical on twisting before Thm 4.8). arXiv v1 is also the same: intro, and §3.8 Theorem 3.25 with the same twist-minimal hypothesis.
issues.printed: The abstract and introduction claim a complete multiplicity determination for irreducible modular ρ̄, with p odd, at its least weight-two level: J_1(N*)[m], or J_1(N) in the abstract. If ρ̄ is unramified at p with scalar ρ̄(Frob_p), its multiplicity is two; other cases have known multiplicity one, and the exceptional cases had known multiplicity ≥2. Before Theorem 4.8, ρ̄ is assumed to have conductor minimal among its twists at every other prime, with twisting said always to achieve this.
issues.correction: In the abstract and introduction, limit the multiplicity claim to ρ̄ that have minimal conductor amongst their twists at primes ≠ p. That is the hypothesis of Theorem 4.8. Twist-minimality at p is automatic in the scalar case, where ρ̄|G_p is unramified. The alternative is to give a separate argument for non-twist-minimal ρ̄. Theorem 4.8 as stated in §4.1 needs no change.
issues.reason:
I rendered pp. 298, 305 and 361–366 and checked them against the text above.

1. The claims do not match. The abstract and introduction claim multiplicity two for every irreducible modular ρ̄ (p odd) at its own minimal weight-2 level. The classical multiplicity-one results cited in Remark 4.9 (Mazur, Gross, Edixhoven, ...) are stated without twist-minimality. Theorem 4.8, however, is proved only under the hypothesis that ρ̄ has minimal conductor among its twists. The only link between the two is the parenthetical "(one can always twist ρ̄ to satisfy these condition)". That remark is true, but it does not show that multiplicity is unchanged by twisting: ρ̄ and ρ̄⊗ψ̄ sit at different levels N(ρ̄)p and N(ρ̄⊗ψ̄)p, with different Jacobians and Hecke algebras.

2. The multiplicity depends on the Hecke algebra. The proof of Theorem 4.8 uses T_pG^0 ≅ T_m and T_pG^e = Hom(T_m, Z_p), so dim J[m] = 1 + (number of generators of ω_{T_m}). Multiplicity two therefore means T_m has type 3. This is a property of T_m, and T_m changes under twisting.

3. A concrete example where T_m changes. Let ρ̄ = ρ̄_0⊗χ̄, with ρ̄_0 twist-minimal and unramified at a prime v ∤ N_0 p, and χ̄ tame of conductor v. Then ρ̄^{I_v} = 0, so every lift has conductor exactly v² and every lift appears at level N(ρ̄)p, with U_v = 0. If ρ̄_0(Frob_v) has eigenvalue ratio ≡ v, then Ribet's level-raised forms (Steinberg at v, level N_0vp) twisted by χ̃ are extra newforms of conductor v² in T_m(ρ̄). They have no counterpart in T_{m_0}(ρ̄_0) at level N_0p. So T_m(ρ̄) corresponds to the unrestricted deformation problem at v, while T_{m_0}(ρ̄_0) corresponds to the unramified one.

4. The proof does not carry over word for word. The proof of Lemma 4.11 lists the non-smooth cases only under twist-minimality. In the example above, R_v ≅ R_v^unrestricted(ρ̄_0|G_v). Its unramified and Steinberg components meet at characteristic-0 points (unramified lifts with eigenvalue ratio v), where H^2(G_v, ad^0ρ) ≠ 0. So "R_v[1/p] formally smooth" fails, and that property is what the text uses when applying Kisin's method to get R̃[1/p] = T[1/p]. The paper's own remark on p. 363 also uses twist-minimality to exclude v ≡ 1 mod p with ρ̄^{I_v} = 0.

5. The result is probably still true. R_v is still a complete intersection, and weight-2 points avoid the intersection locus by Ramanujan. So multiplicity two is plausible at non-minimal level too, but the paper gives no argument for it.

Conclusion: this is a gap in the reduction to the twist-minimal case, and it affects the claim in the abstract and introduction. Theorem 4.8 itself, as stated, is correct. Defence tried and failed. (1) The quantity is not twist-invariant by any formal argument. Twisting ρ̄ = ρ̄_0⊗χ̄ (χ̄ of conductor x ≠ p) changes N(ρ̄), N*, the curve J_1(N*) and the Hecke algebra T. (2) If ρ̄ is not twist-minimal at x, then ρ̄^{I_x} = 0. Every lift then has conductor cond(ρ̄|G_x), so every lift of ρ̄|G_x shows up at level Γ_1(N). After twisting back, m at level N(ρ̄)p also sees non-minimal forms for ρ̄_0. Examples are χ-twists of forms that are Steinberg at x (conductor x²) when the level-raising condition holds, or of ramified principal series of p-power type when x ≡ 1 mod p. So T_m is not the twist of T_{m_0} at level N(ρ̄_0)p. When no such extra forms exist, a Chebotarev/trace argument does identify the two Hecke algebras, but not in general. (3) The paper's proof really does use minimality. On p. 362, Φ is 'the only twists' preserving minimal-conductor lifts only under minimality; when x ≡ 1 mod p and ρ̄ is non-minimal at x, the characters of Z_p⊗(Z/x)^× also qualify. On p. 363 the paper itself says the twist-uniqueness 'is not true when v ≡ 1 mod p and ρ̄ has trivial invariants under I_v' and removes this case by the minimality assumption. Lemma 4.11 lists only the non-smooth cases that can occur for twist-minimal ρ̄. For a non-minimal ρ̄|G_x = χ̄⊗(unramified, Frobenius-eigenvalue ratio ≡ x mod p), R_{x,φ} is isomorphic to the unrestricted fixed-determinant ring of an unramified representation. Its unramified and Steinberg components meet in the generic fibre at the points μ⊕με, where H²(G_x, ad⁰ρ) ≠ 0. So the claim that the generic fibre is formally smooth fails, and with it the stated input to Kisin's R[1/p] = T[1/p]. (4) No nearby statement closes the gap. Remark 4.12 concerns J_H, and the parenthetical '(one can always twist ρ̄…)' only says that a twist-minimal twist exists. The general statement is very plausibly true: the extra local rings are complete intersections of type 1, and modular points avoid the singular locus. But the paper gives no proof of it, so the introduction and abstract claim more than Theorem 4.8 proves. Consequences: §4.1 opens with 'Although this is not needed for our main results', and nothing later cites Theorem 4.8. Only the claim in the abstract and introduction is affected, and the proposed restriction is right and minimal.

issues.locator: §1, description of case Betti, p. 300 (same in arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The Betti description takes reductive G with maximal compact K and maximal Q-split torus A, allowing arbitrary l0 = rank(G) − rank(K) − rank(A). After localization at m in T, it requires l0 + 1 successive cohomological degrees. Citing [9], it assigns length l0 + 1 to the Betti range. For coherent cohomology, l0 depends on allowed πv at infinity, and length l0 is attributed to [10, Theorems 3.4 and 3.5] and infinite L-packets.
issues.correction: "maximal Q-split torus A" should read "maximal Q-split torus A in the centre of G" (the usual A_G). Then l0 = rank(G) − rank(K) − rank(A), with rank meaning absolute rank of the real group, as in §8.4; this is the qualifier the paper itself uses in §8.2, p. 403: "the maximal Q-split torus in the centre".
issues.reason:
I checked the rendered page (p. 300 = PDF p. 4) against the transcription above. Read literally, A is a maximal Q-split torus of G. "rank" must mean absolute rank here: §8.4 computes l0 from rank(SL_n(R)) − rank(SO_n(R)), and with real rank you would get Hilbert modular surfaces wrong. Under that reading my own computations give:
(a) GL2/Q: rank G = 2, rank O(2) = 1, Q-rank = 2, so l0 = −1, which is impossible.
(b) Res_{F/Q}GL2 with F imaginary quadratic: complexified Lie algebra gl2 ⊕ gl2 has rank 4, rank U(2) = 2, Q-rank = 2, so l0 = 0 instead of 1.
(c) Res_{F/Q}PGL2 with F imaginary quadratic, the paper's own Part 1 case: 2 − 1 − 1 = 0, but the paper treats this case as l0 = 1 (Part 1 "l0 equals 1"; §8.3 "n = 2 and l0 = 1").
(d) Remark 5.14 (p. 3xx, "l0 = rank(G) − rank(K) for PGL(2)/H ... equal to the number of complex places of H") has no A term. The literal intro formula would give r2 − 1 there.
With A taken as the Q-split torus in the centre, every value comes out right: GL2/Q gives 0, GL2 over imaginary quadratic F gives 1, PGL2 gives 1 (trivial central torus), and Res GL1 gives r1 + r2 − 1, matching §8.2. So the printed definition is wrong as stated and the fix is the missing "in the centre". It is not one of the 47 bracket errors. It is also in the accepted arXiv v2, so it is not a production artifact. On length, the paragraph does say "length l0 + 1" and then "length l0", but each use is correct under its own meaning: number of degrees versus length of the interval. That part is a stylistic inconsistency, not an error. The paper's main convention elsewhere is "range of length l0", including p. 300 below, and Part 2's "degrees of arbitrary length l0" and "range of degrees of length l0".

issues.locator: §1, paragraph after the Betti/Coherent bullets, published p. 300 (PDF p. 4). arXiv v2 has the same text (cg-v2.txt lines 139–145, 163). arXiv v1 read 'has length l0' with l0 = 1 and 'concentrated in only two consecutive degrees'; the '+ 1' came in with the v2 revision.
issues.printed: The source attributes to [9] a Betti cohomological range of length l0 + 1 for tempered representations. In coherent cohomology, l0 varies with the permitted infinity components π_v; [10, Theorems 3.4 and 3.5] and infinite L-packets give tempered representations a range of length l0. Later it assumes the relevant cohomology lies in a range whose length is l0.
issues.correction: '... the range of cohomological degrees to which they occur has length l0' (the l0 + 1 degrees q0, ..., q0 + l0). Equivalently: in both the Betti and the coherent case, the cohomology lies in l0 + 1 consecutive degrees [q0, q0 + l0], a range of length l0.
issues.reason: Everywhere else the paper uses 'length l0' for a range or complex spanning the l0 + 1 degrees q0, ..., q0 + l0. Examples: the next sentence and the end of p. 300 ('range of length l0'); p. 384 ('occurs in a range of degrees of length l0'); p. 394 (complex 'bounded of length l0'); p. 406 ('[q0, ..., q0 + l0] is the range ...' from Borel–Wallach [9]). The same paragraph asks for cohomology 'concentrated in l0 + 1 consecutive degrees'. So 'has length l0 + 1' in the Betti sentence uses 'length' to mean the number of degrees, which contradicts the next sentence ('range of length l0' in the coherent case). Read literally, one case would have one more degree than the other, which is not what is meant. The intended meaning is clear, and the v1 text ('has length l0' with two consecutive degrees) shows the slip came in with the revision. It is an informal remark in the introduction, and all later statements use the consistent convention.

issues.locator: §1, paragraph before Theorem 1.2, published p. 301 (PDF p. 5). arXiv v2 has the same text (cg-v2.txt line 175). Not in v1, whose intro used 'Barsotti–Tate' instead.
issues.printed: The source takes O as the integer ring of a finite extension of Q_p, with uniformizer ϖ and residue field O/ϖ = k. For v|p, finite flatness of ρ|D_v means that, for every n ≥ 1, the quotient ρ|D_v mod ϖ^n comes from the generic fibre of an O-group scheme that is finite flat. Ordinarity means conjugacy to the subsequently displayed representation.
issues.correction: '... is the generic fiber of a finite flat group scheme over O_{F_v}' (with O-action if wanted). This matches §5.1, p. 368: 'finite flat if there is a finite flat group scheme F/O_{F_v} such that ρ ≅ F(F̄_v)' (§5.1 also requires det ρ|I_v to be cyclotomic, which Theorem 1.2 assumes separately).
issues.reason: In this paragraph O is the coefficient ring. On the standard reading, 'O-group scheme' is a group scheme over Spec O. Its generic fibre lives over Frac(O), and its points carry a G_{Frac O}-action rather than a D_v = G_{F_v}-action, so the definition as written does not make sense. The only sensible base is O_{F_v}, which is how the body of the paper states it (§5.1, p. 368). A charitable reading ('O-group scheme' = group scheme with O-action, base O_{F_v} left implicit) makes the sentence merely terse. That is why confidence is low: this is a wording or notation slip in the introduction, and the intended meaning is clear from §5.1. The main results use the §5.1 definition.

issues.locator: §1, Theorem 1.3, hypotheses (1)–(4), published p. 302 (PDF p. 6). The deduction is in §5.4, last sentence before §5.5, published p. 380 (PDF p. 84). Theorem 5.11 itself is on p. 379. The missing hypothesis is §5.1(3) on p. 369. The levels that depend on it are in §5.2.1(5) on p. 371, and Conjecture A(2) is on p. 374. arXiv v2 has identical text for Theorem 1.3 and §5.1(3). arXiv v1 (Theorem 1.2 there) did not fix the determinant, and its §5.1 begins "After twisting by a global character ... we may assume that for all x ∈ S(ρ̄) such that ρ̄|D_x is reducible, either I_x acts unipotently, is of the form 1 ⊕ ψ, or acts through scalars". That reduction was dropped when the published version moved to PGL with cyclotomic determinant.
issues.printed: Theorem 1.3 assumes Conjecture A, imaginary quadratic F/Q, unramified p ≥ 3, and continuous ρ̄ : G_F → GL_2(k) of cyclotomic determinant: finite flat or ordinary at v|p, modular at N = N(ρ̄), with absolutely irreducible ρ̄|G_{F(ζ_p)}. At ramified x with N_{F/Q}(x) ≡ −1 mod p, it requires reducible ρ̄|D_x or absolutely irreducible ρ̄|I_x. It claims R^min ⥲ T_m for minimal deformations and localized H_1(Y_0(N), O) Hecke operators. §5.4 deduces it from Theorem 5.11; §5.1 lists irreducible, unipotent, ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1}, and N_{F/Q}(x) ≢ −1 mod p local cases.
issues.correction: Add to Theorem 1.3 a hypothesis, and make §5.1(3) exhaustive to match: for each prime x ∤ p at which ρ̄ is ramified, if ρ̄|I_x is reducible then it is either unipotent or semisimple. Equivalently, ρ̄|I_x is never ≅ ψ ⊗ (1 ∗; 0 1) with ∗ ≠ 0 and ψ a non-trivial character. Such a ψ is necessarily quadratic, and this case is the twisted Steinberg type. The analogous twist-minimality assumption "if x ∈ S(ρ̄) and ρ̄|G_x is reducible, then ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ (0)" is imposed in §3.1 (p. 310) for the case over Q. The alternative is to add a fifth local type T: the lift condition ρ|I_x ≅ ⟨ψ⟩ ⊗ unipotent, a matching level K_{Q,x} in §5.2.1(5), and a matching clause in Conjecture A(2). The tangent-space term L_{Q,x} = H^1(G_x/I_x, (ad^0)^{I_x}) and Proposition 5.1 carry over unchanged, because ad^0 does not change under a twist. Both reported corrections are right. Adding the hypothesis is the minimal fix.
issues.reason:
I checked the rendered pages 302, 369–371, 374 and 379–380.

1. The case is possible and falls outside the paper's types. Take x ∤ p. Since det ρ̄ = ε, the restriction det ρ̄|I_x is trivial. Suppose ρ̄|I_x is reducible but not semisimple. Then the unique I_x-stable line is D_x-stable, so ρ̄|D_x is reducible, with characters χ1, χ2 and a non-zero class in H^1(I_x, χ1χ2^{-1}). Because ℓ ≠ p, this group is H^1(I_x/P, k(χ1χ2^{-1})^P), and it vanishes unless χ1|I_x = χ2|I_x = ψ. Together with ψ^2 = 1 this gives ρ̄|I_x ≅ ψ ⊗ (1 *; 0 1) with * ≠ 0. If ψ ≠ 1, the image contains −1 times a matrix of the form (1 *; 0 1), so ρ̄|I_x is not unipotent in the paper's sense (image inside the matrices (1 *; 0 1)). It is not semisimple, so it is not (c). It is not irreducible, so it is not (a). Since D_x is reducible, it is not (d)/M in the intended sense. So it is none of the types S, P, M, H. The deformation conditions (5)–(8) impose nothing at x, §5.2.1(5) defines K_{Q,v} only for types S, P, M, H, and Conjecture A(2) has no clause for this type. The proof of Theorem 5.11 therefore never reaches this case: it needs R^min, Y = Y(K_∅), the tangent bound of Prop. 5.1 with L_{Q,x} = H^1(G_x/I_x, (ad^0)^{I_x}), and Conjecture A.

2. Theorem 1.3's hypotheses do not exclude the case. Hypothesis (4) is satisfied because D_x is reducible.

3. An explicit example. Take E = 11a1, which has split multiplicative reduction at 11 with v_11(Δ) = 5 and surjective mod-7 image. Let χ be the quadratic character of Q(√−11), which is ramified only at 11. Take p = 7 and F = Q(i), so 7 and 11 are inert in F, and set ρ̄ = ρ̄_{E^χ,7}|G_F.
- The determinant is cyclotomic, and ρ̄ is finite flat at 7 (E^χ has good reduction there).
- At x = (11), ρ̄|I_x = χ|I_11 ⊗ (non-trivial unipotent), since 7 ∤ 5.
- The image of G_{F(ζ_7)} is a normal subgroup of SL_2(F_7) with abelian quotient, so it is all of SL_2(F_7) (SL_2(F_7) is perfect). Hence (3) holds.
- N(x) = 121 ≡ 2 mod 7, so (4) holds.
- The Artin conductor at x is x^2 (ρ̄^{I_x} = 0), and the base change of the level-121 newform E^χ gives modularity at Γ_0(N(ρ̄)).
So Theorem 1.3 as printed applies to this ρ̄, but §5 does not cover it.

4. Side remarks. Read literally, the conditional in §5.1(3)(d) is vacuously true when D_x is reducible. That reading makes things no better, because the levels and the type assignment ("we say that ρ̄|D_x is of type S, P, M or H") would then be undefined at x. Twisting ρ̄ by a global quadratic character would reduce this case to type S, as v1 did, but the published paper does not carry out that reduction and it does not transfer the Y_0(N) statement. The conclusion may even fail as stated at Γ_0(N) level: when N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, Γ_0(x^2) also sees principal series π(ψη, (ψη)^{-1}) with η of p-power order, and these are not minimal lifts. I did not verify this possible failure, so I classify the problem as a gap rather than an error.

On locators: C-K1-0's p. 379 for the "follows from" sentence should be p. 380. X-K6-15's aside that Y_0(N) in Theorem 1.3 should be read as Y(K_∅) (K_∅ uses Γ_p(v^c) for types P, M, H) is plausible, but I did not assess it separately. The case exists and is excluded nowhere. Take x ∤ p. Because det ρ̄ is cyclotomic, det ρ̄|I_x = 1. If ρ̄|I_x is reducible and not split, the extension class lies in H^1(I_x, ψ1ψ2^{-1}). The wild inertia group is pro-ℓ with ℓ ≠ p, so this group vanishes unless ψ1 = ψ2 = ψ. Then ψ^2 = 1. With ψ = 1 we get type S. With ψ ≠ 1 we get ρ̄|I_x ≅ ψ ⊗ (non-split unipotent). The line fixed by I_x is D_x-stable, so ρ̄|D_x is reducible and hypothesis (4) of Theorem 1.3 says nothing at x.

This ρ̄ matches none of the lift conditions (5) S, (6) P, (7) M or (8) H on p. 369:
- It is not unipotent.
- It is not a direct sum ψ ⊕ ψ^{-1}.
- ρ̄|D_x is reducible, which rules out M.
- It is not irreducible.
Condition (4) covers only x ∉ S(ρ̄). So R^min puts no condition at x, and that does not match the Selmer condition L_{Q,x} = unramified classes used in Proposition 5.1. The level K_{Q,v} in §5.2.1(5) is defined only for types S/P/M/H. Conjecture A(2) speaks only to S and P, so it gives no local-global compatibility at x for R^min → T_m.

Defence tried and failed:
- Read literally, §5.1(3)(d) is an implication. It is then vacuous whenever ρ̄|D_x is reducible, and §5.1(3) becomes logically equivalent to Theorem 1.3(4). On that reading §5 itself admits the case and leaves it untreated.
- On the intended reading, (a)–(d) list the types, so §5.1(3) excludes the case, but Theorem 1.3 does not.
- Either way, "Theorem 1.3 follows from Theorem 5.11" fails for these ρ̄.
- No nearby statement fills the gap. The §3.1 twist-minimality assumption applies only over Q. The global twist in arXiv v1 was dropped.

Such ρ̄ really occur. Take E = 11a1, which has split multiplicative reduction at 11 with v_11(Δ) = 5, and p = 3 ∤ 5. Twist E by χ_{-11}, which is unramified at 3. Then E^χ has good reduction at 3. Restrict to F = Q(i), where 3 and 11 are inert. At x = (11), ρ̄ = E^χ[3] has cyclotomic determinant and ρ̄|I_x ≅ χ|I_x ⊗ (non-split unipotent) with χ|I_x ≠ 1. It is finite flat at 3, and its image over F(ζ_3) contains SL_2(F_3), so it is absolutely irreducible. N(x) = 121 ≢ −1 mod 3, and ρ̄ is modular via base change of the level-lowered form. So every hypothesis of Theorem 1.3 holds.

Consequences:
- Nothing later in the paper uses Theorem 1.3 except the deduction of Theorem 1.2.
- Theorem 1.2 is unaffected. There ρ is semi-stable, so ρ̄|I_x is unipotent (type S) or trivial.
- Theorem 5.11 is affected only if §5.1(3)(d) is read literally.
- The theorem is expected to hold in the missing case once the right definitions are in place, so this is a gap, not a false statement.

issues.locator: §1, Theorem 1.4, p. 303, versus the standing assumption of §3.1, p. 310 (published version)
issues.printed: Theorem 1.4 claims, for p ≥ 3 and odd continuous irreducible ρ̄ : G_Q → GL_2(k) of Serre level N unramified at p, a quotient X_U of X_1(N) and bundle L_σ with R^min ⥲ T_m and free H^1(X_U, ω⊗L_σ)_m over T_m. In §3.1, reducible ρ̄|G_x at x ∈ S(ρ̄) requires ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ (0), attainable by a twist unramified outside S(ρ̄). Definition 3.1(4) requires ρ^{I_x} to be an R-direct summand of rank one for reducible ρ̄|G_x with x ∈ S(ρ̄) − T(ρ̄).
issues.correction:
Simplest fix: add the §3.1 hypothesis to Theorem 1.4, namely "if x ∈ S(ρ̄) and ρ̄|G_x is reducible, then ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ 0", so the statement matches what §3 proves. Other fixes also work but take more effort:
- Keep the statement general and define R^min in the Diamond sense, i.e. ρ(I_x) ≅ ρ̄(I_x) at such x, as in Cor. 1.5(1). The Hecke side then needs a new type-cutting bundle at those x, e.g. U_x = K_0(x^{max(a1,a2)}) with the character ψ̃1(a)ψ̃2(d).
- State the Hecke side for the twist ρ̄⊗χ̄, with N, X_U, T and m taken from the twist.
Corollaries 1.5 and 1.6 then each need a one-line twisting reduction, which is valid: weight-one modularity, finite image, the minimality in Cor. 1.5(1) and R^min are all unchanged by twisting by the Teichmüller lift of a character unramified at p.
issues.reason:
I checked the page images at pp. 303, 310–311, 338, 340 and 342 against the text. The same wording is in arXiv v2.

(1) Theorem 1.4 as printed covers every odd irreducible ρ̄ that is unramified at p. The whole proof runs under the §3.1 standing assumption. §3.8 (p. 340) says "We now deduce Theorem 1.4, under Assumption 3.9 … we take X_U = X = X_1(N)/H". §3.9.2 (p. 342, and p. 354) removes only Assumption 3.9, the vexing primes. The §3.1 assumption is never removed; the only thing said about it is the one-line twisting remark.

(2) For ρ̄|G_x ≅ ψ̄1⊕ψ̄2 with both characters ramified, ρ̄^{I_x} = 0. So Definition 3.1(4) already fails for ρ̄ over k, and the functor is empty. The R^min of the introduction then has to mean Diamond-minimal (ρ(I_x) ≅ ρ̄(I_x); compare Corollary 1.5(1)), and the §3 machinery does not apply to it directly.

(3) On the Galois side, twisting by the Teichmüller lift of χ̄ does give R^min(ρ̄) ≅ R^min(ρ̄⊗χ̄). The determinant condition and the inertia condition both carry over. On the Hecke side, the Serre level drops at x (from x² to x or 1), and X_U changes with it. The Hecke algebra of ρ̄' = ρ̄⊗χ̄ has no maximal ideal for ρ̄: ρ̄ cannot occur at level N' < N. So the twist does not directly give "X_U a quotient of X_1(N), m corresponding to ρ̄".

(4) Taking the paper's own level structure directly does not work either. For P(ρ̄) (p. 342) the paper uses U_x = {g ≡ (∗ ∗; 0 d) mod x^{c_x}, d of p-power order}, which here has c_x = 2. Take x ≡ 1 mod p and θ a nontrivial character of Z_x^× of p-power order and conductor x. The representation π(ψ̃1θ, ψ̃2θ^{-1}) has conductor 1+1 = 2 and central character ψ̃1ψ̃2, which is trivial on elements d of p-power order. Its newvector is therefore U_x-invariant, it is congruent to ρ̄, and it is non-minimal. Under the §3.1 assumption, by contrast, ψ̄1 is unramified, and such twists raise the conductor to 1+c_x, which excludes them. So the assumption is really used.

Conclusion: the statement of Theorem 1.4 goes beyond what is proved. The theorem is probably still true with a different choice of X_U and L_σ, so this is a gap, not an error. It is minor, and the fix is routine.

Dependencies: Corollaries 1.5 and 1.6 are unchanged by twisting, so they survive. §4 assumes minimal conductor among twists (p. 351), which implies the §3.1 condition. Only Theorem 1.4's generality is affected. Defences I tried, and why each fails. I checked page images for pp. 303, 310, 311, 340 and 342 and read the text of pp. 325–330 and 350–354.

(1) "R^min refers to §3, so the §3.1 assumption is implicit." Theorem 1.4 lists its hypotheses explicitly: p ≥ 3, odd, irreducible (which gives absolute irreducibility for p odd), and unramified at p. These are all the §3.1 standing assumptions except the twist condition. Under the paper's own Def. 3.1(4), a ρ̄ with ρ̄|G_x ≅ ψ̄1⊕ψ̄2, both characters ramified, has ρ̄^{I_x} = 0. No lift then satisfies (4), so the functor is empty and "R^min" means nothing. The intro must therefore intend Diamond-minimality, which is the reading of Cor. 1.5(1): "ρ(I_v) ≅ ρ̄(I_v) or dim ρ^{I_v} = dim ρ̄^{I_v} = 1". The §3 proof never treats that notion.

(2) "By twisting, WLOG." On the Galois side this works. There is a global χ̄ with χ̄|I_x = ψ̄1^{-1}, ramified only at such x, and R^min(ρ̄) ≅ R^min(ρ̄⊗χ̄). On the Hecke side it does not. The twist has a smaller Serre level N' (the x-part drops from x^{a1+a2} to x^{cond(ψ̄2/ψ̄1)}), and its m' corresponds to ρ̄⊗χ̄. Theorem 1.4 requires m to correspond to ρ̄ itself, and ρ̄ does not occur at level N'. The paper says nothing beyond the one-line remark on p. 310, which is the only occurrence of "twist" in §3 apart from the remark on p. 334 about twisting a scalar local ρ̄ to trivial.

(3) "The paper's own X_U works anyway." It does not in general. §3.3 (p. 325) takes X = X_1(N)/H with H the p-part of (Z/N)^×, and §3.9 (p. 342) takes U_x = {g ≡ (* *; 0 d) mod x^{c_x}, d of p-power order} for x ∈ P(ρ̄). Suppose x ≡ 1 mod p and θ is a p-power-order character of Z_x^× of conductor x. Then π(ψ̃1θ, ψ̃2θ^{-1}) has conductor exponent a1+a2 = c_x, because ψ̃iθ^{±1} is still ramified with the same conductor. Its central character ψ̃1ψ̃2 has prime-to-p order, so it is trivial on p-power d, and the newvector is U_x-invariant. This representation is congruent to ρ̄ but not minimal. So Theorem 3.14 ("follows from the choice of N and H") and the p. 341 claim "all minimal lifts … appear in H^0(X_U, ω)" do not give R^min → T_m. Under the §3.1 assumption, ψ̄1 is unramified and such twists raise the conductor, so the assumption is really used. A concrete case exists: p = 3, x = 13, ρ̄|I_x ≅ χ̄ ⊕ χ̄^{-1} with χ̄ of order 4.

(4) Where the proof ends. §3.8 deduces Theorem 1.4 "under Assumption 3.9", and §3.9.2 removes only that assumption (vexing primes). The §3.1 assumption is never removed.

Consequences:
- Only the generality of Theorem 1.4 is affected. The theorem is very likely true with a type-cutting L_σ built with the paper's own §3.9 formalism, so this is a gap rather than a false statement.
- Cor. 1.5 and 1.6 ("immediately deduce") still hold after a routine twist.
- §4 assumes minimal conductor among twists (p. 361), which implies the condition, so it is unaffected.
- The proposed correction (add the hypothesis) is right and minimal.
- A side observation, not part of this candidate: p. 340's "if x^2|N, then U_x = 0" fits the both-ramified case but misses a wildly ramified ψ̄2 under the §3.1 assumption. U_x ∈ T_m still follows from the invariant-line argument in that case.

issues.locator: §1, Corollary 1.5, hypothesis (1), p. 304 (same in arXiv v1 Cor. 1.4 and v2)
issues.printed: Corollary 1.5 is presented as an immediate consequence of Theorem 1.4. It asserts weight-one modularity for continuous ρ : G_Q → GL_2(O) when p ≥ 3, ρ̄ is odd and irreducible, and ρ is unramified at p, subject at every prime v to either ρ(I_v) ~→ ρ̄(I_v) or the condition dim(ρ^{I_v}) = dim(ρ̄^{I_v}) = 1.
issues.reason:
Rendered PDF p.8 = p.304; the printed text matches the transcription. The same statement appears in arXiv v2. I checked the setup the corollary relies on. Def. 3.1(1) (p.307) fixes det ρ = Teichmüller lift of det ρ̄, and R^min is taken with Q=∅. Theorem 1.4 is proved with X_U = X_1(N)/H, where H is the p-part of (Z/N)^× (§3.3). In §3.9, U_x at x ∈ P(ρ̄) requires d to have p-power order. So T_m only sees forms whose nebentypus has order prime to p.

Redoing the counterexample. Take v ≡ 1 mod p with ρ̄|I_v = 1 ⊕ χ̄, χ̄ ≠ 1. Frobenius fixes the trivial isotypic line, so ρ̄|G_v is reducible, v ∈ S−T, and dim ρ̄^{I_v} = 1. Let ρ|I_v = 1 ⊕ [χ̄]θ with θ ≠ 1 of p-power order. Then dim ρ^{I_v} = 1, so (1) holds. Put ψ = det ρ/[det ρ̄], which has p-power order and ψ|I_v = θ. Any twist ρ⊗ε that lifts ρ̄⊗ε̄ with the fixed determinant forces ε = [ε̄]·ψ^{-1/2}, because squaring is bijective on 1+m when p is odd. The standing hypothesis ρ̄^{I_v} ≠ 0 forces ε̄|I_v ∈ {1, χ̄^{-1}}. In both cases (ρ⊗ε)|I_v has characters [ε̄]θ^{-1/2} and [ε̄χ̄]θ^{1/2}, and neither is trivial, so there are no inertia invariants and Def. 3.1(4) fails. So no twist of ρ is a point of any R^min covered by Theorem 1.4. The Hecke side agrees: the twist has conductor v² at v, and the untwisted ρ has non-p'-order nebentypus.

A global example exists. Take p=3, v=13, K=Q(√−14): 13 splits, 3 is unramified, and O_K^× = ±1. Let ψ be a character of order 6 on I_w, unramified at w' and elsewhere. ψ_w(−1) = 1 because 12/6 is even, so ψ extends to a Hecke character. Then ρ = Ind_K ψ is odd, ρ̄ is irreducible (ψ̄ ≠ ψ̄^c at w), ρ is unramified at 3, and (1) holds at 2, 7 (order-2 inertia) and at 13. ρ is modular, but only on X_1(728), not on X_U. So the claimed "immediate" deduction fails for part of the hypothesis. The paper itself says non-minimal lifting is hard (p.304 text after Cor. 1.6).

Corollary 1.5 is not cited again in the paper (grep). Corollary 1.6 assumes minimality, so it is unaffected. The candidate's gap is correct. Its correction's "equivalently" and "only at v ≡ 1 mod p" are overstated, as the correction field explains. I checked the Steinberg case only locally and did not construct a global example. DEFENCE ATTEMPTED AND FAILED. Theorem 1.4 is proved in §3 for R^min as defined in Def. 3.1 with Q = ∅. That ring has a fixed determinant, equal to the Teichmüller lift of det ρ̄ (Def. 3.1(1)), and it requires ρ^{I_x} to be a rank-one direct summand at every x ∈ S−T where ρ̄|G_x is reducible (Def. 3.1(4)). T_m lives on X_U = X_1(N)/H, where H is the p-part of (Z/N)^× (§3.3, p. 2141 of the text). At x ∈ P(ρ̄), the group U_x forces d to have p-power order (§3.9). So T_m sees only forms of conductor dividing N whose nebentypus has no p-part.
The intended deduction runs: twist by ψ^{-1/2}, get a minimal deformation, conclude modularity, twist back. This only works if hypothesis (1) makes some twist of ρ minimal. Two cases show that it does not.

(i) DETERMINANT CASE. Take v ≡ 1 mod p with ρ̄|I_v = 1⊕χ̄, χ̄ ≠ 1, and ρ|I_v = 1⊕[χ̄]θ, with θ ≠ 1 of p-power order. The second alternative of (1) holds. Consider any twist ρ⊗ε that lifts ρ̄⊗ε̄ with the fixed determinant. Since squaring is bijective on 1+m, this forces ε = [ε̄]ψ^{-1/2}. On I_v the twist then has characters [ε̄]θ^{-1/2} and [ε̄χ̄]θ^{1/2}, and neither is trivial. So Def. 3.1(4) fails for every such twist.
A global example, which I re-checked: p = 3, K = Q(√−14), in which 13 splits, 3 is unramified and O_K^× = ±1. Take ψ of order 6 on I_w for one prime w | 13; since ψ_w(−1) = 1, ψ extends to a Hecke character. Then ρ = Ind_K ψ is odd, ρ̄ is irreducible (ψ̄ ≠ ψ̄^c), ρ is unramified at 3, and (1) holds at 2, 7 and 13. This ρ is modular (it is dihedral), but no twist of it is a point of T_m.

(ii) UNIPOTENT-REDUCTION CASE. Take x ≡ ±1 mod p with ρ̄|I_x unipotent and nontrivial, so ρ̄(I_x) ≅ Z/p. Let ρ|I_x = ζ⊕ζ^{-1} with ζ of order p. This occurs as a non-split lattice; I checked the lattice explicitly. Here ρ(I_x) ⥲ ρ̄(I_x), so the first alternative of (1) holds, and det ρ|I_x = 1. But ρ^{I_x} = 0 and the conductor is x^2. Any p-power twist still has no inertia invariants, and a prime-to-p twist destroys ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ 0.
In fact, at a Steinberg-type x the first alternative never yields a minimal ρ. Minimal lifts there have infinite inertia image and satisfy the second alternative instead. I expect global examples to exist (for instance p = 3 tetrahedral or octahedral forms with inertia of order 3 at some prime), but I did not construct a specific one.

In both cases ρ is a non-minimal lift. The paper itself says (p. 304–305) that its method cannot handle such lifts. So the word "immediately" is unjustified for part of the range of hypothesis (1). The conclusion is probably true, as predicted by Fontaine–Mazur, and the examples above are modular by classical results. That makes this a gap rather than a false statement.

CONSEQUENCES. Corollary 1.5 is not used later in the paper. Corollary 1.6 assumes minimality outright, and Theorem 1.4 is unaffected. Only the corollary, as a stated result, is not established in the generality stated.

issues.printed: The source says (1) behaves well for quotients that are non-reduced, taken from power series rings over O. Its example is S_N, defined by S_N := O[(Z/p^N Z)^q]; §6 repeats this description.
issues.correction: Change "non-reduced" to "non-regular" (or "singular", or "not necessarily regular"). For example: "(1) is well behaved for non-regular quotients of power series rings over O (like S_N)". S_N = O[(Z/p^N Z)^q] ≅ O⟦y_1,…,y_q⟧/((1+y_i)^{p^N} − 1) is reduced. It is a 1-dimensional complete intersection that is neither regular nor a domain. Its reductions k[Δ_N] and S_∞/b_N = (O/ϖ^N)[Δ_N] are the rings that are non-reduced. This is a one-word change, and it matches what "balanced" (Definitions 2.1 and 2.2) is built to handle: over a non-regular ring, projective dimension can be infinite, so Auslander–Buchsbaum cannot be used there.
issues.reason:
I checked all six passages on page images (PDF pages 10, 13, 17, 18, 27 and 34; pp. 313–314 at 250 dpi), and every quote matches. All six are also in arXiv v2, so none is a typesetting artifact, and none is one of the 47 bracket errors.

p. 313: Q is a squarefree integer, while C_Q ⊂ E[Q] was defined just before. The moduli condition clearly needs C_Q + α_N(μ_N). Clear misprint.

p. 314: X is the level-N curve, and "Y_Δ(Q; x)" appears on both sides of the slip. Clear misprint.

p. 323: both indices of the displayed spectral sequence are ≥ 0, so it is first-quadrant. The authors' own next sentence calls the dual "third quadrant", which fits only a first-quadrant original. Slip.

p. 306: I redid the check. O[G] ⊂ K[G] ≅ ∏ fields for G finite abelian in characteristic 0, so S_N is reduced. The informal phrase "non-reduced ... (like S_N)" is wrong. The intended property (not regular, not a domain) is clear, and nothing uses the phrase.

p. 330: Theorem 3.14 claims only conditions (2) and (4) of Def. 3.1. These concern x ∉ Q ∪ S(ρ̄) and x ∈ S(ρ̄) − T(ρ̄), where the claim is true: det is unramified at x ∤ NQp, and H is the p-part of (Z/N(ρ̄))^× (§3.3). For x | Q with x ≡ 1 mod p, which is the Taylor–Wiles case, the literal claim fails. So the correct range is x ∤ Qp, as the candidate says. One small point on the candidate's reason: in §3.2–3.3, Q is only squarefree and prime to Np. The failure happens exactly when some x | Q has x ≡ 1 mod p, and the sets Q_N (≡ 1 mod p^N) are such a case. Determinant condition (1) is never claimed for ρ_{n,α}; Thm 3.11 fixes the determinant by a twist. So nothing later depends on this.

p. 309, which I refute: b_N = (ϖ^N) + a_N and a_N ⊂ a. The paper already writes quotients like "H_M/b_N" for H_M/b_N H_M. H is an S_∞/a = O-module through ψ_M, so H/b_N H = H/ϖ^N H, exactly the target in the definition of a patching datum on p. 308. This is harmless shorthand, not an error.

Overall: a genuine but cosmetic bundle. It affects nothing. WHY THE PAPER IS WRONG. O is the ring of integers of a finite extension of Q_p (p. 305), so it has characteristic 0. Take Δ_N = (Z/p^N)^q. Then S_N = O[Δ_N] is free over O, so S_N ⊂ S_N ⊗_O K = K[Δ_N]. By Maschke's theorem in characteristic 0, K[Δ_N] is commutative semisimple, i.e. a finite product of fields. A subring of a reduced ring is reduced, so S_N is reduced. Smallest case, q = N = 1: O[T]/(T^p − 1). Over K, T^p − 1 = (T − 1)Φ_p(T) is separable (its discriminant is ±p^p ≠ 0), so K[T]/(T^p − 1) ≅ K × K(ζ_p) and there are no nilpotents.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE. For q, N ≥ 1, S_N ≅ O⟦y⟧/((1+y_i)^{p^N} − 1). Each relation lies in m^2 of O⟦y⟧: the linear term is p^N·y_i with p ∈ m, the middle terms are divisible by p, and the top term is y_i^{p^N}. So embdim S_N = q + 1 > 1 = dim S_N, and S_N is not regular. It is also not a domain, because K[Δ_N] has more than one factor. Its special fibre k[y]/(y_i^{p^N}) is non-reduced. So "non-reduced ... (like S_N)" misnames the property. The candidate's reasoning and its correction are both right.

DEFENCES I TRIED, ALL FAILED. (a) "Non-reduced" might mean "not necessarily reduced". This strains the words, and even then S_N would not be an example of the feature being singled out. (b) S_N might be redefined somewhere as a torsion ring. It is not: every occurrence (Prop. 2.3(2), proof of Thm 3.14, §5, Thm 6.3, Prop. 6.6, §9) has S_N = O[Δ_N]. (c) Balancedness might be applied over non-reduced rings. The notion is used over S_N itself: Prop. 2.3(5c) says "H_N is finite and balanced over S_N", and later arguments say "d_{S_N}(H_N) ≥ 0". The non-reduced rings S_∞/b_N enter only through base change of the resulting presentation. No reading makes S_N non-reduced.

KIND. This is a false mathematical assertion (that S_N is non-reduced), not a typographical slip. It is repeated verbatim in §2 and §6, but that looks like a copy: the v1 wording "to find a find a" survives in the published §6. The intended word ("non-regular" or "singular") is fairly clear from context. So "misprint" is arguable, and that is how the p. 306 item in the H-part1a-15 bundle is classed. I class it as an error of the harmless kind.

CONSEQUENCES. This is motivational text in an introduction, and nothing refers back to it. Definitions 2.1 and 2.2 are stated for an arbitrary Noetherian local ring S, and no proof uses reducedness or non-reducedness of S_N. That covers Prop. 2.3, Theorems 3.14 and 5.x, Theorem 6.3, Prop. 6.6 and §9. Affects nothing.

RELATION TO H-part1a-15. That candidate bundles six slips. Its p. 306 item is exactly this finding, and its prior verdict already confirmed it with the same correction. Its other items (pp. 309, 313, 314, 323, 330) are separate and were not re-examined here.

SIDE NOTE. The §6 copy on p. 384 also has the duplicated words "to find a find a suitable notion" (also in v2 p. 65 and v1 p. 6). This is a trivial typo and separate from this candidate.

issues.locator: §3.2.3, p. 315 (definition of W_x on H^0(X_Δ(Q;x), ω_A^n)) (published version)
issues.printed: The source defines W_x on H^0(X_Δ(Q; x), ω^n_A) via w_x^* and φ_12^{⊗n}, ending in H^i(X_Δ(Q; x), ω^n_A). It gives W_x f(E, α_{NQ}, C_x) = φ^* f(E/C_x, α'_{NQ}, E[x]/C_x), and uses x : E/E[x] ⥲ E and w_x^2(E, α_{NQ}, C_x) = ⟨x⟩(E, α_{NQ}, C_x) to conclude W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩.
issues.correction: On weight-n sections the identity should read W_x² = x^n⟨x⟩, which is the printed x⟨x⟩ only when n = 1. Stating the identity only for n = 1 would be an equally minimal fix, since every use is in weight one. (The H^i target and '(Q, x)' in the display are E22.)
issues.reason:
I checked the page image at 250 dpi. It shows exactly H^i as the target and "W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩". The arXiv v2 text (cg-v2.txt, lines 675-692) reads the same, and the 2022 Correction covers only the ⟦ ⟧ brackets, so this is not a known error. The paper defines W_x on H^0 in both the sentence before the display and the source of the display. Both maps in the composite (w_x^* and φ_12^{⊗n}) send H^0 to H^0, so the "H^i" target is a slip.

I redid the W_x^2 computation from the paper's own definition, W_x = φ_12^{⊗n} ∘ w_x^*. For a Katz-style section f with f(E, α, C) ∈ ω_E^{⊗n}:
- W_x^2 f(E, α, C) = φ^* ψ^* f(E/E[x], α'', C''), where φ: E → E/C and ψ: E/C → E/E[x], so ψφ is the quotient q: E → E/E[x].
- Let ι: E/E[x] ⥲ E be the identification with ι∘q = [x]. Transported by ι, (E/E[x], α'', C'') becomes (E, x∘α, C). By isomorphism invariance, f(E/E[x], α'', C'') = ι^* f(E, xα, C).
- Hence W_x^2 f(E, α, C) = [x]^* f(E, xα, C).
- [x]^* multiplies invariant differentials by x, so it multiplies sections of ω^{⊗n} by x^n.
- The paper's ⟨a⟩ is pullback along ⟨a⟩ using the canonical identification ⟨a⟩^*ω ≅ ω, so (⟨x⟩f)(E, α, C) = f(E, xα, C).
- Therefore W_x^2 = x^n⟨x⟩. The same thing in sheaf terms: φ_12 ∘ w_x^*(φ_12) is pullback along E → E/E[x], and after (w_x^2)^* = ⟨x⟩^* this is [x]^* = x^n on ω^{⊗n}.

This is consistent with the classical picture: the unnormalized Atkin–Lehner operator in weight k squares to x^k⟨x⟩. The same scalar appears in the paper's own weight-one computation U_x∘V_x = π_1^*⟨x⟩ (p. 319), which uses "x⟨x⟩ f(E, α_N)".

The printed claim is stated in a setting of general weight n: §3.2.3 defines the Hecke action for L = ω^{⊗n} or ω^{⊗n}(−∞), and W_x on ω^n_A. So as a general statement it is false for n ≠ 1. It is correct in weight one, which is what the authors intend.

Every use is in weight one:
- Lemma 3.5, pp. 317–320, on H^0(X, ω_{K/O}): the lower-right matrix entry on p. 318, and "Since W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩, we deduce that xU_x^2 f = ⟨x⟩f" on p. 320.
- Lemma 3.6, pp. 320–321, whose proof reuses Lemma 3.5.
- Theorem 3.30, proof step (1), in §3.9.2 on p. 350: there W_x on ω⊗L_σ is induced from the weight-one W_x on H^0(X_{V_0(x)}, ω_{K/O}).
I found no other occurrence of W_x or of the Fricke map (a grep for W_x, Fricke and Atkin found nothing else). So no proof or stated result is affected, and the proposed correction is right.

I chose "misprint" (a missing exponent n and a wrong index H^i for H^0; the meaning intended is clear in weight one). The W_x^2 part could also be classed as an "error", since it is false as stated for weight n ≠ 1. Defence first. I looked for a reading under which the paper is right.
(a) Could n be fixed to 1 here? No. §3.2.3 (pp. 313–314) says it defines the Hecke action on H^i(X_Δ(Q), L_A) for L = ω^{⊗n} or ω^{⊗n}(−∞), and W_x is defined on H^0(X_Δ(Q;x), ω^n_A). Remark 3.4 on p. 316 then works in general weight n (T_x f = (1+χ(x)x^{n−1})f).
(b) Could the normalisations absorb the factor? No. The φ_12^{⊗n} normalisation is the unnormalised pullback. I checked it on the Tate curve: Σ_C φ_C^* f(E/C) has q^m-coefficient x·(a_{mx} + x^{n−1}a_{m/x}). So xT_x as defined gives the classical T_x in every weight, and the diamond identification ⟨a⟩^*ω ≅ ω is the identity on E. Nothing rescales W_x.
(c) Could "x" mean the operator [x]^* induced by the identification x: E/E[x] ≅ E? That operator equals x^n on ω^{⊗n}, so under this reading the formula would be right. But the paper uses x as a scalar: the matrix entry ⟨x⟩(x+1) on p. 318, and "x^2U_x^2 f = W_x^2 f … we deduce that xU_x^2 f = ⟨x⟩f" on p. 320. So this reading is not faithful for n ≠ 1.

Computation from the paper's own definition. Write W_x f(E,α,C) = φ^* f(E/C, α', E[x]/C). Then W_x^2 f(E,α,C) = φ^*φ'^* f(E/E[x], α'', C''), where φ'φ = q: E → E/E[x]. Take the isomorphism ι: E/E[x] ≅ E with ι∘q = [x]. It carries α'' to x∘α. It carries C'' = (E/C)[x]/(E[x]/C) = {y : xy ∈ C}/E[x] to C. So, by isomorphism invariance, W_x^2 f(E,α,C) = [x]^* f(E, xα, C) = x^n f(E, xα, C) = x^n (⟨x⟩f)(E,α,C). This is consistent with the classical picture: the unnormalised Fricke operator in weight k squares to x^k times a diamond operator. The paper's own weight-one count on p. 319 ("can be identified with x f(E, x∘α_N) = x⟨x⟩f(E, α_N)") shows the same factor [x]^* = x. The H^i target contradicts the sentence just before it and the fact that both maps preserve H^0, so it is a plain slip.

Consequences. W_x appears only on pp. 314–315, 318, 320 and 350 (I grepped for W_x, Fricke and w_x).
- Lemma 3.5 (pp. 317–320) uses W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩ on H^0(X_0(x), ω_{K/O}), which is weight 1: in the lower-right matrix entry on p. 318, and in the step xU_x^2 f = ⟨x⟩f on p. 320.
- Lemma 3.6 (p. 321) reuses that proof.
- Theorem 3.30, step (1) on p. 350, gets W_x on (ω⊗L_σ)_{K/O} from the weight-one W_x on H^0(X_{V_0(x)}, ω_{K/O}).
- p. 344 defines only T_x on ω^n⊗L_σ, not W_x.
- p. 376 ("proceed as in the proof of Lemma 3.5", for homology of Y_0(x)) does not invoke this formula.
So every use is in weight 1, where the printed identity is correct, and no proof or stated result is affected. Both readers' correction (x^n⟨x⟩) is right and minimal.

Kind. I chose "error" because the displayed identity is false as stated for n ≠ 1 (for example over A = O or K/O). The H^i part is a plain misprint. "Misprint" is also defensible for the whole item, since the intended weight-one meaning is clear from how it is used.

issues.locator: §3.2.3, Remark 3.4, p. 316 (published version)
issues.printed: Remark 3.4 asserts transitivity of (Z/NQZ)^× on C_Δ(Q)'s cusps. A nonzero mod p eigenform f of character χ therefore vanishes at none, with T_x(f) = (1 + χ(x)x^{n−1})f for x prime to pNQ, characteristic polynomial X^2 − T_xX + ⟨x⟩x^{n−1}, and representation 1 ⊕ χε^{n−1}. §3.9.2 similarly asserts cusp transitivity for ∏_{x∈T(ρ̄)} GL_2(Z_x) × ∏_{x∈P(ρ̄)} Z_x^× on X_{V_Δ(Q)}, concluding the invariant cusp cohomology is Eisenstein.
issues.correction: The group (Z/NQZ)^× does not act transitively on the cusps. It preserves each fibre of C_Δ(Q) over the cusps of X_0(NQ), and it is transitive only within the fibre over ∞. The T_x (x ∤ pNQ) preserve these fibres. On the fibre over ∞ (the diamond orbit of ∞), a χ-eigenvector satisfies T_x f = (1+χ(x)x^{n−1})f, as printed. On a general fibre, the simultaneous eigenvalues have the form ψ1(x)+ψ2(x)x^{n−1} for characters with ψ1ψ2 = χ. For example, the fibre over the cusp 0 gives χ(x)+x^{n−1}. The associated semisimple representation is ψ1 ⊕ ψ2ε^{n−1}, not always 1 ⊕ χε^{n−1}. A non-zero eigenform can vanish at every cusp outside one fibre. The true statement, which is all that is used, is that every Hecke eigensystem on H^0(C_Δ(Q), ω_k^{⊗n}) is Eisenstein (reducible), so H^0(C_Δ(Q), ω)_m = 0 for non-Eisenstein m. In §3.9.2(2), drop the transitivity parenthetical. H^0(C_{V_Δ(Q)}, ω) is Eisenstein by the same fibre-by-fibre argument, and T_x commutes with G and acts trivially on W_σ, so (H^0(C_{V_Δ(Q)}, ω) ⊗ W_σ)^G is Eisenstein. Candidate X-K2-0's correction is right and essentially minimal. Its "orbit of ∞" equals the fibre over ∞, because in the μ_N-convention the ∞-type cusps (Tate(q), canonical∘[a]) form a single diamond orbit.
issues.reason:
I transcribed both passages from 200-dpi page images. 1. The transitivity claim is false. X_Δ(Q) → X_0(NQ) is the quotient by the diamond operators and by Galois-stable data, so every diamond operator preserves each fibre over a cusp of X_0(NQ). NQ ≥ N ≥ 5, so X_0(NQ) has the two distinct Q-rational cusps 0 and ∞, and in every reading of "set of cusps" there are at least two orbits. Concretely, with Q = ∅, H = 1 and N = 7, X_1(7) has 6 cusps but (Z/7)^×/±1 has only 3 elements. 2. I redid the Tate-curve calculation with the paper's normalisation x T_x f(E,α) = Σ_C φ_C^* f(E/C, α'). At (Tate(q), α with α(μ_M) canonical), the μ_x-quotient is Tate(q^x) with α' = ⟨x⟩α, and φ^*(dt/t) = x·dt/t, so it contributes x^n χ(x) f(q^x). The other x quotients are Tate(ζ^i q^{1/x}) with α' = α. So the constant term is multiplied by 1+χ(x)x^{n−1}, as printed. At (Tate(q^M), ζ_M ↦ q), a cusp over 0, the μ_x-quotient gives the same cusp with parameter q^x and contributes x^n. Each other quotient is Tate(u) with u = ζ_x^i q^{M/x}, and choosing w with w^M = u gives q = ζ'w^x (ζ' ∈ μ_M). So α' = ⟨x⟩ of the same cusp, after rotating the parameter by an M-th root of unity, and these contribute xχ(x). The eigenvalue there is χ(x)+x^{n−1}. This agrees with the classical fact that E_n^{χ,1} has T_x-eigenvalue χ(x)+x^{n−1} and constant term δ(χ)L(1−n,1) = 0 at ∞, while it is non-zero at other cusps. 3. Explicit mod p counterexample within the Remark's generality: N = 7, H = 1, Q = ∅, n = 3, χ = (·/7) (odd, as needed since ⟨−1⟩ acts by (−1)^n), p = 5, x = 3. The fibre over 0 carries a mod 5 χ-eigenvector, which is also a reduction of the char-0 system, since C is finite étale over O. It vanishes at the cusps over ∞, and T_3 acts on it by χ(3)+9 = 8 ≡ 3 mod 5. The Remark predicts 1+χ(3)·9 = −8 ≡ 2 mod 5. 4. Weight 1, relevant to the application: take NQ with two prime factors and ψ1, ψ2 of prime-to-p order, ψ1ψ2 odd. Then E_1^{ψ1,ψ2} gives the eigenvalue ψ1(x)+ψ2(x). This differs from 1+χ(x) by (1−ψ1(x))(1−ψ2(x)), which is non-zero mod p for example when N = 35, p = 13, x = 3. (For N prime in weight 1, the printed formula happens to hold, because χ(x)+1 = 1+χ(x).) 5. Dependence: grep finds only two uses of Remark 3.4, the proof of Lemma 3.7(2) (p. 324, "the action of Hecke on H^0(C_Δ(Q), ω) is Eisenstein (by Remark 3.4)") and §3.9.2(2). Both need only the Eisenstein property, which holds by the corrected fibre-by-fibre statement, so Lemma 3.7(2), its vexing-prime analogue and the results built on them stand. I rate 'affects' as 'the proof' rather than the candidate's 'nothing'. Remark 3.4 itself asserts a false explicit formula and a false non-vanishing claim. The proof of §3.9.2(2) explicitly rests on the false transitivity argument. Repairing it is routine, and no numbered result changes. Minor side note: item (2) on p. 351 cites "(Proposition 3.7 (2))" for what is Lemma 3.7(2). Defence attempts, all failed:
(i) C_Δ(Q) is the whole cusp divisor. The text defines it as "the divisor of cusps", and it fits the sequence with ω(−∞), where ∞ is "the reduced divisor supported on the cusps". It is not only the cusps over ∞.
(ii) Reading "set of cusps" as closed points of the O-scheme, or allowing Galois as well as diamond operators, does not help. X_Δ(Q) is a quotient of X_1(NQ) by diamond operators, so it maps equivariantly to X_0(NQ), where (Z/NQZ)^× acts trivially. The cusps 0 and ∞ of X_0(NQ) are distinct Q-rational points that stay distinct over O (p ∤ NQ). So there are always at least two orbits.
(iii) Only the paper's own normalisation can decide the eigenvalue formula. I redid the Tate-curve computation in its conventions: μ_N-embeddings (§3.2.1), x·T_x = tr(π1)∘φ12∘π2^*, and ⟨a⟩ = pullback by (E,α) ↦ (E, a∘α).
- At (Tate(q), canonical α): the μ_x-quotient is Tate(q^x) with α' = ⟨x⟩α and φ^*(dt/t) = x·dt/t, giving x^n χ(x). The other x quotients, Tate(ζ^i q^{1/x}), keep α' = α, giving x. So the eigenvalue is 1+χ(x)x^{n−1}, which matches the paper at ∞.
- At a cusp over 0, (Tate(Q^N), ζ_N ↦ Q): the μ_x-quotient is the same cusp with parameter Q^x, giving x^n. Each other quotient is Tate(c) with c^x = Q^N. Writing c = w^N gives Q = ζ'w^x. Choosing ζ''^x = ζ' and setting w' = ζ''w gives (Tate(w'^N), ζ_N ↦ w'^x) = ⟨x⟩(Tate(w'^N), ζ_N ↦ w'), giving x·χ(x). So the eigenvalue is χ(x)+x^{n−1}.
- In general, the two values differ by (1−χ(x))(1−x^{n−1}).
Counterexample: N = 7, H = 1 (fine moduli), Q = ∅, n = 3, χ = (·/7). χ is odd, as required since ⟨−1⟩ acts by (−1)^n. Take p = 5 and x = 3. C is finite étale over O. The χ-part of H^0(C, ω_k^{⊗3}) is 2-dimensional, one line on each fibre, and T_3 acts on the two lines by 1+χ(3)·9 = −8 ≡ 2 and χ(3)+9 = 8 ≡ 3 (mod 5). These are distinct. So the eigenform supported on the fibre over 0 vanishes at the ∞-cusps and has T_3 f = 3f, while the Remark predicts 2f. Classically this is E_3^{χ,1}: constant term 0 at ∞ and eigenvalue χ(ℓ)+ℓ^2.
Weight 1, the case actually used: for N prime and Q = ∅ the printed eigenvalue happens to be right, since χ(x)+1 = 1+χ(x), but "cannot vanish at any cusp" is still false. With NQ composite, as with Taylor–Wiles primes Q ≠ ∅, mixed cusps give ψ1(x)+ψ2(x). This differs from 1+χ(x) by (1−ψ1(x))(1−ψ2(x)).
The §3.9.2(2) parenthetical is also always false. The group ∏_T GL_2(Z_x) × ∏_P Z_x^× acts trivially on the U_0-type levels at the primes of Q, of S−(T∪P) and of P (and at the auxiliary prime of footnote 4). Each of these gives at least two cusp classes.
Consequences: grep finds only two uses of Remark 3.4, the proof of Lemma 3.7(2) (p. 322) and §3.9.2(2) (p. 351), and nothing else uses 1 ⊕ χε^{n−1}. Both uses need only the Eisenstein property, which holds on each fibre: T_x = B_x + x^{n−1}A_x, with A_x and B_x in a commutative group algebra and ⟨x⟩ = A_xB_x. Its characters kill p-parts, so every eigensystem is ψ1 + ψ2ε^{n−1}, which cannot match an absolutely irreducible ρ̄ by Chebotarev and Brauer–Nesbitt. So no numbered result changes, but both proofs go through a false assertion and need this routine repair. That is why I set affects to "the proof", not "nothing". Remark 3.4's own explicit claims (transitivity, non-vanishing, the formula and the Galois representation) are false as stated.

issues.reason:
I checked the page images at 200 dpi, and the transcription above is exact. The arXiv v2 text has the same wording at lines 831 and 851.

I redid the computation with the paper's own definitions (§3.2.3, p. 317):
- x T_x = tr(π1)∘φ12∘π2^* and x U_x is defined the same way, so U_x f(E,α,C_x) = (1/x) Σ_{D≠C_x} φ_D^* f(E/D, φ_D α, (C_x+D)/D).
- V_x = φ12∘π2^*, so V_x g(E,α,C) = φ_C^* g(E/C, φ_C α).

This gives (U_x V_x f)(E,α,C_x) = (1/x) Σ_{D≠C_x} φ^*_{D+C_x} f(E/E[x], ·). Identify E/E[x] with E via [x]. In weight 1, [x]^* acts on ω by x, so each term is x f(E, xα) = x⟨x⟩f(E,α). The paper says this too. There are x terms and a factor 1/x, so the total is x⟨x⟩f, not ⟨x⟩f.

Independent check with the Tate curve at the cusp (Tate(q), α_can, μ_x):
- The C = μ_x term of T_x gives V_x F = x⟨x⟩F(q^x). The other x subgroups give U_x F = Σ a_{nx} q^n. Together they recover the classical weight-1 T_x = U + ⟨x⟩V, which confirms the first printed relation.
- Then U_x V_x F = x⟨x⟩F.
- This also matches the paper's own W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩ (p. 317), since V_x = W_x∘π1^*.

With ψ(f,g) = π1^*f + V_x g, the corrected relation gives U_x ψ(f,g) = ψ(T_x f + x⟨x⟩g, −f/x). That is exactly the printed matrix A. Its characteristic polynomial is det(X−A) = X^2 − T_x X + ⟨x⟩, as the proof's (A−α_x)(A−β_x) ≡ 0 needs. The printed relation would instead give the (1,2) entry ⟨x⟩ and the polynomial X^2 − T_x X + ⟨x⟩/x. So the printed matrix agrees with the corrected relation, not with the printed one.

A(f,0)^T = (T_x f, −f/x)^T, so the printed −f does not match the printed matrix either. Since x is a prime different from p, x is a unit in O. So −f/x is non-zero exactly when f is, and the argument goes through unchanged.

This has nothing to do with the 47 known bracket errors. I tried to defend the printed relation and could not.

(1) The paper's own conventions (§3.2.3, pp. 316–317) give a factor x:
- x T_x = tr(π1)∘φ12∘π2^*, and x U_x is defined the same way. So U_x g(E,α,C) = (1/x) Σ_{D≠C} φ_D^* g(E/D, φ_Dα, (C+D)/D).
- V_x = φ12∘π2^*.
- The paper itself says each of the x terms equals x⟨x⟩f, and then divides by 1/x. That gives x⟨x⟩f, not ⟨x⟩f. The step "[x]^* acts on ω by x" is the paper's own; weight 1 has no other normalization that would absorb the factor.

(2) A second check, using only identities the paper itself proves:
- The claim on p. 320, (1/x)π1^*∘tr(π1)∘W_x = U_x + (1/x)W_x, is a true operator identity. Directly, Σ_D φ_D^* g(E/D, φ_Dα, E[x]/D) = xU_x g + W_x g, since C+D = E[x].
- The paper has V_x = W_x∘π1^* (p. 320), W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩ (p. 317) and tr(π1)∘π1^* = x+1.
- So U_xV_x = (1/x)π1^* tr(π1) W_x^2 π1^* − (1/x)W_x^2 π1^* = ⟨x⟩(x+1)π1^* − ⟨x⟩π1^* = x⟨x⟩π1^*.

(3) Tate-curve check at the cusp (Tate(q), α_can, μ_x): V_xF = x⟨x⟩F(q^x) and U_x(Σ b_n q^n) = Σ b_{nx}q^n, so U_xV_xF = x⟨x⟩F.

(4) The only partial defence: in Lemma 3.5, x ≡ 1 mod p, so x ≡ 1 mod m_∅ and the missing factor makes no difference mod m_∅. But the display claims an exact equality of maps over O, which is false.

Consequences:
- The very next display, A = (T_x, x⟨x⟩; −1/x, 0), is exactly what the corrected relation gives. With ψ(f,g) = π1^*f + V_xg, we get U_xψ(f,g) = ψ(T_xf + x⟨x⟩g, −f/x).
- A has characteristic polynomial X^2 − T_xX + ⟨x⟩. The printed relation would give X^2 − T_xX + x^{-1}⟨x⟩ instead.
- So A, the Hensel step, and the V[m]=0 part are all consistent with the corrected relation. The V[m]=0 part uses only the first relation and W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩.
- Lemma 3.6's proof (p. 321) needs exactly X^2 − T_xX + ⟨x⟩ when x ≢ 1 mod p: "T acts via T_{∅,m∅}[X]/(X^2 − T_xX + ⟨x⟩)". It gets this from A, not from the misprinted relation.
- Later arguments that say "as in Lemma 3.5" do not rely on the misprinted relation: p. 331 (§3.5, U_p; states the quadratic relation directly), p. 350 (Thm 3.30(1); cites W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩ and the p. 320 claim), p. 376 (H^1 analogue).
- The vector entry −f contradicts the printed A, whose (2,1) entry is −1/x. It should be −f/x. Since x ≠ p, x is a unit in O, so "non-zero whenever f is" still holds.

I classify both as misprints rather than errors: the intended values are fixed by the paper's own computation and by the next display. Nothing downstream is affected, and both stated results (Lemmas 3.5 and 3.6) stand.

issues.correction: Replace "by length considerations" with "comparing lengths of ϖ^m-torsion submodules for every m". Write M = H^0(X,ω_{K/O})_{m∅}, A = (Im ψ)_m = ker(U_x − α̃_x) and B = ker(U_x − β̃_x), so that A ⊕ B = (Im ψ)_{m∅} ≅ M². Since X is flat over O, M[ϖ] = H^0(X,ω_k)_{m∅} is finite, so each M[ϖ^m] has finite length. The injections restrict to M[ϖ^m] ↪ A[ϖ^m] and M[ϖ^m] ↪ B[ϖ^m], and A[ϖ^m] ⊕ B[ϖ^m] ≅ M[ϖ^m]². So ℓ(A[ϖ^m]) + ℓ(B[ϖ^m]) = 2ℓ(M[ϖ^m]) with each term at least ℓ(M[ϖ^m]), which forces both restricted maps to be isomorphisms. A and B are ϖ-power torsion, so taking the union over m gives the result. An equivalent route works on Pontryagin duals: compare O-ranks first, then the lengths of the torsion submodules. The candidate's proposed correction is right; the ϖ^m-torsion version is the minimal one.
issues.reason:
I checked the page image. The printed sentence justifies the isomorphism by length. But M = H^0(X,ω_{K/O})_{m∅} ≅ (H^0(X,ω)⊗K/O)_{m∅} ⊕ (finite torsion) is a cofinitely generated O-module. It has infinite length whenever there are characteristic-zero weight-one forms at m∅, and those are exactly the cases the paper cares about (for example, dihedral forms). In those cases "ℓ(A)+ℓ(B)=2ℓ(M), ℓ(A),ℓ(B) ≥ ℓ(M)" is ∞ = ∞ and proves nothing. The argument works literally only when H^0(X,ω_K)_{m∅} = 0.

Defence I tried: the paper has no convention that makes "length" meaningful here. It introduces Pontryagin duality only afterwards, before Lemma 3.7, and grepping the paper finds no corank or length convention. So the justification as printed does not apply.

The conclusion is still true, and the fix takes one line (details in the correction field). The rest of the setup holds: ψ is injective on the m∅-part because ψ^∨∘ψ is an isomorphism, α̃_x − β̃_x is a unit, and (U_x − β̃_x)∘π_1^* lands in (Im ψ)_m. Since the statement of Lemma 3.5 is correct, Lemma 3.6, Theorem 3.30(1), Lemma 5.8 and the patching arguments that use it are unaffected. §3.5 (p. ~333) reuses the argument with finite coefficients O/ϖ^m, where lengths are finite, so the printed wording is valid there. This is a minor, routine imprecision rather than a real hole. It counts as a gap under PROTOCOL §18 because the stated reason does not apply as written.

issues.printed: Lemma 3.5's proof claims (1/x)(π1^* ∘ tr(π1) ∘ W_x) = U_x + (1/x)W_x. Using π2 = π1 ∘ w_x, T_x = (1/x) tr(π1) ∘ W_x ∘ π1^* and V_x = W_x ∘ π1^*, it rewrites the earlier identity with π1^* on both sides and concludes by calling π1^* fully faithful. Theorem 3.30 reuses W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩ and (1/x)π1^* ∘ tr(π1) ∘ W_x = U_x + (1/x)W_x.
issues.reason:
I transcribed both passages from the page images (PDF pp. 24 and 54). The deduction as printed is invalid. The displayed relation is an identity of maps H^0(X,ω) → H^0(X_0(x),ω) of the form A∘π1^* = B∘π1^*. Cancelling π1^* on the right to get A = B would need π1^* to be surjective (an epimorphism). "Fully faithful" is meaningless for a linear map, and injectivity does not help. π1^* is not surjective: the proof itself shows that H^0(X,ω)^2_{m∅} (the image of ψ = (π1^*, φ12∘π2^*)) is a direct factor of H^0(X_0(x),ω)_{m∅}. Even read as the pullback functor on sheaves, π1^* is not fully faithful for a finite flat map of degree x+1. The claim is needed exactly off the image of π1^*. It is applied to f ∈ V[m], where V = ker ψ^∨ is a complement to Im ψ, and property (3), tr(π1)W_x f = 0, is turned into −xU_x f = W_x f. So the printed argument leaves a gap. I redid the moduli computation using the paper's own conventions: W_x on p. 315, U_x on X_0(x) from §3.2.3 and p. 319 (where the sum over D ≠ C_x is identified with U_x∘π1^*), and T_x = (1/x)tr(π1)∘W_x∘π1^*. It gives π1^* tr(π1) W_x = xU_x + W_x on all of H^0(X_0(x),ω), so the claim is true and the candidate's correction is right. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors, and the 2022 Correction does not address it. On 'affects': Lemma 3.5 and Theorem 3.30 remain true, and every later use of the identity (Thm 3.30(1) via G-invariants of the level-V operator) goes through once the claim is proved directly. No stated result is affected. But the printed proof of Lemma 3.5 (and of the corresponding step of Theorem 3.30(1)) does not establish its intermediate claim. Under PROTOCOL §18, where 'nothing' means the mathematics is right as intended, I classify this as 'the proof' rather than 'nothing'. 'nothing' is defensible only if one counts the one-line computation as what the authors intended. I checked the page images for p. 318, p. 319, p. 320 and p. 350, and for arXiv v2 p. 18.

Why the defence fails:
- The displayed relation is an identity of maps H^0(X,ω) → H^0(X_0(x),ω) of the form A∘π1^* = B∘π1^*, with A, B endomorphisms of H^0(X_0(x),ω).
- Cancelling π1^* on the right needs π1^* to be surjective. "Fully faithful" does not apply to a linear map. Reading π1^* as the pullback functor on sheaves does not help either: the operators are composed with π1^*, not obtained by applying π1^* to morphisms, and pullback along a finite flat map of degree x+1 is not full anyway.
- π1^* is not surjective. The proof itself makes Im ψ ⊇ Im π1^* a proper direct factor with complement V = ker ψ^∨.
- The claim is needed exactly off Im π1^*. It is applied to f ∈ V[m] to turn property (3), tr(π1)W_x f = 0, into −xU_x f = W_x f. Adding the V_x relation only gives the identity on Im ψ, and x-new forms are not generated by old ones.
- No charitable reading or nearby statement supplies the step. The printed inference is invalid.

The claim itself is true. By the moduli computation above, π1^* tr(π1) W_x = xU_x + W_x holds on the whole space. Consistency checks:
1. On π1^*f it reduces to the paper's xπ1^*T_x = xU_xπ1^* + V_x.
2. On V_x f both sides give x(x+1)⟨x⟩π1^*f. This uses W_x^2 = x⟨x⟩ and U_x∘V_x = x·π1^*⟨x⟩. That value of U_x∘V_x is the one in the matrix A on p. 319 (upper-right entry x⟨x⟩), not the printed "U_x∘V_x = π1^*⟨x⟩", which is the separate candidates H-part1a-1 / X-K2-2.
3. On x-newforms it says W_x = −xU_x. This agrees with the classical a_x = −λ_x x^{k/2−1}, since here W_x = x^{k/2}·w_classical.

The downstream steps are then fine: x²U_x²f = W_x²f = x⟨x⟩f gives xα_x² = α_xβ_x, so α_x ≡ β_x mod m, a contradiction. Theorem 3.30(1) takes the identity on X_{V_0(x)} to X_{U_0(x)} via G-invariants, and the same direct computation works at that level. This is not one of the 47 bracket defects, and the 2022 Correction does not address it.

Affects: Lemma 3.5 and Theorem 3.30 remain true. The printed proof, though, does not establish its intermediate claim, and the repair is a new (short) computation, not a clear-context slip. So I set 'the proof', not 'nothing'.

issues.locator: §3.3, Remark 3.10, footnote 3, published pp. 325–326 (PDF pp. 29–30). The two sheaves printed as ω^2 (in the "naïvely … vanish" sentence and in the displayed H^0(X_H(13)_{F_3}, ω^2) = H^0(X_1(13)_{F_3}, ω^2)^{Z/3Z}) should be ω^2(−∞). arXiv v2 has the same text (cg-v2.txt ll. 1104–1113). arXiv v1 does not have this footnote or example; its only footnote at that point is a different one about representability when p = 3.
issues.printed: Footnote 3 takes H ⊂ (Z/13Z)^× to be the squares and asserts a finite étale stack map X_1(13) → X_H(13) of Galois group Z/3Z. For p ≠ 13, the underlying scheme is said to be the projective line over O, suggesting H^0(X_H(13), ω^2) vanishes. It cites an induced ρ̄ : G_Q → GL_2(F_3) from Q(√−3), with N(ρ̄) = 13, k(ρ̄) = 2, quadratic ε(ρ̄), and conjecture 3.2.4_? of [36]. At p = 3, it asserts H^0(X_H(13)_{F_3}, ω^2) = H^0(X_1(13)_{F_3}, ω^2)^{Z/3Z} is nonzero despite genus zero.
issues.correction: Replace ω^2 with ω^2(−∞) in all three places. The footnote should read: "one would expect H^0(X_H(13), ω^2(−∞)) to vanish" and "H^0(X_H(13)_{F_3}, ω^2(−∞)) = H^0(X_1(13)_{F_3}, ω^2(−∞))^{Z/3Z} is indeed non-zero". An equivalent fix is to localize at the maximal ideal m of ρ̄. The (−∞) version is the minimal correction because it matches the genus-zero heuristic, since Ω^1 ≅ ω^2(−∞).
issues.reason:
I checked the printed text on the rendered pages (PDF 29–30). I then redid the mathematics for Γ_H(13) with H = the squares {1,3,4,9,10,12}, which contains −1.
(1) Invariants. [PSL_2(Z):Γ_H(13)] = 28. The d with d^2 ≡ −1 are 5 and 8, and neither is a square, so there are no order-2 elliptic points. The d with d^2 − d + 1 ≡ 0 are 4 and 10, both squares, so there are 4 order-3 elliptic points. There are 4 cusps. The genus is 1 + 28/12 − 4/3 − 4/2 = 0, which agrees with the paper. So dim M_2(Γ_H(13)) = g + #cusps − 1 = 3 and dim S_2 = 0.
(2) Characteristic 0. In characteristic 0, H^0(X_H(13), ω^2) is 3-dimensional. It is M_2(Γ_0(13)) plus the two Eisenstein series with the quadratic character; S_2(13, χ_quad) = 0. The "naïve" expectation that it vanishes is therefore wrong, even for the coarse scheme. On the stack, deg ω^2 = 14/3. Its pushforward to the coarse P^1 has degree 14/3 − 4·(2/3) = 2, so it is O(2) with 3 sections. The pushforward of ω^2(−∞) has degree −2, so it is Ω^1_{P^1} and has no sections. Only the cuspidal version matches "P^1, hence vanishes" and "genus zero".
(3) Characteristic 3. Mod 3, the printed claim "H^0(X_H(13)_{F_3}, ω^2) is indeed non-zero" is true but trivial. It contains the reduction of (E_2(z) − 13E_2(13z))/(−12) = 1 + 2Σσ(n)q^n − 26Σσ(n)q^{13n}, which has constant term 1 mod 3. So the "However … even though genus zero" contrast shows nothing as printed.
(4) The corrected statement holds. Let f be the weight-2 newform on Γ_1(13) whose character ε has order 6. For d ∈ H, the operator ⟨d⟩ multiplies f by ε(d) ∈ μ_3, and μ_3 ≡ 1 mod (√−3). So f mod (√−3) is a non-zero Z/3Z-invariant element of H^0(X_1(13)_{F_3}, ω^2(−∞)). This is Serre's ρ̄.
Classification. The slip is the omitted "(−∞)". Nothing false is asserted as a mathematical fact: the final non-vanishing is true, and the false claim is labelled a naïve expectation. The intended meaning is clear from "genus zero", from Serre's cuspidal example, and from the paper's own Ω^1 ≅ ω^2(−∞). So I classify it as a misprint, not the "error" the reader proposed. It is a genuine mistake either way. It is a side remark in a footnote, so it affects nothing. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors fixed by the 2022 Correction. 1. The paper's own conventions rule out the charitable reading. The paper always separates ω^n from ω^n(−∞) (e.g. §3.2, and Lemma 3.7 with dim H^0(ω(−∞))_m against dim H^0(ω)_m). It identifies Ω^1 with ω^{⊗2}(−∞) by Kodaira–Spencer (p. 314 of the text). Remark 3.10 itself says H^0(X_R, ω^k) is the space of Katz modular forms, which includes non-cuspidal forms. So H^0(X_H(13), ω^2) means M_2(Γ_H(13)).

2. M_2(Γ_H(13)) is 3-dimensional in characteristic 0. The characters trivial on the squares are 1 and (·/13), and both are even. This gives three Eisenstein series: E_2(z) − 13E_2(13z), E_2^{1,χ} and E_2^{χ,1}. The count matches dim M_2 = g + c − 1 = 0 + 4 − 1 = 3. The stack degree gives the same answer: deg ω^2 = 14/3 on X_H(13), and its pushforward to P^1 has degree 14/3 − 4·(2/3) = 2, so h^0 = 3. Reducing an integral lattice injects into H^0 over F_3 (use 0 → L → L → L/3 → 0), so these forms are also non-zero mod 3.
   - So the printed "naive" expectation fails already over Q.
   - The printed "indeed non-zero" is true but trivially so, and has nothing to do with genus zero.
   - The word "naïvely" cannot rescue the text: the closing contrast ("even though the scheme underlying X_H(13) has genus zero") only has content for cusp forms.

3. With ω^2(−∞) both claims are right.
   - Genus is 0: g = 1 + 28/12 − ν_2/4 − ν_3/3 − 4/2 = 0. Here ν_2 = 0, because the roots ±5 of x^2 + 1 mod 13 are non-squares. ν_3 = 4, because the roots 3 and 9 of x^2 + x + 1 are squares. There are 4 cusps. Riemann–Hurwitz for X_1(13) (genus 2) → P^1 checks out: 2 = 3·(−2) + 4·2.
   - Hence S_2(Γ_H(13)) = 0 over C. Equivalently, the pushforward of ω^2(−∞) is O(−2).
   - Mod 3: take the newform in S_2(Γ_1(13)), whose character has order 6. Modulo (√−3) its character is congruent to (·/13), so it is fixed by H/±1 ≅ Z/3Z. It therefore gives a non-zero class in H^0(X_1(13)_{F_3}, ω^2(−∞))^{Z/3Z}. This is exactly Serre's ρ̄, and it is the stacky mod-3 phenomenon the footnote is describing.

4. Classification. The intended meaning (weight-2 cusp forms, the Ω^1 heuristic) is clear from context and the paper's conventions. The fix is a mechanical insertion of (−∞). So I classify it as a misprint rather than the candidate's "error". "Error" is still defensible, because the heuristic as literally printed is false.

5. Consequences. Footnote 3 is purely illustrative. Nothing later in the paper uses footnote 3 or X_H(13); the only other hits for "(13)" are inside the footnote itself. The main text avoids stacks altogether by adding Γ_1(q)-level. So affects = nothing.

issues.reason: The 'right hand side' is the number dim_K H_1(X_0(Q)_K, ω)_m (with L = O_X). The parallel sentence about the left hand side includes dim_K. Ψ: H^0(X_0(Q), ω) → H_1(X_0(Q), ω) is an isomorphism and is T-linear for n = 1 (p. 323), so it localises at m. Tensoring with K gives dim_K H_1(X_0(Q)_K, ω)_m = dim_K H^0(X_0(Q)_K, ω)_m, and that is the form used in the next display. As printed, a dimension is said to equal a vector space; the missing dim_K is a slip with a clear intended meaning.

issues.locator: §3.3, the continuation of Remark 3.10 (the "fix" paragraph choosing an auxiliary prime q), published p. 326 (PDF p. 30), lines 9–11 of the page. arXiv v2 has the same sentence (cg-v2.txt l. 1079–1080). arXiv v1 does not have this sentence: its footnote 1 in §3 only says the prime's existence is "guaranteed by the Chebotarev density theorem".
issues.printed: The source invokes Chebotarev to obtain the primes: unramified det(ρ̄) at p supposedly ensures the field fixed by ker(ρ̄) does not contain Q(ζ_p), since p ≠ 2. It concludes there are infinitely many q splitting completely in that field with q ≢ 1 mod p, satisfying the required condition.
issues.correction: Replace 'det(ρ̄)' with 'ρ̄': 'Since ρ̄ is unramified at p, the fixed field of ker(ρ̄) is unramified at p, so it does not contain Q(ζ_p), which is ramified at p because p ≠ 2.' The minimal fix is to delete 'det( )'. Both readers' proposed corrections are right.
issues.reason:
The next sentence needs Q(ζ_p) ⊄ L, where L is the fixed field of ker ρ̄. Only then is there a σ with ρ̄(σ) = 1 and χ_p(σ) ≠ 1, which is what gives primes q that split in L with q ≢ 1 mod p. The paper gets this from "det(ρ̄) unramified at p", and that implication is false in general.

Counterexample (checked by hand), p = 3:
- Setup: take K = Q(√−3) = Q(ζ_3) and 𝔮 | 7 (7 splits in K). Let ψ be the quadratic character of (O_K/(√−3)𝔮)^× = F_3^× × F_7^× given by (sign) × (Legendre symbol).
- ψ is trivial on O_K^× = μ_6:
  - ψ(−1) = (−1)·(−1/7) = (−1)(−1) = 1.
  - ζ_3 ≡ 1 mod √−3, and ζ_3 mod 𝔮 has order 3, so it is a square in F_7^×. Hence ψ(ζ_3) = 1.
  - Since h_K = 1, ψ is a ray class character of conductor (√−3)𝔮.
- ρ̄ is absolutely irreducible and odd. Set ρ̄ = Ind_K^Q ψ : G_Q → GL_2(F_3). It is absolutely irreducible because ψ^σ has conductor (√−3)𝔮̄, so ψ^σ ≠ ψ.
- det ρ̄ is unramified at 3. We have det ρ̄ = η_K · (ψ∘V). As a Dirichlet character, ψ∘V(ℓ) = ψ((ℓ)) = (ℓ/3)(ℓ/7), and η_K = (·/3). So det ρ̄ = (·/7), the character of Q(√−7). It is unramified at 3 and odd, since (−1/7) = −1.
- L contains Q(ζ_3). Every element of G_Q \ G_K acts antidiagonally, so it is never the identity. Hence ker ρ̄ ⊂ G_K, and L ⊇ K = Q(ζ_3).

So the stated reason does not give the conclusion. (For comparison, the footnote on the same page mentions Serre's mod-3 example, which is also induced from Q(√−3).)

The conclusion is still true in the paper's setting. Section 3.1 assumes ρ̄|G_p is unramified, so L is unramified at p and cannot contain Q(ζ_p), which is totally ramified of degree p − 1 > 1. The fix swaps det(ρ̄) for ρ̄, i.e. it uses a hypothesis already in force. The mistake is therefore an inadequate justification, not a false statement. Nothing downstream changes.

On the kind: I file this as a gap because the step is asserted with a reason that does not prove it. X-K3-10's "misprint" is also defensible, since the intended reason (ρ̄ unramified at p) is clear from §3.1. WHY THE PRINTED STEP FAILS: in general, knowing that det(ρ̄) is unramified at p does not stop Q(ζ_p) from lying inside L, the fixed field of ker ρ̄. Whether Q(ζ_p) ⊂ L depends on whether ω mod p factors through Gal(L/Q), which can have abelian quotients much larger than the one cut out by det. I checked the reader's counterexample and it holds. Take p = 3, K = Q(√−3), and 7 = 𝔮𝔮̄ (7 splits because −3 ≡ 2² mod 7). Let ψ be the order-2 character of conductor (√−3)𝔮 given by sign on F_3^× times the Legendre symbol on F_7^×.
- ψ is trivial on O_K^× = μ_6: ψ(−1) = (−1)(−1) = 1, and ψ(ζ_3) = 1, because ζ_3 ≡ 1 mod √−3 and an element of order 3 in F_7^× is a square.
- ψ ≠ ψ^c because their conductors differ. So ρ̄ = Ind_K^Q ψ : G_Q → GL_2(F_3) is odd and absolutely irreducible.
- det ρ̄ = η_K·ψ|_{A_Q^×}. On Z_3^× both factors are the character Z_3^× → F_3^× → ±1: for η_K because local norms from Q_3(√−3) are ≡ 1 mod 3. So det ρ̄ is unramified at 3.
- ker ρ̄ ⊂ G_K, so L ⊃ K = Q(ζ_3).
An even simpler example is ω ⊕ ω^{-1}. So 'since det(ρ̄) is unramified' does not justify the claim as written.

DEFENCE: The conclusion itself is true throughout §3. The standing hypothesis of §3.1 (p. 310) is 'Let us suppose that ρ̄|G_p is unramified', and every §3 result assumes it (Cor. 1.5(3), Cor. 1.6). Then L is unramified at p, while Q(ζ_p)/Q is totally ramified at p of degree p − 1 > 1. The parenthetical '(note that p ≠ 2)' is exactly what this ramification argument needs, which is why the intended reason is clear. det(ρ̄) alone would be enough only when Gal(L/Q)^ab is cut out by det, for example when the image contains SL_2(F_p) with p ≥ 3. That is not assumed. The counterexample's ρ̄ is ramified at 3, so it lies outside the paper's setting and does not touch the conclusion.

The rest of the step is fine. If q splits completely in L, then ρ̄(Frob_q) = 1 and the eigenvalue ratio is 1. If also q ≢ 1 mod p, then 1 ≠ q^{±1} mod p. Chebotarev applies because Q(ζ_p) ⊄ L. The printed passage is a slip in the cited reason: it names a true but insufficient consequence (det unramified) instead of the hypothesis actually needed (ρ̄ unramified). It is not a false conclusion.
