issues.locator: §6.1, Theorem 6.3, hypothesis (c), p. 386 (same in arXiv v2, p. 66)
issues.printed: The source assumes perfect S_N/ϖ^N-complexes D_N for every N ≥ 1. Condition (c) provides a surjection φ_N : R∞ → R and, for every n ≥ 1, an R∞-module isomorphism H^{l0}(D_N^□ ⊗_{S_N^□} O/ϖ^n) = H^{l0}(D_N ⊗_{S_N} O/ϖ^n) ≃ H/ϖ^n, using φ_N for the action on H/ϖ^n. These identifications must be compatible as n varies with N fixed.
issues.correction: In Theorem 6.3(c), replace "for each n ≥ 1" by "for each n with 1 ≤ n ≤ N", and "compatible for fixed N and varying n" by "... varying n ≤ N". An equivalent fix asks only for an isomorphism at n = N, because the cases n < N follow by reducing the top-degree cohomology. The Note in the patching-datum definition already uses this step. Proposition 6.6 picks up the fix automatically, since it cites (a)–(d) of Thm 6.3. With the fix, "condition (c) is clear" in the proof of Thm 9.19 is true, and no proof needs any other change. The candidates' correction is right and minimal.
issues.reason:
I checked the rendered pages 386–389 and 426–428 myself.

(1) The printed (c) cannot hold for n > N. D_N is a complex of S_N/ϖ^N-modules, so ϖ^N kills it. For n ≥ N the termwise tensor product is D_N ⊗_{S_N} O/ϖ^n = D_N/(𝔞_N, ϖ^n)D_N = D_N ⊗ O/ϖ^N, which does not depend on n. A derived tensor product would not help either: its cohomology is still killed by ϖ^N. So (c) says ϖ^N kills H/ϖ^n for every n, i.e. ϖ^N H ⊂ ∩_n ϖ^n H. The compatibility clause gives the same thing, since the transition maps H/ϖ^{n+1} → H/ϖ^n would all be isomorphisms. Conclusions (ii) and (iv) make H ≅ H^{l0}(P∞^□)/𝔞 a finite module over the Noetherian local ring R∞. By Krull's intersection theorem ∩ ϖ^n H = 0, so ϖ^N H = 0; with N = 1, ϖH = 0.

(2) A minimal example shows this: take l0 = q = j = 0, R∞ = R = O, H = O, T = k, D_N = O/ϖ^N. Here (a), (b) and (d) hold, but (c) would need O/ϖ^N ≅ O/ϖ^n for all n, which fails for n > N. The expected conclusion (H free) is exactly what the corrected (c) gives.

(3) The application relies on the printed version holding. In the proof of Theorem 9.19 (pp. 426–427), D^1_N is the complex D̃_N/ϖ^N of S_N/ϖ^N-modules, and "its cohomology computes H^*(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_N), O/ϖ^N)^∨_m". Also H^1 = H^{q0}(Y, K/O)^∨_m, which is not killed by ϖ in general: the proof itself uses that H^{l0}(P∞^{1,□}) is p-torsion free. Yet the text says "condition (c) is clear". That is true only for n ≤ N.

(4) The proof of Theorem 6.3 only uses n ≤ N. The level-N datum D_{M,N} uses ψ = the given isomorphism H^{l0}(D_M^□ ⊗ O/ϖ^N) ≃ H/ϖ^N with N ≤ M (p. 388). The datum definition only needs "each N ≥ n′ ≥ 1" (p. 387). Proposition 6.6 only needs n = 1. So the candidate's correction is sufficient, and it matches the application. Hypothesis (b)'s "each n ≥ 1" does no harm, because it only asks for compatible actions.

This is a genuine error in how the hypothesis is stated, not a bracket misprint. On 'affects': I disagree slightly with "a stated result". Theorem 6.3 and Prop. 6.6 are true as printed, just unusable, and no downstream statement is false. What is invalid as printed is the proof of Theorem 9.19 (and so the chain to Theorems 5.16/1.1), which checks a hypothesis that fails. The fix, weakening the hypothesis in the statements of Thm 6.3/Prop 6.6, repairs everything. I checked the rendered pp. 386–391 and 425–428 of the published PDF, the text of arXiv v2 (Theorem 6.3 and the proof of Theorem 9.19), and arXiv v1.

DEFENCE ATTEMPTS, ALL FAIL.
(i) The expression is well-defined for every n. The tensor product is over S_N, and the paper's own convention makes O/ϖ^n = S_0/ϖ^n a quotient of S_N for every n. So nothing in the notation limits n to n ≤ N.
(ii) Reading the tensor product as derived does not help. D_N is a complex of S_N/ϖ^N-modules, so multiplication by ϖ^N is zero on D_N, and hence on the cohomology of D_N ⊗ O/ϖ^n whether the tensor is termwise or derived. For n ≥ N, the termwise D_N ⊗ O/ϖ^n equals D_N ⊗ O/ϖ^N.
(iii) Take N = 1 in the printed (c). It gives ϖ(H/ϖ^n H) = 0 for all n, i.e. ϖH ⊂ ∩_n ϖ^n H. When H is finitely generated this intersection is 0 by Krull, so ϖH = 0. Finite generation is needed anyway: the conclusion H ≅ H^{l0}(P∞^□)/a forces it.
(iv) The simplest model case fails. Take l0 = q = j = 0, R∞ = R = O, H = O, T = k and D_N = O/ϖ^N. Then (1)–(3), (a), (b) and (d) hold, and the intended conclusion (H free) is true. But the printed (c) would need O/ϖ^{min(n,N)} ≅ O/ϖ^n for all n, which is false.

WHY IT MATTERS. The printed Theorem 6.3 and Prop 6.6 are not false: their proofs go through whenever the stronger hypothesis holds. But that hypothesis can never be met in the application. In the proof of Thm 9.19 (p. 427), D^1_N = D̃_N/ϖ^N, "whose cohomology computes H^*(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_N), O/ϖ^N)^∨_m", and H^1 = H^{q0}(Y,K/O)^∨_m, which is finite over O. By (iii), the printed (c) would force ϖH^1 = 0. Yet Theorem 9.19 concludes that H^1 is nearly faithful over R_S. Theorem 5.16 is deduced from this using the characteristic-0 point of R_S given by r, so ϖH^1 ≠ 0. The proof itself (p. 428) also uses p-torsion-freeness of H^{l0}(P∞^{1,□}). So "condition (c) is clear" is false as printed; it is true only for n ≤ N.

THE FIX SUFFICES. Every use involves only n ≤ N:
- D_{M,N} (p. 388) takes ψ to be the given isomorphism for D_M at n = N ≤ M.
- The patching datum (p. 387) records only "N ≥ n′ ≥ 1".
- The extra data and commuting square of Prop 6.6 use only n = 1 ≤ M.
- Hypothesis (b) also says "each n ≥ 1", but that is harmless there, because it only asks for compatible actions.

CLASSIFICATION. The intended range can be recovered from the patching-datum definition, so this is close to a misprint. I call it an error because it is not a one-character slip: the unbounded "n ≥ 1" is written deliberately in (b), (c), (d) and again in §9. As printed, the verification in Theorem 9.19 asserts a condition that fails.

AFFECTS: the proof. No stated result becomes false. Theorems 6.3 and 6.6 only get stronger under the fix, and their existing proofs support it. What fails is the proof of Thm 9.19, and through it the chain to Thms 5.16 and 1.1. The fix repairs it.

SEPARATE ISSUE, NOT PART OF THIS CANDIDATE. Thm 6.3(2) lets H be any R-module. ψ∞ comes from lim H/ϖ^{N_i}H, so it tacitly needs H to be finitely generated (and nonzero, for (iii)). For example, H = K with T = 0 and D_N = 0 satisfies all the hypotheses but not (iv). This is harmless in §9.

The claim on p. 389 that "the image of 𝔞 in End(H^{l0}(P∞^□)) is contained in that of ker(φ∞) by assumption (d)" needs ker(φ_{M_i} mod 𝔡_{N_i}), and φ_{N_i} has no stated relation to φ_{M_i}.
(3) The model is Prop. 2.3(5a), which pairs H_N with φ_N at the same level. It was carried over when 6.3 moved to two indices (M, N).
(4) The application (Thm 9.19, p. 427) chooses the surjections R∞ ↠ R^□_{S_{Q_N}} independently for each N and says "Condition (d) follows from Conjecture B". Conjecture B gives the ker φ_M version. It does not give the φ_N version for M > N. I built a toy case to check: q = 0, j = 1, l0 = 0, R = H = O, D_M = O/ϖ^M, x acting as z + c_M. The corrected (d) holds for arbitrary c_M. The printed (d) forces c_N ≡ c_M mod ϖ^M.
Two points qualify the candidate's reason:
(a) For N ≥ 1 the printed hypothesis is stronger than needed, not weaker. At N = M the printed and corrected versions coincide, and in degree l0 that case already gives what the proof uses: H^{l0}(D ⊗ S_N) = H^{l0}(D ⊗ S_M) ⊗ S_N, and the R∞-actions are compatible by (b). So no conclusion of 6.3, 6.4, 6.6 or 9.19 becomes false. The damage is that the stated hypothesis is ill-formed at N = 0 and, for M > N, differs from what the application verifies.
(b) On p. 427 the application also writes the action on H^*(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M)) through R_{S_{Q_N}} and R∞ ↠ R^□_{S_{Q_N}}. That looks like a matching index slip (it should be Q_M) and could be a separate candidate. I checked the page image (PDF p. 90): the printed text reads exactly as quoted.

DEFENCE ATTEMPTS AND WHY THEY FAIL:
(1) "M, N and n as above" refers to (b): M ≥ N ≥ 0, M ≥ 1, n ≥ 1. But (c) defines φ_N only for N ≥ 1, so the printed condition has an undefined symbol φ_0 when N = 0.
(2) The module belongs to level M. By (c) at level M, together with the (b)-compatibility for the maps to N' = 0, R∞ acts on H^{l0}(D_M^□ ⊗ S_N/ϖ^n) modulo the augmentation ideal through φ_M. φ_N plays no part there.
(3) The proof (p. 388) builds the datum D_{M,N} with φ = (R∞ →φ_M R ↠ R/𝔡_N), and φ∞ = lim φ_{M_i} mod 𝔡_{N_i}. So the final step "image of 𝔞 … contained in that of ker(φ∞) by assumption (d)" (p. 389) directly calls for ker φ_{M_i}.
(4) The one-index model, Prop. 2.3(5a) (p. 307), pairs H_N with φ_N at the same level. The slip is what happens when that clause is carried over to two indices.
(5) One could try to defend the printed index by reading p. 427 literally: there R∞ acts on H^*(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M)) through R∞ ↠ R^□_{S_{Q_N}}. That reading does not hold up. R_{S_{Q_N}} does not act on level-Q_M cohomology, because Q_N and Q_M are different sets of primes; this is H-part2-27. The reading also contradicts (b)+(c).
(6) The printed condition is not the corrected one in disguise when M > N. I built a toy model satisfying (a)–(c): q = 0, j = 1, l0 = 0, R = H = O, R∞ = O⟦x⟧, D_M = O/ϖ^M, x acting as z + c_M, φ_N(x) = c_N ∈ 𝔪. The corrected (d) holds, since z = x − c_M. The printed (d) needs z ∈ (z + c_M − c_N)·(O/ϖ^m)⟦z⟧ with m = min(n, M). Comparing the constant and z-coefficients shows this forces c_N ≡ c_M mod ϖ^m. In §9 the surjections R∞ ↠ R^□_{S_{Q_N}} are chosen independently for each N (via Prop. 8.5). So "Condition (d) follows from Conjecture B" (p. 427) proves the ker φ_M version, not the printed one for M > N. So the text as printed is wrong, and the defence fails.

CONSEQUENCES:
The proof uses (d) only in degree l0, through P_i = D_{M_i} ⊗ S_{N_i}/ϖ^{N_i} with N_i ≥ 1. It never uses N = 0. In degree l0, the N = M instance already gives every other case, and at N = M the printed and corrected conditions coincide. The reason: H^{l0} is a cokernel, so H^{l0}(D_M^□ ⊗ S_N/ϖ^n) = H^{l0}(D_M^□ ⊗ S_M/ϖ^n) ⊗ S_N. The quotient map is R∞- and S_M^□-equivariant by (b). And aug(S_M^□) maps onto aug(S_N^□). So an element of ker φ_M that acts like x̃ upstairs also acts like x downstairs.

It follows that:
- Theorem 6.3 as printed, restricted to N ≥ 1, is still true.
- Its proof needs only this one-line reduction.
- Theorem 6.4, Prop. 6.6 and the application in Theorem 9.19 all go through. The application verifies the corrected (d), which includes the N = M instances.
- No conclusion changes. The mathematics is right as intended.

I therefore set affects to "nothing". This matches how the register records other misprints in hypotheses whose intended reading is clear, e.g. H-part1b-16. If the register instead counts every misprint inside a theorem statement as "a stated result", the earlier verdict's label is the alternative. X-K7-3 classifies this as an error that breaks the proof. That overstates it: the proof survives with the printed hypothesis through the N = M instance. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

issues.printed: Theorem 6.3 takes R∞ in C_O of dimension 1 + j + q − l0, R in C_O, an R-module H, and a finite-dimensional k-complex T in degrees 0, ..., l0 with d = 0 and H^{l0}(T) ⥲ H/ϖ. Theorem 6.4 additionally assumes R∞ is p-torsion free: formal smoothness over O, so R ≃ O⟦x1,...,x_{q+j−l0}⟧, implies H is R-free; irreducibility of R∞[1/p] implies H is nearly faithful over R.
issues.correction:
Theorem 6.3(2) should read: "Let R be an object of C_O, and let H be a non-zero finite R-module." Under (3), being finitely generated over R is the same as being finite over O, which matches Prop. 2.3(1). The reason is that a finite R-module with H/ϖH finite-dimensional is ϖ-adically complete, so it is finite over O by complete Nakayama. Also, for H finite over O, H ≠ 0 holds exactly when H^{l0}(T) ≠ 0.
Theorem 6.3 itself and Theorem 6.4(1) need only finiteness. Non-vanishing is needed for 6.4(2), for 6.3(iii) under the usual convention depth(0) = ∞, and for the use of Lemma 6.2 in the proof. Alternatively, "H ≠ 0" can be added only in 6.4(2).
Theorem 6.4 and Prop. 6.6 inherit the corrected hypothesis.
issues.reason:
Checked on the page images at 110 and 220 dpi. The paper has no global rule that modules are finite: the Notation section only fixes C_O and says what "perfect complex" means. When finiteness is needed elsewhere the authors state it, as in Prop. 2.3(1). I redid the counterexamples.
(A) Finiteness. Take q = j = l0 = 0, so S∞ = S_N = O, O^□ = O and 𝔞 = 0. Take R∞ = R = O (Krull dimension 1 = 1+j+q−l0) and H = K. Then H/ϖ = 0, so T = 0 satisfies (3). Take D_N = 0 and φ_N = id. Conditions (a)–(d) hold trivially, since every cohomology group is 0 = K/ϖ^n K. Conclusion (iv) then gives H^0(P∞) ≅ K, but P∞ is a complex of finitely generated O-modules, so this is impossible. Theorem 6.4(1) applies (R∞ = O is p-torsion free and formally smooth) and would say that K is a free O-module, which is false. If l0 ≥ 1 is wanted, take q = 0 and j = l0; the same argument works with 𝔞 = (z_1..z_j).
The proof uses finiteness explicitly on p. 387: "(As in the proof of Theorem 2.3, one can take 𝔡_N to be the ideal generated by ϖ^N and Ann_R(H)^N)". That step relies on "R/Ann_R(H) ⊂ End_O(H) is finite as an O-module" (p. 307), which needs H finite over O. Finiteness is also needed to identify the limit of the H/ϖ^N H with H when building ψ∞.
(B) Non-vanishing. Take H = 0, T = 0, D_N = 0 and R∞ = R = O. The hypotheses of 6.4 hold and R∞[1/p] = K is irreducible. But 6.4(2) would make 0 a nearly faithful O-module, which is false because Ann = O is not nilpotent. The proof of 6.4(2) on p. 390 itself says "Since H^{l0}(P∞^□) ≠ {0}". Lemma 6.2's proof also assumes that some H^m(P) is non-zero.
Minor point: the proposed "equivalently T ≠ 0" works only through the theorem's own dimension argument. "H^{l0}(T) ≠ 0" is the cleaner equivalent.
Where the theorem is applied (Theorem 9.19, via Prop. 6.6), H = H^{q0}(Y,K/O)^∨_𝔪 is finite over O. It is non-zero because 𝔪 is a maximal ideal of the Hecke algebra, so T ≠ 0. The main results are therefore unaffected. What is wrong is the printed statements of Theorems 6.3 and 6.4 (and Prop. 6.6, which inherits the hypotheses): they are false as printed in these degenerate cases. I checked the page images at 130 dpi, pp. 385–391 and 307–308.

**Defences tried.**
- **Global convention?** There is none. The Notation section (p. 299) only fixes C_O and defines "perfect complex". Elsewhere the authors state finiteness when they need it: in Prop. 2.3(1) (p. 307), and they write "finitely generated" for P∞ in the conclusion.
- **Does (3) force finiteness?** No. It only makes H/ϖ finite-dimensional; H itself need not be finite.
- **Do (a)–(d) force it?** No. They only constrain H/ϖ^n.

**(A) Finiteness fails.**
- Setup: take q = j = l0 = 0. Then S_N = S∞ = O, O^□ = O and 𝔞 = 0. Take R∞ = R = O (Krull dimension 1 = 1+j+q−l0), H = K, T = 0, D_N = 0 and φ_N = id. D_N = 0 is a perfect complex.
- The hypotheses hold: (a) holds because T = 0. (c) holds because H^0(0) = 0 = K/ϖ^n K. (b) and (d) hold trivially, since End(0) = 0.
- Conclusion (iv) would then give H^0(P∞) ≅ K, where P∞ is a perfect complex of finitely generated O-modules. That is impossible.
- Theorem 6.4(1) applies, since O is p-torsion free and formally smooth with 0 variables. It would say that K is a free O-module, which is false.
- For l0 ≥ 1, take q = 0 and j = l0. Then 𝔞 = (z_1..z_j), and H^{l0}(P∞^□)/𝔞 is finite over O, so it again cannot be ≅ K. Taking H = O ⊕ K shows that the proof really produces the ϖ-adic completion of H, not H.
- Two places in the proof use finiteness:
  - p. 387: "(As in the proof of Theorem 2.3 [sic, Prop. 2.3], one can take 𝔡_N to be the ideal generated by ϖ^N and Ann_R(H)^N)". Openness there depends on "R/Ann_R(H) ⊂ End_O(H) is finite as an O-module" (p. 308).
  - p. 388: ψ∞ is built from the H/ϖ^{N_i}H, so it identifies lim H/ϖ^N H with H.

**(B) Non-vanishing fails.**
- Setup: take q = j = l0 = 0, R∞ = R = O, H = 0, T = 0 and D_N = 0.
- R∞ is p-torsion free and R∞[1/p] = K is irreducible. So 6.4(2) says that 0 is a nearly faithful O-module.
- In Taylor's sense ([11]), nearly faithful means Ann is nilpotent. Here Ann_O(0) = O, so this is false.
- The proof on p. 390 itself uses "Since H^{l0}(P∞^□) ≠ {0}", and Lemma 6.2's proof needs some H^m(P) ≠ 0.
- In 6.3, (iv) together with Nakayama forces H^{l0}(P∞^□) = 0. Then (iii) asserts that depth(0) = 1+j+q−l0, which is false under the convention depth(0) = ∞ and undefined otherwise.

**Where the result is used.** Only in the outline of §8.1 (pp. 369–370) and in Theorem 9.19 (pp. 417–419), through Prop. 6.6 and Theorem 6.4(2) with i = 2 and conclusion (iv).
- There H^i = H^{q0}(Y,K/O)^∨_𝔪 (or its χ-version). This is the Pontryagin dual of a cofinitely generated module, so it is finite over O.
- It is non-zero because 𝔪 is a maximal ideal of the Hecke algebra acting on H^*(Y,O/ϖ^n). So T ≠ 0, the patched minimal complex P∞ (with P∞⊗k ≅ T) is non-zero, and by Lemma 6.2 H^{l0}(P∞^□) ≠ 0, hence H ≠ 0.
- So Theorem 9.19, Theorem 5.16 and Theorem 1.1 are unaffected.

**Classification.** Only the printed statements of Theorems 6.3 and 6.4 and Prop. 6.6 are false. They fail in degenerate cases because a hypothesis was left out, and the proof silently uses that hypothesis. By §18 a false statement is an "error". The readers' label "gap" also describes the proof step (𝔡_N and ψ∞), but the statement as printed is false.
- Both proposed corrections work: "finitely generated R-module" (X-K7-4) and "finite over O" (H-part2-4). Each also needs "non-zero" for 6.4(2).

issues.locator: §6.1, Theorem 6.3: the definition of O^□ and M^□ on p. 386 (PDF p. 90), used for S∞^□ and P∞^□ in (i)–(iv) and in the proof on pp. 387–389 (PDF pp. 91–93). The text is the same in arXiv v2, §6.1, pp. 66–67, apart from the bracket. The same reading appears on p. 427: "In the notation of Proposition 6.3, the rings on the right hand side can be written R^□", where the rings are R_{S_{Q_N}}[z_1,…,z_j], i.e. R⟦z⟧.
issues.printed: The source sets O^□ = O[z_1, . . . , z_j]; it defines M^□ := M ⊗_O O^□; it regards A as a quotient by setting z_i to 0. It gives H^{l0}(P∞^□) an R∞⊗̂_O S∞^□ action, defines b_N using ϖ^N, a_N, (z_1^N, …, z_j^N), and asserts cohomology isomorphisms over R∞⊗̂_O S∞. Formal smoothness supplies ı : S∞^□ → R∞ in C_O. It uses dim R∞ = dim S∞^□ − l0 and Lemma 6.2 to get depth_{S∞^□}(H^{l0}(P∞^□)) = dim(S∞^□) − l0 = 1 + j + q − l0.
issues.correction: Read M^□ := M ⊗̂_O O^□, the completed tensor product. This equals ⊗_O whenever M is finitely generated over O, so it changes nothing for S_N, S_N/I, D_N or the finite-level P. In particular S∞^□ = O⟦(Z_p)^q, z_1,…,z_j⟧ and P∞^□ = P∞ ⊗_{S∞} S∞^□, which also fixes H^*(P∞^□). In §9, R^□_{S_Q} = R_{S_Q}⟦z_1,…,z_j⟧, as the paper itself writes on p. 426. The O[…] → O⟦…⟧ bracket is Correction item (10) and is not part of this finding. The candidate also proposes changing "R∞ ⊗̂_O S∞" on p. 387 to "R∞ ⊗̂_O S∞^□". That change is not needed: the maps on cohomology come from P → P′ by base change to O^□, so they are automatically O^□-linear. For these maps, being R∞⊗̂S∞-linear is therefore the same as being R∞⊗̂S∞^□-linear. The candidate's claim that "only S∞^□ is affected" is also incomplete, because P∞^□ and H^*(P∞^□) need the completed product too.
issues.reason:
The paper has no convention that ⊗ means the completed tensor product. The Notation section only defines C_O. The paper also writes ⊗̂ explicitly where it means the completion: in (ii) of this same theorem, in the proof, and in Lemma 4.2. Read literally, S∞^□ = O⟦x_1..x_q⟧ ⊗_O O⟦z_1..z_j⟧ is the algebraic tensor product. For q, j ≥ 1 this ring is not local.

Proof that it is not local:
- A = O⟦x⟧⊗_O O⟦z⟧ is O-flat, so it embeds in A⊗K = O⟦x⟧[1/p]⊗_K O⟦z⟧[1/p].
- That ring maps injectively to coefficient arrays K^{N^q×N^j}, and every element has a coefficient matrix of finite rank.
- The inverse of 1 − x_1z_1 in O⟦x,z⟧ is Σ(x_1z_1)^n. Its coefficient matrix contains an infinite identity block, so the inverse is not in A, and 1 − x_1z_1 is not a unit of A.
- But x_1z_1 lies in the maximal ideal ker(A → k). So the non-units of A do not form an ideal, and A is not local.

So, as printed, S∞^□ is not in C_O. It is not the Noetherian regular local ring that Lemma 6.2 requires ("let S be a Noetherian regular local ring"), and it has no "dim S∞^□ = 1+j+q". P∞ ⊗_O O^□ is likewise not the complete module whose cohomology carries the patched R∞-action.

The intended meaning is clear. The proof uses the completed ring throughout: "open ideal", ı in C_O, the dimension count, Lemma 6.2. On p. 427 the same notation is identified with R⟦z⟧. With the completed ring every step works as written. So this is a notational slip and should be classed as a misprint, not a gap: no step is missing an argument.

One part of the candidate is wrong. On p. 387, "isomorphisms of R∞⊗̂_O S∞-modules" is fine as printed. The induced map on the □-cohomology is (P → P') ⊗ id, which is automatically O^□-linear, so S∞-compatibility suffices. Rendered PDF pp. 90–93 (published pp. 386–389) and read the zoomed crops.

1) Read literally, the definition fails. Even after Correction item (10) (O^□ = O⟦z⟧), M^□ is defined with the plain ⊗_O. Take q = j = 1: S∞ ⊗_O O⟦z⟧ = O⟦T⟧ ⊗_O O⟦z⟧, which embeds in O⟦T,z⟧. Its image consists of power series whose coefficient matrix (c_{a,b}) has finite rank over K. In O⟦T,z⟧ the inverse of 1 − Tz is Σ T^n z^n, whose coefficient matrix is the identity and has infinite rank. So 1 − Tz is not a unit in the plain tensor product. Tz is not a unit either. Hence the ring is not local, so it is not in C_O and not a Noetherian regular local ring. Its Krull dimension is also not 1 + j + q.

2) The proof needs the completed ring at every step:
- "dim R∞ = dim S∞^□ − l0" needs dim S∞^□ = 1 + j + q.
- "By Lemma 6.2 (with S = S∞^□ and P = P∞^□)": Lemma 6.2 needs S Noetherian regular local.
- "since S∞^□ is formally smooth over O, we can and do choose a homomorphism ı: S∞^□ → R∞ in C_O".
- (ii) asks H^{l0}(P∞^□) to be a finite R∞-module carrying an action of R∞ ⊗̂ S∞^□. That action arises as an inverse limit, so it lives on P∞ ⊗̂ O^□, not on P∞ ⊗_O O^□. The latter is in general not complete.

3) Defence tried and rejected. One could argue the paper uses ⊗ to mean ⊗̂ by convention. It does not: it writes ⊗̂ explicitly elsewhere, e.g. Lemma 4.2's B ⊗̂_O C, R_loc, and R∞ ⊗̂_O S∞^□ in the same theorem. So the plain ⊗ is a genuine slip and is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

4) The intended meaning is nonetheless unambiguous from context: the dimension count, formal smoothness, the use of C_O, Lemma 6.2, and p. 426, where R_{S_{Q_N}}⟦z_1,…,z_j⟧ is identified with "R^□_{S_Q} in the notation of Proposition 6.3". With the completed product, every step of Thms 6.3 and 6.4, Prop 6.6 and Thm 9.19 goes through unchanged. So this is a misprint, not a gap, and it affects nothing.

5) The p. 387 wording is correct as printed (see correction).

It reads exactly as quoted, and the "2.3" is a live internal hyperlink. pdftohtml -xml shows its target is PDF page 11 (= p. 307), the page where Proposition 2.3 is stated. The paper numbers everything with one shared counter: in §2 the only labels are Definition 2.1, Definition 2.2 and Proposition 2.3. There is no Theorem 2.3 anywhere in the paper, and grep turns up no other item numbered 2.3 in §2. I also rendered PDF p. 12 (= p. 308). The proof of Proposition 2.3 there makes the same three requirements on 𝔡_N (𝔡_N ⊃ 𝔡_{N+1}; ∩𝔡_N = 0; ϖ^N R ⊂ 𝔡_N ⊂ ϖ^N R + Ann_R(H)), and it gives the example 𝔡_N = (ϖ^N, Ann_R(H)^N) together with the reason these ideals are open. So the cross-reference names the wrong kind of result: the right target is Proposition 2.3. Elsewhere the paper refers to it correctly as "Proposition 2.3", in the proof of Theorem 3.14 area (p. ~). issues.locator: §6.1, proof of Theorem 6.3: definition of patching datum, p. 387, and display on p. 388 (published version)
issues.printed: For (z_1^N,…,z_j^N) ⊂ I ⊂ (z_1,…,z_j), 1 ≤ n′ ≤ N and 0 ≤ N′ ≤ N, the source asserts H^i(P^□ ⊗_{S^□_∞} S^□_{N′}/(I + ϖ^{n′})) = H^i(D^□_M ⊗_{S_M} S_{N′}/ϖ^{n′}) ⊗_{O^□} O^□/I. It invokes (b) for a compatible R_∞-action commuting with S^□_∞ as I, N′, n′ vary, thereby declaring D_{M,N} a level-N patching datum.
issues.correction:
Restrict the third condition to ideals I for which O^□/I is O-flat. The simplest choice is I = (z_1^{a_1},…,z_j^{a_j}) with 1 ≤ a_i ≤ N, or even just I = (z_1^m,…,z_j^m) with 1 ≤ m ≤ N. Make this change both in the definition of a patching datum and in the check for D_{M,N}. With O^□/I free over O, the display holds, since B := O^□/(I+ϖ^{n′}) is then flat over A := O/ϖ^{n′}. The rest of the proof uses only these ideals:
- H^*(P_∞^□) = lim_i H^*(P_i^□ ⊗ S_∞^□/𝔟_{N_i}) uses I = (z^{N_i}).
- The transition maps compare (z^{N_{i+1}}) with (z^{N_i}).
- ψ, and conclusions (i)–(iv), use I = (z_1,…,z_j).
The restricted family is stable under "D mod N′", and the finiteness of patching data still holds. The statements of Theorem 6.3 and Proposition 6.6 are unchanged. H-part2-7's correction is right and minimal. X-K7-10's correction also works, but its extra finiteness objection is unfounded (see reason).
issues.reason:
I confirmed the printed text on the rendered page (p. 388); v2 is the same. Set Y = D_M ⊗_{S_M} S_{N′}/ϖ^{n′}, a bounded complex of free A-modules (A = O/ϖ^{n′}). Since n′ ≤ N and N′ ≤ N, the left side is H^i(Y ⊗_A B). Since O^□ is flat over O, the right side is H^i(Y) ⊗_A B. These two agree for all Y only when B is A-flat.

The reader's own example does NOT satisfy the theorem's hypotheses:
- D_M = (O/ϖ^M →ϖ O/ϖ^M →ϖ O/ϖ^M) is not a complex for M ≥ 3, because d∘d = ϖ^2 ≠ 0.
- With q = 0, j = 2, l0 = 2, condition (d) cannot hold. H^0 contains k⟦z_1,z_2⟧ faithfully, so the image of R_∞ would have dimension at least 2, but dim R_∞ = 1.
- The reader only checked condition (a).

Here is an example that satisfies all of (1)–(3) and (a)–(d):
- q = 0, j = 1, l0 = 1, so S_N = S_∞ = O.
- D_N = (O/ϖ^N →ϖ O/ϖ^N) and T = (k →0 k).
- R_∞ = k⟦z⟧, which has dimension 1 = 1+j+q−l0. It acts on H^*(D_M^□/ϖ^n) ≅ k⟦z⟧ in degrees 0 and 1 via z ↦ z.
- R = H = k, and φ_N sends z ↦ 0.
- (c) holds: H^1(D_N/ϖ^n) = k. (d) holds: S_M^□ and R_∞ have the same image, and the augmentation ideal (z) of S_N^□ and ker φ_N = (z) also have the same image.

Now take N ≥ 2, n′ = 2 and I = (ϖz, z^2). Then (z^N) ⊂ I ⊂ (z), and B = O⟦z⟧/(ϖz, z^2, ϖ^2) = A·1 ⊕ k·z.
- Left side: H^0 = ker(ϖ on B) = span(ϖ, z). Here z acts as 0.
- Right side: H^0(Y)⊗_A B = k⟦z⟧/I = k[z]/(z^2). Here z acts nontrivially.
The two sides are not isomorphic even as O^□-modules. The natural map ϖ⊗z ↦ ϖz = 0 is neither injective nor surjective.

So the proof cannot get the required R_∞-action on the left side from (b) for such I. In this example an action exists anyway, since R_∞ = S_∞^□/ϖ. So this is a flaw in the argument, not a counterexample to the claim, and it is fixed by restricting to monomial I.

I checked what the rest of the proof uses. The passage to H^*(P_∞^□), the transition maps, ψ, (d) and the use of Lemma 6.2 involve only I = (z_1^m,…,z_j^m), so no stated result depends on the general I. The reader's diagnosis, correction and "affects" are right; only their example needs replacing. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. DEFENCE ATTEMPTED AND FAILED. Put Y := D_M ⊗_{S_M} S_{N′}/ϖ^{n′}. It is a bounded complex of free A-modules, where A = O/ϖ^{n′}. Since N′ ≤ N and n′ ≤ N, the left side is H^i(Y ⊗_O O^□/I) = H^i(Y ⊗_A B), with B = O^□/(I+ϖ^{n′}). O^□ = O⟦z⟧ is O-flat, so the right side is H^i(Y) ⊗_O O^□/I = H^i(Y) ⊗_A B. These agree for all such Y exactly when Tor^A(H^*(Y), B) causes no trouble, for example when B is A-flat. That is not true for every I allowed in the text.

Other readings do not rescue the step:
- The display is a plain tensor of a cohomology module with O^□/I. No derived reading gives the left side.
- Hypothesis (b) gives R_∞-actions only on H^*(Y ⊗ O^□), with O^□ not reduced modulo I. These actions live on cohomology, not on the complex. So they do not induce an action on H^*((Y⊗O^□) ⊗^L_{O^□} O^□/I) when O^□/I is not flat.
- No nearby statement restricts I.
- In top degree l_0 the display does hold, by right exactness. But the proof needs every degree: it uses the dimension of H^*(P_∞^□) and then Lemma 6.2.

COUNTEREXAMPLE WITHIN THE HYPOTHESES. I checked this by hand; it is the example in H-part2-7's verdict.
- Take q = 0, j = 1, l_0 = 1. Then S_N = O and O^□ = O⟦z⟧.
- D_N = (O/ϖ^N →ϖ O/ϖ^N) and T = (k →0 k), R = H = k.
- R_∞ = k⟦z⟧, of Krull dimension 1 = 1+j+q−l_0. It acts on H^*(D_M^□/ϖ^n) ≅ k⟦z⟧ by z ↦ z. φ_N sends z to 0.
- Conditions (1)–(3) and (a)–(d) all hold.

Now take M ≥ N ≥ 2, n′ = 2, N′ = 0 and I = (ϖz, z^2). This I lies between (z^N) and (z). Then B = O⟦z⟧/(ϖz, z^2, ϖ^2) = A·1 ⊕ k·z.
- Left side: H^0 = ker(ϖ on B) = span(ϖ, z), and z acts as 0 on it.
- Right side: H^0(Y) ⊗ O^□/I = k[z]/(z^2), and z acts nontrivially.
The two sides are not isomorphic even as O^□-modules. The check with O = Z_3 is: 3(a + bz) = 3a in Z/9 ⊕ (Z/3)z.

X-K7-10's example I = (z^N, ϖz) has O^□/I ≅ O ⊕ k^{N−1}. It shows the same failure in general, but it was not checked against (a)–(d).

X-K7-10'S FINITENESS SUB-CLAIM IS WRONG. The groups depend only on I + ϖ^{n′}O^□, which contains (z_1^N,…,z_j^N, ϖ^N). So they correspond to ideals of the finite ring (O/ϖ^N)[z]/(z_i^N); k is finite by the paper's conventions. Two ideals I and I′ with the same I + ϖ^{n′} both map compatibly to I + I′, so they carry the same action. Hence the paper's claim of "finitely many patching data" is fine as it stands.

CONSEQUENCES. The false display is used only to check that D_{M,N} is a patching datum. After that, the proof uses only I = (z^{N_i}) and (z_1,…,z_j). So restricting to monomial or O-flat I repairs it with no change to any statement. The same applies to Proposition 6.6. Kind: an error, because the displayed identity is false for some admissible I. It is a local error with a routine fix, and it does not reach a stated result. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

issues.locator: §6.1, Theorem 6.3, conclusion (iii), p. 387 (PDF p. 91). arXiv v2 (p. 67) has identical text. arXiv v1 does not contain §6 of Part 2. The p. 401 (§8.1) sentence cited alongside it is NOT a mistake (see reason).
issues.printed: Conclusion (iii) states that H^{l0}(P∞) has R∞-depth 1 + j + q − l0(= dim R∞).
issues.correction: (iii) The R∞-depth of H^{l0}(P∞^□) is equal to 1 + j + q − l0 (= dim R∞).
issues.reason:
Rendered PDF pp. 90–94. In the statement, (i), (ii) and (iv) all concern P∞^□ and H^{l0}(P∞^□). Only (iii) prints P∞ without □. The proof (p. 389) proves depth_{S∞^□}(H^{l0}(P∞^□)) = dim S∞^□ − l0 = 1 + j + q − l0. The proof of Theorem 6.4 (p. 389) uses "Since depth_{R∞}(H^{l0}(P∞^□)) = dim R∞".

The printed statement is false whenever j > 0 and H ≠ 0. P∞^□ = P∞ ⊗_O O^□ with O^□ = O⟦z_1,…,z_j⟧ flat over O. Write M := H^{l0}(P∞^□). Then M = H^{l0}(P∞) ⊗_O O^□, z_1, …, z_j is an M-regular sequence, and H^{l0}(P∞) = M/(z_1,…,z_j)M. Here z_i acts through ι(z_i) ∈ R∞, so R∞ acts on the quotient. Hence depth_{R∞} H^{l0}(P∞) = (1 + j + q − l0) − j = 1 + q − l0. Also dim H^{l0}(P∞) ≤ dim R∞ − j. H is a nonzero quotient of H^{l0}(P∞) by (iv), so the printed value 1 + j + q − l0 cannot hold.

In the application (§9.5, p. 426), j = n²|T| − 1 > 0.

The p. 401 sentence ("the corresponding depth of H^{l0}(P∞) is also exactly l0 less than the classical case") is only a relative comparison. It holds for P∞ (1+q−l0 vs 1+q) as well as for P∞^□, so it is not an error. Not a bracket error.

issues.locator: §6.1, proof of Theorem 6.3, p. 388 (published version)
issues.printed: The proof of Theorem 6.3 selects (M_i, N_i)_{i≥1} using finiteness of the isomorphism classes of level-N patching data for N ≥ 1. Its first requirement is for every i: M_i ≥ N_i; M_{i+1} ≥ M_i; N_{i+1} ≥ N_i.
issues.correction:
Read "M_i ≥ N_i, M_{i+1} > M_i, and N_{i+1} > N_i for all i", exactly as in the proof of Prop. 2.3 on p. 309. The smallest fix is N_{i+1} > N_i, or just N_i → ∞. Together with M_i ≥ N_i this also forces M_i → ∞, so M_{i+1} > M_i is harmless but not needed.

Such a sequence exists by the pigeonhole/König argument the text invokes:
- D_{M,N} mod N' ≅ D_{M,N'} by construction.
- So choose nested infinite sets I_1 ⊃ I_2 ⊃ … of M such that the class of D_{M,k} is constant on I_k.
- Then take N_i = i and strictly increasing M_i ∈ I_i with M_i ≥ i.
issues.reason:
I checked the printed text on the page image. The weak inequalities are really printed on p. 388, and the same text is in v2. As written, the two bullets are satisfied by the constant sequence (M_i, N_i) = (1, 1): 1 ≥ 1, and D_{1,1} mod 1 is D_{1,1} itself, since "D mod N'" for N' = N is the identity operation defined on p. 387–388.

With that sequence the rest of the proof fails:
- ϕ∞ = lim ϕ_i is just ϕ_1 : R∞ ↠ R/𝔡_1, not a surjection onto R.
- The transition maps P_{i+1} → P_{i+1}/(ϖ^{N_i} + 𝔞_{N_i}) ≅ P_i are isomorphisms, so P∞ = P_1. That is a complex of S∞/(𝔞_1 + ϖ) = S_1/ϖ-modules, so it is not a complex of projective S∞-modules.
- ψ∞ only gives H^{l0}(P∞^□)/𝔞 ≅ H/ϖH, not H.
- H^{l0}(P∞^□) is killed by ϖ and 𝔞_1, so its dimension is at most j. The depth claim (iii), 1 + j + q − l0, therefore fails as soon as q ≥ l0.

So the claim "Then P∞ is a perfect complex of S∞-modules … ϕ∞ : R∞ ↠ R" does not follow from the bullets as printed. The argument needs N_i → ∞, which the parallel proof of Proposition 2.3 gets from strict inequalities. The intent is obvious and the fix is one character, so this is a misprint rather than a real gap. It is not one of the 47 known ⟦ ⟧ bracket errors.

The statement of Theorem 6.3 is still true: the corrected choice of sequence exists by the same finiteness argument. Theorem 6.4 and the applications in §9 use only the statement, so nothing downstream is affected. Defence attempted and failed.
- Nothing on pp. 387–389 forces N_i → ∞. The patching-datum definition, the D mod N' operation, the definitions of ϕ∞, P∞ and ψ∞, and the rest of the proof never pass to a cofinal subsequence.
- The inverse-limit construction is used as if the levels grow, but that is never stated.
- The bullets as printed allow the constant sequence (M_i, N_i) = (1, 1). Here 1 ≥ 1, and D_{1,1} mod 1 = D_{1,1}, since D mod N' is defined for 1 ≤ N' ≤ N, which includes N' = N.

With that sequence the conclusions of the proof fail:
- ϕ∞ = ϕ_1 : R∞ ↠ R/𝔡_1, not a map onto R.
- Every transition map P_{i+1} → P_{i+1}/(ϖ^{N_i} + 𝔞_{N_i}) ≅ P_i is an isomorphism, so P∞ = P_1. That is a complex of S∞/(𝔞_1 + ϖ)-modules, not a perfect complex of S∞-modules resolving anything of the stated depth.
- ψ∞ only gives an isomorphism onto H/ϖH, not onto H.
- H^{l0}(P∞^□) is killed by ϖ, so the depth claim 1 + j + q − l0 is false once q + j ≥ l0 ≥ 1.

So the step "Then P∞ is a perfect complex of S∞-modules …" does not follow from the text as printed. It does follow once N_{i+1} > N_i.

The intended meaning is clear:
- the identical construction in Prop. 2.3 uses strict inequalities;
- the authors fixed exactly this slip in §2 between v1 and v2;
- the claimed existence is just as easy with strict inequalities.

So this is a misprint rather than an error or gap. It is not one of the 47 known ⟦ ⟧ bracket errors, and the 2022 Correction does not mention it.

Downstream, the construction is used by:
- the proof of Theorem 6.4 (p. 389), which uses ι and ψ∞ "as in the proof of Theorem 6.3";
- Prop. 6.6, whose proof is omitted as "much the same way as Theorem 6.3";
- §8.1 (p. 5303 of the text file region), which cites the depth information "deduced in the proof of Theorem 6.3".

With the corrected sequence all of these go through unchanged. No stated result changes, because the statements of 6.3, 6.4 and 6.6 remain true.

On 'affects': the protocol's gloss "nothing (the mathematics is right as intended)" could support "nothing", since the intended mathematics is right. I record "the proof" because the proof as printed does not establish the theorem until the inequality is fixed.

issues.locator: §6.1, Theorem 6.4(3), p. 389 (PDF p. 93). arXiv v2 (p. 68) has identical text. arXiv v1 does not contain §6 of Part 2.
issues.printed: Part (3) asserts near faithfulness of H over R whenever the support of H^{l0}(P∞)[1/p] contains every irreducible component of Spec(R∞[1/p]).
issues.correction: (3) More generally, H is nearly faithful as an R-module providing that every irreducible component of Spec(R∞[1/p]) is in the support of H^{l0}(P∞^□)[1/p].
issues.reason:
Rendered PDF pp. 93–94. The proof (p. 390) argues only with P∞^□: "H^{l0}(P∞^□) is nearly faithful as an R∞-module if and only if each irreducible component of Spec(R∞[1/p]) lies in the support of H^{l0}(P∞^□)[1/p]. Part (3) follows immediately."

As printed, the hypothesis can never hold when j > 0 and M := H^{l0}(P∞^□) ≠ 0. H^{l0}(P∞) = M/(z)M with z_1 M-regular (see X-K7-6), so Supp H^{l0}(P∞) ⊂ Supp M ∩ V(ι(z_1)). A minimal prime 𝔭 of R∞ in Supp M is minimal in Supp M, hence lies in Ass M. So ι(z_1) ∉ 𝔭, because z_1 is a nonzerodivisor on M. Hence no irreducible component lies in Supp H^{l0}(P∞)[1/p]. The printed (3) is therefore vacuously true but useless in the case j = n²|T| − 1 > 0 of §9.5. The intended statement is the one the proof gives.

Later uses are unaffected: §9.5 applies Theorem 6.4 to H^{l0}(P∞^{2,□}) with R∞^2 irreducible, which is part (2). Not a bracket error.

issues.locator: §6.1, Theorem 6.4(1), p. 389 (published version)
issues.printed: Part (1) asserts that formal smoothness of R∞ over 𝒪, yielding R ≃ 𝒪[x_1, . . . , x_{q+j−l_0}], makes H free over R.
issues.correction: "(1) If R∞ is formally smooth over 𝒪, so R∞ ≃ 𝒪⟦x_1, …, x_{q+j−l_0}⟧, then H is a free R-module." The change from [ ] to ⟦ ⟧ is one of the 47 known bracket errors. The new point is R → R∞. The conclusion "H is a free R-module" is correct as printed and should stay.
issues.reason:
I checked the rendered PDF page 93 (p. 389), including a 250 dpi crop. Theorem 6.4(1) reads "If R∞ is formally smooth over 𝒪, so R ≃ 𝒪[x_1,…,x_{q+j−l_0}], then H is a free R-module." arXiv v2 (cg-v2.txt, line ~3594) has the same wording, with correct brackets: "so R ≃ O[[x1,…,xq+j−l0]]".

In Theorem 6.3 (p. 386), R∞ and R are separate objects. Hypothesis (1) says R∞ ∈ C_𝒪 has Krull dimension 1+j+q−l_0. Hypothesis (2) says R ∈ C_𝒪 is just some other ring, with an R-module H. Part (iv) on p. 387 gives a surjection φ∞ : R∞ ↠ R. So a formally smooth R∞ is 𝒪⟦x_1,…,x_{q+j−l_0}⟧, since a power series ring over 𝒪 in n variables has dimension 1+n. The proof starts with the correct hypothesis: "Proof Suppose first of all that R∞ ≃ 𝒪[x_1,…,x_{j+q−l_0}]."

As printed, the claim about R is false in general. The proof shows R = R∞/ı(𝔞)R∞, with ker(φ∞) = ı(𝔞)R∞, where 𝔞 is generated by q+j elements. There is also a direct contradiction with the setup. Hypothesis (3) of Thm 6.3 gives H/ϖ ≅ H^{l_0}(T), which is a finite-dimensional k-vector space. Suppose H ≠ 0 were free over R ≅ 𝒪⟦x_1,…,x_m⟧ with m = q+j−l_0 ≥ 1. Then H/ϖ would be free over k⟦x_1,…,x_m⟧ and so infinite-dimensional. So the printed statement only makes sense when q+j = l_0. In the applications R is a Hecke algebra that is finite over 𝒪. The "R" in the "so" clause must therefore be a slip for "R∞". This is not a bracket error; only the [ ] → ⟦ ⟧ part of this line is covered by the 2022 Correction.

Dependence: the text cites Theorem 6.4 only on p. 391 (the paragraph after Prop. 6.6) and on p. 428 (the §9 proof: "by Theorem 6.4 H^{l_0}(P∞^{2,□}) is nearly faithful as an R∞^2-module"). Both uses are of the nearly-faithful parts (2)/(3), not part (1). The proof of (1) already uses the correct hypothesis on R∞, and its conclusion (H free over R, with R = R∞/ı(𝔞)R∞) is correct.

issues.printed: The source assumes S_N/ϖ-isomorphisms H^{l0}(D^1_M ⊗_{S_M} S_N/ϖ) ⟶∼ H^{l0}(D^2_M ⊗_{S_M} S_N/ϖ) for M ≥ N ≥ 0, becoming equivariant under R^1_∞ ⊗_O S^□_N/ϖ ⟶∼ R^2_∞ ⊗_O S^□_N/ϖ after tensoring with O^□ and commuting with the maps to H^1/ϖ ⟶ H^2/ϖ. It claims patched complexes satisfying (i)–(iv) and an R^1_∞/ϖ ⟶∼ R^2_∞/ϖ-isomorphism H^{l0}(P^{1,□}_∞)/ϖ ⟶∼ H^{l0}(P^{2,□}_∞)/ϖ commuting with reduction modulo a+ϖ. The proof is omitted as similar to Theorem 6.3.
issues.correction: Add a compatibility hypothesis. For each M ≥ N ≥ 0 with M ≥ 1, the isomorphism θ_{M,N} at level (M,N), once reduced along S_N/ϖ → S_0/ϖ = O/ϖ (that is, θ_{M,N} ⊗_{S_N} O, which makes sense because H^{l0} is the top degree and so H^{l0}(D_M ⊗ S_N/ϖ) ⊗_{S_N} O = H^{l0}(D_M ⊗ O/ϖ)), should equal θ_{M,0}. Equivalently, the square should also commute when its top arrow is the map induced by θ_{M,N}. The candidate asks instead for compatibility with every natural surjection N → N' ≥ 0. That is a natural, slightly stronger version and it is also correct. Only the case N' = 0 is needed; compatibility across different M is not needed, because pigeonholing takes care of it. Review addition: the conclusion's isomorphism H^{l0}(P^{1,□}_∞)/ϖ ≅ H^{l0}(P^{2,□}_∞)/ϖ must also be linear over (R^1_∞ ⊗̂ S^□_∞)/ϖ ≅ (R^2_∞ ⊗̂ S^□_∞)/ϖ, as hypothesis (3) is, for the top row of its square to be induced.
issues.reason:
I rendered pp. 386–391 and 427–428 and checked them against the patching proof of Thm 6.3 (pp. 387–389).

1. The "same way as Theorem 6.3" proof: build a joint patching datum of level N from (φ^i, ψ^i, P^i) for i=1,2 plus the mod-ϖ isomorphism β, with D_{M,N} carrying β = α_{M,N}. Choose (M_i, N_i) with N_i → ∞ and take limits. The patched β_∞ on H^{l0}(P^1_∞)/ϖ is lim_i α_{M_i,N_i}. By right-exactness of top-degree cohomology, H^{l0}(P_∞)/(a+ϖ) is H^{l0}(D_{M_i}⊗_{S_{M_i}}O/ϖ). So β_∞ mod a equals α_{M_i,N_i}⊗_{S_{N_i}}O, and ψ^i_∞ mod ϖ is the (c) isomorphism of D_{M_i} with n=1.

2. The conclusion square therefore commutes exactly when ψ^2∘(α_{M_i,N_i}⊗O)∘(ψ^1)^{-1} = θ. The hypothesis only gives this for α_{M_i,0}, which never enters the patching because N_i → ∞. Nothing in the statement links α_{M,N} (N ≥ 1) with α_{M,0}. The third bullet only requires R_∞-linearity at each fixed (M,N). The authors state such compatibilities explicitly elsewhere: Thm 6.3 (b) says "compatible with the R_∞-actions" for N ≥ N', and (c) says "compatible for fixed N and varying n". So the omission here looks real, not a convention.

3. Explicit data where every hypothesis holds but the omitted argument gives a square that fails. Take q=1, j=0, l0=0 and R^i_∞ = O[[x,y]]/(y^2), which has dimension 2 = 1+j+q−l0. Take R^i = O, H^i = O^2 and T = k^2. Let D_N = (S_N/ϖ^N)^2 with x acting as [γ]−1 and y as ([γ]−1)·n, where n = [[0,1],[0,0]], and φ_N(x) = φ_N(y) = 0. Conditions (a)–(d) hold, with the same data for i=1,2. Take θ = Id and α_{M,0} = Id, so the square commutes. For N ≥ 1 take α_{M,N} = [[1,1],[0,1]]; this commutes with n, so it is R_∞⊗S_N-linear. The patched β_∞ then reduces to [[1,1],[0,1]] ≠ θ, and the square fails.

Here the literal existential conclusion still holds, because β = Id works. So I have not refuted the statement itself: it is a gap in the omitted proof, not a proven false statement. It does not affect Thm 9.19, where the needed compatibility holds by naturality. Defence attempted, and it fails.

(1) The omitted proof must patch θ as well as the rest. The conclusion needs one isomorphism Θ: H^{l0}(P^1_∞)/ϖ → H^{l0}(P^2_∞)/ϖ. This can only come from the level isomorphisms θ_{M,N}, which have to be added to the level-N patching datum of Theorem 6.3's proof (p. 391). Pigeonholing then picks pairs (M_i, N_i), and Θ is the limit of the θ_{M_i,N_i}. So Θ mod a is θ_{M_i,N_i} ⊗_{S_{N_i}} O.

(2) The vertical maps ψ^i_∞ mod ϖ are the n = 1 isomorphisms of hypothesis (c) for D_{M_i}. This uses (c)'s compatibility "for fixed N and varying n".

(3) The patched square therefore commutes exactly when β∘ψ^1 = ψ^2∘(θ_{M_i,N_i} mod a), where β: H^1/ϖ → H^2/ϖ. The hypothesis only gives this for θ_{M_i,0}. Nothing in the statement links θ_{M,N} to θ_{M,0}. Both are R_∞/ϖ-linear isomorphisms between the same two modules, so they differ by an arbitrary automorphism γ of H^1/ϖ as an R^1_∞/ϖ-module.

(4) The obvious repairs do not work in general. One could twist ψ^1_∞ by γ, but then γ must lift to an automorphism of H^1 as an integral R^1-module. One could twist Θ, but then γ must lift to an automorphism of H^{l0}(P^1_∞)/ϖ as an R_∞/ϖ-module. In general Aut_R(H) → Aut_{R/ϖ}(H/ϖ) and End_{R_∞}(M) → End(M/aM) are not surjective.

(5) A charitable reading does not help. Elsewhere the paper states such compatibilities explicitly: Theorem 6.3(b) covers N ≥ N' and n ≥ n', and (c) says "compatible for fixed N and varying n". Here the square is imposed only for "S_N/ϖ = O/ϖ", i.e. N = 0.

(6) Degenerate check: when q = j = l0 = 0 the conclusion holds trivially, since Θ := ψ^{2,-1}βψ^1 works. I have no counterexample to the statement as printed, so this is recorded as a gap, not an error.

Downstream use: the only use is the proof of Theorem 9.19 (pp. 426–427). There the level isomorphisms are the natural ones H^{l0}(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ) ≅ H^{l0}_χ(Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M), O/ϖ), which exist because χ ≡ 1 mod ϖ. They are functorial in the covers, so they are compatible as N varies and reduce to the N = 0 isomorphism. The paper only says they "give rise to the commutative square required", but the added hypothesis does hold there. Theorem 9.19, and so the main theorems, are unaffected.

issues.printed: Lemma 7.2 claims any γ ∈ G(A^{∞,p}) gives a Hecke action on H_*(X_Δ(Q), O/ϖ^N), N ≤ ∞ with O/ϖ^∞ := O, lifting to T_γ : C → C over R = O[Δ]. The proof regards C(X_K) →^{tr} C(X_{K''}) →^{γ_*} C(X_{K'}) → C(X_K) as R-linear and restricts its composite T̃_γ to C. Section 7.2 similarly takes γ ∈ G(A_F^{∞,p}), constructs T̃_γ through π_1^* ⊗ (φ∘π_2^*) in D^b(R), and lifts to C_n^∨.
issues.correction: Add a hypothesis to Lemma 7.2, and to the Hecke algebra T on p. 393 and the operators T_γ on p. 398: K_Δ(Q)γK_Δ(Q) must be stable under conjugation by K_0(Q), i.e. K_Δ(Q)δ^{-1}γδK_Δ(Q) = K_Δ(Q)γK_Δ(Q) for all δ ∈ K_0(Q). A sufficient condition is that γ commutes with some set of representatives in K_0(Q) of Δ = K_0(Q)/K_Δ(Q). Under this hypothesis the chain map T̃_γ is Δ-equivariant and the proof goes through word for word. The candidate's correction is correct and essentially minimal. The condition "T_γ commutes with Δ on homology" is necessary but does not by itself give a chain-level R-linear map, so the double-coset condition is the natural one to add. It holds for every operator the paper actually uses: good operators at v ∉ S_Q, where K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} and L_Q = ∏_v L_{Q,v}; the diagonal T_{α,k} = T(diag(α,…,α,1,…,1)), V_x and U_x at x ∈ Q in §9, which commute with the diagonal representatives of Δ; the diamond operators; and polynomials in these, such as the projectors P_x and P_i on pp. 394–395.
issues.reason:
R = O[Δ] acts on X_Δ(Q) = X_K by right translation by δ ∈ K_0(Q), which normalizes K = K_Δ(Q). If KγK is the disjoint union of the cosets γ_i K, then r_δ^{-1} T_γ r_δ sends xK to the sum of the x δ^{-1}γ_i δ K. So conjugating T_γ by δ gives T_{δ^{-1}γδ}, which in general is a different operator. If T_γ does not commute with Δ on H_*(X_Δ(Q), A), then no R-linear chain map C → C can induce it. The lemma allows any γ ∈ G(A^{∞,p}), and that includes components at the places v ∈ Q (they do not divide p).

Counterexample inside the paper's own §9 setting, with n = 2. At v ∈ Q, K_{Q,v} is the Iwahori subgroup and L_{Q,v} is the kernel of the character [[a,b],[c,d]] ↦ d/a mod π_v. The Atkin–Lehner element w = [[0,1],[π_v,0]] satisfies w^{-1}[[a,b],[c,d]]w = [[d, c/π_v],[bπ_v, a]]. So w normalizes K_{Q,v} and L_{Q,v}, K w K = wK, and T_w is right translation by w (K' = K'' = K and tr = id in the paper's proof). Since w^{-1} diag(a,b) w = diag(b,a), we get T_w⟨t⟩ = ⟨t^{-1}⟩T_w. Because w² is central, T_w is invertible. If T_w were R-linear, then ⟨t⟩ = ⟨t^{-1}⟩, so ⟨t⟩² = 1. Δ has odd p-power order, so Δ would act trivially on H_*.

But Δ does act nontrivially. Classical check: q = 31, p = 5, Δ = Z/5. By the dimension formula, dim S_2(31, χ) = 8/3 − 2/3 − 1 = 1 for each of the 4 characters χ of order 5. As a consistency check, 2·2 + 4·1 + 8·2 = 24 = g(X_1(31)) − g(X_0(31)) = 26 − 2. So H_1(Y_Δ, O) ⊗ E has χ-isotypic pieces with χ ≠ 1, and Lemma 7.2 fails for γ = w (N = ∞, or N large). Adding auxiliary level at another prime to make the quotient neat changes nothing.

The step of the proof that fails is the implicit claim that C(X_K) → C(X_{K''}) → C(X_{K'}) → C(X_K) is a diagram "of complexes of R-modules". Δ need not act on X_{K'} or X_{K''}, and even when it does, the maps need not be equivariant. The same unjustified R-linearity occurs in §7.2, where the pullback to Y^γ is treated as a morphism in D^b(R).

The paper is aware that the condition matters: p. 395 requires P_x to "commute with the action of the diamond operators". All operators actually used satisfy the condition: diagonal g in §9.2 commutes with torus representatives of Δ. So no main theorem is affected. I class this as an error in the stated generality, not merely a gap, because the lemma as printed is false for some allowed γ. Defence attempted and failed. An R-linear chain map C → C induces an R-linear map on H_*(C) = H_*(X_Δ(Q), A), and the R-action there is the Δ-action by right translation, because the map C → C(X_Δ(Q)) of Lemma 7.1 is R-linear. So the lemma forces T_γ to commute with Δ. Lemma 7.2 is stated for every γ ∈ G(A^{∞,p}), and that is false.

Counterexample inside the paper's own §9 setting. Take n = 2, x ∈ Q, and γ = w = (0 1; π_x 0) at x, trivial elsewhere (x ∤ p, so w ∈ G(A^{∞,p})). A direct computation gives w (a b; πc d) w^{-1} = (d c; πb a). So w normalizes K_{Q,x} (the Iwahori) and L_{Q,x} = {d/a ≡ 1}, and it acts on Δ by δ ↦ δ^{-1}. Hence K' = K'' = K and T_w = w_* is right translation, with w_*∘r_δ = r_{δ^{-1}}∘w_*. Also w^2 = π·I, which is central, so T_w is invertible. R-linearity would then force r_{δ^2} = id on H_*(X_Δ(Q), O). For p odd, δ ↦ δ^2 is bijective on Δ = (Z/p^N)^q, so Δ would act trivially on H_*(X_Δ(Q), O). Taking transfer, dim H_*(X_Δ, K) = dim H_*(X_0, K). That is false in general. For example, with F = Q allowed by the general setting of §7.1, the Euler characteristic gives χ(X_Δ) = |Δ|·χ(X_0) ≠ χ(X_0). In any case, patching needs Δ to act nontrivially.

The failing step in the proof is the claim that T̃_γ is a map of complexes of R-modules. C(X_{K'}) and C(X_{K''}) carry no Δ-action. Computed out, T̃_γ(σ) = Σ_{hK ⊂ KγK} σ·h. This commutes with r_δ exactly when δKγK = KγKδ, which is the candidate's condition. Under that condition the rest of the proof (Tag 08FQ over R) is fine.

The authors evidently meant only operators that commute with Δ: p. 394 says "In practice, the Hecke algebra T will be of the form T^an[U_x : x ∈ Q]", and p. 395 says "a projector P_x which commutes with the action of the diamond operators". The intro to §7.2 on p. 395 speaks of "'good' Hecke operators … together with certain operators at the primes in Q". §7.2 (pp. 398–400) has the same unrestricted γ, and its "element of the right hand side" in D^b(R) likewise needs Δ-equivariance.

Downstream uses:
- Lemma 7.3, Lemma 7.4 and the choice of T on pp. 394–395 use only operators that satisfy the condition.
- §9 (p. 425: "By Conjecture B and the results of Sect. 7.1") uses T_{Q,ψ}, which is generated by diagonal g (Def. 9.1), so the condition holds there.
- §7.2 feeds no stated theorem.

So Lemma 7.2 is false as stated and needs the added hypothesis. No later theorem changes.

issues.locator: §7.1, proof of Lemma 7.1, p. 392 (published version)
issues.printed: The proof invokes [43, Sect. II.5 Lemma 1] for a perfect R-complex C and a quasi-isomorphism C → C(X_Δ(Q)), saying its last flat term is free because R is local. It then uses boundedness and flatness of both complexes to claim H_*(C ⊗_R A) ⥲ H_*(C(X_Δ(Q)) ⊗_R A) for each algebra A over R, by Lemma 2. Here perfect means bounded finite free, while C(Y) denotes O-valued singular chains.
issues.correction:
The singular chain complex C(X_Δ(Q)) is not bounded. It is non-zero in every homological degree i ≥ 0, so it is bounded only below homologically (bounded above cohomologically). Mumford's Lemma 1 therefore does not apply to it as the paper claims. The minimal repair adds finite-dimensionality, which is available in the §7 setting ("covering space X_Δ(Q) → X_0(Q) of manifolds").

Route (a), which makes Lemma 1 unnecessary: Δ acts freely on the Borel–Serre compactification, a compact manifold with boundary. It is Δ-equivariantly homotopy equivalent to a copy of itself inside X_Δ(Q), obtained by removing a collar. Lift a finite triangulation of the quotient. The simplicial chains then form a bounded complex C of finite free R-modules, with a Δ-equivariant quasi-isomorphism C → C(X_Δ(Q)).

Route (b): use dim X_0(Q) = d. Then H_i(C(X_Δ(Q)) ⊗_R M) = H_i(X_0(Q), local system M) = 0 for i > d and every R-module M. So the truncation τ_{≤d}C(X_Δ(Q)) is a bounded complex of flat modules with finitely generated homology. Apply Lemma 1 to it. The resulting map P → τ_{≤d}C lifts to P → C(X_Δ(Q)) because P is a bounded complex of projectives.

In the next sentence, replace "bounded" by "bounded below (homologically)". Mumford's Lemma 2 still holds for such complexes by its mapping-cone proof: an exact complex of flat modules that is bounded above cohomologically has flat cycle modules. The finite generation of H_*(X_Δ(Q), O) is also needed and is not stated; it is standard via Borel–Serre.

The "since R is local" remark needs no change. The §7 introduction (p. 391) fixes Δ = (Z/p^N Z)^q, and in any case a finitely generated flat R-module is projective. That is perfect in the sense of the Notation on p. 306.
issues.reason:
I rendered PDF pages 95–96 and read them; the quoted sentence is exactly as printed, and v2 has the same wording. In the same paragraph the paper uses "bounded" in the two-sided sense: "a perfect complex ... we mean a bounded complex of finite free R-modules". It also defines C(Y) as the complex of O-valued singular chains, which is non-zero in every degree ≥ 0 whenever Y is non-empty. So the statement that C(X_Δ(Q)) is bounded is false under the paper's own definitions. This is not one of the 47 known bracket errors (R = O[Δ] is a genuine finite group ring). The flatness claim is fine: the covering group acts freely, so C_i(X_Δ(Q)) is R-free. I re-derived the key step: a quasi-isomorphism between complexes of flat modules that are bounded below homologically stays a quasi-isomorphism after any base change (mapping cone plus flat cycle modules). So the displayed isomorphism, and both isomorphisms in Lemma 7.1, hold. The proposed correction is right in substance. I could not check the exact wording of Mumford's hypotheses (no copy was available). I am fairly, not fully, sure Lemma 2 there is stated with only K^p = K'^p = 0 for p > n; either way the argument works. I classify this as a minor error, not a misprint, and set "affects" to "the proof" rather than "nothing". The reason is that the same false boundedness is what the proof silently relies on when it cites Mumford Lemma 1 to get a bounded (perfect) C. For an unbounded complex, perfectness does not follow from a lemma about complexes alone; it needs the geometric finite-dimensionality argument described in the correction. The statement of Lemma 7.1 is true. Everything later (Lemma 7.2, the rest of §7.1, the patching in §9) uses only that statement, so no stated result is affected. I rendered PDF pp. 95–98 and read them; the text is exactly as quoted. The paper's own conventions rule out a charitable reading. "Bounded" is two-sided: the Notation on p. 306 defines a perfect complex as a "bounded complex of finitely generated projective R-modules", and the definition just before Lemma 7.1 uses "bounded" the same way. C(Y) is explicitly singular chains, which has a non-zero term in every degree ≥ 0. So the claim that C(X_Δ(Q)) is bounded is false.

Mumford's Lemma 1 requires K^p ≠ 0 only for 0 ≤ p ≤ n. I checked the statement and proof as reproduced in Schnell's lecture notes (Stony Brook MAT615, Lecture 9, Lemma 9.5, credited to Mumford's book). The construction is a descending induction, and the flat "final term" K^0 is a fibre product that uses the fact that nothing lies below degree 0. On a complex that is unbounded in that direction, the induction never ends.

The step is not merely missing a routine citation. As written, it uses only that the map is a covering with group Δ and that the homology is finitely generated. Those two facts would equally "prove" the claim for EZ/p → BZ/p, with Δ = Z/p and R = O[Z/p] local. There C(EZ/p) is a free R-complex with homology O in degree 0. It is not quasi-isomorphic to any perfect complex: otherwise Ext^i_R(O, k) = H^i(Z/p, k) would vanish for large i, but it is k for every i. So the missing ingredient is the finite-dimensional manifold structure of X_0(Q). The §7 setting assumes it, but the proof never uses it.

The rest of the passage is fine. The second sentence (Lemma 2) is correct once "bounded" is read as bounded below homologically. The objection in X-K7-13 that "since R is local" is unjustified does not hold: the §7 introduction on p. 391 says Δ has the form (Z/p^N Z)^q. The explicit "We now assume that Δ is of p-power order. Thus R = O[Δ] is local" on p. 394 only repeats this after the "somewhat general situation".

Consequences: the statement of Lemma 7.1 is true in the paper's setting, by either route in the correction. Everything later uses only that statement: Lemma 7.2 (lifting T_γ through the quasi-isomorphism C → C(X_K) because C is perfect), Lemmas 7.3 and 7.4, the complex D on p. 395, and §9 on p. 425 ("By Conjecture B and the results of Sect. 7.1, there exists a perfect complex D_N ..."). So only the proof of Lemma 7.1 is affected; no stated result is. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors, because R = O[Δ] is a genuine finite group ring.

issues.reason: I checked the rendered page at 300 dpi and the v2 page image, and the transcription above is exact. In §7.1 (p. 392), C(Y) is defined as "the complex of O-valued singular chains on Y", so C is covariant and γ∗ on chains goes the same way as the map of spaces. The paper states γ : X_{K′} → X_{K′′}, and I checked this myself. If g ↦ gγ and k′ ∈ K′, then gk′γ = gγ(γ^{−1}k′γ), and γ^{−1}K′γ = γ^{−1}(γKγ^{−1} ∩ K)γ = K ∩ γ^{−1}Kγ = K′′. So γ∗ maps C(X_{K′}) → C(X_{K′′}). The printed chain line instead has an arrow labelled γ∗ going C(X_{K′′}) → C(X_{K′}). No map in the paper goes that way. The closest valid reading uses right multiplication by γ^{−1} (X_{K′′} → X_{K′}). The composite would then be transfer to K′′, then γ^{−1}, then projection, which is the operator [Kγ^{−1}K], not T_γ. So the printed line is not "the corresponding composition" of the homology line, which does go through K′ first and then K′′ (transfer to K′ ⊂ K, γ∗ to K′′, projection since K′′ ⊂ K). issues.locator: §7.1, proof of Lemma 7.2, last sentences, published p. 393 (PDF p. 97). arXiv v2 has the same wording ("Since C is perfect, the morphism T̃_γ can be lifted to a morphism T_γ : C → C making the diagram commute. (See [Sta14, Tag 08FQ] for example.)"). arXiv v1 has no Lemma 7.2 in this form. The '§7.2, p. 400' part of the candidate is not a mistake. On p. 400 (PDF p. 104) the diagram is explicitly in D^b(R), and the text only says Tag 08FQ lifts T̃_γ "to a morphism of complexes T_γ : C_n^∨ → C_n^∨ that induces the operator T_γ on cohomology". That is correct.
issues.printed: The source calls the diagram R-linear with a vertical quasi-isomorphism. It says perfection of C allows T̃_γ to lift to T_γ : C → C so the diagram commutes, citing [70, Tag 08FQ].
issues.correction: '... can be lifted to a morphism T_γ : C → C making the diagram commute up to homotopy (equivalently, in the homotopy category K(R))'. This is minimal and suffices for everything later. Because C is a bounded complex of finite free modules, Hom_{K(R)}(C, C) → Hom_{K(R)}(C, C(X_K)) is bijective. So a lift exists that is unique up to homotopy, and it induces q_*^{-1} ∘ T_γ ∘ q_* on H_*(C ⊗ A) for every A = O/ϖ^N, since a homotopy survives tensoring.
issues.reason:
Rendered p. 393 and transcribed the passage above. The diagram is the triangle C --T̃_γ--> C(X_K) <--s-- C, described as a diagram "of complexes of R-modules", so "commute" literally means s∘T_γ = T̃_γ on the nose.
(1) The cited reference only gives homotopy. Stacks Tag 08FQ (Lemma 21.44.7, strictly perfect complexes) ends with "a dotted arrow ... making the diagram commute up to homotopy". Perfectness of C makes Hom^•(C,C) → Hom^•(C,C(X_K)) a quasi-isomorphism, which lifts cycles only up to boundaries (homotopy). It does not lift them strictly.
(2) The strict claim is false in general. Over any ring R, take P = R in degree 0 and M with M_1 = R, M_0 = R², d(a) = (a,0). Let s(1) = (0,1), which is a quasi-isomorphism since the cokernel is contractible. Let f(1) = (1,0), which is a chain map. Then s∘g = (0,g(1)) ≠ (1,0) for every g : P → P, so no strict lift exists, although f = d∘h ≃ 0 = s∘0. A strict lift would need, e.g., a surjective quasi-isomorphism, and s cannot be surjective: C is finite free while C(X_K) is free on uncountably many simplices.
(3) The strict claim also fails for some C that is "as in Lemma 7.1". Given any valid (C,s), add the contractible summand R --id--> R in degrees 1,0. Send its generators to a path σ from x to y and to y − x, extended R-linearly. The result is still a perfect complex with a quasi-isomorphism. For generic points x, y, the degree-0 chain T̃_γ(y − x) is supported on Hecke translates of x and y that lie outside the finite support of s(C_0) + R(y−x). So T̃_γ∘s does not factor through s.
Classification: the lemma's statement (the action on homology lifts to a chain map C → C) is true. The homotopy-commutative lift proves it, and later uses (polynomials in the T_γ, Lemma 7.3) need only an endomorphism of C inducing T_γ on homology. The missing "up to homotopy" is a slip whose intended meaning is clear from the cited Tag 08FQ, which states it. I therefore class it as a misprint (wording slip) with affects = nothing, rather than a substantive error. 1) The cited source gives only the weaker statement. Stacks Tag 08FQ is Lemma 21.44.7 (Cohomology on Sites, 'Strictly perfect complexes'). Its conclusion is a dotted arrow 'making the diagram commute up to homotopy', and the proof works in the homotopy category. So the paper's own citation supports only commutativity up to homotopy.

2) Strict commutativity is false in general. Toy example: C = R in degree 0; D_1 = R, D_0 = R⊕R with d(x) = (0,x); q(r) = (r,0), which is a quasi-isomorphism; f(r) = (0,r), which is a chain map. No g : C → C has q∘g = f, since f(C) is not contained in q(C). A strict lift needs something like a surjective quasi-isomorphism. Here q : C → C(X_K) goes from a finitely generated complex into singular chains, which are free of huge rank, so it is never surjective.

3) Strictness also fails for some C that Lemma 7.1 allows, and Lemma 7.2 is stated for any such C. Take any (C, q). Add the contractible summand R e_1 → R e_0 (d e_1 = e_0), sending e_1 to a singular 1-simplex σ and e_0 to ∂σ. This is still perfect with a quasi-isomorphism to C(X_K). Choose σ generic, away from the finite support of q(C_1), its Δ-translates, and the points fixed by the correspondence. Then T̃_γ(σ) is a nonzero positive combination of simplices, none of them in q(C_1) + Rσ, so no strict lift exists (for T_γ not the trivial correspondence).

Defence considered. The paper has no convention that diagrams of complexes commute up to homotopy. The diagram is explicitly one 'of complexes of R-modules', while §7.2 is careful to say 'in D^b(R)'. So as printed the sentence overstates, though the intent (up to homotopy) is clear from the citation. This could also be classed as a misprint.

Consequences. Lemma 7.2 itself only asks for a chain map lifting the action on homology, and the homotopy version gives exactly that. What uses the lift: expressing T ∈ T as a (not necessarily commutative) polynomial in the lifted T_γ; Lemma 7.3 (H_*(lim T^n C) = lim T^n H_*(C) by exactness); Lemma 7.4; the D at the end of §7.1 (H_n(D ⊗ O/ϖ^N) ≅ H_n(X_Δ(Q), O/ϖ^N)_m and so on); and §9's use of 'Sect. 7.1' (p. 431). All of these only need the induced maps on homology of C ⊗ A, and those are the same for homotopic maps. Nothing needs q∘T_γ = T̃_γ∘q on the nose, or the lifts to commute with one another. So no stated result is affected.

issues.locator: §7.1, Lemma 7.4, second sentence, p. 394 (published version)
issues.printed: Lemma 7.4 bounds D’s length by l_0, the cohomological range where lim_→ T^n H^*(C) is nonzero. Its proof invokes Mumford [43], Chap. II.5, Lemma 1 to choose perfect K of length l_0 quasi-isomorphic to C_T. A differential d on D nonzero modulo 𝔪_R from n + 1 to n is then said, by Nakayama, to yield K ≃ L ⊕ J as perfect R-complexes.
issues.correction: Replace the "Moreover" sentence with: "Moreover, if H_n(C_T ⊗_R R/𝔪_R) = lim_→ T^m H_n(X_0(Q), k) vanishes for n outside an interval of length l_0, then D is concentrated in that interval, so its length is at most l_0." This follows at once from the first part of the lemma, and it is enough for the mod-ϖ homology of X_Δ(Q) to vanish outside that interval. Integral vanishing alone only gives length(D) ≤ l_0 + 1. In the proof, the Mumford sentence should not claim length l_0. (The 'd on D' slip is E149.)
issues.reason:
I checked the page image and the v2 text. As printed, the lemma defines l_0 through the integral groups lim_→ T^n H^*(C), where C is the integral chain complex from Lemma 7.1. The paper uses "range/length l_0" to mean degrees q_0..q_0+l_0, so length means max − min.

The first part of the lemma, which is correct (the minimal-complex / Nakayama argument), forces dim D_n/𝔪_R = dim H_n(C_T ⊗ k). So D_n ≠ 0 whenever the mod-𝔪 homology is non-zero in degree n. Universal coefficients give 0 → H_n(C)⊗k → H_n(C⊗k) → Tor_1(H_{n-1}(C),k) → 0, so torsion in the top integral degree produces mod-ϖ homology one degree higher.

Counterexample (redone): take R = O (Δ trivial, which is of p-power order), T = 1, and C = [O --ϖ--> O] in degrees 1, 0. Then H_1(C) = 0 and H_0(C) = O/ϖ, so the integral range is 0. But C⊗k = [k --0--> k] has H_1 = H_0 = k. Any D as in the lemma must have rank 1 in degrees 1 and 0, so its length is 1 > 0.

A geometric instance: a Bianchi manifold with a non-Eisenstein 𝔪 such that H_1(X,O)_𝔪 is non-zero torsion. Then H_2(X,O)_𝔪 = 0, by Poincaré duality, vanishing boundary cohomology at 𝔪, and torsion-freeness of H^1. But H_2(X,k)_𝔪 ⊇ Tor(H_1,k) ≠ 0. The proof's claim that Mumford gives K "bounded of length l_0" fails for the same reason: any perfect complex quasi-isomorphic to C_T contains the minimal one as a summand.

"d on D" is a slip for "d on K", since D is only produced at the end of the induction.

Downstream: the bullets after the lemma on p. 395 use only the first part ("D_n ≠ 0 iff H_n(X_0(Q),k)_𝔪 ≠ 0"). §9.5 (p. 425) gets "D_N concentrated in degrees q_0,…,q_0+l_0" from Conjecture B(4)(a), which is stated with O/ϖ^m coefficients (reducible to k by dévissage, p. 413). So the main theorems are unaffected. Only the "Moreover" clause of Lemma 7.4 and its proof are wrong. The Correction (Invent. Math. 227) fixes brackets only, so this is not one of the 47 known bracket errors. DEFENCE ATTEMPTS
(1) The paper's convention, from the intro ("concentrated in l_0+1 consecutive degrees", "range of length l_0") and §9.5 ("q_0,...,q_0+l_0"), is that length = max − min. Counting terms instead makes no difference: the counterexample below fails under both conventions. It survives only if l_0 counts degrees while length(D) is max − min, and nothing in the paper supports mixing them like that.
(2) Standing hypothesis. §7 opens by saying that the cohomology localised at 𝔪 "is assumed to vanish outside a range of length l_0". Conjecture B(4)(a) is stated with O/ϖ^m coefficients, reducing to k by dévissage (p. 413). If that were the hypothesis, the lemma would be true. But the lemma defines l_0 itself, through the integral groups lim_→ T^n H^*(C). Here C is the O[Δ]-perfect complex of Lemma 7.1, quasi-isomorphic to C(X_Δ(Q)), so these are integral groups. They do not control the mod-𝔪 range.
(3) Reading H^* as cohomology of the dual complex does not help either (see below).

WHY THE PRINTED STATEMENT IS FALSE
The first part of the lemma is correct (minimal complex plus Nakayama). It gives D_n ≠ 0 exactly when H_n(C_T ⊗ k) ≠ 0. Universal coefficients give 0 → H_n(C_T)⊗k → H_n(C_T⊗k) → Tor_1(H_{n-1}(C_T),k) → 0, so torsion in the top integral degree creates mod-ϖ homology one degree higher.
- Abstract example: R = O (Δ trivial), T = 1, C = [O --ϖ--> O] in degrees 1, 0. The integral homology is O/ϖ in degree 0 only (range 0). But C⊗k has k in degrees 1 and 0, so every D satisfying the first part has length 1.
- Geometric example (Bianchi): Q empty, 𝔪 non-Eisenstein, H_1(X,O)_𝔪 non-zero torsion with no characteristic-zero classes at 𝔪 (the torsion phenomenon the paper is built around). Then H_0(X,O)_𝔪 = 0. Also H_2(X,O)_𝔪 = 0: it is torsion-free because X is homotopy equivalent to a 2-complex, and rationally it is H^1_c = H^1 at 𝔪, which is 0. So the integral homology sits in degree 1 only (range 0). But H_2(X,k)_𝔪 ⊇ Tor(H_1,k) ≠ 0, so length(D) = 1.
- Cohomology reading: with cohomology (or the dual complex), the torsion moves to degree 2 alone, so the range is again 0.
- General bound: over the depth-1 ring O[Δ], the bottom degree of D equals the bottom degree of H(C_T). Above the top homology degree, the complex is a finite free resolution of a submodule of a free module, which is free by Auslander–Buchsbaum. So length(D) ≤ l_0 + 1, and this is sharp.
- The proof's first sentence fails too: Mumford's Lemma 1 bounds K by the degree range of the complex it starts from, not by its homology. Any perfect complex quasi-isomorphic to C_T contains the minimal D as a direct summand, so no such K of length l_0 exists in the examples above.

CONSEQUENCES
- The bullets right after the lemma (p. 395) use only the first part ("D_n ≠ 0 iff H_n(X_0(Q),k)_𝔪 ≠ 0").
- §7.2 (the coherent case) does not use the "Moreover" clause.
- The only later use is §9.5 (p. 425): "By Conjecture B and the results of Sect. 7.1, there exists a perfect complex D̃_N ... concentrated in degrees q_0,...,q_0+l_0". That conclusion is true, because Conjecture B(4)(a) gives mod-ϖ vanishing, and together with the first part of Lemma 7.4 this yields the corrected clause. The main theorems are therefore unaffected. Only the "Moreover" clause of Lemma 7.4 and the corresponding proof step are wrong.

This is not one of the 47 bracket errors: the Correction (Invent. Math. 227) fixes brackets only.

VERDICT ON THE PROPOSED CORRECTIONS
Both are right and minimal. The X-K7-18 wording is good. H-part2-9 adds the correct "d on D → d on K" fix. I classify this as an error rather than a misprint because both the printed statement and a proof step fail.

It discusses Pontryagin duals with coefficients E/O, but writes H^{q_0}(X, 𝓔/O)^∨_m for the Betti group identified with H_{q_0+l_0}(X, O)_m. issues.correction: Replace E and 𝓔 with K, the fraction field of O from the Notation section (p. 305): 'minimal polynomial over K of the Teichmüller lift of φ_n(T_i) to \overline{K}', 'coefficients in K/O', 'H^{q_0}(X, K/O)^∨_m' and 'taking coefficients of our sheaves in K/O'.
issues.reason: The Notation section (p. 305) makes O the ring of integers of a finite extension K of Q_p. The paper writes K/O elsewhere, e.g. ω_{K/O} in §3 and H^{q_0}(Y, K/O)^∨_m in Thm 9.19 on p. 426. The only other E in the paper is a local finite extension of Q_p inside a proof in §6 (p. ~367), so E is undefined in §7. The script 𝓔 is the automorphic vector bundle of §7.2 (p. 395). issues.locator: §7.2, p. 395 (published version)
issues.printed: The source specifies an étale cover Y = X_Δ(Q) → X = X_0(Q), whose group is finite abelian p-group Δ. It then places an automorphic bundle ℰ on Y, using a canonical or subcanonical extension in the toroidal setting, and says its pullback is a bundle on X also named ℰ.
issues.correction: "We will be given an automorphic vector bundle ℰ on X (in the case of a toroidal compactification, this will either be a canonical or subcanonical extension) which pulls back to a bundle also denoted by ℰ on Y." An equivalent fix keeps "ℰ on Y" and says "which is the pullback of a bundle also denoted by ℰ on X".
issues.reason:
This is a genuine swap of X and Y. The only map in the setup is f : Y = X_Δ(Q) → X = X_0(Q). On p. 397 (PDF p. 101) the paper restates it as "f : Y → X is an étale map of smooth proper O-schemes". Pullback along f therefore goes from bundles on X to bundles on Y, so a bundle on Y cannot "pull back to" a bundle on X. The rest of the paper uses ℰ the corrected way:
(i) On p. 398 (PDF p. 102) the paper sets ℱ = ℰ^* ⊗_{O_X} ω_X, "a coherent sheaf of O_X-modules". For this to make sense, ℰ has to live on X.
(ii) The Čech complex D computes H^i(Y, f^*ℱ). The paper then says its dual computes H_i(Y, ℰ⊗O/ϖ^n) := H^i(Y, ℰ^*⊗_{O_Y} ω_Y ⊗ O/ϖ^n)^∨. Here ℰ on Y means f^*ℰ.
(iii) On p. 398 the Verdier-duality line reads H^{d-i}(Y, Hom_{O_Y}(f^*ℱ, ω_Y)_A) = H^{d-i}(Y, (f^*ℰ)_A). This explicitly treats ℰ on Y as the pullback f^*ℰ.
I redid the computation. Since f is étale, f^*Ω^1_X ≅ Ω^1_Y, so f^*ω_X ≅ ω_Y. Hence f^*ℱ ≅ (f^*ℰ)^* ⊗ ω_Y, and because f^*ℰ is locally free, Hom(f^*ℱ, ω_Y) ≅ f^*ℰ. Both the corrected sentence and the identification f^*ℱ = ℰ^*⊗ω_Y on Y are consistent. The slip is not one of the 47 known bracket errors. The same text appears in arXiv v2, so it is an authors' slip, not a typesetting defect.
