I confirmed the printed text from the rendered p. 861. The only justification given is the citation of [75], Yamauchi, 'The weight reduction of mod p Siegel modular forms for GSp4'. That source works mod p: its operators involve the Hasse invariant, which exists only in characteristic p. No construction over O/ϖ^m is given for m ≥ 2 with p ≠ 0 in O/ϖ^m, and the claim is false there.

(a) Elliptic analogue. θ does not send forms mod p^2 of weight k to weight k+p+1. Katz's weight congruences show that θf mod p^m has weight ≡ k+2 mod (p−1)p^{m−1} whenever θf ≢ 0 mod p (Chen–Kiming). I checked this for p=5: θE6 is congruent to a form in M_12 = <E4^3, Δ> modulo 5 but not modulo 25.

(b) The Siegel case, computed directly. I coded the degree-2 Siegel Eisenstein coefficients from Cohen's H(k−1,N), with checks E4: 13440, 30240; E6: 44352, 166320. Level-1 forms of weight w are spanned by monomials in E4, E6, E10 and E12. I took p=5 and F=E6, which is 5-integral. The hypotheses allow this: Thm 8.10 explicitly admits k=p+1=6, and Prop 8.9 holds with j=8. ΘF is not ≡ 0 mod 5: at T=[[1,1/2],[1/2,1]] the coefficient is (3/4)·44352 = 33264 ≡ 4 mod 5.

For each weight I computed the saturated 5-adic span of the weight-w forms restricted to the 477 matrices T with n,m ≤ 6. Failure of this test is a rigorous obstruction, and a positive control passes. Results:
- ΘE6 ≡ a weight-12 form mod 5, consistent with Böcherer–Nagaoka and Yamauchi.
- ΘE6 is not congruent mod 25 to any 5-integral level-1 form of weight 12, and it also fails in weights 28 and 32.
- It passes mod 25 only in weight 48 = 6+2+2·20. This matches the Chen–Kiming-type shift 2+2p^{m−1}(p−1).
So with O=Z_5 and m=2, the map asserted in Prop 8.9(1) and Thm 8.10 cannot exist at level 1.

At any prime-to-p level, including X_1(Q), a weight-(12,12) form mod 25 with this q-expansion would give a function on the irreducible Igusa tower. Ichikawa/Katz-type weight congruences would then force 12 ≡ 8 (the p-adic weight of ΘE6) mod 20, which is false.

(c) Nothing downstream breaks. The proofs of Thms 8.10 and 8.11 immediately reduce to m=1, and all uses (§8.8, Prop. 8.25 with Thm 8.11) are over k. So the mistake is confined to the stated generality of Prop 8.9 and Thms 8.10–8.11. It is best classed as an error, a false statement for m ≥ 2, rather than a gap. The computations in (b) were done by a short computer enumeration. DEFENCE ATTEMPTED AND FAILED.
(a) The cited source works only mod p. Yamauchi arXiv:1410.7894v5, §3, begins: "In this section we will define various θ-operators on the space of mod p Siegel modular forms". Prop. 3.9 reads: "Recall the Hasse invariant H_{p−1} = det A ∈ H^0(S_{N,p}, ω^{p−1}). Put Θ := H_{p−1}·Θ̃ ... (1) Let F ∈ M_k(Γ(N), F_p) ... (a) Θ(F) ∈ M_{k+p+1}(Γ(N), F_p)". Prop. 3.12 says: "If F ∈ M_k(Γ(N), F_p), then θ_1^k(F) ∈ M_{(k1+p−1,k2+p+1)}(Γ(N), F_p)". Here S_{N,p} is a component of S_K(N) ⊗ F_p. So the construction needs the characteristic-p Hasse invariant and the Frobenius splitting. The other reference, [27] Flander, is also "(mod p)". Nothing in the paper or in its sources builds Θ or θ_1 over O/ϖ^m when p ≠ 0 there.
(b) One partial defence holds. If m ≤ e, then O/ϖ^m = k[ϖ]/(ϖ^m) is flat over F_p, and Yamauchi's maps extend by base change. So the statement is true in that case, but not for general m.
(c) For m > e the statement is false. Example: p ≥ 11, O = Z_p, m = 2, F = the degree-2 Siegel Eisenstein series E_4, pulled back to X_1(Q). Take k = 4 and j = 6, which satisfies the hypotheses. Cohen's formula gives a(E_4; n,r,m = 1,1,1) = 13440; direct computation also gives 30240 for (1,0,1). So the coefficient of ΘE_4 at Q = [[1,1/2],[1/2,1]] is (3/4)·13440 = 10080 = 2^5·3^2·5·7, a p-unit, and ΘE_4 ≢ 0 mod p.
- Böcherer–Nagaoka (arXiv:1305.0604, Thm 4.1 and Cor. 4.9) show ΘE_4 ≡ F mod p^m with F of weight k+(p−1)p^{m−1} and ρ = det^2. So ΘE_4 is a p-adic Siegel form of weight k+2.
- Suppose G were a mod-p^2 form of weight k+p+1 with the same q-expansion. By the q-expansion principle on the Igusa tower, G and ΘE_4 would agree there, with G transforming by det^{k+p+1} and ΘE_4 by det^{k+2}. Take t a primitive root mod p^2; then t^{p−1} = 1 + p·u with u a unit. This forces p·ΘE_4 ≡ 0 mod p^2, i.e. ΘE_4 ≡ 0 mod p, a contradiction.
- The same happens for elliptic forms: Chen–Kiming (Mathematika 62, 2016) prove θ mod p^m has weight shift 2 + 2p^{m−1}(p−1), which is optimal in some cases when m ≥ 2.
- A sanity check matches the known mod-p kernel: the coefficients of ΘE_4 above all vanish mod 5 and mod 7, as expected because 4 = p−1 (for p = 5) and 4 = (p+1)/2 (for p = 7).
So the maps in Proposition 8.9 do not exist over O/ϖ^m for m > e. Theorems 8.10 and 8.11 are then ill-posed for such m, since they "reduce to m = 1" a map that does not exist.
CONSEQUENCES. Only the mod-ϖ versions are used later:
- The proof of Theorem 8.13 says (p. 865) "we may work with coefficients over a finite field k = O/ϖ", with M = H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j,2)_k)_m on p. 867.
- §8.8 (p. 874) applies Theorem 8.10 to F − X_2F ∈ M over k.
- Proposition 8.25 is stated "modulo p" and is combined with Theorem 8.11 on p. 877.
- Remark 8.23 only mentions Θ.
Theorem 8.13, Theorem 9.1 and the appendix are unaffected; the appendix never uses Θ.

issues.locator: §8.4, proof of Theorem 8.11, p. 862; the argument continues to p. 863. In arXiv:1907.08691v1 it is the proof of Theorem 8.11, pp. 45–46.
issues.printed: The source sets X = X_1(Q), assigns Y to the rank 1 strata, Z to the supersingular locus and S to the superspecial locus, and assumes F has nonzero restriction to Y.
issues.correction:
Read Y as V(h), the closed non-ordinary locus. Then insert: "If F|_Y = 0 then F = hG with G ∈ H^0(X, ω(j−p+1, 3−p)_k), and this group is 0." Also give a reason for "The first term vanishes", which is H^0(X, ω(j−m, 2−m)_k) = 0.

Both follow from one lemma: if a ≥ b and pa − b < 0, then H^0(X, ω(a,b)_k) = 0.

Proof of the lemma, using only what the paper already uses:
1. On each supersingular P^1, ω(a,b) = Sym^{a−b}E ⊗ det^b with E = O(−1)⊕O(p) and det E = O(p−1). So it is a sum of line bundles of degree at most pa − b < 0, and a section vanishes on Z.
2. Z is cut out in V(h) by s ∈ H^0(ω^m). Dividing by s changes pa − b by −(p−1)m, and dividing by h changes it by −(p−1)^2, so the condition is preserved. By Krull, the section is divisible by every power of s on V(h), and then by every power of h on X, so it is 0.

For (j−p+1, 3−p) we get pa − b = p(j+2−p) − 3 < 0. For (j−m, 2−m) we get pa − b = pj − 2 − (p−1)m < 0.

Both weights also have a < 0. So instead one could restrict to Hecke translates of products of modular curves, where every summand has negative degree on both factors.
issues.reason:
1. The printed text matches the image of p. 862 word for word. Earlier in the proof the only assumptions are θ1F = 0 and (for the case sent to [75]) that F is nonzero on the superspecial locus. The proof never assumes or proves that F|_Y ≠ 0.

2. The reduction "it remains to show that the restriction of F to the superspecial locus is nonzero" must hold for every nonzero F. A form F = hF' vanishes on V(h), which contains Z and S, so this case has to be ruled out. The proof of Theorem 8.10 does this explicitly: "After possibly replacing (k,k) by (k−(p−1), k−(p−1)), we may assume that F is not divisible by the Hasse invariant." Theorem 8.11 has no such step. The same trick is not available there, because the lowered weight (j−p+1, 3−p) is outside the range of Prop. 8.9 and Theorem 8.11. What is needed instead is the vanishing H^0(X, ω(j−p+1, 3−p)_k) = 0. This is neither proved nor cited.

3. I checked Yamauchi arXiv:1410.7894v5, whose numbering differs from the paper's citation. Its θ1 non-vanishing result (Thm 4.9) assumes that F is not identically zero on S(0,0). Nothing in it treats forms divisible by the Hasse invariant or proves negative-weight vanishing.

4. I redid the computation. Using E|P^1 = O(−1)⊕O(p) and ω|P^1 = O(p−1), both stated in the paper, the largest summand degree of ω(a,b) on a supersingular P^1 is pa − b. This agrees with the paper's own jp−2 for (j,2). For (j−p+1, 3−p) it is p(j+2−p) − 3 ≤ −3.

5. The second printed sequence ends in H^1(X, ω(j,2)_k ⊗ ω^{−m−(p−1)}), a twist by ω^{−(p−1)}. That is the sequence for 0 → L⊗ω^{−(p−1)} →(h) L → L|_{V(h)} → 0, so Y must be V(h). Theorem 8.10 uses "p-rank 1 strata" in the same loose way for the closure, so this is a clarification, not a separate error.

6. The fix in the correction works. The iteration along Z and V(h) uses only facts the paper already relies on: the Moret-Bailly P^1's, Z Cartier in V(h) (Koblitz), and V(h) reduced (Yamauchi v5 Prop. 3.24). The paper's own unproved "The first term vanishes" needs exactly this vanishing lemma.

7. The claim F|_Y ≠ 0 is in fact true for nonzero F, so Theorem 8.11 as stated is correct. Only the written proof is incomplete. It is used in the proof of Theorem 8.13 ("Combining Proposition 8.25 with Lemma 8.17 and Theorem 8.11 ..."), and through it the main modularity theorem, but those results are unaffected once the step is supplied.

8. arXiv:1907.08691v1 (Theorem 8.11, pp. 45–46) has the same text, with "rank one strata ... We are assuming that the restriction of F to Y is nonzero."

The gap is genuine but minor and easy to fill. DEFENCE ATTEMPTED, FAILS.
(a) Nothing earlier in the proof, or in the statement, gives F|_Y ≠ 0. The only assumptions are θ1F = 0 and, for the case sent to [75, Thm 3.20], F|_S ≠ 0. Then "it remains to show that the restriction of F to the superspecial locus is nonzero" must hold for every nonzero F. A form F = hG vanishes on V(h), which contains Z and S. So that case has to be ruled out.
(b) Theorem 8.10 does rule it out (pp. 861–862): "After possibly replacing (k,k) by (k−(p−1), k−(p−1)), we may assume that F is not divisible by the Hasse invariant." Theorem 8.11 has no such step. The same trick is not available there, because the new weight (j−p+1, 3−p) is outside the theorem.
(c) The charitable reading is "forms of weight with negative entries obviously vanish". That is standard in characteristic 0 and for scalar weights (ampleness). For vector-valued weights mod p it needs an argument, and none is given. The same goes for "The first term vanishes", which is asserted bare.
(d) Yamauchi (arXiv 1410.7894v8) Thms 4.7 and 4.9 assume f is not identically zero on S(0,0). Nothing there handles forms divisible by h.
(e) Y must be V(h): the second sequence, with twist ω^{−m−(p−1)}, is the sequence for multiplication by h.

TRUTH. With the paper's convention ω(j,k) = Sym^{j−k} ⊗ det^k (p. 856) and the P^1 data it quotes (E = O(−1)⊕O(p), ω = O(p−1)), the top summand degree of ω(a,b) is pa − b. This reproduces the paper's own jp − 2 for weight (j,2). A short computer enumeration over p ≤ 101 and 4 ≤ j < p−1 confirms pa − b < 0 for both weights. So the lemma above applies. It needs only facts the main argument already uses: Z is a reduced Cartier divisor in V(h) (Koblitz, [70]), and it is the union of P^1s. Theorem 8.11 is therefore true, and the proof is incomplete.

CONSEQUENCES. Theorem 8.11 is used only in the proof of Theorem 8.13 (p. 877: "Combining Proposition 8.25 with Lemma 8.17 and Theorem 8.11"). Theorem 8.13 feeds Theorem 6.17 (p. 845) and then the main Theorem 9.1. None of these is affected once the lemma is supplied.

issues.printed: The source says F_2|_X ≠ 0 can be arranged by Γ̄ ⊂ SL_2(Z) when j < p − 1. It argues that Γ̄'s level is prime to p, so Γ̄ surjects onto SL_2(F_p). issues.correction: Replace the appeal to Γ̄ with a change of the local frame (ω1, ω2) of E at the superspecial point X by some g ∈ SL_2(F_p). This is Yamauchi's own device: in the proof of his Theorem 4.9 (arXiv v5; Theorem 3.20 in v1–v3) he uses ρ_r((1 a; 0 1)) with a ∈ F_p. The components F_i are taken in the basis δ_n = ω1^{r−n} ω2^n (ω1∧ω2)^{k2}, so they move by Sym^{j−2} of the frame change. For j − 2 ≤ p − 1 that representation is absolutely irreducible under SL_2(F_p), and F|_X ≠ 0. So some F_p-rational frame gives F_2|_X ≠ 0. Whether θ1(F) vanishes at X does not depend on the frame. The frame change should be F_p-rational, as in Yamauchi, and not an arbitrary element of GL_2(k). Yamauchi's normal form A(X) ≡ (t11 t12; t12 t22) mod m^2 involves a Frobenius twist g^{(p)}, and F_p-rational frame changes keep it. The rest of the proof is unchanged.
issues.reason:
Checked against the rendered p. 857 and 861–863 and against Yamauchi arXiv:1410.7894 v1–v6. In v5 the cited Theorem 3.20 is Theorem 4.9. It assumes k1 − 3k2 ≢ 0 mod p. The local term of (4.5) at X is −(k1−3k2)/2·t11F0|X − (k1−3k2)/2·t12F1|X − (k1−3)·t22F2|X. In weight (6,2) the first two coefficients vanish and the third is −3, so F_2|_X ≠ 0 is exactly what is needed. The paper's reduction to that case is correct.

Case for the defence. The paper names the right group, SL_2(F_p). The irreducibility argument is correct: if (gv)_2 = 0 for every g, the span of the orbit would be a nonzero invariant subspace inside the hyperplane x_2 = 0. Γ̄ does surject onto SL_2(F_p) because its level is prime to p. Read charitably, "the action of Γ̄" means ρ acting on the coefficients, which mod ϖ factors through SL_2(F_p), and so amounts to a frame change.

Why the justification still fails. On p. 857, Γ̄ is defined only by the q-expansion symmetry a(F, M.Q) = ρ(M)a(F,Q) for M ∈ Γ̄. That symmetry says F is Γ̄-invariant: Γ̄ lies in the level group and acts trivially on X_1(Q) and on F. It gives no action on the fibre of E at a superspecial point in characteristic p. So "applying an element of Γ̄ to F" leaves F_i|_X unchanged in any fixed frame, and the "since the level of Γ̄ is prime to p" clause proves nothing about X. The step actually needed is the frame change. The paper does not state it, but it is standard and appears in the cited source, restricted there to unipotent frame changes. So this is a gap in the exposition, not a false statement. The proposed correction is right and minimal.

Consequences. Theorem 8.11 is used only at the end of the proof of Theorem 8.13 (p. 877: "Combining Proposition 8.25 with Lemma 8.17 and Theorem 8.11, we obtain a contradiction"), and Theorem 8.13 feeds Theorem 9.1. Weight (6,2) falls inside the range p−1 > j of Theorem 8.13 once p ≥ 11, so the case matters, but the claim F_2|_X ≠ 0 holds with the frame-change argument. Nothing downstream changes.

Side note, a separate citation slip: "[75, Theorem 3.20]" follows the numbering of Yamauchi v1–v3, while "[75, Theorem 4.7]" and the bibliography (v5) follow v4/v5 numbering, where 3.20 is a Lemma and the result is Theorem 4.9.

issues.correction: The expansion 'X^2-coefficient = αβp^{k−2} + O(p^{k−1})' holds when α and β are p-adic units, i.e. in the ordinary case. That is the only case used later, in the 'in particular' of Lemma 8.12. For α, β merely integral, Newton-above-Hodge gives only that the X^2-coefficient has valuation ≥ k−2. That still yields the passage's conclusion that the Q_2-eigenvalues are integral.
issues.reason:
I rendered p. 863 and confirmed the text.

**The X^2-coefficient.** The polynomial's X^2-coefficient is e_2 = αβp^{k−2} + αβ^{−1}p^{j−1} + 2p^{k+j−3} + α^{−1}βp^{2k+j−5} + α^{−1}β^{−1}p^{k+2j−4}. When α and β are units, every term after the first is O(p^{k−1}), using j ≥ k ≥ 2. So the claim is fine in the ordinary case.

**Counterexample under the printed hypothesis.** Nonnegative valuations do not suffice. Take (j,k) = (4,4), so the Hodge weights are 0, 2, 3, 5, and take p = 5, α = 2·5, β = 3·5^2.
- The Frobenius slopes are {1, 4, 1, 4}. The Newton polygon has vertices (0,1,2,6,10), which lie on or above the Hodge polygon (0,0,2,5,10), and the pairing condition s1+s4 = s2+s3 = 5 holds.
- A direct computation gives v(e_2) = 2 but v(αβp^2) = 5. So e_2 − αβp^2 has valuation 2, which is less than k−1 = 3.
- The only other labelling with v(α), v(β) ≥ 0 is v(α) = 4, v(β) = 2. It gives v(αβp^2) = 8 and fails in the same way. Labellings with v(β) = −1 are excluded by the printed hypothesis.
- A filtered φ-module with these slopes and Hodge weights exists, since the Newton point lies in B(GSp4, μ).

So the displayed expansion is false in general for non-ordinary forms. The passage's final conclusion, that the Q_2-eigenvalues are integral, still holds, because v(e_2) ≥ s1+s2 ≥ k−2.

**Why it affects nothing.** The passage is heuristic ('One expects', 'should'). Lemma 8.12 is proved directly on formal q-expansions. Its 'In particular' is stated only for ordinary forms, where the expansion is correct. The displayed expansion is false in general, not merely imprecise, so it is recorded as an error in a motivational passage. The classification is the only uncertain point: one could read 'nonnegative valuation' as a slip for 'unit', which would make it a misprint. The mathematics is not in doubt.

issues.locator: §8.6, Theorem 8.13, statement, pp. 864–865. arXiv v1 (Thm 8.13) has the same text: 'Let A denotes a non-trivial power of the Hasse invariant of weight k'.
issues.printed: The source takes m in the Hecke algebra away from p and A as a nontrivial Hasse-invariant power of weight k. It claims injectivity of H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j,2)_{O/ϖ^m})^{α,β}_m --A--> H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j+k, 2+k)_{O/ϖ^m})_m --π_β--> H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j+k, 2+k)_{O/ϖ^m})^β_m. It defines π_β to project to the summand with nilpotent U − β and Q_2 − αβ, equivalently Z_2 − αβ.
issues.correction: 'Let A denote a suitable power of the Hasse invariant of weight k', i.e. a power A^s of the lift A of h^r from Definition 6.1 with p^{m−1} | s, as in Lemma 6.4. Then A has q-expansion ≡ 1 mod ϖ^m and multiplication by A is Hecke-equivariant away from p.
issues.reason: Definition 6.1 defines h only mod p. A is a noncanonical lift of h^r, and Lemma 6.4 gets Hecke-equivariance of multiplication by A^s on O/ϖ^m-coefficients only when p^{m−1} | s (it cites [32, Thm 6.2.1]). Two things need that equivariance. First, the composite in the theorem is a map between m-localizations. Second, the proof asserts on p. 865 that 'In both results, all of the corresponding maps are equivariant with respect to Hecke operators away from p' to reduce to the socle. For m ≥ 2 and an arbitrary power this equivariance fails: in the GL_2 analogue, multiplication by E_{p−1} mod p^2 does not commute with T_ℓ. The paper's own usage points to the intended hypothesis. The parallel Lemma 8.14 says 'a suitable power'. Theorem 6.17 applies Theorem 8.13 as 'there exists a power A^s of A', with t = r p^{m−1}(p−1), so s = p^{m−1}. So 'nontrivial' is a slip for 'suitable'. Nothing downstream is affected, for three reasons. The application uses s = p^{m−1}. Everything over k = O/ϖ is fine for any power, since h^{rs} has q-expansion 1. And injectivity on O/ϖ^m can in any case be checked on ϖ-torsion, where A acts as h^{rs}.

issues.locator: §8.6, proof of Lemma 8.14, p. 866, first lines. arXiv v1 has the identical text ('U 2 − T U + hpi = 0').
issues.printed: The source names T's action on N as U and claims U^2 − TU + ⟨p⟩ = 0 when acting on the image of M. It concludes that M is ordinary in N and belongs to N_α ⊕ N_β, defining N_γ as the factor with nilpotent U − γ.
issues.correction: U^2 − UT + ⟨p⟩ = 0 on M, i.e. U^2 F − U(TF) + ⟨p⟩F = 0 for F ∈ M, where T is the weight-one operator T_p acting on M.
issues.reason: The composition order in 'TU' is wrong, and the correct relation has T applied first. With T = U + ⟨p⟩V on weight-one forms and UV = 1: U(TF) = U^2 F + ⟨p⟩UVF = U^2 F + ⟨p⟩F, so U^2 − UT + ⟨p⟩ = 0 on M. The printed order fails under both possible readings. First, the paper says T acts on N as U, so T(UF) = U^2 F and the relation would give ⟨p⟩F = 0. Second, as formal q-expansion operators, TU = U^2 + ⟨p⟩VU, so U^2 − TU + ⟨p⟩ = ⟨p⟩(1 − VU) ≠ 0. Here VU(Σa_n q^n) = Σ a_{np} q^{np} ≠ F in general. U does not preserve the image of M, so T∘U is not even defined on it. Read as a Hecke polynomial whose coefficient T commutes with U, the intended meaning is clear. The conclusion also holds with the corrected relation: F = ⟨p⟩^{−1}U(TF − UF), so W = M + UM is U-stable with U(W) ⊇ W, hence W is ordinary. This is a notational slip with no effect on the proof.

issues.printed: Lemma 8.14's proof uses invertibility of U on N_α and TF ∈ N_α ⊕ N_β to obtain VF ∈ N_α ⊕ N_β. From UVF = F ∈ N_β it claims VF ∈ N_α and ⟨p⟩VF = αβU^{-1}F_α. It then obtains TF = (α + β)F, UF = αF, VF = βF, claiming the last equality contradicts the smallest q-expansion exponent whenever β ≠ 1 or F is cuspidal. Alternatively it cites [45] for the absence of a low-weight kernel of θ, with θVF = 0.
issues.correction: "Yet UVF = F ∈ N_α, and so VF ∈ N_α"; the displayed relations should read "TF = (α+β)F, UF = αF, VF = α^{-1}F" (equivalently ⟨p⟩VF = βF); and "the identity VF = α^{-1}F is impossible as soon as either α ≠ 1 or F is a cusp form".
issues.reason:
I checked the page images: the published p. 866 at 110 and 220 dpi, and arXiv v1 p. 48 at 110 dpi. The printed text is as quoted, and arXiv v1 (pp. 48–49) has the same wording.

I redid the computation from the proof's own hypotheses: π_β(F) = (U−α)^m F = 0, so "We are assuming that F = F_α ∈ N_α". U and V are the q-expansion operators, with UV = id and T = U + ⟨p⟩V in weight 1.

(1) Write VF = x_α + x_β in N_α ⊕ N_β. Since U preserves both factors, U(VF) = F ∈ N_α forces Ux_β = 0. U is invertible on N_β because β ≠ 0 (β is an eigenvalue of an invertible matrix). So x_β = 0 and VF ∈ N_α, which is the conclusion the text draws. With "F ∈ N_β" the same step would give VF ∈ N_β instead. So "N_β" must be "N_α".

(2) After the reduction G_α = 0 we have UF = αF. U is injective on N_α and U(VF − α^{-1}F) = F − F = 0, so VF = α^{-1}F. With ⟨p⟩F = αβF this gives ⟨p⟩VF = βF and TF = αF + βF = (α+β)F. That matches the displayed ⟨p⟩VF = αβU^{-1}F_α. The printed VF = βF would force β = α^{-1}, i.e. αβ = 1, since βUF = UVF = F. The reduction explicitly lets ⟨p⟩ act by αβ, which is det ρ̄(Frob_p) and need not be 1. So the ⟨p⟩ has been dropped from the displayed relation.

(3) Write F = Σ a_n q^n. If VF = cF with c ≠ 0, the lowest exponent of VF is p·n0 while that of cF is n0, so n0 = 0 and F is not cuspidal. Comparing constant terms then gives a_0 = c·a_0, so c = 1. With c = α^{-1}, the condition should be "α ≠ 1", not "β ≠ 1".

This correction is right on all three points. As (2) shows, the printed VF = βF is compatible with the rest only when αβ = 1; α = 1 alone is not enough.

The θ argument is unaffected, since θVF = 0 still forces θF = 0. The cusp-form case also still closes. Lemma 8.14 is a warm-up ("a much easier analogue for GL(2)"). The label 8.14 appears nowhere else in the text except at the lemma and its proof heading, and the proof of Theorem 8.13 is separate. So no stated result or later argument changes.

issues.locator: §8.6, proof of Lemma 8.15, pp. 867–868. arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same text at Lemma 8.15, p. 49, with "characteristic zero" in place of "characteristic 0".
issues.printed: The source says nilpotence of Q_2 − αβ makes Q_2 invertible on M. As Q_2 acts through Z_2 in both weights, including τ = (j + k, 2 + k), it claims Q_2 − αβ acts nilpotently on M ⊂ N. By lifting to characteristic 0, it asserts Q_2 is invertible only on N's ordinary part. Later, an isomorphism gives Z_2^2 M = Z_2 M; it concludes Z_2, and consequently U, is invertible on Z_2 M.
issues.correction: The following replacement argument is correct, and it is minimal because it uses only identities the paper already states. On M, which has weight (j,2), Lemma 8.3 gives T ≡ U + Z mod p. On N, which has weight τ = (j+t, 2+t), it gives T ≡ U, and Lemma 8.12 gives Q_2 ≡ Z_2. For m ∈ M, Um = T_N m lies in N and Tm lies in M, so Zm = Tm − Um lies in W := Σ_{i≥0} U^i M. This W is a finite-dimensional U-stable subspace of N. The formal identity Z_2 = UZ (p. 859) gives Z_2 M ⊂ UW. Z_2 commutes with U (p. 869; formally, a(Z_2 UF, Q) = a(UZ_2 F, Q), because M^{-1}.pQ is always integral). Hence Z_2 W ⊂ UW, and by induction Z_2^n W ⊂ U^n W. For j > 2, M = Z_2^n M lies in U^n W for every n. For (2,2), Z_2 M = Z_2^{n−1}(Z_2 M) lies in U^n W, using the paper's own equality Z_2^2 M = Z_2 M. In both cases the space lies in ∩_n U^n W, which is the part of W on which U is invertible, and so it lies in N_α ⊕ N_β by Lemma 8.16. The rest of the proof is unchanged, including the injectivity of M → Z_2 M, which uses only (αβ)^2 ≠ 1. The first sentence of the p. 867 passage should therefore be replaced by this argument, and "as in the previous argument" on p. 868 should point to it.
issues.reason:
This is a genuine gap. The key step, 'Q2 only acts invertibly on the ordinary part of N', is justified only by 'lifting to characteristic 0', and the case (2,2) reuses that step. I redid the computation. For an eigenform of weight (j',k') with Frobenius slopes s1 ≤ … ≤ s4, where s1 + s4 = s2 + s3 = j' + k' − 3, the Hodge weights are 0, k'−2, j'−1, j'+k'−3. The X^2 coefficient is p^{k'−2}·Q2, so Q2 is a unit exactly when s1 + s2 = k'−2. T is a unit exactly when s1 = 0; this uses k' = 2 + t > 2. The slopes (s, k'−2−s, j'−1+s, j'+k'−3−s) with 0 < s ≤ (k'−2)/2 have partial sums s, k'−2, 2k'+j'−3+s and the correct total, so they lie on or above the Hodge polygon. So a Q2-unit eigenform that is not T-ordinary is not excluded by the Galois side. A residual condition does not exclude it locally either. The GL2 analogue: θ^{p−1}f, for f of weight 1 with ρ̄|G_Qp = unr_α ⊕ unr_β, lifts to a non-ordinary crystalline form of weight p², with Hodge–Tate weights {0, (p+1)(p−1)}. Theorem 6.17 uses Hasse powers t = r p^{m−1}(p−1), which can be arbitrarily large. The heuristic in §8.5 (p. 863) does not close the gap. It parametrises the eigenvalues as α, βp^{k−2}, β^{−1}p^{j−1}, α^{−1}p^{k+j−3} with v(α), v(β) ≥ 0, and writes the X^2 coefficient as αβp^{k−2} + O(p^{k−1}). But the term αβ^{−1}p^{j−1} has valuation s1 + s2, which can equal k−2, so 'Q2 unit ⇒ α, β units' does not follow. The obvious formal shortcut also fails. The paper's identity is Z2 = UZ, and Z2 commutes with U, but ZU ≠ UZ formally: a(UF, R) = 0 for non-integral R, so for example the first term of a(ZUF; n,r,m) needs p | m. So U-nilpotence does not force Z2-nilpotence on N. Likewise 'Z2 and hence U' does not follow, since Z does not act on N. Whether Q2 is invertible only on the ordinary part of all of N remains unproven; the lemma needs only the version on W, which the correction proves. On 'affects': 'nothing' would mean the mathematics is right as intended. Here the intended justification fails and the proof needs a new argument, so the right value is 'the proof'. No stated result changes. Lemma 8.15 as stated is true. Its conclusions are used in Lemma 8.17: the statement 'π_β: Z2M → N_β' and M ⊂ N_α ⊕ N_β (with Lemma 8.16), and on p. 871 'the injectivity of Z2 in Lemma 8.15'. From there they feed Theorem 8.13 and Theorem 6.17, and all of these survive. arXiv v1 has the same passage. I tried to defend the paper and could not.

(1) Charitable reading. "Ordinary part of N" can only mean the U-invertible part. That is how p. 866 uses "ordinary subspace of N" in the GL(2) analogue, and the lemma concludes that U is invertible. The needed claim is therefore: a nonzero generalized Q_2-eigenvalue on N implies U is invertible there.

(2) Lifting to characteristic 0. A lifted eigenform of weight (j+t, 2+t) has Hodge–Tate weights 0, t, j+t−1, j+2t−1. A unit Q_2 means s1 + s2 = t, so the Newton polygon touches the Hodge polygon at vertex 2. Then r|G_Qp has a 2-dimensional crystalline piece V_1 with weights {0, t} and slopes {s, t−s}. Since j−1 ≢ 0 mod p−1, V_1-bar^ss must be unr(α) ⊕ unr(β). U invertible needs s = 0.
- For t = p−1 the defence actually works. Breuil and Berger–Li–Zhu (BLZ) for k = p ≤ p+1 say any positive slope reduces to the irreducible ind(ω_2^{p−1}). The paper supplies none of this.
- But Theorem 8.13 claims every nontrivial Hasse power, and Theorem 6.17 uses t = r·p^{m−1}(p−1), so t can be large.
- For (p²−1) | t and slope s > ⌊(t−1)/(p−1)⌋, BLZ gives V_1-bar = ind(ω_2^t)⊗unr = unr(λ) ⊕ unr(−λ). This is compatible with α = −β, which the hypotheses allow: αβ(α²−1)(β²−1)(α−β)(α²β²−1) ≠ 0 whenever α⁴ ≠ 1.
- Example: p = 5, j = 3, t = 24, α of order 8, β = −α. The slopes are (6, 18, 32, 44) against Hodge (0, 24, 26, 50). The Newton polygon touches at x = 2, so Q_2 is a unit, while v(T) = 6 > 0.

So the Galois side does not rule out Q_2-invertible, non-ordinary eigensystems. Whether they occur globally is still open, and so is the claim for all of N. Hence this is a gap, not an error.

(3) Formal shortcut. Z_2 = UZ, but ZU ≠ UZ. For example, the first term of a(ZUF; n,r,m) needs p | m. And Z does not preserve N. So "Z_2 and hence U" (p. 868) does not follow by itself.

(4) No nearby statement fills the gap. Lemma 8.16 only gives N = N_0 ⊕ N_α ⊕ N_β. The p. 806 introduction and Remark 8.18 concede that non-ordinary forms do appear.

Consequences. Lemma 8.15 as stated is true (by the correction above), so no stated result changes. Where the lemma is used:
- Lemma 8.17: the map "π_β: Z_2M ⊂ N_α ⊕ N_β → N_β" (p. 869); "π_β(F) = 0 implies F = F_α ∈ N_α" in the case j > 2; and on p. 871 "the injectivity of Z_2 in Lemma 8.15".
- §8.8 (p. 874 area, "contradicting the injectivity of Z_2: M → N in Lemma 8.15").
- Through these, Theorem 8.13 and Theorem 6.17.
All of them survive. The intended justification fails and a new argument is needed, so 'affects' is "the proof", not "nothing". arXiv v1 has the same text.

issues.locator: §8.6, proof of Theorem 8.13, displayed definition of M just before Lemma 8.15, p. 867. arXiv v1 (1907.08691v1, §8.6) has the same text: 'M = H^0(X1(Q), ω(j,2)_k)_m'.
issues.printed: The source sets M = H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j,2)_k)_𝔪 and N = H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j+k, 2+k)_k)_𝔪, following the preceding proof. It claims αβ ≠ 0 makes Q_2 invertible on M.
issues.correction: M = H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j,2)_k)^{α,β}_𝔪. This is the (α,β)-part, the mod-ϖ version of the source H^0(X_1(Q), ω(j,2)_{O/ϖ^m})^{α,β}_𝔪 of the composite in Theorem 8.13 (p. 865). N stays the full 𝔪-localisation.
issues.reason: The source of the map in Theorem 8.13 (p. 865) carries the superscript α,β. Here 𝔪 is 'the corresponding ideal of the Hecke algebra away from p' (p. 864), so localising at 𝔪 does not fix the eigenvalues of Q_2. Two steps use M and need the (α,β)-part: 'Since αβ ≠ 0, the operator Q_2 acts invertibly on M' (p. 867), and in the proof of Lemma 8.15, 'by assumption we know that Q_2 − αβ is nilpotent' and 'the only generalized eigenvalue of Q_2 is αβ' (p. 868). On the full 𝔪-localisation neither holds in general. The T-socle reduction on p. 865 ('we may work with coefficients over a finite field k') also lands in the (α,β)-part with k-coefficients. So the superscript was dropped, and the meaning is clear from the theorem being proved. Note also that k is both the residue field and the weight of A in the definition of N. Both meanings are defined (k = O/ϖ on p. 865, A of weight k in Theorem 8.13), so this clash reads correctly and is not a separate mistake. Writing O/ϖ in place of k in the corrected M, which avoids the clash, gives the same correction.

issues.locator: §8.6, proof of Lemma 8.15 (case σ = (2,2)), p. 868. arXiv v1 has the same text (Lemma 8.15 proof, p. 49).
issues.printed: Invoking Lemma 8.6 again, the source derives Q_2^2 F = (Z_2 + X_2)X_2 F = X_2^2 F and Q_2^3 F = X_2^3 F = X_2 F. It therefore calls Q_2 F = X_2 F ≠ 0 an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ satisfying λ^2 = 1, contradicting the unique generalized eigenvalue αβ and the assumption (αβ)^2 ≠ 1.
issues.correction: Q_2^3 F = X_2^3 F = X_2 F = Q_2 F, so Q_2F ≠ 0 is an eigenvector of Q_2^2 with eigenvalue 1. Equivalently, since Q_2 is invertible, Q_2^2 F = F. So Q_2^2 − 1 = (Q_2 − 1)(Q_2 + 1) has a nonzero kernel on M, and Q_2 has an eigenvalue λ with λ^2 = 1: F + Q_2F or F − Q_2F is a nonzero ±1-eigenvector. This contradicts αβ being the only generalized eigenvalue, since (αβ)^2 ≠ 1.
issues.reason: By Definition 8.5, mod p we have a(X_2F,Q) = (D/p)a(F,Q), so X_2^3 = X_2. By Lemma 8.6, Z_2X_2 = 0. From these, Q_2(Q_2F) = Q_2(X_2F) = X_2^2 F, and Q_2^2 F = F. So Q_2 swaps F and X_2F. Q_2F is a Q_2-eigenvector only if X_2^2F = λX_2F, i.e. only if X_2F = ±F. That fails, for example, when F has nonzero coefficients at forms Q with both signs of (D/p). So as printed the claim is unjustified. The intended conclusion follows at once from what was just computed: Q_2^2 − 1 kills a nonzero vector. The contradiction with (αβ)^2 ≠ 1 therefore stands. The slip is Q_2 in place of Q_2^2 (or 'Q_2 has an eigenvalue'), and the mathematics is right as intended. It is a false phrase rather than a typographical slip, so 'error' with affects nothing is also defensible. I keep 'misprint' because the fix is immediate from the preceding line.

issues.printed: The source says Z_2 and U commute. For sufficiently large m, for F ∈ ker(π_β) it substitutes (Z_2 − αβ)^m F = (Q_2 − αβ)^m F and claims it may then assume Z_2F = αβF.
issues.correction: Replace F by (Z_2 − αβ)^m F = (Q_2 − αβ)^m F, where m is the largest integer with (Q_2 − αβ)^m F ≠ 0. This vector is nonzero, lies in M ∩ ker(π_β), and satisfies Z_2F = αβF.
issues.reason: For j > 2, Q_2 = Z_2 on M, and Q_2 − αβ is nilpotent on M ('by assumption', proof of Lemma 8.15, p. 867; this is the (α,β)-part). So for m sufficiently large, (Q_2 − αβ)^m F = 0. With that m the replacement gives F = 0, which is useless, because the lemma needs a nonzero form. The intended choice is the last m giving a nonzero vector G. Then (Z_2 − αβ)G = 0. G stays in ker(π_β) because π_β = (U − α)^m is a polynomial in U, which commutes with Z_2, and G ∈ M because Q_2 preserves M. The correction is right.

issues.locator: §8.6, proof of Lemma 8.17(2), p. 870. The same step is needed again for the hypothesis ZF = βF + αF0 of Theorem 8.22(2), p. 873, reached via "In light of Lemma 8.17, to prove Theorem 8.13, it suffices to prove the following."
issues.printed: Lemma 8.17(2)'s proof repeatedly replaces F by (Q2 − αβ)F = (Z2 + X2 − αβ)F to obtain Q2F = αβF, Z2F ∈ Nα. For F = (Fα, 0, F0) ∈ Nα ⊕ Nβ ⊕ N0, it derives X2F = (0, 0, αβF0), Z2F = (αβFα, 0, 0), ZF = (U^{-1}αβFα, 0, G0), G0 ∈ ker U, and G = (Gα − βU^{-1}Gα, 0, G0 − (α + β)F0). Theorem 8.22(2) claims F = 0 in weight σ = (2, 2) if F = Fα + F0, UFα = αFα, X2F = αβF0, ZF = βF + αF0, and αβ(β² − 1)(α²β² − 1) ≠ 0.
issues.correction:
After "replace F by a form such that Q_2F = αβF and Z_2F ∈ N_α", insert the following.

X_2F = Q_2F − Z_2F lies in N. Over k, UX_2 = 0 as formal operators, because a(UX_2F, Q) = a(X_2F, pQ) = p·a(F, pQ) (Lemma 8.3 and Definition 8.5). U is invertible on N_α ⊕ N_β (αβ ≠ 0), so X_2F ∈ ker U ⊂ N_0.

Now compare components of X_2F = αβF − Z_2F, using Z_2F ∈ N_α:
- αβF_β = 0, so F_β = 0;
- Z_2F = (αβF_α, 0, 0);
- X_2F = (0, 0, αβF_0);
- UF_0 = (αβ)^{-1}UX_2F = 0.

The last fact justifies UF = (αF_α + G_α, 0, 0) in the computation of G.

Also add to the conclusion of Lemma 8.17(2): F ∈ M, and ZF = βF + αF_0. The second follows from T ≡ U + Z mod p in weight (2,2) (T = U + Z + pV), TF = (α+β)F and UF = αF_α. It is the hypothesis of Theorem 8.22(2), and §8.8 uses it as "ZF = βF + β^{-1}X_2F". Section 8.8 also uses F ∈ M.

issues.reason:
I rendered p. 859, 872, 873 and 874 and checked the text against the page images.

(1) The claim is printed without its key condition. 'There exists a Q with det(Q) ≢ 0 mod p' says nothing about F, and any Q prime to p satisfies it. What the paragraph proves, as its conclusion on p. 874 states, is that a(F,Q) ≠ 0 for some such Q. The clause 'with a(F,Q) ≠ 0' is missing.

(2) 'In particular' is the wrong connective. Suppose there is a Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0 and p ∤ det(Q). By Definition 8.5 (p. 859), a(X₂F,Q) ≡ (D/p)a(F,Q) ≠ 0, so X₂F ≠ 0 and F₀ = (αβ)⁻¹X₂F ≠ 0. So the existence claim does not imply F₀ = 0; it contradicts it. F₀ = 0 holds only under the opposite assumption, that every Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0 has p | det(Q). In that case every coefficient of X₂F vanishes: either (D/p) = 0 or a(F,Q) = 0, and a(X₂F,Q) = p·a(F,Q) = 0 when Q ≡ 0 mod p. Then X₂F = 0 in characteristic p, so F₀ = 0 because αβ ≠ 0, and ZF = βF + αF₀ = βF.

(3) The same unstated assumption is used again two sentences later. 'By Lemma 8.21, F(Q) consists of a single class [P]' needs (d(Q)/p) = 0 (Lemma 8.21(2), p. 872). That holds for the chosen Q only because of the contrary assumption.

So the printed text states a proof by contradiction without ever stating the contrary assumption, and it misstates what is being proved. Nothing about the conventions makes 'In particular' mean 'suppose not', so this is not a misreading of the text.

On the classification: the missing justification for F₀ = 0 is one line from Definition 8.5 once the assumption is stated. The intended structure is clear from 'we may also assume', from the hint 'F₀ = (αβ)⁻¹X₂F', and from the conclusion on p. 874. That fits the definition of a misprint (a slip whose intended meaning is clear from context) better than 'gap'. Classing it as a minor gap would also be defensible.

The mathematics is unaffected once the assumption is restored. Separate problems in the rest of this proof are recorded under other ids: the reversed display a(F,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q), and the degenerate case d(Q) = 0. Checked on the rendered pages 859 and 872–875 and on arXiv v1 p. 53.

(1) The sentence cannot be read literally. Without "and a(F,Q) ≠ 0", the claim "there exists a Q with det(Q) ≢ 0 mod p" is trivial. The words "In particular ... F₀ = 0" also cannot follow from the intended claim. By Definition 8.5 (p. 859), a(X₂F,Q) = (D/p)a(F,Q) mod p, and we work over k, which has characteristic p. So a Q with p ∤ D and a(F,Q) ≠ 0 would give X₂F ≠ 0, and hence F₀ = (αβ)⁻¹X₂F ≠ 0. Read literally, the connective "In particular" states the opposite of what is true.

(2) The defence fails, but the charitable reading works. The phrase "we may also assume" only makes sense as the contrary hypothesis in a proof by contradiction. In weight (2,2), X₂F = 0 is exactly equivalent to "a(F,Q) = 0 for all Q with p ∤ D". The rest of the paragraph uses this hypothesis without saying so, in both weights. "By Lemma 8.21, F(Q) consists of a single class [P]" needs (D/p) = 0 for the minimal Q, which holds only under the contrary hypothesis. Otherwise Lemma 8.21 allows 0, 1 or 2 classes. The paragraph ends in a contradiction: β²a(F,Q) = 0 when j > 2 and β ≠ 0, or β² = 1 in weight (2,2). The authors then state the conclusion on p. 874: "We may therefore assume that a(F,Q) ≠ 0 for some Q of discriminant D prime to p." So the intended meaning is clear from context. The only step the reader must supply, contrary hypothesis ⇒ X₂F = 0 ⇒ F₀ = 0, follows at once from Definition 8.5 and αβ ≠ 0. This makes it an expository misprint (a missing clause and the wrong connective), not a substantive gap.

(3) Downstream use. The conclusion of this step is used in §8.9 (Theorem 8.22(1), weight (j,2) with j ≥ 4). There, (D/p) = −1 is excluded and "Hence we may assume that (D/p) = 1", which silently needs (D/p) ≠ 0, i.e. p ∤ D, from this step. §8.8 (weight (2,2)) argues on its own through Theorem 8.10 and does not use the conclusion. Theorem 8.22 feeds Theorem 8.13 via Lemma 8.17. Once the passage is read as intended, the mathematics of this step is right, so nothing is affected. The separate issues in the same argument, recorded as other issues, are not part of this finding: the degenerate or minimal-discriminant case, and the ρ(M_Q) versus ρ(M_P)⁻¹ display.

issues.reason:
I checked the display on the rendered page image; it reads exactly as quoted.

Conventions, from pp. 856–858: M.Q = (det M)^{-1} M Q M^T. ρ = Sym^{j−k} is extended to a homomorphism M_2(Z) → End(U). Lemma 8.3 gives a(ZF,Q) = Σ_𝒮 ρ(M)a(F, M^{-1}.Q). On p. 872 this becomes a(ZF,Q) = Σ_{[P]∈ℱ(Q)} ρ(M_P)a(F,P) with M_P.P = Q.

I redid the computation. Normalise Q = [[m, r/2],[r/2, n]] with m a unit, p | r and p | n; this is the case (D/p) = 0, where ℱ(Q) has one element. Then:
- P = M_P^{-1}.Q = [[pm, r/2],[r/2, n/p]], with M_P = diag(1,p).
- When P is p-primitive (v_p(n) = 1), M_Q = diag(p,1) gives M_Q.Q = P.
- So M_Q·M_P = pI, as the paper itself says on p. 874 ("ρ(M_Q.M_P) = ρ(p·I) ... zero in higher weight").

With ρ = Sym^{j−2}, the paper's own Z-identity gives ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q) = ρ(M_Q M_P)a(F,P) = p^{j−2}a(F,P). In characteristic p and weight (j,2) with j ≥ 4, this is 0. So the first printed equality, a(F,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q), would force a(F,P) = 0. That is exactly the opposite of what the next sentence needs: it uses a(F,P) ≠ 0 to get a(F,R) ≠ 0 when P = pR. No step in the text justifies that equality. It holds only in weight (2,2), where ρ is trivial and ρ(pI) = 1. Even taken at face value, the printed line would not give a(F,P) ≠ 0 when j ≥ 4, because ρ(M_Q) = Sym^{j−2}(diag(p,1)) is singular mod p.

The corrected line βa(F,Q) = ρ(M_P)a(F,P) follows directly from the paper's identity. It gives a(F,P) ≠ 0 in all weights. The later chain β²a(F,Q) = ρ(M_P)a(ZF,P) = ρ(M_Q)ρ(M_P)a(F,Q) is fine, because both M_P M_Q and M_Q M_P equal pI.

Also, [Q] ∈ ℱ(P) (needed to define M_Q) is only cited afterwards. This is harmless: Lemma 8.20 has no p-primitivity hypothesis. It does not affect the finding.

This is a real but local slip. Theorem 8.22, Theorem 8.13 (via Lemma 8.17) and the reduction to Q with D prime to p in §§8.8–8.9 all hold once the one-line fix is made. No later result depends on the wrong identity. arXiv v1 (p. 53) has the same text. I checked the display on the rendered page images, both the Duke version (p. 873) and arXiv v1 (p. 53). It reads exactly as quoted.

The paper's conventions:
- M.Q = (det M)^{-1} M Q M^T (p. 857).
- ρ = Sym^{j−k}, extended to a homomorphism M_2(Z) → End(U) (p. 857).
- Lemma 8.3 gives a(ZF,Q) = Σ_𝒮 ρ(M)a(F, M^{-1}.Q). On p. 872 this becomes a(ZF,Q) = Σ_{[P]∈ℱ(Q)} ρ(M_P)a(F,P), with M_P.P = Q.
- a(F, γ.Q) = ρ(γ)a(F,Q) holds only for γ ∈ Γ̄, not for matrices of determinant p.

Defence attempts. None of them survives.
(a) The identity on p. 872 expresses a(ZF,Q) in terms of a(F,P), not the other way round. Nothing in §8 gives a(F,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q).
(b) One could read the display as a garbled form of the identity at P, namely β·a(F,P) = a(ZF,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(F,Q). That needs ℱ(P) = {[Q]}. But this uses P being p-primitive, which the very next sentence derives from the display, so that reading is circular. It also puts β on the other side.
(c) The only other possible source is the Γ̄-equivariance a(F, M_Q.Q) = ρ(M_Q)a(F,Q) applied wrongly to M_Q ∈ 𝒮. That has no Z in it, so it does not produce the display either.

The printed display is false in weight (j,2) with j ≥ 4.
- With ℱ(Q) = {[P]}, the only term in Lemma 8.3 comes from M_P, with P := M_P^{-1}.Q.
- The adjugate pM_P^{-1} is an integral matrix of determinant p, and it sends Q to P. So in the coefficient identity at P we may take M_Q = pM_P^{-1} (writing pM_P^{-1} = s'γ with s' ∈ 𝒮 and γ ∈ Γ̄ gives ρ(s')a(F, s'^{-1}.P) = ρ(pM_P^{-1})a(F,Q)). Then M_Q M_P = M_P M_Q = pI. The paper says the same on p. 874: "ρ(M_Q.M_P) = ρ(p·I) is the identity in weight (2,2) and zero in higher weight".
- Hence ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q) = ρ(M_Q M_P)a(F,P) = p^{j−2}a(F,P), which is 0 in characteristic p when j ≥ 3.
- So the first printed equality would force a(F,P) = 0, the opposite of what the next sentence needs (a(F,P) ≠ 0, to get a(F,R) ≠ 0 when P = pR).
- The printed conclusion a(F,P) = β·ρ(M_Q)a(F,Q) does not give a(F,P) ≠ 0 either: ρ(M_Q) = Sym^{j−2} of a matrix of determinant p is singular mod p.

In weight (2,2), ρ is trivial, and the printed line reduces to the true a(F,P) = a(ZF,Q) = β·a(F,Q). So this looks like the weight-2 line with ρ(M_Q) inserted wrongly. It is a false step, not a mere index slip, so I class it as an error rather than a misprint.

Consequences. The corrected line gives a(F,P) ≠ 0 in every weight, and the rest of the proof survives:
- the minimality argument;
- ℱ(P) = {[Q]}, from Lemma 8.20, which has no primitivity hypothesis, and Lemma 8.21;
- the chain β²a(F,Q) = ρ(M_P)ρ(M_Q)a(F,Q), which is 0 for j > 2 and a(F,Q) for j = 2. This is fine because both products are pI, even though the printed order ρ(M_Q)ρ(M_P) is reversed.

Nothing else in the paper uses the wrong identity. §8.8 and §8.9 start from the output of this proof ("a(F,Q) ≠ 0 for some Q of discriminant D prime to p"). Theorem 8.13, which follows via Lemma 8.17, and Theorem 8.22 itself remain true.

On 'affects': "nothing" would understate it, because the printed step actually fails for j ≥ 4. "the proof" is right: the proof is broken as written, it is repaired locally in one line, and no stated result changes.

issues.locator: §8.7, proof of Theorem 8.22 (first step, the minimal-discriminant choice), p. 873. Also the statement of Theorem 8.22 on p. 873, and Theorem 8.13 on pp. 864–865
issues.printed: Theorem 8.22 concerns characteristic-p Siegel q-expansions of weight σ = (j,2), p − 1 > j. For j ≥ 4 it claims UF = αF, ZF = βF and αβ(β^2 − 1) ≠ 0 imply F = 0. For σ = (2,2), it assumes F = F_α + F_0, UF_α = αF_α, X_2F = αβF_0, ZF = βF + αF_0, αβ(β^2 − 1)(α^2β^2 − 1) ≠ 0, and again concludes F = 0. Its proof chooses minimal-discriminant p-primitive Q, claims 𝓕(Q) has only [P], uses a(F,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q) = β·ρ(M_Q)a(F,Q), and rules out P = pR via a(F,R) ≠ 0 and equal discriminants of P and Q.
issues.correction:
The minimal fix keeps Theorem 8.22 as stated. Add one line before, or in place of, the minimal-discriminant step:

"If a(F,Q) = 0 for every Q with det(Q) ≢ 0 mod p, then ΘF = 0 in weight (2,2), resp. θ1F = 0 in weight (j,2), since both operators multiply the Q-th coefficient by det(Q). Hence F = 0 by Theorem 8.10 (k = 2, p > 3), resp. Theorem 8.11 (p − 1 > j ≥ 4)."

This makes the descent over p-primitive forms unnecessary, and it also covers the constant-term case. Both theorems are already in the paper, and their hypotheses are exactly those of Theorem 8.22.

Acceptable alternatives:
- Add cuspidality to Theorem 8.22, i.e. a(F,Q) = 0 for degenerate Q. This holds in the application, since §6.4 and Theorem 6.17 use H^0(X1(Q), ω(a,2)(−∞)).
- Take Q of minimal nonzero |d|, and dispose of an F supported on degenerate Q by the Θ/θ1 argument above.

Another proposed route, via α ≠ β, is not recommended:
- α ≠ β is not a hypothesis of Theorem 8.22. It comes only from Theorem 8.13.
- For a smaller Γ̄ the Γ̄-classes of degenerate forms can cycle under Z.
issues.reason:
The printed text matches the page images of pp. 873–874. arXiv:1907.08691v1 has word-for-word the same text (§8.7, Theorem 8.22), and the same undecorated Theorem 8.13.

Where the gap is:
- §8.2 (p. 856) takes the index set X to be all positive semidefinite Q, so degenerate Q are included.
- The statement of Theorem 8.22 assumes only "a Siegel modular q-expansion". It does not assume cuspidality, and it does not assume α ≠ β.
- If some degenerate coefficient is nonzero, the minimal |d| is 0. Then R = P/p also has d = 0, and minimality gives no contradiction.

I checked an explicit example myself. Take S = {diag(1,p), [[p,b],[0,1]]} and P = adj(M).Q, with Q = diag(c,0) and p ∤ c.
- Only M = diag(1,p) gives an integral P, namely P = diag(pc,0) = pQ. So R = Q.
- The relations are then β·a(F,Q) = ρ(diag(1,p))·a(F,pQ) = α·ρ(diag(1,p))·a(F,Q).
- In weight (2,2), ρ is trivial, so this gives (β − α)a(F,Q) = 0.
- In weight (j,2), ρ(diag(1,p)) reduces mod p to the projection onto f1^{j−2}. The stabiliser [[1,b],[0,1]] fixes the same line. So if α = β, the relations are consistent and give no contradiction.
- The hypotheses of Theorem 8.22 are αβ(β^2−1) ≠ 0 in part (1) and αβ(β^2−1)(α^2β^2−1) ≠ 0 in part (2). Neither includes α ≠ β.

The step before this one has the same problem. "If F ≠ 0 there is a p-primitive Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0" fails when only a(F,0) ≠ 0, since 0 = p·0. The lemma 8.14 proof on p. 866 handles the analogous constant-term case explicitly ("β ≠ 1 or F is a cusp form"), but Theorem 8.22 does not. Also, p. 865 prints the space without (−∞), while pp. 845–846 have it.

Impact: the application is cuspidal, so Theorems 8.13, 6.17 and 9.1 are not affected. The alternative fix above also appears to prove Theorem 8.22 as literally stated for genuine forms. So the result stands, but the written proof has an unhandled case. The affects value "the proof" is right.

A separate slip in the same passage: the display a(F,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q) is valid only when j = 2. For j > 2 its right-hand side is ρ(pI)a(F,P) = 0. The fact actually needed, a(F,P) ≠ 0, follows instead from a(ZF,Q) = ρ(M_P)a(F,P) = β·a(F,Q) ≠ 0. The printed text matches the page images of pp. 873–874 and is identical in arXiv v1. The defence fails:

1. Degenerate forms are included. §8.2 (p. 856) takes the index set 𝒳 to be all positive semidefinite Q.
2. "Siegel modular q-expansion" occurs only in Theorem 8.22 and is never defined. It must mean the q-expansion of a genuine form, since the proof then uses Theorem 8.10 and Lemma 8.15. Nothing in the statement makes F cuspidal. The spaces M and N (p. 867) and the display of Theorem 8.13 (p. 865) are printed without (−∞).
3. No reading of "minimal discriminant" rescues the step:
   - Minimal |d|: this is 0 whenever some degenerate p-primitive Q has a(F,Q) ≠ 0.
   - Minimal v_p(d), or minimal nonzero |d|: the case where every p-primitive Q in the support is degenerate is still left over.

I checked the failure by direct computation (S = {diag(1,p), [[p,b],[0,1]]}):
- Take p = 5, 7, 11 and Q = c·ℓℓ^T with p ∤ c.
- Exactly one M ∈ S gives an integral P = M^{-1}.Q, as Lemma 8.21 says.
- In every case P = p·R with d(R) = 0 = d(Q). For example, Q = diag(c,0) gives P = pQ.
- So a(F,R) ≠ 0 does not contradict minimality.
- For Q = diag(c,0) the relations reduce to β·a(F,Q) = α·ρ(diag(1,p))·a(F,Q). In weight (2,2) with F0 = 0 this reads (β − α)·a(F,Q) = 0. That is no contradiction unless α ≠ β, and α ≠ β is not among the hypotheses of Theorem 8.22.

The Q = 0 subcase is also not addressed: "a p-primitive Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0" need not exist if only a(F,0) ≠ 0. It is excluded anyway:
- In weight (2,2) with F0 = 0: a(ZF,0) = (p+1)·a(F,0) ≡ a(F,0), so (β − 1)·a(F,0) = 0 and a(F,0) = 0.
- In weight (j,2): a(F,0) is Γ̄-invariant in Sym^{j−2}. That representation is irreducible and nontrivial for SL2(F_p), and Γ̄ surjects onto SL2(F_p) (proof of Theorem 8.11). So a(F,0) = 0.

Consequences. The step's only output is "a(F,Q) ≠ 0 for some Q with p ∤ D" (p. 874).
- §8.8, weight (2,2), does not use it. That argument treats every D directly: (D/p) = −1 is killed by β² ≠ 1, then Θ(F − X2F) = 0, Theorem 8.10 applies, and Lemma 8.15 finishes.
- §8.9 uses it only to meet the hypothesis of Proposition 8.25 (recap on p. 876; "Combining Proposition 8.25 with Lemma 8.17 and Theorem 8.11", p. 877). If no Q with p ∤ det Q carries a nonzero coefficient, then θ1F = 0 trivially and Theorem 8.11 still gives F = 0.

So Theorem 8.22 holds as stated for genuine forms, and Theorems 8.13, 6.17 and the main results are unaffected. In the application F is in any case cuspidal (§6.4, p. 845). Only the written proof has an unhandled case.

Remark 8.23 says a Θ-kernel argument would need a new theorem in nonparallel weight. Theorem 8.11 is in fact enough, because ΘF = 0 implies θ1F = 0.

A separate slip in the same passage: a(F,P) = ρ(M_Q)a(ZF,Q) holds only for j = 2. For j > 2 its right-hand side is ρ(pI)·a(F,P) ≡ 0. The fact actually needed, a(F,P) ≠ 0, follows instead from β·a(F,Q) = a(ZF,Q) = ρ(M_P)·a(F,P).

issues.locator: §8.9, first paragraph (part of the proof of Theorem 8.22(1)), p. 874
issues.printed: In the case σ = (j,2), j ≥ 4, the source chooses p-primitive Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0 and D = d(Q) nonzero. It says (D/p) = −1 gives a(ZF,Q) = 0, contradicting a(F,Q) ≠ 0 and ZF = βZ, and therefore assumes (D/p) = 1.
issues.correction: "the identity ZF = βZ" should read "the identity ZF = βF". Optionally, "D = d(Q) is nonzero" can be clarified to "D = d(Q) is nonzero mod p (prime to p)". That second change only tidies loose wording; it is not a misprint.
issues.reason:
I rendered p. 874 at 130 dpi and read the page image. The quotation above is exact. The phrase 'ZF = βZ' makes no sense as printed: an operator is set equal to a scalar times an operator, applied to nothing. The argument needs the eigen-identity ZF = βF, which is a hypothesis of Theorem 8.22(1) (p. 873: 'suppose that UF = αF and ZF = βF for some α, β with αβ(β²−1) ≠ 0'). The proof then says 'thus have the equalities UF = αF, ZF = βF.'

I redid the argument. Page 872 gives a(ZF,Q) = Σ_{[P]∈F(Q)} ρ(M_P) a(F,P). Lemma 8.21(1) says that when Q is p-primitive with (D/p) = −1, F([Q]) is empty, so a(ZF,Q) = 0. With ZF = βF this gives β·a(F,Q) = 0. Since β ≠ 0 (from αβ(β²−1) ≠ 0), we get a(F,Q) = 0, the stated contradiction. So the intended text is certainly βF.

On 'D is nonzero': the argument also has to rule out (D/p) = 0 before 'Hence (D/p) = 1'. That is supplied by the first part of the proof (p. 873: 'there exists a Q with det(Q) ≢ 0 mod p') and the recap on p. 874 ('a(F,Q) ≠ 0 for some Q of discriminant D prime to p'). In this characteristic-p setting, 'nonzero' is naturally read as nonzero mod p. So this part is imprecise wording rather than a misprint, and the substance of this entry is the βZ → βF typo.

arXiv:1907.08691v1 (§8.9, p. 54 there) has the identical text: 'D = d(Q) is non-zero … the identity ZF = βZ.'

Effect on results: none. The intended step is correct and immediate from Lemma 8.21(1), the p. 872 identity and the hypothesis ZF = βF with β ≠ 0. Theorem 8.22, and through Lemma 8.17 Theorem 8.13 and the results that depend on it, are unaffected.

issues.locator: §8.9 (opening paragraph), p. 874; arXiv v1 §8.9, p. 54 has the same sentence verbatim
issues.printed: The source chooses p-primitive Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0 and nonzero D = d(Q), then assumes (D/p) = 1. It describes the Γ̄ ⊂ SL2(Z) action on discriminant-D binary quadratic forms as having a finite orbit identifiable with a ray class group.
issues.correction: '... has finitely many orbits, and the (finite) set of orbits may be identified with a ray class group.'
issues.reason: Γ̄ is 'the congruence subgroup of SL2(Z) defined in [67]' (p. 857), so it is infinite. The forms here are positive semidefinite with D = r^2 − 4mn ≠ 0, so they are positive definite. The stabiliser in SL2(Z) of a positive definite form is finite (order at most 6), so every Γ̄-orbit is infinite. What is finite, and carries the class-group structure, is the set of Γ̄-orbits (classes). The next paragraph (p. 875) uses exactly that when it says the ray class group 'is partitioned by this process Q → {P,R} into a finite number of cyclic orbits'. The intended meaning is clear, so this is a wording slip.

issues.printed: For σ = (2,2), the source gives a(X_2F, Q) as (D/p)a(F, R), taking D = D_Q as Q's discriminant. Using ZF = βF + β^{-1}X_2F, it derives, for (D/p) = −1, 0 = a(ZF,Q) = βa(F,Q) − β^{-1}a(F,Q) = (β − β^{-1})a(F,Q). With β^2 ≠ 1, it concludes a(F,Q) = 0. issues.correction: Read "a(X_2F,Q) is equal to (D/p)a(F,Q)" and "has D = d(Q) (the discriminant r^2 − 4mn = −4det(Q)) satisfying (D/p) = 0, 1". The same mix-up of det and discriminant appears earlier in the paper. In Lemma 8.4 (p. 859), "(det(Q)/p)" should be "(−det(Q)/p)", which equals ((r^2 − 4mn)/p). In Definition 8.5 (p. 859), "D is the determinant of the quadratic form associated to Q" should say "discriminant", unless "determinant" is taken in Gauss's sense b^2 − ac.
issues.reason:
I checked the page images at 130 dpi and the printed text is as quoted above.

(1) a(F,R): nothing called R is defined in §8.8. Definition 8.5 (p. 859) gives a(X_2F,Q) = (D/p)a(F,Q) mod p. The next display also uses a(F,Q) on the right: a(ZF,Q) = βa(F,Q) + β^{-1}(D/p)a(F,Q). So "R" is a plain typo for "Q".

(2) det versus discriminant. By §8.2 (p. 856), Q = [[m, r/2],[r/2, n]], so det(Q) = mn − r^2/4. The paper itself writes "con(Q⊗Q^∨) = r^2 − 4mn = −4det(Q)" on p. 877, and defines d(Q) as the discriminant on p. 872. That gives (det Q/p) = (−1/p)(D/p), which is wrong for p ≡ 3 mod 4. Example: p = 3 and Q = I. Then x^2 + y^2 has no zeros in P^1(F_3), D = −4, (D/3) = −1, but (det Q/3) = +1. The paragraph defines D as the discriminant two lines earlier and relies on Lemma 8.21 (p. 872, stated for d(Q)) to get a(ZF,Q) = 0 when (D/p) = −1. So "D = det(Q)" contradicts its own definition.

I recomputed the Hecke symbol. The rank-one cosets B = λvv^T (λ ∈ F_p^*, v ∈ P^1(F_p)) contribute Σ_v Σ_λ e(λQ[v]/p) = p·#{zeros of Q in P^1(F_p)} − (p+1). This equals −1 + p((r^2−4mn)/p) when Q ≢ 0, and p^2 − 1 when Q ≡ 0. That matches the second expression in Lemma 8.4, so the symbol in X_2 really is the discriminant symbol. This confirms the correction and shows that the paper's first expression (det(Q)/p) is the same slip. One caveat: Definition 8.5 calls D "the determinant", so the §8.8 wording follows that loose usage. The usage is still wrong against p. 877.

arXiv 1907.08691v1 §8.8 has the same text: "is equal to (D/p)a(F, R), where D = D_Q is the discriminant of Q" and "the only Q with a(F,Q) ≠ 0 have D = det(Q) satisfying (D/p) = 0, 1". The only differences are "have" for "has" and "that" for "then". Definition 8.5 and Lemma 8.4 read the same in v1 as well.

issues.reason: The paper's own convention is Q = [[m, r/2],[r/2, n]] (p. 856), with det(Q) = mn − r^2/4. Page 877 states explicitly 'con(Q ⊗ Q^∨) = r^2 − 4mn = −4 det(Q)'. So (det(Q)/p) = (−1/p)(d(Q)/p), which differs from (d(Q)/p) when p ≡ 3 mod 4. The vanishing just derived comes from two facts, both governed by the discriminant: F(Q) is empty when (d(Q)/p) = −1 (Lemma 8.21, where D = d(Q)), and a(X_2F,Q) = (D_Q/p)a(F,Q). The same paragraph defines D = D_Q as the discriminant two lines earlier. So 'D = det(Q)' contradicts the paragraph's own D. With det(Q) literally, the claim would say (det(Q)/p) ∈ {0, −1} for p ≡ 3 mod 4, so the printed statement is false for those p. The next step uses only the discriminant reading: F − X_2F is supported on Q with (D_Q/p) = 0, i.e. det(Q) ≡ 0 mod p, so Θ(F − X_2F) = 0. Definition 8.5 also calls D 'the determinant', and Lemma 8.4 equates (det(Q)/p) with ((r^2−4mn)/p). Those are the same slip at other places and do not change this locator. The intended meaning is clear.

issues.printed: The source says nonzero a(F, Q) requires D = det(Q) with (D/p) = 0, 1. It puts F − X_2F ∈ M in Θ's kernel and invokes Theorem 8.10 to conclude F − X_2F is zero. It then obtains Z_2F = Z_2X_2F = 0, claiming this contradicts Lemma 8.15's assertion that Z_2 : M → N is injective.
issues.correction:
Replace "F − X₂F ∈ M" by the statement that F − X₂F is (the q-expansion of) a section of weight (p+1, p+1), and apply Theorem 8.10 with k = p+1. The step works as follows.

1. Lemma 8.12 in weight (2,2) gives X₂F = Q₂F − Z₂F. Here Q₂F ∈ M, and Z₂F is the q-expansion of Q₂(hF) ∈ H⁰(X₁(Q), ω(p+1,p+1)_k), where h is the Hasse invariant: in weight (p+1,p+1) ≠ (2,2), Lemma 8.12 gives Q₂ ≡ Z₂, and Lemma 8.8 gives the action.
2. So F − X₂F is the q-expansion of hF − h·Q₂F + Q₂(hF), a section of weight (p+1,p+1). When A = h this is simply "F − X₂F ∈ N".
3. The coefficients of F − X₂F vanish unless det(Q) ≡ 0 mod p, so Θ(F − X₂F) = 0.
4. Theorem 8.10 applies with k = p+1, since p ∤ (p+1)(2p+1). It gives F = X₂F. Then Z₂F = Z₂X₂F = 0 by Lemma 8.6, which contradicts Lemma 8.15 as printed.
5. The contradiction can also be reached without Lemma 8.15. Formally UX₂ ≡ 0, since a(UX₂F, Q) = p·a(F, pQ). So F = X₂F gives 0 = UF = αF_α, hence F = F₀ = (αβ)⁻¹X₂F = (αβ)⁻¹F, which is impossible because αβ ≠ 1.

Replacing M by N alone is not a minimal correction. Theorem 8.13 allows A = h^s for any s ≥ 1, and then N has weight 2 + s(p−1), which is beyond the range of Theorem 8.10 when s ≥ 2. So N has to be taken with A = h, or equivalently one uses the weight-(p+1) section in step 2.

Alternatively, reduce Theorem 8.13 to s = 1. Multiplication by h^{s−1} is injective and is the identity on q-expansions, and it commutes with U, with Q₂ = Z₂ and with the Hecke operators away from p. Hence it commutes with π_β, so π_β∘h^s = h^{s−1}∘(π_β∘h).
issues.reason:
Rendered pages checked: p. 874, and for context p. 859, 861, 864, 865, 867 and 868.

1. F ∈ M. The F of Lemma 8.17(2) is obtained inside M by applying Q_2 − αβ and T − α − β. The last sentence of §8.8 uses "injectivity of Z_2 : M → N", which needs F ∈ M.

2. For nonzero F ∈ M, X_2F is never in M. Suppose X_2F ∈ M.
- Z_2X_2 = 0 over k (Lemma 8.6), so Z_2(X_2F) = 0.
- The map M → Z_2M is injective (Lemma 8.15), so X_2F = 0.
- Then a(F,Q) = 0 whenever Q is p-primitive with (D/p) ≠ 0. So ΘF = 0 coefficient by coefficient, and Theorem 8.10 with k = 2 gives F = 0.
So under the proof's standing assumption F ≠ 0, the claim "F − X_2F ∈ M" is false, not just unjustified. Nothing in §8.8 supports it. The only place the paper puts X_2F in M is the proof of Lemma 8.15, under the opposite hypothesis Z_2F = 0.

3. The paper itself expects this. Lemma 8.17(2) writes F = F_α + F_0 with X_2F = αβF_0 ∈ N_0, a part of N (not M) where U is nilpotent. Remark 8.18 says the "tripled" space in weight (p+1, p+1) "contains nonzero elements in the kernel of Z_2".

4. The correction works, and I redid the computations myself:
- Membership: X_2F = Q_2F − Z_2F ∈ N. Lemma 8.12's computation gives Q_2 ≡ p^{j−2}X_2 + Z_2 ≡ Z_2 mod p in weight (p+1, p+1).
- Theorem 8.10 hypotheses: "p + 1 ≥ k, p ∤ k(2k−1) — so in particular k = 2 and k = p+1 are admissible". Theorem 8.10 is used only here, and Remark 8.23 mentions only an analogue of it. This supports the reading that k = p+1 was meant.
- Kernel of Θ: the vanishing of Θ(F − X_2F) holds under the paper's own conventions for (D/p) and det. When p | D we have det ≡ 0, since det = (4mn − r²)/4.
- General powers: the reduction from h^s to h in the last paragraph of the correction is valid. Steps 1–2 of the correction give a more direct alternative. The example Θ(G^p) = 0 in weight (2p, 2p) shows the extra step is needed for s ≥ 2: Theorem 8.10 fails outside k ≤ p+1.

5. The statement of Theorem 8.13 is still true for all nontrivial powers A. Downstream results that depend on it (Theorem 6.17 and the main theorems) are unaffected once the proof is repaired as above. So only the proof is affected.

6. arXiv:1907.08691v1 has the same text on p. 53. Theorem 8.10 there also lists k = 2 and k = p+1 as admissible.

Unrelated misprint in the same paragraph: "(D/p)a(F, R)" should be "(D/p)a(F, Q)". Rendered and read: pp. 859–874 and v1 p. 53.

DEFENCE ATTEMPTS, all of which fail.

(i) X₂ is not an operator on M. Definition 8.5 (p. 859) defines X₂ only as a formal operator on q-expansions. Mod p it is the twist by (D/p) ≡ (−4det Q)^{(p−1)/2}, so it agrees with ±Θ^{(p−1)/2}, which raises the weight. On M only Q₂ = Z₂ + X₂ acts (p. 867: "the operator Q₂ acts on M either as Z₂ or as Z₂ + X₂"). The one place the paper puts X₂F in M is the proof of Lemma 8.15, under the opposite hypothesis Z₂F = 0. In the proof of Lemma 8.17(2) (p. 870) the paper itself writes X₂F = (0, 0, αβF₀) ∈ N₀ ⊂ N, not in M.

(ii) The claim cannot be justified, and the principle it would need is false. Take any F ∈ M.
- If X₂F ∈ M, then Z₂X₂F = 0 by Lemma 8.6, so X₂F = 0 by the injectivity of Z₂ on M (Lemma 8.15).
- But at this point the proof has F with a(F,Q) ≠ 0 for some Q whose discriminant is prime to p. Since (D/p) = −1 was just excluded, (D/p) = 1, so a(X₂F,Q) = a(F,Q) ≠ 0.
- So "F − X₂F ∈ M" is equivalent to the contradiction the proof is looking for. It cannot be obtained without already finishing the proof. (Because this is a proof by contradiction, no concrete false instance exists, but the inference fails.)
- Moreover, X₂(M) ⊂ M would force X₂M = 0. Every F ∈ M would then be supported on det ≡ 0, so ΘF = 0, so F = 0 by Theorem 8.10 with k = 2. Hence X₂ preserves M only when M = 0, and M ≠ 0 here.

(iii) Reading "M" as a slip for "N" (the paper views M ⊂ N "by abuse of notation", p. 867) works only when N has weight ≤ p+1, that is when A = h. Theorem 8.10's remark "so in particular k = 2 and k = p+1 are admissible" fits that intent. But Theorem 8.13 allows any nontrivial power, and Theorem 6.17 (pp. 845–846) invokes it with a power of weight t = r·p^{m−1}(p−1). In weight (2p, 2p), Θ is not injective: Θ(G^p) = 0 for G of weight (2,2), since det(pQ) ≡ 0. So an extra step is needed, and the text is not a pure misprint. Since it is not a slip with a clear intended meaning, I class it as an error (a step that fails) rather than a gap; "gap" would also be defensible.

THE REPAIR, checked step by step.
- Lemma 8.12 gives Q₂ ≡ Z₂ + X₂ in weight (2,2), and Q₂ ≡ Z₂ in weight (p+1,p+1), where the p-power terms vanish mod p.
- a(F − X₂F, Q) = 0 when (D/p) = 1 (the two coefficients cancel) and when (D/p) = −1 (a(F,Q) = 0 was just shown).
- D = −4·det, so (D/p) = 0 exactly when det ≡ 0. Hence Θ(F − X₂F) = 0.
- Theorem 8.10 with k = p+1 gives F = X₂F, and the printed ending then goes through.

WHERE IT IS USED. §8.8 is the only place Theorem 8.10 is used; Remark 8.23 refers only to an analogue of it. Through Lemma 8.17(2), §8.8 gives Theorem 8.13 in weight (2,2). Theorem 8.13 feeds Theorem 6.17, which feeds §9 (the weight (2,2) modularity lifting, including the abelian-surface application). With the repair, every stated result stays true.

Both routes in the correction are valid: taking A = h (reducing A^s to A as in its last paragraph), so that F − X₂F ∈ N and Theorem 8.10 applies with k = p+1; and the direct route of steps 1–4 through a section of weight (p+1, p+1).

issues.correction:
Replace the appeal to Lemma 8.15 with an argument that uses only the hypotheses of Theorem 8.22(2), all working over k:
- By Definition 8.5, a(X_2F,Q) ≡ (D/p)a(F,Q). With a(UF,Q) = a(F,pQ), this gives UX_2 ≡ 0, because p divides the discriminant of pQ. So UF_0 = (αβ)^{-1}UX_2F = 0.
- Since Z_2 = UZ formally (p. 859), Z_2F = U(βF + αF_0) = β(αF_α + UF_0) + αUF_0 = αβF_α.
- If Z_2F = 0, then F_α = 0. So F = F_0 and X_2F = αβF. Now either X_2³ ≡ X_2 gives αβ((αβ)² − 1)F = 0, or F = X_2F (from the Θ step) gives (αβ − 1)F = 0. In both cases F = 0 because α²β² ≠ 1.

Equivalently, the hypotheses give (Z_2 + X_2)F = αβF, so the argument in the proof of Lemma 8.15 (λ² = 1 against (αβ)² ≠ 1) applies to this F directly. The first step supplies the one-line justification of UF_0 = 0, which is not a stated hypothesis. The relevant part of Lemma 8.15 is its σ = (2,2) sentence; that lemma has no numbered parts. In the only application (F from Lemma 8.17(2), which lies in the (α,β)-part M, with α and β as in Theorem 8.13), Lemma 8.15 applies as cited.
issues.reason:
Defence tried first. It works for the application but not for the statement as printed.

(a) The defence. Theorem 8.22 comes right after "In light of Lemma 8.17, to prove Theorem 8.13, it suffices to prove the following." The §8.8 proof writes "F − X_2F ∈ M", so it treats F as an element of the §8.6 space M. The paper ends with "this completes the proof of Theorem 8.13". In that use, F comes from Lemma 8.17(2). That F lies in M: the proof starts with F ∈ M and only applies Q_2 − αβ and T − α − β, both of which preserve M. And α and β are as in Theorem 8.13. So Lemma 8.15's injectivity of M → Z_2M applies, and the chain Theorem 8.13 → Theorem 6.17 → main theorems is not affected by this step. (Other steps in the same paragraph are recorded as sourceIssues E121.)

(b) Why it is still a gap. Theorem 8.22(2) is stated for any Siegel modular q-expansion with those identities, with α and β chosen afresh subject only to αβ(β²−1)(α²β²−1) ≠ 0. Lemma 8.15 needs α and β "as in Theorem 8.13", which also requires α ≠ β, α² ≠ 1 and the Galois setting, and it needs F in the localized (α,β)-part M, where "the only generalized eigenvalue of Q_2 is αβ" (p. 868). Neither is a hypothesis of Theorem 8.22(2). The factor α²β² − 1 in 8.22(2) matches the remark on p. 868 that Lemma 8.15 is "the point … which uses (αβ)² ≠ 1". So the authors were relying on Lemma 8.15's argument, but the proof cites the lemma, and the lemma's hypotheses do not hold for a general F.

(c) The repair works; I checked it from the printed formulas.
- Page 859 gives U_2 = −1 + pX_2, a(X_2F,Q) ≡ (D/p)a(F,Q) mod p, and Z_2 = UZ.
- Lemma 8.6 gives Z_2X_2 = 0.
- From these, UX_2 ≡ 0 and X_2³ ≡ X_2.
- Then UF_0 = 0 and Z_2F = αβF_α, which gives (Z_2 + X_2)F = αβF.
- If Z_2F = 0, then F = F_0 and X_2F = αβF, which forces F = 0 since αβ ≠ ±1.
So Theorem 8.22(2) is true as stated, given the rest of its proof. Only the justification of this step is missing for the stated generality.

(d) affects. The printed proof of the stated Theorem 8.22(2) cites a lemma outside its hypotheses, so the gap affects the proof. The stated results, 8.22(2) and 8.13, survive. "nothing" would also be defensible, since the paper's only use of the passage (Theorem 8.13) is covered by Lemma 8.15 as cited.

(e) arXiv v1, p. 53, has the same text.

issues.locator: §8.9, paragraph before Lemma 8.24, p. 875; arXiv v1 p. 54 has the same text ('neighbours')
issues.printed: The source describes the operation as sending each binary quadratic form to the two closest neighboring forms. If its orbit contains fewer than two elements, the neighbor pair is allowed multiplicities.
issues.correction: '(if the orbit has at most two elements, this pair of neighbors may have multiplicity)', i.e. 'fewer than three'
issues.reason: Each class has exactly two neighbours counted with multiplicity (Lemma 8.21(3)), and the relation is symmetric (Lemma 8.20). So each orbit is a cycle, and a class's two neighbours are its two cyclic neighbours. In a cycle of size 1 both neighbours are Q itself; the proof of Lemma 8.21 gives the example of class number 1. In a cycle of size 2, {Q,P}, both neighbours of Q are P. In class-group terms, the neighbours of c are c[𝔭] and c[𝔭]^{-1}, and these coincide when [𝔭] has order 2. So the pair has multiplicity exactly when s ≤ 2. The printed condition 'fewer than two' leaves out s = 2. The printed sentence is not false as it stands (it says 'may'), but its threshold is off by one. The later argument (Lemma 8.24) works for every s, so nothing depends on this.

issues.correction:
Replace "we have a(θ₁F,Q) = 0 and θ₁F = 0" with an argument that covers every Q.

(i) Q with (d(Q)/p) = +1: Lemma 8.24 applies to each such Q, with its own s, A and B, so a(θ₁F,Q) = 0.

(ii) Q with (d(Q)/p) = −1: F(Q) is empty (Lemma 8.21), so βa(F,Q) = a(ZF,Q) = 0 and a(F,Q) = 0.

(iii) Q with p | d(Q): this case needs an actual argument. The coefficients do NOT vanish because of a det(Q) factor. That factor in Prop. 8.9(2) is itself wrong (sourceIssues E95): θ₁ has coefficients con(a_Q ⊗ Q). The fix is as follows.
- If Q ≡ 0 mod p, then con(a(F,Q) ⊗ Q) ≡ 0.
- Otherwise F(Q) = {[P]}. Then βa(F,Q) = ρ(M_P)a(F,P), where Q = M_P.P = p^{-1}M_P P M_P^T.
- GL₂-equivariance of the contraction gives con(Sym^{j−2}[M]x ⊗ M.P) = det(M)·Sym^{j−4}[M]con(x ⊗ P). This is ≡ 0 mod p because det M = p.

Hence θ₁F = 0.

A shorter fix: the same identity, applied to each term of a(ZF,Q) = Σ_S ρ(M)a(F, M^{-1}.Q), shows θ₁∘Z ≡ 0 on mod-p formal q-expansions. So θ₁F = β^{-1}θ₁ZF = 0 at once.

The hypothesis "F has a nonzero coefficient a(F,Q) where (D/p) = 1" is not used. The shortcut for case (iii), "a(θ₁F,Q) = det(Q)·con(…) ≡ 0", depends on the wrong det(Q) and has to be replaced as above.
issues.reason:
I checked the text against the rendered pages 861 and 874–877.

DEFENCE. Two parts of the missing step are routine.
- The Q in the proof is generic. Lemma 8.24 is stated for any Q with (D/p) = 1, and the proof never uses the Q from the hypothesis. So the step from one Q to all Q with (D/p) = +1 can be read charitably.
- The (D/p) = −1 case is in the recap paragraph just before the proposition: a(ZF,Q) = 0, which with ZF = βF gives a(F,Q) = 0.
- With the paper's own printed Prop. 8.9(2), θ₁ Σ a_Q q^Q = Σ det(Q)con(a_Q ⊗ Q) q^Q, the p | d(Q) coefficients would also vanish trivially. So under the paper's printed conventions this would be only a terse omission.

WHY THE DEFENCE FAILS. The det(Q) factor is wrong.
- In Yamauchi (arXiv:1410.7894v5, the cited [75]; v8 is the same), θ₁ = H_{p−1}·θ̃₁, where θ̃₁ is a projection of KS^{-1}∘∇. The q-expansion there is A_G(T) = (1/N)A_f(T) ⊗ T, which is linear in T. Only Θ carries det(T).
- The weight count agrees: first order gives +(0,2), and the Hasse invariant gives +(p−1,p−1).
- The paper's own display on p. 876 also has no det(Q).
- This is recorded as sourceIssues E95.

With the correct formula, a(θ₁F,Q) = con(a(F,Q) ⊗ Q) does not vanish automatically when p | d(Q). For example, con(Y^{j−2} ⊗ X²) = 2(j−2)(j−3)Y^{j−4}, and d(X²) = 0. Nothing in the paper shows these coefficients vanish.
- Theorem 8.22's opening argument only finds some Q with p ∤ D and a(F,Q) ≠ 0.
- Even a(F,Q) itself need not vanish for p-primitive Q with p | D, when F(Q) = {[pR]}.

So the final "θ₁F = 0" is asserted without proof for these Q. That is a genuine gap, and it cannot be closed from the printed text.

THE FIX IS SOUND. The identity con(Sym^{j−2}[M]x ⊗ p^{-1}MPM^T) = p·Sym^{j−4}[M]con(x ⊗ P), for det M = p, is equivariance of the second transvectant: Sym^a ⊗ Sym^2 → Sym^{a−2} ⊗ det². I checked it by direct computation in exact rational arithmetic: 1500 random trials with p ∈ {5, 7, 11, 13}, 0 mismatches. The contraction reproduces the paper's normalisation (4, −2) ∝ (2, −1). The paper's own claim that con(Sym^{j−2}[A]x ⊗ Q^∨) = 0 when AQA^t = p^sQ is a special case of this identity (it gives a factor p^s).

USE LATER. Prop. 8.25 is used only in the last sentence of §8.9: combined with Lemma 8.17 and Theorem 8.11 (injectivity of θ₁), it gives the contradiction that proves Theorem 8.22(1), and so Theorem 8.13. The statement of Prop. 8.25 is still true after the repair, so nothing downstream changes. The proof as written, however, does not establish θ₁F = 0.

This issue overlaps with the consequence recorded in sourceIssues E95; case (iii) cannot rest on the det(Q) factor.

issues.locator: §8.9, proof of Proposition 8.25, second display on p. 877; arXiv:1907.08691v1, p. 55
issues.printed: For p > j − 2, the source says contraction on Sym^{j−2} ⊗ Sym^2 has con(f_1^i f_2^{j−2−i} e_1^k e_2^{2−k}) = 0 except when 2 ≤ i + k ≤ j − 4.
issues.correction: "unless 2 ≤ i + k ≤ j − 2". Equivalently, the image f_1^{i+k−2} f_2^{j−2−i−k} lies in Sym^{j−4}, so 0 ≤ i+k−2 ≤ j−4. For p > j−2 the contraction is in fact nonzero exactly when 2 ≤ i + k ≤ j − 2.
issues.reason:
The page fixes the convention just before this display (p. 876 to p. 877). On Sym^2 ⊗ Sym^2, con sends e_1^2 f_2^2 and e_2^2 f_1^2 to −2, sends e_1 f_1 e_2 f_2 to 1, and kills all other monomials. So e_1 pairs with f_2 and e_2 pairs with f_1.

Contracting e_1^k e_2^{2−k} against f_1^i f_2^{j−2−i} therefore uses k copies of f_2 and 2−k copies of f_1, leaving f_1^{i+k−2} f_2^{j−2−i−k}. This needs i+k ≥ 2 and i+k ≤ j−2. The scalar is a product of falling factorials of i and j−2−i, which is a unit when p > j−2.

I checked this by direct computation. I used the GL2-equivariant second transvectant φ_xx ψ_yy − 2 φ_xy ψ_xy + φ_yy ψ_xx, with x = f_1, y = f_2 and e_1 ↦ x, e_2 ↦ y in the ψ slot:
- It reproduces the paper's Sym^2 ⊗ Sym^2 values (4, 4, −2) ∝ (−2, −2, 1), and con(Q ⊗ Q^∨) = 8mn − 2r² ∝ r² − 4mn.
- For j = 4, …, 9 the set of i+k with nonzero contraction is exactly {2, …, j−2}. The printed range {2, …, j−4} is empty for j = 4, 5 and too small for every j.

The printed bound also contradicts the paper's own text in two places:
- For j = 4 it makes con identically zero on Sym^2 ⊗ Sym^2, against the displayed con(Q ⊗ Q^∨) = r² − 4mn = −4 det(Q) just above it.
- In case (1) the paper says "the only monomial which f_1^{j−2} contracts nontrivially with is e_2^2" (i = j−2, k = 0, so i+k = j−2). The printed bound would make that contraction zero.

This is a slip in the upper bound (j−4, the degree of the target Sym, written in place of j−2), so it is a misprint, not an error in the argument.

Effect: none. The proof only needs con(f_1^{j−2} ⊗ e_1^k e_2^{2−k}) = 0 for k = 1, 2, because Q^∨ ≡ m e_1^2 + r e_1 e_2 mod p. Here i+k = j−1 or j, both greater than j−2, so the corrected bound gives exactly this. Case (1) also states the needed fact directly and correctly, and case (2) reduces to case (1). Nothing else cites the display: after the proof, Proposition 8.25 is only combined with Lemma 8.17 and Theorem 8.11 to finish Theorem 8.13, and it does not rely on this display. This correction is right and minimal.
