issues.locator: Appendix (Calegari–Geraghty–Harris, "Bloch–Kato conjectures for automorphic motives"), References, entry [38], p. 893. It is cited twice in the appendix introduction on p. 881: "…compatible families of n-dimensional representations whose existence was only recently proved to exist in [38]" (before Theorem A.1) and "For the families of Galois representations constructed in [38], we prove the following result" (before Theorem A.2). The appendix preprint arXiv:1907.08694v1 (the only version) prints the same entry: "[HLTT] Michael Harris, Kai-Wen Lan, Richard Taylor, and Jack Thorne, Galois representations for regular algebraic cusp forms over CM-fields, in preparation." It is cited there at the same two places. The main-text preprint arXiv:1907.08691v1 does not cite this work.
issues.printed: Reference [38] lists M. HARRIS, K.-W. LAN, R. TAYLOR and J. THORNE's work on Galois representations attached to regular algebraic cusp forms over CM-fields as still in preparation. It ends with the back-reference (881).
issues.correction: [38] M. Harris, K.-W. Lan, R. Taylor, and J. Thorne, On the rigid cohomology of certain Shimura varieties, Res. Math. Sci. 3 (2016), Paper No. 37, doi:10.1186/s40687-016-0078-5. It was also on arXiv as arXiv:1411.6717 (25 Nov 2014, "Version of December 2013").
issues.reason: I rendered p. 893 at 110 dpi, and entry [38] reads exactly as quoted. I also rendered p. 881; the only citations of [38] are the two quoted in the locator. I checked Crossref for doi:10.1186/s40687-016-0078-5. It gives the title "On the rigid cohomology of certain Shimura varieties", the authors Michael Harris, Kai-Wen Lan, Richard Taylor and Jack Thorne, the journal Research in the Mathematical Sciences, volume 3, article number 37, published online 26 Oct 2016 and in print Dec 2016. It is the same work. The arXiv abstract of 1411.6717 says: "We construct the compatible system of l-adic representations associated to a regular algebraic cuspidal automorphic representation of GL_n over a CM (or totally real) field … we impose no self-duality hypothesis". This is exactly the family r_λ(π) that Theorem A.2 uses. So the 2020 paper cites, as "in preparation" and under an old working title, a work that had been on arXiv under its final title since Nov 2014 and in print since 2016. The paper's own wording, "was only recently proved to exist in [38]", also treats the work as finished. The entry does not say where to find the cited work, but the intended reference is clear from the authors and context. That makes it a bibliographic slip, classed as a misprint, not a mathematical error, like the bibliography misprint PAPER-CALEGARI-GERAGHTY-18/E217. No correction exists: Crossref's deposit for doi:10.1215/00127094-2019-0044 (the final issue version, vol. 169, no. 5, 1 Apr 2020) still lists "[38] … Galois representations for regular algebraic cusp forms over CM-fields, in preparation." It shows no update-to/erratum. The appendix arXiv preprint has only v1, with the same text. The work was in print four years before this paper appeared (2016 vs 2020). This correction matches the Crossref record; the arXiv number is included only for completeness.

issues.locator: Proposition 1.3.1, parts (i) and (ii), p. 27
issues.printed: Part i) says each Poincare object belonging to Pn(D^p(R), Q^{[-n]}) admits a cobordant ((-n-a)/2)-connective object. Part ii) says a Lagrangian L -> X for a ((-n-a)/2)-connective (X,q) in Pn(D^p(R), Q^{[-n]}) admits a cobordant Lagrangian L' -> X relative to X with the subsequent properties.
issues.correction: Pn(C, Q^{[-n]}) in both places
issues.reason: The proposition is stated for a general stable infinity-category C: its hypotheses are 'Let C be a stable infinity-category with a bounded t-structure C_{>=0}, C_{<=0}. Let Q be an r-symmetric Poincare structure on C with duality D such that D(C_{<=0}) is contained in C_{>=-d}', and its concluding sentence is 'the canonical map L^{a,b}_n(C,Q) -> L_n(C,Q) is an isomorphism'. There is no ring R in the hypotheses at all, so D^p(R) in parts (i) and (ii) is undefined there. The proof confirms the intended reading, opening 'it suffices to show that every Poincare object (X,q) in Pn(C, Q[-n]) is cobordant to one whose underlying object is ((-n-a)/2)-connective'. What makes this more than cosmetic is that the generality is the whole point: the paragraph immediately preceding the proposition says the argument is cast 'in the setting of a general Poincare infinity-category (C,Q) equipped with a t-structure ... as we shall use this more general setup for a category of torsion modules, which is not itself given by modules over a discrete ring, in Theorem 2.2.4 below'. That application is real and the chain is short: Corollary 1.3.8, which IS stated correctly for a general C, is proved by 'Apply Proposition 1.3.1 in the case of r = infinity, d = 0'; and the proof of Theorem 2.2.4 says 'Hence for both sides of (7) we are in the situation of Corollary 1.3.8', where the two sides of (7) are the direct sum over the primes of S of the perfect derived categories D^p(F_p) of the residue fields, and D^p_S(R), the full subcategory of S-primary torsion perfect R-modules. Neither is D^p(R) - the second is precisely the category of torsion modules the preceding paragraph promised, and the first is a product. So as printed, parts (i) and (ii) fail to cover what Corollary 1.3.8, and through it the devissage Theorem 2.2.4 and hence Theorem 7 and the Berrick-Karoubi conjecture, ask of them. Checked in a rendered clip at 250 dpi: both occurrences print D^p(R).

issues.locator: Example 2.3.14, p. 47
issues.printed: Citing [Lam05, VI Remark 2.31] again, the source identifies 2<1> and <1,-2> as additive generators for the kernel of .<1,3>. It concludes ker( L^s_0(Q_2) --.<1,3>--> L^s_0(Q_2) ) = Z/4 (+) Z/2.
issues.correction: additively generated by 2<1> and <1,-3>
issues.reason: The form <1,-2> is not in that kernel. Over Q_2 the form <1,3> is the norm form of the unramified quadratic extension E = Q_2(sqrt(-3)) - which is the same field whose ring of integers the example is about - so for a unit or non-unit scalar a the form a.<1,3> is the scaled norm form, and a.<1,3> = c.<1,3> in the Witt group if and only if a/c is a norm from E. Since E is unramified, its norm group is exactly the set of elements of even valuation. Hence <a,b>.<1,3> = a.<1,3> + b.<1,3> vanishes if and only if a/(-b) is a norm, that is if and only if v(a) + v(b) is even. For <1,-2> that sum is 0 + 1 = 1, so <1,-2>.<1,3> is not zero; for <1,-3> it is 0 + 0, so <1,-3>.<1,3> is zero, as one also sees directly: <1,-3>.<1,3> = <1,3,-3,-9> = <1,-1> + <3,-3> = 0. The failure of <1,-2> can be confirmed a second way, by computing invariants: <1,-2>.<1,3> = <1,3,-2,-6> has rank 4 and discriminant 36, that is 1 modulo squares, and Hasse invariant (3,-2)(3,-6)(-2,-6) = (+1)(-1)(-1) = +1 at the prime 2, whereas the hyperbolic form of rank 4 has Hasse invariant (-1,-1) = -1; and directly, x^2 + 3y^2 = 2(z^2 + 3w^2) forces a valuation-parity contradiction because both bracketed terms are norms from E and so of even valuation, so the form is anisotropic and in particular not hyperbolic. The stated isomorphism type Z/4 (+) Z/2 is nevertheless correct, with 2<1> and <1,-3> as generators: <1> has order 8 in W(Q_2), 2<1,-3> = 4<1> since <1,1,-3,-3> and <1,1,1,1> agree in rank, discriminant and Hasse invariant, and <1,-3> - 2<1> = <-1,-3> has discriminant 3 and so does not lie in the cyclic group generated by 2<1>; the order is confirmed by counting, the image of multiplication by <1,3> having order 4 and W(Q_2) order 32. Since 2 and 3 differ by one glyph and <1,-3> is exactly the right element, this reads as a typographical slip rather than a mistaken computation. It affects only this step: the conclusion of the example, and the L-group table it feeds, are correct. Checked in a rendered clip of p. 47 at 300 dpi, where the entry is unambiguously <1,-2>.

issues.locator: Example 2.3.14, p. 46
issues.printed: The source gives K discriminant (3). Because (2) does not divide (3), it invokes [Neu99, Corollary III.2.12] to declare (2) prime in R, and therefore the unique dyadic prime.
issues.correction: the cited criterion gives only that (2) is unramified; that it is prime needs in addition that -3 is not a square modulo 8, equivalently that x^2 + x + 1 is irreducible over F_2
issues.reason: Not dividing the discriminant gives unramifiedness, not inertia: an unramified rational prime in a quadratic field is either prime or a product of two distinct primes. The printed inference therefore does not follow, as the field Q(sqrt(-7)) shows - its discriminant is -7, the prime 2 does not divide it, and yet (2) splits, because x^2 + x + 2 factors as x(x+1) modulo 2. The conclusion drawn here is true: in Q(sqrt(-3)) the minimal polynomial x^2 + x + 1 of the Eisenstein unit is irreducible over F_2, equivalently -3 is congruent to 5 and not to 1 modulo 8, so (2) is inert and is the unique dyadic prime, and the example's count d = 1 of dyadic primes is right. Only the justification is incomplete, and the cited Neukirch corollary sits in the section on the different and discriminant, where the statement available is the ramification criterion.

issues.locator: Published §5.3.2–3, p. 20, equations (5.10)–(5.13), Lemma 5.13; arXiv v3 pp. 21–22, same numbered passages
issues.printed: The source associates the spinor representation of SO_10 with a vector bundle S^+ of rank 16 over the classifying stack BSO_10.
issues.correction: Use a Spin/GSpin lift for an actual half-spin vector bundle; distinguish it from the effective projective group PSO_10 and prove the required rigidification, moduli comparison, rational Chow/cohomology/CKgP transport and bundle descent or twists. Items 95–96 are explicit unresolved proof dependencies; /60–65 cannot be consumed as unconditional constructions.
issues.reason: Over C the kernel element −1 of Spin_10→SO_10 acts as −Id on the half-spin module, so that module does not descend to SO_10. The center μ4 of Spin_10 acts faithfully by scalars on S^+ and trivially on its projectivisation and Grassmannian. The resulting Spin quotient has ineffective μ4 inertia; an SO presentation would still have ineffective μ2 inertia. Neither is interchangeable with the moduli stack. Removing the scalar inertia does not descend a bundle on which it acts nontrivially. The printed construction and embedding therefore fail as stated; final Theorem 1.10 and downstream theorem statements are retained as targets with this proof gap, not asserted false.

issues.locator: Lemma 5.6.5 and its proof, pp.85–86, in arXiv:2301.10509v3 (27 March 2025); page image checked
issues.printed: The source concludes reducibility of ρ̄|_{ker(det ρ̄)}. Invoking Dickson’s classification, it gives two possibilities: reducible ρ̄ or G′ ≅ A₄. For the second possibility it puts G₁ = ker(det ρ̄), states ρ̄(G₁)/ρ̄(Z) ≅ Z/2 × Z/2, and derives reducibility of ρ̄|_{ker(det ρ̄)} from this.
issues.correction: The conclusion holds except when d = 3 and the projective image is A₄; then ρ̄|_{ker(det ρ̄)} has projective image Z/2 × Z/2 and is absolutely irreducible. The end of the proof of Theorem 5.2 (p.87), which uses the lemma to find g ∈ ρ̄(G_{F₁}) with det g ≠ 1 and eigenvalue ratio ≠ (det g)^{±1}, needs another argument in that case.
issues.reason: For p odd, a Klein four subgroup of PGL₂(F̄_p) does not fix a line (it would embed in the cyclic group F̄_p^× of a Borel modulo scalars), so its preimage acts irreducibly. Counterexample for every p ≥ 5: let G = 2T ≅ SL₂(F₃) ⊂ SL₂(F̄_p), χ : G → C₃ → F̄_p^× its cubic character (kernel Q₈), and ρ̄ = incl ⊗ χ. Then det ρ̄ = χ² has order 3. An element g ∉ Q₈ has order 3 or 6, with eigenvalues χ(g)ω, χ(g)ω² or −χ(g)ω, −χ(g)ω² (ω a primitive cube root of 1), so one eigenvalue is ±1, which is equivalent to (5.6.1). But ker det ρ̄ = Q₈ acts irreducibly (i and j anticommute). Checked by hand and by a brute-force computation over F₇. The hypotheses of Theorem 5.2 allow this residual image when p ≡ 1 mod 3 (for instance p = 7 and F ⊇ Q(√−7), so that [F(ζ₇):F] = 3); there no unramified place has H²(F_v, ad⁰ρ̄) = 0. The cases d ≠ 3 ([DDT97, Lemma 4.11]) and hence p = 3, 5, which is all §§6–7 use, are unaffected.

issues.printed: The source gives 𝒢_dR a canonical map into the flag variety Fl^std_{G,µ} ≃ G/P_µ. It cites Proposition 3.5 of [Mil90] for constructing automorphic vector bundles by pulling back from Fl_{G,µ} to 𝒢_dR and then descending to S_K.
issues.correction: Fl^std_{G,µ} ≃ G/P^std_µ, and 'by pullback from Fl^std_{G,µ} to 𝒢_dR'
issues.reason: By §2.1 (p. 660), Fl^std_{G,µ} parametrizes parabolics conjugate to P^std_µ, and a base point gives Fl^std_{G,µ}(ℂ) ≃ G(ℂ)/P^std_µ(ℂ). The quotient G/P_µ is the other flag variety, Fl_{G,µ}. The map out of 𝒢_dR comes from 𝒢_dR being the pushout of a P^std_µ-torsor, and it is the map in the diagram S_K ← 𝒢_dR → Fl^std_{G,µ} displayed between the two sentences. Automorphic vector bundles are built from P^std_µ-representations, viewed as G_ℂ-equivariant bundles on Fl^std_{G,µ} (p. 663).

issues.locator: §5.2, p. 732 (also in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: The source defines ellipticity of an endoscopic triple by the condition (Z(Ĥ)^Γ)° ⊂ Z(G).
issues.correction: (Z(Ĥ)^Γ)° ⊂ Z(Ĝ), with Z(Ĥ) viewed inside Ĝ through η, i.e. η((Z(Ĥ)^Γ)°) ⊂ Z(Ĝ).

issues.locator: §1, Introduction, p. 650, with “(so that l_0 = 0)” on p. 651 (also in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: The source describes G(ℝ) acting on X = G(ℝ)/K_∞ with K_∞ ⊂ G(ℝ) maximal compact, assuming compact X_Γ and torsion-free Γ. It sets l_0 = rk G − rk K_∞; it also sets q_0 = ½(dim X − l_0), asserting that l_0 = 0 forces tempered representations into middle degree q_0. It says this holds for complex algebraic X_Γ, including Shimura varieties arising from G, and identifies its own Shimura variety setting with l_0 = 0.
issues.correction: Take X = G(ℝ)/K_∞A_G(ℝ)°, where K_∞ is a maximal compact subgroup and A_G is the maximal ℚ-split torus in the centre of G, as the paper itself does on p. 738 (q(G) = ½ dim G(ℝ)/K_∞A°_∞); equivalently, compute l_0 and q_0 for G/A_G. For the unitary similitude groups of the paper (A_G = 𝔾_m, the scalars) X is then the Hermitian symmetric domain, X_Γ is compact, l_0 = 0 and q_0 = Σ_τ p_τq_τ = dim S_K. The phrase “when G gives rise to a Shimura variety” needs the same convention and, in general, that the centre have the same split rank over ℚ and over ℝ (for G = Res_{F/ℚ}GL_2 with F real quadratic one still has l_0 = 1).
issues.reason: The groups of the paper are unitary similitude groups; their centre contains the ℚ-split torus 𝔾_m of scalars, on which the similitude character is t ↦ t². With K_∞ merely maximal compact, ℝ_{>0} ⊂ Z(ℝ) is not in K_∞, so rk G(ℝ) − rk K_∞ = 1 and dim X = 1 + 2Σ_τ p_τq_τ is odd; hence l_0 = 1, contradicting “l_0 = 0”, and X_Γ cannot be a complex variety. Moreover |ν| is trivial on K_∞ and on every congruence subgroup Γ (ν(Γ) ⊂ ℚ^× ∩ Ẑ^× = {±1}), so it induces a continuous surjection X_Γ → ℝ_{>0}: X_Γ is never compact, contradicting the standing assumption used for Matsushima's formula. The paper uses the correct convention on p. 738. Nothing is affected: the passage is motivational, removing A_G lowers dim X and l_0 by the same amount so that q_0 = dim S_K either way, and Theorem 1.1 is proved for S_K through Theorem 6.3.1.

issues.locator: §1, Remark 1.14, p. 657; the same claim in §4.3, Remark 4.3.14, p. 721 (both also in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: On p. 657 the source says that basic b gives an image which is discrete and cocompact in J_b(ℚ_p), connecting it to uniformization at p of the basic locus via [RZ96]. On p. 721 it repeats that, for the basic Newton stratum, the displayed homomorphism has discrete cocompact image in J_b(ℚ_p) associated with p-adic uniformization.
issues.correction: Let b be basic and let J_b(ℚ_p)^0 = ker(ht) be the open normal subgroup of self-quasi-isogenies of height 0. The image of π_1^proét(𝒮^b_K, x̄) → J_b(ℚ_p), well defined up to conjugacy, is a discrete subgroup contained in J_b(ℚ_p)^0, so it is never cocompact in J_b(ℚ_p). For K^p small, p-adic uniformization [RZ96] writes the basic locus as ⊔_i Γ_i∖𝔐_red; on Γ_i∖𝔐_red the image is the stabiliser in Γ_i of a connected component of 𝔐_red, which is cocompact in the open stabiliser of that component in J_b(ℚ_p) but not in J_b(ℚ_p). It is infinite when the connected components of 𝔐_red are not quasi-compact, and trivial when the basic locus is finite (e.g. for the Harris–Taylor Shimura varieties). The discrete subgroups cocompact (modulo the centre) in J_b(ℚ_p) are the uniformising groups Γ_i themselves, not the monodromy image.
issues.reason: The torsor of Proposition 1.13 (= Proposition 4.3.13, p. 720) parametrises quasi-isogenies ρ : A[p^∞] → 𝕏_b respecting the extra structures. The height of ρ is locally constant and ht(g∘ρ) = ht(g) + ht(ρ) for g ∈ J_b(ℚ_p), so over a connected base the monodromy lies in ker(ht). But p·id ∈ J_b(ℚ_p) is central, respects the extra structures (scaling the polarization by p²) and has height ht(𝕏_b) > 0; hence J_b(ℚ_p)/ker(ht) is an infinite discrete space onto which J_b(ℚ_p)/Γ′ surjects for every subgroup Γ′ ⊂ ker(ht), and no such Γ′ is cocompact. Concretely, in the Harris–Taylor case the basic stratum is finite, each connected component is a geometric point, the pro-étale fundamental group and hence the image are trivial, while J_b(ℚ_p) ⊃ ℚ_p^× is not compact. The remarks are expository and Proposition 4.3.13 is explicitly not used later, so nothing is affected.

issues.locator: §2.1, Example 2.1.1, p. 661 (also in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: The source describes Fl_{G̃,µ̃} as the flag variety classifying subspaces W ⊂ V that are totally isotropic.
issues.correction: The flag variety Fl_{G̃,µ̃} parametrizes Lagrangian subspaces W ⊂ V, that is, maximal (g-dimensional) totally isotropic subspaces.
issues.reason: Fl_{G̃,µ̃} = G̃/P_µ̃ (p. 660). The Hodge structure on V has types (−1,0) and (0,−1), so µ̃ has two weights, each of multiplicity g, and both weight spaces are totally isotropic; hence P_µ̃ is a Siegel parabolic and Fl_{G̃,µ̃} is the Lagrangian Grassmannian of dimension g(g+1)/2. Totally isotropic subspaces of all dimensions form a disjoint union of isotropic Grassmannians, not one flag variety. The use on p. 662, where π_HT records the g-dimensional Hodge–Tate filtration Lie(A) ⊂ C^{2g}, confirms the intended meaning; nothing depends on the wording.

issues.locator: §2.3, proof of Lemma 2.3.6, pp. 671–672
issues.printed: To establish that 𝒫_p is a torsor, the source treats the Hodge-Tate filtration’s type for 𝒱_p ⊗_{ℚ̂_p} Ô_{𝒮_K} as discrete and hence constant on every connected component of 𝒮_K. It therefore reduces verification to classical points, choosing x ∈ 𝒮_K(L, 𝒪_L), where L is finite over E_𝔭 and C is its completed algebraic closure. It attributes the identification of s_{α,p} with s_α via the Hodge-Tate isomorphism to [Bla94].
issues.correction: Apply [Bla94] only at points coming from points of S_K defined over number fields; these meet every nonempty open subset of 𝒮_K. Replace the “discrete invariant” sentence by a closedness argument: over the perfectoid Shimura variety 𝒮_{K^p}, the canonical section of 𝒢_p carries the relative Hodge–Tate filtration to a map 𝒮_{K^p} → Fℓ_{G̃,µ̃}; the preimage of the closed G(ℚ_p)-stable subvariety Fℓ_{G,µ} is closed and G(ℚ_p)-stable, hence descends to a closed subset of 𝒮_K, which contains all number-field points by [Bla94] and is therefore everything; since G → G/P_µ is Zariski-locally trivial, this gives local sections of 𝒫_p. Alternatively, first match s_{α,dR} and s_{α,p} under the relative p-adic de Rham comparison over all of 𝒮_K, deducing this from number-field points by horizontality exactly as in the proofs of Lemma 2.3.7 (p. 672) and Proposition 2.3.9 (p. 674), which do not use Lemma 2.3.6; the printed argument then applies at every classical point.
issues.reason: Blasius's theorem concerns abelian varieties over number fields, and the paper cites it only in that form elsewhere: “At points of S_K corresponding to abelian varieties defined over number fields, this follows from [Bla94]” (proof of Lemma 2.3.7, p. 672) and “… matched at points defined over number fields, and thus globally” (proof of Proposition 2.3.9, p. 674). Here it is applied at an arbitrary point over a finite extension L of E_𝔭, which in general is not defined over a number field (there are uncountably many L-points). In addition, the claim that the type of the Hodge–Tate filtration is locally constant presupposes that the filtration is a G-filtration at every point, which is what the lemma is to prove. The lemma is true and every ingredient of the repair is in §2.3, so only the proof is affected.

issues.locator: §3.3, Proposition 3.3.1 and its proof, p. 682 (also in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: For closed I = [s, r] ⊂ (0, ∞) with rational r, s ∈ ℚ, the source calls 𝒴_I(R, R^+) = Spa(ℛ^{[s,r]}_R, ℛ^{[s,r],+}_{R,R^+}) a sheafy affinoid adic space. It defines ℛ^{[s,r],+}_{R,R^+} by p-adically completing the integral closure of W(R^+)[p/[ϖ^{1/r}], [ϖ^{1/s}]/p] in W(R^+)[p/[ϖ^{1/r}], [ϖ^{1/s}]/p][1/p], and appeals to the argument for Proposition 3.2.1.
issues.correction: Write r = a/b and s = c/e with positive integers a, b, c, e, and let ℛ^{[s,r],+}_{R,R^+} be the p-adic completion of the integral closure of W(R^+)[p^a/[ϖ]^b, [ϖ]^e/p^c] in W(R^+)[p^a/[ϖ]^b, [ϖ]^e/p^c][1/p]. This describes the same rational subset {|p^a| ≤ |[ϖ]^b|, |[ϖ]^e| ≤ |p^c|}, and it agrees with the printed ring whenever ϖ^{1/r} and ϖ^{1/s} exist, since (p/[ϖ^{1/r}])^a = p^a/[ϖ]^b and ([ϖ^{1/s}]/p)^c = [ϖ]^e/p^c. Alternatively, allow only r, s with 1/r, 1/s ∈ ℤ[1/p]: these roots exist because R is perfect, such values are dense in (0, ∞) and stable under multiplication by p, and they suffice for the covering of 𝒴_{(0,∞)}(R, R^+), the Frobenius isomorphisms and the limits defining ℛ̃^r_R and ℛ̃_R on p. 683.

In §3.3, R is only a perfectoid algebra of characteristic p: it contains the p-power roots of ϖ but in general no others. For R the completed perfection of 𝔽_p((t)), with value group |t|^{ℤ[1/p]}, every pseudo-uniformizer has |ϖ| = |t|^{m/p^k}, and ϖ^{1/ℓ} ∉ R for every prime ℓ ≠ p with ℓ ∤ m; so for I = [1, ℓ] the displayed ring is undefined, whatever ϖ is chosen. issues.locator: §3.5, Proposition 3.5.7(1), p. 689, and the same word in its proof, p. 690 (also in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: The source asserts lower semicontinuity of b(·) : |Fℓ_{G,µ}| → B(G). It reduces the task to proving lower semicontinuity for the composite |Spa(R, R^+)| → |Fℓ_{G,µ}| → B(G).
issues.correction: Read "upper semicontinuous" in both places, for the partial order ⪯ on B(G) defined on p. 677. That is, every point x has a neighbourhood on which b(·) ⪯ b(x). Since the image is the finite set B(G, µ^{−1}) by part (2), and κ is constant on it, this is equivalent to the following: for every b ∈ B(G), the set {x : b ⪯ b(x)} is closed. Corollary 3.5.9 (p. 690) and Theorem 1.11 (p. 655) use the proposition in exactly this form.
issues.reason:
The paper orders B(G) on p. 677 by b ⪯ b′ if ν_b ⪯ ν_{b′} and κ(b) = κ(b′). The basic element is the minimum for this order. Read with ⪯, lower semicontinuity would mean that every set {x : b(x) ⪯ b} is closed. In particular the basic stratum would be closed. Corollary 3.5.9 says it "follows immediately" from the proposition, but it states the opposite: the basic stratum is open, and each Fℓ^{⪰b}_{G,µ} = ⊔_{b⪯b′} Fℓ^{b′}_{G,µ} is closed. Theorem 1.11 says the same. The modular-curve example on p. 655 shows that the printed direction cannot hold. There Fℓ = ℙ^1, the strata are ℙ^1(ℚ_p) and Ω², and Ω² is open. Under the printed reading Ω² would also be closed, which is impossible because |ℙ^1| is connected and both strata are non-empty.

The word comes from [KL15, Th. 7.4.5]. There it refers to the y-coordinates of the convex slope polygon (Def. 7.4.1), and the proof shows that near β the polygon lies on or above the polygon at β. With the endpoints fixed, a higher polygon has less spread-out slopes, so it corresponds to a smaller Newton point for ⪯. This does not depend on the sign convention linking bundles to B(G), because ν ⪯ ν′ if and only if −w_0ν ⪯ −w_0ν′. So Kedlaya–Liu's result is exactly upper semicontinuity of b(·) for ⪯. The argument on p. 690 (reduce to representations by [RR96, Lemma 2.2], then apply [KL15, Th. 7.4.5] with Corollary 3.3.4) therefore proves the corrected statement.

Only the name of the property is wrong. The intended statement is clear from Corollary 3.5.9 and Theorem 1.11, it is proved, and it is used correctly. None of the paper's results change. The printed wording of Proposition 3.5.7(1) is still false under the paper's own order, so the misprint sits in a stated result. It should be recorded as a misprint, not as an error. As printed, the statement of Proposition 3.5.7(1) is false; items use the corrected direction.
issues.known: No erratum or published remark was found. The non-compact sequel (Caraiani–Scholze 2024, Theorem 2.7.3) restates the result directly as closedness of Fℓ^{≥b}, which agrees with the corrected reading, and does not repeat the word.

issues.locator: §4.1, proof of Lemma 4.1.8, p. 696 (also in arXiv v1, p. 41)
issues.printed: Using Dieudonné-Manin classification, the source reduces the argument to excluding elements x ∈ A_cris(R) satisfying p^aφ^b(x) = x for positive integers a, b > 0.
issues.correction: … we have to see that there are no nonzero elements x ∈ A_cris(R) with p^aφ^b(x) = x, where a, b > 0 are positive integers.
issues.reason: The sentence is printed exactly as recorded on p. 696. This was checked on the page image, and the text layer agrees. Read literally, the claim is false, because x = 0 satisfies p^aφ^b(x) = x. What the proof needs is that every solution is zero. The reduction runs as follows. By the Dieudonné–Manin classification over F̄_p, it suffices to treat a simple isocrystal D of slope a/b > 0. It has a basis e_1, …, e_b with φ(e_i) = e_{i+1} for i < b and φ(e_b) = p^a e_1. An element Σ x_i ⊗ e_i of D ⊗ B^+_cris(R) is φ-invariant if and only if x_{i+1} = φ(x_i) for i < b and x_1 = p^aφ(x_b). That is, x_1 = p^aφ^b(x_1), and x_1 determines the other coordinates. Multiplying by a power of p puts x_1 in A_cris(R). So (D ⊗ B^+_cris(R))^{φ=1} = 0 is equivalent to the vanishing of every x ∈ A_cris(R) with p^aφ^b(x) = x. The next two sentences prove exactly this: iterating gives x = p^{ma}φ^{mb}(x) ∈ p^{ma}A_cris(R) for every m ≥ 1, and A_cris(R) is p-adically separated, so x = 0. The meaning is clear, and the correction only adds the word "nonzero". Lemma 4.1.8 and Corollaries 4.1.10–4.1.11 are unaffected. arXiv v1 (p. 41) has the same wording, so the slip predates the refereed revision.

issues.correction: In the paper's normalization the block 𝕏_i contributes the entries −λ_i (respectively −λ_i/d) to the Newton point of b, and the F-isocrystal of 𝕏_i has slope −λ_i; so ν_b = (−λ_r, …, −λ_r, …, −λ_1, …, −λ_1) (respectively with −λ_i/d), and ⟨c, ν_b⟩ = −1. Each displayed vector is ν_b^* = −w_0ν_b, the Newton point of the dual isocrystal; the displays and item (2) are correct with ν_b^* in place of ν_b, and ⟨2ρ, ν_b^*⟩ = ⟨2ρ, ν_b⟩.
issues.reason: ν_b is defined by the slope decomposition of (V ⊗ L, bσ) (p. 676); a p-divisible group isoclinic of slope λ has isocrystal slope −λ (p. 692, Example 4.1.3); and for b ∈ B(G, µ^{−1}) the slopes of b on V lie in [−1, 0] (p. 697). Also ⟨c, ν_b⟩ = ⟨c, µ^{−1}⟩ = −1 since c∘µ = id. The printed vectors have nonnegative entries and ⟨c, ·⟩ = +1, so they are not ν_b; e.g. for 𝕏_b = µ_{p^∞} × ℚ_p/ℤ_p (Remark 4.2.12) ν_b = (0, −1), whereas the printed rule gives (1, 0). Since −w_0 permutes the positive roots, every dimension count stands, and item (2) evaluates on the displayed vector, where c pairs to 1. Sign convention only.

issues.locator: §4.2, proof of Proposition 4.2.11, case G = GSp_n/𝒪_F, items (1) and (2), p. 708 (also in arXiv v1, p. 51)
issues.printed: The source gives two contributions to dim Aut_G(𝕏̃_b). (1) For λ_j > λ_i ≥ d/2, it gives d_{i,j} = m_im_j(λ_j − λ_i), matching λ_j/d, λ_i/d in ⟨2ρ, ν_b⟩ as in the EL case; polarization covers d/2 ≥ λ_j > λ_i. (2) For λ_j ≥ d/2 ≥ d − λ_i, i ≠ j, it gives m_im_j(λ_i + λ_j − d), the internal Hom 𝒪_F-module’s dimension from 𝕏_i^∨ to 𝕏_j when j < i. It claims agreement with λ_j/d, 1 − λ_i/d and λ_i/d, 1 − λ_j/d in ⟨2ρ, ν_b⟩ using ⟨c, ν_b⟩ = 1.
issues.correction: Treat the middle slope as a separate case. In (1), require λ_j > λ_i > d/2, and d/2 > λ_j > λ_i in its polarization clause. In (2), require λ_j > d/2 > d − λ_i. Add the following case. Suppose d/2 is a slope λ_i. Then the polarization identifies 𝕏_i with 𝕏_i^∨, and m_i is even. For each λ_j > d/2, the pair {𝕏_i, 𝕏_j} contributes m_im_j(λ_j − d/2) exactly once to each side. On the dimension side, this is the dimension of the internal Hom 𝒪_F-module from 𝕏_i to 𝕏_j; the polarization determines the internal Hom from 𝕏_j^∨ to 𝕏_i^∨ ≅ 𝕏_i. On the root side, let k run over block j and l over the m_i/2 coordinates of block i among the first n/2. For each τ this gives m_jm_i/2 roots e_{τ,k} − e_{τ,l} and m_jm_i/2 roots e_{τ,k} + e_{τ,l} − c, each taking the value (λ_j − d/2)/d at ν_b, so the total over the d embeddings is m_im_j(λ_j − d/2). The block 𝕏_i paired with itself contributes 0 to both sides. With this change, items (1)–(3) and the new case partition both the dimension of Aut_G(𝕏̃_b) and ⟨2ρ, ν_b⟩, and the matching holds case by case.
issues.reason:
Suppose λ_i = d/2 and λ_j > d/2. Then the pair (i, j) satisfies the hypotheses of both (1) and (2). Since 𝕏_i^∨ ≅ 𝕏_i, the internal Hom between 𝕏_i^∨ and 𝕏_j used in (2) is the internal Hom of (1). So one piece of Aut_G(𝕏̃_b), of dimension m_im_j(λ_j − d/2), is counted twice. The root-side matches claimed in (1) and (2) also fail for this pair. Only m_i/2 of the m_i coordinates of ν_b equal to 1/2 lie among the first n/2, so the roots e_{τ,k} − e_{τ,l} give only half the claimed value, and so do the roots e_{τ,k} + e_{τ,l} − c.

Example: take F = ℚ_p (d = 1), G = GSp_4 and ν_b = (1, 1/2, 1/2, 0), which is the p-divisible group of a principally polarized abelian surface of p-rank 1. The slopes are 1, 1/2, 0 with m = 1, 2, 1.
- Root side: e_1 − e_2 contributes 1/2, e_1 + e_2 − c contributes 1/2, 2e_1 − c contributes 1 and 2e_2 − c contributes 0, so ⟨2ρ, ν_b⟩ = 2.
- Dimension side: Hom(𝕏_2, 𝕏_1) has dimension 1, and it determines Hom(𝕏_3, 𝕏_2). The part of Hom(ℚ_p/ℤ_p, μ_{p^∞}) compatible with the polarization has dimension 1. So dim Aut_G(𝕏̃_b) = 2. This agrees with Remark 4.2.13: the p-rank-1 locus of 𝒜_2 is a single central leaf of dimension 2.
- Items (1)–(3) as printed give 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 on the dimension side. Items (1) and (2) each claim a root contribution of 1, where the true value is 1/2.

The printed steps are therefore false whenever d/2 is a slope and 𝕏_b is not isoclinic. In the isoclinic case, (1) and (2) are vacuous. The error cannot be fixed by changing ≥ to >: that leaves the middle-slope pairs uncovered, and they need the separate count given in the correction. Proposition 4.2.11 itself (p. 704) is true. I checked the corrected case division against both ⟨2ρ, ν_b⟩ and the orbit-by-orbit dimension count over many symmetric slope data, with and without a middle slope, and they agreed every time. The printed division over-counts exactly when there is a middle slope together with a slope above d/2. The same passage appears unchanged in arXiv v1.

issues.locator: §4.2, the paragraph before Proposition 4.2.14, Proposition 4.2.14 and the first line of its proof, p. 709 (also in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: The source writes M_{D,∞} ×_{Fℓ_{G,µ}} M_{D,∞} ⊂ M_{D,∞} ×_{Spa(Ĕ,O_Ĕ)} M_{D,∞}. Proposition 4.2.14 asserts that the morphism describing the action, M̂_{D,∞} ×_{Spa(L,O_L)} Aut_G(𝕏̃_b)^ad_η → (M_{D,∞} ×_{Fℓ_{G,µ}} M_{D,∞})^∧ is an isomorphism in the category of perfectoid spaces. Its proof takes a perfectoid affinoid algebra (R, R^+) over Ĕ.
issues.correction: Take both fibre products over Spa(Ĕ(ζ_{p^∞})^∧), the base of M_{D,∞} in Theorem 4.2.4. The target then becomes (M_{D,∞} ×_{Fℓ_{G,µ} ×_{Spa E} Spa(Ĕ(ζ_{p^∞})^∧)} M_{D,∞})^∧, a closed subspace of M_{D,∞} ×_{Spa(Ĕ(ζ_{p^∞})^∧)} M_{D,∞}, and in the proof (R, R^+) is a perfectoid affinoid Ĕ(ζ_{p^∞})^∧-algebra. With these changes the printed proof proves the statement. With the products taken over Spa(Ĕ, O_Ĕ) as printed, the action map is an isomorphism only onto the open and closed subspace lying over the diagonal of Spa(Ĕ(ζ_{p^∞})^∧) ×_{Spa Ĕ} Spa(Ĕ(ζ_{p^∞})^∧) ≅ ℤ_p^× × Spa(Ĕ(ζ_{p^∞})^∧). Equivalently, keep the printed target and enlarge the source by ℤ_p^× = Gal(Ĕ(ζ_{p^∞})/Ĕ), where u ∈ ℤ_p^× acts by (𝒢, λ, ρ, α) ↦ (𝒢, uλ, ρ, α) and twists the structure map by ζ ↦ ζ^u.
issues.reason:
By Definition 4.2.3 and Theorem 4.2.4, M_{D,∞} is a space over Spa(Ĕ(ζ_{p^∞})^∧), because condition (1) of Definition 4.2.3 ties the polarization and α to the fixed p-power roots of unity. The text just before the proposition itself recalls that M_{D,∞} lives over the completion of E(ζ_{p^∞}) (for Ĕ). Aut_G(𝕏̃_b)^ad_η acts on M_{D,∞} by changing only the quasi-isogeny ρ. In the rational description, it composes the map V → (𝕏̃_b)^ad_η(R, R^+) with g and leaves the structure map to the base unchanged. So every pair (x, x·g) in the image has equal structure maps to Spa(Ĕ(ζ_{p^∞})^∧).

The printed target contains other pairs. Take x = (𝒢, λ, ρ, α) over (R, R^+) and u ∈ ℤ_p^× with u ≠ 1, and put y = (𝒢, uλ, ρ, α). Then uλ is again a principal polarization with the same Rosati involution. The quasi-isogeny ρ respects uλ up to the scalar u·c(ρ). The Weil pairing of uλ is the u-th power of that of λ, so α matches it with respect to ζ^u. Hence y is a point of M_{D,∞} over the structure map twisted by ζ ↦ ζ^u. By Proposition 4.2.5, π_HT(y) = π_HT(x), because π_HT depends only on the map V → (𝕏̃_b)^ad_η. So (x, y) lies in M_{D,∞} ×_{Fℓ_{G,µ}} M_{D,∞} ⊂ M_{D,∞} ×_{Spa Ĕ} M_{D,∞}, but it is not in the image. For this pair, the construction in the proof gives the identity isomorphism 𝒢_{1,R} ≅ 𝒢_{2,R}, so g = 1 and x·1 = x ≠ y. The target over Ĕ is therefore a disjoint union of ℤ_p^×-many copies of the image, and the statement as printed is false.

The slip goes beyond the base of one fibre product, since Fℓ_{G,µ} itself is defined over E. The proof, and the proof of Proposition 4.2.23 ('defined over Spa(Ĕ, O_Ĕ)'), work over Ĕ throughout. So this is an error in the statement rather than a misprint, although the intended statement is clear and correct over Ĕ(ζ_{p^∞})^∧.

The proposition is used only in the proof of Proposition 4.2.23 (p. 713), and that use is unaffected. There the fibre of M_{D,∞} over a geometric point ȳ of Fℓ^b_{G,µ} is the product of the profinite set ℤ_p^× with Aut_G(𝕏̃_b)^ad_η ×_{Spa Ĕ} Spa(C, O_C), which has the same dimension. So dim Fℓ^b_{G,µ} = ⟨2ρ, µ⟩ − ⟨2ρ, ν_b⟩ still holds.

issues.locator: §4.2, Remark 4.2.17, p. 710 (used in the proof of Lemma 4.3.15, p. 722; same text in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: The source uses the lemma to extend the main full faithfulness result of [Ber80] beyond the noetherian setting, replacing V by any integral domain R. It argues that extension to R of a homomorphism over K amounts to checking that the entries of specified K-matrices belong to R, a condition testable on valuation rings.
issues.correction: … the same fully faithfulness result holds true for any integrally closed domain R of characteristic p (with G, H p-divisible groups over R of constant Newton polygon) in place of V. Indeed, to check whether a homomorphism over K extends to R, one has to check whether certain matrices over K have entries in R, which can be checked on the valuation rings of K containing R, since R is their intersection.
issues.reason:
The valuation rings of K containing R intersect in the integral closure of R, not in R itself, so the argument only shows that the matrix entries are integral over R. The theorem of [Ber80] being generalised (Th. 4.7.2) assumes the base is connected and normal; its proof uses R = ∩ R_𝔭 over height-one primes. Lemma 4.2.15 (p. 709) likewise assumes R⁺ integrally closed in R. So normality is the hypothesis that matters, and dropping it makes the claim false.

Counterexample: let R = {f ∈ F̄_p[t] : f(0) = f(1)}, the affine line with 0 and 1 glued, with K = F̄_p(t). Let G be the étale p-divisible group of height 1 whose Tate module is the rank-one ℤ_p-local system that is trivial on the normalization A¹ and glued at the node by some u ∈ ℤ_p^× with u ≠ 1. Let H = ℚ_p/ℤ_p. Both are étale, so both have constant Newton polygon. G_K is constant, so Hom_K(H_K, G_K) = ℤ_p. But Hom_R(H, G) = {v ∈ ℤ_p : uv = v} = 0. R is even noetherian, and the same example works after passing to perfections.

The remark is invoked only in the domain case of the proof of Lemma 4.3.15 (p. 722). There it is applied to strictly henselian perfect domains, which need not be normal: the perfection of the strict henselisation of the Whitney umbrella at its pinch point is an example. So that proof has a gap. Lemma 4.3.15 itself still holds, and the gap can be closed as follows. The normalization R′ of R is again a strictly henselian perfect domain with residue field k, and the corrected remark applies to it. Descend the resulting quasi-isogeny from R′ to R along the v-cover R → R′, as in the last paragraph of that proof. The uniqueness this needs comes from the Dieudonné-module computation already given there.

issues.locator: §4.2, proof of Lemma 4.2.16, p. 711 (also in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: The source reduces to simple D = D_λ of slope λ = s/r and sets the remaining task as proving W(V)[1/p]^{φ^r = p^s} = W(K)[1/p]^{φ^r = p^s}.
issues.reason: By §3.1 (p. 676) the simple isocrystal of slope s/r is (L^r, Aσ) with Ae_1 = p^se_r and Ae_j = e_{j−1} for j ≥ 2. A vector x = Σx_je_j of D_λ ⊗ B is φ-fixed iff x_{j−1} = σ(x_j) for 2 ≤ j ≤ r and x_r = p^sσ(x_1), so it is determined by x_1 subject to x_1 = p^sσ^r(x_1), i.e. φ^r(x_1) = p^{−s}x_1. The rest of the proof is symmetric in the sign of s (valuations for s ≠ 0; ℚ_p for s = 0), so Lemma 4.2.16 is unaffected.

issues.locator: §4.2, proof of Proposition 4.2.22, pp. 712–713 (also in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: Proposition 4.2.22 asserts that, for every complete nonarchimedean field K/O_Ĕ, Aut_G(𝕏̃_b)^ad ×_{Spa(O_Ĕ,O_Ĕ)} Spa(K, O_K) has partial properness over Spa(K, O_K) with dimension ⟨2ρ, ν_b⟩. The proof attributes partial properness of the adic generic fiber to Lemma 4.2.15.
issues.correction: Lemma 4.2.15 covers only K of characteristic 0, but the statement also allows K of characteristic p, and the proof uses that case (“by tilting we can assume that K is of characteristic p”, p. 713). For all K, partial properness follows from Proposition 4.2.11: the space maps to the locally profinite set J_b(ℚ_p) with fibres the open perfectoid unit polydisc of dimension d = ⟨2ρ, ν_b⟩ over K, so a (K′, K′^+)-point is an element of J_b(ℚ_p) together with compatible p-power roots of d topologically nilpotent elements of K′; these lie in every K′^+, so the points do not depend on K′^+, which is the criterion of Remark 4.2.20.
issues.reason: Lemma 4.2.15 concerns rings R = R^+[1/p] and extends homomorphisms from R to R^+. If K has characteristic p then K^+[1/p] = 0, the lemma says nothing, and the space lies over the special fibre of Spa(O_Ĕ, O_Ĕ), not the generic fibre. The missing case is easy, the dimension computation uses only the underlying topological space, and Proposition 4.2.23 applies Proposition 4.2.22 only over fields of characteristic 0, so nothing is affected.

issues.printed: The source classifies pairs (A, ρ̃) up to isomorphism, with A ∈ 𝒮_{K_pK^p}(R) taken up to p-power isogeny preserving extra structures and a quasi-isogeny ρ : A[p^∞] ⥲ 𝕏_b ×_{F̄_p} R. issues.locator: §4.3, Remark 4.3.14, p. 721 (also in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: The source allows the displayed map to have noncompact image generally, but asserts compactness if 𝕏 has a slope decomposition or is isogenous to a group with one. It uses this to explain [OZ02, Ex. 4.2], which constructs a p-divisible group on a nonnormal base having no isogenous group with a slope filtration.
issues.correction: … but the image is compact in case 𝕏 is completely slope divisible in the sense of [OZ02, Def. 1.2] (after passing to the perfection of S, such an 𝕏 is pro-étale locally isomorphic to a constant group, so the image lies in a compact open subgroup of J_b(ℚ_p)), or is isogenous to such an 𝕏; this explains [OZ02, Ex. 4.2], where a p-divisible group over a nonnormal base is constructed that is not isogenous to a completely slope divisible one.
issues.reason: A decomposition into isoclinic summands does not force compact image; an isoclinic group is its own slope decomposition. Take G = G_{1,2} (isoclinic of height 3, with a unique α_p ⊂ G and G/α_p ≅ G via Frobenius) and follow [OZ02, Ex. 4.2] with both factors equal to G: on T = ℙ^1 embed α_p(𝒪(−1)) into α_p × α_p ⊂ G × G by (ι_0, ι_∞), take the quotient X_T, and glue its fibres X_0 = G × G/α_p and X_∞ = G/α_p × G, both identified with G × G via Frobenius, over the nodal curve T/(0 ∼ ∞). The resulting isoclinic group has monodromy diag(Fr^{−1}, Fr) ∈ GL_2(D) = J_b(ℚ_p), D = End^0(G), whose powers are unbounded. The remark's own next sentence (cocompact image on the basic stratum, where the group is isoclinic) also contradicts it. For completely slope divisible 𝕏 over a perfect base the group splits canonically into isoclinic pieces, each pro-étale locally constant [OZ02, Prop. 1.3], so the torsor comes from a compact group, as on p. 657. [OZ02, Ex. 4.2] itself asserts only that there is no isogeny to a completely slope divisible group. Proposition 4.3.13 and the remark are not used later.

issues.locator: §4.3, proof of Lemma 4.3.15, case of an integral domain, p. 722, citing Lemma 4.2.16 and Remark 4.2.17 (p. 710); the same passage appears in arXiv v1
issues.printed: Starting with an integral domain R and its fraction field K, the source invokes Lemma 4.2.16 and Remark 4.2.17 for full faithfulness of passage from p-divisible groups over R to those over K. It chooses ψ′_K : G_K → G_{0,K}, an isogeny with degree bounded solely by h, and asserts extension to ψ′ : G → G_{0,R} with the same sort of bound.
issues.correction: Let K̄ be an algebraic closure of K and R̄ the integral closure of R in K̄. R̄ is an integral domain that is integral over the strictly henselian ring R, so it is local and strictly henselian. It is integrally closed and perfect, and its residue field is k, because k is perfect and separably closed and hence algebraically closed. Over K̄, the Dieudonné–Manin classification gives an isogeny ψ′_{K̄} : G_{K̄} → G_{0,K̄} of degree bounded in terms of h. Apply Lemma 4.2.16 on each valuation ring of K̄ containing R̄; the intersection of these rings is R̄. Hence both ψ′_{K̄} and p^N(ψ′_{K̄})^{−1} extend over R̄, so ψ′_{K̄} extends to an isogeny ψ′ : G_{R̄} → G_{0,R̄} of bounded degree. Correcting at k as printed gives a quasi-isogeny ψ_{R̄} : G_{R̄} → G_{0,R̄} that lifts ψ_k and for which p^cψ_{R̄} and p^cψ_{R̄}^{−1} are isogenies. The ring B = R̄ ⊗_R R̄ is perfect and integral over R, and it has a single prime over the closed point, with residue field k. So B is a strictly henselian perfect local ring. The two pullbacks of ψ_{R̄} to B both lift ψ_k, so they agree by the uniqueness of lifts proved at the start of the proof: after inverting p, homomorphisms between constant groups over a connected perfect ring inject into homomorphisms over k. Since R → R̄ is injective and integral, Spec R̄ → Spec R is a v-cover, and [BS17, Th. 4.1(i)] gives R = {f ∈ R̄ : f ⊗ 1 = 1 ⊗ f in B}. Choose R-bases of the Hopf algebras of the p^n-torsion. The matrices of p^cψ_{R̄} and p^cψ_{R̄}^{−1} in these bases then have entries in R, so ψ_{R̄} descends to the required quasi-isogeny ψ : G → G_{0,R}. The case of several minimal primes then applies this to each R/𝔭_i, as printed.
issues.reason:
Two steps of the domain case are unsupported. The statements they are used for are true, so this is a gap and not an error.

(1) Full faithfulness from R to K is taken from Lemma 4.2.16 via Remark 4.2.17. Checking matrix entries on the valuation rings of K that contain R only shows that the entries lie in the integral closure of R. So the argument covers only integrally closed domains. In fact Remark 4.2.17 is false as stated for non-normal domains. Take p odd and the perfection of the nodal cubic y² = x²(x+1). There, the étale group Q_p/Z_p twisted by the sign character of the loop has no nonzero homomorphism to Q_p/Z_p, but it becomes constant over the fraction field.

Strictly henselian perfect domains need not be integrally closed. For a prime ℓ ≠ p, take the perfection of the strict henselisation at the origin of F̄_p[x^ℓ] + yF̄_p[x, y]. This is a strictly henselian perfect domain, and it contains x^ℓ. The element x = xy/y lies in its fraction field and is a root of T^ℓ − x^ℓ, but x is not in the ring, because no x^{p^n} is. The same applies to the rings R/𝔭_i of the general case. For strictly henselian perfect domains the asserted full faithfulness does hold, but only as a consequence of the lemma being proved.

(2) The isogeny ψ′_K is asserted to exist over K, but K is only perfect, not algebraically closed. For example, if R is the perfection of F̄_p[[t]], then x^p − x = t^{−1} has no root in K. Over such a field the Dieudonné–Manin classification does not apply: an étale group whose Tate module carries a nontrivial character of Gal(K̄/K) is not isogenous over K to any group defined over F̄_p. That G_K is isogenous to a constant group depends on G extending over the strictly henselian ring R, and the argument never uses this.

Both steps are repaired by working over the integral closure of R in K̄ and then descending. The descent uses only two things the paper already has: the uniqueness of lifts (called "necessarily unique" on p. 722 and proved in the first paragraph of the proof) and the v-descent [BS17, Th. 4.1(i)] used on p. 723. So Lemma 4.3.15 and Remark 4.3.16 stand, and only their proof is affected. They serve Proposition 4.3.13 (Proposition 1.13 in the introduction), which the paper says is not used later (p. 720).
issues.known: No erratum or later correction of this step is known. The passage is unchanged from arXiv v1 to the published version. Footnote 22 (p. 722) cites [OZ02, Cor. 3.6] for the special case where R is the perfection of a noetherian strictly henselian ring and G is defined over that ring.

issues.locator: §4.4 (Étale cohomology), opening paragraph, p. 726; the same sentence is in arXiv v1, §4.4
issues.printed: The source additionally assumes properness of 𝒮_{K_pK^p} over 𝒪_{E,𝔭} in this section. Citing [Lan11], it says this is equivalent to G being anisotropic over ℚ.
issues.correction: … It is known that this is equivalent to asking that G^ad is anisotropic over ℚ, i.e. that G is anisotropic modulo its centre (equivalently, G has no proper parabolic ℚ-subgroup, or the Shimura varieties Sh_K are compact); cf. [Lan11].
issues.reason: Here G is the PEL group of §4.3 (p. 713), G(R) = {x ∈ End_{B⊗R}(V⊗R) : xx* ∈ R^×}. For t ∈ R^×, the scalar t·id_V is B-linear and has adjoint t, so its similitude factor is t². Hence t ↦ t·id_V embeds 𝔾_m into the centre of G, and G always contains a nontrivial central ℚ-split torus. Read literally, "G is anisotropic over ℚ" therefore never holds, yet the compact PEL Shimura varieties of §6.3 (p. 756) are proper. The intended condition is anisotropy modulo the centre, i.e. G^ad is ℚ-anisotropic. For a connected reductive group this is equivalent to having no proper parabolic ℚ-subgroup. By Borel–Harish-Chandra and Mostow–Tamagawa it is equivalent to compactness of the Shimura varieties, and [Lan11] passes from a proper generic fibre to a proper integral model 𝒮_{K_pK^p} over 𝒪_{E,𝔭}. The page image shows the same loose usage on p. 651 ("an anisotropic unitary similitude group"), so the intended meaning is clear. The working hypothesis of §4.4, and hence of Theorem 4.4.4 (p. 729), is properness of 𝒮_{K_pK^p} itself. The reformulation is used only when §6.3 applies §4.4 to a compact Shimura variety, and it holds in the corrected form. No stated result or proof changes.
issues.known: No published erratum is known for this sentence. Writing "anisotropic" for "anisotropic modulo the centre" is a common abuse of language for similitude groups. The sentence appears unchanged in arXiv v1 (with a comma before "cf.") and in the published version (with a semicolon).

issues.locator: §4.4, proof of Lemma 4.4.1, p. 727 (also in arXiv v1, p. 67)
issues.printed: Spa(C(x), C(x)^+) ∼ lim_j Spa(R_j, R_j^+)
issues.correction: Spa(C(x̄), C(x̄)^+) ∼ lim_j Spa(R_j, R_j^+)
issues.reason: On the page image of p. 727, the first display of the proof reads "Spa(C(x), C(x)^+) ∼ lim_{←j} Spa(R_j, R_j^+)". Both arguments have a plain x with no bar. A magnified image shows this clearly, and the bar on x̄ is clearly printed in "neighborhoods of x̄" in the line just above and in "(R^i f_*G)_x̄" just below, so this is not a text-layer artefact. The statement of Lemma 4.4.1 on p. 726 introduces only C(x̄): a completed algebraic closure of the residue field K(x), with an open and bounded valuation subring C(x̄)^+ lifting K(x)^+. It gives the geometric point x̄ = Spa(C(x̄), C(x̄)^+) → X and the fibre Y_x̄ = (Y ×_X Spa(C(x̄), C(x̄)^+))^∧. No field C(x) is defined in this context. The only other use of the symbol, on p. 684 in §3, belongs to an unrelated argument about points of Spa(R, R^+). The proof takes the limit over a cofinal system U_j = Spa(R_j, R_j^+) of affinoid étale neighbourhoods of x̄. That limit is the geometric point x̄ = Spa(C(x̄), C(x̄)^+), and this is what the next step needs: Y_x̄ ∼ lim_j Y ×_X Spa(R_j, R_j^+). So the display must be read with C(x̄) and C(x̄)^+. The meaning is clear from the context, and the proposed correction is right. The same slip appears on p. 67 of arXiv v1, which is the only arXiv version. The published version did not change this passage. This is not among the recorded misprints E1–E13, none of which is on p. 727. No erratum to the paper is known: the journal page lists none, and Crossref records no update.

issues.printed: The source asserts that, for every i, both canonical arrows H^i(X, ℤ/ℓ^nℤ) ← H^i(𝔛_{𝒪_C}, ℤ/ℓ^nℤ) → H^i(𝒳_C, ℤ/ℓ^nℤ) give isomorphisms.

issues.reason: The étale site of 𝔛_{𝒪_C} is that of its reduced special fibre X ×_{F̄_p} k. The proof treats the first map as H^i(X_0) → H^i(X_0 ×_{F̄_p} k), an isomorphism by invariance under change of algebraically closed base field. Only the arrow is wrong; Theorem 4.4.4 is unaffected.

issues.locator: §5.4: definition of Red^b_n⃗ (p. 739), Remark 5.4.1 and Lemma 5.4.2 (p. 740), identical in arXiv v1; inherited by Lemma 5.5.1 (p. 741), and by the identity before Corollary 5.6.2 and Corollary 5.6.2 itself (p. 749)
issues.printed: On p. 739 the source defines Red^b_n⃗ by composing maps (1), (2), (3): normalized Jacquet functors, transfer along η̃_n⃗, and the Langlands–Jacquet map. It refers to [Shi11], Section 5.5, for their precise definitions. Remark 5.4.1 describes Red^b_n as a normalized Jacquet functor composed with the Langlands-Jacquet map. Lemma 5.4.2 asserts tr π_p(φ^n⃗_p) = tr(Red^b_n⃗(π_p))(φ_p).
issues.correction: Define Red^b_n⃗(π_p) := n-Red^b_n⃗(π_p) ⊗ δ̄^{1/2}_{P(ν_b)}. Here n-Red^b_n⃗ is the composite of maps (1)–(3), and δ̄_{P(ν_b)} : J_b(ℚ_p) → ℂ^× is the character δ̄_{P(ν_b)}(δ) = δ_{P(ν_b)}(γ_0), where γ_0 ∈ M_b(ℚ_p) is an element whose stable conjugacy class matches that of δ and δ_{P(ν_b)} is the modulus character of the parabolic P(ν_b) with Levi M_b ([Shi10, §6]; [Shi11, §5.5]). Remark 5.4.1 then reads Red^b_n(π_p) = e_p(J_b)·LJ(J_{P(ν_b)^op}(π_p)) ⊗ δ̄^{1/2}_{P(ν_b)}, with the Kottwitz sign e_p(J_b) = c_{M_b} as in [Shi11, (5.16)]. Equivalently, keep the untwisted composite and evaluate the right side of Lemma 5.4.2 at φ_p·δ̄^{1/2}_{P(ν_b)} instead of φ_p.
issues.reason: Definition 5.2.2 takes φ^n⃗_p to be the function constructed in [Shi10, §6], and Theorem 5.2.3 holds for that function. In that construction the function transferred to M_H(ℚ_p) is φ′_p := φ_p·δ̄^{1/2}_{P(ν_b)}, not φ_p. The factor comes from |D^G_{M_b}(γ_0)|_p^{1/2} = δ_{P(ν_b)}(γ_0)^{1/2} on ν_b-acceptable elements. For this reason [Shi11, §5.5] gives the name n-Red^b_n⃗ to the composite of exactly the three maps printed on p. 739, and defines Red^b_n⃗ := n-Red^b_n⃗ ⊗ δ̄^{1/2}_{P(ν_b)}. [Shi11, Lemma 5.10], which the proof of Lemma 5.4.2 follows, is stated for this twisted map; its proof ends with tr(LJ(η̃_*π)) evaluated at φ_p·δ̄^{1/2} being equal to tr(LJ(η̃_*π) ⊗ δ̄^{1/2}) evaluated at φ_p. [Car12, §6, before Lemma 6.3] makes the same two-step definition. The paper says Red is "the composition of" the three maps and refers to [Shi11, §5.5] only for those maps, so the printed Red is Shin's n-Red. With it, the correct identity is tr π_p(φ^n⃗_p) = tr(Red^b_n⃗(π_p))(φ_p·δ̄^{1/2}_{P(ν_b)}). The twist is not harmless when b is non-basic. Then s·ν_b is a non-central cocharacter, (sν_b)(p) is central in both M_b and J_b, and δ̄_{P(ν_b)}((sν_b)(p)) is a nontrivial power of p. Comparing absolute values of central characters at this element shows that ρ ⊗ δ̄^{1/2} ≠ ρ for every nonzero virtual representation ρ of J_b(ℚ_p). Twisting by high powers of Frobenius, as in [Shi11, Lemma 6.4], shows the difference is detected by an acceptable φ_p. So Lemma 5.4.2 as printed fails whenever the untwisted composite is nonzero. An example is b µ-ordinary, n⃗ = (n) and π_p an unramified principal series, where J_b = M_b, LJ is the identity and the Jacquet module is nonzero. Lemma 5.5.1, the identity before Corollary 5.6.2 (obtained "making use of Lemma 5.4.2") and Corollary 5.6.2 are stated in terms of Red, so they are off by the same twist. The fix is a one-line change to the definition, and it is clearly what the authors intended, since the proof cites Shin's lemma for the twisted map. Twisting by a character preserves vanishing, so Lemma 5.4.3, Theorem 5.5.7, Corollary 5.6.3 and the main theorems are unaffected.

issues.locator: §5.5, Lemma 5.5.1, p. 742: the last clause of the statement and the sentence of the proof beginning “To check that Π^n⃗_∞ is cohomological” (the same wording is in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: The source asserts that Π^n⃗_∞ is cohomological relative to the trivial algebraic representation. It says verifying this for the trivial representation requires only determining the infinitesimal character of Π^n⃗_∞, obtainable from how the test functions at ∞ are defined.
issues.correction: … and Π^n⃗_∞ is cohomological with respect to Ξ(φ_n⃗), i.e. H^*(𝔤, K_∞; Π^n⃗_∞ ⊗ Ξ(φ_n⃗)) ≠ 0, for one of the discrete L-parameters φ_n⃗ of G_n⃗(ℝ) such that η̃∘φ_n⃗ is equivalent to the parameter of the trivial representation of G. Equivalently, ζ̃_{n⃗,*}(Π^n⃗)_∞ has the infinitesimal character of the trivial representation of 𝔾_n. For n⃗ = (n) this Ξ(φ_n⃗) is the trivial representation. For n⃗ = (n_1, n_2) with n_2 > 0, no Ξ(φ_n⃗) is trivial. In particular Π^n⃗ is regular and C-algebraic, which is all that the later arguments use. In the proof, delete “(for the trivial representation)”.
issues.reason:
The paper builds the test function at ∞ from the endoscopic parameters, not from the trivial representation of G_n⃗. On p. 735, φ^n⃗_∞ is a combination of Euler–Poincaré functions over the parameters φ_{G_n⃗} with η̃∘φ_{G_n⃗} corresponding to the trivial representation of G_ℂ. On p. 737, f^n⃗_∞ is the matching combination of twisted Lefschetz functions f_{𝔾_n⃗,Ξ(φ_n⃗)} ([Shi11, (6.7)]). The twisted trace of Π^n⃗_∞ against f_{𝔾_n⃗,Ξ} vanishes unless Π^n⃗_∞ is Ξ-cohomological, so the argument of the proof shows that each contributing Π^n⃗_∞ is Ξ(φ_n⃗)-cohomological.

For n⃗ = (n_1, n_2) with n_1, n_2 > 0, no such Ξ(φ_n⃗) is trivial. By p. 745, ζ̃ multiplies the i-th block by ϖ^{e_i} with e_i = ε(n−n_i) ∈ {0, 1}; in [Shi11, (6.3)] the exponent is n−m_i ≥ 0 instead. By p. 746, ϖ_∞(z) = (z/z̄)^{δ/2} with δ odd. So if Ξ_i is trivial, the i-th block contributes a run of n_i consecutive exponents centred at e_iδ/2. The n exponents (n+1−2j)/2 of the trivial parameter split into two such runs only with centres n_2/2 and −n_1/2, or −n_2/2 and n_1/2. These have opposite signs, while e_1δ/2 and e_2δ/2 have the same sign or vanish. For example, take n = 3, n⃗ = (2, 1). Each of the three ways of distributing the exponents {1, 0, −1} between the blocks gives a nontrivial Ξ(φ_n⃗).

Read literally, the lemma would therefore force every term with n⃗ ≠ (n) to vanish. That is false in general. In [Shi11, Th. 6.1(ii)] (Case END, ξ may be trivial), the weights of Ξ_1 and Ξ_2 come from a partition of those of ξ, and the endoscopic term Red^b_{m_1,m_2}(π_{H,p}) survives. For a fixed Hecke eigensystem it is not a multiple of the stable term Red^b_n(π_p).

The later results are unaffected. The lemma is used on p. 744 (“Π^n⃗_∞ is cohomological, which implies Π^n⃗ is C-algebraic”, and the regularity of the infinitesimal character in the proof of Theorem 5.5.4), in Corollary 5.5.2, in Corollary 5.5.5, on p. 750 and in the proof of Theorem 5.5.7. All of these need only cohomology for some algebraic coefficient system, or only the form of the terms. The parenthesis “(recall that for us ξ is trivial)” on p. 744 is also correct: it concerns the twist in [Shi11, (6.2)], which is by a character of A_{G_n⃗,∞} and is trivial when ξ is trivial, whatever φ_n⃗ is. So only the stated clause of Lemma 5.5.1 is wrong; Theorems 5.5.4 and 5.5.7 stand.

issues.locator: Corollary 5.5.2 (first assertion) and its proof, p. 743 (added in the published version; arXiv v1 has only Remark 5.5.2, the converse direction)
issues.printed: For fixed φ_{S_fin∖{p}} and φ_p, the source takes a θ-stable automorphic Π^n⃗ of 𝔾_n⃗ satisfying Lemma 5.5.1. Whenever it contributes to tr(φ | ι_ℓ[H_c(𝓘^b_Mant, ℚ̄_ℓ)]), the source says its transfer (Π^n⃗)^S via ζ̃_{n⃗,*} to 𝔾 = 𝔾_n occurs in BC^S([H_c(𝓘^b_Mant, ℚ̄_ℓ)]^{S ur}). The proof appeals to independence of the unramified Hecke characters.
issues.correction: Restate the first assertion for the total contribution of a Hecke eigensystem. Fix φ_{S_fin∖{p}} and φ_p, and put Π^S := ζ̃_{n⃗,*}(Π^n⃗)^S. Suppose the sum of the terms of Lemma 5.5.1 over all θ-stable Π^{n⃗′} (all n⃗′, including n⃗) with ζ̃_{n⃗′,*}(Π^{n⃗′})^S ≅ Π^S is a nonzero function of (f^n)^S. Then Π^S occurs in BC^S([H_c(𝓘^b_Mant, ℚ̄_ℓ)]^{S ur}). A single nonzero term is not enough. The converse assertion is unaffected.
issues.reason:
The proof expresses the trace as a function of (f^n)^S ∈ ℋ^ur(𝔾_n(𝔸^S)) in two ways: once through the terms of Lemma 5.5.1, and once through the Π^S that occur in the cohomology. It then uses linear independence of unramified Hecke characters. For each Π^S this equates only the total coefficient on the automorphic side with the multiplicity on the cohomological side. Remark 5.5.3 notes that several n⃗ can give the same Π^S, and the terms from different n⃗ carry signs that can cancel.

This cancellation happens within the paper's own setting. Take the setting of [Shi11], which satisfies the assumptions of §5.1, in Case END of [Shi11, §6.1]: m_1 > m_2, m_1 + m_2 = n, Π_H = ψ_H ⊗ Π_1 ⊗ Π_2, and Π = ζ̃_{m_1,m_2,*}(Π_H) = n-Ind(Π_M). The terms of Lemma 5.5.1 for n⃗ = (n) (the representation Π) and for n⃗ = (m_1, m_2) (the representation Π_H) have the same Hecke eigensystem. By [Shi11, Th. 6.1(ii), (6.6)], the Π^S-part of the Igusa cohomology is ½(e_1 Red^b_n(π_p) + e_2 Red^b_{m_1,m_2}(π_{H,p})), with e_i = ±1. By [Shi11, Lemma 5.9], Red^b_n(π_p) = e_p(J_b) π_{p,0} ⊗ (X_1 + X_2) ⊗ (⊗_{i>1} π_{w_i}) and Red^b_{m_1,m_2}(π_{H,p}) = e_p(J_b) π_{p,0} ⊗ (X_1 − X_2) ⊗ (⊗_{i>1} π_{w_i}). So only X_2 survives when e_1 = −e_2.

The case e_1 = −e_2 does occur. By [Shi11, Cor. 6.5(ii)], e_1 = (−1)^{n−1}. By [Shi11, Lemma 7.3], for m_2 = 1 exactly one of the two admissible characters χ, χ′ taken as Π_2 gives e_2 = e_1, so the other gives e_2 = −e_1.

Now take b with h(b) = m_2, and take π_{M,w,1} essentially square-integrable (for example, Π_1 supercuspidal at w). Since h < m_1, X_2 = 0. On the other hand, X_1 = LJ_{m_1}(π_{M,w,1}) ⊗ π_{M,w,2} ≠ 0. Then the term of Π in Lemma 5.5.1 is ±½ e_p(J_b) π_{p,0} ⊗ X_1 ⊗ (⊗_{i>1} π_{w_i}), which is nonzero, so Π contributes in the sense set up by the proof. But the Π^S-part of the cohomology is zero in the Grothendieck group, because BC is injective at the split places in S_fin. So Π^S does not occur, and the first assertion fails as printed.

Only the aggregate reading, in which the Hecke eigensystem as a whole contributes, is true, and that is what the proof establishes. Later arguments use only the converse direction or the aggregate form: Corollary 5.5.5, Theorem 5.5.7 (whose vanishing argument applies to every Π^{n⃗′} with the same Π), Corollary 5.6.3, and the proof of Theorem 6.3.1. So no other stated result is affected.

issues.locator: §5.5, Theorem 5.5.4, p. 744, and its proof, pp. 744–745 (arXiv v1, Theorem 5.5.3, restricts to rational primes q ≠ ℓ)
issues.printed: The source requires WD(r_i|_{Gal(F̄_𝔮/F_𝔮)})^{F−ss} ≃ ι_ℓ^{−1} rec(Π_{i,𝔮}|det|^{(1−n_i)/2}) at every place 𝔮 of F. It attributes both the existence of r_i and its local Langlands compatibility to the principal results in [Shi11], [CH13] and [Car12].
issues.correction: Replace “for any place 𝔮 of F” with “for any finite place 𝔮 of F not dividing ℓ”. This is what the cited sources prove, and it is all that is used later. Alternatively, keep every finite place, but define WD at 𝔮 | ℓ through Fontaine's D_pst of the de Rham representation r_i|_{Gal(F̄_𝔮/F_𝔮)}, and add the ℓ = p local–global compatibility theorems to the proof. These are Barnet-Lamb, Gee, Geraghty and Taylor, “Local-global compatibility for l = p, I” (Ann. Fac. Sci. Toulouse Math. 21 (2012)) and “II” (Ann. Sci. Éc. Norm. Supér. 47 (2014), Theorem A), which give the result up to semisimplification; footnote 28 says this suffices. Caraiani, “Monodromy and local-global compatibility for l = p” (Algebra Number Theory 8 (2014), Theorem 1.1), gives it up to Frobenius semisimplification. They are applied to the regular algebraic conjugate self-dual cuspidal pieces of Π_i, exactly as the proof does at places not dividing ℓ.
issues.reason:
On p. 744 the compatibility is asserted at every place 𝔮 of F. The proof on p. 745 takes it from [Shi11], [CH13] and [Car12], but none of these proves it at ramified places above ℓ.

- [Shi11], Theorem 1.2 (Theorems 7.5 and 7.11), proves the isomorphism only at places not dividing ℓ. Above ℓ it gives only potential semistability, crystallinity when Π_𝔮 is unramified, and semistability at Iwahori level.
- [CH13], Theorem 3.2.3, gives (a′) at places prime to ℓ. Above ℓ it gives: de Rham; crystalline, with the crystalline Frobenius matching rec, only when Π_𝔮 is unramified; and semistable at Iwahori level.
- [Car12] treats only places not dividing ℓ.

The finite set S need only contain p, ∞ and the primes where F or the Hecke character ramifies (p. 736; p. 757). So ℓ may lie in S, and Π_{i,𝔮} may be ramified at some 𝔮 | ℓ. The paper also never defines WD at 𝔮 | ℓ. With the standard definition through D_pst, the statement is true at every finite place by the ℓ = p theorems of Barnet-Lamb, Gee, Geraghty and Taylor, and of Caraiani (2014). The paper does not cite them, so the result stands but its proof has a gap.

“Any place” also includes the archimedean places, which are all complex since F is CM; there the display has no meaning. arXiv v1 (Theorem 5.5.3) asserted the compatibility only above rational primes q ≠ ℓ.

Later uses need only places not above ℓ:
- Corollary 5.5.5 (p. 745) uses places above q ∈ Spl ∖ (S ∪ {ℓ}), and Theorem 6.3.1 (p. 759) goes through this corollary.
- Remark 5.5.6, Theorem 5.5.7 (pp. 746–747) and Corollary 5.6.3 (p. 750) use the 𝔭_i above p, and ℓ ≠ p is fixed in §4.4 (p. 726).

issues.printed: The source writes the prime-ideal factorization of p in F as p = ∏_{i=1}^m 𝔭_i, and introduces Π := ζ̃_{n⃗,*}(Π^{n⃗}) together with Π_p = (⊗_{i=1}^m Π_{𝔭_i}) ⊗ Π_{p,0}.
issues.correction: Let 𝔭_1, …, 𝔭_m be the primes of F above u, the prime of 𝒦 over p fixed on p. 740 (p = uu^c in 𝒦). Then u𝒪_F = ∏_{i=1}^m 𝔭_i and p𝒪_F = ∏_{i=1}^m 𝔭_i𝔭_i^c. Write Π_p = ⊗_{i=1}^m (Π_{𝔭_i} ⊗ Π_{𝔭_i^c}) ⊗ Π_{p,0}, following 𝔾(ℚ_p) = (𝒦 ⊗ ℚ_p)^× × ∏_i (GL_n(F_{𝔭_i}) × GL_n(F_{𝔭_i^c})), where Π_{p,0} is a character of (𝒦 ⊗ ℚ_p)^× = ℚ_p^× × ℚ_p^×. Alternatively, keep the printed display and read Π_{p,0} as the component of Π_p on the complementary factor (𝒦 ⊗ ℚ_p)^× × ∏_i GL_n(F_{𝔭_i^c}). The assertion concerns only the factors at the 𝔭_i.
issues.reason:
By §5.1 (p. 730), p is unramified in F and split in 𝒦. So each of the m primes of F^+ above p splits in F, and p𝒪_F = ∏_{i=1}^m 𝔭_i𝔭_i^c has 2m prime factors, not m. On p. 740, 𝔭_i denotes the place of F lying over both the i-th prime of F^+ above p and u. Complex conjugation restricts to the nontrivial automorphism of 𝒦, so 𝔭_i^c lies over u^c, and ∏_i 𝔭_i = u𝒪_F.

Π = ζ̃_{n⃗,*}(Π^{n⃗}) is a representation of 𝔾(𝔸) = 𝔸_𝒦^× × GL_n(𝔸_F) (p. 746), and 𝔾(ℚ_p) = ∏_{w|p} GL_n(F_w) × ℚ_p^× × ℚ_p^× (p. 745). So Π_p has a factor at each of the 2m places of F above p. The printed display copies the decomposition π_p = ⊗_i π_{𝔭_i} ⊗ π_0 of p. 740, which is right for G(ℚ_p) = ∏_i GL_n(F_{𝔭_i}) × ℚ_p^×, because there only the places above u appear. For 𝔾 it is not.

The intended meaning is clear. The proof of Theorem 5.5.7 (p. 747) applies the remark only at the 𝔭_i of p. 740, through G_{n⃗}(ℚ_p) = ∏_i GL_{n⃗}(F_{𝔭_i}) × ℚ_p^×. Theorem 6.3.1(2) (p. 757) states the convention correctly as "the primes 𝔭_i | u of F". The claim at each 𝔭_i follows from Theorem 5.5.4, which gives local–global compatibility at every place of F. The slip therefore changes neither the conclusion of the remark nor any stated result.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 5.5.7, p. 748 (also in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: For a unique such τ, the source names its component in µ_i as µ_{i,τ} and asserts B(G_i, µ_i^{−1}) = B(GL_n/F_{𝔭_i}, µ_{i,τ}^{−1}). It invokes the relative identity B(H/L) = B(L, H), with H reductive over the p-adic field L.
issues.correction: Shapiro's bijection B(G_i) ≅ B(GL_n/F_{𝔭_i}) identifies B(G_i, µ_i^{−1}) with B(GL_n/F_{𝔭_i}, (µ_{i,τ}·z^{c_i})^{−1}), where z(t) = t·I_n and c_i is the number of τ′ ∈ S_i ∖ {τ} at which the signature is (n, 0). Multiplication by the central, Frobenius-fixed element p^{c_i} is a bijection from this set onto B(GL_n/F_{𝔭_i}, µ_{i,τ}^{−1}) which preserves J_b and sends the µ-ordinary element to the µ-ordinary element; that is all the argument and Lemma 5.5.8 need. The printed equality holds exactly when c_i = 0 (e.g. in the Harris–Taylor case).
issues.reason: Let L = F_{𝔭_i}, unramified of degree f = |S_i| over ℚ_p. Under Shapiro's bijection κ_{G_i}(b) = v_L(det b′) and the Newton condition becomes domination by Σ_{τ′∈S_i} µ_{τ′}^{−1}, not by µ_{i,τ}^{−1}. For τ′ ≠ τ one has p_{τ′}q_{τ′} = 0, so µ_{τ′} is trivial for signature (0, n) but equals z for signature (n, 0), which the hypotheses of Theorems 5.5.7 and 6.3.1 allow. Then the Kottwitz invariants differ by n·c_i and the two sets are disjoint when c_i > 0: for f = 2 with signatures (1, n−1) and (n, 0), every element of B(G_i, µ_i^{−1}) has κ = −(n+1), whereas B(GL_n/L, µ_{i,τ}^{−1}) has κ = −1. The remark that the 𝔾_m factor plays no role concerns only µ_0. Theorem 5.5.7 stands, because central translation changes neither J_b nor µ-ordinarity.

issues.locator: §6.1, proof of Proposition 6.1.3, p. 753; the formal model 𝔖_{K_pK^p,U} is introduced on p. 752 (also in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: The source invokes Theorems 6.1.1 and 6.1.2 to claim perversity of the first pushforward in this case, after a shift of ⟨2ρ, µ⟩ = dim 𝒮_{K_pK^p,U}.
issues.correction: First show that 𝔖_{K_pK^p,U} = Spf(R°_{K_pK^p,U}) is the p-adic completion of a scheme of finite type over O_K whose generic fibre is smooth of pure dimension d = ⟨2ρ, µ⟩. R_{K_pK^p,U} is smooth of pure dimension d over K, since 𝒮_{K_pK^p,U} is étale over the Shimura variety; R° is topologically of finite type since R is reduced and K discretely valued; by Elkik's algebraization theorem R° is the p-adic completion of a finite-type O_K-algebra A. Removing from Spec A the closures of the non-smooth locus of the generic fibre and of its components of dimension ≠ d does not change the completion (these closures miss the special fibre, since otherwise the tube would contain such points of 𝒮_{K_pK^p,U}). Then Theorem 6.1.1 applies with 𝓕 = 𝔽_ℓ[d], and Theorem 6.1.2 identifies Rψ𝓕 with the first pushforward.
issues.reason: Theorem 6.1.1 is stated for a scheme X of finite type over O_K and a perverse sheaf on X_η, and Theorem 6.1.2 is stated “in the situation of Theorem 6.1.1”, for the formal completion of such an X. The proof applies them to the formal scheme Spf(R°_{K_pK^p,U}), which is only topologically of finite type, without showing it to be such a completion. A reduction to a global model of the Shimura variety (an affine open in an admissible blow-up of a projective model) works only when 𝒮_{K_pK^p,U} is open in 𝒮_{K_pK^p}, whereas the proof also uses neighbourhoods built from finite étale maps. The missing step is standard (Elkik), so Proposition 6.1.3 and Corollary 6.1.4 stand.

issues.locator: §6.3, Remark 6.3.3, p. 758 (also in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: The source claims uniqueness of τ satisfying p_τq_τ ≠ 0. It says an appropriate choice of the reflex-field prime 𝔭 puts this τ in S_i with 𝔭_i = v.
issues.correction: When the remaining infinite place of F^+ is indefinite, there are exactly two embeddings τ : F ↪ ℂ with p_τq_τ ≠ 0, a conjugate pair τ_0, τ_0c (if that place is definite too there are none, and condition (2) holds trivially). Exactly one of them lies in ⋃_i S_i, since the S_i are indexed by the primes 𝔭_i of F above u and τ_0, τ_0c induce primes above u and u^c respectively. Take u to be the prime of 𝒦 below v and choose ι_p (and with it 𝔭) so that ι_p^{−1} ∘ τ_0 induces v; then τ_0 is the only τ in the sets S_i of Theorem 6.3.1(2) with p_τq_τ ≠ 0, and it lies in S_i for 𝔭_i = v.
issues.reason: Complex conjugation exchanges V ⊗_{F,τ} ℂ with V ⊗_{F,τc} ℂ and the two Hodge summands, so (p_{τc}, q_{τc}) = (q_τ, p_τ) (compare the description of µ on p. 748); the nonzero products p_τq_τ come in conjugate pairs of embeddings, which are the index set of the S_i, so “just one τ” is false. The conclusion of the remark holds because only embeddings inducing primes above u enter the sets S_i and u may be chosen below v. Nothing is affected.

issues.locator: §6.3, proof of Theorem 6.3.1(1), p. 758 (also in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: The source invokes a Hochschild-Serre spectral sequence connecting H^i(𝒮_{K^p}, 𝔽_ℓ) with H^i(S_K, 𝔽_ℓ). It deduces H^i(𝒮_{K^p}, 𝔽_ℓ)_𝔪 ≠ 0 whenever i is the least degree satisfying H^i(S_K, 𝔽_ℓ)_𝔪 ≠ 0.
issues.correction: In particular, if H^i(S_K, 𝔽_ℓ)_𝔪 ≠ 0, then H^j(𝒮_{K^p}, 𝔽_ℓ)_𝔪 ≠ 0 for some j ≤ i; hence RΓ(𝒮_{K^p}, 𝔽_ℓ)_𝔪 ≠ 0, which is all that is used afterwards.
issues.reason: The spectral sequence is E_2^{a,b} = H^a_cts(K_p, H^b(𝒮_{K^p}, 𝔽_ℓ)) ⇒ H^{a+b}(S_K, 𝔽_ℓ), compatible with the Hecke operators away from S ∪ {p, ℓ}. If b_0 is the least b with H^b(𝒮_{K^p}, 𝔽_ℓ)_𝔪 ≠ 0, the least i is ≥ b_0, with equality only when the K_p-invariants of H^{b_0}(𝒮_{K^p}, 𝔽_ℓ)_𝔪 are nonzero. K_p is hyperspecial, not pro-p, and ℓ can divide its pro-order (always for ℓ = 2, and for ℓ ≤ n + 1), in which case a nonzero smooth 𝔽_ℓ-representation can have no invariants but nonzero H^1, and E_2^{1,b_0} can survive to contribute in degree b_0 + 1. The next step uses only that some H^j(𝒮_{K^p}, 𝔽_ℓ)_𝔪 is nonzero, and part (2) uses the spectral sequence only in the valid direction, so Theorem 6.3.1 and its proof stand.

issues.locator: §6.3, proof of Theorem 6.3.1, pp. 758–759, with the set-up of §6.3 (p. 757), Corollary 6.1.4 (p. 753) and the set S of §5, which contains p (pp. 731, 736) (also in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: For (1), the source chooses arbitrary p ∈ Spl_{𝒦/ℚ} ∖ (S ∪ {ℓ}) and splits K = K_pK^p. From H^i(𝒮_{K^p}, 𝔽_ℓ)_𝔪 ≠ 0, it claims the existence of b ∈ B(G, µ^{−1}) with H^i(Ig^b, 𝔽_ℓ)_𝔪 ≠ 0. It then invokes Theorem 5.5.5 to obtain r_{Π^S,ℓ} reducing to the required ρ_𝔪.
issues.correction: Replace 𝔪 throughout by its contraction 𝔪′ = 𝔪 ∩ 𝕋^{S∪{p}} (again maximal): H^i(S_K, 𝔽_ℓ)_𝔪 is a further localization of H^i(S_K, 𝔽_ℓ)_{𝔪′}, so nonvanishing at 𝔪 gives nonvanishing at 𝔪′ and vanishing at 𝔪′ gives vanishing at 𝔪, and Corollary 6.1.4 applies with S ∪ {p} in place of S. The argument then gives a lift that is unramified, with the stated Frobenius polynomial, only at places not above S ∪ {p, ℓ}. To complete part (1), run the construction with a second auxiliary prime p′ ∈ Spl_{𝒦/ℚ} ∖ (S ∪ {ℓ, p}): the two semisimple mod-ℓ representations have the same characteristic polynomials of Frobenius on a set of places of density one, hence are isomorphic by Chebotarev and Brauer–Nesbitt, which gives unramifiedness and the Frobenius polynomial above p as well. In part (2) only the contraction is needed, since unramifiedness of ρ_𝔪 at the 𝔭_i is part of the hypothesis.
issues.reason: In §6.3, p ∉ S, so ℤ[G(ℚ_p)//K_p] is a tensor factor of 𝕋^S (p. 757); but H^i(𝒮_{K^p}, 𝔽_ℓ), H^i(Ig^b, 𝔽_ℓ) and Rπ_{HT*}𝔽_ℓ live at infinite level at p and carry no action of it, so their localizations at 𝔪 are not defined as written, and Corollary 6.1.4 is set up for p ∈ S (K^p = K^p_SK^S with K^S ⊂ G(𝔸_f^S), p. 753). Passing to 𝔪′ cures this. The substantive omission is at p: r_{Π^S,ℓ} comes from Corollary 5.5.5 (cited as “Theorem 5.5.5”), whose set S contains p, so it is known to be unramified with the prescribed Frobenius polynomial only away from p; its behaviour above p is governed by components coming from representations of J_b(ℚ_p), which need not be unramified. Theorem 6.3.1(1) nevertheless asserts both properties at the places above p. The statement is not in doubt: the free choice of p makes the two-prime argument available, and Remark 1.2 (p. 651) notes that part (1) also follows from [Sch15a].

issues.locator: §6.3, proof of Theorem 6.3.1, parts (1) and (2), p. 759 (also in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: In (1), the source uses Poincaré duality with dual Hecke eigenvalues for compact supports, writing [H_c(𝓘^b_Mant, ℚ̄_ℓ)]^{S ur} = [H_c(𝓘^b_Mant, ℚ̄_ℓ)]^{S ur}_𝔪 + [H_c(𝓘^b_Mant, ℚ̄_ℓ)]^{S ur,𝔪}. In (2), it selects b ∈ B(G, µ^{−1}) minimizing d = ⟨2ρ, ν_b⟩ subject to H^i(Ig^b, 𝔽_ℓ)_𝔪 ≠ 0 for an integer i ∈ ℤ. It claims middle-degree concentration and hence a lift r of ρ_𝔪 with BC^p([H_c(𝓘^b_Mant, ℚ̄_ℓ)]^{S ur})_r ≠ 0.
issues.correction: Let 𝔪^∨ be the image of 𝔪 under the involution [K_qgK_q] ↦ [K_qg^{−1}K_q] of 𝕋^S. Since the 𝓘^b_{Mant,m} are smooth of dimension d, Poincaré duality turns the concentration of H^*(𝓘^b_{Mant,m}, ℤ_ℓ)_𝔪 in degree d (b minimal for 𝔪) into concentration of H_c^*(𝓘^b_{Mant,m}, ℤ_ℓ)_{𝔪^∨} in degree d, nonzero for m large; so Lemma 5.5.1 and Corollaries 5.5.2 and 5.5.5 give a lift r of ρ_{𝔪^∨} with BC^S([H_c(𝓘^b_Mant, ℚ̄_ℓ)]^{S ur})_r ≠ 0. ρ_{𝔪^∨} is a twist of the dual of ρ_𝔪 (Frobenius eigenvalues q_v^{n−1}α^{−1}), and the condition λ_a/λ_b ∉ {1, q} is unchanged under inversion and twisting, so ρ_{𝔪^∨} is decomposed generic at the same primes (the paper's remark that the dual ideal satisfies the same hypothesis). Hence in part (2) Lemma 6.2.2 and Theorem 5.5.7 applied to r show that the b minimal for 𝔪 is µ-ordinary, and the proof continues as printed. In part (1), choose b minimal for 𝔪^∨ instead (possible by Poincaré duality on S_K), or obtain ρ_𝔪 from ρ_{𝔪^∨} by dualizing and twisting, as in Caraiani–Scholze, Ann. of Math. 199 (2024), Corollary 5.1.3.
issues.reason: The cup-product pairing makes each Hecke operator adjoint to its transpose, so Poincaré duality identifies H_c^i(𝓘^b_{Mant,m})_𝔪 with the dual (up to twist) of H^{2d−i}(𝓘^b_{Mant,m})_{𝔪^∨}, not of H^{2d−i}(𝓘^b_{Mant,m})_𝔪. Corollary 6.1.4 applied to b minimal for 𝔪 therefore gives concentration of compactly supported cohomology only at 𝔪^∨; “the same discussion with the dual set” would give it at 𝔪 only for a b minimal for 𝔪^∨, and in general 𝔪^∨ ≠ 𝔪. In part (1) the choice of b does not matter, but in part (2) the same b must be minimal for 𝔪, since its µ-ordinarity is fed back into Corollary 6.1.4 at 𝔪, and must carry a lift of ρ_𝔪 in compactly supported cohomology, which is asserted without proof. The paper's own ingredients close the gap, so Theorem 6.3.1 is unaffected.

issues.printed: The source defines Z ≤ Z′ for level-K cusp labels Z = (Z_N, X), Z′ = (Z_{N′}, X′) admitting lifts (Z, X), (Z′, X′) with Z_{−2} ⊂ Z′_{−2}, together with X^∨ ⊂ (X′)^∨. issues.correction: such that Z′_{−2} ⊂ Z_{−2} and (X′)^∨ ⊂ X^∨. In that case, fixing such a lift, the injection (X′)^∨ → X^∨ induces a surjection X → X′ and then inclusions M_{Z′} ⊂ M_Z and P_{Z′} ⊂ P_Z
issues.reason: Theorem 2.5.8(2) says S_Z lies in the closure of S_{Z′} iff Z ≤ Z′, so the deeper label Z must have the larger torus part; for n = 1 the cusps (rk X = 1) lie in the closure of the open stratum (X = 0), and the printed condition would require X^∨ ⊂ 0.
