issues.locator: §7.1–7.2, the series Ψ^{[m]}, Lemma 7.4 and the definitions of Log^t and Exp^t, pp.23–24, in arXiv 2102.01055v2 (10 February 2021, the latest arXiv version, 39 pp.; PDF SHA-256 d7398c4b…67f7); the published article, Invent. Math. 234 (2023), 1197–1250 (54 pp., substantially revised), was not accessible and was not collated, so this finding concerns v2
issues.printed: For integer m, the source defines Ψ^{[m]} = (Ψ^{[m]}_1, ..., Ψ^{[m]}_n) as the t-expansion of multiplication [m] : A → A. Citing [11] III.5.3 Proposition 2(i), Lemma 7.4 claims that Ψ^{[m]}_j has no terms below degree m for j = 1, ..., n. It gives Log^t_j(y) = Σ_{m≥1} ((−1)^m/m) · Ψ^{[m]}_j(y), Exp^t_j(x) = Σ_{m≥1} (1/m!) · ψ^{[m]}_j(x), where ψ^{[m]}_j is the degree-m homogeneous component of Ψ^{[m]}_j.
issues.correction: Take Ψ^{[m]} to be the m-th finite difference of the multiplication maps, Ψ^{[m]} = Σ_{i=0}^{m} (−1)^{m−i} C(m,i) [i], an explicit finite-difference replacement. Take Log^t_j(y) = Σ_{m≥1} ((−1)^{m−1}/m) Ψ^{[m]}_j(y). With these changes the degree-vanishing statement follows from the finite-difference argument preserved in the report. Identification with the unread Bourbaki text is not claimed. Lemma 7.2 still holds, as Ψ^{[m]} is an integral combination. Exp^t is the exponential, and the proofs of Lemmas 7.5–7.7 go through as written.
issues.reason: As defined, Ψ^{[m]} is multiplication by m, whose linear term is m·t_j, so Lemma 7.4 fails already for the additive formal group and m = 2. Then Log^t_j has linear term Σ_m (−1)^m y_j, which does not converge coefficientwise. The printed Exp^t is also wrong in general. For the one-dimensional formal group with logarithm f(t) = t + at² + bt³, the printed Exp^t (degree-m parts of [m], weighted by 1/m!) has cubic coefficient 6a² − 4b, while the true exponential f^{−1} has 2a² − b; the finite differences give the correct 2a² − b, checked by exact computation to degree 4. The sign: with finite differences, Σ ((−1)^{m−1}/m) Ψ^{[m]} equals the logarithm f, while the printed (−1)^m/m gives −f, which is not inverse to Exp^t as Lemma 7.7(ii) asserts. The bounds used later (|b_{j,α}| ≤ ‖α‖^{[K:Q_p]}, m!c_{j,α} ∈ R) hold for the corrected series, so the main results are unaffected. Checked on the page image. Noted by the extraction (gap G4, items formal-low-degree-source, formal-log-source and formal-exp), which proposed a different repair; the finite-difference reading is given here.

issues.printed: The source chooses K-linearly independent v_1, v_2 ∈ ker(f) ∩ R^n and scales them to be primitive. It claims that units b_1, b_2 ∈ R^× satisfying b_1v_1 + b_2v_2 ∈ pR^n ⊆ R^n would give c_1, c_2 ∈ R satisfying b_1v_1 + b_2v_2 = ϖc_1v_1 + ϖc_2v_2, contradicting K-linear independence. It concludes that their images in k^n are k-linearly independent.
issues.correction: Take v_1, v_2 to be two members of an R-basis of the saturated lattice ker(f) ∩ R^n. That lattice is a direct summand of R^n of rank n − 1 ≥ 2, so any basis of it reduces to k-linearly independent vectors.
issues.reason: The step from b_1v_1 + b_2v_2 ∈ ϖR^n to b_1v_1 + b_2v_2 ∈ ϖ(Rv_1 + Rv_2) assumes that Rv_1 + Rv_2 is saturated in R^n. For v_1 = e_1 and v_2 = e_1 + ϖe_2 in R³, both are primitive and K-independent, but v_2 − v_1 = ϖe_2 and their reductions coincide. The lemma itself holds by the corrected choice, so nothing later changes. Checked on the page image. Noted by the extraction (gap G5, item primitive-proof-source).

issues.locator: Introduction §0.3 (Examples), p. 5
issues.printed: The source suggests analogous arguments when p = 3 (respectively p = 7) using real quadratic twists of y² + y = x³ + x² − 7x + 5, with conductor 91 (resp. y² + xy + y = x³ − x² − 19353x + 958713, with conductor 574).
issues.correction: For p = 7 use a curve with good reduction at 7 and a rational 7-isogeny, for example 26b1: y² + xy + y = x³ − x² − 3x + 3 (conductor 26, rational 7-torsion, rank 0). Its real quadratic twists by D with 7 inert in Q(√D) satisfy φ|_{G_7} ≠ 1, ω. Those with root number −1, for example D = 33, 41, 61, have analytic rank 1.
issues.reason: 574 = 2·7·41, and the curve has multiplicative reduction of type I_7 at 7 (PARI: ellglobalred and elllocalred). Since v_7(j) < 0, every quadratic twist has bad reduction at 7, so neither the curve nor any twist satisfies the paper's standing hypothesis that p be a prime of good reduction. The other examples check out: conductors 123, 91, 441 and 1225 are prime to p = 5, 3, 13, 37, and the curves have rational p-isogenies and analytic rank 1.

issues.locator: §5.2, Corollary 5.2.3 and its proof, p. 32
issues.printed: The source claims that for any elliptic curve E over Q admitting a rational 3-isogeny, positive proportions of its quadratic twists have both algebraic and analytic rank 1, and both ranks 0. It says quadratic twisting can secure φ|_{G_p} ≠ 1, ω, and derives the claim from [BKLOS19, Thm. 2.6] together with Corollary 5.2.2.
issues.correction: Corollary 5.2.2 applies only to twists with good reduction at 3 and φχ|_{G_3} ∉ {1, ω}. The argument proves the corollary for E having a quadratic twist with good reduction at 3, using the positive-proportion statements for the subfamily of twists with those local conditions at 3. These follow from BKLOS Thm. 2.1 and §§9.2, 11, not from Thm. 2.6, which counts all twists. For curves with no twist of good reduction at 3 (v_3(j(E)) < 0, or potentially good reduction at 3 of Kodaira type other than I_0^*, e.g. 27a1 and every curve with j = 0) it proves nothing.
issues.reason: E : y² + xy + 3y = x³ has conductor 30, rational 3-torsion (so a rational 3-isogeny) and multiplicative reduction of type I_3 at 3 (PARI). Since v_3(j(E)) < 0, every quadratic twist has multiplicative or additive reduction at 3, so no twist satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem E at p = 3.

issues.printed: The source takes a Dirichlet character θ : G_Q → Z_p^× of conductor C and restricts to C | N (hence p ∤ C). It then uses ψ = φ^{−1}ω and the Katz p-adic L-function functional equation, citing [Kri16, Thm. 27], to claim λ(L_ψ) = λ(L_φ).

issues.locator: §3.3.1, proof of Proposition 3.3.6, p. 20
issues.printed: The source asserts the existence of ψ⁺ ∈ Hom_R(W⁺, (T_E^{(k)})⁺) together with j ∈ {1, 2} with β(ψ⁺(f_j⁺)) ∈ π^{max{d_1,d_2}+r(C_1+C_α)}(R^{(k)})^×. It also claims a ψ⁻ ∈ Hom_R(W⁻, (T_E^{(k)})⁻) satisfying β(ψ⁻(f_{3−j}⁻)) ∈ π^{min{d_1,d_2}+r(C_1+C_α)}(R^{(k)})^× while β(ψ⁻(f_j⁻)) = 0.
issues.correction: What is needed, a pair (ψ⁺, ψ⁻) with q(ψ⁺, ψ⁻) of valuation d_1 + d_2 + 2r(C_1 + C_α), does exist. The possible value vectors (ψ(f_1^±), ψ(f_2^±)) form lattices π^{k−a_1^±}Rε_1^* ⊕ π^{k−a_2^±}Rε_2^* (Smith normal form), and q = det(v, w); since the change-of-basis matrix is invertible, a diagonal or anti-diagonal pair of its entries is a unit, and v, w chosen on those coordinates give valuation ≤ d_1 + d_2 + 2r(C_1 + C_α), made exact by scaling. In the diagonal case pair the two larger invariants (the (1,1) entries), which gives valuation ≤ 2 min(d_1, d_2) + 2r(C_1 + C_α); the other diagonal pairing can give 2 max(d_1, d_2) + 2r(C_1 + C_α). If d_1 + d_2 + 2r(C_1 + C_α) ≥ k the second conclusion is vacuous.
issues.reason: The choice fails for both j under the stated hypothesis. Over Z_3 with r(C_1 + C_α) = 1, d_1 = 0, d_2 = 1, k = 4, W^± = R/27 ⊕ R/9 and f_1 = (1, 0), f_2 = (1, 1), every homomorphism W → R/81 is ψ(x, y) = 3ax + 9by. Killing f_1 forces 81 | 3a and ψ(f_2) = 9b; killing f_2 forces ψ(f_1) = 3a = −9b. So ψ(f_{3−j}) never has valuation 1. Yet q = 27(ab′ − a′b) attains valuation 3 = d_1 + d_2 + 2.

issues.locator: Introduction §0.2, p. 4 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: For torsion 𝔛 over Λ, the source defines λ(𝔛), μ(𝔛) using its characteristic power series. For nonzero 𝓛 ∈ Λ^ur, it defines λ(𝓛), μ(𝓛) using any Λ-element whose generated Λ^ur-ideal equals that of 𝓛.

issues.locator: Remark 5.2.4, p. 32 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: Combining its result with the explicit [BKLOS19] bounds, the source claims simultaneous analytic and algebraic rank 1 for at least 41.6% of its quadratic twists, and simultaneous rank 0 for at least 25%.
issues.correction: The method certifies only twists E_d of 19a3 with good reduction at 3 and χ_d|_{G_3} ∉ {1, ω}, i.e. squarefree d ≡ 2 mod 3, a family of density 3/8 = 37.5%. The claim should be restricted to that family, with the proportions that BKLOS's local-conditions bounds give there (numerically about 15.6% rank 1 and 9.4% analytic rank 0).
issues.reason: BKLOS's 41.6% and 25% are for all twists and count 3-Selmer rank 1 and algebraic rank 0. Converting them needs Corollary 5.2.2, which requires good reduction at 3 and φ|_{G_3} ≠ 1, ω. 19a3 has rational 3-torsion (E[3]^ss = 1 ⊕ ω), so E_d[3]^ss = χ_d ⊕ χ_dω and the condition is χ_d|_{G_3} unramified and non-trivial, i.e. d ≡ 2 mod 3; 3 | d gives additive reduction. PARI counts 0.3751 of squarefree |d| ≤ 3000 in this class. So at most 37.5% < 41.6% of twists can be reached.

issues.correction: For full injectivity, restrict Proposition 2.2 to commutative G; this covers both uses, Proposition 2.3 and Corollary 2.4. Alternatively, retain arbitrary affine smooth G but weaken the conclusion to triviality of the fibre over the trivial torsor. To retain the original full noncommutative statement, supply surjectivity of (^P H)(V) → (^P X)(V) for every G-torsor P over V, where H=Res_{R′/R}(G_{R′}), X=H/G, the groups are twisted by conjugation and X by the induced G-action.
issues.reason: Write H = Res_{R′/R}(G_{R′}) and X = H/G. Surjectivity of H(V) → X(V) shows that the fibre of H¹(V, G) → H¹(V, H) over the trivial class is trivial. When G is commutative this is injectivity, because the map is a group homomorphism. For a noncommutative G, H¹ is only a pointed set. The fibre through the class of a torsor P is the orbit set of (^P H)(V) acting on (^P X)(V), for the twists by P (Giraud III.3.2; cf. Serre, Galois Cohomology, I.§5.4, Cor. 2 (Propositions 35–36, pp.49–51; corrected in REV-ERRATA-PAPER-CESNAVICIUS-19)). The proof checks only the untwisted case. The twisted forms ^P X live only over V, so hypothesis (1) and the affineness of X give no control of their V-points. If P extends to R it is trivial by (2), so the problem is exactly the torsors on V that do not extend. Proposition 2.2 is used only in the proofs of Proposition 2.3 (G = Res_{R′/R}(T_{R′})/T) and Corollary 2.4 (G = T, an R-torus), where G is commutative, so the main theorems are unaffected. Noted by the extraction (gap G-NONABELIAN, items h1-descent and h1-abelian), which did not claim the statement false; neither is it claimed false here. issues.citation: Česnavičius, "Purity for the Brauer group", Duke Mathematical Journal (2019)
issues.reviewReason: Confirmed as a gap, and the printed text is exactly as quoted (p. 4). Proposition 2.2 is stated for "an affine, smooth R-group scheme G" with no commutativity hypothesis, and its proof establishes only that H(V) → X(V) is surjective, where H = Res_{R'/R}(G_{R'}) and X = H/G. For the exact sequence of pointed sets H(V) → X(V) → H¹(V,G) → H¹(V,H), that surjectivity says precisely that the fibre over the neutral class is trivial. For a noncommutative G, H¹ is a pointed set and trivial kernel does not give injectivity: the fibre through the class of a torsor P is computed after twisting, as the orbit set of (^P H)(V) acting on (^P X)(V), and the proof does not treat the twisted forms. The extraction's diagnosis of why the printed hypotheses do not reach them is right: hypothesis (1) together with the affineness of X gives X(V) ≅ X(R) because a map to an affine R-scheme factors through Spec Γ(V,O), but ^P X is only a V-scheme and is not the base change of an affine R-scheme, so neither (1) nor (2) controls its V-points; and by (2) a torsor that extends to R is trivial, so exactly the torsors on V that do not extend are uncontrolled. I verified independently that Proposition 2.2 is invoked in only two places in the paper — the proof of Proposition 2.3, with G = (Res_{R'/R}(T_{R'}))/T, and Corollary 2.4, with G = T an R-torus — and that both are commutative, so the main theorems are untouched. Like the extraction, I do not claim the statement false for noncommutative G; I claim only that the printed proof does not establish it. "Affects a stated result" is therefore the right classification, since the Proposition is asserted in that generality. No later version or erratum corrects it: arXiv 1711.06456 stops at v4, the author's own copy at webusers.imj-prg.fr is dated 27 November 2018 and so predates v4, its text differs from v4 only by reflow, and Crossref's record of doi:10.1215/00127094-2018-0057 carries no update-to, updated-by or relation entry (checked 23 September 2026). The published Duke text is paywalled and was not collated, as the extraction states.

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed, on the page image as well as in the text layer, since pdftotext scrambles the line. Page 119 prints: "Let next R be a general ring; let H ⊂ H_R(F,J) be a finitely generated subideal such that t^h ∈ H." But the hypothesis of Proposition 5.4.13 is (5.4.9), which reads t^h ∈ H_R(F,J) + p_a — the condition evaluated at the point a, not membership in H_R(F,J) itself. I verified the extraction's counterexample: take R = Q[[t]], I = R, a = 1, J = (X²(X−1)), h = 0, n = 1. issues.reviewReason: Confirmed, and I checked it myself rather than inheriting it. The Laszlo annotated edition (SHA-256 1c648d95…58da1, re-fetched 23 September 2026) prints hypothesis (e) of XI Lemma 3.17 as "pour tout y fermé de X, y ∈ Y, l'anneau O_{X,y} est parafactoriel", and I confirmed on the page image that the glyph really is ∈ and not a text-layer corruption of ∉. The proof of 3.17 applies (e) through Théorème 3.12, whose hypothesis 3) is parafactoriality "pour tout voisinage ouvert U de Y dans X et tout x ∈ X − U" — points lying outside every open neighbourhood of Y, hence outside Y; and the proof of 3.17 says just that, that for every open U ⊇ Y the complement X ∖ U consists of finitely many closed points. Under the printed reading (e) would constrain only points of Y, which c) already covers, and would leave the points the proof needs entirely uncovered. Théorème 3.18(iii), which also conjugates 3.12 and 3.13, states the condition in the correct "x ∈ X − U" form. The classification "affects nothing" is right: the application in 3.13(ii) verifies parafactoriality at every closed point of X, so it survives either reading. issues.reason: For x ∉ Supp(𝓜) the stalk is 0, whose depth is +∞, while dim(Supp(𝓜_x)) = dim(∅) = −∞ by the convention just recalled; so the equality fails there although '(S_n) for every n' holds. issues.printed: The proof regards 𝓘_{𝓜,m} as its inverse image in O_X and gives the resulting stalk as (𝓘_{𝓜,m})_x = ∏_{j<dim(O_{X_m,x})} Ann_{O_{X,x}}(H^j_{𝔪(x)}(O_{X,x}, (𝓜|_{X_m})_x)).
issues.correction: The equality holds for the product in O_X of the O_X-annihilators, not for the preimage of the product. Apply Lemma 4.3 to the closed subscheme of X cut out by that product (its support is Y_{𝓜,m}), so that j_{m+1,x} lies in the product as Definition 3.1(ii) requires; or keep the preimage and replace j_{m+1,x} by j_{m+1,x} − b for a suitable b ∈ (j_{1,x},…,j_{m,x}), which changes none of the ideals (j_{1,x},…,j_{i,x}), hence neither secancy, the quotients, nor 𝓙_x.
issues.reason: Each O_{X,x}-annihilator is the preimage of the O_{X_m,x}-annihilator, but with K = (j_{1,x},…,j_{m,x}) the preimage of a product is the product of the preimages plus K, which can be larger. Over A = k[[s,t,u,v,z]]/((s,t) ∩ (u,v)) with K = (z) and the A/K-module (A/K) ⊕ k of support dimension 2, H⁰_𝔪 ≅ H¹_𝔪 ≅ k, so the product of the A-annihilators is 𝔪_A² while the preimage is 𝔪_A² + (z). Read with the preimage, Lemma 4.3 gives only j_{m+1,x} ∈ (product) + K. Proposition 4.4 is unaffected once the step is repaired.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 8.4, claim (2), author PDF p. 25 (the published version p. 24)
issues.printed: For claim (2), the proof deduces from isotropicity that a proper parabolic P ⊂ G exists, citing Definition 8.1.
issues.correction: Definition 8.1 gives parabolics over the local rings. The author’s later stronger semilocal isotropy assumption supplies them globally. Alternatively retain the printed hypothesis: for Noetherian R use a local parabolic and its opposite at each maximal ideal, the corrected finite-polynomial dilation proof of local-parabolic-loop-lifts, and products of lifts that are identity at the other maximal ideals. Descend the finite data to a Noetherian semilocal base for the general case. Theorem 9.1 uses quasi-split groups, which already have a global Borel.
issues.reason: Example: let Ō be the semilocal ring of A¹_Q at two closed points with residue fields L₁ (cyclic cubic) and L₂ = Q(i), and R = {f ∈ Ō : f(q₁), f(q₂) ∈ Q}, a one-dimensional Noetherian semilocal domain with residue fields Q, Q. Milnor patching of M₆(Ō) with M₂(D) and M₃(H) gives an Azumaya R-algebra A of degree 6, where D is a cubic division algebra split by L₁ and H = (−1,−1)_Q. Here A is split over Frac R, and A_{R_{m₁}} ≅ M₂(D′), A_{R_{m₂}} ≅ M₃(H′), by lifting block matrix units along the local normalization, as detailed below. So G = SL₁(A), simply connected of type A₅, is totally isotropic. An R-parabolic would have a single type, since Dyn(G) is constant, proper on both closed fibres SL₂(D) and SL₃(H). Their parabolics are the flags of reduced dimensions in {3} and in {2, 4} respectively, so there is none. Theorem 9.1 is unaffected: it applies Proposition 8.4 to quasi-split G, which has a Borel over R. For the local matrix decompositions in the pinched-ring example, lift a conjugating matrix from the residue splitting field to the local normalization (GL_6 surjects onto its residue GL_6). Conjugated standard block matrix units then belong to the fiber-product algebra and give M_2(D′) or M_3(H′). This supplies the local isotropy assertion; uniqueness of patching alone is not the justification.

issues.locator: CES22 Lemma 6.3 statement, author p.19 and published p.18
issues.printed: Lemma 6.3 takes C to be an R-scheme that is affine and flat.
issues.correction: Require C/R finitely presented as well as flat and affine. Prop.6.5’s smooth affine relative curve has this property.
issues.reason: Set R=Q, C=Spec Q[[t]], Y=V(t)=Spec Q and Z=∅. The fibers are Cohen–Macaulay and pure of dimension one; Y is R-finite and the finite-residue-field point condition is vacuous. Every open containing Y is all of this local spectrum. A quasi-finite map C→A1_Q would be of finite type, hence make Q[[t]] a finitely generated Q-algebra. This is impossible: Q[[t]] is uncountable and every such algebra is countable. The proof’s two sets of closed points outside Y cannot be chosen here. Section 1.7 supplies no standing finite-presentation convention. The main theorem’s actual curve application is unaffected.

issues.citation: Česnavičius–Scholze, "Purity for flat cohomology", Annals of Mathematics 199 (2024), no. 1
issues.reviewReason: Confirmed, and I built a counterexample. Theorem 7.1.2 (p. 87) assumes each O_{X,z} with z ∈ Z is 'either a complete intersection of dimension ≥ d or regular of dimension ≥ d − 1', and concludes that H^i(X,G) → H^i(X∖Z,G) is injective for i < d. At d = 1 the second clause permits dimension 0, i.e. a field. Take X = Spec k ⊔ Spec k, Z one of the two points, G any nontrivial finite locally free group: O_{X,z} = k is regular of dimension 0 ≥ d − 1, the immersion X∖Z ↪ X is quasi-compact, and H^0(X,G) = G(k) × G(k) → H^0(X∖Z,G) = G(k) is not injective. So the theorem as stated fails for d = 1, and the extraction's repair — dimension ≥ max(d−1, 1), i.e. not a field, or d ≥ 2 — is the right one. Every application in the paper has d ≥ 2, so nothing downstream is affected. No later version or erratum corrects it: arXiv 1912.10932 stops at v3, itself the 'final version, to appear in Annals of Mathematics', and Crossref's record of doi:10.4007/annals.2024.199.1.2 carries no update-to, updated-by or relation entry (checked 23 September 2026). The published text is paywalled and was not compared, as the extraction states.

issues.locator: Corollary 2.8 and its proof, pp.499–500, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 487–526 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 3425f269…40e2)
issues.printed: For p > 0, the source asserts the existence of nonnegative integers λ and t satisfying 0 < λ ≤ v², with |disc(NS(X))| = p^t λ |disc(NS(M_H(v)))|. Its proof uses a natural lattice injection Zv ⊕ (v^⊥ ∩ N(X)) ↪ N(X) with torsion cokernel, states the discriminant of Zv ⊕ v^⊥ as v² disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X)), and deduces |disc(N(X))| ≤ v² |disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X))| by the same argument.
issues.correction: λ need not be an integer. With I = [N(X) : Zv ⊕ (v^⊥ ∩ N(X))], one has |disc NS(X)| = p^t (v²/I²) |disc NS(M_H(v))| with t ≥ 0. So λ = v²/I² is a positive rational number with λ ≤ v², and I divides v² because v is primitive. For p ∤ v², for example v² = 2 and p ≥ 3 as in the applications, λ is still a p-adic unit, which is what the later arguments use.
issues.reason: Take v = (1, 0, −1), the Mukai vector of ideal sheaves of length-two subschemes, so M_H(v) = X^[2]. It satisfies condition (C): it is primitive, of rank 1, v² = 2, and gcd(1, 0, −1) = 1. Then v^⊥ ∩ N(X) = NS(X) ⊕ Z(1, 0, 1) with (1, 0, 1)² = −2, so |disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X))| = 2|disc NS(X)|. The proof's first step gives |disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X))| = p^r |disc NS(M_H(v))|. Hence |disc NS(X)| = ½ p^r |disc NS(M_H(v))|, which is not of the form p^t λ with λ a positive integer when p is odd. The proof passes from the equality disc(Zv ⊕ K) = I² disc N(X) to an integer multiplier without controlling I, here I = 2. The inequality stated for p = 0 is correct. Checked on the page image. Noted by the extraction (items 34–35).

issues.locator: Proposition 2.9, p.500, as used in the proof of Theorem 2.10, p.503, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 487–526 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 3425f269…40e2)
issues.printed: Proposition 2.9 takes d positive and Λ ⊂ Λ_2d positive definite of rank 2. It asserts that some positive N and nonzero a, b give a primitive embedding of Λ into Λ_2md for every positive m with (i) m = 1[N] and (ii) m prime to a and b, both quadratic residues modulo m. The proof represents Λ's primitive embedding into Λ_2d by a tuple (V, W, γ, t).
issues.correction: Assume Λ is a primitive sublattice of Λ_2d. In the proof of Theorem 2.10, choose the lattice Λ containing v, w with v² = 2, v·w = 1 to be primitive. For example, in Λ_2d = ⟨2d⟩ ⊕ U with basis h, e, f, take the span of v = e + f and w = kh + e. It is primitive, since (x, y, z) ↦ (z, y − z) retracts it, and its Gram matrix [[2, 1], [1, 2dk²]] is positive definite.
issues.reason: The proof starts from a primitive embedding Λ ⊂ Λ_2d, which the statement does not provide, and the statement fails for non-primitive Λ. In Λ_2 = ⟨2⟩ ⊕ U, the sublattice Λ generated by 2h and 2(e + f) has Gram matrix diag(8, 8). Take m = 1, which satisfies (i) and (ii) for every N, a, b. A primitive embedding of Λ into Λ_2 would give a 2-dimensional subspace of Λ_2/2Λ_2 = F_2³ on which the half-norm Q(x, y, z) = x² + yz vanishes, since Λ has all half-norms even. The nonzero zeros of Q are (0,0,1), (0,1,0) and (1,1,1), and each pairwise sum has Q = 1, so no such plane exists. Noted by the extraction (items 38–41), which also gave the primitive choice above.

issues.citation: François Charles, "Birational boundedness for holomorphic symplectic varieties, Zarhin's trick for K3 surfaces, and the Tate conjecture", Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), no. 2
issues.reviewReason: Confirmed. The proof starts with a primitive embedding not assumed in the statement. The lattice diag(8,8) embeds nonprimitively into ⟨2⟩⊕U but cannot embed primitively: mod 2, x²+yz has three nonzero isotropic vectors and no two-dimensional totally isotropic plane. Taking m=1 satisfies every congruence condition. The explicit split plane fixes the consumer.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 3.1, p.506, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 487–526 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 3425f269…40e2)
issues.printed: The proof invokes Riemann-Roch to assert surjectivity of H⁰(C, 3L|_C) → 3L|_C/(3L|_C − D(p) − D(q)) for every p and q under consideration. It assigns to 3L|_C − D(p) − D(q) the degree 3r − 4 > r = deg(ω_{C/k}), observing that evenness of r implies r > 1.
issues.correction: Pass to 2L before this step, as the proof already allows ("up to replacing L by 2L"), so that r = L² ≥ 4 and 3r − 4 > r holds.
issues.reason: 3r − 4 > r holds only for r > 2. "r is even, so that r > 1" leaves r = 2, the double-plane case, where 3r − 4 = r and the surjectivity argument as written does not apply. The proposition only claims the existence of some L′ with bounded invariants, so doubling L is allowed. Noted by the extraction (item 50), which also leaves the characteristic-two nonreduced-curve argument as an open check.

issues.reviewReason: Rejected. This passage is in the branch C=2C_red with L=O(C), hence r=4(C_red)² is a positive multiple of four (and at least eight by K3 parity). Thus 3r−4>r already holds. issues.locator: Proposition 3.17, p.517, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 487–526 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 3425f269…40e2)
issues.printed: The source asserts that some positive N and nonzero a, b yield a finite set of polarized K3 surfaces (X, H) that are nonsuperspecial, over k, of degree 2md. Here m is positive with (i) m = 1[N], (ii) m coprime to a and b, both quadratic residues modulo m, and (iii) the discriminant of NS(X_k̄) has p-adic valuation bounded by t_0.
issues.correction: There are only finitely many k-isomorphism classes of nonsuperspecial K3 surfaces X over k admitting a polarization H of such a degree 2md with (i)–(iii). The polarized pairs themselves need not be finite in number.
issues.reason: On a fixed eligible (X, H) of degree 2m_0 d, the line bundles H^{⊗ℓ^j} have degree 2(ℓ^{2j} m_0)d. Choose a prime ℓ with a and b quadratic residues modulo ℓ and prime to N, a and b, and let j run through multiples of the order of ℓ² modulo N. Then m = ℓ^{2j} m_0 satisfies (i) and (ii), and (iii) is unchanged. This gives infinitely many pairwise non-isomorphic polarized pairs on one surface; the paper does not require polarizations to be primitive. The proof bounds NS(X_k̄) and then the surfaces. The only use, the proof of Theorem 1.3 on p.523, reads "there exist only finitely many K3 surfaces over k", so the corrected statement is what is used. Noted by the extraction (items 88–89).

issues.locator: §4.1, the definition of N_{α/r}(X) and (4.1), pp.518–519, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 487–526 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 3425f269…40e2)
issues.printed: The source defines N_{α/r}(X) as the inverse image of N(X) under T_{−α/r}, identifies it with the group called CH_{α/r}(X, Z) in [LMS14], and cites [LMS14, Lemma 3.3.3] for (4.1) N_{α/r}(X) = {(ar, D + aα, cω) | a, c ∈ Z, D ∈ NS(X)}.
issues.correction: Define N_{α/r}(X) directly as the lattice (4.1), the twisted Mukai lattice CH_{α/r}(X, Z) of [LMS14], and drop "the preimage of N(X) by T_{−α/r}".
issues.reason: With T_{−α/r}(x) = x ∪ e^{−α/r} and e^{−α/r} = (1, −α/r, α²/(2r²)), one computes T_{−α/r}(ar, D + aα, cω) = (ar, D, (c − (α·D)/r − aα²/(2r))ω). Its last coordinate is not an integer in general, for α ∈ H²(X, Z_ℓ(1)) primitive and r = ℓ^n. So the lattice (4.1) is not the preimage of N(X). Lemma 4.2, Proposition 4.3 and §4.2 compute with the explicit lattice (4.1), so the results are unaffected. Noted by the extraction (§4.1 conventions, items 93–106).

issues.locator: Charles Lemma 4.5, p. 521
issues.printed: The source claims finiteness of the set of prime numbers in question.
issues.correction: Lemma 4.5 holds, with the argument below, after replacing k by a finite extension on which −1 is not a Frobenius eigenvalue on H²(X_k̄, Q_ℓ(1)), and with −1 added to the p_i; it needs Frobenius semisimple on the eigenvalue-1 part (item 111). Let g be the characteristic polynomial of Frobenius on the complement V′ of the invariants. The Cayley transform (F−1)(F+1)⁻¹ is skew-adjoint on V′, so det V′ ≡ g(1)g(−1) modulo squares. Hence disc T(X, Q_ℓ) ≡ −g(1)g(−1)·disc NS(X), a rational number independent of ℓ. The p_i are the primes dividing it. Item 113 states and proves this form.
issues.reason: Each l-adic discriminant is defined modulo l-adic unit squares. A uniform bound on its l-valuation does not compare square classes at distinct primes. A valuation-zero rank-one form can have nonsquare unit coefficient. (cc-442dc5) The repair above supplies the missing rational square class. It is not available over the original k when −1 is an eigenvalue, because the determinant of the (−1)-eigenspace is not fixed by the characteristic polynomial. The finite extension is harmless for Theorems 1.3 and 1.4, since the Tate statement descends (item finite-extension-tate-descent). The finding therefore still affects the proof only.

issues.locator: §5.6, p. 83, Proposition 5.6.1(a) (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The source claims exactly one point of f^{−1}(0) is unramified and all the others have ramification index 3. It therefore gives |f^{−1}(0)| = (p(p+3)−3)/3 for p ≡ 1 mod 4 and (p(p−3)−3)/3 for p ≡ 3 mod 4.
issues.reason: The printed expression is never an integer: deg f = |X*(p)| = p(p±3) ≡ p² ≡ 1 (mod 3) for every prime p ≠ 3, so 3 never divides deg f − 3. The sentence preceding the display gives the correct count, one unramified point together with (deg f − 1)/3 points of ramification index 3. Computing the γ₀-orbits on X*(p) directly confirms it: for p = 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 the fibre has 14, 10, 30, 70, 114, 102, 154 points and γ₀ has exactly one fixed point in each case, matching (deg f + 2)/3 = 14, 10, 30, 70, 114, 102, 154 and not (deg f − 3)/3 = 37/3, 25/3, 85/3, 205/3, 337/3, 301/3, 457/3.

issues.citation: William Y. Chen, "Nonabelian level structures, Nielsen equivalence, and Markoff triples", Annals of Mathematics 199 (2024), no. 1
issues.reviewReason: Recomputed from the paper's own data. By Proposition 5.3.3, deg 𝔣 = |𝕏*(p)| = p(p±3). By Proposition 5.2.20, 𝔣^{−1}(0) is the set of γ₀-orbits on 𝕏*(p), and the ramification index of a point is the size of its orbit; γ₀ acts by (x,y,z) ↦ (xy−z, x, x²y−xz−y). A fixed point has y = x and z = x² − x. (The branch x = −1 forces (−1,−1,2), which is not on 𝕏 for p odd.) Substituting into x²+y²+z²−xyz = 0 gives x²(3 − x) = 0, so for p ≥ 5 the only fixed point in 𝕏*(p) is (3,3,6). γ₀ has order 6 in SL₂(ℤ) and γ₀³ acts on trace coordinates as γ_{−I}, i.e. trivially, so every other orbit has size 3, and |𝔣^{−1}(0)| = (deg 𝔣 + 2)/3. Because deg 𝔣 ≡ p² ≡ 1 mod 3, the printed (deg 𝔣 − 3)/3 is never an integer. A brute-force computation over F_p for every prime 5 ≤ p ≤ 109 finds exactly one fixed point and (deg+2)/3 orbits (14, 10, 30, 70 for p = 5, 7, 11, 13). Riemann–Hurwitz, g = 1 + (deg − |𝔣^{−1}(0)| − |𝔣^{−1}(1728)| − |𝔣^{−1}(∞)|)/2, with the corrected count and the counts of Propositions 5.6.1(b) and 5.6.2, reproduces Theorem 5.6.3's closed formula for every such p (genus 0, 0, 1, 5 at p = 5, 7, 11, 13). With the printed count it gives non-integers (5/6, 5/6, 11/6, 35/6), so Theorem 5.6.3 was computed with the correct value. The TeX (line 4047, \frac{p(p+3)-3}{3}) and the page image both show the printed formula. 'Misprint' would also be a defensible kind, since the preceding sentence gives the right count.

issues.citation: William Y. Chen, "Nonabelian level structures, Nielsen equivalence, and Markoff triples", Annals of Mathematics 199 (2024), no. 1
issues.reviewReason: TeX line 4051 has \pi^{-1}(1728), while the display below it and part (a) use \ff (𝔣). π is not defined in §5.6; elsewhere it denotes the universal cover C → E. The mathematics is right. γ₁₇₂₈ acts by (x,y,z) ↦ (y,x,xy−z), so a fixed point has x = y and 2z = x², and on 𝕏 this gives (x²/4)(8 − x²) = 0. The fixed points in 𝕏*(p) are therefore (±√8, ±√8, 4), two of them, and they exist exactly when 2 is a square mod p, i.e. p ≡ ±1 mod 8. Since γ₁₇₂₈² = γ_{−I} acts trivially, all other orbits have size 2, and the four displayed counts follow. A brute-force computation for 5 ≤ p ≤ 109 matches the display and the fixed-point claim, and Riemann–Hurwitz with these counts reproduces Theorem 5.6.3.

issues.locator: Theorem 1.1.2, last sentence, p. 5 (arXiv v2); the published text was compared at this passage (see publishedText)
issues.printed: The source defines γ−I ∈ Aut(Π) by (a, b) ↦ (a−1, b−1) and asserts that ϕ ◦ γ−I = ϕ allows strengthening the congruences from mod ℓ^k to mod 2ℓ^k.
issues.correction: If ϕ ∘ γ_{−I} ≠ ϕ in Epi^ext(Π,G), i.e. ϕ∘γ_{−I} is not Inn(G)-conjugate to ϕ, then the congruences mod ℓ^k strengthen to mod 2ℓ^k. If ϕ∘γ_{−I} = ϕ in Epi^ext, |Out⁺(Π)·ϕ| equals the degree and no strengthening holds in general.
issues.reason: By Theorem 2.5.2(4) the coarse fibre of M → M(1) over j ≠ 0, 1728 is O/⟨γ_{−I}⟩ for the orbit O = Out⁺(Π)·ϕ, as in the proof of Theorem 4.10.5 and in Corollary 4.12.5, which states the congruence for orbits on Epi^ext/⟨γ_{−I}⟩. Since γ_{−I} is central in Out⁺(Π) ≅ SL₂(ℤ), it fixes O pointwise if it fixes ϕ, and otherwise acts freely. Hence |O| = deg when ϕ∘γ_{−I} = ϕ, and |O| = 2·deg otherwise. Counterexample to the printed version: G = ℤ/2ℤ, c = 1, ℓ = 3 (r = s = j = 0). Then ϕ∘γ_{−I} = −ϕ = ϕ for every ϕ : Π ↠ ℤ/2, but Epi^ext(Π,ℤ/2) is the 3 nonzero vectors of F₂², a single SL₂(ℤ)-orbit of size 3 ≢ 0 mod 2. A nonabelian one: G = S₃, c a 3-cycle, ℓ = 3, j = 1 (r = 1, s = 0). All 3 classes of generating pairs are fixed by γ_{−I} (e.g. τ conjugates (τ,σ) to (τ,σ^{−1})), and they form one orbit of size 3. Checked in the TeX (line 763) and on the page image.

issues.locator: Lemma 2.4.1(a), proof, pp. 21–22 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The proof cites [Sta16, 03I1] for an affine open V ⊂ S with p−1(V ) → V finite étale. It replaces S by V to obtain a finite surjective S′ → S for which CS′ has a section, then repeats the process finitely often, possibly shrinking S further.
issues.correction: The argument must produce, around every point of S, an open neighbourhood over which (AF) holds. In all uses the curve carries a G-invariant relatively ample sheaf, which gives (a) directly: stable marked G-curves and sources of admissible covers (Propositions 2.4.4 and 2.4.6, via Lemma 3.1.3's ω(R)^{⊗3}), their quotients C/ker f (Proposition 2.5.10(f)), and curves over a field (§4.4). Restrict the lemma to this case, or cite local projectivity of such families.
issues.reason: [Stacks 03I1] (generic finiteness of a quasi-finite map) gives only some nonempty open V ⊂ S. Replacing S by V loses the points outside V, and repeating the step yields a stratification of S, not an open cover. Property (AF) and statement (a) are Zariski-local on S but are not inherited from strata. So the proof establishes (a) only over a dense open of S.

issues.locator: Proposition 3.2.2(b), proof, p. 37 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The source describes each arrow in Mg,n → Mg,n−1 → · · · → Mg,1 → Mg,0 = Mg as forgetting a marking, with domain the universal family of its codomain. It therefore calls Mg,n → Mg proper, smooth and representable, with geometrically connected fibres. Later it likewise calls U →Y_K proper and smooth, deducing that it is both open and closed and has connected fibres.
issues.correction: M_{g,n} is the open complement of the n − 1 marked sections in the universal curve over M_{g,n−1}. So M_{g,n} → M_g is representable, smooth, surjective and of finite type with geometrically connected fibres (the fibre is the configuration space of n distinct points on the curve), but not proper. The two connectedness steps (U connected; f*R connected) only need that pr is open and surjective with connected fibres.
issues.reason: The fibre of M_{g,n} → M_{g,n−1} over (C,p₁,…,p_{n−1}) is C − {p₁,…,p_{n−1}}, which is not proper. For an open surjective map with connected fibres onto a connected base the source is connected: a splitting of the source into disjoint opens would map to disjoint open images covering the base. So the conclusion stands.

issues.locator: §4.12, p. 63, proof of Lemma 4.12.2 (last three sentences) (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The proof selects z′ ∈ ⟨z⟩, u′ ∈ ⟨u⟩ with |z′| = ℓ^k and |u′| = ℓ^{k−j}. It claims ℓ^{j+1} does not divide |⟨z′⟩ ∩ ⟨u′⟩| and deduces that ⟨z′^j⟩ ∩ ⟨u′⟩ is trivial. It then asserts ⟨z′^j, u′⟩ ≅ (ℤ/ℓ^{k−j}ℤ)² and concludes ⟨z′,u′⟩ ≅ ℤ/ℓ^kℤ × ℤ/ℓ^{k−j}ℤ.
issues.correction: For j = 0 the argument is complete. For j ≥ 1, ⟨z′⟩ ∩ ⟨u′⟩ can have order ℓ^i with 1 ≤ i ≤ j. Then ⟨z′^{ℓ^j}⟩ ∩ ⟨u′⟩, let alone ⟨z′^j⟩ ∩ ⟨u′⟩, is nontrivial, and ⟨z′,u′⟩ ≅ ℤ/ℓ^k × ℤ/ℓ^{k−j−i}. The printed argument only yields ℤ/ℓ^k × ℤ/ℓ^{k−2j}. That weakens Corollary 4.12.4(a) to ord_ℓ(m′_c) ≤ ⌊(r+s+2j)/2⌋ and Corollary 4.12.5(a) to the modulus ℓ^{⌈(r−3s−2j)/2⌉}, i.e. j replaced by 2j. The printed forms for j ≥ 1 need a further argument.
issues.reason: The hypothesis gives only that ℓ^{j+1} does not divide |⟨z′⟩ ∩ ⟨u′⟩|, i.e. that this intersection has order at most ℓ^j. Subgroups of the cyclic group ⟨z′⟩ form a chain, so a nontrivial intersection lies in every nontrivial subgroup of ⟨z′⟩. A concrete configuration: in ℤ/27 × ℤ/3 with ℓ = 3, k = 3, j = 1, z′ = (1,0) and u′ = (3,1), |u′| = 9 = ℓ^{k−j}. Here ⟨z′⟩ ∩ ⟨u′⟩ = ⟨(9,0)⟩ has order 3, not divisible by 9, yet ⟨z′³⟩ ∩ ⟨u′⟩ ≠ 1, and ⟨z′,u′⟩ ≅ ℤ/27 × ℤ/3 contains no ℤ/27 × ℤ/9. Nothing earlier in the proof rules out ⟨z⟩ ∩ ⟨u⟩ ≠ 1 when j ≥ 1. The paper's main applications take j = 0 and are unaffected: nonabelian simple groups, Corollary 4.12.4(b), and the SL₂(F_ℓ) example of Remark 4.12.6.

issues.locator: Theorem 5.6.4, last sentence, p. 84, and Theorem 1.2.9, last sentence, p. 8 (arXiv v2); in the published text, Theorem 5.6.4, p. 419, and Theorem 1.2.10, p. 310
issues.printed: For p ≥ 13 and p ∉ E_bgs, v2 claims finiteness, for any number field K, of elliptic curves admitting a SL₂(F_p)-structure (Theorem 5.6.4) or an SL₂(F_p)-cover (Theorem 1.2.9), in each case with ramification index 2p. The published statements specify curves over K and structures (p. 419) or covers (p. 310) defined over K, still with ramification index 2p.
issues.correction: Only finitely many j-invariants j(E) ∈ K, equivalently finitely many K̄-isomorphism classes of elliptic curves E/K, admit such a structure or cover. Over K the set of such curves is infinite as soon as it contains, after a finite extension of K, a curve with j ∉ {0, 1728}, since it is closed under quadratic twist. The genus statements are unaffected.
issues.reason: The proof applies Faltings' theorem to the coarse curve M_p‾, so it bounds only its K-points, the j-invariants. (i) For A, B ∈ SL₂(F_p), p odd, with t = tr[A,B], M := (AB − BA)/2 has det M = (2 − t)/4 and MA = A⁻¹M, MB = B⁻¹M (Cayley–Hamilton); at t = −2, M ∈ SL₂(F_p), so γ_{−I} acts on Epi^ext(Π, SL₂(F_p))_{−2} by an inner automorphism. (ii) By Theorem 2.5.2(3),(5), [−1] acts on the fibre through γ_{−I}, so quadratic twisting preserves the SL₂(F_p)-structures of trace −2. (iii) After a finite extension K every point of a nonempty geometric fibre is K-rational; for j ∉ {0, 1728} the twists E^d, d ∈ K^×/K^×², are pairwise non-isomorphic over K. For covers defined over K (the published wording): over a finite extension K containing μ₄, choose a geometrically connected cover and a G-equivariant lift ι of [−1]; ι² ∈ Z(G) = {±I}, so ι has order 2 or 4. In the first case quadratic descent applies; in the second, the Kummer character of a fourth root of d lifts the quadratic character of d, and twisting by ι descends the cover with its constant G-action to E^d, with the same geometric connectedness and ramification 2p. This disproves the universal number-field claim; it does not assert that every twist of every cover descends over an arbitrary initial field.

issues.printed: The source assigns ℜ(s)=ω₁+ω₂+½ω₃+½ω₄ to the B₃ orbit in F₄.
issues.correction: Delete ω₂: ℜ(s)=ω₁+½ω₃+½ω₄. In the Euclidean coordinates of (6.21), the corrected dominant representative is (5/2,1,1/2,0). This is Weyl-conjugate to (2,−1,3/2,1/2), the parameter at ν=1/2 in the B3 complementary series.
issues.reason: Using the explicit fundamental weights (6.21), the printed parameter is (4,3/2,1,1/2), with squared norm 39/2. Ciubotaru’s primary classification [Ci1], §3.2 table continued on manuscript p.14 and §5 p.37, gives B3 parameters (3/2+ν,−3/2+ν,3/2,1/2), 0≤ν<1, in the SAME coordinates (§2.6 p.10). Their squared norms are 7+2ν²<9, so the printed point is not Weyl-conjugate to any member of this complementary series. The nonzero half-integral value is ν=1/2. Its coordinate vector (2,−1,3/2,1/2) first becomes (2,3/2,1,1/2) by a signed permutation and then (5/2,1,1/2,0) by reflection in (1,−1,−1,−1). This equals ω₁+½ω₃+½ω₄. Independent enumeration gives top adjoint Frobenius weight 16 for the printed point, contradicting the p.34 bound 10. The corrected point has multiplicities n_v(10)=1,n_v(9)=0,n_v(8)=2, as needed there. The coordinate classification statement must therefore be repaired, in addition to the index repair E3; no failure of the intended global theorem is asserted.

issues.printed: Part (ii) asserts that W_aV ⊂ V, consisting of ϕ(Frob_u)-eigenvectors whose eigenvalues have weight ≤ a, is stable under (ϕ, N). Part (iii) sets gr_aV = W_aV/W_{a−1}V and asserts, for every i, the isomorphism N^i : gr_{w−i}V → gr_{w+i}V.
issues.correction: With Frob_u a geometric Frobenius (N lowers Frobenius weights by 2, which is what makes W_a in (ii) N-stable), (iii) should read N^i : gr_{w+i}V → gr_{w−i}V, with W_aV the sum of the generalized eigenspaces of weight ≤ a.
issues.reason: The Weil–Deligne relation makes N shift Frobenius weights by 2, down for a geometric Frobenius and up for an arithmetic one. issues.locator: arXiv:2311.15300v1, §4.1, sketch of the proofs of Theorems 4.2–4.3, step (2), p. 11; compare §1.1, p. 3
issues.printed: Step (2) takes a representation τ of ^L G and its associated local system L(Π, τ) on X. It invokes semisimplicity of G to assert that, at every place v of K, the action of Γ_v = Gal(K_v^sep/K_v) on L(Π, τ) gives geometric local monodromy.

Theorem 4.2 is covered by [GHS]; Theorem 4.3 ('The proof of Theorem 4.3 is similar') needs a separate argument or an anchored statement.
issues.reason: Semisimplicity of G makes det(τ∘σ) of finite order, but by Deligne and L. Lafforgue τ∘σ is only a sum of pieces χ ⊗ (pure of weight 0), with χ characters of the constant-field Galois group whose weights are not known to be integers. The paper says so itself on p. 3: 'The genericity hypothesis (1) … should imply that some τ∘σ is irreducible, but this is not known in general. Instead, hypothesis (2) in the statement of Theorem 5.4 provides the anchor that guarantees that only integer weights occur in τ∘σ.' If step (2) held for every cuspidal Π, that anchor would be superfluous. Theorem 4.3 is used in the tempered case of Theorem 5.4 (p. 15).

issues.locator: arXiv:2311.15300v1, Corollary 6.32(1) and its proof, p. 25; used in the proof of Theorem 5.4 (p. 14), Remark 5.8 and Corollary 7.5 (p. 26)
issues.printed: Corollary 6.32 takes the Satake parameter s = s_c s_ν from (6.2) and its spherical G(k)-representation L(s), assuming genericity. Part (1) claims that, if L(s) is unitary, geometricity of s for the adjoint representation of G∨ and those fundamental G∨-representations specified in Proposition 6.31 is equivalent to ν = 0. The proof asserts ν ∈ U0^g under genericity and unitarity.
issues.correction: State (1) for real Satake parameters (s_c = 1, or s_c central in G∨), which is what U0^g covers ('spherical generic representations with real Satake parameter', p. 17). For non-central s_c the unitarity of L(s_c s_ν) is governed, by Barbasch–Moy's reduction, by the centralizer of s_c, and the conclusion can fail; Theorem 5.4 then needs a further argument at such places.
issues.reason: Counterexample for G2. Let s_c ∈ T∨ be the involution with α∨(s_c) = (−1)^a for α∨ = aα1∨ + bα2∨ (α1∨ the short simple coroot); its centralizer has roots ±α2∨ and ±(2α1∨ + α2∨), of type A1 × Ã1. Take ν = ½ω2, s = s_c s_ν. On the positive coroots (a, b) = (1,0), (0,1), (1,1), (2,1), (3,1), (3,2), α∨(s) = −1, q^{1/2}, −q^{1/2}, q^{1/2}, −q^{1/2}, −q, never q^{±1}, and W_s is trivial (Stab(ν) = {1, s_{α1}}, and s_{α1} moves s_c), so X(s) is irreducible by Kato's criterion and L(s) = X(s) is generic. w0 = −1 fixes s_c and negates ν, so X(s) is hermitian; along s_c s_{tν}, t ∈ [0, 1], the same computation shows irreducibility, and at t = 0 the representation is unitarily induced, so X(s) is unitary by the deformation argument of Lemma 6.7. But ν ≠ 0 is half-integral for the adjoint representation, hence for every representation of G2 (Lemma 6.30), and Proposition 6.31 lists none for G2, so (1) fails. The proof's step 'we must have ν ∈ U0^g' is what breaks: ⟨3α1∨ + 2α2∨, ν⟩ = 1, so L(s_ν) is not generic and ν ∉ U0^g. The eigenvalues of Ad(s) are Weil numbers of weights 0, ±1, ±2, so (5.6) does not exclude this s, and the proof of Theorem 5.4, which applies (1) to s_v(σ) with arbitrary compact part, does not cover it. Scoped to v1.

issues.locator: arXiv2311.15300v1, Theorem8.5 pp28–29 and Remark8.7 p30; linked propagation of E11, not a new discovery of its G2 witness
issues.printed: The source asserts the absence of extraneous points for both G₂ and E₆.
issues.correction: Restrict the source-derived list to real/central-compact parameters. The arbitrary-compact theorem needs a new exhaustive centralizer analysis; do not merely add one G2 entry.
issues.reason: E11’s parameter (aα₁+bα₂)(s)=(−1)^a q^(b/2) is unitary and generic by Kato plus its irreducible hermitian path. G2 has trivial connected center; its weight lattice equals its root lattice, so every eigenvalue is an algebraic Weil number of integer weight. Ad(s) has no q-eigenvalue, hence its open nilpotent orbit is0 and s lies in CS(G2,0). Its real part½ω₂ is not0, so it is extraneous under Definition8.4 despite the advertised full geometricity/connected-center hypotheses. The proof treats a set of real parts as real unitary parameters when applying Theorem6.14. This is a local counterexample to the unrestricted list, not a global cuspidal counterexample.
issues.known: Additional consequence of the already confirmed E11 witness, independently confirmed as RT-PAPER-CIUBOTARU-HARRIS-26/1; no new published-version criticism.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 6.18(2), including (17) (v3 p.78; published p.1067)

issues.reason: Let R=Fbar_p[[t]] and k=Fbar_p. Both are strictly henselian and R is a complete regular DVR. Theorem 6.11 identifies K^Sel(−)/p with connective K(−)/p here. issues.locator: Definition 5.14, pp. 42–43 (arXiv 1803.10897v2 only; JAMS text not compared)

issues.reason: Counterexample: for i≥1 let X_i=⊕_{j≥i}Σ^{−j}HF_p with tail inclusions. For fixed j≥1, π_{−j}X_i is F_p for i≤j and zero thereafter, so its tower is nilpotent with exponent j; other homotopy groups vanish. With a common lower bound, any upper truncation has only finitely many relevant homotopy degrees; closure of nilpotent towers under extensions and finite Postnikov dévissage give the corrected converse. The continuity applications use connective or uniformly bounded-below spectra, so Theorems 5.19–5.22 are unaffected.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 2.6(2), the matrix T_{s₂} for n = 9, accepted manuscript p. 14; the relation for e₁₁, p. 16
issues.printed: The source gives T_{s₂} entries (10,10): 1 + q; (10,11): 1; (11,10): q(1+q+q²)/(1+q)²; and (11,11): q²/(1+q). It also states e₁₁ = (q+1)²(q(q²+q+1))^{−1}(T_{s₂}e₁₀ − (q+1)e₁₀).
issues.correction: The (10,10) entry is −1/(1+q), and the relation reads e₁₁ = (q+1)²(q(q²+q+1))^{−1}(T_{s₂}e₁₀ + (q+1)^{−1}e₁₀).
issues.reason: The ⟨e₁₀, e₁₁⟩ block is invariant, and (T + 1)(T − q) = 0 requires trace q − 1 and determinant −q. As printed the trace is (1 + 2q + 2q²)/(1+q). With −1/(1+q) the trace is q − 1 and the determinant is −q²/(1+q)² − q(1+q+q²)/(1+q)² = −q. The Bernstein relation forces the same entry, q − ζ_{β₂}([1,2,0,1]) = −1/(q+1). A symbolic check of the whole n = 9 matrix set shows the quadratic relation for T_{s₂}, the braid relations for s₁s₂ and s₂s₃ and the Bernstein relation for s₂ all fail as printed and all hold with the correction. The displayed matrices therefore do not define an H_B-module as printed; with the correction they do, and Proposition 2.6 and the absolute irreducibility argument go through.

issues.locator: §3.5, proof of Theorem 3.3, after (3.9), accepted manuscript p. 26
issues.printed: The proof asserts Z′ ↪ n-Ind(St_{2,E}|·|^{1/2} ⊗ St_{U(5)}) and claims uniqueness of the irreducible submodule of this induction, because its parameter lies in the chamber opposite the one producing a unique Langlands quotient. It then uses (3.9) for Z or W to identify one of them with Z′.
issues.correction: The induced representation I has at least two irreducible submodules, Y and Z′. Since Y is already identified, the member of {Z, W} that embeds in I is Z′, which gives the same conclusion.
issues.reason: The paper embeds Z′ in I because [1, 0, 2, 1] is the only exponent of j(Z′) with e₁ + e₂ = 1. The same holds for Y: j(Y) (Theorem 2.3(2)) contains [1, 0, 2, 1] once and all its other exponents have e₁ + e₂ = 3, so the same Frobenius reciprocity argument embeds Y in I. So the uniqueness claim is false; the identification of Z survives with the repair above (the same repair is needed for 'the same argument' when m > 5).

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 7.1, accepted manuscript p. 49
issues.printed: The source asserts the existence of Sym^r π_E and its descent to Π, a cuspidal automorphic representation on GL_{r+1}(A_F). It treats Sym^r(π_{E₀} ⊗ χ₀) as a twist of Π_{E₀} and invokes local-global compatibility to conclude Sym^r rec_{F_v} π_v = rec_{F_v} Π_v.
issues.correction: The descent Π is determined only up to Π ⊗ η with η = η_{E/F}, and the comparison over E₀ only up to η∘N_{E₀/F}, so at a place v split in E₀ and inert in E the argument gives rec Π_v ≅ Sym^r rec π_v ⊗ η_v^j with j possibly depending on E₀. Repair: fix Π at a place v₁ with Sym^r π_{v₁} ≇ Sym^r π_{v₁} ⊗ η_{v₁} (one exists, since Π_E is cuspidal) and use E₀ split at v and v₁.
issues.reason: Both Π and Π ⊗ η have base change Sym^r π_E, and both Π_{E₀} and Π_{E₀} ⊗ (η∘N) have the same base change to EE₀.

issues.reviewReason: Rejected as a missing-hypothesis finding. The printed reference to §2.1.3 does not by itself justify the general interchange, but the asserted need to add regularity and nuclear transition maps is false. Use the Banach injective resolution already invoked in the proof. Over the complete discretely valued K, every closed subspace of a Banach space is complemented (Schneider, Nonarchimedean Functional Analysis, Proposition 10.5(a), proof read together with 10.1). Each short exact segment of that resolution therefore splits continuously. The additive completed tensor functor V⊗̂_K− preserves these splittings, giving a split exact tensor resolution without interchanging any inductive limit. Equivalently, the resulting contracting homotopy is preserved. This establishes the needed exactness in the paper’s setting without the proposed extra hypothesis on V. The general nonarchimedean injective-resolution construction remains an explicit supplier contract, not something formally supplied by the cited complex-analytic Prosmans paper. v2 has the same proof paragraph.

issues.printed: For a topological Λ-module M, the source defines M^* := Hom_cont(M,Λ), with weak topology. It identifies Sp_J(Λ)^* naturally with lim←_n LC(X_{n,J},Λ)^*, describing this as an inverse limit indexed countably, whose terms are finite free Λ-modules.
issues.correction: Replace the claimed equality by Sp_J(Λ)^* = Ann(Σ_i LC(X_{J∪{i}},Λ)) inside lim←_n LC(X_{n,J},Λ)^*. A presentation by finite free level modules, when used, needs its own compatible splitting/freeness argument.
issues.reason: Confirmed on rendered p. 38, with the proposed repair narrowed. The inverse limit of LC(X_{n,J},Λ)^* is the dual of LC(X_J,Λ), not the dual of its parabolic quotient. The latter is the annihilator of the parabolic-function subspace. For d=1,J=∅ this is the total-mass-zero subspace of distributions on P^1(K); a Dirac mass lies in the printed right side but not this subspace. Finite-level freeness needs a compatible presentation/proof; it does not follow for arbitrary quotients just by renaming them Sp_{J,n}. v2 p. 38 repeats the incorrect identification.

issues.locator: Proposition 6.11, p. 47 (authors’ manuscript, 7 September 2019)
issues.printed: The source claims that ordinarity of X̃ is equivalent to both X and Y being ordinary.
issues.correction: For the reverse implication, require the smooth centre to have codimension at least two (componentwise), or restrict to the forward implication used for blow-ups of ordinary centres.
issues.reason: The missing restriction has a direct counterexample. Over F_3 let X=P^2 and let Y be the smooth cubic y²z=x³−xz². X is ordinary. The curve is nonsingular, and Cartier kills its invariant differential dx/y: in characteristic 3, the coefficient of x² in x³−x is zero. Hence Y is a nonordinary elliptic curve. As Y is an effective Cartier divisor, Bl_Y X≅X is ordinary. This disproves the printed reverse implication. The paper’s applications to ordinary blow-up centres only need the forward direction. Rendered p. 47 and v2 Proposition 6.11 checked. The original Illusie Proposition 1.6 was not accessed; the counterexample, rather than an unverified quotation, establishes this verdict.

issues.locator: Théorème 5.24 (ii), p. 59 (and Théorème 5.15, p. 55)
issues.printed: Theorem 5.24 asserts in (i) that the R^{ps,δ_M}_B-action on 𝕞_{B,M} factors through R_{B,M}. In (ii) it claims an isomorphism of E^{δ_M}_B[G_{Q_p}]-modules: 𝕞_{B,M} ≃ 𝕞^{δ_M}_B(Π^*(ρ_{B,M})) ⊗ ρ_{B,M} ⊗ Ř_{B,M}.
issues.correction: Part (ii) needs the hypothesis of Theorem 0.18 (ii): p > 3, or p = 3 and B not containing a twist of the Steinberg; and Theorem 5.15, whose proof cites (ii), inherits it.
issues.reason: Neither Theorem 5.24 (ii) nor Theorem 5.15 carries any hypothesis on p, and no standing hypothesis supplies one: chapter 4 assumes only p > 2 (p. 37, footnote 23) and chapter 5 assumes nothing. But the proof of (ii) ends ‘en adaptant le lemme 5.12’ through footnote 32 (p. 60), which needs the semi-simplicity of F ⊗_{R_{B,M}} E_{B,M} and states that Paškūnas's explicit description ‘demande d'exclure les blocs contenant un twist de la steinberg si p = 2, 3’. Accordingly the introduction states the same result as Theorem 0.18 (ii) with ‘Supposons que p > 3’, and footnote 14 (p. 9) relaxes it to p = 3 away from the Steinberg blocks. As printed, the two body statements assert for all p what is proved only under that restriction.

issues.locator: Theorem 1.1(ii), p. 2, against Theorem 5.4(ii), p. 54
issues.printed: Theorem 1.1(ii) claims that p^N kills the map’s kernel and cokernel, where N = N(e,p,r) depends on e, r and is independent of X or n. Theorem 5.4(ii) likewise claims annihilation by p^N, specifying N = N(K,p,r) with dependence on K, p, r.
issues.correction: Do not replace Theorem 1.1(ii) by a purported correction on this evidence. Preserve its N(e,p,r) source statement and separately record the unclosed uniform-descent obligation.
issues.reason: Rejected as an error claim. N(K,p,r) is a weaker statement than N(e,p,r), not a contradiction. Dependence on c(K) alone does not show that c(K) cannot be bounded in terms of e,p. Colmez 2008 §4.1–4.2, pp.148–150, defines this conductor and proves Proposition 4.5. A uniform descent estimate remains a proof obligation; this review neither disproves nor certifies Theorem 1.1(ii).

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 3.2, p.32 (five slips in one proof)
issues.printed: For j ∈ J_i, the source states ϕ(ω_j) = p^jω_j, then claims A ⊂ B; also ϕ(B) ≤ A. Using F^rA = A ∩ F^rB, it reduces p^s-injectivity to the claim that (p^s − p^iϕ)x ⊂ A forces x ∈ A. It later concludes (1 − p^{i−s}ϕ)p^{−s}g_2 ∈ p^{−s−r}A.
issues.correction: ϕ(ω_j) = p^iω_j (equivalently p^{|j|}ω_j); ϕ(B) ⊂ A; (p^s − p^iϕ)x ∈ A; and (1 − p^{i−s}ϕ)g_2 ∈ p^{−s−r}A, without the factor p^{−s}. Also replace the conclusion x∈A in the p^s-injectivity argument by p^s x∈A.
issues.reason: j is a multi-index (j_1 < ⋯ < j_i), so p^j is undefined; the natural Frobenius multiplies each dX/X by p, hence ω_j by p^i, which is also what the parenthesis in the next clause requires ('the map becoming p^s − p^iϕ'). A and B are rings, so ≤ is not a relation between them, and the next sentence writes ϕ(B) ⊂ A. x is an element of B, so (p^s−p^iϕ)x is an element and the conclusion drawn about it is a membership. And g_2 ∈ p^{−[ru]}R^+_ϖ ⊆ p^{−r}A with ϕ(B) ⊂ A already give (1−p^{i−s}ϕ)g_2 ∈ p^{−s−r}A; the extra p^{−s} would give only p^{−2s−r}A, and the next clause subtracts (1−p^{i−s}ϕ)g_1 from f, with g = g_1+g_2 and no such factor. The p^{−s} belongs to the rewriting (1−p^{i−s}ϕ) = p^{−s}(p^s−p^iϕ) used in the last line.

issues.locator: Lemma 2.11(ii), pp.15–16, and Remark 4.3, pp.42–43 (authors’ November 2016 version)
issues.printed: The source claims that t^r:r^[u,v]_ϖ→F^r r^[u,v]_ϖ is an isomorphism up to p^r.
issues.correction: Use a justified coarser arithmetic filtration bound, for example p^(3r), and recompute the downstream numerical losses. The later p^(2r) assertion for the filtered ring also fails for p=2; the p^(2r) bound on the unfiltered smaller annulus is a separate statement.
issues.reason: Take p=2,K=Q_2(ζ_16),i=4,e_0=8,u=3/4,v=3/2. At the Gauss valuation v_2(T)=3/16, P_0=1+(1+T)^8 has valuation 1, whereas t=16 log(1+T) has valuation 5/2 (unique minimum at term k=8). Hence v_2(2P_0/t)=−1/2. Since P_0∈F^1, this disproves the printed bound. More strongly g=P_0/T^5 belongs to F^1 and is integral on the annulus: its endpoint valuations are 9/32 and 1/16, and every Laurent coefficient satisfies the integral bounds. Thus v_2(4g/t)=−7/16, disproving the later 2r bound for the filtered ring too. For the arithmetic annulus, divide an element of F^r by P_0^r analytically; at each endpoint v(P_0)≤1 and v(t/P_0)<2, so the quotient by t^r loses at most 3r. This does not refute the existence of a universal comparison constant, but the printed downstream numerical estimates need recomputation.

issues.locator: §5.1.2, p. 32 (both displays)
issues.printed: It gives two degree definitions: deg(M) := tN(M) − tH(M), followed by deg(M) := deg(det M) = tN(M) − tH(M).
issues.correction: deg(M) := tH(M) − tN(M)
issues.reason: The sign is the wrong way round, and it is printed twice — once for rank 1 and once for rank r — so it is a systematic convention rather than a slip of one character. Three independent checks force tH − tN. (a) The paper's own semistability convention, fixed in §3.2.2, is µ(E′) ≤ µ(E) for strict subobjects, so Definition 5.1's 'weakly admissible = semistable of slope 0' means deg(M′) ≤ 0 for all subobjects; Fontaine's weak admissibility is tH(M′) ≤ tN(M′), which is deg(M′) ≤ 0 only for deg = tH − tN. (b) Remark 5.5(ii) asserts that the Harder-Narasimhan slope of E(M,Fil) equals that of (M,Fil) and that H^1(E) = 0 iff (M,Fil) is acyclic, i.e. iff its slopes are ≥ 0. Take M = F with ϕ(e) = pe, so tN = 1, filtered with Fil^0 M_K = M_K and Fil^1 M_K = 0, so tH = 0: then X_st(M,Fil) = (M ⊗ B_st)^{N=0,ϕ=1} = B_st^{ϕ=p^{-1}} = 0 while X_dR = B_dR/B^+_dR ≠ 0, so H^0(E) = 0 and H^1(E) ≠ 0 and M is not acyclic; but the printed formula gives deg = +1 ≥ 0, which would make it acyclic. (c) The proof of Lemma 5.3 requires that shrinking the filtration strictly decrease the degree, and shrinking decreases tH. Definition 5.13, which defines the same two notions over C directly on the bundle, is unaffected and independently fixes the intended sign.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 4.2.12, p. 17 (arXiv v4)
issues.printed: The proof uses compactness of Q_{W,n} in its induced metric and injectivity of f_n to claim that some s_n ≥ 0 satisfies inf{‖f_n(m)‖ | m ∈ Q_{W,n} ∖ pQ_{W,n}} = p^{−s_n}. It then concludes that p^{s_n} annihilates the p^∞-torsion in R_{W,n} := P_W/f(Q_{W,n}).
issues.correction: The infimum can be 0 and the p^∞-torsion of R_{W,n} can be unbounded, so Lemma 4.2.11 does not apply as stated; the injectivity of (Q_{W,n} ⊗_{A_n} B̃_n)^∧[1/p] → (P_W ⊗_{A_n} B̃_n)^∧[1/p] needs another argument. Theorem 4.2.13, which this proposition serves, is proved independently in [Tsu23, Prop. 6.1].
issues.reason: Take N = M the trivial rank-one module, so Q_{W,n} = A_n·e, P_W = W⟨u⟩·e and f_n the inclusion (any choice of lattices is a scalar multiple). With ū_n = pu^n, the element ū_n^j = p^ju^{nj} is not in pA_n, since every element of A_n has u^{nj}-coefficient of valuation at least j, but ‖ū_n^j‖ = p^{−j} → 0. So the infimum is 0; correspondingly u^{nj} is p^j-torsion and not p^{j−1}-torsion in W⟨u⟩/A_n. Compactness does not help: pQ_{W,n} is not open in Q_{W,n} for the metric induced from P_W (and Q_{W,n} is not compact when k is infinite).

issues.locator: §3.5, after Theorem 3.8, p. 856 (also in arXiv v1, §3.5)
issues.printed: The proof says (49) descends from W_2 to W_3, leaving injectivity of W_3 → ϕ(T) ⊗_{O_E} E to establish. It says this follows from E-linear independence modulo π^{s+1} of {π^i F}_{i=0}^{s} ∪ {Y^i F}_{i=1}^{t−1} ∪ {∏_{j ∈ J}(U_{p_j} − 1) F}_{J ⊂ R, J ≠ φ, R}. It asks the reader to supply the argument, describing it as similar to earlier cases.
issues.correction: The proof of the linear independence has to be written out, as it is for W_1 (pp. 851–852) and for W_2 in both of its subcases (pp. 854–855).
issues.reason: This is the last step of Theorem 3.8, which is the Case 3 analogue of Theorem 2 and the only source of the homomorphism ϕ : T → W_3. issues.correction: The homomorphism φ′ on T_m is not constructed. Either it must be constructed, or the remark must be read with the φ′ of Remark 3.4, whose domain is the subalgebra T′ ⊂ T and whose target is E[π]/π^{r+1}, in which case the ideal I, the isomorphism T_m/I ≅ E[π]/(π^{r_an+1}) and the faithfulness of B as a module over the corresponding ring all have to be restated.
issues.reason: The only φ′ defined in the paper is that of Remark 3.4, p. 852, which has a different domain and a different target. A map of the stated shape need not exist: any Λ-algebra homomorphism W → E[π]/(π^{r_an+1}) must send each ε_i into the annihilator of π, i.e. into E·π^{r_an}, so for r ≥ 2 the product ε_1 ⋯ ε_r maps to 0 while the relation ε_1 ⋯ ε_r + (−1)^{r_an} L*_an(χ)π^{r_an} = 0 forces L*_an(χ) = 0. issues.printed: The source applies φ to the equation, claiming the result lies in m_W^r = E · T^r, described as an E-vector space of dimension 1. It then introduces an explicit computation of the equality for r_an = r.
issues.correction: “… a formula in the 1-dimensional E-vector space m_W^r/m_W^{r+1} = E·T^r (which equals m_W^r when r_an = r) …”
issues.reason: Checked on the page image of p. 843. Take W = E[π, ε_1, …, ε_r]/(π^{r_an+1}, ε_i^2, ε_iπ, ε_1⋯ε_r + (−1)^{r_an}L*_an(χ)π^{r_an}), with T = log_p(u)·π. The only monomial of degree r in the ε_i is ε_1⋯ε_r ∈ Eπ^{r_an}, and ε_iπ = ε_i^2 = 0, so m_W^r is spanned by π^r, …, π^{r_an}. These are linearly independent: dim_E W = 2^r + r_an − 1, with basis 1, π, …, π^{r_an} and the ε_S for S ≠ ∅, R (item w1-dimension). So dim_E m_W^r = r_an − r + 1, which is 1 only when r_an = r. The sentence comes before the case split, and the next sentence treats r_an > r, where the claim is false. The equation obtained by scaling (16) lives in m^r/m^{r+1}, and §5.1 (87) correctly computes modulo m_W^{r+1}. The same sentence is in arXiv v1, which lacks 'when r_an = r'. issues.printed: The source states Σ_{j=1}^r (res_{p_j} κ)(u_i) = 0 in B̄ for r equations. It then deduces (16) det((res_{p_j} κ)(u_i)) = 0 in B_R/mB_R because each matrix row sums to 0. It defines B_R as the T-module spanned by products b(σ_1)⋯b(σ_r) with σ_i ∈ G_{p_i}.
issues.correction: The row-sum argument does not give (16) in B_R/mB_R. It gives vanishing only modulo m·B·B_{p_2}⋯B_{p_r}, where B_{p_j} is the span of b(G_{p_j}). Read (16) as a heuristic. The argument actually carried out is §5.1: Lemma 4.9 (m̂B ⊂ Σ_i (A_i/C_i)m̂^2) rewrites each row sum as an exact zero of elements (A_i/C_i)·(elements of m̂); the A_i/C_i are cancelled, and the determinant is taken in T_m (item determinant-vanishes).
issues.reason: Checked on the page images of pp. 842–843. The entries (res_{p_j}κ)(u_i) are E-combinations b(σ_ij) of values of b on G_{p_j}, and their row sums vanish only in B̄ = B/mB, that is, they lie in mB. Replace one column by the sum of all columns, which is valid in the commutative ring L. This shows only that the determinant of the lifted matrix lies in m·B·B_{p_2}⋯B_{p_r}. That module is not known to lie in mB_R: by Lemma 4.8, B is generated by b(I_{p_k}) for every p_k ∈ R, not only by b(G_{p_1}). After scaling by ∏x_i one would need x_1·B ⊂ m, which is exactly the inclusion the paper says on p. 842 it cannot prove, and believes false for r ≥ 3. Section 5.1 avoids this by using Lemma 4.9, so Theorem 1 is unaffected. The check of §5.1 itself belongs to range 4.

issues.locator: §4.4, proof of Lemma 4.7, p. 864 (also in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: The proof calls the image of I_w in G_w^ab pro-ℓ, with ℓ the rational prime under w, and calls that image trivial at a complex place. It also calls B̄ pro-p because B̄ is a finite-dimensional E-vector space. From these claims it excludes nonzero continuous homomorphisms between the groups and concludes res_{I_w}([κ]) = 0.
issues.correction: The image of I_w in G_w^ab is rec(O_{H_w}^*) ≅ μ_{q−1} × (1 + 𝔪_w). This has an open pro-ℓ subgroup and a finite quotient of order prime to ℓ, possibly divisible by p. B̄ is a finite-dimensional E-vector space, so it is torsion-free and its compact subgroups are finitely generated Z_p-modules. A continuous homomorphism kills the finite part because B̄ is torsion-free, and kills the pro-ℓ part because its image is compact, hence pro-p. So res_{I_w}[κ] = 0.
issues.reason: Both assertions in the printed sentence are false. The tame inertia quotient F_q^* of G_w^ab has order q − 1, prime to ℓ but not to p in general, so the image is not pro-ℓ. A nonzero E-vector space is not compact, so it is not pro-p. And the stated reason, pro-ℓ against pro-p, would not by itself exclude a map from the finite part μ_{q−1} to a p-group. The conclusion is still true, by the torsion-freeness of B̄ as above, and Lemma 4.7 stands. Checked on the page image.

issues.locator: §5, proof of Théorème (5.10), printed p. 293, paragraph beginning « On déduit de (5.8) » (published text, Numdam scan)
issues.printed: The proof claims (5.8) shows that 𝔏 is generated by the square-zero transformations N_s : x ↦ (x, δ_s)δ_s (s ∈ S), with E/(E∩E^⊥) an absolutely irreducible representation of 𝔏. It then derives the theorem from the next lemma.
issues.correction: (5.8) only gives that 𝔏 contains the N_s: the unipotent generators exp(±N_s) lie in the compact image, and so does exp(Z_ℓ·N_s). Let 𝔏' ⊂ 𝔏 be the Lie algebra generated by the N_s. A subspace stable under 𝔏' is stable under every exp(λN_s), hence under the topological generators of the monodromy group, so 𝔏' acts absolutely irreducibly by (5.8). Lemma (5.11) applied to 𝔏' gives 𝔏' = 𝔰𝔭, and therefore 𝔏 = 𝔰𝔭.
issues.reason: For an ℓ-adic analytic group topologically generated by elements exp(N_s), it does not follow formally that its Lie algebra is generated by the N_s. Unlike the real case, the closed subgroup generated by exp(Z_ℓN_s) can be larger than the analytic subgroup of the algebra they generate. The equality is true a posteriori (both algebras equal 𝔰𝔭), and the repair above is immediate. So this is a real but harmless gap: the stated deduction is not valid as written.

issues.reviewReason: Rejected. The deduction is a standard one, not a gap. The image of ρ lies in the Q_ℓ-points of the algebraic subgroup H of Sp generated by the unipotent groups exp(G_a·N_s); in characteristic 0 the Lie algebra of such a group is the Lie algebra generated by the N_s (Chevalley: the Lie algebra generated by algebraic Lie subalgebras is algebraic). A closed subgroup of H(Q_ℓ) has Lie algebra inside Lie(H), so 𝔏 ⊆ ⟨N_s⟩; conversely each exp(Z_ℓ·N_s) lies in the image, so N_s ∈ 𝔏. Hence 𝔏 is exactly the Lie algebra generated by the N_s, as Deligne says, and the sentence before the display points to the Zariski closure for this reason. The reason given here ('the closed subgroup generated by exp(Z_ℓN_s) can be larger than the analytic subgroup of the algebra they generate') is false in this situation. The extraction's alternative argument is also valid; nothing in the paper changes.

issues.locator: §6, (6.10) Préliminaires, printed p. 298, lines 1–6 (definition of H); same convention in (6.12) « μ(g) = q^{−n} » (published text, Numdam scan)
issues.printed: The source defines H ⊂ Ẑ × CSp(ℱ_u, ψ) by q^{−n} = μ(g). It says q is an ℓ-adic unit, so qⁿ ∈ Q_ℓ* is defined for every n ∈ Ẑ. Since ψ takes values in Q_ℓ(−n), it claims that the map from π₁ to Ẑ × CSp, with coordinates the canonical projection to Ẑ and ρ, factors through ρ₁ : π₁(U₀, u) → H.
issues.correction: H = {(a, g) ∈ Ẑ × CSp(ℱ_u, ψ) : μ(g) = q^{−na}}, where n = dim of the fibres and a ∈ Ẑ is a separate letter. Correspondingly, in (6.12), CSp_a = {g : μ(g) = q^{−na}}.
issues.reason: In §6, n is the fibre dimension (X has dimension n+1, and ψ is the cup product with values in Q_ℓ(−n)). The equation uses n also for the Ẑ-coordinate. The generator φ (arithmetic Frobenius) acts on Q_ℓ(1) by q (§2), so an element over a ∈ Ẑ acts on Q_ℓ(−n) by q^{−na}. With the equation as printed, μ = q^{−a}, and ρ₁ would not land in H unless n = 1. With the corrected H, the proofs of (6.11)–(6.13) go through word for word: CSp_a is still an Sp-torsor, Ker(H → Ẑ) = Sp, and F_x lies over −deg(x), so (6.12) is applied to δ^{−1}, which is again an ℓ-adic unit.

issues.locator: §7, proof of (7.1), printed p. 300: (7.1.5), (7.1.5') and the following sentence (published text, Numdam scan)
issues.printed: The source gives (7.1.5) as 0 → ℱ → j_*j^*ℱ → ⊕_{s∈S} Q_ℓ(n−m)_s → 0, calling j_*j^*ℱ constant. It then gives (7.1.5') ⊕_{s∈S} Q_ℓ(n−m) → H¹(D, ℱ) → 0 and says F acts on Q_ℓ(n−m) by the scalar q^{d/2}.
issues.correction: Q_ℓ(m−n) in all three places (as in case B on the same page and in (5.8) b)).
issues.reason: Here n = 2m+1 and d = n+1, so m − n = −d/2. The geometric Frobenius F acts on Q_ℓ(1) by q⁻¹ (§2). Case B on the same page reads « La valeur propre de F agissant sur Q_ℓ(m−n) est q^{d/2} ». On Q_ℓ(n−m) = Q_ℓ(d/2), F acts by q^{−d/2}, which contradicts the stated q^{d/2}. The stalk at s of the cokernel of ℱ → j_*j^*ℱ is Hⁿ/Hⁿ^{I_s}, identified by x ↦ (x, δ_s) with Q_ℓ(m−n) (Picard–Lefschetz, δ_s ∈ Hⁿ(Q_ℓ(m))). The eigenvalue q^{d/2}, which is what (7.1.1) needs, is correct; only the sign of the twist is misprinted.

issues.locator: §8, proof of Théorème (8.2) (Ramanujan–Petersson), printed p. 302 (published text, Numdam scan)
issues.printed: The source identifies these roots as Frobenius eigenvalues on H^{k−1} of a smooth projective variety over F_p of dimension k−1. It cites its Bourbaki talk on modular forms and ℓ-adic representations, exposé 355, February 1969, in volume 179 of Lecture Notes in Mathematics, for a proof under restrictive assumptions, and describes the general case as only slightly harder.
issues.correction: The key geometric input for general N, ε, k ≥ 2 and p ∤ N needs a proof. This means a smooth projective model over F_p (a smooth compactification of the Kuga–Sato variety, with an auxiliary level structure if needed) whose H^{k−1} contains the roots of T² − a_pT + ε(p)p^{k−1} as Frobenius eigenvalues, together with a Hecke/character projector. This was later supplied in the literature, e.g. by A. J. Scholl, « Motives for modular forms », Invent. Math. 100 (1990).
issues.reason: The theorem is stated in full generality, but the paper says explicitly that the needed geometric fact is proved in the cited exposé only under restrictive hypotheses. The general case is dismissed with « n'est pas beaucoup plus difficile » and no argument. The result is true, but its proof in the paper is incomplete for general (N, ε, k).

issues.locator: §3, proof of Corollaire (3.8), printed p. 286, the count of closed points (published text, Numdam scan); page image checked
issues.printed: The source counts qⁿ points of the affine line over F_{qⁿ}, and hence at most qⁿ closed points of degree n. It deduces Σ_x q_x^{−1−ε} ≤ Σ_n qⁿ.q^{n(−1−ε)} = Σ_n q^{−nε} < ∞.
issues.correction: U₀ is an open of P¹, so count on P¹: at most qⁿ + 1 closed points of degree n (at most qⁿ for n ≥ 2), giving Σ_x q_x^{−1−ε} ≤ Σ_n (qⁿ + 1)q^{n(−1−ε)} < ∞.
issues.reason: In (3.1) U₀ is the complement in P¹ of a finite set of closed points, and the reduction after (3.2) only makes U affine; it need not lie in the affine line. Example: q = 2, U₀ = P¹ minus the closed point x² + x + 1 = 0 (affine). The three rational points lie in U₀, and for ε = 5 they alone give Σ_x q_x^{−1−ε} ≥ 3·2^{−6} = 3/64, while Σ_n qⁿ·q^{n(−1−ε)} = Σ_n 2^{−5n} = 1/31 < 3/64; so the displayed inequality fails. Shrinking U₀ is not available here, since (3.8) is a statement about H¹_c(U, ℱ) for the given U. With the count on P¹ the series still converges, so (3.8) is unaffected.

issues.locator: §2, Proposition (2.2.8)(i), p. 195, last line of (i) (published text, Numdam scan)
issues.printed: The source asserts that irreducibility of τ makes this sheaf pointwise ι-pure of weight 2ℛ(τ).
issues.correction: … ponctuellement ι-pur de poids −2ℛ(τ).

Hence the eigenvalues of F_x on 𝓕₀(τ_ℓ) have absolute value q^{−ℛ(τ)·deg x} = N(x)^{w/2} with w = −2ℛ(τ). Sanity check: τ = ω₁ has ℛ = 1 and F_x acts by q^{−deg x}, i.e. the sheaf is 𝐐_ℓ(1), of weight −2, not +2. Only the case ℛ(τ) = 0 is used later ((2.2.9)–(2.2.10)); (3.5.1) repeats the same sign when quoting (2.2.8).

issues.locator: §2, proof of Corollaire (2.2.9), case b), p. 195, last paragraph (published text, Numdam scan)
issues.printed: The source invokes (2.2.9.1) to say Z(X₀, t) is rational, with poles at most simple at t=1 and t=q^{−1}. It argues that absence of a pole at q^{−1} would, by (2.1.12), bound #X₀(𝐅_{q^n}) independently of n, which it calls absurd.
issues.correction: Without a pole at t = q^{−1} (and granting the absence of zeros on |t| = q^{−1}, which (2.1.11)–(2.1.13) also need), the argument of (2.1.11)–(2.1.13) gives q^{−n}#X₀(𝐅_{q^n}) → 0 geometrically, i.e. #X₀(𝐅_{q^n}) = O(ρ^n) with ρ < q, not boundedness. The contradiction then comes from #X₀(𝐅_{q^n}) ~ q^n (e.g. Weil's bound for curves). More simply: H²_c(X, 𝐐_ℓ) = 𝐐_ℓ(−1) gives the factor (1 − qt)^{−1}, and H¹_c cannot cancel it because its weights are ≤ 1.
issues.reason: In (2.1.13) the coefficients a_n = q^{−n}·(mass in degree n) decay geometrically; here a_n = q^{−n}#X₀(𝐅_{q^n}). That gives only #X₀(𝐅_{q^n}) = o(q^n), and nothing in the argument bounds the inverse zeros of Z (eigenvalues on H¹_c) by 1. So 'borné' does not follow as stated, and a lower bound for the point count is needed to reach a contradiction. The assertion itself is classical, as the text says, and this alternative proof is not used elsewhere.

issues.locator: §3, Variante (3.4.9), p. 210 (published text, Numdam scan)
issues.printed: The source deduces from (3.4.1) that every smooth mixed sheaf has a pointwise weight filtration by smooth subsheaves, and that every pure sheaf is geometrically semisimple.
issues.correction: … et que tout faisceau lisse ponctuellement pur sur X₀ normal est géométriquement semi-simple.
issues.reason: The source (3.4.1)(iii) (p. 208) explicitly assumes ℱ₀ lisse and X₀ normal, and normality cannot be dropped. Counterexample: let X₀ be a nodal cubic with split node over 𝐅_q. The normalisation P¹ is simply connected, so π₁(X) has a quotient Ẑ (the loop through the node) on which Frobenius acts trivially. Choose a rank-2 representation of W(X₀) = π₁(X) ⋊ 𝐙 in which π₁(X) acts through Ẑ → 𝐙_ℓ by non-trivial unipotent matrices and Frobenius acts trivially. It is lisse and pure of weight 0 (all Frobenius eigenvalues are 1), but not geometrically semisimple. Similarly, if 'faisceau' is read in the category of all constructible sheaves, 𝐐_ℓ on P¹ has the non-split subsheaf j_!𝐐_ℓ. So the second clause needs the lisse and normal hypotheses of (3.4.1)(iii). The later results (3.4.12)–(3.4.13) correctly carry 'normal'.

issues.locator: §4, proof of Théorème (4.4.9), p. 230 last display and p. 231 first line (published text, Numdam scan)

issues.reason: Let ε = ±1 with (δ,δ) = (δ',δ') = 2ε (by (4.4.8)), so s_δ(x) = x − ε(x,δ)δ. Put a = (δ,δ'). In general Tr(s_δ s_δ') = dim − 2 − 2 + (2/(δ,δ))(2/(δ',δ'))a² = dim − 4 + a². Directly, on span(δ,δ'): s_δs_δ'(δ) = (a²−1)δ − εaδ' and s_δs_δ'(δ') = −δ' + εaδ, giving plane trace a² − 2, and the identity on the orthogonal complement adds dim − 2. Checks: δ' = δ gives s_δ² = 1 with trace dim (the printed formula gives dim + 2), and δ ⊥ δ' gives dim − 4. The conclusion (δ,δ')² ∈ 𝐙 is a square, hence (δ,δ') ∈ 𝐙, is unaffected.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 7.1, p.41 (choice of η_v at finite places) (arXiv v2; the same text is on p.990 of the published version)
issues.printed: For every non-archimedean place v of K, the source chooses η_v := min{1, |t₁(t₁ − 1)|_v, |t₂(t₂ − 1)|_v}. It asserts (µ_{t_i,v}, m_{F,η,v})_v = (µ_{t_i,v}, [F]_v)_v because the potentials of µ_{t_i,v} are constant on radius-η_v disks.
issues.correction: At places v | 2 take η_v := |2|_v · min{1, |t₁(t₁ − 1)|_v, |t₂(t₂ − 1)|_v}. The claim is then true: in the potentially good range the support of µ_{t,v} is a type II point of diameter |Δ_t|_v^{1/6} = |2|_v^{2/3}|t(t − 1)|_v^{1/3} ≥ |2|_v min{1, |t(t − 1)|_v}, and in the bad-reduction ranges of Proposition 3.5 smaller radii are harmless. (7.5) grows by Σ_{v|2} r_v log 2 = log 2, which is divided by 2|F| and absorbed into C(ε).
issues.reason: The claim fails at v | 2 when |t_i(t_i − 1)|_v = 1. There η_v = 1, but µ_{t_i,v} is a point mass at ζ_{a,R} with R < 1. Indeed λ_{t,v}(0) = λ_{t,v}(ζ_{0,1}) = 0 and f_t(ζ_{0,1}) = ζ_{0,1/|4|}, so the support lies in a residue class of ζ_{0,1} other than that of 0. For x ∈ D(a,R), λ(ζ_{x,1}) − λ(x) = log(1/R) > 0, so the non-archimedean term of Proposition 7.3 is positive, not 0. Counterexample: take ω a primitive cube root of 1 and t₁ ≠ t₂ the roots of t² − (6ω² − 4)t − (3ω − 4) = 0 (discriminant 48ω(1 − ω) ≠ 0). Then ψ₃(ω, t_i) = 0, so x = ω ∈ π(E_{t₁}[3]) ∩ π(E_{t₂}[3]) ⊆ F. Also t₁t₂ = 4 − 3ω and (t₁ − 1)(t₂ − 1) = 15 + 3ω are 2-adic units, so |t_i(t_i − 1)|_v = 1 and η_v = 1. The reduction is supersingular (v(j(t_i)) = 25/2 ≥ 8); f_{t_i} conjugated by X ↦ ω + 2^{2/3}X has good reduction, so µ_{t_i,v} is the point mass at the point with centre ω and diameter |2|_v^{2/3}, and each point of F in that disk contributes (2/3) log 2 to the term, which here is divided by |F|. The loss is not O(1/|F|) in general: when |t_i(t_i − 1)|_v = 1 at every place above 2 and b = 0, every torsion image other than ∞ lies in the closed unit disk, the regularized measure at v | 2 is the Gauss point mass, and ĥ_{t_i} · h_{F,η} ≥ (1/3) log 2 whatever F is. (If |x|_v > 1 then |f_t(x)|_v = |x|_v/|4|_v > |x|_v, so torsion images other than ∞ are integral, and the local energy between the point mass at ζ_{a,|2|^{2/3}} and the Gauss point is (1/3) log(1/|2|_v).) The proof of the small-height case of Theorem 8.1 has no room for such a constant, since δ of Theorem 1.5 is ineffective. With the corrected η_v the equality holds and all later statements stand.
