With ⟨φ,φ⟩ = 7.263×10^{−19} and r = 13.78, the unit-vector values are modest: u(i) ≈ 3.76 and u((1+√−3)/2) ≈ 2.44, from the displayed values 4.41046×10⁹ and 2.86296×10⁹. (1) The quotation of (6.6) and of 'Part (6.6) ... follows straight from Theorem 4 and Theorem 5 of [12]' is exact (p.968, p.969). (2) The normalization is fixed. On p.962 the paper says it will 'always' normalize φ by (5.7) with a(1) = 1, and Theorem 4 forces a(1) = 1 through the Shimura relation. I recomputed φ(i) and φ((1+√−3)/2) from the a(p) of Table 1 using φ = 2y^{1/2}Σa(n)K_{ir}(2π|n|y)e(nx) with r = 2·6.889875675. That gives ⟨φ,φ⟩^{−1}φ(i) = 4.41046×10⁹ and ⟨φ,φ⟩^{−1}φ(ρ) = 2.86296×10⁹, which match p.967 to every printed digit. So the object in (6.6) really is the a(1) = 1 form. For the unit vector, u(i) = 3.759, u(ρ) = 2.440, and 1/‖φ‖ = 1.173×10⁹ ≈ 0.47e^{πr/2}. The value ⟨φ,φ⟩ = 7.263×10⁻¹⁹ corresponds to L(1,sym²φ) = 1.148 under ‖φ‖² = 2L(1,sym²φ)/cosh(πr), which is Humphries–Nordentoft (4.5) with q = 1. That is consistent with the Euler product over p ≤ 13, which gives 1.28. (3) What the cited results give. Duke 1988 calls a form 'spectral' when ‖f‖ = 1 on Γ₀(N)\H (p.79), and uses W_{(k/2)sgn n, it} with λ = 1/4 + t² ((2.4), p.77). This matches ⟨F,F⟩ = 1 and W_{(1/4)sgn n, ir/2} in Theorem 4, so t = r/2. Thm 5 (p.85) then gives |b(n)| ≪ r^{A'}ch(πr/4)|n|^{−2/7+ε} for fundamental n. Inserted into (5.16), this gives Weyl(⟨φ,φ⟩^{−1}φ,χ) ≪ r^C cosh²(πr/4)|D|^{3/4−2/7+ε}, so the proof as cited does not yield (6.6). (4) (6.6) is false, not just unproved. Take D = −4 = (1)(−4), which is inside the scope: (5.12) allows d'd < 0, and p.967 uses exactly this case. Here h = 1 and ω = 2, so Weyl = ⟨φ,φ⟩^{−1}φ(i)/2 = u(i)/(2‖φ‖), and (6.6) would force |u(i)| ≪ r^{C+ε}e^{−πr/2} for every even Hecke–Maass form. Odd forms vanish at i. By the local Weyl law at i, Σ_{r_j≤R}|u_j(i)|² + (1/4π)∫_{−R}^{R}|E(i,1/2+it)|²dt ≍ R². From (7.1), E(i,s) = 2ζ(s)L(s,χ₋₄)/ζ(2s), so fourth-moment bounds make the Eisenstein part O(R^{1+ε}). The even forms therefore have Σ|u_j(i)|² ≍ R², which is incompatible with exponential decay. (5) Theorem 2 survives. issues.locator: Appendix A, proof of (A.1): the strategy sentence on p. 983 and the final paragraph on p. 985; the differentiation under the integral sign on p. 984
issues.printed: The proposed proof checks that the two sides of (A.1) obey a differential equation of the same order and that their Taylor coefficients agree through order 2. It claims direct calculation shows agreement between (A.2) and (A.3) at the powers t^s, t^{s+1} and t^{s+2}, which it says exceeds what is required to prove the lemma.
issues.correction: Two unstated routine steps close the proof. (i) Uniqueness. By (A.2), the left side of (A.1) is t^s H(t) with H entire: the double series is dominated termwise using |∫_0^π e^{i(m+μ)θ} sin^{n+s−1}θ dθ| ≤ e^{π|Im μ|}∫_0^π sin^{σ−1}θ dθ, which also justifies integrating termwise. By (A.3), the right side is t^s H̃(t) with H̃ entire. For f = t^s Σ a_ℓ t^ℓ, the equation f″ + (1 − s(s−1)/t²)f = 0 forces a_1 = 0 and ℓ(ℓ+2s−1)a_ℓ = −a_{ℓ−2} (ℓ ≥ 2), and ℓ(ℓ+2s−1) ≠ 0 for ℓ ≥ 1 when Re s > 0. So both sides are determined by their t^s coefficients. These coefficients agree by the duplication formula, and this covers the case where both vanish. (ii) Differentiating twice in t under the integral on p. 984 is justified by dominated convergence: the integrand and its first two t-derivatives are O(sin^{σ−1}θ), σ = Re s, uniformly for t in compact subsets of (0,∞).
issues.reason: The step is terse but no step is false. In the defence of the paper: 'Taylor series' refers to the expansions in powers t^{s+ℓ} that (A.2) and (A.3) actually compute. The authors match coefficients of t^s, t^{s+1}, t^{s+2}, and 'more than what is needed' shows they intend the one-coefficient Frobenius argument at the regular singular point t = 0 (exponents s and 1−s), not a regular-point uniqueness from two Taylor coefficients. So the extraction's framing overstates the problem. What is missing is the explicit statement of the recurrence and the differentiation-under-the-integral justification; items 117/166 and 163–165 supply them. Lemma 7 is true: I verified it numerically, for both signs, complex μ and s, and G = 0.

issues.citation: Duke–Imamoḡlu–Tóth, "Geometric invariants for real quadratic fields", Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), no. 3
issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: Both quoted sentences are on the page images (p. 983, the Proof paragraph; p. 985, the last paragraph before the References). The revision is right, and it is more accurate than the ledger text. I checked the proof independently. (1) The ODE step on p. 984 is correct: the differentiation, the Whittaker equation and the integration by parts all check. The boundary term vanishes because M(2t sin θ) = O(sin^σ θ), σ = Re s > 0. (2) The comparison the authors make is a comparison of coefficients of t^{s+ℓ}, the expansions (A.2) and (A.3) actually compute. The ledger says the paper uses a regular-point uniqueness argument from 'ordinary Taylor coefficients', but the paper never says that, so the ledger's 'is not the missing justification' criticises an argument the paper does not make. (3) The comparison does suffice, once one states the step the paper omits. With 1/4 − λ² = −s(s−1), a solution t^s Σ a_ℓ t^ℓ satisfies ℓ(ℓ+2s−1)a_ℓ = −a_{ℓ−2} and a_1 = 0. The factor ℓ(ℓ+2s−1) is nonzero because Re(ℓ+2s−1) > 0 for ℓ ≥ 1. So one coefficient determines the solution, including s = 1/2 and a_0 = 0. The t^s coefficients agree by the duplication formula: 2πΓ(s) = π^{3/2}2^{2−2s}Γ(2s)/Γ(s+1/2). (4) Numerical checks (mpmath) confirm the argument. (A.1) holds for both signs at (t, μ, s) = (1.3, 1, 1.7), (2.1, 0.4+0.3i, 0.6+0.8i) and (0.7, −1, 0.3), and at μ = 3, s = 2, where both sides vanish. The (A.2) coefficients c_0,…,c_6 at μ = 0.4+0.3i, s = 0.6+0.8i satisfy the recurrence and equal the (A.3) coefficients. So Lemma 7 is true. What is missing is a stated uniqueness principle at the regular singular point t = 0 (exponents s and 1−s). Also missing are the justification of termwise integration in (A.2) and the justification of the two t-derivatives under an improper integral whose integrand is O(sin^{σ−1}θ) at the endpoints. This is a minor gap in the proof, and the result is unaffected. So 'gap' and 'the proof' are right. One overreach in the revision's reason: 'more than what is needed' does not show that the authors meant the one-coefficient Frobenius argument. It is equally consistent with the count of two initial conditions for a second-order equation. Either reading leads to the same verdict.

issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: Checked on the page images. DIT11 p. 959 prints 'pr⁺ = ⅔(U₄∘W₄)+⅓', with left-acting (U₄f)(τ) = ¼Σ_{ν mod 4} f((τ+ν)/4) and (W₄f)(τ) = (2τ/i)^{−1/2}f(−1/4τ), and states the purpose: 'to get forms whose Fourier expansions are supported on n ≡ 0,1 (mod 4)', 'as in [27]'. DIT16 p. 976 prints 'pr⁺ = ⅔WU + ⅓' with left-acting U, W. Conjugating by y^{1/4} turns DIT16's U, W into U₄, W₄ (I checked this; the extra √2 and e^{iπ/4} are what the conjugation produces), so DIT16 applies U first. The printed DIT11 order is wrong. Let f = θ(z)j(4z), which has weight 1/2 on Γ₀(4) and support in n ≡ 0,1 mod 4. Then U₄f = θ(τ)j(τ), because U₄θ = θ and j(4·(τ+ν)/4) = j(τ). Also W₄θ = θ, so W₄U₄f = f. In the printed order, W₄f = θ(τ)j(τ) and U₄(θj) = 746 + 21974457684q + 490845366512384q² + …. I recomputed this from E₄ and E₆ with exact integers. So the printed pr⁺f has a nonzero q² coefficient, although f is already in the plus space. Since W₄² = 1, U₄∘W₄ = W₄(W₄∘U₄)W₄, whose eigenvalue-1 space is W₄(V⁺) ≠ V⁺. Biró's L (p. 142, (A.1)) has the W∘U shape. Its matrices B_w = (1+w, 1/4; 4w, 1) satisfy B_w A_ν^{−1} = (−1, (1+w+ν)/4; −4, w+ν) ∈ Γ₀(4) for ν ≡ 3−w, where A_ν = (ν, −1/4; 4, 0) is the matrix of the ν-th term of W₄∘U₄. For U₄∘W₄ the corresponding products are not integral. On 'affects', the revision is right: 'nothing', not 'the proof'. The intended operator, Kohnen's projection, is unambiguous from the stated purpose. Proposition 2's weight and eigenvalue claims hold for either order. The reason is that U₄∘W₄ = W₄(W₄∘U₄)W₄, W₄ preserves weight-1/2 Γ₀(4)-automorphy, and both operators commute with Δ_{1/2}. DIT11 omits the computation of (2.20) ('we will omit the details', p. 960), and (2.20) holds for the correct operator, given the separate 3/2 normalization of E12. DIT16 uses the correct order. So the slip does not propagate into any proof or stated result.

issues.locator: §2, 'Fuchsian groups and closed geodesics', p. 952
issues.printed: The source calls Γ a group of the first kind if Λ = ℝ, and of the second kind otherwise. It describes ℝ − Λ as a countable union of disjoint open intervals. It defines N_Γ by intersecting the non-Euclidean open half-planes above the geodesics joining the endpoints of those intervals.
issues.correction: Write ℝ̂ = ℝ ∪ {∞} for ℝ in 'Λ = ℝ' and in 'ℝ − Λ'. Define N_Γ as the intersection of the open half-planes bounded by the geodesics joining the endpoints of the intervals of ℝ̂ − Λ, each taken on the side away from its interval. Alternatively, keep 'above' and add the standing normalisation that ∞ ∈ Λ and every component of ℝ − Λ is bounded. This holds for every group in the paper, since each contains a translation.
issues.reason: The limit set lives in ℝ̂. If ∞ ∉ Λ, one interval of ℝ̂ − Λ contains ∞, and the half-plane to keep for it is the inside (below) of the semicircle, not the part above it. With 'above' the definition then gives a set that is not Γ-invariant. In the defence: every group the paper applies this to (Γ_A, PSL(2,Z)) has ∞ as a parabolic fixed point (of T^m), so ∞ ∈ Λ, all intervals are bounded, and 'above' is correct.

issues.citation: Duke–Imamoḡlu–Tóth, "Geometric invariants for real quadratic fields", Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), no. 3
issues.reviewReason: The quotation matches p. 952. The paragraph is set up for an arbitrary nonelementary Fuchsian Γ ⊂ PSL(2,R) with no normalisation. The limit set Λ is a closed subset of ℝ̂ = ℝ ∪ {∞}, so 'Λ = ℝ' should read 'Λ = ℝ̂'. The description 'open half-planes that lie above the geodesics' gives the Nielsen region (Beardon [2, §8.5]: the side of each geodesic away from its interval of discontinuity) only when every component of ℝ̂ − Λ is a bounded interval of ℝ. That means ∞ ∈ Λ and Λ unbounded in both directions. Two cases fail. (a) If ∞ ∉ Λ, the component containing ∞ appears in ℝ − Λ as two rays (−∞,a) and (b,∞). Their geodesics are vertical lines, so 'above' makes no sense, and the correct half-plane is the inside of the semicircle from a to b. (b) If ∞ ∈ Λ but Λ ∩ ℝ is bounded above (or below), there is a ray (b,∞) whose geodesic is the line Re z = b. In either case the literal definition does not give the Γ-invariant hull that the next sentence cites from [2, Thm. 8.5.2]. The defence holds, so affects = nothing is right. Every group the paper uses (PSL(2,Z), and each Γ_A, which contains T^m) has Λ invariant under a translation. So ∞ ∈ Λ, Λ is unbounded both ways, all intervals are bounded, and 'above' is correct. The intended object (the Nielsen region, named and cited) is unambiguous, so the classification as a misprint or imprecision is fair.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 1, p. 958, paragraph after (3.6)
issues.printed: The proof claims the arc joining z to γ(z) meets (x−n_1)²+y² = 1 at z*, because (3.5) gives n_1 − 1 < w < n_1. It similarly claims an intersection z** with (x − n_1 − n_2)² + y² = 1 because n_1 + n_2 − 1 < w_2 < n_1 + n_2.
issues.correction: Insert: by (3.4), γ(z) = S_1(S_2⋯S_ℓ T^m z), and S_ℓT^m z = T^mSz lies on |ζ − m| = 1. Since |S_kζ − N_k| = 1/|ζ − N_k| (N_k = n_1+⋯+n_k), and the open discs |ζ − N_k| < 1 are pairwise disjoint (n_j ≥ 2), induction shows S_k⋯S_ℓT^m z ∈ {|ζ − N_k| < 1} for 1 ≤ k < ℓ. In particular γ(z) lies in the disc about n_1 (on its boundary if ℓ = 1, when z* = γ(z)), while z lies outside it. So the arc from z to γ(z) meets the circle, and it does so exactly once. The same argument, applied to S_{k−1}⋯S_1γ(z) = S_k⋯S_ℓT^m z, justifies each later step.
issues.reason: The stated reason (n_1 − 1 < w < n_1, together with w^σ < 1 ≤ n_1 − 1) shows only that the whole geodesic S_w meets the circle about n_1. It does not show that the arc from z to γ(z) reaches it, i.e. that γ(z) is already inside that disc. The claim is true (the repair above), and I checked it numerically for w = (3+√7)/2: z = 1/2 + (√3/2)i, γ(z) ≈ 2.823 + 0.028i, z* = 5/2 + (√3/2)i, S_1γ(z) = 17/2 + (√3/2)i, which matches Figure 7.

issues.citation: Duke–Imamoḡlu–Tóth, "Geometric invariants for real quadratic fields", Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), no. 3
issues.reviewReason: The quotation matches p. 958. The stated reason, n_1 − 1 < w < n_1 from (3.5), together with 0 < w^σ < 1 ≤ n_1 − 1, shows only that the full geodesic S_w crosses the circle |ζ − n_1| = 1, which it does exactly once. To conclude that the sub-arc from z to γ(z) crosses it, one needs z outside that disc and γ(z) inside it or on it. Nothing in the paper argues the second point. The same applies to the step for z** with w_2 and to the later steps. The claim is true, and the proposed repair is correct. I re-derived it. S_k(ζ) = N_k − 1/(ζ − N_k) gives |S_kζ − N_k| = 1/|ζ − N_k|. So S_k maps the open exterior of the circle about N_k into the open disc. Consecutive centres differ by n_j ≥ 2 (p. 951: a_j ≥ 2), so the open unit discs about the N_k are disjoint, and a point in one disc or on one circle lies strictly outside the others (tangency only at real points). Also S_ℓT^m z = T^mSz lies on |ζ − m| = 1, because |z| = 1. By induction S_k⋯S_ℓT^m z lies in |ζ − N_k| < 1 for 1 ≤ k < ℓ. For ℓ = 1, γ(z) = n_1 − 1/z lies on the circle. Also z = e^{iθ} satisfies |z − n_1| > 1 for n_1 ≥ 2. I checked numerically for w = (3+√7)/2 (D = 28, class I). γ_w = (17 −3; 6 −1) = T^3ST^6S, which agrees with (3.4). z = 1/2 + (√3/2)i, and γ(z) = 2.8226 + 0.0279i lies on S_w with |γ(z) − 3| = 0.180 < 1. z* = 5/2 + (√3/2)i, S_1γ(z) = 17/2 + (√3/2)i, and T^{−9}S_2S_1γ(z) = z. d(z, γ(z)) = 5.53732 = 2 log(8 + 3√7). All of this matches Figure 7. The gap is local and easily filled. The proof is incomplete but the result stands.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 1, last paragraph, p. 959 (the claim 'The conformal class of F_A determines A', Theorem 1, p. 957)
issues.printed: The source says the construction of F_A assigns each elliptic fixed point in F_A a unique nearest point on the boundary geodesic. Using (2.7), it gives (V(n_1), V(n_2), … V(n_ℓ)) as the cycle of hyperbolic distances between consecutive fixed points in H belonging to S_0, S_1, … S_ℓ. It declares this cycle a conformal invariant because conformal equivalence preserves those distances and the boundary geodesic's orientation.
issues.correction: Replace the last paragraph of the proof with the following. A conformal equivalence F_A → F_B, of Riemann orbifolds with their cone points of order 2, is an isometry (pass to the doubles and use uniqueness of the hyperbolic structure). It therefore lifts to φ ∈ PSL(2,R) with φΓ_Aφ^{−1} = Γ_B. Composing with an element of Γ_B (one cusp class), we may take φ(∞) = ∞, so φ(z) = az + b with a > 0. Since Γ_A ⊂ PSL(2,Z), Im γ(N_k + i) = 1/((cN_k+d)² + c²) ≤ 1, with equality exactly for γ ∈ T^{mZ} ∪ T^{mZ}S_k. So the points of maximal height in the ℓ elliptic orbits of Γ_A are N_k + mZ + i, k = 1,…,ℓ, and likewise for Γ_B. Hence a = 1 and the two sets correspond under a translation. Their successive gaps (n_1,…,n_ℓ) therefore agree up to cyclic rotation, and the cycle is a complete invariant of A. Alternatively, keep the distance argument, but prove that the nearest boundary point is unique and gives the stated order. Then define the k-th length intrinsically, as the length of the geodesic arc from P_{k−1} to P_k homotopic to the path through the boundary between their feet, and show that this length is V(n_k). Also state in Theorem 1 that 'conformal class' is taken with the cone points.
issues.reason: A conformal equivalence F_A → F_B preserves only intrinsic data. The distance on F_A between two elliptic points is an infimum over all lifts, and the proof does not show that the chosen lifts attain it or that V(n_k) is the length of an intrinsically characterised arc. Step (i) (uniqueness of the closest point and the resulting order) is stated without argument. The result itself is true, by the normalisation argument above, and V is correct and strictly increasing. So only the proof is incomplete.

issues.citation: Duke–Imamoḡlu–Tóth, "Geometric invariants for real quadratic fields", Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), no. 3
issues.reviewReason: The quotations match p. 959. The proof rests on two things. First, an ordering of the cone points, via a 'unique' nearest boundary point, asserted from 'the above construction'. Second, the claim that the H-distances V(n_k) = d(N_{k−1}+i, N_k+i) between these particular lifts are preserved by conformal equivalence. A conformal (orbifold) equivalence F_A → F_B is an isometry. It preserves distances on the surface and lengths of intrinsically defined arcs, but not distances between arbitrarily chosen lifts in H. The V(n_k) are not surface distances in general. For ℓ = 1 the 'successive' fixed points i and n_1+i are the same point of F_A. For D = 28, class I (cycle (3,6)), F_I has two cone points, [i] = [9+i] and [3+i]. Their distance on F_I is at most V(3) ≈ 2.390, yet the proof's cycle is (V(3), V(6)) ≈ (2.390, 3.637). So V(6) is only the length of one particular geodesic arc, and the proof never characterises that arc intrinsically, for instance by a homotopy class tied to the boundary ordering. The uniqueness of the nearest boundary point and the claim that the induced order is N_0, N_1, …, N_{ℓ−1} are also unargued. So the step fails as written. The theorem is nevertheless true, and I checked the proposed repair. A conformal equivalence of the bordered orbifolds extends to the doubles, which carry unique complete hyperbolic orbifold metrics, so it is an isometry. It lifts to φ ∈ PSL(2,R) with φΓ_Aφ^{−1} = Γ_B. Each Γ_B has one cusp class, so after composing with an element of Γ_B we may assume φ(∞) = ∞, hence φ(z) = az + b with a > 0. For γ ∈ Γ_A ⊂ PSL(2,Z), Im γ(N_k+i) = 1/((cN_k+d)² + c²) ≤ 1. Equality holds only for (c,d) = ±(0,1), i.e. γ = T^j ∈ Γ_A so m | j (the cusp stabiliser is ⟨T^m⟩), or for (c,d) = ±(1,−N_k), i.e. γ = T^{j}S_k with m | j. So the highest points of the elliptic orbits are exactly N_k + mZ + i, all at height 1. φ scales heights by a, so a = 1, and {N'_j} ≡ {N_k} + b mod m. So the gap cycles agree up to rotation, and orientation is kept because φ preserves orientation. Since the cycle is a complete invariant (p. 951), B = A. V(x) = arccosh(1 + x²/2) is correct and strictly increasing, which I checked numerically for x = 2, 3, 6. A precision remark that does not change the verdict: the statement must be read with F_A as a Riemann orbifold, with its ℓ cone points of order 2 (and the cusp) as part of the structure. That is what the paper's 'contains ℓ points of order 2' and its use of hyperbolic distances intend. Forgetting the cone points, every F_A is conformally a punctured closed disc {0 < |z| ≤ 1}, so the bare conformal type carries no information.

issues.printed: L(s; t) = Σ_{n≥1} n^{it} σ_{−2it}(m) m^{−s} = ζ(s + it)ζ(s − it),

issues.reviewReason: The p.963 image, checked at 300 dpi, reads 'L(s; t) = Σ_{n≥1} n^{it}σ_{−2it}(m)m^{−s} = ζ(s + it)ζ(s − it)'. The summation variable is n, but the summand is written in m, and m is not otherwise bound here. issues.locator: §5, Remarks after Theorem 4, p965
issues.printed: The source notes Res_{s=1}E*_{1/2}(z, s) = ½θ(z) and cites [7] for ⟨½θ(z), ½θ(z)⟩ = 6.
issues.correction: '… and ⟨½θ(z), ½θ(z)⟩ = π/2', equivalently ⟨θ,θ⟩ = 2π = area(Γ_0(4)\H), for the product of Theorem 4. The value 6 = [Γ:Γ_0(4)] is ⟨θ,θ⟩, not ⟨½θ,½θ⟩, for the product normalized by 3/π = 1/area(Γ\H). In that normalization ⟨½θ,½θ⟩ = 3/2. Either way the claimed match with ⟨F,F⟩ = 6 does not hold.
issues.reason: The residue claim is right (checked from the constant term Λ(2−2s)2^{1−s}y^{3/4−s/2} and b(m²,s)). For the norm: g(z)=|θ(z)|² is Γ_0(4)-invariant (checked), and ⟨θ,θ⟩=Σ_{i=1}^{6}∫_F g(γ_i z)dµ over coset representatives I, S, ST, ST², ST³, ST²S (bottom rows exhausting P¹(Z/4Z)). Gauss–Legendre quadrature up to y=Y plus the exact cusp tail 3·∫_Y^∞ y^{−3/2}dy = 6Y^{−1/2} gives 6.283185307180 for Y=12 and for Y=20, i.e. 2π to 12 digits; the same code with g≡1 returns area 2π. So ⟨½θ,½θ⟩ = π/2 ≈ 1.571, not 6, and the claimed match between the norm-6 normalization of F and ½θ fails. Defence: the remark is explicitly heuristic ('Perhaps not coincidentally'), and [7] (Chiera, J. Number Theory 122 (2007), which I could not access) may use a normalized Petersson product; even so, no normalization gives ⟨½θ,½θ⟩=6, only ⟨θ,θ⟩=6 with the product divided by π/3. Nothing in the proofs uses it; extraction item 80 repeats the false value.
searched: Crossref record of doi:10.4007/annals.2016.184.3.8, checked 2026-09-23: no update, correction or erratum relation
issues.citation: Duke–Imamoḡlu–Tóth, "Geometric invariants for real quadratic fields", Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), no. 3
issues.reviewReason: The quotation is confirmed on the p.965 image. The paper's definitions: θ(z) = Im(z)^{1/4}Σ_{n∈Z} e(n²z) (p.964), ⟨F,F⟩ = ∫_{Γ_0(4)\H}|F|²dμ (Theorem 4), and dμ = y^{−2}dxdy (p.952). The residue claim is right. Λ(2−2s) has residue ½ at s = 1, which gives the constant term ½y^{1/4}. For n = m², b(m², s) has residue (4π)^{−1/4}m^{−1/2}, consistent with the Shimura relation, and b(n, s) is regular at s = 1 when n is not a square. So the residue is ½θ. The norm value is wrong. I computed ⟨θ,θ⟩ in two independent ways. (i) Rankin–Selberg against the Eisenstein series for the cusp ∞ of Γ_0(4). The constant term of y^{1/2}|Σe(n²z)|² is y^{1/2}(1 + 4Σ_{n≥1}e^{−4πn²y}). Its growth part y^{1/2}, and the matching y^{1/2} growth at cusp 0 (the function is invariant under z ↦ −1/(4z)), cancel in the truncation argument. The residue at s = 1 of 4(4π)^{1/2−s}Γ(s−½)ζ(2s−1) is 1, so ⟨θ,θ⟩ = area(Γ_0(4)\H) · 1 = 2π. (ii) Numerically. I summed ∫_F g(γz)dμ over the coset representatives I, S, ST, ST², ST³ and (1 0; 2 1), with g = y^{1/2}|Σe(n²z)|². I checked numerically that g is Γ_0(4)-invariant, to 1.7e−14. I used Gauss–Legendre quadrature up to height Y and added the cusp tail 6Y^{−1/2}. The result was 6.28318530718 for Y = 12, 20 and 40, and the same code with g ≡ 6 returned the area 2π. So ⟨½θ,½θ⟩ = π/2 ≈ 1.571, not 6. The case for the defence: the remark is heuristic, and [7] (Chiera, JNT 122 (2007)) may normalize its product differently. I could not access [7] to check. That does not save the statement. The remark compares with 'choose F so that ⟨F,F⟩ = 6'. With the product c·∫, F normalized to norm 6 turns the 12 in (5.16) into 2c, so the claimed '2' forces c = 1, the paper's own product, and there ⟨½θ,½θ⟩ = π/2. No standard normalization (none, 1/area(Γ_0(4)\H), 3/π = 1/area(Γ\H), 1/index) gives ⟨½θ,½θ⟩ = 6. With the 3/π normalization one gets ⟨θ,θ⟩ = 6, which suggests θ and ½θ were confused. The claimed coincidence therefore fails. Nothing else in the paper uses the value.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 1, the citation for (6.3), p.968

issues.reason: [58] is Zagier's book Zetafunktionen und quadratische Körper, which has 144 pages (Springer 1981), so it has no p.167. [57] is Zagier, 'A Kronecker limit formula for real quadratic fields', Math. Ann. 213 (1975), pp.153–184, which contains p.167 and develops the minus continued fraction reduction theory used here. So the first citation is almost certainly [57]. I did not see the content of either page. The identity (6.3) itself is correct: I checked it numerically for D = 28 ((3+√7)/2·(3+√7) = 8+3√7) and for the family in E5.

[58] is Zagier's book Zetafunktionen und quadratische Körper (Springer Hochschultext, 1981), which has viii+144 pages, so it has no p.167. Citing the same work twice with 'or' is itself the sign of a slip. Among the paper's references on reduction theory, only [57] contains a p.167: Zagier, 'A Kronecker limit formula for real quadratic fields', Math. Ann. 213 (1975), 153–184. [28] (Hirzebruch) runs 183–281. I read [57] on the page images (author's copy). Its §4 (p.163) sets up the minus continued fraction and the cycle ((b₁,…,b_r)) of a narrow class. On p.167 it displays Σ_{k=1}^{r} log(w_k/w'_k) = log(w₁⋯w_r/w'₁⋯w'_r) = log(A'_r/A_r) = log ε², which is the product-over-the-cycle identity behind (6.3). So [57, p.167] is the intended citation. The identity (6.3) itself is correct, and the proof does not depend on the citation.

issues.locator: Remarks after the proof of Theorem 2, p.969
issues.printed: The source describes Conrey and Iwaniec's paper [10] as providing the best subconvexity bound then known for the L-functions (5.17): both estimates in Proposition 2 have exponent 1/3 + ε in |D|, subject to D being odd.
issues.correction: The Conrey–Iwaniec bounds L(1/2, φ⊗χ_d) ≪ |d|^{1/3+ε} and L(1/2, χ_d) ≪ |d|^{1/6+ε} give the exponent 5/12 + ε of |D| in both estimates of Proposition 2 (for D odd), not 1/3 + ε. The exponent 1/3 + ε is that of the L-function bound.
issues.reason: The printed exponents are built as 7/16 = 1/4 + 3/16 (Burgess) and 13/28 = 3/4 − 2/7 (Duke). Redo the same computation with Conrey–Iwaniec. In (6.5), |D|^{1/4}·|d'|^{1/6}|d|^{1/6} = |D|^{5/12}. In the unit-normalized (6.6), (5.17) gives |b(d)| ≪ |d|^{−1/2+1/6+ε} = |d|^{−1/3+ε}, and then |D|^{3/4}|d'd|^{−1/3} = |D|^{5/12}. Humphries–Nordentoft's bound |W_{χ,f}|² ≪ √D·L(1/2,f⊗χ_{D1})L(1/2,f⊗χ_{D2})/L(1,ad f) gives the same 5/12. In the defence: 1/3 is the exponent in the Conrey–Iwaniec L-function bound, and the sentence may have meant that. The remark lies outside the logical chain.

issues.reviewReason: The quotation is exact (p.969). The |D|-exponent of each estimate in Proposition 2 is 1/4 plus the exponent of the L-value bound, because the relations are exact identities. By Theorem 3, Weyl(E(·,s),χ) = Λ(s,χ_{d'})Λ(s,χ_d), which is |D|^{1/4} times Γ-factors times L(s,χ_{d'})L(s,χ_d). By (5.16)–(5.17), |Weyl(u_φ,χ)|² ≍_r |D|^{3/2}|b(d')b(d)|² ≍_r |D|^{1/2}L(1/2,φ⊗χ_{d'})L(1/2,φ⊗χ_d). This reproduces the printed exponents: 1/4 + 3/16 = 7/16 from Burgess, and 3/4 − 2/7 = 13/28 from Duke's b(n) ≪ |n|^{−2/7}, which corresponds to L(1/2) ≪ |d|^{3/7}. The Conrey–Iwaniec bounds L(1/2,φ⊗χ_d) ≪ |d|^{1/3+ε} and L(1/2+it,χ_d) ≪ |d|^{1/6+ε} (odd conductor) give 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12 in both estimates, not 1/3. An exponent of 1/3 would need L(1/2,χ_d) ≪ |d|^{1/12}, which is far beyond Weyl strength; Lindelöf gives only 1/4. Humphries–Nordentoft (6.7), |W_{χ,f}|² ≍ √D·L(1/2,f⊗χ_{D1})L(1/2,f⊗χ_{D2})/L(1,ad f) up to Γ-factors, gives the same 5/12. In the paper's defence, 1/3 is the exponent of the Conrey–Iwaniec L-function bound, and the next sentence about Young ('the same value 1/3 + ε for the exponent of C') also refers to L-function exponents. Even so, the sentence as printed attributes a false exponent to Proposition 2. It is a remark outside the logical chain.

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed on pp. 973–974. There are three slips. (1) In (8.3), the m=0 term is √y′F_0(z,s)K_{s−1/2}(0), with F_0=E(z,s) and K_{s−1/2}(0)=∞ for Re s>1/2. The correct term is the m→0 limit, y′^{1−s}E(z,s)/(2s−1): on the seed, √y′K_{s−1/2}(2π|m|y′)·y^{1/2}I_{s−1/2}(2π|m|y)→y′^{1−s}y^s/(2s−1). (2) 'Valid when y′>y' should be y′>max_γ Im γz. This is automatic for z in F, the domain in (8.2), so it is harmless. (3) By (5.7), the m-th x′-coefficient of Σ conj(u(z))u(z′) is Σ⟨φ,φ⟩^{−1}conj φ(z)·2√y′a(m)K_{ir}(2π|m|y′). The display on p. 974 omits the √y′. Since (2s−1)/(¼+r²−s(1−s)) has residue 1 at s=½+ir, the √y′ must appear on both sides for the stated conclusion to follow, and that conclusion is correct. All three have a clear meaning, and only m≠0 is used.

issues.locator: §8, display at the top of p.975
issues.printed: For fixed m,n with mn≠0, the source claims Φ(m,n;s) continues meromorphically to Re(s)>0 and satisfies Res_{s=1/2+ir}(2s−1)Φ(−m,n;s)=2Σ_φ⟨φ,φ⟩⁻¹a(m)a(n). The sum includes every Hecke-Maass cusp form φ for Γ having eigenvalue 1/4+r².
issues.reason: By Proposition 3 with −m, Res(2s−1)F_{−m}(z,s)=Σ_φ⟨φ,φ⟩⁻¹2a(−m)φ(z); the proof on p.974 gives the same, Σ2a(m)conj(φ(z))/⟨φ,φ⟩. The n-th Fourier coefficient of F_{−m} is 2y^{1/2}Φ(−m,n;s)K_{s−1/2}(2π|n|y) (the expansion on p.974, which I checked numerically), and that of φ is 2y^{1/2}a(n)K_{ir}. The main term and the y^{1−s} term are holomorphic at s=1/2+ir. So the residue is 2Σa(−m)a(n)/⟨φ,φ⟩, and for odd φ, a(−m)=−a(m). This matches the parity factor in the opposite-sign Kuznetsov formula. The display is only 'for comparison' and is not used later.

I took D=12=(−3)(−4), with classes [1,0,−3] and [−1,0,3], χ=+1 and −1, and γ_Q=[[2,3],[1,2]]. Theorem 4 is unaffected, because its third case is written with (λ/2)∫_{F_A}φdμ, which does not depend on orientation, and the chain Lemma 5 → Proposition 5 → Proposition 6 → Lemma 1 is consistent under the (2.11) orientation. issues.reviewReason: The quotations are confirmed on pp. 978–980. Orientation. p. 978 defines C_Q 'as in [16] using (2.11)', and footnote 8 adds 'Actually, we use g_Q=γ_Q^{−1} in [16]'. DIT11 ((3.1) p. 964, (4.1) p. 966, images checked) takes C_Q from z to g_Qz, with g_Q=±((t+bu)/2, cu; −au, (t−bu)/2)=γ_Q^{−1}, and S_Q counterclockwise for a>0. So in DIT16, C_Q runs from z to γ_Qz. The attracting fixed point of γ_Q is (−b+√D)/(2a), with multiplier ε_D^{−2}. So C_Q is clockwise for a>0, which is the orientation of C_A in §2 (γ_Q=γ_w) and the one Lemma 1 needs. (1) (9.2) holds: mpmath, 4 points including complex s, ratio 1 to 1e−30. Lemma 7 holds for both signs: 5 cases, including complex μ and s. (2) So i∂_zF_m=−½P_m(z,φ), with φ as on p. 980. (9.3) and Lemma 7 then give Φ_m(2√D/c)=2·2^{s−1/2}Γ((s+1)/2)²Γ(s)^{−1}D^{1/4}c^{−1/2}J_{s−1/2}(4π|m|√D/c). Quadrature of (9.3) gives (−½Φ_m)/(c-th term of Lemma 5)=−1.0000000 in 4 cases. So the printed Lemmas 5 and 6 contradict each other under any single orientation. (3) Unfolding by hand, Σ_{Γ\Q_D}χ(Q)∫_{C_Q}P_m=Σ_{Q∈Γ∞\Q_D}χ(Q)∫_{S_Q}f. Take a>0 and S_Q counterclockwise: τ=−b/2a+Re^{iθ}, θ: 0→π, R=√D/2a. Each term is then e(−mb/2a)Φ_m(R). Forms with a<0 contribute the same, because χ(−Q)=−χ(Q) for d<0 and γ_{−Q}=γ_Q^{−1}. By the symmetry b→−b the total is Σ_{c=4a}S_m(d′,d;c)Φ_m(2√D/c). So the printed Lemma 6 is DIT11's counterclockwise statement, and for C_Q from z to γ_Qz it takes a minus sign. (4) Direct computation of Lemma 5. I evaluated F_m by its Poincaré series, differentiating the seed directly rather than through (9.2). Cycle integrals used Gauss–Legendre quadrature, and χ and S_m came from p. 978 and (9.1); my S_m reproduces Lemma 8 in 3240 cases. With C_Q from z to γ_Qz, LHS/RHS was: 1.0000000000 for D=12, m=±1, s=4; 0.99999998 for D=12, m=2, s=3.7; 1.000000008 for D=21, m=1, s=4; and 0.9999999998 for D=28, m=1, s=4.2. With DIT11's orientation it was −1 in every case. So Lemma 5 is right for the paper's orientation, and Lemma 6 is wrong by a sign. The Lemma 4 note has the same problem. On S_Q, √D dz/Q(z,1)=dθ/sinθ, which equals +y^{−1}|dz| only in the counterclockwise direction. Reach. Lemma 6 is a stated lemma, and it is false as printed under the orientation the paper fixes. Under DIT11's orientation, Lemma 5 and the third cases of Propositions 5 and 6 would be false instead. So a stated result is wrong under every reading, not just a step of a proof. Nothing downstream is affected. Proposition 5, Proposition 6 and Theorem 4 are correct under the (2.11) orientation. Theorem 4's d′,d<0 branch is orientation-free through Lemma 1. Only the proof of Lemma 5, as written, would give the opposite sign. The Lemma 4 note is harmless, because Lemma 4 is stated with y^{−1}|dz|.

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed on pp. 979–980. M_{κ,μ}(x)=x^{μ+1/2}(1+O(x)) as x→0. So the φ chosen on p. 980 satisfies φ(y)≍y^{s−1}, which is ≪y^{1+ε} only for Re s>2, while Lemma 5 is claimed for Re s>1. The hypothesis is DIT11's weight-0 one (p. 967: φ=O(y^a), a>1), which that paper needs for G_m=Σφ(Im gτ). In weight 2, the factor |(γτ)′|=Im γτ/Im τ makes φ≪y^ε enough. P_m then converges absolutely, since Σ(Im γτ)^{1+ε} converges. The unfolded sum is Σ_a #{b mod 2a}·∫_0^π|φ(R sinθ)|R dθ ≪ Σ_a a^{o(1)−1−ε} with R=√D/2a, which also converges. So the statement is true, but the proof as written does not cover 1<Re s≤2. The repair is routine: weaken the hypothesis, or prove the lemma for Re s>2 and continue analytically, since both sides of Lemma 5 are holomorphic for Re s>1.

issues.printed: Citing [34], the source gives V_r^+ an orthonormal basis B_r={ψ} of simultaneous eigenfunctions of T_{p²} for primes p>2. From T_{p²}ψ=a_ψ(p)ψ it claims L_d(s+1/2)Σ_{n≥1}b(dn²)n^{−s+1}=b(d)Π_p(1−a_ψ(p)p^{−s}+p^{−2s})⁻¹. It defines a_ψ(n) by (10.2) Π_p(…)⁻¹=Σa_ψ(n)n^{−s}, saying these numbers are always defined because some d has b(d)≠0.
issues.correction: Take B_r to consist of eigenfunctions of Kohnen's plus-space operator at 2 as well, and define a_ψ(2) as its eigenvalue, as in the plus-space Shimura correspondence of [34]/[1]; or restrict (10.2)–(10.4) to odd m and treat 2 separately. Justify b(d)≠0 for some fundamental d: with the full Shimura relation, b(d)=0 forces b(dk²)=0 for all k, and every nonzero n≡0,1 mod 4 is dk² with d fundamental. Note that the a_ψ(m) are real.
issues.reason: With eigenvalues only for p>2, the Euler factor at p=2 in the display and in (10.2) is undefined. So a_ψ(2^k), and hence Shim ψ in (10.3), are not defined by the text, and the nonvanishing claim is asserted without argument. Case for the defence: the plus-space Hecke theory at 2 and the Hecke-equivariant correspondence of Katok–Sarnak [34] and Baruch–Mao [1], which the proof invokes at the end, supply what is missing. The extraction flags this in item 120, but there is no source issue for it.

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed on pp. 980–981. B_r is an eigenbasis only for T_{p²} with p>2. Yet the displayed relation after (10.1), (10.2) and hence (10.3) use a_ψ(p) for every prime, including p=2, and the text never defines a_ψ(2). The a_ψ(2^k) enter (10.4) for even m, and so (10.6). 'For some d, we must have that b(d)≠0' is asserted without argument. Its natural proof, through the Shimura relation and the fact that every n≡0,1 mod 4 is dk², also needs the p=2 part, because the odd-p relations never reach b(4^k d). Case for the defence: Kohnen's plus-space Hecke operator at 2 and the Hecke-equivariant plus-space correspondence of [34]/[1], invoked at the end of the proof, supply what is missing, so Proposition 6 stands. As written, though, the construction is incomplete at p=2. (10.4) also uses silently that a_ψ(m) is real (T_{p²} is self-adjoint) when the Hecke relation is conjugated. That is harmless.

issues.locator: Appendix A, proof of (A.1), p. 984, first display
issues.printed: h″(t) + (1 − (λ²−1/4)/t²) h(t) = (2 sin²θ − 2μ sin θ/t) h(t) + 2i sin 2θ e^{±i(t cos θ)} M′_{μ,λ}(2t sin θ).
issues.correction: h″(t) + (1 − (λ²−1/4)/t²)h(t) = (2 sin²θ − 2μ sin θ/t)h(t) + 2i sin 2θ e^{i(t cos θ)} M′_{μ,λ}(2t sin θ).
issues.reason: The proof restricts to the + signs, and h(t) = e^{i(t cos θ)}M_{μ,λ}(2t sin θ) is defined on p. 983. The derivative of h produces 4i cos θ sin θ e^{i(t cos θ)}M′ = 2i sin 2θ e^{i(t cos θ)}M′. The stray '±' is inconsistent with the next display, which uses e^{i(t cos θ)+iμθ}. Otherwise the display is correct: I rederived 4 sin²θ M″ = (sin²θ − 2μ sin θ/t − (1/4−λ²)/t²)M from the Whittaker equation, which gives 2 sin²θ − 2μ sin θ/t.

issues.citation: Duke–Imamoḡlu–Tóth, "Geometric invariants for real quadratic fields", Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), no. 3
issues.reviewReason: Checked on a 300 dpi crop of p. 984. The first display prints '+ 2i sin 2θ e^{±i(t cos θ)} M′_{μ,λ}(2t sin θ)'. The proof has just restricted to the + signs (p. 983) and defined h(t) = e^{i(t cos θ)}M_{μ,λ}(2t sin θ). The cross term of h″ is 2·(i cos θ)(2 sin θ)e^{i t cos θ}M′ = 2i sin 2θ e^{i t cos θ}M′, so the exponent is +i t cos θ. The '±' cannot be read as covering both signs either: with h = e^{−i t cos θ}M the coefficient would become −2i, so a ± would be needed on the 2i as well. The rest of the display is correct. By the Whittaker equation, 4 sin²θ M″ = (sin²θ − 2μ sin θ/t − (1/4−λ²)/t²)M, and with −cos²θ + 1 this gives 2 sin²θ − 2μ sin θ/t. The next display uses e^{i(t cos θ)+iμθ}, consistent with the + sign. A numerical check agrees: at μ = 0.4+0.2i, s = 0.9+0.3i, θ = 0.8, t = 1.4, h″ + (1 + (1/4−λ²)/t²)h equals the right side with e^{+i t cos θ} to 12 digits, and differs from it with e^{−i t cos θ}. The slip is isolated and affects nothing.

issues.locator: §1.4.3, p. 13, formulas (4)–(6), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 12–13
issues.printed: The source assumes nondegenerate G(F_v)-space pairings ⟨,⟩_{π_v}: π_v ⊗ π_v^∨ → C at every v. It asserts that a constant, written C = C(dg, fac_π, fac_{π^∨}, ∏_v⟨,⟩_{π_v}), gives the factorization ⟨φ, φ^∨⟩_Z = C(…) ∏_v ⟨φ_v, φ_v^∨⟩_{π_v}.
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis that for almost all v the local pairings satisfy ⟨φ_v^0, φ_v^{∨,0}⟩_{π_v} = 1 for the distinguished vectors used to form the restricted tensor products ⊗′π_v, ⊗′π_v^∨ (implicit in fac_π, fac_{π^∨}); only then is ∏_v ⟨φ_v, φ_v^∨⟩_{π_v} a finite product and (6) meaningful.
issues.reason: For factorizable φ = ⊗φ_v, φ_v = φ_v^0 for almost all v; with arbitrary non-degenerate local pairings the factors ⟨φ_v^0, φ_v^{∨,0}⟩ are arbitrary non-zero numbers and the infinite product need not converge. With the normalization, existence of C follows from Schur's lemma (Hom_{G(A)}(π ⊗ π^∨, C) is one-dimensional). Defence: the standard local pairing (7) with spherical vectors normalized by f(1) = 1 satisfies the normalization automatically (vol K_v = 1), and this is what the paper uses later.

issues.locator: §1.4.3, p. 14, sentence after (7), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 13
issues.printed: In case (2) of Hypotheses 1.4.4, the source chooses K_v = ∏_i GL(n_i, O_i) and asserts that pairing (7) is independent of this choice.
issues.correction: Replace 'however, the pairing (7) does not depend on the choice of K_v' by 'changing K_v to bK_vb^{-1} (b ∈ B) multiplies the pairing (7) by δ_B(b); we fix K_v as stated'.
issues.reason: Computation: ∫_{gK_vg^{−1}} F = ∫_{K_v} F(gkg^{−1})dk = ∫_{K_v} φ(gk)dk with φ = F(·g^{−1}); writing g = bk_0 this is δ_B(b)∫_{K_v} φ = δ_B(b)∫_{K_v} F by the G-invariance of ∫_{K_v}. Explicit case: G = GL_2(Q_p), B upper triangular, K = GL_2(Z_p), K′ = diag(p,1)K diag(p,1)^{−1} (hyperspecial, volume 1 for the same Haar measure), F(bk) = δ_B(b) the K-spherical vector with F(1) = 1. For k′ = (a, pb; c/p, d) ∈ K′, F(k′) = |det k′|/max(|c/p|,|d|)² equals 1 if p | c and p^{−2} if c ∈ Z_p^× (probability p/(p+1)), so ∫_{K′} F = 1/(p+1) + p^{−1}/(p+1) = p^{−1} = δ_B(diag(p,1)) ≠ 1 = ∫_K F. Defence: the discrepancy is a constant absorbed into C of (6), so nothing breaks if one K_v is used consistently. Independent check: The quote on p. 14 is accurate. It is also in v4 (p. 13, (1.4.5)) and absent from v3, where the sentence stops at 'we take K_v = ∏_i GL(n_i, O_i)'. For F(bx) = δ_B(b)F(x), the functional Λ_K(F) = ∫_K F dg is G-invariant. If K′ = gKg^{-1} with g = bk_0 (Iwasawa), then ∫_{K′}F dg = ∫_K F(gkg^{-1})dk = ∫_K φ(gk)dk with φ = R(g^{-1})F, which equals δ_B(b)Λ_K(φ) = δ_B(b)Λ_K(F). Here vol(K′) = vol(K) because G is unimodular. I checked the first reading's GL_2(Q_p) example directly. Take K′ = diag(p,1)GL_2(Z_p)diag(p,1)^{-1} and let F be the K-spherical δ_B-function with F(1) = 1 (this is f·f^∨ for the normalised spherical vectors). Then F(k′) = 1 when p | c and p^{-2} when c is a unit; the second case has proportion p/(p+1). So ∫_{K′}F = 1/p ≠ 1 = ∫_K F. The pairing (7) therefore depends on K_v through the positive scalar δ_B(b). The claim is false as stated. It is harmless because the scalar is absorbed into C of (6) once K_v is fixed, which the paper does.
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: The sentence was added in v4 (p. 13, equation (1.4.5)); v1–v3 define the pairing without the independence claim.

issues.locator: §2.1, p. 15, last lines (equivalence of quadruples), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 14
issues.printed: The source declares (A, λ, ι, α) equivalent to (A′, λ′, ι′, α′) if there is an isogeny f : A → A′ prime to □, with λ equal to f^∨∘λ′∘f up to a positive element of Z_(□)^×, satisfying ι′(b)∘f = f∘ι(b) for every b ∈ O_B and α′ = f∘α.
issues.correction: "prime-to-□ quasi-isogeny" (a Z_(□)^×-isogeny as in Lan's isogeny-class formulation), or 'the equivalence relation generated by' the printed relation.
issues.reason: With genuine isogenies the relation is not symmetric: for □ = {p}, if f has degree prime to p and g: A′ → A satisfies g∘f = [N] (N prime to p), then g∘α′ = g∘f∘α = N·α, which is not in the K^□-orbit of α in general (N·1 ∉ K^□ when K^□ ⊂ G(Ẑ^p)). Defence: 'isogeny' for 'quasi-isogeny' is a common abuse and the reference to Lan's representability theorem fixes the meaning.

issues.locator: §2.2, p. 16, definition of the signature of h, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 15
issues.printed: The source says h gives V = L ⊗ C a pure Hodge structure of weight −1. It defines V^0 ⊂ V as the degree 0 Hodge filtration piece, an O_B ⊗ C-submodule, and for each σ ∈ Σ_𝒦 sets a_{σ,i} = dim_C e_i(V^0 ⊗_{O⊗C,σ} C).
issues.correction: V^0 should be V^{−1,0} ≅ V/V^{0,−1} (the summand on which h(z) acts by z; Lan's V_0, the Lie-algebra side of the Kottwitz determinant condition), not the degree-0 Hodge filtration step F^0V = V^{0,−1}.
issues.reason: Convention-free check against §2.6.1/§2.6.3 (p. 21–22): there W = V/V^{0,−1}, Λ_0 ⊗ C = W, and 'e_iΛ_{0,σ} and e_iΛ^∨_{0,σ} are free S′_0-modules of respective ranks a_{σ,i} and b_{σ,i}'. But dim e_i(V/V^{0,−1})_σ = n_i − dim e_i(F^0V)_σ, which with the printed definition is b_{σ,i}, not a_{σ,i} (the weight −1 Hodge filtration is F^{−1} = V ⊃ F^0 = V^{0,−1} ⊃ F^1 = 0). Second check (Deligne's sign convention, h(z) acts on V^{p,q} by z^{−p}z̄^{−q}, the one compatible with weight −1 for an R-algebra homomorphism h): in §2.3, for σ ∈ Σ, h(z) acts on the σ-component V_{i,σ} by diag(z 1_{r_{i,σ}}, z̄ 1_{s_{i,σ}}), so F^0 = V^{0,−1} (h(z) = z̄) has dimension s_{i,σ}, contradicting '(a_{σ,i}, b_{σ,i}) equals (r_{i,σ}, s_{i,σ}) if σ ∈ Σ'. With V^0 = V^{−1,0} both statements hold. Likely origin: Lan's notation V_0 (subscript) for the h(z) = z part read as a Hodge degree. issues.locator: §2.3, p. 17, construction of P from hermitian pairs, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 15–16
issues.printed: The source chooses totally imaginary δ ∈ O prime to p and sets ⟨·,·⟩_i = trace_{𝒦/Q} δ⟨·,·⟩_{V_i}. It defines h_{i,σ} : C → End_R(V_{i,σ}) by h_{i,σ}(z) = diag(z1_{r_{i,σ}}, z̄1_{s_{i,σ}}), and sets Σ = {σ ∈ Σ_𝒦 : p_σ ∈ Σ_p}. It then claims P = (B, ∗, O_B, L, 2π√−1⟨·,·⟩, h) qualifies as a unitary PEL datum.
issues.correction: δ must also satisfy a sign condition tied to the CM type Σ: Im σ(δ) > 0 for all σ ∈ Σ if ⟨·,·⟩_{V_i} is 𝒦-linear in the first variable (Im σ(δ) < 0 for all σ ∈ Σ if linear in the second). Such δ exist (weak approximation), so the fix is to choose δ after Σ.
issues.reason: Positivity axiom of a PEL datum: −√−1 · 2π√−1⟨x, h(√−1)x⟩ = 2π Σ_{σ∈Σ} 2Re(σ(δ) H_σ(x_σ, h(i)x_σ)). With H linear in the first variable: on the r-part (H_σ(x,x) = |x|² > 0, h(i)x = ix) the summand is 2|x|² Im σ(δ); on the s-part (H_σ(x,x) = −|x|², h(i)x = −ix) it is again 2|x|² Im σ(δ). So the form is positive definite iff Im σ(δ) > 0 for every σ ∈ Σ with V_{i,σ} ≠ 0. Σ is determined by the p-adic datum Σ_p and δ only by 'totally imaginary and prime to p', so for a general δ the positivity fails on some V_{i,σ}. The text never states such a condition later (δ reappears in §4.1 only as ⟨·,·⟩_1 = trace δ⟨·,·⟩_V). Defence: the requirement is implicit in the claim that P is a PEL datum and is trivially arranged; alternatively one could flip h_{i,σ} at the offending σ, but that would change the stated relation between (a, b) and (r, s). Independent check: The quote on p. 17 is accurate. δ is only required to be totally imaginary and prime to p, and it is chosen before Σ = {σ : p_σ ∈ Σ_p} is defined. The positivity axiom (p. 14) for the pairing 2π√−1⟨·,·⟩ reads 2π⟨x, h(√−1)x⟩ > 0. On V_i ⊗ R = ⊕_{σ∈Σ} V_{i,σ} we have ⟨x, h(i)x⟩_i = Σ_{σ∈Σ} 2Re(σ(δ)H_σ(x_σ, h_{i,σ}(i)x_σ)). Take H linear in the first variable. On the r-part, h(i)x = ix and H(x,x) = |x|². On the s-part, h(i)x = −ix and H(x,x) = −|x|². In both cases the summand is 2 Im σ(δ)|x|². So positivity holds iff Im σ(δ) > 0 for every σ ∈ Σ with V_{i,σ} ≠ 0 (the reverse sign if H is linear in the second variable). The compatibility ⟨h(z)x, y⟩ = ⟨x, h(z̄)y⟩ holds for every δ, but positivity does not. Replacing δ by −δ, which is allowed, destroys it. Flipping h at the offending σ would contradict the stated equality (a_{σ,i}, b_{σ,i}) = (r_{i,σ}, s_{i,σ}) for σ ∈ Σ. So 'P is a PEL datum' can fail for admissible δ. The fix is trivial: choose δ after Σ with the right signs. Present in v1 (p. 14) and v4 (pp. 15–16).

issues.locator: §2.3.2, p. 18, lines 6–8 of §2.3.2, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 16–17
issues.printed: The source takes finite CM extensions 𝒦_1, …, 𝒦_r of 𝒦 satisfying Σ_{i=1}^r [𝒦_i : 𝒦] = n and sets V′_i = 𝒦_i, of dimension [𝒦_i : 𝒦] over 𝒦. It asserts that 𝒦_i-hermitian structures can be chosen on all V′_i so that the hermitian 𝒦-space ⊕_i V′_i is isomorphic to V.
issues.correction: This must be a hypothesis on (𝒦_1, …, 𝒦_r) ('Suppose each V′_i can be given …'); it holds e.g. when all 𝒦_i = 𝒦, but not for arbitrary CM extensions.
issues.reason: Counterexample: 𝒦 = Q(i), p ≡ 1 mod 4, n = 2, r = 1, 𝒦_1 = Q(i, √2) (CM, 𝒦_1⁺ = Q(√2)), V = 𝒦² with ⟨x, y⟩_V = x_1ȳ_1 + 3x_2ȳ_2 (definite, admissible in §2.3). The 𝒦-hermitian forms on 𝒦_1 for which 𝒦_1 acts by ⟨ax, y⟩ = ⟨x, āy⟩ are Tr_{𝒦_1/𝒦}(αxȳ), α ∈ Q(√2)^×; in the 𝒦-basis {1, √2} their Gram matrix is [[2a_0, 4a_1],[4a_1, 4a_0]] (α = a_0 + a_1√2), of determinant 8N(α). Hence ⊕V′_i ≅ V would force 3 · 8N(α) ∈ N_{𝒦/Q}(𝒦^×). At the place 3 (inert in Q(i) and in Q(√2)), norms from Q_3(i) and from Q_3(√2) have even 3-adic valuation, while 24N(α) has odd valuation: impossible. Equivalently, 𝒦_1 ⊗_{Q} Q_3 splits over 𝒦 ⊗ Q_3 with the involution swapping the factors, so every such trace form is hyperbolic at 3, whereas V ⊗ Q_3 is anisotropic (−3 is not a norm from Q_3(i)). Defence: the only case used for the standing assumption is 𝒦_i = 𝒦 (always possible by diagonalization), and §3.2.4 only uses CM pairs (J_0′, h_0) that exist. Independent check: The quote on p. 18 is accurate. It is stated as a fact for arbitrary CM extensions K_i/K. I verified the counterexample. The K-hermitian forms on K_1 = Q(i, √2) = Q(ζ_8) (with K_1^+ = Q(√2)) compatible with the K_1-action are Tr_{K_1/K}(αxȳ), α = a_0 + a_1√2 ∈ Q(√2)^×. In the basis {1, √2} the Gram matrix is [[2a_0, 4a_1],[4a_1, 4a_0]], of determinant 8N(α). An isometry with V = ⟨1, 3⟩ over Q(i) needs 24N(α) ∈ N(Q(i)^×). But 3 is inert in both Q(i) and Q(√2), so v_3(24N(α)) is odd while local norms from Q_3(i) have even valuation. Equivalently, K_1 ⊗_K K_3 ≅ Q_9 × Q_9 with the involution swapping the factors, so every such form is hyperbolic at 3, whereas V ⊗ Q_3 is anisotropic. V (with δ = i, lattice O², p ≡ 1 mod 4, p ≠ 3) satisfies the §2.3 set-up. The sentence must be a hypothesis on (K_i). The only case the paper needs is K_i = K, where it holds by diagonalisation. Present in v1 (p. 15) and v4 (p. 17).

issues.locator: §2.3, p. 18, lines 3–5, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 16
issues.printed: The source claims ker¹(Q, G) classifies, up to isomorphism, hermitian tuples 𝒱′ = (V′_j, ⟨·,·⟩_{V′_j})_{1≤j≤m} locally isomorphic to 𝒱 at each place of Q.
issues.correction: They classify tuples that are locally similar to 𝒱 at every place (V′_j ⊗ Q_v ≅ c_v·(V_j ⊗ Q_v) with a common c_v ∈ Q_v^× for all j), up to global similitude with a common factor c ∈ Q^×.
issues.reason: G is a similitude group, so H¹(Q, G) and H¹(Q_v, G) classify hermitian tuples up to similitude, not up to isometry. Read literally, the printed sentence makes ker¹(Q, G) trivial: by Landherr's theorem (Hasse principle for hermitian forms over a CM extension), hermitian spaces that are isomorphic at every place are globally isomorphic, so there would be a single class — contradicting the next paragraph, which says the Hasse principle fails in general when dim V_1 is odd. Defence: the intended statement is Kottwitz's [Kot92, §7–§8], which the paper cites. Independent check: The quote on p. 18 is accurate. G = G_P is the similitude group with a common factor ν. From 1 → U → G → G_m → 1 and H¹(Q, G_m) = 1 we get H¹(Q,G) = H¹(Q,U)/Q^×, and likewise locally. So ker¹(Q,G) classifies tuples that are locally similar everywhere, with a common c_v at each v, modulo a common global similitude. With the standard meaning of 'isomorphic' (isometric), tuples locally isometric to 𝒱 everywhere are globally isometric by Landherr's Hasse principle for hermitian forms over K/K^+. The set would then be a singleton, which contradicts the next paragraph: ker¹ ≠ 0 in general when dim V_1 is odd or m > 1. The paper never says that isomorphisms are similitudes. The intended statement is Kottwitz's, and nothing downstream is affected. Present in v1 (p. 14) and v4 (p. 16).

issues.locator: §2.5, p. 20, last lines before (14), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 18–19
issues.printed: The source identifies M̄_{K_r/F} with the normalization of M^tor_{K/F} in M_{K_r/F}, and likewise M̄_{K_r,L/F} with the normalization of M^tor_{K,L/F} in M_{K_r,L}/F.
issues.correction: M̄_{K_r/F} is an open subscheme of that normalization (dense, containing M_{K_r/F}), in general a proper one: the normalization is finite over M^tor_{K/F}, whereas M̄_{K_r/F} is not.
issues.reason: The normalization of M^tor_{K/F} in M_{K_r/F} is finite over M^tor_{K/F}. The paper itself says M̄_{K_r} is étale and quasi-finite but not finite over M^tor_K, and this already holds in characteristic 0: over a boundary point, 𝒜^∨ has a non-trivial torus part and 𝒜^∨[p^r] has fewer geometric points than over M_K, so there are fewer injections L⁺ ⊗ μ_{p^r} ↪ 𝒜^∨[p^r]. Since M̄_{K_r/F} is normal (étale over a smooth scheme) and quasi-finite over M^tor_{K/F}, Zariski's main theorem makes it an open subscheme of the normalization, missing the boundary points where the level structure does not extend. Modular-curve case: over X(1) with the Tate curve at ∞, μ_p ↪ E[p] has p² − 1 geometric choices generically but only p − 1 over the cusp (those onto the canonical μ_p); the normalization X_μ(p) has in addition the (p − 1) cusps ramified of index p, which are not in M̄. Defence: later sections use M̄_{K_r} as defined (sections of ω_{r,κ} over M̄_{K_r}, §2.6.6), not the normalization, and the Koecher principle (20) compares with sections over M_{K_r}; the claim is not used in an essential way, though the definition of cusp forms S_κ(K_r, ψ; R) via D_{∞,r} = M̄_{K_r} − M_{K_r} only imposes vanishing at the boundary present in M̄_{K_r}. Independent check: The quote on p. 20 is accurate; the printed text has 'M_{K_r,L/F}'. The same paragraph says that M̄_{K_r} (resp. M̄_{K_r,L}) is étale and quasi-finite but not finite over M^tor_K. A normalization of the excellent scheme M^tor_{K/F} in M_{K_r/F} is finite over it. So the two statements are incompatible unless M̄_{K_r/F} is finite. It is not finite, even over F. At a boundary point, 𝒜^∨ has a torus part, so 𝒜^∨[p^r] has fewer geometric points. Injections L^+⊗μ_{p^r} ↪ 𝒜^∨[p^r] that do not land in the toric part do not specialise. In the modular-curve analogue, μ_p ↪ E[p] over the Tate curve has p² − 1 generic choices but only p − 1 at the cusp, and the normalization has p − 1 further cusps with ramification index p. M̄_{K_r/F} is normal, quasi-finite and separated over M^tor_{K/F}, and it contains M_{K_r/F} densely (étale maps are open). By Zariski's main theorem it is a dense open subscheme of the normalization, in general a proper one. The paper works with M̄_{K_r} as defined, so the sentence itself carries no weight. A caveat not decided here: the cusp forms S_κ(K_r,ψ;R) = H⁰(M̄_{K_r}, ω(−D_{∞,r})) only require vanishing at the boundary strata present in M̄_{K_r}. §2.6.7's identification of them with classical cusp forms of level K_r therefore cannot rest on this sentence.

issues.locator: §2.5, p. 20, lines 5–3 from the bottom before (14), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 18
issues.printed: The source says a basis of Z_p(1) gives a natural identification of M_{K_r/F} with M_{I_rK^p/F}, and of M_{K_r,L} with M_{I_rK^p,L/F} = S_{I_rK^p}(G, X_P).
issues.correction: The identification induced by a basis of Z_p(1) (i.e. μ_{p^r} ≅ Z/p^r) is defined over F(μ_{p^r}) (in particular on C-points), not over F. Over F, M_{K_r/F} corresponds to the level group I_r′ ⊂ I_r^0 that acts on L⁻ unipotently and on L⁺ with diagonal ν, rather than to I_r.
issues.reason: For (A, α) ∈ M_{I_rK^p}, π_1-stability of the I_r-orbit of α_t: L ⊗ Z/p^r ≅ A_t[p^r] means σ∘α_t = α_t∘g_σ with g_σ ∈ I_r, and I_r acts unipotently on L⁺; so α_t(L⁺/p^r) is a subgroup with trivial Galois action on its graded pieces (constant type), while L⁻ carries the cyclotomic character through ν. For M_{K_r}, φ(L⁺ ⊗ μ_{p^r}) is a μ-type subgroup. These moduli problems agree after trivializing μ_{p^r}, which requires μ_{p^r} ⊂ base; μ_p ⊄ F for p odd since p is unramified in F ⊂ 𝒦′. (Compare Y_μ(N) and Y_1(N) over Q.) Defence: all later uses compare classical forms with automorphic forms over C (or over rings containing μ_{p^∞}), where the identification is valid; v1–v3 wrote 'a basis of Z(1)', suggesting the analytic identification over C was meant.
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: v4 p. 18 identical; v1–v3 say 'The choice of a basis of Z(1) naturally identifies …'.

issues.locator: §2.9.4, p. 32, justification of injectivity of (28), arXiv v5
issues.printed: The source attributes injectivity to the previously mentioned density of S_1 in the special fibre of M^tor_{K,L}.
issues.correction: Injectivity of M_κ(K_r, ψ; R) → V_{κ_p}(K^p, ψ, R) needs (for R flat over Z_p): every connected component of \overline{M}_{K_r,L/R} meets the special fibre, plus p-adic separatedness of H^0. Density of the ordinary locus in the special fibre of M^tor_{K,L} gives this at level K, not directly at level K_r.
issues.reason: The special fibre of \overline{M}_{K_r} already lies over the ordinary locus (a closed immersion L^+ ⊗ μ_{p^r} ↪ A^∨[p^r] in characteristic p forces ordinarity under Hypothesis 2.2.1), and \overline{M}_{K_r} is only quasi-finite over M^tor_K, so the density of S_1 in the special fibre of M^tor_{K,L} does not by itself rule out components of the generic fibre of \overline{M}_{K_r,L} whose closure misses the special fibre (sections supported there would have f_{p-adic} = 0). Defence: the needed fact is standard in Hida's theory (e.g. via the q-expansion principle or irreducibility of Igusa towers, [Hid04, Ch. 8], [Lan18]), and the statement is true; only the justification is too brief.

issues.printed: For R satisfying Equation (32), the source defines O^+ as Z_(p)'s integral closure inside R. It asserts that Frac(O^+) is a number field admitting a rational model of S_κ(K_r, ψ; R) ⊗ Q.
issues.correction: Let O^+ be the localisation at the prime above p (determined by incl_p) of the ring of integers of a number field E_0 ⊂ Frac(R) over which S_κ(K_r, ψ; ·) has a rational model (e.g. E_0 containing K′ and the values of ψ); equivalently, the integral closure of Z_(p) in E_0.
issues.reason: R is a finite O′[ψ]-domain, e.g. R = Z_p or O′. The integral closure of Z_(p) in Z_p is Z_p ∩ \overline{Q}, whose fraction field Q_p ∩ \overline{Q} has infinite degree over Q (it contains √(1 + p^2 k) for all integers k, p odd, hence infinitely many quadratic fields). So Frac(O^+) is never a number field. Defence: any sufficiently large number field works for the definition of 'ordinary complex cusp forms relative to ι' that follows, and O^+ is not used elsewhere in the paper. Independent check: The quote on pp. 33–34 is accurate. R is a finite O′- or O′[ψ]-domain, where O′ is the ring of integers of the finite extension L′ of Q_p (p. 30). So R ⊃ Z_p. The integral closure of Z_(p) in R contains Z_p ∩ Q̄. For odd p, √(1 + p²k) ∈ Z_p for every integer k, and these generate infinitely many quadratic fields. So Frac(O^+) ⊇ Q_p ∩ Q̄ has infinite degree over Q and is never a number field. The intended object is the p-integers of a suitable number field E_0 carrying the rational model. O^+ is used only in this paragraph, to define 'ordinary complex cusp forms relative to ι'. Present in v1–v4 (v4 p. 30).

issues.locator: §2.10.2, p. 35, lines 1–5, arXiv v5
issues.printed: The source takes Δ ⊂ T_H(Z_p) to consist of torsion elements. Using the hypothesis that p is unramified in K, it derives from (12) the identification Δ ≅ ∏_{w|p} ∏_{i=1}^m (k_w^×)^{a_{w,i}} ... and concludes that Δ has order prime-to-p.
issues.correction: Add 'p odd' to the standing hypotheses of §1.4.1, or restrict to p > 2 here.
issues.reason: The standing hypotheses (§1.4.1: p unramified in K, every place of K^+ above p split in K) allow p = 2 (e.g. K = Q(√−7)); then O_w^× ⊃ {±1} and for O_w = Z_2 the torsion of O_w^× is {±1} while k_w^× = 1, so the displayed isomorphism fails and |Δ| is a power of 2, and the decomposition into ω-isotypic pieces over O′ is not available. Defence: p odd is presumably implicit through the cited results of Hida ([Hid02], [Hid04]) and elsewhere in the paper, and all later statements are about p odd in practice; but it is never stated. Independent check: The quote on p. 35 is accurate. The only hypotheses on p (§1.4.1, p. 11) are 'unramified in K, every place of K^+ above p split in K'. p odd is never stated; I searched the text layer. For p = 2, K = Q(√−7) satisfies them (2 splits, K^+ = Q). Then O_w = Z_2, the torsion of O_w^× is {±1} while k_w^× = 1, so the displayed Δ ≅ ∏(k_w^×)^{a_{w,i}} fails. Δ is then a nontrivial 2-group, so it does not have order prime to p. The decomposition of S^ord over O′ into ω-isotypic parts, which needs |Δ| ∈ O′^×, is unavailable. For p odd and unramified the statement is correct: the torsion is the Teichmüller lift of k_w^×. p odd is implicitly needed elsewhere too, e.g. the 1/2 in V_d ⊕ V^d and in (58), but the paper never says so. Present in v1–v4 (v4 p. 31).

issues.printed: The source specifies the map μ ↦ μ(κψ) : ... → S^ord_κ(K_r, ωω_κψ, R[ψ]) ... and defines ω_κ ∈ Δ̂ by κ|_Δ.
issues.correction: S^ord_{κ^cl}(K_r, ωω_κ^{−1}ψ, R[ψ]) with κ the p-adic weight of §2.9.1, ω_κ = κ|_Δ and κ^cl the classical weight with (κ^cl)_p = κ; equivalently keep ωω_κψ but define ω_κ as the restriction of the classical weight to Δ via t ↦ (1, t) ∈ T_{H_0}, which is κ_p^{−1}|_Δ.
issues.reason: By §2.9.4, t·f_{p-adic} = ψ(t)κ_p(t)f_{p-adic} for f ∈ M_κ(K_r, ψ; R); so a classical form of nebentypus χ has Δ acting on its p-adic avatar by χ|_Δ·κ_p|_Δ. If μ lies in the ω-isotypic piece (Δ acting by ω through μ(t·f) = t·μ(f)), then μ(κψ) has Δ-character ω, whence χ|_Δ = ω·(κ_p|_Δ)^{−1} = ωω_κ^{−1}. The printed ωω_κψ differs by ω_κ^2. Case for the defence: the sign depends on which of the two dual characters (κ on T_{H_0} versus κ_p on T_H, related by κ(1, t) = κ_p(t^{−1})) is called κ|_Δ; the paper's text says 'κ as in 2.9.1', which gives the discrepancy. Also S^ord_κ is written with the p-adic weight κ although S_κ requires a classical weight (v1–v3 wrote κ*). This is a cited result of Hida, so only the transcription is at stake.
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: Same ωω_κψ in v1–v4 (v4 p. 31); v1–v3 wrote S^ord_{κ*}.

issues.locator: Proposition 3.2.5(ii), proof, p. 41, arXiv v5
issues.printed: The proof invokes Hida theory to identify V^ord_{κ_p}((G, X); K^p, R) as an R-dual of a finite-rank Iwasawa-algebra module, concluding that f lies in a finite-rank R-module. It derives (ii) from the ordinary locus's Zariski density in S(G, X)'s integral model [Wed99], assuming enough ordinary CM points. It further claims that ordinary points defined over finite fields admit lifts ... into the generic fibre [Moo04, Proposition 2.3.12].
issues.correction: A complete argument: every F̄_p-point of the ordinary locus is the reduction of an ordinary CM point (Serre–Tate canonical lift) and the Igusa tower over it is covered by the Igusa towers (46) of CM pairs and their prime-to-p Hecke translates; hence f mod p vanishes at all F̄_p-points of the reduced Igusa varieties T_{n,1}, so f ≡ 0 mod p; since T_{n,m} is flat over Z/p^m and the value of p·g at a canonical lift depends only on g mod p, induction on m gives f ≡ 0 mod p^m for all m (for R flat over Z_p; general R by the same dévissage), so f = 0.
issues.reason: The printed proof invokes the density of the ordinary locus in the integral model, which is irrelevant for a p-adic form (a function on the formal Igusa tower over the ordinary locus), and never explains how vanishing at the (discrete) set of CM points forces a function on a formal scheme to vanish; the finite-rank remark is not used. Also the Igusa tower of S(J′_0, h_0) must meet every point of each fibre of the Igusa tower, which needs the CM pairs to be taken with all their Hecke translates. Defence: the conclusion is true and the ingredients cited (canonical lifts) suffice once the p-adic dévissage is added; ordinarity of f is not needed for this route.

issues.locator: §4.1.4, p. 45, lines 5–12 (the paragraph after the definition of I(φ, φ^♭, f, s)), in arXiv v5
issues.printed: The source says unfolding [GPSR87] makes (φ, φ′) ↦ I(φ, φ′, f, s) a G_1(𝔸)-invariant pairing for any automorphic representations π, π′ of G_1. Hypothesis 7.3.3 is said to bound the pairing space's dimension by one, with equality when π′ = π^∨ after restriction to U(V). It concludes that ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ = 0 implies I(φ, φ^♭, f, s) = 0 for every s.
issues.correction: For fixed f the map (φ, φ′) ↦ I(φ, φ′, f, s) is not G_1(𝔸)-invariant. Only the trilinear form in (f, φ, φ′) is invariant, and f transforms by the diagonal translation. What is true, using Hypothesis 7.3.3: after unfolding, I depends on (φ, φ′) only through the L² pairings ⟨π(u)φ, φ′⟩, so I ≡ 0 unless π′ ≅ π^∨ (on U(V)). The implication ‘⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ = 0 ⇒ I(φ, φ^♭, f, s) = 0’ is false in general.
issues.reason: By the unfolding (p. 45), I(π(h)φ, π′(h)φ′, f, s) = ∫ f((huh^{-1}, 1))⟨π(u)φ, φ′⟩ du, which differs from I(φ, φ′, f, s) unless f((huh^{-1},1)) = f((u,1)). Concretely, I = c·∏_v Z_v, where Z_v(φ_v, φ^♭_v, f_v) = ⟨π_v(F_v)φ_v, φ^♭_v⟩ with F_v(u) = f_v((u,1)). Take v ∈ S_π (or v = ∞), where the statement allows arbitrary f_v and φ_v. Sections supported in the open cell P_v(U_{1,v} × 1) give arbitrary F_v ∈ C_c^∞(U_{1,v}), for instance F_v = char(g_0K′). Then one can choose φ_v, φ^♭_v with ⟨φ_v, φ^♭_v⟩ = 0 but ⟨π_v(F_v)φ_v, φ^♭_v⟩ ≠ 0, which gives ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ = 0 while I ≠ 0 for Re(s) ≫ 0. Uniqueness of invariant pairings π × π′ → ℂ comes from Schur's lemma, not from multiplicity one. Hypothesis 7.3.3 (π′ occurs with multiplicity one in the cuspidal spectrum) is what makes the L² pairing between π and π′ vanish unless π′ is the realisation of π^∨. Defence: the paper immediately assumes ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ ≠ 0 and uses only (51), which is correct under that assumption. For the specific ramified sections of §4.2.2 one does have Z_v = vol(𝒰_v)⟨φ_v, φ^♭_v⟩. Independent check: The quote on p. 45 is accurate. Replace φ, φ′ by π(h)φ, π′(h)φ′ and change variables (g_1,g_2) ↦ (g_1,g_2)(h,h)^{-1}. This moves (h,h) onto f by right translation, and f is not right-invariant. Equivalently, after unfolding, I(π(h)φ, π(h)φ^♭) = ∫ f((huh^{-1},1))⟨π(u)φ,φ^♭⟩du. Here (h,h) ∈ P, since it stabilises V^d, so f((huh^{-1},1)) = χ(det h)f((u,1)(h,h)^{-1}), which is not f((u,1)) in general. So for fixed f the map is not G_1(A)-invariant. For factorizable data, I = c∏_v⟨π_v(F_v)φ_v, φ^♭_v⟩ with F_v(u) = f_v((u,1)). u ↦ P(u,1) is an open embedding (the paper cites [HLS06] for openness; injectivity holds because (u,1) ∈ P forces u = 1). So at v ∈ S_π or at ∞, F_v can be any function in C_c^∞. Wherever π_v has dimension > 1, one can take ⟨φ_v,φ^♭_v⟩ = 0 and ⟨π_v(F_v)φ_v,φ^♭_v⟩ ≠ 0. That gives ⟨φ,φ^♭⟩ = 0 but I ≠ 0 for Re s ≫ 0, so the displayed implication is false. Uniqueness of invariant pairings on irreducible π × π′ is Schur's lemma, not Hypothesis 7.3.3. The paper then assumes ⟨φ,φ^♭⟩ ≠ 0, and (51), Theorem 4.6.1 and the rest do not use the implication. Same argument in v4 (p. 40); absent in v1.

issues.locator: §4.2.1, pp. 46–47, the displayed identity “d_{n,v}(s, χ_v) I_v(φ_v, φ′_v, f_v, s) = L_v(s + 1/2, π_v, χ_v)” with (53), in arXiv v5
issues.printed: The source asserts in both cases that d_{n,v}(s, χ_v) I_v(φ_v, φ′_v, f_v, s) = L_v(s + 1/2, π_v, χ_v). Its definitions are d_{n,v}(s, χ_v) = d_{n,v}(s) = ∏_{r=0}^{n−1} L_v(2s + n − r, χ_v|_{𝒦^+} η_v^r) and L_v(s, π_v, χ_v) = L_v(s, BC(π_v) ⊗ χ_v∘det).
issues.correction: d_{n,v}(s, χ_v^{-1}) I_v(φ_v, φ′_v, f_v, s) = L_v(s+½, π_v, χ_v^{-1}), with L_v(s, π_v, χ) = L_v(s, BC(π_v) ⊗ χ∘det). Alternatively, keep the printed identity and replace χ by χ^{-1} in the definition of I(χ,s) (inducing from χ^{-1}(det∘Δ(·))δ_P^{-s/n}|ν|^{sn/2}, with the paper's δ_P = |det∘Δ|^n). The first reading's alternative 'χ^{-1}(det∘Δ)δ_P^{s/n}' is right only if δ_P means the true modulus character |det∘Δ|^{-n}. With the paper's δ_P it also flips s ↦ −s.
issues.reason: Right versus left action. Under the right action p acts on V^d by v ↦ vp, the inverse of the left action g·v := vg^{-1}. So χ(det Δ(p))|det Δ(p)|^{-s} = χ^{-1}(det Δ_left(p))|det Δ_left(p)|^{s}, and the paper's I(χ, s) is the left-action induced representation for χ^{-1} used in [GPSR87], [Li92], [HKS96]; the cited computations then give L(s+½, π, χ^{-1})/d(s, χ^{-1}). Direct check for n = 1 at a split unramified v: U(1)(𝒦_v^+) ≅ 𝒦_w^× via the action on V_w, and π_v = β. In (V_d, V^d)-coordinates (u, 1) = ((u+1)/2, (u−1)/2; (u−1)/2, (u+1)/2). The spherical section of Ind(ψ_{w,s}) takes value χ_w(d)χ_{w̄}^{-1}(a)|a/d|^{s+1/2} at a matrix with bottom row (γ, δ), where |d| = max(|γ|, |δ|) and ad = det. Hence f((u,1)) = χ_{w̄}^{-1}(u)|u|^{s+1/2} for |u| ≤ 1 and χ_w(u)|u|^{-s-1/2} for |u| ≥ 1, and ∫ f((u,1))β(u) d^×u = L(s+½, βχ_{w̄}^{-1}) L(s+½, β^{-1}χ_w^{-1}) / L(2s+1, (χ_wχ_{w̄})^{-1}). Equivalently, with Φ = char M_{1×2}(O_w) in (55), f^Φ(1) = L(2s+1, (χ_wχ_{w̄})^{-1}), and the substitution z_1 = xu, z_2 = x factors ∫ f^Φ((u,1))β(u) d^×u into these two Tate integrals. The printed formula predicts L(s+½, β^{±1}χ_w)L(s+½, β^{∓1}χ_{w̄}) / L(2s+1, χ_wχ_{w̄}), which is different for generic unramified χ_v. The corrected characters are exactly those in the p-adic factor of Theorem 4.3.10, L(s+½, π_b ⊗ χ_{2,w}) = L(s+½, π_b ⊗ χ_{w̄}^{-1}) and L(s+½, π̃_a ⊗ χ_{1,w}^{-1}) = L(s+½, π̃_a ⊗ χ_w^{-1}), so the p-adic computation agrees with the corrected unramified formula and the printed one is the odd one out. Defence: the identity is quoted from sources that use left actions, and the discrepancy is the relabelling χ ↦ χ^{-1} (complex conjugation for unitary χ), under which the construction is unchanged in substance. Independent check: The quotes on pp. 46–47 are accurate. I checked independently at n = 1, v = ww̄ split and unramified. I(χ,s) (§4.1.2) with Δ(p) = the V^d-block D restricts on the w-component to Ind(ψ_{w,s}): the w̄-part of Δ(p) is ᵗA^{-1}, so ψ_{w,s} = χ_w(D)χ_{w̄}^{-1}(A)|A/D|^s, and the normalised f(pg) = ψ δ^{1/2}f(g) with δ^{1/2} = |A/D|^{1/2}. This agrees with (55). In polarization coordinates (§4.1.1: (a,b) ↦ (a+b, b−a)), (u,1) = ½[[u+1, u−1],[u−1, u+1]]. So the spherical f with f(1) = 1 gives f((u,1)) = χ_{w̄}^{-1}(u)|u|^{s+1/2} for |u| ≤ 1 and χ_w(u)|u|^{-s-1/2} for |u| ≥ 1. With π_v = β, (51) gives I_v = Σ_{k≥0}X^k + Σ_{k≥1}Y^k, where X = χ_{w̄}^{-1}β(ϖ)q^{-s-1/2} and Y = (χ_wβ)^{-1}(ϖ)q^{-s-1/2}. This sums to (1−XY)/((1−X)(1−Y)) = L(s+½, βχ_{w̄}^{-1})L(s+½, β^{-1}χ_w^{-1})/L(2s+1, (χ_wχ_{w̄})^{-1}). The printed formula predicts denominator d_{1,v}(s,χ_v) = L(2s+1, χ_wχ_{w̄}) and numerator L(s+½, β^{±1}χ_w)L(s+½, β^{∓1}χ_{w̄}). These agree with the computation only when χ_wχ_{w̄}(ϖ) = 1, i.e. χ|_{K^+} is trivial at v, whatever identification of U(1) or BC is used. So the identity holds with χ_v^{-1}. The cause is the right action: the paper's I(χ,s) is the left-action I(s, χ^{-1}) of [Li92]/[GPSR87]. The p-adic factors of Theorem 4.3.10 (L(s+½, π_b ⊗ χ_{w̄}^{-1}), L(s+½, π̃_a ⊗ χ_w^{-1})) match the corrected form. This propagates to the statement of Theorem 4.6.1 (D(χ), L^S(s+½, π, χ_u)), up to the relabelling χ ↦ χ^{-1} = χ̄. Identical in v4 (p. 41) and v1 (p. 39).

issues.locator: Lemma 4.2.3 and its proof, §4.2.2, p. 48, first display of the proof (“for g ∈ U_{1,v} × 1_n, f^-_{L_v}(g) = δ_{−1_n·𝒰_v×1_n}(g)”), in arXiv v5
issues.printed: The source identifies −1_n·𝒰_v × 1_n as the support of f^-_{L_v} on U_{1,v} × 1_n. For g ∈ U_{1,v} × 1_n it asserts f^-_{L_v}(g) = δ_{−1_n·𝒰_v×1_n}(g) … and obtains I_v(φ_v, φ′_v, f_v, χ) = volume(𝒰_v).
issues.correction: Add to the conditions on L_v in §4.2.2 that χ_v(det(1_n − x)) = 1 for all x ∈ L_v, which is possible by shrinking L_v. Fix w := (−1_n, 1_n), or normalise f_{L_v} so that f^-_{L_v}(1) = 1. Then f^-_{L_v}|_{U_{1,v}×1_n} is the characteristic function of −1_n·𝒰_v × 1_n and I_v = vol(𝒰_v).
issues.reason: In (V_d, V^d)-coordinates (u, 1) = p^-·n(X), with p^- block lower triangular with upper-left block (u+1)/2 and X = (u+1)^{-1}(u−1), the Cayley transform. So (−u, 1) = (−1_n, 1_n)(u, 1) = (wp^-w^{-1})·w·n(X), with w = (−1_n, 1_n) and Δ(wp^-w^{-1}) = (u+1)/2 = (1_n − X)^{-1}. Hence f^-_{L_v}((u,1)) = f_{L_v}((−u,1)) = χ_v(det(1_n − X))^{-1}·|det(1_n − X)|^{s+n/2}·δ_{L_v}(X) = χ_v(det(1_n − X))^{-1}δ_{L_v}(X). The paper's two conditions on L_v (𝔘_v ⊇ N(L_v) and P_vwN(L_v) ⊆ P_v(−1_n K_v × 1_n)) do not make χ_v∘det trivial on 1 − L_v. If χ_v is ramified, I_v = ∫_{−𝒰_v} χ_v^{-1}(det(1 − X(u))) du can differ from vol(𝒰_v) and can even vanish. The paper never fixes w: it only says P_vw = P_v(−1_n, 1_n). If w = p_0(−1_n, 1_n) with p_0 ≠ 1, a constant character value χ_s(p_0) also appears. Defence: L_v is only asked to be ‘small enough’, so the extra condition changes nothing else, and later arguments only need I_v to be a nonzero constant. Independent check: The quotes on pp. 47–48 are accurate. The mistake is real. In polarization coordinates, (−1_n,1_n) = [[0,−1],[−1,0]] and (−u,1) = p·(−1_n,1_n)·n(X), where X = (1+u)^{-1}(u−1) and p has V^d-block Δ(p) = (1+u)/2 = (1−X)^{-1}. So with w = (−1_n,1_n), f^-_{L_v}((u,1)) = χ_v(det((1+u)/2))|det((1+u)/2)|^{…}δ_{L_v}(X) = χ_v(det(1−X))^{-1}δ_{L_v}(X) on the support. This is the characteristic function of −𝒰_v × 1 only if χ_v∘det is trivial on (1 − L_v)^{-1}. issues.locator: §4.3.1, (54), p. 50, and the sentence following it (“Then, as explained in [Eis15], f_p ∈ I_p(χ_p, s).”), in arXiv v5
issues.printed: Equation (54) sets f_{p,s}(g) = |ν|_p^{sn/2} ⊗_{w∈Σ_p} f_{w,s}(g_w), g = (ν, (g_w)) ∈ G(ℚ_p). The source then invokes [Eis15] to assert f_p ∈ I_p(χ_p, s).
issues.correction: (54) lies in I_p(χ_p, s) only after restriction to U_4(ℚ_p). To lie in I_p(χ_p, s) on all of G(ℚ_p), the factor |ν|_p^{sn/2} must be replaced by ∏_{w∈Σ_p} χ_{w̄}(ν)^n, reading the absolute values of §4.1.2 as the idelic module of 𝒦 (which makes the centre act unitarily). If |ν| is read as |ν|_{𝔸_ℚ}, the factor is instead |ν|_p^{sn/2}∏_{w∈Σ_p} χ_{w̄}(ν)^n |ν|_w^{-ns}.
issues.reason: For p = (ν, ((A_w, B_w; 0, D_w))_w) ∈ P(ℚ_p), the w̄-component of Δ(p) has determinant ν^n/det A_w, because V^d_{w̄} pairs with V_{d,w} and A_w·ᵗD_{w̄} = ν. Hence χ_p(det Δ(p)) = ∏_w χ_w(det D_w) χ_{w̄}^{-1}(det A_w) χ_{w̄}(ν)^n, while |det Δ(p)|_{𝒦_p}^{-s}|ν|_{𝒦_p}^{sn/2} = ∏_w |A_w^{-1}D_w|_w^{-s}. So I_p(χ_p, s) is induced from ∏_w ψ_{w,s}(p_w)·∏_w χ_{w̄}(ν)^n, whereas (54) transforms by |ν|_p^{sn/2}∏_w ψ_{w,s}(p_w). Test at s = 0 with a central element t = (t_w, t_{w̄}): I_p requires the factor χ_w(t_w)^n χ_{w̄}(t_{w̄})^n, and (54) gives χ_w(t_w)^n χ_{w̄}(t_w)^{-n}. These differ as soon as χ_{w̄}(t_w t_{w̄})^n ≠ 1. Defence: §4 only uses f_U, the restriction to U_4 (see (51)), where ν = 1 and (54) is correct. The similitude part matters only for the Eisenstein series on G_4 via [Eis15]. Independent check: The quote on p. 50 is accurate. For p = (ν,(p_w)) ∈ P(Q_p), unitarity of the similitude gives Δ_{w̄}(p) = ν·ᵗA_w^{-1}, since V^d_{w̄} pairs with V_{d,w}. Hence χ_p(det Δ(p)) = ∏_{w∈Σ_p} χ_w(det D_w)χ_{w̄}^{-1}(det A_w)χ_{w̄}(ν)^n. The factor χ_{w̄}(ν)^n cannot come from |ν|_p^{sn/2}. A decisive test at s = 0 with a central z = (z_w, z_{w̄}), ν = z_wz_{w̄}, which does not depend on how |·| is read: I_p needs the factor χ(z)^n = ∏χ_w(z_w)^nχ_{w̄}(z_{w̄})^n, while (54) gives ∏χ_w(z_w)^nχ_{w̄}(z_w)^{-n}. The ratio is ∏_wχ_{w̄}(ν)^n, which is nontrivial in general. So (54) is not in I_p(χ_p,s) on G(Q_p). It is in I_p after restriction to U_4 (ν = 1), which is all §4 uses through f_U and (51). The first reading's correction checks out: with |·| read as the K-idelic module, |det Δ|^{-s}|ν|^{sn/2} = ∏_w|A_w^{-1}D_w|^{-s}. Versions: v1 prints −sn/2 both globally and in (54). v4 prints +sn/2 globally and −sn/2 in (54). v5 prints +sn/2 in both.
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: v4 (4.3.1), p. 44 and v1–v3 print |ν|_p^{−sn/2}, also inconsistent. The global I(χ,s) had |ν|^{−sn/2} in v1–v3 and |ν|^{+sn/2} in v4–v5. So in v4 the global and local exponents disagreed, and v5 changed (54) to +sn/2 without adding χ_{w̄}(ν)^n.

issues.locator: §4.3.1, inequality (56), p. 51; used in Lemma 4.3.2(i),(ii), p. 52, and in the extension of μ′_w to Γ_R, ᵗΓ_R in §4.3.4, p. 55, in arXiv v5
issues.printed: “t ≥ max_{w∈Σ_p, 1≤i≤r(w)} (1, ord_w(cond(μ_{i,w})), ord_w(cond(χ_w)))), (56)”
issues.correction: t ≥ max_{w∈Σ_p, 1≤i≤r(w)} (1, ord_w(cond(μ_{i,w})), ord_w(cond(χ_w)), ord_{w̄}(cond(χ_{w̄}))), i.e. t must also bound the conductor of χ_{2,w} = χ_{w̄}^{-1}. With r ≥ 2t this also bounds the conductors of the μ′_{i,w}.
issues.reason: Lemma 4.3.2(i) and the support bounds in (ii) need every ν_{i,w} = χ_{1,w}^{-1}χ_{2,w}μ_{i,w} = χ_w^{-1}χ_{w̄}^{-1}μ_{i,w} to be trivial on 1 + 𝔭_w^t. The extension claim in §4.3.4 needs μ′_{i,w} = χ_{w̄}μ_{i,w}^{-1} (i ≤ t(w)) to be trivial on 1 + 𝔭^r. At split p, χ_w and χ_{w̄} are independent, and (56) does not bound cond(χ_{w̄}). Counterexample to Lemma 4.3.2(i): take n = 2, a_w = b_w = 1, so t(w) = 1, r(w) = 2, Γ_w(t) is the set of γ ∈ GL_2(O_w) diagonal mod 𝔭^t, and φ_ν((A, B; C, D)) = ν_1(A)ν_2(D) on 𝔛. With γ_1 = 1 and γ_2 = (1, ϖ^t; 0, 1), φ_ν(Xγ_2) = ν_1(A)ν_2(D + ϖ^tC) = ν_2(1 + ϖ^tC/D)φ_ν(X), while the right side of (i) is φ_ν(X) because μ_w(γ_2) = det γ_2 = 1. Suppose χ_w and μ_2 have conductor ≤ 𝔭^t and χ_{w̄} has conductor 𝔭^{t+1}. Then ν_2 is nontrivial on 1 + 𝔭^t and (i) fails for suitable C. Likewise φ(diag(α, 1)) need not be invariant under α ↦ α + 𝔭^tM, so supp Φ^{(1)} ⊆ 𝔭^{-t}M can fail. Defence: t (and r) are free, ‘sufficiently large’ parameters, so enlarging t repairs everything; possibly χ_w was meant to range over all w | p. Independent check: The quote of (56) on p. 51 is accurate. ν_{i,w} = χ_{1,w}^{-1}χ_{2,w}μ_{i,w} = χ_w^{-1}χ_{w̄}^{-1}μ_{i,w}, with χ_{w̄} viewed on K_w via K_w = K^+_{w+} = K_{w̄} (p. 49). (56) bounds cond(μ_{i,w}) and cond(χ_w) for w ∈ Σ_p only. I checked the counterexample. n = 2, a = b = 1, Γ_w(t) = matrices diagonal mod 𝔭^t, φ_ν((A B; C D)) = ν_1(A)ν_2(D) on 𝔛. γ_2 = (1 ϖ^t; 0 1) gives φ_ν(Xγ_2) = ν_2(1 + ϖ^tC/D)φ_ν(X), while the right side of Lemma 4.3.2(i) is φ_ν(X) (μ_w(γ_2) = 1, det γ_2 = 1). If cond χ_{w̄} = 𝔭^{t+1} and the other conductors are ≤ 𝔭^t, then ν_2 is nontrivial on 1+𝔭^t and (i) fails. The 𝔭^{-t} support bounds in (ii) fail with it. Likewise μ′_{i,w} = χ_{w̄}μ_{i,w}^{-1} (i ≤ t(w)) need not be trivial on 1+𝔭^r, so the extension of μ′_w to Γ_R, ᵗΓ_R on p. 55 is not justified by (56) and (60). Enlarging t repairs everything, since t and r are free. Identical in v4 ((4.3.3), p. 45) and v1.
