issues.locator: §4.3.6, p. 59, display “So Φ((Xg, X)) = Vol(Γ_w)^{-1}Φ_{1,w}(Z′_1, Z″_2)Φ_{2,w}(Z′_2, Z″_1)”, read against the definition (58) of Φ_w on p. 52, in arXiv v5. ; the same mistake at §4.3.6, p. 58 (first paragraph, definition of Z_w) and p. 59 (evaluation of Φ), in arXiv v5; also in v4 pp. 51–52
issues.printed: On p. 52, for X = (X_1, X_2) ∈ Hom_{𝒦_w}(V_w, W_w) = Hom_{𝒦_w}(V_w, V_{d,w}) ⊕ Hom_{𝒦_w}(V_w, V^d_w), the source sets Φ_w(X) = Φ_{χ,μ,w}(X_1, X_2) = vol(Γ_w)^{-1}Φ_{1,w}(−X_1)·Φ_{2,w}(2X_2). On p. 58 it says W_w = V_w ⊕ V_w changes 𝐗 from elements (0, X) to (X, X). On p. 59 it gives Φ((Xg, X)) = Vol(Γ_w)^{-1}Φ_{1,w}(Z′_1, Z″_2)Φ_{2,w}(Z′_2, Z″_1).
issues.correction: In the V_w ⊕ V_w coordinates, an element of Hom(V_w, W_w) with components (Y_1, Y_2) has polarization components X_1 = (Y_1 − Y_2)/2 and X_2 = (Y_1 + Y_2)/2. So the function (58) is Φ_{χ,μ,w}(Y_1, Y_2) = vol(Γ_w)^{-1}Φ_{1,w}((Y_2 − Y_1)/2)Φ_{2,w}(Y_1 + Y_2). At (Y_1, Y_2) = (Xg, X)γ_V = ([Z′_1, Z″_2], [Z′_2, Z″_1]) this is not Vol(Γ_w)^{-1}Φ_{1,w}(Z′_1, Z″_2)Φ_{2,w}(Z′_2, Z″_1). One of two fixes is needed. Either §4.3.1 should define Φ_w := vol(Γ_w)^{-1}Φ_{1,w}(Y_1)Φ_{2,w}(Y_2) in V ⊕ V coordinates (for which §4.3.6–§4.3.10 are the correct computation), and its compatibility with the Eisenstein measure ([Eis15, Lemma 10], §5) must be re-established. Or §4.3.6–§4.3.10 must be redone for the section (58).
issues.reason: Coordinates: ι_d(a) + ι^d(b) = (a, −a) + (b, b) = (a + b, b − a), with V_d, V^d identified with V by the first projection (§4.1.1). Test case n = 1, a_w = 1, b_w = 0 (so γ_V = 1), with χ unramified at w and w̄, μ = μ_{1,w} ramified of conductor 𝔭^c (1 ≤ c ≤ t), β = π_w with β|_{O^×} = μ′ = μ^{-1}, and ν = μ on O^×. For the section (58), f((u,1)) = χ_2(u)|u|^{1/2+s} ∫ Φ_1(x(1−u)/2)Φ_2(x(1+u)) χ_1^{-1}χ_2(x)|x|^{1+2s} d^×x (up to vol(Γ_w)^{-1}). Since supp Φ_1 = O^× and supp Φ_2 = ϖ^{-c}O^×, the integrand vanishes unless |1 − u| = q^{-c}. Substitute z_1 = x(1−u)/2 ∈ O^× and z_2 = x(1+u) ∈ ϖ^{-c}O^×, so that d^×x d^×u = dz_1dz_2/|z_2|^2 and u = (z_2 − 2z_1)/(z_2 + 2z_1) ∈ 1 + 𝔭^c, on which βχ_2 = μ^{-1} is trivial. This gives Z_w = c′·∫_{O^×} μ(z_1) dz_1 · ∫ Φ_2(z_2)(χ_1^{-1}χ_2)(z_2/2)|z_2|^{2s−1} dz_2 = 0. The p. 59 formula instead gives Z_w = Vol^{-1}·vol(O^×)·∫ Φ_2(z)χ_1^{-1}β^{-1}(z)|z|^{s+1/2} d^×z = (nonzero constant)·(Gauss sum)·q^{c(s+1/2)} ≠ 0, in agreement with Theorem 4.3.10 (Z_w = ε(½ − s, π_a ⊗ χ_{1,w})·V_w·⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩, the L-factors being 1). So Theorem 4.3.10 does not compute the zeta integral of the section defined in (58). Defence: the paper is explicit that the V ⊕ V identification differs from the polarization one and rewrites 𝐗 correctly, and the §4.3.6–§4.3.10 computation is correct for the product function in V ⊕ V coordinates, which is presumably the intended section. The factor 2 in Φ_{2,w}(2X_2) turns into Φ_{2,w}(Y_1 + Y_2), so the authors may have had the coordinate change partly in mind. Marcil (arXiv:2311.05466, §4.1) makes the same step with his (37). Independent check: The quotes on pp. 52, 58 and 59 are accurate. §4.1.1 (p. 42): V_d = {(x,−x)} and V^d = {(x,x)}, identified with V by the first projection, and p. 50 builds the basis of W_w from these identifications. So an element with V⊕V components (Y_1,Y_2) has polarization components X_1 = (Y_1−Y_2)/2 and X_2 = (Y_1+Y_2)/2. This is consistent with p. 58's rewriting of 𝐗 = {(0,X)} as {(X,X)}. (58) is therefore Φ_w(Y_1,Y_2) = vol(Γ_w)^{-1}Φ_{1,w}((Y_2−Y_1)/2)Φ_{2,w}(Y_1+Y_2). From (73), (Xg,X)γ_V = ([Z′_1,Z″_2],[Z′_2,Z″_1]) (checked), so p. 59 evaluates Φ as vol^{-1}Φ_1(Y_1)Φ_2(Y_2). That is a different function, and no linear identification of V_d, V^d with V can make the two agree. I redid the n = 1, a_w = 1, b_w = 0 test (γ_V = 1; χ unramified at w and w̄; μ of conductor 𝔭^c, 1 ≤ c ≤ t; π_w a character equal to μ^{-1} on O^×). Φ_1 = μ·1_{O^×}, and Φ_2 is a Gauss-sum function supported on ϖ^{-c}O^×. For (58), Z_w ∝ ∫∫Φ_1(x(1−u)/2)Φ_2(x(1+u))χ_1^{-1}χ_2(x)|x|^{1+2s}χ_2π_w(u)|u|^{1/2+s}d^×xd^×u. On the support, |1+u| = 1 and u ∈ 1+𝔭^c, where π_wχ_2 = 1. The substitution z_1 = x(1−u)/2, z_2 = x(1+u) (Jacobian |x|) is a bijection onto O^× × ϖ^{-c}O^×, and the integral factors through ∫_{O^×}μ(z_1)dz_1 = 0. So Z_w ≡ 0. The p. 59 formula instead gives vol^{-1}·vol^×(O^×)·∫Φ_2(z)χ_1^{-1}π_w^{-1}(z)|z|^{s+1/2}d^×z ≠ 0. This agrees with Theorem 4.3.10, whose value is an ε-factor times 𝔙_w⟨φ_w,φ̃_w⟩, with trivial L-factors. So Theorem 4.3.10, and hence I_p in Theorem 4.6.1, does not hold for the section defined in (58). It is correct for the product section in V⊕V coordinates, whose relation to the Eisenstein measure ([Eis15, Lemma 10], partial Fourier transform in X_2) would have to be re-established. Versions: definition in v4 (p. 46) and v1 (p. 43). The evaluation in v4 (p. 52) and v1 (p. 47) is printed 'Φ((Xg, g))', so v4 also has that misprint. I did not check the first reading's remark about Marcil (arXiv:2311.05466). Second, independent reading of the same mistake: Toy case n = 1, a_w = 1, b_w = 0 (so γ_{V_w} = 1), K_w = Q_p with p odd, all finite-order characters trivial, t = 1, π_w unramified with π_w(p) = α, X := q^{−(s+1/2)}. Then Φ_1 = char(O^×) and Φ_2 = char_O − q^{−1}char_{p^{−1}O}. With the product function Φ' one gets Z = (1 − αq^{−1}X^{−1})/(1 − α^{−1}X) = L(s + 1/2, π̃)/L(1/2 − s, π), as Theorem 4.3.10 predicts. With the literal Φ_w of §4.3.1 one gets Z = (1 − q^{−1})[α^{−1}X/(1 − α^{−1}X) + αX/(1 − αX) + (q − 2)/(q − 1)] − q^{−2}X^{−2}, which also has the pole of L(s + 1/2, π). I confirmed both closed forms by exact enumeration modulo p^5 for p = 3. So the two sections really differ, and Theorem 4.3.10 is about the translated section. Even if Φ is read in the new coordinates, the p. 59 formula also drops the unit constants coming from −X_1 and 2X_2 (∏_iμ_{i,w}(−1)^{n_{i,w}} and ∏_iν_{i,w}(2)^{−n_{i,w}}) and the factor χ_{2,w}(det γ_{V_w}) = χ_{2,w}(−1)^{b_w}. Case for the defence: the authors say explicitly that they switch decompositions ('often convenient … e.g. in [GPSR87]'). v1 (p. 46, (4.3.10)) put an extra change-of-basis-type matrix (½·1_n, −½·1_n; 1_n, 1_n) into the translation, so the need for a translation was recognised. The discrepancy is a right translation of the section by a fixed group element together with unit constants, so the shape of the Euler factor is unaffected provided the Eisenstein measure is built from the matching section. Marcil (arXiv:2311.05466, (37) and p. 23) repeats the same step, also dropping the sign −X_1. Independent check: Quotations checked on the page images (pp. 50, 52, 58-59). By §4.1.1 (p. 42), V^d = {(x,x)} and V_d = {(x,-x)}, and both are identified with V by the first projection (p. 50 uses the same identification for the matrices X_1, X_2). So a homomorphism with V+V components (Y_1,Y_2) has polarization components X_1 = (Y_1-Y_2)/2 and X_2 = (Y_1+Y_2)/2. Then (58) is Phi(Y) = vol^-1 Phi_1((Y_2-Y_1)/2) Phi_2(Y_1+Y_2). It is not the product vol^-1 Phi_1(Y_1)Phi_2(Y_2) that the p. 59 display uses. The block bookkeeping (Xg,X)gamma = ([Z_1',Z_2''],[Z_2',Z_1'']) is itself correct. I re-derived the toy case by hand: n=a=1, b=0, K_w=Q_p with p odd, trivial characters, t=1, pi unramified with pi(p)=alpha, and X=q^-(s+1/2). The product function gives (1-alpha q^-1 X^-1)/(1-alpha^-1 X) = L(s+1/2,pi~)/L(1/2-s,pi), as Theorem 4.3.10 predicts. The literal (58) needs |z_2-z_1|=1 and splits into four cases: v(z_1)=0<v(z_2); v(z_2)=0<v(z_1); z_1,z_2 units with z_1 !≡ z_2 mod p; and v(z_1)=v(z_2)=-1 with z_1≡z_2 mod p but not mod p^2. These give (1-q^-1)[alpha^-1X/(1-alpha^-1X)+alphaX/(1-alphaX)+(q-2)/(q-1)] - q^-2 X^-2. I reran the exact-enumeration check (p=3, mod 3^5), and it matches both closed forms up to truncation (-3.9487 vs -3.9487; -4.798 vs -4.793). A second test, the ramified case of sourceIssues E52 (n=a=1, b=0, chi unramified, mu of conductor p^c): the supports force u=z_1/z_2 in 1+p^c, and the literal zeta integral then contains the factor ∫_{O^x} mu = 0. Theorem 4.3.10 instead gives eps(1/2-s, pi_a⊗chi_1)·Vol·<phi,phi~>, which is nonzero. Theorem 4.3.10 is stated for Z_w built from the translate (73) of the section (58), and (58) is the p-adic section fed into Definition 5.3.2 (p. 85: 'choices ... 4.3 (local choices for v | p)'). So the theorem is false as stated for the section the paper defines. This is an error in a stated result, not only a gap in the proof, and it agrees with sourceIssues E52. The §4.3.6-4.3.10 computation is correct for the product Schwartz function in V_w+V_w coordinates. Whether the Main Theorem survives depends on the Eisenstein measure ([Eis15], Theorem 8.2.2) being built from that section. In the ramified test the literal section would make the p-adic L-function vanish at those characters. Smaller slips: the unit constants from -X_1 and 2X_2 and the factor chi_2(det gamma) = chi_2(-1)^{b_w} are also dropped (p. 58 writes chi_2(g), not chi_2(det g·gamma)). Versions: v4 p. 52 prints 'Phi((Xg,g))'. v1 (4.3.10) puts an extra matrix (1/2, -1/2; 1, 1) into the translation, but v1 (4.3.12) still evaluates Phi((Xg,X)gamma) without it, so v1 was already inconsistent. Reach: a stated result (whether the section whose zeta integral is computed is the section (58) used in the Eisenstein measure).

issues.reason: (66) and (69) give equivariance only under Γ_{R,w}, ᵗΓ_{R,w}, which have level p^r with r ≥ 2t (60). The support of Φ_{1,w} = Γ_w(t) gives only level p^t. So diag(A_1, 1) with A_1 ∈ Γ_{a_w,w}(t) \ Γ_{a_w,w} need not act on φ_w by μ'_w. For example, for u lower unipotent with entries in p^t \ p^r, π_{a_w}(u)φ_{a_w} ≠ φ_{a_w}, since the model function of φ_{a_w} is supported on B_{a_w}Γ_{a_w,w}. In the p. 61 chain the second equality silently replaces (1 0; C 1)(A 0; 0 D) by (1 0; C_1 1)(1 0; 0 D_1). Carrying the factors through gives ⟨φ_w, π̃_w(diag(A^{−1}A_2, D_1^{−1}(1 + CB_2)^{−1}))φ̃_w⟩. Removing A^{−1} and (1 + CB_2)^{−1} needs diag(A, 1) ∈ Γ_{R,w} and diag(1, 1 + CB_2) ∈ ᵗΓ_{R,w}, i.e. 1 + p^{2t}M ⊂ Γ(r), i.e. r ≤ 2t. The next step (levi-coefficient-factorization) needs r ≥ 2t (D_1CA_2 ∈ O for C ∈ p^r). So the printed argument covers exactly r = 2t. Case for the defence: the final formulas (Corollary 4.3.8, Theorem 4.3.10) do hold, and the missing steps are routine once noticed. Marcil 2023 (Lemma 4.1, Lemma 4.2, Proposition 4.3) takes Φ_{1,w} of level p^r and handles the elements γ_0 = (A, AB; 0, 1), γ̃_0 = (1, 0; C, 1 + CB_2) explicitly, which avoids the issue. Independent check: Quotations checked on pp. 60-61. First step of the proof: it applies (66) to diag(A_1,1). But Prop. 4.3.7 only gives A_1 in Gamma_{a_w,w}(t) (level p^t, from supp Phi_{1,w} = Gamma_w(t), p. 51), while (66) holds on Gamma_{R,w} (level p^r, r >= 2t). Second step: the second equality of the p. 61 chain needs diag(A,1) in Gamma_R and diag(1,1+CB_2) in tGamma_R, where A = 1-B_2C_1 = (1+B_2C)^-1 is in 1+p^{2t}M. That requires r <= 2t, while the Levi step needs D_1CA_2 integral, i.e. r >= 2t. So the printed argument covers at most r = 2t, and even there the A_1 problem remains. Beyond the proof, (77) itself is false as stated. Counterexample: b_w=0, a_w=n=2, partition 1+1, K_w=Q_p, all characters trivial, pi_{i,w} unramified, t=1, r=2. Let phi = char(B·Iw_2), where Iw_2 has lower-left entry in p^2. Let phi~ be supported on B·tIw_2 with phi~(k) = [k_22 in O^x] on GL_2(O); it satisfies (67) and (69). Take A_1 = u = (1 0; p 1), which is in Gamma_{a,w}(1), and A_2 = diag(p^-1, p), which is in p^-1 M_2(O). Then Phi^(1)(A_2) = -(1-1/p)/p ≠ 0. Next, <pi(u)phi, pi~(A_2)phi~> = ∫_{k_22 unit} phi(k A_2^-1 u) dk = 0: the bottom row of kA_2^-1u is (p k_21 + k_22, p^-1 k_22), whose ratio has valuation 1. On the other hand <phi, pi~(A_2)phi~> ≠ 0 (the ratio is p^2k_21/k_22). So the left side of (77) is 0, while the right side Vol·Phi^(1)(A_2)·<phi_a, pi~_a(A_2)phi~_a> is nonzero. Corollary 4.3.8 survives. The integrand of (74) is invariant under (Z_1,Z_2) -> (uZ_1,uZ_2) for unipotent u in Gamma_w(t), by Lemma 4.3.2(i) (for Phi_2) and the definition of Phi_1, and this reduces A_1 to level p^r. I checked this step (the first reading's step (i)); steps (ii)-(iii) for the A and 1+CB_2 factors are plausible but I did not check them. The functional equation gives γ(s + 1/2, Π, ψ)^{−1}·∫(Φ^{(1)})^∧(A)|det A|^{−s+a/2}χ_{1,w}(det A)⟨π_{a_w}(A)φ_{a_w}, φ̃_{a_w}⟩ d^×A. Then 1/ε(s + 1/2, Π) = ω_Π(−1)ε(1/2 − s, Π̃) with ω_Π(−1) = ω(−1). Tate check (n = a_w = 1, χ_{1,w} ramified): I_2 = Z(Φ^{(1)}, (πχ_1)^{−1}, s + 1/2), and Z(Φ̂^{(1)}, πχ_1, 1/2 − s) = Vol(O^×), so the printed formula is off by (πχ_1)(−1). Remark 4.3.11 (I_w/V without the pairing) agrees with the corrected formula. Main Theorem 9.2.2's Omega contains no prod_w <phi_w,phi~_w>, even though its proof cites Remark 4.6.2, which does contain it. So the Main Theorem matches the corrected I_p = prod_w L·V_w. v4 (4.3.30) and v4 p. 69 are the same. Reach: a stated result (83), Remark 4.3.12, Theorem 4.6.1, Remark 4.6.2); the Main Theorem 9.2.2 matches the corrected version). Second, independent reading of the same mistake: (1) Remark 4.6.2 gives I_p/(Vol(I^0_{r,V})Vol(I^0_{r,−V})) = L_p · ∏_w⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩_{π_w} / Vol(I^0_{r,V} ∩ I^0_{r,−V}), so Corollary 9.2.1 equals [Main Theorem value] × ∏_{w|p}⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩_{π_w}; the proof of the Main Theorem drops this factor without comment. (2) With the trace-compatible normalisations (Remarks 8.3.9, 8.4.7) Lemma 8.4.9 gives ⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩_{π_w} = Vol(I^0_{w,r} ∩ ᵗI^0_{w,r}) · Vol(I^0_{w,r}ᵗI^0_{w,r}), which depends on r; and Lemma 8.5.3 shows ⟨φ, φ^♭_χ⟩_χ / Vol(I^0_{r,V} ∩ I^0_{r,−V}) is r-independent. The Main Theorem's value is r^1-independent. (3) Source of the double count: (51) (p. 45) defines I_v = Z_v/⟨φ_v, φ^♭_v⟩_{π_v}; Theorem 4.3.10 (p. 64) computes Z_w = [ratio of L- and ε-factors]·𝔙_w·⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩_{π_w} and then says 'and thus I_w = L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w)·𝔙_w·⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩_{π_w}' (83) — the right side is Z_w, not I_w — and Theorem 4.6.1 multiplies this by the global ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ as well. Defence: the Main Theorem, the paper's endpoint, has the right shape; only the intermediate corollaries (and §4.6) carry the extra factor. Independent check: Checked on the page images (pp. 45, 57–58, 64–66, 78, 137–138, 143–145). (51) gives I(φ,φ^♭,f,s) = ⟨φ,φ^♭⟩∏_v I_v with I_v = Z_v/⟨φ_v,φ^♭_v⟩_{π_v}. At w|p, Z_w is the zeta integral with the pair (φ_w,φ̃_w) (p. 58: 'the numerator of the local factor I_{w+} … defined in (51)'), and φ̃_w = φ^{♭,a-ord}_{w,r} (Remark 8.4.8). Theorem 4.6.1 then uses I_p = L_p·∏_w[𝔙_w⟨φ_w,φ̃_w⟩] together with the global ⟨φ,φ^♭⟩, and Corollaries 9.1.8 and 9.2.1 inherit this. By Remark 4.6.2, Cor. 9.2.1's value equals the Main Theorem's value times ∏_{w|p}⟨φ_w,φ̃_w⟩_{π_w}. The proof of the Main Theorem drops this factor without comment. The local pairings are not normalized to 1 at p: the normalization ⟨φ_{v,0},φ^♭_{v,0}⟩ = 1 on p. 44 is only for v ∉ S_π. By Lemma 8.4.9 and its proof (pp. 137–138), ⟨φ^{a-ord}_{w,r},φ^{♭,a-ord}_{w,r}⟩_w = Vol(I^0_{w,r} ∩ ᵗI^0_{w,r})·Vol(I^0_{w,r}ᵗI^0_{w,r}), which depends on r. issues.locator: Remark 4.3.12, pp. 65–66, in arXiv v5; present in v4 p. 58
issues.printed: The source derives I_w/(Vol(Γ_{R,w})·Vol(ᵗΓ_{R,w})) = L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w)⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩_{π_w}/Vol(Γ_{R,w} ∩ ᵗΓ_{R,w}) and claims that both sides are independent of r.
issues.correction: The quantities independent of r are 𝔙_w = Vol(Γ_{R,w})Vol(ᵗΓ_{R,w})/Vol(Γ_{R,w} ∩ ᵗΓ_{R,w}) (the volume of the big cell ᵗΓ_{R,w}Γ_{R,w} = N^-_R(O)L_R(O)N_R(O)) and I_w = L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w)𝔙_w. Neither side of the displayed identity is independent of r: with (72), the right side equals L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w) · q_w^{r·dim N_{R_w}} · ∏_{i=1}^{r(w)}⟨φ_{i,w}, φ̃_{i,w}⟩ (and, with the corrected (83), the left side equals L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w)/Vol(Γ_{R,w} ∩ ᵗΓ_{R,w}), which also grows with r).
issues.reason: By (72) (with the product over all i ≤ r(w)), ⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩ = Vol(Γ_{R,w})∏_i⟨φ_{i,w}, φ̃_{i,w}⟩, with the φ_{i,w} independent of r. Also Vol(Γ_{R,w})/Vol(Γ_{R,w} ∩ ᵗΓ_{R,w}) = [Γ_{R,w} : Γ_{R,w} ∩ ᵗΓ_{R,w}] = |N_{R_w}(O_w/p_w^r)| = q_w^{r·dim N_{R_w}}, since Γ_{R,w} ∩ ᵗΓ_{R,w} is the set of matrices that are in the Levi L_{R_w} mod p^r. This is positive-dimensional unless R_w = GL_n. Case for the defence: the claim becomes true if the test vectors are renormalized so that ⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩ is proportional to Vol(Γ_{R,w} ∩ ᵗΓ_{R,w}), which may be what the global normalization of §8–§9 achieves (Main Theorem 9.2.2 asserts that Ω_{π',χ} = ⟨φ, φ^♭_χ⟩/(Vol(I^0_{r_1,V} ∩ I^0_{r_1,−V})Q) is independent of r_1). As stated with the vectors of §4.3.4, it is false. Independent check: Checked pp. 65-66. The phi_{i,w} do not depend on r, and by (72) (product over all i <= r(w)) <phi_w,phi~_w> = Vol(Gamma_{R,w}) prod_i <phi_i,phi~_i>. Gamma_R ∩ tGamma_R is the preimage of the Levi L_R(O/p^r), and tR is the opposite parabolic, so Vol(Gamma_R)/Vol(Gamma_R ∩ tGamma_R) = |N_R(O/p^r)| = q^{r·dim N_R}. The right-hand side of the remark is therefore L·q^{r dim N_R}·prod<phi_i,phi~_i>, which depends on r unless N_R = 1. The left-hand side (by (83) as printed, or as corrected in sourceIssues E58) also depends on r. What is independent of r is V_w = Vol(tGamma_R Gamma_R) = Vol(N^-(O)L(O)N(O)) (Iwahori factorization), and hence the corrected I_w = L·V_w. v4 p. 58 is the same. Reach: a stated result (remark).

issues.locator: §4.4.2, definition of J_{χ_σ} and Remark 4.4.3, p. 69, in arXiv v5; present in v4 p. 61
issues.printed: The source sets ι(χ_σ)(v(χ_σ)) = J_{χ_σ}(g) := j(g)^{−m+a(χ_σ)} · j'(g)^{−m+b(χ_σ)}ν(g)^{n(m+a(χ_σ)+b(χ_σ))}. Remark 4.4.3 claims that only the archimedean character χ_σ = ||•||^m_σ χ_{0,σ} determines J_{χ_σ}.
issues.correction: The claim holds for the restriction of J_{χ_σ} to U(n, n) (ν = 1). On the similitude group the ν-exponent n(m + a(χ_σ) + b(χ_σ)) depends on the factorization χ = ||•||^m χ_0.
issues.reason: Replacing (m, χ_0) by (m − k, ||•||^k χ_0), which gives a(χ_σ) − k and b(χ_σ) − k, leaves −m + a and −m + b unchanged but changes m + a + b by −3k. Case for the defence: similitude factors are ignored throughout (Remark 4.5.3), and the ν-exponent may itself be a slip. Definition 5.3.2 cites Remark 4.4.3 to say that f_σ does not depend on the factorization. Independent check: Checked p. 69. At sigma, ||z|| = z zbar, so chi_sigma = z^{m-a} zbar^{m-b}. The factorization (m, chi_0) -> (m-k, ||·||^k chi_0) gives a' = a-k and b' = b-k, so -m+a and -m+b are unchanged while m+a+b drops by 3k. Hence J_{chi_sigma}, which is defined on G_sigma = GU(n,n) (p. 68), depends on the factorization through nu(g)^{n(m+a+b)}, and Remark 4.4.3 is false on the similitude group. On U(n,n) it is true. The nu-exponent is probably itself a slip: on the centre, J(t) = t^{n(3a+3b)}, which is not a function of chi_sigma|R^x = t^{2m-a-b}. v4 p. 61 is the same. Reach: nothing (similitude factors are ignored, Remark 4.5.3).

issues.locator: Corollary 4.4.9, last statement, and its proof, p. 73, in arXiv v5; present in v4 pp. 64–65
issues.printed: For every κ† ≤ κ, the source claims unique δ(κ, κ†) ∈ U(p^+_3), having algebraic number fields as fields of definition, satisfying D(κ, χ) = Σ_{κ†≤κ} δ(κ, κ†) ∘ D^{hol}(κ†, χ), with δ(κ, κ) equal to ∏_σ P_{κ_σ,χ,σ}. It attributes the remaining claims to (93) and rationality of that decomposition over a suitable reflex field, citing [Har86, Lemma 7.3.2].
issues.correction: An argument is needed that the component of D(κ, χ)v(χ) in each summand D(κ†) ⊗ D(κ†^♭ ⊗ χ) lies in U(p^+_3)·(v_{κ†} ⊗ v_{κ†^♭⊗χ}). Alternatively, δ(κ, κ†) should be allowed to be vector-valued differential operators, i.e. elements of U(p^+_3) composed with maps between K_3-types.
issues.reason: Each summand is U(p^+_3) ⊗ (minimal K_3-type), and U(p^+_3)·(v ⊗ v) consists of the vectors whose K_3-type component is the highest-weight line. The component of δ(r̃, s̃)·v(χ) in the κ†-summand is a K_3-highest-weight vector of weight κ in S(p^+_3) ⊗ W_{κ†}. When W_{κ†} has dimension > 1 such a vector is in general a combination Σ p_i ⊗ w_i with w_i of lower weight, not of the form p ⊗ v_{κ†}, so neither existence nor the meaning of 'δ(κ, κ†) ∘ D^{hol}(κ†, χ)' follows formally. Case for the defence: with vector-valued operators the decomposition is immediate from (93). The only use, in §8.1 (Proposition 8.1.3 and the proof of Corollary 8.2.4, 'by induction on the size of κ'), needs just that the terms with κ† ≠ κ are killed by the ordinary projector, which holds for such operators as well. The meaning of the order κ† ≤ κ is not explained either. I did not settle this. Independent check: Checked p. 73. The kappa†-component of D(kappa,chi)v(chi) is a K_3-highest-weight vector of weight kappa in D(kappa†)⊗D(kappa†^flat⊗chi), which is S(p_3^+)⊗W_{kappa†}⊗W_{kappa†^flat} as a K_3-module. Writing it as delta(kappa,kappa†)·(v⊗v) with delta in U(p_3^+) requires it to lie in S(p_3^+)⊗(highest-weight line). This is automatic when the minimal K-types are 1-dimensional (e.g. a_sigma, b_sigma <= 1). In general it is not a formal consequence of (93), and for non-Cartan constituents it is not expected. The paper itself stresses, just before, that delta(r~,s~)v(chi) need not lie in the highest-weight space. So 'formal consequences' does not prove the statement as formulated. With vector-valued operators the decomposition does follow, and the first reading reports that the §8.1 uses need only that the terms with kappa† ≠ kappa are killed by the ordinary projector; I did not re-check those uses. v4 pp. 64-65 is the same. Reach: the proof (of the last statement of Corollary 4.4.9 as formulated).

issues.locator: §4.4.12, p. 75, first sentence, in arXiv v5; present in v4 p. 66 and v2/v3 p. 66
issues.printed: For a cuspidal automorphic representation π of GU(V) with anti-holomorphic discrete-series component D_c(τ_σ) at σ, the source asserts that its base change Π to GL(n)_K, ignoring the split centre, is cuspidal and cohomological, with Π^∨ ≅ Π^c.
issues.correction: Π is an isobaric sum of conjugate-self-dual cuspidal representations (cohomological, Π^∨ ≅ Π^c). It is cuspidal only for π with stable (non-endoscopic) parameter.
issues.reason: Endoscopic cuspidal representations of unitary groups, e.g. those whose parameter is a sum of two conjugate-self-dual parameters, have non-cuspidal base change (Mok, KMSW). Case for the defence: the passage is motivational ('in most cases'), and the Hodge types (106) depend only on the archimedean component. Independent check: Checked p. 75. Base change of a cuspidal representation of a unitary group is in general only an isobaric sum of conjugate-self-dual cuspidal representations. Endoscopic cuspidal representations can have discrete series at infinity: for example, holomorphic CM forms on U(1,1) have base change Ind of characters, and Rogawski's endoscopic packets on U(2,1) contain holomorphic discrete series members. The paper itself writes in Remark 9.3.2 'an automorphic representation ... whose base change to GL(n) is cuspidal', which acknowledges that this is an extra condition. v4 p. 66 is the same. Reach: nothing (expository).

issues.locator: §4.4.14, p. 76, and §4.5.4, p. 76 versus Proposition 4.5.6, p. 77, in arXiv v5; present in v4 pp. 67–68
issues.printed: Section 4.4.14 places φ_v in the minimal U_σ-type 1 ⊗ W^∨_{τ_σ} of D_c(κ), assigning T_σ weights −w_0(κ) and −κ to φ_{κ,+} and φ_{κ,−}, respectively. Section 4.5.4 chooses φ_σ ⊗ φ^♭_σ anti-holomorphic in the highest-weight subspace of π_σ ⊗ π^♭_σ's minimal K_σ-type. Proposition 4.5.6 specifies φ_σ = φ_{κ_σ,−}, φ^♭_σ = φ_{κ^♭_σ,−}.
issues.correction: By (90) and §4.4.1, the minimal U_σ-type of D_c(κ) is 1 ⊗ W_{τ_σ}. Either §4.4.1/(90) or §4.4.14 must be adjusted, together with the weights. The vector used in Propositions 4.5.5 and 4.5.6 should be described consistently: the lowest weight vector φ_{κ,−} in Proposition 4.5.6 and (50), but 'highest weight subspace' in §4.5.4.
issues.reason: (90) gives D_c(τ_σ) = U(𝔤_σ) ⊗_{U(k_σ⊕p^+_σ)} W_{τ_σ}, and p. 67 states that its minimal U_σ-type is 1 ⊗ W_{τ_σ}. The weights −w_0(κ), −κ quoted in §4.4.14 are the highest and lowest weights of W^∨_{τ_σ}. For the pairing in Proposition 4.5.5 to be non-zero the anti-holomorphic vector must be dual to the highest weight vector v_κ ⊗ v_{κ^♭⊗χ} of the holomorphic side, i.e. the lowest weight vector of the dual type, consistent with φ_{κ,−}. Case for the defence: the inconsistency is between two dual conventions and the intended vector is clear from (50) and Proposition 4.5.6.

issues.printed: Lemma 4.5.2 asserts ι(m, χ_σ)(D²(m, χ_σ)) ⊂ I_σ(m − n/2, χ). Section 4.5.4 takes f_σ = f_σ(χ_σ, c) ∈ I(χ_{u,σ}, m) … and sets f_σ(χ_σ, c, g) = B(χ_σ, κ_σ)D(κ_σ, m, χ_{u,σ})J_{m,χ_{u,σ}}(g) … . It identifies J_{m,χ_{u,σ}} ∈ C^∞(G_4) as Section 4.4.2's canonical automorphy factor.
issues.correction: Fix one parametrization. J_χ and D²(m, χ_0) of §4.4.2 use χ = ||•||^m χ_0 with χ_{0,σ}(z) = z^{−a}z̄^{−b} algebraic, whereas §4.5.4 and §4.6 use χ = ||•||^m χ_u with χ_u unitary. The two m differ by (a(χ_σ) + b(χ_σ))/2; §5.3.1 calls the first one μ. Say which induced representation, I(χ, s) or I(χ_u, s), and which s contains the image of ι.
issues.reason: With the same letter m used for both factorizations and the argument order of I_σ(·, ·) swapped relative to §4.1.2, one cannot tell which section (107) denotes. Lemma 4.5.2 (proof omitted: 'an easy computation, similar to that in [Har97]') places the image in I_σ(m − n/2, χ), while §4.5.4 and Definition 5.3.2 place f_σ in I(χ_{u,σ}, m). I could not reconcile these without the paper's sign conventions for the tube-domain realization, so I did not verify Lemma 4.5.2. Case for the defence: §5.3.1 explicitly separates μ from m ('We omit the expression of μ and χ_0 in terms of m and χ_u'), so the authors were aware of the two normalizations. Independent check: Checked pp. 69, 76, 83-84. §4.4.2 defines J_{chi_sigma} = J_{m,chi_0} for chi = ||·||^m chi_0 with chi_{0,sigma} = z^-a zbar^-b algebraic. Lemma 4.5.2 puts the image of iota(m,chi_sigma) in I_sigma(m - n/2, chi), with the arguments in the reverse order to §4.1.2's I(chi,s). §4.5.4, (107) and Definition 5.3.2 instead put f_sigma = B·D(kappa,m,chi_{u,sigma})J_{m,chi_{u,sigma}} in I(chi_{u,sigma}, m), where chi = ||·||^m chi_u with chi_u unitary; so J_{m,chi_u} is used with a unitary chi_u, although J was defined for algebraic chi_0. I(chi,s) and I(chi_u,s') differ by a shift of s depending on the factorization, so the two placements cannot both hold with the same m. §5.3.1 introduces mu to separate the two normalizations and says 'We omit the expression of mu and chi_0 in terms of m and chi_u'. The global identity (Theorem 4.6.1) needs all local sections in the same I(chi_u,m), and the proof of Lemma 4.5.2 is omitted, so which section (107) denotes is not established. v4 p. 67 is the same. Reach: the proof (identification of the archimedean section).

issues.locator: Proposition 4.5.6, p. 77, in arXiv v5; present in v4 p. 68
issues.printed: The source attributes Proposition 4.5.6 to Garrett [Gar08] and presents it as the result used for now. Its conclusion is that I_σ(χ_σ, κ_σ) is algebraic and non-zero.
issues.correction: Non-vanishing follows from Proposition 4.5.5. For algebraicity the text itself only reports that [Gar08] proves the integrals 'algebraic up to a predictable power of the transcendental number π, which can be normalized away', for F imaginary quadratic (Remark 4.5.7). The statement needs the normalization (Haar measure at σ and/or the constant B(χ_σ, κ_σ) of (107)) that removes this power of π, and a reference or proof for general CM K.
issues.reason: The paragraph before the proposition says Garrett shows algebraicity 'up to a predictable power of … π', and explicit values are known only when one factor of the extreme K-type is one-dimensional ([Gar08, p. 12]). Remark 4.5.7 says the computation in [Har08, §5] is for imaginary quadratic F and 'the same reasoning applies in general'. B(χ_σ, κ_σ) is only required to be a non-zero algebraic scalar, so it cannot absorb a power of π. Case for the defence: only non-vanishing (and algebraicity up to an explicit normalization) is needed for the construction, and Eischen–Liu (arXiv:2006.04302) later computed these integrals. Independent check: Checked p. 77. The paragraph before the proposition says that Garrett shows the integrals are 'algebraic up to a predictable power of the transcendental number pi, which can be normalized away', gives exact values only when one factor of the extreme K-type is one-dimensional, and gives non-zero algebraic values when both are scalar. Remark 4.5.7 relies on [Har08] for imaginary quadratic F ('the same reasoning applies in general'). The proposition asserts plain algebraicity without fixing the Haar measure or normalizing constant that removes the power of pi. B(chi_sigma,kappa_sigma) is now required to be algebraic (v5 p. 76; v4 said only 'non-zero scalar'), so it cannot absorb a power of pi. Non-vanishing follows from Proposition 4.5.5. Reach: a stated result (the algebraicity part of Proposition 4.5.6).
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: v4 p. 68 same (v4: 'B(χ_σ, κ_σ) is a non-zero scalar'; v5 adds 'algebraic').

issues.locator: Theorem 4.6.1, p. 78, definition of I_p and L_p (and Remark 4.6.2), in arXiv v5; present in v4 p. 69 and v2/v3 p. 68–69 (Proposition 4.6.1); the same mistake at §9.2, Main Theorem 9.2.2, p. 145 (interpolation formula), in arXiv v5; inherited from Theorem 4.6.1 (p. 78); present in v4 at p. 134
issues.printed: The source gives I_p = L_p(s, ord, π, χ) × ∏_w[𝔙_w · ⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩_{π_w}], defining L_p(s, ord, π, χ) := ∏_{w|p} L(s, ord, π_w, χ_w). It also asserts D(χ) · I(φ, φ^♭, f, s) = ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ · I_p(χ, κ)I_∞(χ, ρ^υ)I_S L^S(s + 1/2, π, χ_u) … and I_∞(χ, κ) = ∏_σ I_σ(χ_σ, κ_σ).
issues.correction: I_p = L_p(s + 1/2, ord, π, χ) × ∏_w 𝔙_w (see also sourceIssues E58); I_∞(χ, ρ^υ) and I_∞(χ, κ) denote the same product.
issues.reason: By (83), the local factor at w is L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w). The global identity is evaluated at the same s as L^S(s + 1/2, …). Main Theorem 9.2.2 inherits the shift ('L_p(m, ord, π', χ_u) L^S(m + 1/2, π', χ_u)'). Marcil 2023, Theorem 4.6, writes E_p(s + 1/2, P − ord, π_p, χ_p). Case for the defence: this is a pure naming shift, and L_p(s, ord) could be read as 'the ord-factor attached to the value at s + 1/2'. Independent check: Checked p. 64 and p. 78. (83) says 'L(s+1/2, ord, pi_w, chi_w) is the ratio ... that appear in the formula for Z_w', which defines L(·,ord) with the shift built in. Remark 4.3.11 also calls prod_w L(s+1/2,ord,...) the Euler factor at p. Theorem 4.6.1 instead sets I_p = L_p(s,ord) := prod_w L(s,ord,pi_w,chi_w), in the same identity as L^S(s+1/2). Main Theorem 9.2.2 inherits this as 'L_p(m,ord,pi',chi_u) L^S(m+1/2,...)'. Also I_inf(chi,rho^upsilon) and I_inf(chi,kappa) denote the same product. v4 p. 69 is the same. Reach: a stated result (by a shift of 1/2 in the argument of the p-factor). Second, independent reading of the same mistake: (83) (p. 64) gives the p-adic zeta integral as I_w = L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w)·𝔙_w·⟨φ_w, φ̃_w⟩, and (86) displays this ratio with arguments s + 1/2 and −s + 1/2; Theorem 4.6.1 (p. 78) nevertheless sets L_p(s, ord, π, χ) := ∏_{w|p} L(s, ord, π_w, χ_w) and uses it in I_p at the same s, a half-unit shift; specialising s = m produces L_p(m, …) in the Main Theorem, next to L^S(m + 1/2, …). Defence: the Main Theorem is consistent with Theorem 4.6.1's own (misprinted) definition; the intended meaning is clear from (83), (86) and the parallel L^S(m + 1/2). Independent check: Checked on the page images (pp. 64–65, 78, 145). (83) defines L(s+1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w) as the ratio of L- and ε-factors in Z_w, whose arguments are s+1/2 and −s+1/2 ((86)). Remark 4.3.11 calls ∏_{w|p}L(s+1/2,ord,π_w,χ_w) 'the Euler factor at p'. Theorem 4.6.1 nevertheless defines L_p(s,ord,π,χ) := ∏_w L(s,ord,π_w,χ_w) and puts L_p(s,…) into I_p at the same s as L^S(s+1/2,π,χ_u), a half-unit shift. Specializing at s = m gives L_p(m,ord,π′,χ_u) next to L^S(m+1/2,π′,χ_u) in the Main Theorem. The intended value is L_p(m+1/2,…), i.e. ∏_w L(m+1/2,ord,π′_w,χ_{u,w}). Intended meaning clear from (83), (86) and the parallel L^S(m+1/2). Versions: v4 same; v2/v3 also have I_p = L_p(s,ord,π,χ) and L_p(m,ord,π,χ_u) in the Main Theorem.
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: v4 p. 69 same; v2/v3 Proposition 4.6.1 (p. 68–69): 'I_p = L_p(s, ord, π, χ) := ∏_{w|p} L(s, ord, π_w, χ_w)' with (4.3.24) defining L(s + 1/2, ord, π_w, χ_w), so the shift is present from v2. issues.locator: Theorem 4.6.1, p. 78, in arXiv v5; present in v4 p. 69 and v2/v3 (Proposition 4.6.1)
issues.printed: Assuming unramified vectors at the finite places lying outside S = S_π and a Siegel–Weil section f_s ∈ I(χ, s), the source writes χ = ||•||^m χ_u and asserts D(χ)·I(φ, φ^♭, f, s) = ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ · I_p(χ, κ)I_∞(χ, ρ^υ)I_S L^S(s + 1/2, π, χ_u), with I_S = ∏_{v∈S} D_v(χ)·volume(𝒰_v).
issues.correction: D(χ) · I(φ, φ^♭, f, m) = ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ · ∏_{v|p}D_v(χ) · I_p · I_∞ · I_{S'} · L^{S'∪Σ_p}(m + 1/2, π, χ_u), for f ∈ I(χ_u, m) (equivalently D^{Σ_p}(χ)·I = ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩ I_p I_∞ I_{S'} L^{S'∪Σ_p}(m + 1/2, π, χ_u)), where S' ⊇ S_π ∪ S_χ ∪ S_K is the set of places of §4.2 and I_{S'} = ∏_{v∈S'}D_v(χ)vol(U_v).
issues.reason: The unfolding gives I = ⟨φ, φ^♭⟩∏_v I_v. For v ∉ S' ∪ Σ_p, d_{n,v}(s, χ_v)I_v = L_v(s + 1/2, π_v, χ_v) (§4.2.1), and d_{n,v}(s, χ_{u,v}) = D_v(χ) only at s = m (definition (108): D_v(χ) = d_{n,v}(m, χ_v)). So the identity holds at s = m for sections in I(χ_u, m), the parametrization used in Definition 5.3.2 and Corollary 9.1.8, not for f_s ∈ I(χ, s) with variable s. For v | p, I_v = I_w is given by Theorem 4.3.10, which contains no standard Euler factor and no D_v. So the D_v(χ) (v | p) contained in D(χ) = D^∅(χ) have no counterpart on the right, and L^S (S = S_π, which does not contain p when π_p is unramified) wrongly includes the Euler factors at p. Moreover the unramified computation needs v ∉ S_ram = S_π ∪ S_χ ∪ S_K, and Lemma 4.2.3 is stated for v ∈ S', so S should be S', not S_π. If instead p ∈ S_π, then I_S would include p-adic places with the §4.2.2 value D_v·vol(U_v), which is not what is computed at p. Case for the defence: it is plausible that the intended statement omits the places above p from both D(χ) and L^S (the natural shape for a p-adic L-function, with the modified factor L_p(ord) replacing the Euler factor at p). But the printed formula does not say so, and Corollary 9.1.8 and Main Theorem 9.2.2 reproduce it (with D(χ) and L^S). Independent check: Checked p. 78, p. 47 ((53)), §4.2 (p. 46), Corollary 9.1.8 and Main Theorem 9.2.2 (pp. 144-145). (i) The s-dependence. D_v(chi) = prod_r L_v(2m+n-r, chi^+ eta^r) = d_{n,v}(m, chi_{u,v}) is fixed by m. For f in I(chi,s) with chi = ||·||^m chi_u, the unramified factor is L_v(s+1/2,pi,chi) = L_v(s+m+1/2,pi,chi_u) over d_{n,v}(s,chi) = d_{n,v}(s+m,chi_u). So the printed identity (D(chi) on the left, L^S(s+1/2,pi,chi_u) on the right) can hold only at s = m for sections in I(chi_u,m), which is the parametrization of Definition 5.3.2 and Corollary 9.1.8. (ii) The places above p. D(chi) = D^∅(chi) runs over all finite v, including v|p (108). The factor I_p of Theorem 4.3.10 contains no D_v, and at v|p the section is not unramified. S = S_pi need not contain p (§4.2 even requires p not in S), so L^S wrongly keeps the Euler factor at p. The printed identity is off by prod_{v|p} L_v(m+1/2,pi,chi_u)/D_v(chi), which is not 1 when chi is unramified at p. (iii) At places of S_chi ∪ S_K outside S_pi the sections are those of §4.2.2, with I_v = vol(U_v), so the set should be S' as in §4.2. Main Theorem 9.2.2 reproduces D(chi) (via Corollary 9.1.8) and L^S. v4 p. 69 is the same. Reach: a stated result (Theorem 4.6.1; through Corollary 9.1.8, the form of Main Theorem 9.2.2).

issues.locator: §5.1, p. 79, after the definition of Λ_{X,R}, in arXiv v5
issues.printed: The source defines Λ_{X,R} = lim_i R[X/X_i] and claims compactness of this topological ring.
issues.correction: This is a topological ring, compact when R is compact (e.g. R finite over Z_p).
issues.reason: For a general p-adic ring R (e.g. R = O_{C_p}, or R = Z_p[[T]] with its p-adic topology, both allowed in §5.1) R[X/X_i] ≅ R^{#(X/X_i)} is not compact, and neither is the inverse limit. Defence: compactness is never used. Independent check: Checked p. 79. R is any 'p-adic ring' (p-adic topology). For R = O_{C_p}, allowed since R ⊂ C_p is used throughout, R itself is not compact (its residue field is infinite), and Lambda_{X,R} for X trivial is R. Compactness holds when R is compact, e.g. finite over Z_p, and it is never used. v4 is the same.

issues.locator: §5.3.1, p. 84, paragraph after Definition 5.3.2, in arXiv v5
issues.printed: The source says multiplying an unnormalized measure by the relevant product of local Euler factors at S produces a measure normalized at S.
issues.correction: Multiplying by chi -> prod_{v in S} D_v(chi) gives a pseudo-measure; it is a measure when the elements 1 - eta^r(varpi_v) q_v^{r-n}[varpi_v] (v in S, 0 <= r <= n-1) are units in Lambda_{X_p}. Otherwise state the Main Theorem with the unnormalized measure (I_S = prod_{v in S} vol(U_v)), or in the localized Iwasawa algebra.
issues.reason: For v ∈ S (v ∤ p) at which χ is unramified, D_v(χ) = ∏_r (1 − η^r(ϖ_v) q_v^{r−n} χ(ϖ_v))^{-1}, the evaluation at χ of the inverse of an element of the Iwasawa algebra Λ_{X_p}; that element is a unit only if its reductions at all maximal ideals are non-zero, which fails e.g. for r = n−1 when q_v ≡ ±1 (mod p) and the residual image of [ϖ_v] allows η^r(ϖ_v) q_v^{-1}ζ ≡ 1. Defence: the paper mostly uses D^?(χ) as notation. Independent check: Checked p. 84. For v in S with chi unramified at v, D_v(chi) = prod_r (1 - eta^r(varpi_v) q_v^{r-n} chi(varpi_v))^-1 is the inverse of an element of Lambda_{X_p}, and that element is a unit only if 1 - c_r psi([varpi_v]) is nonzero in every residue field. This fails, for example, for r = n-1 when eta^{n-1}(varpi_v) q_v^-1 ≡ 1 mod p. So multiplying by the Euler factors at S gives in general only a pseudo-measure. The reach is wider than 'nothing'. Corollary 9.1.8 is written with the normalized measure (D(chi)·prod_v I_v), and Main Theorem 9.2.2 keeps prod_{v in S} D_v(chi) inside I_S while asserting that L(Eis, phi⊗phi^flat) lies in Lambda_{X_p,R}⊗T. If the measure of Theorem 8.2.2/Corollary 8.2.4 is the unnormalized one (Corollary 8.2.4 does not say which), integrality in those exceptional cases rests on this unproved sentence. v4 p. 82 is the same. Reach: the proof (of Corollary 9.1.8 / Main Theorem 9.2.2 in the exceptional cases).

issues.correction: If v is a finite place with v ∤ p and v ∉ S, then …; and one must assume that S contains the primes dividing N_0 (and those ramified in K/K^+), so that χ_v is unramified outside S ∪ {p} for all χ ∈ Y_H^class.
issues.reason: S is defined as the set of primes at which K_4^p, K_3^p (subgroups of G_i(A_f^p)) are not hyperspecial, so p ∉ S and the condition literally applies to v | p, contradicting the fourth condition and the ramified p-adic sections of §4.3. Moreover characters of X_p = X_{p,N_0} may ramify at primes dividing N_0, where K_4^p may well be hyperspecial; then I_v(χ_{u,v},m) has no unramified vector. The 'so in particular' is therefore an extra hypothesis, which in §4.2 is built into the definition of S (S ⊇ S_ram = S_π ∪ S_χ ∪ S_K). Defence: the intended meaning is clear from §4.2.

issues.locator: §6.1.3, p. 88, lines 12–16 (the characters κ_h^±), in arXiv v5
issues.printed: The source says h = (h_0,(h_σ)) ∈ H_0(C) acts on Hom_C(∧^d p_h^±, C) by the scalar h_0^{∓d} ∏_{σ∈Σ_K} det(h_σ)^{±2a_σ}. It identifies this character as κ_h^± = (∓d, (κ^±_{h,σ})), κ^±_{h,σ} = (±2a_σ, …, ±2a_σ).
issues.correction: h_0^{∓d} ∏_{σ∈Σ_K} det(h_σ)^{±a_σ}, i.e. κ^±_{h,σ} = (±a_σ, …, ±a_σ) (with the paper's sign pattern; the overall sign depends on which of p_h^± is identified with the nilradical of Lie P_0, cf. sourceIssues E90).
issues.reason: (1) The centre acts trivially on p_h^±. Under (15) (H_0 → G_m × GL(Λ_0^∨), first factor ν), t ∈ R^× ⊂ G(R) maps to (t^2, (t·1_{b_σ})), so the printed character takes the value t^{∓2d}·t^{±2Σ_{σ∈Σ_K} a_σ b_σ} = t^{±2d} ≠ 1, while with a_σ it is t^{∓2d ± 2d} = 1. (2) Direct computation: p_h^± ≅ ⊕_{σ∈Σ} Hom between Λ_{0,σ} (rank a_σ, h acting by h_0 ᵗh_{σc}^{-1}) and Λ^∨_{0,σ} (rank b_σ, h acting by h_σ); the determinant on Hom(Λ_{0,σ}, Λ^∨_{0,σ}) is h_0^{-a_σ b_σ} det(h_σ)^{a_σ} det(h_{σc})^{a_{σc}}, and the product over σ ∈ Σ is h_0^{-d} ∏_{σ∈Σ_K} det(h_σ)^{a_σ}. (3) Modular curve (U(1,1) over imaginary quadratic K, d = 1): the canonical bundle has parallel weight 1 in σ and σc (classical weight 2) and similitude −1, i.e. (−1,(1,1)); the printed formula gives (−1,(2,2)) (weight 4). Defence: κ^D is only used through the intrinsic W_{κ^D} = Hom(∧^d p_h^+, W_{κ^⋆}) in §§6.2–6.5, so the arguments there are unaffected. Independent check: Checked p. 88, with (15) on p. 22, (17) on p. 23 and d = (1/2) sum_{sigma in Sigma_K} a_sigma b_sigma on p. 86. (1) The centre acts trivially on p_h^±. Real scalars t act on Lambda_0^vee by t, with nu(t) = t^2, so under (15) t -> (t^2,(t·1)). The printed character then takes the value t^{∓2d ± 2 sum_{Sigma_K} a_sigma b_sigma} = t^{±2d} ≠ 1; with exponent a_sigma it takes the value 1. (2) Direct computation: h acts on Lambda^vee_{0,sigma} by h_sigma and on Lambda_{0,sigma} by h_0 th_{sigma c}^-1, so the determinant of h on Hom(Lambda_{0,sigma}, Lambda^vee_{0,sigma}) is h_0^{-a_sigma b_sigma} det(h_sigma)^{a_sigma} det(h_{sigma c})^{a_{sigma c}}. The product over the CM type is h_0^-d prod_{Sigma_K} det(h_sigma)^{a_sigma}. So the exponent is ±a_sigma, not ±2a_sigma. The overall sign depends on which of p_h^± is the nilradical (sourceIssues E90). The explicit kappa^D also enters the normalization U^-_{w,j,kappa^D} = |kappa^D'(t_{w,j})|_p U^-_{w,j} in §6.6 (p. 98). Same in v4 and v2. Reach: a stated result (the explicit characters kappa_h^± and kappa^D = kappa* + kappa_h^+).

issues.locator: §6.1.3, p. 88, 'The identification of G(C) with G_0(C) in 2.6.1 identifies Lie(P_0(C)) with P_h and Lie(H_0(C)) with k_h', versus §2.7.2, p. 28, in arXiv v5
issues.printed: On p. 88, the source identifies Lie(P_0(C)) with P_h, where p. 87 gives P_h = p_h^- ⊕ k_h. On p. 28 it says the identification between G(C) and G_0(C) sends Lie(P_0(C)) to k ⊕ p^+, and characterizes holomorphic forms by p^- ∗ f = 0.
issues.correction: One convention throughout; §6 consistently uses Lie(P_0(C)) ↔ P_h = p_h^- ⊕ k_h (holomorphic = annihilated by p_h^-, holomorphic tangent space p_h^+, Ω^d ↔ Hom(∧^d p_h^+, C)), so the §2.7.2 phrase 'k ⊕ p^+' is the likely slip.
issues.reason: The two identifications are incompatible. The sign pattern of κ_h^± on p. 88 (∓d on Hom(∧^d p_h^±,C)) matches the §2.7.2 version: with P_0 = Stab(Λ_0) (§2.7.1), the nilradical of Lie P_0 is Hom(Λ_0^∨, Λ_0)^{sym}, whose ∧^d has character (d, (−a_σ)). Independent check: Checked p. 28 ('identifies Lie(P_0(C)) with k ⊕ p^+, and so f corresponds to a holomorphic form if and only if p^- * f = 0') and p. 87-88 (P_h = p_h^- ⊕ k_h; 'identifies Lie(P_0(C)) with P_h'). The two statements contradict each other. By my computation in sourceIssues E89, the nilradical Hom(Lambda_0^vee, Lambda_0) of Lie P_0 (P_0 = Stab(Lambda_0)) has ∧^d-character (d, (-a_sigma)), so the printed sign pattern of kappa_h^± matches the p. 28 convention, as the first reading says. Which of the two statements is the slip is therefore unclear. Either way it is a local inconsistency. v4 p. 25 and p. 87 are the same. Reach: nothing (sign conventions for kappa_h^±; cf. sourceIssues E89).
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: Same in v4: p. 25 (§2.7.2) and p. 87 (§6.1.3).

issues.reason: With ⟨x,y⟩_V = ᵗx̄ D y (or ᵗx D ȳ), g ∈ GU(V) satisfies ḡ = ν(g) D^{-1} ᵗg^{-1} D, componentwise at w. For M = D ᵗβ^{-1}β^{-1}: w-component of δ̄_p = D^{-1} ᵗM^{-1} D = D^{-2} β ᵗβ D, which equals M^{-1} = β ᵗβ D^{-1} iff D^2 commutes with β ᵗβ; and δ_p^{-1} ḡ δ_p = ν(g)·β[u ᵗg'^{-1} u^{-1}]β^{-1} with u = ᵗβ D^{-2} ᵗβ^{-1}, which need not normalize ᵗI^0. With D^{-1} in place of D, u = 1. The paper gives no proof ('Then'). Defence: the printed formula is right if D is the matrix of the dual pairing or G acts on row vectors, and whenever β_w is diagonal; the convention for 'the hermitian pairing is given by D' is not specified. The middle identity holds in all cases (δ_p ∈ G(Z_p) when the d_i are p-units). Independent check: Checked p. 90 (D = diag(d_i), d_i in K^+, is the Gram matrix of <·,·>_V in the fixed K-basis) and p. 91. The paper's action convention is fixed: §2.1 (<g(v),g(v')> = nu<v,v'>, <gx,gy> = nu<x,y>) is a left action. With that convention and either Gram convention, t g D gbar = nu D gives (gbar)_w = nu D^-1 t g_w^-1 D in each w-component. For delta_p = (1, M): the w-component of delta_pbar is D^-1 tM^-1 D. With M = D tbeta^-1 beta^-1 this is D^-2 beta tbeta D, which equals M^-1 = beta tbeta D^-1 only if D^2 commutes with beta tbeta. Also delta^-1 gbar delta = nu·beta[u tg'^-1 u^-1]beta^-1 with u = tbeta D^-2 tbeta^-1 in GL_n(O_w), which does not normalize tI^0 in general. With M = D^-1 tbeta^-1 beta^-1 one gets u = 1 and all three identities of (125) hold. beta_w is an arbitrary change of O_w-basis of L_w and D is not scalar, so the printed element fails in general. The fix is one symbol (D -> D^-1), and later arguments use only the three properties, so this is a misprint rather than a gap. issues.locator: §6.5.3, p. 96, first paragraph (and the matching signs in §6.3, pp. 93–94), in arXiv v5
issues.printed: The source asserts that (π_∞ ⊗_C W_κ)^{K_h} ≠ 0, for instance for holomorphic π of type (κ,K), implies ξ_{π,∞}(t) = t^{a(κ)} for t ∈ R^×. It also calls g ↦ ||ν(g)||^{-a(κ)} a global section of L(κ)^∨.
issues.correction: With the conventions of §§2.6.3 and 2.7.2 (W_κ = functions on H_0 with right-translation action; forms f with f(gu) = u^{-1}·f(g), i.e. diagonal K_h-invariants), ξ_{π,∞}(t) = t^{−a(κ)}, g ↦ ||ν(g)||^{-a(κ)} is a section of L(κ), and the factors ||ν||^{-a(κ)} in (133), (137), (146), (147) and ||ν||^{a(κ)} in (141) change sign. Alternatively, keep §6 as printed and declare that K_h acts on W_κ contragrediently to §2.7.2.
issues.reason: Under (15), t ∈ R^× maps to (t^2, (t·1)) ∈ H_0, which lies in B_{H_0} and acts on W_κ by κ(t) = t^{a(κ)} (this is how (116) is designed). A diagonal K_h-invariant in π_∞ ⊗ W_κ then forces ξ_{π,∞}(t)·t^{a(κ)} = 1. Likewise, with sections of L(χ) satisfying s(gu) = χ(u)^{-1}s(g), g ↦ ||ν(g)||^{-a(κ)} is a section of L(ν^{a(κ)}) = L(κ). Defence: §§6.3–6.5 are internally consistent with ξ_{π,∞}(t) = t^{a(κ)} (π^♭ = π^∨ ⊗ ||ν||^{a(κ)}, φ'_i·||ν||^{-a(κ)} ∈ π^∨ in (146)), so this is a sign-convention clash between Part I and §6 rather than a failure of an argument. Independent check: Checked p. 28 (f(gu) = u^-1 f(g), U_inf acting on W_kappa by right translation), (17) and (116), pp. 93-94 and p. 96. A central t in R^x maps to (t^2,(t)) in T_{H_0} and acts on W_kappa by kappa(t) = t^{2kappa_0 + sum kappa_{sigma,j}} = t^{a(kappa)}. A diagonal K_h-invariant in pi_inf ⊗ W_kappa (the §2.7.2 and §6.1.2 identification) therefore forces xi_{pi,inf}(t) = t^-a(kappa), not t^a(kappa). Check with (133): under §2.7.2 conventions [phi(gt),phi'(gt)] = t^-2a [phi,phi'](g), so Z_G(R)-invariance of the integrand needs ||nu||^{+a(kappa)}. §6 is internally consistent with the contragredient convention (xi(t) = t^a, pi^flat = pi^vee ⊗ ||nu||^a, (133), (146)). So this is a convention clash with Part I, not a broken argument. v4 is the same. Reach: nothing (sign convention between Part I and §6; the explicit signs of the ||nu||-twists depend on it).

issues.locator: Lemma 6.6.1(ii), p. 98, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 96
issues.correction: T(g)^♭ = T(g^†); away from p, g^† = ν(g)^{-1}ḡ, so T(g^†) = T(ν(g)^{-1})·T(ḡ), which equals T(ḡ) when ν(g) is a local unit.
issues.reason: By §6.2.3, g^† = ν(g)^{-1}δ_p^{-1}ḡδ_p; at ℓ ≠ p this is the central element ν(g)^{-1} ∈ Q_ℓ^× times ḡ. The double coset operator of a central element z_ℓ = ℓ^{-k} is not the identity: it acts on a representation through its central character (which is non-trivial in general, e.g. ξ_{π,∞}(t) = t^{a(κ)} forces non-trivial finite components). Defence: for Hecke operators with unit similitude (in particular for the unitary part of the Hecke algebra) the equality holds; it may be intended as an identity up to the central Hecke operators.

issues.locator: Lemma 6.6.5(ii), p. 100, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 97–98
issues.printed: The source defines S_κ(K_r,R)[λ] by localizing S_κ(K_r,R) over T_{K_r,κ,R} at p_λ ⊂ T_{K_r,κ,R}, the kernel of λ, and calls this the λ-isotypic component. It asserts j_π: π_S^{K_S} ⊗ π_p^{I_r}[λ] ⥲ S_κ(K_r,R)[λ] ⊗_R C = S_κ(K_r,C)[λ]. Here π_p^{I_r}[λ] comprises vectors on which each U_{w,j,κ} has eigenvalue λ(U_{w,j,κ}).
issues.correction: Define π_p^{I_r}[λ] as the generalized eigenspace (the subspace killed by a power of every U_{w,j,κ} − λ(U_{w,j,κ})), matching the localization on the right. Alternatively, keep true eigenspaces on both sides, replace the localization by the λ-eigenspace, and restrict to λ with unit (ordinary) U-eigenvalues or assume the U_{w,j,κ} act semisimply.
issues.reason: R is a field (a finite extension of E(π)), so localization of the finite-dimensional module S_κ(K_r,R) at the maximal ideal p_λ is the generalized λ-eigenspace, which equals the λ-isotypic (eigen)space only if the Hecke algebra acts semisimply. The U_{w,j} need not act semisimply on Iwahori-type invariants (e.g. for GL_2, U_p on the two-dimensional Iwahori invariants of an unramified principal series with equal Satake parameters is a Jordan block). Defence: in the ordinary case used later (Lemma 6.6.10), e_κπ_p^{I_r} has dimension ≤ 1 (Theorem 6.6.9), so the distinction disappears. Independent check: Checked on the page image (p. 100). R is a field (a finite extension of E(π)), so localizing S_κ(K_r,R) at p_λ gives the generalized λ-eigenspace. The left side π_p^{I_r}[λ] is explicitly the true eigenspace ('the subspace of π_p^{I_r} on which each U_{w,j,κ} acts as λ(U_{w,j,κ})'). The lemma has no proof. The two sides differ in general, and not only in exotic cases like equal Satake parameters (the first reading's example). They differ for every π with π_p unramified once r ≥ 3, taking λ with λ(U) = 0. Example (GL_2-type computation, which is the model for each GL_n factor at w|p): I_r ⊂ I^0_r, and I^0_r at a GL_2 factor is Γ_0(p^r). π^{I^0_r} contains the old vectors v_k = π(diag(1,p^{-k}))v_0 (0 ≤ k ≤ r), on which U_p acts by v_k ↦ v_{k−1} (k ≥ 1) and v_0 ↦ a v_0 − c v_1. The characteristic polynomial is x^{r−1}(x² − a x + c), but ker U_p is one-dimensional. So for r ≥ 3 there is a nilpotent Jordan block of size r−1 at eigenvalue 0. The normalizations |κ′(t)|_p^{-1} are scalars and do not change this. Hence for λ extending λ^p_π with λ(U_{w,j,κ}) = 0, j_π(π_S^{K_S}⊗π_p^{I_r}[λ]) is a proper subspace of S_κ(K_r,C)[λ]. The statement as printed is false, so kind 'error' rather than 'gap'. Nothing downstream: only unit eigenvalues are used later (Lemma 6.6.10), where e_κπ_p^{I_r} has dimension ≤ 1 (Theorem 6.6.9), so eigenspace and generalized eigenspace agree. Identical in v4 (p. 97). Reach: a stated result (Lemma 6.6.5(ii) in non-semisimple cases); nothing downstream).

issues.locator: §6.6.8, Theorem 6.6.9 (Hida), p. 101 — whose proof is given in §8.3 (Lemma 8.3.2, Corollary 8.3.3, pp. 128–130) — in arXiv v5; the same mistake at Theorem 6.6.9, p. 101, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 98
issues.printed: Theorem 6.6.9, attributed to Hida, asserts that every representation π_p of G(ℚ_p) has ordinary eigenspace e_κπ_p^{I_r} ⊂ π_p^{I_r} of dimension ≤ 1 for every r. The source directs readers to Section 8.3 for an adaptation of Hida's proof.
issues.correction: Theorem 6.6.9. For any irreducible admissible representation π_p of G(Q_p) and κ satisfying (166) (κ_{σ,a_σ} + κ_{σc,b_σ} ≥ n for all σ), the ordinary eigenspace e_κπ_p^{I_r} has dimension ≤ 1 for every r.
issues.reason: The proof in §8.3 (Lemma 8.3.2) uses irreducibility of π_w and inequality (166) to make |κ_norm|_pδ_w^{1/2} regular; without (166) two Weyl conjugates can both give unit eigenvalues (e.g. for GL_2 in weight one, both roots of X² − a_pX + χ(p) can be units, giving a two-dimensional ordinary space of Iwahori-fixed vectors). Defence: the holomorphic π of §6.6 may be tacitly assumed to have κ in the range (166)/sufficiently regular. Independent check: p. 101: 'Theorem 6.6.9 (Hida). For any representation π_p of G(Q_p), the ordinary eigenspace e_κπ_p^{I_r} ⊂ π_p^{I_r} is of dimension ≤ 1, for any r.' Nothing in §6.6 restricts κ beyond dominance ((16) on p. 22 is only dominance; §6.6.8 takes any holomorphic cuspidal π of type (κ,K_r)), whereas the proof in §8.3 (Lemma 8.3.2, Corollary 8.3.3) assumes π_w irreducible admissible and κ satisfying (166), introduced only in §8.3.1 (p. 126). (166) is genuinely needed: m_{a_w} − m_n = Σ_σ(κ_{σ,a_w}+κ_{σc,b_w}−n), and if this is −1 the corrected character |κ_norm|_pδ_w^{1/2} has equal exponents at t_{a_w} and t_n, so it is fixed by the transposition x = (a_w n); then β_x = β^x is unit-valued, and for π_w = Ind(α) irreducible with α^x ≠ α both α and α^x give ordinary eigenvectors, so the ordinary space is 2-dimensional. The classical instance is weight-one elliptic forms (n = 2), where both roots of X² − a_pX + χ(p) are units. Reducible π_p (e.g. ρ ⊕ ρ) are trivially excluded. Since the printed statement is false without these hypotheses (not merely unproved), the kind should be error (missing hypotheses) rather than gap. The same applies to the claim 'This space has dimension at most one' in §6.6.8 and to Lemma 6.6.10(i) for κ outside (166). Nothing downstream is affected: §§7–9 work with sufficiently regular κ, which satisfy (166). v4 p. 98 is identical (referring to 'Section 8.2 below'). Second, independent reading of the same mistake: For a reducible π_p = π′_p ⊕ π′_p with π′_p ordinary the ordinary eigenspace has dimension 2. The proof in §8.3 works with irreducible admissible π_w (Lemma 8.3.2), and the theorem is applied to local components of cuspidal π.
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: v4 Theorem 6.6.9 (p. 98) is identical and refers to 'Section 8.2 below'. v4 p. 98 identical.

issues.locator: Lemma 6.6.10 (hypothesis on R), p. 102, and its uses in Lemma 6.6.12 and Lemma 6.7.1, pp. 103–105, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 99–101
issues.printed: The source chooses R ⊂ C as either a finite extension of R(λ_π) localized at the prime selected by incl_p, or that ring's p-adic completion. It identifies S^ord_κ(K_r,R)_π as an R-lattice inside ⊕_{π′∈S(K_s,κ,π)} π′^{,ord}_p ⊗ (π′_S)^{K_S}.
issues.correction: Require R to be p-adically complete (or Henselian), or large enough to contain the Hecke eigenvalues of every π′ ∈ S(K_r,κ,π); otherwise replace the localization at m_π by the corresponding direct factor after completion.
issues.reason: If R is a non-complete discrete valuation ring, T^ord_{K_r,κ,R} need not be a product of local rings: e.g. if some Hecke eigensystem λ_{π′} has values in a quadratic extension F of Frac(R) in which p splits, with one prime above p giving λ̄_π and the other not, then T^ord_R contains an order of F with two maximal ideals, its localization at m_π is not finitely generated over R, and S^ord_κ(K_r;R)_π is not an R-lattice; moreover its ⊗E would contain the π″-component with λ̄_{π″} ≠ λ̄_π. When all eigenvalues lie in Frac(R), T^ord_R ⊂ ∏R contains all idempotents of its completion and is a product of local rings, so the statement holds. Defence: from §6.7.8 on R is ‘a sufficiently large finite flat p-adic integer ring’ and in §7 R = O_π is complete; Lemma 6.7.1’s proof uses finiteness (‘H^{d,ord} … are finite R-modules’). Independent check: Checked on the page image (p. 102). Lemma 6.6.10 allows R to be the localization, not completed, of a finite extension of R(λ_π) at the prime given by incl_p. The lemma has no proof. T = T^ord_{K_r,κ,R} is finite over the DVR R, but it need not be a product of local rings unless R is Henselian. Its localization at m_π can then fail to be finitely generated over R. Example of the mechanism: Z_(p)[i] with p ≡ 1 mod 4 has two maximal ideals, and its localization at one of them contains 1/π̄^k for all k. This happens whenever some π′ ≡ π modulo one prime of F′ = F(λ_{π′}) above 𝔭 = the prime of R does not satisfy the congruence at another prime above 𝔭. S_π⊗E then contains the components of the Galois conjugates of π′ whose reductions differ from λ̄_π, so it is not a lattice in ⊕_{π′∈S(K_r,κ,π)}(…). When R contains all Hecke eigenvalues (so T ⊂ ∏R), or R is complete, T contains the idempotents of its completion and the statement holds. The [π]-part is unaffected: for x ∈ S(E)[λ_π] and s ∉ m_π, s acts on x by the unit λ_π(s), so S_π ∩ S(E)[λ_π] = S(R) ∩ S(E)[λ_π] is a lattice. Downstream: Lemma 6.7.1 only pairs against H_{π^♭}, and localizing at s ∉ m multiplies the pairing by units, so the image is the same as for H(R). From §6.7.8 on and throughout §7, R is complete. The defect is a missing hypothesis in a result stated without proof. I keep 'gap' and not 'error' because the failing configuration is generic but no explicit automorphic example is exhibited. Identical in v4 (pp. 99–100). Note also the misprint S(K_s,κ,π) for S(K_r,κ,π) in the same display. Reach: a stated result (stated results (Lemma 6.6.10(ii), 6.6.12(ii)–(iii), 6.7.1 for non-complete R); nothing downstream).
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: v4 pp. 99–101 identical.

issues.locator: Lemma 6.6.12(iii), p. 104 (first pairing), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 100 and in v2 at p. 101 (Lemma 6.5.12(iii))
issues.printed: Part (iii) claims that normalized Serre duality gives perfect pairings equivariant for T^ord_{K_r,κ,R}, using Lemma 6.6.7's isomorphisms: S^ord_κ(K_r;R)[π] ⊗_R H^{d,ord}_{κ^D}(K_r;R)[π] → R and S^ord_κ(K_r;R)_π ⊗_R H^{d,ord}_{κ^D}(K_r;R)_π → R.
issues.correction: Only the pairing of the localizations S_π ⊗ H_π → R is perfect. The pairing of the saturated λ_π-isotypic lattices S[π] ⊗ H[π] → R is perfect after ⊗E but its image is the congruence ideal C(π) (Definition 6.7.2, Lemma 6.7.3), so it is perfect over R iff C(π) = R (no congruences).
issues.reason: Take 𝕋 = {(a,b) ∈ O×O : a ≡ b mod ϖ^n}, S_π = 𝕋 (free of rank one, as under the Gorenstein hypothesis), H_π = Hom_O(𝕋,O) with the perfect evaluation pairing, λ_π = first projection. Then S[π] = 𝕋 ∩ (E×0) = O·(ϖ^n,0) and H[π] = O·λ_π (λ_π is primitive since λ_π(1,1) = 1), and ⟨(ϖ^n,0),λ_π⟩ = ϖ^n, so the pairing S[π]×H[π] → O has image ϖ^nO. The paper itself uses this: Lemma 6.7.3 (c(π) = Q[π]/Q_π generates C(π); if the [π]-pairing were perfect, L[π] = L_π and c(π) would be a unit) and Lemma 7.5.2 (L_φ restricted to S[π] takes values in C(π)). Defence: harmless downstream — no later argument uses perfectness of the [π]-pairing; the statement is a slip for the localized pairing only. Independent check: Quotation checked on the page image (p. 104). The paper's [π]-parts are saturated λ_π-isotypic lattices, not localizations. Lemma 6.6.10(ii) (p. 102) defines S^ord_κ(K_r;R)[π] := S^ord_κ(K_r;R)_π ∩ S^ord_κ(K_r;E)[λ_π], and Lemma 6.6.12 (p. 103) defines H^{d,ord}(K_r;R)[π] := H^{d,ord}(K_r;R)_π ∩ H^{d,ord}(K_r;E)[λ_π], 'where the notation [λ_π] again denotes the λ_π-isotypic component'. H^{d,ord}_{κ^D}(K_r;R) is by definition the R-dual of S^ord_κ(K_r;R) under the normalized pairing (p. 103), and the localizations are direct factors (R complete), so the second pairing S_π ⊗ H_π → R is perfect. The first is not. By T-equivariance the λ_π-part is orthogonal to the other eigen-components. Hence H[π] is the annihilator in H_π of S' := S_π ∩ (⊕_{π'≠π} components), i.e. H[π] = Hom_R(S_π/S', R). So S[π] × H[π] → R is perfect iff S[π] → S_π/S' is onto, i.e. iff S_π = S[π] ⊕ S', i.e. iff π has no congruences; the cokernel is the congruence module. The first reading's rank-one example checks: S[π] = O·(ϖ^n,0), H[π] = O·pr_1, pairing image ϖ^nO. The paper contradicts the statement itself: Lemma 7.5.2 (p. 120) says the restriction of L_φ = ⟨·,φ⟩_{κ,K_r} (φ ∈ H^{d,ord}(K_r,O)[π]) to S^ord(K_r,O)[π] takes values in the congruence ideal C(π), and Lemma 6.7.3/Remark 6.7.4 treat C(π) as non-trivial in general. The perfectness of the [π]-pairing is not used later: Lemma 6.6.12 is cited again only in the list of modifications in Remark 9.3.2. Versions: v4 p. 100 identical; v2/v3 Lemma 6.5.12(iii) reads 'Serre duality induces perfect …'. Reach: a stated result (Lemma 6.6.12(iii), first half); nothing downstream).
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: Identical in v4 (p. 100) and v2 (Lemma 6.5.12(iii), ‘Serre duality induces perfect …’).

issues.locator: §6.7, definition of C(π,M), p. 105, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 102
issues.printed: For any T^{♭,ord}_{K^♭,κ^♭,R}-module M, the source defines C(π,M) as the annihilator of M_{π^♭}/(M[π^♭]+M[π]^⊥), retaining the preceding notation's meanings.
issues.correction: M[π]^⊥ requires a pairing of M with a dual module; for M = 𝕋 (as used for C(π,𝕋) and (153)) it must be read as ker λ_π = 𝕋 ∩ ⊕_{π′≠π}𝕋_E[λ_{π′}], i.e. the annihilator of Hom(𝕋,R)[λ_π] under evaluation.
issues.reason: In Definition 6.7.2, [π]^⊥ is the orthogonal complement for Serre duality between H^{d,ord} on V and on −V; a general module M carries no such pairing. With the reading above, C(π,𝕋) = Ann(𝕋/(𝕋[λ_π]+ker λ_π)), which is what (153) computes. Defence: the intended meaning (the usual congruence module) is standard.

issues.locator: §6.7.5, paragraph after Lemma 6.7.7, p. 106, in arXiv v5 (and ‘as noted above, does not actually depend on χ’, p. 107); absent in v4
issues.printed: The source invokes smoothness of the family of p-adic Hecke characters to claim that neither C(π,χ) nor c(π,χ) varies with χ.
issues.correction: Give an argument, or state the independence as an expectation. A sketch: twisting by χ∘det gives an isomorphism of Hecke algebras 𝕋 ≅ 𝕋_χ carrying λ_{π^♭} to λ_{π^♭⊗χ^{-1}}. It carries the integral lattices to each other up to a single scalar (the CM period), so the congruence modules agree: C(π,χ) = C(π), and c(π,χ) = c(π)·unit. This requires that the twist be integral at p, i.e. that the p-adic CM period be a unit.
issues.reason: C(π,χ) is only defined ‘by analogy’, and the lattices H[π^♭]_χ are defined through the coherent cohomology of the twisted weight κ^♭⋆χ with its own rational/integral structure; smoothness of the family of characters does not by itself compare integral structures of different coherent cohomology groups. Defence: the claim is plausible (scalar changes of lattice do not affect the ratio Q[π,χ]/Q_{π,χ}), and it is exactly what Main Theorem 9.2.2 needs to state c(π′,χ) uniformly. Independent check: Checked on the page image (p. 106): 'However, since the family of p-adic Hecke characters is smooth, it is easy to see that C(π,χ) and c(π,χ) do not depend on χ'. It is repeated on p. 107 ('as noted above, does not actually depend on χ'). C(π,χ) is only defined 'by analogy'. It is the congruence module of the π^♭⊗χ^{-1}∘det-component of the coherent cohomology H^{d,ord}_{κ^♭⋆χ,−V}. That is a different weight with its own integral structure, which the paper says differs from the untwisted one even rationally by a CM period. Smoothness of the character family says nothing about these integral structures. A real argument is needed. For example: (a) twisting by χ∘det gives an isomorphism of Hecke algebras (T ↦ χ(det T)T) and, up to a scalar, of the integral lattices; or (b) under the Gorenstein hypothesis, C(π,χ) = C(π,𝕋_χ) ≅ C(π,𝕋) as in Lemma 6.7.10. The claim is plausible but not proved. Correction to the first reading's note on reach: Main Theorem 9.2.2 does not depend on this claim. It keeps χ in c(π′,χ), and c(π′,χ)·Ω_{π′,χ}/P_{π′,χ} = ⟨φ,φ^♭_χ⟩_χ / Vol(I^0_{r^1,V} ∩ I^0_{r^1,−V}) because Q[π′,χ] = c(π′,χ)Q_{π′,χ} (Lemma 6.7.7 and the proof on p. 145). So the gap affects only the stated independence claim and the motivation in Remark 6.7.12; nothing downstream. New in v5. Reach: a stated result (independence of χ); used in the formulation of Main Theorem 9.2.2).

issues.locator: Theorem 7.1.1, p. 108, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 104
issues.printed: Theorem 7.1.1 asserts a canonical isomorphism T^ord_{K^p,κ_1,R} ⥲ T^ord_{K^p,κ_2,R} for arbitrary characters κ_1, κ_2 on T_H.
issues.correction: For any pair of sufficiently regular characters κ_1, κ_2 of T_H (in the range of Hida’s classicality theorem (32)), there is a canonical isomorphism T^ord_{K^p,κ_1,R} ⥲ T^ord_{K^p,κ_2,R}.
issues.reason: T^ord_{K^p,κ,R} := lim_r T^ord_{K_r,κ,R} is built from classical ordinary cusp forms of weight κ (§7.1). For κ the trivial character, S_κ(K_r;R) consists of holomorphic cusp forms of weight 0, which vanish on a non-compact Shimura variety, so T^ord_{K^p,0,R} = 0, while for regular κ the big Hecke algebra is a non-zero finite free Λ^o-algebra (Theorem 7.2.1). Weight independence holds for the Hecke algebra of p-adic forms and for classical forms only in the range where Hida’s control/classicality theorem applies. Defence: the paper only uses the theorem for sufficiently regular weights (Proposition 7.4.10: ‘if κ^1 is a second sufficiently regular character’), and Remark 7.1.2 refers to Hida’s theorems which carry such a hypothesis. Independent check: Quotation checked on p. 108 (v5): 'Theorem 7.1.1. For any pair of characters κ_1, κ_2 of T_H, there is a canonical isomorphism T^ord_{K^p,κ_1,R} ⥲ T^ord_{K^p,κ_2,R}.' Here T^ord_{K^p,κ,R} := lim_r T^ord_{K_r,κ,R} (p. 108), and T^ord_{K_r,κ,R} = e_κ T_{K_r,κ,R} is the ring obtained by restricting Hecke operators to S^ord_κ(K_r;R) (§6.6.6, p. 101), a submodule of the CLASSICAL cusp forms S_κ(K_r;R) = H^0(M^tor_K, ω_κ(−D_∞)) (§2.6.5; p. 98: T_{K_r,κ,R} ⊂ End_C(S_κ(K_r;C))). So the objects are built from classical forms of the single weight κ, not from p-adic forms of all weights, and there is no standing regularity hypothesis in §7.1 (Theorem 7.2.1(ii) and 7.3.1(ii) impose 'κ sufficiently regular' explicitly, which shows 7.1.1 lacks it). 'Characters of T_H' include dominant non-regular ones: κ with all κ_{σ,i,j} = 0 satisfies (16), and on a non-compact Shimura variety S_0(K_r) = 0 (holomorphic cusp forms of scalar weight 0 vanish), so T^ord_{K^p,0,R} = 0, whereas for regular κ with an ordinary π the big algebra is non-zero (finite free over Λ^o, Theorem 7.2.1(i)). Likewise, below Hida's bound classical ordinary forms of level K_r do not exhaust the family (GL_2 analogue: Hida's lim_r h^ord_k(Np^r) ≅ h^ord(N;Λ) holds for k ≥ 2, not k = 1). Remark 7.1.2 cites Hida's theorems and mentions only (G1)–(G3), not the weight bound of (32) under which those theorems are proved. The missing hypothesis is harmless downstream: the theorem is invoked only for sufficiently regular weights (Proposition 7.3.5 via §7.3.4, Proposition 7.4.10 'if κ^1 is a second sufficiently regular character', Hypothesis 7.3.3 comment). Versions: v4 p. 104 identical ('of T = T_H'); v2/v3 Theorem 7.1.1 'For any pair of characters κ, κ_1' also without hypothesis. Reach: a stated result (as printed); nothing downstream).

issues.locator: Theorem 7.2.1(ii), p. 109, and Theorem 7.3.1(ii), p. 110, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 105 (with Λ_R, Λ_π instead of Λ^o) and in v2/v3 (Theorem 7.1.3(ii))
issues.printed: The control theorem (ii) defines I_κ ⊂ Λ^o_R as the kernel of Λ^o_R → R ⊂ C_p induced by κ. For sufficiently regular κ, it claims the natural map T_{K^p,R} ⊗_{Λ^o_R} Λ^o_R/I_κ → T_{K^p_r,κ,R} is an isomorphism. Theorem 7.3.1(ii) gives the corresponding map 𝕋_π ⊗_{Λ^o_π} Λ^o_π/I_κ → 𝕋_{K^p_r,κ,O_π}.
issues.correction: The isomorphism holds at level r = 1 (target T_{K_1,κ,R}, all nebentypes tame), or at level r for a fixed nebentypus: T_{K^p,R} ⊗_{Λ_R} Λ_R/I_{κψ} ≅ T_{K_r,κ,ψ,R} for ψ of level r (I_{κψ} the kernel of κψ on Λ_R); equivalently T_{K^p,R} ⊗_Λ Λ_{r,κ} ≅ T_{K_r,κ,R} with Λ_{r,κ} = Λ/𝓘_{r,κ} — which is the form actually used in Proposition 7.4.12 (‘T ↠ T ⊗_Λ Λ_{r,κ} = T_{r,κ}’) and in Hida’s (33).
issues.reason: The left side does not depend on r, while T_{K_r,κ,R} acts on S^ord_κ(K_r;R) ⊇ ⊕_ψ S^ord_κ(K_r,ψ;R) over all characters ψ of T_H(Z_p/p^r), whose rank grows with r (for κ sufficiently regular each ψ-part has the rank of the corresponding Λ^o-component). Moreover elements t − κ(t), t in the pro-p part of T, do not act by zero on forms whose nebentypus is non-trivial on the pro-p part, so for r ≥ 2 the natural map T_{K^p,R} → T_{K_r,κ,R} does not factor through Λ^o/I_κ. Defence: ‘K^p_r’ is unspecified; with r = 1 or with the nebentypus built into κ (κ read as a locally algebraic character κψ and the target as the ψ-part) the statement is Hida’s theorem. Independent check: Quotations checked on the page images (Theorem 7.2.1(ii), p. 109; Theorem 7.3.1(ii), p. 110). The target T_{K^p_r,κ,R} is the Hecke algebra of S_κ(K_r;R), which by p. 99 contains the subspaces S_κ(K_r,ψ) for every nebentypus ψ of T_H(Z_p/p^rZ_p); T_{K_r,κ,ψ,R} are its quotients. The source T_{K^p,R} ⊗_{Λ^o_R} Λ^o_R/I_κ does not depend on r. By Hida's control theorem as the paper itself states it ((34), p. 35), each ψ of W trivial on W^{p^{r−1}} gives S^ord_κ(K_r,ωω_κψ,R[ψ]) ≅ 𝒮^ord_ω ⊗ R[ψ]/p_{κψ}, of the same rank as the ψ = 1 part. Since T_{K_r,κ,R} contains the diamond operators separating these ψ, its rank for r ≥ 2 exceeds rank_{Λ^o} T_{K^p,R} = rank_R(T ⊗ Λ^o/I_κ). Moreover t ∈ W acts on the ψ-part through κψ(t), not κ(t), so the natural map does not even factor through Λ^o/I_κ. The statement is correct for r = 1, or at level r with Λ^o/I_κ replaced by Λ/𝓘_{r,κ} (𝓘_{r,ρ} the annihilator of C_r(T,O)·ρ^υ, p. 114). issues.printed: The source invokes Theorem 7.3.1(ii) to claim that tensoring over Λ_π with Λ_π/I_κ yields the isomorphism 𝕋_{K^p_r,κ,O} ⊗_O Î_π ⥲ Hom_O(S^ord_κ(K_r,O)_{m_π},O) = H^{d,ord}_{κ^D}(K_r,O)_π.
issues.correction: Also invoke control for the module of ordinary forms (Hida’s (33): (S^ord_ω ⊗ R[ψ])/p_{κψ} ≅ S^ord_κ(K_r,ωω_κψ,R[ψ])), in the level-r/nebentypus form, and tensor over Λ^o_π with Λ^o_π/I_κ; κ must be sufficiently regular.
issues.reason: Theorem 7.3.1(ii) only identifies 𝕋_π ⊗ Λ^o_π/I_κ with the finite-level Hecke algebra; the right-hand side requires Hom_O(lim_r S^ord_κ(K_r,O)_{m_π},O) ⊗ Λ^o/I = Hom_O(S^ord_κ(K_r,O)_{m_π},O), a separate control statement for forms. Also Theorem 7.3.1 is over Λ^o_π, not Λ_π. Defence: (33) (Hida) provides it for regular weights. Independent check: Quotation checked on the page image (p. 111). Tensoring 𝕋_π ⊗ Î_π ≅ M := Hom_O(lim_r S^ord_κ(K_r,O)_{m_π},O) with Λ/I gives (𝕋_π/I) ⊗ Î_π ≅ M/IM. Theorem 7.3.1(ii) identifies only 𝕋_π/I with the finite-level Hecke algebra. The step also needs M/IM ≅ Hom_O(S^ord_κ(K_r,O)_{m_π},O). The restriction map M → Hom(S_r,O) is surjective (Lemma 6.6.14), but injectivity modulo I is a rank statement about the space of forms. That is Hida's control theorem for forms ((33)–(34), p. 35), used in dual form and at level r with nebentypus (cf. sourceIssues E117). It does not follow from control for the Hecke algebra. For unitary groups there is no perfect q-expansion duality between T and S that would make it follow. The input is available in the paper, but it is not invoked. Minor: Theorem 7.3.1 is over Λ^o_π, while §7.3.4 tensors over Λ_π. Versions: v4 p. 106 identical. Reach: the proof (of the finite-level isomorphisms in §7.3.4 and Proposition 7.3.5).

issues.locator: Proposition 7.3.5 and the sentence before it, pp. 111–112, in arXiv v5; v4 p. 106 (‘a simple rephrasing of the preceding discussion’)
issues.printed: The source presents Proposition 7.3.5, the Minimality Hypothesis, as a consequence of Hypotheses 7.3.2 and 7.3.3, the preceding discussion, and Theorem 7.1.1, referring to the comment after Hypothesis 7.3.3. issues.correction: The derivation (specializing 𝕋_π ⊗ Î_π ≅ Hom_O(lim_r S^ord_κ(K_r,O)_{m_π},O) via the control theorem) gives the finite-level isomorphism only for κ^1 sufficiently regular, and needs the control theorem for the module of forms (Hida’s (33)) in its level-r/nebentypus form, not just Theorem 7.3.1(ii) for the Hecke algebra. The statement should read ‘for every pair (κ^1,r^1) with κ^1 sufficiently regular’.
issues.reason: Theorem 7.3.1(ii) is stated only for κ sufficiently regular and only concerns 𝕋_π; the step ‘tensoring over Λ_π with Λ_π/I_κ gives 𝕋_{K^p_r,κ,O} ⊗ Î_π ≅ Hom_O(S^ord_κ(K_r,O)_{m_π},O)’ (p. 111) also requires Hom_O(lim S,O) ⊗ Λ/I = Hom_O(S_{r},O), a control statement for forms. For non-regular κ^1 the finite-level Hecke algebra need not be a specialization of 𝕋_π at all. Defence: Hida’s (33) supplies module control in the regular range, and the paper only uses sufficiently regular weights. Note also that the v5 Main Theorem 9.2.2 still lists ‘Proposition-Hypothesis 7.3.5’ as a hypothesis, while Propositions 7.4.13 and 7.4.15 no longer assume it. Independent check: Quotation checked on the page images (pp. 111–112). Proposition 7.3.5 is asserted 'for every pair (κ^1, r^1)' and derived from §7.3.4 and Theorem 7.1.1. §7.3.4 gets the finite-level isomorphism from Theorem 7.3.1(ii), which requires κ sufficiently regular. The derivation also needs control at level r (sourceIssues E117) and control for the module of forms (sourceIssues E118). There is no standing regularity hypothesis in §7.3. Elsewhere the paper adds 'sufficiently regular' explicitly (Proposition 7.4.10, Definition 7.4.11, Lemma 7.4.14, Proposition 7.4.15). For non-regular κ^1 the classical finite-level Hecke algebra need not be a specialization of 𝕋_π (cf. sourceIssues E115), so the argument does not cover those pairs. It is not known whether the statement fails there, hence 'gap'. Nothing downstream is affected, since the proposition is used only at sufficiently regular weights. issues.locator: Lemma 7.4.2(1), p. 114, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 108; absent in v2/v3 (Lemma 7.2.2(i), p. 108)
issues.printed: Item 1 specifies measures φ on T with values in 𝒱 and the condition φ(t·f) = ρ^υ(t)·φ(f), f ∈ C(T,O), t ∈ T.
issues.correction: φ(t·f) = ρ^υ(t)^{−1}·(t·φ(f)) for f ∈ C(T,O), t ∈ T, where t acts on 𝒱 through its Λ-module structure (with the translation convention (t·f)(x) = f(xt); with (t·f)(x) = f(t^{−1}x) the scalar is ρ^υ(t)). This is what the stated equivalence φ(f) = φ_{r,ρ}(f·ρ^υ) with Λ-linear φ_{r,ρ} requires. Alternatively keep the v2/v3 condition φ(t·f) = υ(t)·φ(f) and replace the equivalence by φ_{r,ρ} = φ|_{C_r(T,O)·ρ^υ}.
issues.reason: As printed the right side is a scalar multiple of φ(f). Taking f = ψ a finite-order character (t·ψ = ψ(t)^{±1}ψ) gives (ψ(t)^{±1} − ρ^υ(t))φ(ψ) = 0 for all t, so φ(ψ) = 0 unless ψ^{±1} = ρ^υ; since finite-order characters span the locally constant functions (over O with enough roots of unity), φ = 0 whenever ρ^υ has infinite order (e.g. ρ algebraic). Condition (2) (Λ-linear maps into the Λ-module 𝒱) shows the T-action on 𝒱 must appear. The v2/v3 version φ(t·f) = υ(t)·φ(f) was changed in v4 to the degenerate form. Independent check: Quotation checked on p. 114 (v5) and p. 108 (v4): condition 1 reads φ(t·f) = ρ^υ(t)·φ(f), f ∈ C(T,O), t ∈ T, with ρ: T → O^× fixed, so the right side is the scalar ρ^υ(t) ∈ O^× times φ(f); 𝒱 = V^{ord,cusp}_3(K^p,O) is O-torsion-free and p-adically separated. As printed only φ = 0 qualifies, for every ρ (simpler than the first reading's argument): if f ∈ C_r(T,O) and t ∈ T_r then t·f = f, so (1 − ρ^υ(t))φ(f) = 0; if ρ^υ is non-trivial on every T_r (e.g. ρ algebraic, the case of interest since κ = ρ·α(χ) is sufficiently regular) this gives φ(f) = 0 for all locally constant f; if ρ^υ is trivial on some T_r, summing translates gives φ(1_{aT_r}) = [T_r:T_s]·φ(1_{aT_s}) for all s ≥ r, so φ(1_{aT_r}) ∈ ∩_k p^k𝒱 = 0. By density φ = 0 in both cases, while condition 2 (Λ-linear maps C_r(T,O)·ρ^υ → 𝒱) has non-zero solutions, so the equivalence fails. The printed condition drops the action of t on 𝒱. However, the first reading's correction (revert to the v2/v3 form φ(t·f) = υ(t)·φ(f)) does not fit the v4/v5 lemma, which adds 'The equivalence is such that φ(f) = φ_{r,ρ}(f·ρ^υ)': with (t·g)(x) = g(xt) one has t·(fρ^υ) = ρ^υ(t)·(t·f)ρ^υ, so Λ-linearity of φ_{r,ρ} is equivalent to ρ^υ(t)·φ(t·f) = t·φ(f). The v2/v3 form matches instead the older reading φ_{r,ρ} = φ|_{C_r(T,O)·ρ^υ} (no such formula in v2/v3). Intended meaning recoverable from condition 2 and §5.2.2; downstream arguments use condition 2. Versions: v2/v3 Lemma 7.2.2(i) φ(t·f) = υ(t)·φ(f); v4 p. 108 = v5. Reach: a stated result (Lemma 7.4.2(1) as printed is degenerate); nothing downstream, which works with condition (2).
searched: arXiv:1602.01776 v1 (February 2016), v2, v3 and v4 at the same place: v4 p. 108: φ(t⋅f) = ρ^υ(t)⋅φ(f); v2 and v3 p. 108 (Lemma 7.2.2(i)): φ(t⋅f) = υ(t)⋅φ(f), f ∈ C(T,O).
