issues.locator: Proposition A.2 (statement p. 1001; proof p. 1005) with the proof of Proposition A.1 (p. 1002), published version; arXiv v3 pp. 29 and 32. All three passages checked on page images.
issues.printed: The source assumes π_{v0} supercuspidal, excluding the odd Weil representation for ψ_{v0} if n = 1 (p. 1001). It cites [41, Th. 2.2] for supercuspidality of θ_{ψ_{v0}}(π_{v0}), hence cuspidality of Σ (p. 1002). On p. 1005 it invokes Proposition A.1's proof for cuspidality of Θ^aut_ψ(Π_i) on SO_{2n+1}(A), then [36, Prop. A.7] for {Π_{i,S}} ⊂ Irr_{unit,ψ_S-gen,≤c} G_S with some 0 ≤ c < 1/2.
issues.correction: In Proposition A.2, replace 'if n = 1, then π_{v0} is not the odd Weil representation relative to ψ_{v0}' by 'θ_{ψ_{v0}}(π_{v0}) is supercuspidal'. Equivalently, the L-parameter of π_{v0} relative to ψ_{v0} does not contain S_2; for n = 1 this is exactly the printed condition. With this hypothesis the proof works as written. π_{v0} has zero lift to SO_{2n−1}(F_{v0}) (Kudla), so each Θ^aut_ψ(Π_i) is cuspidal (Rallis's tower property) and nonzero (Furusawa), and ILM Prop. A.7 applies. In the proof of Proposition A.1, justify supercuspidality of θ_{ψ_{v0}}(π_{v0}) for the descent of a supercuspidal τ_{v0} by one of two arguments. Either its L-parameter is irreducible (ILM Th. 3.1), so Bakić–Hanzer Prop. 3.5(1) or Atobe–Gan Th. 4.1 with Kudla applies; or apply Jiang–Soudry Th. 2.2(1) to the generic supercuspidal σ with lift τ_{v0}. Proposition A.1 and everything downstream are unaffected, because A.1 applies A.2 only to such descents: Propositions 6.5 and 6.6, Corollary 6.7, Lemmas 6.8–6.12 and Theorems 1.1 and 1.4.
issues.reason: The step fails for n ≥ 2. Jiang–Soudry Th. 2.2(2) (Ann. of Math. 157 (2003), p. 767, read) asserts that for n ≥ 2 every ψ-generic supercuspidal π of Mp_2n has a supercuspidal lift to SO_{2n+1}. This is false. Take n ≥ 2 and σ′ a generic supercuspidal representation of SO_{2n−1}(F_{v0}). By JS Th. 2.2(1), one extension σ′^ε to O_{2n−1} first occurs at Mp_{2n−2}. By the conservation relation n(σ) + n(σ ⊗ det) = 2 dim V (Sun–Zhu, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 28 (2015); checked on O_1 and O_3), the other extension σ′^{−ε} first occurs at Mp_2n. By Kudla, π := θ(σ′^{−ε}) is irreducible and supercuspidal. π is ψ-generic. The open-orbit computation behind JS Cor. 2.2(3) has stabilizer inside SO_{2n−1}, so both extensions of a generic σ′ give Whittaker functionals. Equivalently, θ_ψ(π) is the generic square-integrable subrepresentation of ν^{1/2} ⋊ σ′ (Gan–Savin). That subrepresentation is not supercuspidal. This agrees with Bakić–Hanzer (arXiv:1902.07357, Prop. 3.5(2)): for ψ-generic cuspidal σ whose parameter contains 1 ⊗ S_2, Θ_ψ(σ) is square-integrable and embeds in ν^{1/2} ⋊ (a generic cuspidal representation of the smaller group). It also agrees with the Atobe–Gan first-occurrence theorem. JS's proof of (2) applies the tower principle, a statement about O_{2n−1}-representations, to an SO_{2n−1}-representation. The lifts to Mp_{2n−2} and Mp_2n come from different extensions σ′^{±}, which is exactly the mechanism of the n = 1 exception they note ('supercuspidal Weil representations of SL̃_2(k) do lift to SO_1(k)'). GI's hypothesis mirrors JS's (and ILM Cor. A.8's) exclusion of the odd Weil representation only. For such a π_{v0}, Proposition A.1's argument does not show that Θ^aut_ψ(Π_i) is cuspidal. It can fail: theta lifts to Mp_2n of globally generic cusp forms on SO_{2n−1} with local component σ′^{−ε} at v0 are globally ψ-generic and cuspidal, and have Π_{v0} ≅ π_{v0}, but their lift to SO_{2n+1} is not cuspidal. Their unramified components have exponent 1/2, so ILM Prop. A.7 does not apply and {Π_{i,S}} ⊄ Irr_{≤c}. The isolation argument then breaks. Proposition A.2 is therefore unproved as printed for n ≥ 2 (not shown false), and its application is sound. Existing corrections searched: no erratum found for GI, ILM (Duke 166) or JS (Annals 157). Haan (arXiv:2212.05234, Th. 3.3) restates JS Th. 2.2 with only the n = 1 exception. Bakić–Hanzer describe the phenomenon without mentioning JS or GI. So as far as found, this is new. (Coordinator: recorded as a gap in a stated result, not an error. The false step is the cited Jiang–Soudry Th. 2.2(2), and Proposition A.2 is unproved for such π_{v0}, not shown false.)

issues.printed: The source describes, up to G_2-conjugacy, a projective system of centralizers Z_{G_2}(φ), finite of order 3 and identified with S_φ. Calling this local component-group system S_[φ], it sets C_[φ] = Z_{G_2}(S_[φ]) and claims that these subgroups of G_2(C) form a projective system of simply connected groups of type A_2.
issues.correction: Restrict this construction to the φ = ι′ ∘ ρ with ρ not self-dual, where Z_{G_2}(φ) = μ_3. For self-dual ρ (S_φ ≅ S_3) a separate parametrisation is needed; Theorem 9.1(i) predicts it: the two characters of S_3 trivial on μ_3 go to the lifts from PGL_3 ⋊ Z/2Z, the 2-dimensional representation to the lift from PD^×.
issues.reason: Lemma 2.4(i) (p. 9) states S_{ι′_*(φ)} = S_3 when φ ∈ Φ_ds(PGL_3) is self-dual, and its proof (p. 10) says the centraliser in G_2(C) is μ_3 or S_3 according as φ ≇ φ^∨ or φ ≅ φ^∨. Self-dual discrete φ exist for every p: for φ trivial on W_F and 3-dimensional irreducible on SL_2, ι′ ∘ φ is the subregular SL_2 of G_2(C), which the proposition itself names, and its component group is S_3. For such φ, S_[φ] does not have order 3; C_[φ] = Z_{G_2}(S_3) is the fixed group of an outer involution of SL_3(C), isomorphic to SO_3(C), not simply connected of type A_2; and Irr(S_3) has three elements, so the bijection j : Irr(S_[φ]) → Z/3Z and the map η ↦ π_η of (b)–(c) are not defined. The count is right (three members; PAPER-GAN-SAVIN-23's desiderata list π_gen[1], π_deg[1], π_sc[1], indexed by 1, r, ε of S_3, for the subregular unipotent parameter), so the statement is plausible, but the 'natural bijection' of Proposition 3.2 and Main Theorem (vii) is not constructed for these φ.

issues.locator: Published Forum Math. Pi 11 (2023), e28, §11.2, Proposition 11.6 and proof, p. 33
issues.printed: The source claims that a subsequence of π_n converges to σ.
issues.correction: For irreducible unitary σ weakly contained in ⊕̂_i π_i, [σ] lies in the Fell closure of {[π_i]}. Do not conclude convergence along a subsequence with strictly increasing original indices. Corollary 11.7 remains valid.
issues.reason: Set G = G_2(Q_5), σ = St_G, π_1 = σ and π_n = 1_G for n ≥ 2. The first summand contains σ, so its coefficients already prove weak containment (Definition 11.5). Every increasing-index subsequence is eventually 1_G and cannot converge to St_G, isolated by Proposition 11.3 since rank G_2 = 2. The proof approximates coefficients from the set of summands and imposes no increasing original indices. BHV author version Exercise F.6.4, printed p. 444 / PDF p. 450, gives the correct weak-containment/Fell-closure equivalence. An isolated point in this closure must be a member, so item 118 and the globalization applications survive.

issues.locator: §9, p. 30 (arXiv v1); checked on the page image
issues.printed: The source describes an apparent D_3 system but claims that the Weyl-invariant quadratic form q(s_1, s_2, s_3) = s_1² + s_2² + s_3³ − ¼(s_1 + s_2 + s_3)², in place of the ordinary dot product, realizes C_3. It lists the simple roots as α_1 = (0, 1, −1), α_2 = (1, −1, 0), α_3 = (0, 2, 2).
issues.correction: On the space of characters (s_1, s_2, s_3), where the paper has just written the Weyl action, the invariant form is s_1² + s_2² + s_3² + (s_1 + s_2 + s_3)², and the simple roots are (0, 1, −1), (1, −1, 0), (−1, 1, 1), of type C_3. The printed form, with s_3² for the misprinted s_3³, is the invariant form on the dual space of cocharacters (u_1, u_2, u_3). There the vectors (0, 1, −1), (1, −1, 0), (0, 2, 2) are the images 2α^∨/q(α^∨) of the simple roots, and α_3^∨ = (0, 1, 1).
issues.reason: The paper's reflection for α_3 is r_3(s) = (s_1 + s_2 + s_3, −s_3, −s_2), which is s − ⟨s, α_3^∨⟩α_3 with α_3^∨ = (0, 1, 1) and α_3 = (−1, 1, 1). The computation gives q(r_3 s) − q(s) = (5/4)((s_1 + s_2 + s_3)² − s_1²) ≠ 0, so q is not invariant on characters. A form a|s|² + b(Σs)² is invariant under r_1, r_2, r_3 exactly when a = b. Its inverse matrix I − J/4 gives the printed q on cocharacters. With the roots (0, 1, −1), (1, −1, 0), (−1, 1, 1) and the printed coroots, the Cartan matrix is [[2, −1, 0], [−1, 2, −1], [0, −2, 2]], of type C_3. All this was checked by computation in exact arithmetic. The positive chamber stated next, Re s_1 > Re s_2 > |Re s_3|, is correct, and nothing later uses q.

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed: no proof, sketch or citation in arXiv v1. The result it supports is not routine. Each piece of a Mackey filtration of I_E(s)|_{G_2} is compactly induced from an orbit stabilizer with a positive-valued character (|det|^s times modulus factors, trivial on unipotent elements). So the nondegenerate characters ψ̄_E in I_0 and ψ in J_2 need a further identification (a root exchange or Fourier argument, cf. Lemma 11.4) beyond the orbit count. A consistency check passes: for the closed orbit G_2/P, with P ⊂ P_E, δ_{P_E}|_M = |det|^5 and δ_P = |det|^3 give the normalized exponent s + 5/2 − 3/2 = s + 1, matching J_4 = I_P(s + 1). Reach: Proposition 5.5 rests on it. Through Proposition 5.5 so do §6.3 (weak dichotomy), (6.5) and Lemma 6.4, and hence Theorem 6.1, Propositions 6.6–6.7, Corollary 6.8, Theorem 7.2(i)–(ii), Theorem 8.5 and the later uses of Propositions 6.6–6.7 (§§12, 15). The results are presumably true, so 'the proof' is the right reach. Whether the published version adds a proof is unknown (closed access).

issues.locator: §2.1, p. 6 (arXiv v1)
issues.printed: It assigns rank 1 to nonzero x ∈ O when N(x) = 0, and rank 2 otherwise. In the latter case, it asserts that F[x], the F-subalgebra generated by x in O, is isomorphic to F[t]/(t² − Tr(x)t + N(x)), described as a separable quadratic F-algebra.
issues.correction: State it for trace-zero elements. A nonzero x ∈ O_0 has rank 1 if N(x) = 0 (then x² = 0). Otherwise it has rank 2, and F[x] ≅ F[t]/(t² + N(x)) is a separable quadratic F-algebra. For general x ∉ F, F[x] ≅ F[t]/(t² − Tr(x)t + N(x)), which is separable iff Tr(x)² ≠ 4N(x).
issues.reason: Checked on the page image. The claim fails for x = 1: N(1) = 1 ≠ 0, but F[1] = F. It also fails for x = 1 + n with 0 ≠ n ∈ O_0 and N(n) = 0, which exists because N is isotropic on O_0 for split O. Since n̄ = −n and n² = −N(n) = 0, N(x) = (1+n)(1−n) = 1 and Tr(x) = 2, so F[x] = F ⊕ Fn ≅ F[t]/(t − 1)², which is not separable. The paper uses the notion only for trace-zero elements (V_1 ⊂ V_2 ⊂ O_0 in §2.4) and for quadratic subalgebras (§2.5), where the corrected statement holds (char F = 0).

issues.locator: §8.1, p. 24 (arXiv v1); checked on the page image
issues.printed: The source claims that the nongeneric self-dual representations of PGL_3 consist precisely of J_B(μ). Here B = TU normalizes U, while μ = χ|−|^{1/2} ⊗ 1 ⊗ χ|−|^{−1/2} is a T-character satisfying χ² = 1. It cites [GS04] for irreducibility of θ(τ) in this case and specifies the label τ^+ through θ(τ^+) = θ(τ) and θ(τ^−) = 0.
issues.correction: The nongeneric self-dual irreducible representations of PGL_3 are the trivial representation 1 = J_B(|·| ⊗ 1 ⊗ |·|^{−1}) and the J_B(μ) above. For τ = 1 the extensions 1^± must be labelled by the same convention: θ(1^+) = θ(1), θ(1^−) = 0. This needs θ(1) irreducible and nonzero, which Theorem 8.2(ii) asserts and [GS04]'s functoriality for non-supercuspidal representations supports.
issues.reason: By Langlands classification, a nongeneric self-dual irreducible representation of PGL_3 has a reducible standard module with self-dual exponents of product 1. For {χ|·|^{1/2}, 1, χ|·|^{−1/2}} (χ² = 1) this gives the J_B(μ). For {|·|, 1, |·|^{−1}} it gives the trivial representation, which the paper omits. Ind(χ St_2 ⊗ 1) is irreducible and generic. The trivial representation has φ_1 = |·| ⊕ 1 ⊕ |·|^{−1}, which contains the trivial representation, so Theorems 8.2(ii) and 8.5(i) make claims about 1^± that the paper never defines. Every other τ^ε in Theorem 8.5 is well defined.

issues.locator: §8.3, Theorem 8.2(i), p. 25, and §8.5, Theorem 8.5(iii), p. 27 (arXiv v1); checked on the page images
issues.printed: Theorem 8.2(i) asserts that τ ≠ τ^∨ gives nonzero, irreducible θ(τ^+), preserving genericity, supercuspidality, discrete series status and temperedness. For nonsupercuspidal τ, it claims θ(τ^+) is nonsupercuspidal, with L-parameter obtained from φ_τ via SL_3(C) ⊂ G_2(C). Theorem 8.5(iii) asserts that θ(τ^ε) is generic exactly when τ is generic and ε = +; its proof presents this as a summary of Theorem 8.2.
issues.correction: Restrict the implication 'τ generic (and ε = +) ⇒ θ(τ^+) generic' in Theorem 8.2(i) and Theorem 8.5(iii) to τ tempered or, more generally, to τ for which the G_2 standard module with L-parameter φ_τ composed with SL_3(C) ⊂ G_2(C) is irreducible. The converse direction (θ(τ^ε) generic ⇒ τ generic and ε = +) is correct as stated, by Lemma 8.1(i).
issues.reason: Take τ = Ind_B^{PGL_3}(|·| ⊗ μ ⊗ |·|^{−1}μ^{−1}) with μ unitary, μ ≠ 1 and μ² ≠ 1. No ratio of the three characters is |·|^{±1}, so τ is irreducible, generic and nontempered, with τ ≇ τ^∨. In §3.3's bookkeeping, the G_2 principal series with χ_i = χ ∘ β_i^∨ equal to (|·|, μ, |·|^{−1}μ^{−1}) carries the parameter φ_τ composed with SL_3(C) ⊂ G_2(C). It is reducible because χ_1 = |·| (reducibility along the long root β_1, whose GL_2-Levi induced representation is reducible). By the standard module conjecture (for principal series: the unique generic constituent is a subrepresentation), the Langlands quotient carrying that L-parameter is nongeneric. So 'θ(τ^+) generic' and 'L-parameter of θ(τ^+) = φ_τ composed with SL_3(C) ⊂ G_2(C)' cannot both hold. [GS04] proves that lifts of non-supercuspidal representations respect Langlands functoriality (abstract), and Theorem 1.3(iii) repeats it, so the genericity clause is the one that fails. This is consistent with Lemma 8.1(i): Θ(τ^+) keeps a Whittaker functional through its generic constituent while its cosocle is nongeneric. Theorem 8.5(v) is unaffected, since it uses (iii) only for discrete series τ. arXiv 2102.00372 has only v1. The published version (Invent. Math. 232 (2023)) is closed access and was not read. GS04's abstract (Cambridge Core page) was read.

issues.locator: §10, opening paragraph, p. 31, and Proposition 10.4, p. 33 (arXiv v1); used in Proposition 15.6, p. 54; checked on the page images
issues.printed: The source says Langlands parameterization is available for every parabolic Levi of PGSp6(F), citing Gan–Takeda [GT] for M1 ≅ GSp4. It invokes Shahidi [Sh] to compute generalized principal series reducibility via parameter L-functions. Proposition 10.4 assumes supercuspidal τ of GSp4(F) with trivial central character and std ∘ ϕτ containing the trivial representation, and asserts that I1(s, τ) is reducible precisely for s = ±1/2.
issues.correction: For non-generic supercuspidal τ, Proposition 10.4 needs an input that the paper does not supply. One option: the Plancherel measure of I_1(s, τ) on PGSp_6 depends only on φ_τ, hence equals that of the generic member of the L-packet computed by Shahidi, and Silberger's theory then gives the reducibility point and the discrete series subquotient. Another option is a direct argument for the Saito–Kurokawa τ_ρ, the only non-generic case used (Prop. 15.6). Alternatively, state Proposition 10.4 for generic τ and prove the τ_ρ case separately.
issues.reason: Shahidi's theorem [Sh] applies only to generic supercuspidal inducing data. The only Plancherel-measure result for non-generic supercuspidals of GSp_4 in [GT] (Main Theorem (vi), checked in arXiv:0706.0952) concerns the Levi GSp_4 × GL_r of GSpin_{2r+5}, a type-B group, not M_1 ≅ GSp_4 in PGSp_6. Proposition 10.4 is stated for every supercuspidal τ with trivial central character and std∘φ_τ ∋ 1, and it has no proof beyond the quoted sentence. It is applied in Prop. 15.6 to τ_ρ, which §15.1 calls 'a nongeneric supercuspidal representation of SO_5'; θ(π_ρ) = δ_1(τ_ρ) needs I_1(1/2, τ_ρ) to be reducible with a discrete series constituent. For τ_ρ, std∘φ_{τ_ρ} = 1 ⊕ (φ_ρ ⊗ S_2) does contain the trivial representation. The statement is expected to hold, since Plancherel measures are invariants of tempered L-packets; so affects = the proof, not a stated result. Not among E1–E22. issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 13.8, p. 47, against Proposition 13.7, notes to (3), p. 47 (arXiv v1); checked on the page images
issues.printed: For i = 3, the proof places B̄ in M_2's first GL_2 factor and invokes second Frobenius reciprocity to obtain Ext^i_{M_2}(Ind_{P×B̄}^{G_2×GL_2}(C_c(GL_2)), τ_1^∨ ⊗ τ_2^∨) ≅ Ext^i_{T×GL_2}(Ind_P^{G_2}(C_c(GL_2)), r_B(τ_1^∨) ⊗ τ_2^∨). issues.correction: With B̄ in the second factor, as in Prop. 13.7: Ext^i_{M_2}(piece (3), τ_1^∨ ⊗ τ_2^∨) ≅ Ext^i_{GL_2×T}(Ind_P^{G_2}(C_c(GL_2)), τ_1^∨ ⊗ r_B(τ_2^∨)). The P_2 case goes through unchanged, since τ_2 is also a positive twist of a tempered representation. In the P_23 case the i = 3 term should still vanish, but by a different reason: τ_2 is now the principal-series factor, and its exponent on the second GL_1 is nonzero because s_1 > s_2 > 0. In the P_12 case the i = 3 term can be nonzero (e.g. τ_2 a Steinberg twist by |det|^{1/2}), so the paper's P_12 argument must be rerun with τ_1 and τ_2 exchanged: Θ(σ) is then a quotient of I_P(τ_1), followed by Lemma 13.4. The conclusion Θ(σ) = 0 is not affected.
issues.reason: Three facts put B̄ in the second factor, against the Lemma 13.8 proof. First, the Ω-model: the A_1 factor of ℳ_2, i.e. the second SL_2, since (1)'s notes make the first SL_2 lie in D_5, acts on M_2(O) from the right, and the stabilizer of a point of Ω_2 contains a Borel of the right-acting factor. The proof of Lemma 13.8 applies second adjointness in the first factor throughout, so its i = 3 steps for P_23 and P_12 are argued for the wrong factor.

issues.printed: It gives the action of (g,(α,β)) ∈ G_2 × (GL_2 × GL_2)/GL_1^∇ on f ∈ C_c(Ω) as ((g,(α,β))·f)(X) = δ′(αβ)·f(ᾱ(g^{−1}X)β), with δ′ unknown and g^{−1} acting entrywise on the octonion matrix X. It says (3), including any unknown twist, must match Lemma 13.4 on the correspondence between generic principal series of G_2 and PGSp_6, and that this compatibility uniquely determines δ′.
issues.correction: No character δ′ of M_2 makes the displayed action yield (2) and (3). The twist on each orbit has to be computed, the kind of twist that is not a character of M_2. The sentence 'this determines δ′ uniquely' should be replaced by that computation. Propositions 13.7(2) and (3) as stated appear correct; they pass the functoriality checks.
issues.reason: Reviewer computation. Take the point X_0 of Ω_2 with first column (v_1; v_2), a basis of the null plane V_2, and second column 0. Its stabilizer is S = {(g,[α,β]) : g ∈ P, β ∈ B̄, ᾱ = β_11^{−1}ℓ(g)^⊤}, where ℓ(g) is the matrix of g on V_2; ᾱ may be read as transpose or as adjugate. On S, det α·det β = det ℓ(g)·β_22/β_11. Every character of M_2 is a power of det α·det β. So the displayed action gives C_c(Ω_2) ≅ c-ind_S(|det ℓ|^e|β_22/β_11|^e). The untwisted (3) is c-ind_S(δ_R^{1/2}|_S) = c-ind_S(|det ℓ|^{3/2}|β_22/β_11|^{1/2}), with R = P × (GL_2×B̄)/GL_1^∇, which needs e = 3/2 and e = 1/2 at once. Similarly on the stabilizer of v ⊗ E_11 in Ω_1 (g ∈ Q, α, β ∈ B̄, α_11β_11 = det ℓ), the stated (2) gives |det ℓ|^{5/2}|α_22β_22|^{3/2}, while the display gives |det ℓ|^e|α_22β_22|^e. The same computation with the paper's explicit characters |det m|² and |ν(m)|³ reproduces Props. 13.5 and 13.6 exactly, so the method is sound. Conversely (3) as stated gives I_P(τ) ↔ I_2(τ ⊗ Ind(ω_τ)), which has the cuspidal data of I_13(τ⊗1) (Lemma 13.4). And (2) gives SO_7-parameters {ξ^{±1}|·|^{±1/2}, |·|^{±1}, 1} on both sides, as G_2(C) ⊂ Spin_7(C) requires. So the derivation offered for (2) and (3) fails, while the statements survive.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 1.3, §8, p.226
issues.printed: It applies Proposition 5.1 to X and (A′, L|A′), then says induction on each irreducible component of X′ yields the conclusion after suitable changes to c3 and c2.
issues.correction: Prove the statement for all irreducible X of degree ≤ d in abelian varieties of dimension ≤ g, not only generating ones. If some component X_i of X′ has a point P₁ ∈ X_i° with ĥ(P₁) ≤ c, apply the induction hypothesis to X_i − P₁ ⊆ B_i := ⟨X_i − X_i⟩. That subvariety generates B_i, its degree is bounded by Lemma 2.5, and ĥ(P − P₁) ≤ 2ĥ(P) + 2ĥ(P₁) ≤ 4c for P ∈ X_i° with ĥ(P) ≤ c. Take the Proposition 5.1 constants as min/max over l ≤ c(g)d^{2g} and dim B_i ≤ g, as in the proof of Theorem 1.2.
issues.reason: X lies in a translate A′ + Q, not in A′, and heights are not translation-invariant. The components of X′ need not generate A, while Theorem 1.3 and Proposition 5.1 assume generation. Proposition 5.1 also depends on the exact l = deg_L A′. The repair uses only the parallelogram law and Lemma 2.5, so Theorem 1.3 holds.

issues.citation: Gao–Ge–Kühne, "The Uniform Mordell–Lang Conjecture", Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS (2026)
issues.reviewReason: Confirmed as a gap. The proof of Theorem 1.3 on p.226 applies Proposition 5.1 to X inside (A', L|A') and then 'the induction hypothesis to each irreducible component of X''. Theorem 1.3 and Proposition 5.1 both require the subvariety to generate the ambient abelian variety, and a component of X' generates only the abelian subvariety B_i of X_i - X_i, inside which it sits as a translate; the Neron-Tate height is not translation invariant, and Proposition 5.1's constants depend on the exact degree of the ambient abelian variety. The repair recorded here is sound: when a component has a point P_1 of height at most c, work with X_i - P_1 ⊆ B_i, whose degree is bounded through Lemma 2.5, and use the parallelogram law h(P - P_1) <= 2h(P) + 2h(P_1); the constants are then the min/max over the bounded ranges of l and dim B_i, exactly as in the proof of Theorem 1.2. So Theorem 1.3 stands and the defect is in the written induction.

issues.citation: Garoufalidis, Scholze, Wheeler and Zagier, "The Habiro ring of a number field" (arXiv:2412.04241)
issues.reviewReason: The sentence is on p. 7, and v1 has the same text. R[ζm] has to mean R ⊗_Z Z[ζm]: the Galois-invariance in (8), the Frobenius in (13) (which must fix ζpm while acting on R) and the rank-r statement on p. 7 all require this. For K = Q(i), ∆ = 12 and R = Z[i,1/6], the class of 4 is {4m′ : (m′,6) = 1}. For odd m′, u = i^{m′}⊗ζ4 satisfies u² = (−1)^{m′+1} = 1, so e = (1−u)/2 is an idempotent other than 0 and 1. Since φp(i) = i^p and p² ≡ 1 (mod 4) for p ≥ 5, φp(e_{4pm′}) = e_{4m′}, so this constant family satisfies (13). The factor on that class is therefore not a domain. Since f_m(t, x) = F(t^{1/m}, ζm + x) (p. 12), the specialisation can only mean t^{1/m} = q^ν, i.e. t = q^{mν} = 1 + O(x) at ζm. With q = ζm e^h, V(q^{mν})/(m²h) = V(1)/(m²h) + Σj (νj/m) log zj + O(h), so the constant term gains a factor ∏ zj^{νj/m}, which the proof of Theorem 5 never has to handle. The claim is plausible but not proved, so kind "gap" affecting the (omitted) proof is right.

issues.locator: §1.4, sentence after (15), p. 7 (arXiv 2412.04241v2; the same text is in v1)
issues.printed: The source asserts 𝓗_R̂ ≅ ∏_p 𝓗_{R∧p}. It describes 𝓗_R as the intersection of P_R with 𝓗_R̂ inside P_R̂ and gives 𝓗_R̂ ≅ 𝓗_{Z[1/∆]} ⊗_Z R̂.
issues.correction: 𝓗_R̂ ≅ 𝓗_{Z[1/∆]} ⊗̂_Z R̂, a completed tensor product (e.g. ∏_p (𝓗_{Z[1/∆]} ⊗ R)∧_p), not the plain tensor product.
issues.reason: Take K = Q and ∆ = 1, which the definition on p. 6 allows, so R̂ = Ẑ. The paper identifies 𝓗_Z with ι(ℍ_Z), and (hdecomp) in §5.1 gives ℍ_R ≅ ∏_{n>k≥0} R in coordinates compatible with base change. So the composite 𝓗_Z ⊗_Z Ẑ → 𝓗_Ẑ → 𝓗_{Z_p} has image ι of the image of (∏ Z) ⊗ Z_p → ∏ Z_p = ℍ_{Z_p}. Here ι is injective (§5.1), and ι(ℍ_{Z_p}) ⊂ 𝓗_{Z_p}. That map is not surjective: every element in its image has all coordinates in one finitely generated Z-submodule of Z_p, while Z_p has uncountable Z-rank. So the plain tensor product is not isomorphic to 𝓗_Ẑ via the natural map, and a completed tensor product must be meant. Nothing later uses the plain form.

issues.locator: §4.4, second bullet, p. 53 (arXiv 2412.04241v2; the same text is in v1)
issues.printed: For a root of unity t = ζ ≠ 1, the source computes Li^{(p)}_n(ζ) using the series for Li^{(p)}_n(t/(1−t)). It states convergence when |t| < p^{1/(p−1)} and evaluates at t = t0 = ζ/(1−ζ), with |t0| = 1.
issues.correction: … we use the series expansion of Li^{(p)}_n(t/(1+t)) in powers of t, which converges for |t| < p^{1/(p−1)}, at t = t0 = ζ/(1−ζ). Equivalently, expand Li^{(p)}_n(z) in powers of z/(1−z), as on p. 18.
issues.reason: At t0 = ζ/(1 − ζ), t0/(1 + t0) = ζ but t0/(1 − t0) = ζ/(1 − 2ζ). Moreover, Li^{(p)}_n(t/(1 − t)) is singular at t = 1/2, where |1/2| = 1 for odd p, so its expansion at t = 0 cannot converge at |t0| = 1. With z = t/(1 + t), Li^{(p)}_1 = (1/p)log((1 + t)^p − t^p), and the coefficients of Li^{(p)}_2 have 5-adic valuations growing like j/4. I implemented the method in this corrected form, and it reproduces (271)–(274).

issues.locator: §4.6, last paragraph, p. 57 (arXiv 2412.04241v2; the same text is in v1)
issues.printed: The source considers three representations, all boundary-parabolic, of the (−2, 3, 7)-pretzel knot, valued in the abelian field K = Q(2 cos(2π/7)). It asserts their perturbative series produce an element of HOK[1/7] and describes the associated Bloch-group element as 3-torsion.
issues.correction: The series gives an element of the module H_{R,ξ} for a nonzero 3-torsion ξ, with 2 and 3 inverted in R as Remark 1.8 requires. Only its cube lies in the Habiro ring (Corollary 1.11(b)), and then with 2 inverted: not in HOK[1/7].
issues.reason: The paper's own figures in the same paragraph contradict membership in HOK[1/7]. The denominator of the x^400 coefficient is 2^1997·3^596·7^466, and it drops to 2^1997·7^466 only after cubing, "illustrating part (b) of Corollary 1.11". So the series itself is not in any Habiro ring with 3 uninverted; it is a section of the twisted module attached to the 3-torsion class. Even its cube keeps 2-power denominators, which is incompatible with coefficients in OK[1/7]. (The denominators themselves were taken from the paper, not recomputed.)

issues.locator: §7, Lemmas 7.1–7.2, pp.21–22 (arXiv v3)
issues.printed: The source gives β = √(a−2)/2 and α = O(aK^{−1/2}), claiming an error of O(√K) when α is set to zero. … Lemma 7.2 asserts R⁺(K) = (1/36) K(log K)² + O(K log K).
issues.correction: The lower limit is α = a√(a²−4)/(2√(K−a²)) ≍ a²K^{−1/2}. Dropping it adds the strip 0 ≤ m < a, which contains E_a(K) ≍ a√K points for a ≤ K^{1/4} and E_a(K) = (K/a)(log(a²/√K) + O(1)) for a ≥ K^{1/4}. Lemma 7.1 needs the term −E_a(K). Summed over a, the strip removes K(log K)²·∫_{1/4}^{1/3}(2t − 1/2)dt = K(log K)²/144. So R⁺(K) = (1/48)K(log K)² + O(K log K), the same constant as R⁻(K) in Lemma 7.3.
issues.reason: The substitution in the proof of Lemma 7.1 is x = 2√(K−a²)/√(a²−4)·y, so x = a corresponds to y ≍ a²/(2√K), not aK^{−1/2}. Direct counts at K = 10^10 give N_a(K) − (paper's main term) = −9.4√K, −97√K, −276√K for a = 10, 100, 1000, while the corrected expression agrees to within 1–20√K. Exact values of R⁺(K) for K = 10^6, …, 10^11, fitted as K(c₂L² + c₁L + c₀) with L = log K, give c₂ = 0.0211 (1/48 = 0.0208, 1/36 = 0.0278). (1.6) leaves C_± unspecified and §10 uses only the order (log K)², so the rest of the paper is unaffected.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 6.1, §6.2 (p = 3) and §6.3 (p = 2), p.21 (arXiv v3)
issues.printed: Under 9|k, the proof calls (3,0,0) nonsingular modulo 9 and claims lifts modulo 3ⁿ for n ≥ 2. … Under k ≡ 1 (mod 4), it calls (1,0,0) nonsingular modulo 4 and claims lifts to higher powers of 2.
issues.correction: The two lifts exist only in part of the stated classes: every x ≡ (3,0,0) mod 9 has M(x) ≡ 9 mod 27, and every x ≡ (1,0,0) mod 4 has M(x) ≡ 1 mod 8. Complete the argument with further points. For p = 2 and k ≡ 5 mod 8, use (x₁, 0, 2) with x₁² = k − 4 ≡ 1 mod 8, a 2-adic square. For p = 3, use (3,0,0) when k ≡ 9 mod 27; when k ≡ 18 mod 27, use (3y, 3, 0) with y² = (k − 9)/9 ≡ 1 mod 3; when 27 | k, use (3, 3, x₃) with x₃ a root of x₃² − 9x₃ + 18 − k, whose discriminant 9 + 4k = 9(1 + 4k/9) is a 3-adic square. Each is an exact ℤ_p-point, since the required square roots exist in ℤ₂, resp. ℤ₃.
issues.reason: The gradient of M at (3,0,0) is 6 and at (1,0,0) it is 2, so the lifting needs M(a) ≡ k modulo 27, resp. 8 (Hensel's lemma in the form ‖F(a)‖ < ‖F′(a)‖²). A direct check confirms the two failing classes, k ≡ 18 mod 27 and k ≡ 5 mod 8 (e.g. k = 18, 5). Counting solutions modulo 3⁴ and 2⁶ confirms that Proposition 6.1 itself holds in every admissible class.

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed: p.13 prints V₂ : (x₁,x₂,x₃) ↦ (x₁, x₁x₃ − x₁, x₃).

issues.printed: The source gives V₃(w) = [[1, 0], [−x₂, −1]] w and V₁V₃(w) = Aw + b, where A = [[−1 − x₂², −x₂], [−x₂, −1]]. … It claims x₂ ≠ 0 makes A infinite-order and Aⁿ − I invertible, and that the V₁V₃(p) orbit is infinite for k ≠ 4. … For k = 4 it selects p = (−1, 2, 0) and invokes the same argument for an infinite orbit.
issues.correction: V₃ acts on w = (x₁, x₃) by [[1, 0], [x₂, −1]], so A = [[x₂² − 1, −x₂], [x₂, −1]] with trace x₂² − 2. A has infinite order only for |x₂| ≥ 2, and Aⁿ − I is invertible only for |x₂| ≥ 3, as the paper itself finds for U₂ in §5.2.3. Run the argument with planes x₂ = c, |c| ≥ 3. To show Zariski density for every k, use the points (−t² + k − 4, −t² + t + k − 4, 2) of the parametric family, whose x₂ = −t² + t + k − 4 is unbounded, instead of the single base point (k − 4, k − 4, 2).
issues.reason: x₃ ↦ x₁x₂ − x₃ is linear in w with matrix [[1, 0], [x₂, −1]]. With the correct A the base point p = (k − 4, k − 4, 2) has x₂ = ±1 for k = 5, 3, where A has order 3 and (A² + A + I)b = 0. Its V₁V₃-orbit then has exactly 3 points (checked for k = 3, 5), so the claim "the orbit V₁V₃(p) is infinite if k ≠ 4" fails. For k = 4 and (−1, 2, 0), A is parabolic and Aⁿ − I is singular; the orbit is nevertheless infinite (checked). The density statement for U₁ survives with the repair.

issues.printed: The proof claims |x̂₁| ≥ 2 makes the SL₂(ℤ) element infinite-order. Because it acts away from the origin, it claims an infinite orbit whose Zariski closure includes the conic {x₁ = x̂₁} ∩ V_k.
issues.correction: For |x̂₁| ≥ 3 this is right: the slice is an irreducible conic (k ≠ x̂₁²). For |x̂₁| = 2 the slice is the pair of lines (x₂ ∓ x₃)² = k − 4, the element [[±2, −1],[1, 0]] is parabolic, and for x̂₁ = 2 it preserves x₂ − x₃, so the orbit lies on one line and its Zariski closure is that line, not the slice. The argument only needs a curve in the plane x₁ = x̂₁ in the closure, which still holds.
issues.reason: At x₁ = 2 the equation becomes x₂² + x₃² − 2x₂x₃ = k − 4, and (x₂, x₃) ↦ (2x₂ − x₃, x₂) maps x₂ − x₃ to itself. Such points exist for k = 4 + w² (e.g. k = 5, the point (2, 1, 0)), which (1.5) allows when k is not a square. The finiteness step "infinitely many x̂₁ give infinitely many distinct curves" is unaffected.

issues.reason: Prime-to-p degree alone does not imply tameness of a connected cover. In characteristic 2 take A=F2[[s,t]], U=Spec A[1/(st)], and the monic cubic X^3+sX+t. At the t-divisor the quadratic residue factor X^2+s gives a purely inseparable residue extension of F2((s)), so the cover is not tame. The missing justification is supplied by the finite-group torsor hypothesis, as already outlined in item 99; the lemma itself survives.

issues.citation: Gleason–Lim–Xu, "The connected components of affine Deligne–Lusztig varieties", Inventiones Mathematicae (2026)
issues.reviewReason: Confirmed, with a sharper statement. The counterexample is right: take F = underline(Z_p) x Spa(C,O_C) with the discrete group Z acting by translation. Then |F| = Z_p, |G| = Z_p/Z carries the quotient topology by the first half of the lemma, and every Z-invariant open subset of Z_p is empty or everything (a ball a + p^n Z_p meets every class because Z surjects onto Z/p^n), so |G| is indiscrete and pi_0(G) is a point while the set pi_0(F)/K = Z_p/Z is uncountable. What the proof establishes is that pi_0, being a left adjoint to the inclusion of totally disconnected spaces, commutes with the colimit computed in totally disconnected spaces; under that reading the lemma is true but empty of the content its three noncompact applications need, and under the set-level reading it is false. The applications at Proposition 3.12 (TeX l. 1336), Proposition 6.6(2) (l. 2285) and Lemma 6.12 (l. 2479) all quotient by the noncompact G(Q_p) or Gamma_K and all want the set-level reading; the applications by a compact group - the Iwahori at l. 674 and l. 2409, and the profinite Gamma_K at l. 2495 - are unaffected, since a quotient of a profinite set by a profinite group is again profinite. I add that the conclusions of those three applications are not contradicted: each is an assertion that a torsor under a locally profinite group over a connected base has transitive action on the components of its total space, which is the statement to prove in place of the printed lemma.

issues.locator: §2.5, Definition 2.16(c), p. 525
issues.printed: The source relates two root choices s, s′ for p by σ in Gal(Q̄/Q). For X, Y ∈ K_0(Var_G/R)[(L^{1/r})_{r≥2}], it claims #^{s,χ}_{F_q}(X) = #^{s,χ}_{F_q}(Y) exactly when #^{s′,χ}_{F_q}(X) = #^{s′,χ}_{F_q}(Y), thereby defining an unambiguous relation #^χ_{F_q}(X) = #^χ_{F_q}(Y).
issues.correction: This holds when q = p is a prime not dividing the order m of the values of χ: x^N − p is Eisenstein at every prime of Q(ζ_m) above p, so for each N some σ ∈ Gal(Q̄/Q(ζ_m)) sends s_N to s′_N, and by compactness one σ works for all r. For q = p^k with k ≥ 2 it fails, so the relation must be taken with a fixed system s. Theorems 2.18–2.19 survive: closed points of Spec R with prime residue field, of characteristic prime to m, have Dirichlet density one, which is all Chebotarev density needs; at those points the positive-real-root counts used in Theorem 2.19 and the Tate-root counts used in the proof of Theorem 2.18 agree.

issues.locator: §2.5, Lemma 2.17 and its proof, pp. 525–526
issues.printed: Lemma 2.17 claims that one finite étale extension R′ of R supplies lisse ℓ-adic sheaves Q_ℓ(1/r) on Spec R, representing rth roots of Q_ℓ(1) for every r ≥ 1. Its construction of a continuous ℓ-adic representation of π_1^ét(Spec R′, C), for r ≥ 1, is exp((1/r) log(ρ|π_1^ét(Spec R′,C))).
issues.correction: The formula defines Q_ℓ(1/r) only for r prime to ℓ (or of small ℓ-adic valuation), since exp does not converge on ℓ^{−k}V for large k. The lemma holds for all r with Q̄_ℓ-coefficients: ρ(π_1(R′)) is procyclic with a generator u; choose compatible principal-unit roots u_k of u with u_k^ℓ = u_{k−1}, and set Q_ℓ(1/ℓ^k) = (g ↦ u_k^{a(g)}) where ρ(g) = u^{a(g)}. Theorem 2.18 needs only the finitely many r dividing the denominators of the α_i, β_j, so its proof survives with Q̄_ℓ-coefficients or with ℓ chosen prime to those denominators. The sheaves live on Spec R′[1/ℓ], not Spec R.
issues.reason: Let R ⊂ C be of finite type over Z. The fraction field of R′ is finitely generated over Q, so the cyclotomic character ρ of π_1(Spec R′[1/ℓ]) has open image, which contains 1 + ℓ^m for some m. A Q_ℓ-valued character χ is Z_ℓ^×-valued, and for odd ℓ, (Z_ℓ^×)^{ℓ^k} ⊂ μ_{ℓ−1}·(1 + ℓ^{k+1}Z_ℓ). For k ≥ m, 1 + ℓ^m ∉ μ_{ℓ−1}·(1 + ℓ^{k+1}Z_ℓ), so χ^{ℓ^k} = ρ is impossible. The same bound applies over any fixed finite extension of Q_ℓ.

issues.locator: §3.2, Lemma 3.12 (second assertion) and Corollary 3.13, p. 534
issues.printed: The source asserts ker(Br(P) → Br(P_{F^s}))[r] / Br(F)[r] ≃ Ext²(A, μ_r) as a canonical equivalence.
issues.correction: Replace Br(P)[r] by H²_ét(P, μ_r) (μ_r-gerbes): ker(H²_ét(P, μ_r) → H²_ét(P_{F^s}, μ_r)) modulo the image of H²(F, μ_r) is isomorphic to H¹(F, A^∨[r]) ≅ Ext²(A, μ_r), by Hochschild–Serre with H¹(P_{F^s}, μ_r) ≅ A^∨[r] and H³(F, μ_r) = 0. Corollary 3.13, deduced from it, should be read the same way, and in that form both sides are H¹(F, A^∨[r]). The proof of Lemma 6.7, the only place the corollary is used, concerns μ_r-gerbes and needs only this form.
issues.reason: Let F = Q_5, E : y² = x³ − x (good reduction at 5, E[2] rational), r = 2 and P = A = E. With the unit section and H³(F, G_m) = 0, ker(Br E → Br E_{F^s}) = Br(F) ⊕ H¹(F, Pic(E_{F^s})), and Pic(E_{F^s}) = E(F^s) ⊕ Z equivariantly, so the left side is H¹(F, E)[2] ≅ (E(F)/2)^*. Ẽ(F_5) ≅ Z/2 × Z/4 (8 points, (2, 1) of order 4) and E_1(Q_5) is pro-5, so this has order 4. The right side is H¹(F, E[2]), of order |E[2](F)|² = 16 by the local Euler characteristic formula (Theorem 3.4). The discrepancy is the Kummer term E(F)/2 in 0 → E(F)/2 → H¹(F, E[2]) → H¹(F, E)[2] → 0, which Br(−)[2] loses: H²(E, μ_2) → Br(E)[2] has kernel Pic(E)/2.

issues.printed: The source declares this sequence short exact: 0 → Br(K) → Br(X)_K → H¹(K^sep, Pic(X_{K^sep})) → 0.

Br(K) → Br(X)_K is injective when X(K) ≠ ∅, and the last map is onto when H³(K, G_m) = 0 (for example K local). Lemma 6.5, the only use, needs only exactness at Br(X)_K, which always holds.

issues.locator: §5.1, Lemma 5.1 (a), (c), (d) and the proof of (b), pp. 548–549
issues.printed: Part (a) asserts that any uniformiser π_L in L gives a subfield F(π_L) that is Galois, totally ramified and has degree e over F. Part (c) describes Γ as finite and abelian, a split extension with cyclic quotient of order d/e and cyclic kernel of order e.
issues.correction: Γ is abelian (Frobenius acts on I ≅ μ_e through x ↦ x^q, trivially since μ_e ⊂ F) but need not split, and F(π_L) has the stated properties only for suitable π_L, and only when Γ splits. (d) holds when Γ splits. The formula ξ ↦ (π_L ↦ ξπ_L) in (b) is a field automorphism only when π_L^e ∈ F; the canonical isomorphism is σ ↦ σ(π_L)/π_L mod m_L. Repair: replace L by L′ = L·F_d with F_d the unramified extension of degree d. Then Gal(L′/F) = Γ ×_{Z/f} Z/d, where (g, 1), with g a Frobenius lift of order dividing d, generates a complement of I. Moreover X_{L′/F} ≅ X_{L/F} by Lemma 5.3 applied to Spec O_{L′} → Spec O_L. With this, the uses of the splitting in Lemmas 5.5, 5.7, 5.8, Proposition 5.15 and Theorem 5.20 go through.
issues.reason: F = Q_5, L = Q_5(y) with y⁴ − 20y² + 50 = 0: y² = 5(2 + √2) with 2 + √2 a unit (norm 2) and √2 ∉ Q_5, so Q_5(√2) is unramified quadratic and L/Q_5(√2) is ramified quadratic; e = f = 2 and d = 4. y_1y_2 = 5√2 ∈ Q(y), so Q(y)/Q is cyclic quartic (50 ∈ 2·Q^{×2}) and Γ ≅ Z/4, with I its subgroup of order 2. μ_4 ⊂ Q_5 and the extension is tame, so every hypothesis of §§5.1–5.4 (including μ_{e²} ⊂ F_5) holds, but Z/2 ↪ Z/4 has no complement, and every uniformiser generates L (the only proper subfield is unramified), so F(π_L) has degree 4 ≠ e. Such L occur as T_φ in Proposition 5.25: for M = [A¹/μ_4] over Z_5, the point a = 25u with u a non-square unit gives Q_5(a^{1/4}) of this type. Separately, (a) fails for π_L = 5u with u ∈ O_L^× ∖ O_F in an unramified quadratic L (e = 1).

issues.locator: §5.3, proof of Lemma 5.14, p. 555
issues.printed: The source associates an Azumaya algebra B, of rank r² over a Deligne–Mumford stack X, with a P^r-bundle, the Brauer-Severi variety Y_B —p_B→ X. It asserts that splitting of p_B^*B on X is equivalent to the existence of a section of Y_B → X.

issues.printed: The source gives m/n (m, n∈ℤ, (m, n)=1) ↦ (n/d)⁻¹ m(mod f_d), with d=(n, N). It claims coprimality of n/d with f_d and says the result is determined solely by the class of m/n modulo Γ.
issues.correction: m/n ↦ (n/d)·m (mod f_d) (equivalently m⁻¹(n/d)⁻¹); the printed map is Γ₀(N)-invariant only when (ℤ/f_dℤ)^× has exponent ≤ 2, i.e. f_d | 24.
issues.reason: For γ = (a b; c d′) ∈ Γ₀(N): m′ = am + bn, n′ = cm + d′n, (n′, N) = d, n′/d ≡ d′(n/d) and m′ ≡ am (mod f_d), ad′ ≡ 1 (mod N); hence m′(n′/d) ≡ m(n/d) but (n′/d)⁻¹m′ ≡ a²(n/d)⁻¹m (mod f_d). Example N = 25: γ = (−2 1; −25 12) ∈ Γ₀(25) sends 2/5 to 1/10; the printed invariant gives 2 and 2⁻¹ = 3 (mod 5), the corrected one 2 and 2. Brute force (SCR/t_cusp.py): violations of the printed invariant for N = 25, 49, 50, none of the corrected one for N ∈ {8, 9, 16, 25, 27, 32, 45, 49, 50, 72}. issues.correction: Add the hypothesis that 𝔞₁, 𝔞₂ are prime to D (possible in every class, keeping 𝔫 | 𝔞_i), or replace (3.10) by the exact conditions (A₂/√D)(β − α) ∈ 𝔫𝔞₁⁻¹ and (A₂/√D)(τ̄₂β − τ₂α) ∈ 𝔞₁⁻¹.
issues.reason: The converse divides by √D; at a ramified 𝔭 | 𝔞₁ (or 𝔞₂) the numbers A₁A₂α, A₁A₂β lie in 𝔭 automatically, so (3.10) carries no information there. Counterexample (SCR/t_rho.py, t_rho2.py; recomputed independently by the reviewer): D = −7, N = 2, β = 1, m = 3 (3 inert, h = 1), τ₂ from [2, 1, 1], 𝔞₁ = ℤ14 + ℤ(21+√−7)/2 from [14, 21, 8] (N(𝔞₁) = 14, 𝔞₁ ⊂ (√−7)): the true γ-counts are ρ(1), ρ(2), ρ(4), ρ(8) = 2, 2, 6, 8 while the (α, β)-set of (3.11) has 4, 4, 12, 16 elements (every n with 7 ∤ n doubles; n = 14, 28 agree); with 𝔞₁ from [2, 1, 1] (prime to 7) the two counts agree for all n ≤ 29. issues.locator: Chapter II, §5, normalization of the uniformizing parameter g at an elliptic point, p. 250 (display after 'In general, ω has order 1/u − 1 at x'), Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
issues.printed: ω = (g^{1/u} + higher degree terms) dg/g
issues.correction: ω = (1/u)(g^{1/u} + higher degree terms) dg/g, i.e. ω = d(g^{1/u})·(1 + …); equivalently, keep the printed display with g replaced by u^u·g.
issues.reason: At a Heegner point x with u > 1 the local parameter of X₀(N) is (w − z)^u·(unit), and ω = 2πiη⁴(w) dw. With the printed normalization one gets g = (2πiη⁴(z)(w − z)/u)^u(1 + o(1)), so log|g(y)|_v − u log|2πiη⁴(z)(w − z)|_v → −u log|u|_v ≠ 0, contradicting (5.5) (p. 251), which is what (5.6)–(5.8) use. With the corrected normalization g = (2πiη⁴(z)(w − z))^u(1 + o(1)) and (5.5) holds. Independent check against the non-archimedean normalization Ch. III (8.3) (p. 263, N = 1): from ω^{⊗6} = Δ(dq/q)^{⊗6} and q dj/dq = −E₆j/E₄ one gets ω = dj/(j^{2/3}(j − 1728)^{1/2}) up to a root of unity; at j = 1728 (u = 2) the corrected normalization gives ∂/∂t = 2⁶·3⁴ ∂/∂j and the printed one 2⁸·3⁴ ∂/∂j, and at j = 0 (u = 3) the corrected one gives |2⁹·3^{3/2}| and the printed one |2⁹·3^{9/2}|; (8.3), read on a full-resolution IIIF crop of image 00000269, prints 'α ≡ j(x)^{2/3}(j(x) − 1728)^{1/2} (mod μ₀), j(x) ≠ 0, 1728; ≡ 2⁶ · 3⁴, j(x) = 1728; ≡ 2⁹ · 3^{3/2}, j(x) = 0' — exactly the three values computed with the corrected normalization (the generic value j^{2/3}(j − 1728)^{1/2} is the same for both, since u = 1 there). So (5.5), (5.6)–(5.8) and (8.3) are mutually consistent and only the display on p. 250 is off. Under the paper's standing assumption that D is odd this concerns only D = −3 (u = 3) with r_A(m) ≠ 0. The display on p. 250 was re-checked on imgHR/p250.jpg and a zoomed IIIF crop of image 00000256: it reads 'ω = (g^{1/u} + higher degree terms) dg/g'. (Also recorded by an earlier worker: new (Conrad 2004, §9, conrad.txt pp. 34–38 and 42: the factor u_x^k in (9.4), (9.8) and Theorem 9.2, and the archimedean uniformizer g_{z_v}(z′) = 2πiη⁴(z_v)(z′ − z_v) of Theorem 9.6, which Conrad says is 'exactly the archimedean height contribution which is computed in [GZ, Ch II, (5.3), (5.5)]'; Conrad also says the GZ tangent-vector method is recovered only 'if one avoids the quadratic fields K = Q(√−1) and K = Q(√−3)', but does not name this misprint).)

issues.locator: Chapter III, §1, definition of 𝓜_{Γ₀(N)} (p. 254) and the description of the cusps (p. 255), Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
issues.printed: The source defines 𝓜_{Γ₀(N)} as the algebraic stack of cyclic degree N isogenies (1.1) φ: E → E′ between generalized elliptic curves over S, requiring A = ker φ to meet all irreducible components in every geometric fibre. It takes X as the coarse moduli scheme of 𝓜_{Γ₀(N)}. It describes Cusp(d) using Néron polygon diagrams with A = ker φ isomorphic to μ_d × dℤ/Nℤ.
issues.correction: 'A = ker φ is isomorphic to μ_d × dℤ/Nℤ' holds only when gcd(d, N/d) = 1. In general, at the cuspidal points of Cusp(d) the kernel A is a cyclic group scheme of order N that is an extension of dℤ/Nℤ ≅ ℤ/(N/d)ℤ by μ_d, and it is non-split when f = gcd(d, N/d) > 1 (on a Néron polygon, e.g. ⟨(ζ_N, 1)⟩ ⊂ G_m × ℤ/(N/d)ℤ). The coarse moduli scheme X of (1.1)–(1.2) is still the Deligne–Rapoport and Katz–Mazur model of X₀(N) (Česnavičius 2017, §1.1), so the model itself needs no change; but for N not squarefree the stack 𝓜_{Γ₀(N)} of (1.1)–(1.2) differs from the Deligne–Rapoport stack at these cusps, and Česnavičius' refined Γ₀(N)-structures give the correct moduli description there.
issues.reason: (i) Check: Cusp(d) ≅ Spec ℤ[μ_f] is flat over ℤ, so its geometric points include characteristic-0 points; there μ_d × dℤ/Nℤ ≅ ℤ/d × ℤ/(N/d) is not cyclic when f = gcd(d, N/d) > 1, contradicting the cyclicity condition (1.2) that defines 𝓜_{Γ₀(N)}. On a Néron polygon a cyclic A of order N meeting every component is e.g. ⟨(ζ_N, 1)⟩ ⊂ G_m × ℤ/(N/d), a non-split extension. (ii) Česnavičius, 'A modular description of X₀(n)', Algebra & Number Theory 11 (2017) (arXiv:1511.07475), abstract: 'when a positive integer n is not squarefree, even over ℂ the moduli stack that parametrizes generalized elliptic curves equipped with an ample cyclic subgroup of order n does not agree at the cusps with the Γ₀(n)-level modular stack'. The stack of (1.1)–(1.2) is exactly that naive stack. Katz–Mazur [21] treat [Γ₀(N)] only for elliptic curves and compactify by normalization, so the generalized-elliptic-curve description is not in the cited sources for non-squarefree N. Wording re-checked on imgHR/p254.jpg and p255.jpg ('A = ker φ is isomorphic to μ_d × dℤ/Nℤ'). (Also recorded by an earlier worker: Česnavičius 2017 (for the moduli description at the cusps); the inconsistency with the stated group structure μ_d × dℤ/Nℤ is new. The atlas stage ModularCurvesPartII:R13.2 already routes around it ('Follow Česnavičius' refined description when the naive cyclic-subgroup formulation fails')..)
issues.known: new (for this sentence). The underlying failure of the naive cyclic-subgroup stack at the cusps for non-squarefree N is in print: K. Česnavičius, A modular description of X₀(n), Algebra & Number Theory 11 (2017), §§1.1–1.3 (also Edixhoven 1990, 1.1.1.1, and B. Conrad, Arithmetic moduli of generalized elliptic curves, 2007); none of these comments on this sentence of the paper.

issues.citation: Gross and Zagier, "Heegner points and derivatives of L-series", Inventiones mathematicae 84 (1986), 225–320
issues.reviewReason: Read on p. 255 (image): 'The component Cusp(d) corresponds to diagrams of Néron polygons where A = ker φ is isomorphic to μ_d × dℤ/Nℤ. It has φ(f) geometric points, where f = g.c.d.(d, N/d), and one has an isomorphism Cusp(d) ≃ Spec ℤ[μ_f]'; the definition (1.1)–(1.2) on p. 254 matches the quote. The contradiction is right: Cusp(d) ≅ Spec ℤ[μ_f] has characteristic-0 points, where μ_d × dℤ/Nℤ ≅ ℤ/d × ℤ/(N/d) is not cyclic when f > 1, contradicting (1.2). Česnavičius (arXiv:1511.07475, §1.2) gives exactly this example for N = p²: on the standard p-gon over ℂ the ample cyclic subgroup is ⟨(ζ_{p²}, 1)⟩ ⊂ G_m × ℤ/pℤ, a non-split extension. Error, affects nothing (only Cusp(1) and Cusp(N), where f = 1, are used later) is right. One part of the correction needs changing: Česnavičius §1.1 says the naive stack 'is algebraic, has X₀(n) as its coarse moduli space, and agrees with X₀(n) on the elliptic curve locus'; what differs for non-squarefree N is the stack at the cusps (it is not Deligne–Mumford there, §1.2), not the coarse model. So GZ's model X is the right one and need not be replaced; only the description of A at Cusp(d) (and anything about the stack's automorphism groups at such cusps) is wrong. Česnavičius cites [GZ86] only for the regularity of X at the cusps (Prop. III.1.4), without comment on p. 255, so 'new' stands for this sentence, with the underlying phenomenon known.

issues.locator: Chapter III, §2, paragraph after (2.1), p. 256, Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
issues.printed: The source uses algebraic closedness of k to claim that Hom_S(y, x) does not depend on which diagrams represent x and y.
issues.correction: True for S = W (a complete DVR of characteristic 0 with algebraically closed residue field: two W-diagrams inducing the same W-point are isomorphic, Conrad Theorem 2.6) and hence for the reductions to W/πⁿ of fixed W-diagrams, which is the only way §§4–9 use it; false for general complete local S (e.g. artinian S) at points with Aut_k ≠ ⟨±1⟩, where Hom_S must be defined for chosen diagrams.
issues.reason: Counterexample: p ≥ 5, N = 2, E: y² = x³ − x over 𝔽̄_p with p ≡ 1 (mod 4) (ordinary, j = 1728), A = ⟨(0,0)⟩, which is stable under [i]: (x, y) ↦ (−x, iy); so Aut_k(x₀) = μ₄. The universal deformation ring is W[[T]] with Aut/±1 = ℤ/2 acting faithfully (Conrad p. 12), linearizably T ↦ −T, so the complete local ring of X is W[[T²]] (Conrad Lemma 4.2). Over S = k[ε]/(ε²) the deformations T ↦ 0 (constant) and T ↦ ε both give T² ↦ 0, i.e. the same S-point of X, but they are not isomorphic: the constant one has Aut_S = μ₄, while [i] carries T ↦ ε to T ↦ −ε ≠ ε, so the other has Aut_S = ±1. Hence Card Hom_S(y, y)_{deg 1} is 4 or 2 depending on the representing diagram. Wording re-checked on imgHR/p256.jpg. (Also recorded by an earlier worker: new (Conrad 2004 restricts to W-diagrams: Theorem 2.6 and Lemma 4.2, conrad.txt pp. 6 and 11).)

issues.citation: Gross and Zagier, "Heegner points and derivatives of L-series", Inventiones mathematicae 84 (1986), 225–320
issues.reviewReason: Read on p. 256 (image): 'Using the fact that k is algebraically closed, one can check that the definition of Hom_S(y, x) is independent of the diagrams chosen to represent the points x and y.' The statement is for any complete local S with algebraically closed residue field (p. 255, §2). The counterexample works: for p ≡ 1 (mod 4), p ≥ 5, N = 2, E: y² = x³ − x, A = ⟨(0,0)⟩ is stable under [i], so Aut_k = μ₄; μ₄/±1 acts on the Serre–Tate parameter by q ↦ q⁻¹ (ι(i)² = −1 in ℤ_p), faithfully and linearizably T ↦ −T, and the complete local ring of X is the ring of invariants (Conrad, Lemma 4.2: 'the complete local ring of X at the closed point y₀ of y is the subring of Aut(y₀)-invariants in the universal deformation ring'). Over S = k[ε]/(ε²) the deformations T ↦ 0 and T ↦ ε define the same S-point of X but have automorphism groups μ₄ and ±1, so Hom_S(y, y)_{deg 1} has 4 or 2 elements depending on the diagram. Conrad works only with W-models and notes (text before Theorem 4.1) that 'such models over W are unique up to non-unique isomorphism' (by his Theorem 2.6), which is the case GZ use. Error, affects nothing: right.

issues.locator: Chapter III, §8, convention (8.1), p. 263, Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
issues.printed: Convention (8.1) sets (x · x) = ord_v(α), with α∂/∂t chosen as a basis of T_x X, a free W-module.
issues.correction: (x · x) = ord_v(α), where ∂/∂t = α·(a basis of T_x X); equivalently α^{-1}∂/∂t is a basis of T_x X, or αω_x is a basis of the cotangent line when ω_x is the covector dual to ∂/∂t. This is Conrad's α_x.
issues.reason: (i) Derivation. Take f with ord_x f = 1, write f = T·h with T the integral local parameter of the section x, and normalise g by dg(∂/∂t) = 1. The local symbol of Ch. II (5.1)/(5.3) gives ⟨x, div f⟩_v = log|(f/g)(x)|_v. If ∂/∂t = c·∂/∂T, then (T/g)(x) = c, so the self-intersection that makes (0.2) hold is ord_v(c), with c defined by ∂/∂t = c·basis. (ii) Consistency. With that reading, (8.2) (ord_v α = ½Σ(#Aut_{W/π^n} − #Aut_W) ≥ 0) and (8.3) (α ≡ j^{2/3}(j−1728)^{1/2}, read on the high-resolution scan) are correct. For N = 1 one computes ω = η⁴dq/q = −j^{−2/3}(j−1728)^{−1/2} dj, so ∂/∂t = −j^{2/3}(j−1728)^{1/2}∂/∂j. Under the printed wording, α would be the reciprocal j^{−2/3}(j−1728)^{−1/2}, with ord_v(α) ≤ 0, contradicting (8.2) and (8.3). Conrad's Theorem 8.4 defines (x.x) = ord_v(α_x) with α_xω_x a basis of Cot_x, and his (9.9) and Definition 9.5 show that this equals GZ's ½Σ(#Aut_{W/π^n} − #Aut_W) when v ∤ N. (Also recorded by an earlier worker: Conrad 2004, Remark 8.5 ('Our α_x is the reciprocal of the α in [GZ]').)

issues.locator: Chapter III, §8, sentence before Proposition (8.6), p. 264, Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
issues.printed: The source invokes the action of w_N on ω to claim that, when v|n̄, the vector ∂/∂t generates the submodule (N)^u T_x X.
issues.correction: ∂/∂t spans (N)^{−u} T_x X when v|n̄, i.e. ∂/∂t = N^{−u}·(generator). Equivalently ω_x is N^u times a generator of the cotangent line. With the corrected (8.1) (see PAPER-GROSS-ZAGIER-86/E16) this gives (x·x) = −u·ord_v(N), and hence Proposition (8.6) as printed.
issues.reason: When v|n̄ the kernel of φ is étale at p, and x lies on the fibral component through the cusp 0 = Cusp(1) (Prop. 3.1). Near that cusp the integral parameter is q′ = e^{2πiτ′}, τ′ = −1/(Nτ), attached to the Tate curve Tate(q′^N) with subgroup ⟨q′⟩. From η(−1/(Nτ′)) = (Nτ′/i)^{1/2}η(Nτ′) one gets ω = 2πiη⁴(τ)dτ = −N·η⁴(q′^N)dq′/q′. So ω vanishes to order ord_p(N) along that component: it is N times a generator. Equivalently, on the étale-kernel component the forgetful map (E→E′) ↦ E is inseparable (Frobenius), so ω = π_1^*ω_1 ≡ 0 mod p. The dual vector ∂/∂t is therefore N^{−1}·(generator) when u = 1; for u > 1 the normalisation ω = (g^{1/u}+…)dg/g raises this to N^{−u}. Conrad's Lemma 10.1 independently gives ord_{v,x}(Δ) = 6u·ord_v(N) in exactly this étale case, i.e. Δ(dq/q)^{⊗6} = ω^6 is N^6 times a generator. The printed (8.6) value −u r_𝒜(m) ord_p(N) is correct (Conrad Thm 10.4). It is obtained from the printed '(N)^u' only together with the literal (inverted) wording of (8.1), so the two misstatements cancel. (Also recorded by an earlier worker: new (the underlying fact is Conrad 2004, Lemma 10.1 and Theorem 10.4, which do not comment on GZ's sentence).)

issues.locator: Chapter III, §9, choice of the auxiliary prime q and the order S, p. 265 (inert case), and the ramified analogue (9.8), p. 266, Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
issues.printed: The source chooses an auxiliary prime q satisfying (q/l) = (−p/l) at every prime l|D, and sets S = {α+βj: α∈𝔡^{-1}, β∈𝔡^{-1}𝔮^{-1}𝔫, α≡β mod O_𝔣}. In the ramified case it requires (q/p′) = (−1/p′) at each p′≠p dividing D, together with (−q/p) = −1.
issues.correction: For S (with the congruence α ≡ β) to be an order one needs −pq ≡ 1 (mod l) for every prime l|D, i.e. −pq ≡ 1 (mod D); in the ramified case one needs −q ≡ 1 (mod D/p). Both can be imposed alongside GZ's conditions and still met by Dirichlet's theorem. Alternatively use the congruence α ≡ Xβ with N(X) ≡ −pq (mod D) (Mann's S_X, (A.5)/(A.6)). The sign bookkeeping α ≡ ±β in (9.3), (9.8) and in the proof of (9.7) then applies verbatim.
issues.reason: Let l|D and let 𝔣 be the prime over l. Take α = β ∈ 𝔡^{-1} with a simple pole at 𝔣; then α+βj ∈ S. Its reduced norm is N(α)+pqN(β) = (1+pq)N(β), and ord_l N(β) = −1. So the norm is l-integral only if l | 1+pq. GZ's condition says only that −pq is a square mod l (e.g. −pq ≡ 4 mod l is allowed), so S can contain elements of non-integral reduced norm, and is then not an order. The proof of (9.7) also uses −pq ≡ 1 mod l when it concludes that integrality of mN𝔞 = Nα + pqNβ forces α ≡ ±β mod O_𝔣. With −pq ≡ X² one gets only α ≡ ±Xβ. (Also recorded by an earlier worker: Mann, appendix to Conrad 2004, p. 57 ('certainly one does not get an order in (A.5) using X = 1 unless −pq ≡ 1 mod D'; ramified case: 'take X = 1 (as in [GZ]) by also requiring −q ≡ 1 mod D/p'), and Remark A.7.)
issues.known: W. R. Mann, Appendix A to B. Conrad, Gross–Zagier revisited, in Heegner points and Rankin L-series, MSRI Publ. 49 (2004): in the discussion of (A.5) and (A.6) he writes 'If we had also required −pq ≡ 1 mod D, then we could have taken X = 1 (see Remark A.7). This seems to implicitly be the choice made in [GZ]; certainly one does not get an order in (A.5) using X = 1 unless −pq ≡ 1 mod D', and in the ramified case 'Remark A.7 allows us to take X = 1 (as in [GZ]) by also requiring −q ≡ 1 mod D/p'.

issues.reviewReason: Read on p. 265 (image): 'Fix an auxiliary prime q with (q/l) = (−p/l) for all primes l|D' and 'S = {α+βj: α∈𝔡⁻¹, β∈𝔡⁻¹𝔮⁻¹𝔫, α≡β mod O_𝔣}'; ramified case on p. 266: '(q/p′) = (−1/p′) for all p′ ≠ p which divide D and (−q/p) = −1'. Example: D = −7, p = 3 (inert), N = 1, q = 11 satisfies (11/7) = (−3/7) = 1, but α = β = 1/√−7 gives reduced norm 1/7 + 33/7 = 34/7 ∉ ℤ; q = 23 (−pq ≡ 1 mod 7) gives 70/7 = 10. The same holds in the ramified case with −q. Kind: the assertion that S is an order fails for admissible q, so this is an error (a step that fails) rather than a gap; affects the proof (Prop. (9.7) and (9.11) are right, Mann Theorems A.17 and A.20). This is already in print: Mann's appendix to Conrad's paper says 'If we had also required −pq ≡ 1 mod D, then we could have taken X = 1 (see Remark A.7). This seems to implicitly be the choice made in [GZ]; certainly one does not get an order in (A.5) using X = 1 unless −pq ≡ 1 mod D', and for the ramified case 'Remark A.7 allows us to take X = 1 (as in [GZ]) by also requiring −q ≡ 1 mod D/p'. Items 165, 166 and 170 carry the extra congruence.

issues.correction: From R𝔟 = 𝔟S we get R = 𝔟S𝔟^{-1}. Since jb = b̄j, this puts β in 𝔡^{-1}𝔮^{-1}𝔫𝔟𝔟̄^{-1}𝔞̄, not 𝔡^{-1}𝔮^{-1}𝔫𝔟̄𝔟^{-1}𝔞̄. The printed (9.3) (and the class 𝒜𝔅²[𝔮𝔫^{-1}] of 𝔠′ in (9.5)) holds if 'R𝔟 = 𝔟S' is read as '𝔟R = S𝔟', or equivalently if 𝔟 is replaced by 𝔟̄.
issues.reason: For b1 ∈ 𝔟, b2 ∈ 𝔟^{-1} and α+βj ∈ S: b1(α+βj)b2 = b1αb2 + b1βb̄2 j, and right multiplication by a ∈ 𝔞 gives the factor ā. The β-ideal is therefore 𝔡^{-1}𝔮^{-1}𝔫·𝔟·𝔟̄^{-1}·𝔞̄. issues.printed: The source asserts Hom_{W/π^n}(x^σ, x) ≅ End_{W/π^n}(x)·𝔞 in B for any ideal 𝔞 belonging to 𝒜. It gives (7.4) (x, T_m x^σ) = Σ_{b∈R𝔞/±1, Nb=mN𝔞} ½(1+ord_p(Nb_−)).
issues.correction: In (7.4), (8.5) and §9 the representative 𝔞 ∈ 𝒜 must be prime to p. For the congruences in (9.3) and (9.8) it must also be prime to 𝔡, or those congruences must be read modulo 𝔞O_𝔣. (7.3)(2) itself is fine for any 𝔞.
issues.reason: The proof of (7.4) identifies End_{W/π^n}(x)·𝔞 with {b ∈ R𝔞: D·Nb_− ≡ 0 mod p(N𝔭)^{n−1}}. This holds only when 𝔞 is a unit at p. Otherwise the right-hand sum depends on the representative. Replacing 𝔞 by p𝔞 (same class) sends b ↦ pb and raises every ord_p(Nb_−) by 2, so the inert sum grows by 1 per term and the ramified sum by 2 per term. Similarly, if 𝔣 | 𝔞 in (9.3), then α and β are 𝔣-integral and the congruence mod O_𝔣 is vacuous, while R𝔞 still satisfies α ≡ ±β modulo 𝔞O_𝔣. The equality ord_p(n) = ord_p(Nb_−) in (9.6) and (9.10) also uses p ∤ N𝔞. (Also recorded by an earlier worker: Conrad 2004, Theorem 10.5 (hypothesis 'Let 𝔞 represent the ideal class 𝒜 and be prime to p'); Mann's appendix, proof of Theorem A.17 ('a prime-to-p representative', 'gcd(𝔞, D) = 1').)

issues.locator: Chapter III, §9, proof of Proposition (9.7), p. 266, Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
issues.printed: The source counts 2·u²·δ(n) elements arising from the pair, explaining that b is counted modulo sign.
issues.correction: The number is u²·δ(n): elements b ∈ ⊔_{v|p} R_v𝔞/±1, taken over the 2^{t−1} places v attached to the pair (𝔠, 𝔠′).
issues.reason: Each element has weight ½(1+ord_p Nb_−) = ½ord_p(pn) in (x·T_mx^σ)_v, and ⟨c,T_md^σ⟩_v = −2 log p (x·T_mx^σ)_v. In general there are 4u² generator pairs; up to sign they give 2u²; each lies in the models for δ(n) of the 2^t orders R(𝔟I) (I | 𝔡); and these orders cover each isomorphism class, i.e. each place, twice. Total u²δ(n). The final formula (9.7) is correct (Mann, Theorem A.17). (Also recorded by an earlier worker: new (consistent with Mann's count in the proof of Theorem A.17 and his Remark A.19, which divide out exactly this double overcount).)

Hankel's formula ∫_{c−i∞}^{c+i∞} e^{w} w^{−s} dw = 2πi/Γ(s) (c > 0), with w = uz, gives ∫_{1−i∞}^{1+i∞} z^{−s}e^{uz}dz = 2πi u^{s−1}/Γ(s), which is the value used on the next line. With e^{−uz} the integral would be 0: the integrand is holomorphic for Re z > 0 and decays as Re z → +∞. The final value of V_s(0) is correct.

issues.printed: The source places the point in E(K) and claims that changing the Heegner point x affects it only by a sign.
issues.correction: Up to sign and the addition of a rational torsion point, P_K is independent of the choice of x
issues.reason: The 2^s·h Heegner points of discriminant D are permuted simply transitively by W × Gal(H/K) (Chap. II, p. 239; Chap. I, p. 227), so another choice is x' = w_Q(x^τ). Since w_Q acts on the f-part by the eigenvalue λ_Q = ±1, π∘w_Q − λ_Q π is a morphism X₀(N) → E pulling back ω to 0, hence constant, equal to π(w_Q(∞)): the image of a rational cusp, a torsion point of E(ℚ) by Manin–Drinfeld. So P'_K = λ_Q P_K + h·π(w_Q(∞)). This differs from ±P_K whenever P_K has infinite order and h·π(w_Q(∞)) ≠ 0. For instance N = 11, E = X₀(11), π(0) = (0) − (∞) has order 5, and any K with h_K prime to 5 and P_K non-torsion gives such a case. Heights, ranks and all conclusions of §2 are insensitive to torsion.

issues.locator: Chapter V, §1, proof of Theorem (6.3) of Chap. I, p. 308, Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
issues.printed: The source completes {f} to f_1=f, f_2, …, f_d, a basis for S_2(Γ_0(N)), using normalized newforms and an oldform-space basis. It claims a decomposition into components with the transformation behavior of f_j: c_χ = Σ_{j=1}^d c_χ^{(j)}, satisfying T_m c_χ^{(j)} = a_m(f_j) c_χ^{(j)}.
issues.correction: Decompose only along f: by multiplicity one there is an idempotent e_f ∈ 𝕋⊗ℂ projecting onto the f-isotypical part. Write c_χ = e_f c_χ + (1 − e_f)c_χ with T_m e_f c_χ = a_m(f) e_f c_χ for all m; the two parts are orthogonal for <,> (T_m, (m,N) = 1, self-adjoint with different eigencharacters). The generating series of the second part is a form orthogonal to f, so (Σχ(𝒜)g_𝒜, f) = h^{−1}ĥ(c_{χ,f})(f,f) as claimed.
issues.reason: For an arbitrary basis of the oldspace, 'a_m(f_j)' is not an eigenvalue: for f_j = g(dz) with d > 1, a₁(f_j) = 0 while T₁ = 1, so the relation T_m c^{(j)} = a_m(f_j)c^{(j)} would force c^{(j)} = 0. Moreover the Hecke algebra 𝕋 of p. 306 (all T_m, including U_p for p | N) need not act semisimply on oldforms: for a weight-2 newform g of level M with p ∤ M and p³ | N, U_p acts on span{g(p^j z) : 0 ≤ j ≤ 3} by U_p g = a_p g − p g(pz), U_p g(p^j z) = g(p^{j−1}z) (j ≥ 1), with characteristic polynomial t²(t² − a_p t + p) and a one-dimensional kernel. So the stated decomposition with T_m c^{(j)} = a_m(f_j)c^{(j)} for all m cannot hold in general. Only the f-component is used, and f is new, so the conclusion stands with the idempotent argument of the correction (the form used by Gross–Kohnen–Zagier, Math. Ann. 278 (1987), p. 557).

issues.reviewReason: Page image p. 308: the quoted text is present. The printed decomposition fails for oldforms in two ways. For f_j = g(dz) with d > 1, a₁(f_j) = 0 while T₁ is the identity, so T_m c^{(j)} = a_m(f_j)c^{(j)} forces c^{(j)} = 0. And 𝕋 (generated by all T_m, p. 306) need not act semisimply on oldforms: for g a weight-2 newform of level M, p ∤ M and p³ | N, U_p on span{g(p^j z) : 0 ≤ j ≤ 3} (U_p g = a_p g − p g(pz), U_p g(p^j z) = g(p^{j−1}z)) has characteristic polynomial t²(t² − a_p t + p) and a one-dimensional kernel. The repair in the correction (an idempotent e_f of the algebra generated by the T_m, (m, N) = 1, strong multiplicity one, self-adjointness for the height pairing) is sound and is the form Gross–Kohnen–Zagier use for the same step (Math. Ann. 278, p. 557: 'a finite linear combination of Hecke operators which is the identity on f and 0 on its orthogonal complement'). S.-W. Zhang (Invent. Math. 130, §0.3) repeats the printed formalism in higher weight. The reason's example 'U_p on oldforms when p² | N' is imprecise: in weight 2 with p² ∥ N the old space is U_p-semisimple (from level M the eigenvalues are 0 and the two distinct roots of t² − a_p t + p; from level Mp they are a_p = ±1 and 0); non-semisimplicity needs p³ | N. Kind gap, affects nothing: acceptable (the conclusion stands; one could argue 'the proof'). Proposed set corrects the reason.

issues.locator: Chapter II, §2, p. 241, last paragraph (the sentence leading to the display before (2.23)), Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
issues.printed: The source bases the following conclusion on the claim that T_m fixes every cusp.
issues.correction: Since T_m((∞)) = σ₁(m)(∞) and T_m((0)) = σ₁(m)(0) for (m, N) = 1, we have … (the displayed identity is unchanged). T_m does not fix the other cusps in general: it fixes every cusp for all m prime to N if and only if every f_d = (d, N/d) is at most 2, i.e. if and only if N is divisible neither by 9, nor by 16, nor by p² for a prime p ≥ 5.
issues.reason: For a cusp u/v in lowest terms with d = (v, N) and f = f_d, the Γ₀(N)-class is determined by d and the label (v/d)·u mod f (the corrected label of PAPER-GROSS-ZAGIER-86/E1). For a coset representative (a b; 0 δ) of Γ₀(N)\{γ ∈ R_N : det γ = m}, aδ = m, the image (au + bv)/(δv) reduces by g = gcd(au + bv, δv), which is prime to N; the new denominator has the same d, and since f | v the label becomes (m/g²)·(v/d)·u mod f. Taking the representative (m 0; 0 1) with m prime to v gives the factor m, which is not 1 mod f for suitable m once f ≥ 3. Brute force (plain Python: Γ₀(N)-equivalence tested through γ = M′T^kM⁻¹, all k mod N and both signs): N = 9, m = 2: T₂(1/3) = 3·(2/3), and 1/3, 2/3 are inequivalent cusps of Γ₀(9); N = 25, m = 2: T₂(1/5) = 2·(2/5) + (3/5); N = 16, m = 3: T₃ swaps 1/4 and 3/4; N = 6, 8, 12: every cusp fixed. The cusps ∞ and 0 have f = 1 and are always fixed, and they are the only cusps the argument uses (c = (x) − (∞), T_m((x′) − (0))), so nothing downstream changes.

issues.locator: Chapter III, §1, (1.4) Proposition, p. 255, and the first sentence of the proof of (3.3), p. 257, Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
issues.printed: Proposition (1.4) claims regularity of X over ℤ away from supersingular x in characteristics p|N with Aut_k(x) ≠ ⟨±1⟩. The proof of (3.3) says that resolving quotient singularities at the supersingular points of X over ℤ produces a regular model X^reg.
issues.correction: X is regular except at the points x of characteristic p | N with Aut_k(x) ≠ ⟨±1⟩ that are supersingular or lie on a component 𝓕_{a,b} with a ≥ 1 and b ≥ 1; all those points are singular. The resolution X^reg in (3.3) must also resolve the ordinary ones (points with j = 1728 or j = 0 on 𝓕_{a,b}, a, b ≥ 1, possible when p² | N).
issues.reason: Take N = p², p ≡ 1 (mod 4), and x = (E, A) with E ordinary over k = 𝔽̄_p, j(E) = 1728, on the component 𝓕_{1,1} (A ≅ μ_p × ℤ/p, multiplicity φ(p) = p − 1). The connected and étale parts of A are characteristic, so [i] preserves A and Aut_k(x) = μ₄ ≠ ⟨±1⟩, although x is ordinary. Over the Serre–Tate deformation ring W[[T]], q = 1 + T, the cyclic subgroups of order p² reducing to A are ⟨(x, p)⟩ with x^p = qζ, ζ a primitive p-th root of unity, so the complete local ring of the (regular) stack at x is W[ζ_p][[T]]. The automorphism [i] acts on E[p^∞] by u on the connected part and ū = −u on the étale part (u² = −1 in ℤ_p), hence by q ↦ q^{−1} (T ↦ −T + O(T²)) and ζ ↦ ζ^{−1}: it acts as −1 on the cotangent space ⟨ζ − 1, T⟩, which is not generated by pseudo-reflections. By Serre's criterion (2 invertible) the complete local ring of X at x, the invariant ring, is not regular; explicitly it is W⁺[[X, Y]]/(Y² − ϖ₊X) with X = T′², Y = (ζ − ζ^{−1})T′, T′ = (q − q^{−1})/2, W⁺ = W[ζ + ζ^{−1}], ϖ₊ = (ζ − ζ^{−1})², of embedding dimension 3. The same happens for j = 0, p ≡ 1 (mod 3), where the automorphism of order 3 acts by a primitive cube root of unity on both cotangent directions.

issues.printed: The source chooses a prime q with q ≡ −p(mod D), says (q) = 𝔮·𝔮̄ splits in K, and describes B as K+Kj. For α∈K it gives jα = ᾱj, together with j² = −pq. It claims reduction theory gives a place v dividing p where R consists of α+βj∈B satisfying α∈𝔡⁻¹, β∈𝔡⁻¹𝔮⁻¹𝔫, with α−β integral at every prime dividing 𝔡.
issues.correction: Choose q with pq ≡ −1 (mod D), i.e. −pq ≡ 1 (mod D) (this still gives (q/l) = (−p/l) for l | D, so q splits and B = (D, −pq) is ramified exactly at p and ∞); then the displayed set is an Eichler order of level N and (0.5) holds as printed. Equivalently, keep q ≡ −p (mod D) and replace 'α − β integral at 𝔡' by 'α − pβ integral at 𝔡' in R and in (0.5).
issues.reason: With q ≡ −p (mod D), −pq ≡ p² (mod l) for each prime l | D. Take α = β ∈ 𝔡⁻¹ with a simple pole at the prime 𝔣 | l (and β ∈ 𝔡⁻¹𝔮⁻¹𝔫); then α − β = 0 is integral, and the reduced norm is N(α) + pqN(β) = (1 + pq)N(β) with ord_l N(β) = −1, which is l-integral only if l | 1 + pq, i.e. p² ≡ 1 (mod l). Exact check for D = −7, p = 3 (inert), N = 2, 𝔫 = ((1+√−7)/2), q = 11 ≡ −3 (mod 7), 𝔮 = (2+√−7): the lattice has basis elements of reduced norm 10/7 and 13/7 and is not closed under multiplication, so it is not an order, let alone End_{W/π}(x). With q = 23 (−69 ≡ 1 mod 7), 𝔮 = (4+√−7), it is closed, has integral norms and Gram determinant 36 = (pN)². (0.6)–(0.7) use only norms and are unaffected.

issues.locator: Chapter V, §1, (1.3) Corollary and its proof, p. 309, Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
issues.printed: Corollary (1.3) takes any weight-2 newform f and any conjugate f^α (α∈Gal(ℚ̄/ℚ)). It asserts ord_{s=1}L(f,s)=0 ⇔ ord_{s=1}L(f^α,s)=0, … = 1 ⇔ … = 1, … ≧ 2 ⇔ … ≧ 2, ord_{s=1}L(f,s) ≧ 3 ⇔ ord_{s=1}L(f^α,s) ≧ 3. The proof says all these assertions follow upon proving L(f,1)=0, L′(f,1)≠0 ⇒ L′(f^α,1)≠0.
issues.correction: The fourth equivalence is proved only when L(f,s) has sign −1 (f|w_N = f). For sign +1 the orders are even and it says ord ≥ 4 ⇔ ord ≥ 4, which does not follow from the three facts established (Galois invariance of order 0, of the parity, and of order exactly 1). The corollary should state the fourth line under f|w_N = f.
issues.reason: If the sign is −1, the orders are odd, and ord ≥ 3 ⇔ ord ≠ 1, which is Galois-invariant; if the sign is +1, the orders are even, ord ≥ 2 ⇔ ord ≠ 0 is Galois-invariant, but ord ≥ 3 ⇔ ord ≥ 4 would require knowing that L″(f,1) ≠ 0 is Galois-invariant, which neither the algebraicity of L(f,1)/Ω nor Corollary (1.2) (all L(f,χ,s) have odd order) gives: e.g. with a twist of sign −1, ord L(f,1_K,s) = ord L(f,s) + ord L_ε(f,s) and (1.2) only separates 1 from ≥ 3. The use in §2 (p. 313, orders m or ≥ 3m for A_f) assumes f|w_N = f and is unaffected.

The lead reviewer re-read p. 309: the proof reduces everything to "L(f,1) = 0, L′(f,1) ≠ 0 ⇒ L′(f^α,1) ≠ 0" plus the equal parity of the orders. That gives the first three lines, and the fourth when the sign is −1 (odd orders, so ord ≥ 3 ⇔ ord ≠ 1). When the sign is +1 the orders are even and ord ≥ 3 means ord ≥ 4; nothing in the argument separates order 2 from order ≥ 4. The statement may be true, but it is not proved, so the kind is gap (the reader proposed error) and it affects a stated result.

issues.locator: Lemma 2.2, second paragraph, p.5 of the published version (arXiv v2 Lemma 2.2, p.6)
issues.printed: The source refers to the index of K_X.
issues.correction: m should be the Cartier index of K_X + S at P, the log index. For the plt surface germ obtained by localising at P, this equals the order of the local class group, and the conclusions then hold.
issues.reason: Counterexample. Take X = Spec k[x,y,z]/(xy − z²), the A1 surface singularity with char k > 5, S = V(x, z), Δ = S and P the vertex. Then X is Q-factorial, (X, S) is plt and hence dlt, and P is a codimension-one point of the curve S. The minimal resolution (charts (x,z,y) = (u,uv,uv²) and (st²,st,s)) is crepant, so K_X is Cartier and m = 1. But div(x) = 2S and the ideal (x, z) is not principal at P, so S is not Cartier. Since f*S = S′ + E/2, adjunction gives (K_X + S)|_S = K_S + ½P, not K_S. With m = index(K_X + S) = 2 every clause holds. For a threefold example, multiply by A¹. The only other use is Lemma 4.2 (p.16), which needs only that the different of a plt pair with standard coefficients has standard coefficients; that is unaffected. Checked on the page image. Noted by the extraction (gap-index, item adjunction-index-diagnostic).

issues.printed: The source refers to every one of these discrepancies.
issues.correction: Also fix a finite set I ⊂ [0, 1) and require the coefficients of B to lie in I. Then, over the minimal resolution, the exceptional discrepancies take finitely many values. issues.reason: Counterexample. On the A1 surface S = {xy = z²} with C = V(x, z) and B = bC, 0 < b < 1/2, the minimal resolution is one (−2)-curve E, and K_{S′} + bC′ + (b/2)E = f*(K_S + bC). In the transverse smooth surface calculation, a(E1)=1−b_i and a(E_{r+1})=a(E_r)+(1−b_i), giving the claimed discrepancies.

issues.locator: §2.2, the paragraph before Lemma 2.6, p. 8 (published version; page image checked)
issues.printed: The source sets μm = 4mρG for m ≥ 1 and identifies 2ρG as the usual positive-root sum.
issues.correction: 2ρ_G must be the sum of the positive roots of the dual group Ĝ, that is, the sum of the positive coroots of G, so that μ_m = 4mρ_G is a cocharacter of G (a dominant weight of Ĝ). This is Fu's definition: μ_m := 4mρ_G ∈ X^*(T̂) with ρ_G = ½ Σ_{α∈Φ̂⁺} α ([Fu24], arXiv:2501.00652v1, p. 9 and §3.1, p. 18).
issues.reason: Here μ_m must be a conjugacy class of cocharacters μ: G_m → G, since it indexes the Hecke operator T_{V_μ} through the irreducible Ĝ-representation of highest weight μ (§2.2, p. 6). The sum of the positive roots of G is a character of a maximal torus of G, not a cocharacter. For a group that is not simply laced the two candidates are not even proportional: for type B₂ the sum of the positive roots is 3ε₁ + ε₂, while the sum of the positive coroots is 4ε₁ + 2ε₂. The estimate the proof quotes, |C_m(g,g′) − 1/|[[g]]|| ≤ C/m, is Fu's, and it is proved for Fu's μ_m, built from the roots of Ĝ.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 3.1.1, p. 13 (published version; the same in arXiv v4)
issues.printed: The source claims that H^1(F, N(T, G)) parametrizes conjugacy classes of F-rational tori and that the claimed bijection is readily verified.
issues.correction: T' ↦ [σ ↦ x^{-1}x^σ] is a bijection from G(F)-conjugacy classes of F-rational maximal tori onto ker(H^1(F, N(T, G)) → H^1(F, G)), not onto H^1(F, N(T, G)).
issues.reason: The class of x^{-1}x^σ becomes trivial in H^1(F, G) (it is the coboundary of x), and when H^1(F, G) ≠ 1 (e.g. G = PGL_2) other classes of H^1(F, N(T, G)) record maximal tori of inner forms. issues.locator: Published p275, proof of Lemma9.13(4); author and arXivv4 p39
issues.printed: The source places w over a place belonging to S′.
issues.correction: In the remaining case, w does not lie above S′; first dispose of w above S and exclude S′ minus S.
issues.reason: Assertion (4) says: either w lies above S, or w does not lie above S′ and w(t′₀ − a′_i) > 0. The first case is immediate, and the preceding sentence excludes w above S′ ∖ S. The case left is w not above S′. Only there do the stated valuations hold: S′₀ ⊆ S′ contains every place above which α, γ or a′_i fails to be integral or b′_i fails to be a unit, and b_i is a unit outside S ⊆ S′. At places above S′ they are not controlled. The rest of the argument proves the second alternative in exactly this case, by the identity b′_i(t′₀ − a′_i) = b_i(t₀ − a_i)(α − γt′₀), checked by direct computation with t′₀ − a′_i = (αδ − βγ)(t₀ − a_i)/((γt₀ + δ)(γa_i + δ)) and α − γt′₀ = (αδ − βγ)/(γt₀ + δ).

issues.locator: Published p283, proof of Theorem9.22; author and arXivv4 p47
issues.printed: The source claims that the evaluation on X(k_v) is trivial.
issues.correction: Choose a common integral model carrying the finite subgroup B0. Enlarge S so the old adelic point and the chosen smooth geometrically integral fibre have integral points outside S; choose x-double-prime integral there. Then the finite subgroup evaluates trivially outside S. Use Smeets Proposition6.1 to select finitely many additional approximation places disjoint from S. This repairs the nonproper integrality step conditional on9.17; its separate E4 real branch is not repaired by this argument.
issues.reason: Theorem 9.22 keeps the assumptions of Theorem 9.17, where X is only smooth and irreducible, not proper; Proposition 9.9 applies Theorem 9.17 to the quasi-affine W. For non-proper X an element of Br(X) need not vanish on X(k_v) at almost all v. Take X = 𝔾_m × P^1_k with f the second projection (every fiber ≅ 𝔾_m is geometrically integral), U = P^1_k minus a point, and B = {0, (x, a)} with x the coordinate of 𝔾_m and a ∈ k^* a non-square. Then (x, a) ∈ Br(X), so (x, a) ∈ B₀. At each of the infinitely many places v inert in k(√a), (x, a) takes the value 1/2 at every point with v(x) odd. With x″_v arbitrary k_v-points of X_h, the family (x″_v) need not be orthogonal to B₀, so the next sentence ('By the definition of B₀, the adelic point (x″_v) is orthogonal to (B + f_η^*Br(η)) ∩ Br(X)') fails as written. With integral points it holds: Σ_{v∈S} inv_v β(x_v) = 0 by the orthogonality of (x_v) and its integrality outside S, and β(x″_v) = 0 for v ∉ S. Corollary 9.23 and the later results apply Theorem 9.22 only to proper X, where the printed claim is true, so the gap affects only the non-proper generality of Theorem 9.22 itself.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem9.17, published p281; author/arXivv4 pp44–45, weak9.2 real-place branch
issues.printed: The source claims both openness and closedness.
issues.correction: Replace the real connected-component argument by a valid theorem under the actual hypotheses. Smooth proper over U would suffice, but shrinking U to achieve this changes the polynomials/sign conditions in the restricted Conjecture9.2 assumption. Until a replacement is proved, retain this weak-real branch as a proof gap.
issues.reason: Flatness and properness do not imply openness on real points, even for a smooth total space with geometrically integral fibres. Take y²z=x³−x²z+t z³ over B=A1 minus{4/27}. It is projective and flat with a section [0:1:0]; every fibre is geometrically integral, and the total surface is smooth. On z=1 the map is t=h(x,y)=y²+x²−x³, with strict local minimum at(0,0). More strongly D={x<2/3,h(x,y)<4/27} is a connected component: -1/3<x<2/3 and |y|<sqrt((x-2/3)²(x+1/3)) describe a disk, with all boundary in the excluded fibre and no boundary at infinity. Its image is [0,4/27), not the full base component(-infinity,4/27). It contains smooth-fibre points with t>0 and cannot reach c<0 in that same base component. This refutes exactly the component-surjectivity inference used. It does not disprove Theorem9.17: full real components in a compactification may connect through removed fibres, and a different argument may exist. Strong9.1 and the totally imaginary alternative avoid this step.
