issues.locator: §2.1(a), p. 9, with Corollary 9, p. 12, Theorem A/§0.3, p. 3, and §5.2, p. 20 (both versions); also published §0.6 p.5 (arXiv v3 §0.7 p.4), asserting finiteness of minimal elements in a Newton fibre
issues.printed: Assertion (a) says that a θ-twisted conjugacy class in W̃ meets finitely many W_a cosets. Its justification invokes the finite order of θ acting on V to conclude finiteness of every θ-orbit in Ω.
issues.correction: The statement needs a hypothesis: that (1 − θ)Ω is finite — equivalently, that the fibres of Ω → Ω_θ are finite. It holds automatically for θ = id and whenever Ω is finite (for instance G semisimple), but not in general.
issues.reason: The image in W̃/W_a ≅ Ω of the θ-twisted conjugacy class of w′ is κ(w′) + (1 − θ)Ω, not the θ-orbit of κ(w′), because w ·_θ w′ = w w′ θ(w)^{-1} changes the W_a-coset by ω − θ(ω). Two instances. (i) G = G_m and θ inversion: W̃ = Ω = Z, W_a = 1, all lengths are 0, twisted conjugation sends m to m + 2k, so each of the two classes 2Z and 1 + 2Z meets infinitely many W_a-cosets; every element is of minimal length in its class, so Corollary 9 fails and X_ν is the set of elements of F^× of a fixed parity of valuation, which is not compact. (ii) The case the paper is written for: G = GL_n with the twisted-endoscopy automorphism g ↦ J·(ᵗg)^{-1}·J^{-1} that preserves the standard Iwahori. Then Ω ≅ Z through the valuation of the determinant, θ acts on it by −1, and the twisted class of 1 contains τ^{2k} for every k, where τ generates Ω; all of these have length 0, hence are of minimal length, and all have the same invariants π = (0,0). So again Corollary 9 and the compactness of X_ν fail. The Newton decomposition of Theorem 3 itself is unaffected, and the compactness can be restored by replacing X_ν with a compact core inside one chosen Ω-coset, which the items of this extraction do (see C17 and N20): every minimal element of a Newton fibre is θ-conjugate by an element of Ω into that coset.

Therefore (a) Each θ-twisted conjugacy class of W̃ intersects only finitely many W_a cosets.' The image in Ω = W̃/W_a of the θ-twisted class of w is not a θ-orbit but the coset [w] + (1 − θ)Ω, since Ω is abelian and [xwθ(x)^{-1}] = [w] + (1 − θ)[x]. issues.locator: §5.2, p. 20, and Theorem 22, p. 23 (both versions)
issues.printed: The source uses the Newton decomposition G = ⊔_{ν∈ℵ} G(ν) to assert J(G) = ⊕_{ν∈ℵ} J(G(ν)), together with J(G(ν)) = H̄_R(ν)^*. It says restriction J(G) → ⊕_{(P,τ)∈StP} J_P(Pτ̇) identifies J(G)^rig bijectively with the indicated R-submodule of ⊕_{(P,τ)∈StP} J_P(Pτ̇).
issues.correction: Both indexing objects are products, not direct sums: J(G) = ∏_{ν∈ℵ} J(G(ν)), and the target of the restriction map in Theorem 22 is ∏_{(P,τ)∈StP} J_P(Pτ̇).
issues.reason: Distributions are the R-dual, and Hom_R(⊕_i M_i, R) = ∏_i Hom_R(M_i, R); ℵ = Ω_θ × V^+ and StP are infinite. A concrete witness: for G = G_m with θ = id and ω = 1 the strata are the sets ϖ^m O_F^× indexed by m ∈ Z, and Haar integration over F^× is an invariant distribution that is nonzero on every stratum, so its family of restrictions has infinite support. Compatible families of local distributions are products. Theorem23’s finite θ-stable truncation is not a valid justification: see the separate field-valued support error E14 and finite-relation gap E15.

issues.locator: Theorem 20, pp. 20–21, and through it Theorem 18/Theorem D, p. 20, over the printed coefficient ring (both versions)
issues.printed: The source claims a constant N_ν ∈ N exists for which, whenever n ∈ N satisfies ω(I_{n−1}) = 1, the module J(G(ν))|_{H_R(G,I_n)} admits N_ν[I : I_n] generators.
issues.correction: The primal argument bounds generators of the cocenter image and embeds the restricted distribution image into a free module of rank N_ν[I:I_n]. Over a field this gives the stated dimension bound. Noetherian R gives finite generation at each level, but does not by itself give the printed uniform generator estimate. The retained theorem F3 is field-valued; the arbitrary-ring counterexample remains F6.
issues.reason: The proof produces a surjection ⊕_w H_R(G,I_n)_w ↠ H̄_R(G,I_n;ν) from a free module of rank N_ν[I : I_n] and then dualises; the R-dual of a module generated by N elements embeds in R^N but need not be generated by N elements. An instance inside the paper's own hypotheses (R is any commutative Z[1/p]-algebra and ω any character with open kernel): take G = Q_2^×, θ = id, R = F_3 ⊕ V with V = ⊕_{m∈N} F_3·e_m square-zero, t = e_0 and ω(g) = (1 + t)^{v_2(g)}, whose kernel consists of elements with v_2(g) divisible by 3 and is open, containing I=Z_2^×. For b ∈ Ann_R(t) = V the functional j_b(f) = b∫_I f is (θ,ω)-invariant, and evaluation at 1_I carries the invariant distributions supported on I onto V, which is not a finitely generated R-module. The proposed Noetherian example R=F3[x,z]/(xz,z²), Ann(z)=(x,z), does not refute the existential constant in Theorem20: Ann(z)^d has at most 2d generators, so N_ν=2 works. This fix makes no claim to refute every possible Noetherian uniform estimate.

issues.locator: §1.1, p. 6, with the citation of [10, Proposition 13] (both versions)
issues.printed: It puts V = X_*(Z)_{Gal(F̄/F)} ⊗ R and cites [10, Proposition 13] for W̃ ≅ X_*(Z)_{Gal(F̄/F)} ⋊ W_0 = {t^λ w; λ ∈ X_*(Z)_{Gal(F̄/F)}, w ∈ W_0}.
issues.correction: Use the intrinsic Iwahori–Weyl kernel Λ_IW=Z(F)/Z0 with its finite-kernel affine action. For a torus the comparison is (X_*(T)_I)^σ, not X_*(T)_Gal(Fbar/F). Over the unramified completion use the torus centralizer and descend as in Haines–Rapoport Remark9. For a general group Z_G(A) is a minimal Levi, not necessarily a torus; do not impose a cocharacter semidirect-product formula without the appropriate construction.
issues.reason: Haines–Rapoport's Proposition 13 is stated for a connected reductive group over a strictly henselian discretely valued field, with T the centralizer of a maximal split torus there (a torus, since the group is quasi-split over such a field) and with coinvariants for the inertia; F is not strictly henselian and A is a maximal F-split torus, whose centralizer is a minimal Levi subgroup — for G = GL_m(D) with D a division algebra it is (D^×)^m, which is not a torus, so Hom(G_m, Z) is not a lattice. The paper's §0.3 makes the point that the non-quasi-split case is exactly the subtle one, so quasi-splitness cannot be read into the setup; and §4.3 supplies the objects a correct statement needs, namely S a maximal F̆-split torus defined over F containing A, the isomorphism W̃ ≅ (W̃̆)^σ and Richarz's length comparison. For the norm-one torus T of an unramified quadratic L/F, X_*(T)=Z, inertia acts trivially and Frobenius acts by −1. T(F)/T(F)_0=0=(X_*(T)_I)^σ, whereas X_*(T)_Gal=Z/2. Every torus is quasi-split; imposing quasi-splitness does not repair this. Tensoring with R kills the discrepancy, so the real apartment alone cannot detect it. Thus this is also a concrete integral error in the displayed identification for a quasi-split group, independent of the non-torus defect; it need not change the real apartment V. Haines–Rapoport pp.1–2, Remark9 pp.5–6 and Proposition13 p.8 were reread for the base-field distinction.

This supplies the omitted finite-A argument; it does not fix E14 or extend field dual separation to arbitrary R.

issues.correction: The basic seed has to be taken from a criterion that does not assume a shrunken alcove — [GHN15, Theorem A] (Corollary 3.6.1 with Theorem 4.4.7), which is stated for every element of W̃ — or proved for a t^γ directly; [He15, Theorem 2.27] cannot be quoted as printed.
issues.reason: He15 Theorem 2.27 (arXiv:1511.01386v3, PDF p.37) assumes simple G, a basic class and a shrunken input alcove before giving its Kottwitz/finite-Levi criterion. He21 §6.3, published p.14, applies it to the Theorem 5.5 output a t^γ without establishing that hypothesis. Shrunkenness need not survive that construction; nonregularity of γ alone does not decide it. Critical strips are −1 < ⟨v,α⟩ < 0 for positive α (He21 published p.5). An absolute value in (0,1) discards the root orientation: (0,1) is permitted. In split adjoint A₂ with σ=1, use root coordinates (u,v), base alcove u<0,v<0,u+v>−1 and t^λ(u,v)=(u,v)−λ. The existing negative example remains: λ=ω₂^∨=(0,1), x=s₂s₁,y=1 gives J=∅, J′={s₁}, x′=s₂,z=s₁,γ=λ,y′=1,a=s₁*s₂=s₁s₂. The input has positive-root intervals (−2,−1),(1,2),(0,1), so is shrunken; the output (1−u−v,u) has intervals (1,2),(−1,0),(1,2), so is not. Conversely the actual construction for λ=2ω₂^∨=(0,2),x=s₁,y=s₂ gives J={s₂},ρ_J^∨=ω₂^∨,J′={s₁},x′=s₂,z=s₁,γ=ω₁^∨=(1,0),K={s₂},y′=1 and a=s₁s₂. Here t^λs₂ is left-minimal, η(w)=s₂s₁ and a both have full support, the input intervals are (0,1),(−3,−2),(−2,−1), and the output (1−u−v,u−1) has intervals (1,2),(−2,−1),(0,1). Both alcoves are shrunken although γ is nonzero and singular: a(α₂)=−(α₁+α₂). Thus E1 remains a gap in the cited proof step, not a refutation of the main theorem or a regularity requirement. GHN15 Theorem A, published p.649, has no shrunken hypothesis, but its Levi-obstruction verification (or the restricted class-polynomial route and transport) remains G3's obligation.

issues.printed: The source claims {μ'; μ' dominant and μ' + λ' ≥_Z λ} has exactly one minimal element for the dominance order ≥_Z, and declares its proof complete.
issues.correction: Two steps have to be added: that the set is nonempty, and that it has a minimal element at all.
issues.reason: What the printed proof establishes is that the set is lower directed: for any two of its elements μ'_1, μ'_2 it produces a dominant μ in the set with μ'_1 ≥_Z μ and μ'_2 ≥_Z μ. Both missing steps are standard: μ' = λ − λ' + N·2ρ^∨ is dominant and feasible for N large, which gives nonemptiness (2ρ^∨ = Σ_{α>0}α^∨ lies in Σ_{α∈Δ}Nα^∨ and has ⟨2ρ^∨, β⟩ = 2 for every simple β; the sum Σ_{α∈Δ}α^∨ of the simple coroots alone is not dominant in every type — in G_2 it pairs to −1 with the long simple root); and for a fixed feasible μ'_0 the dominant coweights μ with μ'_0 ≥_Z μ form a finite set, so a minimal element exists. issues.locator: §2.2, p. 5, the standing reduction, with §5.2, p. 9 and §5.4, pp. 10–11 (both versions)
issues.printed: The source cites [GHN15, §2] to reduce questions of nonemptiness and dimension for affine Deligne–Lusztig varieties of arbitrary reductive groups to simple quasi-split groups over F. It therefore assumes G simple and quasi-split over F thereafter.
issues.correction: The reduction must also carry 'of adjoint type', as the cited section does: [GHN15, p. 648] reduces 'to the case where G is quasi-split and semisimple of adjoint type' (§2.2 Reduction to adjoint groups, §2.3, §2.4).
issues.reason: Adjointness is what makes §5 well defined. §5.2 introduces ρ^∨_J, the dominant coweight with ⟨ρ^∨_J, α_s⟩ = 1 for s ∈ J and 0 otherwise — that is, Σ_{s∈J} ω^∨_s — and §5.4 uses the elements w_1 = x z^{-1} t^{λ_w − ρ^∨_J} y' and w_2 = (y')^{-1} z t^{ρ^∨_J} y of W̃ and the element a t^γ of W̃. These require ρ^∨_J ∈ X_*(T)_{Γ_0}, which fails as soon as that lattice is smaller than the coweight lattice: for G = SL_3, split, X_*(T) is the coroot lattice of A_2, and y = s_1 gives J = {s_1} and ρ^∨_J = ω^∨_1 = (2α^∨_1 + α^∨_2)/3 ∉ X_*(T), so t^{ρ^∨_J} is not an element of W̃ at all. The twisted case shifts γ itself out of the lattice: in unramified simply connected ²A_2, with P^∨/Q^∨ = Z/3 and σ acting by −1, taking λ = 3ρ^∨, x = 1, y = s_1 gives J = {s_1}, σ^{-1}(ρ^∨_J) = ρ^∨_{σ^{-1}(J)} = ω^∨_2, and the class of γ in P^∨/Q^∨ is that of ω^∨_2 − ω^∨_1 ≠ 0, so no W_0-translate of it is a coweight of G. That this is a slip in summarising the reduction, and not a restriction the author intends, is clear from §1.2, which describes W̃ as 'the semidirect product of the coweight lattice with the relative Weyl group' — the coweight lattice being X_*(T) exactly for adjoint groups. Two consequences are worth recording: the cited reduction to adjoint groups holds under char k ∤ |π_1(G_ad)| and, after the authors' erratum, only component by component (see E13), and the descent of Theorem 6.1 from G_ad back to G is not written out.

issues.locator: Proposition 3.20, p.27
issues.printed: For a lattice L ⊂ V of rank r, the source asserts that Z(L) meets N_Λ exactly when L ⊂ Λ^♯.
issues.correction: "Moreover, if L is integral, the intersection of Z(L) with N_Λ is nonempty if and only if L ⊂ Λ^♯" (for non-integral L, Z(L) is empty).
issues.reason: Take Λ a vertex lattice of positive type and L = Λ^♯. Then L ⊆ Λ^♯, but no vertex lattice Λ′ contains Λ^♯: it would satisfy Λ^♯ ⊆ Λ′ ⊆ Λ′^♯ ⊆ Λ ⊊ Λ^♯. So Z(L)_red = ∅ by (3.18), and Z(L) ∩ N_Λ = ∅. The proof's first line assumes "L ⊂ Λ^♯ and L is integral". Every use in the paper needs only the valid direction (L ⊄ Λ^♯ ⇒ empty) or has L integral: Proposition 2.12 with Λ_0 = Λ_0^♯, Theorem 4.14, and the start of Theorem 9.7. The printed proof of the valid direction also cites Theorem 3.19(1) where L + Λ may have type 0. Theorem 3.19(4) gives the conclusion there instead.

issues.locator: Lemma 9.6 and its proof, pp.74–75 (authors' final version; same in arXiv v2)
issues.printed: Lemma 9.6 takes a non-degenerate rank n−1 lattice L♭ ⊂ V, setting W = (L♭_F)^⊥. Whenever x ∉ L♭ ⊥ W, it claims a rank n − 1 O_F-lattice L′♭ and x′ ∈ V exist with val(L′♭) < val(L♭), satisfying L′♭ + ⟨x′⟩ = L♭ + ⟨x⟩. The proof takes {ℓ′_1, · · · , ℓ′_n} as a normal basis for L♭ + ⟨x⟩ and claims L′♭ = ⟨ℓ′_1, · · · , ℓ′_{n−1}⟩, x′ = ℓ′_n have the required properties.
issues.correction: The lemma holds when the top fundamental invariant a′_n of L = L♭ + ⟨x⟩ is even. It fails when a′_n is odd and a′_1 + ⋯ + a′_{n−1} = val(L♭) − 1, and must be stated with that exception.
issues.reason: The minor argument correctly gives a′_1 + ⋯ + a′_{n−1} < val(L♭). In the ramified hermitian case the odd invariants come in hyperbolic blocks H_b, so if a′_n is odd then ℓ′_n pairs with ℓ′_{n−1} and ⟨ℓ′_1, …, ℓ′_{n−1}⟩ is degenerate. Any non-degenerate L′♭ with L′♭ + ⟨x′⟩ = L is a rank n − 1 direct summand, so val(L′♭) ≥ a′_1 + ⋯ + a′_{n−1}, and val(L′♭) is even (det ∈ F_0). So when a′_1 + ⋯ + a′_{n−1} = val(L♭) − 1 no admissible L′♭ exists. Example (n = 2): L♭ = ⟨ℓ_1 + πℓ_2⟩ in a hyperbolic plane H_1 = ⟨ℓ_1, ℓ_2⟩, x = ℓ_2. Then val(L♭) = 2 and L = H_1 has invariants (1, 1), but every rank-one sublattice of H_1 has valuation ≥ 2. Same in arXiv v2.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 5.7, pp. 308–310 (for p ≥ 3) (published version)
issues.printed: It defines T̂_U := O_U⟨p^{−α}∂_1, …, p^{−α}∂_d⟩ and introduces c : Δ → T̂_U^×(U) by γ_i ↦ exp(∂_i). It claims an isomorphism with inverse T ↦ exp(∂) − 1, and asserts log(T + 1)/T belongs to the units R⟨p^{−α}T⟩^×.
issues.correction: Use a convergence radius |p|^β with β > 1/(p − 1) (for example β = 1 when p ≥ 3; for p = 2 the paper's α = 2 already works), after a further étale localisation making E and V small for that radius.
issues.reason: With α = 1/(p − 1), the Tate algebra O_U⟨p^{−α}∂⟩ is the closed disc |∂| ≤ |p|^{1/(p−1)}, where exp does not converge: in the variable y = p^{−α}∂ the coefficient of y^{p^k} in exp(∂) has valuation exactly 1/(p − 1) for every k, so exp(∂_i) ∉ T̂_U. Likewise log(1 + T)/T, with T = p^αz, has a unit coefficient at z^{p−1} (it vanishes at T = ζ_p − 1, which lies on that disc), so it is not a unit in R⟨p^{−α}T⟩ and T ↦ exp(∂) − 1 is not defined. The comparison of Koszul complexes goes through on any strictly smaller disc. Theorem 5.5 is not in doubt; the same comparison appears in [5] and [20].

issues.citation: Howe–Klevdal, "Admissible pairs and p-adic Hodge structures II: the bi-analytic Ax-Lindemann theorem", Inventiones Mathematicae (2026)
issues.reviewReason: Checked on the v1 page image (v1 PDF SHA-256 62b77e53…, as the extraction records) and on the arXiv v2 comment ('Section 4 is rewritten to remove an incorrect statement (Lemma 4.1.1 of v1); the main results are unaffected'). Counterexample, as the extraction gives it: G the upper-triangular Borel of GL_2, M the diagonal torus, S = Spa C. Let s be a nonzero section of the stable bundle O(1/2). Its saturation is a line subbundle of degree ≤ 1/2, hence O, so 0 → O → O(1/2) → O(1) → 0 is a non-split extension. The flag O ⊂ O(1/2) is a G-bundle whose Levi push-out is (O, O(1)). It is not isomorphic to (ι∘π)_*𝓔 = O ⊕ O(1), although pro-étale covers of Spa C split. Every E_b (b ∈ G(Q̆_p) is σ-conjugate into M) has a split underlying bundle, so this bundle is not in the image of B(G) either. The v1 proof fails because the torsor of lifts is under the twist Hom(O(1), O) = O(−1), and H^1(FF_C, O(−1)) ≠ 0; Fargues–Scholze II.2.5(ii) treats only slope 0. The extraction's kind, affects and 'known' are right. Its phrase 'holds only on basic strata' is too strong: for example, extensions of O by O(1) always split, so the lemma also holds for flags O(1) ⊂ 𝓔 on non-basic strata. Its claim that later sections use only the basic case checks out: v2 cites Theorem 4.2.2 only for basic [b] (Sections 6.2, 7.3, 8.5 and 10.1, e.g. Bun_G^{[1]} = Bun_M^{[1]} ×_{Bun_M} Bun_G in the proof of Proposition 7.3.3).

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 3.3.1(3), p. 24 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The proof invokes [7, Proposition 3.4.3] to assert that constant lattice type makes the trace filtration on 𝒱 a sequence of local direct summands: trFil^i_ℒ𝒱 = ν_*(Fil^iℒ ∩ M/Fil^iℒ ∩ Fil^1M). It then uses the identifications ℒ/ℒ′ ≅ trFil^0_ℒ ⊗ Ô_X; ℒ′/(ℒ′ ∩ Fil^2M) ≅ trFil^{-1}_ℒ ⊗ Ô_X(1).
issues.correction: Add the descent step. Étale-locally on X, where 𝒱 ≅ O^n, the trace filtration of constant type is a filtration of O^n on X^♢ by finite projective submodules. It therefore defines a map X^♢ → Fl^♢. X is smooth, hence seminormal, so by Scholze–Weinstein Proposition 10.2.3 (the paper's own Proposition 5.0.3(4), whose proof uses nothing from Section 3) this map comes from a unique filtration of 𝒱|_U on X_ét by local direct summands whose pullback is the trace filtration. By uniqueness these filtrations glue to Fil^•𝒱 on X, with Fil^i𝒱 ⊗ Ô_X ≅ trFil^i_ℒ(𝒱 ⊗ Ô_X). Since ν_*Ô_X = O_X, one gets ν_*(trFil^i_ℒ) = Fil^i𝒱. The rest of the proof (Griffiths transversality from Lemma 7.8, and ℒ = M(𝒱, ∇, trFil^•_ℒ) by Scholze's uniqueness Lemma 7.10) then goes through.
issues.reason: Caraiani–Scholze Proposition 3.4.3 (read in arXiv 1511.02418) constructs the Bialynicki-Birula map Gr_{G,μ} → Fl_{G,μ} 'where we regard Fl_{G,μ} as a functor on perfectoid affinoid E-algebras'. So it only shows that the trace filtration of 𝒱 ⊗ Ô is by finite projective Ô-modules over affinoid perfectoids. It says nothing about ν_* or X_ét. The proof then uses what that citation does not give. It writes ℒ/ℒ′ ≅ trFil^0_ℒ ⊗ Ô_X, and it runs Scholze's proof of Proposition 7.9, whose uniqueness Lemma 7.10 computes Ext^1(Fil^0E, ·) for Fil^0E a locally free O_X-module on X_ét. Both need the Ô-filtration to descend to a filtration of 𝒱 on X_ét. An Ô-local direct summand of 𝒱 ⊗ Ô need not a priori be of the form F ⊗ Ô, and the proof never argues that it is. The statement is still true, by the fix above, which uses only tools the paper already has (item 026, item 084).

For a morphism f: (V,L) → (V′,L′) of weight λ over affinoid perfectoid S, the modified bundles E = (V⊗O)_L and E′ = (V′⊗O)_{L′} on FF_S are fibrewise semistable of slope −λ/2. After twisting by O(λ/2)^∨ they are fibrewise semistable of slope 0, so pro-étale locally trivial (Kedlaya–Liu; Fargues–Scholze II.2.19–2.20). Hence E → E′ comes from a map of pro-étale local systems whose rank is constant, since it equals rank f fibrewise. Kernel, image and cokernel are therefore locally direct-summand sub- and quotient bundles, fibrewise semistable of slope −λ/2. Completing at ∞ shows that L ∩ (ker f ⊗ B_dR), f(L) = L′ ∩ (f(V) ⊗ B_dR), and the image of L′ in (V′/f(V)) ⊗ B_dR are B_dR^+-lattices (locally finite projective). So kernels and cokernels exist in HS°(Y), images equal coimages, and ω_ét is exact and faithful.
issues.reason: Checked on the page image. The point-case proof (Part I Lemma 4.3.2) compares slopes of bundles on one curve over C, where B_dR^+(C) is a DVR, so the lattice f(L) and the intersection L′ ∩ (f(V) ⊗ B_dR) are automatically free. Over a family, B_dR^+(R) is not a PID. That these B_dR^+-modules are lattices, and that their formation commutes with restriction to geometric points, is exactly what 'as in the case of a point' skips. The result is true by the argument above, but the paper gives no proof. (The same step appears in the proof of Theorem 7.1.2, p. 40, 'which we can do after restricting to each geometric point'; that is in range 4 and should be checked there.) issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 7.5.2, pp. 47–48 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The proof identifies GrbH−adm H with Hdg(ℓ˘Qp), a subdiamond closed by Lemma 7.4.3. It asserts that G|Hdg(ℓ˘Qp), a neutral G-admissible pair, reduces from G to H compatibly with the canonical reduction of G|GrbH−adm H = H ×H G. The induced neutral H-admissible pair has classifying map s: Hdg(ℓ˘Qp) → GrH, whose image lies in GrbH−adm H, yielding the section s and completing the proof.
issues.correction: Hdg(ℓ) lies in the image of Gr_{H,Q̆_p}, but the induced H-structure is neutral only where the étale line of the sub-pair lies in the G(Q_p)-orbit of ℓ. In general Hdg(ℓ) is the disjoint union, over c ∈ ker(H^1(Q_p, H) → H^1(Q_p, G)) = G(Q_p)\(G/H)(Q_p), of the loci where the H-bundle (E_{b_H})_L lies in the basic stratum Bun_H^{[c]}. Each such locus is open by Theorem 4.2.2, so the piece c = 1, which is Gr_H^{b_H-adm}, is open and closed in Hdg(ℓ) and therefore closed in Gr_G^{b_G-adm}. The Proposition is true; the identification Gr_H^{b_H-adm} = Hdg(ℓ) and the section s hold when the kernel is trivial (for example H a parabolic, a split torus or unipotent).
issues.reason: Counterexample to the identification. Take G = SL_2 and T ⊂ SL_2 the norm-one torus of an unramified quadratic F/Q_p. It is anisotropic and split over Q̆_p, with X_*(T) = Z and Frobenius acting by −1, so B(T) ≅ X_*(T)_Γ = Z/2 = H^1(Q_p, T), while H^1(Q_p, SL_2) = 1. Let ℓ ⊂ W be a line with Stab(ℓ) = T (Chevalley); T fixes ℓ pointwise since X^*(T)^Γ = 0. Take b_H = b_G = g = 1, μ ∈ X_*(T) odd, and L_μ = μ(ξ)·L_0 over C. As a T-bundle, (E_1)_{L_μ} = E_{b′} with κ_T(b′) ≠ 0, so L_μ ∉ Gr_T^{1-adm}. Its push-out to SL_2 is basic with κ = 0, i.e. trivial, so L_μ ∈ Gr_{SL_2}^{1-adm}. Also ℓ ⊗ B_dR^+ = μ(ξ)(ℓ ⊗ B_dR^+) ⊆ L_μ(W), so L_μ ∈ Hdg(ℓ). Hence Hdg(ℓ) ⊋ Gr_T^{1-adm}, and s cannot exist at L_μ. The general description: at a geometric point of Hdg(ℓ), the sub-pair is the Tate pair Q̆_p(n) (a larger lattice would give positive degree inside a slope-zero bundle), so it gives a degree-zero line subbundle of the trivial bundle W ⊗ O, i.e. a constant Q_p-line [w] ∈ (G/H)(Q_p), and the H-reduction is the Q_p-torsor G ×_{G/H} [w]. Lemma 6.3.2's analogue for p-adic Hodge structures is unaffected, because there the étale side is trivialized.

issues.locator: Remark 7.5.3, p. 47 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The source claims that for a subgroup H the map is injective and, using a faithful G-representation, pulls the bG-admissible locus back to the bH-admissible locus. For reductive H it calls the Grassmannian map a closed immersion, deducing Proposition 7.5.2. Its example takes G = GL2 with upper-triangular Borel H, bH = bG = diag(p, 1); g = 1. On the GrG closed Schubert cell for µ = diag(t−1, 1), together with its GrH preimage, the map becomes the open inclusion A1 → P1; on admissible loci it becomes the isomorphism A1 → A1.
issues.correction: Only 'the b_H-admissible locus is contained in the pre-image of the b_G-admissible locus' holds. The b_H-admissible locus is an open and closed part of the Hodge locus (see the issue on Proposition 7.5.2). For reductive H, Proposition 7.5.2 follows from the closed immersion Gr_H → Gr_G only with that extra step. In the example take b_H = b_G = diag(1, p). Then the B-cell {⟨e_1, ξ^{-1}(e_2 + x e_1)⟩ : x ∈ A^1} of type diag(1, t^{-1}) maps by the open inclusion A^1 → P^1 onto P^1 minus ⟨ξ^{-1}e_1, e_2⟩. That is exactly the b_G-admissible locus of the Schubert cell, and it is b_H-admissible, so the admissible loci correspond by A^1 ≅ A^1. With diag(p, 1) as printed, the b_H-admissible locus over the cell is the single point ⟨ξ^{-1}e_1, e_2⟩.
issues.reason: With b = diag(p, 1), E_b = O(−1)e_1 ⊕ O e_2, since isocrystal slopes are negated (Section 6.2; consistent with Proposition 7.3.3 for μ = diag(t^{-1}, 1)). The Schubert cell is P^1 = {L = L_0 + ξ^{-1}(a e_1 + c e_2)B_dR^+}. The GL_2-bundle (E_b)_L is O(−1) ⊕ O(1) for a = 0 and trivial for a ≠ 0 (H^0 is then 2-dimensional over Q_p; equivalently Fil^1 = ⟨a e_1 + c e_2⟩ is weakly admissible iff it is not ⟨e_2⟩). As a B-bundle, the sub-line from e_1 has lattice L ∩ e_1 B_dR = B_dR^+ e_1 whenever c ≠ 0, so the B-bundle is an extension of O(1) by O(−1) and not trivial. Gr_B → Gr_G is bijective on C-points (Iwasawa, since GL_2/B is proper). So every L with a, c ≠ 0 is in the pre-image of the b_G-admissible locus but is not b_H-admissible. The b_H-admissible locus over the cell is the one point ⟨ξ^{-1}e_1, e_2⟩ = Hdg(e_1), consistent with Proposition 7.5.2 and contradicting 'A^1 → A^1'. The same computation with diag(1, p) gives the admissible locus {c ≠ 0} for both GL_2 and B. The pre-image claim also fails for reductive H: in the SL_2/anisotropic-torus example of the Proposition 7.5.2 issue, L_μ lies in Gr_T and is SL_2-admissible but not T-admissible. No later proof uses the remark.

issues.locator: Section 7.5, p. 46, and Lemma 7.5.1, pp. 46–47 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: For a locally spatial diamond Y/Spd ˘Qp, the source asserts that the canonical reduction of G is to H and names the resulting neutral H-admissible pair H. It also says that pulling the universal neutral H-admissible pair back along such an f′ gives H.
issues.correction: Assume Y connected, as in all the paper's uses (Lemma 7.5.1(2); Section 9), or apply the lemma on each connected component with its own H, b_H and g. For connected Y the canonical reduction is neutral. The class of the H-torsor Isom^⊗(ω_y, ω_{y′}) restricted to ⟨𝒢⟩ in the finite set H^1(Q_p, H) is locally constant in y′: on a v-cover trivializing ω_ét(X) for a generator X, it is the GL_n(Q_p)-orbit of the line of a rank-one subobject cutting out H, and these orbits are open. Hence the class is constant.
issues.reason: Remark 7.1.3 stresses that ω_y is faithful even over disconnected Y, so MG(𝒢, y) sees all components; but ω_{y′} for y′ on another component can be a non-trivial form of ω_y on ⟨𝒢⟩. Example: G = SL_2, T the anisotropic norm-one torus of an unramified quadratic F/Q_p, and ℓ ⊂ W with Stab(ℓ) = T. Take b = 1, Y = Spd C ⊔ Spd C, the trivial lattice on the first copy and L_μ = μ(ξ)L_0 (μ ∈ X_*(T) odd) on the second. Both are 1-admissible for SL_2 and ℓ ⊗ B_dR^+ lies in both lattices, so ℓ gives a sub-pair over Y, and MG(𝒢, y_1) ⊆ T for the obvious trivialization at a point y_1 of the first copy. At a point y_2 of the second copy, the étale line of that sub-pair lies in the non-trivial G(Q_p)-orbit of (G/T)(Q_p), because the T-bundle (E_1)_{L_μ} is the non-trivial basic one. So ω_{y_2}∘ℋ is a non-trivial torsor, ℋ is not neutral, and no f′ with f′^*(universal) ≅ ℋ exists.

issues.locator: Lemma 9.3.3, p. 59 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The source says T ⊆ S meets the Hodge generic locus of 𝒢 exactly when MG(𝒢|_T, y) = MG(𝒢, y) at some geometric y in T, equivalently at every such y. The proof ends by choosing an isocrystal of rank one, ℓ ⊆ ω_Isoc∘𝒢(V), underlying a sub-admissible pair for 𝒢|_T but none for 𝒢, and equates this with T ⊆ Hdg(ℓ) ⊊ S.
issues.correction: MG(𝒢|_T, y) = MG(𝒢, y) if and only if T is contained in no single proper Hodge locus Hdg(ℓ) ⊊ S. Hence, if T meets the Hodge generic locus, then MG(𝒢|_T, y) = MG(𝒢, y). When T is a single (geometric) point the converse holds too: a point is Hodge generic iff its motivic Galois group is MG(𝒢, y).
issues.reason: The proof shows that MG(𝒢|_T) is proper iff T lies in one proper Hodge locus. The Hodge exceptional locus (Definition 9.3.2) is the union of all of them. A T contained in the union but in no single member breaks the 'if' direction. Example: T = {t_1, t_2} (a Zariski closed subdiamond) in a connected component of a GL_2 Lubin–Tate/Drinfeld space M_{b,[μ]}, whose generic motivic Galois group is GL_2, with t_1, t_2 CM points whose motivic Galois groups (through ρ_ét) are distinct non-split maximal tori T_1 ≠ T_2. A line that is Hodge on all of T is stabilized by T_1 and T_2. The closed connected subgroup they generate is neither a torus nor inside a Q_p-Borel, so it is GL_2. Hence MG(𝒢|_T) = GL_2 = MG(𝒢), while T lies in the Hodge exceptional locus. A connected example is ({x_1} × S_2) ∪ (S_1 × {x_2}) in a product for G_1 × G_2. The applications are unaffected: Proposition 9.3.4's proof uses the point case, and Theorem 9.1.3's proof (p. 57) uses only the forward direction for T = {z}.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 9.3.5, p. 60 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The source asserts that if Z contains a disk in D_n(L'), it must contain its Gauss point as well, citing Raynaud’s description as an example and relying on algebraic closedness of the residue field.
issues.correction: What is needed is that the residue field k' of L' be infinite. That holds because L' is a finite extension of L ⊇ Q̆_p, so k' ⊇ F̄_p. Algebraic closedness holds only when L is strict.
issues.reason: In Lemmas 9.3.1 and 9.3.5, L is only a p-adic field over Q̆_p (perfect residue field; Section 1.6, p. 12), so the residue field of L' need not be algebraically closed. A rational neighbourhood {|f_i| ≤ |g|} of the Gauss point, normalized so that |g|_Gauss = 1, contains every x ∈ O_{L'}^n whose reduction lies outside the zero set of ḡ ≠ 0, and such points exist when k' is infinite. For finite k' the claim fails: {|x^q − x| ≥ 1} is a neighbourhood of the Gauss point of the unit disc with no L'-points.

issues.locator: Section 2.1.1, p. 14
issues.printed: The source fixes an embedding of a number field L into ℂ. It defines a pure weight-n L-Hodge structure as an L-vector space V bearing a descending filtration F^·V_ℂ on the scalar extension V_ℂ = V ⊗_L ℂ, with V_ℂ = F^pV_ℂ ⊕ \overline{F^qV_ℂ} whenever p + q = n + 1.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 12.4, p. 99
issues.printed: The source claims that Gal(ℚ̄/F_Σ) acts trivially on the components of Sh_{𝒢̃_B}, and therefore c is Gal(ℚ̄/F_Σ)-invariant.
issues.correction: Choose c in the ℚ-subspace of Gal(ℚ̄/F_Σ)-invariant combinations of fundamental classes of components. It is defined over ℚ because Galois permutes the components, and it contains c_η after extension of scalars to ℚ(η): Galois acts on Sh(T_1, h_1) through the reciprocity law of (T_1, μ_1), i.e. by translation by the central elements ([s, s], s), s ∈ 𝔸_{ℚ,f}^×, and η([s, s], s) = η(s^{-1}) = 1 because η is trivial on 𝔸_F^×. The determinant argument then yields a Galois-invariant ℚ-rational c with Res(Ξ_τ(d)) an isomorphism.
issues.reason: Galois does not act trivially on the components of Sh_{𝒢̃_B,K} in general: through the map to Sh(T_1, h_1) it acts by translation by ([s, s], s), and the closure of T_1(ℚ) meets the compact open subgroup in the closure of a finitely generated unit group, which cannot contain the image of an open subgroup of Ẑ^×; so for small K some components are not defined over F_Σ. The Galois-invariance of ξ_0 in Theorem 12.4(ii), and hence Theorems 1(ii) and 3.2(ii), rests on this step; the correction restores it.

It never mentions [30, Theorem D], [30, Remark 6.3], bases, or the constraints of Theorem 2.4 (the TeX of §4.1 has no 'basis'/'bases'). The only place in §4 that recalls [30, Theorem D] together with [30, Remark 6.3] is §4.3.1 (p. 54): 'as stated in [30, Remark 6.3] it would be very difficult to extend the method of [30] for general weights'. The label of §4.3 is sec: application MZV, which differs from the printed sec: application AMZV by one letter, so that is the most likely intended target. §4.4 (Remark 4.14(2), p. 58: 'we cannot find a suitable basis AT'_w for the case w = 3q − 1') is the other relevant passage; a commented-out TeX line in §4.4 even speaks of generalizing [30, Theorem D]. Case for the defence: §4.1's weak Brown theorem for AMZVs only gives the too-large generating set AT_w, and the §4 preamble (p. 43) says sharp bounds for AZ_w are out of reach without ACMPLs. But neither passage gives the 'details' promised about the failure to find the bases required by Theorem 2.4. It is a misdirected cross-reference and nothing depends on it. The published version keeps '§5.1'.

issues.locator: arXiv:2205.07165v2 (10 June 2024), Section 1.1, paragraph after the proof of Proposition 1.3, p. 14 (published: Section 2.1)
issues.printed: The source derives the K-algebra property of 𝒜ℒ from Proposition 1.3, then restricts to arrays whose characters are trivial to infer from the same proposition that ℒ is a K-algebra too.
issues.correction: 'By considering only arrays (ε; 𝔰) with ε_i = 1 for all i, the proof of Proposition 1.3 (or [30, Proposition 2.1]) shows that ℒ is also a K-algebra': when all entries of ε and ϵ equal 1, every entry of each μ'_i, μ''_i is a product of entries of ε and ϵ, hence equals 1.
issues.reason: The character is defined as χ(ε) = ε_1 ⋯ ε_n (p. 9). The statement of Proposition 1.3 only gives (μ'_i; 𝔲'_i) ≤ (ε; 𝔰) + (ϵ; 𝔱), which controls χ(μ'_i) = χ(ε)χ(ϵ), not the individual entries. Applied to CMPLs it therefore only puts the product in the span of ACMPLs of trivial character, which is larger than ℒ (for odd q, ε = (−1, −1) has χ = 1). What is needed, that the μ'_i are all-ones, follows at once from the proof (induction via (1.1)/(1.2)), not from the statement. Case for the defence: the authors sometimes use 'character' for a single entry ε_i (§4.2: 'the character corresponding to q is always 1'), so 'arrays with trivial characters' can mean ε = (1, …, 1), and the missing step is immediate. The claim that ℒ is a K-algebra is not used later in the paper.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 14 image. The ≤ on arrays (p. 8) compares only the character χ(ε) = ε_1⋯ε_n, the weight and the partial sums. So the statement of Proposition 1.3 gives, for ε = ϵ = (1,…,1), only χ(μ'_i) = 1, not μ'_i = (1,…,1). Read literally ('trivial character' = χ = 1, the paper's own definition on pp. 7 and 9), the statement shows that the span of ACMPLs of trivial character is an algebra. That space is a priori larger than ℒ: for odd q it contains Li((−1,−1);(1,1)), which has χ = 1 and lies in AS_2 together with Li(2) and Li(1,1). By Theorem 3.4 it is therefore K-linearly independent of those two, the only CMPLs of weight 2. That ℒ is an algebra follows at once from the proof: in (1.1)–(1.4) every new character entry is ε_1ϵ_1 or an entry of one of the factors, so by induction all entries stay 1. It also follows from [30, Proposition 2.1], which the proof says it follows. So the conclusion is true but is not implied by the result cited. The case for the defence is real: the authors plainly mean 'restrict everything to all-ones arrays', and they use 'character' per entry elsewhere (§4.4, p. 55). Still, 'Proposition 1.3 implies' is not accurate. The claim that ℒ is a K-algebra is never used later (the CMPL specialization in §4.3.2 invokes 'all algebraic relations in §1', not this sentence). The published version (pub. p. 11) keeps the sentence and omits the proof.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 18–21 images. The authors set s_0 = 0 precisely so that j = 0 is covered (s_1 = ⋯ = s_{k−1} = q, including k = 1). Then (Σ′; V′) is empty. The correct step applies no B* at all: summing the Si_{d+1}-relation over d ∈ Z gives the Li-relation directly, and it has no third sum. The printed (1.8) and (1.11) nevertheless keep a type-3 sum with the column (ε_0ε_1; s_0 + 1) = (ε_0ε_1; 1). Here ε_0 is undefined, and with ε_0 = 1 this duplicates the type-2 sum, which is false. issues.locator: arXiv:2205.07165v2 (10 June 2024), proof of Theorem 1.11, p. 25 (published: proof of Theorem 2.11, pp. 19–20, unchanged)
issues.printed: The source invokes Propositions 1.7 and 1.10 for Li(ε′; 𝔰′) = Σ a^{ε′,𝔰′}_{ϵ,𝔱} Li(ϵ; 𝔱), indexed by (ϵ; 𝔱) in AJ_w. It specifies a^{ε′,𝔰′}_{ϵ,𝔱} ∈ A with a^{ε′,𝔰′}_{ϵ,𝔱} ≡ ±1 (mod D_1) when (ϵ; 𝔱) = (ε; 𝔰), and residue 0 (mod D_1) in every other case.
issues.correction: Replace 'From Proposition 1.7 and Proposition 1.10' by an explicit argument. Run the reduction algorithm in the proof of Proposition 1.9 with k = w, and use Proposition 1.7 at every step, including k = 1 in place of C_{Σ,V}(R_1). Then: (i) every coefficient is −1 on a type-1 edge and lies in D_1A otherwise, so a leaf's coefficient is ≡ the contribution of its all-type-1 path mod D_1; (ii) when the m-th q is split off s′_i, choose ε = ε_{h_1+⋯+h_{i−1}+m} in Proposition 1.7(1). Every array on the type-1 chain before the last has an entry > q, so Part 1 applies. After n − ℓ steps the chain reaches (ε; s), which lies in J_w and is not expanded further. So a_{ε,s} ≡ (−1)^{n−ℓ} and a_{e,t} ≡ 0 (mod D_1) for (e; t) ≠ (ε; s). Hence the square matrix has determinant ≡ ±1 mod D_1, which is nonzero.
issues.reason: The claimed congruence is the heart of the strong Brown theorem (the 'second new ingredient' of the introduction), but it does not follow from the results cited. (a) Propositions 1.9 and 1.10 only say that a K-linear combination exists. They carry no integrality and no congruence information, and a D_1-multiple times a K-coefficient need not be ≡ 0 mod D_1. So 'Proposition 1.7 plus Proposition 1.10' does not give the display. (b) Even the proof of Proposition 1.9, followed literally, does not give it: its base case uses the fixed relation R_1, so ε = 1. That inserts the character 1 at the first split, and for h_1 ≥ 2 and ε_1 ≠ 1 the type-1 chain does not reach (ε; s). The coefficient of (ε; s) in that expansion is then ≡ 0, not ±1. The correct argument needs the free parameter ε of Proposition 1.7 chosen target by target, plus tracking that all coefficients are A-integral, and none of this is said. Case for the defence: Proposition 1.7 is stated with a free ε and with D_1-divisible coefficients precisely for this use, the introduction (p. 4) announces 'more precise information about the coefficients', and the completion above uses only the paper's own tools. So Theorem 1.11 is true, and the step is fillable by an expert; it is a gap, not an error.

issues.reviewReason: Quotation checked on p. 25 (and unchanged in the published proof of Theorem 2.11, pp. 19–20). The display does not follow from the results cited. (a) Proposition 1.10 (and Proposition 1.9, from which it follows) says only that Li(ε′; s′) is some K-linear combination of AT_w-elements. It says nothing about integrality or congruences, and a coefficient D_1·c with c ∈ K need not be ≡ 0 mod D_1. What is needed is the reduction algorithm in the proof of Proposition 1.9, with every coefficient tracked. The proof does not say this. (b) That algorithm, run as written, does not give the congruence. Its base case k = 1 with s_1 > q (p. 22) uses C_{Σ,V}(R_1), so the first q split off carries the character 1. Smallest case: q = 3, (ε; s) = (ε_1, ε_2; 3, 1) with ε_1 ≠ 1, so (ε′; s′) = (ε_1ε_2; 4). The base case gives Li(ε_1ε_2; 4) = −Li(1, ε_1ε_2; 3, 1) − Σ b_i Li(1, ϵ_i; 1, t_i). The ±1 falls on (1, ε_1ε_2; 3, 1), and the coefficient of (ε; s) is ≡ 0 mod D_1. Moreover the q − 1 targets (ε_1, ε′ε_1^{−1}; 3, 1) all get the same row mod D_1, so the matrix is singular mod D_1 and the invertibility argument fails. (c) The step can be filled with the paper's own tools, so Theorem 1.11 is true. Proposition 1.7(1) holds for every ε ∈ F_q^× and for k = 1, and its coefficients are −1 (type 1) or lie in D_1A (types 2 and 3). The base-case coefficients −ε^{−1}D_1 and the b_i of Proposition 1.6 also lie in D_1A. In the finite expansion tree, the coefficient of a leaf is the sum over its paths of the product of the edge coefficients. A path with any type-2 or type-3 edge contributes an element of D_1A. There is exactly one path of type-1 edges only. Choose ε so that it ends at (ε; s): when the m-th q is split off s′_i, take ε = ε_{h_1+⋯+h_{i−1}+m}. That path has n − ℓ steps and ends at (ε; s), which is w-admissible and so never expanded. Hence a_{ε,s} ≡ (−1)^{n−ℓ} and every other a ≡ 0 mod D_1. This is a genuine step: the target-dependent choice of the free parameter and the coefficient tracking are both unstated, and a correct but non-trivial argument is missing. It is not an error, because the theorem and its strategy stand. The defence is that Proposition 1.7 is stated with a free ε and D_1-divisible coefficients exactly for this use, the introduction (p. 6, not p. 4 as the claim says) announces 'more precise information about the coefficients', and 'we allow repeated elements' shows that the authors meant different expansions of the same Li(ε′; s′). That makes the step fillable by an expert, and it is a gap, as claimed.

issues.locator: arXiv:2205.07165v2 (10 June 2024), proof of Theorem 1.11, p. 25 (published: proof of Theorem 2.11, pp. 19–20, unchanged)
issues.printed: The source describes AT_w as all ACMPL’s Li(ε; 𝔰) indexed by (ε; 𝔰) ∈ AJ_w. It uses membership (ε; 𝔰) ∈ AJ_w to deduce the bounds s_1, …, s_{n−1} ≤ q, along with s_n < q. It indexes (ϵ; 𝔱) over AJ_w and asserts invertibility of the passage to the set indexed by (ε; 𝔰) ∈ AJ_w consisting of Li(ε; 𝔰).
issues.correction: In all four places, read 'the set of arrays (ε; s) of weight w with s ∈ J_w (s_1, …, s_{n−1} ≤ q, s_n < q)', the index set of AT_w, instead of AJ_w.
issues.reason: AJ_w was defined one page earlier (§1.4.2, p. 24) as the set of arrays of weight w with q ∤ s_i for all i. That is the index set of AS_w, not of AT_w. Read literally, the first sentence contradicts the definition of AT_w in §1.3.2. The expansion of Li(ε'; s') would then run over AS-arrays, where (ε; s) usually does not lie (it contains entries equal to q), so the congruence would make no sense. The intended set is clear from 'which implies s_1, …, s_{n−1} ≤ q and s_n < q'. Same text in the published version.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 25 image. The proof writes AJ_w four times: 'AT_w is the set of all ACMPL's Li(ε; s) with (ε; s) ∈ AJ_w', 'Then (ε; s) ∈ AJ_w, which implies s_1, …, s_{n−1} ≤ q and s_n < q', '(ϵ; t) ranges over all elements of AJ_w', and the transition-matrix sentence. On p. 24 (§1.4.2), AJ_w is defined as the arrays of weight w with q ∤ s_i for all i. That is the index set of AS_w, and it is disjoint from any s with an entry q. AT_w (§1.3.2, p. 23) is indexed by the arrays with s_1, …, s_{n−1} ≤ q and s_n < q, that is, s ∈ J_w. Read literally, the first sentence contradicts §1.3.2, and 'which implies s_1, …, s_{n−1} ≤ q, s_n < q' is false (for example s = (q + 1)). The intended set is unambiguous from that clause and from the structure of the proof. The published text (Theorem 2.11, pp. 19–20) is identical.

issues.locator: arXiv:2205.07165v2 (10 June 2024), Section 2.2.1, Condition (2.1) and the matrix Ψ_{s,Q}, pp. 27–28 (published: Section 3.2.1, Condition (3.1))
issues.printed: The source chooses positive integers 𝔰 = (s_1, …, s_r) ∈ ℕ^r and 𝔔 = (Q_1, …, Q_r) ∈ K̄[t]^r subject to (2.1): (‖Q_1‖_∞/|θ|_∞^{qs_1/(q−1)})^{q^{i_1}} ⋯ (‖Q_r‖_∞/|θ|_∞^{qs_r/(q−1)})^{q^{i_r}} → 0 for 0 ≤ i_r < ⋯ < i_1 with i_1 → ∞. It asserts that Ψ_{𝔰,𝔔} = ( … 𝔏(s_2, …, s_r; Q_2, …, Q_r) … 𝔏(s_r; Q_r) 1 ) ∈ GL_{r+1}(𝕋) satisfies Ψ^{(−1)}_{𝔰,𝔔} = Φ_{𝔰,𝔔}Ψ_{𝔰,𝔔}.
issues.correction: In §2.2.1 (and in the setup §2.3.1 of Theorem 2.4) require Condition (2.1) for every consecutive sub-tuple (s_j,…,s_k;Q_j,…,Q_k), 1 ≤ j ≤ k ≤ r. The simplest sufficient condition is the termwise bound ‖Q_i‖_∞ < |θ|_∞^{qs_i/(q−1)} for all i, which holds in every case the paper uses (Q ∈ F̄_q^×, and γH_s by (2.4)).
issues.reason: Quotation checked on the images of pp. 27–28. The mistake is real. Write c_k := ‖Q_k‖_∞/|θ|_∞^{qs_k/(q−1)}. Then ‖Ω‖ = |θ|^{−q/(q−1)}, since every factor 1 − t/θ^{q^i} has Gauss norm 1. Also ‖f^{(i)}‖ = ‖f‖^{q^i}, and the Gauss norm is multiplicative. So the general term of 𝔏(s_j,…,s_k;Q_j,…,Q_k) has norm ∏_m c_m^{q^{i_m}}, and (2.1) for the whole tuple bounds only the full products. Counterexample: s = (q−1,q−1), Q = (1,θ^{q+1}), so c_1 = |θ|^{−q} and c_2 = |θ|. With i_2 ≤ i_1−1 we get c_1^{q^{i_1}}c_2^{q^{i_2}} ≤ |θ|^{−q^{i_1+1}+q^{i_1−1}} → 0, so (2.1) holds. But the i-th term of 𝔏(s_2;Q_2) = Σ_i (Ω^{q−1}θ^{q+1})^{(i)} has Gauss norm |θ|^{q^i} → ∞. Its constant coefficient alone has absolute value |θ|^{q^i}, so the series does not even converge coefficientwise. The entry 𝔏(s_r;Q_r) of Ψ_{s,Q} is therefore undefined, and the assertion 'Ψ_{s,Q} ∈ GL_{r+1}(𝕋) satisfies Ψ^{(−1)} = ΦΨ' is false for this admissible (s,Q). For q = 2 the example is s = (1,1), Q = (1,θ^3). If some Q_m = 0, (2.1) holds vacuously while a prefix series such as 𝔏(s_1;θ^N) with N large diverges. For the defence: (a) the whole-tuple series 𝔏(s;Q) and, when all Q_i ≠ 0, every prefix series do converge (and are entire). Shifting the prefix indices by r−k and filling the tail with r−k−1,…,0 turns (2.1) into (prefix term)^{q^{r−k}}·C → 0 with C > 0. So (2.3), 𝔏(s;Q) ∈ ℰ and Prop. 2.3, whose MZ-property vector is the first column of Ψ and contains only prefix series, are unaffected. (b) The slip is inherited: CPY19 (arXiv:1411.0124 source, Eq. (2.3.1) and Eq. (E:Ljl)) asserts L_{jℓ} ∈ ℰ for all sub-tuples under the same whole-tuple hypothesis. (c) The published version (Cambridge Core PDF, downloaded 24 Sep 2026, §3.2.1, Eq. (3.1), p. 21) prints the same hypothesis. (d) Every instance the paper uses satisfies the termwise bound c_i < 1, which gives (2.1) for all sub-tuples: Q ∈ F_q^× or γ ∈ F̄_q^× (norm 1), and γH_s by (2.4). The proof of Theorem 2.4 does need the non-prefix series. Ψ' contains 𝔏(s_{i(k+1)},…,s_{ij};…), f in (2.8) contains the tails, and (2.3) is applied to f on p. 33. Reach: I reclassify 'affects' from nothing to a stated result. The false statement is the paper's own assertion in §2.2.1 (the construction extracted as item 28: Ψ_{s,Q} ∈ GL_{r+1}(𝕋) with Ψ^{(−1)} = ΦΨ under (2.1)). Theorem 2.4, read in the generality the paper intends and uses (see E16: general Q satisfying (2.1)), inherits the insufficient hypothesis: for some admissible data the series f_{t;Q} in its conclusion are undefined. No main theorem and no application is affected, because all of them satisfy the termwise bound.

issues.locator: arXiv:2205.07165v2 (10 June 2024), Theorem 3.4, last sentence, p. 35 (no argument in §3.3), used in the proof of Theorem 3.6, p. 36 (published: Theorems 4.4 and 4.6); unchanged in the published version
issues.printed: The source asserts K-linear independence of the ACMPL’s belonging to AS_w.
issues.correction: Add: by the first assertion (with a = 0), the values 𝔏𝔦(s;ε)(θ), (s;ε) with s ∈ J'_w, are K-linearly independent. They all have weight w, so by Proposition 2.3 they are K̄-linearly independent. If Σ_i b_i Li(ε_i;s_i) = 0 with b_i ∈ K, then by (2.7), dividing by π̃^w, Σ_i b_i (γ_{i1}⋯γ_{iℓ_i})^{−1} 𝔏𝔦(s_i;ε_i)(θ) = 0 is a K̄-linear relation. Hence all b_i = 0.
issues.reason: The theorem concerns K-linear relations among the values 𝔏𝔦(s_i; ε_i)(θ) = γ_{i1}⋯γ_{iℓ_i} Li(ε_i; s_i)/π̃^w. A K-linear relation among ACMPLs of different characters is a relation among these values whose coefficients b_i (γ_{i1}⋯γ_{iℓ_i})^{−1} are not in K, so it is not covered by the first assertion. Lemma 3.2 cannot split it by character: its input is a K-relation on the 𝔏𝔦 side. The descent from K̄ to K (Proposition 2.3) is therefore needed, and the paper does not invoke it. Theorem 3.6 ('By Theorem 3.4 the ACMPL's in AS_w are all linearly independent over K') rests on this clause. Case for the defence: Proposition 2.3 is proved in the paper precisely for such descents (it is used inside the proof of Theorem 2.4), so the gap closes in one line.
searched: Crossref record of doi:10.1017/fmp.2024.18, checked 2026-09-24: no update, correction or erratum relation
issues.citation: Im–Kim–Le–Ngo Dac–Pham, "Zagier–Hoffman's Conjectures in Positive Characteristic", Forum of Mathematics, Pi (2024)
issues.reviewReason: I checked the quotation on the p. 35 image; the published Theorem 4.4 and the proof of 4.6 print the same. The proof in §3.3 never addresses this clause. The first assertion gives (with a = 0) the K-linear independence of the values 𝔏𝔦(s;ε)(θ), s ∈ J'_w. By (2.7), Li(ε;s) = π̃^w g^{−1} 𝔏𝔦(s;ε)(θ) with g = γ_1⋯γ_r and g^{q−1} = χ(ε). So a relation Σ b_i Li(ε_i;s_i) = 0 with b_i ∈ K is, after dividing by π̃^w, the relation Σ b_i g_i^{−1} 𝔏𝔦(s_i;ε_i)(θ) = 0. Its coefficients lie in K(F̄_q), and outside K as soon as characters ≠ 1 occur. It is not covered by the first assertion. It cannot be split by character in the manner of Lemma 3.2 either: all the Li(ε_i;s_i) lie in K_∞, and the Galois action of F_q(γ)/F_q fixes them, so no γ is left to separate. Some transcendence input is therefore needed. Proposition 2.3 supplies it at once, since all the values have weight w. Without that step the clause does not follow from what is proved. The paper's implicit route is the p. 42 claim that there is at most one K-relation between π̃^w and the Li's, which has the same unproved passage (E30). Theorem 3.6 ('By Theorem 3.4 the ACMPL's in AS_w are all linearly independent over K') uses exactly this clause, and Theorem A depends on it through Theorem 3.6. The lower bound for Theorem B (Proposition 4.10) does not need this step: S_w consists of CMPLs, and for them γ_{i1}⋯γ_{iℓ_i} ∈ F_q^×, so K-independence of the 𝔏𝔦-values gives K-independence of the Li's directly. Case for the defence: the clause is true, and Proposition 2.3 is in the paper and is used for such descents in the proof of Theorem 2.4, so the fix is one line. It is still an omitted step, not a triviality, because the γ-factors make the Li-version and the 𝔏𝔦-version different statements.

issues.locator: arXiv:2205.07165v2 (10 June 2024), proof of Theorem 3.4, definition of J_0(t; ε), p. 37 (published: §4.3); unchanged in the published version
issues.printed: For (t; ε) ∈ J, the source defines J_0(t; ε) by taking those (t′; ε′) ∈ I for which an index i and an integer j in 0 ≤ j < ℓ_i give (t; ε) = (s_{i1}, s_{i2}, …, s_{ij}; ε, 1, …, 1), together with (t′; ε′) = (s_{i1}, s_{i2}, …, s_{i(j+1)}; ε, 1, …, 1).
issues.correction: … consisting of (t'; ε') ∈ J such that …
issues.reason: For j = ℓ_i − 1 the child (t′; ε′) = (s_i; ε_i) is a leaf, which lies in J = I ∪ {(s_i; ε_i)} but not in I (I consists of proper prefixes). The leaves must be children. They carry the terms a_i(t)(t − θ)^{w−w(t)} coming from the vector v of (2.12), which (3.4)–(3.5) absorb as δ_{s_i;ε_i}^{(−1)}(t − θ)^{w−w(t)} with δ_{s_i;ε_i} := a_i(t). They are also the children with k = 0 (m_{t′} = 0) on p. 39, and the base case m_t = 0 of the induction. With J_0 ⊂ I, the a_i would never enter the system and the conclusion 'a_i(t) = δ_{s_i;ε_i} = 0' would not follow. The meaning is clear from the next sentence, since 'for (t; ε) = (s_i; ε_i), J_0(t; ε) is the empty set' only makes sense for leaves in J.

issues.reviewReason: I checked the quotation on the p. 37 image; the published §4.3 prints the same ('∈ I'). By definition, I consists of ∅ and the proper prefixes of the s_i, all of weight < w. The leaves (s_i;ε_i), of weight w, lie in J = I ∪ {(s_i;ε_i)} but never in I. For j = ℓ_i − 1 the defined child is the leaf (s_i;ε_i), so with '∈ I' no leaf would ever be a child. The system needs the leaves as children. By (2.12), δ = δ^{(−1)}Φ' + v (b = 1), and the component of v at the parent of s_i is a_i(t)Q_{iℓ_i}^{(−1)}(t−θ)^{w−w(t)}. (3.4)–(3.5) absorb this term as the child term δ_{s_i;ε_i}^{(−1)}(t−θ)^{w−w(t)} with δ_{s_i;ε_i} := a_i(t). For depth-one s_i = (w) this is the only way a_i enters (3.5). The proof uses the leaves as children explicitly. On p. 39 the children t' = (t,(m−k)(q−1)) with 0 ≤ k < m include k = 0, that is m_{t'} = 0, a leaf. On p. 40 (Case 1) the children of ∅ run over 0 ≤ k ≤ m, and k = 0 gives t' = (w). The conclusions 'a_i(t) = δ_{s_i;ε_i} = 0' in Case 1 and Subcase 1 need the a_i to enter the system. The intended meaning is therefore clear. (The following sentence, 'for (t;ε) = (s_i;ε_i), J_0(t;ε) is the empty set', concerns the domain J of J_0 and is consistent with either reading, so it is not evidence here.)

The equation for ∅ is (3.5), as the next clause ('a factor γ^{(−1)} on the right hand side of (3.5)') and the passage to (3.9) show. On p. 42 the δ-vector indexed by all of J, including ∅, solves the whole system (3.4)–(3.5), that is (2.12). I do not adopt the second part of the proposed correction ('at most one'). issues.printed: The proof asserts uniqueness up to K^× of a non-trivial relation a π̃^w + Σ_i a_i Li(ε_i; s_i) = 0, where a_i ∈ K and the values satisfy Li(ε_i; s_i) ∈ AS_w; all ε_i = (1, …, 1). It seeks a relation with a ≠ 0, invoking Theorem 1.11 for Li(q−1)^m = Li(1; q−1)^m = Σ_i a_i Li(ε_i; s_i), again requiring a_i ∈ K and membership Li(ε_i; s_i) ∈ AS_w. It presents (−D_1)^{−m} π̃^w − Σ_i a_i Li(ε_i; s_i) = 0 as that relation.
issues.correction: Formulate the uniqueness for what the ABP analysis proves: the K-linear relations a + Σ_i a_i 𝔏𝔦(s_i;ε_i)(θ) = 0 (s_i ∈ J'_w) form a space of dimension ≤ 1, contained in the character-1 class, with all ε_i = (1,…,1). Equivalently, by (2.7), these are the relations aπ̃^w + Σ_i a_i γ_{i1}⋯γ_{iℓ_i} Li(ε_i;s_i) = 0 with a, a_i ∈ K. Then justify the last step. The algebraic theory of §1 respects characters: ≤ on arrays requires equal characters, Proposition 1.3 lands in arrays ≤ the sum array, R_ε is homogeneous, and B*, C, BC multiply characters by χ(Σ). So Propositions 1.7, 1.9, 1.10 and the transition matrix in the proof of Theorem 1.11 are block-diagonal by character, and every weight-w ACMPL of character χ is a K-combination of elements of AS_w of character χ. Li(q−1)^m lies in the K-span of CMPLs of weight w, so its expansion Σ a_i Li(ε_i;s_i) involves only χ(ε_i) = 1. For these, γ_{i1}⋯γ_{iℓ_i} is a (q−1)-th root of 1, hence lies in F_q^× ⊂ K (whatever roots were fixed). So the displayed identity is the K-relation (−D_1)^{−m} − Σ_i a_i (γ_{i1}⋯γ_{iℓ_i})^{−1} 𝔏𝔦(s_i;ε_i)(θ) = 0 with non-zero constant term, to which the uniqueness applies. Alternatively: write 1 = (−D_1)^m Li(q−1)^m/π̃^w as a K-combination of weight-w values 𝔏𝔦(t;1,…,1)(θ). By Proposition 2.3, applied to a maximal K-independent subfamily, every K̄-relation among values of one weight is a K̄-combination of K-relations. By Lemma 3.2 and Subcase 1 (and Case 1), K-relations have zero coefficients at the indices of character ≠ 1. Hence the K̄-relation obtained from Theorem 1.11 has a_i = 0 whenever χ(ε_i) ≠ 1.
issues.reason: The analysis of (3.4)–(3.5) starts from Theorem 2.4, which needs a relation a + Σ_i a_i 𝔏𝔦(s_i; ε_i)(θ) = 0 with coefficients in A. It shows that such relations lie in the character-1 class and form a space of dimension at most one. By (2.7), 𝔏𝔦(s; ε)(θ) = γ_1⋯γ_r Li(ε; s)/π̃^w, and the factor γ_1⋯γ_r ∈ F̄_q (a (q−1)-th root of χ(ε)) lies in K only when χ(ε) = 1. So a K-linear relation between π̃^w and ACMPLs of mixed characters is a relation among the 𝔏𝔦-values with coefficients in K(F̄_q). The analysis does not cover such relations, and Lemma 3.2 cannot split them, because it starts from K-coefficients on the 𝔏𝔦 side and a K-relation among the Li values, which all lie in K_∞, carries no γ to separate. Theorem 1.11 as stated says only that AS_w spans AL_w, with no control on characters. So the expression of Li(q−1)^m could a priori contain elements of AS_w of non-trivial character, and then the 'desired relation' is not one of the relations whose uniqueness was proved. Everything downstream rests on this step: the claim a ≠ 0 for every non-trivial relation (every character-1 relation is proportional to the exhibited one), the existence part, the linear independence of AS_w, Theorem 3.6, and through them Theorems A and B. Case for the defence: the claims are true (they follow from Theorem 3.6), and the missing fact (character homogeneity of the algebraic theory) is visible in its construction: the preorder on arrays requires equal characters. So this is an omitted argument, not a false step.

issues.reviewReason: I checked the quotation on the p. 42 image, and the published HTML (§4.3.2) prints the same text. What the ABP analysis proves: Theorem 2.4 needs (LD), a relation a + Σ a_i 𝔏𝔦(s_i;ε_i)(θ) = 0 with a, a_i ∈ A. Its a_i(t) must lie in F_q[t], because they are used as twist-invariant entries of v and δ_{s_i;ε_i}. Lemma 3.2 splits such a relation into character classes. Case 1 and Subcase 1 kill every class with q−1 ∤ w or χ ≠ 1. Subcase 2 shows that in the class χ = 1 every ε_i = (1,…,1) and the δ-vector is unique up to F_q(t). So what is proved is: the K-relations among 1 and the values 𝔏𝔦(s;ε)(θ), s ∈ J'_w, form at most a line, and that line lies in the character-1 class. By (2.7) such a relation reads aπ̃^w + Σ a_i g_i Li(ε_i;s_i) = 0 with g_i = γ_{i1}⋯γ_{iℓ_i}. Here g_i^{q−1} = χ(ε_i), so g_i ∈ K (indeed g_i ∈ F_q^×) exactly when χ(ε_i) = 1. The paper's sentence ('at most one non-trivial relation aπ̃^w + Σ a_i Li(ε_i;s_i) = 0 with a_i ∈ K … Further ε_i = (1,…,1)') is therefore proved only for Li-relations whose indices all have character 1. A K-relation between π̃^w and ACMPLs of several characters is an 𝔏𝔦-relation with coefficients a_i g_i^{−1} ∉ K. Theorem 2.4 does not apply to it. Lemma 3.2 cannot split it either: π̃^w (q−1 | w) and all Li-values lie in K_∞, so no γ is left to separate them. The final step takes the expansion of Li(q−1)^m from Theorem 1.11. As stated, that theorem, like Propositions 1.7 and 1.9, which record only the tuple inequalities T_k(t) ≤ T_k(s), says nothing about characters. If the expansion contained elements of AS_w of character ≠ 1, the displayed relation would lie outside the class whose uniqueness was proved. Then neither 'a ≠ 0 for every non-trivial relation' (the χ = 1 relation is not shown to be proportional to one with a ≠ 0), nor the existence clause, nor 'ε_i = (1,…,1)' would follow. The induction uses these facts in lower weights ((LW) and the suffix reduction on p. 37). Theorem 3.6 and Theorems A and B depend on them too. The gap can be closed from the paper's own material. The algebraic theory of §1 is character-homogeneous: the preorder ≤ on arrays requires χ(ε) = χ(e) (§1.1), and the products in Proposition 1.3 land in arrays ≤ the sum array. R_ε is homogeneous. B*_{Σ,V} (Lemma 1.5) and C_{Σ,V} (Proposition 1.6) multiply the character of a homogeneous relation by χ(Σ). The type-1/2/3 arrays of Proposition 1.7 keep χ(ε): for example, type 1 replaces ε_k by (ε, ε^{−1}ε_k). In the proof of Theorem 1.11, ε'_i is a block product, so χ(ε') = χ(ε). So the transition matrices of Propositions 1.9, 1.10 and Theorem 1.11 are block-diagonal by character, and the character-χ part of AL_w is spanned by the character-χ part of AS_w. Li(q−1)^m lies in the character-1 part (it is even in the CMPL span, §1.1). So its expansion uses only arrays with g_i ∈ F_q^×, and the displayed identity is the genuine K-relation (−D_1)^{−m} − Σ a_i g_i^{−1} 𝔏𝔦(s_i;ε_i)(θ) = 0, whose constant term is non-zero. A second route: Proposition 2.3 descent with Lemma 3.2 and Subcase 1. Case for the defence: every conclusion is true. The missing fact is structural, and a reader who checks the constructions in §1 can verify it. But the paper never states or uses it, and Remark 3.5 attributes the step to Theorem 1.11 alone. So this is a gap in the proof, not an error in a stated result. E23 is the other half of the same conflation of K-relations among Li's with K-relations among 𝔏𝔦-values; the two fixes are complementary, and the entries should cross-reference each other.

issues.locator: arXiv:2205.07165v2 (10 June 2024), proof of Proposition 4.10, pp. 54–55 (published: proof of Proposition 5.10)
issues.printed: The source embeds S_w into AS_w by setting ϵ = (1, …, 1). It says the algebraic relations of §1 all apply to the CMPL version, specified by Si_d(s_1, …, s_r) = Si_d(1 … 1; s_1 … s_r), together with Li(s_1, …, s_r) = Li(1 … 1; s_1 … s_r). It cites Theorem 4.9 to conclude that S_w is contained in Z_w.
issues.correction: It follows that S_w ⊂ Z_w. By the trivial-character (CMPL) version of Proposition 1.10, every CMPL of weight w is a K-linear combination of the Li(t) with t ∈ J_w, and Li(t) = ζ_A(t) ∈ T_w ⊂ Z_w by Lemma 1.2. Theorem 4.9 by itself gives only S_w ⊂ AL_w = AZ_w.
issues.reason: Theorem 4.9 says AZ_w = AL_w. It gives S_w ⊂ AZ_w, not S_w ⊂ Z_w, and Z_w is in general a proper subspace of AZ_w: dim d(w) < s(w) for q > 2, e.g. d(1) = 1 < s(1) = q − 1. What is needed is the non-alternating analogue: the CMPL version of Proposition 1.10 (or of the bridge). This is not stated or proved. The preceding sentence only asserts that the §1 relations 'hold for CMPL version'. Case for the defence: that sentence signals the intended specialisation, and the claim is true. The products (1.1) and Proposition 1.3 and the relation R_1 only multiply the characters of the inputs, so the algorithm of Propositions 1.7–1.10 applied to an array with trivial characters produces only arrays with trivial characters. The paper uses the same restriction after Proposition 1.3 (p. 14). So only the cross-reference and one sentence of argument are missing; Proposition 4.10 and Theorem B stand.

issues.reviewReason: The quotation matches the images of pp. 54–55 and the TeX. Theorem 4.9 says AZ_w = AL_w. Viewing S_w inside AS_w ⊂ AL_w, it gives only S_w ⊂ AZ_w. For q > 2, Z_w is a proper subspace of AZ_w: by Theorems A and B, dim Z_1 = d(1) = 1 < q − 1 = s(1) = dim AZ_1. Nothing in Theorem 4.9 projects AZ_w onto Z_w, so the cited theorem cannot give S_w ⊂ Z_w. What is needed is the non-alternating inclusion L_w ⊂ Z_w. It follows from the trivial-character version of Proposition 1.10 together with Lemma 1.2: every CMPL of weight w is a K-combination of Li(t) with t ∈ J_w, and Li(t) = ζ_A(t) because all t_i ≤ q. The specialisation is legitimate. In (1.1) and Proposition 1.3 the characters multiply. R_1 and the operators 𝓑*, 𝒞, 𝓑𝒞 with trivial characters create only columns with character 1. So the algorithm of Propositions 1.7–1.10 never leaves trivial characters. The paper already restricts to trivial characters in this way on p. 14 ('By considering only arrays with trivial characters, Proposition 1.3 implies that L is also a K-algebra'). The preceding sentence ('all algebraic relations in §1 hold for CMPL version') signals the intended argument. However, no result states the CMPL version of Proposition 1.10 or L_w ⊂ Z_w, and the explicit reference points to a result that does not give the step. This is a real but minor gap: one sentence and the right cross-reference are missing. Proposition 4.10 and Theorem B stand. The published Proposition 5.10 still says 'by Theorem 5.9'.

issues.printed: The source cites [30, Theorem B] for the bound dim_K Z_w ≥ d(w) when w ≤ 2q − 2.
issues.correction: For w ≤ 2q − 2 we have dim_K Z_w ≥ d(w) (see [30, Theorem D]), as the introduction (p. 4) says.
issues.reason: In Ngo Dac, Ann. of Math. 194 (2021) ([30]), Theorem B states that the MZVs in the subset T⁰_w of T_w (all s_i < q) are linearly independent over K, so dim_K Z_w ≥ d_0(w) := |T⁰_w| for every w; it does not give dim_K Z_w ≥ d(w). The sharp lower bound in weights w ≤ 2q − 2 is [30, Theorem D], which the paper itself cites for it in §0.2.1 (p. 4). The reference is only mis-numbered.

issues.locator: arXiv:2205.07165v2 (10 June 2024), proof of Proposition 4.11, formula (*) and claim H_r, pp. 55–56 (published: proof of Proposition 5.11)
issues.printed: The source takes positive integer tuples U = (u_1, …, u_n) together with W = (w_1, …, w_r), requiring u_n ≤ q − 1, as well as w_1, …, w_r ≤ q. It says direct calculation expresses 𝓑_{ϵ,U}𝒞_{λ,W}(R_ϵ) as [(*)]. It introduces H_r as a claim for arbitrary positive integer tuples U and W = (w_1, …, w_r), the latter of depth r, and for ϵ ∈ (F_q^×)^{depth(U)} with any depth.
issues.correction: Treat U = ∅ separately. Sum the binary relation 𝒞_{λ,W}(R_ϵ) over d. This gives (*) with three changes: U and ε deleted; the ϵ^{−1}D_1-terms kept, now as ζ_A-terms with first column (ϵ; 1); and the four families containing u_n + 1 dropped. The induction for H_r then runs unchanged. In the base case r = 0, use R_ϵ summed over d.
issues.reason: H_r must cover U = ∅. For instance ζ_A(ϵ, λ; q, W) with ϵ ≠ 1 lies in AT_w ∖ AT^1_w and has to be shown to lie in ⟨AT^1_w⟩. But (*) is obtained by applying 𝓑*_{ϵ,U} to the binary relation 𝒞_{λ,W}(R_ϵ) (Lemma 4.4, which needs n ≥ 1), and it contains terms with u_n + 1. For n = 0 the relation 𝒞_{λ,W}(R_ϵ) is not a fixed relation: its D_1-terms are S_{d+1}-terms, and the u_n + 1 terms do not exist. Checked numerically over F_3(θ), d ≤ 4, several W: (*) read literally with U = ∅ is false, while the corrected relation holds. For U ≠ ∅, (*) itself was verified numerically for q = 3 and q = 5, with U of depth ≤ 2 and W of depth ≤ 3 including entries equal to q. This confirms the paper's 'direct calculations' (with 𝓑* for 𝓑, see the next issue). Case for the defence: the proof is announced as a sketch, with full details in [25]; the missing case is immediate once noticed; the proposition is not used for the main theorems.

issues.citation: Im–Kim–Le–Ngo Dac–Pham, "Zagier–Hoffman's Conjectures in Positive Characteristic", Forum of Mathematics, Pi (2024)
issues.reviewReason: The quotation matches the images of pp. 55–56. H_r quantifies over U 'of any depth', and the conclusion ⟨AT^1_w⟩ = AZ_w needs U = ∅. For w ≤ 2q − 2, an element of AT_w ∖ AT^1_w has exactly one entry q, and that entry is not in the last position. When it is in the first position, U = ∅: for example q = 3, w = 4, ζ_A(2, 1; 3, 1) with characters (2, 1) over the tuple (3, 1). Formula (*) is 𝓑*_{ε,U} applied to 𝒞_{λ,W}(R_ϵ) through Lemma 4.4, which needs n ≥ 1. It contains ε_n and u_n + 1, so it is undefined for n = 0. The relation to use is then 𝒞_{λ,W}(R_ϵ) itself, which is binary: its D_1-terms are S_{d+1}-terms. The r = 0 base case has the same issue, but there summing R_ϵ over d suffices. I checked this independently. I evaluated at a generator of F_{3^13} and of F_{5^11}, with d ≤ 6 for q = 3 and d ≤ 4 for q = 5. Every array had depth ≤ d + 1, so no term vanished trivially, and dropping any single term broke the identity. (*) holds for U ≠ ∅ in all 51 cases for q = 3 and all 27 for q = 5, including W with entries equal to q. For U = ∅, the literal reading (drop the u_n + 1 families, keep the D_1-terms at S_d) failed in all 39 and 30 cases. The version with the D_1-terms at S_{d+1} held in every case. Summing it over d gives the claimed ζ_A-relation, because S_0 vanishes on arrays of depth ≥ 2. With this relation the induction goes through: every other term has a non-empty prefix and is covered by H_{r'} with r' < r, or by H_r with a smaller w_1. Case for the defence: the proof is announced as a sketch with details in [25], and the fix is routine. The proposition is not used for Theorems A or B, and its bound also follows from Theorem A. So only the proof is affected. The published Proposition 5.11 replaces (*) by a schematic formula (5.9) with no displayed u_n + 1 terms, but it still does not treat U = ∅ separately.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 5.6, p. 25 (arXiv v3; the same text in v1 and v2)
issues.printed: The proof asserts that in Ā, the ideal generated by the expression (f′_{j+1}) + (f′_{j+1}, …, f′_h)² has the radical of IĀ. It then invokes prime avoidance to choose f″ in (f′_{j+1}, …, f′_h)² for which f′_{j+1} + f″ is a nonzerodivisor in Ā.
issues.correction: Replace the upper index h (= height I) by m (the number of minimal generators): take f″ ∈ (f′_{j+2}, …, f′_m)² ⊆ I². By Nakayama IĀ = (f′_{j+1}, …, f′_m)Ā, so (f′_{j+1}) + (f′_{j+2}, …, f′_m)² has the radical of IĀ, which lies in no associated prime of Ā because IĀ contains a non-zero-divisor; Kaplansky's Theorem 124 then gives f″. Since f″ ∈ I² ⊆ (t)², the new generators keep the form (5.4) and minimality. Theorem 5.6 is true.
issues.reason: When h < m the first h minimal generators need not generate I up to radical. Example: P = O[[t1,t2]], I = (t1(ϖ+t2), ϖt2(ϖ+t2), t1t2), a minimal generating set of the form (5.4) with d = (1, 2, ∞). A = P/I is in C_O(0) (I·P_{(t)} = (t1,t2)), the minimal primes of I are (t1,ϖ), (t1,t2), (t1,ϖ+t2), (ϖ,t2), so h = 2 = n − c and dim A = 1 = c + 1, while m = 3. For j = 1, f1 = t1(ϖ+t2) and Ā = P/(f1) has associated primes (t1) and (ϖ+t2). The printed ideal is (f′_2) and every element of f′_2 + (f′_2)² lies in (ϖ+t2), so it is a zero-divisor: the step fails. With the correction, f2 = f′_2 + (t1t2)² is a non-zero-divisor on Ā.

issues.correction: Ext*_A(O,O) is the cohomology of the complex Hom_O(O⟨X,Y⟩, O) ≅ O⟨η_1,…,η_n⟩ ⊗ O[χ_1,…,χ_m] with d(η_i) = ϖ^{d_i}χ_i (i ≤ m), which is the Koszul complex of ϖ^{d_1}χ_1, …, ϖ^{d_m}χ_m over O[χ] tensored with ∧(η_{m+1},…,η_n). Its H_0-part is the displayed quotient, but the higher Koszul homology is also there. The missing classes are O-torsion, so the conclusions that follow — Ext^c_A(O,O) ≅ O·η_{m+1}⋯η_n ⊕ (torsion) and F^c_A(O) generated by the class of η_{m+1}⋯η_n — are correct.
issues.reason: The sequence ϖ^{d_1}χ_1, …, ϖ^{d_m}χ_m is not O[χ]-regular once two of the d_i are positive, since ϖ^{d_2}χ_2 kills the class of ϖ^{d_1−1}χ_1 modulo ϖ^{d_1}χ_1. Example: A = O[[t1,t2]]/(ϖt1 − t2², ϖt2 − t1²), a complete intersection in C_O(0) (A/ϖA has finite length; A_{(t)} = Frac O) with n = m = 2, d_1 = d_2 = 1. The element χ_2η_1 − χ_1η_2 of degree 3 is a cycle, and d(η_1η_2) = ±ϖ(χ_2η_1 − χ_1η_2), so Ext³_A(O,O) ⊇ O/ϖ ≠ 0, while the displayed module is zero in odd degrees.

issues.locator: Definition of C_O, §2 'Wiles defect', p. 16; used in §4 'Dualizing complexes', p. 21, 5.1, p. 24, §6, and §9 'Complete intersection rings', p. 40
issues.printed: At p. 16, the source defines C_O via pairs (A, λ_A): A is local, complete and noetherian; λ_A : A → O is local and surjective; and A is regular at p_A := Ker(λ_A). At p. 21 it claims that every A belonging to C_O arises as a quotient of a regular ring, specifically a power series ring over O, and therefore possesses a dualizing complex. At p. 40 it writes every local A in C_O as P/I with P := O[[t]].
issues.correction: Require A to be an O-algebra, λ_A a map of O-algebras and morphisms O-algebra maps, as the Introduction (p. 4, 'A a complete local noetherian O-algebra') and the Glossary (p. 80, 'a surjective map in CNL_O') say. Then every A in C_O is O[[t]]/I with I ⊆ (ϖ)(t) + (t)², and §§5–9 apply as written. (Existence of a dualizing complex holds in general by Cohen's structure theorem.)
issues.reason: Under the p. 16 definition the p. 21 and p. 40 claims fail: O = Z_p[√p], A = Z_p[[x]], λ(x) = √p is surjective with kernel (x² − p), A is regular, so A ∈ C_O(1); but A contains no square root of p (reduce mod x), so it is no O-algebra and no quotient of O[[t]]. The proofs of Theorem 5.6, Lemma 5.10, 6.3, Lemma 6.5, Theorem 6.8(2) and Propositions 6.10–6.11 start from A = P/I and so do not cover such A.

issues.printed: The remark assumes oddness of ρ̄ at a real place of F and associates complex conjugation c ∈ G_F to that place, up to conjugacy. For every v with ρ̄(Frob_v) conjugate to ρ̄(c), it claims v is a level raising prime in its terminology and satisfies q_v ≡ −1 (mod ℓ).

issues.reason: ρ̄(c) has eigenvalues 1, −1, so v is level raising iff q_v ≡ −1 (mod ℓ); ρ̄(Frob_v) ~ ρ̄(c) gives det ρ̄(Frob_v) = −1, which equals q_v mod ℓ only if det ρ̄ = ε̄_ℓ. issues.locator: Remark 12.2, second paragraph, second sentence, p. 55
issues.printed: The remark assumes that ρ̄ has projective image PSL_2(k), with |k| ≥ 5 and [F(ζ_ℓ) : F] > 2. It claims the existence of places v where the eigenvalue ratio of ρ̄(Frob_v) is q_v, with q_v ≢ ±1 (mod ℓ), and calls these level raising primes.
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis that some a ∈ F_ℓ^× ∖ {±1} is a square in k (e.g. ℓ ≥ 7, or [k : F_ℓ] even). Then choose λ ∈ k with λ² = a and use Chebotarev in the compositum of F(proj ρ̄) and F(ζ_ℓ), which are linearly disjoint because PSL_2(k) is simple.
issues.reason: An element of GL_2 with class in PSL_2(k) is z·h with h ∈ SL_2(k), so its eigenvalue ratio is μ² for an eigenvalue μ of h; if μ ∉ k then μ^{|k|} = μ^{−1} and a ratio in F_ℓ is ±1. So a ratio in F_ℓ ∖ {±1} must be a square in k. For ℓ = 5 and [k : F_5] odd, 2 and 3 are non-squares; e.g. F = Q with projective image PSL_2(F_5) ≅ A_5: q_v ≢ ±1 (mod 5) forces a ratio of order 4, but A_5 has no element of order 4. The hypothesis [F(ζ_5):F] = 4 > 2 holds. The remark is used in no proof.

issues.locator: Proposition 13.6, p. 62, with 13.1, p. 58 (K∞ ⊆ PGL_2(F ⊗ R) maximal compact); used in Propositions 13.7, 13.10, Lemma 15.3 and Theorem F
issues.printed: Section 13.1 chooses a maximal compact K∞ ⊆ PGL_2(F ⊗_Q R). Proposition 13.6 invokes Proposition 3.7 and Theorem 4.2 of [45] for Verdier duality (C_K)_m ≅ RHom_O((C_K)_m, O[2r_1 + 3r_2]), taking [K_2αK_1] to [K_1α^{−1}K_2].
issues.correction: When F has a real place, K∞ contains the disconnected PO(2) there and Y_K can be non-orientable even at the sufficiently small levels of 13.4; Verdier duality then reads (C_K)_m ≅ RHom_O((C_K ⊗ or)_m, O)[2r_1 + 3r_2], with or the orientation character γ ↦ sign N_{F/Q}(det γ). So Proposition 13.6 (and what rests on it) is proved only when the Y_K are orientable — e.g. F without real places, which covers Theorem G — unless one replaces K∞ by its identity component (restating Conjectures C, D and Theorem F for those spaces) or proves a Hecke-equivariant isomorphism (C_K ⊗ or)_m ≅ (C_K)_m. Newton–Thorne [45] treat CM fields, which have no real places.
issues.reason: Confirmed as an orientation gap. The source’s full real maximal compact is disconnected. This diagnoses the missing orientation coefficient/trivialization; it does not by itself refute every non-Eisenstein localized self-duality.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 3.1, induction step, p. 29 (published); same in arXiv v2
issues.printed: For r > 1, the source claims Z = ⋃_{i=1}^{r−1} Y_i is a normal crossings divisor on X satisfying every hypothesis of the theorem. On Y_r, it makes the same claim about Z_r = Y_r ∩ Z = ⋃_{i=1}^{r−1}(Y_r ∩ Y_i).
issues.correction: State and prove Theorem 3.1 for smooth divisors Y_i that are not necessarily irreducible (or connected), and discard empty intersections. The base case r = 1 works verbatim: for d = 1, Y is a finite set of closed points with separable residue fields, and 0 → C → ⊕_x Ind_{K(x)}^K Q_ℓ/Z_ℓ → Q_ℓ/Z_ℓ → 0 stays exact on G_K-coinvariants because H_1(G, Q_ℓ/Z_ℓ) = 0 for finite G. Z_r is non-empty when d ≥ 2, because X ∖ Y_1 is affine and Y_r is proper of positive dimension, so Y_r meets Y_1. When d = 1 the right-hand column is trivially exact.
issues.reason: The theorem assumes the Y_i are smooth irreducible divisors, and the base case r = 1, d = 1 uses 'the unique point x ∈ Y'. The divisors Y_r ∩ Y_i on Y_r are smooth but in general reducible, and can be empty. For example, on a surface two smooth curves meeting transversally in two points have Y_r ∩ Y_i equal to two points. So the induction applies the theorem outside its stated hypotheses. The argument itself never uses irreducibility beyond the base case, which extends as stated.

Replace K by K^per as allowed; (RS2) then holds by hypothesis, not by characteristic zero. When K is finite, the hyperplane section exists only after a finite extension K′/K, which may be taken of q-power degree for a prime q ≠ ℓ. issues.reason: Theorem 0.10 (Kato's conjecture over finite fields, assuming resolution) is deduced from Theorem 4.19, hence from Theorem 5.12, for a finite field K of characteristic p > 0. There the stated reason for (RS2) is false, since K is not of characteristic 0, and a smooth hyperplane section over the finite field K need not exist. The same gap affects Theorem 0.11 for finitely generated K of positive characteristic. Both steps are repairable as described, so the stated results stand under their resolution hypothesis.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 2.5(b), p. 23; same in arXiv v2 p. 19

issues.reason: For K=F_p(t), its t-adic completion L=F_p((t)) and n=p, the global quotient is countable but L×/L×p is uncountable. issues.locator: Section 2.4, Proposition 2.5, p. 759 (published); arXiv v4: p. 22 (the same)
issues.printed: The source defines H^{O_ℓ}_{ℓ⁻} = H^{w_0}_{ℓ⁻} using a non-degenerate (W_{𝔩⁻}, q) inside (V, q), of dimension 𝔩⁻. Its F-anisotropic kernel is said to have dimension (𝔡_0 − 1) when y_{−κ} lies in the G_{E/F}(1) × G_{n−ℓ}-orbit of a nonzero vector of (V_0, q), the F-anisotropic kernel of (V, q), and dimension (𝔡_0 + 1) when it does not.
issues.correction: Replace y_{−κ} by y_κ (= w_0) in both places. Equivalently: the anisotropic kernel of W_{𝔩⁻} = V_(ℓ) ∩ w_0^⊥ has dimension 𝔡_0 − 1 if (V_0, q) represents q(w_0, w_0) = (−1)^{𝔫+1}κ, and 𝔡_0 + 1 otherwise.
issues.reason: V_(ℓ) = W_{𝔩⁻} ⊕ ⟨w_0⟩ and V_(ℓ) ≅ H^{𝔯−ℓ} ⊕ V_0. By Witt cancellation, W_{𝔩⁻} has Witt index 𝔯 − ℓ (kernel of dimension 𝔡_0 − 1) iff V_0 ≅ ⟨q(w_0)⟩ ⊕ W_0, i.e. iff V_0 represents q(w_0). Equivalently, W_{𝔩⁻} = H′ ⊕ ⟨y_{−κ}⟩ with q(y_{−κ}) = −q(y_κ), whose kernel is that of V_0 ⊕ ⟨−q(w_0)⟩. Scaling by G_{E/F}(1) changes norms only by norms or squares, so the printed rule tests whether V_0 represents −q(w_0). Counterexample: F = Q, V = H² ⊕ ⟨1⟩ (𝔫 = 5, 𝔯 = 2, V_0 = ⟨1⟩), ℓ = 1, κ = 1. Then w_0 = e_2 + ½e_{−2} has norm 1 and W_{𝔩⁻} = ⟨e′_1, e_2 − ½e_{−2}⟩ ≅ ⟨1, −1⟩ is split (kernel of dimension 0 = 𝔡_0 − 1). But y_{−1} has norm −1, which is not a square, so it is in the orbit of no vector of V_0, and the printed rule gives 𝔡_0 + 1 = 2. κ = −1 gives the opposite failure. The authors' commented-out remark in the v4 TeX (Section 4.3: G^{w_0}_{m⁻} is anisotropic when '(−1)^{𝔪+1}κ is not represented by (W_0, q)') uses the corrected criterion. Proposition 2.5 is not cited elsewhere, so nothing downstream depends on it. Checked on the page image.

issues.locator: Section 4.6, (4.47), p. 780 (published); arXiv v4: p. 45 (the same)
issues.printed: For unitary H_{m+a}, the source specifies ρ = … As ⊗ ξ^m.
issues.correction: ρ = As^{(−1)^𝔪} in the notation of Section 2.2: As^+ if 𝔪 = dim W is even, As^− = As ⊗ ω_{E/F} if 𝔪 is odd.
issues.reason: ξ is not defined in Section 4; elsewhere it is the L-embedding of the endoscopic datum. No fixed ξ can work with the exponent m = [𝔪/2]: 𝔪 = 1 gives m = 0 but needs the twisted Asai factor. L(2s + 1, τ, ρ) is the second normalizing factor of the intertwining operator for GL_a × U(W) ⊂ U(W_{𝔪+2a}), and Proposition 5.2 needs L(s, τ_i, ρ) to have a pole at s = 1 for τ_i of the parity opposite to φ_σ. With κ = 1, parameters of U(N′) have every summand of sign (−1)^{N′−1}, so (τ_i, 2) ⊞ φ_σ is a parameter of U(𝔪 + 2a) iff η_{τ_i} = (−1)^𝔪, i.e. iff L(s, τ_i, As^{(−1)^𝔪}) has a pole. Sanity check: U(1,1) with Siegel Levi E^× has normalizing factor L(2s, χ|_{A_F^×}) = L(2s, χ, As^+) (𝔪 = 0). Checked on the page image and in the TeX ('\Asai\otimes \xi^m').
