issues.locator: Section 2.3, (2.7)–(2.9) and the paragraph after (2.9); Section 2.4, before (2.11), pp. 754–757 (published); arXiv v4: pp. 17–21 (the same)
issues.printed: The source identifies H^{O_ℓ} with H^{O_ℓ}_{ℓ⁻} = Isom(W^{O_ℓ}, q)°. It describes (W^{O_ℓ}, q) as non-degenerate, of dimension 𝔩⁻ = 𝔫 − 2ℓ − 1. It also claims that F-rational O_ℓ in the F-stable nilpotent orbit O^{st}_{p_ℓ} correspond bijectively to orbits under G_{E/F}(1) × G_{n−ℓ} of F-anisotropic vectors in (E^{𝔫−2ℓ}, q).
issues.correction: State these for 1 ≤ ℓ ≤ 𝔯, and define the ℓ = 0 case separately as the paper uses it (Gan–Gross–Prasad's restriction case): for an F-anisotropic w_0 ∈ V, F^{O_0}(C_π) is the space of restrictions of forms in C_π to H^{w_0}_{0⁻}(A) = Isom(V ∩ w_0^⊥, q)°(A), and 'O_0' is the G_{E/F}(1) × G_n-orbit of w_0.
issues.reason: For ℓ = 0, p_0 = [1^𝔫] is the zero orbit, a single F-rational orbit, so the orbit correspondence fails. Also V_{p_0} = 1, and (2.7)–(2.8) give F^{ψ_{O_{p_0}}}(φ) = φ and H^{O_{p_0}} = G_n, not a group of dimension-(𝔫 − 1) type. (2.11)–(2.12) do not make sense for ℓ = 0 (no y_ℓ); only (2.13), the stabilizer of the vector J w_0, does. The paper nevertheless uses ℓ = 0 as the restriction case: for anisotropic G_n only p_0 is relevant, yet Conjecture 2.3 and Theorem 5.7 with ℓ_0, ℓ* = 0 pair π with σ on a group of dimension-(𝔫 − 1) type. The intended meaning is recoverable, so nothing downstream fails.

issues.locator: Section 7.2, before Corollary 7.2, p. 809, and the parallel sentence after (6.8), p. 802 (arXiv v4: p. 75; pp. 67–68)
issues.printed: The source says Conjecture 2.3 is automatic here with no datum (H_m, σ), and takes E_τ on the F-quasisplit H*_a(A) as the residual representation. Citing the Ginzburg-Rallis-Soudry descent in [23], it asserts D^{O_{κ_0}}_n(τ; ∅) = F^{O_{κ_0}}_n(E_τ) is cuspidal, nonzero, and automorphic on G*_n(A).
issues.correction: This holds when the first-occurrence space is trivial: G*_n = SO_{2n+1} or U_{2n+1} (𝔪 = 0), and SO_{2n} (𝔪 = 1, H_0 = SO_1 = 1). For G*_n = U_{2n}, a generic π has first occurrence ℓ_0 = n − 1 with p_{ℓ_0} = [(2n−1)1] and H_m = U_1 (m = 0, 𝔪 = 1). Conjecture 2.3 holds with the datum (U_1, χ) for a character χ of U_1(F)\U_1(A) with non-zero Bessel period, as in the U_{2n} case of Section 7.3. The residue is E_{τ⊗χ} on U_{4n+1}, and Corollary 7.2 follows from Theorem 7.1 with this datum. The statement of Corollary 7.2 stands.
issues.reason: For G*_n = U_{2n}, a = N = 2n and H*_a = U_{4n}. Every partition p_κ = [(2κ+1)1^{4n−2κ−1}] of U_{4n} has stabilizer U_{4n−2κ−1} of odd dimension, never U_{2n}. Equivalently, ℓ_0 = (𝔫 − 𝔪 − 1)/2 is not an integer for 𝔫 = 2n, 𝔪 = 0. So F^{O_{κ_0}}_n(E_τ) with E_τ on H*_a does not produce a representation of U_{2n}. Every Bessel partition [(2ℓ+1)1^{2n−2ℓ−1}] of U_{2n} has 𝔪 ≥ 1, so a non-trivial H_m = U_𝔪 always occurs.

issues.locator: Section 5.3, proof of Proposition 5.6 (arXiv v4: p. 54). Corrected in the published version, p. 790.
issues.printed: In arXiv v4, the proof invokes Proposition 5.5 to choose a smooth factorizable φ_{τ⊗σ′} for which the finite local zeta product Z_S(s, φ_{τ⊗σ′}, φ_π, ψ_{O_{κ*}}) does not vanish at s = 1/2. It infers nonvanishing at 1/2 of the normalized Z*_S(s, φ_{τ⊗σ′}, φ_π, ψ_{O_{κ*}}).
issues.correction: Since Z*_S = Z_S / L_S, one needs L_S(s, τ, π, σ; ρ) = Π_{ν∈S} L(s, τ_ν, π_ν, σ_ν; ρ) to be holomorphic at s = ½. The published proof supplies this: by the generic unitary duals of τ_ν, π_ν and σ_ν, as in Appendix B, each L(s, τ_ν, π_ν, σ_ν; ρ) is holomorphic for Re(s) ≥ ½.
issues.reason: If L_S had a pole at ½, then Z_S(½) ≠ 0 would give Z*_S(½) = 0. Local L-factors have no zeros, so only the numerator L(s + ½, τ_ν × π_ν) of (4.47) matters. Its poles satisfy Re(s + ½) ≤ α + β < 1 when the exponents of τ_ν and of the localized parameter of π are < ½ ((B.5)–(B.6)), and this gives holomorphy for Re(s) ≥ ½. The published text (p. 790, 'By using the structures of generic unitary dual of τ_ν, π_ν, and σ_ν ... is holomorphic for Re(s) ≥ 1/2') adds exactly this step. The gap is known: the published version corrects it.

issues.printed: The source uses σ̄ being isomorphic to σ's contragredient σ∨ to conclude that L(s, τ × σ∨) is nonzero and holomorphic at s = 1/2, claiming the same for L(s, τ × σ). It then asserts this behavior for L(s, π×σ) = L(s, τ × σ), the tensor product L-function.
issues.correction: State the conclusion as L(s, τ × σ∨) holomorphic and non-zero at s = 1/2, which is what the argument proves for the sesquilinear period ⟨F^{ψ_{O_ℓ}}(φ_π), φ_σ⟩; for the bilinear GGP period of π ⊠ σ the conclusion is L(1/2, τ × σ) ≠ 0. For orthogonal groups σ∨ ≅ σ (up to the Õ-twist, with the same L-function), so nothing changes there; for unitary groups the two central values differ in general.
issues.reason: For unitary groups BC(σ)∨ ≅ BC(σ)^c, so L(1/2, τ × σ∨) = L(1/2, τ × BC(σ)^c) = L(1/2, τ^∨ × BC(σ)), which is a different central value from L(1/2, τ × BC(σ)); already for GL₁ × GL₁ these are L(1/2, χμ) and L(1/2, χμ⁻¹) for conjugate-self-dual characters, which can vanish independently. The printed 'and so is L(s, τ × σ)' is therefore unjustified for unitary groups; it is harmless for orthogonal groups. The statement is plausibly true with the matching convention, which is how [GGP12, Conj. 24.1] is formulated (bilinear period of π ⊠ σ).

issues.locator: §3.4,printed577;arXivv5 andauthor ri4 PDF16
issues.printed: The source declares two classes in H¹(u → W, Z → G), represented by z₁ and z₂, equivalent when z₂·z₁⁻¹ lies in the image of Z¹(Γ, G¹_sc). It constructs the functor H¹_ab(u → W) : ℛ → Sets with a surjection H¹(u → W) → H¹_ab(u → W), asserting this is an isomorphism if H¹(Γ, G_sc) = 1. It cites Kneser's theorem [Kne65] for p-adic F and says the condition also holds for tori, since G_sc = 1.
issues.correction: Require H1(F,Gprime_sc)=1 for every inner twist occurring in the equivalence fibers. The claimed conclusion remains valid for p-adic F and for tori.
issues.reason: Take G=SL2 over R, Z=mu2. Ordinary H1(R,SL2)=1 by Hilbert90 and determinant surjectivity. Let J=(0,1;-1,0). The strong real forms ±J sigma have square -I and define distinct rigid classes over the same compact inner form. An isomorphism would require gJ=-J conjugate(g). Solving gives g=(a,b;conjugate(b),-conjugate(a)), whose determinant is -|a|²-|b|², never1. Their relative cocycle -I lifts to the simply connected compact twist itself, so D07 identifies them. Hence H1rig->H1ab is not injective despite vanishing for the untwisted Gsc. Corollary3.8 already describes the three rigid classes over two inner forms. (cc-442dc5) Rechecked: the equivalence relation of §3.4 divides by Z^1(Γ, G1_sc) for the twist G1, and H^1(R, SU(2)) ≠ 1 although H^1(R, SL2) = 1. The two cases the paper names (p-adic F by Kneser, and tori) satisfy the corrected hypothesis, so the uses in §4 are unaffected.

issues.citation: Tasho Kaletha, "Rigid inner forms of real and p-adic groups", Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), no. 2
issues.reviewReason: Confirmed, and this is the one finding that reaches a stated result. The criterion is printed as quoted, and the equivalence relation defined four lines above it divides by the image of Z¹(Γ, G¹_sc) — the simply connected cover of the TWIST G₁, not of G — so injectivity needs the vanishing for every inner twist that occurs, and not merely for G_sc. The two cases the paper names are unaffected — Kneser’s theorem gives the vanishing for every simply connected group over a p-adic field, and for a torus every twist has trivial G_sc — so nothing in §4 or the applications moves, which is what the recorded correction says. issues.reviewReason: The page image of p. 37 reads: "Choose any i ∈ I. By (a), the images V_{1,i}, V_{2,i} of U_1, U_2 in X_i are closed and disjoint; they may thus be covered by disjoint open neighborhoods W_{1,i}, W_{2,i}." The disjointness fails for an arbitrary i. Re-derived counterexample: I = {1 ≤ 2}, X_1 = {pt}, X_2 = {a, b} (discrete), X = lim X_i = {a, b}. U_1 = {a}, U_2 = {b} is a disconnection of X, but both images in X_1 are {pt}. The suggested repair is right. If π_i(U_1) ∩ π_i(U_2) ≠ ∅ for every i, these nonempty compact sets form an inverse system (π_{ij} maps the j-th into the i-th). By (c) its limit has a point x, and x_i ∈ π_i(U_k) for every i and k = 1, 2. A closed subset C of X equals ⋂_i π_i^{-1}(π_i(C)): a point outside C has a basic neighbourhood π_i^{-1}(V) missing C, so its i-th coordinate lies outside π_i(C). Hence x ∈ U_1 ∩ U_2, a contradiction. So some i has disjoint images, and the rest of the argument goes through: the pullbacks of W_{1,j}, W_{2,j} contain U_1 and U_2, are disjoint and cover X, so they equal U_1 and U_2. The conclusion of (e) is correct. The authors' errata (part II Appendix A, kl2.txt 9555–9700) do not mention it, so known: new is right.

issues.reviewReason: Page 50 image: 'Corollary 2.5.13. Suppose that A is reduced. Then no two distinct rational subspaces of Spa(A, A+) have the same intersection with Maxspec(A). Proof. We may reduce to the case where A is reduced. By Corollary 2.5.6, we may further reduce to the case A+ = A◦.' Re-derivation: take A = K{T} (reduced) and A^+ = o_K + m_K·o_K{T} = {f ∈ o_K{T} : f mod m_K ∈ k}. This A^+ is open (it contains m_K·A°) and integrally closed: the reduction of an element integral over A^+ lies in k[T] and is integral over k, so it is constant. Let U = {v : v(1) ≤ v(T)} and V = {v : v(T) ≤ 1}; both are rational. On Maxspec(A) (classical points x with |T(x)| ≤ 1), U ∩ Maxspec = U ∩ V ∩ Maxspec = {|T(x)| = 1}. Now let v be the rank-2 point v(Σ a_i T^i) = max_i |a_i|γ^i, with γ > 1 infinitesimal (value group R_{>0} × γ^Z, ordered lexicographically). v is continuous, v(T) = γ > 1, and v(aT^i) = |a|γ^i < 1 for |a| < 1, so v ≤ 1 on A^+ and v ∈ Spa(A, A^+). Then v ∈ U \ V, so U ≠ U ∩ V: two distinct rational subspaces with the same classical points. The printed corollary is therefore false, and the reduction via Corollary 2.5.6 is invalid, because Corollary 2.5.6 concerns the norm, and the passage from A^+ to A° changes Spa. The corrected statement (A^+ = A°) follows from Lemma 2.5.12: apply its one-element case to U ∩ U' ⊆ U and to U ∩ U' ⊆ U'. One flaw in the entry: its correction says '(so that A is reduced)', which is false (see new issue); drop it.

issues.reviewReason: Page 53 image: 'Let I be the set of finite subsets of R+. For each S ∈ I, let Ai be the quotient of Z((z)){S} … Let A+i be the image of Z[[z]]{S} in Ai. This gives the desired affinoid system.' This is printed as described. Counterexample to integral closedness: take R = Q_p(√p), z = p, S = {p√p} ⊂ R^+. Then A_S ≅ Q_p{T}/(T² − p³) = Q_p(√p), but A_S^+ = Z_p[p√p] = Z_p + Z_p·p√p. This does not contain √p, although √p is integral over it ((√p)² = p). So A_S^+ is not integrally closed and (A_S, A_S^+) is not an adic Banach ring. The integral closure still lies in R^+, and every s ∈ R^+ is already in some A_S^+, so replacing A_S^+ by its integral closure leaves the completed direct limit unchanged. Suggested kind is 'gap' rather than 'misprint': the construction as written fails Definition 2.4.1; it is not a typographical slip.

issues.locator: Definition 2.8.1, p. 59 (arXiv 1301.0792v5)
issues.printed: The source declares four conditions equivalent for a Banach ring A: (a) its norm is equivalent to a power-multiplicative norm; (b) it is equivalent to the spectral seminorm; (c) some c > 0 satisfies |x²| ≥ c|x|² for every x ∈ A; and (d) A◦ is a bounded subring.
issues.correction: Conditions (a)–(c) are equivalent and define uniform Banach rings. Condition (d) follows from them and implies that the spectral norm defines the same topology, but it does not imply (a)–(c); it does when A has a topologically nilpotent unit z with |z||z^{−1}| = 1.
issues.reason: For a nonarchimedean field K, the norm equal to |x| for |x| ≤ 1 and |x|(1 + log|x|) for |x| > 1 is submultiplicative, defines the same topology as its spectral norm |·| (so (d) holds), but is not equivalent to it.

issues.reviewReason: Page 59 image lists (a)–(d) as equivalent, with (d) 'The subring A◦ of A is bounded.' The authors' errata (part II Appendix A, p. 189) record exactly this correction. Re-check of the counterexample: f(x) = |x| for |x| ≤ 1 and |x|(1 + log|x|) for |x| > 1, on a nontrivially valued K. It is a nondecreasing function of |x|, so it is nonarchimedean. It is submultiplicative, since (1 + log a + log b) ≤ (1 + log a)(1 + log b) for a, b ≥ 1 and the mixed cases are easy. Its spectral seminorm lim f(x^n)^{1/n} = |x|, so A° = o_K is bounded and (d) holds. But f(x)/|x| = 1 + log|x| is unbounded, so (a) and (b) fail, and f(x²)/f(x)² → 0 as |x| → ∞, so (c) fails.

issues.reviewReason: The p. 73 image matches the quoted text. X is cut out by φ̄^a(U) = A^{−1}U, which U = 0 satisfies, so X parametrizes all invariant m-tuples. The v_j form a basis only on the locus where det U is invertible. The errata (part II App. A, bullet 'Lemma 3.2.6') say the same. Two details in the entry are off. (1) Relative to an invariant basis, d = det U satisfies φ̄^a(d) = d, so locally d lies in F_{p^a}, not F_p (the errata's 'belongs to F_p' is literally right only for a = 1). Nonvanishing is still closed-open, since d^{p^a−1} is idempotent. (2) In the n > 1 paragraph (p. 74), v_j = e_j + Σ_i p^{n−1}U_ij e_i differs from e by the unipotent matrix 1 + p^{n−1}U, which is invertible over W_n(S). Those v_j always form a basis, so the n > 1 scheme needs no restriction. The errata's 'similar considerations apply in the last paragraph' presumably concerns the positive-rank paragraph, where Lang's argument supplies an invertible U and so a point of the closed-open part.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 3.5.9, second paragraph, p. 85 (arXiv 1301.0792v5)
issues.printed: It says G → W(oE)^× → W(κE)^× is constantly 1 and therefore invokes Lemma 3.5.8 to make the 1-cocycle trivial.
issues.correction: Lemma 3.5.8 is about 1 + mL; the cocycle takes values in the kernel U of W(oL)^× → W(κL)^×. Filter U by U_n = U ∩ (1 + p^nW(oL)): U/U_1 ≅ 1 + mL, where Lemma 3.5.8 applies, and U_n/U_{n+1} ≅ mL (additively), where H^1(G, mL) = 0 follows from the almost optimal exactness in the proof of Lemma 3.5.8 (a cocycle of norm δ < 1 bounds a cochain of norm < 1). Trivializing successively and using p-adic completeness gives y.
issues.reason: As written, the lemma is applied to a group it does not cover; the conclusion is right but needs the filtration.

issues.reviewReason: Lemma 3.5.8 (p. 84, image checked) states only H^1(G, 1+m_K) = 0 for K perfect of char p with G acting faithfully and isometrically. In the proof of 3.5.9 the cocycle f(g) = g(w)/w, w = z_1^{-1}z = z_1^{-1}[z̄] + p, takes values in U = ker(W(o_L)^× → W(κ_L)^×) = 1 + W(m_L), which is not 1+m_L; the lemma as stated does not apply. I re-checked the proposed fix: U → (W(o_L)/p)^× = o_L^× has image 1+m_L and kernel U_1 = U ∩ (1+pW(o_L)), so U/U_1 ≅ 1+m_L; for n ≥ 1, 1+p^n x ∈ U iff x ∈ W(m_L) (p^n x has components x_i^{p^n}), and 1+p^n x ↦ x mod p gives U_n/U_{n+1} ≅ m_L additively (surjective via 1+p^n[a]); H^1(G, m_L) = 0 because a cocycle h with max|h(g)| = δ < 1 is dx with |x| ≤ (1+ε)δ < 1 by the almost-optimal exactness shown in the proof of 3.5.8. U is abelian, the n-th correction lies in U_n ⊂ 1+p^nW(o_L), and W(o_L) is p-adically complete, so the product converges to y. Also needed (implicit in the paper): G acts faithfully and isometrically on L (a g trivial on L is trivial on W(o_L) and hence on E = Frac(W(o_L)/I)). The rest of the proof (G-invariant generator w/y, K = L^G, F' ⊆ E^G = F with [E:F'] = #G = [E:F]) checks out. Not in the errata, so 'new' is right.

issues.printed: For every positive integer a, it identifies the φ^a-fixed elements in both Ẽ_L and R̃_L with the unramified extension of Q_p whose residue field is F_{p^a}.
issues.correction: … constitute W(L^{φ^a})[p^{−1}], where L^{φ^a} = {x ∈ L : x^{p^a} = x}; this is the unramified extension of Q_p with residue field F_{p^a} exactly when F_{p^a} ⊆ L (for instance when L is algebraically closed).
issues.reason: Ẽ_L = W(L)[p^{−1}], so its φ^a-invariants are W(L^{φ^a})[p^{−1}], and the proof (via Lemma 4.2.4) shows that R̃_L has the same invariants. Take L the completed perfection of F_p((t)), a perfect analytic field with residue field F_p. An x ∈ L with x^{p²} = x is 0 or a root of unity of order dividing p² − 1, prime to p, and such roots of unity inject into the residue field F_p; so L^{φ²} = F_p and the φ²-invariants of Ẽ_L are Q_p, not Q_{p²}. The uses of the lemma (Proposition 4.3.3, and the proof of Theorem 7.3.7, where L is a completed algebraic closure) take L algebraically closed or a = 1, so they are unaffected.

issues.reviewReason: Page 106 image: Hypothesis 4.2.1 says only 'let L be a perfect analytic field of characteristic p with norm α'. An analytic field is complete for a nontrivial multiplicative norm (§2.2, tex l.1497). So L need not be algebraically closed or contain F_{p^a}. Page 108 image, Lemma 4.2.10: 'for any positive integer a, the elements of Ẽ_L and R̃_L fixed by φ^a constitute the unramified extension of Q_p with residue field F_{p^a}'. Re-derivation: φ^a(Σ p^i[x̄_i]) = Σ p^i[x̄_i^{p^a}], and Teichmüller expansions are unique, so (W(L)[1/p])^{φ^a} = W(L^{φ^a})[1/p]. For R̃_L, φ^a-invariance gives λ(α^s)(x) = λ(α^{p^a s})(x), so x is bounded near 0 and lies in R̃^bd_L ⊂ Ẽ_L by Lemma 4.2.4. Conversely W(L^{φ^a}) ⊂ R̃^int_L, since its Teichmüller coordinates have norm ≤ 1. So both invariant rings equal W(L^{φ^a})[1/p]. Counterexample: L = completed perfection of F_p((t)), with residue field F_p. The roots of X^{p²} − X in L are 0 and roots of unity of order prime to p. These reduce injectively into the residue field (X^{p²} − X is separable mod the maximal ideal), so L^{φ²} = F_p and the φ²-invariants are Q_p ≠ Q_{p²}. The case a = 1 (Q_p) is correct. The authors' errata (part II, Appendix A) do not mention it. The uses of the lemma are with L algebraically closed: Proposition 4.3.3 (L′ algebraically closed) and Theorem 7.3.7 (L a completed algebraic closure). So the entry is right as written.

issues.reviewReason: The page image p. 161 reads '… taut adic spaces locally of finite type over an analytic field K (i.e., covered by the adic spectra of affinoid algebras over K) and Hausdorff strictly K-analytic spaces …'. In this paper 'adic spectrum' means Spa(A, A⁺) for any ring of integral elements A⁺ (§2.4), and Remark 2.4.9 itself uses the pair (K{T}, o_K + m_K·o_K{T}). My own re-derivation: A⁺′ = o_K + m_K A° is open (it contains A°° = m_K A°) and integrally closed in A, because an element integral over it lies in A°, and its reduction in A°/A°° = k[T̄] is integral over k, hence constant. Every continuous rank-one valuation on K{T} has |T| ≤ 1 because T is power-bounded, so both X = Spa(A, A°) and X′ = Spa(A, A⁺′) have real quotient M(K{T}) (quotient map by Definition 2.4.8). Both are affinoid, hence qcqs and taut, and both are sheafy since A is strongly noetherian. X ≅ X′ over K would, by Lemma 8.2.9, give a continuous automorphism of A carrying A° into A⁺′ ⊊ A°, which is impossible because automorphisms preserve A°. Fullness fails concretely: id of M(K{T}) does not lift to X′ → X, since T would have to go into A⁺′. So the functor is not fully faithful on the class the parenthetical describes. With Huber's meaning of 'locally of finite type over Spa(K, K°)', A⁺ must contain the integral closure of the image of K°⟨T⟩, which is A°, so the proposition as Huber states it [79, Prop. 8.3.1] is correct. The defect is the gloss, which is part of the statement. The correction is right.

(i) For the strongly preperfectoid and relatively perfectoid classes, stability under rational localization and finite étale extension follows by applying Theorems 3.6.14 and 3.6.21 after base change to each perfectoid field, resp. algebra. (ii) Closure of the preperfectoid basis under fibred products: given preperfectoid A1 → A2, A1 → A3 with witnessing perfectoid fields K1, K2, K3, pick a point of M(K1 ⊗̂ K2 ⊗̂ K3), which is nonempty by Lemma 2.3.13. Its residue field contains all three fields, and its completed algebraic closure L is a perfectoid field. Each Ai ⊗̂ L = (Ai ⊗̂ Ki) ⊗̂_{Ki} L is perfectoid, so (A2 ⊗̂_{A1} A3) ⊗̂ L is perfectoid by Proposition 3.6.11 (as corrected in part II, Theorem 3.3.13). Uniformity of A2 ⊗̂_{A1} A3 follows because Q_p → L admits a bounded Q_p-linear retraction, so the tensor product embeds strictly into its uniform base change to L.

issues.reviewReason: The page image p. 169 reads 'suppose that A is an integral affinoid algebra over an analytic field. Then on one hand Spec(A) is normal and noetherian, so Zp-ILoc(Spec(A)) = Qp-Loc(Spec(A)) by Remark 1.4.9.' Remark 1.4.9 (p. 23) assumes X normal. My own re-derivation of the nodal example A = K{x,y}/(y² − x²(1+x)), char K ≠ 2, follows. (1) f is y-distinguished of degree 2, so A is free of rank 2 over K{x}. A factorization of f would force (a/x)² = 1+x in K{x}, impossible because 1+x has a simple zero at x = −1 in the disc, so f is prime (K{x,y} is a UFD) and A is a domain. (2) t = y/x satisfies t² = 1+x. If t ∈ A then A → K{t} would be surjective, but A is singular at the maximal ideal (x,y) (f ∈ m², so dim m/m² = 2 > 1), so A is not normal. (3) Following Example 1.4.6, the crosswise double cover B = {(g1,g2) ∈ K{t}² : g1(1) = g2(−1), g2(1) = g1(−1)} is finite étale over A: it is finite, is an isomorphism onto the normalization away from the node, and at the node both complete local rings are K[[u,v]]/(uv). Glueing trivial rank-1 local systems on B by 1 and p across the two nodes gives a Q_p-local system with monodromy p, which is not an isogeny Z_p-local system. Its descent V ⊕ τ*V is then in Qp-Loc(Spec A) but not in Zp-ILoc(Spec A), because pullback preserves Zp-ILoc and V is a direct summand. So the displayed equality is false for integral non-normal A. The remark's conclusion (non-essential-surjectivity) is unaffected, since Example 8.5.17 is smooth.

issues.printed: In (b), it specifies the category of isogeny (c, d)-Zp-local systems on Spec(R0), allowing any subring R0 of R with completed direct perfection equal to R.

issues.reason: The proof ('immediate from Theorem 8.5.6') covers only complete R_0, through Theorem 3.1.15(b), which needs a uniform Banach algebra. For an incomplete R_0 the statement fails: take d = 1, c = 0, K the completed perfection of 𝔽_p((t)), R the completed perfection of K⟨T⟩ and R_0 = K[T] with the restricted norm, whose completed direct perfection is R. The Artin–Schreier–Witt ℤ_p-torsor F(y) − y = [tT] over Spec K[T] is nontrivial (its reduction y^p − y = tT has no solution in K[T], by degree), but it splits over R by y = −Σ_{k≥0} [(tT)^{p^k}], which converges since |t| < 1. So the unipotent rank-2 isogeny ℤ_p-local system attached to it is a nonsplit extension of ℚ_p by ℚ_p over Spec K[T] that splits over Spec R, and base change from (b) to (a) is not fully faithful. The extension is nonsplit even in the isogeny category: if p^m[tT] = F(y) − y with y ∈ W(K[T]), then y − p^m z ∈ W(R)^{F=1} = ℤ_p (z = −Σ_k [(tT)^{p^k}], Spec R connected), so y = p^m z + a with a ∈ ℤ_p, and the m-th Witt component of y is (±Σ_k (tT)^{p^k})^{p^m} + a_m, which is not a polynomial.

Re-derived the counterexample (d=1, c=0, so (0,1)-systems are isogeny Z_p-local systems): K = completed perfection of F_p((t)) (so Hypothesis 5.0.1 holds), R = completed perfection of K<T>, R0 = K[T] with the restricted norm; its direct perfection K[T^{p^-inf}] is dense in R. y^p - y = tT has no solution in K[T] (deg y = n >= 1 gives degree pn != 1; constants give constants), so the ASW torsor of [tT] is nontrivial; z = -sum_k [(tT)^{p^k}] converges in W(R) and F(z) - z = [tT]. Nontriviality must hold after inverting p (Hom/Ext in the isogeny category are tensored with Q), which the entry's reason does not argue; I checked it: if p^m[tT] = F(y) - y with y in W(K[T]), then y - p^m z lies in W(R)^{F=1} = Z_p (R^{F=1} = F_p, Spec R connected), so y = p^m z + a, a in Z_p; the m-th Witt component of p^m z + a is z_0^{p^m} + a_m with z_0 = ±sum_k (tT)^{p^k} (lower components of p^m z vanish, so the Witt addition polynomial contributes nothing else), which is not a polynomial - contradiction. Hence the rank-2 unipotent isogeny local system is nonsplit over Spec K[T] and split over Spec R: (b)->(a) is not full. issues.printed: In (b), with the notation of (a), it identifies the coordinate ring of Z with global sections on the subspace in FF_R defined by t, equips that ring with a uniform norm, and declares the resulting Banach Q_p-algebra perfectoid. Remark 8.8.21 says [45] proves Conjecture 8.8.20 when R = L is an analytic field.
issues.correction: Add to (b) the hypothesis that t has only simple zeros on each fibre FF_x (equivalently that Z is reduced), or conclude only that the uniform completion of the reduced quotient of the coordinate ring is perfectoid. With the extra hypothesis the case R = L follows from the Fargues–Fontaine description of the closed points of the curve; Remark 8.8.21's first sentence holds for (a) and for (b) so amended.
issues.reason: Take R = L algebraically closed, a = 1, F = O(2) (deg F = 2 > 0 and F(−2) = O is globally étale) and t = f^2 with 0 ≠ f ∈ P_{L,1}. The hypothesis of (a) holds, and Z = V_+(f^2) is the first-order thickening of the degree-one point ∞ = V_+(f): its coordinate ring is B^+_dR(K)/(ξ^2), where K is the untilt of L at ∞ and ξ a uniformizer of B^+_dR(K), the completed local ring at ∞. This ring contains the nonzero nilpotent ξ, so it has no power-multiplicative norm and is not perfectoid (perfectoid Banach algebras are uniform, hence reduced). So (b) as stated, and the claim that [45] establishes the conjecture for fields, fail whenever t has a multiple zero; (a) is unaffected.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.2.3(a), p. 28 (arXiv 1301.0792v5)
issues.printed: The proof sets x_{l+1} = x_l − f(x_l)/f′(x_l), placing x_{l+1} ∈ ker(α). It asserts that {x_l} becomes Cauchy in A_i whenever i ∈ I is sufficiently large, and its limit solves f = 0.
issues.correction: Fix i with f_1 invertible in A_i (and f defined over A_i). Choose j ≥ i with |f_0|_j small compared with |f_1^{−1}|_i and the norms of the coefficients (possible because α(f_0) = 0 and the transition maps are submetric). Run Newton's iteration in A_j starting from 0; it converges to a root r_j with |r_j|_j ≤ |f_1^{−1}|_i |f_0|_j. For each k ≥ j the same holds in A_k, and the image of r_j is the unique root of that size, because f(r) − f(r′) = (r − r′)(f_1 + small) and f_1 + small is a unit. Hence α(r) ≤ |f_1^{−1}|_i inf_k |f_0|_k = 0, so the root lies in ker(α), as the criterion of Remark 1.2.7 requires.
issues.reason: Remark 1.2.7 needs a root lying in ker(α). The proof takes the limit in some A_i but never shows that its image in A lies in ker(α). Nor do the iterates x_l ∈ A obviously come from a single A_i in which Newton's method converges: α(f_0) = 0 does not make |f_0|_i small for a fixed i. The statement is true, with the repair above.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.2.4(a), p. 29 (arXiv 1301.0792v5)
issues.printed: The proof selects ǫ > 0 subject to ǫ max{β(e), 1} < 1, then uses β(y − x) ≤ c^{−1}ǫ max{β(x), 1} to conclude β(y − e) < c^{−1}.
issues.correction: Choose ǫ > 0 with cǫ max{β(e), 1} < 1. Then β(x_{l+1} − x_l) ≤ ǫ^{l+1} max{β(x), 1}, so β(y − x) ≤ ǫ max{β(x), 1} < c^{−1}, using β(x) ≤ max{β(e), β(x − e)} ≤ max{β(e), 1}. Hence β(y − e) < c^{−1}.
issues.reason: β is only c-submultiplicative. So from x_{l+1} − x_l = d_l − 2d_l x_l with β(d_l) ≤ c^{−1}ǫ^{l+1}, one gets β(x_{l+1} − x_l) ≤ max{c^{−1}ǫ^{l+1}, cβ(d_l)β(x_l)} ≤ ǫ^{l+1} max{c^{−1}, β(x_l)}, not c^{−1}ǫ^{l+1} max{β(x), 1}. For nonzero e we have β(x) ≈ β(e) ≥ c^{−1}, so the extra factor c^{−1} is lost. With the printed choice of ǫ, β(y − x) < c^{−1} and hence y = e are not justified. Shrinking ǫ fixes this; the rest of the argument (y and e are idempotents, (y − e)² is an idempotent of norm < c^{−1}, so it is 0 and y = e) was checked.

issues.locator: Remark 2.3.9, second bullet, p. 35 (arXiv 1301.0792v5)
issues.printed: The remark asserts equivalence of (a) and (b) when A has characteristic p, arguing that a uniform unit z makes A a Banach algebra over F_p((z)), an analytic field.
issues.correction: If A is of characteristic p and uniform (its norm is equivalent to the spectral seminorm), then (a) and (b) are equivalent: a uniform unit z makes A a Banach algebra over F_p((z)) with |z| = |z|_sp. Without uniformity (b) does not imply (a).
issues.reason: Counterexample. Fix ρ ∈ (0, 1) and let A = F_p((z)) with the norm |Σ a_i z^i| = max{ρ^i (1 + |i|) : a_i ≠ 0}. This norm is nonarchimedean and submultiplicative, since w(i) = ρ^i(1 + |i|) satisfies w(i + j) ≤ w(i)w(j). A is complete: w(i) → ∞ as i → −∞ and w(i) → 0 as i → +∞, so A is a Banach ring. z is a unit, |z^n| = ρ^n(1 + n) → 0, |z|_sp = ρ and |z^{−1}|_sp = lim(ρ^{−n}(1 + n))^{1/n} = ρ^{−1}. So z is a uniform unit and (b) holds. Suppose K → A were a bounded homomorphism from an analytic field. Pick t ∈ K with 0 < |t|_K < 1. Its image is topologically nilpotent in A, so it has z-adic valuation k ≥ 1 (an element of valuation ≤ 0 has |t^n| ≥ 1). Then |t^n|_A ≥ ρ^{nk}(1 + nk) and |t^{−n}|_A ≥ ρ^{−nk}(1 + nk), while boundedness gives |t^{±n}|_A ≤ C|t|_K^{±n}. Multiplying the two bounds gives (1 + nk)² ≤ C² for all n, a contradiction. So (a) fails. The argument in the paper needs |z^n| ≤ C|z|_sp^n for all n ∈ Z, which holds exactly when the norm is equivalent to the spectral norm on powers of z, e.g. when A is uniform.

issues.printed: The source uses α(g) > 0 for every α ∈ Ū and compactness to obtain c = inf{α(g) : α ∈ Ū} > 0. It asserts that, given 0 < ε < c, elements f′_1, …, f′_n, g′ ∈ A with |f′_i − f_i| < ε and |g′ − g| < ε yield generators for the unit ideal, with U = {v ∈ Spa(A, A^+) : v(f′_i) ≤ v(g′) (i = 1, …, n)}.
issues.correction: Take 0 < ε < min(c, d), where d = inf{max(α(f_1), …, α(f_n), α(g)) : α ∈ M(A)} > 0 (Corollary 2.3.6, since f_1, …, f_n, g generate the unit ideal). Then both conclusions hold: for α ∈ M(A), max(α(f′_i), α(g′)) = max(α(f_i), α(g)) ≥ d, so f′, g′ generate the unit ideal; for v ∈ U, α(v)(g) ≥ c > ε gives v(g′) = v(g) and v(f′_i) ≤ v(g′); for v in the primed set, α(v)(g′) = max ≥ d > ε gives v(g) = v(g′) and v(f_i) ≤ v(g). (The remark also tacitly assumes a uniform unit, needed for the projection Spa(A, A^+) → M(A) of Definition 2.4.6.)
issues.reason: Counterexample: A = ℚ_p × ℚ_p with the sup norm (uniform unit (p, p)), A^+ = ℤ_p × ℤ_p, so Spa(A, A^+) has two points 1, 2. Take n = 1, f_1 = (p, p^3), g = (1, p^5) (g is a unit). Then U = {1} (at point 2, p^{−3} > p^{−5}), Ū = {1}, c = 1. Take ε with p^{−2} < ε < 1. (i) g′ = (1, p^2), f′_1 = f_1: |g′ − g| = p^{−2} < ε, but at point 2, p^{−3} ≤ p^{−2}, so the primed set is both points ≠ U. (ii) g′ = (1, 0), f′_1 = (p, 0): |g′ − g| = p^{−5}, |f′_1 − f_1| = p^{−3} < ε, but f′_1, g′ generate ℚ_p × 0, not the unit ideal. Here d = p^{−3}, and ε < min(c, d) excludes both. Downstream uses (Lemma 2.4.13, Lemma 2.4.19(b), Proposition 2.4.24, Remark 2.6.3, Lemma 2.6.5(a), the proof of Theorem 3.6.14(b) 'pick ε as in Remark 2.4.7') only need some small ε and go through with the corrected bound; Proposition 2.4.24 uses only the c-part.

issues.locator: Remark 2.4.4, second paragraph, p. 39 (arXiv 1301.0792v5)
issues.printed: The remark asserts that, for a Banach ring A over an analytic field K, a semivaluation whose values on A^+ are bounded by 1 is continuous precisely when its restriction to K gives a valuation equivalent to K's norm.
issues.correction: Only 'continuous ⇒ restriction to K equivalent to the norm' holds. The correct criterion is the one in the preceding sentence: v (bounded by 1 on A^+) is continuous iff for every x with v(x) ≠ 0 there is n with v(ϖ^n) < v(x), ϖ a pseudo-uniformizer of K, i.e. v(ϖ) is cofinal in the value group.
issues.reason: A = K⟨T⟩, A^+ = o_K⟨T⟩. Let v(f) = (|a_{i_0}|, i_0) for f = Σ a_i T^i with i_0 = ord_T f, valued in ℝ_{>0} × ℤ ordered so that larger T-order is smaller (the composite of the T-adic valuation of K[[T]] with |·| on the residue field K). This is a valuation, bounded by 1 on o_K⟨T⟩, and its restriction to K is |·|. But v(T) < v(ϖ^n) for all n, so it fails the criterion of the previous sentence (and {f : v(f) < v(T)} contains no ball ϖ^N o_K⟨T⟩, since v(ϖ^N) > v(T)): v is not continuous. The consequence the paper draws (continuous morphisms of Banach algebras over K are bounded) is still true, via continuity ⇒ boundedness for K-linear maps. The first paragraph of the same remark has a separate problem (finding E144).

It calls (Di, Di+) → (Ei, Ei+) together with (C, C+) → (Fi, Fi+) rational localizations, using Lemma 2.5.9 to infer Ei+ = Ei◦. From the image of Maxspec(Fi) lying in U ∩ Vi ∩ Maxspec(A), it infers that Di → Fi factors through Ei.
issues.correction: (Di, Di+) → (Ei, Ei+) is the base change of the affinoid localization representing U, so it is only an affinoid localization; it is rational only if U ∩ Vi is a rational subdomain of Vi, which is not known at this point. Theorem 2.5.11 only makes U ∩ Vi ∩ Maxspec(A) a rational subdomain of Maxspec(Di). The claimed factorization of Di → Fi through Ei would need Di → Ei to represent this classical subdomain, which is the assertion (a) being proved. A repair: let Wi ⊆ Vi be a rational subspace with Wi ∩ Maxspec = U ∩ Vi ∩ Maxspec. Then show Wi = U ∩ Vi via Huber's comparison of rigid spaces with adic spaces of the form Spa(A, A°) (Huber 1994, §4), or another argument not relying on (a).
issues.reason: Lemma 2.5.9 applies only to rational localizations. The step from 'Maxspec(Fi) lands in the classical subdomain' to 'Di → Fi factors through Ei' uses the universal property of Ei for classical points, which is statement (a) itself for (Di, U ∩ Vi). The statement of 2.5.14 is standard and presumably true; the gap is in the written proof.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.8.6, first sentence, p. 61 (arXiv 1301.0792v5)
issues.printed: The proof takes a k-basis S of ℓ and claims a unique expansion Σ_{s∈S} as ⊗ [s] for every b ∈ A ⊗K L, with coefficients as ∈ A having finite support.
issues.correction: This holds only when [ℓ : k] < ∞ (then W(ℓ) is finite free over W(k) with basis the [s]). In general the elements Σ as ⊗ [s] (finite sums) form a dense subgroup D of A ⊗K L. The proof shows |b^p| = |b|^p for b ∈ D. For arbitrary b ≠ 0, choose d ∈ D with |b − d| < |b|; then |b^p − d^p| ≤ |b − d|·|b|^{p−1} < |b|^p, so |b^p| = |d^p| = |d|^p = |b|^p.
issues.reason: Take A = K and ℓ/k infinite (e.g. k = F_p, ℓ = an algebraic closure), with distinct s_n ∈ S. The element x = Σ_n p^n [s_n] ∈ L is not a finite K-combination of the [s], because {[s]} is orthonormal in L (the residues s are k-linearly independent), so convergent expansions in it are unique. The lemma is still true by the density argument.

issues.locator: Example 2.8.7, p. 61 (arXiv 1301.0792v5)
issues.printed: The example chooses an analytic field K and arbitrary r > 0, defining A as the closed K-subalgebra inside K{X/r, U} generated by U^n X^{⌈log2 n⌉}, n = 1, 2, . . . . It claims that B is nonuniform for the rational localization (A, A◦) → (B, B+) associated with {v ∈ Spa(A, A◦) : v(X) ≤ 1}, citing [99, Theorem 3.11].
issues.correction: Pick any r > 1. Let A be the closure of the K-subalgebra of K{X/r, U} generated by X and U^n X^{a_n} (n ≥ 1), where a_n is the least integer greater than log2 n. This is Mihara's example, arXiv:1403.7856v1, §2.2 and Theorem 3.11, where a_0 = 1, the index runs over n ≥ 0, and r ∈ (1, ∞).
issues.reason: As printed, X ∉ A. Every generator has U-degree ≥ 1, so every element of A has zero coefficient on U^0 X^j for j ≥ 1. Hence {v : v(X) ≤ 1} is not a rational subset of Spa(A, A°), and the example is ill-posed. Also, once X ∈ A, the condition r > 1 is necessary: for r ≤ 1 the spectral norm of X is r ≤ 1, so X ∈ A° and {v(X) ≤ 1} is all of Spa(A, A°). Then B = A, which is uniform. Mihara v1 (Theorems 2.4 and 3.11) states r ∈ (1, ∞) and includes the generator X (a_0 = 1). There, a_1 = 1 (generator UX), whereas the printed ⌈log2 1⌉ = 0.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 2.8.16(b), monogenic case, p. 65 (arXiv 1301.0792v5)
issues.printed: The proof takes f to be P's resultant and infers that f is invertible in A from B ∈ FÉt(A). Expressing V^{−1} through det(V)^{−1} and V's cofactor matrix, it obtains β′ ≤ cβ, c = c1^{d−1} α(f^{−1}).

issues.reason: Counterexample to the printed constant: A = K, d = 2, P = T(T − λ) with |λ| = R > 1. Then c1 = max{|λ|, 0} = R, f = disc(P) = λ², α(f^{−1}) = R^{−2}, so the printed c = R^{−1} < 1. But Q = 1 has β′(1) = β(1) = 1, so β′ ≤ cβ fails. Correct estimate: by Lagrange interpolation, a_i is bounded by max_j|Q(z_j)| times the coefficient size of Π_{k≠j}(T − z_k) (at most max{1, c1}^{d−1}) divided by |P′(z_j)|. Also |P′(z_j)|^{−1} = |disc|^{−1} Π_{l≠j}|P′(z_l)| ≤ |disc|^{−1} max{1, c1}^{(d−1)²}. Moreover γ(f^{−1}) ≤ α(f^{−1}).

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.8.15, p. 64 (arXiv 1301.0792v5)
issues.printed: The proof chooses a primitive element f in Frac(B), then invokes Lemma 2.4.17 to arrange that its minimal polynomial over Frac(A) lies in A[T]. It names this polynomial P ∈ A[T] and asserts that its resultant does not vanish at α.
issues.correction: Frac(A) and Frac(B) are undefined for a general Banach ring (A need not be a domain; e.g. A = K × K). Instead, after replacing A by a rational localization encircling α, make B free over A and choose f ∈ B whose image in B ⊗A H(α) is primitive (an open condition, Lemma 2.2.13). Take P to be the characteristic polynomial of multiplication by f, which is monic in A[T]; its discriminant (the 'resultant' of P and P′) is nonzero at α. The rest of the argument goes through.
issues.reason: The objects named in the proof do not exist in the stated generality ('any Banach ring A'), so the step selecting P is not justified as written.

issues.locator: Theorem 3.3.7(c) and its proof, pp. 77–78; also the statement of Lemma 3.3.9, p. 78 (arXiv 1301.0792v5)
issues.printed: Part (c) claims that (b) yields a homeomorphism between M(R) and M(W(o_R)[[z̄]^{−1}]/(z)), preserving rational subspaces. It then gives the identification M(R) = {γ ∈ M(o_R) : γ(z̄_0) ≥ p^{−1}}.
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis z̄_0 ∈ R^× to Theorem 3.3.7(c) and Lemma 3.3.9. This is the unit condition the authors' errata add to 'primitive of degree 1', but it is needed already in §3.3, not only 'starting in section 3.6'.
issues.reason: Counterexample. Let R be the completed perfection of F_p{T} with the Gauss norm, |T| = p^{−1}. This norm is multiplicative and bounded by the trivial norm, so o_R = R. Take z = [T] − p. Then z̄_0 = T, z̄_1 = −1 (a unit), and α(xT) = p^{−1}α(x) for all x, so z is primitive of degree 1 in the sense of Definition 3.3.4. Now take γ_0 ∈ M(R), the constant-term seminorm (x ↦ 1 if x(0) ≠ 0, else 0). Then σ(γ_0)([T]) = μ(σ(γ_0))(T) = γ_0(T) = 0. But every point of M(W(o_R)[[T]^{−1}]/(z)) has γ([T]) ≥ p^{−1}, so the homeomorphism of (b) does not carry M(R) into M(W(o_R)[[z̄]^{−1}]/(z)). That space is σ of {γ : γ(T) = p^{−1}}, the spectrum of the completion of R[T^{−1}], not M(R). The proof's identification M(R) = {γ(z̄_0) ≥ p^{−1}} holds exactly when z̄_0 is invertible, since then α(z̄_0^{−1}x) = pα(x). Lemma 3.3.9 evaluates α ∈ M(R) on the Witt components of y ∈ W(o_R)[[z̄]^{−1}], which lie in o_R[z̄^{−1}], and its proof uses α(z̄) = p^{−1} for all α ∈ M(R). Both need z̄_0 ∈ R^×. Example 3.3.8 (a field) and the uses in §3.6 (where the errata impose the condition) are unaffected.

issues.locator: Remark 3.1.6, proof of (d), p. 67 (arXiv 1301.0792v5)
issues.printed: For (d), the proof regards perfectness as evident and reduces the task to establishing that R/I has a spectral seminorm which is a norm. It concludes that ȳ = 0 because ȳ has quotient norm below ε.
issues.correction: Uniformity needs the quotient norm to be equivalent to the spectral seminorm, not just the spectral seminorm to be a norm. The same argument gives this. For any ȳ ∈ R/I and any lift y_n of ȳ^{p^n}, y_n^{p^{−n}} lifts ȳ (I is perfect) and |y_n^{p^{−n}}| = |y_n|^{p^{−n}}. So the quotient norm of ȳ is at most (quotient norm of ȳ^{p^n})^{p^{−n}}, which tends to the spectral seminorm. Hence the quotient norm equals the spectral seminorm and is power-multiplicative.
issues.reason: A Banach ring whose spectral seminorm is a norm need not be uniform (the spectral norm can be strictly weaker than the Banach norm). As written, the proof shows only that the spectral seminorm is a norm.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 6.1.4, last sentence, p. 135 (arXiv 1301.0792v5)
issues.printed: The proof claims convergence of Σ_l a_il to a_i ∈ R̃^∞_R with w = Σ_i a_i v_i, thereby establishing the claim.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 7.3.3(b), p. 148 (arXiv 1301.0792v5)
issues.printed: The proof uses the basis e′_1, …, e′_n of M′ to assert that B′'s maximal minor indexed by J is nonzero in ℰ̃_R/𝔪′, and therefore in ℛ̃^bd_R/𝔪 as well.
issues.correction: Write v_i ≡ Σ_{k∈J} A_ki v_k (mod 𝔪M) for i ∉ J with A_ki ∈ ℛ̃^bd_R/𝔪, and let T = B′_J + A·B′_{J^c} (entries in ℛ̃^bd_R/𝔪) be the matrix expressing e′_1, …, e′_n in the basis (v_j)_{j∈J} of M/𝔪M. Since M′/𝔪′M′ = (M/𝔪M) ⊗ ℰ̃_R/𝔪′ and the e′_j reduce to a basis of it, det T ≠ 0 in ℰ̃_R/𝔪′, hence in ℛ̃^bd_R/𝔪; Nakayama then gives the claim.
issues.reason: The minor of B′ on the rows J need not be nonzero, because the v_i with i ∉ J need not vanish modulo 𝔪. Example: R arbitrary, M = ℛ̃^bd_R with c = 0, M′_0 = W(R) with basis e = 1, generators v_1 = v_2 = e (m = 2, n = 1). Then B = B′ = (0, 1)^T, C = (1, 1), CB = 1, X = 1, and J = {1} is a valid choice (v_1 is a basis of M/𝔪M), yet the J-minor B′_11 = 0. The conclusion that e′_1 = v_2 = e generates M is still true, and the corrected argument above proves it in general.

issues.locator: Proof of Corollary 8.7.10, p. 179 (arXiv 1301.0792v5)
issues.printed: The proof attributes the result directly to Remark 4.2.18 together with Theorem 8.5.12 and Theorem 8.7.8.
issues.correction: Proof. Immediate from Remark 4.2.18 and Corollary 7.3.9 (pointwise semistable of degree 0 = étale), Theorem 8.7.8, and the analogue of Theorem 8.5.12 for étale ℚ_{p^a}-local systems on X and étale φ^a-modules over ℛ̃_{X′} (X′ over 𝔽_{p^a}), which follows from Theorem 8.3.5, Corollary 8.4.7 and Theorem 8.5.6 with d = a exactly as Theorem 8.5.12 follows from Theorem 8.5.8.
issues.reason: Theorem 8.5.12 (p. 173) concerns étale (c, d)-ℚ_p-local systems and (c, d)-pure φ-modules; for c = 0 these are étale φ-modules and, by the ratio-invariance of Definition 8.5.7, ordinary étale ℚ_p-local systems. Corollary 8.7.10 concerns étale ℚ_{p^a}-local systems and vector bundles on FF_X = FF^{(a)}_X, i.e. φ^a-modules over ℛ̃ (Theorem 8.7.8). For a > 1 these differ: the trivial rank-1 ℚ_{p^a}-local system corresponds to O on FF^{(a)}_X (rank 1), whereas as a ℚ_p-local system it has rank a and Theorem 8.5.12 attaches to it a rank-a φ-module. The needed φ^a-version is not stated in §8.5, but Theorem 8.5.6 is stated for φ^d-modules and ℤ_{p^d}-local systems, so the same globalisation argument gives it.

issues.locator: Remark 2.4.4, first paragraph, p. 39 (arXiv 1301.0792v5)
issues.printed: The source calls A Tate when it has a topologically nilpotent unit z. It claims that each c ∈ (0, 1) gives A a Banach ring structure through α(x) = inf{cⁿ : n ∈ Z, z⁻ⁿx ∈ A0}.
issues.correction: Require z ∈ A0 (always achievable by replacing z with a power, since z is topologically nilpotent), and A complete and Hausdorff for "Banach ring". Then α is a submultiplicative nonarchimedean norm defining the topology.
issues.reason: Without z ∈ A0 the set {n : z⁻ⁿx ∈ A0} need not be downward closed, and α can violate the triangle inequality. Take A = ℚ_p(√p), A0 = {a + b√p : a ∈ ℤ_p, b ∈ pℤ_p} (an open bounded subring, a ring of definition), z = √p and c = 1/2. Then α(1) = 1 (n = 0 is allowed), α(√p) = 1/2 (n = 1), but α(1 + √p) = 4: z⁻ⁿ(1 + √p) ∈ A0 only for n ≤ −2 (for n = −1 it is p + √p, whose √p-coefficient 1 is not in pℤ_p). So α(1 + √p) > α(1) + α(√p). Already recorded in the atlas as AdicSpacesPartII/E39 (confirmed by REV-AdicSpacesPartII); the extraction had not listed it. It is separate from the finding on the second paragraph of the same remark.

issues.locator: §3.2 (Proof of Theorem 1.2) and the remark after Theorem 3.4, p. 6 of the author copy results.pdf (Invent. Math. 178 (2009) not compared)
issues.printed: The source proposes deducing hypothesis (D0) from Theorems 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3, then obtaining Theorem 1.2 through Theorem 3.4 and its subsequent remark.
issues.correction: Theorem 3.4 gives only that ρ̄ is modular. Add the passage to weight k(ρ̄) and level N(ρ̄): if the projective image is dihedral, Lemma 6.2(i); otherwise choose i with 2 ≤ k(ρ̄ ⊗ χ_p^i) ≤ p + 1 (p odd; i = 0 when p = 2); Theorem 5.1(1) gives a lift of ρ̄ ⊗ χ_p^i minimally ramified away from p and crystalline of weight k(ρ̄ ⊗ χ_p^i) (k(ρ̄) = 2 when p = 2), Theorem 4.1 makes it modular, and its newform has level N(ρ̄) (twisting by χ_p leaves the prime-to-p conductor unchanged). Untwist: ρ̄ is then modular of level N(ρ̄) prime to p, and Edixhoven's weight theorem (with θ-operators and the Deligne–Serre lifting lemma) gives a newform of weight k(ρ̄) and level N(ρ̄).
issues.reason: Theorem 1.2 asserts that ρ̄ arises from S_{k(ρ̄)}(Γ₁(N(ρ̄))), but Theorem 3.4 concludes 'is modular', and its proof (§8.4) lifts through Theorem 5.1(2), which has weight 2 and a type at p. The introduction (pp. 2–3) presents Theorem 1.2(2) as filling the dyadic scalar case of the qualitative-implies-refined problem, which is exactly the step not written out. Theorems 4.1(2)(i) and 5.1 (p. 9) assume 2 ≤ k(ρ̄) ≤ p + 1 when p > 2, while Serre's weight reaches p² − 1 for odd p; the paper notes (p. 2) that only some twist ρ̄ ⊗ χ_p^i has weight in [2, p + 1]. So for k(ρ̄) > p + 1 the lift is built for the twist, and the untwisting is part of the correction: for instance ρ̄|_{I_p} ≅ χ̄_p ⊕ χ̄_p² has Serre weight p + 3 for p ≥ 5, and only its twist by χ̄_p^{−1}, of weight 2, is in range. Every ingredient is a result of the paper or of Edixhoven's weight theorem, so the theorem stands.

issues.locator: §4.2, proof of Lemma 4.6 (independence of the choice of the g̃_v), p. 44 of the author copy proofs.pdf (Invent. Math. 178 (2009) not compared)
issues.printed: The proof claims independence from g̃_v: replacing it by g̃_v(1 + h_v) changes a_v to g ↦ a_v(g) − (ad(g)(h_v) − h_v) and changes (x_v ∪ a_v) to (x_v ∪ a_v − x_v ∪ δ(h_v)). It invokes x_v ∪ δ(h_v) = −δ(x_v ∪ h_v) to assert that inv((x_v ∪ a_v) + z_v) is unchanged.
issues.correction: For p > 2 one may replace h_v by its trace-zero part (δ kills scalars) and the displayed identity applies. For p = 2 argue instead: δ(h_v) is a 1-cocycle of D_v with values in Ad⁰ whose class is the image of h_v mod Ad⁰ ∈ H⁰(D_v, Ad/Ad⁰) under the connecting map, i.e. lies in L_v (Case 1); since [x] ∈ H¹_{{L_v^⊥}}, x_v ∈ L_v^⊥ and inv(x_v ∪ δ(h_v)) = ⟨[x_v], [δ(h_v)]⟩ = 0 by local Tate duality. So the value of (x, u) is unchanged.
issues.reason: The cup product ∪ is defined only through the pairing (Ad⁰)^*(1) × Ad⁰ → 𝔽(1) → 𝔽_p(1). The lifts of g_v ∈ GL₂(R^{□,ψ}_S)₁ to GL₂(R_u) differ by factors 1 + I_u·M₂(𝔽), so h_v ranges over Ad = M₂(𝔽) (the proof itself later takes "h_v ∈ Ad"), and ad(g)(h_v) − h_v ∈ Ad⁰ for every h_v. For p = 2, Ad⁰ ⊃ Z has no G_F-stable complement in Ad (Lemma 4.3(5)(ii)), so x_v ∪ h_v is not defined when tr h_v ≠ 0 and the identity x_v ∪ δ(h_v) = −δ(x_v ∪ h_v) has no meaning. As printed, the hypothesis [x] ∈ H¹_{{L_v^⊥}}(S, (Ad⁰)^*(1)) — a genuine condition only when p = 2, since L_v = 0 for p > 2 — is never used in showing that (x, u) is well defined; this step is exactly where it is needed. Lemma 4.6 remains true with the correction.

issues.locator: §7.6.1, Corollary 7.8(ii), p. 68 of the author copy proofs.pdf (Invent. Math. 178 (2009) not compared)
issues.printed: Part (ii), for k = 2, assumes πv^{U1(v)} non-trivial, πv^{U0(v)} trivial, and the character of kv∗ factoring through the norm to F∗p. It asserts that ρπ|Dv has weight 2 and becomes crystalline over Qp^nr(µp); if πv is ordinary, it writes ρπ|Iv as (ωp^{k−2}χp ∗ ; 0 1).
issues.correction: … then ρπ|Iv is of the form (εvχp ∗ ; 0 1), where εv = ωp^j is the character of Iv corresponding by local class field theory to the (non-trivial) character of kv∗ ≅ U0(v)/U1(v) through which U0(v) acts on πv^{U1(v)} (the nebentypus at v). In the paper's application (type (B), ψ of kind (ii)) j = k(ρ̄) − 2, so the 'k' of the exponent is the Serre weight of §8.3.3 (B), not the weight 2 of π.
issues.reason: Case (ii) fixes k = 2, so ωp^{k−2} = 1 and the printed form is (χp ∗ ; 0 1), of determinant χp on Iv. But πv has no U0(v)-fixed vector, so the character of kv∗ by which U0(v) acts on πv^{U1(v)}, which is the restriction of the central character to 𝒪v∗, is non-trivial; hence det ρπ|Iv = χp·εv with εv ≠ 1, contradicting the printed form. For an ordinary πv the unramified quotient carries the unit root, so the sub-character on Iv is εvχp. As intended — with the exponent the one of §8.3.3 (B), j = k(ρ̄) − 2 — the statement is right, so the slip affects nothing downstream.

issues.locator: §7.1, proof of Lemma 7.2, case (i) (p > 2), p. 61 of the author copy proofs.pdf (Invent. Math. 178 (2009) not compared)
issues.printed: For p > 2, the source justifies independence of γv,f from f by asserting that the residual representation associated with each f ∈ Sk,ψ(U, O)m remains the same.
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis that for each v ∈ Σ not above p either ρ̄m is ramified at v or N(v) ≢ −1 (mod p) (if N(v) ≡ −1 mod p, a base change in which v acquires even residue degree gives N(v′) ≡ 1 mod p), or fix γv by localising also at an eigenvalue of the operator given by a uniformiser of Dv∗, as the case p = 2 does by taking Uv = Dv∗.
issues.reason: The residual representation determines γ̄v only up to the swap allowed by ρ̄m|Dv. If ρ̄m is unramified at v and N(v) ≡ −1 mod p, let η be the unramified quadratic character of G_{Fv}. Then γ and γη both square to ψv, and ρ̄(Frobv) has eigenvalues {N(v)γ̄(Frobv), γ̄(Frobv)} = {−γ̄(Frobv), γ̄(Frobv)} for both, while γ̄η̄ ≠ γ̄ since p is odd. So the stated fact does not force γv,f = γv,f′. 𝕋ψ(U) contains no operator at v ∈ Σ, so localising at 𝔪 does not fix the eigenvalue of a uniformiser of Dv∗, which determines γv,f by the Remark after Lemma 7.2. Lemma 8.1 makes ρ̄F unramified at every v ∤ p, so in KW's setting the only case left open is N(v) ≡ −1 mod p. Lemma 9.1's map R̄^ψ_S → 𝕋ψ(U)_𝔪, with a fixed γv in the local ring, relies on Lemma 7.2.
issues.known: new for KW II: no published correction found. The same phenomenon in Kisin's §2.2 is recorded as GL2ModularityLifting/E4, corrected in Gee–Kisin, Appendix B.3, by the hypothesis N(v) ≢ −1 mod p

issues.locator: §7.4, proof of Lemma 7.4(1), pp. 64–65 (sentence and commutative diagram) of the author copy proofs.pdf (Invent. Math. 178 (2009) not compared)
issues.printed: The source claims that both the O-module and the image it has in Sk,ψ(U, F) are independent of the character χ of ∆Q, because the first claim shows such χ annihilate (U′Q(A∞F)∗ ∩ t_i^{−1}D∗t_i)/F∗.
issues.correction: … and its image in S_{k,ψ}(U′_Q, 𝔽) … (likewise both bottom entries of the diagram should be S_{k,ψ}(U′_Q, 𝔽)).
issues.reason: The 𝒪-module is S_{W_k(χ),ψ}(U′_Q, 𝒪), of level U′_Q. Since χ has p-power order, χ ≡ 1 mod the maximal ideal, so its reduction lands in S_{k,ψ}(U′_Q, 𝔽). The reduction map is injective, because invariants are saturated. Forms of level U′_Q are not U-invariant, so there is no such injection into S_{k,ψ}(U, 𝔽). The argument compares the images of the reductions for χ and χ′ inside S_{k,ψ}(U′_Q, 𝔽).

issues.locator: §7.6.2, Definition 7.9 and the following paragraph, p. 68 of the author copy proofs.pdf (Invent. Math. 178 (2009) not compared)
issues.printed: The source defines an allowable base change as a totally real solvable F′/F of even degree, unramified above p and split there if ρ̄|Dp is irreducible, satisfying im(ρ̄) = im(ρ̄|F′) and absolute irreducibility of ρ̄|F′(µp).
issues.correction: … such that im(ρ̄|G_F) = im(ρ̄|G_F′) … (and likewise in the next paragraph: 'has the property that im(ρ̄|G_F) = im(ρ̄|G_F′)').
issues.reason: The field F of §7.6.2 is assumed only to give non-solvable image (p = 2) or absolute irreducibility over F(µp) (p > 2). The fields of Lemma 8.1, which make ρ̄F unramified outside p and ρ̄|D℘ trivial, are not asserted to have im(ρ̄|G_F) = im(ρ̄). Read literally, F′ ⊃ F would need im(ρ̄) = im(ρ̄|G_F′) ⊂ im(ρ̄|G_F), so no allowable base change of such an F would exist. The sufficient condition in the next paragraph, linear disjointness from the fixed field of ker(ρ̄|F), yields exactly im(ρ̄|G_F′) = im(ρ̄|G_F).

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 10.1, p. 91 (the morphisms π₁, π₂, β, α, γ), with the definition of R̄^{ψ_F}_F on the same page of the author copy proofs.pdf (Invent. Math. 178 (2009) not compared)
issues.printed: The proof defines R̄^{ψ_F}_F over F for minimal odd deformations of ρ̄_F unramified away from p. Absolute irreducibility of ρ̄ and ρ̄|G_F is said to give CNL_O-algebra maps π₁ : R^{ψ_F}_F → R̄^{□,ψ_F}_F, π₂ : R^ψ_{Q,S} → R̄^{□,ψ}_{Q,S}, β : R^{ψ_F}_F → R^ψ_{Q,S}, α : R̄^{□,ψ_F}_F → R̄^{□,ψ}_{Q,S}, satisfying απ₁ = π₂β. Using π₁(R^{ψ_F}_F) = R̄^{ψ_F}_F together with π₂(R^ψ_{Q,S}) = R̄^ψ_{Q,S}, it obtains the induced CNL_O-algebra map γ : R̄^{ψ_F}_F → R̄^ψ_{Q,S}.
issues.correction: Construct the comparison map only modulo p. By the fourth bullet, τ|_{G_F} (τ the mod-p universal representation over R̄^ψ_{ℚ,S}/(p)) is unramified outside the places above p and ∞, so it is classified by a map β̄ : R^{ψ_F}_F → R̄^ψ_{ℚ,S}/(p); in framed form R^{□,ψ_F}_F → R̄^{□,ψ}_{ℚ,S}/(p), with the frames at w | p, ∞ taken from those at p, ∞. At w | p this factors through R̄^{□,ψ_F}_w, because the restriction R^□_{F_w} → R^□_{ℚ_p} → R̄^{□,ψ}_p kills the ideal of R̄^{□,ψ_F}_w: every 𝒪′-point of the flat reduced ring R̄^{□,ψ}_p restricts to a lift of the same type (A), (B) or (C) over the unramified F_w (Corollary 2.3). At the infinite places oddness is preserved. Hence β̄ factors through γ̄ : R̄^{ψ_F}_F → R̄^ψ_{ℚ,S}/(p), which carries the universal mod-p representation of G_F to τ|_{G_F}. The rest of the proof (finite image of τ, then 3.14 of [31] or Lemma 3.6 of [34]) is unchanged.
issues.reason: R^{ψ_F}_F and R̄^{□,ψ_F}_F classify deformations of ρ̄_F that are unramified outside the places above p. β and α would send the universal deformation over R^ψ_{ℚ,S}, resp. each 𝒪′-point x of R̄^{□,ψ}_{ℚ,S}, to its restriction to G_F, which need not be unramified above primes ℓ ≠ p in S. Theorem 10.1 allows at such ℓ any ring of Theorem 3.1, including the semistable ring of §3.3.4, whose points are (γχ_p ∗; 0 γ). Suppose ρ̄|_{D_ℓ} ≅ (γ̄χ̄_p ∗; 0 γ̄) with ∗ ramified, for example ρ̄ = ρ̄_{E,p} for an elliptic curve E with multiplicative reduction at ℓ and p ∤ v_ℓ(Δ_E), and take the §3.3.4 ring at ℓ. Then every 𝒪′-point x has ρ_x|_{I_ℓ} = γ|_{I_ℓ} ⊗ (1 c; 0 1) with c ≢ 0 mod π. So ρ_x(I_ℓ) is infinite, and ρ_x stays ramified over every finite extension of ℚ_ℓ. Such points exist: R̄^ψ_S is finite (Theorem 10.1) of dimension ≥ 1 (Proposition 4.5), so Corollary 4.7 applies. Composing α with one of them would give an 𝒪′-point of R̄^{□,ψ_F}_F that is ramified above ℓ, which is impossible. So α and β do not exist in this case. The fourth bullet only makes the mod-p representation τ unramified outside p (Lemma 4.2 of [33]), and that is all the correction needs.

issues.locator: §3.2.4, p. 24 of the author copy proofs.pdf (Invent. Math. 178 (2009) not compared)
issues.printed: Section 3.2.4 treats irreducible ρ̄v and weight 2 deformations. It sends p = 2, k(ρ̄v) = 2 to the preceding crystalline case, then assumes p ≠ 2. Citing Savitt, item 3 of th. 6.22 of [54], it identifies the ring as O[[T1, T2]]/(T1T2 − p) when O is sufficiently big.
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis 3 ≤ k(ρ̄_p) ≤ p. When p ≠ 2 and k(ρ̄_p) = 2, the required type (ω_p^{k(ρ̄)−2} ⊕ 1, 0) is trivial, so the weight-two lifts are the crystalline weight-2 lifts of §3.2.3. Their fixed-determinant ring is formally smooth, 𝒪[[T]] (framed: 𝒪[[T₁, …, T₄]]), as in the case p = 2 that §3.2.4 already sends to §3.2.3.
issues.reason: For p odd, §3.2.2(i) (p. 23) gives the weight-two lifts the inertial Weil–Deligne parameter (ω_p^{k(ρ̄)−2} ⊕ 1, 0). At k(ρ̄_p) = 2 this is the trivial type with N = 0, so the lifts are crystalline of weight 2. The case occurs for irreducible ρ̄_p: ρ̄_p|I_p ≅ ω₂ ⊕ ω₂^p, for instance E[p] for an elliptic curve with supersingular reduction at p, has Serre weight 2. Savitt's Theorem 6.22(3) concerns a principal-series type ω̃^i ⊕ ω̃^j with i ≢ j mod p − 1 (as the node LocalGaloisDeformationRings:R08.4/savitt-weight-two-rings records). Here i = k(ρ̄_p) − 2 and j = 0, and k(ρ̄_p) ≤ p for irreducible ρ̄_p, so it applies exactly when 3 ≤ k(ρ̄_p) ≤ p. The two rings differ. The special fibre of 𝒪[[T]] is 𝔽[[T]], a regular domain, while that of 𝒪[[T₁, T₂]]/(T₁T₂ − p) is 𝔽[[T₁, T₂]]/(T₁T₂), which is not a domain. Both are flat domains over 𝒪 of relative dimension 1 with regular generic fibre, which is all Theorem 3.1 asserts, and the paper uses Savitt's explicit form nowhere else. So nothing downstream is affected.

issues.reason: Under (♠), g_∞^{−1}E(R)g_∞ is the algebra of rotation-scalings aI + bJ ≅ C, on which the operator norm of the Euclidean norm is |a + bi|. In Proposition 5.19, either first normalise ε in its class modulo Nr(E^×) so that ord_v ε = 1 at the places where B is ramified and E inert, and ord_v ε = 0 where both are ramified (possible by weak approximation in E; then take π = ε at the inert places), or replace 'τ_v = 1' by 'τ_v = π^k if B is ramified and E inert at v, and τ_v = Π^k if both are ramified, with υ_v = ε/Nr(τ_v)'.

G′(Z_(p))^+ ⊂ G′(Q) ⊂ G′(A^p_f), and in Deligne's formalism it acts through G′(A^p_f): the group acting is G(A^p_f) *_{G(Z_(p))_+} G^ad(Z_(p))^+, (3.7.x) and §4.6. issues.reviewReason: The mistake is in [Ki 2], not in this paper. It is a correction made in print by the author, like E1–E4. The image of footnote 8 (p. 7) reads: 'In fact T_p𝒢* should be replaced by T_p𝒢*(−1), the linear dual of T_p𝒢, in (1.4.2), (1.4.3) and (1.5.11) of loc. cit. We have made this correction here.' The claim's `printed` is not text from this paper. It paraphrases [Ki 2], and its locator should name [Ki 2]. I could not reach the published [Ki 2] (the AMS site returns a Cloudflare page). Kisin's homepage has the author's corrected version of [Ki 2] (shimcorrpub.dvi, footnote: 'This version corrects some mistakes in the published version'). There Thm 1.4.2 reads 𝒢 ↦ 𝔐(𝒢) := 𝔐(T_p𝒢*(−1)), and Cor 1.4.3 and Cor 1.5.11 read L = T_p𝒢*(−1): exactly the three places footnote 8 names. The mathematics: the Weil pairing gives T_p𝒢* ≅ Hom(T_p𝒢, Z_p(1)), so T_p𝒢*(−1) = T_p𝒢^∨. The contravariant crystal D(𝒢) corresponds to V_p𝒢^∨, whose filtration jumps lie in {0,1}, the range of BT^φ_{/𝔖}. With T_p𝒢* the jumps lie in {−1,0}. For 𝒢 = Q_p/Z_p, T_p𝒢* = Z_p(1) is not even in that range. For 𝒢 = μ_{p^∞}, 𝔐(T_p𝒢*) = 𝔐(Z_p) has Fil^1ℳ = Fil^1S·ℳ, whereas Fil^1 D(μ_{p^∞})(S) is all of D(μ_{p^∞})(S). So the printed (1.4.2) of [Ki 2], D(𝒢)(S) ≅ ℳ(𝔐(T_p𝒢*)), is false. The footnote's own correction is right, and this paper uses T_p𝒢*(−1) throughout ((1.1.6), (1.1.7), (1.1.13), (1.2.16)–(1.2.18)). E1–E5 do not record it, and `known` (corrected in print, footnote 8) is accurate.

issues.printed: In (1.1.13) it invokes [Ki 2, 1.4.3(3)] to obtain the W-linear isomorphism (1.1.14) when the stated condition holds. Proof (1.1.19) says the tensors cut out a connected reductive subgroup of GL(T_p𝒢̃′), and cites (1.1.7) for W-linear isomorphisms (1.1.21). issues.correction: In (1.1.13), make the last sentence read: 'If this condition holds and G_{Z_p} is connected (or k is separably closed), then there exists a W-linear isomorphism (1.1.14)'. Prove it from U, not from [Ki 2, 1.4.3(3)]. Isom((U,s_{α,0}), (T_p𝒢̃*(−1), s_α)) is a G_{Z_p}-torsor over Z_p, split over W(k^sep) by [Ki 2, 1.4.3(2)], hence trivial by Lang and Hensel. In (1.1.19), assume G_{Z_p} connected or k separably closed. For connected G and general k, obtain (1.1.21) from Nisnevich's theorem, since the torsor is trivial over K_0 via D(θ).
issues.reason: Throughout §1.1, k is an arbitrary perfect field (1.1.1), and neither (1.1.13) nor (1.1.19) restricts it. Their proofs rest on (1.1.7) = [Ki 2, 1.4.3], which the paper states only under 'k separably closed, or G_{Z_p} connected and k finite'. (The proof cites [Ki 2, 1.4.3(3)]. In (1.1.7), which restates [Ki 2, 1.4.3], the isomorphism is part (2) and part (3) is the filtration statement, so the part number in the cross-reference may also be off; not checkable without [Ki 2].) For general perfect k the relevant G_W-torsors (tensor-preserving isomorphisms, and transporters between conjugate cocharacters) need not be trivial over W(k), since H^1(k, ·) can be non-zero. In (1.1.19) connectedness of the stabiliser is asserted without argument (it follows only if G_{Z_p} is connected). Defence: when G_{Z_p} is connected, the Z_p-structure U shows that the isomorphism scheme in (1.1.13) is a torsor over Z_p, hence trivial by Lang and Hensel for any k. So the gap concerns disconnected G_{Z_p}, and the steps in (1.1.19) that do not come from U, over non-separably-closed k.

issues.reviewReason: The problem is real, and it is worse than a gap: for disconnected G_{Z_p} the last sentence of (1.1.13) is false. In §1.1, 'reductive' allows disconnected groups: (1.1.4)(2) and (1.1.7) state 'G connected' as a separate hypothesis, and [Ki 2, §1.1] defines a reductive group as G with G/G^0 finite étale. Nothing restricts k beyond being perfect (1.1.1). Counterexample, with p odd, k = F_p (so W = Z_p and K = Q_p). Let 𝒢̃ be the étale p-divisible group over Z_p whose T := T_p𝒢̃*(−1) ≅ Z_p^2 has Frobenius acting by the swap τ. Take the tensors v = e_1+e_2 and the form x^2+y^2, whose stabiliser is the finite étale group {1,τ}. That group is reductive in Kisin's sense and contains the Galois image, so the tensors are G_K-invariant. Take U = D(𝒢)(Z_p) = (T ⊗ W(F̄_p))^{τ⊗σ}, with s_{α,0} the images of s_α. The hypotheses of (1.1.11)–(1.1.13) hold: the filtration is trivial, and 𝒢̃ is G_W-adapted. But the isomorphisms (D(𝒢)(Z_p), s_{α,0}) → (T, s_α) form the {1,τ}-torsor with class τ ≠ 0 in H^1(F_p, Z/2), so no isomorphism (1.1.14) exists. The proof cites [Ki 2, 1.4.3(3)], which assumes 'G connected and k finite'. I checked the author's corrected version of [Ki 2], which is all I could reach: there 1.4.3 has four parts, and (3) is precisely the W-linear isomorphism under that hypothesis. So the part number is right, and the claim's aside that it 'may also be off' should be dropped. For connected G_{Z_p} the statement holds for every perfect k, but the proof does not show it for infinite k. The fix: the isomorphism scheme U → T_p𝒢̃*(−1) respecting tensors is a G_{Z_p}-torsor over Z_p, trivial over W(k^sep) by [Ki 2, 1.4.3(2)], hence trivial by Lang and Hensel. (1.1.19) has the same defect. 'these tensors define a connected reductive subgroup' is false when G_{Z_p} is disconnected, and the appeal to (1.1.7) needs its hypotheses. For connected G it can be repaired at any perfect k. The isomorphism for 𝒢′ is a G_W-torsor over W that is trivial over K_0 via D(θ), hence trivial by Nisnevich (Grothendieck–Serre over a DVR). The conjugacy of μ′_0 and gμ_0g^{-1} over W follows from the injectivity of H^1(k,P) → H^1(k,G) and Hensel. No later result is affected. The uses in (1.2.15)–(1.2.19) have k = F̄_p. §1.3 and §2 (including (2.2.3)) have G_{Z_p} connected.

From c = σ^{-1}(b)μ_0(E(0)) and the identity σ(λ(x)) = (σλ)(σx) for a cocharacter λ over W, σ(c) = b·(σμ_0)(σ(E(0))) = b·υ_0(σ(E(0)))^{-1}, since υ_0 = σ(μ_0^{-1}). issues.reviewReason: Checked on p. 15. The torsor Isom((U,s_{α,0}), (U′,s_{α,0})) is split over O_L (both are identified with D(𝒢)), so it is a G_{Z_p}-torsor over Z_p. Its class lies in H^1(Z_p,G) = H^1(F_p, G_{F_p}), which is 0 when G is connected (Hensel, then Lang) but can be non-zero otherwise. Example: G = {1,τ} ⊂ GL(U) (τ the swap) and U′ = (U⊗O_L)^{τ⊗σ}. The s_{α,0} lie in U′^⊗, U′ ⊗ O_L = D(𝒢), and the torsor has class τ ≠ 0. (1.2.15) says only 'reductive', and in this paper that allows disconnected groups ((1.1.4), (1.1.7)). The defence holds: all of (1.2.1)–(1.2.14), which (1.2.15) goes on to use (G(L), X_{υ_0}(b), c_{b,μ}), assumes 'a connected reductive group over Z_p', and in the application K_p is hyperspecial for connected G. So connectedness is implicit. The fix is to state it and to cite Lang and Hensel.

issues.locator: proof of Proposition (1.2.21), first paragraph, p. 17
issues.printed: The source uses π_1(M/Z_G)^Γ → π_1(G^ad)^Γ --(c ↦ σ(c̃) − c̃)--> ker(X_*(Z_G)_Γ → π_1(G)_Γ), with c̃ ∈ π_1(G) lifting c. It places the kernel for π_1(M)_Γ → π_1(G)_Γ ⊕ π_1(M/Z_G)_Γ inside the image of ker(X_*(Z_G)_Γ → π_1(G)_Γ), hence inside the image of π_1(M/Z_G)^Γ, which it calls trivial. It concludes HN-indecomposability of (υ^ad, b^ad).
issues.correction: Replace the first paragraph of the proof by the argument below. Let Q^∨ ⊃ Q^∨_M be the coroot lattices. 0 → Q^∨/Q^∨_M → π_1(M) → π_1(G) → 0 and 0 → Q^∨/Q^∨_M → π_1(M/Z_G) → π_1(G^ad) → 0 are exact and compatible. By (1.2.3), for G and for G^ad, the connecting maps π_1(G)^Γ → (Q^∨/Q^∨_M)_Γ and π_1(G^ad)^Γ → (Q^∨/Q^∨_M)_Γ vanish. So (Q^∨/Q^∨_M)_Γ = ker(π_1(M)_Γ → π_1(G)_Γ) injects into π_1(M/Z_G)_Γ, and π_1(M)_Γ → π_1(G)_Γ ⊕ π_1(M/Z_G)_Γ is injective. Hence (υ^ad, b^ad) is HN-indecomposable.
issues.reason: π_1(G) → π_1(G^ad) is not surjective when Z_G is disconnected (e.g. G = SL_2: π_1(G) = 0, π_1(PGL_2) = Z/2), so 'c̃ ∈ π_1(G) lifting c' need not exist and the second displayed map is not defined as written. The snake-lemma surjection holds only for the image π_1(G)/X_*(Z_G) of π_1(G) in π_1(G^ad). Likewise, ker(π_1(M)_Γ → π_1(M/Z_G)_Γ) contains, but need not a priori equal, the image of X_*(Z_G)_Γ, because π_1(M) → π_1(M/Z_G) has finite cokernel. The printed inclusion is nevertheless true: the kernel is 0, by the corrected argument. So the claim that (υ^ad, b^ad) is HN-indecomposable, and Proposition (1.2.21), stand.

So the lift c̃ required by the second map need not exist, and the map is not defined on π_1(G^ad)^Γ. For the same reason (π_1(M) → π_1(M/Z_G) has finite cokernel), the inclusion of ker(π_1(M)_Γ → π_1(G)_Γ ⊕ π_1(M/Z_G)_Γ) in the image of X_*(Z_G)_Γ is not justified. §1.2 allows any connected reductive G over Z_p, so this is a real hole. The printed argument works only when Z_G is connected. I checked the claim's replacement argument. 0 → Q^∨/Q^∨_M → π_1(M) → π_1(G) → 0 and its analogue for M/Z_G ⊂ G^ad are exact. Γ acts through σ, so the snake lemma for σ−1 gives connecting maps π_1(G)^Γ → (Q^∨/Q^∨_M)_Γ. These vanish because, by (1.2.3) for G and for G^ad, every invariant class lifts to X_*(T)^Γ (resp. X_*(T/Z_G)^Γ). Hence (Q^∨/Q^∨_M)_Γ injects into both π_1(M)_Γ and π_1(M/Z_G)_Γ, compatibly, and the kernel in question is 0. So the HN-indecomposability of (υ^ad, b^ad) and Proposition (1.2.21) stand. But the step as printed fails and must be replaced by a different argument, which is why the reach is 'the proof' (as for the other replaced arguments in this review), not 'nothing'.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on pp. 29, 33–34 and 81–84. §2.1 lets k be any finite extension of k_E. I ⊂ Aut_Q(𝒜_x ⊗ F̄_p) is the geometric group, and I_l = Z(γ_l^n) for n divisible enough. By (2.3.1)–(2.3.3), I_0 ⊗ Q_l ≅ Z(γ_l) = I_{l/k} ≅ I_{/k} ⊗ Q_l, while I ⊗ Q_l ≅ I_l. So (2.3.5) requires dim Z(γ_0) = dim Z(γ_0^n). The first arrow of (2.3.6) silently assumes I_{l/k} = I_l. Counterexample, verified: (G,X) = (GL_2, H^±), p = 5, k = F_5, E: y² = x³+1 (supersingular, a_5 = 0, π² = −5). γ_0 has characteristic polynomial X²+5, so I_0 = Res_{Q(√−5)/Q}G_m has dimension 2. I = B_{5,∞}^× and I_l = Z(−5) = GL_2 have dimension 4. So I_0 ⊗ Q̄ ≇ I ⊗ Q̄. The paper's conventions do not exclude this. (i) Nothing requires k to be large. (ii) The only level condition is 'K^p sufficiently small' (Baily–Borel, representability), and the claim leaves the level out. Since (γ_l) ∈ K^p for any x ∈ 𝒮_K(k) (proof of (2.1.5)), K^p must contain γ. K^p = ⟨γ⟩·K(3) does: modulo 3 it is {1, γ̄}, and det γ̄ ≡ 5 ≢ 1. So every automorphism of a point, which has determinant 1 and finite order, is ≡ 1 mod 3 and therefore trivial. The moduli problem is rigid and the point (E, ε) is F_5-rational. Defence, and its limit: if K^p is neat, then γ ∈ K^p is neat. A root-of-unity ratio of Frobenius eigenvalues would put torsion in every l-adic eigenvalue group, so Z(γ^n) = Z(γ), I_{/k} = I, and (2.3.5) holds for all k. But the paper never assumes neatness and the proof never uses it. The author's own uses fit the k-version. (4.4.6) applies (2.3.5) with 'I the subgroup of Aut_Q(𝒜_x) fixing s_{α,0,x}, s_{α,l,x}' for 𝒜_x over k, which is I_{/k}. The proof of (4.4.13), p. 84, assumes 'r is large enough that I_0, I′_0 have the same dimension as I'.

issues.reviewReason: 𝔻 = lim D_n with D_n = G_m and transitions x ↦ x^{n′/n}. The characters form colim(Z, ·n′/n) ≅ Q. The cocharacters form lim(Z, ·n′/n), and a compatible family (a_n) has a_1 = n·a_n for every n, so a_1 = 0: the cocharacter group is 0. 'Character group Q' is the standard description (Kottwitz, Milne, Reimann). The use of 𝔻 elsewhere is consistent with this reading: Hom(𝔻, T) = X_*(T)⊗Q, and ν(p): 𝔻 → Q is a fractional cocharacter.

issues.citation: Kisin, "Mod p points on Shimura varieties of abelian type", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2017)
issues.reviewReason: By (3.2.2), X_*(G/G̃) consists of isomorphism classes of strictly monoidal functors G_m(k̄) → G/G̃(k̄), and by (3.2.1) the isomorphisms are arbitrary monoidal natural isomorphisms with no algebraicity required. For μ1, μ2 ∈ X_*(T), such an isomorphism is a map η: k̄^× → G̃(k̄) with ∂η_z = λ(z) := μ2(z)μ1(z)^{-1} and η_{zw} = η_z·μ1(z)(η_w). Since ∂^{-1}(T) = T̃ and T acts trivially on the torus T̃, η is an abstract homomorphism k̄^× → T̃(k̄) lifting λ. Such a homomorphism need not be algebraic, so deducing λ ∈ X_*(T̃) takes an argument. The first reading's argument works: λ lands in T∩G^der, and restricting η to torsion gives λ ∈ (X_*(T̃)⊗Ẑ) ∩ X_*(T∩G^der) = X_*(T̃), because the quotient X_*(T∩G^der)/X_*(T̃) is finite. The 'if' direction is formal. The unjustified 'only if' direction is the one that makes the map X_*(G/G̃) → π1(G) well defined, and that is exactly what 'induces' in the statement asserts. The lemma is true.

issues.printed: Part (4) asserts that an abelian cokernel of H̃ → H suffices to equip H^i(Δ, H̃ → H) canonically with an abelian group structure.
issues.correction: (4) If H̃ → H is a braided crossed module (e.g. quasi-isomorphic to a complex of abelian groups with trivial action, as for G̃ → G with G reductive, by [Bo, 3.8]), then H^i(Δ, H̃ → H) has a canonical abelian group structure.
issues.reason: An abelian cokernel alone does not give a canonical group law on H^1. For example, take ∂ = 1: Z/4 → Z/2 with Z/2 acting on Z/4 by inversion. The fibres of H^1 over the classes p ∈ H^1(Δ, Z/2) are H^2(Δ, (Z/4)_p) with p-twisted coefficients, and there is no natural way to add classes lying over different p. In defence: every crossed module to which Kisin applies (4) (G̃ → G, Z_{G̃} → Z_G) is covered by Borovoi. The extraction's R4 item H05 already notes a 'scope correction' to (3.2.7)(4).

issues.reviewReason: (4) is false as stated, already for i = 0. Take the crossed module ∂ = 1: Z/3 → Z/2 with Z/2 acting on Z/3 by inversion (its cokernel Z/2 is abelian), and let Δ = Z/3 act trivially. Then H^0(Δ, H̃→H) consists of pairs (a, h) with a ∈ Hom(Δ, Z/3) and h ∈ Z/2, and there are no identifications. The canonical product coming from the monoidal structure of (3.2.1) is (a,h)(a′,h′) = (a + h·a′, hh′). So H^0 ≅ Z/3 ⋊ Z/2 = S_3, which is non-abelian. The first reading's H^1 example with Z/4 illustrates the same failure. A canonical abelian structure needs a braided (Picard) structure, which forces π0 to act trivially on π1, or a quasi-isomorphism to a complex of abelian groups as in [Bo]. Every application in the paper is covered: (4.4.2) for H̃ → H with H reductive, and Z_{G̃} → Z_G, both via [Bo, 3.8].

issues.reason: The objects of G/G̃(Q̄) multiply in G(Q̄). For a general μ, the Galois conjugates μ^τ need not commute, so (x_τ) ↦ Π_τ μ^τ(x_τ) is neither multiplicative on objects nor Galois-equivariant. issues.reviewReason: 𝔊_{G/G̃} has the elements of G(Q̄)⋊Gal as objects, and a morphism of strictly monoidal categories out of a group is a group homomorphism on objects. The formula (x_τ) ↦ Π_τ μ^τ(x_τ) is multiplicative only if the μ^τ pairwise commute. It is Galois-equivariant only if the order of the product does not matter, since σ permutes the factors. Neither holds for a general μ: in GL_2, take μ = Int(g)(z ↦ diag(z,1)) with g generic over a quadratic field. As printed, Σ a_τ μ^τ_ab~(x) is therefore not a morphism of strictly monoidal categories in the sense of (3.2.1), and the 'semi-direct product with Gal' is not defined. The fix is to replace μ by a G(Q̄)-conjugate lying in a Q-torus T. Proofs later in the paper implicitly do this ('If T ⊂ G is a torus through which μ factors', end of 3.4.2). The (3.3.1) remark ('conjugate cocharacters give isomorphic morphisms') is the intended justification for independence of the choice.

issues.reviewReason: The claim is real. For v = ∞, the pushforward F_μ of ξ_{∞,0} along (3.3.2) has kernel −(μ + cμ) and sends w to μ(−1)⋊c, where μ is the E_p-rational conjugate from (3.3.6). ξ_{∞,ab~} has central kernel w_h and sends w to μ_h(−1)⋊c. Conjugacy in 𝔊_{G/G̃} is equality of objects after Int(g), so the two are generally not conjugate. Concretely, for the modular curve with μ = diag(z,1) and L imaginary quadratic, F_μ has non-central kernel z ↦ diag(z^{-2},1), while w_h is central. The printed step is therefore false, although the lemma's conclusion (conjugate-isomorphic) is true. The reach should be 'the proof', not 'nothing': changing the word needs its own argument that F_μ and ξ_{∞,ab~} are conjugate-isomorphic as morphisms of R-gerbs. Lemma 3.2.3 does not give this, because it concerns functors over k̄ with no Galois part.

issues.reviewReason: The M-Newton condition for an M-dominant λ and a central ν_b holds iff ν_b equals the central projection of the Galois average of λ. Dominance plus centrality alone does not give this, so the printed justification is insufficient. The M-class is also ambiguous. −μ* is G-dominant for an arbitrary Borel B ⊃ T′, but it need not be M-conjugate to −i∘μ_{h_T}, whose class is the one κ_M(i(b)) sees. Example: GL_2 and a CM torus T split at p. Then M = T and ν_b = −μ_{h_T}, which is (−1,0) or (0,−1) depending on i, while −μ* is fixed by B. With the wrong choice, X^T_{−μ*}(b) is empty. The first reading's fill is correct: take λ to be the M-dominant representative of −i∘μ_{h_T}. By (3.1.11), ν_b is the Galois average of −i∘μ_{h_T}; being central, it equals the Z_M-projection of avg(λ), so ν_b ≤_M avg(λ). Together with κ_M(i(b)) = [λ], this gives X^M_λ ≠ ∅, and X^M_λ ⊂ X^G_{−μ}.

issues.reviewReason: X^*(S_L) = Z[Gal(L/Q)]/(1+ι), with ι central because L is CM. So Z_{H̃} ↪ S_L^n requires ι to act by −1 on X^*(Z_{H̃}). By SV2, H̃_R is an inner form of a compact group. The centre is unchanged under inner twisting and lies in an anisotropic maximal torus, so c acts by −1 on it. Equivalently, c acts on the diagram by the opposition involution, and w_0 acts trivially on P/Q. The proof leaves this ingredient unstated.

issues.reviewReason: Admissibility for the auxiliary (G,X) needs the standing hypothesis of (3.3.6), namely a reductive model G_{Z_p}, because X_p(φ) is defined using G_{Z_p}(Z_p^ur). So do 3.4.11 and [LR, Satz 5.3], which works at hyperspecial level. If L is ramified at p, S_L and hence G = (H̃×S_L^n)/Z_{H̃} are ramified at p, and none of this applies. The proof never says L must be unramified at p, but the choice is always possible. H is unramified, so inertia at p acts trivially on its Dynkin diagram, and the field K it cuts out is unramified at p; K is CM or totally real. If K is totally real, then c acts trivially on X^*(Z_{H̃}), which is therefore 2-torsion. One can then use L = K(√−d) with Q(√−d) unramified at p (d = 1 for p odd, d = 3 for p = 2). Then S_L is an unramified torus, and G has a reductive Z_p-model. Also confirmed on the page: 'Hence the lemma holds' should be 'the theorem holds', and 𝕊_0 is used without definition (it should be the weight G_{m,R} ⊂ 𝕊). The lift h̃ exists because the extension of the compact 𝕊/G_m by the compact torus Z_{G,R} splits: Ext^1 of Z(−1) by Z(−1) over Z[Gal(C/R)] is 0.

issues.locator: §3.6.1 (definition of X̃^p(φ), p.52) and proof of Lemma 3.6.2(2), p.54
issues.printed: On p.52 it requires (ε_l(τ_l))_{l≠p,∞} ∈ G̃(Ā^p_f) for every (τ_l)_{l≠p} ∈ ∏ Gal(Q̄_l/Q_l). On p.54 it says ε_l has values in G_{Z_l}(Z̄_l) at almost every l, allowing h_l ∈ G_{Z_l}(Z̄_l).[20] It concludes h = (h_l)_{l≠p} ∈ G(Ā^p_f). Footnote 20 attributes triviality of the class of ε_l to Lang’s Lemma, describing this as less deep.
issues.correction: In (3.6.1) require ε to be adelically trivial: there is (h_l) ∈ G̃(Ā^p_f) with ε_l(τ) = h_l·τ(h_l)^{-1} for the twisted action, for all l. Equivalently, for almost all l, ε_l is the coboundary of some h_l ∈ G̃_{Z_l}(Z̄_l); locally this is automatic, since H^1(Q_l, inner form of G̃) = 0. On p.54 read G̃_{Z_l}(Z̄_l) and G̃(Ā^p_f). With this change the proof of (3.6.2)(2) works as written. The map (g_l) ↦ (g_l,1) still sends X^p(φ) into X^p(φ_ab~), and (3.6.3)–(3.6.10), c_G and the rest of §3.6–3.8 are unaffected.
issues.reason: Lang's lemma trivializes only unramified cocycles, and the integrality condition does not exclude ramified ones. Suppose ker(ρ: G̃ → G) ≠ 1, the non-simply-connected case the section is for. Take (g_l,ε_l) ∈ X̃^p(φ) and replace ε_l by ε_l·c_l, where c_l ∈ Z^1(Q_l, ker ρ) is ramified for infinitely many l (such classes exist by Tate duality and Chebotarev; e.g. G = PGL_2, c_l the quadratic character of Q_l(√l)). Every printed condition still holds, because c_l takes values in the finite central group ker ρ ⊂ G̃(Z̄_l). Suppose this family were h·(x·γ) with h ∈ G̃(Ā^p_f) and γ ∈ G(A^p_f). Then k_l := g_l^{-1}⋆h_l would satisfy ρ(k_l) = γ_l^{-1} and k_l^{-1}τ(k_l) = c_l, so γ_l ∈ G^der(Q_l) and δ(γ_l^{-1}) = [c_l] ∈ H^1(Q_l, ker ρ). But γ_l ∈ G^der(Z_l) for almost all l, and δ(G^der(Z_l)) is unramified for l ∤ |ker ρ|. So X^p(φ_ab~) is not a single G(A^p_f)/G̃(A^p_f)-orbit, and as literally defined π(G,φ_0) is not a π(G)-torsor (3.6.2(2),(3), 3.6.4, 3.6.10). In the paper's defence, the intended object (a restricted product) is clear, and only the definition needs changing.
