issues.reviewReason: Quotations checked on pp.52, 54 (text and fn.20). The page-54 text drops the tildes: it says G_{Z_l}(Z̄_l) and G(Ā^p_f). I tried to show that the paper's own definitions rule out the counterexample. They do not. (i) The only global condition in (3.6.1) is that the values ε_l(τ_l) lie in G̃(Ā^p_f). That constrains the values of ε_l, not whether ε_l is ramified. (ii) Let c_l ∈ Z^1(Q_l, ker ρ) with ker ρ = ker(G̃→G^der), a finite central group. The twisted action (conjugation through G^ad) is trivial on ker ρ. So ε_l·c_l is again a cocycle, and ρ(ε_lc_l) = ρ(ε_l). The pair also gives a morphism in the crossed-module category of (3.2.1), since Hom(h_1,h_2) = {h̃ : h_2 = h̃h_1}. For almost all l, ker ρ(Q̄_l) lies in G̃_{Z_l}(Z̄_l), because ker ρ is finite over Z_l. So (g_l, ε_lc_l) ∈ X̃^p(φ). (iii) Suppose (g_l,1) ∈ X̃^p(φ_ab~) comes from X^p(φ), and suppose (g_l, c_l) = k·(g_lγ_l, 1) with γ ∈ G(A^p_f) and k_l ∈ G̃(Q̄_l); I do not even require k to be integral at almost all l. Put k′_l = (g_lγ_l)^{-1}⋆k_l. Then ρ(k′_l) = γ_l^{-1} and τ(k′_l)k′_l^{-1} = c_l. So γ_l ∈ G^der(Q_l) and δ(γ_l^{-1}) = ±[c_l] ∈ H^1(Q_l, ker ρ). For almost all l, γ_l ∈ G(Z_l) ∩ G^der(Q_l) = G^der(Z_l), whose δ-image consists of unramified classes when l ∤ |ker ρ|. For example, take G = PGL_2 (a Shimura datum with hyperspecial level at any p) and c_l the character of Q_l(√l) for odd l ≠ p. Then δ = det mod squares, and l is never in Z_l^×·Q_l^{×2}. So the class is not in g_0·G(A_f). (iv) The classes that are adelically trivial (those of (g_l,1)) form a subset stable under G(A_f), under G(Q̄)^♮_+ (which acts by right multiplication on the g_l and leaves ε unchanged), and under K^p. Using G(Q)_+ instead of G(Q̄)^♮_+ does not help: in the paper's convention the subscript + means the preimage of G^ad(R)^+, and G(Q̄)^♮_+ ∩ G(Q) = G(Q)_+ ⊂ G(A_f). So the extra classes are never identified with g_0·G(A_f) at any level K^p. Hence for G^der ≠ G̃, taking X^p(φ_ab~) literally makes (3.6.2)(2) non-surjective and (3.6.2)(3) not a bijection. Then π(G,φ_0) is not a π(G)-torsor, so (3.6.4) and (3.6.10) fail as stated, and so does the surjectivity of c_G in (3.7.4). Footnote 20 shows that the author had unramified ε_l in mind. The intended object is clear, and only the definition needs changing.

At p, k′ = (g_p^{-1}⋆i)g^{-1} satisfies τ(k′) = k′ for τ ∈ Gal(Q̄_p/Q_p^ur), because g_p^{-1}φ_ττ(g_p) = 1 there (the strict condition of (3.3.3)/(3.6.1)). So k′ ∈ G̃(Q_p^ur). issues.reviewReason: Quotation checked on p.60. From gψ_{µT}g^{-1} = z·ψ_{µT′} with z_τ = g_+τ(g_+)^{-1}, conjugating by g_+ agrees with twisting by z only if g_+ centralizes the image of ψ_{µT}∘ζ_∞. That fails in general, so the displayed equation is unjustified. (The paper also writes g′_1(gg_+)^{-1} where (gg_+)^{-1}g′_1 would follow.) 'Same connected component' does not follow either. G*(R) = Z_G(R)·ρ(G̃*(R)), because G*^ad(R) is connected. So the image of I(R) in G^ab(R) is the image of Z_G(R), which can be disconnected: for G = GL_2×G_m it is R_{>0}×R^×. The claimed repair is right. g_+ maps into G^ad(Q)_+, which lies in G^ad(R)^+ = ρ(G̃(R)), so g_+ = k·u with k ∈ G̃(R) and u ∈ Z_G̃(C). Then z_c = u·c(u)^{-1}, so z·(ψ_{µT′}∘ζ_∞) = u(ψ_{µT′}∘ζ_∞)u^{-1} and ψ_{µT′}∘ζ_∞ = (gu^{-1})ψ_{µT}∘ζ_∞(gu^{-1})^{-1}. The final claim of (3.6.10) holds. The printed step is a false equation followed by an invalid inference, and it carries the weight of the argument. Its repair needs a new observation (g_+ = ku), so the reach is 'the proof', not 'nothing'.

A τ chosen only to carry s_{α,B,x} to s_α is determined only up to G(Q), and such a τ need not intertwine the Z_{G'}-action on A (defined in [Ki 2, 3.2.2] via the G'(Q)-canonical isomorphism of (4.2.4)) with that on V. Example: a supersingular elliptic curve over F_p with π^2 = −p; γ_0 = π has a torus as centralizer, while γ_0^2 is central, so I_0 = GL_2. Then β(τ) need not commute with γ_l, and τ(γ_l^β) = γ_l^β fails. The same issue affects the next claim, that g_l is determined up to right multiplication by I(Q̄_l) and so γ_l^β up to G(Q_l)-conjugacy. The fix is to use a representative whose own γ_l has centralizer I_l. The equivalence relation allows this, but the text chooses the representative only at p ('After increasing the finite field k'). Lemma 4.3.7 is affected only through the definition of k^β. Once k^β is defined this way, both directions go through, because conjugacy of sufficiently divisible powers suffices and Cent(γ_l) ⊂ I_l.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on p.90. The printed identification π_1(R_{F/Q_p}G)_Γ = π_1(G)_Γ ⊗ Z[Gal(F/Q_p)] is wrong. Over Q̄_p, R_{F/Q_p}G is the product of copies of G indexed by Hom(F,Q̄_p), and Γ permutes these factors while also acting on π_1(G). So π_1(R_{F/Q_p}G) = Ind_{Γ_F}^{Γ} π_1(G), whose Γ-coinvariants are π_1(G)_{Γ_F} (Shapiro's lemma). The diagonal G → R_{F/Q_p}G induces the transfer π_1(G)_Γ → π_1(G)_{Γ_F}, x ↦ Σ_{Γ/Γ_F} g·x. This is multiplication by e for F totally ramified of degree e, and 1+σ+…+σ^{f−1} for F = Q_{p^f}. Composing with the projection back to π_1(G)_Γ gives multiplication by [F:Q_p], so only torsion can be lost, but torsion can be lost. Counterexample: T = U(1) for Q_{p^2}/Q_p, F = Q_{p^2}. Then X_*(T)_Γ = Z/2 and X_*(T)_{Γ_F} = Z, and the map is x ↦ x+σx = 0. Twisting δ = 1 by the nontrivial class of H^1(Q_p,T) = Z/2 (which splits over Q_{p^2}) gives δ' = h_0σ(h_0)^{-1} with κ_T(δ') ≠ 0 = κ_T(δ), although both have the same image in π_1(R_{F/Q_p}T)_Γ. The same happens for GU(V) with dim V even and p inert, where π_1(G)_Γ ⊃ Z/2 is killed by F = Q_{p^2}. The printed step never uses the hypothesis on β at p, so it would 'prove' that every local twist preserves κ_G, which is false. The conclusion κ_G(h_0δσ(h_0)^{-1}) = κ_G(δ) is still true under the lemma's hypotheses. The first paragraph of the proof shows that φ^β = z·φ satisfies (3.3.6)(1), and the κ-part of the proof of (3.4.2) ((3.4.4) pushed to π_1(G) ≅ X_*(G/G̃)) uses only (3.3.6)(1). issues.correction: Replace N_G(M)/M by the absolute Weyl group W(G, T) of a maximal torus T ⊂ M with μ ∈ X_*(T), as in Proposition 1.1.13. Equivalently: some G(Q̄_p)-conjugate μ′ of μ factoring through T makes ([b_M], {μ′}) M-admissible.
issues.reason: The printed statement fails already for split G. Take G = GL_3, M = GL_1 × GL_2 (blocks of sizes 1 and 2), μ = (0,1,0) and b_M = diag(p,1,1), which is basic in M. Since the blocks have different sizes, N_G(M) = M, so W(G, M) is trivial and no w in it helps. The permutation of the first two coordinates, in W(G, T) = S_3, does. The proof transports to the quasi-split inner form and applies Proposition 1.1.13. That proposition gives w* in the absolute Weyl group W(G*, T*), not in N_{G*}(M*)/M*, so the proof establishes the corrected statement. The only use is in the proof of Corollary 1.1.17, p.13, for G not necessarily quasi-split. It cites "Lemma 1.1.13" (the quasi-split Proposition 1.1.13) in the form w ∈ W(G, T). The corrected Corollary 1.1.15 is exactly what that step needs, so the later results stand. Checked on the page images. issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: I checked this on the p.28 image and endorse the proposed revision from gap to error. (1) By §1.3.1 (p.15), G_{V′} = GSp(V′, ψ′). On V′ = V ⊕ V with ψ ⊕ ψ, an element (g, t) ∈ G × T scales the first summand by c(g) and the second by c(t). So (1, a), with a ∈ G_m ⊂ T a scalar, is a similitude only if a² = 1. Hence G × T ⊄ G_{V′}, and the asserted '(G′, X′) ↪ (G_{V′}, H_{V′})' is false. (2) Grant the construction anyway. Then 1 × T is central in G′ and fixes the tensors. It acts on A_{s′_0} ~ A_{s_0} × A_T trivially on A_{s_0} and through T on A_T. So 1 × T ⊂ ker(I_{s′_0} → I_{s_0}), yet I_{s′_0} → T → G^ab maps it onto G^ab, because T is a maximal torus. G^ab ≠ 1: c factors through G^ab and c(a) = a² on the scalars G_m ⊂ G. So the composite does not factor through I_{s_0}. Over Q_ℓ the two composites are (g, t) ↦ t^ab and (g, t) ↦ g^ab, which differ, so the justification 'as this is true over Q_ℓ' is also false. Surjectivity of I_{s′_0} → I_{s_0} never gives a factorization by itself; the kernel has to die. The printed steps are false, not merely unjustified, so the kind is error. It is not a misprint, because nothing in the text points to the fibre product. The lemma survives with the fibre-product construction; I checked each step below. G ×_{G^ab} T lies in GSp(V ⊕ V), because c factors through G^ab. It is connected: (d, t) ↦ (dt, t) is an isomorphism of varieties G^der × T ≅ G ×_{G^ab} T. (h_0, h_T) factors through it, because points of X have a common image in G^ab. The kernel of the map to G is 1 × (T ∩ G^der), which is central and is killed by t ↦ t^ab. I_{s′_0}(Q_ℓ) ⊂ G′(Q_ℓ), where the two composites agree, so the kernel of the faithfully flat map I_{s′_0} → I_{s_0} maps trivially and the map descends. One remark in the first reading's reason does not discriminate: the clause about conjugating T → G by G^ad(Q) is also idle for the fibre product, since (h_0, h_T) always lies in its X′. So that clause is no evidence for which group the authors intended. Lemma 2.2.8 is used in §2.2.7 (p.28).

issues.correction: Uniqueness holds by (1.1.2.3); existence does not. Assume G_{Q_p} quasi-split, in which case [b_μ] exists and satisfies (1.1.3.1) (C02, N16); otherwise assume that [b_μ] exists and satisfies (1.1.3.1). Corollaries 1.3.16 and 1.3.18 and Theorem 3 of the Introduction need the same hypothesis. Also: Theorem 3 (and Corollary 1.3.16): 'Suppose G_{Q_p} is quasi-split. If the special fibre of S is locally integral then the μ-ordinary locus is dense in the special fibre.' This matches the abstract and Theorems 4–5. Alternatively, keep G general but assume that a class [b_μ] with N_ξ(ν̄_G([b_μ])) = μ̄^{-1} exists, and in §1.3.15 replace 'There is a unique [b_μ]' by 'If G_{Q_p} is quasi-split, there is a unique [b_μ]' (it can fail otherwise, e.g. G_{Q_p} = D^×). issues.reason: §1.3.15 allows non-quasi-split G_{Q_p} ('As in (1.1.5) we fix an inner twisting ξ'). For G_{Q_p} = D^×, D the quaternion division algebra, realise D^×(L) as GL_2(L) with Frobenius Ad(Π)∘σ, Π² = p. Then b ↦ bΠ is a bijection B(D^×) → B(GL_2) that raises κ by 1 and both Newton slopes by 1/2. A class with ν = μ̄^{-1} = (0, −1) would give a 2-dimensional isocrystal with the distinct slopes 1/2 and −1/2, each of multiplicity 1, which is impossible. So B(D^×, {μ^{-1}}) is the single basic class, with ν = (−1/2, −1/2). This happens inside the paper's setting: the Shimura curve of an indefinite quaternion algebra over Q ramified at an odd p is of Hodge type with G_{Q_p} = D^×, in agreement with Čerednik–Drinfeld (every point of its special fibre is supersingular). For Theorem 3 and Corollary 1.3.16 the example shows the μ-ordinary locus is undefined rather than that a density assertion is false, since that special fibre is not locally integral.

The global instance (a quaternionic Shimura curve ramified at p) is of Hodge type. For quasi-split G_{Q_p} everything holds: [b_μ] is the image of κ_{T*}^{-1}([μ^{-1}]). The same place also has: Quotation checked on the p.3 image. Theorem 3 is the introduction's form of Corollary 1.3.16 (p.20), which uses the μ-ordinary stratum S_[b_μ] of §1.3.15. §1.3.15 asserts for arbitrary G_{Q_p}, without proof, that 'There is a unique [b_μ] ∈ B(G_{Q_p},{μ^{-1}}) with N_ξ(ν̄_G([b_μ])) = μ̄^{-1}'. Uniqueness is fine by (1.1.2.3). Existence fails for non-quasi-split G. Independent check: take B an indefinite quaternion algebra over Q ramified at p, G = B^× (PEL, hence Hodge type), G_{Q_p} = D^×, G* = GL_2, μ = (1,0). Identify D^×(L) = GL_2(L) with Frobenius Ad(Π)∘σ, where Π = [[0,1],[p,0]] and Π² = p. Then b ↦ bΠ is a bijection B(D^×) → B(GL_2), because (bΠ)σ(bΠ)⋯ = (b·σ_D(b)⋯)·(Πσ(Π)⋯). It raises κ by 1, and it adds the central (1/2,1/2) to Newton points. A class with ν = (0,−1) would give a 2-dimensional isocrystal with the distinct slopes 1/2 and −1/2, each of multiplicity 1. That is impossible, since slope r/s in lowest terms occurs with multiplicity divisible by s. Hence [b_μ] does not exist. The only admissible class is basic, with ν = (−1/2,−1/2), and a check against (1.1.5.2) shows no non-basic class is admissible. So 'the μ-ordinary locus' in Theorem 3 is undefined for such data, and the proof, which goes through §1.3.15, covers only the case where [b_μ] exists. With G_{Q_p} quasi-split everything holds: [b_μ] is the image of κ_{T*}^{-1}([μ^{-1}]), and (1.1.3.1) holds by 1.1.3. Case for the defence: (i) p.2 presents Theorem 3 as a generalisation of Wedhorn and Wortmann, whose setting is hyperspecial, hence quasi-split. (ii) In the D^× test case the hypothesis of Theorem 3 fails at parahoric level: the Čerednik–Drinfeld model is semistable, with nodes where two components meet, so its special fibre is not locally integral. The test case therefore shows that the statement is ill-defined, not that a density assertion is false. No non-quasi-split example with a locally integral special fibre and no [b_μ] is exhibited, so 'false' should not be claimed; 'not established / not well-defined as stated' is accurate. (iii) Reading 'μ-ordinary' as 'the maximal element of B(G,{μ^{-1}})' would need (1.1.3.1) for that class, which the paper does not supply in the non-quasi-split case. On the claim's secondary point: whenever [b_μ] exists, (1.1.3.1) does hold, at least when G is an extended pure inner form of G* (as for D^×). Twisting by a basic x chosen in the Levi M* = Cent(μ̄*) puts a representative of [b_μ] in the Q_p-Levi J_x(M*) with central Q_p-rational Newton point. That point is a routine omission, not part of the mistake. Scope: this is the same defect as ledger E8 (§1.3.15, already 'error / a stated result'), not an independent mistake. It should be recorded by extending E8's locator to Theorem 3 (p.3) and Corollary 1.3.16 (p.20; also Corollary 1.3.18, which applies Corollary 1.3.16), and not counted a second time. One inaccuracy in the claim's correction: Theorem 1 has no quasi-split hypothesis. It assumes that ν_b has a Q_p-rational representative, and quasi-split is a special case.

issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: Checked on the p.19 image: 'C_{D,L} is equivalent to the category Rep_L G_{s0} where G_{s0} = Aut_{{s_α,cris,s0}} D_{s0}'. The Tannakian formalism gives only C_{D,L} ≃ Rep_L H, with H = Aut^⊗ of the L-valued fibre functor (pull back to s0, forget φ). Since the s_α,cris,s0 are values of global morphisms 1 → D^⊗ (Prop. 1.3.12), H ⊂ G_s0, but nothing forces equality. The CM case is covered by the corollary, and there the equality fails. Take (T,h) with T = Res_{K/Q} G_m ⊂ GL_2 = GSp_2, K imaginary quadratic (a Hodge-type datum; the paper itself uses such torus data in 1.3.10), K_p maximal and p unramified. Then a connected component of 𝒮_K ⊗ F̄_p is a point s0, and D_{s0} is H^1_cris of a CM elliptic curve. By Dieudonné–Manin, End(E_λ) ⊗_{Q_p} L is a matrix algebra, so ⟨D_{s0}⟩ ⊗ L is semisimple with rank-one simple objects indexed by slope. H is therefore the torus with character group generated by the slopes: G_m for slopes {1/2} (acting by scalars) and for {0,1}. But G_{s0} ≅ T_L (P(s0) is trivial by Steinberg) has dimension 2. Corollary 1.3.13 is still true (in the CM case it is the F-isocrystal with T-structure given by b_{s0}), and the proof can be repaired. Also, the target of ω_{s0} should be Vec_L: F-Isoc(s0) is only Q_p-linear.

issues.reviewReason: Not a mistake: the two formulas define the same group. Aut(A_s0), the automorphisms in the prime-to-p isogeny category, lies in End_Q(A_s0)^× = Aut_Q(A_s0)(Q). I_s0 is a closed Q-subgroup of Aut_Q(A_s0). A Q-point of Aut_Q(A_s0) that satisfies the Q-rational equations of I_s0 over Q_p lies in I_s0(Q). Hence I_s0(Q_p) ∩ Aut(A_s0) = I_s0(Q) ∩ Aut(A_s0), which is the expression on p.22. Writing Q would match the notation I(Z_(p)) better, but the printed formula is correct. Independent check: Checked on the image: p.21 has 'I_{s0}(Z_(p)) = I_{s0}(Q_p) ∩ Aut(A_{s0})' and p.22 (end of the proof of Lemma 2.1.4) has 'I_{s0}(Z_(p)) = I_{s0}(Q) ∩ Aut(A_{s0})'. These define the same group. Aut(A_{s0}) in the prime-to-p isogeny category lies in (End(A_{s0}) ⊗ Z_(p))^× ⊂ Aut_Q(A_{s0})(Q) ⊂ Aut_Q(A_{s0})(Q_p), so the p.21 intersection makes sense. I_{s0} is a closed Q-subgroup of Aut_Q(A_{s0}), cut out by polynomial equations with Q-coefficients. A Q-point that lies in I_{s0}(Q_p) satisfies those equations, so it lies in I_{s0}(Q). Hence I_{s0}(Q_p) ∩ Aut(A_{s0}) = I_{s0}(Q) ∩ Aut(A_{s0}). The p.21 formula is correct as printed, only less idiomatic, so it should not be recorded as a mistake. I agree with the first reading's rejection.

issues.citation: Kisin–Madapusi Pera–Shin, "Honda-Tate theory for Shimura varieties", Duke Mathematical Journal (2022)
issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p.10 image. The order ⪯_G of 1.1.1 (p.5) asks that ν_2 − ν_1 be a nonnegative linear combination of positive coroots with rational coefficients. It has to be rational there, because Newton points are fractional. With that order, 'μ′ ⪯_G μ and μ minuscule' does not imply that μ′ is conjugate to μ. Example: G = PGL_2, μ = ϖ^∨ (t ↦ diag(t,1)) and μ′ = 0. Then μ − μ′ = α^∨/2, so 0 ⪯ ϖ^∨, but 0 is not conjugate to ϖ^∨. The missing input is that μ′ and μ have the same image in π_1(G), and it is available in context. G is unramified, so the Kottwitz map w_G : G(L) → π_1(G) kills G(W) and N(L). With g = nm we get g^{−1}b_Mσ(g) = (m^{−1}b_Mσ(m))·n″ with n″ ∈ N(L). This element lies in G(W)μ(p)G(W), and m^{−1}b_Mσ(m) lies in M(W)μ′(p)M(W) ⊂ G(W)μ′(p)G(W). Hence μ^♮ = μ′^♮. So μ − μ′_dom is in the coroot lattice, with nonnegative rational and hence integral coefficients on the simple coroots. A minuscule dominant μ is minimal among dominant coweights in its class modulo coroots, so μ′_dom = μ. In the paper's defence, the sentence explains an argument that is cited ([LR87, Lem. 5.2]; alternatives [Kot03], [Kis17]), and that argument gives the integral order. Only the paraphrase, which pins down the order 'in the notation of 1.1.1', is insufficient.

Then continue: if x lies in both kernels, then x ⊗ 1 comes from (X_*(Z_G) ⊗ Q)_{Γ_p} and dies in (π_1(G) ⊗ Q)_{Γ_p}. Now X_*(Z_G)_Q → π_1(G)_Q is injective, because Z_G^0 → G^ab is an isogeny, and Q-coinvariants are exact, so x ⊗ 1 = 0 and x is torsion. By [CKV15, 2.5.12(2)], x = 0.
issues.reason: Taking coinvariants is only right exact, so the printed claim fails in general. Counterexample: G = SU(4)/μ_2, quasi-split over Q_p and split by a quadratic E/Q_p. Γ_p acts on X_*(T) through the diagram involution θ of A_3, and M = T is standard (the centralizer of the maximal split torus). Here X_*(Z_G) = 0. X_*(T) = Q^∨ + Zϖ_2^∨ has basis α_1^∨, α_2^∨, ϖ_2^∨. Since θα_1^∨ = α_3^∨ = 2ϖ_2^∨ − α_1^∨ − 2α_2^∨, we get (θ−1)X_*(T) = Z·2(ϖ_2^∨ − α_1^∨ − α_2^∨). So x = ϖ_2^∨ − α_1^∨ − α_2^∨ has order 2 in π_1(T)_{Γ_p}. Its image in π_1(M̃)_{Γ_p} = (P^∨)_{Γ_p} is ϖ_3^∨ − ϖ_1^∨ = 0. Thus the kernel is nonzero, while the image of X_*(Z_G)_{Γ_p} is 0. The case M = G is even simpler: π_1(G) = Z/2 ⊂ π_1(G^ad) = Z/4, with θ = −1, gives the zero map Z/2 → Z/2 on coinvariants. The conclusion drawn ('so the intersection must be a torsion group') still holds by the argument in the correction. So this is a false intermediate statement that does not break the proof. (Here x maps to the generator of π_1(G)_{Γ_p}, so it is not in the second kernel, which is consistent.)

issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p.10 image, and I re-derived the counterexample. Take G = SU(4)/μ_2, quasi-split over Q_p and split by a quadratic E/Q_p, with M = T the centralizer of a maximal split torus; this is a standard Levi. Then M̃ = T^ad and Z_G ≅ μ_2, so X_*(Z_G) = 0. In fundamental-coweight coordinates P^∨ = Z^3, X_*(T) = {(a,b,c) : a + c even} ⊃ Q^∨, and Γ_p acts through θ, which swaps a and c. So (θ−1)X_*(T) = {(d,0,−d) : d even}. The vector x = (−1,0,1) = ϖ_2^∨ − α_1^∨ − α_2^∨ lies in X_*(T) and has order 2 in X_*(T)_Γ. But x = (θ−1)ϖ_1^∨ is 0 in (P^∨)_Γ. So the kernel of π_1(M)_Γ → π_1(M̃)_Γ is nonzero, while the image of X_*(Z_G)_Γ is 0. (x maps to the nonzero element of π_1(G)_Γ = Z/2, which is consistent with CKV15.) The case M = G fails too: Z/2 → Z/4 → Z/2, with θ = −1 on Z/4, is the zero map on coinvariants. The cause is that coinvariants are only right exact. The printed claim is not idle. The next sentence ('so the intersection must be a torsion group') is deduced from it, so the proof of Proposition 1.1.13 fails at this step as written. That makes 'affects: the proof' the right reach, by the same standard as E5 and E9 (a printed step fails, the result survives after a repair). The conclusion does survive, as the correction shows, so no stated result is affected.

If ξ has ξ(P) = P* and u ∈ R_u(P*)(Q̄_p), then int(u)∘ξ is again an inner twisting with the same property, and it moves ξ(M) to uξ(M)u^{−1}. Concretely, take G = G* = GL_2, P = B upper triangular, M the diagonal torus, and ξ = int(u) with u = (1 a; 0 1) and a ∈ Q̄_p∖Q_p. Then ξ(P) = B, but σ(ξ(M)) = ξ(M) would need u^{−1}σ(u) ∈ N(T), that is σ(a) = a for all σ, which fails. P* has a Q_p-rational Levi factor, and all Levi factors of P* are R_u(P*)(Q̄_p)-conjugate, so after composing ξ with int(u) for some u ∈ R_u(P*)(Q̄_p) we have ξ(M) rational. issues.reviewReason: Confirmed on p.17. The lemma takes an arbitrary mixed-characteristic DVR R and a map s: η → 𝒮_K. Since 𝒮_K is an 𝒪_{E,(v)}-scheme, (i) forces 𝒪_{E,(v)} → R compatible with E → Frac R (s lands in the generic fibre Sh_K, an E-scheme). Suppose E has a second place v' | p and R's valuation restricts to v' on E. Pick y ∈ E with v(y) = 0 and v'(y) > 0. Then 1/y ∈ 𝒪_{E,(v)} but 1/y ∉ R, so s cannot extend. Yet A_η can have good reduction: take a CM point over a number field F, enlarged so that the CM abelian variety has good reduction at a place w | v', and R = 𝒪_{F,(w)}. So (ii) ⇒ (i) fails as literally stated. The proof's first step ('(i) is equivalent to s extending to S → 𝒮_𝒦') tacitly assumes R is an 𝒪_{E,(v)}-algebra compatibly with s. KP18 states its extension property for DVRs R ⊃ 𝒪_E. Every use in the paper satisfies the implicit hypothesis: 1.3.7 (𝒪_{L'}, L' = E_v L), 1.3.10 (𝒪_{E_T,(v')} with v' | v), and p.27 (points over Q̄_p via the fixed embedding).

A point s0 ∈ 𝒮_0(F̄_p) over 𝒪_{E_T,(v')} lifts through an embedding E_T ↪ L̄ inducing v'. By Lemma 1.3.9 for T its class is b_bas(τμ_x^{-1}) with ι_p∘τ inducing v', and this depends on v', not only on v. Example: G = GSp_6 (E = Q), T the CM torus of a sextic CM field K with generic Galois closure, CM type Φ, and p = 𝔭𝔭̄𝔮𝔮̄ with f(𝔭) = 1, f(𝔮) = 2. By Shimura–Taniyama, ι_pΦ = {ψ1,ψ2,ψ3} (H_𝔭 = {ψ1}, H_𝔮 = {ψ2,ψ3}) gives an ordinary reduction. The place of the reflex field E_T induced by ι_p∘τ, with τ swapping only φ3 ↔ φ̄3, gives slopes (0,½,½,½,½,1). Both places lie above v = p. So for [b] ordinary, the printed choice can produce s0 with [b_s0] ≠ [b], and the step 'But then we must have [b_s0] = [b]' fails. The repair is one line and the proposition is unaffected. In 1.2.5 (p.14), μ_T = μ_x is pinned down through ι_p ('the unique cocharacter, which, after base-change along ι_p, is identified with int(g_p)(μ_p)'), and [b] is the image of [b_bas(μ_x^{-1})] computed through ι_p. issues.locator: Corollary 1.3.18 and its proof, p.20
issues.printed: Under p > 2, tame splitting of G, and special parahoric K_p, the source claims one can choose G ↪ 𝒢_V so that S_[b_μ] is dense in 𝒮_{K,k(v)}. The proof attributes this to Corollary 1.3.16 together with [KP18, Cor. 0.3].
issues.correction: Suppose p > 2, G splits over a tamely ramified extension, p ∤ |π_1(G^der)|, and K_p = K°_p is the parahoric attached to a point x ∈ B(G, Q_p) that is a special vertex of B(G, Q_p^ur) (a very special parahoric; this forces G_{Q_p} to be quasi-split, so [b_μ] exists and satisfies (1.1.3.1)). Then, choosing the embedding as in KP18 §4.1.5, 𝒮_{K,k(v)} is normal (KP18, Cor. 0.3), hence locally integral, and Cor. 1.3.16 applies.
issues.reason: KP18 Cor. 0.3 (Publ. IHÉS 128, p.124; checked in the KP18 text) gives normality of the special fibre only 'If K°_p is associated to a point x which is a special vertex in B(G, Q_p^ur)'. It is stated under the introduction's standing assumptions, which include 'p does not divide the order |π_1(G^der)|' (p.122). Neither condition appears in Cor. 1.3.18. A parahoric that is special over Q_p need not be special over Q_p^ur. For the Shimura curve of an indefinite quaternion algebra B/Q ramified at an odd prime p, G_Qp = D^× splits over Q_{p^2} (tame), and K_p = O_D^× is the unique parahoric (the building is a point, so it is special). Over Q_p^ur, however, K_p becomes an Iwahori subgroup of GL_2. There [b_μ] does not exist (E8), and the Čerednik–Drinfeld special fibre has ordinary double points, so it is not locally integral. So the corollary fails in this case when 'special' has its usual meaning over Q_p. Defence: the authors may intend 'special' in KP18's sense (special over Q_p^ur). On that reading only the π_1 hypothesis is missing, and that hypothesis is not automatic for Hodge type (e.g. G^der ≅ SU(1,5)/μ_3 acting through Λ^3, where π_1 = Z/3).

issues.reviewReason: The p.20 image shows the quoted statement and proof. KP18 Cor. 0.3 (p.124 of the KP18 text) gives normality of the special fibre only 'If K°_p is associated to a point x which is a special vertex in B(G, Q_p^ur)'. It sits under the Introduction's standing assumptions (p.122): p > 2, abelian type, tame, and p ∤ |π_1(G^der)|. KMS assume only 'K_p is a special parahoric', which in the usual sense (Tits) means special in B(G, Q_p). By KP18's footnote, special over Q_p^ur (very special) points exist only for quasi-split G_{Q_p}. Counterexample on the Q_p reading: B/Q an indefinite quaternion algebra ramified at an odd p, G = B^× with V = B (Hodge type), and K_p = O_D^× = the stabilizer of O_D ⊂ D. G_{Q_p} = D^× splits over Q_{p^2} (tame), and O_D^× is the unique parahoric; the reduced building is a point, so it is special over Q_p. Over Q_p^ur it becomes Iwahori, not special. π_1(G^der) = 1. Every point of the special fibre is supersingular (basic), and the Čerednik–Drinfeld special fibre has ordinary double points. So no μ-ordinary locus is dense for any choice of embedding; indeed [b_μ] does not even exist here (E8). On the KP18 reading of 'special', the π_1 hypothesis is still missing: SU(1,5)/μ_3 acting through Λ^3 is Hodge type with π_1 = Z/3 and p = 3 > 2. KP18 Cor. 4.6.26 drops that hypothesis, but only for its abelian-type construction, which is not shown there to agree with the normalization of the closure used by KMS. The cited result does not cover the corollary's hypotheses, and on the natural reading the corollary is false.

issues.printed: The source says φ-invariance ensures preservation of the crystalline components {s_α,cris,s0}, yielding γ_{m,s0} ∈ I_{s0}(Q). It also asserts a natural descent of D_{s0} to an F-isocrystal D_{m,s0} over Q_{q^m}, with the φ-invariant tensors {s_α,cris,s0} lying in D^⊗_{m,s0}.
issues.correction: Insert: since s0 is F_q-rational, for an automorphism τ of L̄ extending σ^r, the conjugate s^τ of a lift s of s0 is again a lift of s0, and the s_α,ét are defined over E. By the characterization in Prop. 1.3.7, (1 ⊗ σ^r)(s_α,cris,s0) = s_α,cris,s0 on D_{s0} = D(A_0)_Q ⊗_{Q_q} L. Hence s_α,cris,s0 ∈ D_{m,s0}^⊗, and the linear map γ_{m,cris,s0} = φ^{rm} fixes them, since they are φ-invariant.
issues.reason: φ-invariance alone does not imply invariance under the linear q^m-Frobenius φ_0^{rm} ⊗ 1. For example, let D_0 = Q_p e with φ_0(e) = ue, u ∈ Z_p^× \ {1} (q = p, m = 1). Lang's theorem gives λ ∈ L with σ(λ)u = λ, and λ ∉ Q_p. Then λe ∈ D_s0 is φ-invariant but is moved by the Frobenius endomorphism (multiplication by u). The needed rationality does hold, by canonicity (Prop. 1.3.7), but the paper gives only the φ-invariance reason. The conclusion γ_{m,s0} ∈ I_s0(Q) is correct.

issues.reviewReason: Both quotations are confirmed on the images (p.22 §2.1.5 and p.23 §2.1.7). γ_{m,s0} acts on D_{s0} = D_{m,s0} ⊗_{Q_{q^m}} L as the linear map φ_m^{rm} ⊗ 1, whereas φ^{rm} = φ_m^{rm} ⊗ σ^{rm}. A φ-invariant tensor t is fixed by γ exactly when (1 ⊗ σ^{rm})t = t, i.e. when t ∈ D_{m,s0}^⊗. So φ-invariance alone does not give the conclusion. The first reading's toy example is correct. Take D_0 = Q_p e, φ_0 e = u e with u ∈ Z_p^× \ {1}, and use Lang to pick λ ∈ W(F̄_p)^× with σ(λ)u = λ (then λ ∉ Q_p). The vector λe is φ-invariant, but the linear Frobenius multiplies it by u. The needed rationality, s_α,cris,s0 ∈ D_{m,s0}^⊗, is asserted in 2.1.7 without argument. It is true: s0 is F_q-rational, and transporting a lift s along an automorphism of L̄ extending σ^r yields another lift of s0 (the s_α,ét are defined over E). By the canonicity in Prop. 1.3.7, (1 ⊗ σ^r) then fixes s_α,cris,s0. The conclusion γ_{m,s0} ∈ I_{s0}(Q) is correct. The missing step is a gap in the proof, not an error.

issues.printed: The source says the subalgebra Q^n ⊂ End_{Q̄} V_{Q̄}, acting as scalars on each W_i, descends to L = ∏_{i=1}^k L_i ⊂ End_Q V, a product of fields.
issues.correction: The subalgebra Q̄^n ⊂ End_{Q̄} V_{Q̄} which acts by scalars on each factor W_i descends to …
issues.reason: Checked on the page image (the text layer also has 'Qn'). The Q̄-subalgebra acting by scalars on the isotypic components is Q̄^n. It is Gal(Q̄/Q)-stable, since Galois permutes the W_i, so it descends to an étale Q-algebra L = ∏ L_i of dimension n. The Q-algebra Q^n does not 'descend' to a product of fields L_i; its Galois invariants are just Q^k.

issues.reviewReason: A 400 dpi zoom of p.26 (last line) shows 'ℚ^n' without a bar, while the adjacent End_{ℚ̄} V_{ℚ̄} carry bars. The subalgebra of End_{Q̄} V_{Q̄} acting by scalars on the isotypic components W_1, …, W_n is the Q̄-algebra Q̄^n. It is Gal(Q̄/Q)-stable, because Galois permutes the W_i, so it descends to an étale Q-algebra L = ∏_{i=1}^k L_i of dimension n, with k the number of Galois orbits. The Q-span Q^n of the idempotents is not a Q̄-subspace and cannot 'descend' to fields L_i of degree equal to the orbit sizes. The meaning is clear.

issues.locator: §2.2.7, proof of Proposition 2.2.2, construction of (G″, X″, ι″), p.27
issues.printed: After identifying G′^ad with G^ad, the source defines G″ as the identity component of G′ ×_{G^ad} G. It sets V″ = V ⊕ V′ with ψ″ = ψ ⊕ ψ′, and claims ι and ι′ induce ι″ : (G″, X″) → (G_{V″}, H_{V″}) as an embedding.
issues.correction: Let G″ be the identity component of {(g′, g) ∈ G′ ×_{G^ad} G : c′(g′) = c(g)} = (G′ ×_{G^ad} G) ∩ GSp(V″, ψ″), where c and c′ are the similitude characters. (h_0′, h_0) factors through G″, because c∘h_0 = c′∘h_0′. G″ surjects onto G and G′ with central kernels, and G″^der ≅ G′^der. The rest of the proof is unchanged.
issues.reason: Checked on the page image. G_{V″} = GSp(V″, ψ″) (§1.3.1, p.15). G contains the scalars G_m, via the weight of X, and they map trivially to G^ad, so (1, a) ∈ G′ ×_{G^ad} G for a ∈ G_m, and {1}×G_m lies in the identity component G″. But (1, a) acts on V ⊕ V′ by (a, 1) and scales ψ″ by a² on V and by 1 on V′. It is not a symplectic similitude unless a = ±1. So G″ ⊄ G_{V″}, and 'the embedding ι″ : (G″,X″) → (G_{V″}, H_{V″})', to which 'our previous constructions' are then applied, does not exist as printed. In Noot's Mumford–Tate setting the corresponding group, the Mumford–Tate group of A × A′, automatically satisfies c = c′; the slip comes from reformulating with Shimura data. It is the same kind of slip as in the proof of Lemma 2.2.8 (E5), and the repair is routine.

issues.reviewReason: I checked this on the p.27 image. G_{V″} = GSp(V″, ψ″) (§1.3.1), and a Hodge-type embedding must land there, which the integral-model construction ('our previous constructions') needs. G contains the scalars G_m: for h ∈ X ⊂ H_V, h(r) = r on V_R, and G is defined over Q (compare p.25 and §2.1.3). The scalars map trivially to G^ad, so {1} × G_m ⊂ G′ ×_{G^ad} G, and being connected it lies in G″. The element (1, a) acts on V ⊕ V′ as a on V and 1 on V′, so it scales ψ ⊕ ψ′ by a² on V and by 1 on V′. It is not a symplectic similitude unless a = ±1. So G″ ⊄ G_{V″}, and the printed embedding ι″ does not exist. The step as printed is false, hence an error; the repair is routine and I checked it. c∘h = Nm_{C/R} (or its inverse, consistently) for every point of every Siegel space, so (h_0′, h_0) satisfies c′ = c. The subgroup cut out by c′(g′) = c(g) still surjects onto G and G′ (lift g^ad into G′^der, then multiply by a scalar a with a² = c(g)). It contains the graph of G′^der → G^der, which is its derived group, so G″^der ≅ G′^der still holds. The kernels of the projections, Z_{G′} ∩ ker c′ and Z_G ∩ ker c, are central, so the maps I_{s_0} ← I_{s″_0} → I_{s′_0} and the argument on p.28 are unchanged. Proposition 2.2.2 survives.

issues.locator: §2.2.7, proof of Proposition 2.2.2 (reduction to the accommodating case), p.28
issues.printed: The source replaces γ″ by a power so that γ″^ab ∈ G″^ab(Q), described as γ's image, lifts to z ∈ Z_{G″}(Q), then writes γ″ = γ″_1 z. It uses commutation of z and γ to assert that γ″_1 remains a Weil point, and appeals to the previously treated accommodating case for its image in I_{s′_0}.
issues.correction: Also replace γ″ by γ″^N, taking z^N as the lift of its abelianization, so that γ″_1 becomes γ″_1^N. Choose N to kill the component group of the diagonalizable group Zariski closure of ⟨γ″_1⟩. Then γ″_1^N is neat, and so is its image in I_{s′_0}. Passing from γ″^N back to γ″ is legitimate by [Noo09, Prop. 3.2], since γ″ is neat. Then apply the accommodating case to the image of γ″_1^N.
issues.reason: The accommodating case was proved only for neat Weil points: neatness gives the 'faiblement net' condition needed for [Noo09, Lem. 2.5, 2.6] (p.27). The proof shows that γ″_1 is a Weil point but never that it, or its image in I_{s′_0}, is neat, and neatness is not inherited from γ″. Two lifts z differ by an element of the finite group Z_{G″} ∩ G″^der, and multiplying a neat element by a torsion central element can create eigenvalue ratios that are non-trivial roots of unity. For example, if −1 ∈ Z ∩ G^der does not lie in the torus S = closure of ⟨γ″_1⟩, then the closure of ⟨−γ″_1⟩ is S ∪ (−S). So the reduction as written applies the accommodating case outside its hypotheses. For the defence: the text already replaces γ″ by powers 'as above', and the fix is one more power.

issues.reviewReason: I checked pp.25, 27 and 28. Proposition 2.2.2, and the accommodating case proved on p.27, concern neat Weil points: neatness is what gives the 'faiblement net' input to [Noo09, Lem. 2.5, 2.6]. The reduction on p.28 proves that γ″_1 = γ″z^{-1} is a Weil point and then applies 'the accommodating case considered above' to its image in I_{s′_0}. It never checks that this element is neat, and neatness is not automatic. The lift z ∈ Z_{G″}(Q) of γ″^ab is determined only up to the finite group (Z_{G″} ∩ G″^der)(Q). A cleanest witness: if γ″ is central and ε ≠ 1 lies in that group (for example −1 when G^der = Sp), then z = γ″ε is an admissible lift and γ″_1 = ε^{-1} is a non-trivial torsion element, which is not neat. The conclusion is not in danger: one more power fixes it, and the paper already uses 'replacing γ″ by a power', justified by [Noo09, Prop. 3.2] since γ″ is neat. But the hypothesis of the case being invoked is never checked, so this is a gap in the proof.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 2.2.13, p.29
issues.printed: The source defines M as the identity component in γ's centralizer in G, asserts that M is a Levi subgroup, and concludes that maximal tori T_1, T_2 ⊂ M are conjugate within M.
issues.correction: Delete 'M is a Levi subgroup of G'. M is a connected reductive group containing T_1 and T_2 as maximal tori, so they are conjugate in M(k).
issues.reason: Checked on the page image. Here γ ∈ T_1(k) ∩ T_2(k) is arbitrary, and the identity component of the centralizer of a semisimple element need not be a Levi subgroup. Take G = GSp_4 = GSp(W_1 ⊕ W_2) with W_i symplectic planes and γ = (1 on W_1, −1 on W_2). Then M = GSp(W_1) ×_{G_m} GSp(W_2) has dimension 7 and a 1-dimensional centre, while every proper Levi subgroup of GSp_4 has a central torus of dimension ≥ 2. The assertion is false as stated but idle: conjugacy of maximal tori in the connected group M is all that is used, and in all three applications (p.30) γ is neat or central in I_0.

issues.citation: Kisin–Madapusi Pera–Shin, "Honda-Tate theory for Shimura varieties", Duke Mathematical Journal (2022)
issues.reviewReason: I checked this on the p.29 image. The observation takes an arbitrary γ ∈ T_1(k) ∩ T_2(k). The identity component of the centralizer of a semisimple element is in general only a pseudo-Levi subgroup. Counterexample: G = GSp(W_1 ⊕ W_2) = GSp_4, with W_i symplectic planes and γ = (1 on W_1, −1 on W_2) ∈ Sp_4. Then M = GSp(W_1) ×_{G_m} GSp(W_2) = {(g_1, g_2) ∈ GL_2 × GL_2 : det g_1 = det g_2}, which is connected of dimension 7 with a 1-dimensional connected centre. A proper Levi subgroup L = Z_G(S), with S a non-central torus, has a central torus of dimension ≥ 2, and M ≠ G. So M is not a Levi subgroup. The false clause is idle. The argument uses only that T_1 and T_2 are maximal tori of the connected group M, hence M(k)-conjugate. In the applications on p.30, γ is central in I_0 (so M = I_0) or a neat Weil point (so M is the centralizer of a torus, hence a Levi subgroup).

issues.reviewReason: I checked the p.30 image, and the claim needs narrowing. (a) 'applied with I in place of G' is correct as printed. Apply the observation to I_k with the maximal tori T and j_ℓ^{-1}(T_0), which both contain the central γ_{m,s_0}. If h ∈ I(k) conjugates T onto j_ℓ^{-1}(T_0), then j_ℓ∘int(h) = int(j_ℓ(h))∘j_ℓ, i.e. j_ℓ is conjugated by j_ℓ(h) ∈ I_0(k), exactly as the text says. (b) The real slips are these. σ = j_{ℓ′}∘j_ℓ^{-1} is an automorphism of I_0 preserving T_0, and T ⊂ I is not a subgroup of I_0. So 'σ|_T' should be σ|_{T_0} (Lemma 2.2.11 is applied with S = T_0 and Γ = j_ℓ(neat Weil points)), 'agree on T' should be 'agree on T_0', and 'an element of t ∈ T(k)' should be 'an element t ∈ T_0(k)'. The identification of T with T_0 depends on ℓ, which is exactly what σ compares, so this is not a harmless convention. The meaning is nevertheless clear.

issues.locator: Lemma 2.3.13 and its proof, p. 34 (used in the proof of Corollary 2.3.14, p. 35)
issues.printed: Lemma 2.3.13 assumes s0 ∈ S_{K_p}(F̄_p) and a maximal torus T ⊂ I_{s0}, with (j, x, s0′) supplying a Q̄-isogeny CM lift of s0 relative to T. It asserts that P^T is a T-torsor, and deduces non-emptiness of P^T_ℓ(s0, s0′) from conjugacy of j with i_ℓ by G(Q̄_ℓ).
issues.correction: Add to the hypotheses of Lemma 2.3.13, or build into the definition of a CM lift with respect to T, the following: for m sufficiently divisible, γ_{m,s0} ∈ T(Q) acts on A_{s0′} through j as γ_{m,s0′}. With this, an element of G(Q̄_ℓ) conjugating i_ℓ to j lies in P_ℓ^T(Q̄_ℓ), and the rest of the proof goes through. The lift constructed in the proof of Proposition 2.3.11 has this property (the claim γ_{m,s0} = γ_{m,s0′} proved there). So Corollaries 2.3.14 and 2.3.15 hold if the proof of 2.3.14 starts from that lift.
issues.reason: P_ℓ(s0,s0') ⊂ Isog_ℓ consists of isomorphisms carrying γ_{m,ℓ,s0} to γ_{m,ℓ,s0'}. A G(Q̄_ℓ)-element conjugating i_ℓ to j carries γ_{m,ℓ,s0} = i_ℓ(γ_{m,s0}) to j(γ_{m,s0}), which equals γ_{m,ℓ,s0'} = j(γ_{m,s0'}) only if γ_{m,s0} = γ_{m,s0'} in T(Q). So the step quoted from the proof is incomplete, and the condition is also necessary. If f ∈ P^T(R), R ≠ 0, then f∘γ_{m,s0} = γ_{m,s0'}∘f (f is an isogeny over F̄_p) and f∘γ_{m,s0} = j(γ_{m,s0})∘f (T-equivariance), so γ_{m,s0} = γ_{m,s0'}. Counterexample to the lemma as stated: G = GL_2 = GSp_2 (modular curve, hyperspecial level; PEL type C, so Conjecture 2.3.4 holds by Lemma 2.3.5), s0 ordinary with End^0 = K imaginary quadratic, and T = I_{s0} = Res_{K/Q}G_m. Take (j,x,s0') from Proposition 2.3.11 and let c be complex conjugation on T. By Skolem–Noether, j∘c is GL_2(Q)-conjugate to j, so (j∘c, x, s0') is again a Q̄-isogeny CM lift in the sense of §2.3.7: same image torus, same CM point, still Q̄_ℓ-conjugate to every i_ℓ, still Q̄-isogenous. For it, T-equivariance forces γ_{m,s0} = c(γ_{m,s0}), i.e. γ_{m,s0} ∈ Q^×, which is false for ordinary s0. So P^T = ∅. The defence that the paper only applies the lemma to the lift of Proposition 2.3.11 saves the corollaries, but not the lemma as stated. The printed proof of Corollary 2.3.14 also starts from an unspecified lift.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p.34 image. The lemma asserts that P^T is a T-torsor, and the proof argues that it is non-empty, so non-emptiness is part of the claim. By 2.3.2–2.3.3, P_ℓ(s0,s0′) ⊂ Isog_ℓ consists of tensor-preserving isomorphisms that also carry γ_{m,ℓ,s0} to γ_{m,ℓ,s0′} (m sufficiently divisible). T acts on A_{s0} through T ⊂ I_{s0}. For m divisible, γ_{m,s0} is central in I_{s0}, so it lies in T(Q). T acts on A_{s0′} through j (2.3.9). Let γ′ ∈ T(Q) be the element that acts on A_{s0′} as γ_{m,s0′}. An element g ∈ G(Q̄_ℓ) with int(g)∘i_ℓ = j carries i_ℓ(γ_{m,s0}) to j(γ_{m,s0}), and that equals γ_{m,ℓ,s0′} = j(γ′) only if γ_{m,s0} = γ′. So the quoted step skips a condition. The condition is also necessary. If f ∈ P^T(R) with R ≠ 0, then f∘γ_{m,s0} = γ_{m,s0′}∘f because f is in Isog, and f∘γ_{m,s0} = j(γ_{m,s0})∘f by T-equivariance, so γ′ = γ_{m,s0}. Counterexample: take G = GL_2 = GSp_2 (the modular curve with K_p = GL_2(Z_p); PEL type C, so Conjecture 2.3.4 holds by Lemma 2.3.5). Let s0 be an ordinary elliptic curve with End^0 = K imaginary quadratic, and T = I_{s0} = Res_{K/Q}G_m. Let (j,x,s0′) be any Q̄-isogeny CM lift (Prop. 2.3.11 gives one), and let c be the non-trivial automorphism of T. By Skolem–Noether, j∘c = int(g)∘j with g ∈ GL_2(Q). So j∘c is still Q̄_ℓ-conjugate to every i_ℓ and has the same image torus. h_x still factors through that torus, the image of Sh_{K_{T,p}}(h_x) in Sh(G,X) does not change, and P(s0,s0′) does not change either. Hence (j∘c,x,s0′) is again a Q̄-isogeny CM lift in the sense of 2.3.7, and its γ′ is c(γ′_j). If both lifts had P^T ≠ ∅, then γ_{m,s0} = γ′_j = c(γ′_j) = c(γ_{m,s0}), so π^m ∈ Q for the Frobenius π of s0. That is impossible for ordinary s0, because (π) and (π̄) are powers of the two distinct primes above p. So one of the two lifts has P^T = ∅. Starting from the lift of Prop. 2.3.11, which has γ′ = γ_{m,s0}, it is the twisted one. The defence that the paper applies the lemma only to the lift built in Prop. 2.3.11 saves Corollaries 2.3.14 and 2.3.15, but not the lemma as stated. Also, the proof of 2.3.14 only says 'a Q̄-isogeny CM lift … say (j,x,s0′)'.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on a zoomed p.35 image: 'admitting a lift to Sh_{K_{T,p}}(h_x)'. By 2.3.7, (j′,x′,s0″) is a CM lift only if s0″ lifts to the torus Shimura variety of h_{x′}, which factors through j′(T_R). This is also what [Kis17, 4.2.6] gives, which I checked. The twisted map i_ω identifies Sh(G′,X′) with Sh(G′_ω, X′_ω), where X′_ω = {ω h′ ω^{-1}}, and on it the abelian variety is the twist A_P. So P(s0,s0″) is trivial for points on the twisted locus Sh(h_{x′}). A point lifting to the old Sh(h_x) is a reduction of the old CM locus, where P(s0,s0″) is the I_{s0}-torsor induced from P^T. That torsor is not trivial in general, which is why the twist was made. Meaning clear from the construction.

issues.printed: The source describes the analogue of P(s0, s′0) as a torsor for the units of a product of fields, permitting skew fields among the factors.
issues.correction: … is a torsor under the group of units of a semisimple Q-algebra (a product of matrix algebras over (possibly skew) fields) …
issues.reason: The endomorphism-only automorphism group is the unit group of End_B(A_{s0})⊗Q, e.g. M_g(D_{p,∞}) for A_{s0} = E^g supersingular with B = Q, which is not a product of skew fields. Both triviality arguments given (Zariski density of Q-points of the open invertible locus; 'a product of inner forms of GL_n', up to Weil restriction) work for any semisimple algebra, so the conclusion stands.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p.36 image. When only endomorphisms are respected, the analogue of P(s0,s0′) is a torsor under Aut_B(A_{s0}) = (End_B(A_{s0}) ⊗ Q)^×. End_B(A_{s0}) ⊗ Q is a semisimple Q-algebra: a product of matrix algebras over division algebras, not in general a product of skew fields. For example, on the genus-2 Siegel variety (B = Q), a supersingular A_{s0} ≅ E×E has End^0 = M_2(D_{p,∞}). Both arguments for triviality still work: a torsor under the units of a semisimple algebra is a non-empty open subscheme of an affine space over Q, so it has a Q-point; and the group is a product of Weil restrictions of inner forms of GL_n. The authors' own phrase 'inner forms of GL_n' fits the correct description, so the slip is only in the wording. The conclusion stands.

issues.locator: Proof of Corollary A.7, p. 39
issues.printed: The source chooses dense open immersions U_i ↪ S_i for i = 0, 1, with proper, semi-stable S_i and normal crossings boundary (S_i\U_i) ∪ S_i ⊗_{𝒪_K} k in S_i. It then substitutes U_i for U and S_i for S to assume proper semi-stable S and normal crossing divisor S_0 ∪ D ⊂ S. It obtains the desired map by restricting Proposition A.6's s_0 : 1 → ℰ^{log ⊗} to U.
issues.correction: The reduction step must also make A ×_U U_i extend to a semi-abelian scheme over S_i. One way: take a proper S̄ ⊃ U over which A extends semi-abelianly, and apply [dJ96, 6.5] to S̄ with Z = S̄∖U (and likewise to build U_1). Then the S_i map to S̄ and the extension pulls back. In the application such an S̄ is a toroidal compactification [MP19]. In general one can first pass to the finite étale cover of U trivializing A[N] (N ≥ 3, p ∤ N; this is harmless for proper descent) and use a toroidal compactification of the moduli space [FC] (A polarizable) to get such an S̄. Alternatively, Raynaud's criterion gives semi-abelian reduction at the generic points of S_i∖U_i, and one then extends across the normal-crossings boundary of the regular S_i.
issues.reason: Proposition A.6 is stated in the setting of A.2–A.3, which requires the abelian scheme over U to extend to a semi-abelian scheme over S. That hypothesis produces E^log via [MP19, 1.3.5] and underlies Lemma A.4. [dJ96, Thm 6.5] only provides a semi-stable compactification S_i of U_i, and the pulled-back abelian scheme need not extend semi-abelianly across the new boundary S_i∖U_i. Example: the Legendre family over U = Spec W[λ, 1/λ(1−λ)] with S = U, D = ∅. The choice U_0 = U, S_0 = P^1_W (after a finite extension) satisfies everything the proof asks of de Jong's theorem, but the curve has non-unipotent (−1 times unipotent) monodromy, hence additive reduction, at λ = ∞. So the reduction step as written can fail. The statement of Corollary A.7 is very likely true with the repair above. By p.19, Proposition 1.3.12 (and so this appendix) is used only in (1.3.14) and (1.3.16).

issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p.39 image, and against A.2–A.3 (pp.37–38). Proposition A.6 is stated in the setting of A.2–A.3. That setting requires the abelian scheme over U to extend to a semi-abelian scheme over S, which produces E^log through [MP19, 1.3.5] and hence E^vlog and Lemma A.4. Corollary A.7 assumes this only for the original S ('as above'). The proof replaces (U,S) by (U_i,S_i), where the S_i are the compactifications given by [dJ96, 6.5]. Nothing ensures that A ×_U U_i extends semi-abelianly over the new boundary S_i∖U_i. Since S_i is proper and S need not be, S_i does not in general map to S, so the extension cannot simply be pulled back. Example (p > 2): the Legendre family y² = x(x−1)(x−λ) over U = S = Spec W[λ, 1/λ(1−λ)], with D = ∅. The choice U_1 = U_0 = U and S_0 = S_1 = P^1_W meets every requirement the proof places on de Jong's output: P^1_W is smooth over W, and the disjoint sections 0, 1, ∞ together with the special fibre form a strict normal crossings divisor. But at λ = ∞ the curve is the quadratic twist by the uniformizer of an I_2 curve. It has type I_2^* (additive) reduction, with local monodromy −(unipotent), so it does not extend semi-abelianly over the generic point of the ∞-section, and Proposition A.6 cannot be applied. In the application to Proposition 1.3.12 the base is the non-proper integral model, so new boundary really occurs. The statement of A.7 is very likely true with a repair, so this is a gap in the proof. Per p.19, Proposition 1.3.12 is only used in §1.3 (Cor. 1.3.13, (1.3.14), (1.3.16)).

issues.reviewReason: E4's claim that the printed assertion is 'simply false' is too strong. An action morphism a: 𝒢 × M → M is itself a trivial 𝒢-torsor for h·(g,m) = (gh^{-1}, hm): the shear (g,m) ↦ (g, gm) turns a into pr_2. Concretely, 𝒢_W (identified with 𝒢 ⊗ W in 3.3.9 and in the proof of 4.2.4) acts freely and transitively on the fibres of q^loc via (f,ℱ) ↦ (f∘g^{-1}, gℱ), and m ↦ (f_0, f_0^{-1}m) is a section. What fails is that q^loc is not a torsor for the 𝒢-action on f through V^∨, for which π^loc is a torsor and (4.2.8) is equivariant; so 'π^loc and q^loc are 𝒢-torsors' cannot hold for one and the same action. The proof uses only that q^loc is smooth of relative dimension dim G ('Since q^loc has the required properties, so does q'), and that holds in either reading. KPZ26 §7.3.1(1) is the authors' own erratum and gives the right replacement. Independent check: Quotation checked on p. 187 (zoomed). I re-derived the revision independently. Write q^loc(f,ℱ) = f(ℱ) (see E57). 𝒢_W = Aut(D_x̄, s_{α,0,x̄}) ≅ 𝒢 ⊗ W (3.3.9) acts on M̃^loc_G by h·(f,ℱ) = (f∘h^{-1}, hℱ). This action preserves M^loc_G, because M^loc_G is the flat closure of a G_{K_0}-orbit. It is free, and it is transitive on the fibres of q^loc: if f(ℱ) = f'(ℱ'), then h = f'^{-1}f works. It has the section m ↦ (f_0, f_0^{-1}m), where f_0 is a W-point of the trivial torsor 𝒫. Here f_0^{-1}m ∈ M^loc_G because f_0 carries the orbit closure of y(x) (type μ_h^{-1}) onto M^loc_{G,X} ⊗ O_{E^ur}. So the printed 'q^loc is a 𝒢-torsor' is true for this action, and E4's 'simply false' is too strong. It is false for the V^∨-side action g·(f,ℱ) = (g∘f, ℱ), for which π^loc is a torsor and q^loc is equivariant. No single free 𝒢-action makes both maps torsors unless μ is central, since orbits would lie in the fibres of (π^loc, q^loc), which have dimension dim 𝒢 − dim(orbit of ℱ). The authors' erratum (KPZ26 §7.3.1(1)) is itself loose: the action morphism 𝒢 × M → M is a trivial torsor for h·(g,m) = (gh^{-1}, hm). The proof uses only 'q^loc is smooth of relative dimension dim G', and that holds either way. So the defect is an unspecified or conflated group action, with nothing lost.

issues.reviewReason: Verified on the page images. The failing step is the sentence 'Since K°_p ∩ Ã(G_{Z_(p)})° is contained in the kernel …': an element t of K°_p ∩ Ã° fixes the coset a·j·K°_{2,p} only if j^{-1}(a^{-1}ta)j ∈ K°_{2,p}, which holds for j = 1 (or j normalizing K°_{2,p}) but not in general; the stabilizer of the j-th coset is jK°_pj^{-1} ∩ Ã°. The printed statement then drops j altogether and writes a |J|-th power. arXiv:1512.01149v2 carries the same text. The torsor (4.6.20) is formed by the identical recipe and inherits the error. Independent check: Quotations checked on the images of pp. 202, 203 and 205 (Lemma 4.6.13, the proof's display (4.6.14) and the sentence 'Since K°_p ∩ Ã(G_{Z_(p)})° is contained in the kernel…', (4.6.16), (4.6.20)). Independent check: the j-th piece of (4.6.14) is [Sh(G,X)^+ × Ã(G_{2,Z_(p)}) j K°_{2,p}/K°_{2,p}]/Ã(G_{Z_(p)})° (Cartesian square of Lemma 4.6.10). To pass to Sh_{K°_p}(G,X)^+ the text needs N = K°_p ∩ Ã° to act trivially on this set. An element t ∈ N maps into the normal subgroup K°_{2,p} of Ã(G_{2,Z_(p)}), so t·a·j·K°_{2,p} = a·j·(j^{-1}(a^{-1}ta)j)·K°_{2,p}. This is the same coset only if j^{-1}(a^{-1}ta)j ∈ K°_{2,p}, which fails unless j normalizes K°_{2,p}. So the stabilizer is jK°_pj^{-1} ∩ Ã°, as KPZ26 §7.3.1(3) says, and the |J|-th power at the single level K°_p is not justified. The authors themselves say the description 'is not correct' (credit to Yu Luo and Peihang Wu). The same text is in arXiv v2 (ext/kp_arxiv.txt, 'A(G_{Z(p)})°]^{|J|}' three times). On the revision: (a) is right. (4.6.20) forms the torsor by the same recipe over (4.6.16), so once (4.6.16) is corrected, (4.6.20) as printed is a torsor over the wrong scheme. KPZ26 does not mention it explicitly. (b) is a fair reading of KPZ26's phrase 'component containing (j,X^+)', which is literal only when the image of j in G^ad(Q_p) lifts to some g ∈ G(Q_p). The piece is then the component of Sh_{K°_p}(G,X) through (g,X^+), which is Γ\X^+ with Γ = G(Q)_+ ∩ gK°_pg^{-1}K^p. Caveat: when j does not lift, KPZ26's 'Zariski closure in 𝒮_{K°_p}(G,X)' has no literal meaning either, and a model at level jK°_pj^{-1} is needed. That concerns KPZ26's erratum, not this entry. Housekeeping: the existing entries' 'searched' note says 'the correction of E6 was pointed out by Yu Luo and Peihang Wu'. That should read E6: KPZ26 §7.3.1(3) credits them for Lemma 4.6.13/Cor. 4.6.15, while E7 comes from footnote 8, with no attribution.

issues.locator: §4.6.21, printed p. 205
issues.printed: The source takes a Shimura datum (H,Y) with classical H^ad and cites [20] and [43] 3.4.13 for a central isogeny H̃ → H♯. It says this also depends on Y when H has a type D factor, and characterizes abelian type for (H,Y) by H^der being a quotient of H♯.
issues.correction: Restrict 4.6.21 to Shimura data (H,Y) with (H^ad,Y^ad) of abelian type (KPZ26 p. 80, footnote 8). For these, Deligne's three conditions hold (for type D, the non-compact places are all D^R or all D^H), H^♯ is defined, and (H,Y) is of abelian type iff H^der is a quotient of H^♯.

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed on the page image and against KPZ26 footnote 8. However the only use in this paper (proof of Lemma 4.6.22, via [20] 2.3.10) is for (G_2,X_2) of abelian type, where H^♯ is defined; so no result of the paper is affected. Changed 'affects' from 'a stated result' to 'nothing'. Independent check: The quotation matches the image of p. 205. KPZ26 p. 80 lists three conditions, the third being that for type D the non-compact real places are all D^R or all D^H. Its footnote 8 says that 4.6.21 wrongly asserts H^♯ to be defined for every classical (H,Y), and that the third condition holds when (H^ad,Y^ad) is of abelian type. The assertion is therefore false as stated: a classical datum of type D with mixed D^R/D^H places has no H^♯. The only use in the paper is the proof of Lemma 4.6.22 (p. 206: 'By [20] 2.3.10, we may choose G so that G^der = ∏ Res_{F_i/Q} G_i'^♯'), and the only occurrences of ♯ are on pp. 205–206. There (G_2,X_2) is of abelian type, so (G_2^ad,X_2^ad) is too, and H^♯ is defined for each factor. No result of the paper depends on the false generality, so the revision of 'affects' to 'nothing' is right.

issues.locator: Prop. 0.1, printed p. 122
issues.printed: The source describes 𝒮_{K°}(G,X) := 𝒮_{K_p°}(G,X)/K^p as finite over 𝒪_E and as an extension of Sh_{K_p°}(G,X)_E.
issues.correction: … is a flat O_E-scheme of finite type extending Sh_{K°}(G,X)_E = Sh_{K_p°}(G,X)_E/K^p.
issues.reason: 'Finite' is false: the generic fibre is a Shimura variety of positive dimension in general. The meaning must be 'of finite type', which holds because the models are normalisations of closures in Siegel moduli spaces and their quotients. The quotient by K^p extends Sh_{K°} = Sh_{K_p°}/K^p, not Sh_{K_p°} itself. The body results (Thm. 4.6.23, Remark 4.6.25(a)) contain neither slip. The same text appears in arXiv v2 (1512.01149).

The same wording is in the arXiv text. KPZ26 does not mention it.

issues.locator: §1.2.14, printed p. 135
issues.printed: The source writes Aut(H)(K̃) = H^ad(K̃) ⋊ Ξ and defines Ξ = Ξ_H using automorphisms of the Dynkin diagram. It identifies this group with those H-automorphisms preserving the selected pinning.
issues.correction: Ξ = Ξ_H is the group of automorphisms of the based root datum of H, identified with the automorphisms of H that respect the chosen pinning.
issues.reason: For reductive H with a nontrivial central torus (e.g. H = G_m, whose Ξ is {±1} while its Dynkin diagram is empty), and for semisimple H not simply connected or adjoint (e.g. triality on D_4 does not preserve the character lattice of SO_8), Ξ is not the group of Dynkin diagram automorphisms. The parenthetical identification with pinning-preserving automorphisms is correct, and it is what the paper uses.

issues.reviewReason: Image of p. 135 confirms the wording. H here is an arbitrary split connected reductive group (§1.1.2, §1.2.12), and Aut(H)(K̃) = H^ad(K̃) ⋊ Aut(based root datum). The automorphism group of the based root datum is not in general the automorphism group of the Dynkin diagram. For a torus, e.g. Res_{K'/K}G_m, the diagram is empty but Ξ = Aut(X^•) ≠ 1. For GL_2, which is relevant to U(2) and GU(1,1), the A_1 diagram has no automorphisms, yet transpose-inverse is outer. For SO_8, triality does not preserve the character lattice. Read literally, every torus would be split. The parenthetical identification with pinning-preserving automorphisms is correct, and it is what the paper uses (§1.2.15 ff.; §2.1.4 sets Ξ_H = Aut(R^+)).

issues.locator: §1.2.22, (1.2.23)–(1.2.24) and the composition following it, printed p. 138
issues.printed: The source composes with the equivariant map B(GL(V)_D, K_1^ur) = B(Res_{K_1^ur/K^ur}(GL(V)_D), K^ur) → B(GL(V), K^ur). It describes this as viewing 𝒪_D-lattices of V as 𝒪-lattices in the K-vector space V by restricting scalars. The resulting toral map ι : B(G,K^ur) → B(GL(V),K^ur) is asserted to respect both G(K^ur) and Gal(K^ur/K) actions.
issues.correction: Replace the field K_1^ur by K_1 ⊗_K K^ur = ∏_τ K_1^ur (τ over the f_1 K-embeddings of K_1 ∩ K^ur into K^ur). Equivalently, work over K̃: V ⊗_K K̃ = ⊕_i V_{λ_i,K̃}. Choose σ_i ∈ Γ with σ_iλ_1 = λ_i and define B(H,K̃) → ∏_i B(GL(V_{λ_i,K̃}),K̃) ⊂ B(GL(V ⊗ K̃),K̃) with i-th component σ_i∘(t + ι_1)∘σ_i^{−1}. This is well defined by the Γ_1-equivariance of Prop. 1.2.21 and is Γ-equivariant. Taking inertia invariants gives B(G,K^ur) → ∏_τ B(GL(V)_D ⊗_{K_1,τ} K_1^ur, K_1^ur) = B(Res_{K_1/K}GL(V)_D, K^ur) → B(GL(V),K^ur), which is G(K^ur)- and Gal(K^ur/K)-equivariant, as used in (1.3.11).
issues.reason: If K_1/K has a nontrivial unramified part (f_1 > 1, possible when k is finite), then Res_{K_1/K}(GL(V)_D) ⊗_K K^ur is a product of f_1 copies of Res_{K_1^ur/K^ur}(GL(V)_D ⊗ K_1^ur), and V ⊗_{K_1} K_1^ur has K^ur-dimension dim_K V / f_1. A single chain of lattices in V ⊗_{K_1} K_1^ur is then not a lattice chain in V ⊗_K K^ur, and the single-factor map is neither G(K^ur)- nor Frobenius-equivariant. Example: G = Res_{K'/K}GL_n with K'/K unramified quadratic and V = K'^n (dim_K V = 2n). Here D = K_1 = K', K_1^ur = K^ur, GL(V)_D ⊗ K^ur = GL_n, and G(K^ur) = GL_n(K^ur)². Case for the defence: for k algebraically closed (K^ur = K), or K_1/K totally ramified, the text is correct as written. The intended construction is standard, the existence of the equivariant ι in (1.2.26) and all later uses (§1.3.1, Prop. 1.3.3, §2.3) stand, and §1.3 itself uses the correct product. The same text is in arXiv v2.

Here K_1^ur = K̃^{I_1} is a field. Let f_1 = [K_1 ∩ K^ur : K]. If f_1 > 1, then K_1 ⊗_K K^ur ≅ ∏_τ K_1^ur (f_1 factors), so Res_{K_1/K}(GL(V)_D)_{K^ur} ≅ ∏_τ Res_{K_1^ur/K^ur}(GL(V)_D ⊗_{K_1,τ} K_1^ur). The text keeps only one factor. Also dim_{K^ur}(V ⊗_{K_1} K_1^ur) = e_1·dim_{K_1}V = dim_K V / f_1 ≠ dim_K V, so lattices in V ⊗_{K_1} K_1^ur are not lattices in V ⊗_K K^ur, and the stated map to B(GL(V),K^ur) does not exist. A single-factor map would also be neither G(K^ur)-equivariant nor Frobenius-equivariant, since Frobenius permutes the τ. This case occurs: k may be finite (§1.1.1), and §2.1.1 onward takes K/Q_p unramified. Example: G = Res_{K'/K}GL_n with K'/K unramified quadratic and V = K'^n. Then ρ is K-irreducible and minuscule, D = K_1 = K', K_1^ur = K^ur and G(K^ur) = GL_n(K^ur)², but the construction gives a map from B(GL_n,K^ur)² that sees only one factor and targets an n-dimensional rather than a 2n-dimensional space. The text is correct when k is algebraically closed or K_1/K is totally ramified. The ι of (1.2.26) does exist via the product construction. §1.3 uses the correct product over the embeddings σ: K_{j1} → K̃ ((1.3.11)–(1.3.12), p. 143), so later results stand. Not in the KPZ26 corrections (§1.3.1, §7.3). Same text in arXiv.

So Prop. 1.3.9 and (1.3.10), as used in the proof of Prop. 1.3.3 (p. 143), are not justified as written when k is finite. The statement is true and routine to repair. Either work at a finite tame Galois level, having first obtained the semilinear action over O^ur (or over the completion of O^ur) and descended along the unramified part; or reduce Prop. 1.3.3 to k algebraically closed by the faithfully flat base change O → Ŏ, since closed immersions descend and parahoric group schemes commute with this base change. Moreover the asserted intermediate H¹(𝒦,G)=1 is false in general: for odd p and split G₂, choose ε∈W(k)^× lifting a nonsquare. The Pfister form ⟨⟨ε,u,p⟩⟩ stays anisotropic over the completion of 𝒦 at (p). Apply Springer’s residue criterion first to p (residue field k((u))) and then to u (residue k); the residual binary form ⟨1,−ε̄⟩ is anisotropic. issues.reviewReason: Images of pp. 147–148 confirm the quotes. Step 3 works with O_ℰ-points of the W-group schemes 𝒢, 𝒢_i, 𝒯° and applies Bruhat–Tits results ([11] 4.4.14, 5.2.4, 5.2.11) to G(ℰ), where ℰ = K_0{{u}} has imperfect residue field k((u)). This follows from [11, (1.7.6)] with k algebraically closed, because both are smooth W-models with the same W-points; for p-torsion-free O_ℰ the dilatation's points are exactly that preimage. (b) 'G(ℰ)^1 coincides with the subgroup generated by all parahoric subgroups of G(ℰ) considered in [11, 5.2.11]' needs the 𝒢_i ⊗_W O_ℰ and 𝒯° ⊗_W O_ℰ to be the Bruhat–Tits parahoric and connected Néron group schemes of G_ℰ, with the alcove of x in B(G,K_0) matching one in B(G,ℰ). This holds because ℰ/K_0 has ramification index 1 and G_{K_0} is quasi-split (k algebraically closed) and split by the totally ramified K_0(p^{1/e}), which stays a degree-e field over ℰ; so the relative root system and the affine root valuations do not change. Both are routine, but the paper does not state them. KPZ26 does not correct this; later purity results ([An22], [PR24], cited by KPZ26) cover the statement independently.

issues.printed: The source calls V'_1 ⊗_{K_1} K̃ an irreducible Weyl module and says the preceding argument and construction of ι establish the result. It describes type (b) as analogous and leaves the easier type (c) to the reader.
issues.correction: Type (a): choose a D-basis (e_k) of V_2 adapted to h_2 (orthogonal, or hyperbolic pairs). Then V = ⊕_k V'_1⊗e_k is a decomposition into irreducibles to use in the §1.2 construction. Choose the translation t_k of the k-th copy so that (ι'_1(x)+t_k)_k is self-dual up to a common shift for Tr_{K_1/K}∘Trd(h_1⊗ᵗh_2): shift copy k by −½·val(h_2(e_k,e_k)), pair the hyperbolic copies by t ↦ −t, and absorb the inverse different of K_1/K in the common shift. Then ι(x) ∈ s(B(GSp(V))) for all x by equivariance. Type (b) is the same with D carrying an involution of the second kind. Type (c): V = V_a ⊕ V_a^∨; take the translation on V_a^∨ opposite to that on V_a, so the two lattice chains are dual.
issues.reason: The lemma is proved only in type (a), and there the last step (matching the Satake factorization, including the U(D\V_2,h_2) factor and the multiplicity m, with the per-summand translations of the construction of ι) is asserted without detail. Types (b) and (c) are left to the reader. Also 'V'_1 ⊗_{K_1} K̃ is an irreducible Weyl module' holds only when D = K_1; for D a quaternion algebra (allowed in type (a)) it is two copies. issues.reviewReason: The claim is real, but it is a false step, not merely an omission, so the kind is error. Quotations checked on printed pp. 158–159. By §1.2.15 (p. 136), V_j⊗Q̃_p ≅ ⊕_i V(λ_{ji})^{⊕m_j}⊗Q̃_p, where m_j is the degree of the centralizer division algebra D_j of ρ_j. The printed V'_j = (V(λ_{j1})⊗Q̃_p)^{I_{j1}} has L_j-dimension dim V(λ_{j1}), and the τ's are in bijection with the I-orbits in the Γ-orbit of λ_{j1}. So dim_L V_L = Σ_j dim_{Q_p}V_j / m_j. Hence 'ρ_L can be identified with G_L → ∏_j∏_τ GL(V'_{j,L}) ⊂ GL(V_L)' and 'y = ι(x) ∈ B(GL(V),Q_p) ⊂ B(GL(V_L),L)' are false as soon as some m_j > 1, because the Res_{D/K_1} step of (1.2.17) has been dropped. The case occurs in practice. Check of the first reading's example: G = D^× (D quaternion division over Q_p) acting on V = D by left multiplication, with ψ(x,y) = Trd(x a ȳ), a pure. Then ψ(gx,gy) = Nrd(g)ψ(x,y), ψ is alternating and perfect, G_{Q̄_p} = GL_2 with V = std^{⊕2}, μ = (1,0) gives ρ∘μ ~ diag(a^{(2)},1^{(2)}), scalars lie in G, and G^der is simply connected. So this is a local Hodge embedding (the Shimura-curve situation at a ramified p) with m = 2, dim V = 4 and dim V_L = 2. The same example shows that the first reading's correction is right: O_D⊗W is an Iwahori order in M_2(W), and the O_D-chain {Π^n O_D} gives two copies of the same edge-midpoint chain of GL_2, shifted by one step relative to each other. So y over L is a sum of translates y'+t_i, not a single copy. Omitting the τ-twist in '∏_τ ρ'_{j,L}' is only notational, since the τ's are declared to index the conjugate weights. Prop. 2.3.7 itself is not in doubt, and the repair is routine. KPZ26 does not mention this.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on printed p. 162. The only route offered is to replace ρ by ρ' and 'assume that the point y is hyperspecial'. Its lattice function jumps at the union of the jumps of the summands, so it is a vertex of B(GL(V')) only if every ι_{V_j}(x) is. Example: the standard representation of GSp_{2g} with x Iwahori. The hyperspecial point [V'_{Z_p}] = ⊕_i[pΛ^i] is a sum of different vertices [Λ^i], not of translates of y. So Prop. 2.3.7 applied to ρ' does not give a map to Gr(V'_{Z_p}), and the needed embedding of the lattice-chain local model into Gr(V'_{Z_p}) is not stated. The closed immersion 𝒢_x ↪ GL(V'_{Z_p}) proved in the paragraph does not by itself give a closed immersion of local models. issues.reviewReason: The quotation checks out on the image of printed p. 172. Independent disproof, using only facts the paper recalls in 3.1.2 (p > 2; V maps Ŵ(R) isomorphically onto I_R; φV = p). Since w_0(E([π])) = E(π) = 0, E([π]) ∈ I_{O_K} = VŴ(O_K), say E([π]) = V(y). Put z = p − V(1) ∈ Ŵ(O_K). Then z ≠ 0 (w_0(z) = p) and φ(z) = p − φV(1) = 0. Hence z·E([π]) = z·V(y) = V(φ(z)·y) = 0. So E([π]) is a zero divisor; in fact z kills all of I_{O_K}. This z has ghost vector (p, 0, 0, …), so it is the first reading's Witt vector. I recomputed its components exactly: valuations 1, 2, 5, 14, 41, 122 (p = 3) and 1, 4, 19, 94 (p = 5). For p = 2 they stay 1, consistent with Ŵ not being V-stable at p = 2, which the paper excludes. The failing step is 'φ(z) = 0 and hence z = 0': φ is not injective on Ŵ(O_K). The damage is local. The claim is used only to get the isomorphism (3.2.10), and that needs φ(E([π])) to be a nonzerodivisor, not E([π]), because the map φ*(F)⊗Ŵ(O_K) → φ*(M_{O_K}) multiplies the φ*(T)-part by φ(E([π])). The paper's own computation proves this: w_n(φ(E([π]))) = w_{n+1}(E([π])) ≠ 0 for all n ≥ 0, and the ghost map into ∏O_K is injective. Also φ(E([π])) = φV(y) = p·y, and y is a unit because w_0(y) = (φE)(π^p)/p ∈ O_K^×. So the image of the T-part is pφ*(T⊗Ŵ(O_K)), as (3.2.10) states, and Lemma 3.2.9 stands. KPZ26 §7.3 does not mention this. arXiv v3 has the same text.

issues.locator: Proposition 3.3.13 and its proof, printed pp. 181–182

issues.correction: Strengthen (2): there is an isomorphism T_p𝒢'^∨ ≅ T_p𝒢^∨ taking s'_{α,ét} to s_{α,ét}. More generally, it suffices that (T_p𝒢'^∨, s'_{α,ét}) satisfies 3.3.3 and 3.3.7. Then Proposition 3.3.8 applies to 𝒢' and yields condition (2) of Proposition 3.2.17 (via D ≅ W⊗T_p𝒢^∨ ≅ W⊗T_p𝒢'^∨ with tensors).
issues.reason: Proposition 3.3.8 is proved for a pair (L, s_{α,ét}) satisfying 3.3.3 and 3.3.7. Its proof goes through Corollary 3.3.6, which needs two facts: that the stabilizer of the étale tensors is 𝒢_x with G tame and E_8-free, so that the image of Γ_K lies in 𝒢°(Z_p) by Proposition 3.3.4 and [38]; and that H^1(D^×,𝒢°) = 1 by Proposition 1.4.3. Hypothesis (2) only says that the s′_{α,ét} match s_{α,0} under p-adic comparison. Nothing says the subgroup they cut out in GL(T_p𝒢′^∨) is smooth, let alone a tame Bruhat–Tits stabilizer, and the proof does not show it. Defence: in the paper's only use (Proposition 4.2.2), the s_{α,ét,x′} come from the Shimura datum, so the Tate module with these tensors is isomorphic to the fixed lattice with the s_α and the extra hypothesis holds. KPZ26 lists Proposition 3.3.13 among the results needing 'very good', but does not mention this point. The same text is in arXiv v3.

Û_x̄ is defined in 4.2.2 as the completion of the non-normal 𝒮^−_K, but 4.2.4 is about the normalization 𝒮_K. The proof of 4.2.7 then uses Û_x̄ with x̄ ∈ 𝒮^−_K(k) as mapping to 𝒮_K (4.2.11, p. 188). I checked the implicit step. 𝒮^− is flat over O_(v) and excellent, so Û_x̄ is reduced and p lies in no minimal prime. The completion of 𝒮_K ⊗ O_{E^ur} at a point over x̄ is the normalization of Û_x̄/𝔭 for a minimal prime 𝔭. Each Û_x̄/𝔭 is a flat complete local domain, so it has an O_K-point, i.e. a point x ∈ Sh_K(K) specializing to x̄. By 4.2.2, Û_x̄/𝔭 ≅ M̂^loc_{G,y}, which is normal: R_G is normal (3.3.12, Theorem 2.1.2). The step is standard (cf. [43]), so this is notation plus an implicit routine step.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on p. 187 (zoomed). In the local construction f : D_x̄ ≅ V^∨_{Z_p} ⊗ W and ℱ is a filtration of D_x̄ (a point of M^loc_G ⊂ GL(D_x̄)/P). So f^{-1}(ℱ) does not type-check, whether read as a preimage under f or as the image under f^{-1}. The intended value is f(ℱ). In the global construction f : V^∨ ≅ 𝒱 and the preimage f^{-1}(ℱ) ⊂ V^∨ ⊗ O_S is correct, so the local f runs the opposite way to the global f. On P_h: the paper names this space GL(V_{Z_p})/P_{h^{-1}} (4.1.5; cf. §2.1 'G/P_{μ^{-1}}'), and P_h occurs only in (4.2.10)–(4.2.11) and the line before them. I checked that f^{-1}(Fil^1 H^1) ⊂ V^∨ is the μ_h^{-1}-filtration of V^∨ under the contragredient action. Its stabilizer in GL(V) is P_{h^{-1}}, the stabilizer of the annihilator V^{0,−1} = y, consistent with 4.1.5. The P_h is only an inconsistent name, not an error: P_h and P_{h^{-1}} both stabilize rank-g summands, so they are GL(V_{Z_p})-conjugate, and GL(V_{Z_p})/P_h and GL(V_{Z_p})/P_{h^{-1}} are canonically the same Grassmannian (points matched by their stabilizers). Not corrected in KPZ26.

issues.locator: Corollary 4.2.12 (second sentence) and Corollary 4.2.13 with its proof, printed p. 188
issues.printed: Corollary 4.2.12 assumes K_p = K_p°, described as parahoric, and asserts a stratification of 𝒮_K(G,X) ⊗_{O_E} k by locally closed strata indexed by the μ-admissible set. Corollary 4.2.13 retains K_p = K_p°. Its proof invokes Lang's lemma for π_{F_q} and the smooth connected 𝒢_{F_q} to obtain z̃ ∈ 𝒮̃(F_q) above z.
issues.correction: In Corollaries 4.2.12 (second sentence) and 4.2.13, replace 'K_p = K_p°, i.e. K_p is parahoric' by '𝒢 = 𝒢°, i.e. the stabilizer group scheme 𝒢_x has connected special fibre'. This is the hypothesis of KPZ26 Thm. 7.1.3(3) and of Remark 4.2.14 b). With it, Lang's lemma applies over every F_q and the Adm(μ)-strata are 𝒢_k-stable. For 4.2.13 alone, it would suffice that H^1(F_q, π_0(𝒢_{F_q})) = 0. Under K_p = K_p° this holds for F_q = F_p but not in general.
issues.reason: 𝒢(Z_p) → 𝒢(F_p) → π_0(𝒢_{F_p})(F_p) is surjective by Hensel and Lang, so K_p = K_p° only says that π_0(𝒢_{F_p}) has no nontrivial F_p-point. That is weaker than 𝒢 = 𝒢°, and over F_q (q = p^r) even π_0(F_q) can be nontrivial. Example: T the norm-one torus of Q_p(p^{1/3})/Q_p with p ≡ 2 mod 3, which is tame. Here π_0(𝒯_{F̄_p}) = X_*(T)_{I,tors} = Z/3 with Frobenius acting by −1, so T(Q_p) = 𝒯°(Z_p) although 𝒯 ≠ 𝒯°. So the proof's 'smooth connected group scheme 𝒢_{F_q}' is not justified by the stated hypothesis, and in 4.2.12 π_0(𝒢_k) may permute the Adm(μ)-strata. In the defence: the introduction (pp. 126–127) says the henselization statement needs 'a torsor under a smooth connected group (using Lang's lemma)', so the intended hypothesis is plainly 𝒢 = 𝒢°. Where the corollaries are applied later (Remark 4.2.14 b), Theorem 4.6.23(5)) the group is chosen connected. I have not found a counterexample to the conclusions themselves: in the torus example they hold trivially.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on p. 188 and pp. 126–127; K_p = 𝒢(Z_p) (4.1.6) and K_p° = 𝒢°(Z_p) (4.3.1). Hensel for smooth 𝒢, openness of 𝒢°, and Lang for 𝒢°_{F_p} give 𝒢(Z_p)/𝒢°(Z_p) ≅ π_0(𝒢_{F_p})(F_p). So K_p = K_p° only says π_0(𝒢_{F_p}) has no nontrivial F_p-point. I re-derived the counterexample. Let T = R^1_{L/Q_p}G_m with L = Q_p(p^{1/3}) and p ≡ 2 mod 3, p ≠ 2. T is tame and anisotropic. The Galois closure has group S_3, with inertia A_3 and Frobenius a transposition, and X_*(T) is the augmentation lattice ≅ Z[ζ_3]. Then X_*(T)_I = Z/3 and the transposition acts on it by −1. So π_0(𝒯_{F̄_p}) = Z/3 but its F_p-points are trivial: T(Q_p) = 𝒯°(Z_p) although 𝒯 ≠ 𝒯°. Over F_{p^2}, π_0 and H^1(F_{p^2}, π_0) = Z/3 are nontrivial. So in 4.2.13 (arbitrary F_q ⊃ k_E), 'the smooth connected group scheme 𝒢_{F_q}' does not follow from the hypothesis, and the fibre π^{-1}(z) may be a nontrivial torsor. The geometric strata of 4.2.12 are L^+𝒢°-orbits. Elements of 𝒢(Z̆_p) ∖ 𝒢°(Z̆_p) act on them through conjugation by Ω-elements, which can permute Adm(μ)^K, so descent along π needs 𝒢_k-stable strata. Points in the paper's favour. (a) For q = p the proof does work: π_0 embeds in π_1(G)_I, so it is abelian, |A^σ| = |A_σ|, and H^1(F_p, 𝒢_{F_p}) = H^1(F_p, π_0) = A_σ = 0. (b) The introduction (p. 127) and the later uses (Remark 4.2.14 b), Theorem 4.6.23(5)) show that 𝒢 = 𝒢° is intended. (c) KPZ26 Thm. 7.1.3(3) states the result under 'G = G°'. I also found no counterexample to the conclusions themselves. The statements are unproven as stated, not shown false, and KPZ26 does not list this among its corrections.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 4.3.2, printed p. 189
issues.printed: The source sets Γ_{E_0} = Gal(Q̄_p/E_0) and says π_1(R_{E/E_0}G_m)_{Γ_{E_0}} = Z has no torsion. It concludes that O_E^× has trivial image there and in π_1(T)_{Γ_{E_0}}, so the preceding map takes O_E^× into 𝒯°(O_{E_0}).
issues.correction: Replace Γ_{E_0} by the inertia group I_{E_0} = Gal(Q̄_p/E_0^ur): 'π_1(R_{E/E_0}G_m)_{I} = Z, so κ(O_E^×) = 0, and by functoriality of the Kottwitz map the image of O_E^× lies in ker(T(E_0) → (π_1(T)_I)^σ) = 𝒯°(O_{E_0}).' Alternatively, first enlarge E_0' so that Frobenius acts trivially on π_1(T)_I.
issues.reason: 𝒯°(O_{E_0}) is the kernel of κ_T: T(E_0) → (π_1(T)_I)^σ. Vanishing in the coarser quotient π_1(T)_Γ = (π_1(T)_I)_σ does not in general place an element in 𝒯°(O_{E_0}), since (π_1(T)_I)^σ → (π_1(T)_I)_σ need not be injective. With I in place of Γ_{E_0}, the argument is complete. If Γ_{E_0} is really meant, this is a gap with the same repair.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on p. 189. The claim is real. 𝒯°(O_{E_0}) is the kernel of the Kottwitz map T(E_0) → (π_1(T)_I)^σ. The paper uses the coarser map to π_1(T)_{Γ_{E_0}} = (π_1(T)_I)_σ. The map (π_1(T)_I)^σ → (π_1(T)_I)_σ is injective when π_1(T)_I is torsion-free (the norm argument), but not in general: e.g. A = (Z/2)^2 with σ the swap. So 'image in π_1(T)_{Γ_{E_0}} trivial, hence in 𝒯°(O_{E_0})' does not follow as written. It is not a mere misprint: Γ_{E_0} = Gal(Q̄_p/E_0) is defined explicitly and used twice. The conclusion is true and the repair takes one line. Since E/E_0 is totally ramified, π_1(R_{E/E_0}G_m)_I = Z and κ(O_E^×) = 0, so by functoriality of the Kottwitz map the image lies in ker κ_T = 𝒯°(O_{E_0}). Alternatively, enlarge E_0' further, as the proof permits, so that Frobenius acts trivially on π_1(T)_I; then the printed Γ-argument is valid. Hence the reach is 'gap, the proof' rather than 'misprint'. Not corrected in KPZ26.

issues.reason: Over a base with fibres of characteristic p, and A = Z_(p) with p | |Gal(Fr A′/Q)| when A′ is wildly ramified at p, the identity component of the kernel of a homomorphism of abelian schemes need not be flat. Its special fibre can acquire infinitesimal components such as E[p]°, as for the fixed points of a cyclic permutation on the sum-zero part of E^p. So 'view B as an abelian scheme' is asserted without proof. In the defence: the lemma is applied (4.5.2–4.5.9) to the universal object over the normal, flat scheme 𝒮_K(G,X), where a correct B exists, and the conclusion of the lemma is not in doubt there.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on pp. 192–193. For A = Z_(p) and a base with fibres of characteristic p, the identity component of the kernel of a homomorphism of abelian schemes need not be flat or an abelian scheme. the first reading's example is right: on the sum-zero part K ≅ E^{p−1} of E^p, the fixed points of the cyclic permutation are the diagonal E[p], whose identity component is trivial in characteristic 0 and infinitesimal (E[p]°) in characteristic p. This is exactly what happens when the Galois module A' ⊗ Z_(p) contains the augmentation lattice, as for a wildly ramified cyclic A' (Noether), and then ker(f)° ⊇ 𝒜[p]°-type pieces. A second loose step has the same cause: 'the cokernel of B ⊂ 𝒜^𝒫 is a torsion sheaf, so B ⊗_A A' → 𝒜 ⊗_A A' is an isomorphism' needs that torsion to be killed by an integer invertible in A. Both steps are fine when |Gal(Fr A'/Q)| ∈ A^×, or when A' ⊗ Z_(p) is étale over Z_(p), since then A' is locally free over A[Gal] (normal basis) and taking invariants is exact. In the paper's favour: in 4.5 the lemma is applied to the universal object over the normal flat 𝒮_K(G,X). There B can be taken as the closure of the abelian subvariety of the generic fibre, which extends over a normal base, and nothing suggests the lemma's conclusion fails. Not corrected in KPZ26.

Example: F a non-Galois totally real cubic field, p = 𝔭_1𝔭_2 with f(𝔭_2) = 2, G' of type C compact exactly at σ_1, σ_2 (so E^ad = σ_3(F)), and the isomorphism chosen so that σ_1, σ_2 induce 𝔭_2 and σ_3 induces 𝔭_1. Then T = {σ̃_1, σ̃_2} with both lifts over the same prime 𝔓_2 of K. The Frobenius τ at 𝔭_2 lies in the decomposition group of the degree-one prime v_0 of E^ad and maps σ̃_1 ↔ σ̃_2. For K = F(√a) with the square roots of the conjugates of a independent over the Galois closure F̃, some h ∈ Gal(Q̄/F̃) changes only the lift of σ_2, and then τ(hT) = {σ̃_2, σ̃_1c} ≠ hT = {σ̃_1, σ̃_2c}. So v_0 has a prime of degree 2 in L. For (G_2,X_2) = (G^ad,X^ad) one has E' = E = L, so (3) fails for this choice of K and T. In the paper's defence, the proof of Theorem 4.6.23 uses (3) only to find a place v' with E'_{v'} = E_{2,v_2}, and the argument gives that for the prime induced by the (freely choosable) isomorphism.
