The quotation matches the image of p. 206, and the first sentence of Theorem 4.6.23 is confirmed on p. 208. The same text is in arXiv v2. The gap is real. Fixing C ≅ Q̄_p fixes one decomposition group D_p ⊂ Gal(Q̄/Q), and the argument proves only D_p ∩ Gal(Q̄/E^ad) ⊂ Gal(Q̄/L), with L = E^ad·E(K^×,h_T). That gives one place of L of local degree 1 above the place v_0 of E^ad induced by the embedding. The other places of L above v_0 correspond to h ∈ Gal(Q̄/E^ad); for such a place to have degree 1 one needs D_p ∩ Gal(Q̄/E^ad) to stabilize hT. The condition imposed on T says nothing about hT.

I re-checked the first reading's example:
- F is a non-Galois totally real cubic field (Galois closure F̃ with group S_3), and p = 𝔭_1𝔭_2 with f(𝔭_2) = 2.
- G' is of type C, compact exactly at σ_1 and σ_2, so E^ad = σ_3(F).
- The isomorphism is chosen so that σ_3 induces 𝔭_1 and σ_1, σ_2 induce 𝔭_2. Then D_p fixes E^ad and preserves I_c.
- T must therefore be a whole D_p-orbit of lifts, i.e. {σ̃_1, σ̃_2} over one prime 𝔓_2 of K. A Frobenius τ ∈ D_p swaps σ̃_1 and σ̃_2.
- Take K = F(√a) with √σ_i(a) independent over F̃, and h ∈ Gal(Q̄/F̃) negating only √σ_2(a). Then hT = {σ̃_1, σ̃_2c} and τ(hT) = {σ̃_2, σ̃_1c} ≠ hT.
- So the place of L given by h|_L has degree ≥ 2 over v_0.
For (G_2,X_2) = (G^ad,X^ad) we have E_2 = E^ad and E' = E = L. The later modifications keep the reflex field: G^ab ↪ G'^ab is an injection of Q-tori and G'^ad = G^ad, so E(G',X') = E(G,X). Hence the lemma's output fails (3) for this admissible choice of K and T.

The stated results are nonetheless true, so I reclassify 'affects' from 'a stated result' to 'the proof'. the first reading's repair works: take K = F·K_0 with K_0 imaginary quadratic and p split in K_0, and T = {σ⊗ι_0 : σ ∈ I_c}. Then ι_0(K_0) ⊂ Q_p, so every τ ∈ D_p preserving I_c preserves T, and Gal(Q̄/E^ad K_0) stabilizes T. Hence E(K^×,h_T) ⊂ E^ad·K_0 and E' ⊂ E_2·K_0 (using E^ad ⊂ E_2), in which every prime of E_2 above p splits completely. So Lemma 4.6.22(3) and Theorem 4.6.23 hold with that choice. Moreover, Theorem 4.6.23 only uses one place v' with E'_{v'} = E_{2,v_2}, which the printed argument does give once the isomorphism C ≅ Q̄_p is chosen to induce v_2. KPZ26 Prop. 7.2.10(2) states only 'splits in E'' and fixes v' in §7.1.12; it does not flag this as a correction.

issues.locator: Kisin–Pappas, Integral models of Shimura varieties with parahoric level structure, Publ. Math. IHÉS 128 (2018) ([KP18]), 4.6.21, printed p. 205
issues.printed: The source takes a Shimura datum (H,Y) with classical H^ad and asserts a central isogeny H̃ → H^♯, depending also on Y when H has a type D factor. It characterizes abelian type for (H,Y) by H^der being a quotient of H^♯.
issues.correction: Restrict 4.6.21 (KP18 p. 205) to Shimura data (H,Y) with (H^ad,Y^ad) of abelian type. H^♯ (KPZ26 §7.2.1, pp. 76–77) is defined only when every simple factor of H^ad satisfies Deligne's third condition: for type D, the noncompact real places are all D^R or all D^H. This can fail when H^ad is merely classical (such data are not of abelian type). It holds when (H^ad,Y^ad) is of abelian type [De79, 1.3.10, 2.3.10], and then (H,Y) is of abelian type iff H^der is a quotient of H^♯. KP18 uses H^♯ only in the proof of Lemma 4.6.22, where (G_2,X_2) is of abelian type.
issues.reason: Footnote 8 (p.77) says 'H may not satisfy the third condition above'. It is H (the adjoint factors), not H^♯, that may fail the condition, so the existing correction ('H^♯ need not satisfy the third defining condition') names the wrong object. The existing 'affects: a stated result' overstates the damage: no KP18 result is applied outside the abelian-type case, where the condition holds.

issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: The revision is right and should replace the ledger text. (1) Quotation: the sentence is KP18's published text (Publ. Math. IHÉS 128, printed p. 205, 4.6.21), checked on the image. It is word for word the arXiv wording the first reading quotes, so 'printed' should cite p. 205 rather than 'arXiv version'. (2) Object: KPZ26 §7.2.1 (p. 76) defines H^♯ only for groups H satisfying three conditions. The third says that for type D the noncompact real places are all of type D^R or all of type D^H. Footnote 8 (p. 77) says 'H may not satisfy the third condition above'. So it is H (its adjoint simple factors) that may fail the condition, and then H^♯ is undefined. The ledger's 'H^♯ need not satisfy the third defining condition' names the wrong object. (3) Falsity: a type-D datum whose noncompact places mix D^R and D^H is not of abelian type, and the recalled construction gives it no H^♯. So 'there is a central isogeny H̃ → H^♯ such that (H,Y) is of abelian type iff H^der is a quotient of H^♯' is false as stated for general (H,Y) with H^ad classical. (4) Reach: the only occurrences of ♯ in KP18 are 4.6.21 and the proof of Lemma 4.6.22 (p. 206: 'By [20] 2.3.10, we may choose G so that G^der = ∏ Res_{F_i/Q} G′_i^♯'). There (G_2,X_2) is of abelian type, so the conditions hold ([De79, 1.3.10, 2.3.10], as KPZ26 p. 77 recalls). No KP18 proof or result uses the false generality, so 'affects: nothing' is right and the ledger's 'a stated result' overstates the damage. 'error' is the right kind: the paper states something false, and KPZ26 itself calls it 'incorrectly asserted'.

issues.printed: The source introduces X = Spec k[x, y, x]/(x² + xyz) and calls it a normal surface.
issues.correction: X = Spec k[x, y, z]/(x² + xyz), which is not normal: x² + xyz = x(x + yz), so X is the union of two smooth surfaces meeting along x = yz = 0, and its local ring at the origin is not a domain.
issues.reason: Normality is never used. The rest of the remark holds for this X: T_0X is 3-dimensional, a formal curve (f, g, h) with f(f + gh) = 0 has f = 0 or f = −gh, so f has no t-term, and the tangent cone is Spec k[x, y, z]/(x²). This matches the checkpoint's reading of [P95, Ex. 4.5], a special fibre with two smooth components meeting non-transversally.

issues.citation: Kisin–Pappas–Zhou, "Integral models of Shimura varieties with parahoric level structure, II", Forum of Mathematics, Pi (2026)
issues.reviewReason: Checked on the page image. x² + xyz = x(x + yz), so X is the union of the smooth surfaces {x = 0} and {x = −yz}. They meet along the lines x = y = 0 and x = z = 0 and are tangent at 0, so the local ring at 0 is not a domain. The rest of the remark is right for this X. dim T_0X = 3. If f(f + gh) = 0 in k[[t]], then f = 0 or f = −gh ∈ t²k[[t]]. The lowest-degree form is x², so TC_0X = Spec k[x,y,z]/(x²), whose reduction k[y,z] spans only the plane x = 0. Normality is never used. Independent check: Checked on the p. 31 image: 'Consider the normal surface X = Spec k[x, y, x]/(x² + xyz).' The repeated x is a slip for z. The adjective 'normal' is false: x² + xyz = x(x + yz), so X is the union of the smooth surfaces {x = 0} and {x = −yz}. They meet along {x = 0, yz = 0} (the lines x = y = 0 and x = z = 0) and have the same tangent plane x = 0 at the origin. The local ring at 0 has two minimal primes, so it is not a domain and X is not normal (it is reduced). The rest of the remark is correct for this X. There is no linear term, so dim T_0X = 3. In the domain k[[t]], f(f + gh) = 0 forces f = 0 or f = −gh ∈ t²k[[t]], so every formal curve has tangent in x = 0. The initial form is x², so TC_0X = Spec k[x,y,z]/(x²), and its reduction spans only the plane x = 0. Normality is never used, so the reach is 'nothing'. It is a false assertion, not a typographical slip, so 'error' is the right kind. The first reading's re-check agrees with the ledger text and only makes the intersection locus more explicit. Both are right.

issues.locator: §4.2.9 and proof of Proposition 4.2.10, p.35 (also the 'In particular' sentence of §4.2.9 and Proposition 4.2.10(1))
issues.printed: The source defines membership (ϖ, ϖ′) ∈ W(α) by existence of a weight vector v_ϖ′ with X_α v_ϖ′ ≠ 0. It claims equivalence with ϖ′ and ϖ′ + α both being weights of V(ϖ), and asserts symmetry between (ϖ, ϖ′) ∈ W(α) and (ϖ, ϖ′ + α) ∈ W(−α). As ν and v ∈ V(ν) vary subject to X_α v ≠ 0, it says (ϖ, ϖ′ − α) exhaust W(α).
issues.correction: §4.2.9: the two descriptions of 𝒲(α) differ in characteristic p. Use the weight description (ϖ′ and ϖ′+α are weights of V(ϖ)). Then the 'In particular' symmetry and Proposition 4.2.10(1) hold as printed. Proof of 4.2.10(2): the last sentence is false in characteristic p, since the left inclusion only reaches pairs realised by a nonzero X_α in V(ν)^* = H^0(−w_0ν). Repair it with both inclusions of (4.2.7). The right inclusion gives l ≤ ⟨μ,ϖ⟩ − ⟨λ,ϖ′⟩ for every pair realised by a nonzero X_α in the Weyl module V(ϖ). The left inclusion gives the same bound for pairs realised in H^0(ϖ). On each α-string the minimum is attained at the bottom pair (⟨λ,α⟩ ≤ 0, realised in V(ϖ)) or at the top pair (⟨λ,α⟩ ≥ 0, realised in H^0(ϖ)). Hence 1 ≤ l ≤ l_α in every characteristic. The minuscule pairs alone already give Φ^cur = Φ^tan = Φ^FM, and the characteristic-free equalities k_α = j_α = l_α (Proposition 4.2.13, Remark 4.2.16, Corollary 4.2.19) are unaffected. (The repaired proof uses the right inclusion, contrary to the plan announced in Remark 4.2.8(3).)
issues.reason: I re-derived the E9 counterexample from the page. For GL_2 and V((p,0)) with divided-power basis v_i = F^{(i)}v_0, E v_i = (p−i+1)v_{i−1}, so E v_1 = 0. The weight spaces are one-dimensional, so no vector of weight (p−1,1) has X_αv ≠ 0. F v_i = (i+1)v_{i+1} gives the failure of the symmetry. The repair steps check out: for minuscule ν, V(ν)^* = V(−w_0ν), and X_α is nonzero on the standard SL_2-module.

issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: Checked on the p. 35 image; the quotation is exact. (1) The 'Equivalently' is false in characteristic p. In the GL_2 Weyl module V((p,0)), take v_i = F^{(i)}v_0. Then E v_i = (p−i+1)v_{i−1}, so E v_1 = p·v_0 = 0, although (p−1,1) and (p,0) are weights and the weight spaces are lines. (2) the first reading's addition (i) is right. With the literal definition the 'In particular' symmetry fails too: E v_p = v_{p−1} ≠ 0 but F v_{p−1} = p·v_p = 0. So the proof of 4.2.10(1) needs the weight reading, and with that reading (1) is fine. (3) The last sentence of the proof of 4.2.10(2) is false under either reading. The left inclusion for V(ν), v ∈ V(ν)_{ν'} with X_αv ≠ 0, gives the bound only for the pair (ϖ, −ν'−α), with ϖ = −w_0ν. Transposing, that pair is one where X_α: H^0(ϖ)_{ϖ''} → H^0(ϖ)_{ϖ''+α} is nonzero, because V(ν)^* = H^0(ϖ), not V(ϖ). In H^0(p) = Sym^p, for example, E·y^p = p·xy^{p−1} = 0. (4) the first reading's addition (ii) is right. k_α, j_α and the weight-reading l_α do not depend on the characteristic. The printed proof is valid in characteristic 0, where V(ν)^* = V(−w_0ν) and, by sl_2-theory, X_α is nonzero between adjacent weights of an irreducible module. So k_α ≤ l_α, and k_α = j_α = l_α under the hypothesis of 4.2.13. Minuscule pairs are realised in every characteristic, so Theorem 4.2.3 stands. (5) Against the revision's last sentence, Proposition 4.2.10(2) itself also holds in characteristic p; only its proof needs repair. Let g = (1+εt^{⟨λ,α⟩−l}X_α)t^λ. For v ∈ V(ν)_{ν'}, g^{−1}v = t^{−⟨λ,ν'⟩}v − εt^{−l−⟨λ,ν'⟩}X_αv. The right inclusion of (4.2.7) is part of the definition of S^FM, and it gives l ≤ ⟨μ,ν⟩ − ⟨λ,ν'⟩ whenever X_α: V(ν)_{ν'} → V(ν)_{ν'+α} is nonzero. On an α-string of weights of V(ϖ), ⟨μ,ϖ⟩ − ⟨λ,ϖ'⟩ is affine in the position. So its minimum over the string is at the bottom pair if ⟨λ,α⟩ ≤ 0 and at the top pair if ⟨λ,α⟩ ≥ 0. Bottom pairs are realised in the Weyl module V(ϖ) (right inclusion), and top pairs in H^0(ϖ) (left inclusion). If p does not divide the string length s, this holds in any module: X_{−α}X_αv = s·v for a bottom vector v, and X_αX_{−α}w = s·w for a top vector w. In general it follows from the Weyl (resp. good) filtration of the restriction to the Levi subgroup of α (Donkin, Mathieu). An SL_2 Weyl module has E v_n = v_{n−1} at the bottom, and H^0(n) has E(x^{n−1}y) = x^n at the top. Checks: Γ^p(k^3) = V(pϖ_1) has E_{12}y^{(p)} = x y^{(p−1)} ≠ 0, while Sym^p has E_{12}y^p = 0. Hence l ≤ l_α in characteristic p. So the error breaks the proof of Proposition 4.2.10(2) and the unnumbered 'Equivalently' sentence. Every numbered statement stands, so the reach is 'the proof', not 'a stated result'. Reviewer's decision: the reach stays 'a stated result'. As printed, Proposition 4.2.10(2) is unproved in characteristic p; the repair the independent check proposes (both inclusions of (4.2.7), with the minimum on each α-string at its bottom or top pair) relies, when p divides the string length, on the Donkin–Mathieu theorem on good filtrations restricted to Levi subgroups, whose exact form was not checked here. If that repair holds, the reach drops to 'the proof'. Theorem 4.2.3 and the equalities k_α = j_α = l_α stand in every characteristic.

Here G(K̆)_x = G(K̆)_{x'} (the Iwahori) for every x' on the edge, so x is generic, and x̄ is generic for G^der = SL_2 (stabilizers are Iwahori all along the edge). But G(K̆)_x̄ contains Π = (0 1; π 0), which swaps the vertices, while G(K̆)_x̄' does not for nearby x̄' ≠ x̄. So if 'generic' means generic for G^der, the claimed equality G(K̆)_x̄ = G(K̆)_x̄' is false. If it means generic for the G(K̆)-action on B̄, then 'x̄ also generic' is false. issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 29 image. §3.4.5 lists these hypotheses: G ≅ Res_{K/F}H with H tame, p ∤ |π₁(G^der)|, 𝒢 = 𝒢_x with x generic, and no division-algebra factors of index divisible by p. The last is copied from Prop. 2.2.2. The list omits the blanket hypothesis of §2.2.1 that H is classical. Prop. 2.2.2 needs it, and Prop. 2.2.2 is what supplies the tame K̃ over which x becomes hyperspecial and the Γ-equivariant model used in Prop. 2.4.2. Theorem 3.3.25 and the standard assumptions 3.1.5 both include it. By Remark 3.1.6, a Hodge embedding forces classical type only on factors where μ is nontrivial. So exceptional factors with trivial μ satisfy every listed hypothesis. The omission matters for the construction itself, not only for the proof. Take p = 3, H = (GL_2 × E_6^sc)/μ_3 and ρ_1 = std ⊠ 27. This representation is faithful and minuscule and contains the scalars. With μ = (diag(a,1), 1), ρ_1∘μ = μ_27. H^der = SL_2 × E_6^sc is simply connected, H is split and there are no division algebras. Let the E_6-component of x be the vertex of label 3, x = ω_4^∨/3. Its parahoric fixes only x. Over a tame K̃ with ramification e (3 ∤ e), α_4(x) = 1/3 ∉ (1/e)ℤ, so x never becomes hyperspecial. Hence the K̃, Λ̃ and ρ_Λ̃ of §3.4.5 and Proposition 3.4.6 do not exist. For p ≥ 7 the construction probably works, but the paper proves Prop. 2.2.2 only for classical groups. The first reading's example (μ central on G_m·E_6) satisfies the hypotheses too, but it breaks the construction only with such a choice of x. Defence: 'The proof of Theorem 3.2.15 shows' implicitly brings in the standard assumptions, and the application in §6.1 is classical. So the downstream results are unaffected. Still, Proposition 3.4.6 is not established under its stated hypotheses. 'Gap' is apt: a hypothesis is missing, and the proposition is ill-posed rather than false.

issues.reviewReason: The quotations are on pp. 31, 37 and 38. Read literally, with the W-invariant notion of 'minuscule' that the paper itself uses for weights on p. 36, the condition is vacuous in types B and C. In B_n, P^∨ = ℤ^n is spanned by the minuscule coweights ±e_i, so (2,1,1) = 2e_1 + e_2 + e_3 qualifies, although Remark 4.2.14(2) says no S exists for it. In C_3, (1,1,0) = (½,½,½) + (½,½,−½). But the paper's own usage fixes the meaning. 'The only minuscule coweight is ϖ_1^∨' (p. 37) and '… is ϖ_n^∨' (p. 38) only make sense for dominant coweights. The proof of Theorem 4.2.3 treats exactly μ = rϖ_1^∨ and (r/2,…,r/2). Lemma 4.4.2 produces sums of dominant minuscule μ_θ. So 'dominant' has been dropped, the intended class is clear, and Theorems 4.1.6, 4.2.3, 4.3.2 and 4.4.3 are proved for it. As for E13 and E20, a slip whose intended reading is clear is recorded as misprint / nothing, not as reaching a stated result.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on p. 34. Dualising the right inclusion ℰ^0(ν) ⊂ t^{−⟨μ,ν⟩}φ(ℰ(ν)) gives t^{⟨μ,ν⟩}φ(ℰ(V(ν)^*)) ⊂ ℰ^0(V(ν)^*). For SL_2 and ν = p, V(p) has socle L(p−2), while H^0(p) has socle L(p). (4.2.7) is imposed only on Weyl modules, so the deduction is not justified. On k[ε]-points the two inclusions bound l over different sets of pairs: those realised by a nonzero X_α in H^0(ϖ) for the left inclusion, and in V(ϖ) for the right one (see C-E9). So it is not clear that one implies the other. The remark is harmless: S^FM is defined with both inclusions, the printed proofs use only the left one, and S^FM appears nowhere outside §4 (apart from the introduction).

issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 43 image. The three sums print ⟨α_i^∨, ϖ_{α_i}⟩ with the index of the weight varying, and D^ℝ_n prints 'ϖ_{n−1} for j = 1,…,n; ϖ_n for j = n'. I recomputed the tables. For B_n, ϖ_{n,α_i} = ϖ_n − e_{i+1}, giving δ + λ_{i+1} and δ. For C_n, ϖ_{1,α_i} = e_i, giving r/2 − λ_i. For D^ℝ_n with λ_n ≥ 0, (ϖ_{n−1})_{α_i} = ϖ_{n−1} − e_{i+1} + e_n (i ≤ n−2) gives δ + λ_{i+1}, and the competitor through ϖ_n is larger by λ_n. The vanishing ⟨α_i^∨,ϖ_{α_j}⟩ = 0 holds for i < j (B, D^ℝ) or i > j (C), with ⟨α_j^∨,ϖ_{α_j}⟩ = 1. So (c) holds with the weight fixed at ϖ_{α_j}.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 4.3.10, pp.43–45
issues.printed: The source computes that ⟨β^∨, ϖ_α⟩ ≠ 0 with β ∈ Δ requires β = γ_0, γ_1, γ_m or γ′_0. Here γ′_0 neighbors γ_1, differs from γ_0 and γ_2, and occurs only when γ_1 = α_{n−2}. Minimality gives m_{−γ_1} = 0. Under m_{γ′_0} = 0 it asserts Σ_{β∈Δ}⟨β^∨, ϖ_α⟩ = m_α⟨α^∨, ϖ_α⟩ ≠ 0. Case (2) considers m_{−α_{n−1}} ≠ −m_{−α_n}.
issues.correction: Add the missing case. If ϖ = ϖ_{n−1} (resp. ϖ_n) and α = α_j with j ≤ n−4, then β = α_n (resp. α_{n−1}) also has ⟨β^∨,ϖ_α⟩ = 1. Minimality forces m_β = 0, because (ϖ_{n−1})_{α_n} − (ϖ_{n−1})_{α_j} = e_{j+1} − e_{n−2} ≥ 0 gives k_{−α_n} ≤ k_{−α_j}, and then (α_n, ϖ_{n−1}) would satisfy (a) and (b) with a shorter geodesic. Also: ⟨γ_m^∨,ϖ_α⟩ = 0 for m ≥ 2; read m_{γ_1} for m_{−γ_1}; read Σ_β m_β⟨β^∨,ϖ_α⟩; and in Case (2) read m_{α_{n−1}} ≠ −m_{α_n}.
issues.reason: For a minuscule ϖ, ⟨β^∨, ϖ − Σ_{i≥1}γ_i⟩ is nonzero exactly for γ_0 (+1), γ_1 (−1), and any off-path neighbour of some γ_i with i ≥ 1 (+1). In D_n, α_n is such a neighbour of γ_{m−1} = α_{n−2} on the path α_j → α_{n−1}. Without m_β = 0 for this β, (c) could fail when m_{α_n} = −m_{α_j}. The repair uses only the minimality already in the proof, so the proposition stands.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on pp. 44–45 and by brute force over D_n for n = 4,…,7 (all α ∈ Δ, ϖ ∈ S). For minuscule ϖ, ⟨β^∨, ϖ − Σ_{i≥1}γ_i⟩ is +1 at γ_0, −1 at γ_1, +1 at every off-path neighbour of some γ_i with i ≥ 1, and 0 elsewhere. In particular it is 0 at γ_m when m ≥ 2. The printed list only allows off-path neighbours of γ_1. The computation finds exactly the missed configurations the first reading describes: ϖ ∈ {ϖ_{n−1},ϖ_n} and α = α_j with j ≤ n−4, where β = α_n (resp. α_{n−1}) is an off-path neighbour of γ_{m−1} = α_{n−2}. For n = 5, α = α_1, ϖ = ϖ_4 this gives ϖ_α = (½,−½,½,½,½) and ⟨α_5^∨,ϖ_α⟩ = 1. In that configuration the sum is m_{α_j} + m_{α_n}, so the printed step 'if m_{γ′_0} = 0 then Σ = m_α⟨α^∨,ϖ_α⟩ ≠ 0' is unjustified. The first reading's repair is correct. (ϖ_{n−1})_{α_n} − (ϖ_{n−1})_{α_j} = e_{j+1} − e_{n−2} is a positive root, so k_{−α_n} ≤ ⟨μ,ϖ_{n−1}⟩ − ⟨λ,(ϖ_{n−1})_{α_n}⟩ ≤ k_{−α_j} = min. If m_{α_n} ≠ 0, then (α_n,ϖ_{n−1}) satisfies (a) and (b) with geodesic length 2 < n−1−j, which contradicts minimality. So the proposition stands. As printed, however, the proof omits a case that needs this extra argument. Following the ledger's usage (E22), a missing case in the proof of a result that survives reaches 'the proof', not 'nothing'. The first reading's list of index slips (m_{−γ_1}, the missing m_β, m_{−α_{n−1}} ≠ −m_{−α_n}) is also right.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 53 image. (3.1.10) (p. 17) only shows that the W(k)-lattice attached to x under Gr(d,Λ)(k) → Gr^W_{GL(Λ)}(k) lies in the G(W(k)[1/p])-orbit of Λ_{W(k)}. The paper never writes the bottom map down. On p. 58 it is used untwisted: the attached lattice is M_{W(𝒦),1}, the preimage of the filtration. On p. 53 the paper instead concludes directly that M̃_{0,1} = g·Λ_{W(k)}. But M̃_{0,1} = Im(φ*M_{0,1} → φ*M_0) = φ*(M_{0,1}), as the paper notes further down the same page. With the untwisted reading one gets M_{0,1} = g'·Λ_{W(k)}, and then M̃_{0,1} = σ(g')·Λ_{W(k)}. Since G is defined over Z_p, σ(g') ∈ G(W(k)[1/p]). This one-line Frobenius-twist step is left out. The conclusion s̃_{a,0} ∈ M̃_{0,1}^⊗ is correct, and nothing downstream is affected.

For an O_K-point the filtration lives over O_K, and the natural ideal over 𝔖 is E(x)𝔖. That is not a frame in the paper's sense, since φ(E) ∉ p𝔖, and λ̄ is then only a u-frame morphism in Lau's sense. issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 63 image. Proposition 2.1.5(3) (p. 10) takes G → G' over a base field K, a point x ∈ B(G,K) and an extension K̃. It assumes G is R-smooth over K and concludes 𝒢_x ↪ Res_{Õ/O}𝒢̃'_{x'}. With K = Q_p and K̃ = Q_p it gives 𝒢 → 𝒢'. For 𝒢̃ → 𝒢̃' over Z̃_p it has to be applied with K = Q̃_p, which requires G_{Q̃_p} to be R-smooth. Theorem 6.1.1 assumes R-smoothness over Q_p only. Neither this paper nor KZ25 §2.4 proves that R-smoothness survives a ramified tame base change: KZ25 §2.4.2 records only invariance under F → F̆. Tame descent of Néron models gives only the converse, that T_{Q̃_p} R-smooth implies T R-smooth. The missing input is essential. G^der = G'^der and T'_{Q̃_p} = ∏ Res_{F̃_i/Q̃_p}(split) is R-smooth. So 𝒯̃ → 𝒯̃' is a closed immersion exactly when T_{Q̃_p} is R-smooth, where T_{Q̃_p} is still the centralizer of a maximal Q̆̃_p-split torus. The step cannot be bypassed either. 𝒢 ↪ Res𝒢̃' does follow from 2.1.5(3) with K̃ = Q̃_p. But the proof applies Proposition 5.3.11 to 𝒥 = Res𝒢̃ ↪ GL(Λ̃) of (6.1.6), and then Corollary 5.3.4 via '𝒢 cut out in 𝒥 by endomorphisms'. Both need Res𝒢̃ → Res𝒢̃' to be a closed immersion. Case for the defence: tori built from quasi-tame tori by extensions (Proposition 2.1.5(1),(2)) stay in that class after tame base change. In §7.2, R-smoothness of G comes from that class: Z^c_G is quasi-tame (condition (4)), Lemma 7.2.5 and Lemma 7.2.11. The other uses of Theorem 6.1.1 are to GSp. So the applications I checked are covered, but the theorem as stated (general R-smoothness) is not proved. Gap, not error: I could not construct an R-smooth T with T_{Q̃_p} not R-smooth.

issues.printed: Viewing Λ̃^* as a Z̃_p-lattice inside V ⊗_{Q_p} Q̃_p, the source asserts Λ̃^* = Λ̃^∨. It names L as the chain {(π̃^iΛ̃)^Γ}_{i∈Z} in V. It then gives L^∨ = {(π̃^iΛ̃^*)^Γ}_{i∈Z}, followed by L ⊕ L^∨ = {(π̃^i(Λ̃ ⊕ Λ̃^*))^Γ}_{i∈Z}.
issues.correction: Replace Λ̃^* by the ψ-dual Λ̃^∨ throughout. The (i,γ)-component of Λ̃^∨ is γ(δ_{F_i/Q_p})D_{F̃_i/Q̃_p}^{-1}Λ̃_i^* = D_{Q̃_p/Q_p}D_{F̃_i/F_i}^{-1}Λ̃_i^*, which equals Λ̃_i^* only when D_{Q̃_p/Q_p}O_{F̃_i} = D_{F̃_i/F_i}, e.g. when Q̃_p/Q_p is unramified or every F_i/Q_p is unramified. Then L^∨ = {(π̃^iΛ̃^∨)^Γ}_{i∈Z} (by the identity ((π̃^mΛ̃)^Γ)^∨ = (π̃^{-m}δ^{-1}Λ̃^∨)^Γ) and L ⊕ L^∨ = {(π̃^i(Λ̃ ⊕ Λ̃^∨))^Γ}_{i∈Z}. Λ̃^∨ is a Γ-stable sum of Õ_i-lattices c_{i,γ}Λ̃_i^* with the same stabilizers, so the argument of Theorem 6.1.1 applies to Λ̃, Λ̃^∨ and Λ̃ ⊕ Λ̃^∨.
issues.reason: Counterexample. Take F_1 = Q_p, F_2 = Q_p(√p), W_1 = Q_p^2 and W_2 = F_2^2 with standard symplectic forms, H_i = GL_2, G the common-multiplier subgroup, and x hyperspecial. Then Q̃_p = Q_p(√p) satisfies every requirement of the proof, and F̃_2 = Q̃_p. With standard Λ̃_i one has Λ̃^* = Λ̃, but Λ̃^∨ = Z̃_p^2 ⊕ √pZ̃_p^2 ⊕ √pZ̃_p^2, since δ_{F_2/Q_p} ~ √p and D_{F̃_2/Q̃_p} = 1. The member (π̃Λ̃)^Γ = pZ_p^2 ⊕ √pO_{F_2}^2 of L has ψ-dual p^{-1}Z_p^2 ⊕ √p^{-1}O_{F_2}^2. That is not of the form (π̃^jΛ̃^*)^Γ = p^{⌈j/2⌉}Z_p^2 ⊕ √p^{j}O_{F_2}^2. It is (π̃^{-2}Λ̃^∨)^Γ, as the corrected formula predicts. Case for the defence: if Λ̃_i^* is read as the dual of Λ̃_i for the (i,γ)-component of ψ ⊗ Q̃_p, the claim is a tautology. But the text defines Λ̃_i^* as 'the ψ_i dual'. The δ-normalization of §6.1.8 makes ψ_i-duality agree with ψ-duality over Q_p, and that agreement is not preserved by the ramified base change to Q̃_p.

By §6.1.8, ∨ is the dual for the Q̃_p-bilinear extension of ψ = Σ_i Tr_{F_i/Q_p}(δ_{F_i/Q_p}^{-1}ψ_i). On the summand W_i ⊗_{F_i,γ} F̃_i of V ⊗ Q̃_p this form is Tr_{F̃_i/Q̃_p}(γ(δ_{F_i/Q_p})^{-1}ψ_i). So the (i,γ)-component of Λ̃^∨ is γ(δ_{F_i/Q_p})·D_{F̃_i/Q̃_p}^{-1}·Λ̃_i^*. By transitivity of differents this is D_{Q̃_p/Q_p}·D_{F̃_i/F_i}^{-1}·Λ̃_i^*. It equals Λ̃_i^* only when D_{Q̃_p/Q_p}O_{F̃_i} = D_{F̃_i/F_i}. In the tame case this means e(F̃_i/Q̃_p)(e(Q̃_p/Q_p)−1) = e(F̃_i/F_i)−1, which fails in general. If some F_i/Q_p is tamely ramified, Q̃_p has to contain that ramification, so the case cannot be avoided. I re-derived the first reading's example with p odd, Q̃_p = F_2 = Q_p(√p), π̃ = √p and |Γ| = 2. Then (π̃Λ̃)^Γ = pZ_p^2 ⊕ √pO_{F_2}^2. Its ψ-dual is p^{-1}Z_p^2 ⊕ √p^{-1}O_{F_2}^2, because O_{F_2}^2 is self-dual for Tr(δ^{-1}ψ_2). For every j, (π̃^jΛ̃^*)^Γ = p^{⌈j/2⌉}Z_p^2 ⊕ √p^jO_{F_2}^2, and none of these is that dual. The dual is (π̃^{-2}Λ̃^∨)^Γ. So the claimed L^∨ and L ⊕ L^∨ are false. The proof's own 'Indeed' sentence, read as the tame-descent identity ((π̃^mΛ̃)^Γ)^∨ = (π̃^{-m}δ^{-1}Λ̃^∨)^Γ with δ^{-1}Z̃_p = π̃^{1−e}Z̃_p, actually proves L^∨ = {(π̃^iΛ̃^∨)^Γ}. So the only false step is the identification Λ̃^* = Λ̃^∨. It is a false assertion about two different lattices whose invariant chains differ, not a slip of notation. The defence would read Λ̃_i^* as the dual for the (i,γ)-component of ψ ⊗ Q̃_p. That makes the claim a tautology, but it contradicts the printed definition 'ψ_i dual'. Repair: use Λ̃^∨. It is Γ-stable because ψ is defined over Q_p. Its components are F̃_i^×-multiples of Λ̃_i^*, so they have the same stabilizers in H_i ⊗ F̃_i. The argument of Theorem 6.1.1 therefore applies to Λ̃^∨ and Λ̃ ⊕ Λ̃^∨ unchanged, and the statement of Theorem 6.1.9 stands.

The map x ↦ (left multiplication by x^{-1} on D^{opp,m}) is x^{-1} composed with a right action, so it is the contragredient: V̄ ⊗ Q̄_p ≅ ⊕_φ (std_φ^∨)^{⊕d}. For m = 1 and D = K it is just x ↦ x^{-1}. So ρ̄∘μ has the negated weights {0, −1}. ρ∘μ and ρ̄∘μ can both be standard only if μ is trivial on every factor. Hence the claim that ρ̄ gives a local Hodge embedding (G,μ) ↪ (GL(V̄), ρ̄∘μ) is false. So is the second half of Proposition 6.3.2, whose proof ('the result for ρ̄ is proved in the same way', after setting μ' = μ_d) needs ρ̄∘μ = μ_{d'}. The repair is immediate. Let z : G_m → Z(G) = Res_{K/Q_p}G_m be the scalar cocharacter, which is defined over Q_p. Then ρ̄∘(μ·z^{-1}) = t·(ρ̄∘μ) has weights {1,0}, while μ^ad, the reflex field and the local model are unchanged. This is also what Corollary 6.3.5 needs. G_1 = {(g_1,g_2) ∈ G×G : g_1g_2^{-1} ∈ K^×} ∩ GSp(W), so its Hodge cocharacter (similitude weight 1) has components (μ, μ·z^{-1}) in G × G. The downstream result is sound once Proposition 6.3.2 is restated.

issues.locator: Proof of Corollary 6.3.5, p. 71
issues.printed: The source defines L′ as a periodic chain in W, generated by scaling the lattices Λ′_i := Λ_i ⊕ Λ̄_i. Here Λ_i and Λ̄_i range over determining segments of L and L̄, respectively. It claims Λ̄_i can be chosen to make Λ′_i self-dual for ψ, concluding that L′ is self-dual.
issues.correction: Take Λ̄_i := (Λ_{-i})^⊥ ⊂ V̄ (up to the fixed scalar coming from ξ) and Λ'_i := Λ_i ⊕ Λ̄_i. Then L' = {Λ'_i} is a periodic lattice chain with (Λ'_i)^∨ = Λ'_{-i}, so L'^∨ = L'. The individual Λ'_i are not self-dual. Let ψ' be the form on W^r pairing summand i with summand −i (rescaled by the period). Then Λ' = tot(L') is self-dual for ψ', 𝒢 × 𝒢 → GL(Λ') is very good by Proposition 6.3.2 and Lemma 5.3.9, and 𝒢_1 = (𝒢×𝒢) ∩ GSp(Λ') with Theorem 6.1.1 for GSp(Λ') finish the proof as printed.
issues.reason: V and V̄ are ψ-isotropic and ψ pairs them perfectly, so Λ_i ⊕ Λ̄_i is self-dual exactly when Λ̄_i = Λ_i^⊥. The orthogonal decreases as Λ_i increases. So for i ≠ j in a determining segment, Λ'_i and Λ'_j are incomparable, and no scalar multiples fix this. The resulting family is not a chain once a segment has at least two lattices. Example: D = K = Q_p, m = 2, x in the Iwahori facet. Then Λ'_0 = (O ⊕ O) ⊕ (O ⊕ O) and Λ'_1 = (π^{-1}O ⊕ O) ⊕ (πO ⊕ O), and neither contains the other. The conclusion of Corollary 6.3.5 survives with the corrected chain.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 71 image. From the formula for ψ with τ(d,d') = (d',d), V and V̄ are ψ-isotropic and ψ pairs them perfectly. So (Λ ⊕ Λ̄)^∨ = Λ̄^⊥ ⊕ Λ^⊥, and Λ_i ⊕ Λ̄_i is self-dual iff Λ̄_i = Λ_i^⊥ (up to the fixed scalar from ξ), which forces the choice. The two requirements, that every Λ'_i is self-dual and that the Λ'_i together with their scalar multiples form a chain, are incompatible as soon as a determining segment has two distinct lattices. If Λ'_i ⊂ Λ'_j are both self-dual, then Λ'_j = Λ'_j^∨ ⊂ Λ'_i^∨ = Λ'_i, so they are equal. And π^kΛ'_i is not self-dual for k ≠ 0. Concretely, Λ_i ⊊ Λ_j gives Λ_i^⊥ ⊋ Λ_j^⊥, so Λ'_i and Λ'_j are incomparable. The best one gets is πΛ'_i ⊂ Λ'_j ⊂ π^{-1}Λ'_i. I re-checked the first reading's example (D = K = Q_p, m = 2, x Iwahori): Λ'_0 = (O⊕O)⊕(O⊕O) and Λ'_1 = (p^{-1}O⊕O)⊕(pO⊕O) are incomparable. So 'L' is a self dual lattice chain in W' fails whenever a determining segment for L has more than one lattice, for example for x in the Iwahori facet. The corrected chain Λ'_i := Λ_i ⊕ Λ_{-i}^⊥ is increasing, periodic (Λ'_{i+r} = π^{-1}Λ'_i) and satisfies (Λ'_i)^∨ = Λ'_{-i}. Its tot is, up to permuting and π-rescaling summands, the paper's ⊕_i(Λ_i ⊕ Λ_i^⊥). Rescaling a summand does not change the integral Hodge embedding, so 𝒢 × 𝒢 → GL(tot L') is still very good by Proposition 6.3.2 (as corrected in E69) and Lemma 5.3.9. tot(L') is self-dual for the form on W^r that pairs summand i with summand −i (suitably rescaled). This is the device the paper itself uses on p. 80 for L ⊕ L^∨. (G×G) ∩ GSp is unchanged, because that form is a sum of copies of ψ between paired summands and G×G acts diagonally. The rest of the proof, and Corollary 6.3.5, then go through.

issues.reviewReason: The quotation matches the image of p. 78, and the paragraph is also in arXiv v3. Independent argument: the only F-structure on V′ = V ⊗_Q F comes from the second factor, and ι′|_{G^c} is ι followed by the unit map GL(V) → Res_{F/Q}GL_F(V ⊗_Q F). Under the adjunction Hom_Q(X, Res_{F/Q}Y) = Hom_F(X_F, Y), the F-morphism corresponding to ι′|_{G^c} is ι_F on (Res_{F/Q}H^c)_F. Res_{F/Q}(φ) corresponds to φ composed with the counit (Res_{F/Q}H^c)_F → H^c. So ι′ is fundamental iff ι_F factors through that projection. Over Q̄, V′ ⊗ Q̄ = ⊕_{τ: F→Q̄} V_Q̄, and every factor H^c_{τ′} of G^c_Q̄ = ∏_{τ′} H^c_{τ′} acts on every summand through ι. In a Weil restriction, H^c_{τ′} acts only on its own summand. For [F:Q] ≥ 2 each H^c_{τ′} would then act trivially on some summand ≅ V_Q̄, hence on V, and G^c would act trivially. That contradicts faithfulness, since G^c ⊇ G^der ≠ 1 (G^ad is simple). So the claim fails for every Hodge embedding when F ≠ Q. The Hilbert-modular example (g ↦ (g, σ(g)) on F^2 ⊕ F^2) checks out. ι′ is a genuine Hodge embedding, because the trace form of a totally real F is positive definite; only 'fundamental' fails. Case for the defence: the Deligne liftings of §7.2.3 are fundamental by construction (p. 77: G′ → GL(V) comes from H′ → GL_F(W ⊗_F K); p. 79: 'the Hodge embeddings constructed are fundamental'). So Prop. 7.2.16 does not use the claim. Its only use is implicit, for the centre-modified data in the proof of Prop. 7.2.10 (E81). Hence 'the proof', not 'a stated result'.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on p. 83 (same in arXiv v3). I recomputed the groups. Over F_i, K_S and K both split: H_{F_i} is an inner form of PGL, and K is split above p by choice. So V_i = W_i ⊗ (K ⊗_F F_i) has four isotypic blocks W^{±,(𝔓)} and W^{±,(𝔓̄)}. Z_{H′_i} contains three things: the scalars x; K_S^1, acting by y^{±1} on W^±; and K^1, acting by z^{±1} on the 𝔓- and 𝔓̄-copies. These characters are independent, so the centre is a 3-dimensional torus. By contrast, G_1 of 6.3.4 has centre K^× × K^× (a on V, b on V̄). So G_1 ⊊ G′_i: the paper itself claims only an inclusion here, whereas in case (1) it claims an isomorphism with 6.2.8's G_1, which I confirmed. Lemma 7.2.13 only descends from G′ to (G′ ∩ GSp)^0 with the same derived group. G_1 is not of that form, since G′_i ⊂ Res GSp(V_i,Ψ_i) by Lemma 7.2.8(2). Corollary 6.3.5 gives very-goodness only for 𝒢_1. So the step from 𝒢_1 to 𝒢′_i is missing, as the first reading says. The first reading's repair, and the paper's own sentence 'μ′_i factors through G_1', need one caveat. At an embedding φ of F_i that comes from a compact real place of F, the H^♯-part of h is trivial and h_T (T ↔ I_c, §7.2.3 and [KP18, Lem. 4.6.22]) makes μ_φ central: weight 1 on the 𝔓-copy of W_i and weight 0 on the 𝔓̄-copy. Any G_1 as in 6.3.4 with V_i|_{G_1} a sum of ρ_1 acts by a single scalar on all standard-type blocks W^{+,(𝔓)} and W^{+,(𝔓̄)}. So μ′_i then does not factor through G_1. In that case V_i|_{G′_i} is the sum of two non-isomorphic twists (by z and z^{-1}) of ρ_1, close to the situation of Remark 5.3.8. The missing step is short only when every real place inducing 𝔭_i is noncompact. Prop. 7.2.16 is still very plausibly true, so the kind is gap and the reach is the proof.

issues.locator: Journal Theorem3.10 proof p330, first paragraph; arXiv v2 p23; compare Eq.(4) journal p319
issues.printed: G(ℚ)\G(𝔸_f)/K₀
issues.correction: For a fixed X⁺ take representatives of G(ℚ)_+\G(𝔸_f)/K₀, as in Eq.(4), and form N₁ using all of them.
issues.reason: The proof fixes X⁺ after choosing C, then treats those C-indexed components as all components. For the genus-two Siegel datum GSp₄ and neat principal K(N), N≥3, g=diag(-I₂,I₂) is rational with multiplier -1. Thus 1 and g have the same G(Q) double coset. If they had the same positive-G double coset, taking multipliers would give a positive rational finite unit times a unit congruent1modN equal to -1; the rational unit must be1, contradicting -1≠1modN. This example satisfies real rank2. The missing plus omits a component; using the correct finite set repairs the argument, without changing the theorem.

issues.locator: Rubin, App. B §2, Remark 2.6, p. 153 (Rubin, 1999 author draft of Euler systems); final version: Remark B.2.6, p. 197 (unchanged)
issues.printed: The source says that applying Proposition 2.5(ii) requires finiteness of H^i(G,S) for all i and all finite G-modules S of p-power order. It claims that topological finite generation of the pro-p-part of G suffices.
issues.correction: Finite generation (of a pro-p Sylow subgroup, or of G itself) gives finiteness of H¹ only. Finiteness of all H^i needs a p-cohomological finiteness condition, e.g. a pro-p Sylow subgroup that is finitely presented in all degrees (type p-FP_∞), as in the arithmetic cases of Proposition 2.7.
issues.reason: For a pro-p group P, dim H¹(P,F_p) is the generator rank and dim H²(P,F_p) the relation rank. Finitely generated pro-p groups that are not finitely presented exist, and for them H²(P,F_p) is infinite. If instead 'pro-p-part' means the maximal pro-p quotient, take G = ∏_{n≥1} A_5 with p = 2: that quotient is trivial, but H²(G,F_2) ⊇ ⊕_n H²(A_5,F_2) = ⊕_n Z/2 is infinite, by Künneth, since H¹(A_5,F_2) = 0 and H²(A_5,F_2) = Z/2. The remark is only illustrative (Proposition 2.5(ii) is applied via Proposition 2.7), so nothing downstream is affected. The author's final version (Remark B.2.6, p. 197) has the same wording.

issues.locator: Rubin, Ch. III §5.6, Proposition 5.8(ii) and its proof, p. 50 (Rubin, 1999 author draft of Euler systems); final version: Proposition 3.5.8(ii), pp. 67–68
issues.printed: The source gives H¹(Q(E_{p^∞})/Q, E_{p^∞}) = H¹(ρ_{E,p}(G_Q), (Q_p/Z_p)²), claiming vanishing when ρ_{E,p}(G_Q) = GL_2(Z_p) and finiteness when ρ_{E,p}(G_Q) is an open subgroup of GL_2(Z_p).
issues.correction: … which is zero if ρ_{E,p}(G_Q) = GL_2(Z_p) and p is odd (the scalar c = 2, or any c with c − 1 ∈ Z_p^×, kills it by Sah's lemma). The vanishing of H¹(Q(E_{p^∞})/Q, E_{p^∞}) in Proposition 5.8(ii) needs p > 2, since for p = 2 the group H¹(GL_2(Z_2),(Q_2/Z_2)²) is nonzero; the conclusion that T_p(E) satisfies Hyp(Q_∞,T) holds for p = 2 too.
issues.reason: Let G = GL_2(Z_2), K = ker(G → GL_2(F_2) = S_3) = 1 + 2M_2(Z_2), and V = F_2². Then H¹(S_3,V) = H²(S_3,V) = 0 (V is projective), so inflation–restriction gives H¹(G,V) ≅ Hom_{S_3}(K^{ab}/2, V). K surjects S_3-equivariantly onto K/(1+4M_2) ≅ M_2(F_2) with the conjugation action, and M_2(F_2) ≅ V ⊗ V* ≅ V ⊕ P(1) as S_3-modules, so Hom_{S_3}(M_2(F_2), V) = F_2 ≠ 0. Hence H¹(G,V) ≠ 0 (a direct linear-algebra computation gives dim H¹(GL_2(Z/4),F_2²) = dim H¹(GL_2(Z/8),F_2²) = 1, and inflation is injective). Since H⁰(G,(Q_2/Z_2)²) = 0, the sequence 0 → V → (Q_2/Z_2)² →×2 (Q_2/Z_2)² → 0 gives H¹(G,V) ↪ H¹(G,(Q_2/Z_2)²), which is therefore nonzero. Surjective 2-adic images occur, so (ii) fails as stated at p = 2. The vanishing is used only in Theorem 5.11(ii), whose hypotheses exclude p = 2 and which applies Theorem II.2.10(ii) (stated for p > 2); Theorem 5.16 uses Proposition 5.8(ii) only for Hyp(Q_∞,T), which holds at p = 2. The author's final version (hEulerSystems.pdf, Annals-Studies pagination) has the same statement and proof at pp. 67–68, Proposition 3.5.8(ii).

issues.citation: Kolyvagin, "Euler systems", in The Grothendieck Festschrift, Vol. II, Progress in Mathematics 87, Birkhäuser (1990), 435–483
issues.reviewReason: Quote verbatim at draft p. 50 (proof of Proposition 5.8). Checked independently: with G = GL_2(Z_2), K = 1+2M_2(Z_2), V = F_2^2, V is the projective simple F_2[S_3]-module, so H^1(G,V) = Hom_{S_3}(K,V) ⊇ Hom_{S_3}(M_2(F_2),V), and M_2(F_2) = V⊗V* ≅ V ⊕ P(1) as S_3-module, so this is F_2 ≠ 0. A direct F_2-linear-algebra computation of crossed homomorphisms gives dim H^1(GL_2(Z/4),F_2^2) = dim H^1(GL_2(Z/8),F_2^2) = 1 (and 0 for GL_2(Z/2)); inflation to GL_2(Z_2) is injective, and D^G = 0 for D = (Q_2/Z_2)^2 makes H^1(G,V) → H^1(G,D) injective. So the vanishing fails at p = 2; Sah's lemma with the scalar 2 proves it for p odd. The finiteness claim for open image is fine for all p. Kind error, affects a stated result: correct. Two refinements: (a) only the vanishing needs p > 2 (Hyp(Q_∞,T) holds at p = 2 with x = 1); (b) the downstream sentence is inexact: the vanishing is used in Theorem 5.11(ii), which assumes p ∤ 2r_E|Ẽ(F_p)| and applies Theorem II.2.10(ii), stated for p > 2; Theorem 5.16 uses Proposition 5.8(ii) only for Hyp(Q_∞,T) via Theorem II.3.8(ii), which holds at p = 2. Nothing downstream is affected. Final version: Still present: final version Proposition 3.5.8(ii), p. 67 ('Suppose that ρ_{E,p} is surjective. Then H^1(Q(E_{p^∞})/Q, E_{p^∞}) = 0 and T_p(E) satisfies hypotheses Hyp(Q_∞,T).'), with proof on p. 68: '... which is zero if ρ_{E,p}(G_Q) = GL_2(Z_p), and finite if ρ_{E,p}(G_Q) is open in GL_2(Z_p) (see also Corollary C.2.2).' No p > 2.

issues.locator: Rubin, Ch. III §5.2, proof of Proposition 5.1, p. 48 (Rubin, 1999 author draft of Euler systems); final version: Proposition 3.5.1, p. 65
issues.printed: The proof asserts λ_E(E_1(Q_p)) = pZ_p and uses rank_{Z_p} E(Q_p) = 1 to obtain [λ_E(E(Q_p)) : λ_E(E_1(Q_p)] = [E(Q_p) : E_1(Q_p) + E(Q_p)_tors].
issues.correction: Assume p odd in Proposition 5.1. For p = 2, λ_E(E_1(Q_2)) is 2Z_2 if E_1(Q_2) is torsion-free and 4Z_2 if E_1(Q_2) contains a point of order 2, and the formula must be adjusted by that factor.
issues.reason: The formal logarithm is an isomorphism Ê(p^rZ_p) ≅ p^rZ_p only for r > 1/(p−1), so for p = 2 only from r = 2. Counterexample at p = 2: for E with split multiplicative reduction at 2, E_1(Q_2) ≅ 1 + 2Z_2 (Tate curve) contains −1, and λ_E(E_1(Q_2)) = log(1+2Z_2) = 4Z_2. Then exp*_{ω_E}(H¹_s(Q_2,T)) is off by a factor 2 from the stated value. The proposition is stated for all p in the 1999 draft. The later applications (Theorem 5.11(ii) and Corollary 5.18 have p ∤ 2) are unaffected. The author's final version adds the hypothesis p > 2 (Proposition 3.5.1, p. 65).
issues.known: corrected in the author's final version of the book (hEulerSystems.pdf, Annals-Studies pagination), p. 65, Proposition 3.5.1: "With notation as above, if p > 2 then exp*_{ω_E}(H¹_s(Q_p,T)) = [E(Q_p) : E_1(Q_p) + E(Q_p)_tors]p^{-1}Z_p" (proof: "If p > 2 then λ_E(E_1(Q_p)) = pZ_p")

issues.reviewReason: Quote verbatim at draft p. 48 (proof of Proposition 5.1, including the unbalanced bracket). For p = 2 the formal logarithm is an isomorphism Ê(2^r Z_2) ≅ 2^r Z_2 only for r ≥ 2; λ(Ê(2Z_2)) ⊆ 2Z_2 contains 4Z_2 with index 2/|Ê(2Z_2)_tors|, so it is 2Z_2 if E_1(Q_2) is torsion-free and 4Z_2 if it has a point of order 2. Kind error, affects a stated result (the draft states Proposition 5.1 for all p): correct. Rubin himself added the hypothesis in the final version. Final version: Corrected: final version p. 65, Proposition 3.5.1: 'With notation as above, if p > 2 then exp*_{ω_E}(H¹_s(Q_p,T)) = [E(Q_p) : E_1(Q_p) + E(Q_p)_tors]p^{-1}Z_p', and the proof reads 'If p > 2 then λ_E(E_1(Q_p)) = pZ_p and, since rank_{Z_p}E(Q_p) = 1, we see that ...'.

issues.locator: Rubin, Ch. III §5.9, proof (sketch) of Corollary 5.17, p. 53 (Rubin, 1999 author draft of Euler systems); final version: Corollary 3.5.18, pp. 71–72
issues.printed: The proof takes Σ to comprise the places of Q dividing Np∞ … For v | q with q ∈ Σ and q ≠ p, it claims p ∤ |E(Q_q)_tors| implies absence of p-torsion in E(Q_{∞,v}); it then invokes Proposition 2 of [Gr2] to conclude H¹(Q_{∞,v}, E_{p^∞}) = 0.
issues.correction: Treat v | ∞ separately. H¹(R, E_{p^∞}) = 0 for p odd, so assume p odd in Corollary 5.17 (or handle the real places when p = 2).
issues.reason: Σ contains ∞, and the hypothesis only concerns q | N. For p = 2, H¹_s(R,E_{2^∞}) = H¹(R,E_{2^∞}) ≅ H¹(R,E) ≅ π_0(E(R))^∨, which is Z/2 when Δ_E > 0. Then the local terms at the archimedean places of Q_∞ (totally real for p = 2) do not vanish and the dual sequence written is not justified. Nothing in Corollary 5.17 excludes p = 2 (good ordinary reduction at 2 is allowed). The author's final version (Corollary 3.5.18, pp. 71–72) rewrites the sketch via local duality, Hom(H¹_s(Q_{∞,v},E_{p^∞}),Q_p/Z_p) ≅ lim_← E(Q_{n,v})^, but still treats only finite v | q with q ≠ p; at a real place and p = 2 this limit is E(R)^ ≅ Z/2 when Δ_E > 0, so the gap remains.

issues.locator: Gross, §7, (7.3), p. 247 (Gross, published text, scanned copy)
issues.printed: The source attributes to Tate’s local duality theorem the assertion that (7.3) ⟨,⟩ : H¹(K_λ,E_p) × H¹(K_λ,E_p) ⟶ Z/pZ is both alternating and non-degenerate as a pairing of Z/pZ-vector spaces, citing [M, Ch. I, Corollary 2.3].
issues.correction: … is symmetric and non-degenerate.
issues.reason: For 1-cocycles a, b with coefficients in A, B one has a∪b = −s_*(b∪a) − d(c), where c(σ) = a(σ)⊗b(σ) and s swaps the factors. The Weil pairing is skew (e(y,x) = −e(x,y)), so e_*(a∪b) = e_*(b∪a): the pairing is symmetric. For odd p a non-degenerate symmetric form on a nonzero F_p-space is not alternating. Concretely, at a Kolyvagin prime λ (where Gross uses it, μ_p ⊂ K_λ and E_p ⊂ E(K_λ)), choose P, Q with e(P,Q) = ζ. Then H¹(K_λ,E_p) = H¹(K_λ,ℤ/p)² and ⟨x,y⟩ = x₁∪y₂ − x₂∪y₁, since the cup product on H¹(K_λ,ℤ/p) is alternating. So ⟨x,x⟩ = 2·x₁∪x₂, which is nonzero for x₁ the unramified class and x₂ a ramified class, by non-degeneracy of that cup product (the Hilbert symbol).

issues.correction: The first two cases hold only up to the sign (−1)^{ℓ−1}: N(ζ_{mℓ} − 1) = (−1)^{ℓ−1}(ζ_m − 1) if ℓ | m, and (−1)^{ℓ−1}(ζ_m − 1)^{1−Fr_ℓ^{-1}} if ℓ ∤ m, m > 1. Equivalently use 1 − ζ_m: N(1 − ζ_{mℓ}) = 1 − ζ_m (ℓ | m), (1 − ζ_m)^{1−Fr_ℓ^{-1}} (ℓ ∤ m, m > 1), ℓ (m = 1), exactly; define c̃_{m∞} = N_{Q(μ_{mp})/Q(μ_m)}(1 − ζ_{mp}). Remark 2.1 then reads c̃_{m∞} = 1 − ζ_m for p | m; the printed ζ_m − 1 is right only for p odd.
issues.reason: For ℓ | m the conjugates of ζ_{mℓ} over Q(μ_m) are ζ_{mℓ}ζ_ℓ^j (0 ≤ j < ℓ), so N = ∏_j(ζ_{mℓ}ζ_ℓ^j − 1) = ζ_ℓ^{ℓ(ℓ−1)/2}(ζ_{mℓ}^ℓ − 1) = (−1)^{ℓ−1}(ζ_m − 1). For ℓ ∤ m write ζ_{mℓ} = uv (u ∈ μ_m, v ∈ μ_ℓ); the conjugates are uv^i (1 ≤ i < ℓ), so N = v^{ℓ(ℓ−1)/2}(u^ℓ − 1)/(u − 1) = (−1)^{ℓ−1}(ζ_m − 1)^{1−Fr_ℓ^{-1}}, since u^ℓ = ζ_m and u = Fr_ℓ^{-1}(ζ_m). E.g. N_{Q(μ_8)/Q(μ_4)}(ζ_8 − 1) = 1 − ζ_4, and ζ_6 − 1 = −(ζ_3 − 1)^{1−Fr_2^{-1}} (here Q(μ_6) = Q(μ_3)). Checked numerically: the ratio of the true norm to the printed value is −1 for (m,ℓ) = (4,2), (6,2), (3,2), (5,2) and +1 for (3,3), (6,3), (4,3), (5,3), (9,3). For odd p the sign is invisible, since −1 is trivial in (F^×)^ = H¹(F,Z_p(1)), so the Euler-system claim and Theorems 2.3–2.10 are unaffected. For p = 2, which §2 allows ('Theorem II.3.3 also applies when p = 2', draft p. 37, for Theorem 2.7), the sign is visible in (F^×)^. For m odd, Q(μ_{2m}) = Q(μ_m), and the definition gives both c̃_{m∞} = ζ_{2m} − 1 and c̃_{2m,∞} = N_{Q(μ_{4m})/Q(μ_{2m})}(ζ_{4m} − 1) = −(ζ_{2m} − 1) for the same field. The renormalisation changes each class by ±1, which dies in the χ-parts for nontrivial χ used in Theorems 2.7–2.10, so the stated results survive.

issues.reason: Definition IV.1.1 (draft p. 57) reads 'for every prime q dividing r, M | [K(q) : K(1)], M | P(Fr_q^{-1}|T*;1), and q splits completely in F(1)/K', and the sentence says it restates that definition. Since K(1) ⊂ K(q), [K(q):K] = [K(q):K(1)]·[K(1):K], so M | [K(q):K] does not give M | [K(q):K(1)] when p divides [K(1):K]. The latter is what Lemma IV.1.2(iii)–(iv), Lemma IV.7.3 and the use of these primes in Ch. V require. The same slip is E17 in the proof of Lemma IV.7.3. The author's final version, §5.1, p. 105, reads 'both [K(q) : K(1)] and P(Fr_q^{-1}|T*; 1) are divisible by M'.

issues.locator: Rubin, Ch. V §2, proof of Lemma 2.1, p. 81 (Rubin, 1999 author draft of Euler systems); final version: proof of Lemma 5.2.1, p. 107 (repaired there)
issues.printed: The source asserts κ(G_L) is G_K-stable inside W_{𝔭^d} but lies outside W_{𝔭^{d−1}}. It uses Hyp(K, T)(ii) to claim irreducibility of W_𝔭 = T ⊗ k, then concludes 𝔭^{d−1}κ(G_L) = W_𝔭 and hence κ(G_L) = W_{𝔭^d}.
issues.correction: Replace κ(G_L) and κ(J) by their O-spans. 𝔭^{d−1}·Oκ(G_L) = W_𝔭 gives Oκ(G_L) = W_{𝔭^d} (Nakayama over O/𝔭^d). Then Oκ(J) lies in W_{𝔭^{d−1}} + (τ−1)W_M, and with E22's correction Oκ(J) ≠ Oκ(G_L). So J ≠ G_L, and J has index at least p.
issues.reason: κ(G_L) is the image of a homomorphism G_L → W_M. It is a G_K-stable subgroup, hence a Z_p-module, but not in general an O-module when O ≠ Z_p. If k ≠ F_p, the irreducible k[G_K]-module W_𝔭 can have proper G_K-stable F_p-subspaces (an F_p-form, when the residual representation is realised over a smaller field). So the step '𝔭^{d−1}κ(G_L) = W_𝔭, therefore κ(G_L) = W_{𝔭^d}' is not justified as written; only the O-span is forced. The lemma's conclusion survives with O-spans. The author's final version (p. 107) makes exactly this repair: 'therefore Oκ(G_L) = W_{𝔭^d} … Oκ(J) ⊂ W_{𝔭^{d−1}} + (τ − 1)W_M'. The chain written there still has the slip of E22.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 3.2, (3.16), p.13 (arXiv v1)
issues.printed: The source invokes Lemma 3.1 to claim that every A > 0 and ǫ > 0 satisfy |{β ∈ M : |β^{(i)}| ≤ x^{1/n}, g₁ > A}| ≪_ǫ x^{(n−1)/n+ǫ}A^{−1/2+1/ord(σ)}.

Lemma 3.1 as stated controls the radical g₀ > Z, not the squarefull part g₁ > A. Since Σ_{g>A, g squarefull}g^{−r/n} ≪ A^{1/2−r/n} with r/n = 1 − 1/ord(σ), the proof gives exactly A^{−1/2+1/ord(σ)}.
issues.reason: A squarefull integer g₁ > A can have a tiny radical (for example a large power of 2), so g₁ > A does not give g₀ > A^c for any c > 0, and the statement of Lemma 3.1 does not apply. The exponent −1/2 + 1/ord(σ) written in (3.16) is what summing over g₁ > A yields. The paper also passes from M′ to M silently. The conclusion of Lemma 3.2 is unaffected.

issues.locator: Lemma 4.1 (P3), p.20, and its verification, p.21 (arXiv v1)
issues.printed: Property (P3) asserts γ(w, z₁) = γ(w, z₂) for every non-zero w ∈ O_K and z₁, z₂ ∈ O_K with z₁ ≡ z₂ mod N(w). It further asserts Σ_{ξ mod w} γ(w, ξ) = 0 whenever |N(w)| is not squarefull in ℤ.
issues.correction: Quantify over w ∈ S_f (the domain of γ) and sum over ξ mod N(w): "if |N(w)| is not squarefull, then Σ_{ξ mod N(w)} γ(w, ξ) = 0". The verification needs the degree-one prime p with p ∥ N(β) to be unramified. That holds for w ∈ S_f, since f = (F) contains D_K.
issues.reason: γ(w, ·) is periodic modulo N(w), not modulo w: φ(ξ, β) = (ξ/ϕ(β)) with ϕ(β) = ∏_{σ∈S}σ(β)σ^{−1}(β). So "Σ_{ξ mod w}" is not well defined, and the verification itself sums modulo N(β). For a ramified degree-one prime all conjugates σ(p) coincide, and ∏σ(p)σ^{−1}(p) = p^{2|S|} is a square, so the argument needs p unramified.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on PDF20–21: (P3) sums 'ξ mod w' although γ(w, ·) is periodic modulo N(w) and the verification sums modulo N(β); and it quantifies over all nonzero w although γ is defined on S_f. The correction is right, and the verification needs the degree-one prime p with p ∥ N(β) to be unramified, which S_f guarantees since F ⊇ D_K. One qualification of the stated reason: the conjugates of a ramified degree-one prime all coincide only when it is totally ramified; in general σ(p) = τ(p) whenever σ⁻¹τ lies in the (nontrivial) decomposition group, so ∏σ(p)σ⁻¹(p) can be a square, and that is what the unramified hypothesis rules out.

Its proof uses −(−1)^{χ_{xx₀}(σ)} + 1 = (−1) · (−1)^{|T_x∩T_σ|} + 1. Corollary 2.11 asserts the same identity for j ∈ ℤ_{>0}, x₀ ∈ C, replacing the left sum by ∑_{x∈C, x≠x₀}.
issues.correction: In both statements take x₀ := d₀ ∏_{i∈[s]} p_i(1), the vertex with T_{x₀} = ∅; this is the x₀ of §4 and §5.3. Equivalently, keep x₀ ∈ C arbitrary and put C_T := {x ∈ C : π_i(x) ≠ π_i(x₀) for all i ∈ T}.
issues.reason: Modulo squares xx₀ ≡ ∏_{i∈T_x△T_{x₀}} p_i(1)p_i(2), so χ_{xx₀}(σ) ≡ |(T_x△T_{x₀}) ∩ T_σ| (mod 2). The proof's identity with |T_x ∩ T_σ| therefore holds only when T_{x₀} = ∅, although x₀ is arbitrary in both statements. A counterexample: take s = 1, j = 2, x₀ = p₁(2)d₀, x₁ = p₁(1)d₀, ψ₂(x₀) = 0 and ψ₂(x₁) = ¼·χ_{x₁}. The last is the cochain equal to ¼ ∈ ℚ₂/ℤ₂ off ker χ_{x₁}. It is a cocycle for N(x₁) that vanishes on G_{ℚ(√x₁)}, hence a raw cocycle, with ψ₁(x₁) = ½·χ_{x₁}. For σ with χ_{x₁}(σ) = 1 and χ_{x₀}(σ) = 0, and τ with χ_{x₁}(τ) = 1, the left side is ((−1)^{χ_{x₀}(σ)} − (−1)^{χ_{x₁}(σ)})·¼ = ½. The right side is χ_{p₁(1)p₁(2)}(σ)·ψ₁(x₀)(τ) = 0. Lemma 4.5(ii) asserts ramification index 2 for p in ∏_{x∈S} L(ψ_{k+1}(x)); assuming all decomposition groups of K/ℚ are cyclic and every x ∈ S gives ramification of p in ℚ(√x), it claims residue degree 1 for p in ∏_{x∈S} L(ψ_k(x)).

This local statement is what Proposition 4.4 provides, and it is what the conclusion uses; the global claim on p. 29 is false at a prime p_i(h), where the decomposition group of the whole of K need not be cyclic. The ramification index in the first sentence does equal 2, so nothing is wrong there.
issues.reason: The applications check cyclicity only at p, via Proposition 4.4: S = C − {x₀} with p | d₀, S = C_{p_i(2)} with p = p_i(2) and S = C_{(p_i(1),p_j(2))} with p = p_i(1) (pp. 32–33), and S = C with p | a (p. 37). issues.locator: §8.3, end of the proof that Theorem 8.13 implies Theorem 8.10, p. 93 (arXiv v1)
issues.printed: The source bounds the quantity by Σ_{x ∈ X(a,Q,{Art_k}_{2≤k<m}), π_{S′}(x) ∉ Z_pre,bad} |1 − (d(M_box, m)^{r−k_gap}/R) · Λ(x)|. It divides this sum according to condition (8.22), uses Λ(x) ≤ R for those x that violate it, and declares the proof finished.
issues.correction: Bound the whole sum by Cauchy–Schwarz and the moments (8.20) and (8.21). With μ = R/d(M_box, m)^{r−k_gap}, they give Σ_x (1 − Λ(x)/μ)² = O(e^{−k_gap}) |X(a, Q)|, so Σ_x |1 − Λ(x)/μ| = O(e^{−k_gap/2}) |X(a, Q)|, which fits the error term.
issues.reason: Λ(x) ≤ R gives only |1 − Λ(x)/μ| ≤ d(M_box, m)^{r−k_gap}. Chebyshev's inequality places the x failing (8.22) in a set of density O(e^{−k_gap/2}), so the trivial bound contributes O(d(M_box, m)^{r−k_gap} e^{−k_gap/2}) |X(a, Q)|. Here d(M_box, m) ≥ 2, because L(Q)M_∘(Z) contains √p for the primes p of each Z_j other than π_j(z), and r − k_gap > r/2 > k_gap. So this term is at least 2^{r/2} e^{−r/4} |X(a, Q)|, which is unbounded relative to |X(a, Q)|, and the written step does not close the argument. The moments already computed give the repair above.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 8.2, pp. 42–43, arXiv:1611.02667v3; p. 663 in the version of record
issues.printed: It reduces the task to finding an integer l making [Λ, n + le, 0, ϖ_F^{−l}β] semisimple, and assumes no such integer exists for a contradiction. The definition of a semisimple stratum is said to allow reduction to |I| = 2.
issues.correction: Suppose, for a pair {i,j}, that [Λ, n+le, 0, ϖ_F^{−l}β] fails to be semisimple for infinitely many l. The argument of the proof runs verbatim along that subsequence (simple γ^{(l)} ∈ ⊕A^i equivalent to ϖ_F^{−l}β by [39, Theorem 6.16], ϖ_F^{l}γ^{(l)} → β, [41, Proposition 1.9]) and gives the same contradiction. Hence for each pair the stratum is semisimple for all sufficiently large l; taking the maximum over the finitely many pairs (each block is simple once k_F(ϖ_F^{−l}β_i) < 0) gives the Lemma as stated.
issues.reason: The Lemma asserts semisimplicity for every sufficiently large l, and the reduction to #I = 2 needs, for each pair, a bound beyond which every l works. The existence of a single l, which is all the argument as written yields, gives neither. Monotonicity in l does hold (rescale to level e, then lower the level with Proposition 5.5), but the proof does not say so. The subsequence version of the same argument also repairs it; either fix is a sentence.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 9.16, (ii)⇒(iii), pp. 55–56, arXiv:1611.02667v3; p. 683 in the version of record
issues.printed: To establish (ii)⇒(iii), the source assumes endo-equivalence of Θ and Θ′ and chooses ζ as their matching from Θ to Θ′.
issues.correction: Insert: ζ commutes with σ. Take self-dual realizations of Θ− and Θ′− on a common ε-hermitian space with all blocks of equal F-dimension, for example with hyperbolic E_i-forms on the I_0-blocks. By Theorem 9.9(ii)(b) take equal periods and levels. By Theorem 9.9(ii)(d) the σ-invariant lifts θ, θ′ intertwine with matching ζ. If g intertwines θ with θ′ with matching ζ, then σ(g) intertwines θ^σ = θ with θ′^σ = θ′ and maps V^{σ(i)} to V′^{σ(ζ(i))}, so σζσ is also a matching. Uniqueness in Theorem 8.8 gives σζσ = ζ, as in Remark 8.9.
issues.reason: Assertion (iii) requires ζ to commute with σ. The paragraph before Definition 9.15 proves σ-equivariance only when Θ− ≈ Θ′−, via realizations intertwining in G. Under hypothesis (ii) alone the proof never checks it, yet it uses it: g_i := ḡ_{σ(i)}^{-1} for i ∈ I_− and the I_0-isometries must land in the right blocks for g = Σ g_i to lie in G.

issues.locator: Theorem 10.4, p. 58 (conclusion); proof p. 58, arXiv:1611.02667v3; p. 687 in the version of record
issues.printed: It asserts that some element in G° ∩ P₋(Λ) conjugates θ to θ′.
issues.correction: Then θ is conjugate to θ′ by an element y ∈ G° with yΛ = Λ′ (more precisely yΛ^i = Λ′^{ζ(i)} for all i); when Λ′ = Λ this is an element of G° ∩ P₋(Λ). This is the form stated in Remark 10.5 ("θ is conjugate to θ′ by an element g ∈ G° such that gΛ = Λ′") and used in the proof of Theorem 11.9. In the proof, Theorem 8.15(ii) (stated for two characters on the same Λ) must be applied after transporting θ′ by the element g of the hypothesis.
issues.reason: The theorem allows Λ′ ≠ Λ. Conjugating θ ∈ C₋(Λ, r, β) by y ∈ P₋(Λ) gives a character of yH^{r+1}(β, Λ)y⁻¹ = H^{r+1}(yβy⁻¹, Λ) ⊆ P_{1}(Λ), whereas θ′ lives on H^{r+1}(β′, Λ′) ⊇ P_m(Λ′) for m large. Take θ′ = ^xθ with x ∈ G° (e.g. x in a split torus of SO(V)) moving Λ far away and β with no zero component: all hypotheses hold (g = x, condition (ii)), but P_m(xΛ) ⊄ P₁(Λ), so no y ∈ P₋(Λ) conjugates θ to θ′. issues.correction: N(θ₋, G̃, G) = 2^{max(|I₀| − n₀, 0)}; i.e. N = 1 in the two cases where |I₀| − n₀ = −1: (a) G unitary or orthogonal and I₀ = ∅; (b) G orthogonal and I₀ = {i₀} consists only of a zero component with dim_F V^{i₀} ≤ 2 and dim_an V^{i₀} ≤ 1.
issues.reason: N is a positive integer (it counts f₋ ∈ EP(h, G) with a given GL-endo-parameter, and f_{θ₋} is one). (a) If I₀ = ∅ (all blocks in σ-orbits of size 2, e.g. U(1,1) with β = diag(ϖ⁻¹, −ϖ⁻¹), ϖ ∈ F_o, or SO(2,2) with β = diag(b, b, −b, −b)), every orbit has WT(O) = {[0, 0]} and n is forced by the degree, so N = 1, while n₀ = 1 gives 2^{−1}. (b) If G is orthogonal, I₀ = {i₀} with β_{i₀} = 0 and dim V^{i₀} = 1 (e.g. SO(3) with β = diag(0, b, −b)), the only choice for O = {0} is t = [h|_{V^{i₀}}] forced by herm(f₋) = [h], so N = 1, while n₀ = 2 gives 2^{−1}. In all other cases the formula agrees with a direct count (each i ∈ I₀ with β_i ≠ 0 contributes two Witt classes differing by the maximal element, Proposition 3.13(ii) with Proposition 3.14).

issues.locator: §10.2, first paragraph, p. 58, arXiv:1611.02667v3; p. 687 in the version of record
issues.printed: It assumes i₀ ∈ I with β_{i₀} = 0 and no determinant −1 element normalizing P₋(Λ^{i₀}), then takes g_{i₀} ∈ U(V^{i₀}, h_{i₀}) of determinant −1. It cites Theorem 10.2 for intertwining of θ with θ′ = ^gθ by an element of G°, but claims they are not conjugate in G°, referring to an exercise based on Proposition A.9(ii) together with Theorem 10.2.
issues.correction: Restrict the example to r = 0, or assume instead that the normalizer of P^{r+1}₋(Λ^{i₀}) (equivalently, of θ_{i₀}) in U(V^{i₀}, h_{i₀}) contains no element of determinant −1. The opening claim of §10.2, that such characters exist, is unaffected, since examples with r = 0 exist.
issues.reason: For r ≥ 1 and a non-strict Λ^{i₀}, P^{r+1}(Λ^{i₀}) can have a larger normalizer than P(Λ^{i₀}); the authors note this for O(1,1) in a commented-out remark before Remark 10.5. Counterexample: V = M₂(F) with the quadratic form det, so G° = SO(2,2) is split, its building is a product of two trees, and elements of determinant −1 (such as transposition τ) swap the trees. Take β = 0 (so I = {i₀}), r = 1, and the self-dual lattice sequence Λ of period 3 attached to the point (v₀, x) of the building, where v₀ is a vertex and x lies a third of the way along an edge. Then a₂(Λ) = ϖ_F End_{o_F}(M₂(o_F)), so P²(Λ) is the first congruence subgroup of the stabilizer of the lattice M₂(o_F), which τ normalizes, while no element of determinant −1 normalizes P₋(Λ), because it would move (v₀, x) to a point whose first coordinate is not a vertex. For the trivial character θ of P²(Λ) and any g of determinant −1, y = gτ ∈ G° satisfies ^yθ = ^gθ = θ′, so θ and θ′ are G°-conjugate.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on the page image of p. 4 and against Notation 1.10.1 on p. 10, which reads 'Call such a family is versal if the induced map ℳ → ℳ_{g,n} is dominant and étale.' The §1.3 sentence says it follows that notation, so the two definitions conflict, and the binding one (used in Proposition 2.1.3, Lemma 2.1.4 and Theorem 1.7.1) includes étaleness. The extraction's reason adds that 'dominance alone would not suffice for Corollary 1.3.1'. That is not right as mathematics. For any dominant ℳ → M_{g,n} from a connected variety, the image of π₁(ℳ) in PMod_{g,n} still has finite index: pass to a finite étale scheme cover as in Lemma 2.1.4, then use that a dominant morphism to a normal variety has finite-index image on π₁. The outer-action argument of Proposition 2.1.3 does not use étaleness either. So Corollary 1.3.1 remains true under the weaker reading, and only the paper's route through Lemma 2.1.4 uses étaleness; Theorem 1.7.1 does genuinely need it, because c^*_m must be an isomorphism. The verdict and 'affects: nothing' stand, and the last sentence of the reason should be dropped or replaced by this.

issues.locator: Lemma 2.2.2 and the last paragraph of its proof, pp. 14–15 (arXiv v4)
issues.printed: In Notation 2.2.1's setting, it asserts uniqueness of ρ̃ : Γ̃ → PGL_r(ℂ) making (2.2) commute. It argues from uniqueness of M̄_γ and the identity ρ̃(γηγ⁻¹) = ρ̃(γ)ρ̃(η)ρ̃(γ)⁻¹ for every γ ∈ Γ̃ and η ∈ π₁(Σ_{g,n}, x) that ρ̃(γ) must equal M̄_γ.
issues.correction: Existence holds, with ρ̃(γ) = [M_γ] canonical. Uniqueness holds only among representations whose values ρ̃(γ) lift to matrices conjugating ρ to γ(ρ) in GL_r(ℂ), or under the extra hypothesis that the centraliser of Pρ(π₁(Σ_{g,n})) in PGL_r(ℂ) is trivial, i.e. ρ ⊗ χ ≇ ρ for every nontrivial character χ. In general ρ̃ is determined only up to a 1-cocycle of Γ̃ with values in that finite centraliser, trivial on π₁(Σ_{g,n}).
issues.reason: The displayed identity says that ρ̃(γ) conjugates Pρ to Pρ∘(γ-action) inside PGL_r(ℂ). Schur's lemma pins down M_γ only when the conjugation is required in GL_r(ℂ). Projectively, ρ̃(γ) is determined only up to the centraliser Z of Pρ(π₁) in PGL_r(ℂ), and if a ∈ Z, then aρ̃a⁻¹ also makes (2.2) commute. A counterexample: g = 2, n = 0, ρ: π₁(Σ₂) → Q₈ ⊂ SL₂(ℂ) with (a₁, b₁, a₂, b₂) ↦ (i, j, i, j), which is surjective and irreducible, and MCG-finite because its image is finite. Here Z = Pρ(π₁) = V₄ ⊂ PGL₂(ℂ). The automorphism (a, b) ↦ (a, ba) applied three times and then (a, b) ↦ (ab, b) applied three times fixes [a, b] and sends (i, j) to (j, k): (i,j) → (i,−k) → (i,−j) → (i,k) → (−j,k) → (−i,k) → (j,k). Doing this in both handles gives γ ∈ Mod_{2,1} with ρ∘γ = ωρω⁻¹, where ω = (1+i+j+k)/2, so γ ∈ Γ̃ and ρ̃(γ) = [ω] acts on V₄ by a 3-cycle. For a = [i] ∈ V₄, the representation aρ̃a⁻¹ agrees with ρ̃ on π₁(Σ₂) but not at γ, since [ω] does not commute with [i]. So uniqueness fails. Nothing later uses uniqueness: Lemma 2.2.3, Corollary 2.3.5 and §8.3 use only existence. The same projective-versus-linear Schur slip recurs in the proof of Lemma 2.4.1, recorded separately.

issues.locator: proof of Lemma 2.4.1(1), p. 19 (arXiv v4)
issues.printed: It invokes Schur's lemma to characterize ℙρ(g), for each g ∈ G, as the unique PGL_r(ℂ) element satisfying ℙρ(g)ℙρ(h)ℙρ(g)⁻¹ = ℙρ(ghg⁻¹) for every h ∈ H. This uniqueness is then used to deduce ℙρ(g^{t!}) = id.
issues.correction: Use Schur's lemma in GL_r(ℂ): the displayed relation ρ(h) = ρ(g^{t!})ρ(h)ρ(g^{−t!}) holds in GL_r(ℂ) for all h ∈ H, so ρ(g^{t!}) commutes with the irreducible ρ(H) and is a scalar; hence ℙρ(g^{t!}) = id.
issues.reason: Checked on the page image. The asserted projective uniqueness is false. Take G = H = Q₈ ⊂ SL₂(ℂ) with ρ the inclusion, which is irreducible with det = 1. For g = 1, both id and [i] ∈ PGL₂(ℂ) satisfy X·ℙρ(h)·X⁻¹ = ℙρ(h) for all h, because ℙρ(Q₈) = V₄ is abelian. The conclusion still follows, because the relation the proof actually derives holds in GL_r(ℂ), where Schur's lemma applies. So the lemma and its use in Lemma 2.4.2 are unaffected.

issues.locator: Lemma 6.1.1 and its proof, pp. 33–34 (arXiv v4)
issues.printed: For a nonzero irreducible sub-local system 𝕃 ⊂ R¹π°_*𝕍, it claims that replacing 𝕍 and 𝕃 by 𝕍̄ and 𝕃̄ if needed yields a nonzero v ∈ 𝕃_m ∩ F¹ℋ_m with the rank of ∇̄_m(v) at most rk 𝕃/2.
issues.correction: '… there are a sub-local system 𝕃′ ⊂ R¹π°_*𝕍 isomorphic to 𝕃 (namely ι(q ⊗ 𝕃) for a suitable Hodge-homogeneous q ∈ Q) and a nonzero v ∈ 𝕃′_m ∩ F¹ℋ_m so that ∇̄_m(v) has rank at most rk 𝕃/2'; or simply 'a nonzero v ∈ F¹ℋ_m', which is all the proof of Theorem 1.7.1 uses.
issues.reason: The proof takes v := ι_m(q ⊗ ℓ) with q ∈ Q^{i,j} homogeneous, which lies in the copy ι(q ⊗ 𝕃) of 𝕃, not in the given 𝕃. The literal claim can fail. Suppose V is unitary with a real structure and the weight-one part of R¹π°_*𝕍 has a nonzero flat section. Its fixed part is a real Hodge structure of weight 1, so it contains a real y = y^{1,0} + y^{0,1} with both components nonzero. The trivial rank-one 𝕃 = ℂ·y satisfies 𝕃 = 𝕃̄ and 𝕃_m ∩ F¹ℋ_m = 0, because F¹ ∩ W¹ = ℋ^{1,0}. Such flat sections exist: by the translation of §7 they are exactly failures of the Putman–Wieland property, and Marković's genus-2 counterexample to Putman–Wieland gives them for 𝕍 = f_*ℂ over a finite étale cover of M₂. More generally the claim fails whenever an irreducible real 𝕃 of a single Hodge type occurs in weight one through both q and q̄, taking the diagonal copy. The proof of Theorem 1.7.1 needs only v ∈ F¹ℋ_m, with ∇̄_m(v) computed through ι, so Theorem 1.7.1 is unaffected. Only the auxiliary statement is wrong as printed.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 8.6.1, p. 44 (arXiv v4)
issues.printed: To apply Theorem 7.2.1, it chooses v ∈ Σ_{g,n}, sets Σ_{g,n+1} := Σ_{g,n} \ {v}, and takes finite-index Γ ⊂ Mod_{g,n+1} fixing every σ_i's conjugacy class. It claims projection to the σ_i-isotypic part of ρ₂^∨ ⊗ ρ₁ gives a Γ-stable quotient of H₁(Σ_{g′,n′})^{σ_i}, equivalently a Γ-stable subspace of H¹(Σ_{g′,n′})^{σ_i}, with rank at most (g + 1)/4.
issues.correction: Choose Γ ⊂ PMod_{g,n+1} of finite index with three properties. (a) Γ fixes the isomorphism class of ρ; this is possible because ρ is MCG-finite, and it is the only place that hypothesis enters. (b) Γ preserves K = ker(ρ₁ ⊕ ρ₂). This is automatic from (a) when ρ₁ = soc(ρ), because then ρ₁∘γ ≅ ρ₁ and ρ₂∘γ ≅ ρ₂. (c) Γ induces inner automorphisms of H = π₁(Σ_{g,n}, v)/K, so that Γ lies in the group of Notation 7.1.1 for ϕ : π₁ ↠ H and fixes every σ_i. For γ ∈ Γ choose A_γ with ρ∘γ = A_γ^{-1} ρ A_γ. A_γ preserves ρ₁ when ρ₁ is the socle, as in §8.7, since soc(ρ∘γ) = soc(ρ) as subspaces. Writing A_γ = (a₁ b; 0 a₂), the extension class c : K^ab → Hom(ρ₂, ρ₁) satisfies c∘γ = a₁^{-1} c(·) a₂, so ker(c ⊗ ℂ) ⊂ H₁(Σ_{g′,n′}, ℂ) is Γ-stable. Theorem 7.2.1 is then applied to this Γ, a finite-index subgroup of the group of Notation 7.1.1, with σ_i^∨ in place of σ_i for the dual subspace, which is harmless.
issues.reason: With Γ as printed, Γ need not preserve K, so it need not even act on H₁(Σ_{g′,n′}). Even when it does, nothing makes the kernel of the extension class Γ-stable. The printed choice never uses the hypothesis that ρ is MCG-finite, and without that hypothesis the lemma is false. Example: g ≥ 4 and ρ(x) = (1 f(x); 0 1) for a nonzero homomorphism f : π₁(Σ_{g,n}) → ℂ pulled back from H¹(Σ_g, ℂ). Here ρ₁ = soc ρ and ρ₂ = ρ/ρ₁ are trivial and rk ρ = 2 < √(g+1), yet ρ has infinite image. It is not MCG-finite. The conjugacy class of ρ determines the line ℂf, and PMod_{g,n} acts on H¹(Σ_g, ℂ) through Sp_{2g}(ℤ), which moves any line through infinitely many others. The printed Γ also sits in Mod_{g,n+1} rather than PMod_{g,n+1}. The lemma itself is true: it follows from Theorem 1.2.1, whose proof uses only the socle case, and the repair above is routine.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 8.3.3, p. 40 (arXiv v4)
issues.printed: It constructs a strict normal crossing compactification by taking the finite étale cover C° of M_{g,n+1}, blowing up boundary strata of M̄_{g,n+1} to obtain M̄′_{g,n+1}, and normalizing M̄′_{g,n+1} in C°'s function field to form C̄. Citing Proposition 8.3.2, it reduces the proof to showing that monodromy around C̄'s boundary components is given by products of mutually commuting Dehn twists.
issues.correction: Replace 𝒞̄ by a good compactification Y of 𝒞° (smooth projective with strict normal crossings boundary), for instance a resolution of 𝒞̄, so that Y still maps to M̄′_{g,n+1}. A small loop around a smooth point of the boundary of Y maps into the local (orbifold) fundamental group of a punctured neighbourhood of a boundary point of M̄′_{g,n+1}. By [LLSS20, Lemma 2.1.1] that group is generated, up to the finite stabiliser, by commuting Dehn twists. So a power of the local monodromy is a product of powers of commuting Dehn twists lying in π₁(𝒞°), and Proposition 8.3.2 gives quasi-unipotence as before.
issues.reason: The normalisation 𝒞̄ is in general not a strict normal crossings compactification, and it may not even be a scheme, since M̄′_{g,n+1} is a stack. Near a point where k boundary branches of M̄′ meet, the étale cover 𝒞° restricts to the cover of (Δ*)^k × Δ^m given by a finite-index sublattice Λ of the local fundamental group ℤ^k. Its normalisation is the affine toric variety of the positive orthant with lattice Λ, which is smooth only when Λ is spanned by its intersections with the coordinate rays. For instance, for two disjoint homologous non-separating curves a, b and the level-3 congruence subgroup, T_a^x T_b^y lies in the subgroup iff x + y ≡ 0 mod 3. That lattice is not of this form, before or after blowing up, and gives a cyclic quotient singularity. The Klevdal–Patrikis hypothesis concerns a smooth projective compactification with strict normal crossings boundary. The local monodromy argument works on any such compactification, so Lemma 8.3.3 stands.

issues.locator: Example 9.2.3, p. 48 (arXiv v4)
issues.printed: For each curve (C, x₁, ···, x_n) of genus g with n marked points, and each p, it claims surjections ρ : π₁^ét(C_K̄ \ {x₁, ···, x_n}) → GL_r(𝔽_p) of the kind in Corollary 9.2.2 exist and have no arithmetic lifts to characteristic 0.

issues.locator: §3.5.1, Theorem 3.5.3, published p. 38; arXiv v4 p. 29
issues.printed: The source attributes normality, the domain property and Cohen–Macaulayness to R^τ_ρ̄.
issues.correction: If τ is 1-generic and R^τ_ρ̄ ≠ 0 (equivalently, by the proof, W?(ρ̄,τ) ≠ ∅), then R^τ_ρ̄ is a normal domain and Cohen–Macaulay (and R̄^τ_ρ̄ is reduced with formally smooth equidimensional components); otherwise R^τ_ρ̄ = 0.
issues.reason: The proof treats the nonzero case. Genericity of a tame type does not make it compatible with a fixed rho: a tame central twist can preserve all genericity differences while changing the determinant character required of a lift. An incompatible determinant gives an empty deformation problem. The zero ring is not a domain. Continuation check (2026-09-23, a second, independent reading on the page image): confirmed. The theorem itself says R^τ_ρ̄ = 0 when τ is not 1-generic, and its component count gives R̄^τ_ρ̄ = 0 (hence R^τ_ρ̄ = 0 by Nakayama) whenever W?(ρ̄,τ) = ∅, which happens for 1-generic τ, e.g. when the central characters of W?(ρ̄) and JH(σ̄(τ)) differ. The zero ring is not a domain. The proof (p. 45–46) treats only R^τ_ρ̄ ≠ 0. Defence: the zero case is degenerate and the intended reading is clear; CM and the component statements are vacuous for the zero ring. Reach: a stated result (degenerate case only).

issues.printed: The source defines Σ_w̃ := Σ₀ ∩ w̃(r(Σ₀)) for w̃ ∈ W̃. Citing Figure 2, it asserts that Σ_w̃ is empty exactly when w̃ is not in Adm(η)X⁰(T̲).

issues.reason: Outside that coset the equivalence fails: for w̃ = t_{(1,0,0)}, Σ_w̃ = {(ε₁,0), (ε₁,1), (ε₂,1), (ε₁+ε₂,0)} ≠ ∅, yet t_{(1,0,0)} ∉ W_a X⁰(T) ⊇ Adm(η)X⁰(T) (Bruhat-comparable elements lie in the same W_a-coset; (1,0,0) ∉ Λ_R + Z(1,1,1)). Within W_a t_η X⁰(T) the claim is correct (verified by computer: Σ_w̃ ≠ ∅ exactly for the 25 elements of Adm(η), modulo X⁰). Defence: all uses have w̃ ∈ W̲_a t_{±η}. Independent check: Quote checked on the p. 22 image: 'For w̃ ∈ W̃, define Σ_w̃ := Σ₀ ∩ w̃(r(Σ₀)) … one can check that Σ_w̃ is empty if and only if w̃ is not in Adm(η)X⁰(T)'. By p. 20, W̃ acts on Λ_W × A through W̃^der by the usual action, so t_(1,0,0) acts on Λ_W = Z³/Z(1,1,1) as translation by ε1. r(Σ₀) = Σ₀ with every a flipped. Then Σ₀ ∩ (ε1 + r(Σ₀)) = {(ε1,0), (ε1,1), (ε2,1), (ε1+ε2,0)} ≠ ∅. However, Bruhat-comparable elements lie in the same W_a-coset, so Adm(η) ⊂ W_a t_η. Every element of Adm(η)X⁰(T) therefore has a translation part with coordinate sum ≡ 0 mod 3, and (1,0,0) has sum 1, so t_(1,0,0) ∉ Adm(η)X⁰(T). I checked this independently by computer. I computed Adm(η) from the Bruhat order generated by affine reflections for the dominant base alcove (25 elements, 25 classes mod X⁰) and Σ_w̃ for every w̃ with translation part in a 9×9 box. Inside W_a X⁰(T) = W_a t_η X⁰(T), Σ_w̃ ≠ ∅ exactly for the 25 classes of Adm(η)X⁰, with no mismatch. Outside that coset, 50 of the 324 enumerated classes have Σ_w̃ ≠ ∅. The sentence is an informal remark ('using Figure 2', whose alcoves only represent W_a t_η). Every use has w̃ ∈ W̲_a t_η: Corollary 2.3.11, Lemma 2.3.12, Corollary 2.3.13 and Proposition 3.4.4 via Table 2. So nothing downstream is affected. The proof is 'follows from Corollary 2.3.11 and Proposition 3.4.1', but Corollary 2.3.11 requires w̃ ∈ W̲_a t_η. I rechecked the counterexample. Take f = 1, s = 1, μ deep, A = v^(1,0,0) = diag(v,1,1). This matrix is in Mat_3(F[[v]]) and upper triangular mod v, so by [LLHLM18, Prop. 2.13, Lemma 2.14] it defines 𝔐̄ ∈ Y^{[0,h],τ}(F) for h ≥ 1, semisimple of shape t_(1,0,0), with w̃* = t_(1,0,0). By Prop. 3.4.1 and Def. 2.3.6, V(ρ̄|_{I_K}) = R_1(μ+η+(1,0,0)), which is 3-generic for μ deep. All Jordan–Hölder factors of R̄_w(λ) have the central character given by λ restricted to Z, and W?(ρ̄) = R(JH(V(ρ̄|_{I_K}))) with R shifting the central character by a fixed amount. Compare the admissible shape t_1̲ (Table 2, 'Id' row, 6 weights), where V = R_1(μ+η+(1,1,1)) and the intersection is nonempty, so the central characters match there. For t_(1,0,0) the central character of W?(ρ̄) differs from that case by x ↦ x², which is nontrivial because p > 3. Hence W?(ρ̄,τ) = ∅. But Σ_{t_(1,0,0)} = {(ε1,0), (ε1,1), (ε2,1), (ε1+ε2,0)} ≠ ∅ (recomputed; W̃ acts through W̃^der). The same failure occurs inside Adm(η)X⁰(T). For example, A = v²·Id has shape t_(2,2,2), and Σ_{t_(2,2,2)} = Σ_{Id} has 6 elements. But ρ̄|_{I_K} is the t_1̲ case twisted by a character that changes the central character by x³ ≠ 1, so the left side is again empty. The reader's weaker fix 'w̃* ∈ W̲_a t_η X⁰(T̲)' therefore does not suffice. The applications (Prop. 3.4.4, Lemma 3.5.4, proofs of Lemma 3.5.9 and Thm 3.5.3) all use shapes in Adm^∨(η). issues.locator: Proposition 4.1.1 and its proof, and the phrase 'directed acyclic graph Γ(M)', published p. 76; arXiv v4 pp. 57–58
issues.printed: The source claims that repeatedly substituting σ′ for σ allows one to assume that no σ′ ∈ JH(N) points to σ. It then associates a directed acyclic graph Γ(M) to multiplicity free M.
issues.correction: (i) State and prove that Γ(M) is acyclic: if σ₁ → ⋯ → σ_k → σ₁ were a cycle, take N minimal with σ₁ ∈ JH(N) and N′ ⊂ N maximal; then σ_k ∈ JH(N′) and closedness of JH(N′) forces σ₁ ∈ JH(N′), a contradiction. (ii) Add injectivity of N ↦ JH(N): for multiplicity-free M, JH(N₁ ∩ N₂) = JH(N₁) ∩ JH(N₂), so JH(N₁) = JH(N₂) implies N₁ ∩ N₂ = N₁ = N₂.
issues.reason: The repeated-replacement step terminates only if there is no directed cycle. Acyclicity is asserted afterwards ('directed acyclic graph') without proof, and it is used again in the proof of Theorem 4.2.7(3), condition (2). The proof shows only that N ↦ JH(N) lands in closed sets and is surjective; injectivity is not addressed. In the paper's defence, both facts are elementary, and the fixes above use only what the proof already establishes.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 4.2.4, end of the proof of (4.8), published p. 83; arXiv v4 p. 62
issues.printed: From ⟨ω_κ, α^∨⟩ < 2(h − 1) ⩽ p − 2 for every coroot α^∨ ∈ R^∨, the source puts ω_κ in the lower p-restricted alcove and asserts that L(ω_κ) has no algebraic extensions with any L(ω), ω ∈ X⁰(T).
issues.correction: Replace the last sentence by the following. If Ext¹_G(L(ω_κ),L(ω)) ≠ 0 with ω ∈ X⁰(T), then λ = ω_κ−ω is nonzero, dominant and in W_p·0. For G of type A (here λ+η ≡ w(η)+pν with ν ≠ 0 weakly decreasing), this gives ⟨λ,α0^∨⟩ ⩾ 2(p−h+1) ⩾ 2(h−1), contradicting ⟨ω_κ,α0^∨⟩ < 2(h−1). For GL3 with p ⩾ 5 one may instead note that ⟨ω_κ+η,α0^∨⟩ ⩽ 3+2 ⩽ p, so ω_κ lies in the closure of C0, which meets W_p·0 only in X⁰(T); then apply the linkage principle.
issues.reason: The lemma assumes only p ≥ 2(h−1), and for p ∈ {2h−2, 2h−1} (e.g. h = 3, p = 5) one has 2(h−1) > p−2. For h = 3, p = 5 and ω_κ = (3,0,0), ⟨ω_κ, α^∨⟩ ≤ 3 < 4 for all positive coroots but ⟨ω_κ+ρ, α₀^∨⟩ = 5 = p, so ω_κ is on the upper wall and not in the lower alcove. For h ≥ 4, even p ≥ 2h does not put ω_κ in the lowest alcove, since that needs ⟨ω_κ, α₀^∨⟩ ≤ p−h. In the paper's defence, the conclusion (no extensions with characters) is true under the stated hypotheses by the argument above, and the paper only applies the lemma to GL₃ with p ≥ 5 and large genericity. Independent check: Quotation checked on p. 83 (page image). §4.2.1 works with a general G of Coxeter number h (p. 79), and Lemma 4.2.4 assumes only p ⩾ 2(h−1). Alcoves are open (p. 9: connected components of the complement of the hyperplanes), and C0 is 'the p-restricted lower alcove' (p. 11). p-bounded means ⟨κ,α^∨⟩ < 2(h−1)p (p. 81), so ⟨ω_κ,α^∨⟩ ⩽ 2h−3. For GL3 (h = 3) with p = 5, which is allowed by the lemma and by p > 3 (§1.4), 2(h−1) = 4 > p−2 = 3. Take κ = pω_κ with ω_κ = (3,0,0). It is p-bounded (⟨κ,α0^∨⟩ = 15 < 20), but ⟨ω_κ+η,α0^∨⟩ = 5 = p, so ω_κ lies on the wall H_{α0,1} and not in C0. For general h, lying in C0 needs ⟨ω_κ,α0^∨⟩ ⩽ p−h, i.e. p ⩾ 3h−3. The conclusion (4.8) is still true in type A, the only case the paper uses. Suppose Ext¹_G(L(ω_κ),L(ω)) ≠ 0 with ω ∈ X⁰(T). Then λ := ω_κ−ω is dominant, nonzero and in W_p·0 (mod X⁰). Write λ+η ≡ w(η)+pν with ν a nonzero element of the root lattice. Dominance of λ+η and p > h−1 force ν to be weakly decreasing, so ν1−νn ⩾ 2 and ⟨λ,α0^∨⟩ ⩾ 2p−2(h−1) ⩾ 2(h−1). This contradicts ⟨ω_κ,α0^∨⟩ < 2(h−1). So a false intermediate claim sits in the proof of a true lemma. The lemma is only applied under large genericity, where p is large. Versions: the same sentence is in v3 and v4 (v4 p. 62); v2 has the analogous '< 2(n−1) ⩽ p−2'.
