issues.printed: The source claims that any (S, γ)-abundant r-tuple (Ψ₁, …, Ψ_r) allows S to have a basis {s₁, …, s_r} with θ_S(Ψ_i)(s_j) = 0 whenever i ≠ j, together with exp_λ(θ_S(Ψ_j)(s_j), (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) ⩾ m − m₀ − 𝔣(r)r_R. It calls the first claim immediate from Definition 2.6.5.
issues.correction: Assume 𝔣(r)r_R = 0 (e.g. R̄ absolutely irreducible and r_R minimal), or weaken to: there are elements s_j := Ce_j with AC = λ^c·I (a submodule containing λ^cS), or state it for a suitably chosen tuple rather than every abundant one. The application needs only one good pair, which exists when the O_λ-span of θ_S(G_{S,γ}) is large (cf. E1). At Proof of Theorem 8.3.2, (8.11), published pp. 317–318: Use only what abundance gives: after possibly interchanging Ψ1 and Ψ2, exp_λ θ_S(Ψ1)(λ0^{m_Σ−m_per}s) ⩾ m − m_Σ − 4𝔯_R, and there is a primitive t ∈ S with θ_S(Ψ1)(t) = 0 and exp_λ θ_S(Ψ2)(t) ⩾ m − m_Σ − 4𝔯_R; replace s2 by t in the rest of the proof.
issues.reason: Over O/λ^m with m>4, A=[[λ,1],[0,λ]] has image containing λ²O² and hence λ⁴O². Its total image has index |k|² but its two coordinate projections have indices 1 and |k|; a diagonal matrix with those projections would have index |k|. Right multiplication by a basis change preserves the image, so cannot diagonalize it. Thus the claimed implication from Definition 2.6.5 is false for general linear maps. This example is not presented as a realized Selmer evaluation system, so the finding is a proof gap rather than a counterexample under every global hypothesis. Re-checked on the page image (2026-09-23): revised — confirmed that the inference is invalid, but it is an error in the stated first part of Proposition 2.6.7 (asserted for EVERY abundant tuple), not only a proof gap; the counterexample matrix is realizable whenever θ_S(G_{S,γ}) is all of Hom(S, (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}). Locator is Proposition 2.6.7 (not 2.6.6). Over O_λ/λ^n with n ⩾ 2, A = [[λ,1],[0,λ]] has det λ², image {(λx+y, λy)} ⊇ λ²(O_λ/λ^n)², of index |k|²; its coordinate projections have indices 1 and |k|, so a diagonal matrix with the same image would have index |k|. Column operations (change of basis of S) preserve the image, so no basis diagonalizes A. This A is abundant as soon as 𝔣(2)r_R = 4r_R ⩾ 2, i.e. r_R ⩾ 1 (r_R is any bound from Lemma 2.3.3, and is ⩾ 1 whenever R̄ is reducible). It is realized by actual Frobenius elements whenever θ_S(G_{S,γ}) = Hom(S, (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) (e.g. [F:F⁺] = 1, where Lemma 2.6.4 holds, and θ_S surjective). Case for the defence: in the application the authors are free to choose the pair (Ψ₁, Ψ₂), and a suitable choice (or the one-sided variant) suffices for Theorem 8.3.2 — but the proposition as stated, and its proof, are wrong, and the choice requires control of G_{S,γ} that E1 removes. Reach: a stated result (first part of Proposition 2.6.7; the second part depends on it); the proof of Theorem 8.3.2 (Theorem 1.1.9), which uses it with r = 2). Independent check 1: Quotation checked on p. 135 (PDF p. 29): 'For every (S,γ)-abundant r-tuple … one can choose a basis {s₁,…,s_r} of S such that θ_S(Ψ_i)(s_j) = 0 if i ≠ j and exp_λ(θ_S(Ψ_j)(s_j), (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) ⩾ m − m₀ − 𝔣(r)r_R' with proof 'The first part is obvious from Definition 2.6.5'. The statement is universally quantified over abundant tuples. Definition 2.6.5 (p. 134) asks only that the image of s ↦ (θ_S(Ψ_i)(s))_i contain λ^{m₀+𝔣(r)r_R}((R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ})^{⊕r}. Normalizing by λ^{m₀} (the values lie in λ^{m₀}O/λ^m because S is killed by λ^{m−m₀}), this says: the matrix A ∈ M_r(O/λ^n), n = m − m₀, has image ⊇ λ^c(O/λ^n)^r with c = 𝔣(r)r_R. A change of basis of S acts by A ↦ AC and preserves the image, so a diagonalizing basis exists iff im A is a product of coordinate submodules. Checked: A = [[λ,1],[0,λ]] has Smith form diag(1,λ²), image of index |k|² containing λ²(O/λ^n)², while its coordinate projections are O/λ^n and λO/λ^n (a product would have index |k|). So it is abundant when c ⩾ 2 and not diagonalizable. Also A = [[1,0],[1,λ]] with image {(a,b): a ≡ b mod λ} ⊇ λ(O/λ^n)² is abundant as soon as c ⩾ 1. Does Definition 2.6.5 allow such matrices? It needs c = 𝔣(r)r_R ⩾ 1, i.e. r_R ⩾ 1, and rows that lie in θ_S(G_{S,γ}). r_R is only 'an integer' from Lemma 2.3.3 (any upper bound works), and even the minimal one is ⩾ 1 whenever R̄ is reducible, which the hypotheses of Prop. 2.6.6 allow (R_ℚ irreducible; Lemma 2.3.5(a) or (b), and (b) allows semisimple reducible R̄). The rows are available whenever θ_S(G_{S,γ}) contains Hom(S,(R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) up to less than c: e.g. [F:F⁺] = 1, which §2.4–2.6 allow, where Lemma 2.6.4 holds, with θ_S surjective. So the first part is false as stated. It is TRUE when 𝔣(r)r_R = 0: abundance then means A invertible, and C = A^{−1} works with exponent m − m₀. It is also trivially true for r = 1. The second part is derived from the first. Versions: v1/v2 have no Prop. 2.6.7; the same inference is in the proof of the rank-one theorem ('By the definition of a (S,γ)-abundant pair, we may choose a basis…'). v3 is identical to the published text. Independent check 2: Quote checked on the page image, p. 135 (PDF 29): 'For every (S, γ)-abundant r-tuple … one can choose a basis …', and 'Proof The first part is obvious from Definition 2.6.5.' Definitions checked: exp_λ(x,M) = min{d : λ^d x = 0} (Def. 2.1.6, p. 123); abundance (Def. 2.6.5, p. 134). Set n = m − m₀ and identify Hom(S,(R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) with row vectors over O_λ/λ^n. Then abundance says exactly that the matrix A = (θ_S(Ψ_i)(s_j)) satisfies im A ⊇ λ^c(O_λ/λ^n)^r, with c = 𝔣(r)𝔯_R. The claimed basis exists iff AC is diagonal for some C ∈ GL_r. Column operations preserve im A, and the image of a diagonal matrix is the product of its coordinate projections. Counterexample. Take A = [[λ,1],[0,λ]] with n ≥ 2. Its image {(λx+y, λy)} contains λ²(O_λ/λ^n)² and has index |k|². Its projections have indices 1 and |k|, so no diagonalizing basis exists. A is abundant once c ≥ 2, i.e. r ≥ 2 and 𝔯_R ≥ 1. Arithmetic realization, with [F:F⁺] = 1, where Lemma 2.6.4 does hold. Take F = ℚ(√2,√5) (real, so 𝔠 acts trivially), ℓ = 3, R = ℤ₃(1), j = 2, and m ≥ 5. Let S be generated by κ(1+√2) and κ((1+√5)/2); these are independent modulo cubes (take norms to the two quadratic subfields), so S is free of rank 2. Take γ = 1 (h_γ = 1). Then K ≅ (ℤ/3^m)², θ_S is bijective, and G_{S,γ} = K by Chebotarev. Choose Frobenii Ψ₁, Ψ₂ with rows (3,1) and (0,3). With 𝔯_R := 1, which is a legitimate bound in the sense of Lemma 2.3.3 ('at most 𝔯_R'), the pair is abundant (λ⁴ ⊆ λ²), yet no basis diagonalizes it. If 𝔯_R is instead read as the exact depth, this R gives 𝔯_R = 0. In that case abundance forces A to be invertible and the first part holds. The statement is then false exactly when R̄ is not absolutely irreducible and θ_S(G_{S,γ}) contains the two rows, which is automatic wherever Lemma 2.6.4 holds and θ_S is onto. Versions: v3 is identical. v1 already had the same inference inside the rank-one proof. The first reading's correction (i)–(iii) is sound. Reach to the main theorems: Prop. 2.6.7 is used in Theorem 8.2.2 with r = 1, where the first part is trivially true, and in Theorem 8.3.2 with r = 2 (pp. 317–318, 320). For every λ produced by Lemma 8.1.3 (Prop. 2.7.2(2)) or Lemma 8.1.4 (Lemma 8.1.5(1)), R̄ = R̄₀⊗R̄₁ is absolutely irreducible, so r_R = 0 and Prop. 2.6.7 holds as used. Hence E2 does not affect Theorem 1.1.1 or the prime sets of Theorem 1.1.7 and its rank-one analogue. For a general admissible λ, Definition 8.1.1 requires irreducibility of R_ℚ only in characteristic 0 ((L3)), so R̄ may be reducible and r_R ⩾ 1. The proof of Theorem 8.3.2 (Theorem 1.1.9) must then choose the abundant pair suitably, or use a one-sided variant, instead of 'fixing' an arbitrary one. That is a local repair, available whenever a correct Prop. 2.6.6 is (which E1 undermines only when R_ℚ ≅ R_ℚ^𝔠). E2 alone makes no main theorem false and leaves only a minor gap in the proof of Theorem 1.1.9. Only Theorem 8.3.2 uses the first part with r = 2; it underlies Theorem 1.1.9 and the unstated rank-one analogue of 1.1.7. Theorem 8.2.2 uses Proposition 2.6.7 with r = 1, where the first part is trivially true, so Theorems 1.1.1, 1.1.5 and 1.1.7 are untouched by E2. The failure needs 𝔯_R ≥ 1, i.e. R̄ = R̄₀⊗R̄₁ not absolutely irreducible. Definition 8.1.1 allows this: (L3) is a characteristic-0 condition, (L4) concerns the factors, and (L5-1)(b) allows a semisimple reducible R̄. For such admissible λ the proof of 8.3.2 cites a false statement. Repair where G_{S,γ} is known. Take s₁ := λ₀^{m−m_per}s, which is primitive by footnote 33, so a₁ = 1. Extend it to a basis {s₁,s₂}. Then pick Ψ₁, Ψ₂ with θ_S(Ψ₁) = λ^c s₁* and θ_S(Ψ₂) = λ^c s₂*. This is immediate if θ_S(G_{S,γ}) = θ_S(K) ∩ Hom(S,(R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) and O_λ = ℤ_ℓ; otherwise it needs a short argument about O_λ-spans versus subgroups. Constants (8.11)–(8.13) change harmlessly. The repair presupposes the description of G_{S,γ} that E1 removes when R_ℚ ≅ R_ℚ^𝔠, so E2 and E1 must be repaired together. E2 by itself does not put Theorem 1.1.9 in doubt, and no main theorem is shown false. The same mistake at Proof of Theorem 8.3.2, (8.11), published pp. 317–318: The diagonal basis comes from Proposition 2.6.7, which does not follow from Definition 2.6.5 for r = 2 (E2): the abundant pair with rows λ^{m_Σ}(λ, 1), λ^{m_Σ}(0, λ) (abundant once 4𝔯_R ⩾ 2) admits no such basis. But the proof uses only loc_{w1}(s2) = 0, exp loc_{w2}(s2) ⩾ m − m_Σ − 4𝔯_R and exp loc_{w1}(s) ⩾ m − m_per − 4𝔯_R. These follow from abundance directly: the matrix A′ = λ^{−m_Σ}(θ_S(Ψ_i)(e_j)) over O_λ/λ^{m−m_Σ} has elementary divisors dividing λ^{4𝔯_R}, so A′v has a coordinate of valuation ⩽ 4𝔯_R for every primitive v; and a primitive t spanning the kernel of the unimodular part of the first row has θ_S(Ψ1)(t) = 0 with A′t, hence θ_S(Ψ2)(t), of valuation ⩽ 4𝔯_R. So the threshold m > m_per + m_lat + m_Σ + 8𝔯_R + m_dif is unchanged. For r = 1 (Theorem 8.2.2) Proposition 2.6.7 is correct.

issues.printed: The source chooses a positive integer e_α making the order of (γ′_α)^{ℓ^{e_α}} prime to ℓ, with eigenvalue 1 for h_{(γ′_α)^{ℓ^{e_α}}}. It claims replacing γ′_α with (γ′_α)^{ℓ^{d_α e_α}} produces the required (γ′₀, γ′₁, ξ′).
issues.correction: Take g ∈ Gal(F̄/F′) whose image (γ′₀, γ′₁, ξ′) mod λ^m lifts (γ₀, γ₁, ξ), and replace g by g^{ℓ^k} for ONE k that kills the ℓ-parts (the kernel of reduction mod λ is an ℓ-group) and is divisible by the d_α and by the order of Frobenius on the residue fields involved; then (γ′₀^{ℓ^k}, γ′₁^{ℓ^k}, ξ′^{ℓ^k}) lies in the image, reduces to (γ₀, γ₁, ξ) and satisfies (a)–(e). For (c) one needs ker(h − 1) free of rank one over O_λ/λ^m, not only '1 is an eigenvalue': this follows since h has order prime to ℓ, so ker(h−1) is the image of the averaging idempotent, a free direct summand lifting the rank-one residual kernel.
issues.reason: Choosing powers independently in the two representations need not give an element in the image of the same Galois element. A common power preserves joint-image membership, the residual triple and the required unit conditions. Re-checked on the page image (2026-09-23): confirmed — checked on the page image of p. 136; the triple obtained by independent ℓ-powers of γ′₀, γ′₁ with ξ′ unchanged need not be in the image of the joint homomorphism. Minor and easily repaired; the lemma is true. The previous record's 'printed' field did not quote the faulty step (corrected below). (GI^m) asks for a single element of the image of Gal(F̄/F′) under the joint map (ρ̄₀₊^{(m)}, ρ̄₁₊^{(m)}, ε̄_ℓ^{(m)}). Powers of the components by different exponents ℓ^{d₀e₀} ≠ ℓ^{d₁e₁}, with ξ′ unchanged, correspond to different Galois elements. Defence: the intended argument is obviously the common power (as in arXiv v1/v2), and conditions (a), (d), (e) are Galois-stable (𝒫 ∈ ℤ[T]; eigenvalue conditions invariant under x ↦ x^{ℓ^k}), so nothing beyond the proof is affected. Independent check: Quote checked on the image of p. 136: 'Replacing γ′_α by (γ′_α)^{ℓ^{d_α e_α}}, we obtain the desired element (γ′₀, γ′₁, ξ′).' (GI^m_{F′,𝒫}) asks for ONE element of the image of Gal(F̄/F′) under the joint map (ρ̄₀₊^{(m)}, ρ̄₁₊^{(m)}, ε̄_ℓ^{(m)}). Powering the two components by different exponents ℓ^{d₀e₀}, ℓ^{d₁e₁} and keeping ξ′ gives a triple that in general comes from no single Galois element. The repair is routine. Take g ∈ Gal(F̄/F′) with image (γ′₀, γ′₁, ξ′) lifting (γ₀, γ₁, ξ). Replace g by g^{ℓ^k} with k divisible by d₀, d₁ and by [O_λ/λ : 𝔽_ℓ], and large enough to kill the ℓ-part: the kernel of 𝒢(O_λ/λ^m) → 𝒢(O_λ/λ) is an ℓ-group, and ℓ^k is odd, so the c-component is preserved. The reduction is unchanged, so (a), (d) and (e), which only depend on it, persist; (b) holds by construction. For (c), h has order prime to ℓ, so ker(h−1) is the image of the averaging idempotent: a free direct summand whose rank is the residual multiplicity 1. The printed phrase '1 is an eigenvalue' does not give (c) by itself. issues.printed: Part (4) asserts triviality of the Gal(κ̄/κ)-action on H^{N−2}_ét(DL(V, { , }, N − 1)_κ̄, L((N−2)/2)) for even N. The proof calls N = 2 trivial and cites [31] for the claim that Tate cycles defined over κ span H^{N−2}_ét(DL(V, { , }, N − 1)_κ̄, Q_ℓ((N−2)/2)), thereby obtaining (4).
issues.correction: Add to (4) the hypothesis that the pair descends to F_{p²} over κ, i.e. 𝒱 = 𝒱_0 ⊗_{F_{p²}} κ with {x, y} = −{y, x}^σ on 𝒱_0. More generally it suffices that the κ-Frobenius on ℙ(𝒱 ⊗ κ̄) is a power of the F_{p²}-Frobenius. Then the middle cohomology is spanned by classes of F_{p²}-rational linear subspaces, and (4) holds. Delete 'The lemma is trivial if N = 2' for (4). In Lemma 5.6.2(3) add the verification that the F_p^Φ-forms of the link fibres DL_{s°} given by the 𝔗-twisted Frobenius are split. One route (E9): via the 𝔭-level structure η°_𝔭 of Construction 5.6.1, DL_{s°} ≅ Iso(Λ̄°_𝔭) ⊗ κ, and Frobenius acts on 𝒱_{s°} as a scalar times a power of the F_{p²}-Frobenius, because π_{A°} = i(π_{A0}) once Hom_{O_F}(A0, A°) is κ-rational. Scalars act trivially on ℙ(𝒱_{s°}). At Proof of Lemma 5.6.2(3), published p. 212 (relies on Lemma A.1.4(4), p. 323: Show that Frobenius acts on each link fibre through a κ-rational 𝔽_{p²}-structure. For s° over a finite κ ⊇ 𝔽_p^Φ, identify DL_{s°} ≅ Iso(Λ̄°_𝔭) ⊗_{𝔽_{p²}} κ over κ via the level structure η°_𝔭 of Construction 5.6.1. This needs Frobenius to fix η°_𝔭: after enlarging κ, π_{A°} = i(π_{A₀}) because Hom_{O_F}(A₀, A°) generates A° up to isogeny. Then, using Construction 5.3.6 and the 𝔗-invariance, the 𝔽_p^Φ-Frobenius acts on H^{N−2}_𝔗 through the 𝔽_{p²}-Frobenius of Iso(Λ̄°_𝔭), whose middle cohomology (twisted by (N−2)/2) is spanned by classes of 𝔽_{p²}-rational linear subspaces (Hotta–Matsui). Lemma A.1.4(4) should be restricted to pairs with a κ-rational 𝔽_{p²}-structure.
issues.reason: Let κ=F9, p=3, N=2 and use the form with diagonal (1,t), t∉F3. It becomes an F9 skew-Hermitian form after geometric rescaling and is admissible as defined. Its isotropic projective locus x⁴+t y⁴=0 has four distinct geometric points and no F9 point: fourth powers in F9* lie in F3*. Frobenius permutes the points nontrivially, so it acts nontrivially on H0 (take Q5 coefficients). The actual Shimura fibres may have additional descent data; that is a separate repair. Re-checked on the page image (2026-09-23): confirmed — the N = 2 counterexample (κ = F_9, p = 3, form diag(1, t), t ∉ F_3) is correct; the failure is not special to N = 2 (checked also for N = 4). Admissible κ-forms of a non-degenerate pair differ by twists by the finite unitary group U_N(F_p) (by Lang's theorem every non-degenerate pair is admissible), and these twists act non-trivially on the middle cohomology. N = 2: κ = F_9, p = 3, {x, y} = x_1^3y_1 + t x_2^3y_2 with t ∈ F_9 \ F_3 is admissible (rescale e_1, e_2 by a, b with a^4 = c, t b^4 = c′, where c, c′ ∈ F_9 satisfy c^2 = c′^2 = −1). DL(V, { , }, 1) is the set of lines with x_1^4 + t x_2^4 = 0: four geometric points, none F_9-rational because the fourth powers in F_9^× are {±1} = F_3^× (computer count: 0 rational points for each of the six t ∉ F_3, 4 for t ∈ F_3^×). Frobenius therefore permutes H^0 = L^4 non-trivially (L = Q_5 is 3-coprime with p + 1 = 4 invertible). N = 4: for p = 2, κ = F_4, the split form gives #DL(V, 3)(F_4) = (q²+1)(q³+1) = 45 = 1 + 4·7 + 16 (Frobenius acts trivially on H^2(1); b_2 = 7 for the Hermitian cubic surface), whereas random non-degenerate forms over F_4 (all admissible) give 9, 13, 17, 21, 25, 29 or 33 points, so trace(Frob | H^2(1)) = (# − 17)/4 ≠ 7 and the action is non-trivial. The cited fact (‘spanned by Tate cycles over κ’) is true only when the relevant cycles are defined over κ, i.e. for the split form. Independent check: Checked on pp. 322–323. The lemma is stated for any pair over any κ ⊇ F_{p²} with dim 𝒱^⊣ = 0; it does not even assume admissibility, which holds anyway by Lang. The proof says 'The lemma is trivial if N = 2' and '…is spanned by Tate cycles over κ ([31])'. Re-derived. For N = 2, κ = F_9, {x,y} = x1^σy1 + t x2^σy2, the isotropic points satisfy u^4 = −t. A computer count gives 0 F_9-rational points for each of the six t ∉ F_3 and 4 for t ∈ F_3^×. Frobenius therefore permutes H^0 = L^4 non-trivially, e.g. for L = Q_5 (3-coprime, p+1 invertible). For N = 4, p = 2, κ = F_4, the cubic surface {y,y} = 0 has 45 = 1 + 4·7 + 16 points for the split (Hermitian) form. Random non-degenerate forms give 9, 13, 17, 21, 25, 29 or 33 points, so tr(Frob | H^2(1)) ≠ 7 and the action is not trivial. The cited fact is true only when the Tate classes (F_{p²}-rational linear subspaces) are defined over κ, i.e. for κ-forms that are split. The only use is Lemma 5.6.2(3) (p. 212), whose proof is complete except for (4): the 𝔗-twisted Frobenius defines an F_p^Φ-form of each fibre. So that proof inherits a gap (E9). The needed special case, split forms, is very plausibly true, so Lemma 5.6.2(3) and everything downstream stand. The same mistake at Proof of Lemma 5.6.2(3), published p. 212 (relies on Lemma A.1.4(4), p. 323: Lemma A.1.4(4) asserts that Gal(κ̄/κ) acts trivially on H^{N−2}(DL(𝒱, {,}, N−1)_{κ̄}, L((N−2)/2)) for EVERY pair over κ with 𝒱^⊣ = 0. Admissibility (Definition A.1.1) only provides an 𝔽_{p²}-structure over κ̄, and the claim is false in general. E9's example, re-checked here: κ = 𝔽₉, p = 3, N = 2, {x, y} = x₁^σy₁ + t x₂^σy₂ with t ∉ 𝔽₃. The isotropic points u⁴ = −t are not 𝔽₉-rational, and Frob₉ multiplies u by t² ≠ 1. The 𝔽_{p²}-structure is the fixed space of Φ = 𝔽𝕍⁻¹; here Φ acts on 𝒱 as diag(−1, −t²), not as a scalar. The proof of Lemma 5.6.2(3) invokes exactly this false generality. Construction 5.3.6 only shows that Frobenius preserves Sh(V°, K°_p), i.e. each fibre up to 𝔗; it says nothing about the κ-structure of the fibre. Defence: for the Shimura fibres, Φ^{[κ:𝔽_{p²}]} is the scalar π_{A°}/p^k = τ_∞^c(π_{A₀}/p^k), a root of unity, which acts trivially on ℙ(𝒱_{s°}). So the κ-structure agrees with the 𝔽_{p²}-structure, and Lemma 5.6.2(3) is very plausibly true. The paper does not supply this argument. Lemma 5.6.2(3) is used in Lemma 5.9.3(6) and §6. Independent check: Quotation checked on p. 212: 'Part (3) follows from Lemma A.1.4(4) and Construction 5.3.6.' Construction 5.3.6 (p. 199) says only that Gal(F̄_p/F_p^Φ) acts trivially on Sh(V°, −K°_p) under υ°, and through 𝔗 on T_p. So on the 𝔗-invariant cohomology (Notation 3.5.7) the 𝔗-twisted Frobenius stabilises each link fibre DL_{s°}. Prime-to-p quasi-isogenies identify Dieudonné modules, so this twisted Frobenius acts on V_{s°} ⊗ F̄_p by a σ^f-semilinear bijection that preserves { , }_{s°} up to a scalar. In other words it is the Frobenius of an F_p^Φ-form of a non-degenerate pair. Lemma A.1.4(4), as stated, would then finish the proof. So the proof is complete except for A.1.4(4), which is false in that generality: see E9, whose N = 2 case (F_9) and N = 4 case (F_4: split form 45 points, random non-degenerate forms 9–33 points) I re-ran by computer. What is missing is exactly the check that the forms arising are split, i.e. that the twisted Frobenius is a scalar times a power of the F_{p²}-Frobenius. That holds via η°_𝔭 (Construction 5.6.1) or π_{A°} = i(π_{A0}), and the paper does not give it. So the gap is real and Lemma 5.6.2(3) is very likely true. It is still the same mistake as E9. A.1.4(4) is used only here (grep: its only citation is p. 212). The authors' route is 'A.1.4(4) holds for every κ-form', and restricting A.1.4(4) to split forms (E9's correction) forces precisely the verification this record supplies. Uses of Lemma 5.6.2(3): Lemma 5.9.3(6) (p. 235), Lemma 7.2.5(4) (p. 291), §6.

issues.printed: The source takes N ⩾ 2 and r := ⌊N/2⌋, defining H^prim(Iso(Λ̄_N)_κ̄, Q̄_ℓ) := ker(∪c_1(O_{ℙ(Λ̄_N)}(1)) : H^{N−2}_ét(Iso(Λ̄_N)_κ̄, Q̄_ℓ) → H^N_ét(Iso(Λ̄_N)_κ̄, Q̄_ℓ(1))). It claims a unique irreducible Ū_N(κ⁺)-representation Ω_N isomorphic to ι_ℓ^{−1}H^prim(Iso(Λ̄_N)_κ̄, Q̄_ℓ).
issues.correction: For N = 2 define H^prim as reduced H^0, the kernel of the degree (Gysin) map to H^2 of the ambient ℙ^1, and Ω_2 := St = PS(ε_2^TT), of dimension q. Or restrict the cup-product definition to N ⩾ 3 and set Ω_2 := St. Make the same change in Definition 5.6.3: at N = 2 take the kernel of the Gysin map m^{†°}_!: H^0_𝔗(M̄†) → H^2_𝔗(M̄°), which agrees with the printed definition for N ⩾ 3 when p+1 ∈ L^×. Then (5.13) holds at N = 2. At Definition 5.6.3 and Proposition 5.6.4, display (5.13), published p. 213 (same root cause as E10, Appendix C.2 p. 353): Define H^prim as the kernel of the Gysin map m^{†°}_!: H^{N−2}_𝔗(M̄†_𝔭(V°, –), L(i)) → H^N_𝔗(M̄°_𝔭(V°, –), L(i + 1)), equivalently of ∪ξ followed by the trace to the balloon. issues.reason: The Fermat variety is q+1 points. Cup product H0→H2 is zero, so its kernel is all q+1-dimensional H0, containing constants and not the asserted irreducible q-dimensional Tate–Thompson representation. The reduced H0 has dimension q because q+1 is invertible in the coefficients. Re-checked on the page image (2026-09-23): confirmed (locator relabelled: the published label is Proposition C.2.1, not 'Lemma C.2.1'; definition on p. 353). For N = 2, Iso(Λ̄_2) is the set of q+1 isotropic lines of a hermitian plane over κ (dimension 0), so H^N = H^2 = 0 and the printed kernel is all of H^0, a (q+1)-dimensional permutation representation ≅ 𝟏 ⊕ St of U_2(𝔽_q), not irreducible; so the asserted existence of an irreducible Ω_2 ≅ H^prim fails. Independent confirmation from the paper's own formula (C.1): R_2 = −(χ_2((1,1))/2·R_{(1^2)} + χ_2((2))/2·R_{(2)}) = (R_{(2)} − R_{(1^2)})/2 = ((𝟏 + St) − (𝟏 − St))/2 = St, of degree q; likewise C.2.1(2) singles out St (the unique nontrivial constituent of Ind_{P_2}𝟏). With the reduced H^0 (dimension q) everything in C.2.1 holds at N = 2 and the proof of C.2.1(2) works with [pt] − (q+1)^{−1}·1. Case for the defence: for N ⩾ 3 the cup-product kernel is the standard primitive cohomology and is irreducible (Tate–Thompson); N = 2 is a degenerate case the authors presumably had in mind as 'reduced H^0'. But the paper explicitly allows N ⩾ 2 here and in §5.6 (Definition 5.6.3 is the same kernel construction and Proposition 5.6.4 is stated for N ⩾ 2), and N = 2 is used in the main theorems. Independent check: Checked on pp. 352–355: 'Let N ⩾ 2', the kernel definition, and 'unique irreducible representation Ω_N … isomorphic to ι_ℓ^{−1}H^prim'. At N = 2, Iso(Λ̄_2) is the set of q+1 isotropic lines, of dimension 0, so H^2 = 0 and H^prim = H^0. That is the permutation representation Ind_B^{U_2(F_q)} 1 = 1 ⊕ St of dimension q+1, which is reducible, so the asserted irreducible Ω_2 does not exist. From (C.1), with χ_2 = sgn and z = 2 for both partitions, R_2 = (R_{(2)} − R_{(1²)})/2 = ((1 + St) − (1 − St))/2 = St. C.2.1(2) at N = 2 (P_2 = P_2^{(1)} = B) also singles out St. The same degeneration makes (5.13) in Proposition 5.6.4 false at N = 2, where the left side has an extra Map_{K°_𝔭}(…, 1) (E10). Reach: no written downstream argument uses H^prim or Ω_2 at N = 2. Lemma 6.3.2 (p. 275) assumes N ⩾ 4. Proposition 6.3.1 (p. 272) and Corollary 6.3.5 (p. 279) leave N = 2 to the reader. Proposition 5.6.4(1) survives because 1 and St both have Borel-fixed vectors. So the error is confined to the stated definitions/assertions at N = 2. Versions: v1 and v3 have the same 'It is well-known by Tate–Thompson … unique irreducible' sentence. The same mistake at Definition 5.6.3 and Proposition 5.6.4, display (5.13), published p. 213 (same root cause as E10, Appendix C.2 p. 353): §5.6 assumes only N ⩾ 2. For N = 2 each link fibre DL_{s°} is p + 1 points (Theorem 5.3.4(1)), so H² of the link vanishes and the printed kernel is all of H⁰_𝔗(M̄†). Over s₀ it is the (p+1)-dimensional permutation representation of U(Λ°_𝔭)(𝔽_p) ≅ U₂(𝔽_p) on the isotropic lines, which is 1 ⊕ (p-dimensional irreducible) and contains the constants. Appendix C.2 defines Ω_N as 'the unique irreducible representation' isomorphic to the same cup-kernel, which does not exist for N = 2. Proposition C.2.1(2) singles out the Steinberg-type p-dimensional representation. Hence (5.13) is false at N = 2 under either reading: the left side has an extra copy of Map_{K°_𝔭}(…, 𝟏). Downstream, §6.3 (N = 2r even, r = 1 allowed) uses H^{2r−2}_𝔗(M†_N, O_λ)_𝔪 ≃ O_λ[Sh(V°_N, K°_N)]_𝔪 ⊕ H^prim(M†_N, O_λ)_𝔪 (p. 275), which double-counts constants at r = 1 with the printed definition. Defence: for N ⩾ 3 everything is correct; the N = 2 conclusion (1) of Proposition 5.6.4 (π_𝔭 in an unramified principal series) survives; the fix is definitional. Independent check: Page 213 checked: Definition 5.6.3 takes the kernel of ∪(m^{†°*}ι°_!ξ): H^{N−2}_𝔗(M̄†) → H^N_𝔗(M̄†). §5.6 assumes N ⩾ 2 (p. 211). At N = 2, M̄† is 0-dimensional, so H^2 = 0 and the kernel is all of H^0. Over s0 this is the permutation representation of U(Λ°_𝔭)(F_p) ≅ U_2(F_p) on the p+1 isotropic lines, which is 1 ⊕ St. Ω_2 in C.2 is either undefined (the 'unique irreducible' rep isomorphic to a reducible H^prim) or, by C.2.1(1),(2) and (C.1), St. In either case (5.13) is false at N = 2: the left side has an extra Map_{K°_𝔭}(…, 1). The correction is right. For N ⩾ 4 with p+1 ∈ L^×, restriction H^N(ℙ) → H^N(DL) is injective, so ker(ξ∪) = ker(Gysin). For N = 3 both kernels are all of H^1. For N = 2 the Gysin kernel is reduced H^0. The downstream claim in the reason is wrong. H^{2r−2}_𝔗(M̄†_N)_𝔪 ≃ O_λ[Sh]_𝔪 ⊕ H^prim_𝔪 on p. 275 is in Lemma 6.3.2, which assumes N ⩾ 4. Proposition 6.3.1 and Corollary 6.3.5 treat only N ⩾ 4 and leave N = 2 to the reader (pp. 272, 279). So no written argument uses H^prim or (5.13) at N = 2. Conclusion (1) of Proposition 5.6.4 survives, since both 1 and St have Borel-fixed vectors. Reach: a stated result ((5.13) at N = 2), nothing downstream.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition C.2.1(2), published p. 355 (top); arXiv v3 p. 165
issues.printed: The source places ℙ(Y_N) inside Iso(Λ̄_N), yielding a class in CH^{r−1}(Iso(Λ̄_N)). It claims that subtracting c_1(O_{ℙ(Λ̄_N)_κ̄}(1)) from this cohomology class yields a nonzero member of H^prim(Iso(Λ̄_N)_κ̄, Q̄_ℓ)(r−1).
issues.correction: Replace 'its cohomology class subtracted by c_1(O_{ℙ(Λ̄_N)_κ̄}(1))' with '[ℙ(Y_N)] − (q+1)^{−1}·c_1(O_{ℙ(Λ̄_N)_κ̄}(1))^{r−1}' for r ⩾ 2. For r = 1, use [pt] − (q+1)^{−1}·1 in the reduced H^0; see E10 for the definition of H^prim when N = 2.
issues.reason: The linear cycle has codimension r−1, so subtracting a degree-two class is wrong for r≠2. Its pairing with the complementary hyperplane power is one, whereas the hypersurface hyperplane top degree is q+1; this gives the normalization even at r=2. Page image checked. Re-checked on the page image (2026-09-23): confirmed (published label: proof of Proposition C.2.1(2), p. 355). ℙ(Y_N) ≅ ℙ^{r−1} has codimension r−1 in the (2r−2)-dimensional Iso(Λ̄_N), so its class lies in H^{2r−2}(r−1) while c_1(O(1)) lies in H^2(1): the subtraction is degree-inconsistent unless r = 2. H^{2r}(Iso) is spanned by h^r, and ∪h kills [ℙ(Y_N)] − c·h^{r−1} iff c = ([ℙ(Y_N)]·h^{r−1})/(h^{2r−2}) = deg ℙ^{r−1}/deg Iso = 1/(q+1). Even for r = 2 the coefficient is 1/(q+1), not 1. The 'well-known' nonvanishing is true: if [ℙ(Y_N)] = h^{r−1}/(q+1) then [ℙ(Y_N)]^2 = 1/(q+1), whereas the self-intersection is c_{r−1}(N_{ℙ(Y_N)/Iso}) = ((−q)^r − 1)/(−(q+1)) ∈ ℤ (from c(N) = (1+h)^r/(1+(q+1)h)). Defence: 'subtracted by c_1(…)' can be read loosely as 'minus the appropriate multiple of the appropriate power of the hyperplane class'; the conclusion Ω^{P^{(r)}} ≠ 0 is unaffected. Independent check: Quote checked; the passage runs from the last line of p. 354 onto p. 355. H^prim is defined on p. 353 as ker(∪c_1(O(1)): H^{N−2} → H^N(1)). ℙ(Y_N) ≅ ℙ^{r−1} has codimension r−1 in the (2r−2)-dimensional Fermat hypersurface Iso(Λ̄_N), which has degree q+1. So its class lies in H^{2r−2}(r−1), and subtracting c_1 ∈ H^2(1) is degree-inconsistent for r ≠ 2. Even for r = 2 it is wrong: ([ℙ^1] − h)·h = 1 − (q+1) ≠ 0. H^{2r}(Iso) is spanned by h^r, so [ℙ(Y_N)] − c·h^{r−1} is primitive iff 1 − c(q+1) = 0, i.e. c = 1/(q+1). The difference is nonzero: [ℙ(Y_N)]² = c_{r−1}(N_{ℙ(Y_N)/Iso}) = ((−q)^r − 1)/(−(q+1)) ∈ ℤ, while (h^{r−1}/(q+1))² = 1/(q+1) ∉ ℤ. I rechecked this Chern-class computation from c(N) = (1+h)^r/(1+(q+1)h). The first reading's mathematics is right. But the intended meaning (subtract the multiple of h^{r−1} that projects onto the primitive part) is clear, and the conclusion Ω_N^{P^{(r)}} ≠ 0 stands once the formula is corrected. Following the convention for misprints whose correction leaves the argument intact, 'affects' should be 'nothing', not 'the proof'. Versions: identical in v1/v2/v3 p. 165.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 8.1.7, published p. 307; arXiv v3 Lemma 8.1.7, PDF p. 134; arXiv v1/v2 Lemma 8.1.4, PDF p. 133
issues.printed: The proof claims H^i_ét(Sh(V_{n1}, K^𝔓_{n1}K′^𝔭_{n1,𝔓}K^?_{n1,𝔭})_{F̄}, O_λ)_{𝔪1} has no O_λ-torsion for every i ∈ ℤ. It therefore reduces the task to establishing (8.1), an isomorphism between these groups after ⊗_{O_λ} ℚ̄_ℓ, as ℚ̄_ℓ[Γ_F]-modules in every degree i ∈ ℤ.
issues.correction: Show that the Hecke correspondence T^{•∘}_{n1,𝔭}: H^i(Sh(…K°_{n1,𝔭}), O_λ)_{𝔪1} → H^i(Sh(…K•_{n1,𝔭}), O_λ)_{𝔪1} (integral, Γ_F- and prime-to-𝔓-Hecke-equivariant) is an isomorphism. By the printed local computation, T^{∘•}∘T^{•∘} acts on the π1-part of the source by c(π1) = p^{r1²+r1}∏_{i=1}^{r1}(α_i+p)(α_i+p^{−1})/α_i (Proposition B.4.3(1)), and T^{•∘}∘T^{∘•} acts on the π1-part of the target by the same scalar (one-dimensional K°- and K•-invariants of the same constituent). Since the Satake parameter of BC(π1)_𝔭 is congruent mod λ to that of Π_{1,𝔭}, intertwining genericity mod λ (which presupposes p invertible mod λ) makes every c(π1) a λ-adic unit; hence both composites have unit determinant on the free O_λ-modules H^i(…)_{𝔪1}, are automorphisms, and T^{•∘} is an O_λ[Γ_F]-isomorphism (also 𝕋^{Σ⁺_min∪Σ⁺_𝔓}-linear).
issues.reason: Freeness of source and target and a rational isomorphism do not imply an integral isomorphism: multiplication by λ on Oλ is a counterexample. P5 and the explicit compositions offer the missing integrality input; the full uniform construction remains to be written. Re-checked on the page image (2026-09-23): confirmed — locator corrected (it is Lemma 8.1.7, not a Proposition) and the correction sharpened to an explicit determinant argument using only the paper's own inputs. Torsion-free O_λ[Γ_F]-modules with isomorphic rationalizations need not be isomorphic: Γ = ℤ acting on O_λ² by (1 1; 0 1) and by (1 λ; 0 1) gives rationally conjugate, integrally non-isomorphic lattices (their reductions mod λ are a nontrivial unipotent and the identity). The integral statement is essential: in (8.7) and its rank-one analogue it transports the fixed exponent m_lat, defined at hyperspecial level, to the level-raised Shimura variety at a prime 𝔭 that depends on m; with only a rational isomorphism the lattice discrepancy could grow with 𝔭 and the final choice 'm > m_per + m_lat + …' would be circular. Case for the defence: every ingredient of the repair (the integral correspondences of Definition 5.8.1, Proposition B.4.3(1), intertwining genericity mod λ) is already in the printed proof; only the passage from 'nonzero' to 'unit' and the determinant argument are missing, so the lemma as stated is true. Independent check: Quotation checked on p. 307. The inference 'torsion-free, and isomorphic after ⊗Q̄_ℓ, hence isomorphic as O_λ[Γ_F]-modules' is invalid in general; the first reading's unipotent example is correct. It is not rescued in this setting. If H^{2r₁}_{𝔪₁} ⊗ Q̄_ℓ were isotypic for one residually absolutely irreducible ρ, every Γ-stable lattice would be ≅ T^{⊕μ} (O_λ[Γ] ↠ End(T) by Burnside and Nakayama, then Morita). But localization at 𝔪₁ only fixes the residual eigensystem, so several π₁ with distinct ρ_{BC(π₁)} lifting ρ̄ can contribute, and lattices in such a sum need not be isomorphic. The repair works, and I checked it. I° = T^{∘•}T^{•∘} ∈ 𝕋°_{𝔭} acts on each π₁-part by a scalar that is, up to a power of p, ∏(p + α_i)(p + α_i^{-1}) = P(−p)/(−(p + 1)). Its value for π₁ is congruent mod λ to its value for Π₁ (Chebotarev), and it is a unit because P_{α(Π_{1,𝔭})}(−p) is invertible mod λ (Definition 3.1.5(2)). The same scalar governs T^{•∘}T^{∘•} on the one-dimensional K•-invariants. Hence both composites have unit determinant on the free modules H^i_{𝔪₁}, and the integral, Γ_F- and Hecke-equivariant T^{•∘} is an isomorphism. The lemma is true; the integral statement is essential for the m_lat bookkeeping in (8.7).

issues.locator: Lemma 2.3.5(b) and its proof, published pp. 127–128; arXiv v3 Lemma 2.3.5, p. 15; arXiv v1/v2 Lemma 2.3.4(b), pp. 14–15
issues.printed: Part (b) asserts injectivity of Res_ρ assuming dim_{O_λ/λ} R̄ ⩽ min{(ℓ+1)/2, ℓ−3}, semisimplicity of R̄ over (O_λ/λ)[Γ_F], and Hom_{(O_λ/λ)[Γ_F]}(End(R̄), R̄) = 0. The proof embeds G^i/G^{i+1} in End(R̄) over 𝔽_ℓ[G], then embeds (G^i/G^{i+1}) ⊗ O_λ/λ in End(R̄) ⊗ (O_λ/λ) ≃ End(R̄)^d over (O_λ/λ)[G], setting d := [O_λ/λ : 𝔽_ℓ].
issues.correction: As (O_λ/λ)[G]-modules, End(R̄) ⊗_{𝔽_ℓ} k ≃ ⊕_{σ ∈ Gal(k/𝔽_ℓ)} End(R̄)^{(σ)} (Frobenius twists), k = O_λ/λ, not End(R̄)^d. Replace the last hypothesis of (b) by Hom_{𝔽_ℓ[Γ_F]}(End(R̄), R̄) = 0, equivalently Hom_{k[Γ_F]}(End(R̄)^{(σ)}, R̄) = 0 for every σ ∈ Gal(k/𝔽_ℓ); then the printed proof goes through. As printed, (b) is correct when k = 𝔽_ℓ.
issues.reason: Counterexample with k = 𝔽₂₅, ℓ = 5, m = 2, O_λ = W(𝔽₂₅). Let ζ generate 𝔽₂₅^× (order 24), H = ⟨h⟩ ≅ ℤ/24 acting on k² by χ₁ ⊕ χ₂, χ₁(h) = ζ⁵, χ₂(h) = ζ⁴, and G := A ⋊ H ⊆ GL₂(O_λ/25) with H = {diag([ζ⁵]^t, [ζ⁴]^t)} (Teichmüller lifts) and A = {1 + 5x·e₁₂ : x ∈ 𝔽₂₅} ≅ 𝔽₂₅, on which h acts by ψ = χ₁χ₂^{−1} (ζ). Realize G as Gal(L/F) with 5 unramified in F (any finite group is a Galois group over some number field; choose the S_n-extension of ℚ split at 5), R = (O_λ/25)². Hypotheses of (b): dim R̄ = 2 ⩽ min{3, 2}; R̄ = χ₁ ⊕ χ₂ is semisimple (A acts trivially, |H| prime to 5); End(R̄) = 1 ⊕ 1 ⊕ ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1}, exponents {0,0,1,23} versus R̄ = {5,4}, so Hom_{k[Γ_F]}(End(R̄), R̄) = 0. But the 𝔽₅-linear map A → R̄, x ↦ (x⁵, 0) is H-equivariant (ψ⁵ = χ₁), so H¹(G, R̄) ≅ Hom_H(A, R̄) ≠ 0; since R̄^G = 0, H¹(G, λR) ≅ H¹(G, R̄) injects into H¹(G, R) = ker Res_ρ. So Res_ρ is not injective. (Here (a) fails: no nontrivial scalar in the image.) Defence: the only verification of (b) in the paper (Lemma 8.1.4 via Lemma 8.1.5(2), for Theorem 1.1.7) proves via Jordan types that ρ̄₀⊗ρ̄₁ is not a subquotient of ad(ρ̄₀⊗ρ̄₁); the same argument applies to every Frobenius twist, so Theorem 1.1.7 is not affected; Theorem 1.1.1 uses (a) (Proposition 2.7.2(1)). But Definition 8.1.1 (L5-1) admits primes satisfying only (b), so Theorems 1.1.5 and 1.1.9 as stated rely on the false lemma when O_λ/λ ≠ 𝔽_ℓ. Independent check: Statement and proof checked on the images of pp. 127–128, including 'End(R̄) ⊗ (O_λ/λ) ≃ End(R̄)^d'. G^i/G^{i+1} is only an 𝔽_ℓ-subspace of End_k(R̄), with k = O_λ/λ. As k[G]-modules, End(R̄) ⊗_{𝔽_ℓ} k ≅ ⊕_{σ∈Gal(k/𝔽_ℓ)} End(R̄)^{(σ)}, which is not End(R̄)^d unless every Frobenius twist is isomorphic to End(R̄). I verified the 𝔽₂₅ counterexample by explicit computation. I built G = ⟨diag([ζ]⁵,[ζ]⁴), 1+5e₁₂⟩ ⊂ GL₂(W₂(𝔽₂₅)) with W₂(𝔽₂₅) = (ℤ/25)[√2]; it has order 600 = |A ⋊ H|. A cocycle computation over 𝔽₅ gives dim_{𝔽₅} Z¹(G,R̄) = 6, R̄^G = 0 and dim B¹ = 4, so dim_{𝔽₅} H¹(G,R̄) = 2 = dim_k Hom_H(A,R̄). As characters of h: End(R̄) = ζ^{0,0,1,23} and R̄ = ζ^{5,4}, so Hom_{k[G]}(End R̄, R̄) = 0. The Frobenius twist is ζ^{0,0,5,19} ∋ ζ⁵ = χ₁. The hypotheses of (b) hold: dim 2 ⩽ min{3, 2}, and R̄ is semisimple. Since R̄^G = 0, H¹(G,λR) ≅ H¹(G,R̄) injects into H¹(G,R) = ker Res_ρ. Realizing G as Gal(L/F) inside an S_n-extension is standard. So Lemma 2.3.5(b) is false whenever O_λ/λ ≠ 𝔽_ℓ is allowed. Reach: (L5-1) (p. 303) accepts assumption (b). Proposition 2.6.6 uses it via 'By Lemma 2.3.5, Res is injective', and so do the proofs of Theorems 8.2.2/8.3.2 (p. 310: 'By (L5-1) and Lemma 2.3.4'). Theorems 1.1.5/1.1.9 are therefore unproved for admissible λ with residue degree > 1 that satisfy only (b). Theorem 1.1.7 is safe: Lemma 8.1.5(2)'s Jordan-type argument works for ad(ρ)^{(σ)}, since twisting keeps the unipotent Jordan type and semisimplicity. Theorem 1.1.1 uses (a) through Proposition 2.7.2(1). Versions: identical in v1/v2 (Lemma 2.3.4) and v3.

issues.locator: Proposition 2.6.6, published pp. 134–135; arXiv v3 p. 20; arXiv v1/v2 Proposition 2.5.5, p. 19
issues.printed: The source asserts the existence of an (S, γ)-abundant r_S-tuple.
issues.correction: Add a hypothesis ensuring that the O_λ-span of θ_S(G_{S,γ}) contains λ^c Hom(S,(R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) with c independent of m. This is automatic if [F:F⁺] = 1, holds with c = 𝔣(r_S)r_{Ind R} if R_ℚ ≇ R_ℚ^𝔠, and holds if R extends to R₊ over F⁺ and S lies in the 𝔠-eigenspace on which γ acts on (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} by +1. In the application, choose γ, or separate γ's for the two places in rank one, adapted to the eigenspace decomposition of S.
issues.reason: Consequence of E1: in the example of E1 (F = ℚ(√5, i), ℓ = 3, R = ℤ₃(1), j = 2, S the Kummer class of u = (1+√5)/2 mod 3^m, γ = ρ̄₊^{(m)}(𝔠)) all four hypotheses hold (R_ℚ of rank one; −1 is a nontrivial scalar in the image of Γ_F in GL(R̄) = 𝔽₃^×; γ has order 2; (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} = R̄^{(m)} free of rank one), r_S = 1, m₀ = 0, and G_{S,γ} = {1}, so θ¹_{S,γ}(Ψ) = 0 for every Ψ ∈ G_{S,γ} and no tuple is abundant once m > 𝔣(1)r_R = r_R (r_R = 0 is admissible here since R has rank one). The printed proof is fine except for its appeal to Lemma 2.6.4. Independent check 1: Quotation checked on p. 134 (PDF p. 28): Prop. 2.6.6 asserts an (S,γ)-abundant r_S-tuple exists under: R_ℚ absolutely irreducible; Lemma 2.3.5(a) or (b); order of γ prime to ℓ; (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} free of rank 1. The proof (p. 135) derives this from Lemma 2.6.4. The example of E1 satisfies every hypothesis (see E1 for the §2.1–2.6 conventions): R_ℚ = ℚ₃(1) has rank one; ε̄(Γ_F) = 𝔽₃^× contains the nontrivial scalar −1; γ = ρ̄₊^{(m)}(𝔠) has order 2; h_γ = 1, so (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} = μ_{3^m} is free of rank 1; S = ℤ/3^m·κ(u) has m₀ = 0 and r_S = 1. Recomputed G_{S,γ} = {1}, so θ¹_{S,γ}(Ψ) = 0 for every Ψ ∈ G_{S,γ}. Its image cannot contain λ^{𝔣(1)r_R}Hom(S, R̄^{(m)}) ≠ 0 once m > r_R, and r_R depends only on R (r_R = 0 is admissible here). So the proposition is false for all large m. The proof's only faulty step is the appeal to Lemma 2.6.4. Instances inside the paper's own setting also exist. Take R = R₊|_{Γ_F}. If S lies in the ε-eigenspace and γ acts on (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} ⊂ R̄₊ by −ε, then loc_w(S) = 0 at every γ-associated place and no abundant element exists. If r_S = 2 and S = S₊ ⊕ S₋ meets both eigenspaces, then for every γ one summand is killed by all Ψ ∈ G_{S,γ}, so no γ admits an abundant pair. In the case R_ℚ ≇ R_ℚ^𝔠 the conclusion survives with r_R replaced by the reducibility depth of Ind_F^{F⁺}R (see E1). This item is a direct consequence of E1 and should be recorded as dependent on it (E1's 'affects' already names Prop. 2.6.6) to avoid double counting. Versions: v1/v2 Proposition 2.5.5 (with r_γ, proved from Lemma 2.5.4(2)); v3 is identical to the published text. Independent check 2: Quote checked on the page images: pp. 134–135 (PDF 28–29), 'Then (S, γ)-abundant r_S-tuple exists.' The proof's only nontrivial step is 'It follows from Lemma 2.6.4 …'. In the E1 example (F⁺ = ℚ(√5), F = ℚ(√5,i), ℓ = 3, R = ℤ₃(1), j = 2, μ_Ξ = 1, γ = ρ̄₊^{(m)}(𝔠), S = ⟨κ((1+√5)/2)⟩ mod 3^m), every hypothesis holds. R_ℚ has rank 1, so it is absolutely irreducible. Lemma 2.3.5(a) holds because the image of Γ_F in GL(R̄) = 𝔽₃^× is {±1}, as ζ₃ ∉ F. γ has order 2, prime to 3. (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} = R̄^{(m)} is free of rank 1. S is free of rank 1 over ℤ/3^m, with m₀ = 0. 𝔯_R = 0 here: R̄ is absolutely irreducible, and End(R̄^{(m)}) = O_λ/λ^m. So abundance would require θ_S(Ψ): S → R̄^{(m)} to be surjective. But G_{S,γ} = {1} (recomputed under E1), so θ_S(Ψ) = 0 for every Ψ ∈ G_{S,γ}. No abundant element exists, for every m ≥ 1 (for any bound 𝔯_R, once m > 𝔯_R). The rest of the printed proof (Lemmas 2.3.3–2.3.5, direct summand) is fine; the gap is only the appeal to Lemma 2.6.4. Within §8's own setting the proposition also fails. Suppose R_ℚ ≅ R_ℚ^𝔠 (base change, e.g. Theorem 1.1.1). For S in one 𝔠-eigenspace and γ of the 'wrong' sign, G_{S,γ} = {1}, while all four hypotheses hold by (L3), (L5-1) and Lemma 2.7.1. For S = ⟨s₊,s₋⟩ of rank 2, no abundant pair exists for any γ. An unconditional in-scope instance needs a nonzero H¹_{f,R}(F,R̄^{(m)}), e.g. the rank-one situation of Theorem 1.1.9 for a base-changed pair with △_λ ≠ 0. There H¹_f(F,R_ℚ) is one-dimensional, so its generator lies in a single eigenspace. I have not exhibited such a pair. Versions: v1/v2 Proposition 2.5.5 (with r_γ) relies on Lemma 2.5.4(2); v3 is identical to the published text. Reach to the main theorems: Proposition 2.6.6 is the step in the proofs of Theorem 8.2.2 ('By Proposition 2.6.6 (with m₀ = m_Σ and r_S = 1), we may fix an (S,γ)-abundant element', p. 310) and Theorem 8.3.2 (r_S = 2, p. 317). Here R = R₀⊗R₁, j = 1, and γ is an arbitrary element given by (L5-2). When R_ℚ ≇ R_ℚ^𝔠 the step can be justified with a modified constant. When R_ℚ ≅ R_ℚ^𝔠 it is unjustified, and false for one of the two sign classes of admissible γ. This case includes every instance of Theorem 1.1.1 (base change of Sym^{n₀−1}A₀ ⊗ Sym^{n₁−1}A₁ from F⁺) and base-change pairs in Theorems 1.1.5, 1.1.7 and 1.1.9. In rank one it can fail for every single γ when the Selmer group meets both eigenspaces. So the proofs of Theorems 1.1.1, 1.1.5, 1.1.7 and 1.1.9 have a gap in that case. The gap is repairable for Theorem 1.1.1 (for all but finitely many ℓ, a τ with ρ̄_{A₀}(τ) = −1, ρ̄_{A₁}(τ) = 1, ε̄(τ) = 1 flips the sign without changing (a)–(e)). For base-change pairs at general admissible λ it is not settled by the paper's hypotheses. No main theorem is shown false. Same reach as E1, since the proposition is the channel through which Lemma 2.6.4 enters §8. In 8.2.2 (r_S = 1), the proof fails for a hypothetical Selmer class lying in the 𝔠-eigenspace opposite to the arbitrarily chosen γ. This can happen whenever R_ℚ ≅ R_ℚ^𝔠, which includes all of Theorem 1.1.1. In 8.3.2 (r_S = 2), it fails for every γ when S has one class in each eigenspace, so the single-γ scheme of the paper (𝔭₁ and 𝔭₂ both γ-associated) cannot work. Two γ's of opposite signs are needed. For Theorem 1.1.1 both signs are available when ℓ ≫ 0, so it survives with a modified proof. For 1.1.5 and 1.1.9 at arbitrary admissible λ, and for 1.1.7 via Lemma 8.1.4 (one Frobenius element), the base-change case needs an extra hypothesis or argument supplying a γ of the other sign. For R_ℚ ≇ R_ℚ^𝔠, a version with a bounded loss is plausible but unproved. No main theorem is shown false. Reach: a stated result (Proposition 2.6.6). It is used in the proofs of Theorems 8.2.2 (r_S = 1) and 8.3.2 (r_S = 2).).

issues.locator: §2.7, paragraph before Proposition 2.7.2, published pp. 136–137; arXiv v3 p. 21; arXiv v1 p. 21
issues.printed: For a rational prime ℓ odd and unramified in F, the source defines R_α := (Sym^{n_α−1}_{ℤ_ℓ} H¹_ét(A_{αF̄}, ℤ_ℓ))(r_α) for α = 0, 1 as a ℤ_ℓ[Γ_F]-module. It places R_α in Mod(F, ℤ_ℓ)_fr with rank n_α and describes Ξ_α: R_α^𝔠 ⥲ R_α^∨(1 − α) as its canonical (1 − α)-polarization.
issues.correction: Require ℓ ⩾ n_α (sufficient; then all C(n_α−1, a) are ℓ-units), e.g. 'for ℓ > n₁'.
issues.reason: The polarization is induced from the Weil pairing on H¹ (a perfect alternating pairing on a rank-two lattice T); on Sym^k T the induced pairing pairs x^a y^{k−a} with x^{k−a}y^a by ±a!(k−a)! (or ±1/binom(k,a) if normalized), which is not a unit when ℓ ⩽ k = n_α − 1. Then Sym^k T and its dual (a divided-power lattice) are not homothetic Galois lattices when the image is large (e.g. ℓ = 3, n_α ⩾ 4), so no (1−α)-polarization of R_α exists. Defence: only large ℓ are used. Independent check: Text checked on the images of pp. 136–137: 'For a rational prime ℓ (that is odd and unramified in F) … R_α is an object in Mod(F, ℤ_ℓ)_fr of rank n_α with a canonical (1 − α)-polarization'. A_α is defined over F⁺, so R_α^𝔠 ≅ R_α. A (1−α)-polarization therefore amounts to Sym^k H¹ ≅ Γ^k H¹ as Γ_F-lattices, where k = n_α − 1; the twists match via the Weil pairing. Both are lattices in Sym^k V. For non-CM A_α the image of Γ_F is open in GL₂(ℤ_ℓ), so Sym^k V is absolutely irreducible, and an isomorphism would have to be a homothety. With the basis x^a y^{k−a}, the natural map to the divided powers is multiplication by a!(k−a)!. So the lattices are homothetic iff every binomial coefficient C(k,a) is prime to ℓ. That holds for k < ℓ and fails for ℓ ⩽ k ⩽ 2ℓ−2; examples are ℓ = 3 with n₀ = 4 (C(3,1) = 3) or n₁ = 5 (C(4,2) = 6). The first reading's 'ℓ = 3, n_α ⩾ 4' is slightly too broad. For n_α = 6 every C(5,a) is prime to 3, so a polarization exists; the same happens whenever k = dℓ^e − 1. Only large ℓ are used (Proposition 2.7.2, Lemma 8.1.3). Versions: same text in v1 and v3.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 2.7.2(3), published p. 137; arXiv v3 p. 22; arXiv v1/v2 proof of Proposition 2.6.3(3), pp. 21–22
issues.printed: The proof chooses g ∈ Γ_F with image under (ρ̄_{A₀,ℓ}, ρ̄_{A₁,ℓ}, ε̄_ℓ) conjugate to ((a 0; 0 1), (ab 0; 0 b^{−1}), a^{−1}). For a, b ∈ 𝔽_ℓ^× it requires 𝒫(a^{−1}) ≠ 0; for (i, j) ∈ {r₀, …, 1−r₀} × {r₁, …, −r₁}, excluding (0, 0), (a^{2i}(ab²)^{2j})^{[F′:F⁺]} ≠ 1; for i ∈ {r₀, r₀−1, …, 1−r₀}, (a^{2i−1})^{[F′:F⁺]} ≠ −1; for j ∈ {r₁, r₁−1, …, −r₁}, (a(ab²)^{2j})^{[F′:F⁺]} ≠ −1. It claims that (ρ̄₀₊, ρ̄₁₊, ε̄_ℓ) sends g^{[F′:F⁺]}𝔠 to an image satisfying Lemma 2.7.1(a–e).
issues.correction: Put t := [F′:F⁺], y := g^t𝔠. Then ξ = ε̄_ℓ(y) = −a^{−t} and h_{γ_α} = ρ̄_α(y²) = (ρ̄⁺_α(y))², which depends on the position of ρ̄(g) relative to ρ̄⁺(𝔠). Choose g (possible since the image of Γ_F is {det g₀ = det g₁}) with ρ̄_{A_α}(g) diagonal as displayed in bases in which complex conjugation acts by diag(1, −1). Then h_{γ₀} has eigenvalues a^{2ti} (1−r₀ ⩽ i ⩽ r₀) and h_{γ₁} has eigenvalues (ab²)^{2tj} (|j| ⩽ r₁), and (a)–(e) become: 𝒫(−a^{−t}) ≠ 0; (a^{2i}(ab²)^{2j})^t ≠ 1 for (i,j) ≠ (0,0) (as printed); (a^{2i})^t ≠ −1 for 1−r₀ ⩽ i ⩽ r₀; (a(ab²)^{2j})^t ≠ 1 for |j| ⩽ r₁. Such (a, b) exist for ℓ ≫ 0 when 𝒫 ≠ 0, so (3) holds (with E4).
issues.reason: With the diagonal choice, ρ̄⁺_{A₀}(y) = diag(a^t, −1), ρ̄⁺_{A₁}(y) = diag((ab)^t, −b^{−t}), ε̄_ℓ(y) = −a^{−t}; on Sym^{2r₀−1}(r₀) resp. Sym^{2r₁}(r₁) the squares give the eigenvalues above (the printed second bullet matches them). The printed first, third and fourth bullets do not: e.g. r₀ = r₁ = 1, t = 1, 𝒫 = T² − 1: (i) a of order 4 and b⁴ ∉ {±1, ±a} satisfy all printed bullets, but h_{γ₀} has eigenvalue a^{−2} = −1, violating (d); (ii) a ∉ μ₃ ∪ μ₄ ∪ {±1} with b⁴ = a^{−1} satisfies all printed bullets, but h_{γ₁} has eigenvalue (ab²)^{−2} = a^{−1} = −ξ, violating (e). Moreover, fixing ρ̄(g) only up to conjugacy does not determine h_γ: if complex conjugation swaps the two eigenlines of ρ̄_{A₀}(g), then ρ̄⁺_{A₀}(y)² = a^t·I, h_{γ₀} = a^{−t}·I and (c) fails. Defence: the statement is true and the repair is routine; the second bullet (the multiplicity-one condition) is right, and for 𝒫 = T² − 1 the first bullet is harmless. Independent check: The bullets and 'conjugacy class' were checked on the image of p. 137. Put t = [F′:F⁺] and y = g^t𝔠. Then ξ = ε̄_ℓ(y) = −a^{−t}, because ε̄_ℓ(𝔠) = −1. Also h_{γ_α} = ρ̄_α(y²), independent of the polarization matrix B, since y² ∈ Γ_F. Choose ρ̄_{A_α}(g) diagonal in eigenbases where ρ̄_{A_α}(𝔠) = diag(1,−1); this is possible because the image is all of {det g₀ = det g₁ = ξ^{−1}} and is conjugation-stable. Then h_{γ₀} has eigenvalues a^{2ti} for −r₀ ⩽ i ⩽ r₀−1 and h_{γ₁} has eigenvalues (ab²)^{2tj} for |j| ⩽ r₁. My sign convention gives i ↦ −i relative to the first reading's range 1−r₀ ⩽ i ⩽ r₀; every condition (a)–(e) is invariant under inverting the eigenvalues, so this is immaterial. The printed second bullet is right. The first, third and fourth bullets do not match (a), (d), (e): they should read 𝒫(−a^{−t}) ≠ 0, a^{2ti} ≠ −1 and (a(ab²)^{2j})^t ≠ 1. I checked both counterexamples by hand for r₀ = r₁ = t = 1 and 𝒫 = T²−1. (i) a of order 4 with b⁴ ∉ {±1, ±a} satisfies every printed bullet, yet a² = −1 is an eigenvalue of h_{γ₀}, violating (d). (ii) With b⁴ = a^{−1} and a ∉ μ₄ ∪ μ₃, all printed bullets hold, yet (ab²)^{−2} = a^{−1} = −ξ, violating (e). The conjugacy class alone also does not determine h_{γ₀}: if 𝔠 swaps the eigenlines, then ρ̄_{A₀}(y²) = a^t·I and h_{γ₀} is scalar, so (c) fails. The statement survives, with the corrected conditions, for ℓ ≫ 0 when 𝒫 ≠ 0. Versions: same in v1 (Prop. 2.6.3) and v3.

issues.locator: Remark 3.1.6(2),(3), published p. 140; arXiv v3 p. 24; v1 p. 23
issues.printed: The source interprets (2) as excluding {−‖v‖, −‖v‖−1} from α, and (3) as requiring exactly one occurrence of {‖v‖, ‖v‖−1} in α.
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis ‖v‖² ≠ 1 in L (for (2) it is enough that ‖v‖ ≠ −1 in L).
issues.reason: Let L be a field with char L ≠ 2 and P = P_α unitary. Write P = (T−1)^k R with R(1) ≠ 0. The identity P(T) = (−T)^N P(T^{−1}) gives R(1) = (−1)^{N+k}R(1), so k ≡ N (mod 2); likewise the multiplicity of −1 is even. (3) If ‖v‖ = 1 in L (N even), then 'P(‖v‖) = 0 and P′(‖v‖) invertible' would make 1 a simple root, which is impossible. Yet the pair {1, 1} can appear exactly once: for example ‖v‖ = 7, L = 𝔽_3, N = 2, α = {1, 1}. (2) If ‖v‖ = −1 in L (N odd), then P(−‖v‖) = P(1) = 0 always, so P is never intertwining generic. Yet the pair {1, 1} can be absent: for example N = 1, α = {1}. (1), (4) and the last sentence of the remark are correct. Defence: the remark is an 'easy to see' aside. In every use ‖v‖² ≠ 1 in L: (P2)/(PI2) require ℓ ∤ p(p² − 1) for L = O_E/λ, and Proposition C.2.5 works over ℂ. Independent check: Remark 3.1.6 checked on the image of p. 140. For unitary P with char L ≠ 2, write P = (T∓1)^k R. The functional equation forces the multiplicity of 1 to be ≡ N (mod 2) and the multiplicity of −1 to be even. (3): if ‖v‖ = ±1 in L (N even), the root ‖v‖ always has even multiplicity. So 'P(‖v‖) = 0, P′(‖v‖) invertible' never holds, although the pair can occur exactly once; for example L = 𝔽₃, ‖v‖ = 7, α = {1,1}. (2): if ‖v‖ = −1 in L (N odd), then P(−‖v‖) = P(1) = 0 always, while the pair {1,1} can be absent; for example N = 1, α = {1}. Items (1), (4) and the last sentence are correct, and (2), (3) are correct when ‖v‖² ≠ 1. Uses: the remark is cited only in Proposition C.2.5, over ℂ with q > 1. issues.locator: Construction 3.1.10, published p. 142; arXiv v3 p. 25; v1 p. 25
issues.printed: The source claims that Π ∘ c ≃ Π∨ implies unitarity of the Satake parameter α(Πv) whenever v ∉ Σ+Π.
issues.correction: Assume in addition that the central character ω_Π is trivial on 𝔸_{F^+}^× (true for relevant Π). In general only α(Π_v) = α(Π_v)^{−1} as multisets holds, and at an inert v the product of the entries equals ω_Π(ϖ_v) = ±1.
issues.reason: At an unramified inert v, Π_w ∘ c ≃ Π_w^∨ and c(ϖ_v) = ϖ_v give α(Π_v) = α(Π_v)^{−1} as multisets. Hence (−T)^N P_α(T^{−1}) = (∏α_i)^{−1}P_α(T) with ∏α_i = ω_{Π_w}(ϖ_v). Since ω_Π ∘ c = ω_Π^{−1}, the restriction ω_Π|_{𝔸_{F^+}^×} is quadratic and trivial on norms, so it equals 1 or η_{F/F^+}; in the second case ω(ϖ_v) = −1 and α(Π_v) is not unitary. Explicit counterexample: N = 1, Π = χ a Hecke character of 𝔸_F^×/F^× extending η_{F/F^+} (it exists by Pontryagin duality). Then χ·χ^c = η ∘ Nm = 1, so χ ∘ c = χ^{−1}, but α(χ_v) = {−1} at every inert unramified v, and T + 1 ≠ (−T)(T^{−1} + 1). Defence: the construction is used only for relevant Π. There Definition 1.1.3(3) makes the archimedean central character arg^{Σ(N+1−2i)} = 1, which is incompatible with η_{F/F^+} (the sign character at each real place), so ω_Π|_{𝔸_{F^+}^×} = 1 and the claim holds. Independent check: Construction 3.1.10 checked on the image of p. 142, with Π cuspidal on GL_N(𝔸_F) (p. 138). At an inert unramified v, c(ϖ_v) = ϖ_v and Π∘c ≃ Π^∨ give α = α^{−1} as multisets. Hence (−T)^N P_α(T^{−1}) = (∏α_i)P_α(T), and unitarity (Definition 3.1.3(1)) is equivalent to ω_Π(ϖ_v) = 1. ω_Π restricted to 𝔸_{F⁺}^× is quadratic and trivial on norms, so it is 1 or η_{F/F⁺}. The counterexample works: χ extending η_{F/F⁺} exists by Pontryagin duality and is unramified almost everywhere by continuity. It satisfies χ∘c = χ^{−1}, and α(χ_v) = {−1} is not unitary for N = 1, since that would force α = {1}. For relevant Π (Definition 1.1.3(3)), the archimedean central character is arg^{Σ(N+1−2i)} = 1. This excludes η, which is the sign character at real places, so the claim holds wherever the construction is used. Versions: same in v1 and v3.

issues.locator: Remark 3.2.6 (second sentence), published p. 145; arXiv v3 p. 27; v1 p. 27
issues.printed: The source asserts, assuming Hypothesis 3.2.10, that Q(Π) serves as a strong coefficient field for Π whenever Π ≃ BC(π) and the standard pair (V, π) of Definition 3.2.7 has standard indefinite V.
issues.correction: Either add the hypothesis that ρ_{Π,ι_ℓ} is irreducible for every ι_ℓ and give the descent argument, or delete the sentence. It is never used: all results take a strong coefficient field E as given, and one exists by [16, Proposition 3.2.5].
issues.reason: Hypothesis 3.2.10 only says something when ρ_{BC(π),ι_ℓ} is irreducible, which the remark does not assume and which is not known in general for relevant Π. Even granting irreducibility, the natural Q(Π)_λ-rational object is the φ_Π-eigenpart M of H^{N−1}_ét(Sh(V,K)_{F̄}, Q(Π)_λ). By the hypothesis, M ⊗ ℚ̄_ℓ ≃ (ρ^c)^{⊕d}, and ρ^c is defined over Q(Π)_λ only if the central simple algebra End_{Γ_F}(M) splits. The remark gives no argument for this. Defence: the claim is plausible (for instance, a Frobenius with an eigenvalue of multiplicity one in Q(Π)_λ would split it), and nothing depends on it.

issues.locator: Proposition 3.2.11 and its proof, published p. 146; reference [37], p. 374; arXiv v3 p. 28; v1 p. 27 (Proposition 3.2.10)
issues.printed: Proposition 3.2.11 asserts Hypothesis 3.2.10 for N ⩽ 3, and also for N > 3 provided F+ ≠ Q. Its proof assigns the case N ⩾ 3 with F+ ≠ Q to the forthcoming [37], listed as a work in preparation by Kisin, M., Shin, S.W., Zhu, Y., with a provisional title concerning cohomology of particular Shimura varieties of abelian type.
issues.correction: State the cases N ⩾ 3 with F⁺ ≠ ℚ of Proposition 3.2.11 as conditional on [37] (or on Hypothesis 3.2.10). Carry that condition into Corollaries 8.2.3 and 8.2.5 and into Theorems 1.1.1, 1.1.5, 1.1.7 and 1.1.9 for every n ⩾ 2: they all assume F⁺ ≠ ℚ and use N = n₁ ⩾ 3, not only n ⩾ 3.
issues.reason: For N > 3 the proposition is proved only by a forward reference to a work that the bibliography lists as 'in preparation' with a temporary title. Nothing in the paper establishes it. It is used as a known input: the proof of Corollary 8.2.3 (p. 314) says 'By Proposition 3.2.11 and (c), Hypothesis 3.2.10 is known in this case'. Remark 1.1.10 (p. 113) explains that the assumption F^+ ≠ ℚ for n ≥ 3 in Theorems 1.1.5 and 1.1.9 is there because Hypothesis 3.2.10 is known for N ≥ 4 only when F^+ ≠ ℚ. Defence: the dependence is stated openly. Whether the later Kisin–Shin–Zhu work establishes exactly Hypothesis 3.2.10 in this generality was not checked here. Independent check: Checked on the image of p. 146 and in the bibliography, p. 374: '[37] Kisin, M., Shin, S.W., Zhu, Y.: Cohomology of certain Shimura varieties of abelian type (temporary title) (in preparation)'. The proof says 'The case for N ⩾ 3 when F⁺ ≠ ℚ will be proved in [37]', so N = 3 with F⁺ ≠ ℚ is deferred too; [64], Rogawski's Picard-surface work, covers only F⁺ = ℚ. Theorems 8.2.2/8.3.2 assume Hypothesis 3.2.10 for n and n+1 and are fine as conditional statements. The unconditional results take the hypothesis from Proposition 3.2.11: Corollary 8.2.3 on p. 314 ('By Proposition 3.2.11 and (c), Hypothesis 3.2.10 is known'), Corollary 8.2.5, and Theorems 1.1.1, 1.1.5, 1.1.7 and 1.1.9. All of these assume F⁺ ≠ ℚ and need N = n₁ ⩾ 3, so each depends on [37] for every n ⩾ 2, including n = 2. The KSZ paper that did appear (arXiv:2110.05381, 'The stable trace formula for Shimura varieties of abelian type') proves only a Frobenius–Hecke trace formula. Its §0.2 says: 'We intend to work out the details in a sequel', and lists LTXZZ among the intended applications. So it does not itself establish Hypothesis 3.2.10.

issues.locator: Definition 3.3.4, footnote 11, published p. 147; arXiv v3 p. 28 (footnote 11)
issues.printed: The source gives an equivalent criterion: [F+q : Qp] must be odd for each prime q above p in F+ that remains inert in F.
issues.correction: Delete the footnote or replace it with a correct criterion. Let M be the Galois closure of F, σ the Frobenius at 𝔭 (for ι_p inducing 𝔭), and H ⊆ Gal(M/ℚ) the subgroup generated by the stabilizers of the CM types of F. Then 𝔭 is very special inert iff σc ∈ H. The footnote's condition is equivalent to something else: that some CM type Φ ∋ τ_∞ satisfies σ²Φ = Φ, i.e. ℚ_p^Φ = ℚ_{p²}, which is condition (P3)/(PI3) of §§6–7.
issues.reason: (i) The footnote's condition does not imply very special. Take F = ℚ(√(−(3+√2))) (minimal polynomial x⁴ + 6x² + 7, Galois group D_4, F^+ = ℚ(√2)) and p = 17. Then 17 = 𝔭𝔮 in F^+, with √2 ≡ 6 at 𝔭. At 𝔭, −3 + √2 ≡ 3 is a non-square mod 17, so 𝔭 is inert in F. At 𝔮, −3 + √2 ≡ 8 = 5², so 𝔮 splits in F. 17 is odd and unramified in F (the polynomial discriminant is 2^{10}·7), and 𝔭 has degree 1, so 𝔭 is special inert. The only prime above 17 that is inert in F is 𝔭, of odd degree 1, so the footnote declares 𝔭 very special. But the CM types of F are primitive with reflex fields of real quadratic subfield ℚ(√7) (√7 = √(−3+√2)·√(−3−√2)), so ⋂_Φ F_Φ = ℚ(√7). Hence F_rflx = F(√7) = M and F^+_rflx = ℚ(√2, √7). Since (7/17) = −1, 𝔭 is inert in F^+_rflx/F^+ and is not very special. (ii) Very special does not imply the footnote's condition. Take F a CM octic field with Gal(M/ℚ) = W(B_4) = (ℤ/2)^4 ⋊ S_4 (a generic F = F^+(√−δ) with F^+ an S_4-quartic). Then H = {(ε, π) : Σε_i even}, which has index 2 and contains c, so 𝔭 is very special iff the number of primes of F^+ above p that are inert in F is even. A Frobenius σ = ((1,1,0,0), (2 3)) (it exists by Chebotarev) gives 𝔭 inert of degree 1, 𝔮 inert of degree 2 and 𝔮′ split of degree 1. There are two inert primes, so 𝔭 is very special, but 𝔮 has even degree. Moreover σ² interchanges τ and τ^c for the embeddings above 𝔮, so no CM type is σ²-stable and (P3) fails. Defence: no proof uses the footnote. Lemma 8.1.4 uses only 'φ_𝔭 ∈ Gal(F̄/F^+_rflx)', which is the definition. In the cases of Remark 1.1.8 (F Galois or containing an imaginary quadratic field) the definition and the footnote both reduce to 'special inert'. The footnote does mislead anyone checking hypothesis (a) of Theorem 1.1.7. Independent check: Footnote 11 and the definitions were checked on the image of p. 147. Let M be the Galois closure of F, σ the Frobenius at 𝔭, and H = ⟨Stab Φ⟩, which is normal. Then Gal(M/F_rflx) = Gal(M/F) ∩ H, so a special inert 𝔭 is very special iff σc ∈ H. The footnote's condition is equivalent to the existence of Φ ∋ τ_∞ with σ²Φ = Φ, i.e. (P3). I checked all of this by machine: I enumerated every σ with σ(τ_∞) = τ_∞^c in D₄ and in W(B₄). There the footnote condition is always equivalent to (P3), while 'very special' differs in both directions. (i) D₄: x⁴+6x²+7 has discriminant 2¹⁰·7. Mod 17 it factors as (x−5)(x+5)(x²−3), H = V₄ ∋ c, and ⋂F_Φ = ℚ(√7). Since (7/17) = −1, the degree-one prime inert in F is not very special, though it meets the footnote. Small slip: for F = ℚ(√(−(3+√2))), the inert prime is the one with √2 ≡ −6 mod 17 (−3−√2 ≡ 3); at √2 ≡ 6, −3−√2 ≡ 8 = 5², which splits. The conclusion is unchanged after relabelling. (ii) Explicit W(B₄) instance: F⁺ = ℚ(α) with α⁴−4α²−α+1 = 0, which is totally real with disc 1957 and group S₄, and F = F⁺(√−(α+4)). Since N(α+4) = 197 is not a square in ℚ(√1957), Gal = W(B₄); Frobenius cycle-type frequencies for p < 20000 match. H is the even-sign subgroup, M^H = ℚ(√197) and F⁺_rflx = F⁺(√197). At p = 43, f ≡ (x−3)(x−11)·(quadratic), and the degree-8 polynomial has type [1,1,2,4]. 𝔭 = (43, α−11) is special inert, since −(α+4) ≡ 28 is a non-square, and it splits in F⁺_rflx because 197 ≡ 5² mod 43. So 𝔭 is very special, but the degree-2 prime above 43 is inert in F: the footnote fails, and no CM type Φ ∋ τ_∞ has ℚ_43^Φ = ℚ_{43²}. No proof cites the footnote. Versions: absent in v1/v2; present in v3 (composite definition), where example (i) still refutes it.
searched: arXiv:1912.11942 v1 (December 2019), v2 and v3 (August 2021) at the same place: v1 and v2 (p. 28) have no footnote. v3 p. 28 has the same footnote attached to the v3 definition (F_rflx generated by F and all F_Φ; 𝔭 very special iff some 𝔭′ | 𝔭 of F^+_rflx has degree one). Example (i) refutes it there too, since in that example the v3 F^+_rflx is also ℚ(√2, √7).

issues.locator: Definition 3.3.2, published p. 147 (and its use in Definition 8.1.1 (L5-2), p. 303, and in the choice of 𝔭 in the proofs of Theorem 8.2.2, p. 310, and Theorem 8.3.2, pp. 318–319); arXiv v3 p. 28
issues.printed: It calls Frflx the reflexive closure of F: inside C, this is the field generated by F together with the intersection of the fields FΦ as Φ ranges over the CM types of F.
issues.correction: Make the Chebotarev choice in §8 give (PI3). Options: (1) restore the v1–v3 composite, and correct Remarks 1.1.8 and 3.3.3 for non-Galois F. (2) Define F_rflx := F·F̃_{Φ₀}, where F̃_{Φ₀} is the Galois closure of the reflex field of one fixed CM type Φ₀. Then Frob_𝔭 fixing F⁺_rflx gives σ_𝔭 = c·h with h stabilizing Φ₀ and cΦ₀, hence σ_𝔭² does too, which is (PI3). This keeps F_rflx = F when F is Galois or contains an imaginary quadratic field K (take Φ₀ induced from K). (3) Keep the definition, add Frob_𝔭|_M = c to the Chebotarev conditions, and prove compatibility, e.g. M ∩ F⁺^{(m)}F_S ⊆ F_rflx. Options (1) and (2) narrow 'admissible' and 'very special'.
issues.reason: In the proof of Theorem 8.2.2 (p. 310), γ is taken in the image of Gal(F̄/F^+_rflx) by (L5-2), and then 'by the Chebotarev density theorem' a γ-associated place is chosen whose prime 𝔭 is special inert and satisfies (PI1)–(PI7). Condition (PI3) (p. 287) requires a CM type Φ ∋ τ_∞ with ℚ_p^Φ = ℚ_{p²}, i.e. σ_𝔭² ∈ Stab(Φ). The same choice is made on pp. 318–319. Under the published definition, Frob_𝔭 ∈ Gal(F̄/F^+_rflx) only gives σ_𝔭c ∈ H (the group generated by the CM-type stabilizers), and example (ii) of the footnote-11 issue gives such 𝔭 with no σ²-stable CM type. In addition, a γ-associated place is constrained only on F^{(m)}_+ and F_S, so its Frobenius on M must be imposed separately, and the paper does not address whether that is compatible. Under the v1–v3 definition, a lift of γ to Gal(F̄/F^+_rflx) = Gal(F̄/M^+) acts on M as c, so (PI3) is automatic. Defence: if F is Galois or contains an imaginary quadratic field (Remark 1.1.8), every special inert prime satisfies (PI3). For generic data M is linearly disjoint from F^{(m)}_+F_S over F, and Frob_𝔭|_M = c can be imposed. Independent check: Checked on the images of p. 147 (intersection definition), p. 303 ((L5-2) with F′ = F⁺_rflx), p. 287 ((PI3)) and pp. 310, 318–319. There γ is taken in the image of Gal(F̄/F⁺_rflx), and 'by the Chebotarev density theorem' a γ-associated special inert 𝔭 satisfying (PI1)–(PI7) is chosen; then 'remaining data in Sect. 5.1 with ℚ_p^Φ = ℚ_{p²}'. F_rflx enters the paper only through (L5-2), Lemma 8.1.4 and these choices of γ, so its only role is to deliver (PI3)/(PII3). No hypothesis of Theorems 8.2.2/8.3.2 supplies (PI3) otherwise: not the §7.1 setup, not Hypothesis 3.2.10, not (L1)–(L7). The implicit argument makes Frob_𝔭 fix F⁺_rflx, which is compatible with γ because γ comes from Gal(F̄/F⁺_rflx). Under the published intersection this only gives σ_𝔭 ∈ c·(Gal(M/F) ∩ H), which does not imply (PI3). The explicit W(B₄) field of E31 shows this: 𝔭 = (43, α−11) splits in F⁺_rflx = F⁺(√197), yet no CM type satisfies ℚ_43^Φ = ℚ_{43²}. Chebotarev gives such Frobenius classes a positive density inside the set the argument allows. Under v1–v3, F_rflx is the composite of F and all F_Φ, which equals M since only the identity fixes every CM type. There Frob_𝔭 ∈ Gal(F̄/M⁺) gives σ_𝔭 = c, so (PI3) is automatic. Imposing Frob_𝔭|_M = c directly is compatible when M ∩ F⁺^{(m)}F_S ⊆ F_rflx, e.g. for linearly disjoint (generic) data. It is not implied by (L1)–(L7) in general: if M ⊆ F⁺^{(m)}, then γ fixes Frob|_M. So a full repair may require narrowing (L5-2) and 'very special'. Versions: v1–v3 use the composite, and the change appears only in the published version, together with footnote 11.
searched: arXiv:1912.11942 v1 (December 2019), v2 and v3 (August 2021) at the same place: v1, v2 (p. 28) and v3 (p. 28) define F_rflx as 'the subfield of C generated by F and F_Φ for every CM type Φ of F'. With that definition Remark 3.3.3's 'F contains an imaginary quadratic field ⇒ F_rflx = F' is false for non-Galois F, which is presumably why the published version switched to the intersection.

issues.locator: Lemma 3.4.12 (hypotheses) and proof of (2), published pp. 153, 155; arXiv v3 p. 32; v1 p. 31 (Lemma 3.4.13)
issues.printed: The lemma assumes F+ lies in Qp through τ: F+ ↪ C ≃ Q̄p, and takes p to be the resulting p-adic prime. In proving (2), it uses s = dimκ(ωB∨/κ,τc∞) = dimκ VD(B)τ∞ / pD(B)τc∞.
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis that 𝔭 is inert in F, and read τ as τ̲_∞. For (2), argue directly: Lie_{B,τ_∞} = 𝒟(B)_{τ_∞}/𝚅𝒟(B)_{στ_∞}, so s − r = ℓ(𝒟(B)_{τ_∞}/𝒟(A)_{τ_∞}) − ℓ(𝒟(B)_{στ_∞}/𝒟(A)_{στ_∞}), and στ_∞ = τ_∞^c for 𝔭 inert. This needs no polarization.
issues.reason: As stated, 𝔭 may split in F, and then (2) fails. Take F^+ = ℚ, F imaginary quadratic with p = w_1w_2 split, ϖ = p, E an ordinary elliptic curve over 𝔽̄_p with O_F-action, A = E, B = E/E[w_1], α the quotient map and β: B → E/E[p] ≅ E, so that βα = p. With τ_∞ corresponding to w_1, α_{*,τ_∞} = 0 and α_{*,τ_∞^c} is an isomorphism, so the right side of (2) is 1 − 0 = 1. But B[w^∞] ≅ E[w^∞] for both w, so the Lie ranks agree and the left side is 0. The proof uses σ^{−1}τ_∞^c = τ_∞, i.e. 𝔭 inert. Separately, its first equality s = dim ω_{B^∨,τ_∞^c} needs dim Lie_{B,τ_∞} + dim Lie_{B,τ_∞^c} = rank H^dR_1(B)_{τ_∞^c}, which holds for unitary schemes (a compatible polarization makes B[𝔭^∞] isogenous to its dual) but is not assumed in (2). Parts (1), (3) and (4) are fine; the degree computation in (3)/(4) was checked. Defence: every application (pp. 168, 170, 197, 202, 206, 210) has 𝔭 special inert and unitary A, B, and S ∈ Sch_{/𝔽_{p²}} points to the inert case. Independent check: Lemma 3.4.12 checked on the images of pp. 153–155. The hypotheses only require F⁺_𝔭 = ℚ_p, not that 𝔭 is inert in F. Split counterexample: F⁺ = ℚ, p = w₁w₂, A = E ordinary with O_F-action, B = E/E[w₁], β∘α = [p]. On Dieudonné modules α_{*,τ_∞} ≡ 0 and α_{*,τ_∞^c} is an isomorphism, so the right side of (2) is 1. But B[w^∞] ≅ E[w^∞] for both w, so the Lie ranks agree and the left side is 0. The proof's step 'ω_{B^∨,τ_∞^c} = V𝒟(B)_{τ_∞}/p𝒟(B)_{τ_∞^c}' uses στ_∞^c = τ_∞; by Notation 3.4.10(3) this holds only for 𝔭 inert. I checked the first reading's polarization-free argument: s − r = ℓ(𝒟(B)_τ/𝒟(A)_τ) − ℓ(𝒟(B)_{στ}/𝒟(A)_{στ}), and ℓ(𝒟(B)_τ/𝒟(A)_τ) = dim ker α_{*,τ} because p𝒟(B)_τ ⊆ 𝒟(A)_τ. With στ = τ^c this gives (2). In the split case στ = τ, which gives 0, consistent with the counterexample. All six uses (pp. 168, 170, 197, 202, 206, 210) sit in §§4–5, where 𝔭 is special inert (§4.1). Versions: same in v1 (Lemma 3.4.13) and v3.

issues.locator: Theorem 4.3.5(2) and its proof, published pp. 166, 168; used in the proof of Proposition 4.5.5, p. 180; arXiv v1 p. 40 (Theorem 4.2.5(2)) and p. 50, v3 p. 41 and p. 50
issues.printed: Part (2) asserts that ι restricted to B_{s⋆} is a closed immersion locally on B_{s⋆}, with a canonical normal-bundle identification. The proof calls the map injective and identifies its cokernel with ℋom(ω_{𝒜^∨,τ∞}, im α_{*,τ∞}), concluding (2). On p. 180, Theorem 4.3.5 is cited to assert that ι_sp is a closed immersion Zariski locally on its source.
issues.correction: (2) The restriction of ι to B_{s⋆} is unramified (i.e. étale-locally on B_{s⋆} a closed immersion), with normal bundle ℋom(ω_{𝒜^∨,τ∞}, im α_{*,τ∞}); it is a closed immersion when it is injective on geometric points, e.g. when K^p is sufficiently small (Remark 4.3.6).
issues.reason: The proof only shows that the tangent map T_{B_{s⋆}} → ι^*T_M is injective, i.e. that ι|B_{s⋆} is unramified. Zariski-locally a closed immersion fails whenever ι|B_{s⋆} is not injective on geometric points: B_{s⋆} is proper and irreducible (Theorem 4.3.5(3)), so any Zariski open U ∋ x is dense and ι(U) ∩ V must equal ι(B_{s⋆}) ∩ V for ι|U to be a closed immersion into an open V; if x′ ≠ x has ι(x′) = ι(x) = y, then ι(B_{s⋆}) has two branches at y (or ι is generically non-injective), while U is smooth at x, so U → ι(B_{s⋆}) ∩ V is not an isomorphism. Non-injectivity does occur: for N = 3 each superspecial point of M_𝔭 lies on p + 1 components ι(B_{s⋆}) indexed by the p + 1 neighbouring vertex lattices, and these p + 1 lattices give points of S_𝔭(V, K^p)(F̄_p) over one point of T_𝔭(F̄_p), a set in bijection with Sh(V⋆, (iK^p)K⋆_p) (Proposition 4.4.4); if p + 1 exceeds |Sh(V⋆, (iK^p)K⋆_p)|, two of them coincide and the corresponding B_{s⋆} passes twice through the superspecial point. Remark 4.3.6 (closed immersion for K^p sufficiently small) is consistent with this. Defence: 'locally' can be read étale-locally, which is what the proof gives; every later use (pure codimension ⌊N/2⌋, the normal bundle, the Gysin maps ι_! in Construction 4.4.9, transversality in Theorem 4.6.2) needs only unramifiedness, and in Proposition 4.5.5 the reduction still works: an unramified morphism from a smooth scheme that is bijective on geometric points and on tangent spaces is étale and universally injective, hence an isomorphism. Independent check: Quotation checked on pp. 166, 168, 180 (and Remark 4.3.6, p. 169: closed immersion only 'when K^p is sufficiently small'). The proof of (2) only shows T_{B_{s⋆}} → ι^*T_M injective, i.e. ι|B_{s⋆} unramified; p. 180 then uses (2) as 'locally for the Zariski topology on the source a closed immersion'. That reading is false as soon as ι|B_{s⋆} is not injective on geometric points. Independent proof: let x ≠ x′ in B := B_{s⋆} (over κ = F̄_p) with ι(x) = ι(x′) = y, and suppose U ∋ x is open with ι|U an immersion onto Z. B is proper and irreducible, so U is dense, Z is open in the closed set ι(B), Z = ι(B) ∩ V with V ⊆ M open, and W := B ∩ ι^{-1}(V) → Z is proper. The inverse Z ≅ U ⊆ W is a section of the separated map W → Z, so U is closed in W; it is also open and W is irreducible, hence U = W ∋ x′, contradicting injectivity of U → Z. Non-injectivity occurs: for N = 3 (Vollaard–Wedhorn picture) each superspecial point lies on p + 1 curves ι(B_{s⋆}) indexed by the p + 1 neighbouring vertex lattices, which share the prime-to-p component; if two are equivalent under U(V⋆)(F⁺) (γΛ₁ = Λ₂, γ ≠ 1 by neatness), the curve of Λ₁ passes through the superspecial point twice (at v and γ^{-1}v ≠ v). By pigeonhole this happens when p + 1 > |Sh(V⋆, (iK^p)K⋆_p)|, and for a fixed away-from-p level this cardinality does not grow with p (for odd N, K⋆_p is hyperspecial and the totally definite unitary group of rank 3 is independent of p up to isomorphism), so it happens for all large inert p. Case for the defence: read étale-locally, (2) is true (unramified ⇒ étale-locally a closed immersion, Stacks 04HJ); all later uses (codimension, normal bundle, Gysin maps, transversality) need only unramifiedness, and in Proposition 4.5.5 the reduction still works (a morphism of smooth schemes bijective on geometric points and on tangent spaces is étale and universally injective, hence an isomorphism). So the statement is wrong in the sense the paper itself uses, with no downstream damage.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 4.5.5, first paragraph, published p. 180; arXiv v1 p. 50, v2 p. 50, v3 p. 50
issues.printed: The proof invokes Theorem 4.3.5 to claim that ι_sp is a closed immersion Zariski locally on its source, and that source and target are smooth; it therefore reduces the argument to the subsequent assertion.
issues.correction: Only the source B_𝔭(V_n, −)_sp is known to be smooth (it is étale over B_𝔭(V_n, −_n)); the reduction to (1) bijectivity on κ-points and (2) bijectivity on tangent spaces is valid for an unramified morphism from a smooth scheme, without smoothness of the target.
issues.reason: The target B_𝔭(V_{n+1}, −_{n+1}) ×_{M_𝔭(V_{n+1})} M_𝔭(V_n, −_n) is an intersection of two smooth subschemes of M_𝔭(V_{n+1}); its smoothness is a consequence of the proposition, not an input. The argument survives: if f: X → Y is unramified, X smooth, f bijective on geometric points and on tangent spaces, then at each point Ô_Y → Ô_X is surjective with equal embedding dimension and Ô_X regular, hence an isomorphism; so f is étale and universally injective, hence an open immersion, hence (being surjective) an isomorphism. issues.locator: Construction 4.6.1(1), published p. 185; used in Theorem 4.6.2 (p. 186) and Theorem 7.3.4 (p. 300); arXiv v1 p. 53 (Construction 4.5.1(1)), v3 p. 53
issues.printed: It defines loc′_𝔭: H^i_ét(Sh(V_{n₀}, −_{n₀}K_{n₀,p}) ×_{Spec F} Sh(V_{n₁}, −_{n₁}K_{n₁,p}), L(j)) → H^i_𝔗(M_{n₀} ×_{T_𝔭} M_{n₁}, L(j)) by composing loc_𝔭, the pullback from (4.2) into H^i_𝔗(M^η_{n₀} ×_{T^η_𝔭} M^η_{n₁}, L(j)), and H^i_𝔗(M_{n₀} ×_{T_𝔭} M_{n₁}, RΨL(j)) ⥲ H^i_𝔗(M_{n₀} ×_{T_𝔭} M_{n₁}, L(j)), citing L ≃ RΨL from Theorem 4.2.3.
issues.correction: Define loc′_𝔭 only on classes unramified at 𝔭 (the kernel of the residue map H^i(X_η, L(j)) → H^{i−1}(X_s, L(j−1)), X := M_{n₀} ×_{T_𝔭} M_{n₁} over Z_p^Φ), as the inverse of the injective restriction H^i(X_s, L(j)) ≅ H^i(X, L(j)) → H^i(X_η, L(j)) (proper case; Lan–Stroh otherwise), or fix a splitting (e.g. by the uniformizer p), or work with geometric fibres. The class [ΔSh(V_n, −_nK_{n,p})] is unramified (its closure m_Δ(M_n) is smooth over Z_p^Φ), so Theorem 4.6.2 is unaffected.
issues.reason: M_{n₀} ×_{T_𝔭} M_{n₁} (roman M) is the special fibre over F_p^Φ (Notation 3.3.6(5)) and H^i_𝔗 is the 𝔗-invariant part of its étale cohomology (Notation 3.5.7), i.e. arithmetic cohomology over F_p^Φ, as §7.3 uses (Hochschild–Serre over F_{p²}). The listed maps contain no arrow from H^i_𝔗(M^η_{n₀} ×_{T^η_𝔭} M^η_{n₁}, L(j)) (over Q_p^Φ) to H^i_𝔗(M_{n₀} ×_{T_𝔭} M_{n₁}, RΨL(j)), and none exists canonically onto H^i of the special fibre: for X smooth and proper over the henselian ring Z_p^Φ, proper base change and purity give 0 → H^i(X_s, L(j)) → H^i(X_η, L(j)) → H^{i−1}(X_s, L(j−1)) → 0 (the Gysin map H^{i−1}(X_s)(−1) → H^{i+1}(X) ≅ H^{i+1}(X_s) is cup product with c₁(O(X_s)) = 0 because X_s = div(p)), so the canonical map goes from special to generic, with non-zero cokernel in general (e.g. X = Spec Z_p^Φ, i = j = 1: Kummer classes of p). In Deligne's topos X_s ×_s η, H^i(X_η, L) ≅ H^i(X_s ×_s η, RΨL) ≅ H^i(X_s ×_s η, L) = H^i(Gal(Q̄_p/Q_p^Φ), RΓ(X̄_s, L)), which again differs from H^i(X_s, L) = H^i(Gal(F̄_p/F_p^Φ), RΓ(X̄_s, L)) by the inertia contribution; so the named 'isomorphism' does not hold between the groups the notation denotes. Defence: the intended map is clear on unramified classes, which is all that Theorem 4.6.2 needs; §7.3 localizes at (m₀, m₁), where the residue term may vanish. Independent check: Checked on the zoomed page image, p. 185. The target is H^i_𝔗(M_{n₀} ×_{T_𝔭} M_{n₁}, L(j)) with roman M, which by Notation 3.3.6(5) is the special fibre over F_p^Φ, not the geometric fibre M̄. The middle term H^i_𝔗(𝐌^η_{n₀} ×_{𝐓^η} 𝐌^η_{n₁}, L(j)) is the arithmetic generic fibre over Q_p^Φ. The chain has no arrow from the generic fibre to 'H^i_𝔗(M ×_T M, RΨL(j))', and under every reading one link fails. With RΨ the geometric nearby cycles, there is no canonical map from arithmetic generic-fibre cohomology to arithmetic special-fibre cohomology. With the arithmetic version i^*Rj_*L, the map exists, but 'L ≃ RΨL' is false (i^*R^1j_*L = L(−1)). For X smooth proper over Z_p^Φ, purity and the vanishing of c₁(O(X_s)) give 0 → H^i(X_s, L(j)) → H^i(X_η, L(j)) → H^{i−1}(X_s, L(j−1)) → 0, so the only canonical map runs from special to generic and has nonzero cokernel in general (Kummer class of p). The first reading's analysis is right. As the first reading says, the intended meaning is clear on classes unramified at 𝔭, and [△Sh(V_n, −_nK_{n,p})] is such a class (the proof of Theorem 4.6.2 computes loc′_𝔭 of it through the integral model via (4.8)), so Theorem 4.6.2 survives with the corrected definition. Note for §7: the proof of Theorem 7.3.4 (p. 301) asserts that H^{2n}((Sh×Sh)_{F_𝔭}, O_λ(n)) → H^{2n}_𝔗(M×M, O_λ(n)) is an isomorphism. After localizing at (m₀, m₁) the cokernel is H^0(F_{p²}, H^{2n−1}(X̄, O_λ(n−1))_{(m₀,m₁)}), which need not vanish at a level-raising prime. The argument only needs the specialization-to-generic map applied to the unramified class, so it goes through.
