issues.correction: Let 1_{△Sh(V⋆_n,(i_n−_n)K⋆_{sp,p})} denote the pushforward (sh⋆_↓, sh⋆_↑)_*(1) of the constant function 1 on Sh(V⋆_n, (i_n−_n)K⋆_{sp,p}) (the graph counted with multiplicity), as Theorem 7.3.4 does explicitly ('regarded as the pushforward of the characteristic function along the map Sh(V⋆_n, K⋆_{sp}) → Sh(V⋆_n, K⋆_n) × Sh(V⋆_{n+1}, K⋆_{n+1})'). With this reading Theorem 4.6.2 and its proof are correct.
issues.reason: For n even, B_sp = S_sp ×_{S_n} B_n and (id × π_{n₁}) ∘ b_△ = (b_↓, s_↑ ∘ π_sp): B_sp → B_n ×_{T_𝔭} S_{n+1} is the base change of (s_↓, s_↑): S_sp → S_n ×_{T_𝔭} S_{n+1} along π_n × id, so its pushforward of [B_sp] is (π_n × id)^*((s_↓, s_↑)_*1), which counts multiplicities. Under the uniformizations (Proposition 4.5.9), (s_↓, s_↑) is (sh⋆_↓, sh⋆_↑) × id, and this map need not be injective: the fibre of sh⋆_↓ over a point has p + 1 elements (Lemma 4.5.2(2), (4.13)), which are distinct points of Sh(V⋆_n, K⋆_{sp}) (a common image in Sh(V⋆_n, K⋆_n) plus equality would need an element of U(V⋆_n)(F⁺) fixing the prime-to-p class and Λ⋆_{n,𝔭}, trivial by neatness), and their images under sh⋆_↑ lie in Sh(V⋆_{n+1}, (i_{n+1}−_{n+1})K⋆_{n+1,p}); if p + 1 exceeds the number of points of that Shimura set — the typical situation for fixed K^p and large p — two of them coincide by pigeonhole. At such a point the characteristic function of the image subset is 1 while the left-hand side of the displayed identity is ⩾ 2, so the identity, and hence Theorem 4.6.2 with the literal 'subset' reading, fails. For n odd, sh⋆_↓ = id and both readings agree. Defence: the proof proves the pushforward version, and the only application (proof of Theorem 7.3.4, which applies Theorem 4.6.2 at level (K_sp, K_{n+1}) 'followed by pushforward') uses the pushforward reading, which it states explicitly. Independent check: Checked on pp. 186–188. For n even, B_sp = S_sp ×_{S_n} B_n (Definition 4.5.3), so (id × π_{n₁}) ∘ b_△ = (b_↓, s_↑π_sp) is the base change of (s_↓, s_↑): S_sp → S_n ×_T S_{n+1}, and its pushforward of [B_sp] is (π_{n₀} × id)^*f with f = (sh⋆_↓, sh⋆_↑)_*1, which counts multiplicities. The correspondence is not injective in general. The p + 1 points of a fibre of sh⋆_↓ are distinct (neat level) and share their prime-to-p component. Their images lie in Sh(V⋆_{n+1}, K_♯K⋆_{n+1,p}), whose level at 𝔭 is hyperspecial (n + 1 odd, (Λ⋆)^∨ = pΛ⋆), so its cardinality is bounded independently of p for a fixed away-from-p level; pigeonhole then applies for large p. The theorem itself (not just the proof step) fails under the literal 'subset' reading. The last step of the proof (p. 188, via Theorem 4.4.10) gives LHS − RHS = (ι_{n₀} × id)_!(π_{n₀} × id)^*(T⋆_{n₁,𝔭}(f − 𝟙_△)). Take n = 2, F⁺ ≠ Q so that everything is proper, and L = Z_ℓ. Then B_2 = S_2, and ι_{2!} sends a point to its cycle class, whose degree is 1. Applying the total-degree map H^2_𝔗(M_2 ×_T S_3, L(1)) → L gives d·(|Sh(V⋆_2, K⋆_sp)| − |△|) per point of T. Here d is the common column sum of T⋆_{3,𝔭} = d_{1,p} + d_{0,p}·deg T_{3,𝔭;1} = (−2p² − p + 1) + p(p³ + 1) = (p² − 1)² ≠ 0 (Notation 1.3.1; T_{3;1} has degree p(p³ + 1)). So the difference is nonzero whenever the correspondence is non-injective. The pushforward reading, which §7.3 states explicitly and which is the only one used downstream, makes the theorem and its proof correct.

issues.locator: Theorem 5.4.4(2), published p. 202 (proof pp. 203–204)
issues.printed: The source claims that ι•_κ restricted to B•_{s•} is a closed immersion locally on B•_{s•}.
issues.correction: Add the argument: ι•|B•_{s•} is unramified (injective tangent map, proved) and injective on geometric points. Two points x, x′ with the same image would give γ′γ⁻¹, an automorphism of s• preserving λ• and η^{p•}, which is trivial for neat K^{p°}. Hence it is a closed immersion (B•_{s•} is proper).
issues.reason: The proof only shows that the tangent map is injective and computes its cokernel. Unramifiedness alone gives a closed immersion only étale-locally on the target, not Zariski-locally on the source (a finite étale cover of degree 2 is unramified but not locally on the source an immersion). Remark 5.4.5(1), stated without proof, asserts a closed immersion only for sufficiently small K^{p°}. Defence: the statement is true (indeed stronger) by the rigidity argument above, and only the normal-sheaf formula is used later.

issues.locator: Lemma 5.6.2(2),(3) and proof, published p. 212 (cites Lemma A.1.4(3),(4), p. 323)
issues.printed: Part (2) asserts freeness over L of H^i_𝔗(M̄°_𝔭(V°, –), L) and H^i_𝔗(M̄†_𝔭(V°, –), L) for each i ∈ ℤ. Part (3) asserts triviality when N is even. The proof bases (2) on Lemma A.1.4(3), and (3) on Lemma A.1.4(4) together with Construction 5.3.6.
issues.correction: Either add 'if p + 1 is invertible in L' to (2),(3), or prove that the Fermat hypersurface S has torsion-free ℤ_ℓ-cohomology for every ℓ ≠ p. Weak Lefschetz gives degrees < N − 2 and Gysin degrees > N − 2. In the middle degree, H^{N−2}(S, ℤ_ℓ)_{tors} ≅ H^{N−1}(S, ℤ_ℓ)_{tors} ≅ H^{N+1}(ℙ^{N−1}, ℤ_ℓ)_{tors} = 0. Then deduce (2),(3) for all p-coprime L from the ℚ_ℓ case.
issues.reason: Lemma 5.6.2 puts 'p + 1 invertible in L' only in part (1), but every part of Lemma A.1.4 assumes it ('Suppose that p + 1 is invertible in L'). So for L with ℓ | p + 1 the cited lemma does not apply. Moreover A.1.4(3) is called 'an immediate consequence of (2)', yet A.1.4(2) says nothing about the middle degree N − 2, where freeness needs the torsion argument above. Defence: the statements are true (smooth hypersurfaces have torsion-free ℓ-adic cohomology), and later applications take ℓ large with ℓ ∤ p(p² − 1).

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 5.7.5 ('Third, …'), published pp. 217–218; arXiv v1/v2 proof of Lemma 5.6.5, pp. 73–74; v3 proof of Lemma 5.7.5, p. 75
issues.printed: The proof derives rank_{O_S} H₂ + 1 = rank_{O_S} H₁ and H^dR_1(A•₁/S)^⊥_{τ_∞} ⊆ H₂ from Theorem 5.4.4(4), and rank_{O_S} H₂ ⩾ rank_{O_S} im(pφ•^{−1})_{*,τ_∞^c} + 1 from Lemma 5.7.3(3). Using Lemma 5.7.3(2,5) and (5.14), it concludes (N − j) − j ⩾ 2, equivalently j ⩽ ⌊N/2⌋ − 1.
issues.correction: For N odd the step is right. For N even, H^dR_1(A•₁/S)^⊥_{τ_∞} = 0 and the inequality rank H₂ ⩾ j + 1 is false when j = r − 1 (e.g. N = 2, j = 0: H₂ = 0). Argue instead: by (5.14), im(pφ•^{−1})_{*,τ_∞^c} ⊆ H₂ with rank H₂ = ⌈N/2⌉ − 1 = r − 1, so j ⩽ r − 1 (or: N − j ⩾ rank H₁ = rank H₂ + 1 ⩾ j + 1, so 2j ⩽ 2r − 1).
issues.reason: Lemma 5.7.3(3) gives only im(pφ•^{−1}) ∩ H^dR_1(A•₁)^⊥_{τ_∞} = 0; the '+1' comes from the radical H^dR_1(A•₁/S)^⊥_{τ_∞} ⊆ H₂ being a line, which holds only for N odd: for N even λ•₁ is p-principal and the pairing ⟨ , ⟩_{λ•₁,τ_∞} is perfect (Notation 3.4.7; dim 𝒱_{s•}^⊣ = 0 for N even, p. 200). The component with j = r − 1 does occur (Proposition 5.8.8 sums over δ up to r − 1), and there H₂ = im(pφ•^{−1})_{*,τ_∞^c} exactly. Case for the defence: the conclusion j ⩽ ⌊N/2⌋ − 1 is true in both parities by the corrected argument. Independent check: Checked on pp. 217–218. Lemma 5.7.3(3) (p. 216) gives only im(pφ•^{−1})_{τ∞^c} ∩ H^dR_1(A•_1)^⊥_{τ∞} = 0. The '+1' in 'rank H_2 ⩾ rank im(pφ•^{−1})_{τ∞^c} + 1' comes from the radical H^dR_1(A•_1)^⊥_{τ∞} = 𝒱^⊣_{s•} ⊆ H_2. That radical has dimension 0 for N even and 1 for N odd (p. 200). For N = 2r even and j = r−1, rank H_2 = r−1 = j, so the printed inequality is false. For N = 2 it fails at every point of the diagonal B•_{s•,s•}, where φ• = id and so j = 0 while H_2 = 0. The conclusion j ⩽ ⌊N/2⌋ − 1 is still true. For N even, (5.14) gives j = rank im ⩽ rank H_2 = r − 1. For N odd the printed argument is valid. Reclassified from 'nothing' to 'the proof': this is a false inference in the proof as printed, not a slip of notation, even though the repair is one line and the lemma is unaffected.

issues.locator: Theorem 5.7.8(2), published pp. 223–224; arXiv v1/v2 Theorem 5.6.8(2), p. 77; v3 Theorem 5.7.8(2), p. 78
issues.printed: Part (2) identifies the cokernel of T_{B†_{s•₁}/κ}|_{(π†_{s•})^{−1}(t†)} ⊕ T_{B†_{s•₂}/κ}|_{(π†_{s•})^{−1}(t†)} → ι•*T_{M†_𝔭(V°,K^{p°})/κ}|_{(π†_{s•})^{−1}(t†)} canonically with ζ†*_{t†}((σ*ℋ_{t†}) ⊗_{O_{P(𝒱_{t†})}} O_{P(𝒱_{t†})}(1)). Here it describes ℋ_{t†} as the universal object, the tautological bundle over P(𝒱_{t†}).
issues.correction: Restrict (2) to N even. For N = 2r+1 the cokernel has rank r − j; the paper's own route (restricting Theorem 5.7.7(2)) gives ζ†*_{t†}((σ*(ℋ̄_{s•2}|_{P(𝒱_{t†})})) ⊗ O(1)), where ℋ̄_{s•2}|_{P(𝒱_{t†})} is an extension of ℋ_{t†} by the trivial line bundle 𝒱_{s•}^⊣ ⊗ O, so that its top Chern class is c_{r−j−1}((σ*ℋ_{t†}) ⊗ O(1)) · c₁(O(1)).
issues.reason: Rank count from the rest of the theorem: M†_𝔭 is smooth of dimension N−2; by (1) with j = 0, B†_{s•_i} is a disjoint union of P^{⌊N/2⌋−1}; the intersection component P(𝒱_{t†}) is smooth of dimension ⌊N/2⌋−j−1 and is the scheme-theoretic fibre product. So the cokernel has rank (N−2) − 2(⌊N/2⌋−1) + (⌊N/2⌋−j−1) = N − ⌊N/2⌋ − j − 1: r−j−1 for N = 2r but r−j for N = 2r+1, while σ*ℋ_{t†} ⊗ O(1) has rank dim 𝒱_{t†} − 1 = ⌊N/2⌋ − j − 1. Smallest case N = 3, j = 0: B†_{s•} is a finite set of reduced points on the curve M†, so the cokernel is the 1-dimensional tangent space of M†, whereas dim 𝒱_{t†} = 1 makes ℋ_{t†} = 0. The proof ('(2) follows from Theorem 5.7.7(2) and (ℋ̄^⊣_{s•1}/ℋ̄_{s•2})|_P = (ℋ̄_{s•1}/ℋ̄_{s•2})|_P ≃ O(1)') tacitly replaces ℋ̄_{s•2}|_P by ℋ_{t†} = H₂/(im(pφ•^{−1}) + H^dR_1(A•₁)^⊥_{τ_∞}), which drops the radical 𝒱_{s•}^⊣; that radical is 0 exactly when N is even. Case for the defence: Theorem 5.7.8 is used only in the proof of Proposition 5.8.8, where N is even and the statement is correct. Independent check: Checked on pp. 223–224. From Theorem 5.7.8(1) and the proof, ℋ_{t†} is the universal hyperplane of 𝒱_{t†} (ζ† sends a point to H_2/(im(pφ•^{−1}) + H^dR_1(A•_1)^⊥_{τ∞}), of rank dim 𝒱_{t†} − 1). So (σ*ℋ_{t†}) ⊗ O(1) has rank ⌊N/2⌋ − j − 1. This is consistent with the use of c_{r−j−1} in Proposition 5.8.8 (p. 230). Now count dimensions. M† has dimension N−2. By Theorem 5.5.3(2), B†_{s•_i} is a disjoint union of ℙ^{⌊N/2⌋−1}. The fibre (π†_{s•})^{−1}(t†) ≅ ℙ(𝒱_{t†}) has dimension ⌊N/2⌋ − j − 1. So the cokernel has rank N − ⌊N/2⌋ − j − 1: r − j − 1 for N = 2r (fine) but r − j for N = 2r+1. For N = 3 (so j = 0) no cleanness assumption is needed. M† is a curve, B†_{s•} is a finite set of reduced points, and the cokernel is the 1-dimensional T_{M†} at the point. But dim 𝒱_{t†} = 1 gives ℋ_{t†} = 0. The proof restricts Theorem 5.7.7(2), where σ*ℋ̄_{s•2} has rank ⌈(N−2j)/2⌉ − 1, which is r − j for N odd. It then silently replaces ℋ̄_{s•2}|_ℙ by ℋ_{t†}, dropping the radical 𝒱^⊣_{s•}, which is a line exactly when N is odd (p. 200). The only use is Proposition 5.8.8, where N = 2r is even and r ⩾ 2 (pp. 229–230). So no downstream effect.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 5.9.3(6), published p. 235; arXiv v1/v2 p. 86, v3 p. 87
issues.printed: Using invertibility of p² − 1 in L, the source concludes E_2^{−1,2r}(−1)^{Gal(F̄_p/F_p^Φ)} = 0.
issues.correction: In Lemma 5.9.3(6) replace the hypothesis 'p² − 1 is invertible in L' by '#F_p^Φ − 1 is invertible in L', or assume Q_p^Φ = Q_{p²}. (This does not repair E8.)
issues.reason: E_2^{−1,2r} = ker d_1^{−1,2r} ⊆ H^{2r−2}_𝔗(M̄†_N, L(r−1)), on which Gal(F̄_p/F_p^Φ) acts trivially (Lemma 5.6.2(3)); hence the Frobenius of F_p^Φ acts on E_2^{−1,2r}(−1) by the scalar q^{−1}, q = #F_p^Φ = p^{2f}, and the invariants are the (q−1)-torsion. Q_p^Φ is only required to contain Q_{p²} (§5.1, 'F_p^Φ contains F_{p²}'), and q − 1 = (p²−1)(1 + p² + … + p^{2(f−1)}); e.g. p = 3, f = 2, L = F₅: p² − 1 = 8 is invertible but q − 1 = 80 is not, and the invariants are all of E_2^{−1,2r} ⊗ F₅. Then H¹_sing may have a nonzero image in (J/F_0J)^G and the map H¹_sing → H^{2r−1}(M̄•_N,L(r−1))^G of (6) is not even defined on all of H¹_sing. Case for the defence: §6 imposes (P3) Q_p^Φ = Q_{p²} and (P2) ℓ ∤ p(p²−1), where the step is correct. Independent check: Checked on p. 235. E_2^{−1,2r} ⊆ E_1^{−1,2r} = H^{2r−2}_𝔗(M̄†_N, L(r−1)), on which Galois acts trivially by Lemma 5.6.2(3). So Frob_{F_p^Φ} acts on E_2^{−1,2r}(−1) by multiplication by q^{±1}, where q = #F_p^Φ, and the invariants are the (q−1)-torsion. In §5, F_p^Φ is only required to contain F_{p²} (§4.1: 'F_p^Φ contains F_{p²}'). The condition Q_p^Φ = Q_{p²} is imposed only by (P3) in §6 (p. 264). So with p = 3, F_p^Φ = F_81 and L = F_5 (p-coprime, p²−1 = 8 invertible, q−1 = 80 ≡ 0), the invariants are all of E_2^{−1,2r} ⊗ F_5. That group is typically nonzero; it is the source of the monodromy. The printed vanishing 'as p² − 1 is invertible' is therefore false in that case, not merely unjustified. So the kind is error, not gap. Consequence: J^G may map nontrivially to C^G, so the map H^1_sing → H^{2r−1}(M̄•, L(r−1))^G in (6) is not defined on all of H^1_sing, and Lemma 5.9.3(6) is unproven when F_p^Φ ≠ F_{p²}. Nothing downstream: §6–§7 work over Q_{p²} with ℓ ∤ p(p²−1).

issues.locator: Notation 5.11.1(4), published p. 250; arXiv v1 and v3 same place
issues.printed: For each (?0, ?1) ∈ {°, •, †}², the source defines Q^{?0,?1} as the strict transform under σ of P^{?0,?1}, and asserts it is closed in Q.
issues.correction: For (?0, ?1) ≠ (†, †), Q^{?0,?1} is the strict transform (the closure of σ^{-1}(P^{?0,?1} ∖ P^{†,†})); Q^{†,†} := σ^{-1}(P^{†,†}) = Q^{°,°} ∩ Q^{•,•}, the exceptional locus.
issues.reason: σ is an isomorphism outside P^{†,†} (where P^{°,°} is Cartier), and P^{†,†} lies inside the centre P^{°,°}. So the strict transform of P^{†,†} is empty under any definition: the closure of σ^{-1}(∅), or Bl_{P^{†,†}}P^{†,†} = ∅. Lemma 5.11.3 uses Q^{†,†} as the P¹-bundle over P^{†,†} that forms the diagonal edge of the reduction graph, i.e. σ^{-1}(P^{†,†}). (With the literal Fulton definition, Bl_{Z∩C}Z, even Q^{°,°} would be empty, because the centre C = P^{°,°} is a non-Cartier Weil divisor; the intended convention is the closure of the preimage off P^{†,†}.) Defence: the intended meaning is clear from Lemma 5.11.3(1),(2); a formaliser following the literal definition would get Q^{†,†} = ∅.

issues.locator: Lemma 5.11.3(2), third bullet, and the words 'trivial P¹-fibration' in Lemma 5.11.3(5), published p. 252; arXiv v3 p. 98
issues.printed: The source calls σ : Q^{†,†} → P^{†,†} a trivial P¹-bundle. In (5), it takes f ∈ H²_T(Q̄^{†,†}, O_λ(1)) to represent the cycle class of any T-orbit of sections for σ̄ : Q̄^{†,†} → P̄^{†,†}, described as a trivial P¹-fibration.
issues.correction: σ: Q^{†,†} → P^{†,†} is the (Zariski-locally trivial) P¹-bundle P(pr_0^*N_0 ⊕ pr_1^*N_1) over P^{†,†} = M†_{n0} ×_{T_p} M†_{n1}, where N_α = O(−M°_{nα})|_{M†_{nα}} ≅ O(M•_{nα})|_{M†_{nα}} is the normal bundle of M†_{nα} in M°_{nα} (restricting to O(p+1) on each Fermat fibre M†_{nα} ∩ B°_{s°}). Equivalently, Q^{†,†} = P(N_{P^{†,†}/P^{°,°}}) is the exceptional divisor of Q^{°,°} = Bl_{P^{†,†}}P^{°,°}. It has the two disjoint sections Q^{•,°} ∩ Q^{†,†} and Q^{°,•} ∩ Q^{†,†}, and it is not trivial over any connected component. In (5), 'trivial' should be deleted and f taken to be the class of one of these two sections (or of any section).
issues.reason: Near P^{†,†}, 𝐏 is x0y0 = x1y1 (= p) with M°_{nα} = {xα = 0}, and the ideal of P^{°,°} is pr_0^*O(−M°_{n0}) + pr_1^*O(−M°_{n1}). So 𝐐 embeds in P(pr_0^*O(−M°_{n0}) ⊕ pr_1^*O(−M°_{n1})). A chart computation (x0 = u·x1, y1 = u·y0, p = u·x1·y0) shows σ^{-1}(P^{†,†}) = {x1 = y0 = 0} is reduced, smooth and meets each fibre in a whole P¹, hence σ^{-1}(P^{†,†}) = P(pr_0^*N_0 ⊕ pr_1^*N_1). Since O(M°+M•) = O(div p) ≅ O, O(−M°)|_{M†} ≅ O_{M°}(M†)|_{M†} = N_{M†/M°}, which by Theorem 5.3.4 and Corollary 5.3.5 is O(p+1) restricted to the degree-(p+1) Fermat hypersurface DL(V_{s°}) ⊂ P(V_{s°}). Over a connected proper base, P(A ⊕ B) ≅ base × P¹ iff A ⊕ B ≅ M ⊕ M for a line bundle M (P(E) ≅ P(E′) iff E′ ≅ E ⊗ M), hence, by Atiyah's Krull–Schmidt theorem, iff A ≅ B. Here that would require pr_0^*N_0 ≅ pr_1^*N_1, and restricting to {z} × DL(V_{s°}) for a point z of M†_{n0} would make O(p+1) trivial on a Fermat hypersurface of dimension n1 − 2 ⩾ 1, where it is ample. For example, when n = 2, over a point × Fermat curve C ⊂ P² the bundle is the ruled surface P(O ⊕ O(p+1)|_C), whose sections have self-intersection ±(p+1)², so it is not C × P¹. This matches the analysis of the earlier open question U1. Case for the defence: the bundle is Zariski-locally trivial, the fourth bullet of (2) (two disjoint sections) is correct, and every use found — the decompositions (3)–(5) (Leray–Hirsch with f the class of a section), Lemma 7.2.5(2),(4),(6) and the proof of Theorem 7.2.8(1b)–(1d) — needs only a P¹-bundle with a section. What fails is anything that uses a global trivialisation: e.g. independence of f from the choice of section (the two section classes differ by ±σ^*c1(pr_0^*N_0 ⊗ pr_1^*N_1^{-1})) or f² = 0. No such use was found. Independent check: Checked on p. 252 (third bullet of Lemma 5.11.3(2); (5) 'the trivial ℙ^1-fibration'). Locally, 𝐏 is x0y0 = x1y1 (= p) with M°_{nα} = {xα = 0}. In the chart x0 = u·x1 the blow-up along (x0, x1) gives y1 = u·y0 and p = u·x1·y0, so σ^{−1}(P^{†,†}) = {x1 = y0 = 0} is reduced with fibres ℙ^1. Also I ⊗ O_{P^{†,†}} is free on x0, x1, because the relation y0x0 − y1x1 dies modulo the maximal ideal. Hence Q^{†,†} = ℙ(pr_0^*O(−M°_{n0}) ⊕ pr_1^*O(−M°_{n1}))|_{P^{†,†}}. Since O(M° + M•) = O(div p) ≅ O, O(−M°)|_{M†} ≅ O_{M°}(M†)|_{M†} = N_{M†/M°}. By Corollary 5.3.5 (p. 198) this is (m^{†°})^*O_{M°}(p+1), i.e. O(p+1) on each Fermat fibre, a degree-(p+1) hypersurface in ℙ^{n−1} (Lemma A.1.4(1)). A ℙ^1-bundle ℙ(A ⊕ B) over a connected proper base is trivial iff A ≅ B. Restrict to {z} × C, with C a component of a fibre of M†_{n1} (dimension n1 − 2 ⩾ 1 since n1 = 2r1+1 ⩾ 3). There pr_0^*N_0 is trivial while pr_1^*N_1 = O(p+1)|_C is ample. For n1 = 3 this gives the ruled surface ℙ(O ⊕ O(p+1)|_C) over a Fermat curve, which has a section of self-intersection −(p+1)^2 and so is not C × ℙ^1. The bundle is therefore not trivial over any connected component. Uses: Lemma 5.11.3(3)–(5) feed Lemma 7.2.5(2),(4),(6) (pp. 289–291) and Theorem 7.2.8(1a)–(1d) (pp. 293–295). These need only a ℙ^1-bundle with a Galois-stable section, for Leray–Hirsch and Galois-equivariance of the splitting. The two canonical sections Q^{•,°} ∩ Q^{†,†} and Q^{°,•} ∩ Q^{†,†} (fourth bullet) serve. The class f enters only through the decomposition in (5), which holds for any section class. No argument uses f² = 0 or independence of f from the section. So nothing downstream is affected. issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 6.1.11, published pp. 267–268
issues.printed: The proof says an automorphic representation π′ on U(V′_N)(A_{F⁺}) extends π′^∞ and occurs as a subquotient of parabolic induction from a cuspidal automorphic representation on L(A_{F⁺}). issues.locator: §6.4, local model at 𝔭, published p. 281 (and the computation of H¹_sing on p. 282)
issues.printed: The source chooses the unique x ∈ R^mix for which r^♮_mix(t)v′ = xv + v′, asserts x(s − p^{−2r}) = 0, and gives H¹_sing(ℚ_{p²}, (R^ram)^{⊕N}(r)) = R^ram v/xv ≃ R^ram/(x) = R^cong.
issues.correction: r^♮_mix(t)v = v + xv′ (the monodromy moves the p^{−2r}-eigenvector v towards the p^{−2r+2}-eigenvector v′), and H¹_sing(ℚ_{p²}, (R^ram)^{⊕N}(r)) = R^ram v′/xv′ ≃ R^ram/(x) = R^cong. Equivalently, interchange the eigenvalue labels of v̄, v̄′ (and of s, s′) throughout.
issues.reason: φ_p is an arithmetic Frobenius (the eigen-pair product p^{−4r+2} = ε_ℓ(φ_p²)^{1−N} in the characteristic polynomial (T − s)(T − p^{−4r+2}s⁻¹)Q(T) forces ε_ℓ(φ_p) = p), and [51, Definition 3.3.1] fixes φ_p t φ_p⁻¹ = t^p. With the printed r(t)v′ = xv + v′, conjugating by φ_p² gives x·s/s′ = p²x, i.e. x(s − p²s′) = 0; since s′ = p^{−4r+2}s⁻¹ this is x(s − p^{−2r+2})(s + p^{−2r+2}) = 0, and s − p^{−2r+2} is a unit by (P2), so x(s + p^{−2r+2}) = 0 — not the stated x(s − p^{−2r}) = 0, and it forces x = 0 (every lift unramified) whenever ℓ ∤ p² + 1. With r(t)v = v + xv′ one gets x(s′ − p²s) = 0 ⇔ x(s − p^{−2r})(s + p^{−2r}) = 0 ⇔ x(s − p^{−2r}) = 0 (ℓ odd), as stated. This agrees with [51, proof of Proposition 3.5.2] (arXiv:2108.06998v1, p. 28): in the basis where r^♮(φ_q²) = diag(q^{−N}(1+x)(1+y)⁻¹, q^{−N+2}(1+y)(1+x)⁻¹), r^♮(t) = 1 + (0 0; x_0 0), so t sends the q^{−N}-eigenvector e_1 to e_1 + x_0e_2. issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 6.3.4(3), published p. 285
issues.printed: The source derives (3) from (1) and (P4), describing P_{α(Π_𝔭)} mod λ^m as level-raising special at 𝔭. It identifies H^{2r−1}_𝔗(M̄•_N, O_λ(r)) ≃ H ⊗_{R^ram} R_1(r) as modules over O_λ[Gal(F̄_p/F_{p²})].
issues.correction: Read the left side as localised at 𝔪, and let R_1 ⊆ (R^ram)^{⊕N} be the r^♮_ram(φ_p²)-stable complement of R^ram v ⊕ R^ram v′; inertia acts trivially on it. Then H^{2r−1}_𝔗(M̄•_N, O_λ(r))_𝔪 = E_2^{0,2r−1} = Gr_0 H^{2r−1}_𝔗(M̄_N, RΨO_λ(r))_𝔪 ≅ H ⊗_{R^ram} R_1(r). Proof: (a) F_{−1} and H/F_0 (E_2^{1,2r−2} and E_2^{−1,2r}) have Frobenius eigenvalues p² and 1 by Lemma 5.6.2. By (P4) these are separated modulo λ from the eigenvalues on R_1(r), so H ⊗ R_1(r) ⊆ Gr_0. (b) The {1,p²}-block has zero image in Gr_0: rationally because the monodromy x is nonzero at every characteristic-zero point of R^ram, and integrally because Gr_0 is O_λ-free by part (2).
issues.reason: The symbol R_1 appears nowhere else in the paper, and the displayed isomorphism — which is the entire content of the proof of (3) — is asserted without argument. Defence: with the reading above the isomorphism holds and gives (3): the eigenvalues of r^♮_ram(φ_p²) on R_1 are p^{1−2r}α_i^{±1} (i ≠ the level-raising index), and twisting by ε_ℓ(φ_p²)^r = p^{2r} gives pα_i^{±1}, avoiding 1 and p². Independent check: Quote checked on p. 285: 'Part (3) is a consequence of (1) and (P4) … In fact, we have an isomorphism H^{2r−1}_𝔗(M̄•_N, O_λ(r)) ≃ H ⊗_{R^ram} R_1(r) of O_λ[Gal(F̄_p/F_{p²})]-modules.' In the text layer of pub/v1/v2/v3, R_1 occurs only in this line, so it is never defined. The left side also lacks the localisation at 𝔪 that part (3) concerns. The displayed isomorphism is all the proof of (3) has, and it is not immediate. By Lemma 5.9.3(1), E_1^{0,2r−1} = H^{2r−1}_𝔗(M̄•_N, L(r)) and the odd-degree terms of M°, M† vanish, so H^{2r−1}_𝔗(M̄•_N)_𝔪 = E_2^{0,2r−1} = Gr_0 of H^{2r−1}_𝔪 ≅ H ⊗ (R^ram)^{⊕N}(r) (p. 282). To identify Gr_0 with H ⊗ (complement of R^ram v ⊕ R^ram v′)(r) one needs three things. (i) Frobenius eigenvalues. E_2^{−1,2r} ⊆ H^{2r−2}(M̄†, L(r−1)) and E_2^{1,2r−2}, a quotient of H^{2r−2}(M̄†, L(r)), have Frobenius eigenvalues 1 and p² (Lemma 5.6.2). By (P4) these are separated modulo λ from the eigenvalues p·α_i^{±1} (i ≠ the level-raising index) on the complement, so the complement lies in Gr_0. (ii) The {1, p²}-block H ⊗ (R^ram v ⊕ R^ram v′)(r) contributes nothing to Gr_0. This needs a further argument. For example: at every characteristic-zero point of R^ram ≅ T^ram_𝔪, the monodromy x is nonzero (nontrivial monodromy at 𝔭, cf. p. 277), so the block has no Gr_0 rationally, and Gr_0 is O_λ-free by (2). (iii) The complement on which inertia acts trivially must actually be named. The first reading's reading (R_1 = the φ²-stable complement, i.e. M_1 of [51]) makes the isomorphism true, and (3) then follows. But the paper supplies neither the definition nor steps (i)–(ii), so this is a gap, not a misprint. Versions: the same line is in v1/v2 p. 120 and v3 p. 119.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 6.3.4(5), published pp. 285–286
issues.printed: The proof claims O_λ/λ^m = R^ram/𝔫, reasoning that 𝔫 ∩ O_λ = λ^m O_λ makes the structure map O_λ → R^ram induce this equality.
issues.correction: Add to Theorem 6.3.4(5) the hypothesis that P_{α(Π_v)} mod λ^m is level-raising special at v (Definition 3.1.5) for every v ∈ Σ⁺_lr. Equivalently, ρ̄^{(m)}_{Π,λ,+} satisfies 𝒟^ram at Σ⁺_lr; this holds vacuously if Σ⁺_lr = ∅. In the proof, read 𝔫 O_λ-linearly, as the kernel of O_λ ⊗ T^{Σ⁺∪Σ⁺_p}_N → O_λ/λ^m. With these, ρ_{Π,λ,+} mod λ^m is of type 𝒮^ram, and so R^ram/𝔫 = O_λ/λ^m. The added hypothesis holds in both applications: Theorem 8.2.2 (Σ⁺_lr = ∅) and Theorem 8.3.2 (Σ⁺_lr = {𝔭_1}, by (PII4)).
issues.reason: As defined in Notation 6.1.3, 𝔫 is an ideal of the ℤ[‖v‖^{±1/2}]-algebra T^{Σ⁺∪Σ⁺_p}_N; read literally, λ^m need not lie in 𝔫R^ram when E_λ is ramified over the field generated by the Hecke eigenvalues. Read O_λ-linearly, R^ram/𝔫 is a quotient O_λ/λ^j of O_λ/λ^m, and j = m requires an O_λ-algebra map R^ram → O_λ/λ^m compatible with φ_Π, i.e. (Chebotarev and Carayol) that ρ_{Π,λ} mod λ^m be a lifting of type 𝒮^ram. At 𝔭 this is (P4) (mod λ^m); but at v ∈ Σ⁺_lr the local condition is 𝒟^ram, which demands P_0(T) = (T − ‖v‖^{−N})(T − ‖v‖^{−N+2}) exactly ([51, Definition 3.5.1]), whereas the hypotheses of Theorem 6.3.4 (rigidity (b), §6.1) only give this modulo λ. If Π_v is level-raising special only modulo λ^j with j < m, then R^ram/𝔫 = O_λ/λ^{j′} with j′ ⩽ j, H^{2r−1}/𝔫 ≅ H ⊗ (R^ram/𝔫)^{⊕N}(r) is killed by λ^{j′} (and nonzero since d_ram > 0), and the conclusion (R̄^{(m)c})^{⊕μ} with μ ⩾ 1 fails. Defence: in the applications (§8, pp. 318–319) Σ⁺_lr is either ∅ or {𝔭_1} with 𝔭_1 a previously chosen prime satisfying (PII4), i.e. level-raising special modulo λ^m, so the main theorems are unaffected; Theorem 6.3.4(4) is unaffected. Independent check: Quote checked on pp. 285–286. The problem is real, but the asserted step is false in general rather than merely unjustified, and so is Theorem 6.3.4(5) as stated. So the kind should be 'error'. The argument: 𝔫 is read O_λ-linearly, which is clearly the intended reading. R^ram/𝔫 = T^ram_𝔪/𝔫 is then a quotient O_λ/λ^j of O_λ/λ^m. j = m iff φ_Π mod λ^m factors through T^ram_𝔪 ≅ R^ram. By Chebotarev and Carayol (Assumption 6.1.6), that happens iff ρ_{Π,λ,+} mod λ^m is a lifting of type 𝒮^ram. At v ∈ Σ⁺_lr the local condition is 𝒟^ram, i.e. s = ‖v‖^{−N} exactly: the paper itself writes R^ram = R^mix/(s − p^{−2r}) on p. 281. But Π_v is unramified, since Σ⁺_lr is strongly disjoint from Σ⁺_min ⊇ Σ⁺_Π. The hypotheses of Theorem 6.3.4 constrain Π_v only through rigidity (Definition 6.3.3(2): generalized eigenvalues of r̄♮_v(φ_w) in F̄_ℓ, i.e. modulo λ) and through ℓ ∤ ‖v‖(‖v‖²−1) (p. 264). (P4) is mod λ^m but only at 𝔭, and (P6)/(d) are congruences with no local content at v. So if P_{α(Π_v)} is level-raising special modulo λ^j but not λ^{j+1} with j < m, then R^ram/𝔫 = O_λ/λ^{j′} with j′ ⩽ j. In that case H^{2r−1}_ét(Sh(V′_N,…)_F̄, O_λ(r))/𝔫 ≅ H ⊗ (R^ram/𝔫)^{⊕N}(r) is nonzero (d_ram > 0) and killed by λ^{j′}. It therefore cannot be isomorphic to (R̄^{(m)c})^{⊕μ} with μ ⩾ 1, and (5) is false. The literal (ℤ-linear) reading of 𝔫 fails too, independently, when E_λ is ramified over the field of Hecke eigenvalues; that part is only a notational slip. Reach: §7 never invokes (5). §7.2 uses 6.3.4(1)–(3) (Lemma 7.2.5, pp. 289–291) and 6.3.4(4) (Theorem 7.2.8(2), p. 295). §8 invokes (5) explicitly only in the proof of Theorem 8.2.2 ((8.6), p. 312), where Σ⁺_lr,I = ∅ (p. 310). It invokes (5) implicitly in the proof of Theorem 8.3.2 ('exactly same argument for the parallel claim in the proof of Theorem 8.2.2', p. 319), where Σ⁺_lr,I = {𝔭_1}. There 𝔭_1 satisfies (PII4), 'P_{α(Π_{0,𝔭})} mod λ^m is level-raising special' (p. 298), with the same m, which is exactly the missing hypothesis. So the main theorems are unaffected. Part (4) does not use R^ram/𝔫 = O_λ/λ^m. Versions: the wording '𝔫 ∩ O_λ = λ^m O_λ' is in v1/v2 p. 120 and v3 p. 119.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 7.2.7 and footnote 29, published p. 292
issues.printed: Citing [47, Theorem 2.16 and Theorem 2.18], the proof reduces matters to showing that O_λ qualifies as a very nice coefficient ring, in the terminology of [47, Definition 2.15], for 𝔼^{p,q}_{s,(𝔪₀,𝔪₁)}. Footnote 29 says that although [47] assumes the strictly semistable X is proper over its base, its relevant proofs apply unchanged when 𝐐 is nonproper, because of Lemma 7.2.5(6).
issues.correction: State and prove [47, Theorems 2.16, 2.18] for Λ = O_λ and for strictly semistable 𝐐 that need not be proper, with nearby-cycle cohomology H_𝔗(Q̄, RΨ) in place of generic-fibre cohomology. The inputs are Lemmas 5.11.2, 5.11.3 and 7.2.5(6). Define cl(Q_sp) as the image of the cycle class of Q_sp (the flat closure of 𝐐^η_sp) in C^n(Q, O_λ), i.e. [47]'s e_z. Justify its restriction to Q^{(0)} as the geometric class of Q_sp ×_𝐐 Q̄^{(0)}, as used in Theorem 7.2.8(3), via [47, Proposition 2.19] or a pushforward argument along 𝐌_𝔭(V°_n, K°_sp) → 𝐏. Correct footnote 22: C^r(Q, L) is the coinvariant version of [47]'s A^r(Q, L)^0; the two agree under (N3).
issues.reason: Point (a): the inputs a proof would need are available — Lemma 5.11.2 (specialization isomorphisms via Lan–Stroh [43, Cor. 5.20]), Lemma 7.2.5(6) (compactly supported = ordinary cohomology on the localized strata, which restores Poincaré duality), and finiteness over O_λ. Continuous O_λ-cohomology is the limit of the ℤ/ℓ^ν-cases, as in the proof of [47, Lemma 2.6]. Point (b): Q_sp has dimension n and its singular locus lies over the †-stratum of 𝐌_𝔭(V°_n, K°_sp), which has dimension ⩽ n−2, so the codimension condition (⩾ n+1 in the (2n−1)-dimensional components of Q_κ) is plausible, but the finite map 𝐌_𝔭(V°_n,K°_sp) → 𝐏 need not be an embedding, and the paper says nothing about it. Point (c): under (N3), which the proof itself verifies, invariants → coinvariants is an isomorphism on B^n(Q,O_λ)^0_{(𝔪₀,𝔪₁)} ⊆ H^{2n}(Q̄^{(0)}), so (c) is harmless. In the defence: none of this is likely to fail. But a black-box theorem is being used outside its stated hypotheses with only a one-line justification, and a formalisation must either reprove [47, Theorems 2.16, 2.18] for this setting or supply the extension. Independent check: Quote and footnote 29 checked on p. 292. From arXiv:1511.08268v2: §2 opens 'Throughout this section, the coefficient ring Λ will be either Q_p or Z/p^ν for some ν ≥ 1' (p. 5). §2.2 and §2.4 assume 'X a proper strictly semistable scheme' (pp. 7, 12). Definition 2.15 ((N1)–(N3)), Theorem 2.16, Theorem 2.18 (η^r_𝔪(e_z) = ∂(α_𝔪(z)), with e_z the class of the flat closure z♯) and Proposition 2.19 match the numbering LTXZZ cite. LTXZZ apply them with Λ = O_λ and a possibly non-proper 𝐐. Footnote 29 addresses only properness, and only by assertion. Point (a) is confirmed. In LTXZZ's favour: Lemma 5.11.3 gives strict semistability, Lemma 5.11.2 (via Lan–Stroh) replaces proper base change, Lemma 7.2.5(6) supplies H_c = H after localisation, and O_λ is a limit of O_λ/λ^k. Point (b) needs one correction: cl(Q_sp) is introduced, on p. 291 ('The cycle Q_sp gives rise to a class cl(Q_sp) ∈ C^n(Q, L)'), but its construction is not specified. For [47, Theorem 2.18] to give Proposition 7.2.7 it must be e_z. The proof of Theorem 7.2.8(3) (p. 295) then evaluates it as a geometric class: '∇(cl(Q_sp)) = ∇(cl(Q•_△)) with cl(Q•_△) ∈ H^{2n}_𝔗(Q^{•,•}, O_λ(n))'. That identification is what [47, Proposition 2.19] provides under a codimension condition on the singular locus of Z_i, and neither the proposition nor its hypothesis is mentioned. Point (c) is confirmed: [47] v2 p. 7 has A^j(X_κ,Λ)^? = (B^j(X_κ,Λ)^?)^{G_κ} (invariants), whereas p. 262 here has C^r(Q, L) := B^r(Q, L)^0_{Gal} (coinvariants). Footnote 22 (p. 263) nevertheless equates C^r with A^r(Q, L)^0. This is harmless under (N3), which the proof verifies. None of (a)–(c) is likely to fail, but a black-box theorem is used outside its stated hypotheses with a one-line justification, so 'gap / the proof' is right. issues.locator: Proof of Corollary 7.2.9, published pp. 296–297
issues.printed: The proof cites Theorem 7.2.8 to obtain exp_λ(∂AJ_𝐐(𝐐^η_sp), H¹_sing(ℚ_{p²}, H^{2n−1}_𝔗(Q̄, RΨO_λ(n))/(𝔫₀, 𝔫₁))) = exp_λ((p+1)φ_{Π₀}(I°_{n₀,𝔭})φ_{Π₁}(T°_{n₁,𝔭})𝟙_{Sh(V°_n,K°_sp)}, O_λ[Sh(V°_{n₀}, K°_{n₀})]/𝔫₀ ⊗_{O_λ} O_λ[Sh(V°_{n₁}, K°_{n₁})]/𝔫₁).
issues.correction: The step also needs the natural map H¹_sing(ℚ_{p²}, H_{(𝔪₀,𝔪₁)})/(𝔫₀,𝔫₁) → H¹_sing(ℚ_{p²}, H/(𝔫₀,𝔫₁)) to be injective (in fact an isomorphism), where H := H^{2n−1}_𝔗(Q̄, RΨO_λ(n)). Theorem 7.2.8, through Proposition 7.2.7, only describes the source.
issues.reason: The corollary measures the exponent in H¹_sing of the reduced module, H¹(I, H/(𝔫₀,𝔫₁))^{Gal(F̄_p/F_{p²})}. Theorem 7.2.8(2),(3) computes the image of ∂AJ_𝐐(𝐐^η_sp) in coker Δ^n/𝔫₀ ≅ H¹_sing(ℚ_{p²}, H_{(𝔪₀,𝔪₁)})/𝔫₀. Taking Frobenius invariants does not commute with reduction mod (𝔫₀,𝔫₁) in general, so exponents can drop. The authors prove the corresponding comparison in the analogous Theorem 6.3.4(4), p. 285: 'it suffices to show that the two natural maps … H¹_sing(ℚ_{p²}, H_𝔪)/𝔫 → H¹_sing(ℚ_{p²}, H/𝔫) are both isomorphisms'. Here the comparison is not mentioned. In the defence: it can be proved the same way. Use the decomposition H¹_sing(ℚ_{p²}, H_{(𝔪₀,𝔪₁)}) ≃ H¹_sing(ℚ_{p²}, H^{2r₀−1}(M̄_{n₀}, RΨO_λ(r₀))_{𝔪₀}) ⊗ (¹E^{0,2r₁}_{2,𝔪₁})^{Gal} from the proof of Theorem 7.2.8(2), the mod-𝔫₀ comparison of Theorem 6.3.4(4), and the fact that ¹E^{0,2r₁}_{2,𝔪₁} is free and weakly semisimple (Theorem 6.2.3(2)), so that its invariants commute with reduction. The corollary is very likely correct.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 7.3.4, published p. 301
issues.printed: The source concludes λ₀^e loc_𝔭([Sh(V_n, K_sp)]) = 0, asserting invertibility of the map H^{2n}_ét((Sh(V_{n₀}, K_{n₀}) ×_{Spec F} Sh(V_{n₁}, K_{n₁}))_{F_𝔭}, O_λ(n)) → H^{2n}_𝔗(M_{n₀} ×_{T_𝔭} M_{n₁}, O_λ(n)).
issues.correction: It is an isomorphism only after localization at (𝔪₀,𝔪₁), and this needs an argument. That suffices, since the statement is modulo (𝔫₀,𝔫₁). For the smooth proper model X = 𝐌_{n₀} ×_{𝐓_𝔭} 𝐌_{n₁} over ℤ_{p²}, the localization sequence and absolute purity give 0 → H^{2n}(X_s, O_λ(n)) → H^{2n}(X_{ℚ_{p²}}, O_λ(n)) → H^{2n−1}(X_s, O_λ(n−1)) → 0. After localization H^{2n−1}(X_s, O_λ(n−1))_{(𝔪₀,𝔪₁)} = (V(−1))^{Gal(F̄_p/F_{p²})}, with V := H^{2n−1}(X̄_s, O_λ(n))_{(𝔪₀,𝔪₁)} (the H¹-term vanishes because the localized H^{2n−2} is 0 by Assumption 7.3.2). This is 0, since V is O_λ-free and V(−1) ⊗ E_λ is pure of weight 1.
issues.reason: In the proof's own Hochschild–Serre sequence, H^{2n}_𝔗(M_{n₀}×_{T_𝔭}M_{n₁}, O_λ(n)) is absolute cohomology of the special fibre over F_{p²} (Notation 3.3.6(5)). Without localization it differs from the degree-2n absolute cohomology of the generic fibre over F_𝔭 = ℚ_{p²} by the quotient H^{2n−1}(X_s, O_λ(n−1)). That quotient is nonzero in general: it contains H¹(F_{p²}, H^{2n−2}(X̄_s, O_λ(n−1))), which picks up the Tate classes (for instance powers of an ample class) — so the unlocalized assertion is false. The natural comparison map also runs the other way (restriction from the integral model to the generic fibre). The direction printed is that of loc′_𝔭 in Construction 4.6.1, whose middle arrow H^i(𝐌^η) → H^i_𝔗(M, RΨL) is not spelled out there. In the defence: everything in Theorem 7.3.4 is modulo (𝔫₀,𝔫₁), hence localized at (𝔪₀,𝔪₁), and the localized comparison holds by the weight argument above (the same weight input underlies (7.3)). If H_𝔗(M, ·) is read as Gal(ℚ̄_p/ℚ_{p²})-hypercohomology, the map is an isomorphism by construction, but then the Hochschild–Serre sequence with H¹(F_{p²}, ·) in the same proof needs the localized comparison instead. Either way the theorem stands.

issues.printed: It chooses V′_1 ⊆ V_1 so that k.e ⊗_k V′_1 equals the t-invariant subspace in W. It then claims Γ preserves V′_1, and that irreducibility of ρ1 therefore forces V′_1 = V_1.
issues.correction: Let H be the normal closure of t in Γ. Then ρ1(H) = 1, and V0|_H is semisimple (Clifford) and indecomposable (t acts by one Jordan block), hence absolutely irreducible; so every Γ-stable subspace of V0 ⊗ V1 = V0 ⊗_k V1 (H acting on the first factor) is V0 ⊗ V1′ with V1′ = Hom_H(V0, W) Γ-stable. Hence W = V0 ⊗ V1′ with V1′ = V1.
issues.reason: W^t has the form k·e ⊗ V1′, but g ∈ Γ maps W^t to W^{gtg^{−1}}, not to W^t, so Γ-stability of V1′ is not visible from t-invariants alone; some input such as the normal-closure argument is needed. The statement is true and the repair is short.

issues.locator: Proofs of Theorem 8.2.2 (published p. 310) and Theorem 8.3.2 (p. 317): choice of γ and use of Proposition 2.6.6; arXiv v3 PDF pp. 135, 140
issues.printed: The source invokes (L5-2) and Lemma 2.7.1 to choose (γ1, γ2, ξ), producing γ. Applying Sect. 2.6, it then uses Proposition 2.6.6 with m0 = mΣ and rS = 1 to select an (S, γ)-abundant Ψ ∈ G_{S,γ}.
issues.correction: Choose γ after S and adapted to it. If F_S is Galois over F⁺ with c·s = εs, require that the eigenvalue b(γ) of a lift of γ on (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} equals ε. In the elliptic case (Corollary 8.2.3) this is arranged by replacing γ with γ·ρ̄₊(z), where (ρ̄_{A₀}, ρ̄_{A₁}, ε̄)(z) = (−1, 1, 1); this preserves Lemma 2.7.1(a)–(e). In rank 0, take S inside one c-eigenspace. In rank 1, use γ at 𝔭₁ (with b matching the component of the Abel–Jacobi class with unit coefficient) and γz at 𝔭₂ when the second basis vector lies in the other eigenspace, instead of one abundant pair for a single γ. Base-change situations whose image has no central −1 need a further argument.
issues.reason: This is how E1 (Lemma 2.6.4) enters §8. Let γ̃ run over lifts of γ to Gal(F̃_S/F⁺) and let 2g be the order of γ on F^{(m)}. For a γ-associated place, Ψ_{w^{(m)}} = γ̃^{2g}|_{F_S}, which commutes with γ̃; so G_{S,γ} is contained in the restriction of the σ-fixed part of Gal(F̃_S/F_+^{(m)}), σ = conjugation by γ̃. Suppose ρ̄ extends to r̄: Γ_{F⁺} → GL(R̄) (the base-change situation, e.g. Corollary 8.2.3, where R = Sym^{n0−1} ⊗ Sym^{n1−1}(n) comes from F⁺), and S = O_λ·s with c·s = εs. Then F_S is Galois over F⁺, θ_S(σ(τ))(s) = ε r̄(γ̃) θ_S(τ)(s), and r̄(γ̃) acts on the line (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} by some b = ±1 determined by γ. If εb = −1, then θ_S(Ψ)(s) = 0 for every Ψ ∈ G_{S,γ}: no (S,γ)-abundant element exists, loc_w(s1) = 0 at every γ-associated place, and the 𝔭-bullet of the pairing computation fails. This is the mechanism of E1's example (R = ℤ_3(1), S from a unit of F⁺, γ = complex conjugation). Nothing in Lemma 2.7.1(a)–(e), which is all the proof requires of γ, relates b to the c-sign of S, and γ is chosen without regard to S. Defence: when ρ̄ ≇ ρ̄^c, F_S and F_{S^c} are essentially independent over F_+^{(m)} and G_{S,γ} is as large as Lemma 2.6.4 claims (up to a bounded defect); in the elliptic case of Corollary 8.2.3 (both ranks) the sign can be corrected by the central element as indicated, and in rank 0 a suitable generator of S can be chosen instead. In a base-change situation without a central −1 in the image (e.g. Π_α base changes in Corollary 8.2.5, where (L5-1) comes from Lemma 2.3.5(b)), the rank-one argument, in which s is fixed by the cycle, needs a further idea. The printed proofs address none of this. Independent check: Checked on pp. 133–137, 310, 317–319. The mechanism is correct and hits the printed proofs. Let σ ∈ Γ_{F⁺} be a Frobenius above a γ-associated place, so Ψ = σ^{2g}|_{F_S} (g the order of h_γ). Suppose s ∈ H^1(F, R̄) satisfies c·s = εs for an extension r̄ of ρ̄ to Γ_{F⁺}; r̄ factors through Gal(F₊^{(m)}/F⁺) since ker ρ̄₊ ⊆ ker ρ̄. The cocycle relation on ker r̄ gives s(σ^{2g}) = εr̄(σ)s(σ^{2g}), and by (c) R̄^{r̄(σ)²} is a free rank-one line on which r̄(σ) acts by b = b(γ) = ±1. If εb = −1 then θ_S(Ψ)(s) = 0 for every Ψ ∈ G_{S,γ}; since H^1_ns(F_w, R̄) → R̄ (evaluation at Ψ) is injective, loc_w(s) = 0 at every γ-associated w, and no abundant element exists. In the elliptic setting of Corollary 8.2.3, both signs are admissible. On R̄₁ = Sym^{2r₁}H^1(A₁)(r₁) the fixed line is the middle weight and b₁ = +1. On R̄₀ = Sym^{2r₀−1}H^1(A₀)(r₀), replacing σ by σz with (ρ̄_{A₀}, ρ̄_{A₁}, ε̄)(z) = (−1, 1, 1) (such z exists in Γ_{FF′} for large ℓ) negates r̄(σ), since n₀ − 1 is odd. The element z is central in im ρ̄₊ with z² = 1, so h_γ, ξ, the prime-to-ℓ orders and (a)–(e) of Lemma 2.7.1 are unchanged, while b flips. Since the proofs pick γ from (a)–(e) alone, after S, one of the two admissible choices fails for S in an eigenspace. In rank 0 the hypothetical S may lie in either eigenspace. In rank 1 the Abel–Jacobi class s lies in the eigenspace of the vanishing L-factor when the other Selmer part vanishes. So the reliance on Proposition 2.6.6 is a genuine hole. Repairs. Rank 0: take S c-stable inside one eigenspace and replace γ by γz if needed. Rank 1: a single γ does not suffice when S meets both eigenspaces (then s₂ is invisible at every γ-associated place), but the argument permits different elements at the two primes: take 𝔭₁ γ-associated with b(γ) matching the component of s with unit coefficient, and 𝔭₂ γz-associated. Then loc_{𝔭₁}(s₂) = 0 automatically, loc_{𝔭₂}(s₂) is large, and (PI)/(PII) depend only on h_γ and ξ. The first reading's alternative (a generator with both components) works only if both eigenspaces of the Selmer group are nonzero. When R̄ ≇ R̄^c as Γ_F-modules, F_S and its conjugate are disjoint up to bounded defect (Goursat), and Lemma 2.6.4 holds up to that defect, so the problem is confined to essentially self-dual (e.g. base-change) R. In base-change cases without a central −1 in the image (the setting of Corollary 8.2.5, where (L5-1) comes from Lemma 2.3.5(b)), no repair is available from the paper.

issues.reason: Lemma 8.1.3 assumes F⁺ ≠ ℚ unconditionally and Lemma 8.1.4 has hypothesis (c) F⁺ ≠ ℚ; both need it for (L7) through Corollary D.1.4, which assumes F⁺ ≠ ℚ. Theorem 8.2.2 applies only to admissible λ. So for n = 2 and F⁺ = ℚ, which (c) allows, the proofs establish nothing. In arXiv v1/v2 this case was covered: Definition 8.1.1 defined 'weakly admissible' ((L1)–(L5)), Theorem 8.2.1 treated weakly admissible λ when n = 2, and the elliptic-curve proposition (v1 Proposition 8.1.5) gave weak admissibility for almost all ℓ without F⁺ ≠ ℚ. v3 deleted weak admissibility but left '(c) F⁺ ≠ ℚ if n ⩾ 3'. Defence: the n = 2 case was argued in v1/v2 and Remark 1.1.10 asserts a 'slightly different argument' exists, so the statements are plausibly true; but the published text does not prove them. issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 8.2.2, justification of (8.5), published p. 313; the same for (8.14) in the proof of Theorem 8.3.2, p. 319
issues.printed: The source derives (8.5) from the existence of smooth models for Sh′_n and Sh′_{n+1} over O_{F_w}, asserting that an analogue of Lemma 4.2.4 applies to those models.
issues.correction: For w above ℓ, add the argument that the Abel–Jacobi class of a cycle on a smooth proper O_{F_w}-scheme (F_w/ℚ_ℓ unramified, dimension 2n−1 with 2n ⩽ ℓ−2) lies in the Fontaine–Laffaille subgroup H¹_ns(F_w, −) of Definition 2.2.5 with torsion coefficients, e.g. via Faltings/Fontaine–Messing comparison for H^*(X ∖ Z) with X, Z smooth proper over O_{F_w}, and that Υ_i preserves H¹_ns.
issues.reason: (8.5) is claimed at every nonarchimedean w not above Σ⁺ ∪ {𝔭}, including the ℓ-adic places, and the ℓ-adic bullet of the pairing computation uses it there. Lemma 4.2.4 is a statement for p-coprime coefficient rings (specialization isomorphisms), which gives unramifiedness at w ∤ ℓ but says nothing about crystallinity of torsion classes at w | ℓ. Lemma 2.2.6 identifies H¹_ns with the preimage of the crystalline classes only for free modules, whereas c1 is a torsion class not known to lift. Defence: the needed statement is standard integral p-adic Hodge theory in the Fontaine–Laffaille range guaranteed by (L1), and when F⁺ ≠ ℚ the Shimura varieties are proper. Independent check: Checked on pp. 311–313 and 319. (8.5) is claimed for all w not above Σ⁺ ∪ {𝔭} with Σ⁺_I = Σ⁺_min (so it includes the ℓ-adic places, by (L2)), and the ℓ-adic bullet on p. 311 invokes (8.5) there. The only justification is that Sh′_n and Sh′_{n+1} have smooth models 'for which (an analogue of) Lemma 4.2.4 holds'. Lemma 4.2.4 is a specialization isomorphism for p-coprime coefficients and gives only unramifiedness at w ∤ ℓ. At w | ℓ one needs the torsion class loc_w(c₁) to lie in H^1_ns(F_w, R̄^{(m)c}) in the sense of Definitions 2.2.4–2.2.5, i.e. its extension must be a quotient of lattices in a crystalline representation. Lemma 2.2.6 does not give this, since c₁ is a torsion class obtained through Υ_i and the quotient by (𝔫₀, 𝔫₁). The fact is standard but not in the paper. Faltings' comparison for the good-reduction pair (X, Z) over O_{F_w} (F_w/Q_ℓ unramified, degree 2n − 1 ⩽ ℓ − 2 by (L1)) makes the torsion Abel–Jacobi extension torsion-crystalline. Torsion-crystalline modules in the sense of Definition 2.2.4 are closed under subquotients and direct sums, so the pushout along Υ_i stays crystalline. Same sentence in v1 ('Lemma 4.1.4') and v3.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition A.2.4(2), published p. 328
issues.printed: The proof claims π^{−1}(S) is a singleton for each morphism S → DL(V♯) \ DL(V♯)′, while a special point s has fibre π^{−1}(s) = P(H_s^⊨) ≃ P^{r−1}_κ. It concludes that π is the blow-up of DL(V♯)′ and designates E ⊆ D̃L(V) as its exceptional divisor.
issues.correction: Describe D̃L(𝒱) as the closed subscheme of the ℙ^{r−1}-bundle of hyperplanes H_2 ⊂ H^⊨ over DL(𝒱♯) cut out by H_2 ⊆ 𝒱, i.e. by the vanishing on H_2 of the projection ℓ: H^⊨ → O·1. This needs H^⊨ handled as a subbundle, e.g. through the F_{p²}-structure. Then show that ℓ, as a section of (H^⊨)^∨ (rank r) on the smooth r-dimensional DL(𝒱♯), has as zero scheme exactly the reduced set DL(𝒱♯)′: a transversality check at the (p+1)(p³+1)⋯(p^{2r−1}+1) special points. The standard description of the blow-up along the zero scheme of a regular section then identifies π with Bl_{DL(𝒱♯)′}, gives E as the exceptional divisor and gives O_E(E) ≅ O_E(−1).
issues.reason: A proper morphism that is an isomorphism away from finitely many smooth points and has fibres P^{r−1} over them need not be the blow-up (D̃L(V) could a priori be non-reduced or non-normal along E); the blow-up structure is used for ℒ|_E ≃ O_E(−E) = O_E(1) and for c_1(O(E))|_E = −η in (A.3)–(A.4), which determine the value of the integral. Case for the defence: the deformation argument of Proposition A.1.3(2) presumably adapts to show D̃L(V) smooth, all other steps of (A.1)–(A.5) check out, the case r = 1 is confirmed directly (−p = d•_{1,p}), and the numbers d•_{r,q} are exactly those making Proposition B.3.5(3) factor, so the stated result is very likely correct. Independent check: Quotation checked on p. 328. The inference 'In particular, π is a blow-up along DL(𝒱♯)′' is drawn only from the fibre data: π is an isomorphism off the special points, with fibre ℙ^{r−1} over each. That data does not determine a blow-up. Counterexample: take X a smooth surface and Z the curvilinear length-2 point (x, y²). Then Bl_Z X = {xt = y²s} is an isomorphism off the point with reduced fibre ℙ^1 over it, but it is singular and its exceptional Cartier divisor is 2·ℙ^1. Intersection numbers like those in (A.3)–(A.5), which use O_E(E) ≅ O_E(−1) and c_1(O(E))|_E = −η, would change. The paper gives no scheme-theoretic analysis of D̃L(𝒱). Note also that H^⊨ is a left orthogonal for a pairing σ-linear in the first variable, and in families over non-perfect bases this need not be a subbundle, so the functor as written needs care. A correct route is in the correction. Case for the defence: the result is very likely true. The first reading reports that r = 1 checks directly (−p = d•_{1,p}) and that the numbers d•_{r,q} are the ones that make Proposition B.3.5(3) factor. I did not independently recheck these. The remaining steps (A.1)–(A.5) follow once the blow-up structure is established.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma B.4.5, published p. 350
issues.printed: The source writes (f_1, …, f_s) = (e_1, …, e_s) + (e_{−s}, …, e_{−1}, e_0) (A over v), then asserts that Y is isotropic precisely when ᵗA^c + A + ᵗv^c · v = 0.
issues.correction: Order the basis as (e_{−1}, …, e_{−s}, e_0), or replace A by J_sA (J_s the s×s antidiagonal permutation matrix) in the isotropy equation.
issues.reason: With (e_{−i}, e_j) = δ_{ij} and the displayed ordering, f_j = e_j + Σ_k A_{kj} e_{−(s+1−k)} + v_j e_0, so (f_i, f_j) = A_{s+1−i,j} + (A_{s+1−j,i})^c + v_i^c v_j (form conjugate-linear in the first variable; the other convention gives the same index reversal), i.e. J_sA + ᵗ(J_sA)^c + ᵗv^c v = 0. The count q^{2s} · q^{s²} = q^{s(s+2)} is unaffected since A ↦ J_sA is bijective; the lemma itself was verified by brute force (q = 2, m ≤ 5; q = 3, m ≤ 4).

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma C.2.4, displayed formula for C(α), published p. 362; arXiv v3 p. 169
issues.printed: Invoking [15, Theorem 3.1] together with continuity, the source asserts T_wφ′_α = C(α)φ′_{wα}, with nonzero coefficient C(α) = ∏_{i=r_0+1}^{r} ( (α_i − q^{−1})/(α_i − 1) ∏_{|α_j|<|α_i|} (α_i − q^{−2}α_j)/(α_i − α_j) ∏_{j=1}^{i−1} (α_iα_j − q^{−2})/(α_iα_j − 1) ).
issues.correction: Add 'where α_1 := q' (as in the proof of Lemma C.2.2(2)) and restrict the middle product to j ⩾ 2. Equivalently, C(α) = ∏_{i=r_0+1}^{r} ( (α_i − q^{−3})/(α_i − 1) · ∏_{j⩾2, |α_j|<|α_i|} (α_i − q^{−2}α_j)/(α_i − α_j) · ∏_{j=2}^{i−1} (α_iα_j − q^{−2})/(α_iα_j − 1) ).
issues.reason: Rank-one check r = 2, r_0 = 1: G = U(V′_4), V′_4 = H ⊕ V′_2 with V′_2 anisotropic. For the torus t_a (a on e_2, ā^{−1} on e_{−2}) the unipotent radical of P_min has F⁺-dimension 4 + 1 with weights ā^{−1} and N(a)^{−1}, so δ_{P_min}(t_ϖ) = |ϖ|_F^{−3} = q^6 and the trivial representation is a subrepresentation of I(𝟏′_2 ⊠ α̲_2) at α_2 = q^{−3}. The long intertwining operator must kill the spherical vector there (otherwise T_w would be an isomorphism I(q^{−3}) ≅ I(q^3), impossible since 𝟏 is a sub of the first and not of the second), so C must vanish at α_2 = q^{−3}; the printed C = (α_2 − q^{−1})/(α_2 − 1)·[undefined j = 1 term] does not (without the j = 1 term it is finite and nonzero at q^{−3}). Macdonald's formula confirms: both maximal parahorics of U(V′_4) (stabilizers of vertex lattices of type 1 and 3) have reductive quotient U_1 × U_3 over 𝔽_q, so the Iwahori–Hecke algebra has both parameters q^3 (|U_3(𝔽_q)/B| = q^3 + 1) and c(α) = (α − q^{−3})/(α − 1), the analogue of (α − q^{−1})/(α − 1) for U(1,1) whose vertices have parameter q. With α_1 := q the printed j = 1 factor is (qα_i − q^{−2})/(qα_i − 1) = (α_i − q^{−3})/(α_i − q^{−1}), and (α_i − q^{−1})/(α_i − 1) times it gives (α_i − q^{−3})/(α_i − 1). Defence: only C(α) ≠ 0 is used, and every factor of the correct formula is finite and nonzero for |α_i| > 1, so Lemma C.2.4 is unaffected. Independent check: Quote checked on p. 362. α = (α_2,…,α_r), so α_1 in ∏_{j=1}^{i−1} is undefined. The first reading's computation of the correct long-root factor is right. U(V′_4) has relative root system BC_1 with root spaces of F⁺-dimension 4 and 1, so δ^{1/2}(t_ϖ) = q^{±3}. Its two maximal parahorics (vertex lattices of types 1 and 3) both have reductive quotient U_1 × U_3 over 𝔽_q, and [K:I] = q³+1. So c = (α − q^{−3})/(α − 1), which vanishes where the trivial representation embeds. The first reading also shows that the printed formula is exactly correct if α_1 := q, as in Lemma C.2.2(2), where α = (q, α_2, …, α_r) on p. 358: (α_i − q^{−1})/(α_i − 1) · (qα_i − q^{−2})/(qα_i − 1) = (α_i − q^{−3})/(α_i − 1). That reading is the natural one: BC(𝟏′_2) = St_2 has parameters {q, q^{−1}}, and the formula copies the C.2.2(2) formula, where the middle product is written over j > 1. The version history supports this. v1 p. 169 printed the U(1,1) factor (1 − q^{−1−2s_i})/(1 − q^{−2s_i}) with no j = 1 term, which really was wrong. v2 p. 170 added ∏_{j=1}^{i−1}, which with s_1 = 1/2 (α_1 = q) turns (1 − q^{−1−2s_i}) into (1 − q^{−3−2s_i}): a repair whose α_1 was never written down. So the published formula is correct up to an undefined symbol (α_1 = q) and an implicit j ⩾ 2 in the middle product. That makes it a misprint, not an error. The alternative reading, which drops j = 1, is the v1 error. Only C(α) ≠ 0 is used, and it holds under every reading, so 'nothing' is right.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition D.1.3, published p. 366 (definition of K_{w_0,0}); arXiv v3 p. 172
issues.printed: The proof takes w_0 to be the rational prime below w, defines K_{w_0,0} := ∏_{v|w_0} U(Λ)(O_{F⁺_v}), and calls this a hyperspecial maximal subgroup in G(ℚ_{w_0}).
issues.correction: Either add to Proposition D.1.3 the hypothesis that no place of F⁺ above the rational prime w_0 below w lies in Σ⁺ (i.e. w_0 ∉ Σ := {p | Σ⁺_p ∩ Σ⁺ ≠ ∅}), or explain how to treat places v | w_0, v ≠ w, lying in Σ⁺ (where V_v may be non-split and K_v arbitrary). For Corollary D.1.4 the extra hypothesis is harmless: Chebotarev supplies infinitely many admissible w, hence w with w_0 not below any given finite Σ⁺′.
issues.reason: The statement only requires w ∉ Σ⁺ ∪ Σ⁺_ℓ with w split in F; other places v of F⁺ above w_0 may belong to Σ⁺ (Σ⁺ is an arbitrary finite set containing Σ⁺_bad). For such v, Λ is only given away from Σ⁺ (U(Λ)(O_{F⁺_v}) is undefined), V_v need not be split, and K_v is an arbitrary factor of K_{Σ⁺}; then K_{w_0,0} is not defined/hyperspecial, G_{ℚ_{w_0}} may be non-quasi-split, and the smooth integral model 𝒮(G̃, h̃)_{K^{w_0}} over W(F̄_{w_0}), the Igusa varieties and the Mantovan formula used afterwards are not available as described. The subsequent definitions (Σ := {p | Σ⁺_p ∩ Σ⁺ ≠ ∅}, (K_T)_p maximal for p ∉ Σ, test functions φ_Σ ⊗ φ^Σ on G(𝔸^{∞,w_0}) × J_b(ℚ_{w_0})) are consistent only with w_0 ∉ Σ. Note w_0 is automatically unramified in F (else Σ⁺_{w_0} ⊆ Σ⁺_bad ⊆ Σ⁺, contradicting w ∉ Σ⁺). Defence: Hodge cocharacter μ is trivial at the places v | w_0 other than w, so a variant with non-hyperspecial level at those places might be made to work, and the only application (Corollary D.1.4) can choose w with w_0 ∉ Σ; but as written the proposition is proved only under the extra hypothesis. Independent check: Quote checked on p. 366. Proposition D.1.3 (p. 365) allows any finite Σ⁺ ⊇ Σ⁺_bad, requires V_v split only for v ∉ Σ⁺_∞ ∪ Σ⁺, and only asks that w ∉ Σ⁺ ∪ Σ⁺_ℓ with w split in F. Nothing prevents another place v | w_0 from lying in Σ⁺. For such v, Λ (given only away from Σ⁺) is undefined, U(V_v) need not be quasi-split, and K_v is an arbitrary factor of K_{Σ⁺}. So K_{w_0,0} := ∏_{v|w_0} U(Λ)(O_{F⁺_v}) is neither defined nor hyperspecial, and the smooth projective model 𝒮(G̃, h̃)_{K^{w_0}} over W(F̄_{w_0}) and the Mantovan/Igusa argument are unavailable as written. Shrinking K_v does not help with F̄_ℓ coefficients and non-hyperspecial targets. The rest of the proof (Σ := {p | Σ⁺_p ∩ Σ⁺ ≠ ∅}, (K_T)_p maximal for p ∉ Σ, test functions φ_Σ ⊗ φ^Σ on G(𝔸^{∞,w_0}) × J_b(ℚ_{w_0}), p. 367) is consistent only with w_0 ∉ Σ. Σ⁺_bad is the union of the Σ⁺_p for p ramified in F (p. 120), so w_0 is unramified in F, as the first reading says. Reach: D.1.3 is used only in Corollary D.1.4 (p. 368), whose proof produces infinitely many admissible w, so one can take w_0 ∉ Σ for any given Σ⁺′ (as Definition D.1.1 requires). Footnote 9 (p. 146) and the introduction's remark on p. 110 refer only to the method. The statement is probably true by a variant with non-hyperspecial level at the definite places above w_0, but it is proved only under the extra hypothesis. Versions: same sentence in v1 (Theorem D.1.3) p. 171, v2 p. 172, v3 p. 172.

issues.printed: The source claims α_i/α_j ∉ {1, ‖w‖} for i ≠ j in F̄_ℓ whenever the rational prime ℓ is sufficiently large. Choosing λ over ℓ in E, it invokes Chebotarev for any residual representation ρ̄_{Π,λ} of ρ_{Π,λ} to produce infinitely many nonarchimedean w in F⁺ outside Σ⁺ ∪ Σ⁺_ℓ, split in F, where (D.1) is decomposed generic.
issues.correction: Apply Chebotarev to ρ̄_{Π,λ} × ε̄_ℓ (i.e. in the compositum of the field cut out by ρ̄_{Π,λ} with F(ζ_ℓ)), producing places u of F of degree one over ℚ with ρ̄_{Π,λ}(Frob_u) conjugate to ρ̄_{Π,λ}(Frob_w) and ‖u‖ ≡ ‖w‖ (mod ℓ); then the ratios of the roots of φ(H_{u|_{F⁺}}) are the α_i/α_j mod λ, which avoid 1 and ‖u‖.
issues.reason: Decomposed genericity at the new place w′ = u|_{F⁺} requires that no ratio of roots equals ‖w′‖ in F̄_ℓ. Conjugacy of ρ̄(Frob_u) with ρ̄(Frob_w) controls the ratios (they equal α_i/α_j mod λ) but not ‖u‖ mod ℓ; ε̄_ℓ(Frob_u) is not determined by ρ̄_{Π,λ}(Frob_u) (conjugate self-duality relates Frob_u and Frob_{u^c}, not ε̄_ℓ(Frob_u) alone). So ratio ≠ ‖w‖ does not give ratio ≠ ‖w′‖ unless ‖w′‖ ≡ ‖w‖ mod ℓ is also imposed. Defence: the fix is routine and standard; the conclusion is correct.

issues.printed: The source claims projectivity of N_p over Z_p[Γ] because that ring is hereditary. It also asserts N_p ⊗ Q_p ≅ (𝓕_n)^𝒞_p ⊗ Q_p, citing torsion-freeness and the finite-index inclusion of N_p in (𝓕_n)^𝒞_p ≅ (Z_p[Γ])^n.

issues.reason: For 𝒞 the abelian |Γ|′-Γ-groups, (𝓕_n)^𝒞 = 𝓕_n^ab, and Corollary 3.10 of the paper gives 𝓕_n^ab ≅ (Z[Γ]/(Σ_g g))^n with no Γ-invariants, whereas (Z_p[Γ])^n has invariants Z_p^n. The argument goes through unchanged: finite-index Γ-sublattices of a lattice over the hereditary order Z_p[Γ] are projective with the same rational span, hence isomorphic (Serre, Linear representations, §16, Theorem 34, Corollary 2).

issues.locator: Statement of Theorem 5.12, p. 30, against Theorem 5.15 (p. 31), Theorem 6.2 (pp. 32–33) and Theorems 7.4–7.5 (pp. 35–36) (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: Theorem 5.12 takes an integer u ≥ 0 and asserts countable additivity of µ_u on A, the algebra generated by U_{C,H}. Theorem 5.15 takes an integer u and gives µ_u(V_{C,H}) = … . Theorem 6.2 introduces a random Γ-group X_u distributed according to µ_u and states its assertion for any integer u.

Its proof applies Lemma 5.10 to f_n(H, ℓ) = µ_{u,n}(U_{𝒞_ℓ,H}), g_n(H) = |Sur_Γ(𝓕_n, H)|/(|Aut_Γ(H)||Y(H)|^{n+u}) and g(H) = |Aut_Γ(H)|^{−1}|Y(H)|^{−u}. The inequality g_n ≤ g holds for every u, because |Sur_Γ(𝓕_n, H)| ≤ |Y(H)|^n by Corollary 3.8. Corollary 5.9 only needs u > −n. For u < 0, X_{u,n}, f_n and P_{u,n} are defined only for n > −u, so Lemma 5.10 and the proof are read for those n. Nothing else in the argument uses u ≥ 0.
issues.reason: For u < 0, Theorems 5.15, 6.2 and 7.4–7.5 evaluate µ_u on Borel sets V_{𝒞,H} and integrate against µ_u. issues.locator: Theorem 4.12, (4.14), p. 24, and its proof, (4.17), p. 25; (5.13) in the proof of Theorem 1.2, p. 30; Theorem 5.15, p. 31 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: Equation (4.17) gives λ(C, H, G) = lim_{n→∞} h_{H⋊Γ}(G)^{m(C,n,H,G)}|Y(G)|^{−n} for G ∈ A_H. Otherwise it asserts λ(C, H, G) > 0 and deduces m(C, n, H, G) → ∞ as n → ∞. For finite admissible H of level C and integer u, Theorem 5.15 gives µ_u(V_{C,H}) = 1/(|Aut_Γ(H)||Y(H)|^u) ∏_{G∈A_H} ∏_{i=1}^∞ (1 − λ(C,H,G) h_{H⋊Γ}(G)^{−i}/|Y(G)|^u) ∏_{G∈N} e^{−|Y(G)|^{−u}λ(C,H,G)}.
issues.correction: Add to (4.14), (5.13) and Theorem 5.15 the hypothesis that H has Property E in the category of level-𝒞 Γ-groups. Equivalently, λ(𝒞, H, G) = 0 for every G ∈ 𝒜_H on which Γ acts trivially. When the hypothesis fails, Prob((X_{u,n})^𝒞 ≅ H) = 0 for every n, and μ_u(U_{𝒞,H}) = μ_u(V_{𝒞,H}) = 0. In the proof, (4.17) and "m → ∞" hold for G with G^Γ ≠ G.
issues.reason: 𝒜_H contains Z/p with trivial H⋊Γ-action. §7.1 speaks of "G ∈ A_H with trivial H-action", and (4.13) needs it. For such G, |Y(G)| = 1, and every sub-H-extension D of an admissible E has Y(D) = Y(E), hence D = E. So Corollary 4.8 gives (h^m − 1)/(h − 1) = Σ_E 1/|Aut_{Γ,H}(E, π)| with m independent of n, i.e. h^m = 1 + λ by (4.10). Hence (4.17) fails whenever λ ≠ 0. The finite-n formula (4.13) is right: its k = 0 factor 1 − 1/|Y(G)|^{n+u} vanishes, so the probability is 0 for every n. It must be: by Proposition 3.13 every (X_{u,n})^𝒞 has Property E, and λ ≠ 0 for such a G exactly when H has a non-split central level-𝒞 Γ-extension by Z/p with trivial action. The limit formula instead contributes ∏_{i≥1}(1 − λh^{−i}), which is never 0. Example: Γ = Z/2, p = 3, 𝒞 the 3-Γ-groups of 3-class ≤ 2, H = F_3² with σ = −1. Then λ(Z/3 trivial) = 2 (the Heisenberg group, |Aut_{Γ,H}| = 1) and λ(Z/3 sign) = 1. The formula gives 2.70·10^{−3} at u = 0 and 4.50·10^{−4} at u = 1. Two helper agents independently enumerated the random quotients: exhaustively at n = 2 and by Monte Carlo at n = 3, 4. F_3² never occurred, while the frequencies of 3^{1+2}_+, Z/3 and Z/9 matched (4.13). For H = F_3⁴, λ = 728 and the formula is negative (−1.42·10^{−4} at u = 0). With 𝒞 all finite 3-Γ-groups, Theorem 7.4 gives μ_u(V_{𝒞,F_3²}) = 0, contradicting Theorem 5.15, which it cites. Unaffected: (4.13); the existence and weak convergence in Theorem 1.2; Theorems 5.12 and 6.2; §7.1 (at abelian level E^Γ = 1); and Theorems 7.4–7.5, which assume H of the form 𝓕_n^𝒞/[Y(S)].

Its proof concludes lim_{q→∞, q≡a (mod |G|²)} Σ_{0≤n≤b} N(E, Γ, q^n, F_q(t)) / Σ_{0≤n≤b} |E_Γ(q^n, F_q(t))| = 1 + O_G(b^{−1}).
issues.correction: State the inner limit as lim sup and lim inf over q. For each b both lie within O_G(1/b) of [H : H^Γ]^{−1}, so lim_{b→∞} lim sup_q = lim_{b→∞} lim inf_q = [H : H^Γ]^{−1}; the same holds for Corollary 1.5. In the second display on p. 41 the numerator should be E_3 b^{d_Γ(q)−2} + (E_1 − E_2) q^{−1/2}.
issues.reason: The proof gives the ratio as (π_{G,c}(q,b′) + O_{b,G}(q^{−1/2}))/(π_Γ(q,b′) + O_{b,G}(q^{−1/2})). Theorem 10.4 controls π_{G,c}(q,b′) − π_Γ(q,b′) only up to O_G(b′^{d_Γ(q)−2}). The numbers of Frobenius-fixed components are integers that depend on q, and nothing in §§10–12 shows that they are eventually constant on a residue class of q. Components in which some inertia class occurs fewer than M times are not classified by the lifting invariant; Proposition 12.7 only bounds how many there are. issues.locator: Lemma 9.3, p. 38, with the definition of E_Γ(D, Q), p. 3, and the second display of the proof of Theorem 1.4, p. 40 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: On p. 3, E_Γ(D, Q) denotes totally real Γ-extensions of Q up to isomorphism, with rDisc K = D. Lemma 9.3 asserts Σ_{K∈E_Γ(D,Q)} |Sur_Γ(Gal(K^{un,∞}/K), H)| = 1/[H : H^Γ] N(H, Γ, D, Q). On p. 40, the source sets H trivial in Lemma 10.2 to obtain Σ_{n=0}^b |E_Γ(q^n, F_q(t))| = Σ_{n=0}^b #Hur^n_{Γ,Γ∖{1}}(F_q).
issues.correction: Either take E_Γ(D, Q) to be the set of surjections Gal(Q̄/Q) → Γ with the stated conditions (Γ-extensions K ⊂ Q̄ with their identification, not up to isomorphism), or multiply the right-hand sides of Lemma 9.3 and of the p. 40 display by |Z(Γ)|/|Γ|.
issues.reason: A Γ-extension is K/Q with a chosen isomorphism α : Gal(K/Q) ≅ Γ (p. 3). (K, α) and (K, inn(γ) ∘ α) are isomorphic via γ ∈ Gal(K/Q), so isomorphism classes correspond to Sur(Gal(Q̄/Q), Γ)/Inn(Γ), with orbits of size [Γ : Z(Γ)]. N(H, Γ, D, Q) counts surjections, and so does #Hur^n(F_q), since the marked point kills automorphisms. For H = 1, Lemma 9.3 asserts |E_Γ(D, Q)| = N(1, Γ, D, Q). Check: x³ − 4x + 1 has discriminant 229, three real roots and Galois group S_3 (PARI), and the narrow ray class group of Q(√229) is Z/3. So this is the only totally real S_3-field with rDisc = 229, and |E_{S_3}(229, Q)| = 1, while N(1, S_3, 229, Q) = |Aut S_3| = 6. |Sur_Γ(Gal(K^{un,∞}/K), H)| is the same for α and inn(γ) ∘ α, so the moment ratios of Conjecture 1.3, Theorem 1.4 and Corollary 1.5 are unchanged. For abelian Γ there is no discrepancy.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 5.10, pp. 29–30 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: It defines Λ using finite Γ-groups H up to isomorphism, of level ℓ, requiring both H^{C_{ℓ−1}} ≃ H̃ and, for at least one n, f_n(H, ℓ) > 0. It then asserts Σ_{H∈Λ} g(H, ℓ) = lim_n Σ_{H∈Λ, i(H)≤n} g(H, ℓ) ≤ lim_n Σ_{H∈Λ, i(H)≤n} 2/c(u, ℓ, H̃) f_n(H, ℓ) ≤ …
issues.correction: The second step needs f_n(H, ℓ) > 0 for every H ∈ Λ with i(H) ≤ n, not only for some n. Add to Lemma 5.10 the hypothesis that f_n(H, ℓ) > 0 implies f_{n′}(H, ℓ) > 0 for n′ ≥ n, and replace i(H) by max(i(H), n_0(H)), where n_0(H) is the first n with f_n(H, ℓ) > 0.
issues.reason: By Corollary 5.9, for n ≥ i(H) either f_n = 0 or f_n ≥ (c/2) g. So g ≤ (2/c) f_n needs f_n > 0 at that n. The hypothesis holds in both applications, Theorem 5.12 and Theorem 6.2. Killing x_{n+1} gives 𝓕_{n+1}/[Y(S̃ ∪ {y})] ≅ 𝓕_n/[Y(S)] with y ∈ 𝓕_{n+1} and Y(y) = Y(x_{n+1}) (Lemma 3.1). The event {X^{𝒞_ℓ} ≅ H} depends only on the images of the relations in a finite quotient, so it is open, and positivity at n implies positivity at n + 1.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 3.17, function-field case, p. 19 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: For a function field K with constant field F_{q^r}, the source gives O_K^× = F_{q^r}^×. It infers O_K^×/O_K^{×p} = 1 from the absence in K of nontrivial pth roots of unity.
issues.correction: Work with the complete curve C_K, since G̃_{K,p} (maximal unramified pro-p extension, no condition at ∞) is its p-part. Then V = {α : div(α) ∈ p·Div(C_K)} gives V/K^{×p} ≅ F_{q^r}^×/p ⊕ Pic(C_K)[p] = Pic⁰(C_K)[p], because μ_p ⊄ K. Pic⁰(C_K)/p is a Γ-direct summand of G̃_{K,p}^{ab}/p. So (3.20)–(3.21) hold with O_K^× replaced by the constants and Cl(O_K) by Pic⁰(C_K), and the lemma follows.
issues.reason: O_K is the integral closure of F_q[t] (p. 4), and its unit group has rank (number of places over ∞) − 1. For a totally real K with Γ ≠ 1 that rank is |Γ| − 1 ≥ 1. Example: K = F_5(t)(√(t²+2)), where ∞ splits. ε = t + √(t²+2) has norm −2 ∈ F_5^×, so it is a non-constant unit. With p = 3 (p ∤ 40, μ_3 ⊄ K), O_K^×/O_K^{×3} ≠ 1. The statement of Lemma 3.17 is unaffected.

issues.printed: The source claims any pair of these elements anticommutes because r is odd, and each squares to 0. It argues that the v_i are isotropic except when ζ_i = −1, and that not all ζ_i can be −1 because their product is 1 with r odd. It concludes that every a ∈ A^1 commuting with s has a^2 = 0 and hence is non-invertible.
issues.correction: The claim that every a ∈ A^1 commuting with s̃ has a^2 = 0 is false; a different argument is needed that no element of C^1(𝒱) centralizes s̃ when 1 is not an eigenvalue of s (e.g. via the image of such an element in O(𝒱) ∖ SO(𝒱), which forces −1 to be an eigenvalue, and then a separate analysis of the (−1)-eigenspace, whose volume element anticommutes with its odd part). Also 'commutes with s' should read s̃.
issues.reason: Counterexample to the intermediate claims: q ≡ 1 mod 3, ζ a primitive cube root of unity, 𝒱 six-dimensional split with s = diag(ζ,ζ,ζ,ζ^{−1},ζ^{−1},ζ^{−1}) on eigenvectors x_1,x_2,x_3 (eigenvalue ζ) and y_1,y_2,y_3 (eigenvalue ζ^{−1}), B(x_i,y_j) = δ_ij/2. Then x_1x_2x_3 and y_1y_2y_3 are admissible monomials (product of eigenvalues 1, r = 3), but in the fermionic model (x_i ↦ creation, y_i ↦ annihilation) a = x_1x_2x_3 + y_1y_2y_3 has a^2 = −(n_1n_2n_3 + (1−n_1)(1−n_2)(1−n_3)) ≠ 0, so the monomials do not anticommute and a^2 ≠ 0. (Monomials sharing a factor, e.g. v_1v_2v_3 and v_1v_4v_5 with orthogonal vectors, even commute.) In this example a is still non-invertible and the stated conclusion of the paragraph (no element of C^1(𝒱) centralizes s̃) is expected to hold (for s^2 = 1 it is in [32, Lemma 8.9]), so Proposition 7.9 is plausibly true, but the argument as written is invalid.

issues.reason: Test (5.13) on n = u_{e_i}(t), 2 ≤ i ≤ 5. By (5.3) with A = 0, Ω_ψ(n)φ(a, 0) = φ(a, atX_{e_i}): N_𝒥 vanishes on the single root vector atX_{e_i}. By (5.8), Ω′_ψ(n)φ′(Y) = ψ(tY_i)φ′(n ⋆ Y), with (n ⋆ Y)_i = Y_i since n ⋆ changes only the coordinate 7 − i. So the left side carries ψ(+tY_i). On the right side, (n, a).0 = atX_{e_i} has trace 0 and ⟨atX_{e_i}, atX_{e_i}⟩ = 0, leaving ψ(−⟨n ⋆ Y, atX_{e_i}⟩/a) = ψ(−tY_i). The proof of Theorem 5.9(3) (p. 29) writes the phase with +Σ Y_iA_i/a. Only with that sign does its germ constant ψ(2(Y_{2,0} − A_{15,0})(Y_{5,0} − A_{12,0}) + 2(Y_{3,0} − A_{14,0})(Y_{4,0} − A_{13,0})) equal I^+(φ, φ′) as defined with Y · A of Proposition 5.5. With the printed − sign the same computation gives (Y_{2,0} + A_{15,0})(Y_{5,0} + A_{12,0}) + …, and Theorem 5.9(3) would fail for general φ′. The alternative repair, a sign error in (5.8) instead, would force changes to Proposition 5.5 and to the computation on p. 29 as well, so the printed (5.13) is the likelier slip. Either way the paper is internally inconsistent here. The fundamental lemma (Theorem 5.9(2)) is unaffected, because 1_{Y′(𝒪_F)} is even. With the corrected sign, Proposition 5.7, Theorem 5.9 and Theorem 1.13 hold as the paper intends.

issues.locator: §3.3, the sketch for the families j = n + in0, p. 651 (published version)
issues.printed: For f whose degree in each variable is bounded by d ≥ 1, the source asserts a permissible j = n + in0 with 0 ≤ n0 ≤ 2d³ + 1. It then chooses n0 ≥ 1 to avoid the obstacle, bounding n0 − 1 by the total degree of Gm and, via standard resultant estimates, by 2dψ(m)² ≤ 2d³.
issues.correction: The obstacle must be avoided for every m with ψ(m) ≤ d at once, so the sketch as written gives n0 − 1 ≤ Σ_{m: ψ(m) ≤ d} 2dψ(m)² ≤ 2d⁴ (there are at most d such m, as ψ(m) ≥ m), that is some 1 ≤ n0 ≤ 2d⁴ + 1. The bound 2d³ + 1 needs a further argument.
issues.reason: Permissibility needs Gm(n + in0, n − in0) ≢ 0 in n for every m ≤ M, as in the proof of Lemma 3.2. The sketch shows that the obstacle can occur only when ψ(m) ≤ d and, for one such m, excludes at most deg Gm ≤ 2dψ(m)² values of n0. For d ≥ 3 more than one m qualifies (m = 1, and m = 2 since ψ(2) = 3), and the excluded sets need not coincide: for d = 3 the union bound is 2·3·(1 + 9) = 60 > 54 = 2d³. The existence of some n0 bounded polynomially in d is unaffected; whether 2d³ + 1 itself holds is not settled here.

issues.locator: §7, in the proof of Proposition 7.17, the non-superspecial supersingular case; independently checked only in author manuscript (25 December 2021).
issues.correction: the middle expression is 2(p² + p − 1)/(p(p² − 1)); the two summands of the numerator are transposed
issues.reason: The displayed series is (2/(1-p^{-2}))(h(p^{-1}+1)/p² + hp/p⁴ + hp²/p⁶ + ···). Summing the geometric tail, the bracket is h((p+1)/p³ + 1/(p²(p-1))) = h(p²+p-1)/(p³(p-1)), and multiplying by 2p²/(p²-1) gives exactly (h/(p-1))·2(p²+p-1)/(p(p²-1)). At p = 3 this is 22/24 = 11/12, which is where the constant 11/12 comes from and shows the bound is sharp there; numerically, with h = 1 and p = 3 the series is (9/4)(4/27 + 1/18) = 0.4583… = (11/12)·(1/2), confirming it. The printed 2(p²-p+1)/(p(p²-1)) equals 7/12 at p = 3, so as printed the first inequality of the chain is false, although the final bound 11/12 that the proof uses is correct. The same computation carried out for the two superspecial cases of the same proof reproduces the printed constants exactly, 61/62 at p = 5 in case (1) and 17/20 at p = 5 in case (2), which confirms the method.

In this setup the positive determinants det L and det L'_1 have the same rational square class: local isometry away from p makes the valuation differences even there, and the p-discriminant exponent is the even type. issues.printed: The source gives generators for (B ⊗ F(V)×)^H: the subgroup (B ⊗ F×)^H and the elements N_{H/H_x}(b ⊗ f_x), ranging over every x ∈ V^(1) and b ∈ B^{H_x}.

issues.reason: Without roots of unity the elements N_{H/H_x}(b ⊗ f_x) need not be H-invariant, and invariants of the tensored sequence are only left exact, so generation of (B ⊗ Div V)^H does not lift. Counterexample (item /64): H = C₂ acting on A¹_R by t ↦ −t, B = Z/2, x = (t), f_x = ct. Then H_x = H, and h(1 ⊗ ct) − 1 ⊗ ct = 1 ⊗ (−1), which is nonzero in R(t)^×/R(t)^{×2} (if −1 = (f/g)², then f² + g² = 0, whose leading coefficient is a positive sum of real squares). issues.locator: §9.1, p. 19, in arXiv:1711.02189v3 (20 September 2018); the same text in the published version, §9.2, p. 966
issues.printed: It defines BJ^r_kY := (Hom(D^r_k, Y) × A¹_C)/G_{m,C}, using the action r · (t ↦ f(t), s) := (t ↦ f(rt), rs). Local Taylor coefficient coordinates are said to readily identify BJ^r_kY with a weighted projective space over Y, making it projective whenever Y is. For projective Y, this is asserted to compactify J^r_kY functorially.
issues.correction: Remove the closed locus of pairs (f, 0) with f a constant jet before taking the quotient (equivalently, take the relative weighted Proj). The result is a bundle of weighted projective spaces over Y containing J^r_kY as the chart s ≠ 0. Functoriality holds for maps that send nonconstant jets to nonconstant jets (immersions, open embeddings, automorphisms); an arbitrary morphism induces only a rational map.
issues.reason: Over a point of a curve with k = r = 1 the fibre of the printed quotient is A²/G_m with weights (1, 1): the origin is an orbit in the closure of every other orbit, so the orbit space is not P¹, which is the quotient of A² minus the origin. A constant map Y → Y′ sends every boundary point (nonconstant jet, s = 0) to (constant jet, 0), so the printed functoriality fails.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 4.3, p. 9, in arXiv:1711.02189v3 (20 September 2018); the same text in the published version, p. 955
issues.printed: Citing Hwang–To [14, Th. 2], the source asserts that γ · W ∩ X ∩ B(R) has volume growing exponentially with R, taking B(R) to be a hyperbolic ball with radius R.
issues.correction: The volume of the positive-dimensional projection of U (equivalently of (γ · W) ∩ D) to Ω, inside a hyperbolic ball B(R) ⊂ Ω, grows exponentially with R.
issues.reason: γ · W is a subset of Ω × X, so "γ · W ∩ X" is not defined, and on the quotient side the statement is false (a ball in a finite-area modular curve has area at most that of the curve). Hwang–To's theorem concerns analytic subvarieties of the Hermitian symmetric domain, and the counting argument needs growth upstairs, across translates of the fundamental domain.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 27.3, p. 182 (also arXiv v3)
issues.printed: For G=SOn, the source claims that the spinor norm embeds G(Fv)/G(Fv)+ in Fv× modulo squares. It derives the assertion from the spinor norm being surjective on SOn−1 when n−1⩾2.
issues.correction: For (G, H) = (SO3, SO2) and Π ≅ Π ⊗ χ, where χ := η_{K/F}∘θ, K = F(√−disc V_H) and θ is the spinor norm, Theorem 27.1 and (31.3) of Theorem 31.11 are false, and with them Theorem 30.1 and Corollaries 31.4 and 31.8: with the components σ′ at the places of R∖{q} fixed, the H-period of Π against Σ vanishes identically for every Σ whose archimedean weight at q has one sign (when K_q = C), so a one-sided admissible U gives average 0, not 1/τ(G) = 1/2; and (27.1) fails for suitable a. They fail whenever Π ≅ Π ⊗ χ, also when K splits at q: then the sign depends on σ′ alone, and a suitable singleton U′ gives average 0 or 1. The weak subconvex bound (1.4) still holds, losing at most a factor 2. With the added hypothesis 'if (G, H) = (SO3, SO2), then Π ≇ Π ⊗ χ' the statements hold: χ is then the only character of ε trivial on the image of H(A), and ∫_{[G]}[a]χ = 0 because multiplication by χ carries Π into the orthogonal Π ⊗ χ. Remark: the same sentence also asserts local surjectivity of the spinor norm on SO_{n−1} at every place. That is false at a real place where V_H is definite and V is not (θ(H_q) = 1 while θ(G_q) = {±1}; at q this happens for (SO(2,1), SO(2)) and (SO(3,1), SO(3)), both quasi-split), even when n − 1 ≥ 3. For dim V_H ≥ 3 the conclusion is recovered globally (Kneser: θ(G(F)) = F^× ∩ θ(G(A))), so there only the proof is affected.
issues.reason: (a) Images. For SO2 = SO(V_H) with V_H an anisotropic plane, θ(SO2(F_v)) = N(K_v^×)F_v^{×2}, of index 2 in F_v^×/F_v^{×2} wherever K_v is a field. The spinor norms of G(F)H(A)G(A)⁺ lie in F^×N(A_K^×)(A^×)² = ker η_{K/F}, while θ(SO3(F_v)) = F_v^×/F_v^{×2}. So χ is a non-trivial automorphic character of G(A), trivial on G(F), H(A) and G(A)⁺, and non-trivial on ε = G(F)G∞⁺U\G(A) once θ(U) ⊆ ker η_{K/F}. Then the image of H(A) in ε is ker χ, of index 2, and (27.1) ⟺ ∫_{[G]}[a]χ = 0. (b) Example. F = Q, D an indefinite quaternion division algebra, G = PD^× = SO(D⁰, Nrd), K ⊂ D imaginary quadratic, H = K^×/Q^× = SO(K^⊥ ∩ D⁰), so χ = η_K∘Nrd. Π = JL(π(ψ)) for a Hecke character ψ of K with ψ|_{A^×} = η_K (trivial central character), D ramified only at primes where π(ψ) is supercuspidal (these are non-split in K, so K embeds in D), and Π_∞ = D_k with k even, tempered and generic as §25.7 requires. Then Π ⊗ χ ≅ Π. (c) Vanishing. χ is trivial on H(A), so ∫_{[H]}φΣ̄ = ∫_{[H]}(χφ)Σ̄. By multiplicity one, multiplication by χ is an involution M = ⊗M_v of Π. M_∞ commutes with PGL₂(R)⁺ and anticommutes with diag(1, −1), which swaps D_k^±, so M_∞ = c·sgn(n) on SO(2)-weight n; at finite v toric multiplicity one (Tunnell–Saito) gives ℓ_v∘M_v = ±ℓ_v, with a sign independent of Σ outside R (at split v, χ_v = 1; at inert v, Σ_v is trivial). Hence, with σ′ fixed, the global H-period vanishes for every Σ of one sign of weight at q, and L(Π, Σ) = 0 by (25.1). Taking the finite places of R non-split in K (single supercuspidal points, allowable by Theorem 24.5) and U a nice interval on the vanishing side of [h^∧] ∩ image(O_stab) = R∖{0}, F_h is non-empty (Lemma 31.9) and every term of (31.3) is 0. Directly, with T′ = u ⊗ ū for an M′-eigenvector u, ∫_{[G]}[a]χ = ±c(∫_{O⁺}a − ∫_{O⁻}a), non-zero for a supported near one sheet of the nilcone. This matches the root numbers: flipping the sign of the weight multiplies the archimedean root number of L(½, ψΩ)L(½, ψ^cΩ) by −1. (d) (1.4). [a] ⩾ 0 and ε/im H(A) injects into A^×/Q^×N(A_K^×) ≅ Z/2 (Kneser for dim V = 3), so the left side of (27.1) is at most twice the right, and the upper-bound half of the argument gives L(Π, Σ) = o(C^{1/4}). issues.locator: Lemma 24.10, the example after it, p. 166, and Example 24.7, p. 165 (also arXiv v3)
issues.printed: The source claims that in the PGL2(F) example, f := (α^{−n}+α^{−n+2}+...+α^n)/n satisfies the lemma when n∈Z⩾1 is sufficiently large relative to ε. Example 24.7 gives Θ^unit ≅ C^(1) ∪ [q^{−1/2}, q^{1/2}]/∼ and Θ^nt ≅ (q^{−1/2}, 1) ∪ (1, q^{1/2})/∼.
issues.correction: Drop the example, or replace it by a function bounded on Θ^unit ≅ C^(1) ∪ ([q^{−1/2}, q^{1/2}] ∪ [−q^{1/2}, −q^{−1/2}])/∼; the lemma is proved independently by Urysohn and Stone–Weierstrass. Example 24.7 itself omits the negative real interval: Θ^unit is as just stated, and Θ^nt ≅ ([q^{−1/2}, 1) ∪ (1, q^{1/2}] ∪ [−q^{1/2}, −1) ∪ (−1, −q^{−1/2}])/∼, which also includes the endpoints q^{±1/2}. For odd n the example function also fails f ⩾ 1 on the negative part of Θ^nt.
issues.reason: The first requirement is |f| ≤ 2 on Θ^unit, which contains the real points α ∈ [q^{−1/2}, q^{1/2}] (complementary series, trivial and Steinberg). There f(α) ≥ α^n/n, and at α = q^{1/2} this is q^{n/2}/n → ∞, so f fails the first requirement for n large. It does satisfy the other two: f ≥ (n+1)/n on the real points, and ∫_{C^(1)} f² = (n+1)/n². The bound is needed in Step 5 of §24.4 because the Steinberg representation, in D′, has infinitesimal character α = q^{1/2}. Checked on the page image of p. 166. Amended after RT-PAPER-NELSON-VENKATESH-21/12(iii): for η the unramified quadratic character, η∘det (α = −q^{−1/2}), St ⊗ η∘det and the twisted complementary series π(η|·|^s, η|·|^{−s}), 0 < s < ½, are unitary with trivial central character and lie in the unramified principal-series component, so α = −q^{±s}, 0 ⩽ s ⩽ ½, lies in Θ^unit; and f(−α) = −f(α) for odd n. The closure of Θ^nt still meets Θ⁰ only in {±1}, a null set, so Lemmas 24.8 and 24.10 survive.
