issues.locator: §3, proof of Theorem 3.1, p. 148, the paragraph on the case 2 ∈ sc(π) (published version; the same in arXiv v2)
issues.printed: For π of weight 2 with 2 ∈ sc(π), the source claims that substituting 2 for 3 in the earlier argument establishes the existence of Sym^{n−1} π.
issues.correction: After running the argument with 3 replaced by 2, conclude by the case just treated (weight 2 and 2 ∉ sc), not by Proposition 3.11. Lemma 3.4 at p = 2 gives π″ of weight 2 with 2 ∉ sc(π″), so the first case gives Sym^{n−1}π″. Theorem 2.1 at p = 2 then gives Sym^{n−1}π′, and BLGGT14 Theorem 4.2.1 gives Sym^{n−1}π.
issues.reason: The argument being repeated ends with 'Then Proposition 3.11 implies that Sym^{n−1}π″ exists' (p. 148), and Proposition 3.11 assumes 2, 3 ∉ sc(π″). With 3 replaced by 2, Lemma 3.4 is applied at the prime 2. It controls π″_2 (rec π″_2 = ω_1 ⊕ ω_2), and for l ≠ 2 it only preserves the Steinberg and supercuspidal types (property (4)). So if π_3 is also supercuspidal, then 3 ∈ sc(π′) (π′ ∼ π at 3) and 3 ∈ sc(π″), and Proposition 3.11 does not apply. The repair uses only what has been proved: π″ has weight 2 and 2 ∉ sc(π″), which is the case treated first. (The repeat also needs a ≥ 3 in KW I Lemma 6.3 at 2, i.e. 2^a > 5 for Lemma 3.4; this follows, as in the 3-adic case, from 2^a > 2n − 1 and n ≥ 3.)

issues.locator: §1.17, proof of Proposition 1.22(3), p. 24
issues.printed: The source invokes reduction modulo ϖ together with Hensel’s lemma to obtain α′_ṽ ∈ R(ṽ, Θ, ρ̄_ṽ)/(ϖ) satisfying det(X − σ_{ṽ,1}(φ_ṽ)) ≡ ∏_{i=1}^{n_1}(X − q_ṽ^{i−1}α′_ṽ) mod ϖ.
issues.correction: Take α_ṽ = (−1)^{n_1+1} det σ_{ṽ,1}(φ_ṽ). Then det(X − σ_{ṽ,1}(φ_ṽ^{n_1})) = (X − α_ṽ)^{n_1} already in R(ṽ, Θ, ρ̄_ṽ) (check at Q̄_p-points, which suffices since the ring is reduced and p-torsion-free). α_ṽ is independent of the Frobenius lift, because det σ_{ṽ,1} is unramified (Θ ∘ N_{k_{n_1}/k(ṽ)} = 1).
issues.reason: Since q_ṽ is a primitive n_1-th root of unity mod p, the displayed product is X^{n_1} − α′^{n_1}, so Hensel's lemma needs an n_1-th root of (−1)^{n_1+1} det σ̄_{ṽ,1}(φ_ṽ) in the residue field, which the hypotheses do not provide. Example: n_1 = 2, q_ṽ ≡ −1 mod p, k = 𝔽_p and a non-square value. The proof also never shows that α does not depend on the Frobenius lift, as the statement claims. The statement is true.

issues.locator: Introduction to Part II, p. 66
issues.printed: The source says that when n is even, a group G of the required kind does not exist.
issues.correction: such a group G does not exist if n ≡ 2 mod 4; it exists for n odd and for n ≡ 0 mod 4.
issues.reason: A definite unitary group in n variables for K/ℚ, quasi-split at all finite places, exists iff there is a hermitian form whose discriminant is positive and a local norm at every finite place. For n ≡ 0 mod 4, d = 1 works. For n ≡ 2 mod 4 the class (−1)^{n/2}d would be a local norm at every finite place but not at ∞, contradicting the product formula for the Hilbert symbol. The statement sits in a heuristic sketch; the paper works over fields with [F⁺ : ℚ] even.

issues.locator: Proposition 5.4 and its proof, arXiv v2 pp. 39–40; the same step in the proof of Lemma 5.7, p. 42
issues.printed: The source says PSL₂(F_{p^a}) has an element of order t₁ with t₁ ≠ p, infers that t₁ divides either p^a − 1 or p^a + 1, and concludes p^a > M. It also claims that the projective image is dihedral or contains SL₂(F_{l^a}), where l^a > t.
issues.correction: For an odd coefficient prime the printed strict bound holds; only the prime 2 needs a correction. From t₁ | ℓ^a ± 1: if ℓ is odd, ℓ^a ± 1 is even and t₁ is odd, so 2t₁ | ℓ^a ± 1 and ℓ^a ≥ 2t₁ − 1 > M. If ℓ = 2, one gets only 2^a ≥ t₁ − 1, and 2^a > M fails exactly when t₁ = 2^a + 1 is a Fermat prime with t₁ − 1 ≤ M. So Proposition 5.4 should read ℓ^a > M for ℓ odd and 2^a ≥ t_i − 1 for ℓ = 2 (or assume t_i > M + 1). Every use needs only the weaker bound: Theorem 5.9 is applied at p ≥ 5, where the strict bound holds, and uses l^b ≥ t₁ − 1 ≥ p^{a₀(p)} > max(4r, 5) at other primes; Lemma 5.7 uses l^a ≥ t − 1 > 4r + 1.
issues.reason: Equality p^a = t₁ − 1 = M is possible: for p = 2, M = 16 and t₁ = 17 (a Fermat prime), 2⁴ ≡ −1 mod 17, so PSL₂(F₁₆) contains elements of order 17, and nothing in the argument forces a larger field. The strict inequality is not proved in that case.

issues.printed: The source requires π_v, π′_v and σ_v to be Iwahori-spherical in (12). In (13), it takes Σ to consist of π’s ramified places and sets S = S_p ∪ Σ. It uses P for conjugate self-dual group determinants of G_{K,S}, sets V₀ = ∏_{v∈Σ} ι_ṽ^{−1}(Iw_ṽ) × ∏_{v∉Σ} G(O_{F_v}), and invokes the automorphy hypothesis to obtain p_∞ ∈ Supp H_{G,∞}.
issues.correction: Add the places where σ (or σ′) is ramified to S, with the unramified lifting ring for r̃ (formally smooth of dimension 4), D unramified and V₀ Iwahori there. The dimension formulas keep their form, and Theorem 4.1 is expected to hold as stated.
issues.reason: In Lemma 5.8 the theorem is applied with π = γπ, which is tamely dihedral of order p at v₀ (Theorem 5.5(3)), and σ = Sym^{r−1}σ′ with σ′_{v₀} an unramified twist of Steinberg (Lemma 5.7(3)). After the base change in (12), γπ is Iwahori-spherical with N = 0 above v₀, hence unramified there, so those places are not in Σ; Sym^{r−1} of a Steinberg twist has N ≠ 0 for r ≥ 2, and base change does not remove that. Then t is not a point of P, the map P → R of Corollary 4.3 is not defined (r̃ ⊗ s is ramified outside S), and T has no G(O_{F_v})-fixed vectors. So the printed proof does not cover the case in which the paper uses the theorem, and the printed route to Theorem 5.5, and through it to Theorems 5.9, 6.4 and A, has a gap with a routine repair.

issues.locator: §5.3, Step 3 of the proof of Theorem B, pp. 21–22; and §6, Step 3 of the proof of Theorem 6.2, (6.2), p. 23 (HAL printed page; the journal PDF was not available)
issues.printed: It defines m_i ∈ Z^{≥0} for s_i as the largest index with (s_{i1},...,s_{im_i}) in I(s_j) for some j ≠ i. Setting m := max_i m_i, it asserts the existence of distinct tuples s_1 and s_2 with m_1 = m_2 = m.
issues.correction: First dispose of a relation with only one index: a_1Γ_{s_1}ζ_A(s_1)=0 is impossible since ζ_A(s_1)≠0 [24, Theorem 4] and a_1Γ_{s_1}≠0. Otherwise at least two indices occur, m_i is defined, and the argument runs as printed. The same remark justifies 'for some a_1,a_2∈K^*' in (6.2).
issues.reason: With a single index there is no j≠i, so m_i is undefined and two tuples with m_1=m_2=m do not exist. Step 3 gives no contradiction then: f_∅(θ)=0 is the hypothesis, and the isolated tails only force divisibility. The case is trivial by nonvanishing (stated in §1), but neither proof mentions it. Likewise, (6.2) presupposes that both (w) and (k,q−1) occur.

issues.locator: Proposition II.3.4 and its proof, p. 259 (also arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The source presents Cyc Sp^gen → Cyc Sp = Sp^{BT} ×_{∏_{p∈P} Sp^{BC_{p^∞}}} ∏_{p∈P} Cyc Sp_p. It says that retaining the underlying spectrum and its T-action lifts the induced Cyc Sp^gen → ∏_{p∈P} Sp^{BC_{p^∞}} to Cyc Sp^gen → Sp^{BT}.
issues.correction: Drop the identification. Cyc Sp (Definition II.1.6(i)) asks each φ_p to be T ≅ T/C_p-equivariant, while the fibre product only records φ_p as a C_{p^∞}-equivariant map. The natural functor Cyc Sp^gen → Cyc Sp does exist: it is the one of §II.6, Cyc Sp^gen ⊆ CoAlg_{(Φ^{C_p})}(TSp_F) → CoAlg_{(−^{tC_p})}(Sp^{BT}) ≃ Cyc Sp (Lemma II.5.8), where the residual T/C_p-action on Φ^{C_p}X makes each Frobenius T-equivariant. On bounded below objects X^{tC_p} is p-complete (Lemma I.2.9) and C_{p^∞} → T is a p-adic equivalence, as the proof of Theorem II.4.11 uses, so there the two notions of Frobenius agree.
issues.reason: Both sides are categorical fibrations over Sp^{BT}, so an equivalence would give equivalences of fibres. Over X = KU with trivial T-action the fibres are ∏_p Ω^∞W_p^{hT} and ∏_p Ω^∞W_p^{hC_{p^∞}}, with W_p = map(KU, KU^{tC_p}). W_p is a rational KU-module, as KU^{tC_p} is rational (Example I.2.3(iii)), so W_p^{hC_{p^∞}} ≃ W_p, BC_{p^∞} being rationally a point. The fibre of W_p^{hT} → W_p is Σ^{−2}W_p^{hT} (Gysin sequence; W_p is complex oriented), and W_p^{hT} ≠ 0 because the non-zero map KU → KU^{hC_p} → KU^{tC_p} is T-equivariant (as in Example II.1.2(ii)). Being 2-periodic, Σ^{−2}W_p^{hT} has non-zero homotopy in non-negative degrees, so Ω^∞W_p^{hT} → Ω^∞W_p is not an equivalence. The authors' Remark II.1.3 notes the same difference between T- and C_{p^∞}-equivariant Frobenius maps outside the p-complete bounded below case.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem B.3, p. 383 (also arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The criterion is applied to C = Δ/T = Δ ×_{Λ∞} Λ∞/T, using U_t := C[t, t+1), t ∈ T, as a cover. It describes C[a, b) by pairs (S, ϕ) with ϕ(S) ⊆ [a, b) ⊆ T, says finite intersections again have this form with b ⩽ a+1, and concludes that U1 ∪...∪Un is weakly contractible.
issues.correction: Use closed intervals U_t = C[t, t+1], which do cover C: a simplex (S_0, ϕ_0) → … → (S_k, ϕ_k) has all ϕ_i(S_i) inside ϕ_k(S_k) ⊆ [ϕ_k(min), ϕ_k(min) + 1]. For a ≤ b ≤ a + 1, C[a, b] ≅ Δ/[k] (k + 1 the number of points of T in [a, b]) has a terminal object. Add the U_t for consecutive t_0 < t_1 < … of T ∩ [−N, N] in increasing order: (U_{t_0} ∪ … ∪ U_{t_{n−1}}) ∩ U_{t_n} = C[t_n, t_{n−1} + 1] is contractible, so each window is weakly contractible by the pushout step, and C is the filtered union of the windows. The last line of the induction should read U_0 ∪ … ∪ U_n.
issues.reason: The half-open U_t do not cover C: for T = Z (n = 1) and S = [1], ϕ(k, 0) = k, ϕ(k, 1) = k + 1 is non-decreasing and Z-equivariant on Z × [1], but ϕ({0} × S) = {0, 1} lies in no [t, t + 1). And the criterion needs every finite intersection weakly contractible, while U_0 ∩ U_1 = C[1, 1) is empty (so is any C[a, b) with b ≤ a, which the reduction to Δ/[k−1] with k ≥ 1 silently excludes). The theorem is true, by the argument above.

issues.locator: Theorem 1.2, p. 208 (also arXiv v2)
issues.printed: Theorem 1.2 asserts that, for a map A → Ā between connective unital associative algebras in Sp, a nilpotent kernel of π0 A → π0 Ā makes the square with rows K(A) → TC(A) and K(Ā) → TC(Ā) homotopy cartesian.
issues.correction: … such that π_0A → π_0Ā is surjective with nilpotent kernel …
issues.reason: The Dundas–Goodwillie–McCarthy theorem is for nilpotent extensions; the notation Ā and Theorem 1.1 ('a surjection … with nilpotent kernel') show the intent. Without surjectivity the statement fails for HZ → HQ (kernel zero): the fibre of K(Z) → K(Q) is ⊕_p K(F_p), which is connective, while TC(Z) is (−2)-connective and TC(Q) = HQ^{hT} (all Tate constructions vanish rationally) has π_{−2} = Q, so the fibre of TC(Z) → TC(Q) has π_{−3} ⊇ Q.

issues.locator: Example I.2.3(iii), p. 220 (also arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The source displays π∗(KU^{tCp}) ≅ KU∗((x))/[p](x) ≅ KU∗((x))/((x−1)^p − 1), and identifies the multiplicative group law’s p²-series as [p²](x) = (x−1)^{p²} − 1.
issues.correction: [p](x) = (1 + x)^p − 1 and [p²](x) = (1 + x)^{p²} − 1, the series of the multiplicative formal group law x + y + xy (or ±((1 − x)^p − 1) for x + y − xy).
issues.reason: A p-series has zero constant term, but for odd p, (x − 1)^p − 1 has constant term −2, so it is no p-series (for p = 2 it is (1 − x)² − 1, a unit multiple of [2](x) for x + y − xy, so harmless). The paper itself writes π_*KU^{tC_p} ≅ π_*KU((t))/((t+1)^p − 1) on p. 329.

issues.locator: p. 351 (definition of a Frobenius lift, and the sentence on TC(X)_p^∧), p. 352 (Proposition IV.3.4 and the sentence before it), p. 353 (Lemma IV.3.5 and its proof); also arXiv v2
issues.printed: It defines a Frobenius lift as a C_{p^∞}-equivariant factorization ϕ_p: X → X^{tC_p} through ϕ̃_p: X → X^{hC_p}. For bounded below X it states TC(X)_p^∧ = TC(X_p^∧) = TC(X_p^∧, p) and automatic extension to a T-action. Proposition IV.3.4 gives bounded below p-complete X with such a lift a pullback with rows TC(X) → ΣX_{hT} and X → X, using tr and id − ϕ̃_p. Lemma IV.3.5 asserts a pullback with rows X^{hT} → X^{hT} and X → X for every p-complete p-cyclotomic X with a lift.
issues.correction: Assume a T-action and a T-equivariant lift. Proposition IV.3.4: X p-complete and bounded below, with a T-action and a T ≅ T/C_p-equivariant φ_p: X → X^{tC_p} (equivalently, a p-complete bounded below cyclotomic spectrum, since X^{tC_ℓ} = 0 for ℓ ≠ p by Lemma I.2.9; equivalently, a p-cyclotomic spectrum whose C_{p^∞}-action extends to T), with a Frobenius lift φ̃_p: X → X^{hC_p}, which may be taken C_{p^∞}-equivariant and is then automatically T ≅ T/C_p-equivariant; the conclusion is the pullback with tr: ΣX_{hT} → X, and TC(X) ≃ TC(X, p). Lemma IV.3.5: X p-complete with a T-action and a T ≅ T/C_p-equivariant φ̃_p: X → X^{hC_p}; neither bounded below nor φ_p is used. On p. 351 read 'cyclotomic' for 'p-cyclotomic'; under that reading the sentence that the action 'extends automatically' is vacuous.
issues.reason: Definition II.1.1(ii) gives a p-cyclotomic spectrum only a C_{p^∞}-action, and the Frobenius lift of p. 351 is only C_{p^∞}-equivariant, yet both statements use X^{hT}, ΣX_{hT} and the transfer, and the proof of Lemma IV.3.5 starts from 'the T ≅ T/C_p-equivariant map ϕ̃_p'. TC(X) is defined only for cyclotomic spectra (Definition II.1.8), which suggests that 'cyclotomic' was meant on p. 351. The bridging claim that the C_{p^∞}-action extends automatically to a T-action is false for p-cyclotomic spectra, as the paper's own Remark II.1.3 (pp. 240–241) says: 'not every C_{p^∞}-action on a p-complete spectrum extends to a T-action, since a C_{p^∞}-action can act non-trivially on homotopy groups'. Example: X = H(F_p[C_{p^∞}]) with C_{p^∞} acting by translation is bounded below and p-complete (an HF_p-module, so p·id = 0). F_p[C_{p^∞}] is free over F_p[C_p], so X^{tC_p} = 0, φ_p = 0 is forced, and φ̃_p = 0 is a C_{p^∞}-equivariant Frobenius lift. A T-action acts trivially on π_* (BT is simply connected), so its restriction to C_{p^∞} would act trivially on π_0 = F_p[C_{p^∞}], but translation does not; no T-action extends the given one. The two results are therefore ill-posed on their stated hypothesis class, where X^{hT} and X_{hT} are undefined; the example does not make a conclusion false. The corrected forms hold: a C_{p^∞}-equivariant lift of a T-equivariant φ_p is automatically T-equivariant, because the mapping spectra into the p-complete X^{hC_p} and X^{tC_p} are p-complete and Z^{hT} ≃ Z^{hC_{p^∞}} for p-complete Z (p. 266). Theorem IV.3.6 and the rest of the paper are unaffected: (Σ^∞_+LY)_p^∧ has a T-action, and Corollary IV.3.3 gives a T-equivariant lift. Found by the red team RT-PAPER-NIKOLAUS-SCHOLZE-18 (finding 3) and confirmed by its verifier, who checked the page images of pp. 240–241 and 351–353.

issues.printed: The source asserts convergence of f = sum_{i,j,k>=0} c_{i,j,k} (y - y_n)^i (log(f_1/f_{1,n}))^j (log(t/t'_n))^k for any n >= 0, provided the sections d_{i,j,k}, i,j,k = 0,1,..., lie in B^{H_{r(n)}} and have uniformly bounded norms after multiplication by p^{(n-1)(i+j+k)}.

issues.reason: The sequence is introduced and its growth bounded as d_{i,j,k}, and then the series that is asserted to converge is written with c_{i,j,k}, which the theorem never defines. The intended reading is unambiguous - the c_{i,j,k} of the corresponding Lubin-Tate statement, Theorem 5.2.8 on p. 59, play exactly this role there, and this theorem is stated as its Drinfeld-side twin with 'Same proof as [Pan22, Theorem 4.3.9]' - so it is a renaming that was not carried through the display. Checked in a clip of p. 65 rendered at 300 dpi: the hypothesis prints d_{i,j,k} twice and the display prints c_{i,j,k}, so this is not an artifact of PDF text extraction.

issues.locator: Theorem 5.3.17, part (1) of the first list, p. 67
issues.printed: The theorem asserts existence of a continuous natural operator d-bar^{k+1}_Dr : O^{la,chi}_LT --> O^{la,chi}_LT tensor_{O^{sm}_LT} (Omega^1_LT)^{tensor k+1}, formally interpreted as (d_{Fl'})^{k+1}. The first listed property instead names d-bar^{k+1}_LT as O^{D_p^*-sm}_LT-linear.
issues.correction: (1) d-bar^{k+1}_Dr is O^{D_p^*-sm}_LT-linear
issues.reason: The theorem constructs d-bar^{k+1}_Dr, and every other occurrence in it - part (2) of the first list, and both parts of the 'Moreover' list on the same page - prints Dr; only this one prints LT. It is more than cosmetic because d-bar^{k+1}_LT is a different operator, constructed in Theorem 5.2.16 on p. 61, and the property asserted here is false of it: that theorem states d-bar^{k+1}_LT is O^{sm}_LT-linear, linear over the GL_2(Q_p)^0-smooth sections, and the two subsheaves O^{sm}_LT and O^{D_p^*-sm}_LT of O^{la}_LT are different, neither containing the other. Indeed if d-bar^{k+1}_LT were linear over the D_p^*-smooth sections its kernel would contain them, whereas Theorem 5.2.16(2) computes that kernel as the GL_2(Z_p)-locally algebraic subsheaf Sym^k V(k) tensor omega^{-k,sm}_LT . t^{n_1}, built from the GL_2-smooth sections. The whole point of Subsection 5.3 is that the two towers exchange the roles of the two groups, which is why a subscript slip of exactly this kind matters when read literally. Checked in a clip of p. 67 rendered at 320 dpi: part (1) unambiguously prints the subscript LT.

Corollary 6.1.21 asserts a commuting diagram of Fontaine operators N_W : W_{0,0} -> W_{k,-k}, taking W to be ker f, X, Y or coker f.
issues.correction: Read B^+_dR/(t^{k+1}) for B^+_dR/(t^k) in all five places of Proposition 6.1.20, as in 6.1.12 ('Let W be a flat Banach B^+_dR/(t^{k+1})-module'), 6.1.17 and 6.1.19. Corollary 6.1.21 then compares the Fontaine operators N_W : W_{0,0} -> W_{k,-k} of ker f, X, Y and coker f.
issues.reason: For a B^+_dR/(t^k)-module W one has t^kW = 0, so W_k = t^kW/t^{k+1}W = 0 and its summand W_{k,-k} is 0. Proposition 6.1.20 itself is meaningful as printed, since being Hodge-Tate of weights 0, k is a condition on W_0 alone, but then it misses the case the paper applies. Then (1) holds (non-split), (2) holds (ψ has infinite order, so the G-semisimplification is not in μ_{p−1}), (3) is vacuous; but the line ē_{12} of (Lie SL_2)^*(1) has character ωψ = 1 (the computation in the proof of Lemma 11.4), so h⁰ ≥ 1.

issues.locator: §1 Introduction, p. 2 of the author version (17 June 2019), last lines of the paragraph before Theorem 1.1. This defines the T used in Thm 1.1(2), Remark 1.1 and the p. 4 control theorem. HAL v3 (6 Jan 2018) does not have this sentence. Its introduction names only U ('an Hecke operator U at p associated to the double classe K_Kli(p)diag(1,p,p,p^2)K_Kli(p)', v3 p. 2), and its Thm 1.1 uses a bare 'ord'. So the sentence is new in the author version. HAL v3 §7 also lacks the comparison T = T_{p,1} + (1+p+p^2+p^3)T_{p,0} that the author version gives on p. 37.
issues.printed: The source associates a Hecke operator T at p to K_p diag(p^2, p, p, 1)K_p, asserting that it acts on the cohomology of X_K.
issues.correction: Suggested rewording: 'There is also a corresponding Hecke operator T at p, a modification of the double coset operator T_{p,1} = K_p diag(p^2,p,p,1)K_p, which acts on the cohomology of X_K. T is the normalized composite of the parahoric double cosets GSp4(Z_p)diag(p,p,p,1)GSp4'(Z_p) ⋆ GSp4'(Z_p)diag(p,1,1,1)GSp4(Z_p) (§7). It acts as p^{3-r}(T_{p,1} + (1+p+p^2+p^3)T_{p,0}), with T_{p,0} = pK_p. For r = 2 and k ≥ 2 it is congruent to pT_{p,1} mod p, so its ordinary part is that of the normalized double coset operator.' Besides the Hecke-algebra identity, the normalization p^{3-r} (a factor p when r = 2) is needed. K_p diag(p^2,p,p,1)K_p and K_p diag(1,p,p,p^2)K_p are indeed the same double coset: the two matrices are Weyl-conjugate with the same similitude p^2.
issues.reason:
Checked on the page images of pp. 2, 3, 4, 37 and 38.
(1) The discrepancy is real. §7, p. 37 says 'The Hecke operator T is related to the classical Hecke operator T_{p,1} = GSp4(Z_p)diag(1,p,p,p^2)GSp4(Z_p) … This suggests to replace T_{p,1} by a composition (denoted T) of two double cosets', and 'an elementary computation reveals that T = T_{p,1} + (1+p+p^2+p^3)T_{p,0}'. p. 38: 'The Hecke operator T that we use acts like p^{3-r}(T_{p,1} + (1+p+p^2+p^3)T_{p,0})'. The body then works only with T = T1∘T2 (p. 39 'We let T = T1 ◦ T2'; §8; §11.1.1).
(2) I checked the identity by counting degrees, using footnote 8's chains G → G/H1 → (G/H1)/H2. There are 1+p+p^2+p^3 choices of H1 and p+1 of H2. H2 ≠ G[p]/H1 gives L = ker of type (1,p,p,p^2), each counted once, so deg T_{p,1} = p(1+p+p^2+p^3). H2 = G[p]/H1 gives multiplication by p, counted 1+p+p^2+p^3 times. The eigenvalue formula on p. 38 also checks out: p^{3-r}[p^{-1}Σ − p^{-3}αδ + (1+p+p^2+p^3)p^{-3}αδ] = p^{2-r}Σ + p^{1-r}(1+p+p^2)αδ.
(3) The p. 2 sentence is written in parallel with the one for U, where 'associated to' is meant literally: §10, p. 57 says U 'corresponds to the operator p^{3-r}U_{Kli(p),1}'. Read the same way, the sentence identifies T with the normalized double coset operator, and that is inaccurate. The difference p·(1+p+p^2+p^3)·T_{p,0} is nonzero.
(4) Case for the defence. The sentence says 'associated to', not 'equal to'. The introduction itself, on p. 4, says T is built from the factorization diag(p^2,p,p,1) = diag(p,p,p,1)·diag(p,1,1,1) as T1 and T2. §7 gives the exact definition and states the relation. So the intended meaning is clear from context, which makes this a slip or imprecision (misprint class), not a false statement.
(5) Consequences: none. For r = 2, v(αδ) = k+1, so the normalized term p(1+p+p^2+p^3)T_{p,0} has eigenvalue (1+p+p^2+p^3)p^{-2}αδ, of valuation k−1. The paper itself notes (p. 38) 'T and pT_{p,1} are congruent modulo p for k ≥ 2'. Integrally, this term is p^{k-1} times an automorphism, because the central element p acts through a prime-to-p central automorphism of X_K. Theorem 1.1(2) and Remark 1.1 assume k > p+1 ≥ 3. So the T-ordinary part equals the pT_{p,1}-ordinary part, and both results are true under either reading. Nothing later in the paper uses the intro sentence; every proof uses the T of §7.

issues.locator: §1 (Introduction), p. 2, the paragraph that sets up Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 (author version, 17 June 2019). HAL v3 (p. 2) has the same omission, worded slightly differently: "a toroidal compactification of the Siegel threefold of level some open subgroup K = ∏ K_ℓ ⊂ GSp4(A_f) such that K_p = GSp4(Z_p)". That version also drops "compact".
issues.printed: It defines X_K → Spec Z_p as a toroidal compactification for the Siegel threefold with level a compact open K = ∏_ℓ K_ℓ ⊂ GSp4(A_f), assuming K_p = GSp4(Z_p).
issues.correction: Read "given by a neat compact open subgroup K = ∏_ℓ K_ℓ ⊂ GSp4(A_f) such that K_p = GSp4(Z_p)". This is the standing hypothesis of §5.2.1 (p. 23) and §6.1.1 (p. 26). A second option, also adding "for a good polyhedral cone decomposition", is not needed. Theorem 1.1 is about cuspidal cohomology, and by Theorem 6.1.5.1(2) (Rπ_*O = O and, in the form corrected in sourceIssues E40, (Rπ)_*I_Σ' = I_Σ, plus the projection formula and common refinements) that cohomology does not depend on which toroidal compactification is chosen. So the minimal correction is the single word "neat".
issues.reason:
The omission is real. I checked the page images of p. 2 of the author version and of the HAL v3 intro. The list of conditions on K is only "compact open, K = ∏K_ℓ, K_p = GSp4(Z_p)", and "neat" does not appear. Everything the proof uses is built for neat K. The only occurrences of "neat" in the paper are p. 23, §5.2.1 ("Let K ⊂ GSp4(A_f) be a neat compact open subgroup. We let S_K = …") and p. 26, §6.1.1 ("Let K ⊂ GSp4(A_f) be a neat compact open subgroup. We assume that K = K^p K_p and that K_p = GSp4(Z_p)"). Y_K, the compactifications of Theorem 6.1.5.1, the Hecke correspondences and all later sections rest on §6.1.1. That includes Theorems 11.2.1 and 11.3.1 and Theorem 14.8.1, which together give Theorem 1.1 (p. 73: "In order to complete the proof of theorem 1.1 …"), and Theorem 15.2.1, which gives Theorem 1.2. The paper has no descent to non-neat level; no text mentions stacks, coarse spaces or taking invariants.

The defence is partial but substantial. (i) In the paper's own terminology, "the Siegel threefold of level K" is only ever defined for neat K (§5.2.1, §6.1.1). The same intro sentence also speaks of "the semi-abelian scheme" over X_K and "the relative Cartier divisor of the boundary", which assume a fine moduli scheme. A careful reader therefore infers neatness, and the intended meaning is clear from context. §15.1 and §15.2 (pp. 106–107) likewise reintroduce "K = ∏K_ℓ … a compact open subgroup. We assume as usual that K_p = GSp4(Z_p)" without saying "neat". There it plainly means the standing assumption of §6.1.1. (ii) Read literally for a non-neat K, such as level 1 with X_K taken as a Faltings–Chai stack, the claims are not proved. When p divides the order of the finite quotient K/K', taking invariants is not exact. The perfect amplitude-[0,1] claim of Theorem 1.1 and the integral statement in point 2 would then need an argument the paper does not give. When p does not divide that order, a descent argument works easily, but none is written.

So this is a genuine slip in the printed statement, not a mathematical failure. It is a misprint rather than a gap, and it affects nothing rather than a stated result, because under the intended hypothesis the proved results are exactly Theorems 1.1 and 1.2. Nothing later relies on the intro passage with non-neat K; the only back-reference, on p. 6, just uses the complex M.

issues.locator: §1 Introduction, p. 6 of the author version (the paragraph starting 'As a replacement of H^0(X_K, Ω^{(0,2)}(−D) ⊗ Q_p/Z_p)'). The same text is in HAL v3 on printed p. 5 (PDF p. 6).
issues.printed: The source proposes replacing H^0(X_K, Ω^{(0,2)}(−D) ⊗ Q_p/Z_p) by H^0(M ⊗^L_{Λ,2} Q_p/Z_p), with M from theorem 1.1. It claims the latter’s p-divisible classes arise from H^0(X_{Kli}(p)_K, Ω^{(0,2)}(−D)), hence from classical automorphic forms.
issues.correction: Both occurrences should read H^0(M ⊗^L_{Λ,0} Q_p/Z_p), i.e. specialise M at k = 0 (weight (0,2)), not at k = 2 (weight (2,2)).
issues.reason:
I checked the printed text on a 300 dpi page render. Both occurrences clearly show the subscript "Λ,2" under ⊗^L; this is not an artefact of the text layer.

The paper's own conventions:
- p. 3 says: "For each integer k, there is a map k : Λ → Z_p extending the character z ↦ z^k of Z_p^×".
- Theorem 1.1(1) says: M ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Q_p = RΓ(X_{Kli}(p)_K, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D) ⊗_{Z_p} Q_p)^{U−ord}, where Ω^{(k,2)} comes from Sym^k St ⊗ det^2 St.
- p. 3 also says M is the U-ordinary part of the cohomology of F^κ ⊗ Ω^{(0,2)}(−D).
- §9.4 (p. 56) gives F^{n,n}_k ≅ (ω_{H_n})^k, which is the highest-weight quotient of Ω^{(k,0)}.
- Theorem 11.3.1(3) (p. 71) gives f RΓ(X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ≃ f RΓ(X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), F^κ ⊗ ω^2(−D)) ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Z_p.

So ⊗_{Λ,2} specialises to Ω^{(2,2)} (Sym^2 ⊗ det^2). The paragraph is about Ω^{(0,2)} = det^2, the abelian-surface weight, which is k = 0.

I redid the check that the claim holds after the correction. Let M_0 = M ⊗^L_{Λ,0} Z_p. It is perfect over Z_p with amplitude [0,1], so there is an exact sequence 0 → H^0(M_0) ⊗ Q_p/Z_p → H^0(M_0 ⊗^L Q_p/Z_p) → H^1(M_0)[p^∞] → 0. The last term is finite, so the maximal p-divisible subgroup is H^0(M_0) ⊗ Q_p/Z_p. Also H^0(M_0) ⊗ Q_p = H^0(X_{Kli}(p)_K, Ω^{(0,2)}(−D) ⊗ Q_p)^{U−ord} by Theorem 1.1(1) at k = 0. This is exactly the stated claim, and with k = 2 it would concern Ω^{(2,2)} instead. Part (2) of Theorem 1.1 (k > p+1) plays no role here.

The slip may come from BCGP-style notation, where abelian surfaces have weight (2,2). In this paper, however, the weight is Ω^{(k,r)} = Sym^k ⊗ det^r and specialisation is written ⊗_{Λ,k}, so the text is wrong under its own conventions.

HAL v3 (printed p. 5) has the identical text with "Λ,2" in both places, and its Theorem 1.1 uses the same ⊗^L_{Λ,k} and z ↦ z^k convention. I could not check the published Duke text.

issues.locator: §2, standing hypothesis, p. 7 (author version, 17 June 2019), as applied with R = Λ = Z_p[[Z_p^×]] (defined in §9.3, p. 56) in §11.3: Theorem 11.3.1(1),(2) (p. 71) and its proof (last line of p. 72: "We deduce from lemma 2.1.2 ..."). HAL v3 has the same text: the §2 hypothesis (HAL v3, printed p. 6, PDF p. 7) and the same "We deduce from lemma 2.1.2" step (HAL v3, printed p. 62, PDF p. 63).
issues.printed: Section 2 assumes R complete, local and noetherian, with maximal ideal 𝔪_R and finite R/𝔪_R, for its ordinary projectors on complexes. Section 9.3 puts Λ = Z_p[[Z_p^×]] and takes κ : Z_p^× → Λ^× universal. Theorem 11.3.1’s proof invokes lemma 2.1.2 for local finiteness of U on RΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), 𝔉^κ ⊗ ω^2(−D)); part (2) declares fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), 𝔉^κ ⊗ ω^2(−D)) perfect over Λ and concentrated in degree [0, 1].
issues.correction: State §2 for a complete semi-local noetherian ring R whose residue ring R/rad(R) is finite. Take m_R to be the Jacobson radical rad(R), and let "perfect" mean a bounded complex of finite projective (not finite free) R-modules. Equivalently, use the fact that such an R is a finite product ∏ R_{m_i} of complete local rings with finite residue fields, and apply §2 factor by factor. For p odd, Λ = ∏_{χ mod p−1} e_χΛ with e_χΛ ≅ Z_p[[T]], so applying §2 factor by factor is right and minimal. Replacing m_R by the Jacobson radical is not enough alone. The basis argument of Lemma 2.3.1 must be done factor by factor, and the "finite free" in the definition of C_perf / Prop. 2.2.1 must become "finite projective".
issues.reason:
(1) Checked on the rendered pages: the §2 standing hypothesis requires R to be local. Λ = Z_p[[Z_p^×]]. For odd p, Z_p^× ≅ μ_{p−1} × (1+pZ_p). X^{p−1}−1 splits into distinct linear factors over Z_p by Hensel's lemma, so Z_p[μ_{p−1}] ≅ Z_p^{p−1}, and Λ ≅ Z_p[[T]]^{p−1}. So Λ has p−1 maximal ideals and is not local. The paper allows any p: it treats p = 2 and p ≥ 3 separately elsewhere (p. 37: "When p ≥ 3 ... When p = 2"), and footnote 23 uses residue classes mod p−1. For p = 2, Λ is local.
(2) §2 really is used with R = Λ, not R = Z_p. Local finiteness over Z_p would fail for Λ-linear U on a module like Λ, because F_p[[Z_p^×]] is infinite-dimensional. The topology on 𝔉^κ = lim_n 𝔉^κ_{∞,n} (p. 56) comes from ker(Λ → Λ_n), which for n = 1 is the Jacobson radical. The step "We deduce from lemma 2.1.2 ..." reduces modulo colim_m RΓ(X_1, 𝓕^k_{m,1} ⊗ ω^2). That is M ⊗ Λ/m_k with m_k = ker(Λ → F_p, [z] ↦ z^k mod p), and this maximal ideal depends only on k mod (p−1). So Lemma 2.1.2, stated for local R, is used outside its hypotheses. Read literally, one fixed k > p+1 only gives local finiteness on the e_{χ_k}-component. Theorem 11.3.1(2), perfectness over Λ, likewise needs Prop. 2.2.1 over the non-local Λ.
(3) The repair is routine. Every §2 proof works factor by factor on e_χΛ. For example, Lemma 2.3.1 picks a basis of M/𝔪_R over the residue field, which needs locality, and this can be done on each factor. Since k > p+1 is arbitrary, every class mod p−1 is covered. The stated results stand. What is missing is a justification in the proof. 1. The mismatch is real. For p odd, Z_p^× = μ_{p−1} × (1+pZ_p), so Λ = Z_p[μ_{p−1}][[T]]. Also Z_p[μ_{p−1}] ≅ Z_p^{p−1}, because x^{p−1}−1 splits into distinct factors over Z_p. So Λ has p−1 maximal ideals and is not local. For p = 2, Λ = Z_2[{±1}][[T]] is local, so the problem only arises for odd p. The paper allows odd p, and it handles weights in residue classes mod p−1 (footnote 23, p. 91). Nothing in the paper extends §2 to semi-local rings. The only mention of semi-locality is for the Hecke algebra in §15.2, via [41] lem. 2.12.

2. The defence mostly works, so this is only a gap. The proofs of Lemmas 2.1.1–2.1.3 and Prop. 2.2.2 never use locality; they go through word for word with m_R = rad(Λ) = (p, [γ]−1). The paper's own argument on p. 72 in fact uses this reading. By §9.3, F^{∞,1}_κ = colim_m F^{m,1}_κ is 𝔉^κ reduced modulo ker(Λ → Λ_1 = F_p[(Z/p)^×]) = rad(Λ), and Λ_1 ≅ F_p^{p−1}. So F^{∞,1}_κ = ⊕_{k mod p−1} F^{∞,1}_k. The proof establishes local finiteness for every k > p+1, which covers every residue class mod p−1, before invoking Lemma 2.1.2. The ideals ker(Λ→Λ_n) also define the rad(Λ)-adic topology. So Thm 11.3.1(1) is correct once Lemma 2.1.2 is read with the Jacobson radical.

3. What does not carry over. Lemma 2.3.1 (and so Prop. 2.3.1) picks a basis of M/m_R over the field R/m_R, but Λ/rad(Λ) is not a field. Prop. 2.2.1 relies on [55] (Mumford) lem. 1, p. 44. Over a non-local ring that lemma gives a first term that is finite flat, i.e. projective, not free. So Thm 11.3.1(2), which the proof never argues explicitly and which presumably comes from Prop. 2.2.1 over Λ, holds in the standard sense of "perfect" (finite projective). It need not hold in §2's literal sense ("complexes of finite free R-modules"). A complex of finite free Λ-modules in [0,1] has the same Euler characteristic on every component. Nothing forces that here: Prop. 13.4.1 only says the relevant dimension difference is locally constant on each residue class mod p−1.

4. What uses the passage: Thm 11.3.1(1) and (2); through them Thm 1.1 (a perfect complex of Λ-modules), §15.2 (the perfect complex f RΓ(...)_m), and Thm 15.2.1. Thm 15.2.1's proof specializes at an arbitrary large weight k, so it works on every component. Every stated result stays true with the standard meaning of "perfect" once §2 is extended as above (a routine extension). So the damage is confined to the proof.

issues.reason: I rendered p. 9 at 400 dpi and it reads exactly as quoted, with 𝔪_R^n/𝔪_R^{n−1} in the first term. So this is not a text-layer artefact. Because 𝔪^n ⊂ 𝔪^{n−1}, the printed quotient 𝔪^n/𝔪^{n−1} does not make sense, and no convention in the paper would make it correct. Redoing the computation degreewise: the surjection M^i/𝔪^n M^i → M^i/𝔪^{n−1} M^i has kernel 𝔪^{n−1}M^i/𝔪^n M^i. Tensoring 0 → 𝔪^n → 𝔪^{n−1} → 𝔪^{n−1}/𝔪^n → 0 with the flat module M^i gives 𝔪^{n−1}/𝔪^n ⊗ M^i ≅ 𝔪^{n−1}M^i/𝔪^n M^i, since 𝔪^k ⊗ M^i ≅ 𝔪^k M^i by flatness. This gives the corrected sequence, which is what the induction in the proof needs. 𝔪^{n−1}/𝔪^n is a finite-dimensional R/𝔪-vector space, because R is noetherian. So 𝔪^{n−1}/𝔪^n ⊗ M^• is a finite direct sum of copies of M^• ⊗ R/𝔪, and its cohomology is finite. The same paper has the correct form in Lemma 2.1.2 on p. 8: "𝔪_R^{n−1}/𝔪_R^n ⊗_R M → M/𝔪_R^n → M/𝔪_R^{n−1} → 0". This correction is right. The error does not affect the argument: the intended sequence is clear from context and from Lemma 2.1.2, and the proof works with it. issues.printed: The proof uses descending induction for H^i(C(f)) = 0. Assuming vanishing for i ≥ n + 1, it invokes E_2^{p,q} = Tor^R_{−p}(H^q(M^•), R/m_R) ⇒ H^{p+q}(M^• ⊗_R R/m_R) to obtain H^n(C(f))/m_R ↪ H^n(C(f)/m_R) = 0, then deduces H^n(C(f)) = 0 via Nakayama’s lemma.
issues.correction: Replace M^• by C(f) in the displayed spectral sequence. It should read: "Using the (Künneth) spectral sequence E_2^{p,q} = Tor^R_{−p}(H^q(C(f)), R/m_R) ⇒ H^{p+q}(C(f) ⊗_R R/m_R) we see that H^n(C(f))/m_R ↪ H^n(C(f)/m_R) = 0."
issues.reason: In Prop. 2.2.2, M^• is the source of f : M^• → N^•. The displayed formula is copied word for word from the display in the proof of Prop. 2.2.1, where M^• was the complex of that proposition. As printed, it is the spectral sequence of the source complex, and that says nothing about H^n(C(f)). I redid the argument. C(f) is a bounded complex of flat modules, so C(f) ⊗_R R/m_R computes the derived tensor product, and the Künneth spectral sequence (Weibel 5.6.4, which the paper cites as [83]) gives E_2^{p,q} = Tor_{−p}(H^q(C(f)), k) for p ≤ 0. The term E_2^{0,n} = H^n(C(f))/m_R has no outgoing differentials, because they land in columns p > 0, which are zero. Its incoming differentials are d_r from E_r^{−r, n+r−1}, which are subquotients of Tor_r(H^{n+r−1}(C(f)), k) with r ≥ 2. These vanish by the induction hypothesis, since n+r−1 ≥ n+1. So the edge map H^n(C(f))/m_R → H^n(C(f)/m_R) is injective, and its target is 0 because the cone of f⊗1 is acyclic. H^n(C(f)) is finite by Prop. 2.2.1, so Nakayama gives H^n(C(f)) = 0. The descending induction can start because C(f) is bounded. So the argument is correct once C(f) replaces M^•. The index Tor_r(H^{n+r−1}(C(f))) used above is right. Only the name of the complex is wrong, so this is a misprint. The same text appears in HAL v3.

issues.locator: §3.1, proof of Proposition 3.1.1, second paragraph, p. 12 of the author version (PDF p. 12). HAL v3 has the same sentence word for word ("There is a surjective map of coherent sheaves over X : OX → OX̄red and we denote by IX its kernel"), but it sits in the paragraph just before Proposition 3.1.1 on printed p. 10 (PDF p. 11), followed by "If X has reduced special fiber then IX = mOk OX".
issues.printed: It asserts a surjection 𝒪_𝔛 → 𝒪_{X̄^{red}} of coherent sheaves on 𝔛 and defines 𝔍_𝔛 as its kernel.
issues.correction: Delete "coherent" and read: "There is a surjective map of sheaves of 𝒪_𝔛-modules 𝒪_𝔛 → 𝒪_{X̄^{red}}; we denote by 𝔍_𝔛 its kernel." The two sheaves are coherent over 𝔛 only when k is discretely valued. The rest of the proof stands as printed.
issues.reason:
I transcribed the sentence from the page rendered at 250 dpi. §3.1 lets k be "a complete non-archimedean field" with no discreteness assumption. The section's results are also used later over non-discretely valued fields: Corollary 3.1.1 is applied "over the non-archimedean field (k(x), k(x)+)" for a maximal rank-1 point x (proof of Prop. 3.4.1, p. 15).

Counterexample: take k = C_p and X = Spa(C_p, O_{C_p}), which is separated and of finite type. It has the formal model 𝔛 = Spf O_{C_p}, whose underlying space is a single point. Then X̄ = Spec(O_{C_p}/m) = Spec F̄_p, which is already reduced. So the printed map is O_{C_p} → F̄_p on global sections, and its kernel is 𝔍_𝔛 = m_{C_p}.

For 𝒪_{X̄^{red}} to be a coherent 𝒪_𝔛-module, the kernel of 𝒪_𝔛 → 𝒪_{X̄^{red}} must be of finite type. On a one-point space that means m_{C_p} must be a finitely generated O_{C_p}-module. It is not. In a valuation ring every finitely generated ideal is principal. If m = (π), then |π| would be the largest absolute value below 1. But |p^{1/n}| = p^{-1/n} tends to 1, so no such largest value exists. Equivalently, F̄_p = O_{C_p}/m is not finitely presented. The claim that this is a map of coherent sheaves is therefore false for non-discretely valued k. For discretely valued k it is true, because 𝔛 is then noetherian.

The mistake is harmless. The proof uses only two facts, and neither needs coherence:
1. 𝒪^{++} = colim 𝔍_𝔛.
2. Čech cohomology equals cohomology for 𝔍_𝔛 on separated models.
Fact 2 follows because H^i(𝔘, 𝔍) = 0 for i > 0 on an affine 𝔘 = Spf A. This comes from the exact sequence 0 → 𝔍 → 𝒪_𝔛 → 𝒪_{X̄^{red}} → 0. Both 𝒪_𝔛 and the quasi-coherent sheaf 𝒪_{X̄^{red}} on the affine scheme have no higher cohomology. Also A → (A/mA)_red is surjective on sections, so H^1(𝔘, 𝔍) = 0 as well. The colimit result cited as [19] prop. 3.1.10 applies to arbitrary sheaves. So this is a false side remark, not a failed step. I class it as an error rather than a misprint because the word states a property that fails, rather than being a typing slip. The defence fails. §3.1 says "Let k be a complete non-archimedean field" and puts no discreteness hypothesis on k. The paper uses §3 over non-discretely valued fields: Corollary 3.1.1 is applied over completed residue fields k(x) in the proof of Prop. 3.4.1 (p. 15), and Lemma 3.2.2 is applied to cohomology over C_p in §13.3 (p. 89). No convention makes 𝒪_{X̄^{red}} coherent over 𝔛. It is generated by one section, 1, whose annihilator is 𝔍_𝔛, so coherence would need 𝔍_𝔛 to be of finite type.

Simplest counterexample: 𝔛 = Spf O_k. Then 𝔍_𝔛 = m_{O_k}. For a non-discrete valuation, m_{O_k} is not finitely generated, because a finitely generated ideal of a valuation ring is principal. So k̃ = O_k/m is finitely generated but not finitely presented over the coherent ring O_k, and is not coherent.

The same failure happens on every formal model 𝔛 of every non-empty X. Suppose 𝔍_𝔛 = (f_1,…,f_r) on an affine Spf A. Each f_j has some power in mA, so its sup norm on the generic fibre is below 1. Every element of (f_1,…,f_r)A then has sup norm at most max_j |f_j|_sup < 1. But m ⊂ 𝔍_𝔛 contains constants a with max_j |f_j|_sup < |a| < 1, which is a contradiction. The HAL v3 sentence "𝔍_𝔛 = m_{O_k}𝒪_𝔛" shows the same thing directly. When O_k is a DVR, A is noetherian and the statement is true.

Why this is harmless: the proof never uses coherence. Repeating the proof of the first isomorphism needs only three facts.
(a) 𝒪_𝒳^{++} = colim_𝔛 𝔍_𝔛. Elements of 𝔍_𝔛 have a power in m𝒪_𝔛, so they have |f| < 1. Conversely, a section with |f| < 1 on an affinoid is topologically nilpotent, so it lies in 𝔍_𝔛 on a suitable model.
(b) [19] prop. 3.1.10 and the reduction to finite coverings. These are purely topological statements.
(c) H^i(𝔘, 𝔍_𝔛) = 0 for i > 0 on affine opens 𝔘 = Spf A (so H^i = Ȟ^i on the separated 𝔛). This follows from 0 → 𝔍 → 𝒪_𝔘 → 𝒪_{Ū^{red}} → 0. Here 𝒪_𝔘 is acyclic on affines (it is lim 𝒪/ϖ^n, with Mittag-Leffler), 𝒪_{Ū^{red}} is quasi-coherent on the affine scheme Ū^{red}, and A → (A/mA)_red is surjective.

Consequences: Proposition 3.1.1 is correct for arbitrary k with the word "coherent" deleted. Deleting that word is the right, minimal correction. Prop. 3.1.1 itself is never cited later in the paper; a search of the whole author version finds no citation. Prop. 3.4.1 uses Corollary 3.1.1, whose proof relies on [26] and Theorem 3.1.1, not on Prop. 3.1.1. The mistake is nonetheless real, because Prop. 3.1.1 itself is stated for arbitrary k. It is a false descriptive claim rather than a typographical slip, so I class it as an "error" with affects "nothing". Some readers might call it a misprint, since the intended meaning ("surjective map of sheaves") is clear.

issues.printed: The source cites [69], thm. 2.22 for the locally ringed space identification (𝒳, O^+_𝒳) = lim_𝔛(𝔛, O_𝔛), over all formal models 𝔛. Using [19], prop. 3.1.10, it concludes H^i(𝒳, O^+_𝒳) = lim_𝔛 H^i(𝔛, O_𝔛), and then Ȟ^i(𝒳, O^+_𝒳) = lim_𝔛 Ȟ^i(𝔛, O_𝔛).
issues.correction: H^i(𝒳, O^+_𝒳) = colim_𝔛 H^i(𝔛, O_𝔛) and Ȟ^i(𝒳, O^+_𝒳) = colim_𝔛 Ȟ^i(𝔛, O_𝔛): direct limits over the filtered system of formal models, with pullback transition maps H^i(𝔛, O_𝔛) → H^i(𝔛', O_{𝔛'}) for 𝔛' → 𝔛.
issues.reason: The paper writes 'colim' for direct limits throughout: O^{++}_𝒳 = colim_𝔛 I_𝔛 later in this same proof, colim_n on pp. 13-14, and many more. It writes 'lim' for inverse limits: lim_n in §3.2, and lim_𝔛(𝔛, O_𝔛) for the space itself. Cohomology is contravariant in 𝔛, so the groups H^i(𝔛, O_𝔛) form a direct system. For a limit of quasi-compact quasi-separated spaces, cohomology of the colimit of pulled-back sheaves is the colimit of the cohomologies; that is the cited result. An inverse limit is not the right object. The next step, Čech cohomology computed with finite coverings, also commutes with filtered colimits. The intended meaning is clear and the proof is fine with colim.

issues.locator: §3.2, proof of Proposition 3.2.1 (injectivity when 𝒳 is proper), p. 13 (author version, 17 June 2019)
issues.printed: The proof seeks a normal proper formal model 𝔛 carrying a locally free ℱ that induces ℱ⁺. Raynaud’s theory supplies 𝔛′ with an affinoid cover 𝔘′ refining 𝒰 on generic fibers; normalizing 𝔛′ in 𝒳 gives 𝔛. It says ℱ⁺ descends to locally free ℱ on 𝔛′ and cites [52], lemma 2.6 for properness. For an affine cover 𝔙 of 𝔛 with generic fiber 𝒱, it identifies Ȟⁱ_𝒱(𝒳, ℱ⁺) with Hⁱ(𝔛, ℱ), declaring this finite over 𝒪_k.
issues.correction: "The sheaf ℱ⁺ comes from a locally free sheaf ℱ on 𝔛", where 𝔛 is the normalisation of 𝔛′ in 𝒳. This matches the paragraph's opening sentence ("a normal proper formal model 𝔛 ... a locally free sheaf ℱ on 𝔛") and the later use of Hⁱ(𝔛, ℱ).
issues.reason:
The printed text is exactly as quoted. The symbol is a fraktur X with a prime (𝔛′), so this is not a text-layer artefact. Four points support a misprint.

(1) It contradicts the framing sentence of the same paragraph, which asks for a normal model 𝔛 with ℱ⁺ coming from a locally free ℱ on 𝔛. The rest of the proof uses ℱ on 𝔛: the affine covering 𝔙 of 𝔛, Ȟⁱ_𝒱(𝒳, ℱ⁺) = Hⁱ(𝔛, ℱ), and finiteness because 𝔛 is proper.

(2) As mathematics, the claim on 𝔛′ is false in the sense the proof needs, which is ℱ(𝔙) = ℱ⁺(𝔙_η), i.e. sp_*ℱ⁺ = ℱ. On an affine piece Spf A of a model with reduced generic fiber, O⁺(Spf A_η) = A°, the integral closure of A in A[1/p]. This equals A exactly when A is integrally closed there. So on a non-normal 𝔛′ we get sp_*O⁺ = ν_*O_𝔛 ≠ O_𝔛′. This is not even invertible. Suppose A° = A·a. Since 1 ∈ A°, we have 1 = ba with b ∈ A, and a² = ca with c ∈ A. Cancelling the unit a gives a = c ∈ A, so A° = A. Already for ℱ⁺ = O⁺, the sheaf on 𝔛′ is therefore not locally free. On the normal 𝔛, O_𝔛(𝔙) = O⁺(𝔙_η). So the gluing matrices in GL_r(O⁺) descend, and ℱ is locally free on 𝔛. This is why the normalisation is taken.

(3) HAL v3 (p. 11) had the sentences in the other order and without "locally free": "The sheaf ℱ⁺ comes from a sheaf ℱ on 𝔛′. We can then replace 𝔛′ by its normalisation 𝔛 in 𝒳. This is still a formal model." The 2019 revision moved the sentence after the normalisation step and added "locally free", but did not change 𝔛′ to 𝔛. That is a leftover from editing.

(4) The intended argument is correct once 𝔛 is read, so no gap remains. The only later use I found, in the construction of the map "ext" ("by proposition 3.2.1, this defines the map ext", p. 100), relies on the statement of Proposition 3.2.1, which is unaffected.

issues.locator: §3.2, proof of Proposition 3.2.1, injectivity part (𝒳 proper), p. 13 of the author version (17 June 2019), last paragraph of the proof. HAL v3 has the same argument on pp. 11–12 (printed), with "finite dimensional Q_p-vector space" where the author version has "k-vector space", and with the sentences in a slightly different order ("The sheaf 𝓕^+ comes from a sheaf F on 𝔛′. We can then replace 𝔛′ by its normalisation 𝔛 in 𝒳. This is still a formal model.").
issues.printed: For complete non-archimedean k with integers O_k, the proof seeks a lattice Im(H^i(𝒳,𝓕^+) → H^i(𝒳,𝓕)) by expressing H^i(𝒳,𝓕^+) as finite type over O_k plus torsion. It takes a Raynaud model 𝔛′ whose cover refines 𝒰, asserts that its normalization 𝔛 remains a formal model, and says 𝓕^+ comes from locally free F on 𝔛′. Citing [52], lemma 2.6 for properness, it identifies Ȟ^i_𝒱(𝒳,𝓕^+) with H^i(𝔛,F) and declares it finite over O_k.
issues.correction:
The proof as written needs k to be discretely valued, or k to be algebraically closed (more generally, stable with divisible value group, by the Grauert–Remmert finiteness theorem). Under those hypotheses the normalisation of an admissible formal model is again admissible. The paper's only use of the result is over C_p, where this holds.

For arbitrary k, replace the claim "finite type plus torsion" by boundedness, which is all that is needed:
- 𝒳 is reduced, so the Čech complex Č(𝒰, ℱ^+) is termwise bounded in the Banach complex Č(𝒰, ℱ).
- H^i(𝒳, ℱ) is finite-dimensional, so B^i is closed. Hence the image of Ȟ^i_𝒰(𝒳, ℱ^+) in H^i(𝒳, ℱ) is bounded.
- By Lemma 3.2.2, c·Im(H^i(𝒳, ℱ^+) → H^i(𝒳, ℱ)) lies inside that bounded image.
- Therefore ∩_n p^n Im = 0, which gives injectivity.

This is the argument the paper itself uses in Lemma 14.7.1. There "lattice" just means "bounded".

Two further remarks:
1. The application is over C_p, not Q_p (§12.1: "the base ring for our constructions is O the ring of integers of C_p"; the space 𝒳_Kli(p) lives over Spa(C_p, O)).
2. Stability of k alone, without a divisible value group, does not seem enough: the obstruction already appears for a tame extension without defect in which |L*| is not contained in |k*| and |k*| is dense.

A separate small slip: "locally free sheaf ℱ on 𝔛'" should read "on 𝔛".
issues.reason:
I rendered p. 13 at 220 dpi and transcribed the passage. The field k is an arbitrary complete non-archimedean field (§3.1, p. 11), and Proposition 3.2.1 is stated for all i ≥ 0.

Counterexample to the intermediate claim, for i = 0:
- Take p odd, k the completion of Q_p(p^{1/p^∞}), with value group Γ_k = Z[1/p]. Since 1/2 ∉ Z[1/p], √p ∉ k, so L = k(√p) has degree 2.
- 𝒳 = Spa(L, O_L) = Spa(k⟨T⟩/(T²−p)) is finite étale over Spa(k, O_k). So it is of finite type, smooth, separated and proper. Take 𝓕 = O_𝒳 and 𝓕^+ = O_𝒳^+.
- For a, b ∈ k, v(a + b√p) = min(v(a), v(b) + 1/2), because the two values lie in different cosets of Z[1/p]. So O_L = O_k ⊕ I·√p with I = {b ∈ k : v(b) > −1/2}.
- Finitely generated submodules of k over the valuation ring O_k are principal. I is not principal, because −1/2 ∉ Γ_k and I has no element of minimal valuation. So H^0(𝒳, 𝓕^+) = O_L is torsion-free and not finitely generated. It is therefore not "the sum of a finite type O_k-module and a torsion group", since any torsion part inside O_L is 0.
- The step "We can replace 𝔛′ by its normalisation … This is still a formal model" also fails. For the model 𝔛′ = Spf O_k⟨T⟩/(T²−p), the normalisation is Spf O_L. If O_L were topologically of finite type, the images t_i of the variables would generate a finite free O_k-submodule M = O_k[t_i]. M is closed in L because all norms on L are equivalent. Then the image of O_k⟨T⟩ would be M, so O_L would be finitely generated, which is false. In fact 𝒳 has no normal formal model of finite type at all.

The proposition's conclusion still holds here: ∩ p^n O_L = 0, and L → lim_n L/p^nO_L is an isomorphism because L is complete. It also holds in general, by the Banach/Čech boundedness argument given in the correction. So only the proof is affected, not the stated result.

I classify this as an "error" rather than a "gap": the printed intermediate claims are false for general k, not just left unproved.

The proposition is applied over C_p, not Q_p. Part III works over Spa(C_p, O) (p. 73: "the associated analytic adic space over Spa(Cp, O)"), and the proposition is used in the proof of Theorem 14.7.1 (pp. 99–100). C_p is algebraically closed, so the normalisation there is of finite type, and the finiteness of H^i(𝔛,F) for proper admissible 𝔛 holds. The paper's application is therefore unaffected. I checked the page image. §3.1 lets k be any complete non-archimedean field, and §3.2 only fixes p as a topologically nilpotent unit of k. With that generality the step "replace 𝔛' by its normalisation 𝔛 … This is still a formal model" can fail, and so can the claim that H^i(𝒳, ℱ^+) is "finite type + torsion".

**Counterexample.** Let p be odd, let k be the completion of Q_p(p^{1/p^∞}), and let L = k(√p).
- The value group of k is Z[1/p], and 1/2 is not in it, so [L:k] = 2, e = 2, f = 1.
- Since v(a) and v(b) + 1/2 can never be equal, v(a + b√p) = min(v(a), v(b) + 1/2). Hence O_L = O_k ⊕ J·√p, where J = {b : v(b) > −1/2}.
- J is not finitely generated, because Z[1/p] ∩ (−1/2, ∞) has no least element. So O_L is not finitely generated over O_k.
- Equivalently: m_k O_L = m_L, so O_L/m_k O_L = F_p has dimension 1, whereas a free module of rank 2 would give dimension 2.

Take 𝒳 = Spa(L, O_L), which is finite étale over Spa(k, O_k), hence smooth, proper and separated. Take ℱ = O and ℱ^+ = O^+, and i = 0.
- H^0(𝒳, O^+) = O_L. It is torsion-free and not of finite type, so the intermediate claim is false.
- Any normal formal model is Spf A with O_L ⊆ A ⊆ L° = O_L, so A = O_L.
- O_L is not topologically of finite type. If O_L/p were a finitely generated O_k/p-algebra, it would be finite (it is integral), and topological Nakayama would make O_L finitely generated. So no normal formal model exists, and "This is still a formal model" fails.

The proposition itself still holds here: lim_n L/p^n O_L = L.

**Defence tried and rejected.** The author version says "k-vector space" (HAL v3 said "Q_p-vector space"), so general k really is intended. No nearby statement restricts k.

**Consequences.** Proposition 3.2.1 is cited only once, in the proof of Theorem 14.7.1 (p. 99, continued "by proposition 3.2.1" at the top of p. 100), for the proper space 𝒳_Kli(p) over Spa(C_p, O). C_p is algebraically closed, so the Grauert–Remmert theorem makes the normalisation admissible. Coherent cohomology of proper admissible formal schemes over O_{C_p} is finitely presented. The paper's argument therefore works there.

Even over C_p, the proof literally shows only that c·H^i(𝒳, ℱ^+) lies in a finitely generated submodule. That is not quite "finite type + torsion" over a non-noetherian O, but it gives the needed boundedness.

The boundedness argument above proves Proposition 3.2.1 for every k. So no stated result changes: only the proof, in the generality stated in §3, is wrong. I classify this as an error rather than a gap, because a concrete counterexample shows the intermediate assertions are false, not merely unproved.

issues.locator: §3.2, proof of Lemma 3.2.3, p. 14 of the author version (17 June 2019). HAL v3 (hal-01393374v3) has the same text on printed p. 12 (PDF p. 13); the only difference is that the sequence is in parentheses: "(cz_0, cz_1 + d(t_0), cz_2 + d(t_0 + t_1), ···)".
issues.printed: The source sets Im_α(z_{α+1}) to the image in Z^i(K•_α), writes Im_α(z_{α+1}) − z_α = d(w_α) ∈ B^i(K•_α), and lifts cw_α to t_α ∈ K^{i−1}. It claims convergence in Z^i(K•) of cz_0, cz_1 + d(t_0), cz_2 + d(t_0 + t_1), ···, with limit lifting c(x_α).
issues.correction: The sequence should be cz_0, cz_1 − d(t_0), cz_2 − d(t_0 + t_1), …, that is y_α = cz_α − d(p_α(t_0 + ⋯ + t_{α−1})) ∈ Z^i(K•_α), where p_α : K• → K•_α is the projection. You could instead keep the + sign and take t_α to be a lift of −cw_α, or define w_α by z_α − Im_α(z_{α+1}) = d(w_α). With the corrected sign, (y_α) is a compatible family, so it gives an element of lim_α Z^i(K•_α) = Z^i(K•), and this element lifts (c x_α).
issues.reason:
I checked page 14 of the author version at 250 dpi, and the printed signs are as quoted. The HAL v3 page 12 image shows the same signs.

Let π_α : K•_{α+1} → K•_α be the transition map. The paper's convention is π_α(z_{α+1}) − z_α = dw_α and p_α(t_α) = cw_α. Write T_α = t_0 + ⋯ + t_{α−1} and let s_α = cz_α + d p_α(T_α) be the printed sequence. Then π_α(s_{α+1}) = c z_α + c dw_α + d p_α(T_α) + d p_α(t_α) = s_α + 2c·dw_α. So the printed family is not compatible, and it gives no element of lim Z^i(K•_α).

A concrete counterexample: take the constant system K•_α = K• = [O_k → O_k] with d = id, in degrees i−1 and i. Take c = 1, all x_α = 0, and the allowed lifts z_α = α. Then w_α = t_α = 1 and s_α = 2α. This is neither compatible nor p-adically convergent. With the corrected sign y_α = α − α = 0.

In general, with the minus sign, π_α(y_{α+1}) = cz_α + c dw_α − d p_α(T_α) − c dw_α = y_α. Also y_α ≡ cz_α modulo boundaries, so its class is c x_α. So the argument works once the sign is fixed.

This is a sign slip whose intended meaning is clear, so it is a misprint. The lemma is true, and the proof is repaired by flipping the sign. The only place the lemma is used is as "the lemma below" in the proof of Proposition 3.2.1, p. 14. That proposition is then used at p. ~96 (ext map) and is unaffected. I could not compare the published Duke text, which is paywalled.

issues.locator: §3.4, proof of Proposition 3.4.1, p. 15 (first paragraph of the proof); HAL v3: same proposition number, p. 14, identical wording
issues.printed: The proof cites [40], coro. 1, page 44, and [70], thm. 9.1 for the result after inverting p, then asserts O^{++}_{T^an_Σ} ≃ f_⋆O^{++}_{T^an_{Σ′}}. For i > 0 it seeks R^i f_⋆O^{++}_{T^an_{Σ′}} = 0, claiming R^i f_⋆O^{++}_{T^an_{Σ′}}/p = 0 suffices: multiplication by p would be surjective and the sheaf is torsion.
issues.correction:
What the argument actually needs is that O^{++}_{T^an_Σ}/p → Rf_⋆(O^{++}_{T^an_{Σ′}}/p) is a quasi-isomorphism, including in degree 0. Then multiplication by p is bijective on R^i f_⋆O^{++} for every i > 0, and a torsion sheaf on which p is injective is 0.

- For i ≥ 2 the printed vanishing is already enough: R^{i−1}f_⋆(O^{++}/p) = 0 makes p injective on R^i f_⋆O^{++}.
- For i = 1 one must add the degree-0 step f_⋆(O^{++}_{T^an_{Σ′}}/p) = O^{++}_{T^an_Σ}/p. Together with f_⋆O^{++} = O^{++}, this makes f_⋆O^{++} → f_⋆(O^{++}/p) surjective. That surjectivity is equivalent to p being injective on R^1 f_⋆O^{++}.
- Alternatively, a bound on the p-power torsion of R^1 f_⋆O^{++} would do, but the paper proves none.

The degree-0 step comes from the proof's own fibre computation:
- H^1(f^{−1}(U_n), O^{++}) = 0 gives H^0(f^{−1}(U_n), O^{++}/p) = H^0(f^{−1}(U_n), O^{++})/p.
- H^0(f^{−1}(U_n), O^{++}) = H^0(U_n, O^{++}), by the degree-0 part of [40] Coro. 1 through Cor. 3.1.1.
- Pass to the colimit, then use Prop. 3.3.1 and Lemma 3.3.1 for i = 0, and the same generisation argument at non-maximal points.

The correction is minimal: the fix changes "surjective" to "bijective" and adds the i = 0 case to the fibre computation. Nothing else changes.
issues.reason:
I transcribed the text from a 220 dpi render of p. 15. Proposition 3.3.1's proof shows that 'R^i f_⋆O^{++}/p' in this paper means R^i f_⋆(O^{++}/p). The fibrewise computation later in the proof indeed gives H^i(f^{−1}(U_n), O^{++}/p) = 0 for i > 0. Since p is invertible on the analytic space, 0 → O^{++} →p O^{++} → O^{++}/p → 0 is exact. The long exact sequence then gives only what the proof says: p is surjective on R^i f_⋆O^{++} for i > 0. But a p-divisible torsion sheaf need not vanish (Q_p/Z_p is an example), and the proof proves no bound on the torsion. So 'surjective + torsion ⇒ 0' is a non sequitur. Injectivity is what is needed. For i ≥ 2 it follows from R^{i−1}f_⋆(O^{++}/p) = 0. For i = 1, the p-torsion of R^1 f_⋆O^{++} is coker(f_⋆O^{++} → f_⋆(O^{++}/p)), and the proof never controls it: its fibre computation only treats i > 0 and never compares f_⋆(O^{++}/p) with O^{++}/p. The author makes exactly this degree-0 step explicitly in Prop. 14.4.1.1, p. 95: 'We look at the sequence for i = 0. Since (π)_⋆O^{++}/p = O^{++}/p … the map … is surjective. This implies that for all i > 0, multiplication by p is an isomorphism'. That confirms the argument in §3.4 is incomplete as printed and that the proposed fix is the right one. The correction is sound: the isomorphism f_⋆(O^{++}_{T^an_{Σ′}}/p) = O^{++}_{T^an_Σ}/p together with f_⋆O^{++} = O^{++} gives the surjectivity. It uses only ingredients already present. The statement of Prop. 3.4.1 is true. Its only later use is the statement, in the proof of Prop. 14.4.1.1 (pp. 94–95), so no stated result is affected. HAL v3 (p. 14) has word-for-word the same argument. The published Duke version could not be checked. I transcribed the passage from a 130 dpi render of author p. 15 and compared it with a render of HAL v3 PDF p. 14.

Notation: in this paper 'R^i f_⋆O^{++}/p' means R^i f_⋆(O^{++}/p). The proof of Prop. 3.3.1 on p. 14 says so ('R^k f_⋆O^{++}/p^n is the sheaf associated to the presheaf U ↦ H^k(f^{−1}(U), O^{++}/p^n)'). The fibre computation also gives exactly this: H^i(f^{−1}(U_n), O^{++}) = 0 for i > 0 implies H^i(f^{−1}(U_n), O^{++}/p) = 0 for i ≥ 1.

The failing step: p is invertible on the analytic space, so 0 → O^{++} →p O^{++} → O^{++}/p → 0 is exact. The long exact sequence, with R^i f_⋆(O^{++}/p) = 0 for i > 0, gives what the text says: p is surjective on R^i f_⋆O^{++} for i ≥ 1, and bijective for i ≥ 2. But 'p-surjective + torsion ⇒ 0' is false in general; Q_p/Z_p is p-divisible torsion. For i = 1 the kernel of p on R^1 f_⋆O^{++} is coker(f_⋆O^{++} → f_⋆(O^{++}/p)), and the proof never controls it. In fact R^1 f_⋆O^{++} = colim_n R^1 f_⋆O^{++}[p^n] = coker(O → f_⋆(O/O^{++})). So its vanishing is exactly a degree-0 statement about f_⋆(O/O^{++}), and the proof omits it.

Defences tried, all of which fail:
1. Reading 'R^i f_⋆O^{++}/p' as the cokernel of p only makes the sentence a tautology. The inference 'surjective + torsion ⇒ 0' is still invalid.
2. 'Torsion' comes only from inverting p ([40] + [70] Thm 9.1). That gives unbounded torsion. No bounded-torsion or derived-completeness result is cited, and derived Nakayama would also need the degree-0 mod-p statement.
3. The integral statement f_⋆O^{++} = O^{++} ('it follows easily') says nothing about f_⋆(O^{++}/p).

The author supplies the missing step himself when he reuses the result. In Prop. 14.4.1.1 (p. 95) he writes: 'We look at the sequence for i = 0. Since (π_{Σ′,Σ})_⋆O^{++}/p = O^{++}/p and O^{++} ↪ (π_{Σ′,Σ})_⋆O^{++}, we deduce that the map … is surjective. This implies that for all i > 0, multiplication by p is an isomorphism'. That is exactly the correct argument, and it confirms that the one on p. 15 is incomplete.

Consequences:
- The statement of Prop. 3.4.1 is true. The fix uses only ingredients already in its proof.
- A grep of both versions finds only one other citation of Prop. 3.4.1: p. 95 (HAL v3 p. 89), where the proof of Prop. 14.4.1.1 uses its statement ('By proposition 3.4.1, we deduce that Rπ_⋆O^{++}_{M_{σ∩Σ}} = O^{++}_{M_σ}').
- No stated result is affected.

HAL v3 has the identical argument on printed p. 13 (PDF p. 14).

issues.locator: §3.4, proof of Proposition 3.4.1, p. 15 (paragraph "First assume that x is a maximal point ..."). HAL v3 (hal-01393374v3) has the same Proposition 3.4.1 and word-for-word the same sentence on its p. 13.
issues.printed: The proof sets U_0 = x′ × T^{rig}_{2,σ}, chooses T_2 ≃ G^s_m for integer s and p̲ = (p, ···, p) ∈ T^{an}_2(Q_p), and declares {U_n = p̲^n U_0}_{n∈N} a neighborhood basis at x in x′ × T^{an}_{2,σ}. For all i > 0 and n ≥ 0 it seeks H^i(f^{-1}(U_n), O^{++}_{x′×T^{an}_{2,Σ″}}) = 0, reducing to U_0 by the p̲-action.
issues.correction: Tie the choice of p̲ to σ. Take a cocharacter λ ∈ X_*(T_2) in the interior of σ, for example the sum of the primitive generators of the rays of σ. This lies in the interior because σ spans X_*(T_2)_R. Put p̲ = λ(p). Equivalently, choose the isomorphism T_2 ≃ G_m^s so that (1,…,1) lies in the interior of σ. Such an isomorphism exists because GL_s(Z) acts transitively on primitive vectors. With the opposite sign convention for σ^∨, use −λ instead. Then ⟨χ,λ⟩ ≥ 1 for every nonzero χ ∈ σ^∨ ∩ X^*(T_2). Let χ_1,…,χ_r generate σ^∨ ∩ X^*(T_2) and let N = max_j ⟨χ_j,λ⟩. Then {|χ_j| ≤ |p|^{nN} for all j} ⊂ U_n ⊂ {|χ_j| ≤ |p|^n for all j}. So the U_n are cofinal among the neighbourhoods of the rational point 0 in the fibre x′ × T^{an}_{2,σ}. The rest of the proof is unchanged, because translation by λ(p) is an automorphism of the whole situation: f_2′ is T_2-equivariant and automorphisms preserve O^{++}.
issues.reason:
I checked the printed text on the rendered page (p. 15 at 130 and 220 dpi). The page has p̲ with an underline, and the quote above is accurate.

Setup (p. 15): σ spans X_*(T_2), T_{2,σ} = Spec Z[σ^∨ ∩ X^*(T_2)], and U_0 = x′ × T^{rig}_{2,σ} = {|χ| ≤ 1 for all χ ∈ σ^∨}. For t = λ(p) we have y ∈ t^n U_0 ⇔ |χ(t^{-n}y)| ≤ 1 ⇔ |χ(y)| ≤ |p|^{n⟨χ,λ⟩}. So the U_n shrink to the closed-orbit point 0 exactly when ⟨χ,λ⟩ > 0 for every nonzero χ ∈ σ^∨, that is, when λ ∈ int σ. Here p̲ = (p,…,p) means λ = (1,…,1) in the chosen coordinates. The paper says only "Fix an isomorphism T_2 ≃ G_m^s" and never ties the choice to σ. Note that σ need not be smooth: only Σ′ is assumed smooth, so there is no canonical identification with (1,…,1) ∈ σ.

There is already a counterexample with s=1. With σ = R_{≥0}(−1) and T_{2,σ} = Spec Z[t^{-1}], we get p^nU_0 = {|t^{-1}| ≤ |p|^{-n}}, which increases. That example depends on the direction of the action, so I also checked a stronger one that fails under either sign convention. Take s=2 and σ = cone(e1, e1−e2). Then σ^∨ is generated by u = (0,−1) and v = (1,1), and T_{2,σ} ≅ A^2. The pairings are ⟨u,(1,1)⟩ = −1 and ⟨v,(1,1)⟩ = 2. So p̲^{±n}U_0 = {|u| ≤ |p|^{∓n}, |v| ≤ |p|^{±2n}}, and neither family is a neighbourhood basis of 0. The printed claim is therefore false for some admissible choices of the isomorphism. This is a genuine but minor gap, not a text-layer artefact.

Proposition 3.4.1 itself is true and the fix is immediate. The later use of Proposition 3.4.1, on p. 95 in §13 (Rπ_⋆O^{++}_{M_{σ∩Σ′}} = O^{++}_{M_σ}, independence of the toroidal compactification), relies only on the statement, so it is unaffected. I checked the printed text on the rendered page (p. 15 at 130 and 220 dpi). The page has p̲ with an underline, which the text layer drops. HAL v3 p. 13 has the same passage.

Setup (p. 15). X_*(T_2) = X_*(T) ∩ σ_R, and σ spans X_*(T_2). So T_{2,σ} = Spec Z[σ^∨ ∩ X^*(T_2)] has a unique fixed point 0, and U_0 = {|χ| ≤ 1 for all χ ∈ σ^∨}. For t = λ(p) we have y ∈ t^n U_0 ⇔ |χ(t^{-n}y)| ≤ 1 ⇔ |χ(y)| ≤ |p|^{n⟨χ,λ⟩}. The printed choice p̲ = (p,…,p) means λ = (1,…,1) in coordinates that the paper fixes with no reference to σ. The U_n shrink to 0 exactly when ⟨χ,λ⟩ > 0 for all nonzero χ ∈ σ^∨, i.e. when λ lies in the interior of σ.

Defences I tried, none of which works:
(1) Sign convention. Take s = 2 and σ = cone(e1, e1−e2). This σ is even smooth, and only Σ′ is assumed smooth anyway. Its dual σ^∨ is generated by (0,−1) and (1,1), and T_{2,σ} ≅ A^2. The pairings with (1,1) are −1 and 2. So p̲^{±n}U_0 = {|u| ≤ |p|^{∓n}, |v| ≤ |p|^{±2n}}, and neither family is a neighbourhood basis of 0. Reversing the convention for σ^∨ only swaps the two signs, so it does not help. Also, neither (1,1) nor (−1,−1) lies in σ = {(a+b, −b) : a, b ≥ 0}.
(2) Charitable reading, "an isomorphism suitably adapted". The text says only "Fix an isomorphism ... for some integer s", with no condition. The decomposition T = T_1 × T_2 is itself an arbitrary choice, so no canonical coordinates exist.
(3) Other statements in the paper or cited sources. The proof cites [40] only for the cohomology of the toroidal embedding, not for this step.
So the sentence as written is false for some admissible choices. Because the choice is the author's to make and a good one always exists, this is a local gap in the proof, not an error in the result.

Consequences. Proposition 3.4.1 is true: the corrected choice restores the argument without changing anything else. Its only later use is on p. 95, in the proof of Proposition 14.4.1.1 (§14.4, independence of the toroidal compactification: "By proposition 3.4.1, we deduce that Rπ_⋆O^{++}_{M_{σ∩Σ′}} = O^{++}_{M_σ}"). That proof uses only the statement. This use is in §14.4, not in §13 as said above. The correction is right and minimal, in either of its two equivalent forms. The s = 1 counterexample above depends on the direction of the sign convention; the s = 2 example above fails under either convention.

issues.locator: §4.1.3, Proposition 4.1.3.1, p. 16 (author version, 17 June 2019); the same text is in HAL v3, printed p. 14 (PDF p. 15)
issues.printed: Proposition 4.1.3.1 assumes h : X → S embeddable and a local complete intersection with pure relative dimension n, and asserts f^!𝒪_X = ω_{X/S}[n], with ω_{X/S} the determinant of 𝕃_{X/S}. The proof attributes this to the definition of f^! in [32], thm 8.7.
issues.correction: h^!𝒪_S = ω_{X/S}[n]. Two symbols are wrong: the letter f should be h, and 𝒪_X should be 𝒪_S. The proof's "definition of f^!" is the generic functor from §4.1.2, applied here to h.
issues.reason: I checked the rendered page image, not the text layer (page 16 at 150 dpi, and HAL v3 PDF p. 15). The statement is in italics and reads "then f^!𝒪_X = ω_{X/S}[n]". Inside the proposition only h : X → S is named. By §4.1.2 on the same page, f^! for f : X → Y is a functor D^+_qcoh(𝒪_Y) → D^+_qcoh(𝒪_X), so it takes objects on the target. That makes h^! a functor from D^+_qcoh(𝒪_S) to D^+_qcoh(𝒪_X), and h^!𝒪_X has the wrong type. Reading f as h does not fix it; the argument also has to be 𝒪_S. The slip probably comes from the paragraph just before, which defines lci for a generic "f : X → S". The corrected statement is the standard one. For a smooth h of relative dimension n, h^!𝒪_S = Ω^n_{X/S}[n]. For an lci h, 𝕃_{X/S} is perfect in degrees −1 and 0 with virtual rank n, and its determinant ω_{X/S} = det(L^0) ⊗ det(L^{−1})^{−1} generalises Ω^n. The paper uses exactly this form on p. 17: the proof of Corollary 4.1.3.1 opens "We have h^!𝒪_S = ω_{X/S}[n]" (image checked) and then computes h^!𝒪_S = f^!(g^!𝒪_S) = f^!(ω_{Y/S}[n]) = f^!(𝒪_Y) ⊗ f^*ω_{Y/S}[n]. HAL hal-01393374v3 has the same wrong text word for word (Proposition 4.1.3.1, with [29] cited in place of [32]). I could not check the published Duke text.

issues.locator: §4.2.3, proof of Lemma 4.2.3.1, top of p. 18 (author version). HAL v3 has the identical sentence (§4.2.3, pp. 15–16 printed).
issues.printed: The source calls f_⋆ det 𝕃_{X/Y} = Hom(f_⋆𝒪_X, 𝒪_Y) → 𝒪_Y the residue map. It says this sends ω ∈ f_⋆Ω^1_{X/S}, with local ideal generators (t_1, ···, t_n) of ℐ_X over Y, to Res[ω, t_1, ..., t_n].
issues.correction: … which associates to ω ∈ f_⋆Ω^n_{X/S} = f_⋆ω_{X/S}, where n is the relative dimension, and to (t_1, …, t_n) … the function Res[ω; t_1, …, t_n].
issues.reason: X ↪ X ×_S Y is a regular immersion of codimension n into a smooth Y-scheme of relative dimension n, and the ideal has n local generators t_1, …, t_n. Hartshorne's residue symbol Res[ω; t_1, …, t_n] ([32] III.9) is defined for relative n-forms ω ∈ Ω^n_{X×_S Y/Y}, whose restriction to X is Ω^n_{X/S}. This matches the determinant ω_{X/Y} of the rank-n complex [Ω^1_{Y/S} ⊗ 𝒪_X → Ω^1_{X/S}] used in the same paragraph. A 1-form is only right when n = 1. The paper writes ω_{X/S} for the determinant and never uses Ω^1 for top forms, so this is a slip with clear intended meaning.

issues.locator: §5.1.1 (The dual group of GSp4), p. 20
issues.printed: It chooses {e1 − e2, −2e1 + e3, −e1 − e2 + e3, −2e2 + e3} as positive roots, compact α1 = e1 − e2, α2 = −2e2 + e3, ∆ = {α1, α2}, and half-sum ρ = (−1, −2; 0). It gives α1^∨ = f1 − f2, α2^∨ = f2, ∆^∨ = {α1^∨, α2^∨}, and asserts the root-datum isomorphism i : X*(T) → X_*(T) has matrix (1 1 1 / 1 0 1 / 1 1 2) in bases e1 = (1,0;1), e2 = (0,1;1), e3 = (0,0;2); f1 = (1,0;0), f2 = (0,1;0), f3 = (−1/2,−1/2;1/2), citing [65], lemma 2.3.1.
issues.reason:
I redid the computation. A character (a1,a2;c) pairs with a cocharacter (b1,b2;d) as a1b1 + a2b2 + cd, and I checked that the f_i are dual to the e_i.

**Positive roots and ρ.** In (t1,t2)-exponents the printed positive roots are t1/t2, t1^−2, (t1t2)^−1 and t2^−2. They form a positive system; λ = (−1,−2) is regular dominant for it. Half their sum is (−1,−2;0), so ρ is right.

**The printed ∆ is wrong.**
- −e1−e2+e3 = (e1−e2) + (−2e1+e3), and −2e2+e3 = (e1−e2) + (−e1−e2+e3). So −2e2+e3 is a sum of two positive roots and is not simple.
- The coroot of −2e2+e3 = (0,−2;0) is −f2, not f2: ⟨−2e2+e3, f2⟩ = −2.
- ⟨ρ, −f2⟩ = 2, which is its height. The simple coroots f1−f2 and −f1 both pair with ρ to give 1.
- ⟨e1−e2, −f2⟩ = +1 > 0, so {e1−e2, −2e2+e3} is not a base of any positive system.

**The printed matrix.** It is symmetric, so rows and columns read the same way. It gives i(e1) = f1+f2+f3, i(e2) = f1+f3, i(e3) = f1+f2+2f3. So i(e1−e2) = f2, which is the printed α2^∨ but a negative coroot for the printed positive system. And i(−2e2+e3) = f2−f1, which is not in the printed ∆^∨. For the correct base, i(−2e1+e3) = −f1−f2. So the printed i is not a based isomorphism for the author-version choices.

**Images in ∆^∨.** The image f2 does lie in the printed ∆^∨ (it is the printed α2^∨); only f2−f1 does not. Neither image lies in the correct ∆^∨ = {f1−f2, −f1}. This does not change the conclusion.

**HAL v3.** HAL v3 had the upper-triangular positive system on printed p. 17 (PDF p. 18): positive roots {e1−e2, 2e1−e3, e1+e2−e3, 2e2−e3}, α2 = 2e2−e3 and α2^∨ = f2. The same matrix is on printed p. 18 (PDF p. 19). There everything is consistent: i(e1−e2) = f2 = α2^∨ and i(2e2−e3) = f1−f2 = α1^∨. HAL v3 has a different typo, e2 = (1,0;1). The revision negated the three non-compact roots and added ρ, but left ∆, the coroot of α2 and i as they were. So the inconsistency was introduced by the revision; HAL v3 itself was consistent (its matrix is on printed p. 18).

**Affects nothing.** ∆, α1, α2, α2^∨ and ∆^∨ appear only in §5.1.1; I grepped the whole text. The printed i still sends every root to a coroot and satisfies the transpose condition, so it is an unbased root-datum isomorphism, and a based one for the upper-triangular Borel. The identification of the dual group with GSp4(C) is therefore still valid. It is used only through semisimple conjugacy classes c_Θ in §5.1.3 and §5.1.5, which do not depend on the choice of base. ρ and 'our choice of positive roots' are used later (§5.1.6), and both are printed correctly. I checked this by hand and by direct computation. The pairing is (a1,a2;c)·(b1,b2;d) = a1b1 + a2b2 + cd, and the f_i are dual to the e_i.

**No reading makes the printed §5.1.1 consistent.**
- The printed Δ = {e1−e2, −2e2+e3} is not a base of any positive system: ⟨e1−e2, (−2e2+e3)^∨⟩ = ⟨(1,−1), (0,−1)⟩ = +1 > 0.
- In the printed list, −2e2+e3 = (e1−e2) + (−e1−e2+e3), so it is not simple. The simple roots of the printed list are e1−e2 and −2e1+e3.
- α2^∨ = f2 is wrong in every system: ⟨−2e2+e3, f2⟩ = −2, so the coroot is −f2.
- The printed i sends α1 to f2 and α2 to f2 − f1. The pair {f2, f2 − f1} is not the printed Δ^∨ = {f1−f2, f2}. So the stated based isomorphism fails for the printed data.

**Defence attempt.** The printed list and ρ = (−1,−2;0) do agree with each other, and Remark 5.1.2.1 holds for them. But the paper's only later uses of "our choice of positive roots" require e2−e1 to be positive:
- §5.1.6 (p. 22) says: "0 ≥ λ2 > λ1 and C is the dominant chamber corresponding to our choice of positive roots". The same range for holomorphic λ appears on p. 24, and the embedding into H^0(Ω^(λ2−λ1−1, 2−λ2)) gives λ = (1−k−r, 2−r; ·).
- For λ = (−5, −2), λ pairs with the coroots of the printed positive roots as (−3, 5, 7, 2). The signs are mixed, so λ is neither dominant nor antidominant under either sign convention.
- For the lower-Borel system the same pairings are (3, 5, 7, 2), all positive.
- The normalizing region "−λ1 ≥ λ2 ≥ λ1" in §5.1.6 lies in the half-plane λ2 ≥ λ1, where e2−e1 is non-negative on λ.
- In §15.2.1 (λ2 = 0 > λ1), both chambers positive for λ contain e2−e1. For λ = (−5, 0) the printed pairings are (−5, 5, 5, 0). So the printed chamber is not one of the "two choices for C", and π(λ)^h would be ill-defined as written.
- The printed α2 = −2e2+e3 and the printed matrix are exactly right for the lower-Borel system.
- On the other side, §15.2.2 says "(−λ1+1, 2; −c) is dominant for the Levi M_Si". That is the standard upper-Borel convention for GL2 highest weights, and the same phrase appears in HAL v3. It does not refer to "our choice".
So no charitable reading rescues the printed list.

**How the error arose.** HAL v3 used upper-triangular conventions throughout, with holomorphic λ1 > λ2 ≥ 0. The revision negated λ but updated §5.1.1 only in part: it negated the non-compact roots, kept e1−e2, computed ρ from that mixed list, and kept the old α1^∨, α2^∨ and matrix.

**Consequences.** Δ, Δ^∨ and i only fix the identification of the dual group with GSp4(C). That identification is used only through semisimple conjugacy classes (c_Θ in §5.1.3 and §5.1.5), which do not depend on the base. In §5.1.6 and §15.2.1 the intended holomorphic chamber is clear from the stated range of λ. No stated result or proof changes once the correction is made, so this affects nothing downstream.

**On §5.1.6.** The statement in the "Affects nothing" paragraph that ρ and 'our choice of positive roots' are used later (§5.1.6) and both are printed correctly is wrong for §5.1.6. The correct §5.3 formula is λ = (1−k−r, 2−r; k+2r). The main text on p. 24 actually prints (1−k+r, …), which is a separate slip; the correct form appears in Remark 5.3.1.
