issues.locator: §9.1.1, proof of Lemma 9.1.1.1, pp. 54–55 (both slips are on p. 55; ψ_T is defined on p. 54)
issues.printed: The source says h′ deforms G̃^D[p^n]|_T to G̃[p^m]_{T′}, alongside H^D_m|_{T′}. Citing [37], thm VII, 4.2.5, it uniquely extends the surjection ψ_T : G̃^D[p^m]|_T → H^D_m|_T, whose target is étale and locally Z/p^mZ, to ψ_{T′} : G̃^D[p^m]|_{T′} → H^D_m|_{T′}. It also describes the nonzero locus of s ∈ H^0(Z′, L^{(p−1)}) as an open (Z′)^m of Z, and calls (Z′)^m → X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^{m−1})_1 affine via an affine open immersion into Z′ followed by a finite map.
issues.correction: Replace "a deformation G̃[p^m]_{T′} to T′ of G̃^D[p^n]|_T" with "a deformation G̃^D[p^m]|_{T′} to T′ of G̃^D[p^m]|_T". This is the Cartier dual of the deformation G̃[p^m]_{T′} of G̃[p^m]|_T. The essential fix is p^n → p^m, with the dual used consistently. The second change is optional: "the open subscheme (Z′)^m of Z" could read "of Z′", which is what the argument proves and what the next sentence uses. The printed "of Z" is not actually false, though.
issues.reason:
First part: a genuine misprint. The map being deformed is ψ_T : G̃^D[p^m]|_T → H^D_m|_T (p. 54), and its extension is ψ_{T′} : G̃^D[p^m]|_{T′} → H^D_m|_{T′}. So Illusie's theorem needs a deformation of the source G̃^D[p^m]|_T. Here n is the p-adic truncation level of X_n and has nothing to do with m. As printed, G̃[p^m]_{T′} (order p^{4m} away from the boundary) cannot be a deformation of G̃^D[p^n]|_T (order p^{4n}) when n ≠ m, and the dual is used on one side only.

HAL v3 (PDF p. 46, printed p. 45) shows where the slip came from. There p^n appears throughout: "ψ_R : G̃^D[p^n]|_R → H^D_m|_R", "a deformation of G̃[p^n]_{R′} to R′ of G̃^D[p^n]|_R", and "ψ_{R′} : G̃^D[p^n]|_{R′} → H^D_m|_{R′}". The author version changed ψ_T, ψ_{T′} and the first group to p^m but left G̃^D[p^n]|_T. So the revision was incomplete. This correction is right.

Second part: this is at most a wording slip, not an error. It is true that s lives on Z′, so the reason given only makes (Z′)^m open in Z′, and the next sentence uses the open immersion (Z′)^m ↪ Z′. But the printed claim is also literally true. Points of (Z′)^m have C an extension of multiplicative groups by multiplicative groups, so C is multiplicative, and that locus U is open in Z. On U, the order of C[p^{m−1}] is locally constant. Both C[p^{m−1}] and H_{m−1} lie in the finite flat group G[F^{m−1}]. By Cartier duality, the condition C[p^{m−1}] ⊂ H_{m−1} says that a homomorphism from a finite flat group to an étale group vanishes, and that condition is open and closed. So Z′ is open and closed in Z near (Z′)^m, and (Z′)^m is open in Z. HAL v3 has the same "(Z′)^m of Z" wording.

Neither slip affects the logic. The proof works once the obvious indices are read in. Nothing downstream depends on the wording: Remark 9.1.1.2, §9.1.2, §9.2, and Lemma 9.5.1 ("Similar to the proof of lemma 9.1.1.1") use only the statement "étale and affine". Separately, the author version gives the number 9.1.1.1 to both a Remark and this Lemma.

issues.locator: §9.1.1, proof of Lemma 9.1.1.1 (the affineness part, case n = 1), p. 55 of the author version (17 June 2019). HAL v3 has the same text on printed pp. 45–46 (PDF p. 46), where "Verschiebung" is misspelt "Vershiebung".
issues.printed: The source defines closed Z′ ⊂ Z by C[p^{m−1}] = H_{m−1}, with connected order p quotient C/H_{m−1} and invertible conormal ℒ. Differentiating V : (C/H_{m−1})^{(p)} → C/H_{m−1} gives s ∈ H^0(Z′, ℒ^{(p−1)}). It describes the nonzero locus as an open (Z′)^m of Z where the quotient is multiplicative, and calls (Z′)^m → X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^{m−1})_1 affine because (Z′)^m ↪ Z′ is an affine open immersion and Z′ → X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^{m−1})_1 is finite.
issues.correction:
For m ≥ 2, replace the definition of Z′. In all cases, give the reason why ℒ is invertible. (It is enough to treat n = 1, as the paper does.)

m = 1. Here H_0 = 0, so Z′ = Z. C ⊂ G[F] is killed by F. So locally C ≅ Spec R[x]/(x^p − ax) with a = 0, and ℒ ≅ R/aR = R is invertible. With this sentence added, the printed argument is correct.

m ≥ 2. Let Z′ be the closed subscheme of Z where H_{m−1} ⊂ C and F kills C/H_{m−1}; in Oort–Tate terms, a = 0. Both conditions are closed, so Z′ is finite over X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1. On Z′ the conormal sheaf ℒ of C/H_{m−1} is ≅ R/aR = R, so it is invertible. The differential of V gives s ∈ H^0(Z′, ℒ^{⊗(p−1)}), and its non-vanishing locus (Z′)^m is where C/H_{m−1} is multiplicative. So (Z′)^m → Z′ → X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1 is affine.

The map H_m ↦ C = H_m embeds X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 in Z, because μ_{p^m} is killed by F^m. The image lies in (Z′)^m: C/H_{m−1} ≅ H_{m−1}[p] is multiplicative, hence killed by F. On (Z′)^m, C is multiplicative of order p^m. There, the three conditions "C is étale-locally μ_{p^m}", "C[p] has order p" and "C[p^{m−1}] = H_{m−1}" are equivalent, and they cut out an open and closed subscheme. That subscheme is X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1, since both represent the subgroups H_m with H_m[p^{m−1}] = H_{m−1}. So the map X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 → X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1 is affine.

Two alternative fixes:
- Keep Z′ = {H_{m−1} ⊂ C}, write C/H_{m−1} = G^L_{a,b} in Oort–Tate form, and replace s by the section b of L^{⊗(1−p)}. Its non-vanishing locus is the multiplicative locus, and a = 0 there.
- Replace {H_{m−1} ⊂ C} by its reduction. On a reduced base, a connected group of order p has a nilpotent, hence a = 0. X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 is reduced, being étale over the smooth X^{≥1}_1, so it lies in the reduction.

The same change repairs the proof of Lemma 9.5.1.
issues.reason:
What the step claims. The affineness half of Lemma 9.1.1.1 is reduced to n = 1. Z → X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1 is the finite scheme of subgroups C ⊂ G[F^m] of order p^m. Z′ is defined as "the closed subscheme of Z where C[p^{m−1}] = H_{m−1}". The proof then makes two claims.
(a) Z′ is closed in Z, so Z′ is finite over X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1.
(b) C/H_{m−1} is connected of order p over Z′, and its conormal sheaf ℒ is invertible; no other reason is given. The differential of V then gives s ∈ H^0(Z′, ℒ^{⊗(p−1)}), whose non-vanishing locus (Z′)^m is the multiplicative locus.
From these, (Z′)^m → Z′ → X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1 is affine, and X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 is open and closed in (Z′)^m.
Connectedness is true: H_{m−1} ⊂ G[F^{m−1}] ⊂ G[F^m], and G[F^m] is infinitesimal. So C and C/H_{m−1} are connected wherever H_{m−1} ⊂ C.

Why "connected of order p" gives no reason. Over an F_p-algebra R, a group of order p is locally Oort–Tate: Spec R[x]/(x^p − ax) with ab = 0. Its conormal module is I/I² = Rx/(ax) ≅ R/aR. Connectedness says only that a vanishes at every point, i.e. that a is nilpotent. If a is nilpotent and non-zero, R/aR is not invertible. Such a group is still killed by F^m once a^{1+p+⋯+p^{m−1}} = 0. The paper knows only that Z is finite over a smooth base; it does not claim Z is reduced. Invertibility holds exactly where a = 0, i.e. where F kills the group. On a reduced base, connectedness does imply a = 0.

m = 1. Here H_0 = 0, so Z′ = Z under any reading. C ⊂ G[F] is killed by F, so a = 0 and ℒ is invertible. The step is correct and only the reason is missing.

m ≥ 2, literal reading. Suppose C_T[p^{m−1}] = H_{m−1,T}. Since C ⊂ G[F^m] ⊂ G[p^m], multiplication by p^{m−1} induces a monomorphism C/H_{m−1} ↪ H_{m−1}[p]. Both are finite flat of order p, so C/H_{m−1} ≅ H_{m−1}[p] is multiplicative. Then C is multiplicative with C[p] of order p, so C is étale-locally μ_{p^m}. Conversely, every H_m gives such a C. So the literal locus is X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 itself. On it, ℒ is invertible, s is nowhere zero, and (Z′)^m = Z′.

This locus is not closed in Z; Remark 9.1.1.2 itself says it is not finite over the base. The usual argument that equality of two finite flat subgroups of the same order is a closed condition does not apply here. The reason is that C[p^{m−1}] is not flat over Z: the literal condition is the closed condition H_{m−1} ⊂ C together with the open condition that C[p^{m−1}] has order p^{m−1}.

Suppose the locus were closed. Then it would be finite over the base. The map is étale (first half of the lemma), so it would be finite locally free of locally constant rank. But the rank is p at ordinary points: the lifts of a cyclic H_{m−1} ⊂ μ_{p^m}² are the p points of P¹(Z/p^m) over a point of P¹(Z/p^{m−1}). The rank is 1 at points of p-rank 1, where the multiplicative part is μ_{p^m} (Remark 9.1.1.2). The ordinary locus is dense, being the complement of the Hasse divisor in a scheme étale over the smooth X^{≥1}_1. This is a contradiction.

The missing points can be identified. Let x be a geometric point of X^{≥1}_Kli(p^{m−1})_1 of p-rank 1, over k. Write E for the local-local p-divisible group of height 2 and dimension 1 at x. Then G_x[F^m] = μ_{p^m} × E[F^m] and H_{m−1} = μ_{p^{m−1}} × 0. Over k, the only order-p subgroups of G_x[F^m]/H_{m−1} = μ_p × E[F^m] are μ_p × 0 and 0 × E[F]. Indeed, such a subgroup is μ_p or α_p. Hom(μ_p, E[F^m]) = 0 and Hom(α_p, μ_p) = 0. And E[F] is the only subgroup of order p of E[F^m], since E is one-dimensional. So {H_{m−1} ⊂ C} has two points over x.
- C = μ_{p^m} lies in the literal locus.
- C = μ_{p^{m−1}} × E[F] is killed by p^{m−1}, so it does not.
The literal locus is open in {H_{m−1} ⊂ C} and étale over the base. Hence, along a trait from an ordinary point to x, at most one of the p lifts can specialise into it. The others specialise to μ_{p^{m−1}} × E[F].
So under the literal reading, claim (a) is false, and the step assumes the finiteness it was meant to supply.

m ≥ 2, closed reading. The last sentence of the proof ("X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 is the open and closed subscheme of (Z′)^m where C ≅ μ_{p^m}") only has content if (Z′)^m can be strictly larger than X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1. That holds for Z″ = {H_{m−1} ⊂ C}. For example, take H_{m−1} = μ_{p^{m−1}} × 0 and C = μ_{p^{m−1}} × μ_p at an ordinary point. Z″ is closed and finite, but ℒ is not invertible on it.

Counterexample. Take x as above, and let E_0 be a supersingular elliptic curve over k, so that E ≅ E_0[p^∞]. Let Spec A be the scheme of order-p subgroups of E[p]. This is the fibre over E_0 of the finite flat degree-(p+1) Γ_0(p) map of Katz–Mazur. Its only k-point is E[F]. So A is Artin local with residue field k and length p+1. Let D ⊂ E[p]_A be the universal subgroup, D ≅ Spec A[t]/(t^p − at). The locus V(a) where F kills D is where D = E[F]_A, which is the closed point. So aA = m_A ≠ 0, and ω_D ≅ A/aA = k is not free over A. Since E[p] = E[F²] ⊂ E[F^m], the group C = μ_{p^{m−1}} × D ⊂ G_x[F^m]_A is flat of order p^m, contains H_{m−1}, and has C/H_{m−1} ≅ D. The conormal sheaf commutes with base change. So the conormal sheaf of C/H_{m−1} on Z″ is not invertible at C = μ_{p^{m−1}} × E[F]. Under this reading, claim (b) is false.

Conclusion. For m ≥ 2 the printed step fails under both readings. The literal Z′ is not finite over the base, and the closed Z′ does not carry an invertible ℒ. The argument works as written only on a closed subscheme the text does not define. Examples are the locus where F also kills C/H_{m−1}, or the closure of X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_1 in Z, which is reduced. So this is an error in the proof. The lemma itself is still true, with the fix given in the correction.

What is affected. Lemma 9.5.1 (p. 57) is proved as "Similar to the proof of lemma 9.1.1.1", for G′ over X_par. Its p-rank-1 points have the same shape, so it has the same flaw, and the same fix repairs it. The affineness is used in three places:
- in §9.1.2, where the vertical maps are "étale and affine";
- in §9.2, to form 𝔛^{≥1}_Kli(p^∞) ("It exists because the transition maps are affine");
- in Remark 9.3.1.
All of these still hold. No stated result changes.

I checked the rendered p. 57, and the text matches the quote above, with the symbol ℭ_𝔜 (fraktur C). The definition does not bound the order of L.

In detail:
(1) Every subgroup of G[p] is totally isotropic in G[p²]. Take x, y ∈ G[p] and write x = p·x̃. Then e_{p²}(x, y) = e_{p²}(x̃, y)^p = e_{p²}(x̃, py) = 1.
(2) Suppose L is totally isotropic with |L[p]| = p³. Then |L| = p³·|pL| ≤ p⁴, so |L| is p³ or p⁴. Order is locally constant for finite flat L, so the literal ℭ_𝔜(p^m) has an extra open and closed piece where L ⊂ G[p] has order p³.
(3) This piece is not empty. Take an ordinary point with G[p] = μ_p a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ Z/p e ⊕ Z/p f, where a pairs with e and b pairs with f. Let H_1 = μ_p a and L = μ_p b ⊕ Z/p e ⊕ Z/p f. Then L ∩ H_m ⊂ L ∩ H_1 = 0. Also H_1^⊥ = μ_p a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ Z/p f, so L ∩ H_1^⊥ = μ_p b ⊕ Z/p f. That gives L/(L ∩ H_1^⊥) ≅ Z/p, not Z/p², so the second claim of Lemma 10.1.1 fails. More generally, L ∩ H_1 = 0 forces L ≠ H_1^⊥, so the quotient always has order p on this piece.
(4) The proof of Lemma 10.1.1 needs |L| = p⁴ for "pL = L[p]^⊥". The inclusion pL ⊂ L[p]^⊥ always holds, and |L[p]^⊥| = p, so equality holds exactly when |pL| = p.
(5) Proposition 10.2.1 fails literally. Its proof needs "the kernel of G/L[p] → G/L is étale of order p". Also, ℭ(p^m) = ℭ² ×_{𝔛^{m-et}_{par,Kli}(p^m)} ℭ¹ only parametrises isogenies G → G' → G'' of degree p³·p = p⁴, while on the extra piece G → G/L has degree p³.

The intended meaning is clear from the paper itself. Footnote 16 on p. 60 (in the proof of Lemma 10.3.2) says "the universal rank p⁴ subgroup L". The proof of Proposition 10.2.1 uses an étale kernel of order p for G/L[p] → G/L. The parallel definitions on p. 44 (§7, the correspondence D: "an extension of an étale group scheme locally isomorphic to Z/pZ ⊕ Z/p²Z by ... µ_p") and in §13.2.1 ("locally ... isomorphic to (Z/pZ)² ⊕ Z/p²Z") both state the isomorphism type. So this is an omitted condition, not a real mathematical error.

Effect: ℭ_𝔜(p^m) is only used on pp. 57–60. It appears in Lemma 10.1.1, Proposition 10.2.1 and Lemmas 10.3.1–10.3.2, where the 1/p³ trace normalisation and the deformation computation assume |L| = p⁴. As literally stated, Lemma 10.1.1 and Proposition 10.2.1 are false. The U-operator itself is built from ℭ(p^m) via ℭ¹ and ℭ², which never mention L, so the operator and everything after §10.3 are unaffected once the obvious correction is made.

HAL v3 (p. 47, §10.1) has different text: "Let ℭ_𝔜(p^m) be the moduli over 𝔜_{Kli}(p^m) of triples (G, H_m, L) where L ⊂ G[p²] is totally isotropic L ∩ H_m = {0}, and pL ∩ H_m^⊥ = {0}", with the matrix diag(1,p,p,p²). That definition also has no order condition. It is even weaker, since L = {0} satisfies it. So the defect was already there in v3, in a different form. Defence attempted and failed.
(a) The paper's own convention does not make "totally isotropic" mean Lagrangian. §5.1.2 calls W = <e1> a "totally isotropic direct factor". §6.1.4 says "totally isotropic direct factors L ⊂ V1 of rank 2", giving the rank separately. In §6.1.5.2 the set C contains isotropic factors of every rank.
(b) The conditions do not force the order. For x ∈ L and y ∈ L[p], e_p(px, y) = e_{p^2}(x, y) = 1, so pL ⊂ L[p]^⊥, which has order p. Hence |L| is p^3 or p^4, and every subgroup of G[p] is isotropic for e_{p^2}. The case |L| = p^3 (L = L[p]) does occur. Take an ordinary point with G[p] = μ_p a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ Z/p e ⊕ Z/p f, H_m = μ_{p^m} a and L = μ_p b ⊕ Z/p e ⊕ Z/p f. Then L ∩ H_m ⊂ L ∩ H_1 = 0.
(c) Brute force for p = 2 on (Z/4)^4 with the standard symplectic form and H_1 = <2a>, by a short computer enumeration. There are 16 = p^4 subgroups of order p^4, each with L/(L∩H_1^⊥) ≅ Z/4. There are also 8 = p^3 extra subgroups of order p^3, each with quotient of order p.
(d) On this extra piece the literal statement of Lemma 10.1.1 fails, because the quotient has order p and is not Z/p^2. Its proof uses "pL = L[p]^⊥", which needs |pL| = p. Worse, G/L = G/H^⊥ with H = L^⊥ is the paramodular quotient of the Klingen chain in §6.1.2–6.1.3. The polarization descended from p^2λ has degree p^2, so t_2(G, H_m, L) = (G/L, ...) does not lie in 𝔜^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^m). In fact this piece is just ℭ^1(p^m)|_𝔜. So the literal definition is wrong. The intended meaning is still clear from the context:
- U is "associated to the matrix diag(p^2,p,p,1)", which is U_{Kli(p),1} of §5.1.4.
- The statement of Lemma 10.1.1 forces |L| = p^4.
- The proof of Proposition 10.2.1 factors G → G/L[p] → G/L, where the second map has an étale kernel of order p.
- Footnote 16 on p. 60 speaks of "the universal rank p^4 subgroup L".
- The parallel definitions state the type: D in §11.1.1 (p. 67; the "p. 44, §7" given above is a wrong locator), Lemma 11.1.1.4 on p. 68 (L_n of type Z/p^n ⊕ Z/p^{2n} by μ_{p^n}), and §13.2.1 on p. 85.
This is an omitted condition in a definition, not a step asserted without proof, so "misprint" fits better than "gap".

Consequences: ℭ_𝔜(p^m) is used only on pp. 57–60, in Lemma 10.1.1, the maps t_1 and t_2, Proposition 10.2.1, and Lemmas 10.3.1–10.3.2. All of these hold once the definition is corrected. So no later result depends on the defective wording. Following PROTOCOL §18 ("nothing (the mathematics is right as intended)"), I set affects = nothing. issues.locator: §10.1, proof of Lemma 10.1.1 (the 'classical fact' paragraph), p. 57 of the author version (17 June 2019)
issues.printed: The proof claims finite flat M → S over p-nilpotent S is BT of level n exactly when p^n kills M and every M_s is BT of level n. For n = 1 it assumes S over Spec F_p, then uses pG = 0 to factor F : G → G^(p) through Ker(V : G^(p) → G). To obtain faithful flatness of G → Ker(V : G^(p) → G), it cites surjectivity from the hypotheses and flatness from the fiber criterion, saying arbitrary n is similar.
issues.correction: Write M for G in the two sentences that prove the classical fact: "By assumption, M is killed by p and it follows that the Frobenius map F : M → M^(p) factors into a map M → Ker(V : M^(p) → M). We have to prove that the morphism M → Ker(V : M^(p) → M) is faithfully flat." That is all nine occurrences of G/G^(p) in those two sentences. "Throughout" must stop there. In the next paragraph of the same proof ("L[p] ⊕ H1 = G[p]"), G correctly means the universal abelian surface and should stay as it is.
issues.reason: I rendered p. 57 at 150 dpi, and the page image confirms the printed text word for word. The paragraph states the fact for an arbitrary finite flat M → S, but the proof then says "G is killed by p" and works with F : G → G^(p), V : G^(p) → G. In §10.1, G is the abelian scheme in the triples (G, H_m, L) with L ⊂ G[p^2]. That abelian surface is not killed by p. It is also not the object the fact is about: the fact is applied to L and its subquotients to reduce Lemma 10.1.1 to geometric points. The same proof uses G for the abelian surface again a few lines later (G[p]). So the letter G here is a slip for M. With M in place of G I redid the argument and it is correct. If M is killed by p, then V∘F = [p] = 0, so F factors through Ker V. Surjectivity onto Ker V is a fiberwise statement: fibers of a BT_1 satisfy Im F = Ker V, and taking kernels commutes with base change. Faithful flatness then follows because M is flat and finitely presented over S and each fiber map M_s → (Ker V)_s is a surjective homomorphism of finite group schemes over a field, hence flat (fiberwise flatness criterion, EGA IV 11.3.10). The proof of the other half, Ker F = Im V, is left to "a similar argument" in the paper and is not considered here. Nothing downstream uses the letter G in this paragraph, so the statement and logic of Lemma 10.1.1 and everything built on it (the U-correspondence in §10.2 onwards) are unaffected. issues.correction:
Add one step saying why ℭ(p^m) (and hence ℭ_𝔜(p^m)) is lci. The shortest fix keeps the proof of Lemma 10.2.2.

(a) The map q'_2 : ℭ(p^m) → ℭ^2(p^m) is the base change of q_2 : ℭ^1(p^m) → 𝔛^{m-et}_{par,Kli}(p^m), and q_2 is étale. The reason: on ℭ^1, Ker(G'→G) is the image of H_1, so it equals K(λ')^m. On that open-closed piece, p_2 : 𝔛_{Kli}(p) → 𝔛_par is an isomorphism onto 𝔛^{m-et}_par, since G = G'/K(λ')^m. So ℭ^1 and 𝔛^{m-et}_{par,Kli}(p^m) are both étale over 𝔛^{m-et}_par. It follows that the composite ℭ(p^m) → ℭ^2(p^m) → 𝔛_{Kli}(p) is étale. The argument of Lemma 10.2.2 then gives: ℭ(p^m) is lci over Spf Z_p, so ℭ_𝔜(p^m) is Cohen–Macaulay.

(b) Another route, the one HAL v3 takes, also works. Over the interior, r_1 is finite flat of degree p: its fibre is the set of order-p subgroups C ⊂ K(λ') with C ∩ K(λ')^m = 0, which is a torsor under Hom(K^et, K^m), locally μ_p. So r'_1 : ℭ → ℭ^1 is finite flat with lci fibres, and ℭ_𝔜 is lci by Lemma 10.2.2 for i = 1.

An alternative correction gets r_1 flat by miracle flatness. That needs 𝔛^{m-et}_{par,Kli}(p^m) to be regular, which the paper never establishes, so the direct torsor description is preferable.

The statement of Lemma 10.3.1 is unchanged.
issues.reason:
I checked the page images for pp. 58–61 of the author version. The text layer matches the page.

As printed, the justification is inadequate. Lemma 10.2.2 is stated and proved only for ℭ¹(p^m) and ℭ²(p^m). ℭ_𝔜(p^m) is the restriction of the fibre product ℭ² ×_{r_1,q_2} ℭ¹ (Prop. 10.2.1). A fibre product of lci formal schemes is not lci in general unless one of the two maps is flat or étale. The author version never proves the step that is needed: it states neither that r_1 is flat nor that q_2 is étale. That makes this a gap in the sense of PROTOCOL §18: a step asserted without an adequate proof.

The conclusion is true, and I redid it both ways. Along the way I recomputed the fibres.
- r_1 has degree p: its fibre is the splittings torsor.
- q_1 has degree p^3: it parametrizes hyperplanes H^⊥ ⊂ F_p^4 not containing H_1, and there are p^3+p^2+p+1−(p^2+p+1) = p^3 of them.
- So t_1 has degree p^4. This agrees with the rank p^3 of each Serre–Tate component on p. 60 times the p components counted in footnote 16. On the ordinary locus it also agrees with t_2 being étale.

One might think CM needs an extra flatness step, because the composite is not étale over ℭ¹. But ℭ(p^m) is étale over ℭ²(p^m), since q_2 is étale. So the lemma's own "étale over 𝔛_Kli(p)" argument extends directly, and flatness of r_1 is one sufficient fix, not a necessary one. The flatness route (b) of the correction is still mathematically valid.

HAL v3 (hal-01393374v3, pp. 49–50) does not have this text. It has no Lemma 10.2.2, and its proof of Lemma 10.3.1 argues instead that "This boils down to the flatness of the maps r_1 and q_1 over the interior". It proves r_1 finite flat as "a standard fact". Its q_1 step has a weakness: it deduces flatness from "the fiber is flat". So the gap was introduced by the rewrite into the miracle-flatness argument (Matsumura, CRT Thm 23.1, printed as "chap. 23, thm. 2.3.1"). The published Duke text could not be compared.

Dependence: Lemma 10.3.1 is used only in Lemma 10.3.2 (the normalized trace (1/p^3)Tr_{t_1} over the interior). Neither lemma is cited later by number. The U-operator is built from Lemmas 10.3.3 and 10.3.4, which use Lemma 10.2.2 only for ℭ^i. So only this proof is affected.

Side observation, outside this issue and not fully checked: q_2 is étale but seems not finite. Over the open-closed locus {H'_1 = K(λ')^m}, for m = 1 its fibres have p points at ordinary points and 1 point at p-rank-1 points. That suggests the parenthetical "q_2 and q_1 are proper" (p. 58) is wrong for q_2. U_1 does not need q_2 to be proper. I checked the page images for pp. 57–61 of the author version and pp. 49–50 of HAL v3. The text layer matches the pages.

Defence attempted. The best charitable reading is "by (the proof of) Lemma 10.2.2": the object is lci because it is étale over 𝔛_{Kli}(p). That reading does not hold up. Lemma 10.2.2 is stated and proved only for ℭ^1 and ℭ^2, and its only input is "étale morphisms ℭ^i(p^m) → 𝔛_{Kli}(p) by construction". ℭ(p^m) is a fibre product, not one of the ℭ^i. Its natural map through ℭ^1 is not étale in characteristic p: r'_1 has μ_p-torsor fibres. Its map through ℭ^2 is étale only because q_2 is étale. The author version never states that q_2 is étale or that r_1 is flat. HAL v3 did prove r_1 finite flat, but that argument was removed in the rewrite. A fibre product of lci formal schemes is not lci in general. So the citation does not justify the step. The missing step is small but not a slip of notation, so "gap" (PROTOCOL §18) is the right kind, not "misprint".

The conclusion is true. I checked both routes:
- (a) q_2 is étale, because source and target are étale over 𝔛^{m-et}_par. That uses the open-closed component of 𝔛_{Kli}(p)|_{𝔛^{m-et}_par} where C = K(λ')^m, which p_2 maps isomorphically onto 𝔛^{m-et}_par.
- (b) r_1 is finite flat of degree p over the interior, as a splitting torsor.

The degrees are consistent: q_1 has degree p^3 (p^3+p^2+p+1 − (p^2+p+1) = p^3), r_1 has degree p, and t_1 has degree p^4. This matches the normalisations 1/p^2 (Lemma 10.3.3) · 1/p (Lemma 10.3.4) = 1/p^3 (Lemma 10.3.2). It also matches the rank-p^3 local rings on p. 60 times the p components of footnote 16. The other inputs of miracle flatness in Matsumura, CRT Thm 23.1 (printed as "chap. 23, thm. 2.3.1") are fine: 𝔜^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^m) is étale over the smooth 𝔜, so it is regular, and t_1 is finite between equidimensional schemes.

Consequences. Lemma 10.3.1 is used only in Lemma 10.3.2, the normalized trace (1/p^3)Tr_{t_1} over the interior. Neither lemma is cited by number later. U = U_1∘U_2 is built from Lemmas 10.3.3 and 10.3.4, which rely on Lemma 10.2.2 only for ℭ^i and are unaffected. So only this proof is affected, and no stated result changes.

On "affects": since the printed justification does not cover the object and a new argument is needed, "the proof" is more accurate than "nothing". The underlying facts are solid. Confidence is medium only because the omission is small, and a reviewer could treat it as an implicit extension of Lemma 10.2.2.

issues.printed: The proof obtains finiteness from properness and the claim that a characteristic p abelian surface of p-rank at least 1 has finitely many order p subgroups. It then asserts regularity of 𝔜^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^m) and Cohen-Macaulayness of ℭ_𝔜(p^m) by Lemma 10.2.2, invoking [53], chap. 23, thm. 2.3.1 for flatness.
issues.correction: "Flatness follows from [53], §23, Thm. 23.1", i.e. Matsumura, Commutative Ring Theory, §23 "Flatness and fibres", Theorem 23.1 (miracle flatness): a local homomorphism A → B of Noetherian local rings with A regular, B Cohen–Macaulay and dim B = dim A + dim B/m_A B is flat. Most likely "thm. 23.1" was mistyped as "thm. 2.3.1".
issues.reason: I rendered p. 60 at 110 dpi. The image reads "Flatness follows from [53], chap. 23, thm. 2.3.1." with a bold [53], so this is not a text-layer artefact. [53] is Matsumura's Commutative Ring Theory. That book has chapters 1–11 and numbered sections §1–§33, and its theorems are numbered by section (Theorem 23.1, 23.2, …). No result anywhere in it is numbered with three parts like "2.3.1". "Chap. 23" is loose wording for §23 "Flatness and fibres", which sits in Chapter 8 "Flatness revisited". Theorem 23.1 is the miracle-flatness criterion, and a web search agrees: the standard citation for miracle flatness is "Matsumura, CRT, §23, Theorem 23.1". This is exactly the tool the proof needs: a finite (so quasi-finite) map from a Cohen–Macaulay source to a regular target. So the citation as printed points to a theorem that doesn't exist, and the intended one is Theorem 23.1. The paper has no numbering convention of its own that would make "thm. 2.3.1" correct. The bibliography names CRT, and Matsumura's other book, Commutative Algebra, uses (n.X)/Theorem-N numbering, so it doesn't match either. HAL v3 (6 Jan 2018, p. 50, Lemma 10.3.1) does not have this text. There the flatness is proved directly, by showing that the fibres of q1 are torsors under a group étale-locally isomorphic to the finite flat H1^⊥ and that r1 is finite flat. Matsumura ([49] in v3) is listed in the v3 bibliography, but I found no citation of it in the text layer. So the misprint was introduced when this proof was rewritten for the 2019 version. The published Duke text could not be checked. Side remarks, not part of this item: Theorem 23.1 also needs dim O_{ℭ,x} = dim O_{𝔜,y}, which the paper leaves implicit. Lemma 10.2.2 as stated covers ℭ^1(p^m) and ℭ^2(p^m) (lci over Spf Z_p), not the composite ℭ(p^m) directly. Neither point bears on the citation misprint.

issues.printed: The source says definition over the whole ordinary locus suffices: the boundary's intersection with the non-ordinary locus has codimension 1 in the special fiber, with a boundary flat over Spf Z_p. Equivalently, it assigns that intersection codimension at least 2 in Spec O_{ℭ^1(p^m),x} for closed x of ℭ^1(p^m).
issues.correction: "… is of codimension 1 in the special fiber of the boundary (codimension 2 in the special fiber of ℭ^1(p^m)), and the boundary is flat over Spf Z_p …"
issues.reason: Printed text confirmed. Dimension count: the special fibre of ℭ^1(p^m), finite over X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^m) away from the boundary, has dimension 3. Its boundary D_s has dimension 2. On the toric-rank-1 stratum, p-rank = 1 + p-rank of the elliptic abelian part, so non-ordinary means that elliptic curve is supersingular, a codimension-1 condition in D_s. The toric-rank-2 strata are ordinary. So D ∩ (non-ordinary) has dimension 1: codimension 1 in D_s but codimension 2 in the ambient special fibre. Read as the special fibre of ℭ^1(p^m), which is the natural reading, "codimension 1" is false. The appeal to flatness of the boundary shows the author meant D_s: codimension 1 in D_s and D flat give codimension 2 in D, hence at least 2 in Spec O_{ℭ^1(p^m),x} (in fact 3). The parenthetical conclusion, codimension ≥ 2 in the 4-dimensional local rings, is true either way, so the Hartogs-type extension of Θ is unaffected. This is a wording slip, not an error. Confidence is only medium because a charitable reader can take "the special fiber" to mean the boundary's.

issues.correction:
1. Replace "p^{6+2r+k} p_1^!Ω^{(k,r)}" with "p^{6+2r+k} s_1^!Ω^{(k,r)}".
2. The second component of s_2 should be ((G/L)[p])/L′, meaning the image of (G/L)[p] in (G/L)/L′, that is ((G/L)[p]+L′)/L′.
3. Every "G[p]/L" (in the lift of g_2, in the second projection of T‴, and in "G[p]/L ⊂ L′") should read (G[p]+L)/L ≅ G[p]/(L∩G[p]). This is the image of G[p] in G/L, and it is the notation the author himself uses in the condition on L′. On the mod-p ordinary locus this group is G[p]^m/L^m ≅ μ_p, so it is multiplicative of order p, as the Klingen datum requires.
issues.reason:
I checked each part against the page image and redid the reasoning.

(1) The correspondence 𝔥 in the proof of Lemma 11.1.1.3 is defined only with the projections s_1 and s_2, and the same sentence gives Θ the target s_1^!. So "p_1^!" is a leftover from the notation of §7.1 (Lemmas 7.1.1 and 7.1.2 use p_1, p_2). This part is an unambiguous misprint.

(2) L is an extension of Z/p⊕Z/p^2 by μ_p. Its étale quotient has exponent p^2, so L is not contained in G[p], and G[p]/L is not literally defined. The intended group is the image of G[p] in G/L. On the mod-p ordinary locus (X_1^{ord}, where the reduced base forces L[p] = L∩G[p] to be flat of order p^3), I recomputed:
- L[p] maps onto G[p]^{et}, and L[p] ∩ G^m = L^m, which is μ_p.
- Hence G[p]/L[p] = G[p]^m/L^m ≅ μ_p, which is multiplicative of order p.
The author's revisions support this reading. HAL v3 wrote "L′ ∩ G[p]/L ≠ {0}" and "G[p] ⊂ L+L′". The author version changed these to "L′ ∩ (G[p]/(L∩G[p])) ≠ {0}" and "G[p]/L ⊂ L′", but left the other occurrences of "G[p]/L" unchanged.

(3) "(G/L[p])/L′", read literally as G/(L[p]), is an abelian scheme, not a subgroup of (G/L)/L′. The intended group is the image of (G/L)[p]. HAL v3 already wrote "G/L[p^2]" for (G/L)[p^2]. The author version added the parentheses in "(G/L)[p^2]" but not here.

The mathematics works with the intended meanings:
- H′ is the image of G[p] and has order p. Since L′∩H′ ≠ 0, we get H′ ⊂ L′.
- So the composite G → G/L → (G/L)/L′ kills G[p] and factors through [p].
- Its multiplicative kernel has order p^2, so on ω it is p times an isomorphism. This gives p^{k+2r} on Ω^{(k,r)}.
- With p^6 from the fundamental classes and the normalization p^{-(3+r)} twice, the normalized operator is divisible by p^k. It is therefore 0 mod p for k ≥ 1, exactly as stated.

A caveat: "G[p]/L" is used consistently (three times) and its meaning is clear, so one could call it an abuse of notation rather than a misprint. The p_1^! and the missing parentheses are genuine misprints either way.

HAL v3 (p. 56) has the same "(G/L, G[p]/L)", "(G/L[p])/L′" and "p_1^!", with further sloppiness ("G/L + L′", "G/L[p^2]").

issues.locator: §11.1.1, proof of Lemma 11.1.1.4, p. 68 (author version, 17 June 2019)
issues.printed: The proof uses T^{1,et} = T′ and says every G → G/L in T^{n,m} factors through multiplication by p, deriving T^{n,et} = T^n mod p^k as in Lemma 11.1.1.3. It states Tr ∘ U^n ∘ i = pT^{n,et}, explaining p by the p multiplicative order p subgroups H disjoint from a given L_n, H ∩ L_n = {0}. Lemma 11.1.1.4 asserts Tr ∘ U^n ∘ i = pT^n mod p^k on H^0(𝔛^{ord}, Ω^{(k,r)}) for all n ≥ 0.
issues.correction:
Replace "will factor through multiplication by p on G" with "has kernel L ⊇ G[p]^m, the multiplicative part of G[p]". Then do the count step by step instead of copying Lemma 11.1.1.3.

Why L ⊇ G[p]^m holds for every chain in T^{n,m}:
- A T1^m step has H1 ⊇ G_i[p]^m.
- A T1^et∘T2^m step has kernel G_i[p].
- A chain made only of T′ = T1^et∘T2^et steps whose L^m is not cyclic already contains G[p]^m.
- If L^m is cyclic, then |L^m| = p^n and L is Lagrangian, so L has the T^{n,et} type (μ_{p^n}; Z/p^n ⊕ Z/p^{2n}).

The count uses Lemmas 7.1.1 and 7.1.2. Write M_i for a step's multiplicative-order exponent, F_i for its fundamental-class exponent, and δ = F_i + rM_i − 3 − r. The four step types give:
- T1^et T2^et: δ = 0
- T1^et T2^m: δ = r−1
- T1^m T2^et: δ = r−2
- T1^m T2^m: δ = 2r−3

A chain's normalized coefficient is then divisible by p^{Σδ + k·min(j1,j2)}, where (p^{j1}, p^{j2}) are the elementary divisors of L^m, and min(j1,j2) ≥ 1 on T^{n,m}. So T^{n,et} ≡ T^n mod p^k when r ≥ 2. That is the standing hypothesis of §11.1.1, and the lemma should state it.

An equivalent alternative correction:
- T ≡ T′ mod p^k when r ≥ 2, since the other three pieces carry p^{k+r−1}, p^{k+r−2} and p^{k+2r−3}.
- Inside T′^n the printed claim is literally true: L ⊇ L_1[p], and L_1[p] + G[p]^m = G[p].

How this compares with another proposed correction:
- The equivalent fix above is right and complete.
- The other proposed correction names the right fact (L ⊇ G[p]^m) but understates the rest: it takes divisibility of the differential by p to be all that the argument of Lemma 11.1.1.3 uses. Lemma 11.1.1.3 also takes p^3 per step from fundamental classes, and T1^m and T2^m steps do not supply that. Only det^r makes up the difference, and that needs r ≥ 2.

Aside: the lemma itself only needs pT^{n,m} ≡ 0 mod p^k. The same count seems to give this already for r = 1, because each T1^m step makes the whole differential divisible by p. So r ≥ 2 is needed for the proof's intermediate claim, not necessarily for the lemma. The requirement n ≥ 1 (the lemma fails at n = 0) is a separate item, sourceIssues E85.
issues.reason:
The page image of p. 68 matches the quoted text. Read literally, the sentence is false. I checked the counterexample myself. Take an ordinary G, for example the canonical lift, with G[p^∞] = μa ⊕ μb ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)e ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)f, where a pairs with e and b pairs with f. Let L = μ_{p²}a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ (Z/p)f.
- L is isotropic for e_{p²}: e_{p²} is trivial on G[p]×G[p], ⟨a,f⟩ = 0, and the annihilator of L^m in G^et[p²] is exactly (Z/p)f. Its order is p^4, so L is Lagrangian.
- L[p] = μ_p a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ Z/p f has order p^3, with K = L[p]^⊥ = μ_p a. So L is the T_{p,1} chain T1^m ∘ T2^m, and it lies in T^{1,m}.
- G[p] ⊄ L, since e is missing.
There are other counterexamples: the T1^m T2^et chains H1 + ⟨e + αã⟩ with α ≠ 0 also lie in T^{1,m} and do not contain G[p].

The true statement is weaker: every T^{n,m} chain satisfies L ⊇ G[p]^m, so the differential is still divisible by p. But the appeal to "reasoning as in lemma 11.1.1.3" does not transfer. That proof gets p^6 from two T‴-type steps, each with fundamental class p^3. On T1^m and T2^m steps the fundamental class is an isomorphism (Lemmas 7.1.1 and 7.1.2). The missing powers are recovered only through extra det^r factors, which needs r ≥ 2. For example, T1^m T2^et has normalized coefficient p^{k+r−2}, and that hypothesis is not in the lemma.

I recomputed the coefficients p^{k+r−1}, p^{k+r−2}, p^{k+2r−3} of the pieces T1^et T2^m, T1^m T2^et and T1^m T2^m of T and confirmed them. I also found that T1^et T2^m consists only of the T_{p,0} chains L = G[p]. The corrected argument is sound.

The conclusion holds for n ≥ 1 and r ≥ 2. Its only use is Corollary 11.1.1.2 (r ≥ 2, k ≥ 2, n large), which then feeds Proposition 11.1.3/Theorem 11.2.1, so no stated downstream result is affected.

HAL v3 does not have this lemma. There, Corollary 11.1.1.2 (r ≥ 2, k ≥ 1) proves injectivity by a different argument, a local representation-theoretic p-stabilisation. So this passage is new in the 2019 version. The printed claim is false even for n = 1. Take an ordinary G with G[p^∞] = μ a ⊕ μ b ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)e ⊕ (Q_p/Z_p)f, where a pairs with e and b with f.

First counterexample: L = μ_{p²}a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ (Z/p)f.
- L is Lagrangian in G[p²], and L[p] = (μ_p a)^⊥.
- It is the chain T1^m∘T2^m. This is the same L as in the counterexample above.
- Its multiplicative part is μ_{p²} ⊕ μ_p, so it lies in T^{1,m}.
- The e-direction is missing from G[p], so G → G/L does not factor through [p].

Second family: the T1^m∘T2^et chains (μ_p a ⊕ μ_p b ⊕ Z/p f) + ⟨e + αã⟩ with α ≠ 0 also lie in T^{1,m} and do not contain G[p].

I checked this by a short computer enumeration with p = 3, over all 40 order-p lines H, with H1 = H^⊥ and H1 ⊂ L ⊂ p^{-1}H:
- 108 T1^et T2^et chains, each with L^m = μ_p. These are exactly T^{1,et}.
- 36 T1^et T2^m chains, all with L = G[p].
- 12 T1^m T2^et chains: 4 with L = G[p] and 8 with G[p] ⊄ L.
- 4 T1^m T2^m chains, each with |L^m| = p³ and G[p] ⊄ L.
- All 48 chains of T^{1,m} contain G[p]^m. Of these, 12 do not contain G[p].

The defence fails.
- If T meant T′, the claim would be true. But the proof itself writes T^{1,et} = T′, so T^{1,m} = T − T′ is nonzero over 𝔛^ord.
- The paper identifies T with T′ only on H^0(X_1^ord), that is mod p, through Lemma 11.1.1.1. It never does so mod p^k.
- No nearby statement supplies T ≡ T′ mod p^k. That congruence follows from the local computations in the proofs of Lemmas 7.1.1 and 7.1.2 (T1^m: p^{k+2r} with the fundamental class an isomorphism; T2^m: p^r with the fundamental class an isomorphism), but it holds only for r ≥ 2, and the paper does not state it.
- "Reasoning as in 11.1.1.3" does not transfer either, because that proof takes p^6 from two T′′′-type fundamental classes.

The conclusion does hold with r ≥ 2, by the corrected count.

Downstream: Lemma 11.1.1.4 is used only in the injectivity half of Corollary 11.1.1.2 (r ≥ 2, k ≥ 2, n large). That corollary feeds Corollary 11.1.3.1 (r ≥ 2, k > p+1). Both stay within the valid range, so no stated result is affected.

issues.locator: §11.1.1, Lemma 11.1.1.4, p. 68 (author version, 17 June 2019)
issues.printed: Lemma 11.1.1.4 claims Tr ◦ U^n ◦ i = pT^n mod p^k on H^0(𝔛^ord, Ω^(k,r)) for every n ≥ 0. The preceding text makes 𝔛^ord_Kli(p) → 𝔛^ord finite étale of rank p+1 and defines its trace Tr : H^0(𝔛^ord_Kli(p), Ω^(k,r)) → H^0(𝔛^ord, Ω^(k,r)). The proof gives Tr ◦ U^n ◦ i = pT^{n,et}, attributing p to the number of multiplicative order p subgroups H satisfying H ∩ L_n = {0} for fixed L_n.
issues.correction: Replace "For all n ≥ 0" with "For all n ≥ 1". At n = 0 the correct identity is Tr ∘ i = (p+1)·Id. Other hypotheses the lemma may need, such as r ≥ 2 for T^{n,et} ≡ T^n mod p^k, are a separate issue and not part of this correction.
issues.reason:
I checked the page image at 220 dpi, and the statement reads "n ≥ 0". Take n = 0. Then U^0 = Id and T^0 = Id, so the left side is Tr ◦ i. Here i is pullback along 𝔛^ord_Kli(p) → 𝔛^ord, and the paper says just above the lemma that this map is finite étale of rank p+1. This matches §9.1.1: H ⊂ G[p] is étale-locally μ_p, and on the ordinary locus G[p]^mult ≅ μ_p^2 has p+1 such lines. The trace of a pullback along a finite étale map of degree p+1 is multiplication by p+1, so Tr ◦ i = (p+1)·Id. The right side is p·T^0 = p·Id. The difference is Id. That is not ≡ 0 mod p^k for k ≥ 1, the standing range in §11.1.1 (Lemmas 11.1.1.1–3 need k ≥ 1, Corollary 11.1.1.2 needs k ≥ 2), because H^0(𝔛^ord, Ω^(k,r)) is a nonzero p-adically separated module. The printed statement is therefore false at n = 0. No normalisation convention rescues it: T^0 = Id whatever the normalisation of T, and renormalising Tr by 1/(p+1) would break the case n ≥ 1. The proof's count fails at the same place. L_0 ⊂ G[p^0] is 0, so all p+1 multiplicative H satisfy H ∩ L_0 = {0}, not p of them. For n ≥ 1 the count p is right: L_n ∩ G[p]^mult is the line μ_p ⊂ μ_p^2, and H must avoid it, which leaves p of the p+1 lines. The lemma is used only in the proof of Corollary 11.1.1.2, "Applying lemma 11.1.1.4 for n large enough"; a grep finds no other citation. So the fix to n ≥ 1 changes nothing downstream. HAL v3 (hal-01393374v3) does not contain this lemma or the rank-(p+1) sentence. Its §11.1.1 stops at Lemma 11.1.1.3 and Corollaries 11.1.1.1–2 (Corollary 11.1.1.2 there assumes k ≥ 1), and it proves injectivity by a p-stabilisation / Hecke-polynomial argument. The published Duke version could not be checked. On 'affects': I would record 'a stated result', not 'nothing'. The printed Lemma 11.1.1.4 is itself a stated result that is false in its n = 0 case, and its proof fails there too. The reach stops at that lemma: no later result depends on the n = 0 case. I checked this against the page image at 250 dpi. The statement reads "n ≥ 0".

**Why n = 0 fails.** U^0 = Id and T^0 = Id, so the claim at n = 0 says Tr ∘ i ≡ p·Id mod p^k. Here i is pullback along 𝔛^ord_Kli(p) → 𝔛^ord. The paper says in the sentence just before the lemma that this map is finite étale of rank p+1. That matches §9.1.1, where H ⊂ G[p] is étale-locally μ_p: on the ordinary locus G[p]^0 ≅ μ_p², which has p+1 lines. Ω^(k,r) on the Klingen space is pulled back from 𝔛^ord, so Tr ∘ i = (p+1)·Id. The difference from p·Id is Id. Now M = H^0(𝔛^ord, Ω^(k,r)) is nonzero, p-torsion-free and p-adically separated. So M ≠ p^k M for every k ≥ 1, and Id is not ≡ 0 mod p^k. The statement is vacuous only for k = 0, and the lemma sets no condition on k.

**The proof fails at the same place.** L_0 ⊂ G[p^0] is 0 and T^{0,et} = Id, so all p+1 multiplicative H satisfy H ∩ L_0 = {0}, not p of them. For n ≥ 1 the count of p is right: L_n ∩ G[p]^0 is the line μ_{p^n}[p] = μ_p inside μ_p², and H must avoid it, which leaves p choices.

**Defences tried, none works:**
- Normalisations: the powers U^0 and T^0 are the identity whatever normalisation U and T carry (p^{3−r}U_{Kli(p),1} and p^{−3−r}).
- Tr: it is the plain trace map, as stated. Rescaling it by 1/(p+1) would break the cases n ≥ 1.
- i: it is the canonical pullback from p. 67.
- The rank: the paper's own count of p+1 is correct.
- k in "mod p^k" is the weight, so the congruence has content for every k ≥ 1.

**Who uses the lemma.** A grep finds a single citation, in the proof of Corollary 11.1.1.2: "Applying lemma 11.1.1.4 for n large enough, we find that Tr(f∘(i))(F) = pF = 0 mod p^k". This passes to the limit f = lim U^{n!}, e = lim T^{n!}, which only needs n ≥ 1. Corollary 11.1.1.2 is later used in Corollary 11.1.3.1 (the left vertical map), again without the n = 0 case. So "n ≥ 1" is the right and minimal fix, and it changes nothing downstream.

**On 'affects'.** The printed Lemma 11.1.1.4 is a stated result that is false as printed (its n = 0 case), and its proof fails there too. So I record "a stated result", with the reach stopping at the lemma itself; no later result depends on n = 0. This is an error rather than a misprint because the proof's own count shows the author did not treat n = 0; it is not an evident typographical slip.

issues.locator: §11.1.1, proof of Corollary 11.1.1.2 (surjectivity part), p. 68 of the author version. HAL v3 has the same gap on p. 57 (PDF p. 58), in older notation: "By lemma 11.1.1.3, feT'U^{-1}G = fT'U^{-1}G = fUU^{-1}G = G." There the single symbol T' stands for i, T'' and T'''.

Since f commutes with U and U is bijective on fM (Lemma 2.1.3), we get f∘T''' = f∘U. Hence f∘i∘T = U∘f∘i, and so f∘i∘T^n = U^n∘f∘i. The module is killed by p and T is locally finite on it (Prop. 7.4.1.1). So for x ∈ (1−e)M we have T^{N!}x = 0 when N ≫ 0, which gives U^{N!} f i x = 0 and therefore f i x = 0. Equivalently: f i e x = lim f i T^{N!} x = lim U^{N!} f i x = f i x. This correction is right and minimal. I checked the rendered page image. The chain goes from f i(e x) to f T''' U^{-1}G = f i(x) and silently drops the projector e. Lemma 11.1.1.3 (U∘T''' = U∘U) does not by itself justify this.

Defence attempts:
(a) Lemma 2.1.4, which says maps commute with ordinary projectors, needs the same operator T acting equivariantly on source and target. Here the map i goes from T on H^0(X_1^{ord}) to U or T''' on H^0(X_Kli^{ord}(p)_1), so the lemma does not apply.
(b) The element x = T''U^{-1}G is not known to lie in eM already. We have T^n T'' = T'' T'''^n, but the paper never shows that T''' preserves the f-part. So e cannot simply be deleted.
(c) No statement anywhere in the paper gives the intertwining relation f∘i∘T = U∘f∘i. I searched for "◦ i", "i ◦" and "equivariant".

The missing step is still true and follows in two lines from facts on pp. 67–68 (the diagram, Lemma 11.1.1.3, Lemma 2.1.3). I checked each step of this argument:
- T'''∘i = i∘T∘... more precisely T'''∘i = i∘T''∘i = i∘T.
- U f T''' = f U U = U f U, and U is injective on fM, so f T''' = f U.
- By induction, f i T^n = U^n f i.
- On (1−e)M with M killed by p, Lemma 2.1.3 gives T^{N!} = 0 locally.
- So U^{N!} f i x = 0, and f i x = 0.
Nothing is false; the argument is only incomplete. So this is a genuine minor gap, not a misprint and not an error.

Later uses: Corollary 11.1.1.2 feeds the left vertical map in the proof of Corollary 11.1.3.1(2) (p. 70). Through that it feeds Theorem 11.2.1(4)–(7), Corollary 11.2.1 and Theorem 11.3.1. The injectivity half also uses surjectivity through Nakayama. Once the gap is filled, all of these stand. So no stated result is affected.

issues.locator: §11.2, Theorem 11.2.1, point 6, p. 70 (author version, 17 June 2019); HAL v3: Theorem 11.2.1, point 6, printed p. 60 (PDF p. 61)
issues.printed: Point 6 asserts, for every k ≥ C, that eH^i(𝔛, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) → eH^i(𝔛^{≥1}, Ω^{(k,r)}(−D)) gives a bijection in degree i = 0 and an injection in degree i = 1.
issues.correction: eH^i(𝔛, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) → eH^i(𝔛^{≥1}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)): the weight on the target should be (k,2), not (k,r).
issues.reason:
I checked the page image at 200 dpi, and the printed text is as quoted: the source has weight (k,2) and the target has weight (k,r).

The r in point 6 is not unbound: the theorem opens with "For k > p + 1 and r ≥ 2 :", so r is the theorem's general r ≥ 2. The misprint still stands, for these reasons:

(a) Ω^{(k,r)} = Sym^k ω_G ⊗ det^r ω_G (p. ~27). The map in point 6 is the natural restriction from 𝔛 to 𝔛^{≥1}, and restriction cannot change the sheaf. For r ≠ 2 there is no natural map Ω^{(k,2)} → Ω^{(k,r)} (multiplying by Ha^m would only reach r = 2 + m(p−1), and the paper never uses it here). With general r, the i = 0 bijectivity would compare ordinary forms of different weights.

(b) Point 6 is the r = 2 complement of point 5 (r ≥ 3). Its proof, "The point 6 also follows by induction on n from corollary 11.1.3.1" (p. 71), relies on Cor 11.1.3.1(4) (p. 69): "eH^i(X_1, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) → f H^i(X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p)_1, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) is bijective for k ≥ C and i = 0 and injective ... i = 1". That in turn comes from Prop 8.2.1 (p. 53): "For all k ≥ C, eH^0(X_1^{≥1}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) = eH^0(X_1, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) and the map eH^1(X_1, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) → eH^1(X_1^{≥1}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) is injective." Both have weight (k,2) on both sides.

(c) The later use is also at r = 2. Theorem 11.3.1(4) (p. 71) states "eH^i(𝔛, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) → H^i(fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), 𝔉^κ ⊗ ω^2(−D)) ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Z_p) is bijective for i = 0 and injective for i = 1". Its proof (p. 73) says "proposition 2.2.2 and theorem 11.2.1 imply directly the points 3 and 4". Section 11.3 says "We specialize to r = 2".

HAL v3 has the identical point 6 (printed p. 60). In HAL v3, Corollary 11.2.1 had the same kind of mismatch: eH^0(X, Ω^{(k,2)}...) → fH^0(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,r)}...). The author version corrected that corollary to (k,2) on both sides (p. 71) but left point 6 unchanged. This supports reading point 6 as a leftover typo.

Affects nothing: the intended r = 2 statement is clear from the proof and its sources, and the only later use (Theorem 11.3.1(4)) needs only r = 2. The published Duke version was not checked.

issues.locator: §11.2, end of the proof of Theorem 11.2.1, p. 71 (author version). HAL v3 has the same text (printed p. 60).
issues.printed: The proof obtains points 4 and 5 from Corollary 11.1.3.1 with Proposition 2.2.2. It attributes point 6 to induction on n using that corollary and obtains point 7 by applying Proposition 2.2.2 again.
issues.correction: Finally, 7 follows from Proposition 2.2.1 applied to fN^•. fN^• is in C^{flat}(Z_p), concentrated in degrees [0,1], and fN^• ⊗ F_p computes fRΓ(X^{≥1}_Kli(p)_1, Ω^{(k,r)}(−D)). By Corollary 11.1.3.1(5) that complex is perfect of amplitude [0,1] (so it has finite cohomology) for r ≥ 2 and k ≥ C.
issues.reason: Proposition 2.2.2 (p. 9) is Nakayama's lemma for complexes: a map in C^{flat}(R) that is a quasi-isomorphism mod m_R is a quasi-isomorphism. Using it requires a map to or from a complex already known to be perfect. For r ≥ 3, point 7 follows from points 4 and 5 by composing quasi-isomorphisms with eRΓ(𝔛, …). For r = 2, point 6 gives only a bijection for i = 0 and an injection for i = 1, so no such quasi-isomorphism is available. Proposition 2.2.1 is the perfectness criterion: M^• in C^{flat}(R) in degrees [a,b] with M^• ⊗ R/m_R of finite cohomology is quasi-isomorphic to a perfect complex in degrees [a,b]. Its hypotheses are exactly those of Corollary 11.1.3.1(5), with the same range k ≥ C and r ≥ 2 as point 7. The mod-p reduction of fN^• is f(N^•/p) by Lemma 2.1.4. So the intended argument is clear and complete once the reference is corrected to 2.2.1. The printed 'another application of proposition 2.2.2' is a wrong cross-reference, not a gap.

(iii) U^m does not change the weight. The other three corners of the square are at weight k, the left U^m arrow starts from 𝓕^k_{1,1}, and the right vertical arrow goes into 𝓕^k_{m,1}. So 𝓕^κ_{1,1} must be 𝓕^k_{1,1}.
(iv) The section says "We specialize to r = 2", so Ω^{(k,r)} literally equals Ω^{(k,2)}. This is a leftover symbol, not an error.
HAL v3 (pp. 61–62) has the same double (−D), the same 𝓕^k_{1,1}(−D), the same Ω^{(k,r)} and the same 𝓕^κ_{1,1} diagram corner. In HAL v3 the quasi-isomorphism display itself also read "fRΓ(…, 𝓕^κ_{1,1} ⊗ ω²(−D))". The author version corrected that display to 𝓕^k_{1,1} but left the diagram corner as 𝓕^κ_{1,1}, which supports reading the corner as a misprint.

The gap concerns only the Igusa-type sheaves on p. 72. Before [50] Thm 8.6 can be used for F^κ_{m,n} ⊗ ω^2(−D), its hypothesis has to be checked: the sheaf must be formally subcanonical in the sense of [50] Def. 8.5, and the theorem, which is stated for sheaves on the whole toroidal compactification, has to be localised to the open X^{*,≥1}_{Kli}(p). This needs an argument because the sheaf is only quasi-coherent: f: X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^m)_n → X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p)_n is affine and étale but not finite (Lemma 9.1.1.1, Remark 9.1.1.2).

A sufficient sketch:
- Every boundary fibre of π lies in the ≥1 locus, and G has constant multiplicative rank along it. So over the formal completion along a fibre, H_m lies in the multiplicative part of G̃[p^m], which is pulled back from C_{Φ,δ}. Hence X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p^m) and IG(p^m) become finite étale there, with trivial tame part and unipotent (p-power) monodromy. This gives E_0 a finite filtration with constant graded pieces, as Def. 8.5(2) requires.
- Alternatively, split the sheaf along Ha. Over the ordinary locus the covers are finite étale (deeper-level Lan models). Over V(Ha^l), f is étale and universally bijective, so it is an isomorphism.

No change to any statement is needed.

(1) The cited theorem is not limited to automorphic vector bundles at spherical and paramodular level. That description fits only the paper's restatement, Thm 6.2.2.1. I downloaded Lan's paper [50] (kwlan.org/articles/cpt-ram-nbl.pdf). Its Thm 8.6 applies to any quasi-coherent sheaf E on M^tor_{H,Σ} that is "formally canonical (resp. formally subcanonical) over R" (Def. 8.5). It works at any neat level H and over any O_{F_0,(p)}-algebra R. So Ω^{(k,r)}(−D) on the Klingen-level compactification is covered. The paper itself uses this for X_Kli(p) → X*_Kli(p) in §14, where it shows that X^{≥1}_Kli(p) is the preimage of X*^{≥1}_Kli(p). Colimits and the quotients by Ha^l then follow from the long exact sequence. So the citation in the proof of Thm 11.2.1 is not a gap.

(2) For Thm 11.3.1 the citation does not apply as written. Lan's Def. 8.5(2) requires, at each boundary point x̄, a finite filtration of E_{0,x̄} whose graded pieces are pullbacks of finite R-modules. So E must be of finite type near the boundary.
- As an O-module, F^κ_{m,n} is the pushforward along X^{≥1}_Kli(p^m)_n → X^{≥1}_Kli(p)_n (and the finite Igusa torsor). That map is affine, étale and quasi-finite but not finite: Remark 9.1.1.2 says it is an isomorphism over the p-rank-1 locus and has degree p or p+1 over the ordinary locus. The p-rank-1 locus meets the boundary (toric rank 1 with supersingular abelian part). There, for m ≥ 2, F^κ_{m,n}⊗ω^2(−D) is not of finite type, because an affine quasi-finite map with a coherent pushforward would be finite. So it is not formally subcanonical.
- The Ha-torsion right-hand sheaves do not have the form in Def. 8.5(2) either.
- The paper checks none of this, and F^κ_{m,n} exists only on the p-rank ≥ 1 open.

The conclusion that is actually needed is very likely true and can be recovered as described in the correction. So this is a gap in the proof, not an error in any stated result. Defence, part 1. The citation in the proof of Thm 11.2.1 is not a gap. The cited theorem is not only about automorphic vector bundles on the spherical and paramodular compactifications; that describes only the paper's own restatement, Thm 6.2.2.1 on p. 30. [50] itself (Lan, IMRN 2017; author's compilation read from kwlan.org) is much more general:
- Thm 8.6 reads: "Suppose R is an O_{F0,(p)}-algebra, and suppose that E is a quasi-coherent sheaf over M^tor_{H,Σ} that is formally canonical (resp. formally subcanonical) over R ... Then R^i(∮_{H,Σ})_* E(−nD′) = 0 for all i > 0 and n > 0 (resp. n ≥ 0)."

The paper's proof of Thm 6.1.5.1 (p. 29) says that X_Kli(p) is built in [49] and [50] by normalisation, and on p. 101 the paper itself applies [50] to X_Kli(p) → X*_Kli(p). (There it cites "thm. 8.9", but 8.9 is a Remark in [50].) Ω^{(k,r)}(−D) is the subcanonical extension of an automorphic bundle, which is the intended case. Three further points are formal:
- X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p) is the preimage of the open X^{*,≥1}_{Kli}(p) (p. 101), and relative vanishing is local on the target.
- Reduction mod p^n follows from flatness.
- R^iπ_* commutes with the Ha-colimit, and the quotient term follows from the long exact sequence.

So the p. 71 claim, and its implicit use in Cor. 11.1.3.1, is covered by the cited source.

Part 2, what remains. On p. 72 the sheaf F^κ_{m,n} = (π_{m,n})_*(O_{IG(p^m)_n} ⊗ Λ_n)[κ_{m,n}] is a pushforward along a non-finite affine étale map, so it is not coherent. The paper never checks Def. 8.5 for it, and Lan's proof via [17, Thm 3.9] works with formal completions along fibres; for a non-coherent sheaf that step does not follow formally. The paper itself takes a separate argument for the analogous non-finite sheaves in Part III: Prop. 12.9.2.1, plus smallness via [3] A.1.3.1 in Lemma 12.9.2.1. That contrast suggests the one-line citation on p. 72 is not enough. My local analysis (see the correction) indicates the vanishing is true, so this is an omitted verification rather than an error.

Consequences. The acyclic resolutions give the two-term flat complexes behind Thm 11.3.1 (U locally finite; fRΓ perfect over Λ in degrees [0,1]; the control maps 3 and 4). These feed Thm 1.1 and §14.8. Because the missing step can be filled, only the proof is affected.

Repair: only the Thm 11.3.1 citation needs one. Affineness from Lemma 9.1.1.1 plus the local structure at the boundary is the right approach and close to minimal, but it needs to be combined with [50] Def. 8.5, as described above.

Its proof ends with a quasi-isomorphism for all k ≥ 0 and obtains points 3 and 4 from Proposition 2.2.2 and Theorem 11.2.1. issues.correction:
Add a proof of point 2. The following argument is close to minimal.

(i) Pass to the limit over n in the resolutions, as in the proof of Thm 11.2.1. This gives a two-term representative M• in degrees [0,1]. Its terms are Λ-flat and complete, because 𝔉^κ is invertible over O ⊗̂ Λ (§9.3). So M• lies in C^flat(Λ), and fM• is a termwise direct summand of it.

(ii) For p odd, write Λ = Z_p[μ_{p−1}] ⊗ Z_p[[1+pZ_p]] ≅ ∏_{i mod p−1} Λ_i, using the idempotents of Z_p[μ_{p−1}]. Each Λ_i ≅ Z_p[[T]] is complete local noetherian with residue field F_p. For p = 2, Λ ≅ Z_2[C_2][[T]] is already local.

(iii) For each i, choose k ≡ i mod p−1 with k ≥ C. Then e_i fM• ⊗ Λ_i/m_i = fM• ⊗_{Λ,k} F_p. The mod-p quasi-isomorphism proved just above (equivalently, point 3 ⊗^L F_p) identifies this with fRΓ(X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p)_1, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)). That complex has finite cohomology by Cor. 11.1.3.1(5), or by Thm 11.2.1(7) together with point 3.

(iv) Prop. 2.2.1 over Λ_i then shows that e_i fM• is quasi-isomorphic to a perfect complex in degrees [0,1]. Taking the product over i, fM• is perfect over Λ in degrees [0,1].

Only finiteness of the cohomology mod m_i is needed. The amplitude [0,1] comes from the representative itself.

Every ingredient of the repair is already in the paper, so the result stands and 'affects' is 'nothing'. My confidence is medium only because this is a minor omission in the write-up rather than a failing step. Defence attempted and failed.

(a) The proof establishes point 1: "We deduce from lemma 2.1.2 that U is locally finite …". Its only other conclusion is the closing sentence, which names points 3 and 4 only. Point 2 is never mentioned. The proof does not cite Prop. 2.2.1, which is the only perfectness criterion in §2. Unlike the proof of Thm 11.2.1 ("They are objects of C^flat(Z_p) by construction"), it also never says that the limit complex is Λ-flat and complete.

(b) A charitable reading does not rescue it. The proof of Thm 11.2.1 itself gets its perfectness point 7 "by another application of proposition 2.2.2", which should be 2.2.1. So "proposition 2.2.2" in the closing sentence might loosely stand for §2.2 as a whole. Even so, that sentence claims only points 3 and 4.

(c) The intended argument is the one given in the correction. The introduction (p. 3) says the integral control theorem for k ≫ 0 is used "to show that M is a perfect complex". It is not carried out anywhere else in the paper. Footnote 24 on p. 101 cites "theorem 11.3.1, point 2" as the place where the degrees [0,1] are established.

(d) The fix works, so the statement is true. For each maximal ideal of Λ one picks k ≥ C in the matching class, which is always possible. Reduction modulo that ideal gives fRΓ(X^{≥1}_{Kli}(p)_1, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)), by the mod-p comparison proved in the text on pp. 72–73. That complex is finite by Cor. 11.1.3.1(5), and Prop. 2.2.1 applies.

(e) The semi-local point is correct. For p odd, μ_{p−1} ⊂ Z_p and p−1 is prime to p, so Z_p[μ_{p−1}] ≅ Z_p^{p−1} and Λ ≅ Z_p[[T]]^{p−1}. This ring is not local, while §2 assumes a complete local noetherian ring. Applying §2 factor by factor is routine. The same issue affects the use of Lemma 2.1.2 for point 1; this overlaps with sourceIssues E5.

- Thm 1.1 (M is perfect of amplitude [0,1]).
- Lemma 14.8.4 (Euler characteristics are "locally constant functions of k … by theorem 11.3.1").
- Footnote 24.
- §15.2: the Hecke-generated subalgebra is a finite Λ-algebra, the localisation uses [41] lem. 2.12, and Thm 15.2.1 concerns the Euler characteristic of the perfect complex, hence Thm 1.2.

issues.locator: §12.2.2, proof of Lemma 12.2.2.1, p. 74 (author version, 17 June 2019); HAL v3 §12.2.2, Lemma 12.2.2.1, PDF p. 64
issues.printed: The proof assumes c, f are units, derives HT(e_2) = \frac{a}{c} HT(e_3), and says HT(e_2) generates Fil^{can}_ε, complemented by the span of HT(e_4). Earlier it gives the HT matrix rows (0 a c e), (0 b d f), with ad − bc = 0 and cf − de a unit in R_ε.
issues.correction: "... We deduce that HT(e_2) = (a/c) HT(e_3) and that Fil^{can}_ε is generated by HT(e_3), a direct factor is provided by the submodule generated by HT(e_4)."
issues.reason: I redid the computation. The columns of the printed 2×4 matrix are HT(e_1) = 0, HT(e_2) = (a,b), HT(e_3) = (c,d) and HT(e_4) = (e,f). The relation ad − bc = 0 agrees with J from §5.1: J = [[0,A],[−A,0]] with A antidiagonal, so e_1 pairs with e_4 and e_2 pairs with e_3. A Lagrangian kernel containing e_1 therefore lies in ⟨e_1,e_2,e_3⟩. Suppose c is a unit. Then b = ad/c, so HT(e_2) = (a, ad/c) = (a/c)·HT(e_3), as printed. Hence Fil^can_ε = ⟨HT(e_2), HT(e_3)⟩ = R_ε·HT(e_3). This is free of rank one because c is a unit. HT(e_3) and HT(e_4) form a basis of R_ε^2 because det[[c,e],[d,f]] = cf − de is a unit, so HT(e_4) spans a direct complement. HT(e_2) = (a/c)HT(e_3) generates Fil only when a is a unit, and nothing forces that. So the printed "generated by HT(e_2)" is wrong under the stated assumptions; the correct generator is HT(e_3). The same holds in the other case (d, e units), where HT(e_2) = (b/d)HT(e_3). The paragraph right after the proof supports this reading: X(p^n,ε) is covered by X(p^n,ε,e_2) and X(p^n,ε,e_3), where HT(e_2), respectively HT(e_3), generates Fil. The case the proof treats (cf − de a unit) is exactly the HT(e_3) chart. The HT(e_2) chart corresponds to af − be being a unit; minors that use column 1 vanish, and ad − bc = 0. This is not a text-layer artefact: the page images of both versions clearly print HT(e_2). The lemma's statement still holds (locally free of rank one, locally a direct summand), because the corrected argument proves it. The later uses at pp. 81–84 (the X(p^n,ε,e_2)^?, X(p^n,ε,e_3)^? covering and the Mayer–Vietoris-type sequence) depend only on the lemma and the covering, both of which are correct. So the misprint is a one-symbol slip (e_2 for e_3) and affects nothing downstream.

issues.locator: §12.4 (Group action), p. 75, 2nd paragraph, first line (author version). This is not in HAL v3: HAL v3 (printed p. 64 = PDF p. 65) reads 'We let 𝔗_{w'} be the formal scheme in groups defined by ...' with no range for w'. The slip was introduced in the author version.
issues.printed: For rational w' ≥ 0, the source defines the formal group 𝔗_{w'} by 𝔗_{w'}(R) = Z_p^×(1 + p^{w'}R), R in Adm. It identifies the identity component 𝔗^0_{w'} with the functor 𝔗^0_{w'}(R) = 1 + p^{w'}R on Adm.
issues.correction: For all rational numbers w' > 0
issues.reason: For w' = 0 the definition does not give a group. Take R = O ∈ Adm: 1 + p^0 R = 1 + O = O, which contains 0, so 𝔗_0(O) = Z_p^× · O = O is not a subgroup of O^×. Formally, 1/(1+X) does not converge in O⟨X⟩, so R ↦ 1 + R is only a formal monoid. For w' > 0, p^{w'}R is topologically nilpotent in the p-adically complete R, so 1 + p^{w'}R is a group. Every later use has w' > 0: §12.3 says 'positive rational numbers w' ≤ w', and §12.6.2 says '0 < w' ≤ w ≤ ε', which governs §§12.6–14. The intended range is therefore clearly w' > 0.

issues.locator: §12.6.2, proof of Lemma 12.6.2.1, p. 76 (author version). HAL v3 has the same sentence (printed p. 65 = PDF p. 66). In HAL v3, however, 𝔏^{κ_A} was defined through 𝔗^0_w-invariants, so the sentence matched that version's definition. It became inconsistent when the author version switched the definition to 𝔗^0_{w'}.
issues.printed: Using the Section 12.5 cover, the source identifies 𝔉𝔏^+_{n,ε,w,w'}|_{Spf R} with (1 0; p^w𝔅(0,1)_R 1) × (1 + p^{w'}𝔅(0,1)_R). It assigns the action of 𝔗^0_w to the second factor and concludes 𝔊^{κ_A,w}(Spf R × Spf A) ≃ R⊗̂A⟨X⟩.
issues.correction: The action of 𝔗^0_{w'} is on the right term.
issues.reason: On the same page, π_1 : 𝔉𝔏^+_{n,ε,w,w'} → 𝔉𝔏_{n,ε,w} is a 𝔗^0_{w'}-torsor, and 𝔏^{κ_A} = ((π_1)_*O ⊗̂ A)^{𝔗^0_{w'}}, with invariants 'taken with respect to the diagonal action of 𝔗^0_{w'}'. The right factor is 1 + p^{w'}𝔅(0,1)_R = 𝔗^0_{w'}, on which 𝔗^0_{w'} acts simply transitively. That simple transitivity is what gives 𝔊^{κ_A,w}(Spf R × Spf A) ≃ R⊗̂A⟨X⟩. 𝔗^0_w is only a subgroup (w ≥ w'), and its invariants alone would not give that isomorphism. The subscript should be w'.

issues.locator: §12.6.2, paragraph after the proof of Lemma 12.6.2.2 (definition of 𝔉^{κ_A,w}), p. 77 of the author version. HAL v3 is different (printed p. 65 = PDF p. 66): it reads '(π_3)_⋆𝔊^{κ_A,w} is 𝔎𝔩𝔦(ℤ/p^nℤ)-equivariant. We define a Banach sheaf 𝔉^{κ_A,w} = ((π_3)_⋆𝔊^{κ_A,w})^{𝔗_{w,n}}', with no second expression. HAL v3 also defined 𝔏^{κ_A} using 𝔗^0_w invariants, which explains the leftover w.
issues.printed: The source takes the finite projection π_3 : 𝔛(p^n,ε) → 𝔛_Kli(p^n,ε), calls (π_3)_⋆𝔊^{κ_A,w} equivariant for 𝔗_{w,n}, and defines the Banach sheaf on 𝔛_Kli(p^n,ε) × Spf A by 𝔉^{κ_A,w} = ((π_3)_⋆𝔊^{κ_A,w})^{𝔗_{w,n}} = (π_⋆𝒪_{𝔉𝔏^+_{n,ε,w,w'}} ⊗̂ A)^{𝔗_{w,n}}.
issues.correction: Replace 𝔗_{w,n} by 𝔗_{w',n}, as defined in §12.4. This is essential in the second expression, (π_⋆𝒪_{𝔉𝔏^+_{n,ε,w,w'}} ⊗̂ A)^{𝔗_{w',n}}. It is harmless but consistent in the other two places. This matches the analytic definition on p. 79, (π_⋆𝒪_{𝓕𝓛^+_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'}} ⊗̂ A)^{𝒯_{w',n}}.
issues.reason:
§12.4 (p. 75) defines 𝔗_{w',n} = 𝔗_{w'} ×_{𝔗_{w'}/𝔗^0_{w'}} 𝔎𝔩𝔦(ℤ/p^nℤ). It says that the 𝔗^0_{w'}-action on 𝔉𝔏^+_{n,ε,w,w'} (a 𝔗^0_{w'}-torsor over 𝔉𝔏_{n,ε,w}) extends to an action of 𝔗_{w',n}. With the dummy variable renamed, 𝔗_{w,n} is a subgroup of 𝔗_{w',n} that contains only 𝔗^0_w ⊆ 𝔗^0_{w'}.

First expression: 𝔗^0_{w'} already acts trivially on 𝔊^{κ_A,w} = (π_2)_⋆((π_1)_⋆𝒪 ⊗̂ A)^{𝔗^0_{w'}}, and 𝔗_{w,n} maps onto 𝔎𝔩𝔦(ℤ/p^n). So ((π_3)_⋆𝔊)^{𝔗_{w,n}} equals the 𝔎𝔩𝔦-invariants, which equal ((π_3)_⋆𝔊)^{𝔗_{w',n}}. That expression is therefore correct even as printed.

Second expression: this one is wrong for w' < w. In the local chart of §12.5, 𝔉𝔏^+ = 𝔉𝔏 × (1 + p^{w'}𝔅(0,1)). Invariants of 𝒪 ⊗̂ A under the diagonal action of 𝔗^0_w = 1 + p^w(·) only impose κ_A-equivariance along the smaller group. They give a strictly larger sheaf, namely functions on the 𝔗^0_{w'}/𝔗^0_w-torsor 𝔉𝔏^+/𝔗^0_w, not π_⋆𝔏^{κ_A}. With 𝔗_{w',n} one gets the intended sheaf, as in the p. 79 definition.

The cause is a leftover from HAL v3, where w and w' played swapped roles (𝔏^{κ_A} was defined with 𝔗^0_w). A separate minor point, not part of this issue: π in the second expression is the map to 𝔛(p^n,ε) (p. 76), so strictly one means π_3∘π.

issues.locator: §12.7.2, paragraph before Lemma 12.7.2.2 and the statement of Lemma 12.7.2.2, p. 78
issues.printed: The source defines 𝓕𝓛^+ → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n, e_1)^+ to parametrize rank 1 locally split flags Fil ω_G and trivializations ρ ∈ Grω_G = ω_G/Filω_G^(18). Lemma 12.7.2.2 descends 𝓕𝓛^+_{n,ε,w,w'} to an open 𝓕𝓛^+_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'} over the same base. Its conditions are (Filω_G ∩ ω_G^{mod,+})_w = Fil^{can}_w and ρ in ω_G^{mod,+}/(Filω_G ∩ ω_G^{mod,+}), reducing to HT_4(1) in Gr^{can}_{w'}.
issues.correction: Replace 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n, e_1)^+ with 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n, ε)^+ in both places.
issues.reason: The page image confirms the printed e_1 in both places; this is not a text-layer artefact. Under the paper's own notation the second argument of 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n, ·) is the rational number ε ∈ [0, n−1/(p−1)] ∩ Q. See §12.7.1, p. 77: "We denote by 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε) ⊂ 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n) the quotient of 𝒳(p^n,ε) by 𝔎𝔩𝔦(Z/p^n) and by 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε)^+ ⊂ 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n)^+ the quotient of 𝒳(p^n,ε) by 𝔎𝔩𝔦(Z/p^n)^+". e_1 is the first basis vector of (Z/p^nZ)^4 (§12.2.2). The only spaces indexed by basis vectors are 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i) for i ∈ {2,3}, which take three arguments. No 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n, e_1) is defined anywhere: a search of the text finds only these two occurrences. ε is the right base, for three reasons. (1) FL^+_{n,ε,w,w'} lies over 𝒳(p^n,ε), which is the space that is quotiented to give 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε)^+. (2) The second condition uses HT_4(1). On p. 78 this map is defined only "Over 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε)^+ … obtained via the map ψ", where ψ is the universal trivialization of H_n^D. So the base has to be the '+' space at level ε. (3) The companion Lemma 12.7.2.1, immediately before, descends to FL → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε). The notation cannot be read charitably. P_Kli is the stabiliser of ⟨e_1⟩ (§5.1.2, p. 20), but that is already encoded in the subscript "Kli", and "e_1" is not an admissible value for the ε slot. Even if one read it as 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n)^+, the notation is still undefined; ε is the reading that agrees with everything around it. Nothing downstream uses 'e_1'. On p. 79 the projection is π : FL^+_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'} → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε), the composite through the '+' space, followed by T_{w',n}-invariants. Corollary 13.2.2.1 (p. 86) uses only FL^+_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'}. The proof of Lemma 13.3.2.1 (p. 89) defines its own FL^+ as the G_m-torsor over FL → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε). That is a separate minor inconsistency ('+' vs no '+'), not part of this finding. So the slip changes no statement or argument. HAL v3 has the same text: PDF p. 68 (printed p. 67), "Let us denote by 𝓕𝓛^+ → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n, e_1)^+ the moduli space of flags …" and "Lemma 12.7.2.2. — The space 𝓕𝓛^+_{n,ε,w',w} descends to an open-subspace of 𝓕𝓛^+ → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n, e_1)^+ …". The v3 lemma has a different subscript order and a condition "ρ reduces to the element HT(1)", but the e_1 slip is the same.

issues.printed: The source calls the 𝒰-Čech complex for ℒ^{κ_A} ⊗ ω^r bounded and projective over Banach A[1/p]-modules, computing RΓ(𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε), 𝒢^{κ_A,w} ⊗ ω^r). It says 𝔎𝔩𝔦(ℤ/p^nℤ) acts on it, and the invariant direct summand computes RΓ(𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε), ℱ^{κ_A,w} ⊗ ω^r).
issues.correction: "... which computes RΓ(𝒳(p^n,ε), 𝒢^{κ_A,w} ⊗ ω^r) (= RΓ(ℱℒ_{n,ε,w}, ℒ^{κ_A} ⊗ ω^r))". The subscript Kli should be dropped from 𝒳.
issues.reason: The paper puts 𝒢^{κ_A,w} on the full level space, not on the Klingen quotient. On p. 78 it says: "We denote by 𝒢^{κ_A,w} the Banach sheaf generic fiber of 𝔊^{κ_A,w} over 𝒳(p^n,ε) × Spa(A[1/p],A)". Here 𝔊^{κ_A,w} = (π_2)_* ℒ^{κ_A} over X(p^n,ε) × Spf A (§12.6.2, p. 76). The Klingen-level sheaf is the separate sheaf ℱ^{κ_A,w} = ((π_3)_* 𝔊^{κ_A,w})^{T_{w,n}}, with π_3 : X(p^n,ε) → X_{Kli}(p^n,ε) (p. 77). The display just above the proposition (p. 79) is exactly the corrected identity: RΓ(𝒳(p^n,ε), 𝒢^{κ_A,w}⊗ω^r) = RΓ(ℱℒ_{n,ε,w}, ℒ^{κ_A}⊗ω^r). The proof takes a covering 𝒰 of ℱℒ_{n,ε,w}, so its Čech complex computes RΓ(ℱℒ_{n,ε,w}, ℒ^{κ_A}⊗ω^r), which equals RΓ(𝒳(p^n,ε), 𝒢⊗ω^r). The next sentence takes 𝔎𝔩𝔦(ℤ/p^nℤ)-invariants to reach the Klingen level. That step only makes sense if the complex is still at full level 𝒳(p^n,ε), which matches the second display, RΓ(𝒳_{Kli}, ℱ⊗ω^r) = RΓ(𝔎𝔩𝔦(ℤ/p^nℤ), RΓ(ℱℒ_{n,ε,w}, ℒ⊗ω^r)). The same pattern appears in Corollary 12.9.2.1 on p. 80: H^i(𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε), ℱ⊗ω^r(−D)) = H^0(Kli(ℤ/p^n), H^i(𝒳(p^n,ε), 𝒢⊗ω^r(−D))). One charitable reading is RΓ(𝒳_{Kli}, (π_3)_*𝒢), which gives the same thing because π_3 is finite. But the paper always writes that pushforward explicitly, so as printed the formula names a space the sheaf does not live on. It is a subscript slip, not a mathematical error: the corrected argument goes through unchanged. HAL v3 (printed p. 68, PDF p. 69) has the identical sentence ("𝒰-Chech complex ... computes RΓ(𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε), 𝒢^{κ_A,w} ⊗ ω^r)"), so the slip was there in 2018 and was not fixed by June 2019. Whether the Duke version fixes it cannot be checked because that text is paywalled.

issues.printed: The proof describes a stratification of 𝔛(p^n,ε) by a selection of locally split Lagrangian factors W in V = ℤ^4. It assigns W = {0} to the dense open stratum outside the boundary D, then treats one-dimensional and two-dimensional W.
issues.correction: '… indexed by a subset of the set of all totally isotropic locally direct factors W of V = ℤ^4.'
issues.reason:
V = ℤ^4 carries a symplectic form of rank 4, so a Lagrangian direct factor has rank exactly 2. The strata listed immediately afterwards, however, are W = {0}, W one-dimensional and W two-dimensional. Only the last of these are Lagrangian.

The paper's own boundary index set is 'the set of totally isotropic direct factors W ⊂ V' (§6.1.5.2, p. 27; see also §5.1.2). The standard stratification of a toroidal compactification of a Siegel threefold is indexed the same way. The word 'Lagrangian' is therefore a slip for 'totally isotropic', and the intended meaning is clear from the list that follows.
