HAL v3 has the same text, with [47] (Lan, Higher Koecher principles) in place of [51]: the proposition is on printed p. 70 (PDF p. 71) and the items on printed p. 71 (PDF p. 72).
issues.printed: The proof identifies the completions of 𝔛(p^n,ϵ) and 𝔐̄_W(p^n,ϵ)/Γ_W along ℨ_W(p^n,ϵ)/Γ_W and calls its image in 𝔛(p^n,ϵ)^⋆ closed and finite over Spf 𝒪. Formal functions is invoked to reduce vanishing to H^i(𝔐̄_W(p^n,ϵ)/Γ_W, 𝒪_{𝔐̄_W(p^n,ϵ)/Γ_W}(−ℨ_W(p^n,ϵ)/Γ_W)) = 0 for i > 0, W two dimensional, and H^i(\widehat{𝔐̄_W(p^n,ϵ)}^x, 𝒪_{𝔐̄_W(p^n,ϵ)}(−𝔅_W(p^n,ϵ)) for one-dimensional W, closed x ∈ 𝔛_W(p^n,ϵ), and i > 0. It defines the latter completion from itself along the fibre at x and invokes [3], proposition 8.2.2.4 and [51], sect. 4.
issues.correction: Item 1 should read H^i((𝔐̄_W(p^n,ε)/Γ_W)^∧, O(−D)) = 0 for i > 0. Here ^∧ is the formal completion along 𝔷_W(p^n,ε)/Γ_W, and D is the whole boundary 𝔐̄_W∖𝔐_W, which is where O_𝔛(−D) restricts to. The printed ideal of 𝔷_W/Γ_W is the wrong sheaf. This is exactly AIP's H^q(Z̃_{V'}, O(−D)). Two smaller slips: item 2 needs "= 0", and the hat-M^x there should be defined as the completion of 𝔐̄_W(p^n,ε), not of itself, along the fibre. The arguments of [3] Prop. 8.2.2.4 and [51] §4 need not be redone for the models 𝔐̄_W(p^n,ε): neither the level p^n, nor ω^mod, nor the Hodge–Tate condition enters the local models in a way that breaks them. Pointing to the argument of [3] Prop. 8.2.2.4 and [51] §4 is an adequate proof, because the needed local models are stated on p. 82, so no gap needs recording. Minimal fix: correct item 1 as above and add "= 0" in item 2.
issues.reason:
I rendered pp. 82–83 at 130 and 250 dpi. Item 1 has no hat, while item 2 has one.

(a) The missing completion in item 1 is a notational slip. The theorem on formal functions computes the completion of the coherent sheaf R^iπ_*𝒪(−D) along the image of ℨ_W/Γ_W, which is finite over Spf 𝒪. The toroidal fibre over a 0-dimensional cusp is the union of strata whose cones meet the interior of the positive cone. That union is closed and equals ℨ_W/Γ_W. So the completion equals H^i of the completion of 𝔛 along ℨ_W/Γ_W. By the p. 82 sentence, that is the completion of 𝔐̄_W/Γ_W along ℨ_W/Γ_W. The paper itself separates 𝔐̄_W/Γ_W from this completion on p. 82. Moreover, the uncompleted quotient is not a reasonable object: Γ_W acts on the torus part M_W by group automorphisms and fixes the identity section, so it does not act freely or properly there. AIP's own version ([3] p. 678) says "it suffices to prove that H^q(Z̃_{V'}, 𝒪_{Ẑ}(−D)) = 0", with Z̃_{V'} = Ẑ_{V'}/Γ, the completed object. So the intended meaning is clear from context: a misprint. The same applies to the self-referential definition under item 2.

(b) The "repeat the arguments" step is not a genuine gap. The "equivalent to" step is correct once the completions are read in. The two local statements depend only on the local structure that Pilloni records from [63] thm 4.1:
- Two-dimensional W: this stratum lies in the ordinary locus, where 𝔛(p^n,ϵ) → 𝔛(p^n) is an open immersion. The local model is the completion along ℨ_W of a relative torus embedding for a torus isogenous to Hom(Sym²V/W^⊥, G_m), divided by a neat Γ_W. This is exactly AIP's situation with trivial abelian part. Their Kempf-type argument (Γ-admissible polarization function h, the finite flat maps Φ_ℓ, and the round-down ⌊ℓ^{-1}sD_h⌋ = −D) needs only the fan and the lattice. Replacing the lattice by an isogenous one (adjoining p^n-th roots of the q-parameters) rescales h and changes nothing.
- One-dimensional W: the fan is R_{≥0} and Γ is trivial, since GL_1 is {±1} and the level is neat. 𝔐̄_W is a line-bundle total space over the elliptic curve 𝔅_W (a G_m-torsor with 0 adjoined). The completed cohomology is ∏_{k≥1} H^i(𝔅_{W,x}, N^k), where N is the conormal bundle, which is isogenous to 𝒪(2O) and has positive degree. Hence H^1 = 0 by cohomology and base change on an elliptic curve, which is the [Mum70]-vanishing step of AIP's proof.

§12.9.1 says openly that it "follows [3] section 8 closely". Deferring a verbatim-applicable argument to one's own earlier paper is not an unproved step. Neither the level p^n, nor ω^mod, nor the Hodge–Tate condition enters the local models in a way that breaks the argument. Checked against AIP [3] (author PDF, pp. 46–50). Its proof of 8.2.2.4 reads: "By the theorem of formal functions it suffices to prove that H^q(Z̃_{V'}, O_{Ẑ_{V'}}(−D)) = 0." In AIP, Ẑ is the formal completion and Z̃ = Ẑ/Γ. D sums D_ρ over all rays ρ, explicitly "not simply over the set Σ(1)^o as in the definition of W_Σ". Pilloni's 𝔷_W is a "closed codimension 1" subscheme and its quotient by Γ_W is the closed W-stratum, so it is AIP's W (the interior-ray part), not D. The divisor D_ρ of a boundary ray, such as ρ = x², meets 𝔷_W: the orbit of the cone ⟨x²,y²⟩ lies in both. So O(−𝔷_W) differs from O(−D) on the completion, and item 1 as printed is the wrong group. Also, 𝔐̄_W/Γ_W without completion is not even defined, because Γ_W does not act properly on the torus part; the preceding sentence uses the completion. The intended object is clear from context, since the proposition is about O(−D) and item 2 correctly uses O(−𝔅_W), the full complement. So this is a misprint.

Defence of the "repeat the arguments" step:
(i) W two-dimensional. Pilloni states on p. 82 that the boundary lies in the ordinary locus, where 𝔛(p^n,ε) → 𝔛(p^n)^mod is an open immersion and 𝔛(p^n)^mod → 𝔛(p^n) is an isomorphism. So ω^mod and the HT condition play no role there. The model is the normalisation of the toroidal compactification at full level p^n: a torus embedding with the character lattice uniformly rescaled, which is still smooth for the fan. AIP's own 8.2.2.4 already treats such a normalised level-p^n model, X_1(p^n)(v). Its inputs all survive a finite normalisation: a smooth admissible decomposition, a polarisation function h, the [C-S] splitting, freeness of Γ, and ampleness of O(D'_h) (from FC V.5.8, or AIP's alternative argument via the boundary).
(ii) W one-dimensional. The torus has rank 1 and Γ_W is trivial. The completion is a line bundle over the elliptic curve 𝔅_W completed along its zero section. The cohomology of O(−𝔅_W) is then the product over k ≥ 1 of H^i(𝔅_W, L^k), with L isogenous to O(2O) and hence ample. This vanishes by Mumford §16, which is the argument AIP use in their first proof of Thm 8.2.2.3.
One caveat the text does not address: §12.1 takes O = O_{C_p}, which is not noetherian, so EGA III formal functions needs a routine descent to a finite extension. Everything is finitely presented, so this is standard.

Downstream use: Lemma 12.9.2.1 (p. 83) → Cor. 12.9.2.1 → Prop. 12.9.1 (vanishing of H^i_cusp for i > 1) → §13. The intended statement is right and the proof goes through with the corrected item 1, so nothing downstream is affected.

issues.printed: The proof derives degree 0 concentration of Čech(𝔘_i, 𝔏^{κ_A}⊗ω^r(−D))[1/p] from Theorem 12.9.2.1. For 𝔘 = 𝔘_2∪𝔘_3 on 𝔉𝔏_{n,ε,w}, it introduces the sheaf 𝔏^{κ_A}(−D)) and says the corresponding Čech complex computes RΓ(ℱℒ_{n,ε,w}, ℒ^{κ_A}⊗ω^r(−D)). It identifies this with the two-term complex of sections of π_⋆𝒢^{κ_A}⊗ω^r(−D) on 𝒳(p^n,ε,e_2)^⋆ and 𝒳(p^n,ε,e_3)^⋆ mapping to sections on their intersection, hence gives degrees 0 and 1.
issues.correction: Add the missing step. Write 𝔛_2, 𝔛_3 for 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_2)^⋆, 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_3)^⋆. The intersection 𝔛_2 ∩ 𝔛_3 is the inverse image in 𝔛_2 = 𝔛(p^n)^{⋆−mod} ×_{𝔛(p^n)^{⋆−HT}} 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_2)^{⋆−HT} of the locus in the affine 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_2)^{⋆−HT} = Spf A⟨s_{1,j}/(s_{2,4}p^ε)⟩ where s_{3,4}/s_{2,4} is a unit. That locus is again affine: it is the locus where s_{2,4} and s_{3,4} are both invertible and s_{1,j} ∈ p^ε det ω^mod. Projectivity and the isomorphism on generic fibres are preserved by this open base change, so Theorem 12.9.2.1 also applies to 𝔛_2 ∩ 𝔛_3 with the small sheaf π_⋆𝔊^{κ_A,w}⊗ω^r(−D) restricted to it. Hence the Čech complex of the mixed intersections 𝔘_2 ∩ 𝔘_3, after inverting p, is also concentrated in degree 0. Only with this does the Mayer–Vietoris total complex reduce to the displayed two-term complex. This correction is right and essentially minimal. As a separate harmless misprint, the display writes 𝒢^{κ_A} for 𝒢^{κ_A,w}.
issues.reason:
The proof only establishes acyclicity for the two pieces. It says "We deduce from thm 12.9.2.1 that Čech(𝔘_i, …)[1/p] is concentrated in degree 0" for i ∈ {2,3}. That rests on Lemma 12.9.1.3, which gives each 𝔛(p^n,ε,e_i)^⋆ a projective map to an affine that is an isomorphism on generic fibres. The Čech complex of 𝔘 = 𝔘_2 ∪ 𝔘_3 is quasi-isomorphic to the Mayer–Vietoris total complex [Čech(𝔘_2) ⊕ Čech(𝔘_3) → Čech(𝔘_2∩𝔘_3)]. Acyclicity on the pieces alone gives exact sequences 0 → H^0 → H^0(X_2)⊕H^0(X_3) → H^0(X_23) → H^1 → 0 and H^{j+1}(FL) ≅ H^j(X_23) for j ≥ 1. So the claimed concentration in degrees 0 and 1 is equivalent to H^j(X_2∩X_3, π_⋆𝒢⊗ω^r(−D)) = 0 for j ≥ 1, and the text never states or proves this.

Defence attempted. The intersection is not affine, because the pieces themselves are only projective over affines, not affine. It is affinoid on the generic fibre, but π_⋆𝒢 is a Banach sheaf on the minimal compactification, not a coherent sheaf. Being affinoid therefore gives no acyclicity; Theorem 12.9.2.1 with a formal model is what supplies it. The strategy in the §12.9 introduction ("covered by two affines") shows this is what the author meant. The analogous argument in §14 (proof on p. 91 onward) has no such gap, because there the covering opens are genuinely affine and D(s_1)∩D(s_2) = D(s_1 s_2). Here the gap is filled by one line, since Theorem 12.9.2.1 applies to the intersection exactly as to the pieces (see the correction). So the step is asserted without justification, but it is true.

Downstream: Lemma 12.9.2.1 → Corollary 12.9.2.1 → Proposition 12.9.1 (vanishing of H^i_cusp(†,κ_A,r) for i > 1) → §13.4 (C_cusp(A_l) concentrated in degrees 0 and 1; Proposition 13.4.1) and footnote 24 in §14. None of these is endangered, because the gap is routinely filled.

issues.locator: §13.1.1 (Slope decomposition), condition 4 in the definition of an h-slope decomposition, p. 84 of the author version (17 June 2019). HAL v3: §13.1.1, printed p. 72 (PDF p. 73), same wording.
issues.printed: Point 4 asserts that Q^⋆(U) is invertible on M^{>h} whenever every root of the polynomial Q has valuation strictly greater than h; Q^⋆ denotes Q's reciprocal polynomial.
issues.correction: Minimal fix: replace "with roots of valuation strictly greater than h" by "with roots of valuation ≥ −h". This is Urban's "Q of slope ≤ h" ([81] §2.3.1), whose reciprocal Q^⋆ has all its roots of valuation ≤ h. An equivalent form: P(U)|_{M^{>h}} is invertible for every nonzero polynomial P whose roots (in k̄) all have valuation ≤ h. Variants of this correction that add the side condition "Q(0) a unit" or "Q(0) ≠ 0" are also right and equivalent; these side conditions are harmless but not needed. Rescaling Q does not affect invertibility, and a root 0 (valuation +∞ ≥ −h) only lowers the degree of Q^⋆.
issues.reason:
The printed text matches the page image at 150 dpi exactly. In HAL v3 condition 4 is word-for-word the same; only condition 3 differs, lacking "(in an algebraic closure of k)". The text layers of HAL v1 and v2 give the same condition 4.

Why the printed condition fails:
- The paper uses "reciprocal" in the standard sense, X^d Q(1/X) (compare §5.1.5, p. 23: "the roots of the reciprocal of Θ(Q_ℓ(X))").
- For Q = c∏(X−α_i) this gives Q^⋆(U) = c∏(1−α_i U). Its invertibility only says that U − β is invertible for β = 1/α_i, and these have v(β) < −h. That is the wrong condition.

Counterexample: k = Q_p, M = k^2, U = diag(1,p), h = 1/2.
- Decomposition A: M^{≤h} = 0 and M^{>h} = M. Condition 3 is vacuous. For condition 4, Q^⋆(U) = diag(c∏(1−α_i), c∏(1−pα_i)). Here v(α_i) > 1/2, so 1−α_i and 1−pα_i are units, and a root α_i = 0 gives a factor 1.
- Decomposition B: M^{≤h} = ke_1 (eigenvalue 1, valuation 0 ≤ 1/2) and M^{>h} = ke_2. It also satisfies conditions 1–4 as printed.
- So the uniqueness asserted right after the definition ("By [81], coro. 2.3.3 ... it is unique") is false under the printed definition.
- Reading "reciprocal" as 1/Q does not rescue it. Then Q(U) must be invertible when v(root) > h, and Q = X−p kills e_2, so neither A nor B qualifies and no decomposition exists at all.

Checked against [81] (Urban, Ann. of Math. 174 (2011), §2.3.1, from the Annals PDF):
- Urban says Q is of slope ≤ h "if Q(0) ∈ O_L^× and if the roots of Q^*(X) := X^d Q(1/X) ... have their slope ... less or equal to h".
- His condition (4) reads: "For any polynomial Q of slope ≤ h, the restriction of Q^*(u) to M_2 is an invertible endomorphism of M_2".
- So Urban requires roots of Q of valuation ≥ −h, not > h, and the proposed correction states exactly that.
- Equivalence with the P(U) form: P ↦ P^⋆ is a bijection, up to scalars, between polynomials with P(0) ≠ 0 and roots of valuation ≥ −h and polynomials with roots of valuation ≤ h, and P^⋆⋆ = P.
- Under the corrected condition, uniqueness holds even with Pilloni's condition 3. Take P = the characteristic polynomial of U on M_1. P(U) kills M_1 and is invertible on M_2'. This forces M_1 ⊂ M_1', and M_2 ⊂ M_2' follows the same way.
- In the counterexample the correction rules out A: Q = 1−X gives Q^⋆(U) = diag(0, p−1).

Why it affects nothing:
- The intended notion is clear from the citation of [81] and from the use of Serre [72] and Coleman [14] for existence.
- The later uses all rely on the standard notion: Prop. 13.1.3.1, §13.2–13.3, Lemma 14.7.1, Rem. 14.8.1 (H^{>0} = (1−f)H) and "0-slope decomposition is functorial" (§14, near p. 107).
- The Duke version was not available to compare. The printed text matches the page image at 130 dpi. The paper defines "reciprocal" as X^d Q(1/X). This is its only meaning in the paper: the Hecke polynomial Q_ℓ(X) = 1 − T_{ℓ,2}X + … has "reciprocal" with roots the Hecke parameters (§5.1.5, p. 23; also p. 32).

Defence attempts, all failing:
(a) Literal reading. For Q = c∏(X−α_i) with v(α_i) > h, Q^⋆(U) = c∏(1−α_iU). Its invertibility only excludes eigenvalues 1/α_i, which have valuation < −h, so this is the wrong condition.
(b) "Roots" read as roots of Q^⋆ (valuation > h). Then eigenvalues of valuation > h are excluded from M^{>h}, the opposite of what is wanted.
(c) Reading Q(U) in place of Q^⋆(U) gives the same opposite condition.
No sign convention rescues it: v(p) = 1 is fixed on the same page.

Counterexamples to the uniqueness claimed in the next line (I checked both):
- M = k, U = 1, h = 0. Both (M^{≤0}, M^{>0}) = (M, 0) and (0, M) qualify, since Q^⋆(1) = c∏(1−β_j) is a unit when v(β_j) > 0.
- M = k², U = diag(1, p), h = 1/2. Both (0, M) and (ke₁, ke₂) qualify.
Under the printed definition, existence also fails for h < 0. Take M = k, U = 1, h = −1. Condition 3 forces M^{≤−1} = 0, and Q = X − 1 (root of valuation 0 > −1) gives Q^⋆(U) = 1 − U = 0. So the claim in §13.1.3 that [72] gives a slope decomposition would also fail as printed.

Urban's definition, checked in the local copy of Ann. Math. 174, §2.3.1: Q is of slope ≤ h if Q(0) ∈ O_L^× and the roots of Q*(X) := X^d Q(1/X) have valuation ≤ h. His condition (4) is "For any polynomial Q of slope ≤ h, the restriction of Q*(u) to M_2 is an invertible endomorphism". This is exactly the correction.

Uniqueness holds under the corrected definition together with Pilloni's condition 3. Let P be the characteristic polynomial of U on M₁. Its roots are nonzero, since condition 3 excludes eigenvalue 0 (valuation +∞). P(U) kills M₁ and is invertible on M₂', which gives M₁ ⊂ M₁'. The argument is symmetric, and M₂ ⊂ M₂' follows the same way.

Later uses, all of which import the standard notion from its sources:
- the uniqueness sentence ([81] Cor. 2.3.3) and the definition of M^{=h} and M^{<h} (p. 84);
- existence via [72] and Prop. 13.1.3.1 via [14] Part A (pp. 84–85);
- the finite slope part in Cor. 13.2.4.2 (p. 87);
- (M^•)^{≤h} for a compact operator in Lemma 14.7.1 and Thm 14.7.1 (p. 99);
- "0-slope decomposition is functorial" (p. 102), which is [81] Lemma 2.3.2.
Nothing in the paper argues from condition 4 as printed. Every claim is right for the intended notion, which the citation of [81] identifies. So this is a sign or inequality slip in the definition ("≥ −h" printed as "> h"), not a failing step. It affects nothing, though a formaliser must use the corrected definition. It is not an "error" affecting "a stated result": the uniqueness claim after the definition is false only under the literal misprinted definition; it is true under the intended one.

issues.locator: §13.2.1, proof of Lemma 13.2.1.1, last paragraph of p. 85 of the author version. HAL v3 (printed p. 74 = PDF p. 75) has the same sentence. Its preceding sentence is worded '(In case G and G_1 have bad reduction, …)'.
issues.printed: For semi-abelian G and G_1, the source interprets T_p(G), T_p(G_1) as Tate modules of the associated 1-motives. It chooses bases of T_p(G) ≃ ℤ_p^4 together with T_p(G_1) ≃ ℤ_p^4, chosen to lift the moduli-problem bases of G[p^n], G_1[p^n], and says suitable bases of ω_G, ω_{G_1} respecting the canonical filtration give the displayed diagram.
issues.correction: Choose bases e_1,…,e_4 of T_p(G) and f_1,…,f_4 of T_p(G_1), adapted to ξ, so that ξ = diag(1,p,p,p^2) (i.e. f_1 = ξ(e_1)) and e_1 lifts a generator of H_n ⊂ G[p^n]. Then f_1 lifts a generator of the level subgroup H_{n+1} = t_2-image ⊂ G_1[p^{n+1}].
issues.reason:
The moduli problems here are the Klingen-level ones. By p. 77, 𝒳_Kli(p^n,ε) 'parametrizes pairs (x,H_n)', and t_2 lands in 𝒴_Kli(p^{n+1}). So no basis of G[p^n] is provided, only the cyclic subgroup H_n. For G_1 the relevant level is p^{n+1}, not p^n: the next page speaks of 'the group generated by the image [1,p,p,p^2](e_1) in G_1[p^{n+1}]'.

Moreover, if bases of G[p^n] and G_1[p^n] were both prescribed independently, ξ could not in general be put in diagonal form. The subsequent computation needs exactly the diagonal form plus the fact that e_1 lifts a generator of H_n, which gives p_1(e_1) ∈ p^ε.

The intended choice exists. Write T = T_p(G) ⊂ T_1 = T_p(G_1) with T_1/T ≅ L. The vector e_1 is primitive in T_1, because p^{-1}e_1 mod T lies in H_n[p] \ {0} and L ∩ H_n = 0. Take elementary-divisor bases (p,p,p^2) of T/ℤ_p e_1 ⊂ T_1/ℤ_p e_1, lift them, and correct the lifts in T by multiples of e_1. This gives ξ = diag(1,p,p,p^2) with f_1 = e_1.

A charitable reading is also possible: lift the geometric point to full level 𝒳(p^n), resp. 𝒳(p^{n+1}). Under it the sentence is merely loose rather than false. Either way, the intended argument is clear from the rest of the proof. Hence this is a misprint (imprecise wording), not a gap. Confidence is medium because the classification between an imprecision and a misprint is a judgement call.

issues.locator: §13.2.1, definition of the correspondence and proof of Lemma 13.2.1.1, p. 85 of the author version. The same text is in HAL v3 (printed pp. 73–74 = PDF pp. 74–75), apart from the wording '(G,H_n) ∈ 𝒴_Kli(p^n)'.
issues.printed: The source introduces t_1 : C|_{𝒴_Kli(p^n)} → 𝒴_Kli(p^n) for triples (G, H_n, L), with totally isotropic L ⊂ G[p^2], étale-locally (ℤ/pℤ)^2 ⊕ ℤ/p^2ℤ, and L ∩ H_n = {0}. Its rule is (G, H_n, L) ↦ (G, H). It also defines t_2 : C_n|_{𝒴_Kli(p^n)} → 𝒴_Kli(p^{n+1}) by (G, H_n, L) ↦ (G/L, p^{−1}H_n + L/L). Lemma 13.2.1.1's proof takes a rank one point (K, 𝒪_K) of C_n with isogeny ξ : G → G_1.
issues.correction: t_1(G,H_n,L) = (G,H_n). The map is t_2 : C|_{𝒴_Kli(p^n)} → 𝒴_Kli(p^{n+1}), (G,H_n,L) ↦ (G/L, ([p]^{-1}(H_n) + L)/L). In the proof, read 'a rank one point of C_ε'.
issues.reason:
(1) 'H' is not defined in §13; the level subgroup here is H_n. '(G,H)' is a leftover from the Klingen-level-p correspondence of §10 ('The construction is parallel to section 10').

(2) 'C_n' is not defined in §13. There the objects are C|_{𝒴_Kli(p^n)}, its compactification C, and C_ε = C ×_{t_1} 𝒳_Kli(p^n,ε), which is the space Lemma 13.2.1.1 is about. The parallel proof of Lemma 13.2.2.1 (p. 86) says 'a rank one point of C_ε'. The symbol C_n is later defined in §14.2 for a different object (the n-fold iterate of the correspondence over 𝒳_Kli(p)).

(3) 'p^{-1}H_n + L/L' is shorthand with missing parentheses for the image in G/L of [p]^{-1}(H_n) + L. I checked that this is the right level-p^{n+1} subgroup. L ≅ (ℤ/p)^2 ⊕ ℤ/p^2, so L[p] has order p^3. Since L ∩ H_n = 0, L[p] ⊕ H_n[p] = G[p]. Then L ∩ [p]^{-1}(H_n) = L[p], because pL ⊂ L meets H_n trivially. The image therefore has order p^{n+4}/p^3 = p^{n+1}.

The image is generated by the class of any y with py generating H_n. That class has order p^{n+1}, because p^n y ∈ H_n \ {0} is not in L. So the image is cyclic, as a Klingen p^{n+1} structure must be. It agrees with p. 86, 'the group generated by the image [1,p,p,p^2](e_1) in G_1[p^{n+1}]'.

All of these are notational slips with clear intended meaning.

issues.correction: 𝒰'_i ⊂ 𝒳(p^{n+1}) ×_{𝒳(p^n)} ℱℒ_{n,ε,w}, and '… stable under the action of 𝔎𝔩𝔦(ℤ/p^{n+1}ℤ)'
issues.reason: By §12.7.2 (p. 78), ℱℒ_{n,ε,w} lies over the full-level space 𝒳(p^n,ε). 𝒳(p^{n+1}) → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^{n+1}) ×_{𝒳_{Kli}(p^n)} 𝒳(p^n) is generically a covering with group ker(Kli(ℤ/p^{n+1}) → Kli(ℤ/p^n)), so ℱℒ_{n+1,ε+1,w+1} is not a subspace of it and '\overline{𝒰_i} ⊂ 𝒰'_i' makes no sense. The second slip is the group. The translates added are under 𝔎𝔩𝔦(ℤ/p^{n+1}ℤ), and the displayed factorization takes (Čech(𝒰',…))^{𝔎𝔩𝔦(ℤ/p^{n+1}ℤ)}, so stability under 𝔎𝔩𝔦(ℤ/p^{n+1}ℤ) is what is needed. 𝔎𝔩𝔦(ℤ/p^nℤ) does not even act on this fibre product. The intended meaning is clear from the first paragraph and from the factorization.

issues.printed: For finite slope f ∈ H^i(C(n',ε',w',κ_A,r)), the source asserts the local existence on A of nonzero P(X) ∈ A[X], with P(0) = 0 and f = P(U)f. It defines the extension into H^i(C(n,ε,w,κ_A,r)) as P(Ũ)f.
issues.correction: Write P(X) = X·Q(X) and set ext(f) := Ũ(Q(U)f), which equals Q(U)(Ũf).
issues.reason: Ũ goes from H^i(C(n',ε',w',…)) to the different space H^i(C(n,ε,w,…)), so its powers, and hence P(Ũ), are undefined as written. The only sensible reading is Ũ∘Q(U) with P = XQ. Then res∘ext(f) = (res∘Ũ)Q(U)f = U Q(U) f = P(U)f = f. The result does not depend on the choice of P: Ũ Q1(U)f = Ũ Q1(U)P2(U)f = Ũ Q2(U)P1(U)f = Ũ Q2(U)f. Also ext∘res = Q(U)∘Ũ∘res = Q(U)U = P(U) = id on finite-slope classes, as the paper claims. This is a notational slip with clear intended meaning; the corollary is unaffected.

issues.locator: §13.3.1, proof of Proposition 13.3.1.1, first sentence, p. 88 (author version). HAL v3 has the same text on printed p. 76.
issues.printed: The proof treats ℱ^{κ,w} as a Banach subsheaf of 𝒪_{ℱℒ_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'}} and defines ℱ^{κ,w,++} = ℱ^{κ,w} ∩ 𝒪^{++}_{ℱℒ_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'}}, explaining ++ as the topologically nilpotent sections.
issues.correction: Replace ℱℒ_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'} by ℱℒ^+_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'} in both places: ℱ^{κ,w} ⊂ π_⋆𝒪_{ℱℒ^+_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'}} and ℱ^{κ,w,++} = ℱ^{κ,w} ∩ π_⋆𝒪^{++}_{ℱℒ^+_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'}}, where π : ℱℒ^+_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'} → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε).
issues.reason: A 600 dpi render confirms there is no '+' on ℱℒ in either subscript; the '++' in the second place is the superscript of 𝒪. The paper defines no space ℱℒ_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'}. The four-index space is ℱℒ_{Kli,n,ε,w} (Lemma 12.7.2.1). The extra index w' belongs only to the 𝒯-torsor ℱℒ^+_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'} (Lemma 12.7.2.2), always written with '+' (pp. 75, 78, 86). The definition on p. 79 reads ℱ^{κ_A,w} = (π_⋆𝒪_{ℱℒ^+_{Kli,n,ε,w,w'}} ⊗̂ A)^{𝒯_{w',n}}. The π_⋆ in the correction only makes precise the usual abuse of calling this a 'subsheaf of the structural sheaf'; the actual slip is the missing '+'.

issues.locator: §13.3.1, proof of Proposition 13.3.1.1, p. 88 (author version, 17 June 2019); HAL v3: same proposition number, printed pp. 76–77 (PDF pp. 77–78)
issues.printed: Citing Proposition 14.4.1.1^{(22)}, the proof states R^i(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = (t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = 0 for i > 0. It then claims the trace Tr : (t_1)_⋆𝒪_{C_ε} → 𝒪_{𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε)} induces the map Tr : (t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} → 𝒪^{++}_{𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε)}.
issues.reason: I checked the page image (p. 88). The printed chain "R^i(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = (t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = 0 for all i > 0" is what is on the page; it is not a text-layer artefact. The middle term has no index i, so read literally the chain says two things: the pushforward (t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} is 0, and R^i equals R^0. Both are wrong. The pushforward is not zero: the very next sentence defines the restricted trace Tr : (t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} → 𝒪^{++}_{𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε)} on it, and that trace is what builds p^3U on the ++ complexes. The cited result, Proposition 14.4.1.1(2) (p. 94), says R(t_{n,1})_⋆𝒪^{++} = (t_{n,1})_⋆𝒪^{++}. That means the higher direct images vanish; it does not mean the pushforward itself vanishes. Also, on p. 85 (§13.2.1) the paper recalls "the map (t_1)_⋆𝒪_C → R(t_1)_⋆𝒪_C is a quasi-isomorphism." So the author meant R^i(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = 0 for i > 0 and ran together two ways of writing it. The proposed correction fits the paper's own conventions. HAL v3 has a similar slip: its PDF p. 78 (printed p. 77) reads "R^i(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = (t_1)_⋆𝒪_{C_ε} = 0 for all i > 0", with no ++ on the middle term. The author version added the ++ but still left the equation "= (t_1)_⋆… = 0" in place. The proof only needs the vanishing of R^i for i > 0, so the argument goes through as intended. No later result depends on the literal reading. One separate point, not part of this misprint and not assessed: Proposition 14.4.1.1(2) is stated for t_{n,1} : C_n → 𝒳_{Kli}(p), while it is applied here to C_ε → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε). So the scope of the citation is a separate question.

issues.locator: §13.3.1, proof of Proposition 13.3.1.1, p. 88 of the author version (the citation of Prop. 14.4.1.1 with footnote 22). The cited Prop. 14.4.1.1(2) is on p. 94 (§14.4.1). HAL v3 has the same citation, without the footnote, on printed p. 76, and states Prop. 14.4.1.1(2) the same way (still only at level p) on printed pp. 81–82.
issues.printed: The proof cites Proposition 14.4.1.1 for R^i(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = (t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = 0, i > 0. Footnote 22 dismisses circularity because the later proposition uses only Section 3.4. That proposition states, for t_{n,1} : C_n → 𝒳_{Kli}(p), R(t_{n,1})_⋆𝒪_{C_n} = (t_{n,1})_⋆𝒪_{C_n} and R(t_{n,1})_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_n} = (t_{n,1})_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_n}.
issues.correction: Minimal fix: state Prop. 14.4.1.1(2) for any Klingen level p^n (n ≥ 1), for the map t_1 : C_{Σ'} → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n)_Σ of §13.2.1, with Σ' chosen smooth, because Prop. 3.4.1 needs that and §13.2.1 does not say it. The conclusion is R(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_C = (t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_C, i.e. R^i(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_C = 0 for i > 0. The proof is word for word the same. The 𝒪-version is the "standard computation" already recalled on p. 85. The ++-version comes from the local toroidal charts (Kuga–Sato variety times a torus), Props. 3.4.1 and 3.3.1, the p-dévissage, and the factorisation of t_1 as C_{Σ'} → C_Σ → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n)_Σ (a change of cone decomposition, then a finite map). Restricting over 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε) needs no extra work: higher direct images are local on the target and C_ε = t_1^{-1}(𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε)).
issues.reason:
I rendered pp. 85, 88, 92 and 94 and checked the text. In §13 the correspondence depends on n. On p. 85, C|_{Y_Kli(p^n)} is 'the moduli space of (G, H_n, L) where (G, H_n) is a point of Y_Kli(p^n)', and t_1 : C_{Σ'} → 𝒳_Kli(p^n)_Σ. The proof of 13.3.1.1 uses t_1 : C_ε → 𝒳_Kli(p^n, ε) and needs R^i(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = 0 for i > 0.

Prop. 14.4.1.1 is stated only for t_{n,1} : C_n → 𝒳_Kli(p), the n-fold iterate of the U-correspondence at Klingen level p. §14.1 says: '𝒳_Kli(p) is the analytic Siegel threefold of Klingen level at p'. In the remark on p. 92, the author identifies C_1 with 'the correspondence C|_{Y_Kli(p)} considered in section 13.2.1', which is §13's C in the case n = 1 only.

The case n > 1 cannot be avoided. On p. 55, ε lies in [0, n − 1/(p−1)], and §13.2.2 requires w ≤ ε. A w-analytic κ may need w ≥ 1, which forces n > 1. Cor. 13.2.4.2 allows changing (n, ε, w) only among admissible triples.

As stated, 14.4.1.1 does not formally imply the level-p^n claim. On the abelian locus, C^{(p^n)} = C_1 ×_{Y_Kli(p)} Y_Kli(p^n): because H_n is cyclic, L ∩ H_n = 0 exactly when L ∩ H_n[p] = 0. But no base-change result is available for the ++ sheaves or across the toroidal boundary. So the cited proposition does not cover the step as written.

The step is nonetheless very likely true. The proof of 14.4.1.1 uses nothing specific to level p. The author also 'recall[s]' the non-++ statement (t_1)_⋆𝒪_C ≅ R(t_1)_⋆𝒪_C at level p^n on p. 85, without a reference. So this is a minor gap: the cited result is stated for a different space. The proof is affected, but the stated result is not.

Footnote 22 only addresses circularity. It does not address the level. Lemma 14.3.1(2), cited in the same sentence, is fine: it is a pointwise statement about L alone, so it transfers via (G, H_n, L) ↦ (G, H_n[p], L).

A separate, unrelated slip: the printed '(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}_{C_ε} = 0' should read 'R(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++} = (t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++}, i.e. R^i = 0 for i > 0'. Defence first.
(i) For n = 1 the citation is literally correct. §14.2 (p. 92) says C_n|_{𝒴_Kli(p)} is "obtained by iterating n times the correspondence C_1|_{𝒴_Kli(p)} (which is the correspondence C|_{𝒴_Kli(p)} considered in section 13.2.1)". So the author treats the §13.2.1 correspondence as the level-p^n member of the same family.
(ii) Nothing in the proof of 14.4.1.1 (pp. 94–95) depends on the level. On the interior t_1 is finite. The boundary input is the toroidal chart computation (Prop. 3.4.1, Prop. 3.3.1) plus a finite map g. Footnote 22 points the reader to that proof.
(iii) §13.2.1 (p. 85) already "recall[s] that the map (t_1)_⋆𝒪_C → R(t_1)_⋆𝒪_C is a quasi-isomorphism" at level p^n.
So the mathematics is not in doubt.

The defence still does not make the text literally right.
- The ++-statement is stated and proved only for t_{n,1} : C_n → 𝒳_{Kli}(p). Here it is applied to the level-p^n map t_1 : C_ε → 𝒳_{Kli}(p^n,ε), and no level-p^n ++-statement appears anywhere.
- Taking n = 1 does not cover the use. §13 needs general n: w-analytic κ needs w ≤ ε ≤ n − 1/(p−1), and §13.4 takes n, ε, w large.
- Base change from level p does not give it formally either. On the interior, C at level p^n is C_1 ×_{Y_Kli(p)} Y_Kli(p^n), because H_n is cyclic, so L ∩ H_n = 0 exactly when L ∩ H_n[p] = 0. But the content sits at the boundary, and R(t_1)_⋆𝒪^{++} does not formally commute with that finite base change.
So a reader must redo the proof at level p^n. That makes it a genuine but minor gap: a citation used beyond its stated scope, filled routinely.

Consequences. The vanishing is needed to identify RΓ(C_ε, t_1^⋆(−)^{++}) with RΓ(𝒳, (t_1)_⋆t_1^⋆(−)^{++}), so that the ++-trace can define p^3U on the ++ complexes. That gives slopes ≥ −3 in all degrees in Prop. 13.3.1.1. The degree-0 bound (slopes ≥ 0) uses a separate q-expansion argument and is unaffected. Downstream: Prop. 13.3.1.1 → Cor. 13.3.3.1 (pp. 90–91) → Cor. 14.7.1 (p. 100) and Lemma 14.8.4 (p. 102, "with equality if k ≥ 3 by corollary 13.3.3.1") → the main classicity and dimension results. The extension is routine, so no stated result is affected, and affects = the proof. Confidence is medium only because it is a judgement call whether a verbatim-transferable citation counts as a gap.

issues.printed: The proof cites Proposition 14.4.1.1 for R^i(t_1)_⋆O^{++}_{C_ε} = (t_1)_⋆O^{++}_{C_ε} = 0, i > 0, then restricts trace to ++ and constructs p^3U on RΓ(X_Kli(p^n,ε), F^{κ_A,w,++} ⊗ (ω^{++})^r). With an affinoid cover U such that FL_{Kli,n,ε,w} is affinoid over each member, it cites Lemma 3.2.2 to claim bounded p-torsion for kernel and cokernel of H^i(C^{•,++}) → H^i(X_Kli(p^n,ε), F^{κ,w,++} ⊗ (ω^{++})^r).
issues.correction:
Two auxiliary statements are needed, and the paper proves neither.

(a) A bounded-torsion Čech-vs-derived comparison (a version of Lemma 3.2.2) for the ++-lattice F^{κ,w,++}⊗(ω^{++})^r of the Banach sheaf F^{κ,w}⊗ω^r on X_Kli(p^n,ε). Refine the covering so that each member pulls back to X(p^n,ε) as an affinoid over which FL^+_{n,ε,w,w'} is trivialised. There F^{κ,w,++} is locally the completed direct sum of copies of O^{++} (Lemma 12.6.2.1, generic fibre, since |κ|=1 on T^0_{w'}). At Klingen level it is the Kli(Z/p^n)-invariants of its pushforward along the finite map π_3.

We assume that there exists F^+ ⊂ F a locally free sheaf of O_X^+-modules such that F = F^+ ⊗ O_X". p. 13: "Let U be a finite affinoid covering of X, such that F^+|_U is trivial." So d_1 commutes with the unnormalised transport along any isomorphism of ω, including the rational one ξ*. It also commutes with t_i^* and with Tr.

Hence d_1∘U_top = p^{-r}·p^{k+r+1}·U_bottom∘d_1 = p^{k+1}U_bottom∘d_1.

Scalar check: for ξ* = c·Id, the top transport is c^{k+2r}p^{-r} and the bottom transport is c^{-2-k}c^{2(k+r+1)}p^{-(k+r+1)} = c^{k+2r}p^{-(k+r+1)}. Their ratio is p^{k+1}.

(3) The printed square is false. It would force (p^{k+1} − p^{-k-1})·U∘d_1 = 0. But take a finite-slope class f that is not classical (Uf = αf with α ≠ 0 and d_1f ≠ 0). Then U(d_1f) = p^{-k-1}α·d_1f ≠ 0.

(4) The cited source does not rescue the statement; it explains where the slip came from. [3] is Andreatta–Iovita–Pilloni, Annals 2015; I read the homepage PDF. Its Prop. 7.2.3 (p. 35) prints Θ_αU_{p,i} = α(d_{g−i})^{⟨κ,α∨⟩+1}U_{p,i}Θ_α, with d_i = diag(p^{-1}1_{g−i}, 1_i) (p. 10). For g = 2 and α = t_1/t_2 this gives ΘU = p^{-(k+1)}UΘ, which is exactly Pilloni's p^{-k-1}. But [3] itself uses the other direction elsewhere:
- its §2.5 formula δ_iΘ_α = α(d_i)^{⟨κ,α∨⟩+1}Θ_αδ_i has δ on the left;
- its proof of Prop. 7.3.1 uses U_{p,g−i}Θ_α(f) = p^{k_{i+1}−k_i−1}Θ_αU_{p,g−i}(f).
Both mean ΘU = p^{k+1}UΘ, which agrees with the correction.

(5) Consequences. Proposition 13.3.3.1 is used only in the proof of Corollary 13.3.3.1. With the corrected factor, the bottom operator p^{k+1}U has slopes ≥ k−2 in every degree (Prop. 13.3.1.1 gives U slopes ≥ −3) and ≥ k+1 on H^0. The triangle of Corollary 13.3.2.1 then gives parts 1–3 with exactly the printed thresholds <k−2, <k+1 and <k+1. With the printed p^{-k-1}U, the bottom slopes are only ≥ −k−4 and nothing follows. Corollary 13.3.3.1 then feeds Corollary 14.7.1 (p. 100) and Lemma 14.8.4 (p. 102; 'equality if k ≥ 3', i.e. slope 0 < k−2), and both are right with p^{k+1}.

Classification. This is a sign misprint, not an error: the intended factor is fixed by the thresholds of Corollary 13.3.3.1, and the paper never uses the wrong sign. It is copied from the swapped formula in [3], Prop. 7.2.3. Still, the displayed Proposition 13.3.3.1 is false as printed, so affects = a stated result (the proposition itself). Nothing downstream is affected.

issues.locator: §13.4 (The spectral variety), displayed formula in the second paragraph, just before Proposition 13.4.1, p. 91 (author version). HAL v3 has the same text on printed p. 79 (PDF p. 80).
issues.printed: The source asserts H^i((κ, α^{−1})^⋆ C_cusp(A_l)) = H^i_cusp(κ, r)[U = α] for every κ : Spa(C_p, O) → Spa(A_l[1/p], A_l), together with α^{−1} ∈ C_p^× defining (κ, α^{−1}) : Spa(C_p, O) → Spa(A_l[1/p], A_l) × G_m.
issues.correction: There are two faults. (i) Notation: 'H^i_cusp(κ, r)' should read 'H^i_cusp(†, κ, 2)'. The complex is built from C_cusp(n,ε,w,κ_{A_l},2), and r is not defined in §13.4. (ii) Mathematics: the fibre at the point does not compute the eigenspace. The correct statement localises at α^{−1} instead of taking the fibre there: H^i(Lκ^*C_cusp(A_l))_{(α^{−1})} ≅ H^i_cusp(†,κ,2)_{(α)}, the generalised α-eigenspace of U. Equivalently, for the support: (κ,α^{−1}) lies in Supp H^•(C_cusp(A_l)) iff α is a U-eigenvalue on H^•_cusp(†,κ,2). That support statement is all the definition of Z_l needs. If a pointwise formula is wanted, for x = (κ,α^{−1}) there is an exact sequence 0 → coker(U−α | H^i_cusp(†,κ,2)_{(α)}) → H^i(Lx^*C_cusp(A_l)) → ker(U−α | H^{i+1}_cusp(†,κ,2)_{(α)}) → 0. Another proposed reading gives the same correction, but with the exact sequence shifted by one (that is the x^! form); its example (α only on H^0) fails only in degree −1 under the standard derived x^*. The passage is a false statement, not just an unproved one, so it is an error, not a gap.
issues.reason:
I transcribed the formula from the page image, and HAL v3 prints the same formula. In §13.1.2 the G_m/A^1 coordinate X is inverse to the eigenvalue (det(1−XŨ)), and the sheaf over the spectral variety is the slope part N^• with X acting as U^{−1}. My own check: the derived pullback along κ is N^•_κ, which computes the generalised eigenspaces (base change, since N^• is perfect over O_V). Pulling back further to X = α^{−1} tensors with the Koszul complex in degrees −1 and 0. That gives the long exact sequence above: H^i(fibre) is an extension of ker(U−α | H^{i+1}) by coker(U−α | H^i). So the printed equality fails in general. If α is a U-eigenvalue on H^0_cusp, then H^{−1}(fibre) = ker(U−α|H^0) ≠ 0, while the right side is 0 in degree −1. If α occurs on H^1 but not on H^0, then H^0(fibre) ≠ 0 = H^0[U=α]. The underived, termwise reading also fails. It depends on the representative Ũ. Explicit counterexample: N^0 = C_p^2 with U a Jordan block at α, N^1 = C_p with U = α, and d(e2) = 1. Then H^0 = ⟨e1⟩ with U = α, but the termwise fibre is acyclic. Another proposed reading has a long exact sequence with an index shift: the cocone/x^! version, 0 → coker(H^{i−1}) → H^i → ker(H^i) → 0. With the standard derived tensor, its example (α on H^0 only) gives H^{−1}(fibre) ≠ 0 rather than H^1(fibre) ≠ 0. The conclusion still holds, in degree −1. What the text actually uses does hold. By derived Nakayama, the support of H^•(C_cusp(A_l)) is the set of pairs (κ,α^{−1}) with α a U-eigenvalue on H^•_cusp(†,κ,2), so the definition of Z is fine. Proposition 13.4.1 ('corollary of the discussion above and proposition 13.1.3.1') needs only Prop 13.1.3.1 with h = 0 applied to C_cusp(n,ε,w,κ_{A_l},2), plus independence of n,ε,w. It does not use the fibre formula. Its only later use is in Lemma 14.8.4 (p. 102), where it enters only through local constancy of the Euler characteristic. DEFENCE ATTEMPTED. In §13.1.2 (p. 84) the paper sets up a complex of coherent sheaves 𝓜^• over Z̃ ⊂ A^1 × Spa(A,A^+), 'the universal eigenspace of M^• for the action of Ũ'. The coordinate X satisfies P̃(X) = det(1 − XŨ), so X acts as U^{−1}, and the point (κ,α^{−1}) corresponds to the eigenvalue α. Nothing in §13.1–13.2 or in the cited sources ([14] Coleman, [9] Buzzard, [81] Urban) identifies the fibre at a point with an eigenspace. Buzzard's machine gives the fibre as the eigenspace quotient coker(U−α), not the eigenspace itself. I tested every reading of '(κ,α^{−1})^⋆':
(a) Derived fibre. Lx^*N = N ⊗^L O/(X−α^{−1}) = cone(U^{−1}−α^{−1} : N → N), where N = Lκ^*C_cusp(A_l) is the finite-slope part of C_cusp(n,ε,w,κ,2). This gives the exact sequence in the correction. Toy check, computed by hand: take N = C_p in degree 1 with U = α. The map U^{−1}−α^{−1} is 0, so the cone is N[1] ⊕ N and H^0(fibre) = C_p. But H^0[U=α] = 0. In general, in degree 0 the fibre has dimension dim H^0[U=α] + dim H^1[U=α]. So the formula fails at every α that is a U-eigenvalue on H^1_cusp(†,κ,2), which is the case the paper is about. It also fails in degree −1 whenever α occurs on H^0. Another way to see it: every derived fibre has Euler characteristic 0, while dim H^0[U=α] − dim H^1[U=α] is not 0 in general.
(b) Termwise fibre of the complex. This depends on the representative Ũ and fails the same way.
(c) Fibre x^*H^i(C) of the cohomology sheaves. For i = 1 this is coker(U−α | H^1_{(α)}), whose dimension equals that of H^1[U=α]. For i = 0 base change fails wherever H^1(C) has κ-torsion, i.e. where the dimensions jump. Lemma 14.8.4 exists precisely to rule out such jumps.
(d) '[U=α]' read as the generalised eigenspace. This is right only for the localisation, not for the fibre at the point.
So no faithful reading makes the display true. Separately, the r is a leftover of the general-r notation H^i_cusp(†,κ_A,r) (p. 83), and the † is missing.
CONSEQUENCES. 'Z_l' is defined as the support of H^•(C_cusp(A_l)). That, and 'quasi-finite and locally finite', need only the support description and Z_l ⊂ Z̃; the support description holds by derived Nakayama. Proposition 13.4.1 ('corollary of the discussion above and proposition 13.1.3.1') follows from Prop. 13.1.3.1 with h = 0, applied to C_cusp(n,ε,w,κ_{A_l},2), together with Cor. 13.2.4.2 (independence of n,ε,w on the finite-slope part). Neither step uses the display. The only later reference to §13.4 is Lemma 14.8.4 (author p. 102: 'by theorem 11.3.1 and proposition 13.4.1'), and it uses only the local constancy of the Euler characteristic. I searched the text: the glued Z → W and H^•(C_cusp) are never used again. Remark 1.2 mentions the finite-slope theory in passing, but no numbered result depends on this display. So the mathematics as intended (support, generalised eigenspaces) is right, and no result or proof is damaged.

issues.printed: The source takes (G, H) ∈ 𝒴_{Kli}(p) and totally isotropic L_n ⊂ G[p^n], requiring L_n to be étale-locally (ℤ/p^nℤ)^2 ⊕ ℤ/p^{2n}ℤ and to satisfy L_n ∩ H = {0}.
issues.correction: L_n ⊂ G[p^{2n}] (a Lagrangian subgroup: its order p^{n}·p^{n}·p^{2n} = p^{4n} is half the order p^{8n} of G[p^{2n}]).
issues.reason: I checked this on page 92 rendered at 110 and 220 dpi. The page really prints "L_n ⊂ G[p^n]" next to "(ℤ/p^nℤ)^2 ⊕ ℤ/p^{2n}ℤ", so this is not a text-layer artefact. The printed text contradicts itself. A group scheme locally isomorphic to (ℤ/p^n)^2 ⊕ ℤ/p^{2n} has sections of order p^{2n}, so for n ≥ 1 it cannot lie in G[p^n]. For n = 1 it would require a ℤ/p^2 inside G[p]. The paper's own later text uses G[p^{2n}]: (1) the same paragraph says C_1 is the correspondence C of §13.2.1 (p. 85), which reads "L ⊂ G[p^2] ... isomorphic to (ℤ/pℤ)^2 ⊕ ℤ/p^2ℤ", and G[p^2] matches G[p^{2n}] at n = 1. (2) The proof of Corollary 14.3.1 (p. 94) says "L_i locally isomorphic to ℤ/p^{2i} ⊕ (ℤ/p^i)^2 and totally isotropic in G[p^{2i}]". (3) The proof of Lemma 14.6.1 (p. 97) says "|m_i|_x ≥ |p^{2n}|_x since L_n ⊂ G[p^{2n}]". (4) The ordinary-case analogue in the proof of Lemma 11.1.1.4 (p. 68) says "L_n ⊂ G[p^{2n}] is a totally isotropic subgroup". The order count also works: L_n has order p^{4n}, exactly Lagrangian in G[p^{2n}], which fits the double coset diag(1, p^n, p^n, p^{2n}) = U^n that comes from iterating C_1 n times. HAL v3 (6 Jan 2018) has the same wording on printed p. 80 (PDF p. 81), which I checked on the page image. The proposed correction L_n ⊂ G[p^{2n}] is right.

issues.printed: The proof bounds H_n's degree below by n − 2(n − ϵ + 1/(p−1)). It asserts that p^{k−1} : H_n[p^k]/H_n[p^{k−1}] → H_n[p^{n−1}] = H_1 give morphisms inducing generic-fiber isomorphisms. Citing [20], coro. 3, p. 13, it concludes deg H_1 ≥ (1/n) deg H_n ≥ 1 − (2/n)(n − ϵ + 1/(p−1)).
issues.correction: p^{k−1} : H_n[p^k]/H_n[p^{k−1}] → H_n[p] = H_1 (the same as p^{n−1}H_n on the generic fiber)
issues.reason:
This is a real misprint. By §12.7.1 (p. 77), X_Kli(p^n, ϵ) parametrizes pairs (x, H_n), where H_n ⊂ G_x[p^n] is locally isomorphic to Z/p^nZ and is generated by e_1. The map to X_Kli(p) sends H_n to its subgroup of order p. So H_1, the Klingen subgroup whose degree is v_x(δ_H), is H_n[p] = p^{n−1}H_n, which has order p. H_n[p^{n−1}] has order p^{n−1}, and it is the level-p^{n−1} group H_{n−1}, not H_1. The two agree only when n = 2.

Checking the step myself: on the generic fiber, H_n[p^k]/H_n[p^{k−1}] ≅ Z/p. Multiplication by p^{k−1} maps it isomorphically onto H_n[p], which is also ≅ Z/p. For n ≥ 3 it cannot be an isomorphism onto H_n[p^{n−1}], a group of order p^{n−1}. So the sentence as printed is false.

With H_n[p] the argument works. Fargues [20], coro. 3 says that a morphism of finite flat group schemes that is a generic isomorphism does not decrease degree. Hence deg(H_n[p^k]/H_n[p^{k−1}]) ≤ deg H_1 for each k. Since degree is additive along the filtration 0 ⊂ H_n[p] ⊂ … ⊂ H_n[p^n] = H_n, we get deg H_n ≤ n·deg H_1. Also deg H_n + deg H_n^D = n and deg H_n^D ≤ 2(n − ϵ + 1/(p−1)). Together these give deg H_1 ≥ 1 − (2/n)(n − ϵ + 1/(p−1)), exactly as printed.

The error is only the exponent in one target group. The rest of the proof, the statement of Lemma 14.1.1 and Remark 14.1.1 are unaffected, and later uses of the lemma depend only on the bound, which is correct. HAL v3 (p. 80) has the same "H_n[p^{n−1}] = H_1", there with the phrase "are generic isomorphisms". It also has the separate slip "deg H_1 ≥ (1/n) deg H_n^D", which the author version fixes to deg H_n.

issues.locator: §14.4.2 (Cohomological correspondences for classical sheaves), p. 95 of the author version (17 June 2019). HAL v3 has the same wording word for word in §14.4.2, printed p. 83 (PDF p. 84).
issues.printed: Section 14.4.2 divides by p^{n(3+r)} to define U^n, calling this consistent with Section 10.4. It asserts U^n : (t_{n,1})_⋆ t^⋆_{n,2} 𝓕^{++} → p^{−3n} 𝓕^{++}. It explains the target p^{−3n}𝓕^{++}, rather than p^{−3n−nr}𝓕^{++}, by claiming degree at least one for the kernel L_n of G → G_n, citing Lemma 14.3.1, 2.
issues.correction: "... is that the kernel L_n of the isogeny G → G_n has degree at least n." Justification to add: C_n is C_1 iterated n times (p. 92). So G → G_n factors through the filtration L_1 ⊂ ... ⊂ L_n used in the proof of Cor. 14.3.1. Each graded piece L_i/L_{i−1} is the kernel of a C_1-point of G/L_{i−1}. δ_{L_n} is the product of the δ_{L_i/L_{i−1}}, so deg L_n = Σ deg(L_i/L_{i−1}). For each piece, deg = deg p(·) + deg (·)[p]/p(·) + deg (·)/(·)[p] ≥ 1, by Lemma 14.3.1(2) and non-negativity of the degree. Hence deg L_n ≥ n. Equivalently: prove the case n = 1 as printed, then use U^n = U∘···∘U, which the paper states a few lines later.
issues.reason:
I re-did the computation. F = Ω^{(k,r)} = Sym^k ω_G ⊗ det^r ω_G (p. 43 / §3). The unnormalized correspondence uses the differential Ω^+_{G_n} → Ω^+_G of G → G_n = G/L_n. On Sym^k this map is integral. On det^r it is multiplication by δ_{L_n}^r, where v_x(δ_{L_n}) = deg L_n|_x (§14.3, v_x(p) = 1, no division by n). The factor p^{3n} in the normalization belongs to the trace, as in §10.4, where the trace is normalized by p^{−3} and ω^r by p^{−r}. So after dividing by p^{n(3+r)}, the image lies in p^{r·deg L_n − nr − 3n}F^{++}. For r > 0, landing in p^{−3n}F^{++} needs deg L_n ≥ n. The printed reason, "degree at least one by lemma 14.3.1, 2", covers only n = 1: Lemma 14.3.1 is stated for points of C_1 only (p. 93). For n ≥ 2 it gives only p^{r−3n−nr}F^{++}, which is not p^{−3n}F^{++}. So the justification as printed falls short for n ≥ 2. The claimed conclusion is still true, via the filtration (additivity of the degree is already used in the proof of Corollary 14.3.1, p. 94) or via iteration. This is not a text-layer artefact: I checked the page image, and "one" and "lemma 14.3.1, 2" are printed that way. It is also not a convention issue: deg L_n is defined unnormalized, and on the relevant component deg L = 1, so the bound deg L_n ≥ n is exactly what is needed. Nothing later depends on the slip. Prop. 14.5.1 uses U^n only on F, not F^{++}. Prop. 14.6.1 gets its integrality from Lemma 14.6.1 directly. Cor. 14.6.1 and Remark 14.6.1 use only the n = 1 bound U: F^{++} → p^{−3}F^{++}. This correction is right, and nothing is affected. Two side notes, outside this issue: (1) for r < 0 the det^r map is δ^r with negative valuation, so the p^{−3n} claim implicitly assumes r ≥ 0. (2) On p. 92 the definition of C_n reads "L_n ⊂ G[p^n]", which should be G[p^{2n}] (compare p. 94 and Lemma 14.6.1). I tried to defend the text; it fails.

(1) The degree is not normalised by n. §14.3 (p. 93) defines deg L_n|x = v_x(δ_{L_n}) with v_x(p) = 1.

(2) What the claim needs. On 𝓕 = Ω^{(k,r)} = Sym^k ω ⊗ det^r ω (pp. 24, 30), the unnormalised correspondence has three parts:
- the differential of G → G_n, which is integral on Sym^k Ω^+;
- the factor δ_{L_n}^r on det^r;
- the integral trace on 𝒪^{++}.
The factor p^{3n} in the normalisation belongs to the trace. That matches §10.4, where the trace is normalised by p^{-3} and ω^r by p^{-r}. After dividing by p^{n(3+r)}, the image lies in p^{r·deg L_n − nr − 3n}𝓕^{++}. For r > 0, landing in p^{−3n}𝓕^{++} therefore needs deg L_n ≥ n. The reason as printed only gives deg L_n ≥ 1, hence only p^{r−nr−3n}𝓕^{++}. That is not enough once n ≥ 2.

(3) Lemma 14.3.1 is stated only for points of C_1 (p. 93). So "by lemma 14.3.1, 2" does not by itself bound deg L_n for n ≥ 2.

(4) No charitable reading rescues the sentence. It speaks explicitly of "the kernel L_n of the isogeny G → G_n". The parallel n = 1 statement on p. 88 ("ξ^⋆ : t_2^⋆(ω^{++})^r → p^r t_1^⋆(ω^{++})^r by lemma 14.3.1, 2") is correct. This suggests the sentence was written for n = 1 and not updated when n was introduced.

The conclusion itself is true. It follows from the filtration/additivity argument that the paper already uses in the proof of Cor. 14.3.1 (p. 94), or from "Obviously, U^n is the n-th iterate of U = U^1" (p. 95) together with the n = 1 case. So this is an inadequate justification for n ≥ 2, i.e. a gap. It is not a false statement. One could also call it a misprint ("one" for "n"). But changing that one word would still leave the n ≥ 2 case without a proof, because Lemma 14.3.1(2) alone does not give deg L_n ≥ n. So I classify it as a gap. The correction above is correct and minimal.

What later uses this passage:
- Prop. 14.5.1 and 14.5.2 use U^n only on 𝓕, not on 𝓕^{++}.
- Prop. 14.6.1 gets its integrality on V from Lemma 14.6.1. On W it only needs the image in 𝓕(U).
- Cor. 14.6.1 and Remark 14.6.1 use only the n = 1 bound U : 𝓕^{++} → p^{−3}𝓕^{++}, which the printed reason does cover.
- A search of the whole text finds no other use of p^{−3n}𝓕^{++} for n ≥ 2.
So nothing depends on the gap.

Two side remarks outside this issue:
- The bound implicitly needs r ≥ 0. For r < 0, δ^r has negative valuation.
- On p. 92, "L_n ⊂ G[p^n]" should read G[p^{2n}], because L_n ≅ (Z/p^n)^2 ⊕ Z/p^{2n}.

issues.locator: §14.4.2 (p. 95); Lemma 14.6.1 and Proposition 14.6.1 (p. 97); Corollary 14.6.1, Remark 14.6.1, Corollary 14.6.2 (pp. 97–99); Theorem 14.7.1 (p. 99); Corollary 14.7.1 (p. 100). The r ≥ 0 hypothesis is stated only at the start of §13.3 (p. 88).
issues.printed: For F = Ω^(k,r) or Ω^(k,r)(−D), §14.4.2 divides by p^{n(3+r)} and asserts U^n : (t_{n,1})_* t^*_{n,2} F^{++} → p^{−3n} F^{++}, rather than p^{−3n−nr}F^{++}, using degree at least one for L_n. Lemma 14.6.1 gives factors p^{n−α} and p^{k(n−α)+r(3n−α)} when |δ_{L_n}|_x ≤ |p^{3n−α}|_x. Section 13.3 takes (k, r) ∈ Z≥0 × Z≥0, while §§13.3.2, 6.2.1 allow Z≥0 × Z. Theorem 14.7.1 claims bijectivity of restriction at slope <k+2r−3 for ε ∈ [0, 1[∩Q without restricting r.
issues.correction:
Assume r ≥ 0 throughout §14. The simplest fix is to open §14.4.2 with "Let F be any of Ω^(k,r) or Ω^(k,r)(−D) with (k,r) ∈ Z≥0 × Z≥0". That covers every statement listed in the locator, and the printed statements and proofs are then correct.

Refinements, if a sharper fix is wanted:
- Lemma 14.6.1 and Proposition 14.6.1 are true exactly when k + r ≥ 0.
- For r < 0 the §14.4.2 bound p^{−3n} must be weakened, for example to p^{−n(3−2r)}. The shift "n−3" in Remark 14.6.1 and the "p^{−3}" in the proof of Corollary 14.6.1 then change the same way.
- Theorem 14.7.1 very likely holds for every r ∈ Z, so it needs no hypothesis in its statement.
- Corollary 14.7.1 needs r ≥ 0 anyway, because it uses Corollary 13.3.3.1 and Proposition 13.3.1.1, which are proved under the r ≥ 0 of §13.3.
issues.reason:
I checked the page images. The text is as quoted, with no condition on r in §14. Ω^(k,r) is defined for r ∈ Z (§6.2.1, restated in §13.3.2), and §14.4.2 says "any of Ω^(k,r)". Only §13.3 says r ≥ 0. The sentence "instead of p^{−3n−nr}F^{++}" in §14.4.2 shows that the author implicitly takes r ≥ 0.

I redid the computation. In the diagonal basis the normalized map on Sym^k⊗det^r has entries m1^{a+r}m2^{k−a+r}·p^{−n(3+r)}. Here d = v(m1m2) = deg L_n lies in [n,3n], since deg L[p]/pL = 1 and pL, L/L[p] have order p. Also 0 ≤ v(m_i) ≤ 2n. For r ≥ 0 every step of the paper is fine. For r < 0 the factor (m1m2)^r has valuation rd ≤ r(3n−α), so the proof step "multiply v(m1m2) ≥ 3n−α by r" goes the wrong way.

The extreme case d = 3n does occur. Take G ordinary with multiplicative part ⟨e1,e2⟩ and Weil pairing e1↔e4, e2↔e3. Take H = ⟨e3/p⟩ and L = ⟨e2/p^2, e1/p, e4/p⟩. The lattice T+⟨e2/p^2, e1/p, e4/p⟩ is self-dual for p^2⟨,⟩, so L is totally isotropic of type (Z/p)^2⊕Z/p^2. Also L∩H = 0, L∩G^m ≅ Z/p^2⊕Z/p, deg L = 3 and ξ* = diag(p,p^2). With the other labelling e1↔e3, e2↔e4, the subgroup ⟨e2/p^2, e1/p, e3/p⟩ with H = ⟨e4/p⟩ does the same job. A brute-force count for p = 2 found 30 such L at an ordinary point. Their multiplicative parts are Z/2 (24 of them), (Z/2)^2 (3) and Z/4⊕Z/2 (3), so d = 3 does occur.

For (k,r) = (0,−1) and n = 1:
- The normalized map on this component is p^{3r}·p^{−(3+r)} = p^{−5}. The trace on ++-sections is integral. So the claim "lands in p^{−3}F^{++}" in §14.4.2 fails.
- Lemma 14.6.1 with α = 1 predicts p^{r(3n−α)} = p^{−2}, but the actual factor is δ^{−1} = p^{−3}. So the lemma is false as printed.
- Proposition 14.6.1 predicts n(−5+2ε'), but the V-part at d = 3n gives only −5n.

HAL v3 has the same text: §14.4.2 on p. 83 and Lemma 14.6.1 on p. 84 are verbatim the same, Theorem 14.7.1 on p. 87 has no r condition, and §13.3 and §13.3.2 read the same.

On 'affects': this affects a stated result, since printed statements are false for parameters the paper allows: the §14.4.2 bound and Lemma 14.6.1, and Proposition 14.6.1 when k+r < 0. The proofs of Theorem 14.7.1 and Corollary 14.7.1 do not cover r < 0. Nothing downstream is affected, though. The only later use is Theorem 14.8.1 with r = 2, which feeds Theorem 1.1. Corollary 14.7.1 is not cited anywhere else. I checked the page images (author pp. 88, 89, 93–100 and 62; HAL v3 p. 84). There is no condition on r anywhere in §14.

The defence partly succeeds. The author clearly means r ≥ 0:
(a) §13.3 opens with "(k,r) ∈ Z≥0×Z≥0", and §14 continues it. Corollary 14.7.1 combines Theorem 14.7.1 with Corollary 13.3.3.1, which is proved under that hypothesis.
(b) The §14.4.2 sentence "lands in p^{−3n}F^{++} instead of p^{−3n−nr}F^{++} ... degree at least one" only makes sense for r ≥ 0.
(c) §14 is only ever used with r = 2: Theorem 14.8.1, which feeds Theorem 1.1. HAL v3's Theorem 14.8.1 assumes r ≥ 2.
(d) §10.4, whose normalisation §14.4.2 cites, is not the source of the problem. There the det map is exactly p, so (1/p^r) works for every r.

But the statements as printed are not restricted. Ω^(k,r) is defined for all r ∈ Z (§6.2.1), §13.3.2 repeats "(k,r) ∈ Z≥0 × Z", and §14.4.2 says "any of Ω^(k,r)". For r < 0 the numbered statements are false.

Computation. Let d = v(δ_{L_n}), which lies in [n, 3n], and let 0 ≤ v(m_i) ≤ 2n. The entries of the map on Sym^k ⊗ det^r are m1^{a+r}·m2^{k−a+r}. Their smallest valuation is r·d + k·min v(m_i), and min v(m_i) ≥ d − 2n. So the entries have valuation at least (k+r)d − 2kn. Compared with the lemma's k(n−α) + r(3n−α), the difference is (k+r)(d − (3n−α)). Hence Lemma 14.6.1 holds iff k + r ≥ 0 (for α > 0). A grid check in python agrees.

Explicit counterexample. Use the symplectic basis ⟨e1,e4⟩ = ⟨e2,e3⟩ = 1. Take an ordinary point with multiplicative part ⟨e1,e2⟩ and H = ⟨e3/p⟩, which is étale. Let n = 1 and L = ⟨e2/p², e1/p, e4/p⟩.
- L is totally isotropic in G[p²]: the only nonzero pairing is e1/p with e4/p, and p²·(1/p²) = 1 ∈ Z.
- L ≅ Z/p² ⊕ (Z/p)² and L ∩ H = 0.
- L ∩ G^m ≅ Z/p² ⊕ Z/p, so d = 3 and ξ* = diag(p, p²).
For (k,r) = (0,−1):
- The normalised factor is p^{−3}·p^{−(3+r)} = p^{−5}, not p^{−3}. So the §14.4.2 claim fails.
- Lemma 14.6.1 with α = 1 predicts p^{−2}, but the actual factor is p^{−3}.
- Proposition 14.6.1 fails for any 0 < ε < ε'. Near x, t_1 is étale, so a section p^a·e with 0 < a < 2ε', supported on the branch through y = (G,H,L), is valid. Its restriction to t_2^{−1}(X_ε) vanishes, because (H+L)/L is étale of degree 0 < ε. Its U-image p^{−5+a}e does not lie in p^{−5+2ε'}F^{++}.

The main theorem very likely survives:
- If r < 0 ≤ k + r, Lemma 14.6.1 and Proposition 14.6.1 hold as printed. Corollary 14.6.1 then needs only some fixed constant c with U(F^{++}) ⊂ p^{−c}F^{++}, and c = 3 − 2r works because d ≤ 3n.
- If k + r < 0, the smallest normalised valuation is n(k+2r−3), attained at d = 3n. So slopes are at least k + 2r − 3, and Theorem 14.7.1 holds vacuously.
So only the auxiliary statements (§14.4.2, Lemma 14.6.1, Proposition 14.6.1, Remark 14.6.1) are false for some r < 0. The proofs of Corollaries 14.6.1–14.6.2 and Theorem 14.7.1 do not cover r < 0, and Corollary 14.7.1 is unproved for r < 0. Nothing downstream is affected.

I set 'affects' to "a stated result" because numbered statements are literally false for parameters the paper allows. It could be argued down to "nothing", since the intended r ≥ 0 is evident. In HAL v3 the passages are verbatim the same.

issues.locator: §14.5, Remark 14.5.1, p. 96 of the author version (17 June 2019), the last paragraph of §14.5. HAL v3 has the same text on printed p. 84 (PDF p. 85), with Ω^(k,r) in place of ℱ: "... sections of H^i(𝒳_Kli(p)_ε′, Ω^(k,r)) for any ε′ > 0 ...".
issues.printed: Remark 14.5.1 uses Lemmas 14.1.1, 14.1.2, Corollary 13.2.4.2 and the preceding proposition to identify finite slope classes in H^i(𝒳_Kli(p^n, ε), ℱ), for every ε > 0 and n, with classes in H^i(𝒳_Kli(p)_ε′, ℱ) for every ε′ > 0, making the analogous claim for cuspidal cohomology.
issues.correction: "... as sections of H^i(X_Kli(p)_{ε'}, F) for any ε' ∈ ]0,1[ ...", equivalently "for any 1 > ε' > 0". This is the minimal fix. Adding "(and ε ∈ ]0, n − 1/(p−1)])" is not needed: §12.7.1 (p. 77) defines X_Kli(p^n, ε) only for ε ∈ [0, n − 1/(p−1)] ∩ Q, so that range is already implicit.
issues.reason:
I checked the printed text on the rendered pages. §14.1 (p. 92) defines 𝒳_Kli(p)_ε = {|δ_H| ≤ |p^ε|} with no range for ε, and recalls that v_x(δ_H) = deg H_x ∈ [0,1] at rank-1 points. This holds at boundary points too, where the degree is computed through the semi-abelian part G^0, as on p. 93. So for ε′ > 1 no rank-1 point satisfies v(δ_H) ≥ ε′. A condition |f| ≤ |p^ε′| survives passing to the rank-1 generization, so 𝒳_Kli(p)_ε′ = ∅ and H^i(𝒳_Kli(p)_ε′, ℱ) = 0. Nonzero finite slope classes exist (for example classical small-slope forms in H^0), so they cannot be "thought of" as sections there. The remark is therefore literally false for ε′ > 1.

At ε′ = 1, p. 100 says "By definition 𝒳^{≥1}_Kli(p) = 𝒳_Kli(p)_1". The argument the remark cites does not reach this case. Prop. 14.5.1 and Prop. 14.5.2 assume ε < 1 and continue classes only to ε′ ∈ ]0,ε[, and the dynamics in Cor. 14.3.2 needs [a,b] ⊂ ]0,1[. §14.8 compares with 𝒳^{≥1} separately: Lemma 14.8.2 gives only injectivity in H^0 and surjectivity in H^1, and only for the ordinary part f.

So the correct range is ε′ ∈ ]0,1[, and the context makes this clear. The remark says "using ... the above proposition", which works with ε′ < ε < 1. Every use of the remark takes ε′ < 1: Theorem 14.7.1 with ε ∈ [0,1[, Cor. 14.7.1 (which cites the remark), and Lemma 14.8.2 with ε ∈ ]0,1[. I therefore class this as a misprint (a slip in the quantifier range) rather than a gap. No step of any proof fails in the intended range. Restricting ε to ]0, n−1/(p−1)] is not needed: that is only the definitional range of 𝒳_Kli(p^n,ε) from §12.7.1 (p. 77), so "for any ε > 0" is not a mistake. My confidence is medium because a reader could count this as harmless informal phrasing rather than a recordable slip; the mathematics above is not in doubt. I checked the rendered pages 76–77, 91–102 of the author version and pages 79, 83–84 of HAL v3.

Conventions (p. 92): X_Kli(p)_ε is the locus where |δ_H| ≤ |p^ε|, and at rank-1 points v_x(δ_H) = deg H_x ∈ [0,1]. So a larger ε gives a smaller space. Nothing on p. 92 bounds ε. On p. 100 the paper itself says: "By definition X^{≥1}_Kli(p) = X_Kli(p)_1". Under the paper's own conventions, then, ε' = 1 is a legitimate value, and so is any ε' > 1.

What the cited results give: Prop. 14.5.2, "the above proposition", assumes ε < 1 and extends a class only to ε' with ε > ε' > 0. It relies on Cor. 14.3.2, where [a,b] ⊂ ]0,1[. Lemma 14.1.1 places X_Kli(p^n, ε) inside X_Kli(p)_{ε''} with ε'' = max{0, 1 − (2/n)(n − ε + 1/(p−1))}. This ε'' is always below 1, because n − ε + 1/(p−1) ≥ 2/(p−1). Together these ingredients reach every ε' ∈ ]0,1[, and no others.

Where the printed range fails:
(a) ε' > 1. The degree of an order-p group is at most 1, and at bad-reduction points it is computed through G^0 (p. 93). So v(δ_H) ≤ 1 at every rank-1 point. X_Kli(p)_{ε'} is a rational open subset, so if it were non-empty it would contain rank-1 points. Hence it is empty and H^i = 0. Read literally, the remark would then identify non-zero finite-slope classes (for example classical small-slope eigenforms in H^0) with sections of the zero group, which is false.
(b) ε' = 1. The space is X^{≥1}_Kli(p), where Prop. 14.5.2 does not apply. The paper handles this space separately in §14.8, and only for the slope-0 part in weight (k,2). There, Lemma 14.8.2 gives only injectivity on H^0 and surjectivity on H^1. Bijectivity comes later, from the dimension count in Lemmas 14.8.3–14.8.4. If the remark were meant to cover ε' = 1, that machinery would be unnecessary. So ε' = 1 is not intended, and the cited results do not cover it.

Defence (why this is a slip, not an error or gap): the intended range ]0,1[ is clear from context. The remark itself cites a proposition that works only on ]0,1[. The paper also habitually writes "ε > 0" when it means ε ∈ ]0,1[ (for example Cor. 14.6.1, "Let ε > 0", whose proof calls Prop. 14.5.1, which needs ε < 1). Every downstream use takes ε' < 1:
- Cor. 14.7.1: "see also remark 14.5.1", combined with Thm. 14.7.1 for ε ∈ [0,1[ ∩ Q and Cor. 13.3.3.1.
- Lemma 14.8.2: uses Prop. 14.5.2 for ε, ε' ∈ ]0,1[ ∩ Q.
- Lemma 14.8.4: compares d_i^{†'}(k) with d_i^†(k), where d_i^† is defined for ε ∈ [0,1[ ∩ Q.
With ε' restricted to ]0,1[, the remark follows from the cited ingredients. So the printed text is genuinely too broad, but nothing in the paper depends on the excess range. That fits PROTOCOL §18's definition of a misprint better than that of a gap.

issues.locator: §14.5 (Analytic continuation), first paragraph, definition of res_{ε,ε′}, p. 96 of the author version (PDF p. 96)
issues.printed: For ε′ ≥ ε, the source defines res_{ε,ε′} : RΓ(X_Kli(p)_ε, F) → RΓ(X_Kli(p)_{ε′}, F) using X_Kli(p)_ε ↪ X_Kli(p)_{ε′}. Wherever defined, it asserts U^n_{ε,ε′} ∘ res_{ε″,ε} = U^n_{ε″,ε′}; it also gives res_{ε′,ε″} ∘ U^n_{ε,ε′} = U^n_{ε,ε″}.
issues.correction: "induced by the inclusions X_Kli(p)_{ε′} ↪ X_Kli(p)_ε". The map res_{ε,ε′} : RΓ(X_Kli(p)_ε, F) → RΓ(X_Kli(p)_{ε′}, F) and the condition ε′ ≥ ε are correct as printed. Only the direction of the inclusion is reversed.
issues.reason:
I checked this on rendered page images, not just the text layer. The misprint is real.

1. The definition on p. 92 (§14.1) reads: "We let X_Kli(p)_ε ⊂ X_Kli(p) be the locus where |δ_H| ≤ |p^ε|". Since v_x(δ_H) = deg H_x, this is the locus where deg H ≥ ε. Raising ε shrinks the locus, and X_Kli(p)_0 is the whole space. So ε′ ≥ ε gives X_Kli(p)_{ε′} ⊂ X_Kli(p)_ε.

2. The rest of the author version uses the same convention:
- Lemma 14.1.1 and its proof conclude deg H_1 ≥ 1 − (2/n)(n−ε+1/(p−1)), which says the map lands in X_Kli(p)_{index}, a set bounded below in deg H.
- Prop 14.5.1 and Prop 14.5.2 (p. 96) take ε > ε′ > 0, g ∈ H^i(X_Kli(p)_{ε′}, F) and res_{ε′,ε} g = f ∈ H^i(X_Kli(p)_ε, F), so the restriction goes from the larger space X_{ε′} to the smaller X_ε.
- The uniqueness argument factors H^i(X_{ε′}) → H^i(X_ε) → H^i(X_{ε′}), with res as the first arrow.
- Cor 14.6.2 and Thm 14.7.1 (p. 99) restrict from X_Kli(p) = X_0 to X_Kli(p)_ε.
- The proof of Lemma 14.7.1 needs closure(U_{i,ε′}) ⊂ U_{i,ε} for ε < ε′.

3. The two composition rules on p. 96 also fit these source and target spaces.

So the stated source, target and condition ε′ ≥ ε are right. The restriction RΓ(X_ε) → RΓ(X_{ε′}) is pulled back along the inclusion X_{ε′} ↪ X_ε. The printed map X_ε ↪ X_{ε′} does not exist in general, and even if it did, pulling back along it would give a map in the opposite direction.

HAL v3 (PDF p. 84, printed p. 83) has the same sentence word for word. However, HAL v3 (PDF p. 81, printed p. 79) defines X_Kli(p)_ε as the locus where |δ_H| ≥ |p^ε|. Under that definition the inclusion X_ε ↪ X_{ε′} is literally correct, and the inconsistency is in the definition instead. The author version fixed the definition to "≤" but did not update this clause, so the misprint is new in the 2019 author version. The published Duke text could not be checked.

Nothing later relies on the wording of this clause. Every later use (Props 14.5.1–14.5.2, §14.6, Lemma 14.7.1, Thm 14.7.1, §14.8) uses res with the correct source and target.

issues.locator: §14.6, Corollary 14.6.1 (statement p. 97, proof p. 98), author version of 17 June 2019. The same missing restriction on ε appears in Corollary 14.6.2 and Lemma 14.7.1 (p. 99). HAL v3 has the same text: Cor. 14.6.1 "Let ε > 0" and Cor. 14.6.2 / Lemma 14.7.1 with no restriction on ε, on printed pp. 85–86. In HAL v3, Thm 14.7.1 has no ε-range at all.
issues.printed: Corollary 14.6.1 assumes ε > 0, f ∈ H^i(𝒳_Kli(p)_ε, 𝓕), Uf = af and v(a) < 2r + k − 3, claiming a compatible system (f_n) ∈ lim_n H^i(𝒳_Kli(p), 𝓕/p^n𝓕^{++}) lifting f with U(f_n) = a(f_n). Its proof chooses α = 2r+k−3−2ε′(r+k)−v(a) > 0 and uses Proposition 14.5.1 to arrange 0 < ε < ε′, that proposition assumes ε < 1. Corollary 14.6.2 and Lemma 14.7.1 impose no ε condition; Theorem 14.7.1 uses ε ∈ [0, 1[∩ℚ. The source identifies X^{≥1}_Kli(p) = X_Kli(p)_1.
issues.correction: In Corollary 14.6.1 replace "Let ε > 0" with "Let 0 < ε < 1". In Corollary 14.6.2 and Lemma 14.7.1 add "ε ∈ ]0,1[" (ε = 0 is trivial there, so [0,1[ also works, matching Theorem 14.7.1). This is the right and minimal fix. The only non-vacuous case it removes is ε = 1: X_Kli(p)_ε = {deg H ≥ ε}, deg H ≤ 1, so X_ε is presumably empty for ε > 1. It is also the hypothesis the paper itself uses in Prop. 14.5.1/14.5.2 (ε < 1), Thm. 14.7.1 (ε ∈ [0,1[) and Lemma 14.8.2 (ε ∈ ]0,1[).
issues.reason:
I checked the rendered pages 91–100. By §14.1 (p. 92), 𝒳_Kli(p)_ε = {|δ_H| ≤ |p^ε|} = {deg H ≥ ε}, with deg H ∈ [0,1]. By p. 100, 𝒳_Kli(p)_1 = 𝒳^{≥1}_Kli(p), the non-empty locus where p-rank ≥ 1 and H is multiplicative, so ε = 1 is a real case of the printed statement "Let ε > 0".

The proof's first step shrinks ε below ε′ using Prop. 14.5.1, which explicitly requires ε < 1. It cannot use a larger ε′ instead: ε′ must satisfy 2ε′(r+k) < 2r+k−3−v(a), so ε′ < 1. If ε′ ≥ 1, then α < 0 and Prop. 14.6.1 gives no convergence. Nothing in the proof handles ε = 1.

The analytic-continuation method also cannot be adapted at ε = 1:
- The dynamics of Cor. 14.3.2 need [a,b] ⊂ ]0,1[.
- Lemma 14.3.1(5) shows the correspondence only preserves deg H = 1.
- For every ε′ < 1, the space 𝒳_Kli(p)_{ε′} contains points with supersingular (p-rank 0) reduction. For example, take G with p-divisible group that of E1×E2 (supersingular reduction, small Hasse valuation w) and H = can(E1), so deg H = 1−w. Isogenous quotients G/L_n keep p-rank 0, so they have no multiplicative H′. Hence no U^n maps 𝒳_{ε′} into 𝒳_1.
- In Lemma 14.7.1, U is not compact on H^i(𝒳_1, 𝓕), so the factorisation through a strictly smaller 𝒳_{ε′} is unavailable, and even the ≤h part is not defined by the paper's slope theory.

For i = 0, the statement at ε = 1 would say that every U-eigenform on 𝒳^{≥1}_Kli(p) of slope < 2r+k−3 is classical. The paper proves nothing like this. It treats ε = 1 only for weight (k,2) and slope 0, by the separate argument of Thm 14.8.1 (Lemmas 14.8.2–14.8.4). The analogue for modular curves (Katz forms on the ordinary locus) is false. I could not prove the Siegel statement false at ε = 1, so this is a gap rather than a proven error.

Downstream, all uses have ε < 1 (Thm 14.7.1 with ε ∈ [0,1[, then §14.8), so no later result is affected. Only the three over-stated results are unproven, at ε = 1. Checked on rendered pages 92, 96–101 (author version) and 84–88 (HAL v3).

1. The proof fails at ε = 1. The corollary's α > 0 forces 2ε′(r+k) < 2r+k−3−v(a). With v(a) ≥ −3 (Prop. 13.3.1.1), this gives ε′ < (2r+k)/(2r+2k) ≤ 1. So for ε ≥ 1 we have ε ≥ ε′, and the step "We can assume 0 < ε < ε′ … by proposition 14.5.1" needs analytic continuation from X_ε to a smaller ε. Prop. 14.5.1 (p. 96) explicitly requires "ε < 1". Its proof uses Cor. 14.3.2, which only covers [c,d] ⊂ ]0,1[. The torsion-coefficient map of Prop. 14.6.1 cannot replace it either, because it needs ε < ε′ with α > 0.

2. The case ε = 1 is real, not vacuous. Page 92 defines X_Kli(p)_ε as the locus |δ_H| ≤ |p^ε|, i.e. deg H ≥ ε with deg H ∈ [0,1]. Page 100 says "By definition X^{≥1}_Kli(p) = X_Kli(p)_1", the generic fibre of the non-overconvergent p-rank ≥ 1 formal locus. On this locus the correspondence gives no improvement. The new subgroup is H′ = (H+L)/L = (G[p]+L)/L, and Lemma 14.3.1(5) gives deg H′ ≥ deg H = 1, so X_1 maps to itself and no neighbourhood X_ε′ (ε′ < 1) is pushed into it.

3. At ε = 1 the statement is probably false, not just unproved. In degree 0, H^0(X_1, F^{++}) is p-adically separated, and lim_n H^i(X, Ω/p^n Ω^+) = H^i(X, Ω) (Prop. 3.2.1, as used in the proof of Thm. 14.7.1). So the conclusion would make every U-eigenform on X^{≥1} with v(a) < 2r+k−3 classical. The analogous statement for modular curves is false. On the ordinary-canonical locus of X_0(p), take any g with Ug = 0 (for example f − VUf). Then F = Σ a^m V^m g converges for v(a) > 0 and satisfies UF = aF. This gives an infinite-dimensional a-eigenspace, whereas the classical eigenspace is finite-dimensional. I have not built such a counterexample for the Siegel–Klingen case, so I record this as a gap rather than an error.

4. The paper itself treats ε = 1 as separate. Theorem 14.7.1 is stated only for ε ∈ [0,1[, and this bound was added after HAL v3. Remark 14.8.1 keeps a slope > 0 part of H^i(X^{≥1}). Theorem 14.8.1 proves only slope-0 classicity at ε = 1, by a dimension count through colim_{ε<1} (Lemmas 14.8.2–14.8.4). That detour would be unnecessary if 14.6.2 + 14.7.1 held at ε = 1.

5. Lemma 14.7.1 has the same problem. Its proof needs U to be compact on X_ε, via some ε′ > ε with the correspondence mapping X_ε into X_ε′. At ε = 1 this is impossible, so the slope decomposition "(M^•)^{≤h}" is not even available.

Consequences: the passage is used only in Thm. 14.7.1 (ε ∈ [0,1[; ε = 0 is trivial because the restriction is the identity), Cor. 14.7.1 (overconvergent, i.e. ε < 1, via Remark 14.5.1), and §14.8 (ε ∈ [0,1[ or ]0,1[). No later result invokes ε ≥ 1, so the main theorems stand once the hypothesis is added. Only the printed statements of 14.6.1, 14.6.2 and 14.7.1 overreach.

I redid the computation. Write β = 2r+k-3-2ε'(r+k), so α = β - v(a). By Proposition 14.6.1, U^m_{ε,0} sends F^{++}|_{X_ε} to F/p^{mβ}F^{++}. Multiplying by a^{-m} then gives a well-defined map to F/p^{mβ-m·v(a)} = F/p^{mα}.
(1) Top row: a^{-n}U^n_{ε,0} lands in F/p^{nα}. This matches the print.
(2) Commutativity of the upper square. On the left, a^{-1}U sends f to a^{-1}Uf = f in p^{-3-v(a)}F^{++}, because Uf = af in p^{-3}F^{++}. So the middle arrow x has to satisfy x∘(a^{-1}U) = a^{-n}U^n_{ε,0}. That forces x = a^{-(n-1)}U^{n-1}_{ε,0}. With the printed label the composite is a^{-n-2}U^n_{ε,0}, which is wrong.
(3) Targets. With a^{-(n-1)}, the middle row sends p^{-3-v(a)}F^{++} to F/p^{(n-1)β-3-v(a)-(n-1)v(a)} = F/p^{(n-1)α-3-v(a)}, and the bottom row lands in F/p^{(n-1)α}. Both match the printed targets exactly. With a^{-n-1} they would be F/p^{(n-1)α-3-3v(a)} and F/p^{(n-1)α-2v(a)}, so each is off by 2v(a), as the reader said.

It is also not a text-layer artefact: the page image shows a^{-n-1}. HAL v3 (PDF p. 86, printed p. 85) has the identical diagram with the same two labels, so the typo survived the 2019 revision; the Duke text could not be checked. Once the labels are read correctly the argument is complete, and the rest of the proof uses only the correct f_n = a^{-n}U^n f. That includes the second diagram (a^{-n}U^n, U) and the projective system in F/p^{nα-3-v(a)}. Corollary 14.6.1 and later results in §14.6 do not depend on the label.

issues.locator: §14.6, Corollary 14.6.2 and its proof, p. 99 (author version, 17 June 2019). HAL v3 has the same proof word for word (printed p. 86 = PDF p. 87); its statement says "roots a of P in Q̄_p" where the author version says "in ℂ".
issues.printed: The proof defines Q = −a_0^{−1}(X^m + a_{m−1}X^{m−1} + ··· + X), asserts Q(U)f = f, and takes f_n = Q(U)^n f by the method of Corollary 14.6.1. Its statement assumes P = X^m + a_{m−1}X^{m−1} + ··· + a_0 ∈ O[X] of degree m, P(U)f = 0, and v(a) < 2r + k − 3 for every root a of P in ℂ.
issues.correction:
(i) Misprint: read Q = −a_0^{−1}(X^m + a_{m−1}X^{m−1} + · · · + a_1X). This is what Prop. 14.5.2 on p. 96 prints ("+ · · · + a_1X"). With it, P(U)f = 0 is equivalent to Q(U)f = f. Also, a_0 ≠ 0 follows from the root hypothesis, since v(0) = ∞, so Q is defined.
(ii) Missing estimate, to add to "as in the proof of corollary 14.6.1":
- Let s_max be the largest valuation of a root of P. Choose ε′ so that β := 2r+k−3−2ε′(r+k) > s_max. The hypothesis on the roots makes this possible, and it is where that hypothesis enters.
- Write Q = Σ_{i=1}^m b_i X^i with b_i = −a_i/a_0. Each a_i is ± the elementary symmetric function of degree m−i in the roots, so v(a_i) ≥ v(a_0) − i·s_max, i.e. v(b_i) ≥ −i·s_max.
- Hence Q^n = Σ_{j=n}^{mn} c_j X^j with v(c_j) ≥ −j·s_max.
- By Prop. 14.6.1, U^j_{ε,0}f is defined in H^i(X_Kli(p), F/p^{jβ}F^{++}). So f_n := Σ_j c_j U^j_{ε,0}f is well defined in H^i(X_Kli(p), F/p^{n(β−s_max)}F^{++}).
- The rest goes exactly as in Cor. 14.6.1 with α = β − s_max. After rescaling, Q(U)f = f integrally in p^{−C}F^{++}|X_ε. Then f_n ≡ f_{n−1} and P(U)f_n ≡ 0, each up to a bounded loss p^{−C′}.
The statement of Cor. 14.6.2 is correct as printed.
issues.reason:
I checked the printed text on the page image at 250 dpi: the last term inside the bracket is a bare "X", not "a_1X". With a bare X, Q(U)f = f does not follow from P(U)f = 0 unless a_1 = 1. The intended a_1X is clear from Prop. 14.5.2's proof on p. 96, which prints "+ ··· + a_1X".

The substantive point is a gap. Cor. 14.6.1 (p. 98) sets f_n = a^{−n}U^n_{ε,0}f ∈ H^i(X, F/p^{nα}F^{++}) with α = β − v(a) > 0. The gain p^{nβ} comes from Prop. 14.6.1 (p. 97) and is set against a single denominator a^{−n}. Copying this literally for Q(U)^n bounds the coefficients only by a_0^{−n}O. That gives the modulus p^{n(β−v(a_0))}, which needs v(a_0) = Σ v(root) < β. That is much stronger than the hypothesis "every root has v < 2r+k−3" as soon as m ≥ 2. I checked an example with p = 3 and P = (X−3)^2, taking β = 1.5, so each root has valuation 1 < β. The naive exponent n(β − v(a_0)) = −0.5n goes to −∞. The true exponent min_j(jβ + v(c_j)) = 0.5n goes to +∞. A short computer check over 60 random products of linear factors and n ≤ 6 found no violation of v(c_j) ≥ −j·s_max.

So "as in the proof of corollary 14.6.1" does not cover the step. The needed Newton-polygon bound on the coefficients of Q(X)^n (or a reduction to generalized eigenvectors, which also needs its own argument) is not stated. The hypothesis being on the roots rather than on a_0 shows the author intended the correct estimate. The statement is therefore true and only the proof is incomplete.

Downstream: Cor. 14.6.2 is used only in Theorem 14.7.1 (p. 99). That theorem concerns slope < k+2r−3, where P can have several roots whose valuations add up to more than β, so the refined estimate is really needed there. Since the corrected proof gives the statement as printed, no stated result changes. HAL v3 has the identical proof text, including the bare "X". Defence first. The paper is right about the statement but not about the proof as written.
(a) The bare "X" is a genuine slip. If a_1 ≠ 1, then Q(U)f = f does not follow from P(U)f = 0. The intended a_1X is clear from Prop. 14.5.2, p. 96.
(b) The step "as in the proof of corollary 14.6.1" does not go through on its own. In Cor. 14.6.1 (p. 98), f_n = a^{−n}U^n_{ε,0}f ∈ H^i(X, F/p^{nα}F^{++}) with α = β − v(a) > 0: one scalar a^{−n} is set against the gain p^{nβ} from Prop. 14.6.1 (p. 97). For Q(U)^n = Σ c_jU^j, the only bound visible from the data is b_i ∈ a_0^{−1}O, which gives v(c_j) ≥ −n·v(a_0). That yields the modulus p^{n(β−v(a_0))}, which needs v(a_0) = Σ v(roots) < β. For m ≥ 2 this is much stronger than the hypothesis. Example: P = (X−p)^2 and β ∈ (1,2). Each root has v = 1 < β, but the naive exponent n(β−2) goes to −∞. The coefficient of X^n in Q^n is (2/p)^n, of valuation −n, so the true exponent is ≥ n(β−1), which goes to +∞.
(c) The printed proof never uses the hypothesis on the roots, and any correct proof must. A charitable reading takes α = β − s_max, which gives the right modulus, but it still leaves the key bound v(c_j) ≥ −j·s_max unstated.
(d) No nearby result supplies it. Prop. 14.5.2 works in characteristic 0 and needs no estimate. [38] (Kassaei) is cited only for the idea. Reducing to generalised eigenvectors would need the same kind of estimate for (X−a)^k, which the paper does not prove either.
Checks:
- The bound v(c_j) ≥ −j·s_max is correct. A short computer check (p = 3, 300 random polynomials with integer roots of mixed valuations, repeated roots included, n ≤ 6) found no violation.
- In 178 of those cases the naive condition v(a_0) < β fails while the refined exponent min_j(jβ + v(c_j)) is positive.
- The terms c_jU^j_{ε,0}f are well defined mod p^{j(β−s_max)}; they need not vanish there.
Consequences:
- The only later use of Cor. 14.6.2 is the proof of Theorem 14.7.1 (p. 99: "we obtain (f_n) … by corollary 14.6.2"). There f lies in the slope < k+2r−3 part and P can have several roots, or a repeated root, whose valuations add up to more than β. So the refined estimate is really needed there.
- Cor. 14.7.1 and Theorem 14.8.1 depend on Cor. 14.6.2 through Theorem 14.7.1 (checked by grep; 14.8.1's reduction is on p. 100).
- The corrected proof gives Cor. 14.6.2 exactly as stated, so no stated result changes.
- The proposed correction (a_1X, plus choosing ε′ with β > s_max and the elementary-symmetric-function bound) is right and minimal.
- Judgement call: one could argue the estimate is routine and file this as a misprint with nothing affected. But a required estimate is missing, the hypothesis is never used, and the literal analogy fails, so "gap" fits better.
