issues.locator: §14.7, proof of Lemma 14.7.1, p. 99 (author version, 17 June 2019). HAL v3 has the same text at §14.7, Lemma 14.7.1, p. 86. It has the same U_{ε,ε′}, the same Ũ_{ε′,ε}, the same condition U(𝒳_{ε′}) ⊂ 𝒳_ε and the same parenthetical. The only difference is that v3 says 'Let 𝒵^i((M^•)^{≤h}) ⊂ M^i.' without 'be the cocycles of slope less than h'.
issues.printed: The proof chooses ε < ε′ with U(𝒳_Kli(p)_{ε′}) ⊂ 𝒳_Kli(p)_ε and labels the return arrow after restriction U_{ε,ε′}, while its compact Čech representative is Ũ : M^• --res--> N^• --Ũ_{ε′,ε}--> M^•. It calls 𝒵^i((M^•)^{≤h}) ⊂ M^i the finite-dimensional space of cocycles of slope less than h. From bounded M^{+i} it obtains a lattice M^{+i} ∩ 𝒵^i((M^•)^{≤h}), and identifies its bounded image with H^i(𝒳_Kli(p)_ε, 𝓕)^{≤h} ∩ V′.
issues.correction:
Replace the last sentence with this argument. Let c ∈ H^i(𝒳_ε,𝓕)^{≤h} ∩ V′. Then c = [z] with z ∈ 𝒵^i(M^{+•}). The slope projector π_{≤h}: M^• → (M^•)^{≤h} is a chain map and is the identity on H^{≤h}, so c = [π_{≤h}(z)]. The projector is continuous (the paper states this for the analogous complex in the proof of Prop. 13.3.1.1, p. 89) and M^{+i} is open and bounded, so π_{≤h}(M^{+i}) ⊂ p^{-N}M^{+i} for some N. Hence H^{≤h} ∩ V′ lies in the image of p^{-N}(M^{+i} ∩ 𝒵^i((M^•)^{≤h})), which is bounded. The parenthetical should therefore say "whose p^{-N}-multiple contains H^{≤h} ∩ V′", not "which is H^{≤h} ∩ V′".

There is also a separate index slip, a misprint. In the §14.5 convention, U^n_{ε,ε′}: RΓ(𝒳_ε) → RΓ(𝒳_{ε′}) is defined when t_{n,2}t_{n,1}^{-1}(𝒳_{ε′}) ⊂ 𝒳_ε. So the second arrow should be U_{ε′,ε}, which matches the Ũ_{ε′,ε} in the next display. The hypothesis should be U(𝒳_ε) ⊂ 𝒳_{ε′}, that is t_{1,2}t_{1,1}^{-1}(𝒳_Kli(p)_ε) ⊂ 𝒳_Kli(p)_{ε′}. By Cor. 14.3.2 such an ε′ > ε exists for ε ∈ ]0,1[. For ε = 0 one may take ε′ = 0, since compactness then comes from Ū′_i ⊂ U_i alone, and the case is trivial in Thm 14.7.1 anyway. Both fixes are minimal and use only facts stated in the paper.
issues.reason:
1) The parenthetical equality is false in general. The image of M^{+i} ∩ 𝒵^i is always contained in H^{≤h} ∩ V′, but the reverse inclusion can fail, because π_{≤h} need not preserve M^{+•}. Counterexample, with a U-stable integral lattice and h = 3/2. Take M^0 = Ky and M^1 = Ka ⊕ Kb with d(y) = b, Ua = pa, Ub = p²b and Uy = p²y. Take M^{+0} = Oy and M^{+1} = O(a+b)/p ⊕ Ob. This is a subcomplex and U-stable, since U((a+b)/p) = p·(a+b)/p + (p−1)b. Then (M^•)^{≤h} = Ka in degree 1, so H^1 = H^{≤h} = K[a]. V′ = image of M^{+1} = p^{-1}O[a]. But M^{+1} ∩ Ka = Oa, whose image O[a] is strictly smaller than H^{≤h} ∩ V′. So as written, the proof only bounds a subset of the set it needs to bound. The lemma is still true, via continuity of π_{≤h} as in the correction; that continuity is stated and used in the proof of Prop. 13.3.1.1. 2) Notation. §14.5 writes the source first: U^n_{ε,ε′}: RΓ(𝒳_ε) → RΓ(𝒳_{ε′}). The §14.7 map goes RΓ(𝒳_{ε′}) → RΓ(𝒳_ε), yet it is labelled U_{ε,ε′}, while the next display writes Ũ_{ε′,ε}; the proof is inconsistent with itself. With ε < ε′ we have 𝒳_{ε′} ⊂ 𝒳_ε. By Lemma 14.3.1(5) the correspondence never lowers deg H, since (G[p]+L)/L = (H+L)/L, both of order p. So the printed condition U(𝒳_{ε′}) ⊂ 𝒳_ε always holds and says nothing. What is actually needed is t_2t_1^{-1}(𝒳_ε) ⊂ 𝒳_{ε′}, which Cor. 14.3.2 provides. Effect on later results: Lemma 14.7.1 is used only in the proof of Theorem 14.7.1 ('Using lemma 14.7.1, we deduce that res∘ext = id'), which feeds Corollary 14.7.1 and §14.8. The lemma's statement is true once the fix is made, so no stated result changes. The earlier HAL version v3 (p. 86) has the identical text. Defence attempted, and it fails.

(1) The parenthetical. The image of M^{+i} ∩ 𝒵^i(M^{≤h}) is always contained in H^{≤h} ∩ V′, but equality is not a formal consequence and fails in general. A class [z] with z ∈ 𝒵^i(M^+) has representatives in 𝒵^i(M^{≤h}) exactly of the form π(z) + d(M^{≤h,i-1}). None of these need lie in M^{+i}, because π_{≤h} need not preserve M^{+•}. It does not help that M^+ is Ũ-stable, since π is only a limit of K-polynomials in Ũ.

I checked a counterexample by hand. Take h = 3/2, M^0 = Ky and M^1 = Ka ⊕ Kb, with dy = b, Ua = pa, Ub = p²b and Uy = p²y. Take M^{+0} = Oy and M^{+1} = O(a+b)/p ⊕ Ob. This is a U-stable subcomplex, since U((a+b)/p) = p(a+b)/p + (p−1)b. Then:
- H^1 = H^{≤h} = K[a];
- V′ = p^{-1}O[a];
- M^{+1} ∩ Ka = Oa, whose image O[a] is strictly smaller than H^{≤h} ∩ V′.
So, as written, the proof bounds only a subset of the set it has to bound.

No nearby statement fills the step directly. The missing ingredient, continuity of the slope projector, is stated and used by the paper itself in the proof of Prop. 13.3.1.1 (p. 89: "Its image (C^{•,++})^{=a} under the continuous projection C^• → (C^•)^{=a} is again open and bounded"). With it the lemma follows. Boundedness of H^{≤h} ∩ V then gives injectivity, because the kernel of the map to lim_n H^i(𝓕/p^n𝓕^+) is H^{≤h} ∩ ⋂_n p^nV.

I classify this as a gap rather than an error because the intended claim, boundedness of H^{≤h} ∩ V′, is true with a short fix. One could argue for "error", since the parenthetical identity is false in general.

(2) The indices. X_ε is the set where deg H ≥ ε (p. 92), so 𝒳_{ε′} ⊂ 𝒳_ε for ε < ε′. By Lemma 14.3.1(5), deg H′ = deg(G[p]+L)/L ≥ deg H, because (H+L)/L = (G[p]+L)/L, both of order p. So the printed hypothesis U(𝒳_{ε′}) ⊂ 𝒳_ε always holds and is not the one needed. Neither reading of U(S), as t_2t_1^{-1}(S) or t_1t_2^{-1}(S), makes it the needed condition t_2t_1^{-1}(𝒳_ε) ⊂ 𝒳_{ε′}. The label U_{ε,ε′} contradicts both §14.5 (source index first; see also U^n_{ε,0} on p. 98) and the Ũ_{ε′,ε} printed two lines later. The intent is clear from context, so this part is a misprint.

(3) Consequences. Lemma 14.7.1 is cited only once: in the proof of Theorem 14.7.1 (p. 100, "Using lemma 14.7.1, we deduce that res∘ext = id"). Corollary 14.7.1 and §14.8 (Thm 14.8.1) depend on it through Theorem 14.7.1. The lemma's statement is true with the fix, so no stated result is affected.

issues.correction: "... respectively only have eigenvalues of non-negative p-adic valuation", i.e. every eigenvalue α satisfies v(α) ≥ 0 (is p-adically integral). "Positive" here is the French usage (≥ 0), not the strict inequality.
issues.reason:
I checked the printed text on the rendered image of p. 102, and it reads exactly as quoted. (1) What the proof shows (p. 103): "We assume that U_{Kli(p),2} f = αf with v(α) < 0 ... We want to deduce that f = 0." It uses v(α) < 0 in the step "there exists n' such that p^n ∈ α^{-n'}O". So the proof gives only v ≥ 0 and says nothing when v(α) = 0.

(2) The strict reading is false under the paper's own normalisations.
- Lemma 5.1.5.1: T_{p,2} acts on the spherical line by α+β+γ+δ.
- Prop. 5.1.5.1: on the 4-dimensional Klingen invariants of a generic spherical π_p, the U_{Kli,2}-eigenvalues are the Weyl orbit of α+β, namely α+β, α+γ, β+δ, γ+δ.
- Corollary 14.9.1: a π_p contributing to eH^i has valuations (0,0,k+1,k+1). The Klingen eigenvalue α+γ then has v(α)=0 and v(γ)=k+1 ≥ 1, so it is always a p-adic unit.
- For k=0, a weight-2 form attached to an abelian surface of p-rank ≥ 1 has T_{p,2}-eigenvalue a_p, which is a unit.

(3) The paper's own usage points to ≥ 0. Elsewhere it writes "non-negative" for ≥ 0 (Remark 13.3.1.1 "only non-negative slopes"; proof of Lemma 14.8.4 "non-positive"/"non-negative").

(4) Later results only use v ≥ 0. I redid the Newton-polygon step behind Corollary 14.9.1.
- Spherical case: take e1 = α+β+γ+δ (v ≥ 0 by the proposition). T-ordinarity with k ≥ 1 forces v(e2) = 0, since e2 = Θ(T) − p^{-1}(1+p)αδ. Also v(e3) = v(e1)+k+1 and v(e4) = 2k+2. The slopes are therefore (0,0,k+1,k+1).
- Klingen case: αβ is a unit (f-ordinary, U = p·U_{Kli,1}) and v(α+β) ≥ 0, which forces v(α) = v(β) = 0 for all k ≥ 0.
Both cases need only v ≥ 0, and Lemma 14.8.3 cites only Corollary 14.9.1. So nothing downstream breaks; only the statement of Prop. 14.9.1 is misworded.

(5) HAL v3 has no §14.9 and no such proposition: §14.8 is followed directly by §15. Its counterpart, in §11.1.1 (HAL v3 p. 58), says instead "The roots are p-adic integers ... It can be proved in an elementary way (by an analysis of the integral properties of the Hecke operators)". That is the v ≥ 0 statement, which confirms what was intended.

Citing Theorem 11.3.1 and Proposition 13.4.1, it calls d_1(k) − d_0(k), together with d_1^{†,′}(k) − d_0^{†,′}(k) locally constant in k ∈ Z_{≥0}.
issues.correction: d_i^{†,′}(k) = dim_ℂ H^i_{cusp}(†, k, 2)^{=0}, the slope-0 part for U, which is the same as dim_ℂ f H^i_{cusp}(†, k, 2) with f the ordinary projector attached to U. HAL v3 writes it the second way.
issues.reason:
I checked the page image at 200 dpi. The formula is printed as "d_i^{†,′}(k) = dim_ℂ H^i_cusp(†, k, 2)", with no ordinary projector f and no =0 superscript.

By §12.8.1, p. 79, H^i_cusp(†, κ_A, r) is the whole overconvergent locally analytic cohomology, colim_{n,ε,w} H^i(X_Kli(p^n, ε), F^{κ_A,w} ⊗ ω^r(−D)). This is a colimit of cohomologies of Banach complexes (Prop. 12.8.2.1). It is not a finite-slope or ordinary part, so its dimension is not finite in general. The ordinary part is finite-dimensional, as p. 102 itself says.

Taken literally, the definition breaks every later step of the proof:
(a) "d_0^{†,′}(k) = d_0^†(k)" would compare the dimension of the whole space with d_0^† = dim f H^0(X_Kli(p)_ε, ·), a finite number.
(b) The appeal to Cor. 13.3.3.1 only makes sense on the slope-0 part. Slope 0 < k+1 always holds, which gives the isomorphism in degree 0 and the injection in degree 1. Slope 0 < k−2 holds exactly when k ≥ 3, and the proof says "with equality if k ≥ 3".
(c) Prop. 13.4.1 (p. 91) is explicitly about k ↦ dim_ℂ H^1_cusp(†, k, 2)^{=0} − dim_ℂ H^0_cusp(†, k, 2)^{=0}.
Remark 14.8.1 identifies f H^i with H^i^{=0}. So the intended definition is clear, and the proof holds once the =0 (equivalently f) is added. This correction is right.

HAL v3 does not have the same text. There the matching argument sits inside the proof of Theorem 14.8.1 (HAL v3 p. 87, PDF p. 88), which I checked on the page image. It defines "d_i^†(k) = dim f H^i_cusp(†, k, r)" with the projector f. So the omission appeared when the argument was rewritten for the 2019 author version.

Lemma 14.9.2 gives restriction isomorphisms for i = 0 and injections for i = 1, for n ∈ ℤ_{≥0} ∪ {∞}, using Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)/p^n on X → 𝔛^{≥1} and Ω^{(k,2)}(−D) ⊗ 𝓘^{−3}/p^n on X_{Kli}(p) → (𝔛_{Kli}(p))^{≥1}.
issues.correction: Restrict the statement to i ∈ {0,1}: "For all k ≥ 0 and i ∈ {0,1}, the Hecke operators T_{p,2} and U_{Kli(p),2} acting on H^i(X, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗ C and H^i(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗ C … only have eigenvalues of valuation ≥ 0." Add the same restriction to Corollary 14.9.1. For the fH^i part of the corollary the restriction costs nothing: once Theorem 14.8.1 is proved, fH^i(X_{Kli}(p)) ⊗ Q_p = 0 for i ≥ 2. This is the minimal correction, and it is all that is ever used. The only citation is in the proof of Lemma 14.8.3 (p. 102). There Corollary 14.9.1 is applied to eH^i(X) and fH^i(X_{Kli}(p)) inside the claim that eH^i → fH^i "are isomorphisms for i ∈ {0,1}". Lemma 14.8.4, Theorem 14.8.1 and everything after them depend only on those degrees and are unaffected.
issues.reason:
The printed text is confirmed on the page images. In the statement of Proposition 14.9.1, i is free. The only paper-wide restriction is a sentence of focus in §5.3, p. 25: "Our main focus will be on the case r = 2, i ∈ {0, 1}". It is not a standing convention, since §14 does treat other degrees (for example, Lemma 14.8.2 proves that complexes are concentrated in degrees 0 and 1).

1. **The proof cannot be extended to i ≥ 2.** It needs the restriction map from H^i(X_{Kli}(p), ·) to H^i((𝔛_{Kli}(p))^{≥1}, ·) to be injective. In degrees ≥ 2 the target is zero. The image of these opens in the minimal compactification is covered by two affines, as in the proof of Lemma 14.8.2, and the cuspidal sheaves have no higher direct images to the minimal compactification (the paper cites [50], thm. 8.6 in the proof of Theorem 11.3.1). So the restriction maps vanish in degrees 2 and 3. Lemma 14.9.2 is correct as stated: codimension-2 complement in a Cohen–Macaulay scheme gives an isomorphism in degree 0 and injectivity in degree 1 only.
2. **Degrees 2 and 3 are not vacuous.** The canonical bundle is Ω^{(0,3)}(−D). By Serre duality, H^3(X, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) is dual to H^0(X, Ω^{(k,1−k)}). For k = 0 this is H^0(X, det ω), the scalar Siegel forms of weight 1. These can be non-zero at suitable prime-to-p level (for example, products of theta constants θ_mθ_n at level Γ_2(4,8)). So the i = 3, k = 0 case of the proposition, as printed, is a real claim that the paper does not prove.
3. **The i ≥ 2 case is probably true, but not shown here.** It should follow from Newton-above-Hodge for the attached crystalline Galois representations, whose Hodge–Tate weights are {0, 0, k+1, k+1}. In the weight-1 example the parameters of the dual system have valuations (0, 0, 1, 1). So this is a scope gap, not a false statement. The intended meaning is probably i ∈ {0,1}.

'affects' = "a stated result" is appropriate only in the narrow sense that the printed scope of Proposition 14.9.1 (and of Corollary 14.9.1) has to be restricted; no later result depends on i ≥ 2.

Side note: "positive p-adic valuation" means ≥ 0 (French usage); the proof only rules out v(α) < 0.

HAL v3 (6 Jan 2018) has no §14.9: §14.8 is followed directly by Part IV. The whole section, including Proposition 14.9.1 and Lemma 14.9.2, was added after v3, so there is nothing to compare. The published Duke version could not be checked. I checked pp. 102–104 on rendered page images; the printed text is as quoted.

The defence fails, for three reasons.
(a) No convention restricts i. The paper's only general remark is in §5.3, p. 25: "Our main focus will be on the case r = 2, i ∈ {0, 1}". That states a focus; it sets no convention. The sentence that opens §14.9 defines the Hecke action on H^i for every i, and the proposition then quantifies only over k.
(b) The method cannot reach i ≥ 2. Lemma 14.9.2 is correct: a codimension-2 complement in a Cohen–Macaulay scheme gives depth 2, so H^0 is an isomorphism and H^1 is injective, via SGA2 exp. III. It says nothing in higher degrees, and in fact the restriction maps vanish there. As the proof of Lemma 14.8.2 shows, the image of the p-rank ≥ 1 locus in the minimal compactification is covered by two affines. The paper also uses (citing [50]) that cuspidal sheaves have no higher direct images to the minimal compactification. So H^i((𝔛_{Kli}(p))^{≥1}, ·) = 0 for i ≥ 2, and the injectivity the argument needs fails as soon as H^i(X_{Kli}(p), ·) ≠ 0.
(c) The unproved cases are not vacuous. By Kodaira–Spencer, K_X = Ω^{(0,3)}(−D). Serre duality then makes H^3(X, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) dual to H^0(X, Ω^{(k,1−k)}). For k = 0 this is M_1, the scalar forms of weight 1. It is non-zero at suitable neat prime-to-p level: by Igusa, θ_mθ_n is a weight-1 form for Γ_2(4,8), for p odd. So the case i = 3, k = 0 of the printed statement is a real claim, and the paper does not prove it.

The mistake is still mild. The missing degrees are probably true: the attached Galois representations would have Hodge–Tate weights {0,0,k+1,k+1}, and Newton-above-Hodge would give the bound. So I found no counterexample, and I class this as a scope gap rather than an error. The proof's first line, "Let i ∈ {0,1}", shows what the author intended. A reader could therefore reasonably call it a misprint, in which case affects = nothing. I keep it as a gap because the printed statement asserts unproved cases, and a formaliser must use the restricted statement. 'affects' = "a stated result" only in that narrow sense: the printed scope of Proposition 14.9.1 and Corollary 14.9.1 shrinks, and no later result changes.

Side note, not part of this issue: "positive p-adic valuation" is French usage for ≥ 0. The proof only rules out v(α) < 0.

issues.locator: §14.8, proof of Lemma 14.8.3, p. 102 (author version, 17 June 2019), using Lemma 5.1.5.2 on p. 22. HAL v3 does not have this text: it has no Lemma 14.8.3 and no Lemma 5.1.5.2. At the corresponding point (v3 p. 57), v3 argues through "the projection to the ordinary line", citing [23] coro. 3.2.2 and 3.2.4, with no distinctness hypothesis.
issues.printed: The proof considers irreducible smooth admissible π_p of GSp_4(Q_p) occurring in eH^i(X, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) or fH^i(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)). It assigns the Hecke parameters (α, β, γ, δ) valuations 0, 0, k + 1, k + 1 up to ordering, citing corollary 14.9.1, proposition 5.1.5.2 and lemma 5.1.5.2. The latter requires 4 distinct members of {αβ, βδ, αγ, γδ} and asserts an isomorphism π_ℓ^{GSp_4(Z_ℓ)} ↪ π_ℓ^{Kli(ℓ)} →^{π_{αβ}} (π_ℓ^{Kli(ℓ)})_{αβ}.
issues.correction: The other natural approach, verifying the hypothesis of Lemma 5.1.5.2, cannot work because that hypothesis can genuinely fail. The minimal fix is to weaken Lemma 5.1.5.2 so that it only needs αβ ∉ {αγ, βδ, γδ}, and to take (π^{Kli})_{αβ} to be the generalized ℓ^{-1}αβ-eigenspace of U_{Kli(ℓ),1}, with the projection taken along the other generalized eigenspaces. That space is 1-dimensional. In the proof of Lemma 14.8.3, add that the valuations (0, k+1, k+1, 2k+2) of (αβ, αγ, βδ, γδ) make αβ a simple eigenvalue. The ordinary projector f for U = p·U_{Kli(p),1} is then exactly this projection.
issues.reason:
Page images of pp. 21, 22 and 102 checked. Conventions (p. 21): αδ = βγ. The Weyl group W (order 8) permutes positions while keeping the pairs {α,δ} and {β,γ}, so the W-orbit of αβ is {αβ, αγ, βδ, γδ}. These are the eigenvalues of U = p^{3−r}U_{Kli(p),1} = pU_{Kli(p),1} for r = 2 (§10, "U corresponds to the operator p^{3−r}U_{Kli(p),1}"), and f is the ordinary projector of U (§14.8).

Corollary 14.9.1 gives valuations 0, 0, k+1, k+1. Because αδ = βγ, each pair must contain one unit, so after a Weyl move v(α) = v(β) = 0 and v(γ) = v(δ) = k+1. Then αγ and βδ both have valuation k+1. With δ = βγ/α, we get βδ = αγ exactly when β² = α², i.e. β = ±α. Nothing in the valuations or the other hypotheses rules this out.

Explicit case: α = β = u and γ = δ = p^{k+1}/u, with u a p-adic unit (e.g. a unit Weil number of weight k+1). This satisfies αδ = βγ = p^{k+1}. All ratios ξ^{-1}ξ' lie in {1, p^{±(k+1)}}, so none equals p for k ≥ 1, and Prop. 5.1.5.2 makes π_p generic spherical. Yet the set {αβ, βδ, αγ, γδ} = {u², p^{k+1}, p^{k+1}, p^{2k+2}/u²} has only 3 elements, so the hypothesis of Lemma 5.1.5.2 fails. The same happens for β = −α (δ = −γ). The proof never checks this hypothesis. The set is W-stable, so a different "suitable order" cannot rescue it.

The stated result still holds. αβ is the only unit eigenvalue of U, so its generalized eigenspace is well defined and one-dimensional, and the spherical vector projects to it nontrivially. The relevant c-factors involve only the ratios α/γ, α/δ, β/γ, β/δ and their inverses, which have valuation ±(k+1), never 0 or 1. The Levi root α/β, where the degeneracy sits, does not enter. So this is a gap in the proof: a lemma is applied without checking its hypothesis, which can fail. It is easily repaired, and Lemma 14.8.3 is not affected. Conventions (p. 21): αδ = βγ, and U = p^{3−r}U_{Kli(p),1} with r = 2 (p. 38). By Proposition 5.1.5.1 the eigenvalues of U on π_p^{Kli(p)} are the W-orbit of αβ, namely {αβ, αγ, βδ, γδ}. This set is W-stable, so no reordering helps. e is the T-ordinary projector and f the U-ordinary projector.

The valuations (0, 0, k+1, k+1) are compatible with αδ = βγ only if one member of each dual pair is a unit. So after using W we may take v(α) = v(β) = 0 and v(γ) = v(δ) = k+1. Then v(αβ) = 0, v(αγ) = v(βδ) = k+1 and v(γδ) = 2k+2. Using δ = βγ/α, αγ = βδ ⟺ α² = β² ⟺ α = ±β. Neither the valuations, the hypotheses of Theorem 14.8.1 (which puts no condition on π) nor anything else in the paper excludes this. It would be a repeated Frobenius eigenvalue, or two opposite ones, among the unit roots. So the hypothesis of Lemma 5.1.5.2 is neither checked nor implied, and the proof as written does not cover such π_p.

Defence attempted: the needed fact is still true, so only the proof is affected. The hypothesis of Proposition 5.1.5.2 (ξ^{-1}ξ' ≠ p) does hold for k ≥ 1, since valuation differences are 0 or ±(k+1). So π_p is generic spherical. Only αβ has to be a simple eigenvalue, and the valuations guarantee that. The argument: π^{Kli} ≅ (π_N)^{M(Z_p)} (Borel–Casselman, Klingen parabolic P = MN). The summand σ of π_N whose central character gives the αβ-eigenvalue splits off as a direct summand because that character differs from the other three. By Frobenius reciprocity π embeds in Ind_P^G σ. The spherical vector v0 goes to a nonzero spherical function F, and F(1) ≠ 0 because G = P·GSp4(Z_p). F(1) is the image of v0 in σ^{M(Z_p)}, which is 1-dimensional, so v0 ↦ π_αβ(v0) is nonzero, hence an isomorphism of lines.

The T-ordinarity side is also consistent: Θ(T) = (αβ+αγ+αδ+βδ+γδ) + p^{-1}(1+p+p²)αδ is a unit iff αβ is a unit, because v(p^{-1}αδ) = k ≥ 1. So the claim that eH^i → fH^i is an isomorphism holds, and Lemma 14.8.3, Lemma 14.8.4 and Theorem 14.8.1 all stand. Downstream, Lemma 14.8.3 is used only in the proof of Lemma 14.8.4, which completes Theorem 14.8.1.

Aside: the p. 22 Klingen paragraph writes "αβ = γδ". This is inconsistent with αδ = βγ on p. 21. Read literally it would make αβ = γδ, so Lemma 5.1.5.2's set could never have 4 distinct elements. It is a separate misprint.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 14.9.2, p. 103 of the author version; not in HAL v3 (§14.9 does not exist there; v3's §14 ends at 14.8)
issues.printed: The proof invokes [SGA], exposé III, section 3, asserting Cohen-Macaulayness for 𝔛 and 𝔛_Kli(p) and describing the open subsets 𝔛^{≥1} and (𝔛_Kli(p))^{≥1} as having codimension 2.
issues.correction: … and 𝔛^{≥1} and (𝔛_Kli(p))^{≥1} are opens whose complements (the p-rank-0 loci, contained in the special fibre) have codimension 2 (≥ 2 suffices).
issues.reason: Read literally, the statement is false: a non-empty open subset has codimension 0. The SGA2 exp. III argument (H^0 iso and H^1 injective) needs depth ≥ 2 of the coefficient sheaves along the closed complement Z. That follows from Cohen–Macaulayness plus codim Z ≥ 2. The author uses the correct wording elsewhere, e.g. p. ~81/Cor. 11.2.1: 'the complement of 𝔛^{≥1} in X is of codimension 2'. The intended claim is also true for Klingen level. The p-rank-0 locus of X_Kli(p)_{F_p} is 1-dimensional: the supersingular curves, plus P^1-fibres over the finitely many superspecial points, where α_p ⊂ α_p^2. So it has codimension 2 in the 3-dimensional special fibre, which is what matters for the /p^n coefficients. This is a wording slip with clear intended meaning. Confidence is only medium because some readers would treat 'open of codimension 2' as acceptable shorthand rather than a misprint.

issues.locator: §14.9.1 ("proof of proposition 14.9.1 assuming lemma 14.9.1"), last paragraph, p. 103 last two lines continuing to p. 104 line 1 (author version, 17 June 2019)
issues.printed: The proof rescales g to obtain h = 0. It claims that each n ≥ 0 admits n′ with p^n ∈ α^{−n′}𝒪, so g′ = α^{−n}U^{n}_{Kli(p),2} g′ vanishes in H^i((𝔛_{Kli}(p))^{≥1}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)⊗𝓘^{−3}/p^n)⊗𝒪. It concludes that the image of g vanishes in H^i(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)⊗𝓘^{−3}/p^n)⊗𝒪.
issues.correction: "For any n ≥ 0, there exists n′ such that α^{−n′} ∈ p^n𝒪 (i.e. n′·|v(α)| ≥ n), and we deduce that g′ = α^{−n′}U^{n′}_{Kli(p),2} g′ is zero in H^i((𝔛_{Kli}(p))^{≥1}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)⊗𝓘^{−3}/p^n)⊗𝒪". This contains two slips: the membership is reversed, and the unprimed exponent n in α^{−n}U^n should be n′.
issues.reason:
Checked on the page image, so this is not a text-layer artefact. The setup is v(α) < 0, α^{−1}U g′ = g′ (h = 0), and U = U_{Kli(p),2} preserves the integral lattice H^i((𝔛_{Kli}(p))^{≥1}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)⊗𝓘^{−3})⊗𝒪 (Lemma 14.9.1). The proof needs g′ to lie in p^n times that lattice.

(1) The inclusion is reversed. Because v(α) < 0, α^{−n′}𝒪 = {x : v(x) ≥ n′|v(α)|}. So "p^n ∈ α^{−n′}𝒪" means n ≥ n′|v(α)|, which n′ = 0 already satisfies, and it gives nothing. What the argument needs is α^{−n′} ∈ p^n𝒪, i.e. n′|v(α)| ≥ n, which some n′ satisfies. Then g′ = α^{−n′}U^{n′}g′ lies in p^n·(lattice), so it maps to 0 mod p^n.

(2) The printed formula α^{−n}U^n g′ uses n where n′ is meant. The identity itself is true, but it only puts g′ in α^{−n}·(lattice), of valuation n|v(α)|. That is ≥ n only when |v(α)| ≥ 1, which need not hold. The n′ just introduced is otherwise never used, so n′ is clearly intended.

With both fixes the argument goes through unchanged: Lemma 14.9.2 injectivity for i ∈ {0,1}, then the limit over n gives g = 0, hence f = 0. So Proposition 14.9.1 and Corollary 14.9.1, and anything later that uses them, are unaffected, so 'affects' = nothing.

issues.reason: The page image confirms the subscript 𝔛^{≥1}, the spherical-level formal scheme. issues.locator: §15.1, Proposition 15.1.1 and its proof, p. 106 of the author version; used in §15.2, p. 107 (the H^{Np}-action on fRΓ and the localisation at 𝔪), and hence in Theorem 15.2.1 and Theorem 1.1(3). HAL v3 has the same proof (pp. 88–89 printed). There the Proposition reads only "We have operators T_{ℓ,0}, T_{ℓ,1} and T_{ℓ,2} acting on RΓ(...)". But the §15.1 opening ("We construct an action of the Hecke algebra") and the §15.2 sentence "The algebra H^{Np} acts on the perfect complex fRΓ(...)" are already in HAL v3.
issues.printed: Proposition 15.1.1 asserts that H_ℓ = Z[T_{ℓ,0}, T_{ℓ,0}^{-1}, T_{ℓ,1}, T_{ℓ,2}] acts on RΓ(𝔛_{Kli}(p)^{≥1}_K, 𝔉^κ ⊗ ω²(−D)) for ℓ ≠ p with K_ℓ = GSp_4(Z_ℓ). Its proof builds T'_{ℓ,i} and sets T_{ℓ,2} = ℓ^{−3}T'_{ℓ,2}, T_{ℓ,i} = ℓ^{−6}T'_{ℓ,i} with indices i = 0, 1. Section 15.2 asserts an H^{Np}-action on fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), 𝔉^κ ⊗ ω²(−D)), whose generated Λ-algebra is finite and semi-local, and defines the direct factor for 𝔪 using [41], lemma 2.12.
issues.correction: The proof has to add the following. (1) T_{ℓ,0}, T_{ℓ,1} and T_{ℓ,2} commute as endomorphisms in D(Λ), not only on cohomology groups. This is what [41] lem. 2.12 needs. (2) T_{ℓ,0} is invertible. This is easy: its correspondence has degree 1 (p_1 is an isomorphism), its inverse comes from ℓ^{-1}GSp_4(Z_ℓ), and ℓ^{-6} lies in Z_p^×. Since H_ℓ = Z[T_{ℓ,0}^{±1}, T_{ℓ,1}, T_{ℓ,2}] is a polynomial ring (§5.1.3), (1) and (2) are exactly what a ring map H_ℓ → End needs. (3) The operators for different ℓ commute, so that H^{Np} = ⊗'H_ℓ acts. (4) They commute with U, so that they preserve the direct factor fRΓ. §4 does not supply these checks: §4.3 defines and constructs cohomological correspondences but has no rule for composing them. So the proof needs a composition and base-change step. One way: compare the composite correspondences on the interior, where they are finite étale and the Hecke relations are classical, then extend over the boundary with the argument of Prop. 7.2.1 ("maps of locally free sheaves that coincide on a dense open coincide"). The proof in §15.2.5 also uses a fifth fact: the action is compatible with specialisation (Thms 11.3.1 and 14.8.1) and with Harris's classical action (Cor. 15.2.3.1). This is the equivariance in Theorem 1.1(3).

I rendered pp. 21 and 107, and HAL v3 p. 89, and checked them directly.

1. The rule is compatible with the local theory. I computed with exact fractions: the eigenvalues in Lemma 5.1.5.1 (ℓ^{-3}αδ; ℓ^{-1}(αβ+αγ+αδ+βδ+γδ) − ℓ^{-3}αδ; α+β+γ+δ) with αδ = βγ give exactly the coefficients of det(1−X·diag(α,β,γ,δ)). So under Θ the coefficients of Q_ℓ(X) are: −Θ(T_{ℓ,2}); ℓ(Θ(T_{ℓ,1}) + (ℓ²+1)Θ(T_{ℓ,0})); −ℓ³Θ(T_{ℓ,2})Θ(T_{ℓ,0}); ℓ⁶Θ(T_{ℓ,0})².

2. When it fails. If Θ(T_{ℓ,2}) = tr ρ̄(Frob_ℓ) ≠ 0, the X³ coefficient fixes Θ(T_{ℓ,0}), and then the X² coefficient fixes Θ(T_{ℓ,1}). If tr ρ̄(Frob_ℓ) = 0, only Θ(T_{ℓ,0})² is fixed. The substitution T_{ℓ,0} ↦ −T_{ℓ,0}, T_{ℓ,1} ↦ T_{ℓ,1} + 2(ℓ²+1)T_{ℓ,0} leaves every coefficient unchanged; I checked this for 200 random rational inputs. For p odd and ℓ ≠ p, the two characters are different.

3. The case really occurs. A ρ̄ that shows up in this cohomology is odd, so complex conjugation has eigenvalues (1,1,−1,−1), trace 0 and ν = −1. By Chebotarev there are infinitely many ℓ ∤ Np with ρ̄(Frob_ℓ) in that class. For ℓ = 5, both Θ(T_{ℓ,0}) = +ℓ^{-3} and −ℓ^{-3} (with the matching T_{ℓ,1}) give Θ(Q_ℓ(X)) = 1 − 2X² + X⁴ = det(1 − X·ρ̄(c)). So the rule allows infinitely many characters of ℋ^{Np}. The sentence "Θ_𝔪 is thus defined by the rule" is therefore false, and "the associated maximal ideal" is not pinned down by what is printed. Nothing in the paper excludes odd p.

4. Why no result is affected. The intended meaning (the natural character attached to ρ̄ in GSp4, including its similitude) is clear. The proof in 15.2.3–15.2.5 uses Θ_𝔪 only through "Θ_{π_f} congruent to Θ_𝔪". It uses this to see, by comparing characteristic polynomials, that the Galois representation of π_f reduces to the irreducible ρ̄, which rules out the Yoshida and Saito–Kurokawa cases and the Eisenstein-type contributions. That argument works for every 𝔪 that satisfies the printed rule, so Theorem 15.2.1 holds for each of them.

Classification: I call it an error, meaning a false claim that the rule determines Θ_𝔪, with no effect on the results. It could also reasonably be recorded as a gap in the definition. I checked the rendered pages 21 and 107 and HAL v3 p. 90. §5.1.3 gives Q_ℓ(X) = 1 − T_{ℓ,2}X + ℓ(T_{ℓ,1}+(ℓ²+1)T_{ℓ,0})X² − ℓ³T_{ℓ,2}T_{ℓ,0}X³ + ℓ⁶T_{ℓ,0}²X⁴, and H_ℓ = Z[T_{ℓ,0}^{±1}, T_{ℓ,1}, T_{ℓ,2}]. Write det(1 − Xρ̄(Frob_ℓ)) = 1 − a1X + a2X² − a3X³ + a4X⁴. For g in GSp4, a3 = ν·a1 and a4 = ν². Comparing coefficients gives Θ(T2) = a1, ℓΘ(T1) + ℓ(ℓ²+1)Θ(T0) = a2, ℓ³a1Θ(T0) = a3 and ℓ⁶Θ(T0)² = a4.

If a1 ≠ 0, the rule fixes Θ(T0) = ℓ^{-3}ν and then Θ(T1). If a1 = 0, only Θ(T0)² is fixed. The substitution T0 ↦ −T0, T1 ↦ T1 + 2(ℓ²+1)T0 then leaves Θ(Q_ℓ) unchanged, which I checked numerically. So for p odd there are two distinct characters at that ℓ, because Θ(T0) is a unit. Example: p = 3, ℓ = 5, eigenvalues (1,1,−1,−1) with ν = −1. The solutions (T0,T1,T2) mod 3 are (1,0,0) and (2,1,0).

This is not a rare edge case. When ν(c) = −1, as for the Galois representations of Siegel forms, ρ̄(complex conjugation) has eigenvalues ±1,±1 and trace 0. By Chebotarev, infinitely many ℓ ∤ Np then have tr ρ̄(Frob_ℓ) = 0. So for p odd, "thus defined by the rule" is false, and "the associated maximal ideal" is not well defined. For p = 2 the two choices coincide.

Defence tried: Lemma 5.1.5.1 does supply the natural choice T_{ℓ,0} ↦ ℓ^{-3}αδ, but §15.2 never states it and calls the rule alone a definition. The problem is harmless for the results, which is why affects is "nothing". Theorem 1.2 in the introduction (p. 3) starts from a maximal ideal m with an associated absolutely irreducible ρ̄. That direction is unambiguous. The proof of Theorem 15.2.1 uses m only through "Θ_{π_f} is congruent to Θ_m", which appears in Corollary 15.2.3.1, the boundary argument on p. 109 (ρ_f ⊕ ρ_f is not congruent to ρ̄), Proposition 15.2.4.1 (the irreducibility of ρ̄ excludes Yoshida and Saito–Kurokawa packets) and §15.2.5. Each of these needs only that the Q_ℓ-values match det(1 − Xρ̄(Frob_ℓ)), via Brauer–Nesbitt and Chebotarev. So the theorem and its proof hold for every m satisfying the rule. I class this as an error rather than a gap because the assertion is false, not merely unproved. This correction is right and is consistent with Lemma 5.1.5.1.

issues.printed: The source gives 𝔤 = 𝔨 ⊕ 𝔭 as the Cartan decomposition of the complex Lie algebra of GSp4 and identifies 𝔨 with the complex Lie algebra of M_Si. It regards V_{(−λ1+1,2;c)} as a representation of 𝔨 and K∞. For a (𝔤, K∞)-module W it introduces cohomology H^•(𝔭, K∞; W), citing [30], sect. 4.1.1; Theorem 15.2.2.1 uses H^i(𝔭, K∞; π(λ)^h ⊗ V_{(−λ1+1,2;−c)}).
issues.correction: The cohomology meant is H^•(𝔓, K∞; W), the (𝔓, K)-cohomology of Harris [30] and of Blasius–Harris–Ramakrishnan [4]. Here 𝔓 ⊃ 𝔨 is the parabolic subalgebra 𝔨 ⊕ 𝔭^± of the Hodge decomposition. In this paper's notation this is presumably 𝔭_h = 𝔤^{(0,0)} ⊕ 𝔤^{(1,−1)} of Remark 5.2.1.1, which is conjugate to 𝔭_Si. It should not be denoted by the Cartan complement 𝔭 just introduced, and Theorem 15.2.2.1 should be read with the same change.
issues.reason: Checked on the page images. The Cartan complement 𝔭 in 𝔤 = 𝔨 ⊕ 𝔭 is not a Lie subalgebra ([𝔭,𝔭] ⊂ 𝔨) and does not contain 𝔨 = Lie(K∞). So relative Lie algebra cohomology H^•(𝔭, K∞; W) is undefined with this 𝔭. Reading it as the complex Hom_{K∞}(∧^•𝔭, W) would give (𝔤, K∞)-cohomology, which cannot be meant. The coefficient V_{(−λ1+1,2;−c)} is only a P_Si-module, viewed as a 𝔨-module, not a 𝔤-module. The statements of Theorem 15.2.2.1 (H^0 for π(λ)^h, H^1 for π(λ)^g) are those of [4] Thm 3.2.1 for coherent (𝔓, K)-cohomology. The citation of [30] §4.1.1 and the parabolic 𝔭_h of Remark 5.2.1.1 make the intended object clear, so this is a notation clash (𝔭 used for two things), not a mathematical error. Whether 𝔓 is 𝔨 ⊕ 𝔭^+ or 𝔨 ⊕ 𝔭^− depends on the holomorphy convention, which I could not check against [30] (not accessible); hence the ± in the correction.

issues.reason:
I checked this on the page images, not the text layer. At 300 dpi, p. 108 of the author version shows the H^0 display with the subscript 𝔪 ("…(−D))_𝔪 = ⊕…") and the H^1 display without it ("…(−D)) = ⊕…"). HAL v3, printed p. 91, has the same two displays.

As printed, the H^1 statement is false in general. Its right side depends on 𝔪, since it keeps only the π_f with Θ_{π_f} ≡ Θ_𝔪. Its left side does not depend on 𝔪. Two maximal ideals whose sets of contributing π_f are non-empty and disjoint would therefore give the same group two different values. Also, without localisation, H^1(Ω(−D)) can contain boundary classes: the image of H^0(Ω^{(k,2)} ⊗ O_D) is the kernel of the map to H^1(Ω^{(k,2)}).

The intended meaning is clear from the context:
- The sentence just before the corollary introduces "the localized cohomology groups H^i(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_𝔪".
- The parallel H^0 display carries the subscript 𝔪.
- The proof opens by saying it must show that "the natural map H^1(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_𝔪 → H^1(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)}) is injective". It does this by showing H^0(Ω^{(k,2)} ⊗ O_D)_𝔪 = 0: boundary eigenforms have reducible Galois representations, and ρ̄ is irreducible.

I redid the deduction. Localisation is exact, so the kernel of H^1(Ω(−D))_𝔪 → H^1(Ω)_𝔪 is a quotient of H^0(Ω ⊗ O_D)_𝔪 = 0. So H^1(Ω(−D))_𝔪 ≅ (interior H^1)_𝔪. By Theorem 15.2.3.1, taking 𝔪-parts of the Hecke-module decomposition keeps exactly the π_f with Θ_{π_f} ≡ Θ_𝔪. This proves the localised statement.

The only later use is §15.2.5 (p. 109), the proof of Theorem 15.2.1, and it applies the corollary to the localised groups f H^i(X_Kli(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_𝔪 ⊗ Q̄_p. The misprint does not reach any later result.

On 'affects': PROTOCOL.md §18 defines "nothing" as "the mathematics is right as intended". That is the case here, so it affects nothing, not a stated result. Only the printed H^1 formula of the corollary is wrong, and the intended statement is what is proved and used.

I could not compare the published Duke version (paywalled, revised 15 Oct 2019).

issues.reason: Checked on the page image at 250 dpi. Two of the three sub-claims hold. (1) The displayed three-term sequence is only exact in the middle. It is not a short exact sequence: that would need H^0(Ω) → H^0(Ω⊗𝒪_D) to be injective and the map onto H^1(Ω(−D)) to be surjective, i.e. H^1(Ω(−D)) → H^1(Ω) to be zero. The argument needs the next term. The kernel of H^1(Ω(−D)) → H^1(Ω) is the image of H^0(Ω⊗𝒪_D), so the vanishing of H^0(Ω⊗𝒪_D)_𝔪, proved next, gives the injectivity. The intended long exact sequence is clear. (2) The third term is printed S^{tor}_K with no Σ, while the other two terms have S^{tor}_{K,Σ}. S^{tor}_K is not defined, so the Σ was dropped. (3) Not a mistake: the unlocalised target is fine. H^1(Ω(−D))_𝔪 is a Hecke direct factor of H^1(Ω(−D)), and the map is Hecke-equivariant. So the kernel of H^1(Ω(−D))_𝔪 → H^1(Ω) is (ker)_𝔪 = image of H^0(Ω⊗𝒪_D)_𝔪, and injectivity into H^1(Ω) is equivalent to injectivity into H^1(Ω)_𝔪. The group is a genuine misprint, but the correction should not insist on the localised target. The proof goes through as intended.

issues.reason:
I checked the page image at 110 and 300 dpi. It prints "λ_1 ≥ R" with no minus sign, so the text layer is right. The author version flipped the sign convention. §15.2.1 (p. 107) says "The case of interest to us is λ_2 = 0 and 0 > λ_1". §15.2.2 fixes "λ = (λ_1, λ_2; c) with λ_2 = 0, 0 > λ_1" and uses the character (−λ_1+1, 2; −c). §15.2.3 (p. 108) sets "k = −λ_1 − 1". Theorem 15.2.3.1 then assumes "For every integer k ≥ R − 1 (see thm. 15.2.2.1, 2.)", and Corollary 15.2.3.1 assumes "For k ≥ R − 1".

Redoing the computation: k ≥ R − 1 ⇔ −λ_1 − 1 ≥ R − 1 ⇔ −λ_1 ≥ R. As printed, with λ_1 < 0, "λ_1 ≥ R" picks out the bounded band R ≤ λ_1 < 0 of small weights. If R > 0 it is empty. The theorem needs the reverse: sufficiently regular weights, |λ_1| large. As printed it does not give "k ≥ R − 1", so the cross-reference fails. Within the paper's own conventions the printed text is a sign misprint.

HAL v3 (p. 90, PDF p. 91) has the same words "if λ_1 ≥ R". There it is consistent, because v3 has "λ_2 = 0 and λ_1 > 0", "V_{(λ_1+1,2;c)}" and "k = λ_1 − 1", so k ≥ R − 1 ⇔ λ_1 ≥ R. The author version changed the signs everywhere except this line. The same section has other sign leftovers, which are separate issues. Proposition 15.2.4.1 (p. 109) still says "with λ_1 > 0". Page 107 prints "V_{(λ_1+1,2;−c)}" and "V_{(−λ_1+1,2;c)}" next to "(−λ_1+1,2;−c)". The inequality "−λ_1 ≥ λ_2 > −λ_1" in §15.2.1 is self-contradictory. I could not check the published Duke text.

Effect: none downstream. Theorem 15.2.2.1 is quoted from [4] (Blasius–Harris–Ramakrishnan). Its only users are Theorem 15.2.3.1 and Corollary 15.2.3.1. Both state their hypothesis correctly as k ≥ R − 1, and the proof of Theorem 15.2.1 (§15.2.5) only specializes "at a very large weight k". The intended meaning is clear from the cross-reference.

issues.printed: The proof assumes automorphy of π_f ⊗ π(λ)^h, saying the argument also works for π_f ⊗ π(λ)^g. It asserts that the associated global A-packet Π is generic in the classification of [1], p. 78, hence stable and tempered, and identifies its infinite component as the L-packet {π(λ)^g, π(λ)^h} using [4], prop. 5.3.7.
issues.correction: "We claim that ψ is of general type ([1], p. 78, case (a): stable, semisimple). Hence S_ψ = 1 and ψ is trivial on Arthur's SL(2,ℂ), so the local packet Π∞ = Π_{ψ∞} is the L-packet of the archimedean L-parameter. Since it contains the limit of discrete series π(λ)^h, this parameter is tempered and Π∞ = {π(λ)^g, π(λ)^h} ([4], prop. 5.3.7)." Temperedness of the whole global packet should not be claimed.
issues.reason: I checked Arthur [1], Clay library copy, pp. 77–78. The six families on p. 78 are headed "(a) Stable, semisimple (general type)", with S_ψ = 1. Remark 2 on p. 77 says explicitly: "if ψ belongs to Ψ_{ss,2}(G, χ), the generalized Ramanujan conjecture (applied to the groups GL(2) and GL(4)) implies that the representations in the packet Π_ψ are tempered". So Arthur says semisimple (general type) parameters give tempered packets only conditionally on the generalized Ramanujan conjecture. For these non-regular weights (π∞ a limit of discrete series) Ramanujan was not known, so the assertion "Π is ... tempered" is unproved. It is not needed. The next step ("Π∞ is an L-packet") follows from ψ being semisimple (trivial on SL2), which general type gives. The archimedean parameter is tempered because the packet contains π(λ)^h. Multiplicity one follows from S_ψ = 1. The paper also writes "generic type" where Arthur says "general type", a naming slip. The conclusion of the proposition is unaffected, given Arthur's classification as announced, on which the paper explicitly relies.

issues.printed: The source computes π_⋆Ω^{(k,2)}|_D = ω^{k+2}(−cusp) for k ≠ 0 and ω^2 for k = 0, with ω^{k+2} the weight k + 2 modular-form sheaf. It then identifies H^0(S^{tor}_{K,Σ}, Ω^{(k,2)} ⊗ 𝒪_D) ≃ H^0(S_K^{(1),⋆}, ω^{k+2}(−cusp)), or ≃ H^0(S_K^{(1),⋆}, ω^2) if k = 2, and states T_{ℓ,2} = 2T_ℓ there by [22], IV, satz 4.4.
issues.reason:
I checked the rendered p. 109 at 250 dpi, so this is not a text-layer artefact. The page does print "(resp. ≃ H^0(S_K^{(1),⋆}, ω^2) if k = 2)". The sentence just before it sets out two cases: π_⋆Ω^{(k,2)}|_D = ω^{k+2}(−cusp) if k ≠ 0, and ω^2 when k = 0. The "resp." clause must therefore cover the second case, k = 0. That is the only value where ω^{k+2} = ω^2, and the only case with no (−cusp) twist. With k = 2 the paper's own formula gives ω^4(−cusp), not ω^2.

I also checked that the preceding sentence, not the "resp." clause, is the correct one, using the paper's convention. By p. 1402 of the text layer (the definition Ω^{(k,r)} = Sym^k ω_G ⊗ det^r ω_G), Ω^{(k,2)} = Sym^k ω ⊗ det^2 ω, which is classical weight (k+2, 2). Near a 1-dimensional cusp ω_G restricts to ω_E ⊕ (torus part). The Siegel Φ-operator keeps the top component, giving ω_E^{k+2}. For a vector-valued weight (k > 0), Φ(f) is cuspidal, which explains the (−cusp) twist. For k = 0 (weight (2,2)) the result is ω^2 with no twist. This matches the preceding sentence. There is no reading of the paper's conventions under which "k = 2" is right, so it is a misprint for k = 0.

Effect: the corollary assumes k ≥ R − 1 with R a large constant, and its only use (§15.2.5, proof of Theorem 15.2.1) specialises "at a very large weight k". So the k = 0 case never arises there. The argument (T_{ℓ,2} = 2T_ℓ, giving a reducible ρ_f ⊕ ρ_f that is not congruent to ρ̄) is also the same in both cases. Nothing downstream depends on the parenthetical.

HAL v3 has the same text: PDF p. 92 (printed p. 91) reads "(resp. ≃ H^0(S_K^{(1),⋆}, ω^2) if k = 2)", with the reference cited as [20] instead of [22].

issues.reason:
I checked this on the rendered page (p. 109, 110 and 250 dpi crops). The page prints "with λ_1 > 0", so this is not a text-layer artefact. In the author version the sign convention of §15.2 is flipped relative to HAL v3. §15.2.1 (p. 107) says: "The case of interest to us is λ_2 = 0 and 0 > λ_1. We now make these hypothesis." π(λ)^h and π(λ)^g are defined only under this hypothesis. §15.2.2 repeats "For λ = (λ_1, λ_2; c) with λ_2 = 0, 0 > λ_1", and uses V_{(−λ_1+1,2;−c)}. §15.2.3 (p. 108) sets "k = −λ_1 − 1". §5.1.6 of the author version also uses "0 ≥ λ_2 > λ_1" for holomorphic (limits of) discrete series. So "λ_1 > 0" contradicts the standing hypothesis under which the objects in the proposition are defined. §15.2.5 then applies the proposition (together with Cor. 15.2.3.1) at a very large weight k = −λ_1 − 1, so there λ_1 = −k − 1 < 0 and the printed hypothesis fails. With "λ_1 < 0" everything matches.

HAL v3 prints the same words ("Let λ = (λ_1, 0; c) ∈ X(T) + (2, 1; 0) with λ_1 > 0.", p. 91). There they are consistent, because HAL v3's §15.2.1 says "The case of interest to us is λ_2 = 0 and λ_1 > 0" and §15.2.3 sets "k = λ_1 − 1". So the phrase is a leftover from the old convention.

The proof of the proposition never uses the sign of λ_1. It uses Arthur's classification, the L-packet {π(λ)^g, π(λ)^h} from [4] prop. 5.3.7, and the reducibility of Galois representations in the Yoshida and Saito–Kurokawa cases. So the intended mathematics is unaffected.

There are related leftovers from the same convention change, not part of this finding: Theorem 15.2.2.1(2) on p. 108 still reads "if λ_1 ≥ R", which should be −λ_1 ≥ R to match k = −λ_1 − 1 ≥ R − 1. On p. 107, §15.2.2 writes V_{(λ_1+1,2;−c)} and V_{(−λ_1+1,2;c)} next to V_{(−λ_1+1,2;−c)}. The inequality in §15.2.1, "−λ_1 ≥ λ_2 > −λ_1", is itself garbled.

issues.printed: The proof of theorem 15.2.1 proposes specialization at a very large k. It invokes theorem 11.3.1 for fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), 𝔉^κ ⊗ ω²(−D))_𝔪 ⊗_{Λ,k} Q_p = fRΓ(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_𝔪 and asserts that only degrees 0 and 1 have cohomology.
issues.correction: Then fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), 𝔉^κ⊗ω^2(−D))_𝔪 ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Q_p ≅ fRΓ(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_𝔪 ⊗_{Z_p} Q_p by theorems 11.3.1(3) and 14.8.1, i.e. Theorem 1.1(1) localised at 𝔪 using the Hecke-equivariance in Theorem 1.1(3). This corrected chain is right and minimal: 11.3.1(3) tensored with Q_p gives ≅ fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_𝔪 ⊗ Q_p, and 14.8.1 then passes to X_{Kli}(p). A side remark: Corollary 15.2.3.1 is stated in §15.2's setting K_p = GSp_4(Z_p), but the next display applies it at level K^pKli(p). This is harmless: Theorem 15.2.3.1 ([30]) and the corollary's boundary argument, which uses only T_ℓ for ℓ ∤ Np and the modular-curve boundary strata, do not depend on the level at p.
issues.reason:
I rendered pp. 71, 73, 100, 107–109 and checked each image against the text layer.

(1) Theorem 11.3.1 (p. 71) covers only two things:
- point 3: the p-rank ≥ 1 formal scheme 𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p). For all k ≥ 0 it gives fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ≃ fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), 𝔉^κ⊗ω²(−D)) ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Z_p.
- point 4: the spherical-level eH^i(𝔛, ·). For k ≥ C this map is bijective only for i = 0 and injective for i = 1.
Neither point mentions the classical Klingen-level scheme X_{Kli}(p).

(2) The comparison with X_{Kli}(p) is Theorem 14.8.1 (p. 100): fRΓ(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗^L_{Z_p} Q_p → fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗^L_{Z_p} Q_p is an isomorphism for all k ≥ 0. The author says this himself on p. 73, right after proving Theorem 11.3.1: "In order to complete the proof of theorem 1.1 of the introduction, we still have to obtain a control theorem for characteristic 0 classes of weight k ≥ 0. This will be obtained at the end of the next part of this work in theorem 14.8.1." So Theorem 11.3.1 alone cannot justify the equality in §15.2.5.

(3) The right-hand side is missing ⊗Q_p. X_{Kli}(p) lives over Z_p (the intro has X_K → Spec Z_p, and Theorem 14.8.1 needs ⊗_{Z_p} Q_p). As printed, a Q_p-complex is set equal to a Z_p-complex. The next display does add "⊗ \bar Q_p".

(4) The equality is true once ⊗Q_p is added: combine 11.3.1(3), localised at 𝔪 and tensored with Q_p, with Theorem 14.8.1. This is exactly Theorem 1.1(1). So the mathematics holds and the proof of Theorem 15.2.1 goes through; only the citation and notation slipped.

(5) Comparing with HAL v3 shows how this happened. There the right-hand side was eRΓ(X_K, ·)_m, and even that version was not fully covered by 11.3.1(4), which is only injective for i = 1. The author moved the comparison to Klingen level but kept the old reference.

This is a misprint, not an error: a wrong or incomplete cross-reference plus a missing ⊗Q_p. The statement itself is correct, and the right justification is stated in the paper and flagged by the author on p. 73.

Side remark: Corollary 15.2.3.1 is stated for S_K at spherical level, but here it is used at level K^pKli(p). The underlying result [30] holds at any level, so this is harmless. Checked on rendered page images: author p. 109, p. 71 (Thm 11.3.1), p. 100 (Thm 14.8.1), and HAL v3 PDF p. 93.
(1) The citation is incomplete. Theorem 11.3.1 is only about the formal scheme 𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p) (the p-rank ≥ 1 locus). Point 3 gives fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ≅ fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), 𝔉^κ⊗ω^2(−D)) ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Z_p. Point 4 concerns eH^i(𝔛, ·) at spherical level, is surjective only for i = 0, and does not concern X_{Kli}(p) at all. The author himself says, just after the proof of 11.3.1 (p. 73): "In order to complete the proof of theorem 1.1 ... we still have to obtain a control theorem for characteristic 0 classes of weight k ≥ 0. This will be obtained ... in theorem 14.8.1." Theorem 14.8.1 (p. 100) is exactly fRΓ(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗^L_{Z_p} Q_p ≅ fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D)) ⊗^L_{Z_p} Q_p. So 11.3.1 alone does not give the printed equality, and the missing input is 14.8.1.
(2) The right-hand side is missing ⊗Q_p. Here X_{Kli}(p) (roman) is the toroidal compactification over Spec Z_p (§6.1, §7.1: "normal and lci over Spec Z_p"), the same object as in Theorem 14.8.1. So the right-hand side is a Z_p-complex, which may have p-torsion, while the left-hand side is a Q_p-complex.
Defence tried: no reading makes 11.3.1 by itself cover the classical Klingen-level cohomology, so the printed justification is inadequate. However, the intended statement is clear: it is Theorem 1.1(1) localised at 𝔪, which the paper proves. The missing ⊗Q_p is repaired by the very next display, which tensors both H^0 and H^1 with Q̄_p. So this is a slip in the cross-reference and in the notation, not a false step. It is a misprint (a wrong name/reference with clear intended meaning), not an error; "gap" would be the most one could argue for.
Consequences: the passage is used only in this proof of Theorem 15.2.1. issues.printed: The proof specializes at very large k and states fRΓ(𝔛^{≥1}_{Kli}(p), 𝔉^κ ⊗ ω^2(−D))_m ⊗_{Λ,k} Q_p = fRΓ(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_m citing theorem 11.3.1, with cohomology only in degrees 0 and 1. Invoking corollary 15.2.3.1 and “proposition prop 15.2.4.1”, it asserts fH^0(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_m ⊗ Q̄_p = ⊕_{π_f} f(π_f^{K^p Kli(p)}) = fH^1(X_{Kli}(p), Ω^{(k,2)}(−D))_m ⊗ Q̄_p.
issues.correction:
Minimal fix: replace "specialize at a very large weight k" with "specialize at every sufficiently large weight k". It is enough to take one such k in each residue class mod p−1, which is one point on each of the p−1 connected components of Spec Λ, Λ = Z_p[[Z_p^×]] ≅ ∏_{p−1} Z_p[[T]], for p odd. For p = 2 the ring Λ is local and one k is enough. The rest of the argument applies unchanged to every such k. The proof should then conclude: χ(M_m) restricted to the component of k equals Σ(−1)^i dim H^i(M_m ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Q̄_p) = dim fH^0 − dim fH^1 = 0, so χ(M_m) = 0.

An alternative fix needs more work. One shows that M_m is supported on the single component singled out by ρ̄. The central operator T_{ℓ,0} ∈ H_{Np} acts through the group element of ℓ in Λ times a tame character, and the tame character cannot absorb ω^{i−j}, which is ramified at p. One then takes k in that class. The printed text does neither of these.
issues.reason:
Defence attempted. Λ = Z_p[[Z_p^×]] (§1 and §9.3; §13.4 again: "Λ = Z_p[[Z_p^×]] is the one-dimensional Iwasawa algebra"). The paper fixes an arbitrary prime p (§6.1). For p odd, Z_p[μ_{p−1}] ≅ Z_p^{p−1}, so Λ ≅ ∏_{p−1} Z_p[[T]] and Spec Λ has p−1 connected components. The Euler characteristic of a perfect Λ-complex is a locally constant rank function, i.e. an element of K_0(Λ) = Z^{p−1}. The paper itself treats Euler characteristics this way in the proof of Lemma 14.8.4: "are locally constant functions of k ∈ Z_{≥0} by theorem 11.3.1". The map k: Λ → Z_p sends ζ ∈ μ_{p−1} to ζ^k, so it lands on the component e_{ω^k}. One specialisation M_m ⊗^L_{Λ,k} Q_p therefore gives χ(M_m) on the component of k mod p−1 only.

The charitable reading "any large k" is not what the text says. The defence that M_m sits on one component does hold, but only through an unstated Hecke/Galois argument. T_{ℓ,0} acts on 𝔉^κ through κ(ℓ), so Θ_m fixes the character ψ̄·ω^{±i}, and ψ̄ is unramified at p. Even then, the single weight k has to be chosen in the right class, and the printed proof never says so. For p = 2, Z_2[C_2] is local, so Spec Λ is connected and the printed argument is complete. The flaw is therefore real only for odd p.

The fix is right and minimal. Theorem 11.3.1(3) holds for all k ≥ 0, Theorem 15.2.3.1 and Corollary 15.2.3.1 for all k ≥ R−1, and Proposition 15.2.4.1 for all admissible λ. None of these depends on k mod p−1, so the displayed equality dim fH^0 = dim fH^1 holds for every large k. In a class that does not support M_m, both sides are 0. The missing last line "hence χ = 0" is an immediate consequence of the display and is not a separate gap.

Consequences: Theorem 15.2.1 (= Theorem 1.2) is the last result of the paper, and nothing later uses it. The stated result stays true, and only the written proof is incomplete for odd p.

issues.locator: Lemma 3.12, p. 1267 (statement; proof ends p. 1268). The lemma takes its range of t from the opening of Lemma 3.11, p. 1266: "let t ∈ F_v as a point in T_0(F_v)". Its only use is in the proof of Lemma 4.3, p. 1273.
issues.printed: Lemma 3.12 takes a place λ′ of Q(ζ_N) over an odd prime l′ ≠ l not dividing N, under the preceding assumptions. Viewing V_{λ′,t} as a G_{F_v}-representation, it asserts that the N in WD(V_{λ′,t}) = (r_1, N) is maximally nilpotent.
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis v(t) < 0. The corrected statement: let v be a place of F above l, and let t ∈ F_v with v(t) < 0 (so t lies in T_0(F_v) and is v-adically close to ∞). Then the monodromy operator of WD(V_{λ′,t}|G_{F_v}) is maximally nilpotent. This is the hypothesis v_K(a) < 0 of Harris–Shepherd-Barron–Taylor, Lemma 1.15, whose argument the proof cites. It also holds wherever the lemma is used: Lemma 4.3 (p. 1273) assumes v(t) < 0 at every l-adic place. With this hypothesis the cited argument works. The restriction of V_{λ′} to the punctured formal neighbourhood of t = ∞ over W(F̄_l) is lisse, because l ∤ N. So inertia at v acts through its tame Z_{l′}-quotient by exp(v(t)·t_{l′}·N_∞), where N_∞ is the logarithm of the monodromy at ∞. That monodromy is maximally unipotent by Corollary 3.5: the loop around t = ∞ is the N-th power of the loop around t′ = ∞, and it is still a single Jordan block. A nonzero multiple of a maximally nilpotent operator in characteristic 0 is again maximally nilpotent, so the corrected statement follows.
issues.reason: As printed, the lemma covers every t ∈ T_0(F_v), because the only standing condition on t is the one from Lemma 3.11 (p. 1266). The statement is false for t = 0, and more generally for any t ∈ O_{F_v} with t^N − 1 a unit. For such t the hypersurface X_1^N + … + X_N^N = N t X_1⋯X_N has good reduction at v. At a singular point of the reduction the partial derivatives give X_i^N = t X_1⋯X_N for every i, because N is invertible (l ∤ N). Taking the product over i gives (1 − t^N)(X_1⋯X_N)^N = 0, which forces every X_i = 0. The paper uses this same good reduction in Lemma 3.11(2). Since l′ ≠ l, smooth proper base change makes H^{N−2}_et(Y_t ×F̄_v, Z[ζ_N]_{λ′}) unramified at v. Because ζ_N ∈ F, the H_0-action is defined over O_{F_v}, so the χ-eigenspace V_{λ′,t} is also unramified. Hence WD(V_{λ′,t}) has N = 0. But V_{λ′,t} has rank n ≥ 2 (Proposition 3.2, p. 1257), so by Definition 3.6 N = 0 is not maximally nilpotent: its minimal polynomial is X, not X^n. For t = 0 this is completely explicit: V_{λ′,0} is a sum of n characters on which Frobenius acts by Jacobi sums (proof of Lemma 3.9, p. 1262), all unramified at v. A direct check on small Dwork hypersurfaces (N = 3 over F_7 and F_13, N = 5 over F_11) gives singular reduction exactly when t^N ≡ 1. The proof only covers v(t) < 0. It appeals to the monodromy around ∞ and to Harris–Shepherd-Barron–Taylor Lemma 1.15(2), whose statement assumes v_K(a) < 0. Remark 3.13 (p. 1268) also reads the lemma as a statement about v(t) < 0. The recorded correction is right and sufficient. The main theorems are unaffected, because the only application, Lemma 4.3 (p. 1273), has v(t) < 0 at every l-adic place, and there l′ ≡ 1 mod N and l′ > 2ln + 5 (Proposition 4.1, p. 1269). This is an error, not a misprint: a stated lemma is false as printed, not merely mistyped. The intended hypothesis can still be recovered from the context.

issues.locator: Theorem 1.4, p. 1241, and its proof in the final paragraph of §4 (after Remark 4.4), p. 1274. The cited result is ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2(4): Ann. of Math. 197 (2023), p. 1030, and arXiv:1812.09999v1, p. 109. The v1 numbering (Definition 6.2.28) is the one Qian cites.
issues.printed: Theorem 1.4 assumes that l is odd. Its proof claims that the corresponding hypotheses on r̄ imply every required condition apart from decomposed genericity.
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis l > n to Theorem 1.4. This is the second sentence of condition (4) of ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2; the fourth hypothesis of Theorem 1.4 copies only the first sentence. With l > n added, the proof on p. 1274 works as written. For odd primes l < n with l ∤ n, the paper does not prove Theorem 1.4 (the case l | n is already excluded by the enormity hypothesis). Proving it there would need an ordinary automorphy lifting theorem for such l. Neither ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2 nor its later adequate-image version (Miagkov–Thorne, arXiv:2203.04520v2, Theorem 1.3) provides one: both require p > n.
issues.reason:
**How the proof goes.** On p. 1274, Theorem 1.1 is used to make r̄|G_{F'} ι-ordinarily automorphic, and then ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2 is applied at p = l to ρ = r|G_{F'}. The paper says that conditions (3) and (4) of that theorem, apart from decomposed genericity, "follow from the corresponding conditions of r̄".

**The missing condition.** Condition (4) of ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2 reads: "There exists σ ∈ G_F − G_F(ζ_p) such that ρ̄(σ) is a scalar. We have p > n." This is the published text on p. 1030, and it is the same in arXiv v1, p. 109. The fourth hypothesis of Theorem 1.4 reproduces the first sentence and drops the second. Nothing in the hypotheses of Theorem 1.4 implies l > n:
- The enormity hypothesis excludes only l | n. ACC+ notes after Definition 6.2.29 that ad⁰ contains the scalars when p | n.
- Enormity puts no lower bound on l in terms of n. For l ∤ n, large subgroups such as SL_n(F_{l^r}) with r large are enormous.
- The other hypotheses (ordinarity, decomposed genericity, the scalar element) do not involve n.

**The bound is needed in ACC+.** The bound p > n is not a removable formality. It is used in the proof of Theorem 6.1.2 in §6.6: at the Ihara-avoidance places, n pairwise distinct characters trivial modulo the uniformiser are chosen, and §6.2.15 on level-raising deformations assumes p > n.

**What is affected.** For odd primes l < n with l ∤ n, Theorem 1.4 is asserted without proof. The first such case is n = 4, l = 3. No counterexample is known, and the statement may well be true there. So this is a gap in the range of a stated result, not a false statement.

**What is not affected.** With l > n added, the published argument proves the theorem. Theorem 1.1 is also unaffected: there ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2 is applied at the auxiliary prime l′, which Proposition 4.1 (p. 1269) chooses with l′ > 2ln + 5 > n.

**Defence considered.** The introduction (p. 1241) says Theorem 1.4 is obtained by combining Theorem 1.1 with ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2. One could read that as importing the cited theorem's hypotheses implicitly. This reading does not hold up: Theorem 1.4 lists its hypotheses explicitly, copying conditions (1)–(4) of the cited theorem except for this one sentence, and the proof asserts outright that those conditions follow.

**Version history and later use.** arXiv v1 has the same omission, and there Theorem 1.4 says only "Let l be a prime number". The journal version added "odd" but not l > n. One later paper applies Theorem 1.4 as printed under the sole restriction p ∤ 2n (A'Campo, Rigidity of automorphic Galois representations over CM fields, arXiv:2202.14022v4, Corollary 1.0.5), so it inherits the gap for odd p < n.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.3, final paragraph, first line of p. 1250 (the sentence begins "For the second condition, we" at the foot of p. 1249).
issues.printed: The source says the required check is N ∤ l^{r/2} − 1 = l^{2^{t_0−1} ∏_{i=1}^{m} p_i^{t_i}} − 1 when t_0 > 0.
issues.correction: need to verify that N ∤ l^{r/2} + 1 = l^{2^{t_0−1} ∏_{i=1}^{m} p_i^{t_i}} + 1. Both minus signs should be plus signs.
issues.reason: The second condition of Lemma 2.3 (p. 1248) says: when r is even, N ∤ l^{r/2} + 1. The final paragraph of the proof checks this condition. It sets out to prove it ("For the second condition, we need to verify that ..."), and both cases end with the plus sign. If m > 0, then M_1 divides l^{r/2} − 1 and M_1 is an odd divisor of N greater than 1, so "N ∤ l^{r/2} + 1". If m = 0, then N = M_0 = AB and r = 2^{t_0}, and by construction "M_0 = N ∤ l^{2^{t_0−1}} + 1". The target is printed with −1 in both places, and that is not the statement the proof needs. It is true, but it follows at once from the minimality of r, since r/2 < r. So the sign is a misprint. The intended statement is clear from the lemma, from the opening words of the sentence and from the two conclusions that follow, and the argument itself proves the plus-sign version. Neither the lemma nor the proof is affected. A minor point: the caveat "(if t_0 > 0)" is always satisfied, because the construction takes t_0 > 2, so r = 2^{t_0} ∏ p_i^{t_i} is always even. This sentence is not in arXiv v1. There, the proof of this condition simply reads "M_1 | l^{2^{t−1}∏ p_i^{t_i}} − 1 yields a contradiction with N | l^{r/2} + 1" (arXiv v1, p. 9). So the misprint entered when this paragraph was rewritten for publication.

issues.locator: Section 4, proof of Theorems 1.1 and 1.4, the paragraph after Proposition 4.1 beginning "On the side of characteristic l", p. 1270 (arXiv v1, p. 22, same wording, where Lemma 3.9 is numbered 3.8). It restates the third bullet of the choice of N at the start of Section 4, p. 1268.
issues.printed: The source includes the assumptions F_{l^2} ⊂ k(λ) and n | #(k(λ)^×).
issues.correction: Write n = l^a m with l ∤ m, as the paper does at the start of Section 4 (p. 1268). The sentence should read: "We also assumed that F_{l^2} ⊂ k(λ) and m | #(k(λ)^×)". Equivalently, k(λ) contains all n-th roots of unity in characteristic l, because μ_n(F̄_l) = μ_m. Nothing else changes: the x ↦ x^{l^a} map is a bijection on k(λ)^×, so (k(λ)^×)^n = (k(λ)^×)^m.
issues.reason: The group k(λ)^× is cyclic of order l^r − 1, which is prime to l. So the printed condition n | #(k(λ)^×) can hold only when l ∤ n. Take n = l = 3: then 3^r − 1 ≡ 2 mod 3 for every r. Theorem 1.1 allows l | n; it has no enormity hypothesis. (In Theorem 1.4 enormity forces l ∤ n, because when l | n the scalars have trace zero, so ad^0 has nonzero invariants.) So as printed, the sentence is false in some cases the theorem covers. It is also not what was assumed. The third bullet on p. 1268 requires F_{l^2}F' ⊂ F_l(ζ_N) = k(λ), where F' is generated by all m-th roots ("hence n-th roots") of elements of F_{l^s}. This gives the two facts the paragraph needs. (i) μ_m ⊂ k(λ). This is exactly the hypothesis of Lemma 2.1 that the finite field contains all n-th roots of unity. The proof of Lemma 2.1 on pp. 1244–1245 writes n = l^a m and uses the exact sequence with kernel Z/mZ, so it needs only this. (ii) Every element of F_{l^s} has an m-th root in k(λ), hence an n-th root in k(λ), since l^a-th powers are a bijection. So det r̄ takes values in (k(λ)^×)^n. The deduction from Lemma 3.9 uses only F_{l^2} ⊂ k(λ). Nowhere else is n | #(k(λ)^×) used; Lemma 3.7 and Proposition 3.8 involve only the order of l mod N. A small case confirms the corrected reading. For n = l = 3 we have m = 1, and the bullet asks for F_9F_{3^s} ⊂ F_3(ζ_N). Cubing is then an automorphism of k(λ)^×, and every k(λ)^×-valued character has a unique cube root. For n = 6, l = 3 the corrected condition 2 | 3^r − 1 always holds, while the printed 6 | 3^r − 1 never does. The intended meaning is clear from the paper's own set-up, and the argument is correct as intended. So this is a misprint (n for its prime-to-l part m) that affects nothing. It is not an error that affects the proof, as the original record said.

issues.locator: §4, proof of Theorems 1.1 and 1.4, paragraph beginning "On the other side of characteristic l′" (checking the hypothesis of Lemma 2.1 at λ′), p. 1270; uses Lemma 3.9 and formulas (3.1)–(3.3), pp. 1262–1264
issues.printed: The source states det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′} = (χ_cyc)^{n(n−1)/2} with image in F^×_{l^2}. Applying Lemma 3.9 at l′, it concludes that (det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′})^∨ ⊗ (det V[λ′]), regarded as a G_{F(ζ_N)}-representation, has image in (k(λ′)^×)^n.
issues.correction: Prove the step from the Frobenius computation inside the proof of Lemma 3.9, not from the statement of the lemma. Let v be a place of F(ζ_N) not dividing Nll′, and let q = #k(v). By (3.1), det V[λ′](Frob_v) = (q^{(N−3)/2} ∏_j g(v,b_j))^n · q^{−n(n−1)/2}. For geometric Frobenius on H^1, det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′}(Frob_v) = q^{n(n−1)/2}. So (det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′})^∨ ⊗ det V[λ′] sends Frob_v to (q^{(N−2n−1)/2} ∏_j g(v,b_j))^n. The exponent (N−2n−1)/2 is an integer because N is odd. By (3.2)–(3.3), ∏_j g(v,b_j) lies in Q(ζ_N) (in Q(ζ_N)^+ when n = 2) and is a unit at λ′, so the base reduces into k(λ′)^× = F_{l′}^×. By Chebotarev, the character takes values in (k(λ′)^×)^n. With the paper's own sign for det Symm^{n−1}, the value is instead (q^{(N−3)/2} ∏_j g(v,b_j))^n, which is also an n-th power. The clause "which have image in F^×_{l^2}" should refer to l′, not l: the character takes values in F_{l′}^×, and for even n those values are in general n-th powers only in F_{l′^2}^×.
issues.reason: Lemma 3.9 at λ′ gives only det V[λ′](G_F) ⊂ (F_{l′^2}^× k(λ′)^×)^n. Here k(λ′) = F_{l′} because l′ ≡ 1 mod N. On the l side the paper imposed F_{l^2} ⊂ k(λ), but no such condition is available at λ′. Knowing that an element of F_{l′}^× is an n-th power in F_{l′^2}^× does not make it an n-th power in F_{l′}^×. For example, every element of F_{l′}^× is a square in F_{l′^2}. The two determinants also cannot be treated one at a time. Take n even with n | l′−1, as Lemma 2.1 needs. The character χ̄_cyc is onto F_{l′}^× on G_{F(ζ_N)}, because F(ζ_N) is unramified at l′. So there are places v with q a non-square mod l′. At such a v, det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′}(Frob_v) = q^{±n(n−1)/2} is not an n-th power in F_{l′}^×, and so det V[λ′](Frob_v) is not one either. Only their quotient is an n-th power, because the half-integral powers of q cancel as in (3.1). The paper never states this cancellation. When n is odd, the proof of Lemma 3.9 already gives n-th powers in k(λ′)^×, so the gap concerns even n only. The conclusion is true and the stated theorems are unaffected. In every case (3.1) holds and ∏_j g(v,b_j) reduces into F_{l′}. Neither det V[λ′](Frob_v) nor q^{n(n−1)/2} is an n-th power in F_{l′}^×, while their quotient is one and equals (q^{(N−2n−1)/2} ∏_j g(v,b_j))^n. issues.locator: §4, proof of Theorems 1.1 and 1.4: Lemma 2.1 is applied at the auxiliary prime λ′ in the paragraph beginning "Now, apply Lemma 2.1" and the paragraph beginning "On the other side of characteristic l′", p. 1270. The hypothesis of Lemma 2.1 is on p. 1244, and the choice of l′ is in Proposition 4.1, p. 1269.
issues.printed: The source asserts that the condition required by Lemma 2.1 is checked in the subsequent argument.
issues.correction:
Add the condition l′ ≡ 1 mod n to Proposition 4.1, so that l′ ≡ 1 mod Nn (N and n are coprime). These primes have Dirichlet density 1/φ(Nn) > 0. The other conditions on l′ exclude only a finite set or a set of density 0, and the fourth condition still follows from the second and third. The later uses of l′ impose no congruence condition that could conflict: the Section 3 hypotheses, Proposition 3.8, and the first paragraph of the proof of ACC+ Corollary 7.2.4. With this condition, k(λ′) = F_{l′} contains μ_n and Lemma 2.1 applies as stated.

Alternatively, the gap closes without any new condition on l′. Put d = gcd(n, l′−1). Then (F_{l′}^×)^n = (F_{l′}^×)^d, and F_{l′} contains μ_d, so Lemma 2.1 with exponent d gives ψ_0 with ψ_0^d = χ. Build an n-th root ψ of χ one primary component of the cyclic group F_{l′}^× at a time:
- if v_p(n) ≤ v_p(l′−1), then n/d is prime to p, and the p-part of ψ is the p-part of ψ_0 raised to an inverse of n/d modulo p^{v_p(l′−1)};
- if v_p(n) > v_p(l′−1), then the p-part of χ is trivial, and so is the p-part of ψ.
Equivalently, the proof of Lemma 2.1 goes through with Z/mZ replaced by μ_n(F_{l^r}), which is cyclic of order gcd(m, l^r−1).
issues.reason:
Lemma 2.1 (p. 1244) assumes that the finite field F_{l^r} contains all n-th roots of unity. Its proof uses this to identify the kernel of x ↦ x^n on F_{l^r}^× with Z/mZ, where n = l^a m.

In §4 (p. 1270) the lemma is used to produce two characters: χ_1 valued in k(λ)^× and χ_2 valued in k(λ′)^×. For λ the paper states that n | #(k(λ)^×); this comes from the choice of N, up to replacing n by m. For λ′ nothing corresponding is said, and the paragraph on λ′ checks only that the determinant quotient takes values in (k(λ′)^×)^n.

Since l′ ≡ 1 mod N, the prime l′ splits completely in Q(ζ_N), and also in Q(ζ_N)^+ when n = 2, so k(λ′) = F_{l′}. Since l′ > 2ln + 5 > n, F_{l′} contains μ_n exactly when n | l′−1. Proposition 4.1 (p. 1269) imposes only l′ ≡ 1 mod N. Because gcd(N, n) = 1, this says nothing about l′ modulo n. So the hypothesis of Lemma 2.1 is not verified, and it can fail whenever n ≥ 3; for n = 2 it holds automatically.

Small cases:
- n = 3, N = 401 (odd, prime to 3l for l ≠ 401, and greater than 100n + 100). The least prime l′ ≡ 1 mod 401 is 3209, which is 2 mod 3, so F_3209 has no primitive cube root of unity.
- n = 4, N = 503. The least prime l′ ≡ 1 mod 503 is 3019, which is 3 mod 4, so μ_4(F_3019) = {±1}.
In both cases Lemma 2.1 does not apply as stated, but the required root still exists. Cubing is bijective on F_3209^×. In the second case the fourth powers equal the squares, a group of odd order on which the fourth-power map is bijective.

In general the conclusion of Lemma 2.1 holds for every finite field. Both repairs above are valid, and either is sufficient for this point. So this is a missing verification in the proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.4, which share this construction; neither theorem is affected. A separate question is whether the determinant quotient at λ′ really lands in (k(λ′)^×)^n. That is not addressed by this repair and is recorded separately.

issues.printed: The source asserts that V_{λ,t} is de Rham as a G_F-representation. It derives (2) from good reduction of Y_t over the residue field of F and, for (3), uses t ∈ 𝔪_F to assert (V_{λ,0} ⊗_{τ,F} B_cris)^{Gal(F̄/F)} ≅ (V_{λ,t} ⊗_{τ,F} B_cris)^{Gal(F̄/F)}.
issues.correction: Replace F with F_v throughout. Read “a de Rham representation of G_{F_v}”, “the maximal ideal of O_{F_v}” and “t ∈ 𝔪_{F_v}”. Take the invariants in the displayed isomorphism under Gal(F̄_v/F_v). By Remark 2.5 (p. 1251), the display is D_{cris,τ}(V_{λ,0}) ≅ D_{cris,τ}(V_{λ,t}), so the tensor product is taken over the maximal unramified subfield: ⊗_{τ,F_v^0} B_cris. Reading ⊗_{τ,F_v} would fail when F_v/ℚ_l is ramified, because B_cris is not an F_v-algebra in that case.
issues.reason:
The page image matches the recorded text exactly, so this is not a text-layer artefact. On p. 1266, v is a place of the number field F above l, and the lemma takes t ∈ F_v as a point of T_0(F_v). So V_{λ,t} is the fibre of the lisse sheaf V_λ at a local point, which makes it a representation of G_{F_v}. It need not come from a representation of G_F.

The rest of the lemma is written locally. The embeddings in (1) are σ : F_v ↪ \overline{ℚ(ζ_N)_λ}, and the hypotheses of (2) and (3) are stated with O_{F_v} and 𝔪_{F_v}. Lemma 3.12, on the same page, explicitly treats V_{λ′,t} as a G_{F_v}-representation. A number field F has no maximal ideal in the sense needed for good reduction, and t ∈ 𝔪_F makes no sense for t ∈ F_v.

The slip comes from a partial change of notation. In arXiv v1 (p. 19), F denotes a finite extension of ℚ(ζ_N)_v, which is a local field. There the corresponding lemma (Lemma 3.10, p. 20) consistently writes G_F, O_F, 𝔪_F and ⊗_{σ,F} B_cris. The published version renamed this local field F_v but did not carry the change through the lemma.

The displayed module in the proof of (3) is the D_{cris,τ} of Remark 2.5. It feeds into Lemma 2.4, which is stated with ⊗_{τ,F_v^0} B_cris, so F_v^0 is the right subscript for the tensor product. The meaning is clear from the statement and the surrounding text, and nothing depends on the slip.

issues.locator: Section 4, proof of Theorem 1.1, the paragraph after Proposition 4.1 that begins "On the other side of characteristic l′", p. 1270. The same sentence appears unchanged in arXiv v1, p. 22. The representation r̄_{E,l′} is defined in the opening paragraph of Section 4, on p. 1268.
issues.printed: The source gives det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′} = (χ_cyc)^{n(n−1)/2} and says its image lies in F_{l′²}^×.
issues.correction: det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′} = χ̄_cyc^{−n(n−1)/2}, where χ̄_cyc is the mod-l′ cyclotomic character. The paper defines r̄_{E,l′} as H^1_ét(E, F_{l′}) (p. 1268). The printed formula holds instead for the l′-torsion E[l′], that is, for the Tate-module convention. In that convention r_{E,l} is the Tate module and the automorphic object is its dual, as in ACC+, Corollary 7.2.4. The rest of the argument is unchanged, because both characters take values in F_{l′}^× ⊂ F_{l′²}^×.
issues.reason: By the Weil pairing, ∧²E[l′] ≅ μ_{l′}, so det E[l′] = χ̄_cyc. H^1_ét(E_{Q̄}, F_{l′}) is the F_{l′}-dual of E[l′], so its determinant is χ̄_cyc^{−1}. The same follows from Frobenius eigenvalues. At a prime p ≠ l′ of good reduction, geometric Frobenius acts on H^1 with eigenvalues α, β, where αβ = p. The paper uses χ_cyc in the standard sense (compare the central-character identity on p. 1273), so χ_cyc sends geometric Frobenius to p^{−1}. Now take any 2-dimensional representation whose Frobenius eigenvalues are a and b. The eigenvalues on Symm^{n−1} are a^{n−1−i}b^i for 0 ≤ i ≤ n−1, whose product is (ab)^{n(n−1)/2}. Hence det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′} = χ̄_cyc^{−n(n−1)/2}. The printed identity is false in general. For n = 2 it would say det r̄_{E,l′} = χ̄_cyc, whereas the true determinant is χ̄_cyc^{−1}. These differ by χ̄_cyc², which is nontrivial on G_{F(ζ_N)}: there l′ > 5 and l′ is unramified in F(ζ_N), so χ̄_cyc maps G_{F(ζ_N)} onto F_{l′}^×. The slip is harmless, and its intended meaning is clear. The next sentence uses only that this determinant is a power of the mod-l′ cyclotomic character, so that its values lie in F_{l′}^× ⊂ F_{l′²}^×, and that holds for either sign. Moreover, the two candidates differ by χ̄_cyc^{n(n−1)} = (χ̄_cyc^{n−1})^n, an n-th power. So the n-th-power statement drawn from it with Lemma 3.9 does not depend on the sign. The paper's H^1 convention is itself consistent with the automorphy input in Proposition 4.1: ACC+, Corollary 7.2.4 proves automorphy of the dual of Symm^m of the Tate module, which is Symm^m H^1. The exponent n(n−1)/2 appears to have been carried over from the Tate-module convention; the introduction (p. 1244) also speaks of "the Tate module of an elliptic curve". Since the paper fixes both r̄_{E,l′} and χ_cyc explicitly, the sign is not a matter of convention within the paper.
