issues.reviewReason: The page image on p. 1257 shows a bar over the whole of W(k)[1/p]. So the paper fixes an isomorphism between ℂ and the algebraic closure of W(k)[1/p], not with W(k)[1/p] itself. Such an isomorphism exists by Steinitz's theorem. Both fields are algebraically closed of characteristic 0, and both have cardinality 2^{ℵ_0}, hence transcendence degree 2^{ℵ_0} over ℚ. This cardinality condition holds when k is finite, or more generally when |k| ≤ 2^{ℵ_0}. The paper does not name k at this point. The companion's blowup lemma (Lemma 2.1 of arXiv:2103.00106v1, pp. 4–5) only needs char k ∤ N, so a finite field of characteristic prime to N can be taken. The base change W(k)[T, U^±] → ℂ[T] needs a ring map from W(k) to ℂ. The paper's map is the composite W(k) ⊂ W(k)[1/p] ⊂ \overline{W(k)[1/p]} ≅ ℂ. This is the same device as the "fixed embedding τ : W → ℂ" in the companion preprint (arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 21). The recorded objection is that W(k)[1/p] is a finite unramified extension of ℚ_p and so is not algebraically closed. That is true, but it concerns a formula the paper does not print. arXiv v1 (p. 13) prints the same formula, with the same bar. There is no misprint here and the proof is unaffected.

issues.locator: Lemma 4.2 of L. Qian, "Ordinarity of local Galois representation arising from Dwork motives", arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 20. This preprint is reference [14] of the paper and exists only in this version. The paper does not cite Lemma 4.2. It refers only to the main theorem of [14], in Remark 3.13 (p. 1267) and Remark 4.4 (p. 1273). Lemma 3.12 (p. 1266) does not cite [14]. In arXiv v1 of the paper, Lemma 3.10(4) (v1, pp. 20–21) was proved as "the main theorem of [Qia21]". The published version dropped that part.
issues.printed: Lemma 4.2 takes a characteristic 0 local field F_v over ℚ_p and semistable r : Gal(F̄_v/F_v) → GL_n(ℚ̄_p). For every τ : F_v^0 ↪ ℚ̄_p, it assumes that N on (r ⊗_{τ,F_v^0} B_st)^{Gal(F̄_v/F_v)}, of dimension n, has smallest vanishing power N^j = 0 at j = n. It concludes that r is regular and ordinary, attributing the assertion to Lemma 2.2 (2) of [BLGHT09].
issues.correction:
Add the Hodge–Tate hypothesis of BLGHT Lemma 2.2(2), in shifted form: for every embedding τ : F_v ↪ ℚ̄_p there is an integer k_τ such that the τ-labelled Hodge–Tate weights of r are k_τ, k_τ+1, …, k_τ+n−1, each with multiplicity one. Then r is regular and ordinary.

The case k_τ = 0 is exactly BLGHT Lemma 2.2(2), with conclusion "ordinary of weight 0". The general case follows by twisting by a crystalline character with τ-labelled weight −k_τ; the twist changes neither semistability nor N. It also follows directly from the same weak-admissibility argument.

The proof of the preprint's Theorem 1.1 must then check this hypothesis for V_{λ,t^{-1}}. It holds: the theorem assumes maximally unipotent monodromy at ∞ for every conjugate σχ, and this forces the Hodge numbers of each eigenpart to be 1 in n consecutive degrees.
issues.reason:
Lemma 4.2 omits a hypothesis of the result it quotes. BLGHT Lemma 2.2(2) also assumes that for every τ the τ-labelled Hodge–Tate weights are exactly 0, 1, …, n−1, each with multiplicity one. Without that hypothesis the statement is false already for n = 2 over ℚ_p.

Counterexample. Let D have basis e1, e2 with φ(e1) = p·e1, φ(e2) = p²·e2, N(e2) = e1 and N(e1) = 0. Then Nφ(e2) = p²·e1 = pφN(e2), so Nφ = pφN. Give D the filtration Fil⁰ = D, Fil¹ = Fil² = Fil³ = ⟨e1+e2⟩, Fil⁴ = 0.
- t_H(D) = 0 + 3 = 3, and t_N(D) = v_p(p·p²) = 3.
- The only nonzero proper N-stable subspace is ker N = ⟨e1⟩. There t_H = 0 ≤ 1 = t_N.
- So D is weakly admissible. By Colmez–Fontaine it is D_st(V) for a 2-dimensional semistable V with Hodge–Tate weights {0, 3} and N ≠ 0, so N is maximally nilpotent and V is regular.
- A G_{ℚ_p}-stable line in V would give a (φ,N)-stable line in D, or a rank-one quotient, with t_H = t_N. The only candidates are ⟨e1⟩ (t_H = 0, t_N = 1) and D/⟨e1⟩ (t_H = 3, t_N = 2).
- Hence V is irreducible and not ordinary, although it satisfies every hypothesis of Lemma 4.2.

Why the weights matter. When N is maximally nilpotent, the only (φ,N)-stable flag is ker N ⊂ ker N² ⊂ …. Because N maps each graded piece isomorphically onto the previous one and Nφ = pφN, the φ-slopes of the graded pieces are s, s+1, …, s+n−1. An ordinary flag needs rank-one admissible pieces, so ordinarity forces the labelled weights to be consecutive. Conversely, if the labelled weights are k_τ, …, k_τ+n−1, then t_H(D) = t_N(D) fixes s. Weak admissibility then forces each ker N^j to carry the lowest j weights at every τ and to be admissible. This gives the ordinary flag.

How far the error reaches.
- The false stated result is Lemma 4.2 itself.
- The preprint's proof of its Theorem 1.1 (pp. 20–23) applies Lemma 4.2 without ever computing Hodge–Tate weights, so that proof has a gap. The gap can be filled. In the limiting mixed Hodge structure at ∞, N has type (−1,−1) and commutes with H_0. Take v in a suitable Deligne component I^{p,q} of the χ-eigenspace. Then v, Nv, …, N^{n−1}v span that eigenspace, so its Hodge numbers are 1 in the n consecutive degrees p, p−1, …, p−n+1. By the de Rham comparison, and because the hypothesis holds for every σχ, these are the labelled Hodge–Tate weights. So Theorem 1.1 itself survives.
- For the family chosen in the paper, the consecutive weights are proved directly in Lemma 3.10(2) and Lemma 3.11(1) (pp. 1265–1266).
- The published paper uses neither Lemma 4.2 nor the main theorem of [14]. It gets ordinarity at l for v(t) < 0 from Lemma 4.3 (p. 1272), through Varma's local-global compatibility and Steinberg local components. Remark 3.13 (p. 1267) says the full strength of the main result of [14] is not needed.
- arXiv v1 of the paper used that main theorem in Lemma 3.10(4), where the consecutive weights were available from Lemma 3.10(1).
- So no stated result of the paper is affected.

issues.printed: The source takes (Y, N) log smooth over (W[T]′, ℕ, 1 ↦ T), requiring Spec W[T]′ to be an affine open in Spec W[T] containing T = 0. Theorems 1.6 and 3.2 identify the limit with ℍ^i(dR_{Ȳ/(W,ℕ,1↦0)})[1/p]. It also asserts finite generation over W of every ℍ^j(dR_{Ȳ/(W,ℕ,1↦0)}), citing truncation and preservation of coherence by proper pushforward.
issues.correction: Add to Theorems 1.6 and 3.2 the hypothesis that Y is proper over Spec W[T]′. It is enough that the fibre Ȳ be proper over W, or, more minimally, that ℍ^i and ℍ^{i+1} of the log de Rham complex of Ȳ over (W, ℕ, 1 ↦ 0) be finitely generated W-modules. With that hypothesis the printed proof is complete. Steps (i) and (ii) hold for every log smooth Y: the short exact sequences (3.5)/(3.6) are just the long exact sequence for multiplication by p^n on a complex of p-torsion-free sheaves, so the cited proper base change is not needed there. Finite generation is used only in step (iii), where it gives lim_n ℍ^i/p^n = ℍ^i and makes the limit over multiplication by p of ℍ^{i+1}[p^n] vanish. The only application is to the family (Y, N) of Remark 2.4, a blowup of a projective scheme over Spec W[T]′, so it is proper. The companion's Theorem 1.1 and the main paper are therefore unaffected by this correction.
issues.reason:
As printed, Theorems 1.6 and 3.2 are false, so this is an error rather than a gap: the step that fails is the finite-generation claim in (iii). A small case shows this.

Take Y = A^1 over W[T] (so W[T]′ = W[T]), with the log structure pulled back from (W[T], ℕ, 1 ↦ T). Y is strict and smooth over the base, so it is log smooth. Then Ȳ is A^1_W with the chart 1 ↦ 0. For a strict morphism the log differentials are the ordinary ones, so dR_{Ȳ/(W,ℕ,1↦0)} is the complex W[x] → W[x]dx.

Its first cohomology is the direct sum over k ≥ 1 of (W/kW)·x^{k−1}dx. That module is torsion and not finitely generated, so the right-hand side ℍ^1(...)[1/p] is 0.

By step (i) of the proof, which is valid here, the level-n crystalline group is H^1 of W_n[x] → W_n[x]dx, namely the direct sum over k of (W_n/kW_n)·x^{k−1}dx, with surjective transition maps. The classes ξ_n = Σ_{j=1}^{2n} p^{⌊j/2⌋} x^{p^j−1}dx form a compatible system, because the terms with j > 2n vanish mod p^n. For every r, p^r ξ is nonzero at level n = 2r+2: there the coefficient of x^{p^{2r+2}−1}dx is p^{2r+1}, which is nonzero in W/p^{2r+2}. So ξ is not torsion, and the left-hand side (lim_n H^1)[1/p] is nonzero; in fact it is infinite-dimensional. The two sides differ for i = 1.

In general, the limit of (3.6) identifies lim_n ℍ^i(dR_{Ȳ_n}) with an extension of the Tate module of ℍ^{i+1} by the p-adic completion of ℍ^i. This agrees with ℍ^i after inverting p exactly when finiteness holds, and properness supplies finiteness.

The author clearly intended properness: the proof invokes "proper pushforward", and the companion's GAGA statements, Theorem 1.8 (p. 4) and Proposition 3.6 (p. 18), assume it explicitly. But the section states the comparison for an arbitrary log smooth (Y, N), and only "in particular" applies it to the family of Remark 2.4. The stated result therefore has to be restricted. The correction, adding properness, is right. Since the statement as printed has a counterexample, this is an error in a stated result rather than a gap in the proof. Neither version of the main paper uses the comparison outside the proper case.

From Lemma 3.10 (4) and v_l(t) < 0 for any v_l | l, it calls V_{λ,t} ⊗ χ_1^{−1} regular ordinary and r̄|_{G_{F′}} ordinarily automorphic. issues.correction:
Hypothesis (5) of ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2 needs a regular algebraic cuspidal π that is ι-ordinary at every place above the prime, in the sense of Geraghty's Definition 5.3. An automorphic lift that is only ordinary as a Galois representation is not enough. So "ordinarily automorphic" has to be defined on the automorphic side, as in the published Definition 1.3 (p. 1241), and both applications of Theorem 6.1.2 need that input.

(i) The auxiliary prime l′. Sym^{n−1} r_{E,l′}|G_{F′} is polarizable and ordinary above l′, because E has good ordinary reduction at l′. Geraghty's Lemma 5.9 then gives ι′-ordinary automorphy (published, p. 1273).

(ii) V_{λ,t}, which is not polarizable. Prove ι-ordinarity directly, as in the published Lemma 4.3.
- Write V_{λ′,t} ≅ r_{l′,ι′}(π) with ι′ compatible with ι, so that V_{λ,t} ≅ r_{l,ι}(π).
- At each v | l we have v(t) < 0, and Lemma 3.12 shows that WD(V_{λ′,t}|G_{F′_v}) is a single Jordan block.
- Varma's bound WD(r_{l′,ι′}(π)|G_{F′_v})^{F-ss} ≺ ι′^{−1}rec(π_v|det|^{(1−n)/2}) compares partial sums of block sizes, and the two sides have the same semisimplification. So rec(π_v|det|^{(1−n)/2}) is also one block, and π_v ≅ Sp_n(ψ_v|·|^{(1−n)/2}) is a twist of Steinberg.
- The labelled Hodge–Tate weights are consecutive, so the automorphic weight is parallel. Geraghty's ordinarity conditions for this Steinberg representation then scale linearly in j, and they reduce to the single condition at j = n on val_l(ι^{−1}ψ_v(ϖ_v)^n) = val_l(ι^{−1}φ_{π,v}(ϖ_v)).
- That condition is fixed by the continuous, hence unit-valued, l-adic character r_{l,ι}(φ_π) = det r_{l,ι}(π)·ε^{n(n−1)/2}, whose Hodge–Tate weights are nλ_τ.

So V_{λ,t} ⊗ χ_1^{−1} is ι-ordinarily automorphic, and hypothesis (5) holds in the proof of Theorem 1.4. The Galois-side ordinarity taken from the companion preprint (v1 Lemma 3.10(4)) is then no longer needed, and the published version drops it. The conclusions "ordinarily automorphic" in the published Theorems 1.1 and 1.4 are to be read as ι-ordinary automorphy in the sense of the revised Definition 1.3.
issues.reason:
In arXiv v1, Definition 1.3 (p. 2) calls r̄ ordinarily automorphic when it has an automorphic lift that is "potentially semistable and ordinary with regular Hodge-Tate weights" at every place above l. This is a condition on the Galois side. Under this definition the last sentence of the proof of Theorem 1.1 (p. 24) is correct: Lemma 3.10(4), from the companion preprint, gives Galois ordinarity of V_{λ,t} when v(t) < 0.

The gap is where this Galois-side notion is used in ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2. Hypothesis (5) of that theorem requires π itself to be ι-ordinary in Geraghty's Hecke-theoretic sense. This happens twice:
- On p. 24, for Sym^{n−1} r_{E,l′} ("ordinarily automorphic by our choice of l′").
- On p. 26, for V_{λ,t} ⊗ χ_1^{−1} in the proof of Theorem 1.4, where only conditions (3) and (4) are checked.

Passing from "automorphic and ordinary at l as a Galois representation" to "π is ι-ordinary" is the converse direction of ordinary local–global compatibility. Geraghty's Lemma 5.9 proves it only for polarizable representations. ACC+ Theorem 5.5.1 and Corollary 5.5.2 give only the opposite direction. The Sym^{n−1} case is polarizable, so a citation repairs it. V_{λ,t} is built from a character of H_0 chosen to break self-duality, so it is not known to be polarizable, and it needs a new argument.

The published version identifies exactly this problem in Remark 4.4 (p. 1274), crediting J. Thorne, and supplies Lemma 4.3. I checked Lemma 4.3 against Varma's Definition 1 and Theorem 1 (arXiv:1411.2520):
- A one-block Galois side forces a one-block automorphic side, because (n) is maximal for the order and the semisimplifications agree.
- For a twist of Steinberg with parallel weight, the conditions for 1 ≤ j ≤ n are proportional to j, so only j = n matters.
- The j = n condition says that the normalised central Hecke eigenvalue is an l-adic unit. That follows from r_{l,ι}(φ_π) being a continuous l-adic character.

Small case: n = 2, F′_v = Q_l, λ_τ = 0, the Tate-curve shape. Here r_{l,ι}(φ_π) has Hodge–Tate weight 0, so φ_π has finite order and ψ_v(l)^2 is a unit. Hence π_v = Sp_2(ψ_v|·|^{−1/2}) has a unit U_l-eigenvalue and is ι-ordinary, consistent with the ordinarity of a Tate curve.

The gap therefore affects only proofs. The published version proves Theorems 1.1 and 1.4 in the stronger, automorphic-side sense. Its new restriction to odd l comes from §2 and is unrelated to this point. The phrase "ordinarily automorphic" on its own does not show where the gap is, so the quotation above cites the sentences that invoke Theorem 6.1.2.

A separate bookkeeping remark on Lemma 4.3 (p. 1273), outside this finding: the paper's normalisations are the geometric Artin map and Hodge–Tate weight −1 for the cyclotomic character, as in the proof of Lemma 3.11. With these, a unit-valued l-adic character with labelled Hodge–Tate weights k_τ satisfies val_l(ι^{−1}φ_v(ϖ_v)) = val_l(∏_τ τ(ϖ_v)^{k_τ}). For example, with n = 1, φ = ‖·‖^{−M} and r = ε^{−M}, both sides equal f_v·M. So the exponent −nλ_τ printed there should carry the sign that matches Geraghty's normalisation of the target. Since the same exponent is printed on both sides, the conclusion is unaffected.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.1, second step (Poitou–Tate duality), p. 1246
issues.printed: The source specifies a pairing ⟨·, ·⟩ : Ш²(F_2, ℤ/mℤ) × Ш¹(F_2, μ_m) → ℚ/ℤ. For any finite F_1/F_2, x ∈ Ш¹(F_1, μ_m) and y ∈ Ш²(F_2, ℤ/mℤ), it asserts the compatibility ⟨x, Res(y)⟩ = ⟨Cor(x), y⟩.
issues.correction: Write the compatibility in the order in which the pairing is defined: ⟨Res(y), x⟩_{F_1} = ⟨y, Cor(x)⟩_{F_2} for x ∈ Ш¹(F_1, μ_m) and y ∈ Ш²(F_2, ℤ/mℤ), where the left side is the analogous Poitou–Tate pairing over F_1. Alternatively, define the pairing on Ш¹ × Ш² from the start.
issues.reason: The pairing is declared on Ш²(F_2, ℤ/mℤ) × Ш¹(F_2, μ_m), with the Ш² argument first, but both brackets of the compatibility put the Ш¹ element first: x ∈ Ш¹(F_1, μ_m) before Res(y) ∈ Ш²(F_1, ℤ/mℤ), and Cor(x) ∈ Ш¹(F_2, μ_m) before y. Since the two groups are different, the transposed bracket has only one meaning, and transposing introduces no sign; with the order fixed the identity is the standard adjunction between restriction and corestriction. The next step is sound: if Cor(x) = 0 for all x ∈ Ш¹(F_1, μ_m), then Res(y) pairs to zero with all of Ш¹(F_1, μ_m), so Res(y) = 0 by perfectness over F_1. arXiv:2104.09761v1 has the same wording.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.1, second step (construction of L₁), p. 1248
issues.printed: The source applies [5], Lemma 4.1.2, to F₀F₂(μ_{2^r})/ℚ, choosing S to consist of p and ∞.
issues.correction: Apply [5, Lemma 4.1.2] to the normal closure over ℚ of F₀F₂(μ_{2^r}), with the same S = {p, ∞} and the same local conditions (E_p/ℚ_p at p, ℝ/ℝ at ∞). This gives a totally real Galois extension L₁/ℚ that is linearly disjoint over ℚ from that normal closure, and hence from each of its subfields. In particular L₁ is linearly disjoint over ℚ from F₂(μ_{2^r}) and from F₀F₂. Only these two disjointness properties are used afterwards. The first shows that F₁ = F₂L₁ and F₂(μ_{2^r}) are linearly disjoint over F₂. The second shows that L₁L₂ and F₀F₂ are linearly disjoint over L₂, so L₁L₂ ∩ F₀ = ℚ. The rest of the proof is unchanged.
issues.reason:
Clozel–Harris–Taylor, Lemma 4.1.2 (Publ. Math. IHÉS 108, p. 116), assumes that the field D to be avoided is a finite Galois extension of the base, and its proof on p. 117 uses this. For each Galois subextension D_i of D with simple Galois group, it chooses a prime v_i that does not split completely in D_i. The soluble extension E it builds is split at every v_i. Since D and E are both Galois, E ∩ D is Galois with soluble group, so if it were nontrivial it would contain some D_i, which is impossible.

In the first step of the proof of Lemma 2.1 (p. 1245) the lemma is applied to F₀, which is Galois over ℚ, so that step is fine. In the second step (p. 1248) it is applied to F₀F₂(μ_{2^r}), where F₂ = ML₂. Here F₀ and L₂ are Galois over ℚ, but M is an arbitrary CM field: the statement of Lemma 2.1 on p. 1244 does not assume that M is Galois over ℚ, and arXiv:2104.09761v1 only assumes that M is Galois over a CM field F. So F₀F₂(μ_{2^r}) need not be Galois over ℚ. For example, take M = K(i) with K a non-Galois totally real cubic field and F₀ = ℚ. Then F₀F₂(μ_{2^r}) = K·L₂(i, μ_{2^r}) is Galois over ℚ only if it contains the Galois closure of K, and nothing in the construction of L₂ ensures this. So the printed application does not meet the hypothesis of the cited lemma.

Trying to defend the paper: in its only application (p. 1270), Lemma 2.1 is used with M = F(ζ_N) and F₀ = F^avoid F₂^avoid F^suff(ζ_N). This F₀ is Galois over ℚ and contains F(ζ_N), because F^avoid is the normal closure of a field containing F. So there F₀F₂(μ_{2^r}) = F₀L₂(μ_{2^r}) is Galois and the citation is literally valid. The defence therefore saves every use of the lemma in the paper, but not the proof of Lemma 2.1 in the generality stated.

The gap closes at once by passing to the normal closure, because linear disjointness from a field implies linear disjointness from each of its subfields. The later deductions only need the special case of the paper's own second bullet on linear disjointness, applied with D = L₁. So Lemma 2.1 and everything built on it stand, and the kind "gap" and the reach "nothing" are both correctly stated. The wording is identical in arXiv:2104.09761v1, which is the only arXiv version. The published paper is the final version, and no erratum is known.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.6(2), p. 1251: the two "without loss of generality" reductions (F replaced by F̃, then F by Ẽ and F_1 by E_1 = ẼF_1), and the last sentence of the page
issues.printed: The source says that H ∩ F̃′_s = F permits application of [1], Lemma 7.1.6 (3).
issues.correction:
Apply [1, Lemma 7.1.6(3)] with m = n − 1 to the original pair (F, F_1) of Lemma 2.6, not to the reduced pair (Ẽ, E_1). The original pair satisfies both standing hypotheses of that lemma, because they are hypotheses of Lemma 2.6: r̄(G_F̃) ⊃ SL_2(F_l), and F_1/F is linearly disjoint from F̄^{ker r̄} over F. Also l > 2n + 5 > 2(n − 1) + 3. For n = 1 there is nothing to prove: Symm^0 r̄ is trivial, and any prime p ≠ l that splits completely in F_1 is decomposed generic for it.

The extra hypothesis of part (3) comes from the case being treated. In the reduced setting, H = Ẽ·F̄^{ker ad r̄} is Galois over Ẽ with group ad r̄(G_Ẽ). The normal closure F̃′_s of E_1 over ℚ is also Galois over Ẽ, and H ∩ F̃′_s = Ẽ. So restriction identifies Gal(HF̃′_s/F̃′_s) with Gal(H/Ẽ). That is, ad r̄(G_{F̃′_s}) = ad r̄(G_Ẽ) ⊃ PSL_2(F_l). Since F̃′_s is Galois over ℚ and contains F_1, it contains the normal closure F̃_1 of F_1. Hence ad r̄(G_{F̃_1}) ⊃ PSL_2(F_l), and [1, Lemma 7.1.6(3)] shows that Symm^{n−1} r̄|G_{F_1} is decomposed generic.

Alternatively, keep the reduced pair and note that the proof of [1, Lemma 7.1.6(3)] uses only ad r̄, the hypothesis of (3) and l > 2m + 1. It never uses linear disjointness from F̄^{ker r̄}. The other standing hypothesis, r̄(G_Ẽ) ⊃ SL_2(F_l), does hold for the reduced pair. After the first reduction F is Galois over ℚ, so r̄(G_Ẽ) is normal in r̄(G_F) ⊃ SL_2(F_l) with abelian quotient. Since SL_2(F_l) is perfect for l ≥ 5, it follows that SL_2(F_l) ⊂ r̄(G_Ẽ).
issues.reason:
[1, Lemma 7.1.6] (Ann. of Math. 197 (2023), p. 1090) has two standing hypotheses on a pair (F, F′). First, r̄(G_F̃) ⊃ SL_2(F_l). Second, F′/F is linearly disjoint over F from F̄^{ker r̄}, the field cut out by r̄ itself. Part (3) adds the hypothesis ad r̄(G_{F̃′}) ⊃ PSL_2(F_l).

The proof of Lemma 2.6(2) makes two reductions "without loss of generality". First it replaces F by F̃ and F_1 by F̃F_1. Then it replaces F by Ẽ and F_1 by E_1 = ẼF_1. It checks only that E_1 is linearly disjoint over Ẽ from H′, and H′ depends only on ad r̄. The quoted sentence then applies [1, Lemma 7.1.6(3)] to the renamed pair (Ẽ, E_1), since F̃′_s is the normal closure of E_1. For that pair, the disjointness of E_1 from Ẽ·F̄^{ker r̄} over Ẽ is neither checked nor true in general.

Example:
- Let F = F_0(ζ_l), where F_0 is a quartic field whose normal closure has Galois group A_4 and is linearly disjoint from ℚ(ζ_l). Then K := F̃ is cyclic cubic over F.
- Let r̄_0 be the restriction to G_F of the mod l representation of an elliptic curve over ℚ with surjective mod l image. Then det r̄_0 = 1 and r̄_0(G_F̃) = SL_2(F_l).
- Let χ : G_F → μ_3 be a cubic character, with fixed field L, that is ramified at a prime of F above a rational prime unramified in H′. This is possible because H′ depends only on ad r̄_0, and such a χ exists by the Grunwald–Wang theorem.
- Put r̄ = r̄_0 ⊗ χ.

Since SL_2(F_l) has no quotient of order 3, Goursat's lemma gives r̄(G_F̃) ⊃ SL_2(F_l). Since det r̄_0 = 1, we get ker r̄ = ker r̄_0 ∩ ker χ, so Gal(F̄^{ker r̄}/F) ≅ SL_2(F_l) × μ_3. Hence L is the only cubic abelian subextension of F̄^{ker r̄}/F. Also L ⊄ H′ ⊇ Ẽ, by ramification.

Let F_1 be one of the two cubic subfields of KL other than K and L. Then F_1/F is Galois. It meets neither F̄^{ker r̄} nor H′; for H′, note that otherwise KF_1 = KL ⊂ H′. So every hypothesis of Lemma 2.6(2) holds. Yet E_1 ⊇ KF_1 = KL ⊇ L, so E_1 ∩ Ẽ·F̄^{ker r̄} ⊇ ẼL ≠ Ẽ. The same failure already occurs after the first reduction.

So the lemma is cited outside its stated hypotheses, in the case that carries all of part (2); the other case ends in a contradiction on p. 1252. The conclusion survives. The original pair satisfies every hypothesis of [1, Lemma 7.1.6], and the extra hypothesis of part (3) follows from H ∩ F̃′_s = Ẽ. Moreover, the proof of part (3) in [1] never uses disjointness from F̄^{ker r̄}.

Lemma 2.6(2) is therefore true as stated. But the printed proof needs this short argument, and the paper does not contain it. This is a gap in the proof, not a false result. The argument in arXiv v1 is the same, citing [1, Lemma 7.1.5(3)] in the older numbering, which has the same standing hypotheses.

issues.locator: Proposition 3.2, proof, first sentence, p. 1257
issues.printed: The source infers local freeness from smoothness and properness of the family.
issues.correction:
Smoothness and properness give only that the sheaves are locally constant. For V_λ and V[𝔫] this comes from smooth proper base change, and for V_B and V′_B from Ehresmann's theorem. Because the bases are connected, every stalk is then isomorphic to the stalk at one complex point, using the comparison with V_B stated just before the proposition. Local freeness needs three further facts.
(i) The integral cohomology of a smooth hypersurface Y_t ⊂ ℙ^{N−1} is torsion-free, by the Lefschetz hyperplane theorem and Poincaré duality. So H^{N−2}(Y_t, ℤ[ζ_N]) = H^{N−2}(Y_t, ℤ) ⊗ ℤ[ζ_N] is free. By the universal coefficient theorem, H^{N−2}(Y_t, ℤ[ζ_N]_λ) and H^{N−2}(Y_t, ℤ[ζ_N]/𝔫) are obtained from H^{N−2}(Y_t, ℤ) by tensoring, and they are also free.
(ii) For V_λ and V[𝔫], #H_0 = N^{N−2} is invertible in ℤ[ζ_N]_λ and in ℤ[ζ_N]/𝔫. So the χ-eigenpart is the image of an idempotent. It is a direct summand of a free module over a local ring, or over a finite product of local rings, and is therefore free.
(iii) For V_B and V′_B, N is not inverted. The χ-eigenpart is then a finitely generated submodule of a free module over the Dedekind ring ℤ[ζ_N], hence projective, that is, locally free in the sense of commutative algebra.
In every case the rank equals the dimension over ℚ(ζ_N) of the χ-eigenspace at t = 0. By Deligne's Proposition I.7.4 this dimension is n.
This argument gives only projective stalks for V_B and V′_B, not stalks free over ℤ[ζ_N] itself. The paper uses only their completions at λ and their reductions V_{B,t}/λ and V_{B,t}/𝔫 for λ, 𝔫 prime to 2N, and these are free of rank n.
issues.reason:
The printed sentence cannot hold as stated. A smooth proper family gives locally constant higher direct images, but their stalks can have torsion: an Enriques surface has H²(X, ℤ) ≅ ℤ^10 ⊕ ℤ/2. So local freeness needs the fibres' integral cohomology to be torsion-free, and it needs the χ-eigenpart to be a direct summand or at least projective. The paper gives neither.
I tried to defend it and the defence fails. The second sentence of the proof checks only the fibre over 0 through Proposition I.7.4 of [7]. That result counts dimensions over a field of characteristic 0 and gives the rank, not freeness. The paper says it adapts the proof of Lemma 4.1 of [4], and that proof does get freeness at t = 0 over ℤ[ζ_N, 1/2N]. But it inverts 2N, so it does not cover V_B or V′_B, whose coefficient ring is ℤ[ζ_N]. Nothing else in the paper supplies torsion-freeness or a direct-summand argument. The companion preprint (arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 2) also asserts local freeness only "by standard comparison results".
The missing facts are standard, so the conclusion is correct. Everything used later concerns localizations or reductions at primes prime to 2N, where the stalks are free of rank n. So the kind is gap, and nothing downstream is affected.

issues.locator: Paragraph after Proposition 3.2 (the case n = 2), p. 1257
issues.printed: The source uses locally constant V_λ, V[𝔫], V_B with coefficients ℤ[ζ_N]^+_λ, ℤ[ζ_N]^+/𝔫, ℤ[ζ_N]^+, respectively. It identifies V_λ ⊗_{ℤ[ζ_N]^+} ℤ[ζ_N], V[𝔫] ⊗_{ℤ[ζ_N]^+} ℤ[ζ_N], V_B ⊗_{ℤ[ζ_N]^+} ℤ[ζ_N] identify respectively with the cited source’s U_λ, U[𝔫], U_B.
issues.correction: For V_B, read coefficients ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N]^+ and V_B ⊗_{ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N]^+} ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N] ≅ U_B. Nothing changes for V_λ and V[𝔫]. Here λ is a prime and 𝔫 a nonzero ideal of ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N]^+, so both are prime to 2N. Hence ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N]^+_λ = ℤ[ζ_N]^+_λ and ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N]^+/𝔫 = ℤ[ζ_N]^+/(𝔫 ∩ ℤ[ζ_N]^+).
issues.reason:
I checked this against the page image. The sentence is printed exactly as recorded and is not an artefact of the text layer. The meaning is clear: the paper means to use the sheaves of [4, §4] for n = 2.

In [4, §4] these sheaves are cut out by an idempotent e with the prefactor 1/(2#H_0), where #H_0 = N^{N−2}. So e only exists once 2N is inverted, and [4] defines V_B = [e]^* R^{N−2}π_* ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N]^+. Its perfect alternating pairing takes values in ℤ[ζ_N, 1/(2N)]^+. U_B is the χ-summand of R^{N−2}π_* ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N], and the projection isomorphism V_B ⊗_{ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N]^+} ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N] ≅ U_B is stated over these rings. So [4] gives no ℤ[ζ_N]^+-structure on V_B, and the printed ℤ[ζ_N]^+ misstates what [4] defines. By contrast, [4] defines V_λ and V[𝔫] only for primes λ and nonzero ideals 𝔫 of ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N]^+. The paper uses the same convention on p. 1256, so those two coefficient rings are correct as printed.

No argument is affected. For n = 2, V_B is used only through V_B/λ and V_B/𝔫 with λ and 𝔫 prime to 2N: in Corollary 4.7 of [4] as quoted on p. 1257, in Lemma 3.7 and in Proposition 3.8. It is also used through the unipotence of monodromy at ∞ in Lemma 3.12, which does not depend on the coefficient ring. Proposition 3.2's claim that V_B is locally free over ℤ[ζ_N] concerns the case n > 2, where V_B is defined over ℤ[ζ_N] as χ-isotypic invariants.

The wording is identical in arXiv:2104.09761v1, p. 13. The published article is the final version, and no erratum is known.

issues.locator: Lemma 3.3(2), proof, p. 1257 (argument concluded on p. 1258)
issues.printed: The source reduces the argument to proving that monodromy around 0 on R^{N−2}p_*ℂ has characteristic polynomial equal to a power of (X − 1).
issues.correction:
The reduction is invalid. It has to be replaced by an argument that finds the eigenvalues of ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) itself, not those of its N-th power. The semistable-model argument that follows is still valid, but it proves only that the monodromy of ρ_t around t = ∞ is unipotent.

To prove (2), identify V′_B ⊗ ℂ with a hypergeometric local system on ℙ^1 − {0, 1, ∞}. There are two ways to do this:
- as [4] does for its Lemma 4.3(3), by citing Katz (Another look at the Dwork family, Theorem 5.3, together with Exponential sums and differential equations, Theorem 8.4.11);
- through the Picard–Fuchs equation and Levelt's theorem, as in A'Campo (arXiv:2407.16481v1, Lemmas 2.4.5 and 2.5.4 and Proposition 2.5.7).

The second route describes only the pull-back to the t-line, so it determines V′_B only up to a twist by a character ψ of the deck group μ_N. The hypotheses of §3 make n prime to N, so no nonzero translate of {b_1, …, b_n} in ℤ/Nℤ equals the set itself. Hence the hypergeometric system is not isomorphic to any nontrivial twist of itself, its pull-back is irreducible, and the eigenvalues at 0 from part (1) force ψ = 1.

Let e_1, …, e_n be the entries of (a_1, …, a_N) that remain after one copy of each residue that occurs is removed. Then ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) is conjugate to the companion matrix of ∏_k (X − ζ_N^{±e_k}), where a single sign, the same for every k, is fixed by the conventions for characters and loops. For the exponents chosen in §3 the only repeated residue is 0, which occurs n + 1 times. So every e_k = 0, and ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) has characteristic polynomial (X − 1)^n and a single Jordan block. This also gives Corollary 3.5 directly.
issues.reason:
For T ≠ 0 the fibre of Z_0: T(X_1^N + ⋯ + X_N^N) = N X_1⋯X_N is Y_{1/T}. So Z_0 is the Dwork family Y of §3 in the coordinate T = 1/t, not the family Y′ over the t′-line, and its monodromy around T = 0 is the monodromy of ρ_t around t = ∞. The covering t ↦ t′ = t^N is totally ramified over t′ = ∞. A small loop around t = ∞ therefore maps to a conjugate of γ_∞^{±N}, and the pull-back of V′_B is V_B. The blow-up from Lemma 2.1 of [14] and the local monodromy theorem (reduced divisor, e = 1) thus prove only that ρ_{t′}(γ_∞)^N is unipotent, that is, that the eigenvalues of ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) are N-th roots of unity.

The argument never uses the exponents a_j, and for other characters of H_0 the conclusion it claims is false. Take N = 5 and (a_1, …, a_5) = (1, 2, 2, 0, 0). Then Σa_j ≡ 0, a_N = 0, {b_1, b_2} = {1, 2} and n = 2.
- The proof of (1) applies word for word and gives det ρ_{t′}(γ_0) = ζ_5^{±3} ≠ 1.
- The fibres over μ_N have only ordinary double points, and the fibre dimension N − 2 = 3 is odd. By Picard–Lefschetz, ρ_{t′}(γ_1) is unipotent.
- Since γ_0γ_1γ_∞ = 1, det ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) ≠ 1, so ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) is not unipotent, although the argument of (2) applies to this character word for word.

The same failure occurs for every odd N ≥ 5. Let (a_j) consist of each residue other than −b_1, …, −b_n once, together with n extra entries e_1, …, e_n that avoid the −b_j. Then Σb_j ≡ −Σe_k mod N and det ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) = ζ_N^{±Σe_k}. Any such choice with Σe_k ≢ 0 therefore breaks the argument; an example is b = {1, N − 3} with e = (1, 1).

No reading of the paper rescues the step. The deck-group action on the limit at t = ∞, which would supply the missing eigenvalues in the way part (1) does at t = 0, is never computed. The extra facts (1), (3) and det = 1 do not fix the eigenvalues at ∞ when n ≥ 2. Lemma 3.4 cannot help, because it takes (2) as input.

For the paper's exponents the nonzero entries are distinct and 0 occurs n + 1 times, so every e_k = 0. This is why the statement of Lemma 3.3(2) is still true although its proof fails. A'Campo's Proposition 2.5.7 agrees: on the t-line the monodromy at ∞ is a single unipotent Jordan block. For the counterexample character his parameters give eigenvalues 1 and ζ_5^{±3} at t′ = ∞.

The same step appears in arXiv:2104.09761v1, proof of Lemma 3.3(2), pp. 13–14. Part (2) is used for the eigenvalues at ∞ in Lemma 3.4, and hence in:
- Corollary 3.5;
- the l-power order of the reduction of ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) in the proof of Lemma 3.7 (p. 1259);
- det(γ_∞) = 1 on p. 1260;
- maximal unipotence at ∞ in Lemma 3.12 (p. 1268).
All of these stand once (2) is proved as in the correction. BLGHT's Lemma 4.3(3) had deferred exactly this point to Katz and wished for a direct argument. The printed direct argument does not supply one.

issues.locator: Lemma 3.3(3), statement p. 1257; proof of (3), p. 1258
issues.printed: The source attributes the proof of (3) to the argument for [4], Lemma 4.3, part 2.
issues.correction:
Keep the Picard–Lefschetz half of the cited argument. The fibre over t′ = 1 has N^{N−2} ordinary double points, and H_0 permutes them simply transitively. So on the χ-part, ρ_{t′}(γ_1) − 1 has image in the line spanned by the χ-projection of a single vanishing cycle, and rank(ρ_{t′}(γ_1) − 1) ≤ 1.

Replace the symplectic step with either of the following arguments.

(a) Determinant. By (1), (2) and γ_0γ_1γ_∞ = 1, det ρ_{t′}(γ_1) = ζ_N^{−(b_1+⋯+b_n)}. Moreover b_1+⋯+b_n ≡ a_1+⋯+a_N ≡ 0 mod N, for three reasons:
- {b_1,…,b_n} is the complement of {−a_1,…,−a_N} in ℤ/Nℤ;
- the nonzero a_j are pairwise distinct;
- the elements of ℤ/Nℤ sum to 0 when N is odd.
This agrees with the explicit list of the b_j on p. 1254. Write ρ_{t′}(γ_1) = 1 + v ⊗ f. Then det ρ_{t′}(γ_1) = 1 + f(v) = 1, so f(v) = 0 and (ρ_{t′}(γ_1) − 1)^2 = f(v)(ρ_{t′}(γ_1) − 1) = 0. Hence ρ_{t′}(γ_1) is unipotent.

(b) Odd-dimensional Picard–Lefschetz. The fibres have odd dimension N − 2, so the cup product on H^{N−2} is alternating. The vanishing cycles are therefore isotropic, and they are pairwise orthogonal because the double points are distinct. Hence (γ_1 − 1)^2 = 0 on all of H^{N−2} of the fibre, and so also on its χ-part.

Finally, [4] gives only dim ker ≥ n − 1, so the exact equality dim ker(ρ_{t′}(γ_1) − 1) = n − 1 needs one more step. If ρ_{t′}(γ_1) = 1, then ρ_{t′}(γ_0) = ρ_{t′}(γ_∞)^{−1} would be unipotent. This contradicts (1), because no b_j is 0 in ℤ/Nℤ.
issues.reason:
The proof of [4, Lemma 4.3(2)] has two steps.
- Picard–Lefschetz theory shows that ker(γ_1 − 1) has rank at least n − 1. This part carries over unchanged to the family Y′ with the character χ.
- Unipotence then follows from the sentence "As γ_1 acts as a symplectic transformation we conclude that it has characteristic polynomial (X − 1)^n". This works in [4] because the χ-part there becomes, after extending scalars, the sheaf Ṽ_B, which carries a perfect alternating pairing, and ρ̃ takes values in Sp_n. In effect the step uses det = 1.

Neither step can be replaced by a symplectic structure in the present setting. The cup product pairs the χ-part of H^{N−2} only with the χ^{−1}-part. Also χ^2 ≠ 1 on H_0: since N is odd, χ^2 = 1 would force all the a_j to be congruent mod N, but the a_j take both values 0 and 1. Symplecticity of γ_1 on the whole of H^{N−2} constrains only the pair of χ- and χ^{−1}-parts, and gives no information on det ρ_{t′}(γ_1). There is no alternative self-pairing either. Lemma 3.1 with α = −1 gives {−b_j} ≠ {b_j}, so the eigenvalues of ρ_{t′}(γ_0) are not closed under inversion. Hence the monodromy on V′_B, which is irreducible because no b_j is 0, preserves no nonzero bilinear form. Avoiding such self-duality is the stated purpose of the choice of the a_j (p. 1255). So the step the "same" proof relies on is not available.

I also looked for another reading and found none. The paper never computes det ρ_{t′}(γ_1), and it never uses the odd-dimensional form of the Picard–Lefschetz formula. Lemma 3.4 shows ρ(γ_1) = BA^{−1} with corner entry C_n, but C_n is not identified with 1. The remark det(γ_1) = 1 on p. 1260 is stated after the lemma and without proof. The needed facts are easy to supply: I checked that b_1 + ⋯ + b_n ≡ 0 mod N from the printed a_j for all n from 3 to 29 and many admissible N, and this also matches the printed list of the b_j. So the statement of Lemma 3.3(3) is correct and only its proof is incomplete.

Unipotence is really used later:
- Lemma 3.7 needs the residual image to be generated by transvections, which is the hypothesis of the classification theorem in [18].
- p. 1260 uses det(γ_1) = 1.
Lemma 3.4 and the irreducibility argument after Definition 3.6 need only rank(ρ_{t′}(γ_1) − 1) = 1.

issues.locator: Lemma 3.7, p. 1259: the first assertion (about ρ̄_{t′}) in the case n = 2, and the first sentence of the proof. The relevant definitions are Y′ and V′_B on p. 1256 and the n = 2 convention on p. 1257.
issues.printed: For even r and n > 2, the source assumes N ∤ l^{r/2} + 1. It concludes ρ̄_{t′}(π_1(T′_0(ℂ), t′)) = SL(V′_{B,t}, /λ), together with ρ̄_t(π_1(T_0(ℂ), t)) = SL(V_{B,t}/λ). Its proof credits [4], Lemma 4.6, with resolving n = 2.
issues.correction:
Restrict the first assertion, about ρ̄_{t′}, to n > 2. For n = 2 only the second assertion is needed: the image of ρ̄_t is SL(V_{B,t}/λ). This is [4, Corollary 4.7], because Sp_2 = SL_2, and the paper already cites it for this purpose on p. 1257.

Alternatively, keep the n = 2 case of the first assertion but state explicitly that for n = 2 the symbols T′_0 and V′_B denote the family Ỹ → T̃_0 of [4] and its sheaf Ṽ_B. In that family t̃^{−1} multiplies the middle term X̃_{(N+1)/2}^N, whose exponent in χ is 0. [4, Lemma 4.6] is a statement about Ṽ_B.
issues.reason:
The definition on p. 1256 holds for every n ≥ 2. It sets Y′ : X′_1^N + ⋯ + X′_{N−1}^N + t′^{−1}X′_N^N = N X′_1⋯X′_N and V′_B = (R^{N−2}π̃′_*ℤ[ζ_N])^{χ,H_0}. The n = 2 convention on p. 1257 replaces only V_λ, V[𝔫] and V_B by the sheaves of [4]. It does not replace V′_B.

The paper identifies the two families by X′_N = tX_N and t′ = t^N. Under this identification, the deck transformation t ↦ ζ_N t of T_0 − {0} → T′_0 acts on Y − Y_0 as the element ξ = (1, …, 1, ζ_N^{−1}) of H. Transport the action to the Fermat fibre over t = 0. There ρ_{t′}(γ_0) acts on the χ_i-line by ζ_N^{±(a_N+i)}, for i ∈ {b_1, …, b_n}.

For n > 2 the character on p. 1253 has a_N = 0, which gives Lemma 3.3(1). For n = 2 it has a_N = N − 1, and {b_1, b_2} = {(N−1)/2, (N+1)/2} (p. 1254). The eigenvalues of ρ_{t′}(γ_0) are then ζ_N^{±(N−3)/2} and ζ_N^{±(N−1)/2}. So det ρ_{t′}(γ_0) = ζ_N^{∓2}, which is a primitive N-th root of unity because N is odd. Since l ∤ N, it remains ≠ 1 modulo λ. Hence for n = 2 the image of ρ̄_{t′} does not lie in SL, and the first assertion is false for the sheaf the paper defines.

There is an equivalent way to see this. In [4, §4] the family Ỹ over T̃_0 = T′_0 lets t̃^{−1} multiply the middle coordinate, where χ has exponent 0. The two deck elements differ by (1, …, ζ_N, …, 1, ζ_N^{−1}) ∈ H_0, with ζ_N in position (N+1)/2. On this element χ takes the value ζ_N^{0−(N−1)} = ζ_N. So for n = 2 the paper's V′_B is the sheaf Ũ_B of [4] twisted by a character of order N that factors through the deck group. In particular V′_B ⊗ ℚ has no ℚ(ζ_N)^+-form: the eigenvalues ζ_N^{(N+1)/2} and ζ_N^{(N+3)/2} of γ_0 are not stable under complex conjugation. Yet p. 1258 takes λ to be a prime of ℤ[ζ_N]^+ when n = 2. The cited [4, Lemma 4.6] concerns Ṽ_B, not this sheaf.

The best defence is to read V′_B for n = 2 silently as Ṽ_B of [4]. The citation of [4] and the choice of λ in ℤ[ζ_N]^+ point that way, and under that reading the lemma is true. However, it is not what pp. 1256–1257 define, so the defence fails on the text as written. The defect is notational in origin, but the printed statement is false.

The damage is limited to the statement of Lemma 3.7. For n = 2 the second assertion is [4, Corollary 4.7], as p. 1257 notes. Proposition 3.8 (p. 1261) uses only that second assertion, and no later argument uses ρ̄_{t′} for n = 2.

The arXiv version has the same wording and definitions (the lemma is numbered 3.6 there).

The substitution used for (3.2) gives σ(g(v,b)) = t(c^{(q−1)/N})^{−b} g(v,−b). The prefactors cancel in the product because b_1 + b_2 ≡ 0 mod N, and {−b_1, −b_2} = {b_1, b_2}, so σ fixes g(v,b_1)g(v,b_2). More directly: for n = 2, b_1 = (N−1)/2 and b_2 = (N+1)/2 ≡ −b_1 mod N, so the identity g(v,a)g(v,−a) = q displayed on p. 1263 (N odd, a ≠ 0) gives g(v,b_1)g(v,b_2) = q ∈ ℚ. A third route treats the Gauss sums as algebraic numbers in ℚ(ζ_N, ζ_p) and uses Gal(ℚ(ζ_N, ζ_p)/ℚ(ζ_N)^+). There a σ with σ(ζ_N) = ζ_N^{−1} and σ(ζ_p) = ζ_p does exist, because ℚ(ζ_N) and ℚ(ζ_p) are linearly disjoint over ℚ (p ∤ N).
issues.reason:
The step fails under the paper's own conventions. The additive character ψ takes values in the p-th roots of unity in Q̄_l (p. 1262). The primes l and p are distinct and prime to N, so ℚ_l(ζ_N, ζ_p) is unramified over ℚ_l. Every σ ∈ G_{ℚ_l} therefore acts on it as a Frobenius power Frob_l^m (m ∈ Ẑ), sending ζ_N to ζ_N^{l^m} and ζ_p to ζ_p^{l^m}.

Let r be the order of l mod N. An element of G_{ℚ_l(ζ_N)^+} sending ζ_N to ζ_N^{−1} exists only when −1 is a power of l mod N, that is, when l^{r/2} ≡ −1 mod N; it then has m ≡ r/2 mod r. The extra condition σ(ζ_p) = ζ_p requires m ≡ 0 modulo the order s of l mod p. Both hold for some m exactly when gcd(r, s) divides r/2, i.e. when v_2(s) < v_2(r). This fails for a positive proportion of primes p.

Two concrete cases satisfy the §3 hypotheses for n = 2 (p. 1259: l an odd prime, N odd and prime to 2l, N > 300):
- N = 307, l = 613 = 2N − 1, p = 5. Here l ≡ −1 mod N forces m to be odd, while 613 ≡ 3 mod 5 has order 4, which forces 4 | m.
- N = 301, l = 3, p = 5. Here 3 has order 42 mod 301 and 3^{21} ≡ −1 mod 301, so m ≡ 21 mod 42 is odd, while 3 has order 4 mod 5.

A direct search of the relevant finite cyclic Galois groups confirms that no σ exists in either case. So (3.3) as printed is not established for the places v above such p. The second line of (3.3) uses σ(ζ_p) = ζ_p essentially, since it leaves ψ(x) unchanged.

When −1 is not a power of l mod N, ℚ_l(ζ_N)^+ = ℚ_l(ζ_N). Then no element of G_{ℚ_l(ζ_N)^+} sends ζ_N to ζ_N^{−1}, so the requested σ does not exist either, but the n = 2 claim is already (3.2).

Defences considered:
- Reading ℚ_l as ℚ throughout the passage would make every step correct (third route). But the paper uses ℚ_l(ζ_N) consistently, in (3.2) and in the statement to be shown, together with Q̄_l-valued ψ, so this is not a slip in one symbol.
- The conclusion does follow from the identity g(v,a)g(v,−a) = q printed a few lines earlier, since b_2 = −b_1. The paper never draws this conclusion, however; it rests the n = 2 case on the nonexistent σ.

Hence the step is wrong but locally repairable. The asserted membership is true, since the product equals q. A numerical check of g(v,(N−1)/2)g(v,(N+1)/2) = q for (N, q) = (11, 23), (15, 31) and (307, 1229) agrees.

Reach: Lemma 3.9 stands, and so do the main results. At both primes where §4 applies the lemma, −1 is not a power of the prime mod N: l satisfies N ∤ l^{r/2} + 1 (p. 1268), and l′ ≡ 1 mod N (Proposition 4.1). There ℚ_l(ζ_N)^+ = ℚ_l(ζ_N), so (3.2) suffices. arXiv:2104.09761v1, p. 18, has the same sentence.

issues.locator: Remark 3.13, p. 1268
issues.printed: The source attributes to the proof of [14] the assertion that v(t) < 0 makes V_{λ,t} semistable as a G_{F_v}-representation, with maximally nilpotent N in its Weil-Deligne representation.
issues.correction: Claim only what the proof in [14] gives. Take t ∈ F_v with v(t) = −d < 0 and write t^{−1} = uπ^d, where u is a unit and π is a uniformiser. Then V_{λ,t} is potentially semistable. It becomes semistable on restriction to G_{F′}, where F′ = F_v(π^{1/e}) is the totally ramified extension of [14, Theorem 1.4]. The integer e comes from a toroidal subdivision and is not controlled. The rest of the sentence holds as printed: the monodromy operator N of WD(V_{λ,t}) can be computed from D_st over F′, and it is maximally nilpotent. The argument of [14] gives semistability over F_v itself only when v(t) = −1. In that case the blow-up of [14, Lemma 2.1], base-changed along T ↦ t^{−1}, is already a semistable model of Y_t over O_{F_v}. For v(t) ≤ −2 the claim needs a separate argument. One option is a semistable model of Y_t over O_{F_v}; this means gluing compatible semistable resolutions of the local models uπ^d = Z_1⋯Z_r. Another is to combine two facts: ℓ′-adic inertia acts unipotently on the whole middle cohomology, as in the proof of Lemma 3.12, and the traces of inertia on D_pst do not depend on ℓ, by Ochiai's theorem.
issues.reason:
The remark cites the proof of the main theorem of [14]. That proof works throughout over an auxiliary ramified extension:
- Theorem 1.4 and Theorem 2.3 of [14] (arXiv:2103.00106v1, pp. 3 and 9) give a semistable model of the Dwork hypersurface only over O_{F′}, where F′ = F(π^{1/e}).
- The integer e comes from the subdivision theorem of Kempf, Knudsen, Mumford and Saint-Donat (pp. 11–12), and it is never shown to be 1.
- Only the case of valuation −1 is settled over F itself (p. 8, after Remark 2.2). The same page notes that the naive base change for d ≥ 2 has local form uπ^d = Z_1⋯Z_r, which is not semistable.
- Section 4 of [14] (p. 19) reduces at the start to proving that V_{λ,t^{−1}} is regular and ordinary as a G_{F′}-representation. The operator N is then computed on D_st over F′, using Tsuji's comparison theorem for the model over O_{F′} (pp. 20–21).
- Lemma 4.1 of [14] descends from F′ to F only the properties de Rham, regular and ordinary, never semistability.
- The main theorem of [14] is itself stated for an arbitrary finite extension F_0, and its proof replaces F_0 by F′.

Attempts to defend the text:
1. Read "semistable" as "potentially semistable". This would make the sentence correct, but the paper keeps the two notions apart: its Theorem 1.4 (p. 1241) requires r|_{G_{F_v}} to be "potentially semistable". The remark also offers its claim as the p-adic analogue of the unipotent ℓ′-adic inertia of Lemma 3.12, which points to genuine semistability. So the missing word is not a plain misprint.
2. Look for the claim elsewhere in the paper. Nothing supplies it. Remark 4.4 proves only ordinarity, via local–global compatibility, and ordinarity in the sense of [1] does not imply semistability over F_v.

The statement about N is correct. The Weil–Deligne representation of a potentially semistable representation can be computed from D_st over any extension over which it becomes semistable. F′/F_v is totally ramified, so the maximal unramified subfield is unchanged, and [14] shows N is maximally nilpotent on each embedding component. The semistability claim is plausible, but the cited proof does not establish it.

Nothing depends on the remark. It says itself that the result of [14] is not needed. The main proof uses the ℓ′-adic Lemma 3.12, through Lemma 4.3, and Remark 4.4 refers back to Remark 3.13 only for ordinarity. The remark does not appear in arXiv v1. There, Lemma 3.10(4) cited [14] only for "regular and ordinary". The published paper is the final version, and arXiv has no later version of either paper.

issues.printed: The source applies Lemma 2.1 with F = F, M = F(ζ_N), F_0 = F^avoid F_2^avoid F^suff(ζ_N). It obtains finite CM Galois E/F with E = LM, L/ℚ totally real Galois and linearly disjoint from F_0 over ℚ, and χ̄_1 : Gal(F̄/E) → (ℤ[ζ_N]/λ)^×, χ̄_2 : Gal(F̄/E) → (ℤ[ζ_N]/λ′)^× satisfying (χ̄_1 × χ̄_2)^n ≅ (det V[λλ′]) ⊗ det(r̄ × Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′})^∨ as G_E-modules.
issues.correction: Apply Lemma 2.1 twice, and enlarge the field to be avoided before the second application. First apply it to M = F(ζ_N), F_0, k(λ) and the characteristic-l component of the character. This gives a totally real Galois field L_1/ℚ with L_1 ∩ F_0 = ℚ and a character χ̄_1 of G_{L_1M}. Then apply it to the CM field L_1M, the finite Galois extension F_0L_1/ℚ, k(λ′) and the restriction to G_{L_1M} of the characteristic-l′ component. This gives L_2 with L_2 ∩ F_0L_1 = ℚ and a character χ̄_2 of G_{L_1L_2M}. Put L = L_1L_2 and E = LM, and restrict χ̄_1 to G_E. Then L ∩ F_0 = ℚ: since L_2 and F_0L_1 are linearly disjoint over ℚ, L_1L_2 and F_0L_1 are linearly disjoint over L_1 (by the second property of linear disjointness listed at the start of §2), so L_1L_2 ∩ F_0 ⊂ L_1L_2 ∩ F_0L_1 = L_1, and hence L_1L_2 ∩ F_0 = L_1 ∩ F_0 = ℚ. Because F_0 is Galois over ℚ, this gives linear disjointness. The other hypotheses of Lemma 2.1 must still hold at λ and at λ′; that is a separate question. Alternatively, state Lemma 2.1 for characters with values in a finite product of finite fields. Its proof then goes through factor by factor: the kernel of the n-th power map is a finite product of cyclic groups with trivial action. The first step can kill the finitely many nonzero local classes of all factors at once, using the least common multiple of their orders. The second step kills every locally trivial H² at once if F_1 is chosen linearly disjoint from F_2(μ_{2^R}), where 2^R is the largest 2-power order that occurs.

Lemma 2.1 (p. 1244) gives an n-th root of a single character with values in one finite field F_{l^r}. Its proof starts from the Kummer sequence 0 → ℤ/mℤ → F_{l^r}^× → (F_{l^r}^×)^m → 0 with n = l^a m and l ∤ m, which only makes sense in one characteristic. The character that needs a root here takes values in (ℤ[ζ_N]/λλ′)^× = k(λ)^× × k(λ′)^×. This is a product of two finite fields of different characteristics l and l′, so one application of the lemma as stated cannot give both χ̄_1 and χ̄_2. The arXiv version (arXiv:2104.09761v1, Lemma 2.1 and p. 22) states the lemma the same way and contains the same sentence.

The best defence is that two applications are meant: the paper checks the hypotheses separately, “on the side of characteristic l” and “on the other side of characteristic l′”. But the text does not say how the disjointness conclusion survives. Two independent applications with the same F_0 give L_1 and L_2, each meeting F_0 only in ℚ, and this does not control L_1L_2 ∩ F_0. For example, ℚ(√2) and ℚ(√3) each meet ℚ(√6) only in ℚ, but their composite contains √6. The disjointness is used later: the paper derives from L ∩ F_0 = ℚ that E and F^avoid F_2^avoid F^suff are linearly disjoint over F (pp. 1270–1271), and this feeds the conditions of Proposition 4.1 and the choice of the auxiliary field. So the second application has to avoid F_0L_1, not just F_0. This is exactly the device the paper uses to build L_1 at the end of the proof of Lemma 2.1 on p. 1248, where L_1 is chosen linearly disjoint from F_0F_2(μ_{2^r}), and the same calculation L_1L_2 ∩ F_0 = L_2 ∩ F_0 = ℚ appears there.

The other reading, that Lemma 2.1 is applied once to a character with values in a product of fields, also fails as written, because the lemma is not stated in that generality, although its proof extends. Nothing elsewhere in the paper fills the gap. The repair is routine, so the existence of E, χ̄_1 and χ̄_2, and hence Theorem 1.1, is unaffected. But the proof as written cites the lemma outside its stated scope and leaves out the step that keeps the disjointness. This point is separate from the roots-of-unity hypothesis at λ′ and from the divisibility condition n | #k(λ)^× at λ. The published version is final, arXiv has only v1, and no erratum is known.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 1.1, p. 1273: first sentence of the paragraph after the application of [1, Theorem 6.1.2]. The same identification appears in the outline on p. 1242 ("and conclude that V_{λ,t} is automorphic"), in the first sentence of the proof of Lemma 4.3 ("Write V_{λ,t} = r_{l,ι}(π)", p. 1273), and in Remark 4.4 ("V_{λ,t} ≅ r_{l,ι}(π) is ι-ordinarily automorphic", p. 1274).
issues.printed: The source concludes automorphy of V_{λ,t} as a representation of G_{F′}.
issues.correction:
Replace the sentence with the following. The semisimplification V_{λ,t}^{ss} is isomorphic to r_{l,ι}(π). Here π is the regular algebraic cuspidal representation with V_{λ′,t} ≅ r_{l′,ι′}(π), namely the output of [1, Theorem 6.1.2] twisted by the character corresponding to the Teichmüller lift of χ̄_2. The isomorphism ι′ must be chosen so that ι and ι′ induce the same embedding of ℚ(ζ_N) into ℂ through λ and λ′. If they do not, replace π by its conjugate σπ under a suitable σ ∈ Aut(ℂ); σπ is again regular algebraic and cuspidal.

Then apply the argument of Lemma 4.3 to V_{λ,t}^{ss}. That argument uses only three things: V_{λ′,t} ≅ r_{l′,ι′}(π), the Hodge–Tate weights of V_{λ,t}, and det V_{λ,t}. The representation V_{λ,t}^{ss} has the same Hodge–Tate weights and the same determinant. It follows that V_{λ,t}^{ss} ⊗ χ_1^{−1} is an ι-ordinarily automorphic lift of r̄|G_{F′}. To see that it is a lift, intersect the integral lattice with a composition series of V_{λ,t}. The graded pieces form a lattice in V_{λ,t}^{ss}, and its reduction is isomorphic to V[λ]_t ≅ χ̄_1 ⊗ r̄|G_{F′} because V[λ]_t is semisimple.

When r̄|G_{F′} is absolutely irreducible, as in Theorem 1.4, V_{λ,t} is irreducible. Then V_{λ,t}^{ss} = V_{λ,t} and the printed sentence holds as stated.
issues.reason:
Under Definition 1.3 (p. 1241), a representation is automorphic when it is isomorphic to some r_{l,ι}(π), and r_{l,ι}(π) is semisimple by construction (p. 1240). So the printed sentence claims in particular that G_{F′} acts semisimply on V_{λ,t}. Lemma 4.3 and Remark 4.4 use the sentence in exactly this form.

The only way to pass from λ′ to λ is to compare Frobenius characteristic polynomials and then apply Chebotarev and Brauer–Nesbitt. That identifies only V_{λ,t}^{ss} with r_{l,ι}(π). Semisimplicity of the Galois action on the étale cohomology of the fibre Y_t is not known.

The defences fail as follows.
(i) In Theorem 1.1, r̄ is only assumed semisimple. So V[λ]_t ≅ χ̄_1 ⊗ r̄|G_{F′} may be reducible and cannot force V_{λ,t} to be irreducible.
(ii) V_{λ′,t} is irreducible because its reduction χ̄_2 ⊗ Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′}|G_{F′} is absolutely irreducible. But irreducibility of r_{l,ι}(π) is not known for a non-polarizable π over a CM field, and irreducibility is not known to be independent of the prime.
(iii) The maximally nilpotent monodromy of V_{λ,t} at places above l (Remark 3.13) makes V_{λ,t} indecomposable, not semisimple.
(iv) No other part of the paper states or proves semisimplicity of V_{λ,t}. The arXiv v1 contains the same sentence ("And so V_{λ,t} is automorphic").

The comparison also needs two facts the paper leaves unstated.
First, at places of good reduction the characteristic polynomial of Frobenius on the χ-eigenspace has coefficients in ℚ(ζ_N) and does not depend on the coefficient prime. This follows from the Lefschetz trace formula applied to Frobenius composed with elements of H_0: H_0 acts trivially on the cohomology of Y_t outside the middle degree (weak Lefschetz and Poincaré duality), and χ is nontrivial.
Second, ι and ι′ must induce the same embedding of ℚ(ζ_N). Lemma 4.3 needs this as well, since its proof uses a single π for both primes, via r_{l′,ι′}(π).

With the correction, Theorems 1.1 and 1.4 still hold. When r̄ is reducible, the argument of Remark 4.4 gives local ordinarity only for V_{λ,t}^{ss}.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 4.3, first paragraph, p. 1273
issues.printed: The proof invokes Lemma 3.12 to give WD(V_{λ′,t}|G_{F′_v}) ≅ WD(r_{l′,ι′}(π)|G_{F′_v}) a maximally nilpotent N, concluding that it is Steinberg.
issues.correction:
Under the hypotheses of Lemma 4.3, the only comparison available is V_{λ′,t}^{ss} ≅ r_{l′,ι′}(π). Here ι′ is chosen so that ι′ (through λ′) and ι (through λ) induce the same complex embedding of ℚ(ζ_N). The comparison follows from the equality of Frobenius characteristic polynomials across the compatible system, together with Chebotarev and Brauer–Nesbitt, because r_{l′,ι′}(π) is semisimple.

Replace the sentence by the following argument, which needs no new hypothesis.
1. By Lemma 3.12 (with v(t) < 0), the Frobenius-semisimplified Weil–Deligne representation of V_{λ′,t}|G_{F′_v} is Sp_n(ψ) for a character ψ of W_{F′_v}. Its Weil-group semisimplification is therefore the segment ψ, ψ|·|, …, ψ|·|^{n−1}.
2. The semisimplified Weil–Deligne representation depends only on the semisimplification of the Galois representation. So WD(r_{l′,ι′}(π)|G_{F′_v})^{ss} is the same segment.
3. By Varma's Theorem (1ss), which applies because v ∤ l′, the same holds for ι′^{−1}rec_{F′_v}(π_v|det|_v^{(1−n)/2})^{ss}. Hence the cuspidal support of π_v|det|_v^{(1−n)/2} is a single segment of n characters.
4. Since π is cuspidal, π_v is generic. By Zelevinsky's classification, a generic irreducible representation is an irreducible product δ(Δ_1) × ⋯ × δ(Δ_k) of essentially square-integrable representations whose segments are pairwise unlinked. Splitting one segment into k ≥ 2 pieces always produces two juxtaposed pieces, which are linked. So k = 1.
5. Hence π_v ≅ Sp_n(ψ_v|·|^{(1−n)/2}) is Steinberg, without using Varma's monodromy bound.

Alternatively, at the one place where the lemma is applied, in the proof of Theorem 1.1 (pp. 1272–1273), V_{λ′,t} is irreducible. This is because ρ = V_{λ′,t} ⊗ χ̃_2^{−1} has absolutely irreducible reduction Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′}|G_{F′}. So V_{λ′,t} ≅ r_{l′,ι′}(π), and the printed isomorphism holds there.
issues.reason:
Lemma 4.3 assumes only that V_{λ,t} is automorphic. In the sense of Definition 1.3 this means V_{λ,t} ≅ r_{l,ι}(π). Comparing Frobenius polynomials across the compatible system then gives only V_{λ′,t}^{ss} ≅ r_{l′,ι′}(π).

The representation r_{l′,ι′}(π) is semisimple by construction (p. 1240; Varma, Introduction). But V_{λ′,t} is not known to be semisimple, since semisimplicity of the étale cohomology of the Dwork fibre is not known.

Maximal monodromy does not pass to the semisimplification. A nonzero proper G_{F′}-stable subspace W of V_{λ′,t} is inertia-stable, hence N-stable, so it is some ker N^k. Then N on W ⊕ V_{λ′,t}/W has two Jordan blocks. So the printed claim that WD(r_{l′,ι′}(π)|G_{F′_v}) has maximally nilpotent N is equivalent to V_{λ′,t} being irreducible. Nothing in the statement or proof of the lemma supplies this. With a smaller N on the Galois side, Varma's bound ≺ gives no information, so the printed deduction fails in the generality of the lemma.

Attempts to defend the paper:
- V_{λ,t} ≅ r_{l,ι}(π) does not imply irreducibility of r_{l,ι}(π). The non-polarizable case is exactly the setting of the paper.
- Monodromy density for the family gives irreducibility only for generic t, not for every t with v(t) < 0.
- The gap is filled only at the lemma's application in the proof of Theorem 1.1. There the residual representation of V_{λ′,t} ⊗ χ̃_2^{−1} is stated on p. 1272 to be absolutely irreducible, and Theorem 6.1.2 of ACC+ even gives V_{λ′,t} ≅ r_{ι′}(π′) directly.

The lemma remains true as stated, by the repair above. Its ingredients are:
- Lemma 3.12, which gives the Weil-group semisimplification as a single segment;
- Varma's semisimplified compatibility at v ∤ l′;
- Shalika's genericity of the local components of a cuspidal π;
- Zelevinsky's classification of generic representations, which forces the twisted Steinberg representation.

The remainder of the proof uses only V_{λ,t} ≅ r_{l,ι}(π), the Hodge–Tate weights of Lemma 3.11 and the central character, so it is unchanged. Lemma 4.3 and Theorems 1.1 and 1.4 are therefore unaffected; only the written proof needs repair.

issues.correction: WD(r_{l′,ι′}(π)|_{G_{F′_v}})^{Frob−ss} ≺ ι′^{−1} rec_{F′_v}(π_v |det|_v^{(1−n)/2}), where ι′ : Q̄_{l′} ≅ ℂ is the isomorphism for which V_{λ′,t} ≅ r_{l′,ι′}(π).
issues.reason: The left side is the l′-adic representation r_{l′,ι′}(π), just identified with V_{λ′,t} (the introduction, p. 1244, also writes V_{λ′,t} = r_{l′,ι′}(π)), but the right side is transported by the unprimed ι : Q̄_l ≅ ℂ. The cited result is Varma's Theorem 1 ([17], arXiv:1411.2520, p. 1), applied with coefficient prime l′ and isomorphism ι′ at a place v | l (so v ∤ l′); it bounds WD(r_{l′,ι′}(π)|G_{F_v})^{Frob−ss} by ι′^{−1} rec_{F_v}(π_v|det|_v^{(1−n)/2}), with the same isomorphism on both sides, and the order ≺ (Varma, Definition 1) compares Weil–Deligne representations over one common coefficient field. As printed the display compares a representation over Q̄_{l′} with one over Q̄_l and has no meaning. The next step needs only that the monodromy of rec_{F′_v}(π_v|det|_v^{(1−n)/2}) is a single Jordan block, which is unchanged by transport along a field isomorphism, so the conclusion that π_v is Steinberg, and everything after it, is unaffected.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 4.3, second paragraph, p. 1273
issues.printed: The source assigns π weight (−λ_τ)_τ, meaning λ_{τ,i} = −λ_τ for fixed τ. It reduces the proof to val_l(ι^{−1}(ψ_v(det(α^{(n)}_{ϖ_v})))) = val_l(∏_{τ:F′_v↪Q̄_l} τ(ϖ_v)^{−nλ_τ}). It gives r_{l,ι}(φ_π) Hodge-Tate weight (nλ_τ)_τ and, because its image consists of l-adic units, asserts val_l(ι^{−1}(φ_{π,v}(ϖ_v))) = val_l(∏_{τ:F′_v↪Q̄_l} τ(ϖ_v)^{−nλ_τ}).
issues.correction: In the conventions the paper uses, π has weight (λ_τ)_τ, that is, λ_{τ,i} = +λ_τ for all i. Both the identity to be shown and the identity obtained should read val_l(ι^{−1}φ_{π,v}(ϖ_v)) = val_l(∏_{τ:F′_v↪Q̄_l} τ(ϖ_v)^{nλ_τ}), where ψ_v(det α^{(n)}_{ϖ_v}) = ψ_v(ϖ_v)^n = φ_{π,v}(ϖ_v). For general j the condition is val_l(ι^{−1}ψ_v(ϖ_v)^j) = val_l(∏_τ τ(ϖ_v)^{jλ_τ}). Once both signs are corrected, dividing by n and multiplying by j works as before, the argument closes, and Lemma 4.3 holds.
issues.reason:
The page image of p. 1273 matches the quoted text. The paper uses the conventions of Allen et al. [1], Ann. of Math. 197 (2023):
- Art sends uniformizers to geometric Frobenius (p. 906), and HT_τ(ε) = {−1} (p. 907).
- For π of weight λ, HT_τ(r_ι(π)) = {λ_{τ,1}+n−1, …, λ_{τ,n}} ([1, Theorem 6.1.1(5)(b), p. 1029]).
- For the central character, HT_τ(r_ι(ω_π)) = Σ_i λ_{τ,i} and det r_ι(π) = r_ι(ω_π)ε^{n(1−n)/2} ([1, p. 987]).

The paper's Lemma 2.4 (p. 1250) and Definition 1.2 (p. 1240) use the same normalisation. The proof of Lemma 3.11 (pp. 1266–1267) uses it too: there V_{λ,0} ≅ ⊕_i Q̄_l(−M(a_τ)−i) on inertia, with weights {M, …, M+n−1}, and Lemma 3.11(3) gives the ordinary weight λ_{τ,i} = M(a_τ). So consecutive weights {λ_τ, …, λ_τ+n−1} mean λ_{τ,i} = +λ_τ.

The proof itself uses this convention. It computes the weight of r_{l,ι}(φ_π) = det r_{l,ι}(π)·χ_cyc^{n(n−1)/2} as nλ_τ, which requires HT(χ_cyc) = −1; with the opposite sign it would get nλ_τ + n(n−1). By [1, p. 987], weight nλ_τ also forces Σ_i λ_{τ,i} = nλ_τ, not −nλ_τ.

The last step has the wrong sign. Let φ be an algebraic Hecke character and let h_τ be the τ-weight of r_{l,ι}(φ). On F′_v^×, r_{l,ι}(φ)∘Art_v = ι^{−1}φ_v·∏_τ τ(·)^{a_τ}. Near 1 the character φ_v is trivial and ε∘Art_v(u) = N(u), which gives a_τ = −h_τ. The left side takes unit values, so evaluating at ϖ_v gives val_l(ι^{−1}φ_v(ϖ_v)) = val_l(∏_τ τ(ϖ_v)^{+h_τ}). As a check, take φ = ||·||: then r_{l,ι}(φ) = ε, and val_l(q_v^{−1}) = −f_v = val_l(∏_τ τ(ϖ_v)^{−1}), whereas the printed rule gives +f_v.

The target identity has the same wrong sign. Suppose Geraghty labels weights dually, so that "(−λ_τ)" is literally correct in his notation. The target still cannot be right. At j = n the normalised operator is central, so its condition holds either for every π of these Hodge–Tate weights or for none, and ι-ordinary ones exist. Also, [1, Corollary 5.5.2, p. 1028] and Matsumoto (arXiv:2312.01551v3, Lemma 4.34(2), pp. 46–47, from Geraghty's proofs of Lemmas 5.4 and 5.7) apply Geraghty's Definition 5.3 to π of weight λ in the sense of [1] without any change. Matsumoto's criterion requires val_l(ι^{−1}χ_i(ϖ_v)) = e_v^{−1}Σ_τ(λ_{τ,n+1−i}+i−1+(1−n)/2). The constituents of Sp_n(ψ_v|·|^{(1−n)/2}) are ψ_v|·|^s for s = (1−n)/2, …, (n−1)/2, and for parallel weight the criterion reduces to val_l(ι^{−1}ψ_v(ϖ_v)) = val_l(∏_τ τ(ϖ_v)^{λ_τ}).

Both printed identities are false whenever Σ_{τ|v} λ_τ ≠ 0, which happens here: for n = 2, λ_τ = M(a_τ) = (N−3)/2 > 0. The two sign errors cancel, so Lemma 4.3 is unaffected. The passage does not appear in arXiv v1.

issues.locator: Remark 4.4, p. 1274
issues.printed: The source invokes “Theorem 5.5.1 or [1]” to conclude that V_{λ,t}, as a G_{F′_v}-representation, is ordinary at every l-adic place v of F. It also says that deducing ι-ordinary automorphy of V_{λ,t} from automorphy and ordinarity of its l′-adic realization appears invalid.
issues.correction: Read “Theorem 5.5.1 of [1]” (whose form for a single ι-ordinary automorphic representation is [1, Corollary 5.5.2]), “for any l-adic place v of F′”, and “ordinary as l-adic representation”, meaning ordinary at the l-adic places of F′.
issues.reason: There are three slips. First, the paper has no Theorem 5.5.1; in [1] Theorem 5.5.1 is the local–global compatibility theorem for ordinary parts, so “or” should be “of”. Second, the remark restricts V_{λ,t} to G_{F′_v}, so v must be a place of F′; the paper states the same assertion with “any l-adic place of F′” on p. 1243 and in Lemma 4.3 on p. 1273. Third, V_{λ,t} is the λ-adic realisation with λ above l, so it is an l-adic representation. The superseded argument, at the end of the proof of Theorem 1.1 in arXiv:2104.09761v1 (p. 24), deduced ordinary automorphy from V_{λ,t} being automorphic and ordinary at the l-adic places when v(t) < 0 (arXiv:2104.09761v1, Lemma 3.10(4), the main theorem of [14]). The published paper also uses ordinarity of V_{λ′,t} at the l′-adic places (v(t) > 0 there), but only to make V_{λ′,t} automorphic through the lifting theorem; it says nothing about π at the l-adic places. The “local-global compatibility result in this direction” that needs polarizability goes from Galois ordinarity to ι-ordinarity at the same prime, and the paper applies it in that form ([8, Lemma 5.9]) to Sym^{n−1} r_{E,l′} on p. 1273. So the remark makes sense only with “l-adic”. The remark is not used in any proof.

issues.locator: Remark 4.4, p. 1274
issues.printed: The source invokes “Theorem 5.5.1 or [1]” for ordinarity of V_{λ,t} as a G_{F′_v}-representation at every l-adic place v of F, and calls this another proof of the principal result of [14].
issues.correction: First fix the misprints: "Theorem 5.5.1 or [1]" should read "of [1]", and "l-adic places v of F" should read "of F′". Then make the deduction only when the residual representation V[λ]_t ≅ χ̄_1 ⊗ r̄|G_{F′} of V_{λ,t} is absolutely irreducible and decomposed generic. Twisting by a character preserves both properties, so this is the same as asking that r̄|G_{F′} be absolutely irreducible and decomposed generic. That holds in the setting of Theorem 1.4, but not in general in Theorem 1.1. Under this condition, cite the single-representation result [1, Corollary 5.5.2], or equivalently [1, Theorem 5.5.1] together with [1, Lemma 6.2.11] after the soluble base change used in that corollary's proof. The conclusion then covers only the global points t produced in the proof, and only on the decomposition groups of F′ at places above l. For those points it gives the conclusion of the main theorem of [14]. It does not give it for every t of negative valuation over every finite extension of an l-adic field containing ζ_N.
issues.reason:
[1, Theorem 5.5.1] is stated on p. 991 and restated on pp. 1026–1027 of the Annals version. It concerns Galois representations valued in ordinary Hecke algebras. It carries the standing hypothesis that F contains an imaginary quadratic field in which l splits, and it assumes [F^+:ℚ] > 1, a non-Eisenstein maximal ideal (by Definition 2.3.6, an absolutely irreducible residual representation) and a decomposed generic residual representation. The version for a single automorphic representation is [1, Corollary 5.5.2] on p. 1028. It requires the residual representation to be decomposed generic and irreducible. That corollary was added at a referee's request and appears first in the June 2022 arXiv revision; it is not in the December 2018 version that the paper cites.

The remark presents its conclusion as a consequence of the proof of Theorem 1.1, where r̄ is only semisimple. For a reducible r̄, or one that is not decomposed generic, the residual representation χ̄_1 ⊗ r̄|G_{F′} fails these hypotheses. A polarized local–global result such as Geraghty's cannot replace them, because V_{λ,t} is deliberately not self-dual. Irreducibility also matters for a second step. Transfer from the auxiliary prime l′ gives only V_{λ,t}^{ss} ≅ r_{l,ι}(π), and ordinarity of the semisimplification does not imply ordinarity of V_{λ,t}, because the order of the characters in the ordinary flag is prescribed. An absolutely irreducible residual representation makes V_{λ,t} irreducible and so closes this step.

Defence: in the setting of Theorem 1.4 the remark is correct. The proof of that theorem on p. 1274 shows that r̄|G_{F′} is absolutely irreducible, using linear disjointness from F^{avoid}, and decomposed generic, using [1, Lemma 7.1.7]. The remark, however, is not restricted to that setting.

The phrase "another way of proving the main result of [14]" overstates what is shown. [14, Theorem 1.1] (arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 2) proves ordinarity for every t of negative valuation over every finite extension of a local field containing ζ_N. The remark covers only the global points given by Moret-Bailly's theorem.

The remark is not used anywhere. [1, Theorem 6.1.2(5)] (p. 1030) needs π to be ι-ordinary, which Lemma 4.3 supplies, and does not need Galois ordinarity of r_ι(π).

In [13] the colon after “Neukirch, J.” makes the co-authors Schmidt and Wingberg part of the title; the title itself is right, since “Cohomology of global fields” is Chapter VIII (pp. 425–520) of Neukirch–Schmidt–Wingberg, Cohomology of Number Fields, which contains Theorem 8.6.7, the result cited for Poitou–Tate duality on p. 1246. The published entry omits the book title and drops the page range 425–520 given in arXiv:2104.09761v1; [12] is Chapter IX of the same book and also omits the book title. [4] gives no year (the arXiv version printed 2009, also wrong; the volume is Publ. RIMS 47 (2011)). The title of [17] has “representations” in the plural. Every cited work can still be identified, and every internal reference (for example Theorem 8.6.7 of [13], Lemma 4.1.2 of [5], Theorem 20 of [15]) points to the intended source, so no argument is affected. The entry for [1] is dealt with together with the citations of [1].

issues.locator: Companion preprint (Qian, Ordinarity of local Galois representation arising from Dwork motives), proof of Lemma 2.1, regularity of U_k, arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 6
issues.printed: The source claims that f_j = 0 forces a_j = 0, ∀j < k when all coefficients vanish, using l ∤ N.
issues.correction: … from f_j = 0 since char(k) ∤ N.
issues.reason: The page image confirms the sentence is printed as recorded, so this is not a text-layer artefact. The l is a math-italic l, the same glyph as the index function l(x) of p. 5, and ∤ is typeset correctly. For j < k the variable x_j does not occur in the product ∏_{l(k)≤s≤N, s≠i} x_s, so f_j = ∂f/∂x_j = −N a_j^{N−1}. The step f_j = 0 ⇒ a_j = 0 therefore needs N to be a unit in k̄: the point q is a k̄-point, and the Jacobian is read in m/m² ⊗_{k(m)} k̄. That condition is char(k) ∤ N, which is the standing hypothesis of §2 ("In this section we always assume char(k) ∤ N and N > 1", arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 4). It also follows from the assumption on p. 1 that the residue characteristic p of F does not divide N, since k is the residue field of F. Here char(k) means the residue field k, not the index k that appears in the same sentence. The companion never introduces a prime l. On p. 5 the letter denotes the index function l(x). Its only other use is the phrase "the l-adic representation V_{λ,(uπ)^{-1}}" on p. 8, where it loosely stands for the residue characteristic of λ, and by p. 1 that is p = char(k). Under either reading the intended hypothesis is char(k) ∤ N, so the meaning is clear and the argument is unaffected. There is no later version of the companion: arXiv has only v1. The published paper (Invent. Math. 231 (2023)) cites the companion only as a 2021 preprint and does not reproduce this argument; it only invokes Lemma 2.1 on p. 1257.

issues.locator: Companion preprint (L. Qian, Ordinarity of local Galois representation arising from Dwork motives), paragraph following the statement of Theorem 2.3 ("The idea of the proof goes as the following"), arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 9
issues.printed: The source defines 𝕏_{de} by base change of 𝕏_d through W[R, U^{±1}]′ → W[S, U^{±1}]′, T → S^e. It specifies Spec W[S, U^{±1}]′ by (S^{de}U)^N ≠ 1 inside Spec W[S, U^{±1}].
issues.correction: … where 𝕏_{de} is the base change of 𝕏_d along W[R, U^{±1}]′ → W[S, U^{±1}]′, R ↦ S^e, U ↦ U.
issues.reason: The page image shows the formula exactly as recorded, so this is not an artefact of the text layer. The recorded quotation writes X for the blackboard-bold 𝕏 of the source, a harmless difference. The meaning is clear from p. 8. There 𝕏_d is defined by base-changing the blow-up 𝕏 of U T(X_1^N + ⋯ + X_N^N) = N X_1⋯X_N along W[T, U^{±1}]′ → W[R, U^{±1}]′, T ↦ R^d. So 𝕏_d is a blow-up of U R^d(X_1^N + ⋯ + X_N^N) = N X_1⋯X_N over Spec W[R, U^{±1}]′, and T no longer occurs in its base ring. The map W[R, U^{±1}]′ → W[S, U^{±1}]′ must therefore be given by R ↦ S^e. The two substitutions compose to T ↦ R^d ↦ S^{de}. This is exactly the map W[T, U^{±1}] → W[S, U^{±1}]′, T ↦ S^{de}, of Proposition 1.5 (arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 3). It turns the equation into U S^{de}(X_1^N + ⋯ + X_N^N) = N X_1⋯X_N, which matches the condition (S^{de}U)^N ≠ 1 defining Spec W[S, U^{±1}]′ in the same sentence. Taken literally, 'T → S^e' is not even a ring map out of W[R, U^{±1}]′. Read as the composite substitution for T, it would give the wrong exponent, S^e instead of S^{de}. The printed arrow → should also be ↦, as in every other substitution on pp. 8–9. The later argument uses only 𝕏_{de} over W[S, U^{±1}]′ with the equation involving S^{de}, so nothing depends on the slip. The published paper (Invent. Math. 231 (2023)) does not reproduce this passage; it cites the companion only as a 2021 preprint.

issues.locator: Companion preprint L. Qian, "Ordinarity of local Galois representation arising from Dwork motives", proof of Theorem 1.1 in §4, passage from the algebraic to the analytic setting, arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 21. The same disc is used again in the monodromy step on arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 23 (the base point s with (s^{de}u′)^N ≠ 1, and "over the punctured unit disc"). The family Y comes from Remark 2.4, arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 13.
issues.printed: The source chooses (S, ℕ, 1 ↦ T) as the radius 1 complex analytic disc about 0, with coordinate T. It defines π^an : Y^an → S by pulling the analytic space of Y back from the affine line to S.
issues.correction: Let S be an open disc centred at 0 whose radius is at most |τ(u′)|^{−1/(de)}. This is the common absolute value of the points where (T^{de}τ(u′))^N = 1. On p. 23, replace "the punctured unit disc" by S ∖ {0}. Over this S the map π^an : Y^an → S is proper and log smooth, so [Ill94] 2.2.2 and 2.2.3 apply. For every s ∈ S ∖ {0} the condition (s^{de}u′)^N ≠ 1 then holds automatically. Under t = 1/(τ(u′)T^{de}), a loop around T = 0 in S ∖ {0} goes to a loop in the region |t| > 1 that winds de times around t = ∞. So the identification of the monodromy with ρ_s(γ_∞)^{de} goes through. Nothing else changes, because the argument only uses a neighbourhood of T = 0. Alternatively, take u′ in Remark 2.4 to be the Teichmüller lift [ū] of ū, which Remark 2.4 allows because any lift of ū will do. Then τ(u′) is a root of unity, all excluded points lie on the unit circle, and the open unit disc can be kept as printed.
issues.reason:
The printed sentence matches the page image. By Remark 2.4 (p. 13), Y is defined only over Spec W[T]′, the open subscheme of Spec W[T] where (T^{de}u′)^N ≠ 1. Here u′ ∈ W^× is any lift of the reduction ū of u. The scheme Y is a blow-up of u′T^{de}(X_1^N + ⋯ + X_N^N) = N X_1⋯X_N that is an isomorphism away from T = 0.

The removed fibres really are singular. For λ ≠ 0, the hypersurface λ(X_1^N + ⋯ + X_N^N) = N X_1⋯X_N is singular exactly when λ^N = 1. At a singular point the partial derivatives force λX_i^N = X_1⋯X_N for every i, and taking the product of these equations gives λ^N = 1. Conversely, if λ^N = 1, a point with every X_i ∈ μ_N and X_1⋯X_N = λ is singular. After base change along the embedding τ : W → ℂ fixed on p. 21, the excluded points are therefore the de·N values of T with (T^{de}τ(u′))^N = 1. All of them have absolute value |τ(u′)|^{−1/(de)}.

Nothing forces this radius to be at least 1. For example, u′ = [ū](1 + p) is an admissible lift. Since τ([ū]) is a root of unity and τ(1 + p) = 1 + p, we get |τ(u′)| = 1 + p for every τ. The excluded points then lie on the circle of radius (1 + p)^{−1/(de)} < 1, strictly inside the printed unit disc. For such a u′, Y^an is not defined over all of S and π^an is not proper over S, so [Ill94] 2.2.2 cannot be applied with S the unit disc. The condition (s^{de}u′)^N ≠ 1 on p. 23 shows that these points were not excluded from S.

The monodromy step on p. 23 fails in the same way. Take a base point s beyond the excluded circle. A loop around 0 through s is carried by t = 1/(τ(u′)T^{de}) into the region |t| < 1 around t = 0. Its monodromy is then a power of the monodromy around t = 0, not ρ_s(γ_∞)^{de}.

The missing restriction on the disc, or on the choice of u′, is always available, and the argument is local at T = 0. So this is a gap, not an error, and Theorem 1.1 of the companion is unaffected. However, the step as printed is invalid for some admissible choices of u′, so the proof needs the amendment above. The reach is therefore the proof, not nothing. The published main paper does not depend on this passage beyond the stated theorem. Its own Lemma 3.3(2) (published p. 1257) specialises U ↦ 1 and works over 𝔸^1 ∖ μ_N, where the excluded points lie on the unit circle, so that separate argument is not affected.
