issues.locator: Companion preprint arXiv:2103.00106v1 (27 February 2021), Remark 1.2, p. 2; not a statement of the published main paper
issues.printed: The source claims that 0 ∈ {a_1, …, a_N} ensures that the minimal polynomial of ρ_s(γ_∞) is (X − 1)^n.
issues.correction: Delete this sufficient condition. Retain the maximal-unipotent-monodromy hypothesis for every coefficient-conjugate character in Theorem 1.1. For Qian's selected character use the separately proved published Corollary 3.5 (item 049), with coefficient-conjugation compatibility. A criterion for other characters must follow the actual Jordan-block multiplicities, not the occurrence of 0 in an exponent vector.
issues.reason: Take N = 5 and a = (1,2,2,0,0), with Σa_i = 0 mod 5. A'Campo, arXiv:2407.16481v1, Definitions 2.1.1–2.1.2 (pp. 7–8), reconstructs this tuple up to permutation from α = (0,3), β = (1,2): −α = (0,2) and the complement of −β is {0,1,2}. Proposition 2.1.3 gives rank two, and Proposition 2.5.7 (pp. 19–20) gives Jordan blocks at t = ∞ of sizes equal to the multiplicities of α. The two multiplicities are one, so monodromy is the identity and its minimal polynomial is X−1, not (X−1)². Multiplication by a unit modulo 5 preserves distinctness of α, so all coefficient conjugates give the same obstruction. Dualizing for the cohomological action convention preserves the identity operator. Moreover a simultaneous translation a_i ↦ a_i + c leaves the H_0-character unchanged and can always make one entry 0, so zero occurrence is not an intrinsic sufficient condition. The false remark does not refute the conditional Theorem 1.1 or the published potential-automorphy results; E11's independent Hodge–Tate proof boundary is retained.

issues.locator: Lemma 5.12 and its proof, pp.285–287 (published version)
issues.printed: The proof takes m ∈ M(𝔽̄_p) with m̂ := ad_M(m) in Z_{M^ad}(ad_M(U)). From #F | e and the construction of U[e], it infers φ_m(U[e]) = {1}, equivalently m ∈ Z_M(U[e]). It declares the lemma proved by choosing U′ = U[e] and c(N) = e^{k(N)}.
issues.correction: The argument proves the inclusion Z_{M^ad}(ad_M(U)) ⊆ Z_M(U[e])/Z(M). This is what the applications use, and it suffices there. In Lemma 5.11 the Tate hypothesis gives Z_M(V[e]) = Z(M), hence Z_{M^ad}(ad_M(V)) = 1 and so Z_{M^ad}(Û) = 1. Either restate Lemma 5.12 as this inclusion, or supply a separate argument for the equality on U′.
issues.reason: The lemma asserts Z_{M^ad}(ad_M(U′)) = Z_M(U′)/Z(M) for U′ = U[e]. That needs, for every m with ad_M(m) centralising ad_M(U[e]), that m centralises U[e]. The proof takes m centralising the image of the larger group U. Then φ_m is a homomorphism U → F killed by U[e]. For m only centralising ad_M(U[e]), φ_m is a homomorphism U[e] → F, and U[e] need not lie in its kernel, because homomorphisms of U[e] to F need not extend to U. The inclusion needed for the stated equality is therefore not established.

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed as a gap. Lemma 5.12 (p.285) asserts, for a bounded-index U′ ≤ U, the equality Z_{M^ad}(ad_M(U′)) = Z_M(U′)/Z(M), and the proof (pp.286–287) takes m ∈ M(F̄_p) with ad_M(m) ∈ Z_{M^ad}(ad_M(U)) — the centraliser of the image of the whole of U — shows that φ_m : u ↦ mum^{-1}u^{-1} is a homomorphism U → F(F̄_p) with #F | e, and concludes m ∈ Z_M(U[e]). With U′ = U[e] that gives Z_{M^ad}(ad_M(U)) ⊆ Z_M(U[e])/Z(M), and since ad_M(U[e]) ⊆ ad_M(U) the centraliser on the left of the asserted equality is the larger one, so the equality does not follow. The recorded repair is the inclusion the proof does establish; it fits the use I read at the top of p.285, where Lemma 5.11 needs only the triviality of a centraliser of an image.

issues.locator: Definition 2.10, printed p. 114 (PDF 15), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical (main2.tex line 542)
issues.printed: The source describes the ideles as a topological ring whose topology is the restricted product topology.

issues.correction: For n ≥ 0, ζ(−n) = (−1)^n B_{n+1}/(n+1); equivalently ζ(0) = −1/2 = B_1 and ζ(−n) = −B_{n+1}/(n+1) for n ≥ 1. (The printed formula is right only with the other convention B_1 = +1/2.)
issues.reason: From Lemma 2.7 at s = −n and Theorem 2.4: (−n−1)ζ(−n) = L(f,−n−1) = (−1)^{n+1}f^{(n+1)}(0) = (−1)^{n+1}B_{n+1}, so ζ(−n) = (−1)^n B_{n+1}/(n+1). With the paper's own B_1 = −1/2 (Remark 2.5, generating function t/(e^t−1)), the printed formula gives ζ(0) = +1/2, but ζ(0) = −1/2 (Mathlib riemannZeta_zero). For n ≥ 1 the two agree because B_{n+1} = 0 for n+1 odd ≥ 3. Mathlib's riemannZeta_neg_nat_eq_bernoulli states the corrected form. The 'in particular' clauses (rationality; vanishing at even n ≥ 2) are unaffected; Theorem 2.13 is unaffected since its k = 1 case carries the factor 1 − p⁰ = 0. (Also recorded by an earlier worker: DirichletPadicLFunctions.json DirichletPadicLFunctions/E5.)

issues.locator: Remark 2.18, printed p. 117 (PDF 18), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical (main2.tex lines 630–636)
issues.printed: The source claims that the theorems give (1−η(p)p^{k−1})L(η,1−k) ≡ (1−η(p)p^{ℓ−1})L(η,1−ℓ) (mod p^m) for every Dirichlet character η with conductor prime to p. It identifies the Riemann zeta case with the generalised Kummer congruences.
issues.correction: For η nontrivial (conductor D > 1 prime to p) the congruence holds in 𝒪_L, because ζ_η is an integral measure. For η trivial (the Riemann zeta function) ζ_p is only a pseudomeasure: the congruence holds (p odd) only when (p−1) ∤ k, or in general after smoothing: (1−a^k)(1−p^{k−1})ζ(1−k) ≡ (1−a^ℓ)(1−p^{ℓ−1})ζ(1−ℓ) (mod p^m) for a prime to p.
issues.reason: Counterexample: p = 3, m = 1, η trivial, k = 2, ℓ = 4 (k ≡ ℓ mod 2). (1−3)ζ(−1) = (−2)(−1/12) = 1/6 and (1−27)ζ(−3) = (−26)(1/120) = −13/60; the difference 1/6 + 13/60 = 23/60 has 3-adic valuation −1, so the two values are not even congruent mod 3 (both have denominators divisible by 3, as von Staudt–Clausen predicts when (p−1) | k). Integrating the congruence x^k ≡ x^ℓ (mod p^m) against ζ_p is not allowed since ζ_p ∉ Λ(ℤ_p^×). Smoothing by a = 2: (1−2²)/6 = −1/2 and (1−2⁴)(−13/60) = 13/4 differ by 15/4, of 3-adic valuation 1, as the integral measure x⁻¹Res μ_a predicts. For (p−1) ∤ k take a a primitive root mod p, so 1−a^k and 1−a^ℓ are units with a^k ≡ a^ℓ (mod p^m), and divide. (Also recorded by an earlier worker: PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras.json PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras/E13; DirichletPadicLFunctions.json DirichletPadicLFunctions/E10.)

issues.locator: Remark 2.1, definition of L_p(V,s), printed p. 107 (PDF 8), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical (main2.tex line 306)
issues.printed: L_p(V,s) := det(Id − φ^{−1}p^{−s} | D_cris(V))^{−1}
issues.correction: L_p(V,s) := det(Id − φ·p^{−s} | D_cris(V))^{−1}, with D_cris(V) = (B_cris ⊗_{ℚ_p} V)^{𝒢_{ℚ_p}} (covariant, as in the cited Berger [7] and Benois [6]); this matches the factor det(Id − Frob_ℓ^{−1}ℓ^{−s} | V^{I_ℓ})^{−1} used at ℓ ≠ p.
issues.reason: Test on V = ℚ_p(1), the cyclotomic character, whose L-function should be ζ(s+1): at ℓ ≠ p, Frob_ℓ^{−1} acts by ℓ^{−1}, giving (1 − ℓ^{−1−s})^{−1} as the text's convention requires. D_cris(ℚ_p(1)) = ℚ_p·(t^{−1} ⊗ e) and φ(t) = pt, so φ acts by p^{−1}; then det(1 − φp^{−s}) = 1 − p^{−1−s} (correct Euler factor of ζ(s+1)) whereas the printed det(1 − φ^{−1}p^{−s}) = 1 − p^{1−s} (Euler factor of ζ(s−1)). Equivalently, for unramified V, D_cris(V) = (V ⊗ ℚ̂_p^{ur})^{𝒢} and φ = 1 ⊗ σ corresponds to the geometric Frobenius Frob_p^{−1} on V, so φ (not φ^{−1}) plays the role of Frob_ℓ^{−1}. The printed formula would be right only for a contravariant D_cris, which neither cited reference uses.

issues.locator: Proposition 2.9(i) and its proof, printed pp. 113–114 (PDF 14–15), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical (main2.tex lines 505–526)
issues.printed: The source asserts a correspondence of Dirichlet characters χ with characters χ : Π_{ℓ prime} ℤ_ℓ^× → ℂ^× that are continuous, claiming that its two constructions are mutually inverse.
issues.correction: The identification is between primitive Dirichlet characters (equivalently, Dirichlet characters modulo induction to a larger modulus) and continuous characters of Π_ℓ ℤ_ℓ^×; the reverse procedure should factor the character through (ℤ/Nℤ)^× with N minimal (the conductor). The same applies to the uniqueness of χ in κ_{χ,s} and in Proposition 2.11.
issues.reason: A character χ mod N and the character it induces mod NM give the same continuous character on Π_ℓ ℤ_ℓ^× (both are χ composed with the projection), so the map from all Dirichlet characters is not injective; the converse construction 'factors through a finite quotient (ℤ/Nℤ)^× for some large enough N' depends on the chosen N and returns the given χ only if N is its conductor. The notes later require primitivity explicitly (Theorem 2.16 '(primitive)', Theorem 5.1).

issues.locator: §2.4.2, display (2-3) and the following sentence, printed p. 115 (PDF 16), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical (main2.tex lines 566–569)
issues.printed: The source defines L : Hom_cts(ℚ^×\𝔸^×, ℂ^×) → ℂ, κ_{χ,s} ↦ L(χ,s). It interprets L in Tate’s framework as the integral of κ_{χ,s} with respect to Haar measure on ℚ^×\𝔸^×.
issues.correction: With the identification of Proposition 2.9 (χ on Π_ℓ ℤ_ℓ^× is χ composed with the projection to (ℤ/Nℤ)^×), Tate's zeta integral of κ_{χ,s} produces L(χ⁻¹,s) = L(χ̄,s); to obtain L(χ,s) one must attach κ_{χ⁻¹,s} to χ (or map κ_{χ,s} ↦ L(χ̄,s)).
issues.reason: For ℓ ∤ N, the uniformiser idele π_ℓ = (1,…,ℓ at ℓ,…,1) equals ℓ·u with u = (ℓ^{−1} at ∞ and at q ≠ ℓ, 1 at ℓ) ∈ ℝ_{>0} × Π_q ℤ_q^×, so κ_{χ,s}(π_ℓ) = ℓ^{−s}χ(ℓ^{−1} mod N) = χ̄(ℓ)ℓ^{−s}. Tate's unramified local integral ∫_{ℚ_ℓ^×}1_{ℤ_ℓ}(x)κ_ℓ(x)d^×x = (1 − κ(π_ℓ))^{−1} = (1 − χ̄(ℓ)ℓ^{−s})^{−1}, the Euler factor of L(χ̄,s). The sentence is heuristic ('can be viewed as') and nothing later depends on it (the p-adic interpolation formulas of Theorems 2.15–2.16 are proved concretely in §5 with χ evaluated directly on ℤ_p^×), but a formalisation of the idelic dictionary (GlobalNumberFields Layer 9) must fix this inversion.

issues.locator: Definition 3.3(2), printed p. 118 (PDF 19), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical (main2.tex, def:orthonormal)
issues.printed: The source calls a family (e_i)_{i∈I} an orthonormal basis of B, for a set I, when the map ℓ⁰_∞(I,L) → B, (a_i)_{i∈I} ↦ Σ_{i∈I} a_i e_i is an isometry.
issues.correction: …such that (a_i) ↦ Σ a_i e_i is an isometric isomorphism (a surjective isometry) ℓ⁰_∞(I,L) ≅ B.
issues.reason: An isometry need not be onto: in B = 𝒞(ℤ_p,L) the family e_n = (x choose 2n) gives an isometry ℓ⁰_∞(ℕ,L) → B (by Mahler's theorem the norm of Σa_n(x choose 2n) is sup|a_n|), but its image misses (x choose 1), so it is not a basis. The standard notion (Serre's orthonormal bases of p-adic Banach spaces, which is what the existence statement quoted in Remark 3.4 produces) requires the map to be an isometric isomorphism onto B; the Colmez source text itself was not re-read here. The paper's later assertion that the (x choose n) 'form an orthonormal basis' (after Definition 3.20) is true in the corrected sense, which Mahler's theorem (uniqueness+existence of the expansion) gives.

issues.locator: Definition 3.5, strong-topology bullet, second sentence, printed p. 119 (PDF 20), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical
issues.printed: The source describes this as the least fine topology in which convergence of (µ_j)_j ⊂ B* is equivalent to uniform convergence, understood for continuous functions on B.
issues.correction: The strong (operator-norm) topology is the topology of uniform convergence on the unit ball of B (equivalently on bounded subsets of B), not on all of B.
issues.reason: Take B = L = ℚ_p and µ_n(x) = p^n x. Then v*(µ_n) = n → ∞, i.e. µ_n → 0 strongly, but sup_{x∈B}|µ_n(x)| = ∞ for every n (take x = p^{−n−k}), so µ_n does not converge to 0 uniformly on B. Indeed a sequence of linear functionals converges uniformly on all of B only if it is eventually constant. (Also recorded by an earlier worker: PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras.json PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras/E9.)

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed at Definition 3.5, printed p. 119: 'converges uniformly (in the usual sense of continuous functions on B)'. With µ_n = p^n·id on ℚ_p, µ_n → 0 in norm but sup_B |µ_n| = ∞.

issues.locator: Remark 3.6, first sentence, printed p. 119 (PDF 20), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical (rem:strong topology)
issues.printed: The source asserts completeness of B* for each of the two topologies.
issues.correction: B* is complete for the strong topology. For the weak topology it is in general NOT complete when B is infinite-dimensional (its completion is the algebraic dual); only bounded weakly Cauchy nets/sequences converge (Banach–Steinhaus), and the closed unit ball (e.g. M(G,𝒪_L)) is weakly compact since L is locally compact.
issues.reason: For B = c₀(ℕ,ℚ_p) choose an algebraic linear functional ℓ with ℓ(e_n) = p^{−n} (extend from the span of the e_n by a Hamel basis); it is discontinuous. For every finite F ⊂ B there is a continuous ℓ_F (factor through finitely many coordinates injective on span F) agreeing with ℓ on F; the net (ℓ_F)_F is weakly Cauchy (eventually constant at each vector) but its only possible weak limit is ℓ ∉ B*. The packet lead gives the same construction; I re-derived it. (If 'complete' is read as 'sequentially complete' the weak statement is true by Banach–Steinhaus, but the paper does not say so.) (Also recorded by an earlier worker: PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras.json PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras/E10.)

issues.locator: Remark 3.11, locally constant truncations, printed p. 120 (PDF 21), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical
issues.printed: The source claims p-adic approximation of any continuous φ ∈ 𝒞(G,𝒪_L) by locally constant truncations given by φ_n(x) = Σ_{a∈(ℤ/p^nℤ)} φ(a)1_{a+p^nℤ_p}(x).
issues.correction: For a general profinite G: by compactness and uniform continuity, for each n choose an open subgroup H_n with |φ(x)−φ(y)| ≤ p^{−n} when x−y ∈ H_n, and set φ_n = Σ_{[a]∈G/H_n} φ(a)1_{aH_n} (finitely many cosets, representatives chosen); then ‖φ−φ_n‖ ≤ p^{−n}. The displayed formula is this for G = ℤ_p, H_n = p^nℤ_p.
issues.reason: Remark 3.11 is stated for an arbitrary profinite abelian G, where residue classes a+p^nℤ_p indexed by ℤ/p^nℤ do not exist (e.g. G = ℤ_p × ℤ_p or G = ℤ_p^×). The density conclusion is true for every profinite G (Mathlib ContinuousMap.exists_finite_approximation_of_mem_nhds_diagonal), so only the justification is incomplete. issues.locator: Remark 3.35, printed p. 130 (PDF 31), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 (main2.tex, remark after (eq:integrate pseudo-measure)) identical
issues.printed: The source claims that this produces exactly one homomorphism Q(G) → C_p, whose value on a pseudomeasure is the expression (3-11).
issues.correction: The ring homomorphism ε_χ : Λ(G) → C_p, µ ↦ ∫_G χ·µ, extends to a localisation of Λ(G) only if every inverted element has nonzero image; in general it does NOT extend to the total quotient ring Q(G). What is true: on the Λ(G)-module of pseudomeasures, (3-11) is the unique additive map E with E(µ) = ε_χ(µ) for µ ∈ Λ(G) and E(µλ) = ε_χ(µ)E(λ).
issues.reason: Counterexample meeting the remark's hypotheses: p = 3, G = Z_3, Λ(G) = Z_3[[T]] with [1] ↦ 1 + T (a domain), χ(x) = 4^x, a nontrivial continuous character, so ε_χ(F) = F(3). The element s = T − 3 is nonzero, hence a non-zero-divisor, but ε_χ(s) = 0; a ring homomorphism F : Q(G) → C_p extending ε_χ would give 1 = F(s)F(s^{−1}) = 0. (Checked by hand; the same obstruction exists for G = Z_p^× and many characters.) Reach: the claim in Remark 3.35); nothing downstream, since (3-11) is used directly and its independence of g is proved separately. (Also recorded by an earlier worker: PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras.json, PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras/E1.)

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 3.36(iii), printed p. 131 (PDF 32), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical
issues.printed: The proof chooses an integer a ≠ 1 coprime to p and claims that [a] −[1] meets the hypothesis in part (ii), making it a non-zero-divisor.
issues.correction: Take an integer a prime to p with a ∉ {1, −1} (e.g. a = p + 1), so that a^k ≠ 1 for all k > 0; then [a] − [1] satisfies the hypothesis of (ii).
issues.reason: a = −1 is an integer ≠ 1 prime to p, and ∫_{Z_p^×} x^k·([−1] − [1]) = (−1)^k − 1 = 0 for every even k, so (ii) does not apply. Indeed ([−1] − [1])([−1] + [1]) = [1] − [1] = 0 in Λ(Z_p^×) with both factors nonzero (their images in O_L[(Z/p)^×] are nonzero as −1 ≢ 1 mod p for odd p), so [−1] − [1] is a zero divisor and the concluding step fails for this choice. Reach: Lemma 3.36(iii) remains true with the corrected choice. (Also recorded by an earlier worker: PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras.json, PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras/E3.)

issues.locator: Theorem 8.2(a) and the first sentence of its proof, printed p. 160 (PDF 61), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical
issues.printed: Part (a) asserts that A_0 is a pseudomeasure, whereas A_n ∈ Λ(Z_p^×) for every n ≥ 1. The source identifies A_0 with xζ_p/2.
issues.correction: (a) x^{−1}A_0 is a pseudomeasure (A_0 = xζ_p/2 ∈ Q(Z_p^×), the twist by the character x of the pseudomeasure ζ_p/2; equivalently (g[g] − [1])A_0 ∈ Λ(Z_p^×) for all g ∈ Z_p^×), and A_n ∈ Λ(Z_p^×) for n ≥ 1.
issues.reason: By Definition 3.34 a pseudomeasure λ satisfies ([g] − [1])λ ∈ Λ(Z_p^×) for all g, i.e. as a function on weight space it can have a pole only at the trivial character. Twisting by x is a ring automorphism of Λ(Z_p^×) with x·([g] − [1]) = g[g] − [1], so xζ_p has its pole at κ = x^{−1} (where ∫κ·(xζ_p) = ∫1·ζ_p), not at 1; since ζ_p really has a pole at the trivial character (Theorem 7.1(ii), Lemma 7.5: ∫1·([a]−[1])ζ_p = −(1 − p^{−1})log_p(a) ≠ 0), ([g] − [1])·xζ_p ∉ Λ for g ≠ 1. Moreover no pseudomeasure A_0 can satisfy (b): for k = (p−1)p^m (even, ≥ 4) the character x^{k−1} lies on the component ω^{−1} ≠ 1, where a pseudomeasure µ/([a]−[1]) has |∫x^{k−1}·λ| ≤ ‖µ‖ because |a^{k−1} − 1| = |ω(a)^{−1} − 1| = 1; but |½(1 − p^{k−1})ζ(1−k)| = |B_k/(2k)| = p^{m+1} → ∞ by von Staudt–Clausen. So (a) and (b) as printed are incompatible; the construction A_0 = xζ_p/2 is right and only the word 'pseudomeasure' is wrong.

issues.locator: §10.5, definition of c_m and the sentence 'The cyclotomic units form an Euler system for the representation Zp(1)', printed pp. 171–172 (PDF 72–73), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical
issues.printed: With m = Dp^n and n ≥ 1, the source defines cm := (ξm^{−1} − 1)/(ξm − 1) ∈ O×Q(µm) and presents it as extending the Section 10.2 cyclotomic units cn(−1), where D = 1.
issues.correction: Use non-torsion cyclotomic elements: Rubin's c̃_m = N_{Q(µ_{mp})/Q(µ_m)}(1 − ξ_{mp}), or its smoothings c̃_m^{σ_a − 1} (primes dividing a added to Σ), which satisfy Definition 10.16 including the ℓ = p relation at n = 0. The family c_m(a) := (ξ_m^a − 1)/(ξ_m − 1) (a ∉ {0, ±1} prime to m) is non-torsion but its norm from Q(µ_{pm′}) to Q(µ_{m′}) carries the factor 1 − σ_p^{−1}. The norm relations of the printed display should read N(c_{mℓ}) = c_m for ℓ | m and N(c_{mℓ}) = c_m^{1 − σ_ℓ^{−1}} for ℓ ∤ m (σ_ℓ the Frobenius at ℓ in Gal(Q(µ_m)/Q)), not '(1 − ℓ^{−1})c_m', and after δ: cores(z_{mℓ}) = (1 − σ_ℓ^{−1})z_m with σ_ℓ acting through Gal(Q(µ_m)/Q), not through its action on the coefficients ℤ_p(1). (Revised by the review; the extraction's correction led with c_m(a).)
issues.reason: ξ^{−1} − 1 = −ξ^{−1}(ξ − 1), so c_m = −ξ_m^{−1} is a root of unity (and c_n(−1) = −ξ_{p^n}^{−1} likewise). Its Kummer class z_m = δ(c_m) is torsion and vanishes in H^1 ⊗ Q_p; e.g. its Coleman power series is −(1+T)^{−1}, whose ∂log is the constant −1, killed by 1 − φ∘ψ, so Col(c(−1)) = 0. This family cannot be the Euler system 'at the heart of Rubin's proof' or give ζ_p in the later paragraph. Norm relation for 1 − ξ_{mℓ}, ℓ ∤ m: write ξ_{mℓ} = αβ with α ∈ μ_m, β of order ℓ; then α^ℓ = ξ_m, α = σ_ℓ^{−1}(ξ_m), and ∏_{β′ ≠ 1}(1 − αβ′) = (1 − α^ℓ)/(1 − α) = (1 − ξ_m)/σ_ℓ^{−1}(1 − ξ_m). (Also recorded by an earlier worker: research/blueprint/packets/EulerSystemsCyclotomicMainConjecture.json, EulerSystemsCyclotomicMainConjecture/E2.)

issues.locator: §9, paragraph after (9-3), printed p. 163 (PDF 64), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical; contradicted by the paper's own §12.1, printed p. 177 (PDF 78)
issues.printed: The source asserts compactness over Zp for all infinite-level modules, reasoning that they are limits of compact Zp-modules. It equips them naturally with continuous Γ = Gal(F∞/Q) or Γ+ = Gal(F+∞/Q) actions and, consequently, continuous Λ(Γ) or Λ(Γ+) actions.
issues.correction: U_{∞,1} and U_{∞,1}^+ are compact Z_p-modules (hence Λ(Γ)-, resp. Λ(Γ^+)-modules); U_∞ and U_∞^+ are compact abelian groups with continuous Γ- (resp. Γ^+-) actions but not Z_p-modules: U_∞ = μ_{p−1} × U_{∞,1} and U_∞^+ = μ_{p−1} × U_{∞,1}^+.
issues.reason: The previous paragraph itself says U_n and U_n^+ 'are only Z-modules', so the justification 'inverse limits of compact Z_p-modules' does not apply to U_∞, U_∞^+. Directly: U_n = μ_{p−1} × U_{n,1} (Teichmüller; residue field F_p), and the norm N_{K_n/K_{n−1}} acts on μ_{p−1} ⊂ Q_p by ζ ↦ ζ^p, a bijection, so U_∞ ≅ μ_{p−1} × U_{∞,1} (same for the plus parts). Since p − 1 is a unit of Z_p, multiplication by p − 1 is bijective on any Z_p-module, but it kills the nontrivial subgroup μ_{p−1} ⊂ U_∞ (p odd); so no Z_p-module structure extends the Z-module structure of U_∞. §12.1 (printed p. 177) says so: 'whilst there is a natural action of Z on U∞ by u ↦ u^a ..., this does not extend to an action of Zp', and proves U_∞ = μ_{p−1} × U_{∞,1}.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 12.22(i), printed p. 188 (PDF 89), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical
issues.printed: Citing Lemma 12.21(ii), the source gives (p − 1)D_n^+ = (p − 1)D^+_{n,1} ⊂ U^+_{n,1} with Z[Γ_n^+]-generator (wγ_{n,a})^{p−1}. It then cites Lemma 12.20 to claim that its p-adic closure, (p − 1)C^+_{n,1}, has the same generator over Z_p[Γ_n^+].
issues.correction: By Lemma 12.21(ii), (p − 1)D_n^+ ⊂ U^+_{n,1} is generated as a Z[Γ_n^+]-module by (wγ_{n,a})^{p−1}. By Lemma 12.20 (applied to its finitely many Γ_n^+-conjugates) the p-adic closure of (p − 1)D_n^+ is Z_p[Γ_n^+]·(wγ_{n,a})^{p−1}. This closure is (p − 1)C_n^+ (the image of the compact C_n^+ = closure of D_n^+ under x ↦ x^{p−1}), and (p − 1)C_n^+ = C^+_{n,1}, because U_n^+ = μ_{p−1} × U^+_{n,1}, x ↦ x^{p−1} kills μ_{p−1}, and p − 1 is invertible on the Z_p-module C^+_{n,1}.
issues.reason: With the Part II convention X^+_{n,1} = X_n^+ ∩ U^+_{n,1} (the text itself uses D^+_{n,1} = V^+_{n,1} ∩ D_n^+ in §13), (p − 1)D^+_{n,1} is in general a proper subgroup of (p − 1)D_n^+. Example p = 5, n = 1: D_1^+ = ⟨−1, γ⟩ with γ = γ_{1,2} = ξ^2 + ξ^3 = (−1 − √5)/2 ≡ 2 mod 𝔭_1; ±γ^k ≡ 1 mod 𝔭_1 iff (+, 4 | k) or (−, k ≡ 2 mod 4), so D^+_{1,1} = ⟨−γ^2⟩ and 4D^+_{1,1} = ⟨γ^8⟩ ≠ ⟨γ^4⟩ = 4D_1^+ (γ is not a root of unity). The index [ (p−1)D_n^+ : (p−1)D^+_{n,1} ] divides p − 1, so the p-adic closures in the pro-p group U_{n,1} coincide (in the example Z_5γ^8 = Z_5γ^4) and the lemma is true.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 12.23, printed p. 188 (PDF 89), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical
issues.printed: The source invokes Lemma 12.22 to reduce the task to computing Col on (ξ^b_{p^n}γ_{n,a})_{n≥1} ∈ U_{∞,1}, with a, b ∈ Z_p^×. Since a ∈ Z_p^× is arbitrary, it claims Col sends C_{∞,1} to I(Γ)ζ_p and C^+_{∞,1} to I(Γ^+)ζ_p.
issues.correction: Fix a ∈ Z a topological generator of Z_p^× and w = ω(a)^{−1} ∈ μ_{p−1}. Then C^+_{∞,1} = Λ(Γ^+)·(wγ_{n,a})_n (Lemma 12.22) and C_{∞,1} = Z_p(1) × C^+_{∞,1} (from D_n = ⟨ξ_{p^n}⟩ × D_n^+, Lemma 12.18(ii)). Col kills Z_p(1) = {(ξ^b_{p^n})_n : b ∈ Z_p} and μ_{p−1}, so Col((ξ^b_{p^n}wγ_{n,a})_n) = Col(c(a)) = ±([σ_a] − [1])ζ_p. As σ_a topologically generates Γ (and its image generates Γ^+), I(Γ) = Λ(Γ)([σ_a] − [1]) and I(Γ^+) = Λ(Γ^+)([σ_a] − [1]); hence Col(C_{∞,1}) = I(Γ)ζ_p and Col(C^+_{∞,1}) = I(Γ^+)ζ_p.
issues.reason: (1) γ_{n,a} ≡ a mod 𝔭_n (Lemma 12.21), so (ξ^b γ_{n,a})_n ∉ U_{∞,1} unless a ≡ 1 mod p; the factor w is missing (harmless since Col(w) = 0 by Lemma 12.3). (2) b must range over Z_p (Z_p(1) is not {(ξ^b) : b ∈ Z_p^×}), and a cannot be arbitrary: Lemma 12.22 and Theorem 10.15 are stated for a fixed topological generator. The step from the single generator to the whole ideal needs the principal-augmentation-ideal property of the procyclic groups Γ, Γ^+, which the text does not invoke. (3) Lemma 12.22 describes only C^+_{∞,1}; the decomposition C_{∞,1} = Z_p(1) × C^+_{∞,1} needed for part (i) is not stated or proved. The theorem itself is correct.

issues.reason: Take L = ℚ_p(√p), ϖ = √p, M = Λ/(ϖ). A map with finite kernel and cokernel becomes an isomorphism after localising at the height-one prime (ϖ) (finite Λ-modules are killed by a power of (ϖ, T) ⊄ (ϖ), and T is a unit in Λ_(ϖ)), so it preserves the length at (ϖ). issues.locator: Definition 13.19(1), printed p. 196 (PDF 97), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical
issues.printed: The definition requires V to admit a finite saturated filtration Fil^i invariant under G_Q. On Fil^i/Fil^{i+1}, it prescribes the action of I_{Q_p}, the inertia subgroup of G_{Q_p}, to be the cyclotomic character raised to its i-th power.
issues.correction: … a saturated, finite filtration Fil^iV by G_{ℚ_p}-stable subspaces (stable under a decomposition group at p) …, as in Greenberg [36]; the local condition 𝓛^Gr_{v_p} uses only the restriction to the decomposition group.
issues.reason: For an elliptic curve E/ℚ with good ordinary reduction at p, V = V_pE is irreducible as a G_ℚ-representation (standard: a G_ℚ-stable line would give an infinite chain of cyclic p-power ℚ-isogenies, contradicting finiteness of the ℚ-isogeny class), so its only G_ℚ-stable filtrations are trivial, whose single graded piece V is not acted on by I_{ℚ_p} through a power of χ (inertia acts by (χ ∗; 0 1)). Yet it is Greenberg's basic ordinary example, with Fil^1 = V_p(Ê) (the formal group) stable only under G_{ℚ_p}. As printed, Definition 13.19(1) and Conjecture 13.21 would exclude the 'representations attached to arithmetic objects' the section is about. The example ℚ_p(n) (one-dimensional) is unaffected. issues.locator: Remark 13.7, printed p. 192 (PDF 93), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical
issues.printed: The source uses density of O_L[Γ] in Λ(Γ) and the Hausdorff property of Λ(Γ) to claim that linearity and continuity extend the action to Λ(Γ) on X_∞.
issues.correction: Because 𝒳_∞ is a compact (profinite) ℤ_p-module on which Γ acts continuously — 𝒳_∞ = lim← 𝒳_∞/U over open Γ-stable subgroups U, and Γ acts on each finite p-group 𝒳_∞/U through a finite quotient — the ℤ_p[Γ]-action extends uniquely by continuity to ℤ_p⟦Γ⟧ = Λ(Γ). The coefficients are ℤ_p (or tensor 𝒳_∞ with O_L), not O_L.
issues.reason: Extending an action from the dense subring by continuity needs the target 𝒳_∞ to be complete Hausdorff and the action to be (uniformly) continuous for the Λ(Γ)-topology; Hausdorffness of Λ(Γ) itself plays no role. Moreover 𝒳_∞ is a pro-p group, i.e. a ℤ_p-module, not an O_L-module, so O_L[Γ] (L a general finite extension as in §13.1) does not act on it. The asserted conclusion (a Λ(Γ)-module structure with ℤ_p-coefficients) is correct.

issues.locator: Example 13.22 with Conjecture 13.21(ii), printed p. 198 (PDF 99), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical
issues.printed: The source identifies Greenberg’s p-adic L-function here with ∂^nζ_p, the n-th Kubota–Leopoldt twist, and consequently describes the conjecture as essentially Theorem 13.8 with a twist.
issues.correction: For n > 0 even, Theorem 13.8 is equivalent to ch_{Λ(Γ^+)}(𝒳_∞^+(−n)) = Tw_n(I(Γ^+)ζ_p) = Tw_n(I(Γ^+))·∂^nζ_p (Tw_n: [g] ↦ χ(g)^n[g]). Conjecture 13.21(ii) with L_p(ℚ_p(n)) = ∂^nζ_p, read literally, would assert ch = (∂^nζ_p), which is false; Greenberg's formulation needs the correction factor Tw_n(I(Γ^+)) (coming from H⁰(𝓕, W_n) = W_n ≠ 0 for n even), or the conjecture must exclude/adjust this case.
issues.reason: ζ_p is a pseudo-measure with a pole at the trivial character, not an element of Λ(Γ^+) (node DirichletPadicLFunctions:L1/arithmetic-not-integral: 'There is no μ ∈ M with Iwasawa.integral δ Q μ = ζ_p', on ℤ_p^×; ζ_p is even, and Λ(Γ)^+ ≅ Λ(Γ^+)); Tw_n is a ring automorphism of Λ(Γ^+) (n even, so χ^n factors through Γ^+), hence ∂^nζ_p = Tw_n(ζ_p) ∉ Λ(Γ^+) and (∂^nζ_p) is a fractional ideal not contained in Λ(Γ^+), whereas a characteristic ideal is an integral ideal. Twisting Theorem 13.8 (char(M(−n)) = Tw_n(char M)) gives Tw_n(I(Γ^+))·∂^nζ_p, which differs from (∂^nζ_p) exactly in the component of the character x^{−n}. The word 'essentially' hides this; the packet node EulerSystemsCyclotomicMainConjecture:L3/tate-twisted-selmer-formulation records it in its hypotheses, but node SelmerIwasawaCohomology:L4/greenberg-conjecture-tate-twists repeats the literal claim. (Also recorded by an earlier worker: new (noted, not filed as an issue, in the hypotheses of EulerSystemsCyclotomicMainConjecture.json node EulerSystemsCyclotomicMainConjecture:L3/tate-twisted-selmer-formulation).)

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed at Example 13.22, printed p. 198. ∂^nζ_p has a genuine pole at the character x^{−n}: the numerator (a^n[a] − [1])∂^nζ_p evaluated at x^{−n} is the residue term −(1 − p^{−1})log_p a ≠ 0. So (∂^nζ_p) is not an integral ideal, and twisting Theorem 13.8 gives Tw_n(I(Γ^+))·∂^nζ_p.

issues.locator: Appendix A.1, Theorem A.3, printed p. 200 (PDF 101), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; proof on printed p. 206; arXiv v2 identical
issues.printed: The source asserts that integers λ≥0, µ≥0, ν ≥0 and n0 exist with en = µpn + λn + ν for every n ≥n0.
issues.correction: There exist integers λ ≥ 0, µ ≥ 0 and ν (an arbitrary integer, possibly negative), and n₀, such that e_n = µp^n + λn + ν for all n ≥ n₀.
issues.reason: The proof gives ν = c + c', where c comes from Lemma A.9 (|Y∞/ω_n| = p^c|𝒜/ω_n|, c ∈ ℤ, and c < 0 happens whenever 𝒜/ω_n is larger than Y∞/ω_n) and c' is the constant of Proposition A.10. Nothing in the argument makes the sum non-negative, and Washington's Theorem 13.13 (the source the text follows, [81, §13]) puts no sign on ν. Proposition A.10's constant can itself be negative. Take p = 3 and 𝒜 = Λ/(g), g = T⁴ − 3 (distinguished, prime to every ω_n). Then #𝒜/ω_n𝒜 = ∏_{ζ^{3^n}=1} |(ζ−1)⁴ − 3|_3^{−1}. ζ = 1 gives valuation 1. The two ζ of order 3 give (ζ−1)² = −3ζ, so (ζ−1)⁴ − 3 = 3(3ζ² − 1), valuation 1 each. The φ(3^k) roots of order 3^k, k ≥ 2, have v((ζ−1)⁴) = 2/3^{k−1} < 1, contributing 4 in total. So log₃ #𝒜/ω_n𝒜 = 4n − 1 for n ≥ 1: λ = 4, µ = 0, 'ν' = −1. I did not check whether this module occurs as some Y∞ satisfying (H), so this is recorded as an unsupported claim (gap), not a disproved one. The integer ν of the standard statement is the target that stage IntegralIwasawaTheory:L2 already specifies ('**nu is an integer**'). (Also recorded by an earlier worker: new (anticipated by the atlas stage description IntegralIwasawaTheory:L2, which stresses that ν is only an integer).)

issues.locator: Appendix A.2, Conjecture A.15, printed p. 207 (PDF 108), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical
issues.printed: The source asserts µ = λ = 0 and interprets this as boundedness of #Cl(Fn) as n →+∞.
issues.correction: … we have µ = λ = 0. In other words (by Theorem A.3), the p-parts #(Cl(F_n) ⊗ ℤ_p) = p^{e_n} are bounded as n → +∞.
issues.reason: By Theorem A.3, e_n = µp^n + λn + ν for large n, so µ = λ = 0 if and only if e_n = v_p(#Cl(F_n)) is bounded. The full class number also has a prime-to-p part, about which Iwasawa theory says nothing. Boundedness of #Cl(F_n) implies µ = λ = 0, but the converse would need the prime-to-p parts of the class numbers along the tower to stay bounded, which neither the notes nor Iwasawa's theorem provide (for abelian F, Washington's theorem controls one prime ℓ ≠ p at a time). So the 'in other words' asserts an equivalence that does not follow, and it replaces Greenberg's conjecture by a different, a priori stronger statement. (Also recorded by an earlier worker: new (the same point is flagged in the atlas stage description IntegralIwasawaTheory:L4: 'do not replace it by bounded full class numbers').)

issues.locator: Appendix A.2, opening paragraph, printed p. 206 (PDF 107), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical
issues.printed: The source presents Corollary 13.16 as an earlier application of Iwasawa’s theorem in the main conjecture discussion, asserting that in a Zp-extension, coprimality of any one class number to p implies coprimality of every other one.
issues.correction: Corollary 13.16 is about the tower F_n⁺ = ℚ(μ_{p^n})⁺: if p ∤ h₁⁺ then p ∤ h_n⁺ for all n. The general principle 'if one layer has class number prime to p, so do all layers' holds for ℤ_p-extensions satisfying hypothesis (H) (one prime above p, totally ramified). It follows from Proposition A.6 and Lemma A.7, not from Theorem A.3, and it is false for general ℤ_p-extensions.
issues.reason: Counterexample: F = ℚ(i), p = 5, F∞ = F·ℚ∞ the cyclotomic ℤ₅-extension. Here h(F) = 1. Both primes above 5 = (2+i)(2−i) are totally ramified in F_n/F, since 5 is totally ramified in ℚ_n/ℚ and [F_n : F] = 5^n. Chevalley's ambiguous class number formula for the cyclic extension F_n/F gives #Cl(F_n)^{Gal(F_n/F)} = h_F·∏_v e_v / ([F_n : F]·[E_F : E_F ∩ N F_n^×]) = 1·5^n·5^n/(5^n·1) = 5^n. The unit index is 1 because E_F = μ₄ has order prime to 5 while E_F/(E_F ∩ N F_n^×) is killed by 5^n. Hence 5 | h(F₁) although 5 ∤ h(F₀). Corollary 13.16's proof (printed p. 194) uses only Proposition 13.15 (= Proposition A.6) and Nakayama's lemma.

issues.printed: The proof claims binomial expansion leaves only the constant 1 in each expression indivisible by p, with these constants adding to p. It concludes ϕk+1(T) ≡ pϕk(T) (mod g).
issues.correction: In particular φ^{k+1}(T) ≡ pφ^k(T)·u (mod g) with u ≡ 1 (mod p); for p odd u = 1 + p·(poly), because Σ_{i=0}^{p−1}(pQ_k + 1)^i = p + pQ_k·p(p−1)/2 + p²(…). So φ^{k+1}(T) ∈ pφ^k(T)Λ + gΛ, and this is all the next step uses.
issues.reason: The congruence as printed is false. Take p = 3, g = T − 3 (distinguished, d = 1, n₀ = 0) and k = n₀ = 0. In V = Λ/(g) ≅ ℤ₃ (T ↦ 3), φ¹(T) = (1+T)³ − 1 ↦ 63, while pφ⁰(T) = 3T ↦ 9. The two agree only up to the unit 7 ≡ 1 (mod 3). The deduction Q_{n₀+1} ≡ 0 (mod p) goes through with the corrected form, since p is a non-zero-divisor on V, so the lemma stands.

issues.locator: Appendix B.2.1, footnote 16, printed p. 208 (PDF 109), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record; arXiv v2 identical
issues.printed: The source describes Deligne’s criterion for a motivic L(M, s): with L∞(M, s) its infinity Euler factor, s = j is critical exactly when both L∞(M, s) and L∞(M, 1−s) are free of poles at j.
issues.correction: … s = j is critical for L(M, s) if neither L∞(M, s) nor L∞(M^∨, 1−s) has a pole at s = j, where M^∨ is the dual motive.
issues.reason: Taken literally, the printed criterion contradicts the next sentence of the text. For M = M(f), f of weight k+2 with trivial character, L∞(M,s) = Γ_ℂ(s) = 2(2π)^{−s}Γ(s), and L∞(M,1−s) = Γ_ℂ(1−s) has poles at s = 1, 2, 3, …, so no j + 1 with 0 ≤ j ≤ k would be critical, whereas the text says the critical values are L(f,χ,j+1), 0 ≤ j ≤ k. With M^∨ ≅ M(k+1), L∞(M^∨, 1−s) = Γ_ℂ(k+2−s) has poles at s ≥ k+2, and the criterion gives exactly 1 ≤ s ≤ k+1. For M = ℚ(0) (the ζ example in the footnote) M^∨ = M, so that example is unaffected.

issues.printed: The proof uses geometric expansions for the summands to write the left side as −(1/p)Σ_{ξ∈µ_p}Σ_{n≥0}(1+T)^nε_D^{nc}ξ^n = −Σ_{n≥0}(1+T)^{pn}ε_D^{pcn}, and claims that summing yields the right side of (5-4).

issues.locator: §12.1, paragraph before Corollary 12.6, printed p. 180 (PDF 81), Essential Number Theory 4 (2025) version of record (page image checked); arXiv v2 identical

issues.printed: The proof uses the pseudomeasure property of ζ_p to assert ([g] − [1])ζ_p ∈ Λ(Γ) for every g ∈ Γ. It concludes by identifying I(Γ) as the topological ideal generated by those [g] − [1].
issues.correction: Use that I(Γ) = ([σ_a] − [1])Λ(Γ) is principal for a topological generator σ_a of the procyclic group Γ ≅ ℤ_p^× (p odd). This is stated for ℤ_p^× in the proof of Lemma 3.38. Then I(Γ)ζ_p = Λ(Γ)·([σ_a] − [1])ζ_p ⊆ Λ(Γ). The same holds for Γ^+.
issues.reason: The set {λ ∈ Λ(Γ) : λζ_p ∈ Λ(Γ)} is an ideal containing every [g] − [1]. The printed argument needs it to be closed in order to contain the topological ideal they generate, and that is not shown: multiplication by ζ_p is not a map Λ(Γ) → Λ(Γ). The principal-ideal argument avoids the point. The proof of Theorem 12.23 uses the same ingredient without citing it (E75).

For the real part, if x = lim v_i is real then x² = lim v_iv̄_i is a limit of real units, and x is the unique square root of x² in the pro-p group U_{n,1} (2 is a unit in ℤ_p).
issues.reason: The definitions in the notes take the closure first and then the plus and principal parts. The proof uses the other order. The two agree, but this needs the short argument above; it is not 'by definition'.

issues.locator: Corollary 1.9 i) and ii), arXiv v2 p. 5; Corollary 1.4 (i) and (ii), Annals p. 301
issues.printed: The source calls $\overline{A}_{g,r,d}(z_1, \ldots, z_{2g})=q^{2(1+(g-1)r^2} A_{g,r,d}(z_1^{-1}, \ldots, z_{2g}^{-1})$ the Poincaré dual of $A_{g,r,d}$ and asserts $\text{dim}\; H^{1 + (g-1)r^2} (\Lambda^{st}_{r,d}, \mathbb{C})=\text{dim}\; H^{1 + (g-1)r^2}(Higgs_{r,d}^{st}, \mathbb{C})=A_{g,r,d}(0)$. Both displays also occur in the published version.
issues.reason: Write D = 1+(g−1)r². The published proof (§6.11, pp. 351–352) gives the corrected statement. Higgs^st_{r,d} and Λ^st_{r,d} are unions of affine fibrations of ranks n⁺_i = D and n⁻_i over the components Z_i of the G_m-fixed locus, with dim Z_i = D − n⁻_i. So |Higgs^st(F_q)| = q^D Σ_i |Z_i(F_q)|, and by Poincaré duality on each Z_i, |Λ^st(F_q)| = Σ_i q^{n⁻_i}|Z_i(F_q)| = q^D A_{g,r,d}(σ_X^{−1}), not q^{2D}A_{g,r,d}(σ_X^{−1}). The top degree of Λ^st, of dimension D, is 2D; H^{2D} counts its irreducible components, and it is the degree whose dimension is A_{g,r,d}(0). Rank one: Higgs^st_{1,d} = Pic^d(X) × H⁰(X, Ω_X) and Λ^st_{1,d} = Pic^d(X). With A_{g,1,d} = ∏_i(1 − α_i) and ∏_i α_i = q^g, q^g A(α^{−1}) = A(α) = |Pic^d(X)(F_q)|, while the printed exponent gives q^g times too much; and dim H^{2g}(Pic^d) = 1 = A(0), while dim H^g(Pic^d) = C(2g, g). (g, r, d) = (1, 2, 1), for an elliptic curve E: Λ^st_{2,1} = E (Atiyah) and A_{1,2,1} = (1 − α_1)(1 − α_2), so q·A(α^{−1}) = |E(F_q)|; and dim H²(E) = 1 = A(0), while dim H¹(E) = 2. The '2(' of (ii)'s degree appears to have moved into (i)'s exponent.

The only proof offered is that it is 'completely parallel to that of Theorem 1.1', whose conclusion is in K_g. This is a gap in the justification, not a disproof of the stronger statement.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 5.5, p. 844
issues.printed: The source invokes Proposition 5.3 to obtain π_1^et(γ′_0)(σ)=τ′στ′^−1.
issues.correction: Before applying Proposition 5.3, check its hypotheses for γ′. From Lemma 2.2, ι′_et γ′ = ι′_et, so γ′ lies over k′_et, where k′ is the base field of W′. For every factor p_i: W′ → C′_i, Theorem 4.7(c) gives (p_i ι′)_et r(γ′)_et = (p_i ι′)_et γ′ = (p_i ι′)_et. Theorem 3.2 then gives p_i ι′ r(γ′) = p_i ι′, hence ι′ r(γ′) = ι′ and r(γ′) = id_{X′}. X′ is smooth and geometrically connected over k′ with a factor-dominant immersion into a product of non-rational hyperbolic curves (finite étale covers of hyperbolic curves are hyperbolic).
issues.reason: Proposition 5.3 applies only to automorphisms γ with r(γ) = id over the base field. The proof applies it to the base-changed γ′ from Lemma 2.2 without checking this. Lemma 2.2 is stated without uniqueness, so r(γ′) = id is not automatic. The check above supplies it.

issues.locator: Theorem A.8 proof, p. 857, formula after holim X=lim_n Tot^n Π*X; v2 TeX lines 2186–2189
issues.printed: Tot^n Π*X = ∏_(u∈I_n) X_(i_0)
issues.correction: The product describes the cosimplicial replacement (Π*X)^n. Tot^n is its partial totalization, defined by compatible maps from the truncated/coskeletal simplices; after the appropriate fibrant replacement these form the totalization tower.
issues.reason: Degree n of the cosimplicial replacement is not its n-th partial totalization. For the inverse diagram of two equal discrete two-point spaces indexed by a single arrow, the degree-one product has 2^3=8 elements (three arrows including identities), whereas Tot^1 imposes the arrow compatibility and has 2 elements. Use the genuine totalization tower for the cited Bousfield–Kan spectral sequence.

issues.locator: Appendix A.2.3, p. 858, relative cylinder projection; v2 TeX line 2218
issues.printed: The source calls X∧I → X a trivial fibration.
issues.correction: Use that X∧I→X is a weak equivalence and that the endpoint map is a cofibration in the undercategory. This is a cylinder object; do not assert that this particular projection is a fibration.
issues.reason: Take constant X={a,b,c}, with distinguished points a,b. The cylinder is {a}⊔{b}⊔Δ[1], projecting its interval component to c. The outer horn Λ²_0→Δ[1] with vertices (0,1,0) has valid edges 01=(0→1), 02=(0→0), but no 2-simplex filler, because 1→0 is absent. Hence the projection fails the horn-lifting property even as a constant pro-map. The weak-equivalence cylinder suffices for homotopy classes into a fibrant target; this does not disprove A.9 or A.10.

issues.locator: §4, Theorem 4.17 and its proof, p. 272 (published); arXiv v1, p. 21
issues.printed: The source asserts that B is uniformly finite projective over A exactly when B ⊗A A/ϖ is uniformly finite projective over A/ϖ. It attributes the first part to [15], Theorem 5.3.27, and describes the remainder as easy.
issues.correction: The 'if' direction needs an argument: lift an approximating map (A/ϖ)^r → B/ϖB with cokernel killed by a small power of ϖ to A^r → B, and kill the cokernel by an almost Nakayama lemma for a tight ideal (Gabber–Ramero, Lemma 5.1.6), using the p-power roots of ϖ available over K°.
issues.reason: Uniform finite projectivity over A/ϖ does not formally give it over A; the ϖ-adic completeness of A must be used through a Nakayama-type argument that the paper leaves out.

issues.reviewReason: Theorem 8.5 holds for every fan, including the complete fan of ℙ¹, for which X^ad_Σ is (ℙ¹)^ad (a complete fan's formal generic fibre is the analytification). The Frobenius φ(x_0 : x_1) = (x_0^p : x_1^p) preserves ∞ and 𝔸¹ = ℙ¹ ∖ {∞} at every level, so lim_φ |𝔸^{1,ad}_K| is an open subset of lim_φ |ℙ^{1,ad}_K|, and the homeomorphism of Theorem 8.5(iii) carries |𝔸^{1,ad}_{K♭}|, the complement of π^{-1}(∞) = {∞}, onto it. That is Theorem 1.5, so the introduction's statement is covered by the body and there is no gap; the exhaustion by rescaled discs is an alternative, not a missing step.

issues.citation: Scholze, "On torsion in the cohomology of locally symmetric varieties", Annals of Mathematics 182 (2015), 945–1066
issues.reviewReason:
The quote matches p. 957 and arXiv v2 p. 15.

The counterexample in the reason works:
- Take R^+ as the integral closure of 𝒪_K + R°°. Its image in R°/R°° = k[T^{1/p^∞}] is integral over k, so it lies in k, and T ∉ R^+.
- R°/R^+ is killed by m_K, so R^+ → R° is almost surjective.
- The rank-two specialization x of the Gauss point with |T(x)| = 1^+ lies in Spa(R, R^+) but not in Spa(R, R°). So the image of Spa(R, R°) → Spa(R, R^+) is not even closed, while V(ker) = V(0) is everything.

The correction matches ECD v4 Definition 5.7(ii), which I read.

One point for the lead. The parenthetical 'The paper applies the notion only with S^+ = S°' is not something the paper states. It should read instead: every use (Corollary 3.2.20, Lemma 2.2.9(ii), Theorem 3.3.18(ii), Theorem 4.1.1(ii), §4.2 p. 1022) concerns a map that is already a Zariski closed embedding built by Lemma 2.2.2 (a boundary, or a pullback of one). So the false implication 'strongly Zariski closed ⇒ Zariski closed' is never used downstream.

issues.reviewReason:
The published text on p. 984 reads 'In particular, X*(ε) → X* is an admissible blowup in the sense of Raynaud.' arXiv v2 p. 38 has 'blow-up'. In the TeX the sentence sits after \end{lem}, so the locator 'the sentence after Lemma 3.2.13' is right.

The mistake is real:
- Spf((R⊗̂ℤ_p^cycl)⟨u⟩/(uH̃a − p^ε)) is flat by Lemma 3.2.10, so it is exactly the chart of the blow-up of (H̃a, p^ε) on which H̃a generates.
- The paper itself says on p. 984 that on generic fibres 𝒳*(ε) ⊂ 𝒳* is the open subset where |Ha| ≥ |p|^ε. An admissible blow-up would be an isomorphism on generic fibres.

Misprint with affects 'nothing' is acceptable, since nothing later uses properness.

issues.citation: Scholze, "On torsion in the cohomology of locally symmetric varieties", Annals of Mathematics 182 (2015), 945–1066
issues.reviewReason:
The quote matches p. 986 and arXiv v2 p. 40. The degree slip is real:
- the same proof, p. 987, says 'Both vertical maps are finite étale of degree p^{g(g+1)/2} (using that m ≥ 1)';
- Corollary 3.2.23 normalises by 1/p^{(m′−m)g(g+1)/2}.
The degrees p^{g(g+1)/2} and p^{g(g+1)/2+g} are right.

The correction and reason, however, repeat 'finite locally free' integrally, and that is false for 0 < ε < 1/2: F̃ is not flat (see my newIssues entry on the same sentence). Reword the correction as: 'F̃_𝔛(p^{-1}ε) and F̃_𝔄(p^{-1}ε) are finite, and after inverting p finite étale of degree p^{g(g+1)/2}, resp. p^{g(g+1)/2+g}.' Run the degree argument on generic fibres, via 𝒳(p^{-1}ε) ≅ 𝒳_{Γ_0(p)}(ε)_a → 𝒳(ε) (Theorem 3.2.15(iii)), or integrally over 𝔛(0). Item 39 repeats the integral claim; see itemChanges.

issues.reviewReason:
The quote matches p. 1020 and arXiv v2 p. 69. The whole proof of (i) for G is that sentence, and nothing in the construction compares R^+_{K^p}, built from the Zariski-closed subspaces of the Siegel 𝒴*_{K^p}(J), with the finite-level rings R^+_{J,K_p}. So 'affects: the proof' is right.

The gap appears fillable without Bhatt–Scholze 7.4. I checked the argument at the rational level but not the plus-ring identifications in full:
1. 𝒱_J is the preimage of 𝒱_{J,K_p} := the preimage in 𝒳^{u*}_{K_pK^p} of the Siegel affinoid.
2. colim_{K_p} R_{J,K_p} → R_{J,∞} has dense image. Chain the density of Lemma 2.2.2 with part (i) for G′, since the Siegel finite-level rings factor through R_{J,K_p}.
3. |𝒱_J| → |𝒱_{J,K_p}| is surjective, so the spectral norms agree. This gives R°_{J,∞} = the completion of colim R°_{J,K_p}.
The correction says 'e.g.', so it stands.

One inaccuracy in the reason: it calls X**_{K_pK^p} 'normal varieties'. The paper defines X^{u*}_K (\uast, an underlined star) as the scheme-theoretic image of X*_K in Y*_{K′} (p. 1018) and does not claim it is normal.

issues.locator: §3.3, the paragraph before Lemma 3.3.9, p. 1008; Theorem 3.3.18(i), p. 1012, and the last sentence of its proof, p. 1014 (published); arXiv v2: before Lemma III.3.9, p. 58; Theorem III.3.18(i), p. 62; its proof, p. 63. Same text in both.; with its consequences Theorem 4.1.1(i), Lemma 4.3.3 and the proof of Theorem 4.3.1, pp. 1018–1030
issues.printed: For a subset J ⊂ {1, …, 2g} having cardinality g, the source defines the projective homogeneous coordinate s_J and the open affinoid Fl_J ⊂ Fl by |s_{J′}| ≤ |s_J| for every J′. It asserts transitive permutation of these Fl_J by GSp_{2g}(ℤ_p). On p. 1014 it says stability of the desired property under GSp_{2g}(ℚ_p) gives it on Fl_{g+1,…,2g} and hence every Fl_J.
issues.reason:
Why the transitivity fails. Take g = 2, coordinates (a_1, a_2, b_1, b_2) with ψ = Σ(a_i b′_i − a′_i b_i), and J = {1,2} versus J′ = {1,3}.
- For W ∈ Fl(ℚ_p) with primitive integral Plücker vector, W ∈ Fl_J iff s_J(W̄) ≠ 0 in 𝔽_p, i.e. iff W̄ is transversal to the complementary coordinate plane.
- The complement of {1,2} is span(e_3,e_4), a Lagrangian. Exactly p³ Lagrangians W̄ ⊂ 𝔽_p^4 are transversal to it (graphs of symmetric maps).
- The complement of {1,3} is span(e_2,e_4), a symplectic plane. Of the (p+1)(p²+1) Lagrangians of 𝔽_p^4, exactly (p+1)² meet it: each meets it in one of its p+1 lines ℓ, and ℓ lies in p+1 Lagrangians. That leaves p³ − p.
- GSp_4(ℤ_p) acts compatibly with reduction, and LG(ℤ_p) → LG(𝔽_p) is surjective. So no γ ∈ GSp_4(ℤ_p) carries Fl_{12} onto Fl_{13}, although Fl_{13} is nonempty (W = span((1,0,0,1),(0,1,1,0)) is Lagrangian with |s_{13}| = |s_{12}| = 1 = max).

Why the Lagrangian Fl_J cover Fl. Every Lagrangian over a field is transversal to one of the 2^g coordinate Lagrangians. Applied to the reduction of a normalised Plücker vector over the valuation ring of a point, this shows that the maximum of |s_J| is always attained at a Lagrangian J.

Where the proof breaks. The last step of the proof of (i) ('and then for all Fl_J') reaches only the orbit of Fl_{g+1,…,2g}, i.e. the Lagrangian J. I did not decide whether 𝒱_J is affinoid perfectoid for non-Lagrangian J: Fl_{13} is a finite union of rational pieces of Lagrangian Fl_{J′}, but that does not make its preimage affinoid. The same restriction applies to Theorem 4.1.1(i), Lemma 4.3.3 and the proof of Theorem 4.3.1, which rest on Theorem 3.3.18(i); since the 2^g Lagrangian charts cover Fl, every later use goes through (found independently by two review readers).

issues.locator: §3.2.1, Corollary 3.2.6 (the displayed formula) and its proof, pp. 977–978; Proposition 3.2.8(i)–(ii) and its proof, p. 979 (published); arXiv v2: Corollary III.2.6, p. 33; Proposition III.2.8, p. 34. Same text in both.
issues.printed: The source asserts, for every flat p-adically complete ℤ_p^cycl-algebra R′ receiving R → R′, that C_m(R′) = {s ∈ A[p^m](R′) | s ≡ 0 mod p^{(1−ε)/p^m}}. Its proof uses the action of F on R/p^{1−ε} to obtain s = 0 ∈ C_m(R/p^{(1−ε)/p^m}). The proof of Proposition 3.2.8 claims (i), (ii) follow immediately from Corollary 3.2.6’s displayed formula.
issues.correction:
Only the inclusion ⊇ holds in general. Equality holds when x^{p^m} ∈ p^{1−ε}R′ implies x ∈ p^{(1−ε)/p^m}R′, for example when R′ is integrally closed in R′[1/p] (R′ = 𝒪_K).

The uniqueness of C_m and Proposition 3.2.8(i)–(ii) remain true, by Lemma 3.2.4 as in the paper's proof of Proposition 3.2.8(iii). Suppose C, C′ ⊂ A[p^m] both agree with ker F^m modulo p^{1−ε}. Then the universal point of C gives a point of A[p^m]/C′ over the p-adically complete flat R-algebra 𝒪(C). That point vanishes modulo p^{1−ε}, so it is 0, and C ⊂ C′.
issues.reason:
Counterexample:
- Take R = 𝒪_C, A = E_{𝒪_C} for an ordinary elliptic curve E over ℤ_p, ε = 0 (Ha is invertible) and m = 1. Then C_1 = E[p]° ≅ μ_p.
- Take R′ = {(a,b) ∈ 𝒪_C × 𝒪_C : a ≡ b mod p^{1/(p−1)}}. It is flat, and p-adically complete, since p²(𝒪_C)² ∩ R′ ⊂ pR′ and R′ is closed.
- s = (ζ_p, 1) ∈ μ_p(R′) = C_1(R′), because v(ζ_p − 1) = 1/(p−1).
- s ≡ 0 mod p^{1/p} would need (ζ_p − 1, 0) ∈ p^{1/p}R′, i.e. v((ζ_p − 1)/p^{1/p}) = 1/(p−1) − 1/p ≥ 1/(p−1). That is false. The example also works for p = 2.

The failing step is the extraction of p^m-th roots: F^m(s) = 0 modulo p^{1−ε} says that the coordinates x of s satisfy x^{p^m} ∈ p^{1−ε}R′.

The paper uses the formula over 𝒪(C_m), which need not be normal, in two places: in the uniqueness argument ('it is enough to prove that the final formula holds for any C_m') and in Proposition 3.2.8(i)–(ii). The same root extraction on p. 987 ('thus s modulo p^{(1−ε)/p} is 0') is harmless there, since only geometric points (S = 𝒪_K) are needed.

issues.locator: §3.2.2, proof of Theorem 3.2.15, p. 986 (published); arXiv v2: proof of Theorem III.2.15, p. 40. This is the sentence of E4; this entry concerns 'locally free', not the degree.
issues.printed: The source concludes that F̃_{𝔛(p^{−1}ε)} and F̃_{𝔄(p^{−1}ε)} are finite, locally free maps of degree g(g + 1)/2.
issues.correction: F̃_{𝔛(p^{−1}ε)} and F̃_{𝔄(p^{−1}ε)} are finite, and they become finite locally free (indeed finite étale) of degrees p^{g(g+1)/2} and p^{g(g+1)/2+g} after inverting p. For 0 < ε < 1/2 they are not flat. For ε = 0 they are finite locally free.
issues.reason:
Work modulo the maximal ideal of ℤ_p^cycl. This ideal contains p^{1−ε}, so F̃ there is the relative-Frobenius-type map of Lemma 3.2.14:
- For ε > 0 it goes from Spec R̄[u]/(u·Ha) to Spec R̄[u′]/(u′·Ha), where R̄ is smooth of dimension d = g(g+1)/2.
- It is Frobenius on R̄ and sends u′ ↦ u^p.

Take a point y with Ha(y) = 0 and u′(y) = 0. Let R′ be the Frobenius fibre, of length p^d, with Ha ∈ its maximal ideal. The fibre over y is R′[u]/(uHa, u^p) = R′ ⊕ ⊕_{i=1}^{p−1}(R′/Ha)u^i, of length ≥ p^d + p − 1.

Over an ordinary point of the same component {u′ = 0} the fibre is R′, of length p^d. That component is connected to the non-ordinary locus, and the ordinary locus is dense in each component of the special fibre. So the rank jumps and the map is not flat.

The paper never uses integral flatness:
- p. 987 says the maps are finite étale on the good-reduction generic fibre;
- Corollary 3.2.22(i) claims only that ϕ[1/p] is finite and flat, and factors ϕ = τ∘ψ with τ not an isomorphism integrally;
- the traces in Corollary 3.2.23 are taken after inverting p.

issues.locator: §3.1, Definition 3.1.1 and the two sentences after it, p. 971; §3.2.2, the paragraph defining 𝒳_{K_p}, p. 983 (published); arXiv v2: Definition III.1.1 and the remark after it, pp. 27–28; p. 37. Same text in both (TeX l. 918, 924).
issues.printed: The source defines Γ_0(p^m) = {γ ∈ GSp_{2g}(ℤ_p) | γ ≡ (∗ ∗; 0 ∗) mod p^m, det γ ≡ 1 mod p^m}. It describes the added requirement det γ ≡ 1 mod p^m as slightly nonstandard, and uses the symplectic similitude factor to assert that X*_{Γ_0(p^m)} is naturally over ℚ(ζ_{p^m}).
issues.correction: The extra condition should be on the similitude factor, c(γ) ≡ 1 mod p^m, where γ^tJγ = c(γ)J. Then c(Γ_0(p^m)) = 1 + p^mℤ_p and X*_{Γ_0(p^m)} is naturally a ℚ(ζ_{p^m})-scheme.
issues.reason:
For γ ∈ GSp_{2g}, det γ = c(γ)^g. So the printed condition gives c(Γ_0(p^m)) = {c ∈ ℤ_p^× : c^g ≡ 1 mod p^m}; every such c occurs, e.g. via γ = diag(1,…,1,c,…,c).

This is larger than 1 + p^mℤ_p whenever x ↦ x^g is not injective on (ℤ/p^m)^×. For example, take g = 2, p odd and γ = diag(1,1,−1,−1): it is block upper-triangular with c(γ) = −1 and det γ = 1.

The similitude factor on X_{Γ_0(p^m)} is then determined only up to such c, so there is no tautological ζ_{p^m}, and X*_{Γ_0(p^m)} is not naturally over ℚ(ζ_{p^m}). The paper needs that structure: p. 983 defines 𝒳_{K_p} from X_{K_p} ⊗_{ℚ(ζ_{p^m})} ℚ_p^cycl 'using the tautological element ζ_{p^m} ∈ ℚ_p^cycl and ζ_{p^m} ∈ 𝒪_{X_{K_p}}, given by the symplectic similitude factor'.

The context makes the intended condition clear. For g = 1 the two conditions agree. Extraction item 26 reproduces 'det γ'; see itemChanges.

issues.locator: §2.3.2, proof of Corollary 2.3.5, p. 963 (published); arXiv v2: proof of Corollary II.3.5, p. 20. Same text in both.
issues.printed: The source says it must still establish the almost-isomorphism property for A → Hom_{A_0^{1/p^∞}}(g^{1/p^∞}A_0^{1/p^∞}, A). It claims the explicit expression for A and the u^i basis reduce this to the next lemma.
issues.correction:
The reduction to Lemma 2.3.6 needs a bound that is uniform in i.

The bound: take C ∈ ℤ_{≥0} with C·v(f) ≥ v(g) for the finitely many height-one primes containing f. Then, by normality of the A_0^{1/p^n}, g^e m ∈ fA_0^{1/p^∞} implies f^{Ce} m ∈ fA_0^{1/p^∞}.

Now let φ ∈ Hom(J, A) and choose k with C/p^k ≤ ε. Then (uf)^{C/p^k}φ is supported on finitely many u^i, namely those near the support of φ(g^{1/p^k}). Lemma 2.3.6 then applies to finitely many summands. The corollary stands.
issues.reason:
J = g^{1/p^∞}A_0^{1/p^∞} is not finitely generated, so Hom(J, ⊕_i M_i) = lim_k ⊕_i M_i, with transition maps multiplication by g^{1/p^k − 1/p^{k+1}}. This can be strictly larger than ⊕_i Hom(J, M_i), which is all that Lemma 2.3.6 controls.

Example, within the corollary's hypotheses: A_0 = 𝔽_p[x,y], f = x, g = xy. Define φ(g^{1/p^k}) = Σ_{j=1}^{k−1} x^{1+1/p^k−1/p^j} y^{1/p^k} u^{j+1}. It is compatible:
- g^{1/p^k−1/p^{k+1}}φ(g^{1/p^{k+1}}) = φ(g^{1/p^k});
- the new j = k term becomes x·y^{1/p^k}u^{k+1} = 0, since f·u^i = 0 for i ≥ 1.
Its u-support is unbounded, so φ is not in the image of A. It is only almost in the image: (uf)^ε φ has finite support.

I checked the bound in the correction with divisorial valuations on the normal noetherian A_0^{1/p^n}; the proof of Lemma 2.3.6 (p. 965) uses the same kind of constant C.

issues.locator: §2.2, Lemma 2.2.8, p. 957 (published); arXiv v2: Lemma II.2.8, p. 15.
issues.printed: Lemma 2.2.8, citing [43, Prop. 3.6.9(c)], asserts almost surjectivity of R° → S° whenever R → S is a surjection between perfectoid K-algebras.
issues.correction: [43, Prop. 3.6.9(c)] covers only characteristic 0, for strict homomorphisms of perfectoid uniform Banach ℚ_p-algebras; a surjection is strict by the open mapping theorem. In characteristic p the statement follows from the paper's own Lemma 2.2.5, applied to the Zariski closed subspace V(ker(R → S)), or from [43, Remark 3.1.6] as used in [43, Prop. 3.6.9(a)].
issues.reason: In §2.2, K is any perfectoid field, and the lemma is stated for perfectoid K-algebras. Kedlaya–Liu arXiv:1301.0792v5 (9 May 2015), Proposition 3.6.9(c), reads: 'Let ψ : A → B be a strict homomorphism of perfectoid uniform Banach ℚ_p-algebras. Then ψ is almost optimal and ψ(A) is perfectoid.' I did not check the Astérisque 371 numbering. The paper says it does not need this lemma.
issues.known: Recorded in the atlas as PerfectoidSpaces/E19 (against Étale cohomology of diamonds, which cites the same proposition; its locator notes that this paper's Lemma II.2.8 carries the same citation). Not corrected in print.

issues.locator: §3.2.5, proof of Lemma 3.2.30, p. 999 (published); arXiv v2: proof of Lemma III.2.30, p. 51. Same text in both (TeX \mathcal{Y}_m^\ast\setminus\partial twice).
issues.printed: The source derives from the preceding statement an adic-space map 𝒴*_m ∖ ∂ → Spa(S_∞, S_∞^+) in the sense of [55, Def. 2.1.5], then combines maps to obtain 𝒴*_m ∖ ∂ → Spa(U, U^+).
issues.correction: 𝒴*_∞ ∖ ∂ in both places.
issues.reason: The lemma concerns the tilt of 𝒴*_∞ ∖ ∂. The map to Spa(S_∞, S_∞^+) uses that S_∞^+ is the completion of colim S_m^+, which maps to functions on 𝒴*_∞ ∖ ∂ but not on the finite-level 𝒴*_m ∖ ∂. issues.printed: The source asserts that |h| ≤ |p|^{C+1} defines an open set inside U disjoint from the boundary, and concludes that this set is empty.
issues.correction: '… an open subset of U that is contained in the boundary (it does not meet U ∖ ∂); thus, it is empty.'
issues.reason: On U ∖ ∂ one has |h| ≥ |p|^C > |p|^{C+1}, so the set misses U ∖ ∂ and lies in the nowhere dense boundary. An open set that does not meet the boundary need not be empty. issues.locator: §4.2, proof of Corollary 4.2.3, p. 1024 (published); arXiv v2: proof of Corollary IV.2.3, p. 72
issues.printed: Assuming failure of the last statement, the source selects the largest violating codimension c among the H̃_i, then the smallest i < d attaining c. It asserts codim H̃_i = c < d − i and codim H̃_k > c when k < i. It claims E^j(H̃_k) vanishes when j < c with j + k < d, since otherwise codim H̃_k ≤ j < c together with j + k < d would contradict the selection of c.
issues.correction: choose the minimal one, c (the minimal codimension among the H̃_i with i < d and codim H̃_i < d − i).
issues.reason: Call H̃_k violating if k < d and codim H̃_k < d − k. With c the maximal violating codimension, neither step of the proof holds. First, a violating H̃_k with k < i has codimension ≤ c and ≠ c (i is minimal), so < c; this contradicts 'the codimension of H̃_k for k < i is greater than c'. Second, 'codim H̃_k ≤ j < c' is no contradiction with a maximal c. That second step is what kills the differentials d_r : E_r^{c−r,i+r−1} → E_r^{c,i} into the codimension-c term (their sources have j = c − r < c and j + k = i + c − 1 < d), so the argument needs it. With c minimal both steps hold. For k < i, a violating H̃_k has codimension ≥ c and ≠ c; a non-violating one has codimension ≥ d − k > d − i > c. A nonzero E^j(H̃_k) with j < c and j + k < d would make H̃_k violating with codimension ≤ j < c. The targets E^{c+r}(H̃_{i−r+1}) have codimension ≥ c + r in any case (Venjakob). So a codimension-c subquotient of E^c(H̃_i) survives into H̃^BM_{2d−i−c} = 0, the intended contradiction. Checked on a render of the published page and in the v2 TeX.

issues.printed: For compact X_K, the source claims all of [17, Conj. 1.5] follows, apart from obtaining non-strict codimension inequalities where strict ones are requested. It gives l_0 = d and q_0 = 0 and also points to [17, Th. 1.4].
issues.correction: (Note that here l_0 = 0 and q_0 = d.)
issues.reason: With the Calegari–Emerton/Calegari–Geraghty invariants l_0 = rk G(ℝ) − rk K_∞ − rk A (A the maximal ℚ-split central torus) and q_0 = (dim_ℝ X − l_0)/2, a group as in §4 has G(ℝ) with a compact Cartan subgroup (it has a compact inner form, §4 opening paragraph) and no split centre. So l_0 = 0 and q_0 = dim_ℂ X_K = d. For G = Sp_{2g}: rk Sp_{2g}(ℝ) = g = rk U(g), so l_0 = 0 and q_0 = g(g+1)/2 = d. These are the values under which Corollary 4.2.3 (vanishing above d, codimension ≥ d − i below d) matches the conjecture's statement around the middle degree q_0; with l_0 = d and q_0 = 0 it would not. I did not reopen [17] (network limited to errata); the definitions are the ones quoted in the atlas (PAPER-CALEGARI-GERAGHTY-18 items def-l0 / l0-invariant, PAPER-CARAIANI-SCHOLZE-17/E14, and the CompletedCohomologyPartII decomposition).

issues.printed: Corollary 5.1.11 takes T_cl from Theorem 4.3.1 and asserts that every continuous quotient T_cl → A with discrete A admits a unique continuous h-dimensional G_{F,S}-determinant D valued in A. The proof says the open ideal I = ker(T_cl → A) includes an intersection of finitely many I_{K,k} = ker(T_cl → T_{K,k}), by the topology’s definition, and treats this as proving the result.
issues.correction: Take T_cl = T_{cl,m} with m > n if F is totally real and m ≥ n if F is CM. With this hypothesis every weight mk (k ≥ 1) in the topology is in the range of Corollaries 5.1.7/5.1.10.
issues.reason: Theorem 4.3.1 fixes an arbitrary integer m ≥ 1 and topologizes T by the maps to End(H^0(𝒳*_{K_pK^p}, ω^{⊗mk} ⊗ ℐ)) for all k ≥ 1, so weight m itself occurs. The determinants with values in T_{K,k} come from Corollaries 5.1.7/5.1.10, which fix 'k > n, resp. k ≥ n', because Proposition 5.1.1 and Theorem 5.1.2 need π_∞ to be the holomorphic discrete series π_k. For m ≤ n (resp. m < n) an open ideal may contain only intersections involving I_{K,mk} with mk ≤ n (resp. < n), for which the paper supplies no determinant. So the corollary as stated is unproved for small m. The paper's only use is repaired by the author himself: the proof of Corollary 5.2.6 (p. 1045) takes 'the topological ring T_{K^{S^+}} defined as in Theorem 4.3.1 for m large enough' (there m is Theorem 4.3.1's weight multiplier, while §5.2 uses m for the coefficient exponent in ℤ/p^m). Nothing downstream is affected.

issues.locator: §5.3, the paragraph between Corollary 5.3.5 and Lemma 5.3.6, p. 1050 (published); arXiv v2: before Lemma V.3.6, p. 95
issues.printed: The source chooses a new rational prime with ℓ ≠ p and ℓ ≥ 3, requiring that ℓ not divide [F̃ : F]. It concludes that F̃ and F^{cycl_ℓ} are linearly disjoint.
issues.correction: Also require I_{0,ℓ} = I_0. This is possible: by construction (p. 1048) I_{0,ℓ} = I_0 for infinitely many ℓ, and only finitely many ℓ divide [F̃ : F].
issues.reason: The proof of Lemma 5.3.6 works with this ℓ. It asserts that A[T^{±1}] → ∏_{χ : ℤ_ℓ → W(𝔽̄_p)^×, Ĩ_{0,χ} = I_0} A is injective, and derives I^{4(d+1)} = 0 for the preimage I of ∏ Ĩ_χ from that injectivity. Injectivity holds when the index set is infinite: a Laurent polynomial over A vanishing at infinitely many ℓ-power roots of unity, whose differences are units in W(𝔽̄_p), is 0 (Vandermonde). The condition Ĩ_{0,χ} = I_0 (so I_0·A ⊂ Ĩ_χ) is also what lets the twisted determinant factor through Gal(F̃·F^{cycl_ℓ}/F), since P_g is defined only modulo I_0. By construction, for a given ℓ only the ideal I_{0,ℓ} is known to occur as Ĩ_{0,χ} for infinitely many χ. So I_0 is guaranteed to occur infinitely often only when I_{0,ℓ} = I_0; for another ℓ the index set may be finite or empty, and then I need not be nilpotent. The earlier primes ℓ, ℓ′ (p. 1048) were chosen with this condition ('with I_{0,ℓ} = I_{0,ℓ′} = I_0'); the new one is not.

issues.locator: §5.3, proof of Lemma 5.3.10 (the claim Q_m ∈ S[XT^m]), pp. 1053–1054 (published); arXiv v2: proof of Lemma V.3.10, p. 98
issues.printed: The source places Q′ in S[[X, XT]], hence in S[T][[X]], and states Q′Q_0 ∈ S[T, X]. It expands Q′ = Σ_{a≥0} Q′_a(T)X^a with coefficients Q′_a(T) ∈ S[T], asserting Q′_aQ_0 = 0 once a is sufficiently large. Since Q_0 ∈ S[T] has 1 as its constant coefficient, it concludes Q′_a = 0 and therefore Q′ ∈ S[T, X].
issues.correction: Swap the roles of X and T: Q′ ∈ S[[T, XT]], so Q′ ∈ S[X][[T]]; write Q′ = Σ_{a≥0} Q′_a(X)T^a with Q′_a(X) ∈ S[X]; then Q′_aQ_0 is the T^a-coefficient of Q′Q_0 = Q, hence 0 for a large, and as Q_0 ∈ S[X] has constant coefficient 1 (so is a non-zero-divisor) Q′_a = 0.
issues.reason: Here Q_m = 1 for m < 0 and Q′ = ∏_{m>0} Q_m with Q_m ∈ S[[XT^m]]. For m ≥ 2, XT^m ∉ S[[X, XT]], since monomials X^{i+j}T^j there have T-degree at most their X-degree; but XT^m = T^{m−1}(XT) ∈ S[[T, XT]]. The paragraph before establishes Q_0 ∈ S[X] ('Q ≡ Q_0 mod T so, in particular, Q_0 ∈ S[X]'), so 'Q_0 ∈ S[T]' contradicts it. In the printed X-expansion the X^a-coefficient of Q′Q_0 is Σ_b c_bQ′_{a−b}(T), where Q_0 = Σ c_bX^b, not Q′_aQ_0, so the step fails as written. After the swap it is correct.

issues.locator: §5.3, proof of Lemma 5.3.8 (multiplicativity of D^{(m)}), the display before Lemma 5.3.12, p. 1055 (published); arXiv v2: p. 99
issues.printed: The source invokes the multiplicity of D_0^{(m)} to express the target identity as D_0^{(m)}((1 − U(x + y) + Uxy)(1 + Ux + U²x² + ⋯)(1 + Uy + U²y² + ⋯))|_{U=1} = 1. It sets f = (1 − U(x + y) + Uxy)(1 + Ux + U²x² + ⋯)(1 + Uy + U²y² + ⋯) ∈ 1 + US[G][U], reducing multiplicativity of D^{(m)} to the subsequent lemma.
issues.correction: f = (1 − U(x + y) + Uxy)(1 + Uy + U²y² + ⋯)(1 + Ux + U²x² + ⋯), i.e. multiply by (1 − Uy)^{−1} before (1 − Ux)^{−1}.
issues.reason: Lemma 5.3.12 requires f|_{U=1} = 1. S[G] is non-commutative when G is (in the application G = Gal(F̃/F)), and the printed f has f|_{U=1} = (1 − x)(1 − y)(1 − x)^{−1}(1 − y)^{−1}, a commutator. Example: x = εg, y = δh with ε² = δ² = 0 and gh ≠ hg gives f|_{U=1} = 1 + εδ(gh − hg) ≠ 1. With the factors reversed, f|_{U=1} = (1 − x)(1 − y)(1 − y)^{−1}(1 − x)^{−1} = 1 and still f ≡ 1 mod I. Since D_0^{(m)} is multiplicative with commutative values, D_0^{(m)}(f) does not depend on the order, so the desired equation is unchanged and the reduction works. ('multiplicity' is also a slip for 'multiplicativity'.)

issues.locator: §5.4, proof of Corollary 5.4.2, p. 1059 (published); arXiv v2: proof of Corollary V.4.2, p. 103
issues.printed: The source says that a twist by a character 𝔸_F^× → ℤ/2ℤ, whose archimedean components are prescribed, makes π′ occur in H^i(X_K, ℳ_{ξ,K}) ⊗_{ℤ̄_p} ℂ. It adopts this occurrence as an assumption for the remaining argument.
issues.correction: Allow the quadratic character η to ramify at an auxiliary finite set S′ of places disjoint from S. Run the argument with S ∪ S′ to get σ_{π⊗η}, and put σ_π = σ_{π⊗η} ⊗ η^{−1}. Doing this for two choices of η with disjoint auxiliary sets, and comparing by Chebotarev and Brauer–Nesbitt, shows that σ_π is unramified outside S.
issues.reason: For π′⊗η to occur at a level K = K_SK^S, η must be unramified outside S. A quadratic Hecke character with prescribed archimedean components that is unramified outside S need not exist. Example: F = ℚ, p = 5, S = {5}, n = 1, π = π′|·|^{−1} with π′ an odd character of order 4 and conductor 5 (regular L-algebraic, unramified outside S). Here X̃_K ≅ Ẑ^×/K and X_K ≅ Ẑ^×/{±1}K (K_5 = 1 + 5ℤ_5, K_ℓ = ℤ_ℓ^× for ℓ ≠ 5), so π′ occurs in H^0(X̃_K) but not in H^0(X_K), which sees only even characters. The only quadratic characters of ℚ^×\𝔸^× unramified outside 5 are 1 and the character of ℚ(√5), and both are even, so no admissible twist exists. issues.locator: §5.4, proof of Corollary 5.4.2, p. 1060 (published); arXiv v2: proof of Corollary V.4.2, p. 103
issues.printed: The source asserts that the first kernel is contained in the second for the maps T_{F,S} → T_{F,S}(K, ξ, i) and T_{F,S} → ∏_{m≥1} T_{F,S}(K, ξ, i, m), respectively. Invoking Theorem 5.4.1 together with [19, Example 2.32], it deduces a continuous determinant D of G_{F,S}, of dimension n, valued in T_{F,S}(K, ξ, i)/I with I nilpotent.
issues.correction: The true containment is the reverse: ker(T_{F,S} → ∏_m T_{F,S}(K, ξ, i, m)) ⊂ ker(T_{F,S} → T_{F,S}(K, ξ, i)). So T_{F,S}(K, ξ, i) is a quotient of B = im(T_{F,S} → ∏_m T_{F,S}(K, ξ, i, m)). Theorem 5.4.1 (N uniform in m) and [19, Example 2.32] give a determinant on B/(B ∩ ∏_m I_m), whose ideal has N-th power 0. Its push-forward along B ↠ T_{F,S}(K, ξ, i) is a determinant with values in T_{F,S}(K, ξ, i)/Ī, with Ī^N = 0.
issues.reason: Put H^i = H^i(X_K, ℳ_{ξ,K}). There is a Hecke-equivariant exact sequence 0 → H^i/p^m → H^i(X_K, ℳ_{ξ,K}/p^m) → H^{i+1}[p^m] → 0. An operator killing every H^i(X_K, ℳ/p^m) kills every H^i/p^m, hence kills H^i (H^i is finitely generated over a finite extension of ℤ_p, so ∩_m p^mH^i = 0); this gives the reverse containment. The printed containment would need an operator killing H^i to kill H^{i+1}[p^m] too. That fails whenever a Hecke eigensystem occurs in the torsion of H^{i+1} but not in H^i. Example in the setting of Theorem 5.4.1, which allows stacky levels: F = ℚ, n = 1, p = 2, K = Ẑ^×, i = 1. Then X_K = [pt/{±1}], H^1(X_K, ℤ_2) = 0 and H^1(X_K, ℤ/2) = ℤ/2, so the first kernel is all of T and the second is not. The same step recurs in the proof of Corollary 5.4.4 and in footnote 29; Remark 5.4.5 calls the result for im(T → ∏_m …) 'slightly stronger', which is consistent only with the corrected direction. The stated results, including I^N = 0, remain true.

issues.locator: proof of Lemma 2.9 (existence of generic points), p. 13 (arXiv:1709.07343v4, 14 April 2026)
issues.printed: The source considers the cofiltered family of opens U ⊂ X/R satisfying U ∩ Z ≠ ∅ and having quasicompact preimage in X. To establish existence, it seeks a point in their intersection. Each preimage is open and quasicompact, hence compact Hausdorff in the constructible topology. It argues that their nonemptiness makes their intersection nonempty, and consequently the U’s also have a nonempty intersection.
issues.correction: Intersect with Z. With π : X → X/R, the sets π⁻¹(U) ∩ π⁻¹(Z), for basic opens U meeting Z, are closed in the constructible topology of X (π⁻¹(U) is quasicompact open, π⁻¹(Z) is closed, hence pro-constructible), nonempty, and cofiltered (U₁ ∩ U₂ ∩ Z ≠ ∅ by irreducibility of Z, and the basis is stable under finite intersections). By compactness of the constructible topology they have a common point x. Then π(x) ∈ Z lies in every basic open meeting Z, so it is a generic point of Z.
issues.reason: A point of the intersection of the U’s need not lie in Z, so nonemptiness of that intersection does not give a generic point of Z. Example within the lemma’s hypotheses: X = X/R = Spec of a DVR {η, s}, R the diagonal, Z = {s}; the only open meeting Z is the whole space, so the intersection is {η, s} and contains η ∉ Z. (The conclusion of the lemma is unaffected: the repaired argument is the same compactness argument with π⁻¹(Z) added.)

issues.reviewReason: The image of p. 13 prints exactly the quoted argument: it proves only that the intersection of the basic opens U meeting Z is nonempty, which does not give a point of Z. issues.locator: proof of Lemma 2.10 (existence of generic points), p. 13 (arXiv:1709.07343v4, 14 April 2026)
issues.printed: The source seeks a generic point for each irreducible closed Z̄ ⊂ X/R. It identifies this with nonemptiness of the intersection of the quasicompact opens V0 ⊂ X/R satisfying V0 ∩ Z̄ ≠ ∅. Compactness in the constructible topology is then used to make the intersection of their preimages in X nonempty and to conclude the claim.
issues.correction: Equivalently, the intersection of Z̄ with all quasicompact open V₀ ⊂ X/R meeting Z̄ (and having quasicompact preimage) is nonempty. This follows from compactness of the constructible topology of the (reduced to quasicompact, hence spectral) X applied to the cofiltered family of nonempty constructibly closed sets π⁻¹(V₀) ∩ π⁻¹(Z̄); a point of Z̄ in all such V₀ is a generic point since these V₀ form a basis.
issues.reason: The asserted equivalence is false as a logical step: a point in the intersection of the V₀ need not lie in Z̄, and then it does not give a generic point of Z̄ (same Spec-of-a-DVR example as for Lemma 2.9: the intersection is the whole space for Z̄ = {s}). The repair is immediate by adding π⁻¹(Z̄), which is pro-constructible.

issues.locator: proof of Proposition 3.5, p. 15 (arXiv:1709.07343v4, 14 April 2026)
issues.printed: The source asserts R° ⊂ ⋃_{k≥0} Φ^{−k}(R₀), from which it deduces R° ⊂ ϖ^{−n}R₀ and the required boundedness.
issues.correction: Only topologically nilpotent elements are covered: for x ∈ R°, ϖx is topologically nilpotent, so (ϖx)^{p^k} ∈ R₀ for k ≫ 0, i.e. ϖR° ⊂ ⋃_k Φ^{−k}(R₀). Together with a uniform bound ⋃_k Φ^{−k}(R₀) ⊂ ϖ^{−c}R₀ (proved with integral exponents, see PerfectoidSpaces/E7 for the preceding fractional-exponent step) this gives R° ⊂ ϖ^{−1−c}R₀, so R° is bounded.
issues.reason: The inclusion fails for an arbitrary open bounded subring R₀: take K the completion of 𝔽_{p²}((t^{1/p^∞})), R₀ = 𝔽_p + tK° (open, bounded subring), and λ ∈ 𝔽_{p²} \ 𝔽_p. Then λ ∈ K° but λ^{p^k} ∈ {λ, λ^p} ⊄ R₀ for all k (elements of R₀ have constant term in 𝔽_p), so λ ∉ ⋃_k Φ^{−k}(R₀). The proposition itself is true (uniformity of perfect complete Tate rings is standard).

issues.locator: Proposition 4.4 and its proof, pp. 20–21 (arXiv:1709.07343v4, 14 April 2026)
issues.printed: Proposition 4.4 characterizes κ-small perfectoid X by a covering with fewer than κ open affinoids U = Spa(A, A+), each having A of cardinality below κ. It further asserts that such a covering forces the cardinality of |X| to be below κ.
issues.correction: For the 'if' direction require fewer than cf(κ) covering affinoids (e.g. countably many, since cf κ > ω), or a uniform bound sup #A < κ, or κ regular; without this one only gets that every open affinoid has ring of cardinality < κ. The finite-product addendum likewise needs uniformly bounded (e.g. quasicompact) factors.
issues.reason: Lemma 4.1 allows singular κ, e.g. κ = κ(ω₁) of cofinality ω₁ < κ (and the paper says an uncountable strong limit suffices in §4). Let K_α (α < ω₁) be perfectoid fields with #K_α < κ cofinal in κ; the disjoint union of the perfectoid closed discs over the K_α is covered by ω₁ < κ affinoids whose rings have cardinality < κ, but it has at least sup #K_α = κ points (its classical points), so it is not κ-small. (For the finite-product addendum the atlas finding PerfectoidSpaces/E40 gives a separate example: a disjoint union of ω₁ field points Spa(K_α) over a fixed field is κ-small, but its self-product has unboundedly many points.)

issues.printed: Lemma 7.2(iii) calls the sheaf functor F ↦ Γ(X, F) exact, explaining exactness as preservation of every finite colimit.
issues.correction: (iii) The functor F ↦ Γ(X, F) on sheaves (of sets) on X commutes with coequalizers. This is exactly what the proof of (i)⇒(iii) establishes ('We have to see that Γ(X, −) commutes with coequalizers') and what (iii)⇒(iv) uses (cokernels of abelian sheaves are coequalizers of sheaves of sets). Γ preserves finite coproducts only when X is connected.
issues.reason: Counterexample: X = {a, b} with the discrete topology is spectral and every open cover splits (each component is a point), so (i) and (ii) hold. Sheaves on X are pairs of sets and Γ(X, F) = F_a × F_b. For F = G = the terminal sheaf, Γ(X, F ⊔ G) has 4 elements while Γ(X, F) ⊔ Γ(X, G) has 2, so Γ does not commute with finite colimits. In general Γ(X, F ⊔ G) = ⊔ over clopen decompositions X = U ⊔ V of F(U) × G(V).

issues.printed: The source claims a left adjoint X ↦ X^wl for the inclusion of w-local perfectoid spaces, with w-local morphisms, into qcqs perfectoid spaces. It calls X^wl → X the adjunction map and asserts that it is pro-étale.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 7.13, p. 34 (arXiv:1709.07343v4, 14 April 2026)
issues.printed: The source considers f, g : T_1 → T_2 between the factorizations under consideration and asserts that their equality locus T ⊂ T_1 is clopen. More specifically, from T_1 = ⊔_{i∈I} U_i it obtains T = ⊔_{i∈J} U_i for a subset J ⊂ I, and says X^wl → T_1 factors over T.
issues.correction: T ∩ U_i is an open and closed subset of U_i, not necessarily ∅ or U_i, so T need not be a union of members U_i (and, for an arbitrary basis B, need not be an object of C). To equalize f and g inside C: cover the quasicompact open T by finitely many B_k ∈ B, note that the cover {B_k} of T splits after pullback to the w-local space X^wl, and use T′ = ⊔_k B_k → T ⊂ T_1. (For B = rational subsets of an affinoid perfectoid space, clopen subsets of rational subsets are rational, so T itself lies in C.)
issues.reason: A map U_i → T_2 = ⊔_j V_j over X is the same as a decomposition of U_i into clopen pieces W_j ⊂ V_j, so f and g can agree on a proper clopen part of a disconnected U_i. Example: X = {a, b} discrete, B = all subsets, T_1 = T_2 = X ⊔ X with X^wl = X mapping to the first copies, f = id, g = id on the first copy and on the second copy sending a to a but b to the first copy; then T = (first copy) ⊔ {a} is not a union of the U_i. The conclusion 'C is cofiltered' remains true by the argument in the correction.
