issues.locator: Example 11.12, surjectivity step, p. 58 (arXiv:1709.07343v4, 14 April 2026)
issues.printed: The source reduces to affinoid Z and asserts that every continuous map |Z| → T, with T compact Hausdorff, factors through the profinite component set π0(Z).
issues.correction: Replace 'affinoid' by '(strictly) totally disconnected' (allowed, since one is looking for a pro-étale cover Z̃ → Z anyway: Lemma 7.18 gives an affinoid pro-étale strictly totally disconnected cover). Then each connected component of |Z| is |Spa(K′, K′⁺)|, which has a dense generic point, so any continuous map to the Hausdorff space T is constant on it; since |Z| → π₀(Z) is a quotient map onto a profinite set, |Z| → T factors continuously through π₀(Z), and the rest of the argument (Z̃ = Z ×_{π₀(Z)} (π₀(Z) ×_T S)) is unchanged. The claimed full faithfulness is unaffected.
issues.reason: The assertion is false for general affinoid Z. Take Z = Spa(K⟨T^{1/p^∞}⟩, O_K⟨T^{1/p^∞}⟩), the perfectoid closed unit disc over K. Its ring of global functions is a domain (the Gauss norm is multiplicative), so |Z| has no nontrivial clopen subsets and π₀(Z) is a point. By the paper's own Proposition 13.9, |Z| → |Z|_B is a continuous surjection onto a compact Hausdorff space, and |Z|_B is not a point (the Gauss point and the point T = 0 give different seminorms). So with T = |Z|_B, the element of T(Z) = C⁰(|Z|, T) given by this map, that is a map Z → T × Spa(K, O_K), does not factor through π₀(Z).

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 11.26, p. 66; the same sentence recurs in the proof of Proposition 12.20, p. 76 (arXiv:1709.07343v4, 14 April 2026)
issues.printed: The source reduces the task to proving an isomorphism Spa(C, O_C) → Y_0°. It defines Y_0° ⊂ Y_0 as the open subfunctor attached to the maximal point and declares that point open.
issues.correction: The maximal point η of |Y_0| need not be open. Take Y_0° := Y_0 ×_{|Y_0|} {η} instead. The set {η} is the intersection of the quasicompact opens containing η, so it is pro-constructible and generalizing, and Y_0° → Y_0 is a quasicompact injection: a spatial diamond by Proposition 11.20, or a sub-v-sheaf as in Proposition 12.15 for 12.20. R_0° = R_0 ×_{Y_0} Y_0° is then the fibre of R_0 over the rank-one point of Spa(C, C⁺), namely S × Spa(C, O_C). The rest of the argument (the profinite group G, the finite étale covers and their extension to a clopen subset of Y) never uses openness.
issues.reason: Counterexample: Y = Y_0 = Spa(C, C⁺), which is strictly totally disconnected and so satisfies the hypotheses of Proposition 11.26. Here C⁺ ⊂ O_C is the preimage of a valuation ring W of the residue field k of C whose value group is ⊕_{n≥1} ℚ, ordered by the sign of the last nonzero coordinate. Such W exist, e.g. for C the completed algebraic closure of k((t)) with k an algebraic closure of 𝔽_p(x_1, x_2, …), using the monomial valuation. The convex subgroups H_n = ⊕_{i≤n} ℚ increase and exhaust the group, so the points of Spa(C, C⁺) form the chain C⁺ ⊂ V_1 ⊂ V_2 ⊂ … ⊂ O_C with ⋃_n V_n = O_C. A rational subset containing the rank-one point has the form {V : h_1, …, h_m ∈ V} with h_j ∈ O_C, and all the h_j already lie in some V_N ≠ O_C. So no open set is {O_C}: the maximal point is not open.

issues.locator: proof of Proposition 14.7 (vanishing of R^iλ_{Y*}λ_Y^*F), p. 85 (arXiv:1709.07343v4, 14 April 2026)
issues.printed: The source chooses the least failing i and a nonzero α ∈ H^i(X_v, λ∗_Y F). A v-cover f : X′ → X kills α, and X′ is assumed affinoid perfectoid. It then uses a Čech spectral sequence to obtain α from a differential-kernel class in (λ∗_Y F)(X′ ×X . . . ×X X′), with i + 1 copies of X′.
issues.correction: For i ≥ 2 the passage to a Čech cocycle needs H^q((X′ ×_X ⋯ ×_X X′)_v, λ_Y^*F) = 0 for 0 < q < i (with at least two factors), or at least the vanishing of the corresponding E_∞-terms. Minimality of i gives vanishing only on strictly totally disconnected spaces. On the fibre powers, minimality and Proposition 14.8 only identify these groups with H^q_ét, which the proof does not show to vanish. An extra argument is needed, for example vanishing of these étale groups for a suitable choice of X′, or a hypercover form of the approximation-and-splitting step. The case i = 1, and so the statement for sheaves of groups, is unaffected.
issues.reason: In the Čech-to-derived spectral sequence E₁^{p,q} = H^q((X′^{×_X(p+1)})_v, λ_Y^*F) ⇒ H^{p+q}(X_v, λ_Y^*F), the hypothesis f^*α = 0 only removes the E^{0,i}-component of α. α lies in the Čech part E^{i,0} only if its components in E^{p,i−p}, 1 ≤ p ≤ i−1, vanish. The fibre powers are affinoid perfectoid but in general not strictly totally disconnected. For example, take X = Spa(C, O_C) and X′ = Spa(C′, O_{C′}) with C′ the completed algebraic closure of the Gauss-norm completion of C(t). Then X′ ×_X X′ is connected (Lemma 14.6) but has two rank-one points on which |t⊗1 − 1⊗t| is 0 and 1 respectively. So it is not of the form Spa(K, K⁺), and the induction hypothesis does not apply to it.

issues.locator: proof of Lemma 15.3, p. 90 (arXiv:1709.07343v4, 14 April 2026)
issues.printed: The source uses p^{n−1} ≥ n to deduce ϖ^p|p. To prove surjectivity of Φ : R◦/ϖ → R◦/ϖ^p, it takes f ∈ R◦ and asserts that x^p − ϖ^p x − f defines a finite étale R-algebra, which therefore admits a section.
issues.correction: Choose n with p^{n−1} > n, so that p/ϖ^p is topologically nilpotent. Then the derivative −ϖ^p(1 − (p/ϖ^p)x^{p−1}) is a unit in R[x]/(x^p − ϖ^p x − f) and the algebra is finite étale.
issues.reason: With only ϖ^p | p (equality p^{n−1} = n is allowed: n = 1 for every p, and p = n = 2), the polynomial may have a double root: ϖ^p = p and f = 1 − p give x^p − px + p − 1, which vanishes to order 2 at x = 1.

The derivative is px^{p−1} − ϖ^p, which is a unit only if p/ϖ^p is topologically nilpotent. I checked the example: x^p − px − (1 − p) vanishes with its derivative at x = 1. issues.locator: proof of Theorem 19.5(ii), p. 112 (arXiv:1709.07343v4, 14 April 2026)
issues.printed: The source uses Theorem 19.2 to assert vanishing on both sides for A = j! A0, taking A0 ∈ D+ét (U, Λ) and defining U = Y \ {s} ⊂ Y by removing the closed point s ∈ Y.
issues.correction: Give a separate argument that RΓ(Y′_n, f_n* j_! A₀) = 0 for the annuli f_n : Y′_n → Y = Spa(C′,C′⁺). Two routes: an explicit computation over the rank-≥2 point, or a comparison of Y′_n with its canonical compactification over Y (to which Theorem 19.2 does apply) for sheaves pulled back from Y.
issues.reason: Theorem 19.2 requires f proper, but f_n : Y′_n = {|t|ⁿ ≤ |ϖ| ≤ |t|^{1/n}} → Y is not proper when C′⁺ ≠ O_{C′}, which is exactly the case in which U ≠ ∅. The valuative criterion of Proposition 18.3 fails. Pick u ∈ O_{C′}^× whose residue is not in C′⁺/C′°° and τ ∈ C′ with τⁿ = ϖu. The continuous k-embedding C → C′ with t ↦ τ gives Spa(C′,O_{C′}) → Y′_n over the identity of Spa(C′,C′⁺). It does not extend to Spa(C′,C′⁺) → Y′_n, since tⁿ/ϖ ↦ u ∉ C′⁺. For non-proper qc maps the vanishing of RΓ(−, j′_!) can fail; for example, for the open immersion Spa(C′,O_{C′}) ⊂ Spa(C′,C′⁺) one gets RΓ = Λ. So the cited theorem does not justify the step. The statement being proved may still be true.

issues.locator: proof of Proposition 20.16, (i)⇒(ii), p. 120 (arXiv:1709.07343v4, 14 April 2026)
issues.printed: The source claims f ∗ A is constant with perfect values above Sj = Uj \ Uj−1, indexed by j = 0, . . . , n. It cites containment of Uj \ Uj−1 in the image of Uj,i \ Uj−1,i.
issues.correction: An extra argument is needed. For example: lift generalizations along the étale map Y_i → Y (and the quasi-pro-étale surjection X → Y_i) to show that all cospecialization maps of A between points of S_j are isomorphisms. Then f*A|_{f⁻¹(S_j)}, which is constant on the finitely many constructible pieces f⁻¹(S_j) ∩ (preimage of U_{k,i} ∖ U_{k−1,i}), k ≥ j, all with the same value B_j, is constant after refining by clopen pieces. Constancy for an arbitrary strictly totally disconnected X′ → Y then follows by v-descent, as in Proposition 20.13.
issues.reason: Constancy of f*A is known only over the preimages in X of the pieces U_{k,i} ∖ U_{k−1,i} of |Y_i|. A point of f⁻¹(S_j) may lie over U_{k,i} ∖ U_{k−1,i} with k > j: for instance take Y_i = Y ⊔ Y with U_{0,i} one copy, so f⁻¹(S_0) meets both pieces. The stated reason, that every point of S_j has a preimage in the j-th piece, identifies the stalks over S_j but does not by itself make f*A constant on the whole preimage of S_j. The gluing between pieces still has to be controlled.

There T^♢ ×_{Spd O} S is the diamond of the punctured open unit disc over the untilt S^♯, an analytic adic space smooth over S^♯. issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 27.6, pp. 166–167 (arXiv:1709.07343v4, 14 April 2026)
issues.printed: In characteristic p, the source invokes [dJ96, Theorem 4.1, Theorem 6.5] on de Jong’s alterations to reduce, after a finite extension of k, to a normal crossing boundary divisor Z over k. Dimension induction and smooth pullback are said to give an isomorphism outside finitely many k-points, the most singular ones. It then reduces to Spec K ,→ Spec O and claims a direct computation handles this immersion.
issues.correction: Three things need supplying. (a) The descent from the altered situation back to X, e.g. cohomological descent along proper hypercovers built from alterations, with proper base change (27.5) on both sides; an alteration may have degree divisible by ℓ, so no trace splitting is available. (b) The explicit purity/Kummer computations of Rj_*F_ℓ and Rj_{T*}F_ℓ along the normal-crossing strata, and the dimension induction in the strictly semistable case. (c) The base case Spec K ↪ Spec O.
issues.reason: These steps are only asserted. Reduction along an alteration is not formal, since the alteration is not an isomorphism and its degree is not controlled. The final comparison is left as 'a direct computation'.

issues.locator: §8, warning before Proposition 8.3, p. 41 (arXiv:1709.07343v4, 14 April 2026)
issues.printed: The source claims that quasiseparated X implies quasiseparated X → ∗, using algebraicity of T and SGA 4 VI Proposition 2.2. It also claims quasicompact X → ∗ implies quasicompact X by SGA 4 VI Proposition 1.3: choosing any quasicompact Y ∈ T, it regards X × Y → X as a cover and X × Y as quasicompact whenever X → ∗ is quasicompact.
issues.correction: X → ∗ quasicompact implies X quasicompact provided the final object ∗ is covered by some quasicompact object Y (Y → ∗ surjective); then X × Y → X is a cover by a quasicompact object. This holds for (small) sheaves on Perfd, since every perfectoid space pro-étale-locally maps to the quasicompact Spa(ℚ_p^cycl) ⊔ Spa(𝔽_p((t^{1/p^∞}))^∧), and on X_proét for quasicompact X, but not for X_proét with X not quasicompact.
issues.reason: X × Y → X is a cover only if Y → ∗ is surjective (for Y = ∅ it is not), and the implication fails in general algebraic topoi. Counterexample in one of the paper's own settings (algebraic by Proposition 8.3): T = small sheaves on X_proét for X = ⊔_{n∈ℕ} Spa(C, O_C). The final object is X, so X → ∗ is the identity and quasicompact, but X is not quasicompact (its cover by the components has no finite subcover). In the cases used later (sheaves on Perfd/Perf) the corrected hypothesis holds, so later uses are unaffected.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 13.13, p. 81 (arXiv:1709.07343v4, 14 April 2026)
issues.printed: The source reduces verification to stalks and chooses y ∈ |Y|^B. It asserts cofinality of the clopen neighborhoods of y and uses a standard limit argument to deduce (Rf∗f∗F)_y = RΓ(f⁻¹(y), f∗F).
issues.correction: Open and closed neighbourhoods of y are cofinal only when |Y|^B is totally disconnected (e.g. profinite). What is true, and presumably intended (cf. the proof of Lemma 2.6, 'the open neighborhoods are cofinal with the closed neighborhoods'), is that closed neighbourhoods are cofinal and, as f : |Y| → |Y|^B is closed (quasicompact source, Hausdorff target), the sets f⁻¹(U) are cofinal among the open neighbourhoods of the fibre f⁻¹(y). The identity (Rf∗G)_y = RΓ(f⁻¹(y), G|) then needs a separate justification, e.g. a tautness statement for the closed quasicompact subset f⁻¹(y) ⊂ |Y| (colim_{W ⊃ f⁻¹(y)} H^i(W, G) = H^i(f⁻¹(y), G)), or a reduction to a profinite base via a surjection S → |Y|^B and Y ×_{|Y|^B} S (spatial, Proposition 13.12) together with descent along S → |Y|^B. The text supplies neither.
issues.reason: Counterexample to the cofinality claim within the hypotheses: Y = Spa(K⟨T^{1/p^∞}⟩, O_K⟨T^{1/p^∞}⟩) is affinoid perfectoid, hence a quasicompact separated diamond. Its ring is a domain (multiplicative Gauss norm), so |Y| is connected, and |Y|^B, a continuous image of |Y| (Proposition 13.9), is connected; it has at least two points (the Gauss point and the point T = 0 differ on |T|). In a connected Hausdorff space with two points the only open and closed neighbourhood of y is the whole space, which is not inside the open neighbourhood of y missing the other point, so open and closed neighbourhoods are not cofinal. The same happens for T̲ × Spa(K, O_K) with T = [0, 1] (Example 11.12). I have not found the conclusion of 13.13 to fail; only the step is unsupported.

issues.printed: The source extends the result to a coefficient ring Λ annihilated by n prime to p, provided every M ∈ D(Λ) satisfying R Hom_Λ(M, Λ) = 0 satisfies M = 0. It says this condition can fail, citing Λ = O_K for spherically complete K and the residue field M = k.
issues.correction: … for example if Λ = O_K with K spherically complete and non-discretely valued (e.g. the spherical completion of C_p), and M = k the residue field. Note that this O_K is not killed by any n, so the example illustrates the ring-theoretic condition only, not a coefficient ring in the scope of the remark.
issues.reason: For K = Q_p (spherically complete, being locally compact), Λ = Z_p and M = F_p, Hom(F_p, Z_p) = 0 but Ext^1_{Z_p}(F_p, Z_p) = Z_p/p ≠ 0, so RHom_Λ(M, Λ) = F_p[−1] ≠ 0 and the example fails. For non-discrete K it works. O_K is then a maximal valuation ring (Kaplansky), so K/O_K is injective (Matlis), and RHom(k, O_K) = [Hom(k,K) → Hom(k,K/O_K)] = [0 → (O_K : m)/O_K] = 0, because (O_K : m) = O_K when the value group is dense. Separately, O_K is torsion-free, while the remark restricts to Λ killed by n prime to p.

issues.printed: The source defines G^L_{a,b}(A) = {f ∈ L ⊗_R A | f^{⊗2} = a ⊗ f} and prescribes the multiplication f₁ ⋆ f₂ = f₁ + f₂ + b ⊗ f₁ ⊗ f₂.

issues.citation: Stefan Schröer, "There is no Enriques surface over the integers", Annals of Mathematics 197 (2023), no. 1
issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 14 image and in the TeX ("f_1\star f_2=f_1+f_2+ b\otimes f_1\otimes f_2"). With f²=af, g²=ag and h=f+g+cfg, h²−ah=(c²a²+3ca+2)fg=(ca+1)(ca+2)fg. With ab=2 this vanishes for c=−b (ca=−2), but for c=+b it equals 12fg. Over Z with (a,b)=(1,2) and f=g=1, the printed law gives 4, and 4²≠4. With the minus sign, (R,1,2) gives Z/2 (symmetric difference of idempotents) and (R,2,1) gives μ₂ via u=1−f, as the paper states. The group law is used nowhere else.

issues.locator: proof of Proposition 5.5, p. 16 (arXiv v3, identical to the author version of 19 July 2022; the published pagination was not seen)
issues.printed: The proof invokes Hensel's Lemma to lift every F₂^alg-valued point of 𝔜 → S to an A-valued point. Proposition 5.4 is then said to provide a family of canonical covers 𝔛 ⊗ A → 𝔜 ⊗ A, implying good reduction of X_F over A and yielding a contradiction.
issues.correction: Compare the covers over ℤ₂ instead of A = W(F̄₂): 𝔜(F₂) is non-empty (constant Num and Corollary 7.3 give 25 points), so a canonical cover exists over ℤ₂ (Proposition 5.4(ii)). Over ℚ₂ it differs from the cover over ℤ[1/2] by a class c in ℚ₂^×/ℚ₂^{×2} = ⟨−1, 2, 5⟩. Twist the global cover by the unit u ∈ {1, −1, 2, −2} of ℤ[1/2] with cu ∈ {1, 5}, and the local cover by the unramified class 5 if needed (the étale algebra ℤ₂[z]/(z² − z − 1)). The twisted generic K3 surface then has smooth proper models at every prime, which are projective (local projectivity from a section and constant Num), and Fontaine's theorem applies. Items /176–/179 and /184 give the steps.
issues.reason: The cover over A is not the base change of the cover over ℤ[1/2]. Over F = Frac(A) the two differ by a class in H¹(F, ℤ/2) = F^×/F^{×2}. That group is infinite: for a unit u, 1 + 2u is not a square, and 1 + 2u and 1 + 2u′ have the same square class exactly when u ≡ u′ mod 2. Twisting the global cover realizes only the classes of −1, 2 and −2. So good reduction of the cover over A says nothing about X_F. Fontaine's theorem also needs a scheme, while 𝔜 is an algebraic space.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on the p. 16 image and in the TeX. The global cover 𝔛 exists only over Z[1/2], and A=W(F̄₂) is not a Z[1/2]-algebra, so '𝔛⊗A' is undefined. The cover over A given by Proposition 5.4(ii) is unique, since H¹(A,Z/2)=0 (A strictly henselian). X_F differs from its generic fibre by a class in F^×/F^{×2}, which the paper never controls, so 'whence X_F has good reduction' does not follow. The group F^×/F^{×2} is indeed infinite: squares of units are ≡[x] (Teichmüller) mod 4, and 1+2u has Witt coordinates (1,ū²,…). Fontaine's Remark (a) (scan p. 3) asks for a proper smooth scheme model, while 𝔜 and 𝔛 are algebraic spaces. The statement of Proposition 5.5 survives by the repair.

issues.locator: proof of Proposition 9.3(v), p. 25 (arXiv v3, identical to the author version of 19 July 2022; the published pagination was not seen)
issues.printed: The source writes MW(J/P¹) = J(F) = Pic⁰_{Y_F/F}(F) = Pic⁰(Y_F), taking F to be the function field of P¹. It justifies the last identification by Br(F) = 0, attributed to Tsen's Theorem.
issues.correction: Br(F) ≠ 0 for F = F₂(t). Instead: over F̄₂(t) Tsen's theorem holds, so L ↦ (L − (deg(L|Y_F̄)/2)R)|Y_F̄ is a surjective Galois-equivariant map Pic(Ȳ) → MW(J̄/P̄¹) for an F₂-rational two-section R. Since Pic(Ȳ) has trivial Galois action (constant Picard scheme), so does MW(J̄/P̄¹), and Galois-fixed sections descend: MW(J/P¹) = MW(J̄/P̄¹).
issues.reason: Tsen's theorem concerns k(t) with k algebraically closed. Br(F₂(t)) is non-zero: the cyclic algebra of F₄(t)/F₂(t) and t is non-split, since norms from F₄(t) have even valuation at t = 0. So Pic⁰_{Y_F/F}(F) = Pic⁰(Y_F) is not justified as printed. The statement (v) itself survives by the correction; /94 records it.

issues.locator: proof of Proposition 9.5, p. 27 (arXiv v3, identical to the author version of 19 July 2022; the published pagination was not seen)
issues.printed: The proof says the maps in (10) send (P − O) − (1 + (P · O))J_ā ∈ W to Θ₁^* ∈ W_ā^*, the dual basis element. Preservation of the intersection pairing is then used to assert that (Θ₁^* · Θ₁^*) ∈ ℚ lies in 2ℤ.
issues.correction: The restriction W → W_ā^* is not an isometry. Argue instead: under the hypothesis, the image of W in W_ā^* is W_ā + ℤΘ₁^*; since W is unimodular, every x ∈ W_ā ⊗ ℚ pairing integrally with W lies in W, and Θ₁^* does. So Θ₁^* ∈ W, and (Θ₁^*)² = −1 contradicts the evenness of W.
issues.reason: Orthogonal projection onto W_ā ⊗ ℚ does not preserve the form, so evenness of W says nothing directly about the norm of the image of an element. The dual-lattice argument gives the stated contradiction; /97 records it.

issues.locator: proof of Lemma 1.1, p. 5 (arXiv v3 = author version of 19 July 2022)
issues.printed: The source sets X′ = X ⊗ E together with P′ = Pic_{X′/E}, regarding both as k-schemes. It declares the right-hand term zero because R¹pr_*P′ vanishes, referring to the later arguments for Lemma 1.4.
issues.correction: P′ = Pic^τ_{X′/E} = P ⊗_k E, so that the norm maps H¹(k, pr_*P′) to H¹(k, P). Delete the vanishing claim. The five-term exact sequence 0 → H¹(k, pr_*P′) → H¹(E, P′) → H⁰(k, R¹pr_*P′) already makes the first map injective, and that is all the argument uses (pr*(l) ↦ 0, hence pr*(l) = 0 and n·l = N(pr*(l)) = 0).
issues.reason: With P′ the whole Picard scheme, l maps to 0 in H¹(k, Pic_{X/k}) from the start, because T ⊂ Pic_{X/k} is a sub-torsor, so the argument would say nothing about l ∈ H¹(k, P). The vanishing claim is false in general. Lemma 1.4's argument concerns G_m, but P′ can be non-reduced, and E = κ(a) can be inseparable: a torsor under a non-reduced group may have no separable point. Take k = F₂(c), E = k(√c) and P′ = μ₂, the τ-part of an ordinary Enriques surface (/37). Squares in E ⊗_k A = A ⊕ A√c lie in A, so the class of √c in (E⊗A)^×/(E⊗A)^{×2} ⊂ H¹(E ⊗ A, μ₂) is nonzero for every nonzero k-algebra A. Hence R¹pr_*μ₂ ≠ 0.

issues.locator: Theorem 2.1(ii) and its proof, p. 8 (arXiv v3 = author version of 19 July 2022)
issues.printed: The source leaves (ii) unproved, claiming it follows directly from (i) together with the definitions.
issues.correction: Let D_i, D_j be distinct components of S_a with geometric components C_i = D_i ⊗_{κ(a)} Ω and C_j. The labels are (D_i·D_j) on S over k and (C_i·C_j) on S_Ω. Since (D_i ∩ D_j) ⊗_{κ(a)} Ω = C_i ∩ C_j, we get (D_i·D_j) = [κ(a):k]·(C_i·C_j). So (ii) needs κ(a) = k whenever S_ā is reducible, and this holds. By (iii), κ(a)/k is purely inseparable, of degree q say. E ⊗_k Ω is local of length q, so D_i ⊗_k Ω = q·C_i as divisors on the smooth surface S_Ω, and (D_i·D_j) = q²(C_i·C_j). S_ā is connected, so some pair has (C_i·C_j) > 0, and comparing the two formulas gives q = 1.
issues.reason: The definitions alone do not give (ii). At a closed point with κ(a) ≠ k, intersection numbers on S are multiplied by [κ(a):k]. The missing equality κ(a) = k needs the argument above, which uses the smoothness of S. In the paper's only application (Proposition 3.1, over a finite field), (iii) gives κ(a) = k directly, so no later result is affected.

issues.locator: proof of Theorem 2.1, p. 9 (arXiv v3 = author version of 19 July 2022)
issues.printed: Assuming r ≥ 2, the proof calls C₁ + … + C_{r−1} as well as C₂ + … + C_r negative-definite curves. It invokes the preceding paragraph to conclude again that Γ(S_ā) → Γ(S_a) is an isomorphism of graphs.
issues.correction: Show directly that distinct components have distinct classes. For i ≠ j, (C_i − C_j)·C_i = C_i² − (C_i·C_j) < 0, since C_i² < 0 (Zariski's lemma, r ≥ 2) and (C_i·C_j) ≥ 0. So [C_i] ≠ [C_j] in Num_{S/k}(Ω), and since Galois acts trivially on Num, it fixes every C_i.
issues.reason: Injectivity on the two sub-curves shows only that σ ∈ Aut(Ω/κ(a)) fixes every C_i except possibly by exchanging C₁ and C_r, because neither sub-curve contains both. For r = 2 the sub-curves are C₁ and C₂ separately, and nothing excludes [C₁] = [C₂]. The conclusion is right, and the fix takes one line.

issues.locator: Introduction, p. 3 (third displayed theorem); the same claim opens §10, p. 27 (arXiv v3 = author version of 19 July 2022)
issues.printed: The theorem, citing Thm. 10.4 and Thm. 10.5, counts exactly eleven isomorphism classes of Weierstraß equations y²+a₁xy+… = x³+a₂x²+… with a_i ∈ F₂[t]. They define geometrically rational elliptic surfaces with fibration φ : J → P¹ and constant Pic_{J/F₂}, and at most one rational a ∈ P¹ whose fiber J_a is semistable or supersingular.
issues.correction: There are exactly fourteen such Weierstraß equations up to isomorphism: the eleven of Theorems 10.4 and 10.5 and the three recorded in the Theorem 10.4 issue. The paper shows only that every such surface is among its eleven, not that each has constant Picard scheme; the review's exhaustive search confirms that all fourteen do (for geometrically rational J, constant Picard scheme is equivalent to #J(F₂) = 25).
issues.reason: Theorems 10.4 and 10.5 say that under assumptions (i)–(ii) of §10 the fibration 'is given by exactly one of' the listed equations, and their proofs derive only necessary conditions. The converse would need Theorem 9.4, whose hypotheses include descent of every geometric Mordell–Weil section, and that is never checked. The TeX never cites Theorem 9.4 (\ref{constant pic}). The main theorem uses only the necessary direction, which /115 and /117 state correctly. Moreover the list itself is incomplete (Theorem 10.4 issue), so the count 'eleven' is wrong, not only unproved.

issues.locator: Theorem 10.4, p. 29, and its proof, p. 31 (twisted semistable case); the count in the introduction to Section 10, p. 28 (arXiv v3 = author version of 19 July 2022)
issues.printed: The source claims φ:J→P¹ has exactly one of eight listed Weierstraß equations modulo coordinate changes and automorphisms of P¹. For a twisted semistable fiber it states r_c≤2, n_c=2r_c+2 and (11): r_a+i+r_c=11, hence r_c≥11−i−r_a≥7. It lists I₁*+E₄+I₄, III*+E₄+I₂, III*+E₂+Ĩ₂, II*+E₄+I₁, II*+E₂+Ĩ₁ as the possibilities, and on p. 28 counts exactly eleven such equations.
issues.correction: The twisted case also gives I₂*+E₄+Ĩ₂, I₃*+E₄+Ĩ₁ and IV*+E₄+Ĩ₂. Theorem 10.4 has eleven models, not eight, and §10 has fourteen equations in all. The additional models, with fibres over t=0, 1, ∞, are: y²+txy+t³y=x³+x² [I₂*+E₄+Ĩ₂, Δ=t¹⁰, j=t²]; y²+txy+t³y=x³+tx² [I₃*+E₄+Ĩ₁, Δ=t¹¹, j=t]; y²+txy+t²y=x³+t²x² [IV*+E₄+Ĩ₂, Δ=t⁸(t²+t+1), j=t⁴/(t²+t+1), plus I₁ over t²+t+1=0]. Theorem 10.5 is correct. Proposition 11.1 (p. 33) and the key-reduction proposition of §11 take their elliptic column from Theorem 10.4. The proof of Theorem 15.1 reduces every fibration to I₁*+I₄ or I₂*+III+III. All of these must treat the three configurations; I₃* is never mentioned in §§11–15. On an Enriques surface Y, the multiple fibres would lie over the unstable and the E₄ points, because Ĩ₁ and Ĩ₂ are semistable. Until then the proof of the main theorem has a gap at this point. Whether the configurations occur on a non-exceptional Enriques surface over F₂ with constant Picard scheme is not settled here.
issues.reason: Checked by hand for y²+txy+t³y=x³+x². Δ=t¹⁰. At t=0 (Tate's algorithm): the reduction y²=x³+x² is singular at (0,0), and b₂=t², so the fibre is additive; v(a₆)=∞, v(b₈)=6, v(b₆)=6. The change y↦y+x gives a₂=t, a₄=t³ and P(T)=T³+T²=T²(T+1). Then a_{3,2}=a_{6,4}=0, and a_{2,1}X²+a_{4,3}X+a_{6,5}=X²+X has distinct rational roots. So I₂* with c=4, all seven components defined over F₂, 15 points. At ∞: y²+xy+y=x³+s²x², Δ′=s², node at (1,1) with tangent polynomial T²+T+1, so non-split I₂, 6 points. At t=1: y²+xy+y=x³+x² is smooth ordinary with 4 points (E₄). Total 25, so the trace of Frobenius on NS(J̄) is 10 and Pic_{J/F₂} is constant. Condition (ii) holds: only Ĩ₂ is semistable, and E₄ is ordinary. The other two models are checked the same way: I₃* at t=0 after three steps of the I_n* loop, and IV* at t=0 (Y²+Y distinct roots, c=3). Independent checks (scripts S/tate2.py, brute.py, classify.py, lcheck.py): (1) all 2²¹ equations were enumerated through their 2¹⁸ representatives with a₂=0 (every equation becomes one via x↦x+a₂), with Tate's algorithm at every place; this gives exactly 14 isomorphism classes, taken modulo the 512 coordinate changes of degree ≤(2,1,3) and PGL₂(F₂), that satisfy (i) and (ii); these are the 11 printed and the 3 above, one class per configuration; (2) for every class, the L-function of the generic fibre was computed from naive point counts at all places of degree ≤8; it equals (1−2T)^r with r=8−Σ(m_v−1), which confirms the component counts and the Galois-trivial Mordell–Weil action independently of Tate's algorithm; (3) for all 2¹⁸ normalised equations, Ogg's formula (v(Δ)≥e, δ=0 for I_n, IV, IV*) and Σ deg(v)·v(Δ)=12 hold. The proof's other claims were also reproduced: II*+E₂+E₄, I₃*+E₄+E₄ and IV*+E₄+I₃ are excluded, d₁=1 and 1+t are equivalent in the I₄* case, the second I₁* solution is twisted, and α=1 gives E₂. The error is the unexamined twisted case ('the argument is similar'): the tuples (r_a,i,r_c)=(7,2,2) and (8,2,1) yield these configurations.

issues.locator: proof of Proposition 9.5, p. 26 (arXiv v3 = author version of 19 July 2022)
issues.printed: The proof seeks triviality of the action of G=Gal(F₂^alg/F₂) on Γ=Γ(J_ā). Because Γ is a tree, it claims fixing every terminal vertex suffices. For IV and IV*, it says two other terminal vertices remain besides v₀∈Γ.
issues.correction: For IV the dual graph (§2: an edge for each pair of meeting components) is a triangle, not a tree, and has no terminal vertices. Argue directly: Θ₀ is fixed, and a section defined over F₂ through a second component fixes it. The third component is then fixed as well.
issues.reason: The three components of IV pass through one point, so they meet pairwise. The lattice argument (A₂ is not unimodular) still gives such a section, so the conclusion stands.

issues.locator: proof of Proposition 9.5, p. 26 (arXiv v3 = author version of 19 July 2022)
issues.printed: The source says that a sole additional terminal vertex must also be fixed, and claims this resolves Kodaira types III, III* and II*.
issues.correction: For III* (Ẽ₇) and II* (Ẽ₈) there are two further terminal vertices, of multiplicities 1 and 2, resp. 2 and 3. The count 'at most one further' is right for the multiplicity-one vertices only.
issues.reason: Ẽ₇ has three terminal vertices (multiplicities 1, 1, 2) and Ẽ₈ has three (1, 2, 3).

issues.locator: proof of Proposition 9.3(iv), p. 25 (arXiv v3 = author version of 19 July 2022)
issues.printed: Using Lemma 4.3, the source says the relevant φ^{−1}_ind(a) are neither semistable nor supersingular. It concludes that among the three rational points, only one b∈P¹ permits φ^{−1}_ind(b), and consequently J_b, to be semistable or supersingular.

issues.locator: Proposition 11.2 and its proof, p. 34 (arXiv v3 = author version of 19 July 2022)
issues.printed: Under the hypotheses of Proposition 11.1, Proposition 11.2 excludes fibers of Kodaira type I8. It also asserts existence of ψ : Y → P1 as a genus-one fibration whose multiple fibers 2F satisfy F · ϕ⁻¹_ind(0) = 1.
issues.correction: Add 'Assume Y is non-exceptional', as in Proposition 11.3, so that the partner fibration ψ comes from Proposition 4.4(iii). Alternatively cite Cossec–Dolgachev 1989, Theorem 3.4.1 directly. It supplies ψ unless Ȳ is extra-special of type Ẽ₈, and the (−2)-curves of such a surface form the tree T_{2,3,7} with ten vertices (Martin–Mezzedimi–Veniani, arXiv:2201.05481, Definition 1.1), which contains no cycle, so no fibre of type I₈.
issues.reason: The proof gives no source for ψ. In the paper the only one is Proposition 4.4(iii), stated under 'Suppose p=2, and that the Enriques surface Y is non-exceptional'. Proposition 11.1's standing assumption does not include non-exceptionality: that enters only in its second part ('If moreover…'), and Proposition 11.3 adds it explicitly. So the proof does not cover exceptional Y. Harmless for the main theorem: Proposition 11.2 is applied only in Propositions 11.3 and 11.4, both for non-exceptional Y. Checked in the TeX and on the page image.

issues.locator: proof of Proposition 11.3, case IV, p. 38 (arXiv v3 = author version of 19 July 2022)
issues.printed: The proof places the ψ-vertical curves C′1 and C′2 in ψ⁻¹_ind(0), with multiplicities m1, m2 ≥ 1. From 2 ≥ ϕ⁻¹_ind(∞) · ψ⁻¹(0) ≥ C′0 · (m1C′1 + m2C′2) = m1 + m2 ≥ 2 it deduces that ψ⁻¹(0) is simple too, yielding a contradiction.
issues.correction: Also treat the case where C′₁+C′₂ lies in ψ⁻¹(∞), the simple fibre already containing C₁+⋯+C₅. That fibre would contain D₅ and a disjoint, non-adjacent A₂, hence at least 8 components. II*, IV* and I₈ are already excluded, and Ẽ₇ has no such pair of subgraphs, so it is a simple I₄*. In D̃₈ the only A₂ not adjacent to a D₅ consists of a branch vertex (multiplicity 2) and an end vertex (multiplicity 1). This gives 2 = ϕ⁻¹_ind(∞)·ψ⁻¹(∞) = C′₀·ψ⁻¹(∞) ≥ 2+1 = 3, a contradiction. The printed argument covers the other case, t≠∞, where ψ⁻¹(∞) and ψ⁻¹(t) would both be simple, although ψ has two multiple fibres over rational points.
issues.reason: The word 'say' presumes that C′₁+C′₂ lies in a ψ-fibre different from ψ⁻¹(∞), and nothing excludes ψ⁻¹(∞). The embedding is realizable in D̃₈ (D₅={Θ₀,Θ₁,Θ₂,Θ₃,Θ₄} with centre Θ₂, A₂={Θ₆,Θ₇}), and there ψ⁻¹(∞) is simple with m=2. So the printed text does not rule the case out, but the intersection count above does. Checked on the page image of p. 38 and the dual graphs in the TeX.

issues.locator: proof of Proposition 12.2, p. 42 (arXiv v3 = author version of 19 July 2022)
issues.printed: The proof assumes R̃ ≡ C8*, giving (R̃·C8) = 1. For 2 ≤ i ≤ 6 it gives (R̃·Ci) = 0; among j ∈ {0, 1, 7}, precisely one satisfies (R̃·Cj) = 1, in addition to j = 8. It says (R̃ · C7) = 1 would give R̃ ≡ C7* + C8* ≡ C1*, a contradiction, and therefore assumes (R̃ · C0) = 1 without loss of generality.
issues.correction: R̃·ϕ⁻¹(∞)=2 leaves 15 incidence patterns. Their classes in A_S, computed with N⁻¹ from (14): C₈* exactly for {R̃·C₀=R̃·C₈=1} and {R̃·C₁=R̃·C₇=1}; C₇* exactly for {R̃·C₀=R̃·C₇=1} and {R̃·C₁=R̃·C₈=1} (all other R̃·C_i=0); every other pattern gives 0 or C₁*. The symmetries C₀↔C₁ and C₇↔C₈ of the graph (13) preserve S (C₀=2F−C₁−2(C₂+⋯+C₆)−C₇−C₈) and permute these four patterns transitively. So one may assume R̃·C₀=R̃·C₈=1 and R̃·C_i=0 otherwise, and the rest of the proof is unchanged.
issues.reason: R̃≡C₈* does not force R̃·C₈=1. The two-section with R̃·C₁=R̃·C₇=1 is R̃=C₁*+C₇*+nR*+F*, which is ≡C₈* because C₁*≡C₇*+C₈* mod S. Moreover, once R̃·C₈=1, the option j=1 is not 'without loss of generality': it gives R̃≡C₇*, contradicting R̃≡C₈*. Verified in exact arithmetic (S/rv4_lattice.py) and on the page image of p. 42. The conclusion used afterwards (R̃=C₈*+nR*+F*) is correct after the symmetry reduction.

issues.printed: Over an algebraically closed k with any characteristic p ≥ 0, the source invokes [17], Theorem A to call Y non-exceptional. Proposition 4.4 is then cited for a further genus-one fibration ψ : Y → P1 satisfying ϕ⁻¹(∞) · ψ⁻¹(∞) = 4.

issues.locator: Proposition 11.1, table (12), p. 33, and the proof of Theorem 15.1, pp. 49–50 (hence Theorem 5.1) (arXiv v3 = author version of 19 July 2022)
issues.printed: For a genus-one fibration ϕ : Y → P¹, Proposition 11.1 asserts that table (12) lists the possible configurations over rational t = 0, 1, ∞, modulo automorphisms of P¹.
issues.correction: Add the configurations I₂*+E₄+Ĩ₂, I₃*+E₄+Ĩ₁ and IV*+E₄+Ĩ₂ to the elliptic column of (12), coming from the three Jacobians that Theorem 10.4 omits, and exclude them on non-exceptional Enriques surfaces over F₂ with constant Picard scheme before concluding Theorem 15.1.
issues.reason: The elliptic column of (12) is taken from Theorem 10.4, whose list is incomplete (previous issue), and §§11–15 never treat the three omitted configurations (I₃* does not occur after §10). On such an Enriques surface the multiple fibres would lie over the unstable point and the E₄ point, because Ĩ₁ and Ĩ₂ are semistable. Whether these configurations can occur is not settled by the review, so the printed proof of the main theorem has a gap at this step.

issues.locator: Lemma 5.3, Proposition 5.2, Theorems 5.7 and 5.8, pp.25–31
issues.printed: Proposition 5.2 takes m ∈ Z_{>0} with Z(m) ≠ ∅ and, for odd b, requires √(m/D) ∈ Z for fixed D as in Theorem 2.4. Lemma 5.3 uses the same restriction and invokes [BK03, Theorem 4.11, (4.73), (4.74)] because d_0 and k do not depend on m. Theorems 5.7 and 5.8 derive bounds from Proposition 5.2 for, respectively, every m represented by (L, Q) and every positive integer m.
issues.correction: For b odd and m/D not a square, add this to the proof of Lemma 5.3. In [BK03, Thm. 4.11(ii)] (r odd), the m-dependence through d_0 = d_0(m) enters as log|4m/D_0²| − 2L′(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ)/L(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ). By the functional equation of L(s, χ_{D_0}), this is log m + 2L′(χ_{D_0}, κ − 1/2)/L(χ_{D_0}, κ − 1/2) + O(1): the log|D_0| terms cancel. The logarithmic derivative at κ − 1/2 ≥ 2 is bounded by |ζ′/ζ(2)|, and the χ_{d_0}-factors of σ_m(s) are bounded uniformly as in the proof of Proposition 5.2. So Lemma 5.3 (with O(1) uniform in m) and Proposition 5.2 hold for every m with Z(m) ≠ ∅. That is what Theorems 5.7–5.8 assert, and what Proposition 6.4 and Lemma 7.6 use.
issues.reason:
Theorem 5.8 is proved from equation (3.1), Proposition 3.2 and Proposition 5.2, so for b odd its proof covers only m ∈ D·(Q^×)². It is then applied to arbitrary integers:
- in Proposition 6.4 to M = Q(λ) for a difference λ of two lattice vectors ("Theorem 5.8(i) implies X^{b/2} ≪ −log|Q(λ_x)| ≪ A(M) ≪ M^{b/2} log M");
- in Lemma 7.6 to m = a_1(n)², a square but not in general D times a square.
Both feed Theorem 6.1 and Theorem 7.1, hence the main theorem for every odd b ≥ 3. For b even, d = (−1)^{r/2}det(L) does not depend on m and there is no gap. BK03 Theorem 4.11 was read in arXiv:math/0204100v2 (p.27): its r-odd formula contains log|4m/D_0²| and −2L′(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ)/L(χ_{D_0}, 3/2 − κ).

issues.locator: §7.3, construction of μ, p.43
issues.printed: Given a_n ≠ 0, the source sets a_i = 0 throughout n + 1 ≤ i ≤ e^{e^{p^n}} and assigns a_i = 1 at i = ⌈e^{e^{p^n}}⌉. It claims Σ_{i≤n} a_ip^i ≡ μ mod p^N with N ≥ e^{e^{p^n}}, giving an integer x_n of size O(p^n) approximating μ mod p^N with N double-exponential in its size. It further claims the resulting lattice Λ has property 2.
issues.correction: Make the gaps double-exponential in the discriminant rather than in x_n: after a_n ≠ 0, set a_i = 0 for n < i < exp(exp(C·p^{2c(n+1)})) with C depending only on L (so that exp(C·p^{2c(n+1)}) exceeds the discriminant of L_n below). Then property (2) of Lemma 7.11 holds with L_n = span_Z{e_j + x_nf_j}, and the example stands.
issues.reason: Property (2) of Lemma 7.11 needs N_i ≥ e^{e^{D_i}}, where D_i is the discriminant of the approximating sublattice L_i. Here L_i = span_Z{e_j + x_nf_j : 1 ≤ j ≤ c}, with e_j, f_j orthogonal and Q positive definite. So D_i ≍ Π_j (Q(e_j) + x_n²Q(f_j)) ≥ x_n^{2c} ≥ p^{2cn}, because a_n ≠ 0 forces x_n ≥ p^n. The printed choice gives only N ≈ e^{e^{p^n}}, which is far below e^{e^{D_i}}, so the proof of Lemma 7.11 (m_i < e^{D_i} and (Y_Λ.Z(m_i)) > N_i ≥ e^{e^{D_i}} > e^{m_i}) does not apply. "Double-exponential in the size of x_n" is not double-exponential in D_i ≍ x_n^{2c}. The example is illustrative and not used for the main results.

issues.reason: dim A = 2^{b+1} (the paper's own 2^{2+3−1} = 16 for b = 3), so dim A^+ = 2^b = 2^{2n−1}, and A^+ ~ B^{2^n} forces dim B = 2^{n−1}. issues.reason: With n = g − a − b and X = Θ_{g−a} ∩ L − Θ_{g−b}, the kernel F of Q_ℓ[n] → IC_X has hypercohomology in degrees [−e, e], so H^k(X, Q_ℓ[n]) ≅ IH^k exactly when k ∉ [−e−1, e]. issues.locator: Proof of Corollary 2.20, p. 12, arXiv v1 (final journal text not obtained)
issues.printed: The proof writes O(R1 + R2 + 2R∩) = κ^{−m}L with m ≤ e(L), then invokes Corollary 2.4 to conclude finiteness of the possible choices of R·.

For p ≤ 2g − 2 it needs a separate proof. Until then, Corollary 2.20, Lemma 3.7, Proposition 3.8 and Theorems 3.9 and 1.3 are established only in characteristic 0 or p > 2g − 2, and Case 2 of Theorem 4.4 over a fixed F_q (where g → ∞) needs them for all g. issues.reason: R1, R2 and R∩ may be non-reduced (for instance D1^r − S = 2p and D2^r − S = p give R∩ = p and R1 = p), so the total multiplicity of R1 + R2 + 2R∩ at a support point can be any integer up to deg ≤ 2g − 2. Corollary 2.4 fails when such a multiplicity is divisible by p (E2: the family 5P + Q ∈ |6∞| in characteristic 5), and its proof, Proposition 2.3, needs every total weight nonzero in k. The support of R1 + R2 + R∩ has h⁰ = 1, so the argument goes through whenever all total weights, which are at most 2g − 2, are nonzero in k.

issues.locator: arXiv:1405.7294v1 (28 May 2014), §§2.6 and 2.7: the definition of the anticyclotomic p-adic L-function, the definition of Λ, Conjecture 2.7.1 and Proposition 2.7.2
issues.printed: The source asserts L^S_𝔭(f) ∈ O[[Γ]] for an anticyclotomic p-adic L-function with an interpolation condition for ψ ∈ Σ^c_𝔭, and defines Λ = O[[Γ]]. Conjecture 2.7.1 asserts Ch_Λ(f,K,S) = (L^S_𝔭(f)) in Λ ⊗_{Z_p} Q_p. Proposition 2.7.2 asserts, under the preceding hypotheses, Ch_Λ(f,K,S) ⊆ (L^S_𝔭(f)) in Λ ⊗_{Z_p} Q_p.
issues.correction: The published version reads: O^ur is the ring of integers of the completion of the maximal unramified extension L^ur of L; L^S_𝔭(f) ∈ O^ur[[Γ]] and the unit W of w(f,ψ) = ψ(W) lies in O^ur[[Γ]]^×; Λ = O[[Γ]] and Λ^ur = O^ur[[Γ]]; Conjecture 2.7.1 reads "Ch_Λ(f,K,S) and L^S_𝔭(f) generate the same ideal of Λ^ur ⊗_O L" and is called essentially the Iwasawa–Greenberg main conjecture; Proposition 2.7.2 reads "the ideal of Λ^ur ⊗_O L generated by Ch_Λ(f,K,S) is contained in the ideal generated by L^S_𝔭(f)".
issues.reason: The interpolation formula defining L^S_𝔭(f) has the p-adic period Ω_p^{4n} of a CM elliptic curve E_0 in it, and Ω_p is a unit of the completion of the maximal unramified extension, not of O; the same is true of the two-variable function 𝓛^{Σ,Hida}_{f_0,K,ξ} ∈ O^ur[[Γ_K]] of Wan's theorem, to which the deduction of Proposition 2.7.2 specialises. So the element L^S_𝔭(f) of the preprint's Conjecture 2.7.1 and Proposition 2.7.2 need not lie in O[[Γ]] and those two statements are not the ones the sources prove. The published version's own deduction makes this explicit: it specialises Wan's inclusion of ideals of O^ur[[Γ_K]] ⊗_O L along O^ur[[Γ_K]] → Λ^ur and concludes about ideals of Λ^ur ⊗_O L. Everything else in the preprint and the published version agrees: the 19 numbered statements carry the same numbers and, apart from these coefficient rings, the same text.
issues.known: Corrected in the published version, Ann. of Math. (2) 191 (2020), 329–354, §§2.6–2.7 (pp. 342–346), which introduces O^ur and Λ^ur and restates Conjecture 2.7.1 and Proposition 2.7.2 over Λ^ur ⊗_O L. The items of this extraction use the published form.

issues.citation: Skorobogatov–Sofos, "Schinzel Hypothesis on average and rational points", Inventiones Mathematicae (2023)
issues.reviewReason: The counterexample is literally correct: M=0, n₀=0, Q=t+1 makes the family {t+1}, and m=0 gives the value 1. But a modulus in 'm≡n₀ (mod M)' is by universal convention nonzero, and negative M is harmless. The paper itself treats M as positive wherever it matters: Definition 1.8 says M∈ℕ and uses φ(M); Theorem 1.9, from which Theorems 1.5 and 1.2 are derived, says 'M be positive integers'; Corollary 1.6, Proposition 2.8 and Corollary 2.9 take M∈ℕ, and ℕ={1,2,…} in this paper. The instructions exclude harmless conventions, and recording this against the authors would be unfair. I judged only the p. 675/677 occurrence. The Proposition 6.7 p. 730 occurrence ('a multiple of 8a₁a₂a₃', where 0 is a multiple) is outside my range, but the same convention argument applies. Independent check: Checked on the images of p. 675 (Theorem 1.2: 'Fix integers n₀ and M'), p. 677 (same standing assumption) and p. 730 (Proposition 6.7: 'Let M be a multiple of 8a₁a₂a₃'). In all three places M is used only as a modulus ('m ≡ n₀ (mod M)', 'P ≡ Q (mod M)', 'coprime to M'). A modulus is read as a positive integer by the standard convention of analytic number theory. Negative M is harmless, since mod M means mod |M|. The paper states the positivity wherever it is used quantitatively: Theorem 1.9 ('n, d_1,…,d_n, M be positive integers', p. 680), from which Theorems 1.5 and 1.2 are derived; Definition 1.8 (M ∈ ℕ, with φ(M) and M^{1−n}); Corollary 1.6; Proposition 2.8; Corollary 2.9. Here ℕ = {1,2,…} (p. 684: 'd_1,…,d_n ∈ ℕ', used on p. 685 as 'd_i ⩾ 1'). The ledger's counterexample for Theorem 1.2 (M = 0, n₀ = 0, Q = t+1) is literally valid, but only under the degenerate reading 'congruence modulo 0 = equality', which no reader would adopt there. For Proposition 6.7, M = 0 does not even give a counterexample. P ≡ Q (mod 0) forces P = Q, and m ≡ n₀ (mod 0) forces m = n₀. (Q_ij(n₀), 0) = 1 forces Q_ij(n₀) = ±1, so the fibre at n₀ is a smooth conic. Every prime divides 0, so the hypothesis gives local points at every prime, hence at ℝ by Hilbert reciprocity. Hasse–Minkowski then gives a ℚ-point, so the conclusion holds. This is a harmless convention, not a mistake that should be recorded against the authors. The first reading's proposed rejection is correct.

On p. 694 it asserts |f(t)| ≤ Σ_{m|t} log m ≤ (log t)τ(t) for f = E_z and f = Λ_z, and attributes ‖S_{E_z}‖_∞ ≪_C 𝓜^d H(log H)(log z)^{−C} in (3.3) to Corollary 3.3.
issues.correction: Add after (3.1): 'Here Λ(n) := Λ(|n|) for n ∈ ℤ∖{0} and Λ(0) := 0; for all n ∈ ℤ put Λ_z(n) := −Σ_{d≤z, d|n} μ(d) log d (so Λ_z(0) = −Σ_{d≤z} μ(d) log d) and E_z := Λ − Λ_z, both even.' In the proof of Proposition 3.8, use |f(t)| ≤ τ(|t|)log|t| for t ≠ 0 and |f(0)| ≤ z log z. For (3.3), write S_{E_z}(α) = E_z(0) + T(α) + T(−α) with T(α) = Σ_{1≤c≤B} E_z(c)e^{icα}, apply Corollary 3.3 to T, and bound E_z(0) = Σ_{d≤z} μ(d)log d ≪_C z(log z)^{−C} (Lemma 3.2 at α = 0 plus partial summation). Theorem 3.1, Proposition 3.8 and Lemma 3.9 then hold as printed with this convention. Lemma 3.10 already uses it.
issues.reason: G_{k,m}(H;d) sums Λ(P(k))Λ(P(m)) over P > 0 in a box, and P(k) takes both signs for a positive proportion of P when k is small. S_{E_z} is a sum over |c| ≤ (d+1)𝓜^d H, but Corollary 3.3 only bounds sums over r ∈ ℕ ∩ [1,y]. Under the usual extension Λ(n) = 0 for n ≤ 0, the natural (divisibility-defined, hence even) Λ_z gives E_z(−c) = −Λ_z(c). At α = 0 the negative half is then −Σ_{c≤B}Λ_z(c) = −B + o(B), for example when z = H^{1/2}, since Σ_{d≤z}μ(d)log d/d → −1. So ‖S_{E_z}‖_∞ ≫ B and (3.3) fails. Theorem 3.1 is then false. Numerical check (my own): for d = 1, k = 1, m = 2, H = 2000, G/(2H²) = 0.997 with Λ even but 0.749 with Λ = 0 on n ≤ 0. For d = 2, k = 1, m = 3, H = 160 the ratio to the stated main term is 0.969 versus 0.687. No non-even convention rescues the section: Lemma 3.10 (p. 696) counts c with k1 | P_c(k), which is blind to sign, so it computes the even Λ_z-sum. If Λ_z is also set to 0 on n ≤ 0, Proposition 3.8's proof goes through but Lemma 3.10's main term is wrong. Defence: the paper's Λ_z definition already makes sense and is even on Z, and the repair is routine. But the paper never states the convention, and its proofs write log t for t ≤ 0 and omit the c = 0 term. Revision: the printed quotation is made verbatim (the old one spliced two sentences), the proof steps that need the convention are pinpointed, and numerical evidence and the Lemma 3.10 consistency argument are added. Kind and reach are unchanged. §4 then counts |P(m)| prime for negative values, which θ_P does not; that is handled outside this range (items 40/101, E1/E10).

issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: Quotation checked on the page images (p. 690, p. 691, and p. 694 at 300 dpi). All four quoted passages are verbatim. The (3.3) quotation stops before the second bound '≪_{δ1} H(log H)^{1+dδ2−C}'. An ellipsis there would be cleaner, but nothing is misquoted. Substance: the paper defines Λ, Λ_z and E_z only for r ∈ ℕ ('Recall that for r ∈ ℕ …'; Corollary 3.3 sums over r ∈ ℕ ∩ [1,y]). But (3.1) evaluates Λ at P(k), which is negative on a positive proportion of the box. S_F is defined for F : ℤ → ℝ over |c| ≤ (d+1)𝓜^d H, so (3.3) needs E_z on all of ℤ. (i) Under the standard extension Λ(n) = 0 for n ≤ 0, Theorem 3.1 is false. For d = 1 and k = 1 < m, the region where P(1), P(m) > 0 is c0 > −c1, which has area 3/2 out of 2, so G_{1,m} ~ (3/4)·(stated main term). My own C computation (independent of the first reading's scripts) gives the ratio G/main as even Λ vs zero-extended Λ: d=1, (k,m)=(1,2), H=2000: 0.9974 vs 0.7491 (the first reading's figures reproduced); H=10^4: 0.9994 vs 0.7498; (1,3), H=10^4 (singular series 2): 0.9985 vs 0.7494; (2,5), H=5000: 0.9984 vs 0.8744. d=2, (1,3), H=160: 0.9694 vs 0.6874 (the first reading's figures reproduced); H=300: 0.9796 vs 0.6909. d=3, (1,2), H=60: 0.9929 vs 0.6677. In each case the zero-extended ratio tracks the box fraction with P(k), P(m) > 0 (0.75, 0.875, 0.70, 0.66). (ii) Step (3.3) fails under that convention. Λ_z, defined by divisibility, is even, so E_z(−c) = −Λ_z(c), and at α = 0 the negative half contributes −Σ_{c≤B} Λ_z(c) = B·Σ_{d≤z} μ(d)log d/d + O(z log z) → −B. Computed: B = 4·10^6, z = 1000 gives S_{E_z}(0)/B = −0.940 zero-extended vs +0.060 even. B = 4·10^7, z = 20000 gives −0.972 vs +0.028. (iii) No other convention rescues §3. If Λ_z is also zero-extended, (3.3) and Proposition 3.8 hold, but Lemma 3.10 is then false. Its proof, (3.4) and p. 697, counts c ∈ [−H,H]^{d+1} with k1 | P_c(k), which does not see the sign. Computed for d=1: (k,m,H,z) = (1,2,2·10^4,10) and (1,3,2·10^4,12) give an even Λ_z-sum / Lemma 3.10 main term of 1.0000 but a zero-extended ratio of 0.7500. (iv) Under the even convention the repair works. For t ≠ 0, E_z(t) = −Σ_{d|t,d>z} μ(d)log d, and both |E_z(t)| and |Λ_z(t)| are ≤ τ(|t|)log|t|. Also |Λ_z(0)| = |E_z(0)| ≤ z log z ≤ H log H, so S_{|f|}(0) keeps its bound. S_{E_z}(α) = E_z(0) + T(α) + T(−α), with T the one-sided sum of Corollary 3.3. Also E_z(0) = Σ_{d≤z} μ(d)log d ≪_C z(log z)^{−C} by partial summation from Lemma 3.2 at α = 0. So (3.3) holds, and Lemma 3.9 uses the same (3.3). Defence considered: the main term 2^d H^{d+1}∏ p/(p−1) counts the whole box, and Lemma 3.10 is sign-blind, so the even reading is recoverable. But the paper never states it. The p. 691 wording restricts Λ to ℕ, the proofs write log t for t ≤ 0, and the c = 0 term is dropped. The same sign blindness gives a genuinely false statement in Lemma 3.14 (E1). So this is a gap, not a misprint. It reaches the stated Theorem 3.1, whose statement must gain the convention. The kind, the reach and the revised text are right.

issues.citation: Skorobogatov–Sofos, "Schinzel Hypothesis on average and rational points", Inventiones Mathematicae (2023)
issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: Revision accepted; checked on the page images. Lemma 4.1 (p. 704) asserts the equality Σ_P θ_P(x)² = 2Σ_{1⩽m<k⩽x, k≡m≡n₀ (mod M)} ∏_i 𝒢_{k,m}(H; d_i) + O(xH^{d+n}(log H)^n). By (1.4) (Definition 1.8, p. 679), θ_P counts only the m for which every P_i(m) is prime, with weight ∏ log P_i(m), so the primes are positive. The proof (pp. 704–705) starts from '1_primes(j) log j ⩽ Λ(j) … the sum over the P_i in our lemma is at most' Σ_P(Σ_m ∏Λ(P_i(m)))² = Σ_{k,m} ∏𝒢_{k,m}. It then bounds the diagonal k = m by (log H)^n Σ_m ∏_i Σ_{P_i} Λ(P_i(m)) ≪ xH^{d+n}(log H)^n (Lemma 3.14 with Ω = 1) and ends 'which is sufficient for the proof' (p. 705). No lower bound is ever given, so only '⩽' is proved. The quotation in the revision matches the page; the ledger's old 'printed' was a paraphrase. Lemma 4.4 (p. 707: 'Taking sufficiently large A in Theorem 3.1 and using Lemma 4.1 yields Σθ_P(x)² = 2^{d+1}H^{d+n}T₀(x) + …') and (4.5) (p. 709: 'Combining Lemma 4.5 with Lemma 4.4 gives') are equalities that rest only on Lemma 4.1, so the extended locator is right. The lower bound is not a formality. 𝒢_{k,m} (3.1, p. 690) satisfies Theorem 3.1 only with Λ even (E4), so it also counts P(k) or P(m) equal to −ℓ^α. For m = 1 these are a positive proportion of the box (for d = 1, c₀ + c₁ < 0 on 1/4 of it). The crude bound (defect ⩽ ∏𝒢 for each pair) gives only O(x²H^{d+n}), which is not inside O(xH^{d+n}(log H)^n) once x > (log H)^n, and §4.4 works in exactly that range. I re-derived the sketch in the correction. For 1 ⩽ m < k, P(m) ⩽ 0 forces c_d m^d ⩽ HΣ_{j<d} m^j ⩽ dHm^{d−1}, i.e. c_d ⩽ dH/m, and P(k) ⩽ 0 forces c_d ⩽ dH/k < dH/m. Since P(k) ≡ P(m) (mod p) for p | k − m, the two-form sieve in (c₀, c₁) has local factor ∏_{p|k−m} p/(p−1). With 0 ⩽ ∏G⁺ ⩽ ∏𝒢 and ∏𝒢 − ∏G⁺ ⩽ Σ_i(𝒢_i − G⁺_i)∏_{j≠i}𝒢_j, each pair then contributes ≪ m^{−1}H^{d+n}∏_{p|k−m}(p/(p−1))^n. By Lemma 4.3 the sum over m < k ⩽ x is ≪ x log x ≪ xH^{d+n}(log H)^n (the H^{d+n} factor comes along, and log x ≪ log log H). Proper prime powers give H^{d+n−1/2+o(1)} per pair. So the equalities are very likely true, and the right label is 'gap' affecting only the proof. In (4.1) (p. 703) Σθ² enters with a plus sign, and §4.4 (p. 714) uses (4.5) only to bound the right side of (4.1) from above, so the proved upper bound is all that is needed and Theorem 1.9 is unaffected (E1 is a separate issue). For θ^Λ the printed argument is an identity plus the diagonal bound, so restating the lemmas for θ^Λ (items 40 and 88) is also correct. Minor: the proof of Lemma 4.1 ends on p. 705, so the locator could read pp. 704–705.

issues.locator: Corollary 1.10, pp. 680–681, and the sentence before it ('From Theorem 1.9 and Markov's inequality one immediately deduces…'), p. 680
issues.printed: The source asserts, simultaneously for every x with (log|P|)^{A₁} < x ≤ (log|P|)^{A₂}, that irreducible P ∈ ℤ[t] satisfying P > 0 and deg(P) = d obey Σ_{m∈ℕ∩[1,x], P(m) prime} log P(m) = (∏_{ℓ≤log x}(1−ℓ^{−1}Z_P(ℓ))/(1−ℓ^{−1}))x + O(x/(log x)^c). Among polynomials with |P| ≤ H, it allows at most O(H^{d+1}(log log H)^{c−1/2}) exceptions.
issues.correction: Either state Corollary 1.10 pointwise in x or supply a maximal inequality in x. Pointwise version: for every H ≥ 3 and every x, #{P ∈ ℤ[t]: P > 0, deg P = d, |P| ≤ H, (log|P|)^{A₁} < x ≤ (log|P|)^{A₂}, |θ_P(x) − 𝔖_P(x)x| > x/(log x)^c} ≪ H^{d+1}(loglog H)^{c−1/2}. Irreducibility is not needed. This follows from Theorem 1.9 (n = M = n₀ = 1) and Markov on the dyadic ranges H/2^k ≥ H^{1/2} with some A₁' ∈ (1, A₁). The printed form, one exceptional set for all x, needs a bound for the average over P of sup_x |θ_P(x) − 𝔖_P(x)x|, which the paper does not prove.
issues.reason: Markov applied to Theorem 1.9 gives, for each fixed x, at most #Poly(H)·R(x,H)·(log x)^c/x ≪ H^{d+1}(loglog H)^{c−1/2} exceptions. The natural reading of the corollary, however, puts 'for all x' inside a single exceptional set of P. Moving from the H-range to the |P|-range is routine (dyadic argument above). The existing reason lists it as a second obstruction; it is not one. The real gap is uniformity in x, and the obvious repairs fail. θ_P is increasing and 𝔖_P(x)≪loglog x, so a P-independent grid for x with ratio 1+δ, δ≍(log x)^{−c}/loglog x, controls the intervals between grid points. That grid needs ≍(loglog H)^{1+c}·logloglog H points on [(log H)^{A_1},(log H)^{A_2}]. A union bound with Markov then gives H^{d+1}(loglog H)^{2c+1/2+o(1)}. Even with Chebyshev and the stronger V(x,H)≪x²/log x of §4 it gives H^{d+1}(loglog H)^{3c+o(1)}. Both exceed the trivial H^{d+1}. The paper nowhere proves a sup-in-x statement; Lemma 4.10 and §4.5 also work at fixed x. This remains a missing argument, not a proven falsity. For the defence: the lead-in sentence ('immediately deduces') suggests the authors meant the pointwise statement, which is correct.

issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: The quotation matches pp. 680–681. Theorem 1.9 with n = M = n₀ = 1 gives R(x,H) ≪ x/√(log x) for (log H)^{A₁} < x ≤ (log H)^{A₂} and A₁ > 1. Markov at a fixed x then gives at most #Poly(H)·R(x,H)(log x)^c/x ≪ H^{d+1}(log x)^{c−1/2} ≪ H^{d+1}(loglog H)^{c−1/2} exceptions. Passing from the H-range to the |P|-range is routine, as the revision says. Split |P| dyadically into H_k = H/2^k ≥ H^{1/2} and use Theorem 1.9 with some A₁' ∈ (1, A₁); since x ≥ (log|P|)^{A₁} ≥ (log H_k)^{A₁'}, each piece contributes ≪ H_k^{d+1}(loglog H)^{c−1/2}. Polynomials with |P| < H^{1/2} number O(H^{(d+1)/2}). Irreducibility is never needed. So the old ledger reason's second obstruction ('nor replace H by |P|') is not one, and the revision is right to drop it. The real gap is uniformity in x. The sentence puts 'for all x' before a single exceptional set of P, and the lead-in ('a form of the Bateman–Horn conjecture valid for almost all polynomials') confirms that this stronger reading is meant. The obvious repair fails. θ_P is increasing and 𝔖_P(x) ≤ ∏_{ℓ≤log x}(1−1/ℓ)^{−1} ≪ loglog x, so a grid with ratio 1+δ, δ ≍ (log x)^{−c}/loglog x (plus the O(loglog H) jump points e^ℓ of 𝔖_P), controls the gaps. That grid has ≍ (loglog H)^{1+c}·logloglog H points. The union bound then gives H^{d+1}(loglog H)^{2c+1/2+o(1)} with Markov. It gives H^{d+1}(loglog H)^{3c+o(1)} with Chebyshev and the intended §4 bound V(x,H) ≪ x²/log x (p. 703, printed there as x²/(log x)^{−1}). Both exceed the trivial count H^{d+1}. The paper contains no maximal inequality in x: Theorem 1.9, §4 and Lemma 4.10 are all at fixed x. So the uniform statement is unproven, not shown false. The pointwise statement is correct and immediate. The revised issue is accurate: kind gap, affects a stated result.

issues.citation: Skorobogatov–Sofos, "Schinzel Hypothesis on average and rational points", Inventiones Mathematicae (2023)
issues.reviewReason: 'A subset ℳ′ ⊂ ℳ of density 1' is the standard phrase for relative density 1 in ℳ. 'When 𝒫 is ordered by height' fixes the ordering, which ℳ inherits, not the denominator. The next sentence names the ambient set explicitly ('positive density in ℤ^{d+1}') when the ambient is meant. Example 5.6 on the next page shows the authors know that ℳ misses a positive proportion of 𝒫, so the reading 'density 1 in 𝒫' is excluded by the paper itself. The proof gives exactly relative density 1 in each ℳ_i. This is a harmless convention, not a slip. Independent check: The quotation checks out on p. 719, and Theorems 5.8 (p. 722) and 6.1 (p. 725) use the same wording. It is not a mistake. 'A subset ℳ′ ⊂ ℳ of density 1' has its standard meaning, relative density 1 in ℳ. This matches the paper's '100% of' usage in Theorems 1.1–1.2, which is always relative to the named family. 'When 𝒫 is ordered by height' fixes the ordering, which ℳ ⊂ 𝒫 inherits. It does not fix a denominator. Measuring the density in 𝒫 would make no sense: ℳ′ ⊂ ℳ, and Example 5.6 (p. 720) shows that ℳ can miss a positive proportion of 𝒫, so that reading would make the theorem false in a way the authors plainly know about. When the ambient set is meant, the next sentence names it ('positive density in ℤ^{d+1}'). The proof gives exactly the relative statement: 100% of each of finitely many ℳ_i, hence of ℳ = ∪ℳ_i, since #ℳ_i(H) ≤ #ℳ(H). This is a harmless convention, so E15 should be rejected.

issues.reviewReason: For odd t ∈ ℤ_2 and m ≥ 2, t^s ≡ 1 (mod 2^{m+1}), because (ℤ/2^{m+1})^* has exponent 2^{m−1} = s. So P(t) = 2^m(1 + 2a(2^m−3) + 4Q(t)) with an odd cofactor, and v_2(P(t)) = m exactly. For even t there is no solution. So every 2-adic solution has valuation m, which is never divisible by 2^m (2^m > m): the printed sentence is false for every m, but the intended claim (2^m | P(t), so P(t) is not a unit and U_m(ℤ_2) = ∅) is clear and correct. issues.locator: Published Remark 5.9(2) p. 722
issues.printed: In (2), the source uses the Bouniakowsky property of each P_i(t, m_i) to choose, for every p ∉ S, a t_p ∈ ℤ_p with P_i(t_p, m_i) ∈ ℤ_p^*, giving inv_p(χ, P_i(t_p, m_i)) = 0. Multiplication over i = 1, …, n is then said to yield a ℤ_p-point of U_m above t_p.
issues.correction: Since (P_1(t,m_1),…,P_n(t,m_n)) is a Schinzel n-tuple, P_1⋯P_n mod p is not divisible by t^p − t. Hence there is one t_p ∈ ℤ_p with P_i(t_p,m_i) ∈ ℤ_p^* for every i. Then inv_p(χ,P_i(t_p,m_i)) = 0 for all i, and by Lemma 5.1 U_m has a ℤ_p-point over t_p.
issues.reason: The product step needs one t_p for all i. Bouniakowsky for each P_i separately does not give it: t and t+1 are each non-vanishing somewhere on 𝔽_2, but t(t+1) vanishes on all of 𝔽_2. The hypothesis m ∈ 𝒫 (Schinzel) gives the common t_p, so the remark's claim is true and only the stated reason is inadequate. Revision: 'affects' should be 'nothing', not 'the proof'. Remark 5.9(2) is motivation (local solubility and absence of a Brauer–Manin obstruction). It is not used in the proof of Theorem 5.8, which handles primes p ∉ S ∪ {q_i} directly on p. 724 via q_i ∈ ℤ_p^*, nor anywhere later (Remark 6.2 cites only (5.2)).

issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: The quotation checks out on p. 722, and the revision is right. The product step needs one t_p that works for every i at once. Counterexample: P_1 = t and P_2 = t+1 are each Bouniakowsky, but t(t+1) vanishes on all of 𝔽_2, and 2 ∉ S for many cyclic K (e.g. ℚ(ζ_7)^+). Lemma 5.1 then gives the ℤ_p-point and inv_p(χ,P_i(t_p,m_i)) = 0 for all i. So the remark's conclusions are true, and only the stated reason is inadequate. Nothing depends on the remark. The proof of Theorem 5.8 (p. 724) treats p ∉ S ∪ {q_i} directly, since q_i is a unit and p is unramified. Remark 5.9 is cited nowhere else (a text search finds only its own occurrence), and Remark 6.2 cites only (5.2). So 'affects: nothing' is correct, not 'the proof'.

issues.printed: The source derives log P_ij(m) = O_{d_ij}(log(Hx)) from P_ij(m) = O_{d_ij}(Hx^{d_ij}), and consequently asserts 0 ⩽ θ_P(x) − θ̃_P(x) ≪_{n,d_ij} (log(Hx))^n in (6.7).

In the average on p. 732, treat the tuples with a repeated polynomial separately. They make up a proportion ≪H^{−2} of Poly(H), and for them |C_P−2^{1−n}θ_P| ≤ θ_P ≪ x(log H)^n. issues.reason: Confirmed; only the counterexample in the reason needs sharpening. θ_P (Definition 1.8) carries the condition m≡n₀ (mod M), so for P₁=P₂=t+1, θ_P(x)∼x log x/φ(M) (not x log x). A fully admissible instance of Proposition 6.7: a=(1,1,−1), n₁=n₂=1, n₃=0, M=8, n₀=0, Q₁₁=Q₂₁=t+1. Every P≡Q (mod 8) and m≡0 (mod 8) give P₁₁(m)≡1 (mod 8), a 2-adic square, so the conic P₁₁(m)x²+P₂₁(m)y²−z²=0 has the ℚ₂-point (1,0,√P₁₁(m)), and the hypothesis holds. issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: The quotation is on p. 731 (checked on the image), and the arXiv v3 TeX has the same text. θ̃_P has the extra condition P_ij(m)≠P_rs(m) for (i,j)≠(r,s), so θ_P−θ̃_P is the sum of ∏log P_ij(m) over those m for which two of the primes P_ij(m) coincide. The printed argument bounds each term by (C log(Hx))^n, but it never bounds how many such m there are. If the tuple has two equal polynomials, every m counts, and θ̃_P=0. The proposed instance satisfies every hypothesis of Proposition 6.7. With a=(1,1,−1), a₁a₂a₃=−1 is square-free and the signs are not all equal. M=8 is a multiple of 8a₁a₂a₃, n₀=0, and Q₁₁=Q₂₁=t+1 has Q(0)=1, which is coprime to 8. Suppose P≡Q (mod 8) and m≡0 (mod 8). Then P₁₁(m)≡P₂₁(m)≡1 (mod 8), so P₁₁(m) is a non-zero square in ℚ₂, and (1,0,√P₁₁(m)) is a ℚ₂-point of P₁₁(m)x²+P₂₁(m)y²−z²=0. The tuple P=(t+1,t+1) is Schinzel: (t+1)² mod ℓ has one root, and mod 2 it is t²+1, which t does not divide. P lies in Poly(H) for every H≥1. Also θ̃_P=0, while θ_P(x)=Σ_{m≤x, 8|m, m+1 prime} log²(m+1) ∼ (x log x)/4. For x=(log H)^5, which lies in the range of (6.8), the ratio θ_P/(log(Hx))² tends to infinity. So (6.7) is false for admissible P in exactly the range where it is used. The remedy holds. For pairwise distinct P_ij, each pair agrees at no more than max(d_ij,d_rs) values of m, which gives (6.7) with constant ≤ n²·max d_ij·C^n. The tuples with a repeated polynomial need d_ij=d_rs, Q_ij≡Q_rs (mod M) and d_ij+1 ≥ 2 coincident coefficients, so they make up a proportion ≪H^{−2} of Poly(H). For them, C_P=θ̃_P=0 and θ_P ≪ x(log(Hx))^n ≪ x(log H)^n, since x ≤ (log H)^{3n}. Their contribution to the average on p. 732 is therefore ≪ H^{−2}x(log H)^n = o(1), and Proposition 6.7 is unaffected. The only use of (6.7) is that average.

issues.locator: Remark after Definition 1.8, top of p. 680
issues.printed: The source claims convergence of 𝔖_P(x) as x → ∞ for fixed P, citing the number-field version of the prime number theorem as the basis of the argument. It further asserts that absolute convergence requires every P_i to be linear.
issues.correction: Add the Bateman–Horn hypotheses: 'for a fixed P with P_1,…,P_n irreducible and pairwise distinct'. With them both sentences are correct. For general P allowed by Definition 1.8 neither holds: take (t+1, t+1), where the product diverges to ∞; (t+1)(t+3), where it tends to 0; or t², where it converges absolutely although P is not linear.
issues.reason: I confirm the existing counterexample: n=2, M=1, P_1=P_2=t+1 is a Schinzel pair, Z_{P_1P_2}(ℓ)=1, each factor is (1−1/ℓ)^{−1}, and 𝔖_P(x)~e^γ loglog x→∞. Such tuples lie in Poly(H) whenever d_i=d_j and Q_i≡Q_j. The second sentence also fails literally: n=1, P=t² (Schinzel, since Z(ℓ)=1≠ℓ) has every factor equal to 1, so the product converges absolutely although P is not linear. Under the Bateman–Horn hypotheses both claims are right. Convergence follows from the prime ideal theorem for ℚ[t]/(P_i) and partial summation. Absolute convergence forces linearity: Σ_i(π_i−1), a sum of permutation characters of the Galois group of P_1⋯P_n minus trivial characters, vanishes identically only if every π_i is trivial. Defence: the preceding sentence ties 𝔖_P to 'the Hardy–Littlewood singular series associated to Schinzel's Hypothesis' ([6]), and the PNT for number fields presupposes irreducible factors, so the intended scope is recoverable. If the reviewer weights this context heavily, 'misprint' (a missing hypothesis whose meaning is clear) is also defensible. The remark is never used; the paper works with the truncated product throughout.

issues.citation: Skorobogatov–Sofos, "Schinzel Hypothesis on average and rational points", Inventiones Mathematicae (2023)
issues.reviewReason: Revised on re-reading; independent check: The quotation matches the top of p. 680 (image). The claim is made 'for a fixed P', where P is as in Definition 1.8 (p. 679): any tuple with P_i > 0, n₀ ∈ ℤ and M ∈ ℕ. Counterexample to the first sentence: n = 2, M = 1, P₁ = P₂ = t+1. This is a Schinzel pair (Z_{P₁P₂}(ℓ) = 1 ≠ ℓ) and lies in Poly(H) whenever d₁ = d₂ and Q₁ ≡ Q₂. The prefactor is 1 and each factor is (1−1/ℓ)/(1−1/ℓ)² = (1−1/ℓ)^{−1}, so 𝔖_P(x) ~ e^γ loglog x → ∞. Irreducibility is also needed for n = 1: P = (t+1)(t+3) is Schinzel (Z(2) = 1, Z(3) = 2), and its product ≍ 1/loglog x → 0. The second sentence also fails literally: P = t² (n = 1, Schinzel) has every factor equal to 1, so the product converges absolutely although P is not linear. Under the Bateman–Horn hypotheses (P_i irreducible and pairwise distinct) both sentences are true. For such tuples Z_{∏P_i}(ℓ) = Σ Z_{P_i}(ℓ) for all but finitely many ℓ. The prime ideal theorem with partial summation gives conditional convergence. Absolute convergence holds iff Σ_i(π_i − 1) = 0, where π_i are the permutation characters of the Galois group. Each π_i − 1 is a genuine character, so this sum vanishes only if every P_i is linear; otherwise Chebotarev gives a positive density of ℓ with Z ≠ n. The defence: the preceding sentence ties 𝔖_P to the Hardy–Littlewood singular series for Schinzel's Hypothesis ([6]), and the PNT for number fields presupposes irreducible factors, so the intended scope can be recovered. But the missing hypothesis is stated nowhere, and the paper's own averages range over tuples where the remark fails. I keep 'error'; 'misprint' is a defensible alternative. The remark is never used, since the paper works only with the truncated product, so the issue affects nothing. The revision is accurate.

issues.locator: Published Theorem 1.5 p. 677, Eq. (1.3) ('for all H ⩾ 3'); cf. its proof p. 717 ('when H ≫_{d,n,A} 1')
issues.printed: Theorem 1.5 fixes A > 0 and claims, under Theorem 1.2's hypotheses and for every H ⩾ 3, ♯{P ∈ Poly(H): P is Schinzel, ♯S_{n+A}(P) ⩾ (log|P|)^{A/3}} / ♯{P ∈ Poly(H): P is Schinzel} = 1 + O((log log log H)^{d−n}/√(log log H)).
issues.correction: State (1.3) for H ≥ H_0(d, n, A, M) as the proof gives, or replace log log log H by max(1, log log log H). With the latter, bounded H is absorbed into the implied constant.
issues.reason: For d > n the error term is 0 at H = e^e ≈ 15.15, very small near it, and negative for odd d−n below e^e. The ratio is < 1 there. Take n = 1, d_1 = 2, M = 1, A = 3, Q = 0 and P = 2t² + t + 1. P is Schinzel (P(0) = 1) with |P| = 2, but S_4(P) = {m ∈ ℕ: m ≤ (log 2)^4} = ∅ while (log|P|)^{A/3} = log 2 > 0, so P is excluded. For all H ∈ [15, 16) the family and the ratio (< 1) are the same, while the error term → 0 as H → e^e. So no implied constant works for 'all H ≥ 3'. For large H the theorem is unaffected. Noticed while checking the proof on p. 717; the statement is on p. 677.

issues.citation: Skorobogatov–Sofos, "Schinzel Hypothesis on average and rational points", Inventiones Mathematicae (2023)
issues.reviewReason: Checked on p. 677: (1.3) is asserted 'for all H ⩾ 3' with error O((log log log H)^{d−n}/√(log log H)), and Poly(H) is defined for real H ≥ 1. The Notation paragraph (p. 683) only assumes that iterated logarithms are well defined, and log log log H is well defined, and negative, on [3, e^e). So the convention does not rescue the statement. The proof on p. 717 explicitly works 'when H ≫_{d,n,A} 1'. For d > n the error term vanishes at H = e^e ≈ 15.154. Example: n = 1, d_1 = 2, M = 1, A = 3, Q = 0. P = 2t² + t + 1 is Schinzel, since it is positive and P(0) = 1 is a non-root mod every ℓ, and |P| = 2. Its set S_4(P) = {m ∈ ℕ : m ≤ (log 2)^4 ≈ 0.23} is empty, while (log 2)^{A/3} = 0.69 > 0, so P lies in the denominator but not the numerator for every H ≥ 2. By exhaustive count the ratio is 8794/10299 ≈ 0.854 for every H ∈ [15, 16), while (log log log H)/√(log log H) = −0.0038 at H = 15, 0 at e^e and +0.0082 at H = 15.5. So 1 − ratio = 0.146 cannot be ≤ C·|error| as H → e^e, for any C. If H were restricted to integers, a constant ≥ 39 (forced at H = 15) would cover this, but the paper treats H as real. Only the range is wrong. The asymptotic content is untouched and the fix is routine, so misprint/nothing is the fair classification rather than an error in a stated result.

issues.locator: Corollary 1.7, p. 678; proof p. 679
issues.printed: The source claims that (x, y, z, t) ∈ ℕ⁴ solves to x² − ay² = P(t)z² satisfying max{x, y, z, t} ≤ |a|^{1/2}|P|^{1/2}(log |P|)^{d/2+ε}. It later asserts that (x₁, y₁, z₁) = (bx₀, y₀, bz₀) gives a nonzero solution to x² − ay² = pz².
issues.correction: Either add 'a not a square' (the proof is then complete once x₀y₀z₀ ≠ 0 is noted, as above), or state the conclusion as the proof gives it: t ∈ ℕ and (x,y,z) ∈ ℤ_{⩾0}³ ∖ {(0,0,0)}, which for square a is trivial via (b,1,0). For square a with x,y,z ⩾ 1 the statement appears true but needs a different argument. The prime-value argument cannot work, since then x > P(t)/2.
issues.reason: In this paper ℕ={1,2,…}. Corollary 1.6 and Theorem 3.1 fix d∈ℕ. Definition 1.8 and Proposition 2.8 take M∈ℕ and use φ(M). Theorem 1.4 with all d_ij=0 would be false. So (x,y,z,t)∈ℕ⁴ requires x,y,z≥1, but the proof only produces a 'non-zero solution'. For a=b² (a₀=1) it provably cannot do better. Holzer's bounds for (−1,1,p) are |x₀|,|y₀|≤√p and |z₀|≤1. The value z₀=±1 would need x₀²−y₀²=p, so x₀=(p+1)/2>√p. Hence every Holzer-bounded solution has z₀=0, i.e. (x₁,y₁,z₁)=(b,1,0) up to sign. More strongly, every solution of x²−b²y²=pz² with z≠0 has x≥p/2 (one factor of (x−by)(x+by)=pz² is divisible by p), far above (|a|p)^{1/2}. A brute-force check confirms this: for a=1,4,9 and the first primes p≡1 (mod 8a), the least x with y,z≥1 is (p+1)/2. So for square a the printed statement is not established by the argument. Defence: if ℕ is read as containing 0 and 'solution' as nontrivial, which the proof's 'non-zero solution' suggests, the corollary is correct as proved; for square a the conic has the obvious point (b:1:0). But with 0∈ℕ the printed statement is trivial via x=y=z=0, so on either reading the formulation needs a fix. The reviewer may prefer 'misprint' on the nontrivial-solution reading. The case of non-square a, the one of interest, is fully proved once x₀y₀z₀≠0 is noted.

issues.citation: Skorobogatov–Sofos, "Schinzel Hypothesis on average and rational points", Inventiones Mathematicae (2023)
issues.reviewReason: Both quotations match pp. 678–679 (images). ℕ = {1,2,…} in this paper: p. 684 says 'd_1,…,d_n ∈ ℕ', used on p. 685 as 'Since d_i ⩾ 1', and ℤ_{⩾0} is written when 0 is wanted (p. 685). So '(x,y,z,t) ∈ ℕ⁴' requires x,y,z,t ⩾ 1, but the proof only produces a 'non-zero solution' (x₁,y₁,z₁) ∈ ℤ³. Non-square a: the missing step is easy. If y₀ = 0 then x₀² = pz₀². If x₀ = 0 then −a₀y₀² = pz₀², and p ∤ a₀. If z₀ = 0 then x₀² = a₀y₀² with a₀ ≠ 1 squarefree. In each case valuation parity forces (x₀,y₀,z₀) = 0. So after taking absolute values the solution lies in ℕ⁴ and the corollary holds. Square a = b² (a₀ = 1): the step fails. Holzer's bounds for (f₁,f₂,f₃) = (−1,1,p) are |x₀|,|y₀| ≤ √p and |z₀| ≤ 1. z₀ = ±1 would need x₀² − y₀² = p, i.e. |x₀| = (p+1)/2 > √p. So every Holzer-bounded solution is (k,±k,0) with 1 ≤ |k| ≤ √p, and (x₁,y₁,z₁) = (bk,±k,0) has z = 0 ∉ ℕ. Even the paper's weaker combined bound max ≤ (|a₀|p)^{1/2} forces z₀ = 0. Worse, the prime route cannot be repaired. Any solution of x² − b²y² = pz² with x,y,z ⩾ 1 has x > p/2, because p divides x−by or x+by. But p/2 > b√p since p ≡ 1 (mod 8a). Brute force confirms this. For a = 1, 4, 9 and the first 8 primes p ≡ 1 (mod 8a), every nonzero Holzer-bounded solution has z = 0 (e.g. p = 17: 16 solutions, all z = 0). The least x with x,y,z ⩾ 1 is exactly (p+1)/2 (e.g. (9,8,1) for p = 17, a = 1). The printed statement is not shown false, however. An exhaustive search over all t, z (not only prime values P(t)) found solutions in ℕ⁴ within |a|^{1/2}|P|^{1/2}(log|P|)^{d/2+0.01} for most random P of height ≤ H. Rates: a=1, d=1: 193/200 (H=10⁴), 198/200 (10⁶), 100/100 (10⁹). a=1, d=2: 199/200 (10⁶), 100/100 (10⁹). a=4, d=1,2 (H=10⁶): 199/200, 200/200. a=9, d=3 (H=10⁶): 100/100. These solutions come from values P(t) with a divisor near √P(t), mostly with z = 1 or 2. A heuristic count (≈ log|P| values of t, each succeeding with probability ≈ (log|P|)^{−0.086}, by Ford's results on divisors in intervals) suggests the statement holds for 100% of P. So for square a the corollary is plausibly true but unproven: the step 'non-zero solution ⇒ solution in ℕ⁴' is invalid there, and no quick repair is available. Hence error, affecting a stated result. Defence: if the intended object is a rational point of the conic bundle x² − ay² = P(t)z² in ℙ² × 𝔸¹, then for square a the points (b:1:0; t) are trivial. On that reading the corollary is trivially true and only its formulation ('ℕ⁴') is at fault. With 0 ∈ ℕ and no non-triviality condition, x = y = z = 0 would make the statement vacuous. So on every reading the formulation needs a fix. The reviewer may prefer 'misprint' on the non-trivial-projective-point reading.

issues.correction: In Corollary 1.6 write 'fix d, M ∈ ℕ and n₀ ∈ ℤ' (as in Theorem 1.2 and Definition 1.8). In the proof of Corollary 1.7 take M = 8|a| (or n₀ = 8|a|).

issues.reviewReason: Both quotations match p. 678 (image): Corollary 1.6 'fix d, n₀, M ∈ ℕ', and the proof of Corollary 1.7 'we use Corollary 1.6 with n₀ = 0 and M = 8a', where Corollary 1.7 allows any a ∈ ℤ ∖ {0}. issues.reviewReason: Checked at 300 dpi on p. 695: 'where the implied constant does not depend on k, m, H, R, Ω and z.' Lemma 3.9 fixes d, δ1, δ2 and quantifies over z, H, A, k, Ω and R, with k ≤ (log H)^{δ2}, H^{δ1} ≤ z ≤ H and Ω ≤ H. It evaluates only P(k). issues.locator: (3.6) in the proof of Lemma 3.11 p. 699; applied in the proofs of Lemma 3.11 (p. 699) and Lemma 3.14 (p. 703)
issues.printed: The source states Σ_{t⩽T, gcd(t,q)=1} μ(t) log t/t = −q/φ(q) + O_A((log T)^{−A}); it also gives Σ_{t⩽T, gcd(t,q)=1} μ(t)/t = O_A((log T)^{−A}) in (3.6), attributing both to the prime number theorem and citing [51, Ex. 17, p. 185].
issues.correction: State (3.6) for 1 ⩽ q ⩽ T^C (C fixed; implied constants depending on A and C). Proof: μ·1_{(·,q)=1} = μ∗1_{q^∞}. For a ⩽ √T use Σ_{b⩽y}μ(b)/b ≪_A (log y)^{−A} and Σ_{b⩽y}μ(b)log b/b = −1 + O_A((log y)^{−A}), which gives −Σ_{a|q^∞, a⩽√T}1/a + O((log T)^{−A}(q/φ(q))(1 + Σ_{p|q}log p/(p−1))). For a > √T use the uniform boundedness of both partial sums and Rankin's trick: Σ_{a|q^∞, a>√T}(1+log a)/a ≪ T^{−1/4}exp(O((log q)^{0.6})) ≪ T^{−1/5}. Finally Σ_{a|q^∞}1/a = q/φ(q). In Lemma 3.11 this is applied with T/q ⩾ q in place of T. In Lemma 3.14 the factor Ω^{−d−1} makes the range Ω > (log H)^{A+2} trivial.
issues.reason: No range of q is printed for (3.6). Lemma 3.11 (q ⩽ T^{1/2}) is deduced from (3.6) with T/q in place of T, which needs q ⩽ T/q, i.e. uniformity for q up to T. The proof of Lemma 3.14 uses (3.6) with T = z = H^{1/4} and q = Ω ⩽ H = T⁴. Both uses need uniformity in q well beyond the range q ⩽ T^{1/2} stated for Lemma 3.11. The estimates do hold in these ranges (argument in the correction), so no result is affected. I could not check the wording of the cited exercise; if it states uniformity in q, only the range is left unstated.

issues.reviewReason: The quotation of (3.6) is confirmed on p. 699. No range of q is given, and the subscript O_A suggests uniformity in q, but some restriction is needed. For q = ∏_{p⩽T} p the only admissible t ⩽ T is t = 1, so the first sum is 0 instead of −q/φ(q) ~ −e^γ log T, and the second is 1 instead of O((log T)^{−A}). The printed proof of Lemma 3.11 does rely on uniformity. The lemma is stated for all q ⩽ T^{1/2} with constants depending only on A, and it follows from (3.6) with T' = T/q in place of T, using log(qt) = log q + log t. Here q ⩽ T^{1/2} ⩽ T', so (3.6) is needed uniformly for q ⩽ T' (the log q·O((log T')^{−A}) term is absorbed by changing A). Assuming (3.6) only for q ⩽ T'^{1/2} would cover only q ⩽ T^{1/3}. The uniform statement is true: I checked the argument in the correction. The identity μ·1_{(·,q)=1} = μ∗1_{q^∞} holds because the Dirichlet series is ζ(s)^{−1}∏_{p|q}(1−p^{−s})^{−1}. Then use |Σ_{b⩽y}μ(b)/b| ⩽ 1 and the boundedness of Σμ(b)log b/b for a > √T, and Rankin with σ = 1/2 (∏_{p|q}(1−p^{−1/2+ε})^{−1} = T^{o(1)} for q ⩽ T^C). Also q/φ(q), Σ_{p|q}log p/(p−1) ≪ log log T. One point of the first reading's reason is overstated. Lemma 3.14 (p. 703) does apply (3.6) with T = z = H^{1/4} and q = Ω up to H = T⁴, but there the error is multiplied by 2^dH^{d+1}/Ω^{d+1}. For Ω > (log H)^{A+2} the trivial bound |Σ_{k₁⩽z}μ(k₁)log k₁/k₁| + Ω/φ(Ω) ≪ (log H)² already suffices, so that use needs uniformity only for q ⩽ (log T)^{O(A)}. The step that needs uniformity beyond q ⩽ T^{1/2} is the deduction of Lemma 3.11. The paper states no uniformity and gives no argument for it, and the step is true, so the label 'gap' affecting nothing is right. Caveat: I could not access Montgomery–Vaughan [51, Ex. 17, p. 185]. If that exercise states the estimate uniformly for q up to T (or with explicit dependence on q), the issue reduces to an omitted range, which is a misprint.

issues.locator: Lemma 3.14 statement pp. 701–702
issues.printed: The source asserts the ensuing result for every H ⩾ 1, A > 0, natural k and Ω, and R ∈ (ℤ/Ω)[t], provided Ω ⩽ H and k ⩽ (log H)^δ.
issues.correction: … and all R ∈ (ℤ/Ω)[t] of degree at most d such that k ⩽ (log H)^δ and Ω ⩽ H … (as in Lemma 3.9).
issues.reason: If R has a nonzero coefficient of t^j with j > d, no P of degree d satisfies P ≡ R (mod Ω), so the left side is 0 while the right side need not be: e.g. d = 1, Ω = 2, R = t² + 1, k = 2 gives R(2) = 5 coprime to 2 and main term H². The proof invokes Lemma 3.9, which assumes deg R ⩽ d, and both applications satisfy it (Ω = 1 in Lemma 4.1; R_i of degree ⩽ d_i in Lemma 4.9). So the omission is a slip whose meaning is clear.
