issues.citation: Skorobogatov–Sofos, "Schinzel Hypothesis on average and rational points", Inventiones Mathematicae (2023)
issues.reviewReason: The quotation is confirmed on pp. 701–702. Lemma 3.14 ranges over 'all R ∈ (ℤ/Ω)[t]' with no degree bound, whereas Lemma 3.9 (p. 695), which its proof invokes, says 'all R ∈ (ℤ/Ω)[t] of degree at most d'. The paper reads P ≡ R (mod Ω) coefficientwise: the proof of Lemma 3.9 writes R(t) ≡ Σ_{j⩽d} r_j t^j (mod Ω), and Lemma 4.9 takes R_i to be the reduction of P_i in (ℤ/W)[t] (p. 713). The counterexample is valid. Take d = 1, Ω = 2, R = t² + 1, k = 2; then Ω ⩽ H, and k ⩽ (log H)^δ once H is large. No P of degree 1 is congruent to R mod 2, so the left side is 0. But gcd(R(2), 2) = gcd(5, 2) = 1, so the right side is 2H²/(2·φ(2)) + O_A(H²(log H)^{−A}) = H² + o(H²). Both uses satisfy the missing hypothesis: Lemma 4.1 takes Ω = 1, and Lemma 4.9 applies the lemma to R_i ∈ (ℤ/W)[t] with deg R_i ⩽ d_i (p. 713). The intended hypothesis is clear from Lemma 3.9, so this is a misprint that affects nothing. It is independent of E1 (the sign of P(k)).

issues.reason: This is downstream of E1: the proof feeds the positive-prime sum ∑* into the printed Lemma 3.14, whose main term is really that of the both-signs sum. The statement itself is false for θ_P, not merely unproved. Take n = d_1 = M = 1 and P = at + b with 1 ≤ a ≤ H, |b| ≤ H. Suppose P(m) = −p with p > log x prime. If a prime ℓ ≤ log x divided both a and b it would divide p, so none does. Hence S_P(x) = ∏_{ℓ|a, ℓ≤log x}(1 − 1/ℓ)^{−1} ≥ 1. For m ≤ x and a < H/m, as b runs over [−H, −am−1] the value P(m) runs bijectively over [−(H−am), −1]. So Σ_P S_P(θ^Λ_P − θ_P) ≥ Σ_{m≤x} Σ_{a<H/m} (ϑ(H−am) − ϑ(log x)) = (1/2 + o(1))H² log x by the PNT, since Σ_{a<H/m}(H − am) = H²/(2m) + O(H). With item 46 this gives Σ_P S_Pθ_P ≤ main − (1/2 + o(1))H² log x + O(H²), which is not main + O(H²) once log x → ∞ (e.g. x = (log H)^{A_2}). E1's reason says only that Lemma 4.9 'inherits the error'. This entry records that the printed Lemma 4.9 is false by a factor log x in its error term, and that §4.4 as printed relies on it; the reviewer may merge it into E1. Same text in the arXiv v3 source.

issues.reviewReason:
Statement confirmed on p. 712. θ_P (1.4, p. 679) counts only positive prime values, with weight log P_i(m). Independent argument with n = d_1 = M = 1, so P = at + b, 1 ≤ a ≤ H, |b| ≤ H. Then S_P(x) = ∏_{ℓ≤log x}(1 − Z_P(ℓ)/ℓ)/(1 − 1/ℓ) is 0 if some ℓ ≤ log x divides gcd(a,b), and otherwise equals ∏_{ℓ|a, ℓ≤log x}(1 − 1/ℓ)^{−1} ≥ 1. For fixed m and a, as b runs over [−H, H] the value am + b runs over the window [am − H, am + H]. When am < H the window contains the negative primes −p with p ≤ H − am. θ^Λ counts these and θ does not. For p > log x the gcd condition is automatic, so S_P ≥ 1 on them. Summing, Σ_P S_P(θ^Λ_P − θ_P) ≥ Σ_{m≤x}Σ_{a<H/m}(ϑ(H − am) − ϑ(log x)) = (1/2 + o(1))H² log x. The PNT is uniform here because H/m ≥ H/(log H)^{A_2} → ∞. The same windowing also gives Σ_P S_Pθ^Λ_P = 2xH²∏γ_1 + O(H²), because Σ_{a≤H}S(a) = H∏γ_1 + O(W log log x) with W ≤ x² (S(a) is W-periodic). Hence Σ_P S_Pθ_P = main − (∏γ_1/2 + o(1))H² log x + O(H²). At x = (log H)^{A_2} the deficit is ≍ A_2 H² log log H, which is not O(H^{d+n}) = O(H²). So Lemma 4.9 is false as printed, not merely unproved.

Exact numerics (C code; the fast window formula was checked against brute force over all (a, b, m) for H = 60) show the ratio to H² is stable in H and grows like log x. For H = 10^5: (ΣS_Pθ_P − main)/H² = −0.93, −2.24, −3.60, −4.74, −6.16, −7.62 at x = 3, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000; here x = 1000 = (log H)^{2.83}. Over the same x, (ΣS_Pθ^Λ_P − main)/H² lies in [−0.03, 0]. The negative-prime part is 0.91, 2.19, 3.48, 4.51, 5.74, 6.82, against (∏γ_1/2)(log x + γ_E) = 0.84, 2.16, 3.48, 4.53, 5.77, 6.88. The rest of the θ-deficit comes from prime powers, O(xH^{3/2}). For H = 10^6 and x = 3, 10, 30, 100 the θ values are −0.92, −2.21, −3.53, −4.60 and the θ^Λ values are ≤ 0.001 in size.

The cause is E1: the proof applies Lemma 3.14, whose main term is really that of the both-signs sum Σ Λ(|P(k)|). With θ^Λ in place of θ the printed proof goes through, including the gcd-removal step (|P(m)| is then a power of a prime dividing M, cost O(H^{d_i} log H)). The correction is sound. θ_P ≤ θ^Λ_P and S_P ≥ 0 keep the upper bound Σ S_Pθ_P ≤ main + O(H^{d+n}). For the lower bound, the mean of θ^Λ_P − θ_P over the box is ≪ (log H)^n Σ_{m≤x}(Σ_i d_i/m + x^{d/2}H^{−1/2}) ≪ (log H)^n log x: the proportion with P_i(m) < 0 is ≤ d_i/m, and prime-power values are rare. With S_P ≪ (log log x)^n, 2x times the loss is ≪ x^{1+n/A_1}(log x)(log log x)^n H^{d+n} ≪ x²H^{d+n}/log x, since x > (log H)^{A_1} and A_1 > n. So §4.4 and Theorem 1.9 stand. Kind error: Lemma 4.9 is a numbered statement that is false. The entry overlaps E1, whose reason only says Lemma 4.9 'inherits the error'. It can be merged into E1 if the reason there is sharpened to say that Lemma 4.9 is false for θ_P with a deficit ≍ H^{d+n} log x.

issues.locator: Published proof of Theorem 5.3 pp. 719–720 and proof of Theorem 5.8 p. 723
issues.printed: On p. 719 the source defines ℳ by m ∈ 𝒫 and m ≡ m_0 (mod M). On p. 720 it writes ℳ = ∪_{i=1}^n ℳ_i, with each ℳ_i comprising all degree-d Bouniakowsky P(t) satisfying P(t) ≡ Q(t) (mod M) and (Q(n_0), M) = 1. On p. 723 it expresses ℳ as a finite union of ℳ_j, each comprising all Schinzel n-tuples subject to a congruence m ≡ m_0 (mod M).
issues.correction: Add an integral form of Lemma 5.2. If N ∈ U(ℤ_p), there is M ≥ 1 such that U_{ν,m}(ℤ_p) ≠ ∅ whenever ν ∈ ℤ_p, m ∈ ℤ_p^{d+1} (resp. ℤ_p^{d+n}) and max(|ν−g(N)|_p, |m−h(N)|_p) ≤ p^{−M}. Proof: U(ℤ_p) is an open neighbourhood of N in U(ℚ_p), and the smooth map f is open on ℚ_p-points [21, p. 80]. For K Galois it also follows from Lemma 5.2 as stated: K⊗ℚ_p ≅ L^g with isomorphic factors, so a unit that is a norm from (K⊗ℚ_p)^* equals N_{L/ℚ_p}(y) with y ∈ 𝒪_L^*, and z = (y,1,…,1) ∈ 𝒪_K⊗ℤ_p. Use this form when choosing M_p. In Theorem 5.8, take t_p = n_p, which satisfies (5.2) by (5.4) and (5.6). Then ℳ ∩ {m ≡ m_0 (mod M)} = 𝒫 ∩ {m ≡ m_0 (mod M)}, as both proofs assert.
issues.reason: By construction, ℳ_i = ℳ ∩ ∏_p𝓑_{N_p} = ℳ ∩ {m ≡ m_0 (mod M)}, which is contained in 𝒫 ∩ {m ≡ m_0 (mod M)}. Equality needs every m ∈ 𝒫 in the class to have U_m(ℤ_p) ≠ ∅ for p ∈ S (and, for Theorem 5.8, a ℤ_p-point satisfying (5.2)). Lemma 5.2 as stated gives only U_{ν,m}(ℚ_p) ≠ ∅. U is not proper over V, and a ℚ_p-point with unit norm need not be integral: for p odd and K⊗ℚ_p ≅ ℚ_p(√p) × ℚ_p(√(εp)) with ε a non-square unit, ε is a norm from (K⊗ℚ_p)^*, but norms from (𝒪_K⊗ℤ_p)^* are only (ℤ_p^*)². Both conclusions of the theorems use the equality. Corollary 2.9 and Proposition 2.8 count full congruence classes, which gives positive density of ℳ. Theorem 1.2 gives 100% of the full class, and passing to ℳ_i requires ℳ_i to be a positive proportion of that class. In §6.3 (p. 733) the authors state the integral version explicitly, where it follows from properness; §5 lacks it. The results stand, because K is cyclic and the fix is short.

issues.citation: Skorobogatov–Sofos, "Schinzel Hypothesis on average and rational points", Inventiones Mathematicae (2023)
issues.reviewReason: All three quotations check out on pp. 719, 720 and 723. By CRT, ∏_{p∈S}𝓑_{N_p} ∩ ℤ^{d+1} = {m ≡ m_0 (mod M)}, so ℳ_i = ℳ ∩ {m ≡ m_0} = {m ∈ 𝒫 : m ≡ m_0, U_m(ℤ_p) ≠ ∅ ∀p ∈ S}. The proofs then treat ℳ_i as the whole set 𝒫 ∩ {m ≡ m_0}: 'our new set ℳ consists of all m ∈ 𝒫 such that…', and on p. 720 'each ℳ_i consists of all Bouniakowsky polynomials … ≡ Q (mod M)'; p. 723 is the same for Schinzel tuples. That equality needs U_m(ℤ_p) ≠ ∅ for every such m, together with (5.2) in Theorem 5.8. Lemma 5.2 (p. 718) and (5.5) (p. 723) give only U_{ν,m}(ℚ_p) ≠ ∅. U → V is not proper, and Lemma 5.2 is stated for arbitrary K. For non-Galois K, a unit that is a local norm need not be the norm of an integral element. The first reading's example works: for p odd and K⊗ℚ_p ≅ ℚ_p(√p) × ℚ_p(√(εp)), ε = N(1/√p, √(εp)). But an integral z with unit norm has both components units, whose norms lie in (ℤ_p^*)², and ε is not a square. The equality is used twice as written. First, positive density: Corollary 2.9 and Proposition 2.8 count whole congruence classes. Second, passing from 100% of 𝒫 ∩ class (Theorem 1.2) to 100% of ℳ_i. The local-norm step at p ∈ S only needs ℚ_p-points, so it is fine. In §6.3 (p. 733) the authors do state the integral version, deducing it from properness (f(U(ℤ_p)) = f(U(ℚ_p)) ∩ V(ℤ_p)). That argument is not available in §5, and §5 has no substitute. The step is true and the fix is short, so the stated theorems stand; this is a gap in the proof. It is distinct from E14, which is about separate versus joint openness in the proof of Lemma 5.2. E14's correction mentions an integral version only in passing and does not record that the §5 proofs need it.

issues.reviewReason: The quotation checks out on p. 721. Reference [9] (p. 737) is Brown–Parry, 'The imaginary bicyclic biquadratic fields with class-number 1', which lists the 47 imaginary ones. As printed, the count is false. The real field ℚ(√2,√3) has class number 1: by Kuroda's formula for real V4-fields, h = Q·h(ℚ(√2))h(ℚ(√3))h(ℚ(√6))/4 = Q/4 with Q ∈ {1,2,4}, which forces h = 1. Equivalently, ℚ(√2,√3) = ℚ(ζ_24)^+ and h^+ divides h(ℚ(ζ_24)) = 1. If 'biquadratic' is read as 'quartic', cyclic fields such as ℚ(ζ_5) (h = 1) are extra counterexamples. The sentence is about totally imaginary K, and the citation makes the intended meaning clear. The example ℚ(√−1,√2) = ℚ(ζ_8) itself is correct.

issues.reason: As written, 'the product of all the terms' covers the symbols, signs and logs but not the distinctness indicator. The one pairwise condition that involves both h and k cannot be put into 𝓕₁, 𝓕₂ or 𝒢. It is automatically enforced by the Jacobi symbol, but the paper does not say so. The claim is true, and the proof needs this one-paragraph observation.

issues.reviewReason: The quotations are on pp. 732–733 (checked on the images). T_{S,P} in (6.6) sums over m with all P_ij(m) prime and pairwise distinct. η_P (Definition 6.4) has no distinctness condition, and 𝓕₁, 𝓕₂, 𝒢 are defined as 'the product of all the terms' of the rewritten summand, i.e. the Jacobi symbols and the reciprocity signs. So T_{S,P} is not literally a case of η_P, and the paper does not say how the distinctness indicator is absorbed. The fix works. The indicator is ∏ 1[P_a(m)≠P_b(m)] over pairs. A pair containing h but not k goes into 𝓕₁, a pair containing k but not h into 𝓕₂, and a pair containing neither into 𝒢. The pair {h,k} needs no factor, because the separated symbol (P_h(m)/P_k(m)) vanishes when these two primes are equal. The reciprocity rewrite is only needed where all the primes are distinct and odd (they are prime to M, and 2|M). The signs involve only primes indexed by S₁∪S₂∪S₃, and h lies in a complement, so each sign factor goes into 𝓕₂ (if it involves k) or 𝒢. All factors have modulus ≤1 and depend only on the values, as Definition 6.4 requires. The step is true but not justified as written.

It justifies this by coprimality of P_ij(n₀, m₀) with M and by U_{ν,m}(ℤ_p) ≠ ∅ for p ∈ S whenever m ≡ m₀ (mod M) and the integer ν satisfies ν ≡ n₀ (mod M).

issues.reason: Proposition 6.7 assumes 'M be a multiple of 8a₁a₂a₃'. The M_p come from (6.9) and are only said to be positive integers, and the 'legitimate because' list omits this hypothesis. In the defence: the fix is immediate, and the proof of Proposition 6.7 uses only 2a₁a₂a₃|M (for p_ij∤2a₁a₂a₃). The reciprocity signs need no condition mod 8, because they are absorbed into F₂. issues.reviewReason: The quotations are on p. 734 (checked on the image). Proposition 6.7 (p. 730) assumes that M is a multiple of 8a₁a₂a₃. In §6.3, M=∏_{p∈S}p^{M_p}, where the M_p are only the positive integers given by the analogue of Lemma 5.2 in (6.9). Because a₁a₂a₃ is square-free, 8a₁a₂a₃ | M comes down to M_2 ≥ 3+v₂(a₁a₂a₃), and nothing guarantees this. The 'legitimate because' sentence checks coprimality and local solubility, but it never checks this hypothesis. Defence: the fix is immediate, because (6.9) still holds when M_p is increased. Also, the proof of Proposition 6.7 only uses that every prime factor of 2a₁a₂a₃ divides M. That makes the p_ij=P_ij(m) prime to 2a₁a₂a₃ and puts the local solubility at p|2a₁a₂a₃ that Lemma 6.6 needs into the hypothesis. The quadratic-reciprocity signs are functions of the primes and go into 𝓕₂ or 𝒢, so they need no fixed residue mod 8. The step is incomplete as written, but a single sentence fixes it.

issues.locator: Published §6.3 p. 734 (last statement of Theorem 6.1, p. 725)
issues.printed: The source says the final assertion of Theorem 6.1 follows by the method used for Theorems 5.3 and 5.8.
issues.correction: Add: ∏_{p∈S}U(ℤ_p)≠∅. For each p∈S, take constant polynomials (plus a point of the conic) with P₁₁=U₁, P₂₁=U₂ and all other P_ij=1. Here (U₁,U₂)=(a₂,−a₁) with the point (1:1:0) if p∤a₁a₂; (1,−a₂a₃) with (0:1:a₂) if p|a₁; and (−a₁a₃,1) with (1:0:a₁) if p|a₂. So the finite cover contains at least one ball. The corresponding ℳ_r equals the set of Schinzel tuples m≡m₀ (mod M) with ∏P_ij(n₀,m₀) prime to M, which has positive density by Proposition 2.8. Hence ℳ, and with it ℳ′, has positive density.
issues.reason: The §5 argument ('ℳ=∪ℳ_i, each ℳ_i has positive density by Corollary 2.9') presupposes that the cover is non-empty, i.e. U(ℤ_p)≠∅ for every p∈S. If some U(ℤ_p) were empty, ℳ=∅ and 'ℳ′ has positive density in ℤ^{d+n}' would be false. In §5 non-emptiness is trivial (P ≡ 1). Here it needs the short local construction above, which the paper does not give. The statement is true, and Theorem 1.4 depends on it.

issues.citation: Skorobogatov–Sofos, "Schinzel Hypothesis on average and rational points", Inventiones Mathematicae (2023)
issues.reviewReason: The sentence is on p. 734. The model argument in §5 (end of the proof of Theorem 5.3 on p. 720, and p. 724 for Theorem 5.8) writes ℳ=∪ℳ_i with each ℳ_i a congruence class of Schinzel tuples, and gets positive density from Corollary 2.9 or Proposition 2.8. This needs the finite cover to be non-empty, i.e. ∏_{p∈S}U(ℤ_p)≠∅. If it were empty, ℳ=∅ and the last claim of Theorem 6.1 would fail. In §5 non-emptiness is trivial: the constant polynomial 1 is the norm of 1, so the invariants vanish. That does not carry over to §6. With every P_ij≡1, the conic a₁x²+a₂y²+a₃z²=0 can have no ℚ_p-point (e.g. x²+y²−3z² at p=3). Neither §6.3 nor §6.4 checks this, and Theorem 1.4 ('positive proportion') depends on it. The statement is still true. For p∈S, let U_i be the product of the values of the block-i polynomials, which can be any p-adic units since n₁,n₂>0, and take U₃=1. If p∤a₁a₂, take U₁=a₂, U₂=−a₁, with the point (1:1:0). If p|a₁, then p∤a₂a₃; take U₂=−a₂a₃, with the point (0:1:a₂). If p|a₂, take U₁=−a₁a₃, with the point (1:0:a₁). Using constant polynomials with these values gives N_p∈U(ℤ_p).

issues.printed: The theorem defines λ_Smyth(Σ, F) with positive numbers a_1, …, a_N. The separation argument in its proof yields nonnegative a_1, …, a_N and F(x) ≥ λ_N − N^{−1} + Σ_{i≤N} a_i log|Q_i(x)| for x ∈ Σ outside the roots of Q_i with i ≤ N. At such roots, the proof claims the inequality because its left side is finite while its right side is −∞.
issues.correction: Discard the Q_i with a_i = 0, so that the remaining coefficients are positive as the definition requires. At points x ∈ Σ that are roots only of discarded Q_i, the right side is then finite, and the inequality needs an argument. If x is a limit point of Σ, use continuity. If x is an isolated point of Σ, perturb, for example by giving the relevant Q_i a small positive coefficient at a small cost in λ. On compact parts the cost is at most η times an upper bound for log|Q_i|; outside a sufficiently large compact set, growth condition (5.11) absorbs the finitely many added logarithmic terms. Let the resulting loss in λ tend to zero.
issues.reason: When a_i = 0 the term a_i log|Q_i(x)| is 0 · (−∞), not −∞. At a root x of such a Q_i that is not a root of any Q_j with a_j > 0, the right side is finite. The Dirac measure δ_x is not in M_N, since ∫ log|Q_i| dδ_x = −∞, so the separation inequality does not cover x, and the printed justification ("the right is −∞") fails. The definition of λ_Smyth also demands positive coefficients, which the separation argument does not supply. The conclusion λ(Σ, F) = λ_Smyth(Σ, F) is expected to survive the repair. Noted by the extraction (item 114), which left the perturbation as an outstanding step. issues.reason: A one-point component need not be isolated. Σ = {0} ∪ ⋃_{n≥1}[1/(2n+1), 1/(2n)] ∪ [1, 6] is compact, has countably many components and capacity greater than 1 (it contains [1, 6], of capacity 5/4). Its component {0} is not isolated, and 0 lies in no compact finite union of intervals inside Σ, because every neighbourhood of 0 meets gaps of Σ. So the printed decomposition fails. With one-point components in place of isolated points the decomposition holds (the other components are countably many closed intervals, and Σ_k is the union of the first k of them), and the argument that μ gives this countable set measure 0 is unchanged. issues.correction: Write Q=B+N with B=Q₀+Σ ε_iT_i. For every shift N′∈[0,N), minimality gives a root α with |B(α)+N′|<a/2. Each root contributes an open interval of real shifts of length at most a. At most n such intervals cover [0,N), hence N≤na, proving (4.9).
issues.reason: At k=0 the printed assertion contradicts the defining lower bound |Q(α)|≥a/2 for every root. If n=0 there are no roots and the minimal shift is N=0; the division by n is used only for n>0. Verified against Definition 4.6 and the page image.

issues.printed: The introduction says E=F[β] is a sum of fields, each stable under the involution, and identifies this with β being elliptic semisimple in the Lie algebra of G. In §1 (ii), it asserts compactness of the G-normalizer of P for the classical groups under consideration.
issues.correction: Both fail when G is orthogonal (F = F₀, ε = +1) and the null block V⁰ (β₀ = 0) has dimension 2 with h|V⁰ isotropic: then G_E has the factor SO(V⁰) = SO(1,1)(F) ≅ F^×, a split central torus, so β is not elliptic, and the maximal parahoric o_F^× of that factor has non-compact normalizer F^×. The correct condition is that G_E has compact centre.
issues.reason: SO(1,1)(F) = {diag(t, t⁻¹)} in a hyperbolic basis is ≅ F^×, commutes with β (β acts by 0 on V⁰) and lies in the centre of G_E = ∏ G_{E_i}; its maximal compact subgroup o_F^× is normal in F^×. Miyauchi–Stevens state that a factor SO(1,1)(F) of G_E 'can only happen when G is an even-dimensional orthogonal group and β_i = 0, dim_F V^i = 2' and add 'G_E has compact centre' to the definition of cuspidal type for this reason. (Also recorded by an earlier worker: Miyauchi–Stevens 2014.)

issues.locator: §2.2, proofs of Lemma 2.10 (arXiv v2 p. 12, TeX 1206-1210) and Lemma 2.12 (p. 12, TeX 1247)
issues.printed: Lemma 2.10 asserts local constancy of Λ″ ↦ a₀(Λ″) along the segment except at a discrete, hence finite, set: its intersections with building walls. Lemma 2.12 asserts that deleting every building wall from [Λ,Λ′,Λ″] partitions it into disjoint convex polygons.
issues.correction: Use only the walls of I(G̃, F₀) that do not contain the segment (resp. the affine plane of the triangle). Walls containing it do not separate its points, and the rest of each proof is unchanged.
issues.reason: The image of I(G̃_E, F₀) often lies inside walls of I(G̃, F₀). Example: V = V¹ ⊕ V², dim_F V^i = 2, E_i/F unramified quadratic; in an adapted apartment of GL₄(F) the points of I(G̃_E) are (a,a,b,b), which lie on the walls x₁ − x₂ = 0 and x₃ − x₄ = 0, and b₀ = o_{E₁} ⊕ o_{E₂} is constant. The segment from (0,0,0,0) to (1/2,1/2,0,0) meets a wall at every point, so the literal set of the proof is the whole segment and 'removing all walls' leaves nothing. The segments and triangles used in §4 lie in the image of I(G̃_E, F₀), so they are of this kind whenever some E_i/F has residue degree > 1.

The facet, and so a_0 (Remark 2.11/[BL]), is fixed by the sign vector, which is constant between consecutive crossing points, a The entry is corrected as the review found necessary.

issues.locator: §3.3, proof of Lemma 3.10, arXiv v2 p. 18 (same in v1)
issues.printed: The source chooses g = diag(ϖ_E, ϖ_E⁻¹) or diag(ϖ_E⁻¹, ϖ_E) according to the case, then asserts gxg⁻¹ ∈ P_1(Λ^M_{o_E}). It proceeds using g ∈ G_E to intertwine φ.
issues.correction: g = diag(ϖ_E, ϖ̄_E⁻¹) or diag(ϖ_E⁻¹, ϖ̄_E) (i.e. diag(ϖ_E, −ϖ_E⁻¹), diag(ϖ_E⁻¹, −ϖ_E) when E/E_0 is ramified); these lie in G_E and still satisfy gxg⁻¹ ∈ P_1(Λ^M_{o_E}).
issues.reason: In a basis e_1,e_2 of the plane with f(e_1,e_1)=f(e_2,e_2)=0, diag(a,b) is an isometry iff a·b̄ = 1. The paper fixes ϖ̄_E = −ϖ_E when E/E_0 is ramified (§2.1), so diag(ϖ_E, ϖ_E⁻¹) has multiplier ϖ_E·(ϖ̄_E)⁻¹ = −1 and is only a similitude; the second case (𝔟_0(Λ^M) = [[o_E,𝔭_E⁻¹],[𝔭_E,o_E]]) occurs only for E/E_0 ramified, and the first case also occurs for E/E_0 ramified with f skew-hermitian, so the printed g is not in G_E exactly in the ramified cases (for E = F = F_0 it is fine). With the corrected g, gxg⁻¹ = [[1,−ϖ_E²],[0,1]] resp. [[1,0],[−ϖ_E³,1]], which lie in P_1(Λ^M_{o_E}) (𝔟_1 = 𝔭_E M_2(o_E), resp. [[𝔭_E,o_E],[𝔭_E²,𝔭_E]]); x itself lies in G_E in both cases (b + ε'b̄ = 0 checked).

issues.printed: Using Lemma 3.9’s notation, the source reduces to |Δ| = 1 and 𝒢 ≃ SL_2(F_3). It chooses an E-basis that is self-dual and splits Λ^m_{o_E}, claiming an identification of 𝔟_0(Λ^m_{o_E}) with [[o_E,o_E],[𝔭_E,o_E]].
issues.correction: 𝒢_i may contain an SL_2(F_3) factor together with other factors (e.g. GL factors when Λ^M is not maximal, or two SL_2(F_3) factors for Sp_{2n}(F) with F = F_0, ε = −1), and V^i may have E-dimension > 2, so one cannot restrict to 𝒢_i ≃ SL_2(F_3) with a 2×2 matrix model. Argue on each SL_2(F_3) factor separately: it acts on a hyperbolic plane W spanned by two vectors of the splitting self-dual basis; take x ∈ P_1(Λ^m_{o_E}) acting on W as the displayed unipotent and trivially on W^⊥, and g acting on W as the (corrected, PAPER-STEVENS-08/E10) torus element and trivially on W^⊥; then g ∈ G_E, and gxg⁻¹ ∈ P_1(Λ^M_{o_E}) because Λ^M splits along the basis, so 𝔟_1(Λ^M) ∩ End(W) = 𝔟_1(Λ^M|_W).
issues.reason: In the proof of Lemma 3.9 'we fix i and omit it', so 𝒢 = 𝒢_i and Δ is its full set of simple roots; |Δ| = 1 and 𝒢 ≃ SL_2(F_3) is then a restriction on the whole block, which the preceding sentences do not justify. The completion above uses only the splitting basis and the blockwise structure of split lattice sequences.

issues.locator: §3.3, proof of Lemma 3.9, parenthesis after the citation of [DM, page 129], arXiv v2 p. 17 (same in v1)
issues.printed: The source lists as the only quasi-simple exceptions types B_2 and F_4 over a field with 2 elements, and G_2 over a field with 3 elements.
issues.correction: G_2 over the field of 2 elements is also an exception; none of these can occur for classical groups over residue fields of odd characteristic, so the argument is unaffected.
issues.reason: Chevalley commutator formula for G_2 (a short, b long) over F_2, where 2 = 0 and 3 = 1: [x_a,x_b] ∈ x_{a+b}x_{2a+b}U_{3a+b}U_{3a+2b}, [x_a,x_{a+b}] ∈ U_{3a+b}U_{3a+2b}, [x_a,x_{2a+b}] ∈ U_{3a+b}, [x_b,x_{3a+b}], [x_{a+b},x_{2a+b}] ∈ U_{3a+2b}, other pairs commute. So N = ⟨x_{a+b}(1)x_{2a+b}(1), U_{3a+b}, U_{3a+2b}⟩ is normal with 𝒰/N abelian, hence [𝒰,𝒰] ⊆ N has order ≤ 8 < 16 = |∏_{α∈Σ⁺∖Δ}𝒰_α|. (G_2(2) is not quasi-simple, but neither is B_2(2) ≅ S_6, which the paper lists, so '(quasi-simple)' refers to the type.) Digne–Michel p. 129 was not available to check whether the omission is inherited.

issues.printed: On p. 32 the source defines J⁺_P = H¹(β,Λ)(J⁺(β,Λ) ∩ P), with P = P̃ ∩ G. On p. 33 it restricts κ_P to J⁺_P ∩ M = J⁺(β,Λ) ∩ M and writes κ_P|_{J⁺(β,Λ)∩M} = κ^{(0)} ⊗ ⊗ κ̃^{(j)}, taking κ^{(0)} to be an irreducible representation of J⁺(β^{(0)},Λ^{(0)}).

With P⁺, M⁺ everything is consistent (Corollary 5.10(ii) and 5.11 already use (M⁺,P⁺) and J⁺ ∩ M⁺). For unitary and symplectic groups P = P⁺, M = M⁺. issues.printed: The source defines exact subordination by minimality among properly subordinate self-dual decompositions. If P°(Λ_{𝔬_E}) is maximal parahoric in G_E, it identifies the decomposition as V=W^{(0)} with M=P=G. Otherwise it claims that exact subordination makes the group 𝔐_J of §1 equal to M ∩ G_E.
issues.correction: Definition 6.5 should also require that P°(Λ_{𝔬_E}) ∩ M be a maximal parahoric subgroup of G_E ∩ M (and, for the conclusion N_Λ ⊆ P(Λ_{𝔬_E}) in the trivial-decomposition case, that G_E have compact centre — the SO(1,1) failure of that part is chunk A's PAPER-STEVENS-08/E1). With this, 𝔐_J = M ∩ G_E and N_Λ = N_N(𝔐_J ∩ P_J) as claimed.
issues.reason: For G = SO_{2n}(F) split (n ≥ 2), β = 0 and Λ the self-dual chain {M ⊂ M^*}, M = L₀ ∩ L₁ with L₀ = ⟨e_i,f_i⟩ and L₁ = ⟨ϖ^{−1}e₁, ϖf₁, e_i, f_i (i ≥ 2)⟩ (see PAPER-STEVENS-08/213), the only properly subordinate decomposition is the trivial one (e₁ and f₁ jump at the same index), so it is exactly subordinate in the printed sense with M = P = G; but P°(Λ) is not maximal parahoric, Morris's 𝔐_J is the Levi GL₁ × SO_{2n−2} ≠ G_E, and the element t = diag(ϖ, 1,…,1, ϖ^{−1}) (on e₁, W₀, f₁) intertwines λ_P = ρ (P°(Λ) ∩ U and P°(Λ) ∩ U_l lie in P₁(Λ), so the identity intertwines at t) while J°_P N_Λ J°_P is compact (N_Λ normalizes the parahoric P°(Λ) of G_E, whose normalizer is the compact stabilizer of its facet). So Proposition 6.15 fails for the printed definition. Note: with the corrected definition some Λ (such as this one) admit no exactly subordinate decomposition; Miyauchi–Stevens and Kurinczuk–Stevens handle this in the exhaustion by choosing Λ with minimal P°(Λ_{𝔬_E}) (chunk E). issues.locator: Ann. of Math. 186 (2017), Theorem 4.2.1 and Step 4 of its proof, pp. 121–122; page image checked
issues.printed: The source assumes universal P-resolvability of S for primes P satisfying char(X) ⊆ P. In Step 4 it invokes Theorem 3.3.6 to enlarge a so that its factorization consists of S̄ → S′, a tame Galois covering, followed by a : S′ → S, a P-alteration.
issues.correction: Either assume char(S) ⊆ P, which is how Theorem 4.3.1 uses the theorem, or keep char(X) ⊆ P and run Step 4 over S₀ := S minus the fibres over char(S) ∖ char(X) (finitely many, as in §4.3.2), which contains f(X) and has char(S₀) = char(X). Apply Theorem 3.3.6 to S̄ ×_S S₀ → S₀, obtaining a P-alteration and a Galois covering that is tame over S₀. Extend to S by normalization and closure of the modification, and resolve with the P-resolvability of S. Tameness is needed only over f(X), since X̄ lies over S₀ and Step 10 uses tameness of the action on X̄.
issues.reason: Theorem 3.3.6 yields a P^w_{S̄/S}-alteration, where P^w_{S̄/S} is the wild primes set of S̄ → S, a subset of char(S). With only char(X) ⊆ P it may contain primes outside P, at which S̄ → S can be wildly ramified although X is empty there. Then 'a P-alteration' does not follow as written. The paper's main results apply the theorem only through Theorem 4.3.1, where char(S) ⊆ P. Exposé X §3.3.3 defines universal ℓ′-resolvability only for ℓ invertible on the scheme, so its Theorem 3.4 assumes char(S) ⊆ {ℓ}′. Temkin's printed char(X) hypothesis is more general; the identification with that source holds only under the base hypothesis.

issues.printed: The source ends the argument if p|eLi/Ki; otherwise it asserts p|fLi/Ki. It then says p = char(K̃i) divides [L̃i : K̃i] and uses K̃i = (K̃i)u to conclude that L̃i/K̃i is not tame.
issues.correction: 'p, the residual characteristic exponent of the valued field K̃_i (that is, exp.char of the residue field of K), divides [L̃_i : K̃_i]'. The field K̃_i itself has characteristic p_i, which is 1 when i < n.
issues.reason: In §2.6.2, p_i = exp.char(k̃_i) equals 1 for i < n and p for i ≥ n. When p_i = 1 the reduction to this case is reachable: L_i/K_i is then automatically tame and defectless, so [L : K] = e_{L_i/K_i}·f_{L_i/K_i}, and p can divide f with p ∤ e. For example, take K̃_i strictly henselian of mixed characteristic (0, p) and L̃_i a degree-p extension of it. Then char(K̃_i) = 0 ≠ p. The argument survives with the corrected reading: K̃_i = (K̃_i)^u has separably closed residue field of characteristic p, so an extension of degree divisible by p cannot be tame.

issues.correction: For separable input, prove the separately stated separable variants of 3.2.12 and 3.3.6 using a maximal separable P-extension. Supply separably P-closed implies separably P-tame through perfection; then Step 4 has a separable P-alteration.
issues.reason: The unrestricted maximal P-extension can contain a purely inseparable closure when char K belongs to P; its selected finite K_x need not be separable. issues.printed: The source describes $\LL_G(U^2)$ as the Levi formed from $\TT$ by adding the roots ±x_1, ±y_3, ±y_1, ±y_3.
issues.correction: The four root pairs are ±x_1, ±x_3, ±y_1, ±y_3: the second entry should be ±x_3, not a second ±y_3.
issues.reason: As printed the list names only three distinct root pairs, which cannot give the derived group SL_2^4 asserted two lines later. Computing directly in the E_8 root system with the simple roots of (12.1) and the roots x_1, x_2, x_3, y_1, y_2, y_3 of (12.3): U is orthogonal, has order 4 and equals s_{x_1}s_{x_2+x_3}s_{-x_1-x_2}s_{y_1}s_{y_2+y_3}s_{-y_1-y_2} exactly, L_G(U) has 24 roots, and the centraliser of the identity component of T^{U^2}, that is the set of roots orthogonal to the fixed space of U^2, consists of exactly eight roots, namely ±x_1, ±x_3, ±y_1, ±y_3. These four are orthogonal and satisfy U^2 v = -v, so they span the (-1)-eigenspace of U^2 and give SL_2^4. The deleted proof in the source file makes the same statement: 'x_1, x_3, y_1, y_3 are orthogonal and generate the (-1)-eigenspace of U^2'.

issues.printed: The source associates an étale F-algebra to the permutation action of Γ_F on simple roots. When G is semisimple, it identifies that algebra's units naturally with the F-rational points of T^can_G.
issues.correction: … and if G is adjoint or simply connected, the F-rational points of T^can_G are naturally identified with the units in this algebra. In those cases X^*(T^can_G) is the permutation module on the simple roots, respectively on the fundamental weights, so T^can_G ≅ R_{E/F} G_m. For other semisimple G the claim fails.
issues.reason: Counterexample: quasi-split, non-split SO_4, e.g. G = SO(3,1) over R (semisimple, neither adjoint nor simply connected). T_can = G_m × SO(2), so T_can(R) = R^× × S^1. Complex conjugation swaps the two simple roots e_1 ± e_2, so the étale algebra is C with units C^×. The groups R^× × S^1 and C^× are not isomorphic even abstractly: C^× is divisible, while (−1,1) has no square root in R^× × S^1. Over a number field the same happens for SO(H ⊕ N_{E/F}): T_can(F) = F^× × E^1 versus E^×. The claim is not used later; published §9 defines global pseudoroots as idele class characters of T_can directly. (Versions: present in both versions.)

issues.locator: published version: §4.3, formula (4.3.1), p. 193 (checked on the page image); identical in arXiv:1407.2346v1 (9 July 2014), §4.3, (4.3.1), p. 13
issues.printed: The source gives the explicit formula (4.3.1) br(h)(K^σ, gK^σ) = ((h ∗ ᵖ⋯ ∗ h)(K, gK))^{1/p}.
issues.correction: br(h)(K^σ, gK^σ) = ((h ∗ h^σ ∗ ⋯ ∗ h^{σ^{p−1}})(K, gK))^{1/p}, using the norm product rather than the p-fold self-convolution. The two agree when h is σ-invariant.
issues.reason: By §3.4 the unique extension of Br^p from H(G,K)^σ is Br~(h) = Br(h ∗ h^σ ∗ ⋯ ∗ h^{σ^{p−1}}). The norm product is σ-invariant, and Br kills N·H(G,K), so this map is additive and Frobenius-semilinear. br(h) is its coefficientwise p-th root, as one sees by expanding h over the F_p-structure. The restriction of h^{∗p} to fixed pairs is not even multiplicative when h is not σ-invariant. Counterexample: p = 2, H_0 = GL_1(F_v) with residue characteristic ≠ 2, G = H_0 × H_0 with σ swapping the factors, K = O_v^× × O_v^×. K is σ-plain, G^σ = H_0 diagonally, H(G,K) = k[t_1^{±1}, t_2^{±1}] and H(G^σ,K^σ) = k[t^{±1}] are domains, and Br(Σ c_{mn} t_1^m t_2^n) = Σ c_{mm} t^m. For h = t_2 we have h ∗ h^σ = t_1t_2, so br(t_2) = t, a unit as it must be, since t_2 is a unit and br is a ring homomorphism. But h ∗ h = t_2^2 vanishes at every pair (K, gK) with g ∈ G^σ, so the printed formula gives br(t_2) = 0. Only the displayed formula is wrong. The definition of br (via Br~ and the F_p-structure) is correct, and (4.3.1) is not used later: §8.15, p. 219, works from the definition. (Versions: the same formula is printed in the arXiv preprint (v1, the only version), and the extraction's search found no erratum or corrigendum on the Annals article page.)

issues.locator: published version: proof of Theorem 4.4, p. 194 ('If C_* is bounded…') and step (3), (4.4.4), p. 196; also the proof of Theorem 6.5, p. 204 (checked on the page images); identical in arXiv:1407.2346v1 (9 July 2014), pp. 14–15 and 21
issues.printed: The source claims bounded C∗ makes hvE and vhE converge to the total homology of C^Smith∗. In (3), it uses vhE^1_ij = H_j(X/K) and vanishing of H∗(X/K) in high degrees to claim convergence of (4.4.4) vhE^1_ij = H_j(X/K) ⟹ H∗(Tot(C^Smith)). Theorem 6.5 attributes convergence to a bound on the cohomological dimension of [G]_K′ independent of [K′].
issues.correction: Run the comparison with a bounded complex. Replace the singular chains C_*(X/K) by a bounded complex of permutation k[σ]-modules that carries the H(G,K)^σ-action and is σ-equivariantly quasi-isomorphic to C_*(X/K). For example, take cellular chains of a finite-dimensional σ-stable, K-equivariant triangulation compatible with all finite levels, as §1.4 suggests ('a compatible triangulation of X'). Alternatively, argue with sheaf-theoretic Smith theory, which uses the hypothesis that X/K has finite cohomological dimension. Either way both spectral sequences then converge to the same homology, and the conclusions of Theorems 4.4, 5.8 and 6.5 follow as stated.
issues.reason: C_*(X/K) is the singular chain complex (the vertical differential 'is the standard singular differential'), which is unbounded. Each total degree of C^Smith then has infinitely many terms. With the direct-sum totalisation the row filtration is bounded below and exhaustive, so steps (1) and (2) are fine. The column filtration is not bounded below, however, and vanishing of H_j(X/K) for large j does not make vhE converge to the same homology. Example: G = K = 1, and X a locally finite mapping telescope of S^1 ⊂ S^3 ⊂ S^5 ⊂ ⋯ with the free action of σ = ζ_p. X is locally compact, contractible and has a free σ-action. Every singular simplex has trivial stabiliser, so each C_j(X) is k[σ]-free and hvE^1 = 0, giving H_*(Tot) = 0. But vhE^1 = H_0(X) = k in row 0, so vhE^2_{i0} = T^i(k) = k for every i, and with one row there are no further differentials. Thus vhE^∞ ≠ 0 does not compute H_*(Tot), although H_*(X) vanishes in positive degrees. Such an X has infinite covering dimension, so the theorem's hypothesis of finite cohomological dimension excludes it. The proof, however, never uses that hypothesis beyond the vanishing of H_*(X/K) in high degrees. The same step recurs in the proof of Theorem 6.5, with cochains. (Versions: the same text is in the arXiv preprint (v1, the only version), and the extraction's search found no erratum on the Annals article page.)

issues.printed: The source claims (a) implies (b). Starting with χ as specified in (b), it invokes (a) to say (4.4.3) χ ◦ Br occurs as an eigenvalue of (4.4.1) restricted to H(G, K)^σ.
issues.correction: Add to Theorem 4.4(b) the hypothesis that H^*(X/K) be finite-dimensional over k, or at least that its generalised eigenspaces for H(G,K)^σ be. This holds for X/K = [G]_K in §5. Then a composition factor χ∘Br gives an H(G,K)^σ-eigenspace. That eigenspace is H(G,K)-stable and finite-dimensional, so it contains an H(G,K)-eigenvector, whose character is (χ∘Br~)^{1/p} by uniqueness (§3.4). Without the hypothesis, (a) yields only that χ∘Br is a composition factor.
issues.reason: (a) gives χ∘Br only as a composition factor (simple subquotient) of H^*(X/K) restricted to H(G,K)^σ. For infinite-dimensional modules a composition factor need not be an eigenvalue. Example: A = k[t] acts on M = k[t, t^{−1}], and M^* = Hom_k(M, k) has the character t ↦ 0 as a composition factor, being the dual of the subquotient k[t]/tk[t] of M. Yet M^* has no eigenvector with eigenvalue 0, since t is invertible on M. The step from an A^σ-eigenvector to an A-eigenvector also needs finite-dimensionality. Theorem 4.4 assumes only finite cohomological dimension, which bounds degrees but not dimensions. The applications are unaffected: Theorem 5.8's proof itself notes that H^*([G]_K) is finite-dimensional, and Theorem 6.5 works with localisations at finite level. With these changes, (7.2.6) holds, (a) and (b) correspond under (2.9.2) (α0 is the parameter of δ^{1/2}), and (7.4.4)–(7.4.5), (7.5.3)–(7.5.5) and Theorem 8.10 hold as printed. Equivalently, keep (7.2.1) and §7.4(a) but read S*(f) via λ ↦ λ(ϖ_v)^{-1}. Then (a) corresponds to (δ^{1/2})^{-1}, and (7.5.3) must read t_θ^{-1}·ρ^-_G(Frob_v).

So δ = |Σ_G|_v = Σ_G⊗q_v^{-1} has parameter Σ*_G(q_v)^{-1}, and the δ^{1/2} of (b) corresponds to an element whose square is Σ*_G(q_v)^{-1}, the inverse of (a)(i). The conditions (b)(ii) and (a)(ii) likewise match only after inversion. (2) Take G = PGL_2, T = 1_{K diag(ϖ,1) K} and λ(x) = diag(x,1). Then S*(T)(diag(ϖ,1)) = q, since n ∈ ϖ^{-1}O, and S*(T)(diag(ϖ^{-1},1)) = 1. Check: S(T) = δ^{1/2}S*(T) is √q at both points, hence W-invariant. With λ ↦ λ(ϖ_v) and the coordinate a = λ on Â = T̂ ⊂ SL_2, S*(T) = qa + a^{-1}. The printed twist (7.2.1) is s∗a = q/a, and qa + a^{-1} is not invariant under it unless q_v ≡ 1 mod p; it is invariant under a ↦ 1/(qa). So (7.2.6) fails in the reading that (7.5.2) uses: there hv0 = Σ_{a} S*h(a)θ(a) = S*h(t_θ). (3) In the other reading, S*(T) = q/a + a and α0 = √q. For θ with θ(diag(ϖ,1)) = μ, (7.5.2) gives χ_θ(T) = qμ + μ^{-1}. The Satake class of this character is that of μ√q, which is also the classical parameter of J(θ) = Ind_norm(θδ^{-1/2}). But (7.5.3) gives μ/√q, whose T-eigenvalue is μ + q/μ. So no single reading makes (7.2.1)/(7.2.6), §7.4(a) and (7.5.3) all true. issues.locator: Published version: §9.2 Remark, p. 221 (preprint §7.8)
issues.printed: The source denies the existence in this case of an L-group homomorphism G_m ⋊ Γ_Q → SL_2 × Γ_Q. It argues that complex conjugation must project to an order 2 element of SL_2 normalizing, but not centralizing, a nontrivial torus, and that no such element exists.
issues.correction: There is no homomorphism of L-groups G_m⋊Γ_Q → SL_2×Γ_Q that is nontrivial on G_m = Ĥ, and in particular no σ-dual homomorphism.
issues.reason: (h,γ) ↦ (1,γ) is a homomorphism of L-groups, and so is any map that kills G_m. The argument given works only when the image of Ĥ is a nontrivial torus. issues.locator: Keel99 Lemma5.2, printed p.281; repeated as a paraphrase in Witaszek22 published p.701
issues.printed: h⁰(L⊗m)>0
issues.correction: Use h⁰(L⊗m)≥2 for some m>0, with nef numerical dimension one on a normal projective surface over an algebraically closed field. Growing h⁰ in the application supplies this stronger hypothesis.
issues.reason: Take an elliptic curve E/C and a nontorsion M in Pic⁰(E). On P_E(O⊕M), L=O(1) is nef, L²=0 and L·fibre=1. For every m>0, H⁰(L^m)=⊕_{i=0}^m H⁰(E,M^i) has dimension1. Its unique section vanishes along a section of the ruled surface, so no positive power is generated. The source assumption gives κ=0 here. The resolution/moving-pencil proof and the positive Euler slope below repair Witaszek’s actual application. (cc-442dc5) Verified: over an algebraically closed field where Pic⁰(E) has a non-torsion point M (for example C), L = O(1) on P_E(O ⊕ M) is nef and effective with L² = 0 and L·fibre = 1, and h⁰(L^m) = 1 for all m > 0, so L is not semiample. The paper's own paraphrase on p.701 ('Q-effective nef line bundles of numerical dimension one on normal projective surfaces over algebraically closed fields are semiample') is false for the same reason. In the application, χ(O(mL)) grows linearly and h² is bounded (Keel's Lemma 5.4), so h⁰(mL) grows and the stronger hypothesis holds.

issues.correction: Let Γ be the maximal prime-to-p quotient of that tame quotient. This Γ is free pro-prime-to-p on δ_1, …, δ_k with δ_1⋯δ_kδ_∞ = 1. Since |F| is prime to p, φ factors through it.
issues.reason: In characteristic p the tame fundamental group of P¹ minus a finite set S is not pro-prime-to-p. Grothendieck's comparison (SGA 1, XIII, 2.12, which the paper cites) describes only its maximal prime-to-p quotient as the prime-to-p completion of the topological fundamental group. For example, for p ≥ 5 the tame fundamental group of P¹ ∖ {0, 1728, ∞} has as quotients the groups PSL₂(F_ℓ), ℓ ≠ p, of modular covers X(ℓ) → X(1), ramified with indices 2, 3, ℓ, and these orders are divisible by p for suitable ℓ. The definition and the proof of Theorem 3.13 only use homomorphisms to F and its lift F̃_c, whose orders are prime to p. These factor through the prime-to-p quotient, so nothing changes. Noted by the extraction (item 56).

issues.reason: By Lemma 3.11, u ↦ I_{F,π,K}(φ,u) is a homomorphism from μ_L to H_2(F,c)[|μ_K|], so I(ρ,1) = 1 for every ρ. With u = 1 and h ≠ 1 the count in the numerator is zero for every X, so the limit is 0, not 1, whenever H_2(G′,c)[|μ_Q|] ≠ 1. The paper has such cases. For a generator u, evaluation at u identifies the homomorphisms μ_L → H_2(G′,c)[|μ_Q|] with H_2(G′,c)[|μ_Q|], since |μ_Q| divides |μ_L|, which is the intended stratification. issues.locator: arXiv:2108.09722v1 (22 Aug 2021), proof of Proposition 3.6, first case, p. 16; page image checked
issues.printed: The argument starts with tr(A^{K/k})_K ≠ A. Corollary 3.5(i) supplies k_{A,X} := k_A ∈ I(K/k), with tr(A^{K/k′})_K = A equivalent to k_{A,X} ⊆ k′ for each k′ ∈ I(K/k). Using the conditions Stab⁰(X) = 0, T_A(X) = A, it asserts that being special for A/K/k′ is equivalent to k_{A,X} ⊆ k′.
issues.correction: Only 'X special for k′ ⇒ k_A ⊆ k′' holds: X ⊆ tr(A^{K/k′})_K + a + C with C ⊆ Stab⁰(X) = 0 and T_X = A forces tr(A^{K/k′})_K = A. For k′ ⊇ k_A, choose an isogeny Φ : A → A₀ ⊗_{k_A} K with A₀ over k_A and run the second case over the base k_A: Φ(X) is special for k′ iff it is defined over k′, iff k′ contains the field k_{Φ(X)⊆(A₀)_K} ∈ I(K/k_A) of Corollary 3.5(ii) for K/k_A. Take k_{A,X} to be that field, which contains k_A.
issues.reason: The converse fails. Take char k ≠ 2, K an algebraic closure of k(s, t), k′ the algebraic closure of k(s) in K, and A = E ⊗_{k′} K with E : y² = x(x−1)(x−s). A has trivial K/k-trace (j(E) ∉ k), so this is the first case, and k_A = k′. Let P ∈ A(K) have x(P) = t and X = {P}. Then Stab⁰(X) = 0, and T_X = A because P is not torsion (torsion points lie in E(k′)). The printed claim makes X special for A/K/k′, but specialness would give P ∈ E(k′) + A_tor = E(k′), whereas x(P) = t ∉ k′. The proposition itself holds by the corrected argument, and Proposition 3.1 uses only its statement.

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed on the page image of p. 16. The printed claim 'X is special for A/K/k′ iff k_{A,X} ⊆ k′' with k_{A,X} = k_A fails in the 'if' direction. Example: take k′ ⊇ k_A, so that A ∼ A₀ ⊗_{k′} K; let C ⊂ A₀ be a curve over k′ with trivial stabilizer that generates A₀, and X = C_K + P with P ∈ A₀(K) ∖ A₀(k′). Then Stab⁰(X) = 0 and T_X = A. If X = Y_K + τ with Y over k′ and τ torsion, uniqueness of the translate gives P − τ ∈ A₀(k′), and τ ∈ A₀(k′) since k′ is algebraically closed, a contradiction. So X is not special although k_A ⊆ k′. The repair recorded (pass to A₀ over k_A and use Corollary 3.5(ii)) restores Proposition 3.6; 'the proof' is the right scope.

issues.locator: arXiv:2108.09722v1, proof of Proposition 5.4, p.25 (page image checked), use p.26
issues.printed: The source asserts that each of 𝒜′ and ℬ is an abelian scheme over S.
issues.correction: Use the Néron model 𝒜′_N of A′ and ℬ_N=𝒜×_S𝒜′_N of B. The generic isomorphism A×A′→B⊆A×A is (x,t)↦(x,t−x), with inverse (x,y)↦(x,x+y). Thus the summation h is the second projection, smooth and flat. The arrow ℬ_N→𝒜×_S𝒜 is an extended homomorphism, not an asserted immersion. Take 𝒴 to be the closure of Y in ℬ_N; its map to 𝒜′_N is surjective by properness and generic dominance. Projectivity and symmetric relatively ample rigidified bundles come from abelian-scheme-projectivity. For prime-to-p torsion, 𝒯 is smooth, so Proposition 2.1 and Proposition 4.2 apply, and Lemma 4.1(4) applies to h*ℒ_{𝒜′_N}. Compute heights on ℬ_N using good-reduction-height; height-properties transports small points and height zero back to the generic inclusion B⊆A×A.
issues.reason: The sentence identifies closures of generic abelian subvarieties with abelian schemes. In characteristic p, distinct finite flat order-p subgroups can meet trivially generically and coincide at a special point: an extended homomorphism is then a generic closed immersion with a special infinitesimal kernel, and its image closure has a multiple nonreduced fibre. The verifier supplies a trivial-trace instance, not just the constant Moret–Bailly mechanism: take a generically ordinary non-isotrivial abelian surface over a projective curve in the interior of the fine moduli space A_{2,n} in characteristic p, meeting the p-rank-one stratum. The positive-degree Hasse bundle forces a nonordinary fibre, excluding a constant surface factor; an elliptic factor and its elliptic quotient would both be isotrivial by good reduction on a projective curve, so the generic trace is trivial. After finite separable base change split the p+1 generic μ_p lines; at a p-rank-one fibre ker F=μ_p×α_p has only two order-p subgroup schemes, so two closures G,H coincide. The generic diagonal map into (𝒞/G)×(𝒞/H) has trivial kernel, but has kernel of length p there. Its closure has fibre multiplicity p by specialization/projection of cycles and is not smooth. The ambient generic fibre has good reduction and trivial trace. With X equal to this generic abelian subvariety, the paper’s setting applies. The endpoint survives by the Néron-model repair. Full moduli existence details remain the documented counterexample route of the verifier, not a new formalized construction.

issues.locator: arXiv:2108.09722v1, first paragraph of the proof of Proposition 3.6, p.16 (page image checked)
issues.printed: The source describes φ as bijective.
issues.correction: First construct F=k_{A,X} over K̄/k̄, using E18 for Corollary 3.5(i) and E1 for the first case. Let F″ be the algebraic closure inside K̄ of the compositum of all σ(F), σ∈Aut(K̄/K), and set k_{A,X}=F″∩K. No finiteness of the orbit is assumed. F″ is stable under Aut(K̄/K). For x∈F″ all roots of its minimal polynomial over K lie in F″ (including multiplicities in inseparable characteristic), so its coefficients lie in F″∩K. Thus F″ is algebraic over k_{A,X}, which is algebraically closed in K. For relatively algebraically closed k′⊆K, its algebraic closure k̄′ in K̄ is stable under Aut(K̄/K); consequently X is special over k′ iff F⊆k̄′ iff F″⊆k̄′ iff k_{A,X}⊆k′.
issues.reason: Noninjectivity: take algebraically closed k, K=k(s,t), ℓ prime different from char k, u=s^(1/ℓ)+t and F=acl(k(u))⊆K̄. A K-automorphism sends s^(1/ℓ) to ζs^(1/ℓ), ζ≠1, and u,σu are algebraically independent. If f∈F∩K is transcendental over k, both u and σu are algebraic over k(f), a contradiction. Thus F∩K=k, just as for k itself. For a constant elliptic E/k, a point P with x(P)=u makes {P} special over F but not over k, since all torsion of E lies in E(k). The corrected general reduction depends on E18 and E1 for the algebraically closed case. It uses all conjugates, not an unproved finite orbit, and the minimal-polynomial argument handles inseparability.

Independence gives trdeg(k(b,τb,c)/k)=2e−d₁, hence the new defect δ′=2δ−d₁+a, with a≤d₁−δ. Equality would make the loci of c over k₂ and τk₂ equal after extension to acl(k₂τk₂), since both contain the locus over that field with the same dimension. Lemma 3.4 then descends this locus to k, contradicting dim locus=d₁−δ<d₁. Thus 0≤δ′<δ. Induction descends A₂ up to isogeny to k, and Lemma 3.3 over k₁ descends A₁. issues.locator: Yu arXiv:1807.04659v5 (18 July 2022), §3.3.1, p. 18, Théorème 3.3.1, and its use on p. 20
issues.printed: Theorem 3.3.1 declares T ↦ J_e^T, viewed as a function of T ∈ 𝔞_B, quasi-polynomial according to [Ch15, Définition 4.5.3].
issues.correction: The restriction of T ↦ J^T_e to lattice points T ∈ Hom(X^*(B), Z) ≅ Z^n is a quasi-polynomial in the sense of [Ch15, Déf. 4.5.3]. The same applies on p. 20 to the right-hand side via [Ch15, Prop. 4.5.5]: the equality holds for all lattice T with T_1 ≥ ⋯ ≥ T_n. T = 0 is a lattice point, so J_e = P_n^e(X_1) follows unchanged.
issues.reason: In Yu 𝔞_B = Hom(X^*(B), R) is real (§3.1.1). Ch15 Déf 4.5.3 (author p. 25, image read) defines quasi-polynomials on 𝔞_B as Σ_{ν∈f} p_ν(T) q^{⟨ν,T⟩} with p_ν polynomials and ν ∈ (2πi/log q)X^*(B) ⊗ Q, so they are real-analytic in T. J^T_e depends on T only through the indicators τ̂_P(H_B(δx) − T) with H_B(δx) in a lattice, so it is locally constant off the hyperplanes ϖ(T) ∈ (1/n)Z. It is not constant: by (3.3.7), for d(T) ≥ max(0, 2g−2) it counts T-semistable bundles of degree e, and this number is unbounded as d(T) → ∞ (already for n = 2 via L_1 ⊕ L_2). A non-constant locally constant function on the open chamber cannot be real-analytic, so the statement is false for real T. The inconsistency is inherited from Ch15, whose Example 4.5.4 counts floor functions as quasi-polynomial and whose Prop. 4.5.5 is stated on a lattice. The proof of Théorème 3.2.4 compares the two sides only at deep lattice points and evaluates at T = 0, so no result is affected.

issues.locator: Yu arXiv:1807.04659v5 (18 July 2022), Appendix B, p. 79
issues.printed: The source claims that T ↦ J^T_{p,e} and T ↦ J̃^T_{p,e} become quasi-polynomial for sufficiently large d(T), citing Théorème 3.3.1 together with [Ch15, Théorème 5.2.1 et Théorème 6.1.1.2].
issues.correction: For J̃^T_{p,e} cite [Ch15, Théorème 6.1.1, assertion 4] (assertion 2 only gives the F^G-form of the kernel for large T). For the group integrals J^T_{p,e}: if p(0) ≠ 0 then J^T_{p,e} = J̃^T_{p,e} for d(T) large, by (B.0.1). If p(0) = 0 then J^T_{p,e} = 0, since an endomorphism with zero constant term in its characteristic polynomial is not an automorphism. So each J^T_{p,e} agrees for large d(T) with a quasi-polynomial, and Σ_p J^T_{p,e} = J^T_e there.
issues.reason: Théorème 3.3.1 concerns only the unrefined J^T_e, and Ch15 Thm 5.2.1 and 6.1.1 treat only the Lie algebra (Ch15 pp. 29–32 read). Neither gives quasi-polynomiality of the characteristic-polynomial pieces of the group trace, which the displayed chain J_e = Σ_p J_{p,e} = Σ_{p(0)≠0} J̃_{p,e} needs. The fix above uses only facts already on p. 79, so the conclusion stands.

issues.locator: Yu arXiv:1807.04659v5 (18 July 2022), Appendix A, p. 75, Lemme A.2 (proof p. 76). It is applied 'pour tout e ∈ Z' in §5.3.3, p. 41, to obtain (5.3.6), and the proof of Théorème A.4 (p. 77) rests on (5.3.6).
issues.printed: Lemma A.2 takes μ_0 ∈ X_M^G and a (G,M)-family (c_Q)_(Q∈P(M)) on a domain containing μ_0^Z. For every L ∈ L(M), it requires c_M^Q … to be independent of Q ∈ P(L), and assumes c_Q(λμ_0) = c_Q(λ). It concludes that lim_(λ→1) Σ_(Q∈P(M)) 1̂^e_Q(λμ_0)c_Q(λμ_0) vanishes unless μ_0 ∈ X_G^G. On p. 41 the source applies Lemma 4.2.8 for e = −1 and Lemma A.2 for every e ∈ Z.
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis gcd(e,n) = 1. The proof then goes through with d_Q = 1̂^e_Q(λμ_0)θ_Q(λ) (E24) and the vanishing Σ_(Q∈P(L)) 1̂^e_Q ≡ 0 on proper Levis L for gcd(e,n) = 1 (proposed new item). Consequently (5.3.6) is established only for (e,n) = 1, and Théorème A.4 and Corollaire A.5 are proved only in the form 'J_e and P_n^e are the same for all e prime to n'. For gcd(e,n) > 1 the same-order statement (Théorème 1.4) rests on Mellit [Me17]. The main results (Théorèmes 1.1–1.3) use only coprime e and are unaffected.
issues.reason: Counterexample: n = 2, M = T, c_Q ≡ 1 (a constant (G,M)-family, invariant under every μ_0, with c_M^L independent of Q), e = 0 and μ_0 = (i,−i) ∈ X_M^G, which is not central. By Prop. 5.2.1, 1̂^0_B(λ) + 1̂^0_(B̄)(λ) = 1/(1−λ_1/λ_2) + 1/(1−λ_2/λ_1) ≡ 1, so the limit is 1 ≠ 0. The failure also occurs where Théorème A.4 has nontrivial content: for n = 10, M = GL_5×GL_5 and e ∈ {2,4,6,8}, Σ_Q 1̂^e_Q(μ_0) = 1 at a generic noncentral μ_0. In general, for μ_0 ∈ X_L^G the term d_L of Yu's argument is proportional to Σ_(Q∈P(L)) 1̂^e_Q(μ_0), which is nonzero whenever (n/gcd(m_j)) | e; the 'même argument' of Lemme 4.2.8 works only when the monomials λ^{I^e_Q} do not depend on Q, as for e = −1. Numerical checks (mpmath, 60–150 digits): with random μ_0-periodic root-product families and μ_0 on walls of proper Levis, the limit is O(x) → 0 for every coprime e and converges to stable nonzero values for non-coprime e, for example −12.04 and 11.86 in GL_4 with e = 0 and e = 2. The statement is confirmed on the page image (p. 75); the image of the application is from p. 41.

issues.locator: Yu arXiv:1807.04659v5 (18 July 2022), §1, p. 3, Théorème 1.1(1), last sentence ('De plus, si on pose deg t = 2 et deg z_i = 1, le terme de poids dominant de P_(g,n) est t^{(g−1)n²+1}…'); §7, pp. 64–75, contains no proof
issues.printed: The source names t^{(g−1)n²+1} as the dominant-weight term of P_(g,n), specifying deg P_(g,n) = 2((g−1)n²+1) and deg(P_(g,n) − t^{(g−1)n²+1}) < 2((g−1)n²+1).
issues.correction: Supply the proof. (i) A_(g,n) has the unique top term t^{(g−1)n²+1}, with coefficient 1: the Higgs moduli is smooth and connected of dimension 2(g−1)n²+2, and one applies Deligne's weights and a curve with multiplicatively independent Weil numbers; alternatively use Mellit's formula. (ii) Every correction term of (7.2.2) is a rational multiple of a product Π_j C_(s_j)(X_(k_j)) with all s_j < n and Σ s_jk_j ≤ n. By induction its weight is 2Σ_j k_j((g−1)s_j²+1) ≤ 2((g−1)(n−1)n + n), which is less than 2((g−1)n²+1) for g ≥ 2.
issues.reason: A search of the TeX finds the assertion only in the statement on p. 3: §7.2 proves existence, uniqueness and integrality, and §7.3 proves the J_g-divisibility, but neither mentions the weight. The assertion is true: the argument above is complete given (i), and an exact computation (A_(g,n) from Mellit's formula, P_(g,n) from the recurrence) gives top term exactly t^{(g−1)n²+1} with coefficient 1 for g = 2, n ≤ 4 and g = 3, n ≤ 3.

issues.locator: Yu arXiv:1807.04659v5 (18 July 2022), §7.3, p. 74: proof of Lemme 7.3.1 (cone condition for I_(g,n)) and the existence of Q_(g,n) ('par récurrence, le lemme précédent et le lemme de Gauss')
issues.printed: The proof says a monomial of I_(g,n)(q,1,z_1,…,z_g) violating the condition would yield a contradiction by examining the monomials q^m z^n in the product of I_(g,n)(q,1,z) with J_g(q,1,z) for which m + Σ min{n_i,0} is minimal.
issues.correction: Use, for each S ⊆ {1,…,g}, the linear functional φ_S(t^m z^u) = m + Σ_(i∈S) u_i. The lowest φ_S-parts multiply, so ord_S(FG) = ord_S(F) + ord_S(G). Moreover ord_S(J_g) = 0, and m + Σ min(u_i,0) = min_S φ_S. Hence ord_S(I) = ord_S(A) ≥ 0 for every S. The same argument gives the cone condition for Q_(g,n).
issues.reason: The function φ(t^m z^u) = m + Σ min(u_i,0) is only superadditive (φ(xy) ≥ φ(x) + φ(y)). The φ-minimal monomials of I·J could therefore a priori cancel, and the printed argument does not rule this out. With the S-linear functionals, a minimal monomial of I with S = {i : u_i < 0} survives in I·J. The conclusion is true: the cone condition was confirmed for I_(g,n) and Q_(g,n) for g ≤ 3.

issues.locator: Theorem 4.19, p. 101, read together with the definition of maximal variation in section 1.6, p. 16 (author manuscript dated 21 August 2024; identical in arXiv:2108.05625v4)
issues.printed: Theorem 4.19 takes K to be a number field or a one-variable function field and S quasi-projective over K. It assumes pi : X -> S is a smooth relative curve with genus g > 1 and maximal variation, and asserts relative Bogomolov for i^m_alpha : X^m_{/S} -> J^m_{/S} whenever m >= dim S + 1. Section 1.6 defines maximal variation for quasi-projective integral S over a noetherian ring R by requiring its moduli map S -> M_{g,R} to be generically finite.
issues.correction: In the function-field case the hypothesis must be maximal variation over the field of constants k, not over K: the moduli morphism must be generically finite on a projective model of S over k. (Corrected by REV-PAPER-YUAN-26: the clause 'equivalently the family must not become isotrivial over the constant field' overstated this. Generic finiteness of the moduli morphism on a k-model implies non-isotriviality over k but is strictly stronger as soon as dim S > 0 - a family over a surface whose moduli image is a curve is non-isotrivial and not maximally varying - and the two agree only in the case dim S = 0 of the counterexample below. What the proof of Theorem 4.19 actually needs is the bigness input of Theorem 4.5 over k, for which maximal variation over k is a sufficient hypothesis; the paper does not prove it necessary.) The number-field case needs no change.
issues.reason: As stated the theorem is false in the function-field case. Because S is a quasi-projective variety over K, the base ring in the section 1.6 definition is R = K, so 'maximal variation' means that S -> M_{g,K} is generically finite. Take k any field, K = k(t), and S = Spec K, so that dim S = 0. Let C be a smooth projective curve of genus g >= 2 over k and let X = C x_k K be the constant family, with alpha any line bundle of positive degree. The hypothesis is then satisfied vacuously: S = Spec K is its own dense open and Spec K -> M_{g,K} is quasi-finite, so the family has maximal variation over K. Part (1) with m = 1 >= dim S + 1 therefore asserts the relative Bogomolov conjecture for i_alpha : X -> J. But that fails: by the definition recalled on p. 100 the canonical height is the one attached to the adelic extension of L over k, and every point of C(kbar), viewed in X(Kbar), is a constant section of a constant family and so has canonical height 0; C(kbar) is infinite, hence Zariski dense in the curve X_{Kbar}. So for every epsilon > 0 the set of points of height at most epsilon is Zariski dense, contradicting the conclusion. The defect is only in the hypothesis, and the paper's own proof shows what the hypothesis should be: it states 'Similar to Proposition 4.18, we need the bigness of the adelic line bundles over k instead of over K, where k = Z if K is a number field and k is the field of constants if K is a function field of one variable', and the bigness input it invokes, Theorem 4.5, requires maximal variation over that same k. Proposition 4.18, on p. 100, is stated correctly and carries bigness on S/k as an explicit hypothesis; it is Theorem 4.19 that fails to upgrade 'maximal variation' to match. The number-field case is unaffected: there k = Z, and for S a variety over a number field K generic finiteness of S -> M_{g,K} is equivalent to that of the induced morphism on a Z-model, since passing to the model adds one to the dimension of the source and of the image alike. Consistently with this, the paper's main uniform theorem is stated with an explicit non-isotriviality condition of its own (section 4.3.2), so the isotrivial case is excluded there and that theorem is not affected.

issues.citation: Xinyi Yuan, "Arithmetic bigness and a uniform Bogomolov-type result", Annals of Mathematics 203 (2026), no. 1
issues.reviewReason: Confirmed, and the counterexample is decisive. Every element of it is verbatim on the page. Theorem 4.19 (p. 101) reads ‘Let K be either a number field or a function field of one variable. Let S be a quasi-projective variety over K. Let π : X → S be a smooth relative curve over S of genus g > 1 with maximal variation … (1) the S-morphism i^m_α for any m ⩾ dim S + 1’, and §1.6 (p. 16) defines maximal variation as generic finiteness of the moduli morphism S → M_{g,R}, ‘i.e. there is an open and dense subscheme U of S such that the induced morphism U → M_{g,R} is quasi-finite’. With K = k(t) and S = Spec K the hypothesis holds vacuously, S being its own dense open and a morphism from a point being quasi-finite, and m = 1 ⩾ dim S + 1 is allowed; but for a constant family X = C ×_k K of genus g ⩾ 2 the points of C(k̄) are constant sections of canonical height 0 and are Zariski dense in X_{K̄}, so the relative Bogomolov conclusion fails. This is the familiar reason function-field Bogomolov statements exclude isotrivial families. The paper’s own proof shows what was meant, in the same paragraph: ‘Similar to Proposition 4.18, we need the bigness of the adelic line bundles over k instead of over K, where k = Z if K is a number field and k is the field of constants if K is a function field of one variable.’ One clause of the recorded correction overstated the repair and this review has corrected it in place: generic finiteness of the moduli morphism on a k-model implies non-isotriviality over k but is strictly stronger once dim S > 0, and the two coincide only in the dim S = 0 case of the counterexample. That distinction matters here, because the open handoff on the errata register for this paper (PR #2299) raises the same objection against the parallel clause in the register’s own E1, and the two should be reconciled together. Checked at the locator in the author manuscript of 21 August 2024, which this review re-downloaded from the author’s page: its SHA-256 is b36f4860…a813e, the hash the extraction records, so the text is the same one. The published Annals version (203 (2026), no. 1, 15–119) is subscription-only and was not obtained by this review either, as the extraction’s own `gaps` entry says; arXiv:2108.05625 ends at v4, which is older than this manuscript.

issues.locator: Section 3.3.2, p. 50 (the displayed integration formula for the total Green function of Phi_S)
issues.printed: The source specifies the total Green function g~_{Phi_S} on S^an by g~_{Phi_S}(v) = int_{X^an_v} log||1||_{Delta,a} c_1(O(Delta)_a)^2 for each v in S^an that is a discrete or archimedean valuation.
issues.correction: the domain of integration is the analytic fibre of the fibre square, int_{(X x_S X)^an_v}
issues.reason: The integral is ill-typed as printed. The metrized line bundle O(Delta)_a is attached to the diagonal Delta in X x_S X and lives on that fibre square, and c_1(...)^2 is a top-degree Chambert-Loir measure only on a two-dimensional analytic space, whereas X^an_v is the analytification of a curve over H_v. The paper's own parallel formula fixes the intended domain: section 3.3.1, p. 48, defines the same invariant as phi(C) = - int_{(C x C)^an} g_{Delta,a} c_1(O(Delta-bar)_a)^2, over the product, and p. 50 asserts that its displayed value 'is exactly the phi-invariant of X_{H_v}', so the two domains have to agree. That the rest of the sentence is right is confirmed by the sign bookkeeping: log||1||_{Delta,a} = -g_{Delta,a}, so the corrected integral is -int g_{Delta,a} c_1^2 = phi, which is what Theorem 3.6(5) then uses. Two pages later, on p. 52, the paper integrates over X^an_{H_v} correctly, with a single c_1 in the integrand.

issues.locator: Section 3.3.1, p. 49 (the base-change recipe for delta)
issues.printed: For split semistable reduction, the source identifies delta(C) with the node count of the minimal regular model over O_K. Otherwise, for a finite extension K' of K giving C split semistable reduction, it specifies delta(C) = delta(C_{K'})/[K' : K].
issues.correction: delta(C) = delta(C_{K'})/e(K'/K), with e the ramification index (equivalently, K'/K must be required totally ramified)
issues.reason: False as printed, and the two halves of the one sentence contradict each other. Let C already have split semistable reduction over K and let K'/K be unramified of degree f > 1. By the first half, delta(C) is the number of nodes of the minimal regular model over O_K. Over O_{K'} the reduction is still split semistable and the minimal regular model base-changes etale-locally, so it has the same nodes and delta(C_{K'}) = delta(C). The second half then gives delta(C) = delta(C)/f, forcing delta(C) = 0 for every such curve. The recipe is not even well defined as printed, since taking K' = K and K' unramified quadratic give answers differing by a factor 2. With the ramification index it is consistent: a node with local equation t_1 t_2 = pi^m becomes t_1 t_2 = pi'^{em} after a degree-e ramified extension, so delta scales by exactly e. That delta is the raw uniformizer-normalized length, with no residue-degree factor, is fixed by the paper's own conventions: p. 47 normalizes the local Green functions by log e_v, and section 4.5.1, p. 86, writes the global invariants as delta(C) = deg(Delta_S) and phi(C) = sum_v phi_v(C) deg(v), carrying the residue degree separately in deg(v). This is an internal inconsistency in one sentence and is independent of how the conventions of [Zha3] compare with this paper's.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 3.10, p. 57 (the sentence introducing the adelic divisor Phi-bar)
issues.printed: Invoking Theorem 3.6, the source asserts existence of an adelic divisor Phi-bar in Div^(M/Z) whose underlying divisor on M is 0. At every discrete or archimedean valuation v in S^an_v, its total Green function has value g~_{Phi-bar}(v) equal to phi(X_{H_v}).
issues.correction: at any discrete or archimedean valuation v in M^an is equal to phi(C_{H_v}), and the citation is to section 3.3.2 rather than to Theorem 3.6
issues.reason: The sentence was transplanted from section 3.3.2 without renaming its objects, and picked up a stray subscript on the way. Three things are wrong and all three are visible on the page. First, 'v in S^an_v' is self-referential, v occurring as both the element and the subscript; the source sentence in section 3.3.2, p. 50, correctly reads 'at any discrete or archimedean valuation v in S^an'. Second, neither S nor X is in scope here: the proof of Theorem 3.10 opens by fixing M = M_{g,N,Q} and a tautological stable relative curve C -> M-bar, and the same sentence writes Div^(M/Z), 'underlying divisor 0 on M' and phi : M(C) -> R, while the S and X of the preceding proof belong to the arithmetic case of Theorem 3.2, which ends two sentences earlier at 'It remains to prove Theorem 3.10'. So the base is M and the curve is C. Third, Theorem 3.6 is the intersection identity for the triple Deligne pairing; it neither constructs Phi_S nor computes its total Green function. Both of those are section 3.3.2, which defines Phi_S = div^(s) and gives the integration formula that the sentence is asserting. The proof is unaffected.

issues.locator: Proof of the arithmetic case of Theorem 3.2, p. 57, and the sketch at the end of section 1.4, p. 14
issues.printed: pi_*<omega_{X/S,a}, omega_{X/S,a}> = (2/(3g-1)) O(Phi_S) + nef = (2/(3g-1)) O(c_0) + nef + eff
issues.correction: the step needs, and does not cite, the non-negativity of the phi-invariant at the non-archimedean places
issues.reason: The second equality asserts that Phi_S - O(c_0) is an effective adelic divisor on S/Z. Since O(c_0) is pulled back from Spec Z, its total Green function is c_0 above the archimedean place and 0 above every finite place, so effectivity needs g~_{Phi_S}(v) >= c_0 archimedean and g~_{Phi_S}(v) >= 0 at every non-archimedean v in S^an. Theorem 3.10, which is what is cited, supplies only the archimedean half, for compact Riemann surfaces. The non-archimedean half is true - it is Cinkir's bound phi(Gamma_v) >= (1/39) l(Gamma_v) >= 0, which the paper quotes as Theorem 3.7 - but Theorem 3.7 is stated only over a base field k, section 3.2 having explicitly excluded k = Z, so the fact needed here is nowhere cited at this point. The gap is therefore in the exposition rather than in the mathematics: the missing input is a graph-theoretic bound the paper already has. The same elision occurs in the outline at the end of section 1.4.

issues.locator: Section 1.6, p. 16 (definition of a stable curve)
issues.printed: The definition calls a curve stable when it is semistable of arithmetic genus g > 1 and every rational irreducible component of C_kbar meets the remaining irreducible components in at least three points.
issues.correction: any SMOOTH (nonsingular) rational irreducible component, as in Deligne-Mumford Definition 1.1(iii)
issues.reason: As printed the definition excludes genuine stable curves. Take C over kbar irreducible and rational with exactly two nodes, both self-intersections. It is reduced with only ordinary double points, so semistable by the paper's own definition, and its arithmetic genus is 0 + 2 = 2 > 1. It is a stable curve in the standard sense - its only component is singular, so the Deligne-Mumford condition on nonsingular rational components is vacuous, and omega_C is ample - and it is a point of the boundary of Mbar_2. But its unique component is rational and meets OTHER irreducible components in 0 < 3 points, so the printed condition fails. The paper treats its own section 1.6 and [DM, section 1] as interchangeable, saying on p. 41 'We refer to [DM, Sec. 1] (or our Sec. 1.6) for quick definitions of stable curves', and then defines Mbar_g as the moduli of stable curves, whose boundary contains exactly the curves the printed definition rules out. Section 3.3.4 confirms the intended notion by counting nodes 'of type 0', where the partial normalization is connected, i.e. self-nodes of a single component. Every later use is the Deligne-Mumford notion, so nothing downstream is affected.

issues.citation: Xinyi Yuan, "Arithmetic bigness and a uniform Bogomolov-type result", Annals of Mathematics 203 (2026), no. 1
issues.reviewReason: Confirmed, and the counterexample is correct. Page 16 reads ‘curve is called stable if it is semistable with arithmetic genus g > 1, and any rational irreducible component of C_k̄ intersects other irreducible components at three or more points’, with no smoothness qualifier. An irreducible rational curve with two self-nodes is reduced with ordinary double points, has arithmetic genus 0 + 2 = 2 > 1, is stable in the sense of Deligne–Mumford — its only component is singular, so DM’s condition on nonsingular rational components is vacuous — and is a boundary point of M̄₂; but its unique component meets other components in 0 < 3 points, so the printed condition excludes it. The recorded correction, ‘any SMOOTH (nonsingular) rational irreducible component, as in Deligne–Mumford Definition 1.1(iii)’, is exactly right, and for a connected curve of arithmetic genus ⩾ 2 it is equivalent to the branch count 2s + r ⩾ 3 on each rational component. It is worth recording that this is the correct form of the same point: the errata register’s E4 for this paper carries instead the clause ‘a rational component with a self-node meets them in at least one’, which the two-self-node curve refutes, and which the open handoff PR #2299 objects to on exactly that ground. issues.locator: Theorem 2.3, p. 28, with its proof in section 2.2.3, p. 32
issues.printed: Part (a) assumes a smooth relative curve pi : X -> S with genus g > 0. It asserts existence of an adelic line bundle omega_{X/S,a}, declaring it nef and determined uniquely up to isomorphism.
issues.correction: the proof establishes this only for g > 1; for g = 1 both the normalization and the nefness are unproved
issues.reason: The stated hypothesis is g > 0 but the proof supports only g > 1, in two independent ways. First, the normalization: section 2.2.3 pins down beta-bar_2, and hence O(Delta)_a, by an isomorphism whose coefficient is (2g-2), which vanishes at g = 1, so the condition it is meant to impose becomes vacuous and neither beta-bar_2 nor beta-bar_1 is determined. The appendix flags exactly this degeneration: Theorem A.1, p. 105, states the characterizing properties in terms of c_1(O(x)) and then says 'Note that if g > 1, the first two properties are equivalent to the following', the omega-version, which is what Theorem 2.3(2) encodes. Second, the nefness asserted in (a) is proved nowhere for g = 1: the only proof of nefness in the paper is Theorem 2.10(1), whose formula carries 1/(4g(g-1)) and is meaningless at g = 1, and Theorem 2.10 opens by assuming g > 1. The paper itself notices the mismatch without resolving it, remarking on p. 40 'Note that we require g > 1 in this section, while we only require g > 0 in the previous section.' A repair is available inside the paper's own toolkit, since the condition used in section 3.3.3 has coefficient 2 - 1 = 1 and so survives g = 1. The g = 1 case of Proposition 2.7 and Theorems 2.8 and 2.9, which rest on Theorem 2.3 under the same standing hypothesis, is affected in the same way; every application in sections 3 and 4 has g > 1.

issues.locator: Section 2.1, p. 20 (definition of strongly nef)
issues.printed: The source defines a strongly nef adelic line bundle as one isomorphic to a limit, in the boundary topology, of nef hermitian line bundles. For an adelic divisor, the corresponding requirement is equality to such a limit of nef adelic divisors.

issues.reason: Theorem 4.5(4) introduces T as the image of Y -> S and assumes that the composition T -> S -> M_{g,k} is generically finite; the whole purpose of that hypothesis, as against the ambient maximal-variation hypothesis on X -> S, is to allow T to be a proper subvariety of S. When T is strictly smaller than S the fibre of Y -> S over the generic point of S is empty, so the sentence as printed is vacuous. The argument imported from part (3) also fails literally: the positive term there is (pi_J^* pi_*<omega_a,omega_a>|_Y)^{dim S} times a power of Theta|_Y, and on Y that first class is pulled back from T, so its (dim T + 1)-st power vanishes and the term is identically zero whenever dim T < dim S. With dim T throughout, the term is the degree of Theta|_Y on the generic fibre of Y -> T times (pi_{T*}<omega_a,omega_a>)^{dim T}, which is positive by Theorem 3.2 applied over T - which is exactly what the hypothesis on T buys. The statement of Theorem 4.5(4) is correct and the corrected step is immediate.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 4.2(2), pp. 65-66, and proof of Theorem 4.10, p. 83
issues.printed: The proof asserts the inclusion {x in (X^m)_y(overline{k(y)}) : h_{L_m}(x) <= epsilon d deg(M|y)} into Z_y(overline{k(y)}).
issues.correction: a strict inequality, h_{L_m}(x) < epsilon deg(M|y); equivalently halve epsilon in the claim
issues.reason: What the displayed derivation establishes is 0 <= deg(pi_x)(h_{L_m}(x) - epsilon d deg(M|y)) for x outside Z_y, because a nonzero effective section gives only the non-strict bound. issues.locator: Section A.1, p. 102 (the condition equivalent to admissibility of a Green function)
issues.printed: The source identifies the condition with the current equation (i/pi) ddbar g_D = dmu_Ar - delta_D on C.
issues.correction: (i/pi) ddbar g_D = deg(D) dmu_Ar - delta_D
issues.reason: The identity fails on total mass for every divisor of degree other than 1. The left side is exact, so it integrates to 0 over the compact surface C. The paper's own normalization makes mu_Ar a probability measure: dmu_Ar = (i/2g) sum_j alpha_j wedge alpha_j-bar for an orthonormal basis of the pairing <alpha,beta> = (i/2) integral alpha wedge beta-bar, so its total mass is (1/g) times g, namely 1; and delta_D has total mass deg(D). As printed the right side integrates to 1 - deg(D). The factor is also forced by the two neighbouring definitions: admissibility of a metric is defined three lines earlier as c_1(L,||.||) = deg(L) dmu_Ar, and Poincare-Lelong for ||1|| = exp(-g_D), the paper's own convention, gives c_1(O(D),||.||) = (i/pi) ddbar g_D + delta_D, so substituting admissibility produces the deg(D). The non-archimedean twin, Proposition A.2 on p. 108, correctly carries deg(L). Nothing downstream breaks, because every subsequent use is for a divisor D = x_0 of degree 1.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition A.5, p. 118, and one step of the existence proof of Theorem A.1, p. 113
issues.printed: Appendix A assumes genus g > 0 throughout; this hypothesis accompanies Theorem A.1, Proposition A.2, Theorem A.3, and Proposition A.5.
issues.correction: two steps need g > 1 and are unproved at g = 1
issues.reason: Two steps silently require 2g - 2 to be nonzero. First, the proof of Proposition A.5 computes c_1(omega_{C/K}, ||.||_a) = i_*((2g-2) mu) and then appeals to the defining equation of dmu_a, which for L = omega reads c_1(omega, ||.||_a) = deg(omega) dmu_a = (2g-2) dmu_a; at g = 1 this is 0 = 0 and determines nothing. The asserted formula nevertheless appears to be true at g = 1 - good reduction gives the single vertex measure, and a Tate curve with an n-cycle graph gives uniform probability measure on the edges - so this is a gap rather than a false statement, and the fix is to run the argument with a degree-1 line bundle instead of omega. Second, the existence half of Theorem A.1 concludes on p. 113 that 'The constancy of this integral with L = omega_{C/K} is exactly what we need for (2) of Theorem A.1'; but property (2) as stated integrates against c_1(O(x), ||.||_x), and the omega-version is equivalent to it only under the paper's own proviso on p. 105, 'Note that if g > 1, the first two properties are equivalent to the following'. That the author was tracking the g-dependence is clear from the neighbouring uniqueness proof, which inserts '(for g > 0)' exactly where it is needed; these two steps do not survive g = 1.
