issues.locator: Proposition 3.15 (p. 156), in its proof on p. 157; checked on the page image
issues.printed: For a geometric point s of M_n, the source identifies q_1^{-1}(s) with the order-p subgroups of E_s. It counts p + 1 of them when car(k(s)) ≠ p, but just one, namely the Frobenius kernel, when car(k(s)) = p.
issues.correction: In characteristic p the fibre has one point (the kernel of Frobenius) if E_s is supersingular and two points (the kernel of Frobenius and the étale subgroup of order p) if E_s is ordinary.
issues.reason: For ordinary E_s over an algebraically closed field of characteristic p, E_s[p] ≅ μ_p × Z/p has exactly two subgroup schemes of order p. Deligne's own Proposition 4.3 (p. 162) says that for a p-isogeny between curves with invertible Hasse invariant either its kernel or the kernel of its dual is étale, and the special fibre of M_{n,p} has two components (F and V). issues.printed: For p > 2 the proof deduces that the unramified character γ_{v,f}, a square root of ψ_v with ρ_f|D_v of the form (χ_pγ_{v,f} ∗; 0 γ_{v,f}), does not depend on f from the single fact that the residual representation of the forms in the localisation at m does not depend on f.

issues.reason: The two candidates are γ and γη, η the unramified quadratic character. Their residual semisimplifications are {χ̄_pγ̄, γ̄} and {χ̄_pγ̄η̄, γ̄η̄}. Since p > 2, η̄ ≠ 1, and the two sets coincide exactly when χ̄_p|D_v = η̄, that is when v ∤ p and N(v) ≡ −1 mod p. Then a split ρ̄_m|D_v ≅ γ̄ ⊕ γ̄η̄ is compatible with both candidates, while a non-split one still singles out γ̄ as its unramified quotient. The Hecke algebra of the lemma contains only the operators at places outside S ⊇ Σ, so the maximal ideal does not see the sign. Whether forms of both signs actually occur in one localisation (as level raising suggests when N(v) ≡ −1 mod p) was not decided.

By BLGGT A.2, r_{l,ι}(χ) = r_{l,ι}(χ₀) ε_l^{−w} with χ₀ of finite order, so r_{l,ι}(χ)(c_v) = (−1)^w χ_v(−1), and µ(c_v) = (−1)^{n−1+w} χ_v(−1). Counterexample for w odd: n = 1, F imaginary quadratic, ψ the Hecke character of a CM elliptic curve (weight (1, 0)). (ψ, ψ|_{𝔸_ℚ}) satisfies the printed conditions, since ψ|_{𝔸_ℚ} has sign (−1)^1 at ∞. But r_{l,ι}(ψ|_{𝔸_ℚ}) = r_{l,ι}(ψ)∘V (V the transfer) takes c to r_{l,ι}(ψ)(c²) = 1, so µ(c) = +1. A pairing on a line is symmetric, so (r_{l,ι}(ψ), µ) is not polarized, let alone totally odd. The same happens for the base change of a newform of odd weight k (w = k − 2). Patrikis (Math. Ann. 362, p. 8 of arXiv v2) gives the general sign as ω_ι(c_v) = (−1)^w ω_v(−1), consistent with this correction.

issues.locator: Published §2.5, Lemma 2.5.1, p. 189; n(r,N)=rank N in preceding paragraph
issues.printed: Lemma 2.5.1 uses maximum rank of N as a uniqueness criterion for a pure Weil–Deligne extension of the fixed semisimple Weil representation.
issues.correction: Pure extension is unique up to equivalence by TY Lemma 1.4(4). Rank N alone does not characterize it in arbitrary dimension. Use purity’s full family of monodromy-power isomorphisms, or a proved sufficiently refined criterion in the intended restricted rank.
issues.reason: For q=4, fix an unramified semisimple Weil representation whose geometric Frobenius is diag(8,2,2,1/2,1/2,1/8), with weights (3,1,1,−1,−1,−3). Let N_p have chains (0,1,3,5),(2,4), and N_i have chains (0,1,3),(2,4,5), each sending an entry to the next. Both satisfy FNF^−1=N/4 and have rank 4, the maximum allowed by the graded dimensions (1,2,2,1). N_p is pure of weight 0 with strings of lengths 4 and 2. N_i has strings of length 3 centred at weights 1 and −1, is not pure, and has N_i³=0 while rank N_p³=1. Thus the maximizing WD class is not unique even up to equivalence. Literal uniqueness of a matrix N must also be replaced by equivalence.

issues.locator: §3A dimension of Y^(i,j), p.1610; also arXiv v1 §3.1, p.8
issues.printed: The stated dimension of a nonempty two-index stratum omits the m smooth Z-coordinates of the local model.

issues.reason: On the special fiber, imposing i X-coordinates and j Y-coordinates to vanish already kills both product equations, leaving 2n+m−i−j free coordinates. issues.locator: Published 2004 chapter, §3, Remark after Proposition 3.5, pp. 121–122, (3.22)
issues.printed: The source places the poles, when F=ℝ, at −r∈ℤ_{≤0}, imposing r≡a mod2. Its residue identity reads Res_{s=−r}z(s,ω)=c_rD^rδ₀.
issues.correction: In the chapter's convention ω(x) = x^{−a} (3.18), for which L(s, ω) = π^{−s/2}Γ(s/2) for both a (3.19): the poles are at s = −r with r ≡ 0 mod 2, and the residue is c_r D^{a+r}δ₀ ∈ S′(ωω_{−r}) (the constant term extends x^{−a−r}d^×x). The printed statement is right for the other common normalisation ω = sgn^a.
issues.reason: For a = 1, Proposition 3.5 gives z(s, x^{−1}; x e^{−πx²}) = ∫ e^{−πx²}|x|^s d^×x = π^{−s/2}Γ(s/2), with poles at s = 0, −2, −4, …, not at odd −r. Directly, the Taylor term f^{(k)}(0)x^k/k! contributes ∫_{|x|<1} x^{k−1}|x|^{s−1}dx, nonzero only for k odd, with a pole at s = 1 − k and a residue proportional to f^{(k)}(0), i.e. to D^{a+r}δ₀ with r = k − 1 even. This matches the chapter's own complex statement, residue D^{a+r}D̄^{b+r}δ₀, and the eigencharacter: D^{a+r}δ₀ ∈ S′(x^{−a−r}) = S′(x^{−a}|x|^{−r}) for r even.

issues.locator: Appendix A, proof of (A.1): the strategy sentence on p. 983 and the final paragraph on p. 985; the differentiation under the integral sign on p. 984
issues.printed: The proof attempts to establish uniqueness from a common differential equation and agreement of the first three expansion coefficients.
issues.correction: Two unstated routine steps close the proof. (i) Uniqueness. By (A.2), the left side of (A.1) is t^s H(t) with H entire: the double series is dominated termwise using |∫_0^π e^{i(m+μ)θ} sin^{n+s−1}θ dθ| ≤ e^{π|Im μ|}∫_0^π sin^{σ−1}θ dθ, which also justifies integrating termwise. By (A.3), the right side is t^s H̃(t) with H̃ entire. For f = t^s Σ a_ℓ t^ℓ, the equation f″ + (1 − s(s−1)/t²)f = 0 forces a_1 = 0 and ℓ(ℓ+2s−1)a_ℓ = −a_{ℓ−2} (ℓ ≥ 2), and ℓ(ℓ+2s−1) ≠ 0 for ℓ ≥ 1 when Re s > 0. So both sides are determined by their t^s coefficients. These coefficients agree by the duplication formula, and this covers the case where both vanish. (ii) Differentiating twice in t under the integral on p. 984 is justified by dominated convergence: the integrand and its first two t-derivatives are O(sin^{σ−1}θ), σ = Re s, uniformly for t in compact subsets of (0,∞).
issues.reason: The step is terse but no step is false. In the defence of the paper: 'Taylor series' refers to the expansions in powers t^{s+ℓ} that (A.2) and (A.3) actually compute. The authors match coefficients of t^s, t^{s+1}, t^{s+2}, and 'more than what is needed' shows they intend the one-coefficient Frobenius argument at the regular singular point t = 0 (exponents s and 1−s), not a regular-point uniqueness from two Taylor coefficients. So the extraction's framing overstates the problem. What is missing is the explicit statement of the recurrence and the differentiation-under-the-integral justification; items 117/166 and 163–165 supply them. Lemma 7 is true: I verified it numerically, for both signs, complex μ and s, and G = 0.

issues.locator: Yu arXiv:1807.04659v5 (18 July 2022), §3.3.1, p. 18, Théorème 3.3.1, and its use on p. 20
issues.printed: The trace is asserted to be quasipolynomial in a real height parameter while invoking a lattice-based definition.
issues.correction: The restriction of T ↦ J^T_e to lattice points T ∈ Hom(X^*(B), Z) ≅ Z^n is a quasi-polynomial in the sense of [Ch15, Déf. 4.5.3]. The same applies on p. 20 to the right-hand side via [Ch15, Prop. 4.5.5]: the equality holds for all lattice T with T_1 ≥ ⋯ ≥ T_n. T = 0 is a lattice point, so J_e = P_n^e(X_1) follows unchanged.
issues.reason: In Yu 𝔞_B = Hom(X^*(B), R) is real (§3.1.1). Ch15 Déf 4.5.3 (author p. 25, image read) defines quasi-polynomials on 𝔞_B as Σ_{ν∈f} p_ν(T) q^{⟨ν,T⟩} with p_ν polynomials and ν ∈ (2πi/log q)X^*(B) ⊗ Q, so they are real-analytic in T. J^T_e depends on T only through the indicators τ̂_P(H_B(δx) − T) with H_B(δx) in a lattice, so it is locally constant off the hyperplanes ϖ(T) ∈ (1/n)Z. It is not constant: by (3.3.7), for d(T) ≥ max(0, 2g−2) it counts T-semistable bundles of degree e, and this number is unbounded as d(T) → ∞ (already for n = 2 via L_1 ⊕ L_2). A non-constant locally constant function on the open chamber cannot be real-analytic, so the statement is false for real T. The inconsistency is inherited from Ch15, whose Example 4.5.4 counts floor functions as quasi-polynomial and whose Prop. 4.5.5 is stated on a lattice. The proof of Théorème 3.2.4 compares the two sides only at deep lattice points and evaluates at T = 0, so no result is affected.

issues.locator: Yu arXiv:1807.04659v5 (18 July 2022), Appendix A, p. 75, Lemme A.2 (proof p. 76). It is applied 'pour tout e ∈ Z' in §5.3.3, p. 41, to obtain (5.3.6), and the proof of Théorème A.4 (p. 77) rests on (5.3.6).
issues.printed: The lemma concludes that the translated cutoff-family limit vanishes at every noncentral parameter under its family and translation hypotheses. Its subsequent use permits all integer degrees, although the coprime-degree restriction needed by the counterexample check is absent.
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis gcd(e,n) = 1. The proof then goes through with d_Q = 1̂^e_Q(λμ_0)θ_Q(λ) (E24) and the vanishing Σ_(Q∈P(L)) 1̂^e_Q ≡ 0 on proper Levis L for gcd(e,n) = 1 (proposed new item). Consequently (5.3.6) is established only for (e,n) = 1, and Théorème A.4 and Corollaire A.5 are proved only in the form 'J_e and P_n^e are the same for all e prime to n'. For gcd(e,n) > 1 the same-order statement (Théorème 1.4) rests on Mellit [Me17]. The main results (Théorèmes 1.1–1.3) use only coprime e and are unaffected.
issues.reason: Counterexample: n = 2, M = T, c_Q ≡ 1 (a constant (G,M)-family, invariant under every μ_0, with c_M^L independent of Q), e = 0 and μ_0 = (i,−i) ∈ X_M^G, which is not central. By Prop. 5.2.1, 1̂^0_B(λ) + 1̂^0_(B̄)(λ) = 1/(1−λ_1/λ_2) + 1/(1−λ_2/λ_1) ≡ 1, so the limit is 1 ≠ 0. The failure also occurs where Théorème A.4 has nontrivial content: for n = 10, M = GL_5×GL_5 and e ∈ {2,4,6,8}, Σ_Q 1̂^e_Q(μ_0) = 1 at a generic noncentral μ_0. In general, for μ_0 ∈ X_L^G the term d_L of Yu's argument is proportional to Σ_(Q∈P(L)) 1̂^e_Q(μ_0), which is nonzero whenever (n/gcd(m_j)) | e; the 'même argument' of Lemme 4.2.8 works only when the monomials λ^{I^e_Q} do not depend on Q, as for e = −1. Numerical checks (mpmath, 60–150 digits): with random μ_0-periodic root-product families and μ_0 on walls of proper Levis, the limit is O(x) → 0 for every coprime e and converges to stable nonzero values for non-coprime e, for example −12.04 and 11.86 in GL_4 with e = 0 and e = 2. The statement is confirmed on the page image (p. 75); the image of the application is from p. 41.

issues.locator: Author Chapter IV PDF, Theorem 1.18, p.12, version accessed 2026-10-05; published-book collation unavailable
issues.printed: K_n(A) ⊗ Q ≅ K_n(F)
issues.correction: K_n(A) ⊗ Q ≅ K_n(F) ⊗ Q for n≥2. The rank table is unchanged.
issues.reason: Take A=F=ℚ and n=2. The displayed even-degree rank makes K₂(ℚ)⊗ℚ zero. Localization gives K₂(ℚ)→⊕_p K₁(𝔽_p)→K₁(ℤ)→K₁(ℚ); the final map is the injection {±1}→ℚ×, so the first map is onto the nonzero, indeed infinite, direct sum of finite residue-field unit groups. Thus the literal integral right-hand side cannot equal the zero rationalized left-hand side. issues.locator: §3.5, Proposition 3.5.7(1), p. 689, and the same word in its proof, p. 690 (also in arXiv v1)
issues.printed: Paraphrase of the issue: the proposition and proof describe the Newton map as lower semicontinuous for their chosen order.
issues.correction: For the order fixed on B(G), the Newton map is upper semicontinuous: locally b(y)≤b(x). Its finite image has constant κ, so upper unions are closed. This agrees with Corollary3.5.9 and Theorem1.11.
issues.reason:
The paper orders B(G) on p. 677 by b ⪯ b′ if ν_b ⪯ ν_{b′} and κ(b) = κ(b′). The basic element is the minimum for this order. Read with ⪯, lower semicontinuity would mean that every set {x : b(x) ⪯ b} is closed. In particular the basic stratum would be closed. Corollary 3.5.9 says it "follows immediately" from the proposition, but it states the opposite: the basic stratum is open, and each Fℓ^{⪰b}_{G,µ} = ⊔_{b⪯b′} Fℓ^{b′}_{G,µ} is closed. Theorem 1.11 says the same. The modular-curve example on p. 655 shows that the printed direction cannot hold. There Fℓ = ℙ^1, the strata are ℙ^1(ℚ_p) and Ω², and Ω² is open. Under the printed reading Ω² would also be closed, which is impossible because |ℙ^1| is connected and both strata are non-empty.

The word comes from [KL15, Th. 7.4.5]. There it refers to the y-coordinates of the convex slope polygon (Def. 7.4.1), and the proof shows that near β the polygon lies on or above the polygon at β. With the endpoints fixed, a higher polygon has less spread-out slopes, so it corresponds to a smaller Newton point for ⪯. This does not depend on the sign convention linking bundles to B(G), because ν ⪯ ν′ if and only if −w_0ν ⪯ −w_0ν′. So Kedlaya–Liu's result is exactly upper semicontinuity of b(·) for ⪯. The argument on p. 690 (reduce to representations by [RR96, Lemma 2.2], then apply [KL15, Th. 7.4.5] with Corollary 3.3.4) therefore proves the corrected statement.

Only the name of the property is wrong. The intended statement is clear from Corollary 3.5.9 and Theorem 1.11, it is proved, and it is used correctly. None of the paper's results change. The printed wording of Proposition 3.5.7(1) is still false under the paper's own order, so the misprint sits in a stated result. It should be recorded as a misprint, not as an error. As printed, the statement of Proposition 3.5.7(1) is false; items use the corrected direction.

issues.printed: Paraphrase of the issue: the ordinary-class assertion assumes existence for a general inner form; the density statement adds local integrality.
issues.correction: The ordinary class is unique if it exists. For a quasi-split p-adic group its existence follows from the supplied theorem; for general inner forms existence must be assumed and can fail for a division-algebra multiplicative group. Density claims therefore need this existence or quasi-split hypothesis in addition to local integrality.
issues.reason: §1.3.15 allows non-quasi-split G_{Q_p} (its setup allows an inner twisting). For G_{Q_p} = D^×, D the quaternion division algebra, realise D^×(L) as GL_2(L) with Frobenius Ad(Π)∘σ, Π² = p. Then b ↦ bΠ is a bijection B(D^×) → B(GL_2) that raises κ by 1 and both Newton slopes by 1/2. A class with ν = μ̄^{-1} = (0, −1) would give a 2-dimensional isocrystal with the distinct slopes 1/2 and −1/2, each of multiplicity 1, which is impossible. So B(D^×, {μ^{-1}}) is the single basic class, with ν = (−1/2, −1/2). This happens inside the paper's setting: the Shimura curve of an indefinite quaternion algebra over Q ramified at an odd p is of Hodge type with G_{Q_p} = D^×, in agreement with Čerednik–Drinfeld (every point of its special fibre is supersingular). For Theorem 3 and Corollary 1.3.16 the example shows the μ-ordinary locus is undefined rather than that a density assertion is false, since that special fibre is not locally integral.

issues.printed: Paraphrase of the issue: after choosing an arbitrary full lattice M0, the proof bounds an effective over-lattice by a power of the uniformizer depending only on the Newton polygon.
issues.correction: Include the Frobenius denominator of the chosen lattice. Over a coefficient DVR with Frobenius preserving the DVR and fixing π, assume an effective lattice exists and ΦM0⊂π^(−d)M0 with d≥0. The minimal effective over-lattice is Σ_(i=0)^(h−1) Φ^i M0 for rank h, and lies in π^(−d(h−1))M0. This field-level repair does not remove the proper-cover or local-freeness obligations over general bases.
issues.reason: Over an algebraically closed residue field, take rank two with Φ(x,y)=(σ(x)+π^(−N)σ(y),σ(y)) and standard M0. In equal characteristic choose a residue-field element u with u−u^q=1, which exists over the algebraic closure. The shear g=[[1,uπ^(−N)],[0,1]] satisfies b=g σ(g)^−1, so this is σ-conjugate to the identity and its Newton polygon is always (0,0). Any effective M containing M0 contains Φ(e2)−e2=π^(−N)e1. Containment in π^(−c)M0 therefore forces c≥N, while N is arbitrary. Zink author-copy Lemma9 pp.11–12 bounds the number of iterates by h−1 using a minimal stable lattice, the residue-field dimension and Nakayama; it does not bound these arbitrary input denominators. issues.locator: ECD, author PDF dated 14 April 2026 (the text the register cites as arXiv:1709.07343v4), proof of Theorem 25.1, p. 160; against Lütkebohmert 1995, Theorem 5.3, p. 197, and Remark 6.7, p. 211
issues.printed: The source cites [Lüt95, Theorem 5.3] to embed X in a rigid-analytic curve X′ that is proper and smooth.
issues.correction: The cited theorem is over the fraction field of a complete discrete valuation ring and gives a compactification étale-locally on the base and locally on the curve. For the algebraically closed C of the proof one needs its extension to nondiscretely valued fields, which Remark 6.7 of Lütkebohmert's paper asserts without proof. A global embedding is not needed: the cone is a direct sum of contributions at the finitely many frontier points, so it suffices to embed a neighbourhood of each frontier point into a proper smooth curve, which is what the theorem provides once it is available over C. Footnote 7 of ECD names [GW21] for a different treatment of this case.
issues.reason: Theorem 5.3 reads: 'Let K be the field of fractions of a complete discrete valuation ring R. Let f_K : X_K → S_K be a smooth rigid curve fibration. Then, étale locally on S_K and locally on X_K, there exists a smooth projective S_K-compactification.' Remark 6.7 reads: 'Throughout the paper we always assumed that the valuation of the base field is discrete.' An algebraically closed nontrivially valued field has a divisible value group and is not discretely valued, and a compactification of open pieces of X is not an embedding of X. So the cited theorem does not justify the sentence as written. The statement of Theorem 25.1 is not put in doubt.

issues.locator: Theorem 4.4 (The Law of Biquadratic Reciprocity), p. 45, arXiv v3
issues.printed: The source asserts χπ(λ)χλ(π) = (−1)^((Nλ−1)/4 · (Nπ−1)/4) when π, λ ∈ D are primary and relatively prime.
issues.correction: χπ(λ) = χλ(π) · (−1)^(((Nλ−1)/4)·((Nπ−1)/4)), that is χπ(λ) χλ(π)^(−1) = (−1)^(((Nλ−1)/4)·((Nπ−1)/4)); the product of the two characters is not a sign in general.
issues.reason: In ℤ[i] take the primary primes π = −1 + 2i (norm 5) and λ = −3 (norm 9). Modulo π, i ≡ 3 and −3 ≡ 2 ≡ 3^3 = i^3, so χπ(λ) = −i; modulo 3, π^2 = −3 − 4i ≡ −i, so χλ(π) = −i. The product is (−i)^2 = −1, while the printed right side is (−1)^(2·1) = 1; the quotient is 1, as the corrected law requires.

issues.locator: Chapter 7, Exercise 7.5, printed p. 120 (author's PDF)
issues.printed: The source requires aij = 0 whenever i > j, and also aii ≥0. For every j < i it imposes aij < aii, except that aii = 0 forces every aij = 0.
issues.correction: The third condition should constrain the entries above each pivot: 0 ≤ aji < aii for all j < i whenever aii > 0 (a zero diagonal entry imposes nothing, as the source's own example with a33 = 0 and a13 = 3 shows). As printed, for j < i the entry aij lies below the diagonal and is already 0, so the condition is vacuous, and nonnegativity of the entries above the pivots is missing; pivots of a rank-deficient matrix also need not lie on the diagonal.
issues.reason: With the printed conditions both upper triangular matrices with rows (1, 2), (0, 1) and (1, 0), (0, 1) would be in Hermite form, and they have the same row lattice ℤ², contradicting the uniqueness the exercise presupposes; the exercise's own example (rows (1, 2, 3), (0, 3, 6), (0, 0, 0)) is consistent only with the corrected reading (2 < 3 above the pivot 3).

issues.locator: Definition 1, p. 1 (Spring 2014 lecture 4)
issues.printed: Definition 1 calls a non-singular B = [b1, . . . , bn] ∈Rm×n a Hermite normal form (HNF) matrix precisely when indices 1 ≤i1 < . . . < ih ≤m exist with bi,j̸ = 0 ⇒(j < h) ∧(i ≥ij), described as strictly decreasing column height, and when 0 ≤bij,k < bij,j for every k > j.
issues.correction: b_{i,j} ≠ 0 ⇒ (j ≤ h) ∧ (i ≥ i_j), and 0 ≤ b_{i_j,k} < b_{i_j,j} for all k < j; 'non-singular' should read 'full column rank on its first h columns', since zero columns are allowed.
issues.reason: With j < h the h-th column would have to vanish, contradicting h being the number of nonzero columns; in a lower-triangular form the entries b_{i_j,k} with k > j are zero (column k starts below row i_j), so the reduction must be over k < j, as the gloss 'all elements at rows i_j are reduced' and the lecture's own algorithm indicate.

issues.locator: Definition and proof of the Theorem, p. 1
issues.printed: The source chooses ρ1, . . . , ρµ1 as the roots of greatest ord. In σµ1 = ρ1 . . . ρµ1 + (other products), it asserts that every other product of µ1 factors has strictly smaller ords.
issues.correction: The roots with the smallest ord ν1 must be chosen, and the other products have strictly larger ords; then ord σ_{µ1} = µ1ν1 by the ultrametric equality. Also: N(i_j) = ord c_{i_j} (printed ord c_{i+j}); c_{n−i} = ±σ_i (printed c_i = ±σ_i); the segment has slope −ν_{j+1} (printed −νj + 1); and ord σ_M (printed ord M). In the interior-index condition M counts roots, so compare it with cumulative multiplicities Σµ, not Σµν. The coefficient point lies on or above the polygon; the polygon ordinate itself lies on the edge.
issues.reason: With ν1 < ⋯ < νm the smallest ord, the product of the µ1 roots of largest ord would have the largest ord among products of µ1 roots, so it does not dominate σ_{µ1}; the next line's conclusion ord σ_{µ1} = µ1ν1 uses the roots of ord ν1. For f = (x − 1)(x − p) over ℚ_p: σ_1 = 1 + p has ord 0 = ν1, the smaller ord.

issues.locator: arXiv v1 §1 p.1; compare published 2025 text §1 p.623 / PDF1
issues.printed: The source attributes to Markoff [8] the assertion that the integer-solution graph is a tree, and consequently connected.
issues.correction: Markoff's tree theorem is about the positive solutions M (equivalently, the nonzero integer solutions up to the sign changes of two coordinates). The graph on all nonzero integer solutions is a disjoint union of four trees, one for each sign pattern with product +1, and is not connected.
issues.reason: The moves R_i preserve the sign pattern of a nonzero integer solution: for (−a, −b, c), R₃ gives 3(−a)(−b) − c = 3ab − c and R₁ gives 3(−b)c + a = −(3bc − a). So (1, 1, 1) and (−1, −1, 1) lie in different components.
issues.known: Corrected in the published 2025 text, printed p.623: it explicitly says positive integer solutions.

These are supplied in the proof steps of three-squares-auxiliary-prime and three-squares-lattice-point.

issues.reviewReason: CKMR §2, printed p.402 (PDF p.3): an algebraic series is a power series ('suite algébrique') iff the leading nonzero coefficient satisfies a_v(0) ≠ 0. issues.locator: Remark 6, p. 13 of arXiv:2108.07577v2
issues.printed: The source treats weight 4 as a tr`es ramiﬁ´ee case whose residual representation is flat over an extension of even ramification index. It claims a contradiction because the lemma chooses the ramification type at 2 so that the resulting representation becomes flat over a cubic extension.
issues.correction: The operative fact is that a très ramifiée ρ̄ : G_{ℚ₂} → GL₂(𝔽̄₂) is finite flat over NO finite extension of ℚ₂ of odd ramification index (KW I, proof of Theorem 9.1, p. 19). Since the new 2-adic member becomes crystalline with Hodge–Tate weights {0, 1}, so its reduction finite flat, over K = ℚ₄(χ′) with e(K/ℚ₂) = 3, the new residual representation is not très ramifiée and has weight 2.
issues.reason: Up to twist a très ramifiée representation is given by a Kummer class x ∈ ℚ₂^×/ℚ₂^{×2} of odd valuation, and over K it is finite flat exactly when v_K(x) = e(K/ℚ₂)·v(x) is even. So it is flat over some extensions of even ramification index (for instance ℚ₂(√x)), and that is compatible with becoming flat over a further extension; being "flat over an extension with even ramification index" gives no contradiction with flatness over a cubic extension. The contradiction needs non-flatness over every extension of odd ramification index.

issues.locator: the definition of "minimal lift" (p. 6), Lemma 2.1 (p. 11) and Pasos 3–4 (pp. 12–13) of arXiv:2108.07577v2
issues.printed: The source calls a lift minimal when it stays unramified at every prime ℓ̸ = p at which ρ is unramified. It then claims that the new family omits pi from its ramification set, which remains within S1 ∪{2, 3}, allowing Lemma 2.1 to apply.
issues.correction: The lifts in Pasos 3–4 must be minimal in KW I's sense (for ℓ ≠ p, ρ(I_ℓ) → ρ̄(I_ℓ) bijective unless ρ̄(I_ℓ) is projectively cyclic of order p), which the cited source of Theorem 1.9(1)–(3), KW I Theorem 5.1(1)–(2), provides. Then ρ(I_N) ≅ ρ̄(I_N) = κ̄ ⊕ κ̄^N, the type at N is again that of Ind κ, and Lemma 2.1 applies to each new family.
issues.reason: Lemma 2.1 assumes that the inertial type at N is that of Ind κ, but Paso 3 checks only that the ramification set stays inside S₁ ∪ {2, 3}. Under DP's definition (unramified wherever ρ̄ is) a lift of ρ̄_{p_i} could have type Ind(κε) at N with ε of p_i-power order (possible, as N ≡ 1 mod p_i), which is not the type of Ind κ; for the dyadic lifts of Paso 4, ε could have even order, and the last step of Lemma 2.1's proof ("the inertia group at the prime N has even order contradicting … an odd order character") would no longer apply.

issues.locator: Paso 2, p. 11 of arXiv:2108.07577v2
issues.printed: The source cites Theorem 1.9 (4) to obtain a weight 2 crystalline lift ρ(2) q whose image at N is dihedral of order 2q.
issues.correction: "… a crystalline lift ρ^{(2)}_q of weight 2 whose inertial type at N is that of Ind κ": then ρ^{(2)}_q(I_N) is cyclic of order q and the projective image of D_N is dihedral of order 2q, which is all that Lemma 2.1 uses (its hypothesis is stated for the inertial type).
issues.reason: The determinant of a weight-2 lift is ψχ_q with ψ of finite order, so det ρ^{(2)}_q(Frob_N) = ψ(N)·N, which is not a root of unity; hence ρ^{(2)}_q(D_N) is infinite and cannot be dihedral of order 2q. Even Ind κ has image of order 2q only when κ is trivial on the Frobenius attached to N. The proof of Lemma 2.1 speaks in the same way of "a ramified character of order q", where only its restriction to inertia has order q.

issues.locator: §3.2 (Proof of Theorem 1.2) and the Remark after Theorem 3.4, p. 6 of the author's preprint results.pdf (Invent. Math. 178 (2009) not compared)
issues.printed: The source derives Theorem 1.2 from Theorem 3.4 and its subsequent remark. It also claims Theorem 3.4 makes (D0) imply Serre’s conjecture for S-type ρ̄ in odd characteristic when N(ρ̄) is odd, and in characteristic 2 when k(ρ̄) = 2.
issues.correction: Theorem 3.4 gives only that ρ̄ is modular. The passage to weight k(ρ̄) and level N(ρ̄): if the projective image is dihedral, Lemma 6.2(i); otherwise choose i with 2 ≤ k(ρ̄ ⊗ χ_p^i) ≤ p + 1 (p odd; i = 0 when p = 2); Theorem 5.1(1) gives a lift of ρ̄ ⊗ χ_p^i minimally ramified away from p and crystalline of weight k(ρ̄ ⊗ χ_p^i) (k(ρ̄) = 2 when p = 2), Theorem 4.1 makes it modular, and its newform has level N(ρ̄) (twisting by χ_p leaves the prime-to-p conductor unchanged). Untwist: ρ̄ is then modular of level N(ρ̄) prime to p, and Edixhoven's weight theorem (with θ-operators and the Deligne–Serre lifting lemma) gives a newform of weight k(ρ̄) and level N(ρ̄). This covers the dyadic scalar case that the introduction says Theorem 1.2(2) fills.
issues.reason: Theorem 3.4 concludes "is modular" and its proof (§8.4) lifts with Theorem 5.1(2), which gives weight 2 and a type at p, so the weight k(ρ̄) and level N(ρ̄) of Theorem 1.2 are asserted without an argument in the paper. The introduction (pp. 2–3) says Theorem 1.2(2) fills the missing case of the qualitative-implies-refined problem at 2 (ρ̄|_{D₂} scalar, projective image not dihedral), which is exactly the step not written out. Theorems 4.1(2)(i) and 5.1 assume 2 ≤ k(ρ̄) ≤ p + 1 when p > 2 (p. 9), and only some twist ρ̄ ⊗ χ_p^i has weight in that range (p. 2), so for odd p the argument ends with an untwisting (Edixhoven's weight theorem). Every ingredient is a theorem of the paper or of Edixhoven's weight theorem, so the result stands.

issues.locator: Remark 6.6 and Theorem 6.7(ii), p. 39 (arXiv v2); p. 154 (version of record)
issues.printed: The source credits Coleman with constructing p-adic functions Li_{k,p}(z) and states that they are locally analytic on C_p∖{1}.
issues.correction: Li_{k,p} must be Coleman's polylogarithm Li_k (Coleman function with Li_1(z) = −log_p(1 − z), z dLi_k/dz = Li_{k−1}, Li_k(z) = Σ z^n/n^k near 0), not the modified Li_k^{(p)}(z) = Li_k(z) − p^{−k}Li_k(z^p), and the branch must be fixed (the character sums do not depend on it).
issues.reason: Locally analytic solutions of the differential equations are determined only up to locally constant functions, and changing Li_{k,p} by a constant on one residue class changes the right side (ColemanIntegration:L3/coleman-functions-versus-locally-analytic). With the Euler factor printed, Li_{k,p} = Li_k^{(p)} would give the factor (1 − θ(p)p^{−k})^2 for p ∤ N, contradicting the case k = 1 (Theorem 6.1).

issues.locator: §6.2, (6.2), Lemmas 6.4 and 6.5 and the proof of Theorem 6.1(ii), pp. 36-38 (arXiv v2); pp. 149-153 (version of record)
issues.printed: The source factors a non-trivial Dirichlet character θ as χη, assigning conductor p^n to χ and conductor D, prime to p, to η. It defines L_p(θ,1) := ∫_{Z_p^×} χ(x)x^{−1}·μ_η = ∫_{Z_p^×} x^{−1}·μ_θ.

issues.locator: Published Lemma 4.1 proof, p.384
issues.printed: The source claims rigidity for A when a basis of A[3] is specified.
issues.correction: Use a polarization-preserving full-level moduli problem. An unpolarized abelian variety with full level 3 need not have trivial automorphisms. For forgetting polarization, supply a separate bounded field-of-definition argument; CM.2 does not infer the absolute unmarked degree equality.
issues.reason: Take a CM abelian surface whose CM field has an infinite unit group. Infinite-order integral units congruent to 1 modulo 3 act as origin-preserving automorphisms and act trivially on A[3]. Polarization-preserving automorphisms are finite and level at least 3 kills their torsion. This distinction is exactly why the polarized stabilizer cannot be exported as an unmarked absolute field-degree identity.

issues.reason: For an ordinary f the shape ρ̄_f|G_{Q_p} ≅ ψ̄ ⊕ ψ̄^{−1}ε̄^{1−k} determines k mod p − 1 up to replacing k by p + 1 − k (the companion), and gcd(p − 1, k − 1) = gcd(p − 1, p − k) is the same for both. This was confirmed by matching the characteristic polynomials of T_2 and T_3 on S_52 and on S_100 (twisted by ℓ^{99}) mod 151; no other pair (k, 152 − k) with 12 ≤ k < 76 matches, and the self-pair k = 76 = (p+1)/2 has (150, 75) ≠ 1. Since (150, 51) = (150, 99) = 3, hypothesis (2) of Theorem 2.1 fails at 151. (Theorem 3.1 does apply at 151, through the non-ordinary pair (60, 94).) The same search finds pairs with gcd 1 at 107, 139, 173, 179, 191 and 193.

issues.locator: Lemma 5.6.5 and its proof, pp.85–86, in arXiv:2301.10509v3 (27 March 2025); page image checked
issues.printed: The source claims reducibility of ρ̄|_{ker(det ρ̄)}. It invokes Dickson’s classification to obtain either reducible ρ̄ or G′ ≅ A₄. For the A₄ case it defines G₁ = ker(det ρ̄), asserts ρ̄(G₁)/ρ̄(Z) ≅ Z/2 × Z/2, and deduces reducibility of ρ̄|_{ker(det ρ̄)}.
issues.correction: The conclusion holds except when d = 3 and the projective image is A₄; then ρ̄|_{ker(det ρ̄)} has projective image Z/2 × Z/2 and is absolutely irreducible. The end of the proof of Theorem 5.2 (p.87), which uses the lemma to find g ∈ ρ̄(G_{F₁}) with det g ≠ 1 and eigenvalue ratio ≠ (det g)^{±1}, needs another argument in that case.
issues.reason: For p odd, a Klein four subgroup of PGL₂(F̄_p) does not fix a line (it would embed in the cyclic group F̄_p^× of a Borel modulo scalars), so its preimage acts irreducibly. Counterexample for every p ≥ 5: let G = 2T ≅ SL₂(F₃) ⊂ SL₂(F̄_p), χ : G → C₃ → F̄_p^× its cubic character (kernel Q₈), and ρ̄ = incl ⊗ χ. Then det ρ̄ = χ² has order 3. An element g ∉ Q₈ has order 3 or 6, with eigenvalues χ(g)ω, χ(g)ω² or −χ(g)ω, −χ(g)ω² (ω a primitive cube root of 1), so one eigenvalue is ±1, which is equivalent to (5.6.1). But ker det ρ̄ = Q₈ acts irreducibly (i and j anticommute). Checked by hand and by a brute-force computation over F₇. The hypotheses of Theorem 5.2 allow this residual image when p ≡ 1 mod 3 (for instance p = 7 and F ⊇ Q(√−7), so that [F(ζ₇):F] = 3); there no unramified place has H²(F_v, ad⁰ρ̄) = 0. The cases d ≠ 3 ([DDT97, Lemma 4.11]) and hence p = 3, 5, which is all §§6–7 use, are unaffected.

issues.locator: Theorem 6.3 proof, claimed cohomology/base-change identity for a framing ideal I, author-hosted journal PDF p.92
issues.printed: The construction obtains actions on cohomology after every allowed framing quotient I by commuting cohomology with tensor by O□/I.
issues.correction: Supply the compatible cohomology actions at these framing quotients directly as part of the decorated finite patch datum, or prove a sufficient flatness/derived action lifting statement. The present P8 construction takes the former input. The displayed tensor identity is not valid for all the allowed I.
issues.reason: Let A=O/π² and consider the perfect two-term A[[z]] complex with differential π. Take I=(z²,πz), lying between (z²) and (z). Before quotient its H⁰ is πA[[z]], isomorphic to k[[z]] as a module. Its tensor with A[[z]]/I retains a nonzero formal class π⊗z, but the natural cohomology base-change map kills that class. After quotient the differential also kills the nonzero class z, which is outside the image of the natural map. In fact z acts nontrivially on the tensor H⁰, and acts trivially on H⁰ of the quotient complex, so even the modules are not isomorphic. The issue is coefficient Tor from a nonflat framing quotient, not a convention on cochain indexing.

issues.locator: §3, Variante (3.4.9), p. 210 (published text, Numdam scan)
issues.printed: The source claims geometric semisimplicity for every pure sheaf.
issues.correction: … et que tout faisceau lisse ponctuellement pur sur X₀ normal est géométriquement semi-simple.
issues.reason: The source (3.4.1)(iii) (p. 208) explicitly assumes ℱ₀ lisse and X₀ normal, and normality cannot be dropped. Counterexample: let X₀ be a nodal cubic with split node over 𝐅_q. The normalisation P¹ is simply connected, so π₁(X) has a quotient Ẑ (the loop through the node) on which Frobenius acts trivially. Choose a rank-2 representation of W(X₀) = π₁(X) ⋊ 𝐙 in which π₁(X) acts through Ẑ → 𝐙_ℓ by non-trivial unipotent matrices and Frobenius acts trivially. It is lisse and pure of weight 0 (all Frobenius eigenvalues are 1), but not geometrically semisimple. Similarly, if 'faisceau' is read in the category of all constructible sheaves, 𝐐_ℓ on P¹ has the non-split subsheaf j_!𝐐_ℓ. So the second clause needs the lisse and normal hypotheses of (3.4.1)(iii). The later results (3.4.12)–(3.4.13) correctly carry 'normal'.

issues.locator: proof of Proposition 25.4, p. 161 (arXiv:1709.07343v4)
issues.printed: The source claims that the closed points form a very dense subset of the Zariski–Riemann spaces of fields, explaining this by expressing those spaces as cofiltered limits of projective varieties.
issues.correction: Argue valuation-theoretically: for k algebraically closed, every nonempty locally closed subset of ZR(k′/k) contains a closed point. Given V₀ ∈ U₀ ∩ Z with U₀ = {V ⊇ A}, A finitely generated over k, a minimal valuation ring W with A ⊆ W ⊆ V₀ (Zorn) has residue field algebraic over k, hence is closed, and lies in U₀ ∩ Z. Then vanishing of stalks at closed points forces vanishing, since supports of sections are locally closed.
issues.reason: A cofiltered limit of Jacobson spectral spaces along uncountable index systems need not inherit the property that every nonempty locally closed (not only constructible) subset has a closed point: an inverse limit of nonempty sets of closed points can be empty. The stated reason does not give the conclusion used (vanishing of a complex of arbitrary, non-constructible sheaves).

issues.correction: Require the terminal object to be quasicompact, or require a quasicompact object Y with an epimorphism Y→*. An arbitrary quasicompact Y need not cover the terminal object. Retain the algebraic-topos quasiseparatedness implication.
issues.reason: In the algebraic topos of sheaves on the infinite discrete space ℕ, the terminal object is not quasicompact: its cover by singleton-open subobjects has no finite subcover. Its identity is a quasicompact morphism, since every base change is an identity on a quasicompact object. SGA VI 1.8(i) confirms that isomorphisms are coherent. The source proof incorrectly calls X×Y→X a cover for any quasicompact Y; a singleton-open Y is a counterexample.

issues.locator: Chapter 3, proof of Lemma 3.2, printed p. 13 (PDF p. 14), the estimate of |σ_k(Σ_j a_ij x_j)| for a complex embedding σ_k, r₁ < k ≤ r₁ + r₂
issues.printed: The bound for the imaginary part uses the interval half-length A_{k+r₁,i}.
issues.correction: It should be A_{k+r₂,i}. The imaginary part of σ_k is, up to sign, the coordinate τ_{k+r₂} = Im σ_{k+r₂}, since σ_{k+r₂} is the conjugate of σ_k and the τ with indices r₁ + r₂ < k ≤ r₁ + 2r₂ are the imaginary parts. The next line of the display bounds the term by N·Y·max_j|σ_k(a_ij)|, which holds for A_{k+r₂,i}, so the argument is unaffected.
issues.reason: The indices r₁ < k ≤ r₁ + r₂ shifted by r₁ give 2r₁ < k + r₁ ≤ 2r₁ + r₂, which are the indices of imaginary parts only when r₁ = r₂. For K = ℚ(∛2) (r₁ = 1, r₂ = 1) they agree; for K = ℚ(i) (r₁ = 0, r₂ = 1), k = 1 and A_{1,i} is the real-part half-length, not the imaginary one.

issues.correction: Choose one convention consistently. With Lemma 2.2’s degree-normalised local absolute values, Definition 2.4 is already the absolute logarithmic height, so Definition 2.7 should simply use H = exp h without a second degree root. Alternatively use relative local absolute values, replace the sum in Lemma 2.2 by [L:K] log |x|_v and Lemma 2.5 by h_L = [L:K] h_K; then Definition 2.7 is correct. issues.reason: Let K = ℚ and L = ℚ(√2), and take P = [2:1]. Under Lemma 2.2, the sum of the archimedean logs over L is log 2 and the finite contributions to the height vanish, so Definition 2.4 gives H_L(P) = H_K(P) = 2 as Lemma 2.5 says. Definition 2.7 then gives 2 over K and √2 over L, contradicting its claimed independence. Under Mathlib’s relative convention H_L(P) = 4 and H_K(P) = 2, and the degree root restores equality.

issues.locator: Exact author preprint infart2.pdf, printed/PDF p18, §4.2 projective representative conditions(1)–(2) before equation(41). Author-linked preprint dated February5,1995, 25 PDF/printed pages, SHA256 36b3079bb5277f819fbc0083d5020d774c8cb1cf6559fc82eebd5028510c31b3. Only this exact copy was visually verified; no assertion about the unread published version of record.
issues.printed: The source takes S_p inside Z^(r+s) with zero excluded, yet labels vector entries up to b_p throughout. Under Condition(2), all vectors in V_p, zero included, are quantified over, and β may be any scalar in F_p.
issues.correction: Write each vector as (b₁,…,b_(r+s)). For the computable surviving subspace V′_p, choose exactly one bounded integral lift of each one-dimensional subspace of V′_p; equivalently, every nonzero a∈V′_p has a unique representative b∈S_p with a=β(b mod p) for some β∈F_p^×. Then the required coverage also holds for V_p minus zero, since V_p⊆V′_p. Zero requires no projective representative; if V′_p={0}, take S_p empty. This states a sufficient corrected representative construction, not a claim that the full numerical point-recognition procedure is certified.
issues.reason: At a=0, every b∈S_p satisfies the printed congruence with β=0, so uniqueness fails whenever S_p has at least two elements; with S_p empty existence fails. Even when S_p has one element the zero clause does not express a projective class. For example a two-dimensional F₂ surviving space has three projective classes, all representing zero when multiplied by0. The missing nonzero scope is essential to the literal condition. The b_p notation is independently dimensionally inconsistent with Z^(r+s) and the r+s-term sum(41).

issues.locator: Lemma 5.1, Corollaries 5.2 and 5.4, published §5 pp.995–997; preprint v3 pp.10–11
issues.printed: Claims that taking diagonalizable-group fixed schemes commutes with the normal cone and consequently that the fixed cone has no points outside a group-fixed vertex.
issues.correction: The general comparison is false. Require and prove suitable smooth hypotheses, or replace the cone step by an independent argument. For the full fixed subscheme of a tame finite-order automorphism, the review supplies a restricted true statement and an independent proof; this does not restore the claimed comparison for arbitrary invariant Z.
issues.reason: Take char k≠2, X=𝔸², g(u,v)=(−u,−v), Z=V(uv). This is a reduced invariant Cartier divisor and D=µ₂ is reduced. N_ZX=Spec k[u,v,t]/(uv), with g(t)=t, so (N_ZX)^D=Spec k[t]. But X^D=Z^D=Spec k and N_(Z^D)(X^D)=Spec k. The proof substitutes vector-space coinvariants for the algebra quotient by the ideal of differences defining fixed schemes.

issues.locator: Hypothesis 4.7(ii), p. 22 of arXiv:1805.08448v1
issues.printed: After adjoining the representation’s trivializing field K(T) to the auxiliary infinite tower, condition(ii) asks for a Galois element whose coinvariants on T are free of rank one over R.
issues.correction: Take τ in G_{K_{p^∞}}, with K_{p^∞}=⋃_m K_{p^m} and K_{p^m}=K(μ_{p^m},(O_K^×)^{1/p^m})K(1), and require T/(τ−1)T≃R. The field fixed by τ must omit the additional trivializing extension K(T).
issues.reason: K(T) is by definition the minimal Galois extension of K such that G_{K(T)} acts trivially on T, so every τ ∈ G_{K(T)_{p^∞}} ⊆ G_{K(T)} acts trivially on T and T/(τ − 1)T = T, which is isomorphic to R only when T has rank one. The finite-level Hypothesis 3.2(ii) takes τ ∈ G_{K_M}, and Remark 4.9 asserts that Hypothesis 4.7 gives Hypotheses 3.2(i) and (ii) for T/p^mT, which is true for τ ∈ G_{K_{p^∞}} ⊆ G_{K_{p^m}} and false in rank at least two for the printed group.

issues.locator: 1999 course draft Chapter IX §1, p.133; also book-format author copy §9.1 p.175 (PDF p.181)
issues.printed: The source takes the largest abelian extension of K with ramification confined to N.
issues.correction: For the isolated-initial-class example take the maximal abelian extension unramified at every prime dividing N.
issues.reason: The printed extension contains the cyclotomic Z_p-extension because p divides N, contrary to the following parenthesis. For a nontrivial extension ramified only at N, the Euler-factor product is empty, hence is 1, and the family c_F=0 for F≠K requires c_K=0. With no ramification at N and class number one, every nontrivial finite abelian extension ramifies at a prime outside N, where the stipulated factor vanishes; the claimed arbitrary c_K family then works.

issues.locator: Archived author copy, Proposition 3.4.4(ii), p.27 (PDF p.33)
issues.printed: The source asserts that Γ(S) admits an isomorphism, without a canonical choice, to an ideal of R.
issues.correction: Evaluation identifies Γ(S) with a submodule of the cyclic hub stalk. It is isomorphic to an ideal if the hub stalk is free of rank one, or if R is principal artinian. The unrestricted complete noetherian local assertion needs such additional hypotheses.
issues.reason: Let R=Z_p and take the graph with one vertex and no edges, with S(v)=R/pR. The sheaf is locally cyclic, its vertex is a hub and monodromy is trivial. Γ(S)=R/pR is nonzero torsion, whereas every ideal of the domain R is torsion-free. The proof’s injection into a cyclic module does not imply injection into R.

issues.locator: Author-hosted 356-page manuscript, SHA-256 9ab9efbd0df251bfa3b610d1d1d88a8dfb1bdf7c397bd04f4c277280d98ae905, printed p. 292, proof of VIII.4.1, reindexing square after VIII.4.2. Published passage unavailable.
issues.printed: The source calls the map obtained by pulling back along g cartesian.
issues.correction: The diagram commutes. Do not assert a cartesian square for arbitrary finite-set reindexing.
issues.reason: Take H=Q=1, W=C2, C=Vect_L and the trivial W-equivariant tensor family. End(id_C)=L and every left function ring is L. For I={1,2}, J={1}, g:I->J the fold map, the left vertical arrow is id_L; the right is diagonal restriction Map(W^2,L)->Map(W,L). Both horizontal maps send scalars to constant functions. The pullback consists of (a,f) with f(w,w)=a; off-diagonal values are arbitrary. In particular (0,f) with f(1,t)=1 and f zero elsewhere lies in the pullback but not in the image of L. Thus the square is commutative and not cartesian. Over F2 it has 8 pullback elements versus 2 source elements. The subsequent fusion proof only uses commutativity.

issues.locator: Proposition 3.3 proof, journal p. 240; arXiv v2 p. 11; author proof p. 112
issues.printed: The proof infers finiteness of the split-torus rational-point cokernel from its valuation lattice.
issues.correction: Use compactness of that cokernel. A surjective map of split tori has full-rank, finite-index image on the valuation lattice; compact unit representatives then give a compact set surjecting onto the cokernel. Compactness suffices for the subsequent Levi and Iwasawa steps.
issues.reason: Over F_q((t)), the pth-power map G_m to G_m is surjective and central as a scheme morphism, but E-times/(E-times)^p is infinite: units 1+t^n for distinct positive n prime to p have distinct classes. Its valuation quotient is finite and its unit quotient compact. Thus the asserted finiteness is false in the explicit field range of section 3, while Proposition 3.3 remains correct.

issues.locator: Proposition 3.3 proof, journal p. 239; arXiv v2 p. 11; author proof p. 111
issues.printed: The proof identifies the full inverse image of a maximal split torus with a maximal split torus and allows an unspecified parabolic containing it.
issues.correction: Choose a maximal split torus in the inverse image, mapping surjectively onto the target split torus, and choose a minimal parabolic containing the target torus. Its centralizer is the required Levi; the source centralizer and inverse-image parabolic give the central Levi map and unipotent isomorphism used in the proof.
issues.reason: Projection G_m times A to G_m, for a nontrivial anisotropic E-torus A, is surjective central. The full inverse image of G_m is G_m times A and is not split. The split-subtorus choice repairs this. Also an arbitrary larger parabolic need not have the displayed centralizer as its Levi; minimality supplies this identification and compactness modulo the maximal split torus.

issues.locator: Adjacent formula (4-1), finite branch and definition of e, journal p. 240; arXiv v2 formula (4.1), p. 11; author proof p. 112
issues.printed: The finite square-class dimension branch uses two plus the ramification index defined by the ideal generated by two.
issues.correction: For characteristic zero and residue characteristic two, use two plus [F:Q_2], equivalently two plus ramification index times residue degree. For odd residue characteristic the dimension is two; characteristic two has the infinite branch as corrected in E10.
issues.reason: Take the unramified quadratic extension of Q_2, with residue field F_4 and ramification index e=1. Let U_j=1+2^j O_F. Squaring maps U_2 onto U_3. Modulo U_3 the squares from U_1 correspond to the image of a to a+a^2 in F_4, which has size two. Hence U_1/U_1^2 has size eight, and the odd-order residue units do not change the square quotient. The valuation factor doubles it to sixteen, of dimension four, whereas the displayed 2+e gives three. This unused adjacent result does not alter any planned target.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem IX.7.2, p. 335, author-hosted manuscript (SHA-256 9ab9efbd…); reduction to quasi-split G
issues.printed: The quasi-split reduction uses a Kaletha z-embedding with torus quotient and connected centre.
issues.correction: The step is justified for E of characteristic 0 (Kaletha’s §5 assumes F p-adic). It cannot be applied uniformly in characteristic p: for G = SL_p, no embedding G ↪ G′ with torus quotient D and Z(G′) a torus has Z(G′)(E) → D(E) surjective. Thus the deduction of B(G) ↪ B(G′) and of centre detection via Kaletha Fact 5.5 requires another argument for this case and for the general non-smooth-centre range.
issues.reason: From 1 → Z(G) → Z(G′) → D → 1 (fppf), coker(Z(G′)(E) → D(E)) ≅ ker(H¹_fppf(E, Z(G)) → H¹(E, Z(G′))). For Z(G) = μ_p in characteristic p, H¹_fppf(E, μ_p) = E^×/E^{×p} is infinite, while H¹(E, T) is finite for a torus T over a local field; so the kernel is infinite. Fact 5.5’s proof uses exactly this injectivity. In characteristic p connectedness of Z(G′) does not force a torus (μ_p is connected; SL_p ↪ SL_p × G_m has connected centre μ_p × G_m and surjective Z(G′)(E) → D(E)), but the next step, a basic b₀ with G_{b₀} quasi-split via Kottwitz 10.4, needs a central torus, and for SL_p × G_m the inner form SL₁(D) is not reached.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 10.15, p. 1354, published article
issues.printed: The lifting argument asserts ker(u) ∩ im(p_{π′}) = {0} for the arbitrary surjection u : E′ → E between smooth representations and the natural isotypic projector p_{π′}.
issues.correction: Replace that assertion by a splitting of the surjection on the semisimple V-isotypic summands. Naturality of the projectors makes the restricted map surjective, and complete reducibility permits a G-equivariant lift. This repairs the proof route without changing the projectivity statement.
issues.reason: Take the trivial group and its one-dimensional representation V over a characteristic-zero field, E′ = V ⊕ V, E = V and u(x,y)=x. issues.printed: Invoking [13], Theorem 2, the source concludes that χ·χ_0^{−Σ m_i d_i} has finite order as a character on both D and π̃.
issues.correction: Tate's Theorem 2 gives only that χ·χ_0^{−Σ m_i d_i} has finite image on the inertia group of D. Since χ = ⟨χ_0⟩^a·(finite order) by class field theory and χ_0 has open image on inertia, this forces a = Σ m_i d_i, and only then is χ·χ_0^{−Σ m_i d_i} of finite order on π̃ and on D.
issues.reason: A character ψ of D with C(ψ) ≅ C need not have finite order: every unramified ψ (for instance Frobenius ↦ 1 + l) has C(ψ) ≅ C, because x ↦ φ(x)/x is surjective on the units of the completed maximal unramified extension. The conclusion is right, but only through the global form of χ, which Faltings states just before.

issues.locator: section 4.2.3, p. 12 (arXiv v3)
issues.printed: For f ∈ Fq(X) − Fq, the source asserts geometric irreducibility of the pull-back sheaf Lψ(f), with conductor equal to 1 plus the number of poles of f plus their total multiplicity.
issues.correction: On the maximal lisse open, write ψ=ψ_can(b·), b≠0. Then C(L_ψ(f))=1+#{x:v*_x(bf)>0}+Σ_x v*_x(bf). On a deliberately smaller open the conductor as defined in this source includes all its omitted geometric points. The raw pole-order expression is only an upper bound. Over a prime field the scaling b does not change modified orders. Artin–Schreier trivial phases give a geometrically constant rank-one sheaf, conductor 1 on P¹; rank-one sheaves, including the constant one, remain geometrically irreducible.
issues.reason: The raw Swan/pole multiplicity formula fails already for f=X^p, whose sheaf has Swan order 1 and maximal-open conductor 3, not p+2. For the canonical character f=X^p−X is geometrically trivial. Triviality does not contradict the source’s rank-one geometric irreducibility claim: the error is the conductor formula. The open-locus and character-normalization qualifications prevent repeating the packet’s overgeneralization.

issues.locator: Chapter 1, proof of Theorem 1.6, printed p. 11 (arXiv v1)

issues.locator: §3.2, Theorem 3, p. 32 of the authors' copy (J. Algebra 219 (1999), 16–79)
issues.printed: For every G-group H, the Zariski topology on H^n (closed sets: intersections of finite unions of algebraic sets over G) is said to be T1, i.e. all singletons are closed.
issues.correction: Singletons {v} are closed when each coordinate of v lies in (the image of) G, since then {v} = V({x_i v_i⁻¹}); in particular the topology is T1 when H = G (or ι_H is onto). For a G-group H with H ≠ G it need not be T1.
issues.reason: Take G = 1 and H = F(a, b), n = 1. Coefficient-free equations in one variable are x^k = 1, whose solution sets in the torsion-free group H are {1} (k ≠ 0) and H (k = 0); so the closed sets are ∅, {1}, H and finite unions, and the closure of {a} is H. With G = ⟨a⟩ < H = F(a, b) the automorphism of H fixing a and sending b to b a preserves every algebraic set over G, so b and b a have the same closure.

issues.locator: §2.7, Definition 6 and the remark following it, p. 9 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: After defining regular standard quadratic equations (including the equation [x₁,y₁][x₂,y₂] = 1 explicitly), the paper says that equivalently S = 1 is regular iff κ(S) ≥ 4 and S has a non-commutative solution, or S is [x, y]d = 1; it then remarks that a consistent equation with κ(S) ≥ 4 and positive genus (orientable case) has a non-commutative solution and is therefore regular.
issues.correction: The equivalent formulation must also list [x₁,y₁][x₂,y₂] = 1, and the remark must exclude it: that equation has κ = 4 but no non-commutative solution.
issues.reason: For S = [x₁,y₁][x₂,y₂] (atoms r₁ = [x₁,y₁], r₂ = [x₂,y₂], no coefficient d) every solution φ satisfies r₂^φ = (r₁^φ)⁻¹, so [r₁^φ, r₂^φ] = 1: every solution is commutative in the sense of Definition 5. The paper itself acknowledges this on p. 99, where it notes that this equation has no solution in general position and treats it as [x₁,y₁] = [y₂,x₂] over G ∗ F(x₂,y₂).

issues.locator: arXiv:1011.3392v1, §2.2, p.9, character specification immediately after the pairing; printed image checked
issues.printed: The finite-field additive character into complex units is described as injective and determined by a qth root of unity for general q.
issues.correction: Choose a nontrivial character of Fp and compose it with Tr_{Fq/Fp}. It is generally noninjective; the induced residue pairing is nevertheless nondegenerate.
issues.reason: The additive group of F_{p^f} has exponent p. Any homomorphism to C× has image in μ_p and cannot be injective if f>1. Finite-field trace pairing, rather than injectivity of the scalar character, proves nondegeneracy.

issues.locator: arXiv:1011.3392v1, §2.1, p.7, test-function spanning assertion and footnote 4; printed image checked

issues.locator: §14, proof of Theorem 14.2, printed p. 247 of the IAS retypeset edition (PDF p. 253), just before Corollary 14.3; the Springer LNM 114 original was not collated
issues.printed: The proof asserts that the places where M′ splits are even in number, and deduces ∏_v h_v=1.
issues.correction: Since the algebra M′ does not split (is ramified) at an even number of places, the product ∏_v h_v equals 1.
issues.reason: h_v = −1 exactly at the places where G′_{F_v} is not isomorphic to GL(2,F_v) (printed p. 241), so ∏ h_v = (−1)^{#nonsplit places}. issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 2, printed pp. 126–127 (PDF pp. 4–5): definition of the class c and the sentence 'Moreover, as l splits in K, one has that ρ(Frobl) is the identity matrix'

issues.correction: Impose λ ≡ 1 modulo 4D·f·σ(f) (a σ-stable modulus, e.g. 4D·Norm(f)·O_K). Then χ(Λ)=χ(σΛ)=1, ρ(Frob_l)=1 and the trace is zero; ℓ is also prime to N, as Corollary 8 needs in Theorem 9.
issues.reason: ρ(Frob_l)=diag(χ(Λ),χ(σΛ)). The congruence λ≡1 mod f gives χ(Λ)=1, but χ(σΛ)=1 needs σλ≡1 mod f, i.e. λ≡1 mod σ(f). If χ is ramified at a prime Q with σ(Q) not dividing f, the class c does not constrain λ modulo σ(Q), and Chebotarev produces Λ in c with χ(σΛ)≠1. Then the trace 1+χ(σΛ) is nonzero in characteristic two. Lemma 2 remains true with the corrected modulus.

issues.locator: Lemma 1.13, torus-normaliser case in its proof, published p. 8; also arXiv 2108.07577v2, p.8
issues.printed: The source denies that the latter subgroups are normal in G.
issues.correction: Diagonalise H itself. A nonscalar abelian H has two character lines; normality of H makes G permute them. The permutation character factors through the cyclic cyclotomic quotient and kills its square subgroup. The original torus need not contain H.
issues.reason: In characteristic greater than 2 let A=diag(1,−1), W=(0 1;1 0), G=⟨A,W⟩ and H=⟨−I,W⟩. Then |G|=8, |H|=4 and H is normal: AWA⁻¹=−W∈H. The quotient G/H is cyclic of order 2, but W is not diagonal. Thus the claimed group-theoretic assertion is false, even under reducible H and cyclic G/H. This refutes the proof step, not the Galois lemma.

issues.locator: p. 425, proof of Lemma 1.18 (positive dimension of fibres); also p. 425, proof of Lemma 1.18 (last paragraph)
issues.printed: The proof says that some index i satisfies dim_k(Λ_λ ∩ p^iΛ_0/Λ_λ ∩ p^{i+1}Λ_0) > 1 in its argument about fibres.
issues.correction: Replace ∩ by +: for λ < Nω_1, dim_k((Λ_λ + p^iΛ_0)/(Λ_λ + p^{i+1}Λ_0)) > 1 for some i (e.g. i = 0). Every hyperplane 𝓔_1 ⊂ Λ_0 containing Λ_λ + pΛ_0 extends to a point of π^{−1}(p^λ), so the fibre surjects onto ℙ^{d−1,p^{−∞}} with d = #{j : l_j ≥ 1} ≥ 2. Also: Replace ∩ by + in both places: dim_k (Λ_λ + p^iΛ_0)/(Λ_λ + p^{i+1}Λ_0) > 1 (this holds at i = 0 when λ < Nω_1), and lines L in this space give the lattices Λ_λ + p^{i+1}Λ_0 + L̃, which extend to full chains. Equivalently, dim (p^{-1}Λ_λ ∩ Λ_0)/Λ_λ = #{j : m_j ≥ 1} ≥ 2, the fibre of π_2 from the preceding paragraph.
issues.reason: For λ = (l_1 ≥ … ≥ l_n ≥ 0) with Σ l_j = N, Λ_λ ⊂ Λ_0 and Λ_λ ∩ p^iΛ_0 = ⟨p^{max(l_j,i)}e_j⟩, so the printed dimension is #{j : l_j ≤ i}. For n ≥ 2 this exceeds 1 for every λ once i ≥ l_1, including λ = Nω_1, whose fibre is a single point by the first part of the lemma. Moreover these subquotients lie inside Λ_λ, while points of π^{−1}(p^λ) are chains of lattices between Λ_λ and Λ_0, so lines in them do not give points of the fibre. With + the dimension is #{j : l_j ≥ i+1}, which for i = 0 is at least 2 exactly when l_2 ≥ 1, i.e. λ ≠ Nω_1. The intended argument is then correct. The same text is in v2 (with 𝓔_λ) and v3. It is classified as a misprint (∩ for +); a verifier could argue for 'error', since the step fails as printed.

issues.correction: Use Im(H^*_{S̄^-_λ}(A) → H^*(A)), as in [MV07, Th. 3.6]. Fix k = (2ρ,λ). Parity and degree give H^k_{S̄^-_λ}(A) = H^k_{S^-_λ}(A) and H^k(S̄_λ,A) = H^k_c(S_λ,A). The composite H^k_{S̄^-_λ}(A) → H^k(A) → H^k(S̄_{λ′},A) is the isomorphism of (2.2.10) (hyperbolic localization at ϖ^λ) for λ′ = λ. It is zero for λ′ ≠ λ of the same degree, since a nonempty closed G_m-stable S̄^-_λ ∩ S̄_{λ′} contains some ϖ^η with λ ≤ η ≤ λ′. Hence H^k(A) = ⊕_{(2ρ,λ)=k} Im(H^k_{S̄^-_λ}(A) → H^k(A)), which gives H^* ≅ ⊕_λ H^*_c(S_λ,−).
issues.reason: By Proposition 2.5, S̄^−_λ − S^−_λ = ∪_{λ′>λ} S^−_{λ′}. By (2.2.10) and Proposition 2.7, H^k_{S^−_{λ′}}(A) = 0 unless k = (2ρ,λ′) > (2ρ,λ). So the printed Fil′_{<λ} vanishes in degree (2ρ,λ) and cannot split off the λ-piece. Morally it is ⊕_{λ′>λ}, which lies inside Fil_{≥λ} instead of complementing it. Counterexample to the claimed complementarity: GL_2, A = IC_{(1,0)} = Q̄_ℓ[1] on P^1, λ = (0,1). Here Fil_{≥λ} = H^*(A), because S_{<λ} ∩ P^1 = ∅. But Fil′_{<λ} is the image of H^*_{pt}(A) with pt = ϖ^{(1,0)}, which is H^1 ≠ 0. The corollary is right by the MV argument the proof cites. Same text in arXiv v3.

issues.locator: p. 437, item (2) before Lemma 2.12
issues.printed: The source claims that no parahoric subgroup properly contains Q_{1/2}.
issues.correction: Delete item (2), or state: Q_{1/2} is the parahoric of −θ/2, whose reductive quotient contains the SL_2 of the affine roots ±(θ^∨+1). It is maximal unless the simple factor containing θ is of type A_n with n ≥ 2.
issues.reason: Q_{1/2} is the parahoric of −θ/2 (the v2 discussion identifies −μ/2 as a vertex). The affine roots vanishing there are ±(θ^∨ + 1) and the roots orthogonal to θ. These have full rank only if the roots orthogonal to the highest root have rank r − 1, which fails in type A_n, n ≥ 2, where they have rank n − 2. For SL_3, θ = (1,0,−1) pairs to 1 or 2 with every positive root. So −θ/2 lies on the single wall θ^∨ + 1 = 0, inside an edge, and Q_{1/2} is properly contained in the parahorics of the edge's two vertices. Type A is covered by the paper: θ ∈ M (p. 439) and Lemma 2.11 includes it. The claim is not used in any proof.

issues.locator: p. 439, proof of Lemma 2.11 (μ = θ): display for π^{-1}(S_0 ∩ Gr_{≤μ}) and (2.2.13)
issues.correction: With Y = ∪_{wμ<0} ŪwP̄_μ/P̄_μ, π^{-1}(S_0 ∩ Gr_{≤μ}) = [φ^{-1}(Y) \ π^{-1}(∪_{wμ<0} S_{wμ} ∩ Gr_{≤μ})] ⊔ [π^{-1}(Gr_0) ∩ φ^{-1}(Ḡ/P̄_μ − Y)], where π^{-1}(Gr_0) ≅ Ḡ/P̄_μ is the section at infinity. So (2.2.13) should read RΓ_c(π^{-1}(S_0 ∩ Gr_{≤μ}), Q̄_ℓ[d]) = RΓ_c(Y, Q̄_ℓ[d−2]) ⊕ RΓ_c(Ḡ/P̄_μ − Y, Q̄_ℓ[d]); the sequence splits since all terms are in even degrees. Comparison with (2.2.12) then gives H^i(𝒞) = H^i_c(π^{-1}(S_0 ∩ Gr_{≤μ}), Q̄_ℓ[d]) for i ≠ 0 and H^0_c(S_0, IC_μ) ≅ Q̄_ℓ^{|Δ_θ|}.
issues.reason: Cells of Ḡ/P̄_θ: for β = wθ > 0 the dimension is ht θ + ht β − 1; for β < 0 it is ht θ − ht(−β); and d = 2 ht θ. With the printed (2.2.13), H^i_c vanishes for i > 0, yet H^i(C) = H^{i+d}(Ḡ/P̄_μ) ≠ 0 whenever some positive β ∈ Wθ has height 1 + i/2. In degree 0 both sides have dimension |Δ_θ|, which would give H^0_c(S_0, IC_μ) = 0. Check for SL_3: Ḡ/P̄_θ is the flag variety and C = Q̄_ℓ[2] ⊕ Q̄_ℓ^2 ⊕ Q̄_ℓ[−2]. The printed (2.2.13) gives Q̄_ℓ[2] ⊕ Q̄_ℓ^2, so H^0_c(S_0, IC_θ) = 0 and the degree-2 term would be negative. The corrected formula gives H^0_c = Q̄_ℓ^2 = V_θ(0). The final conclusion (and the [NP01, §8] computation it defers to) is right. The same display is in arXiv v2 and v3.

issues.locator: p. 35, proof of Theorem 8.3, second paragraph
issues.printed: The proof appeals to induction to show that L|⋃_{μ<λ}Gr_{≤μ} is ample, although it has not yet shown that the union is representable.
issues.correction: Before invoking Keel, show that Y = ∪_{μ<λ}Gr_{≤μ} is the perfection of a proper algebraic space. Here Y is the image sheaf of ⊔_{μ<λ}Gr_{≤μ}, equivalently the closed complement of Gr_λ. The map ⊔Gr_{≤μ} → Y is a v-cover. Its equivalence relation is given by the closed intersections Gr_{≤μ} ×_{Gr_{≤λ}} Gr_{≤μ'}. So Y is the iterated pushout of the Gr_{≤μ} along these intersections. Affine-locally this pushout is A1 ×_{A12} A2, which is perfect and satisfies A1 ⊗_A A2 = A12. On finite-type models the pushout is a proper algebraic space by [Ar70, 6.1]. Next, every subvariety of Y lies in some Gr_{≤μ}, where L is ample, so E(L|_Y) = ∅. Keel's Lemma 1.8, applied inductively over the pieces, then makes L|_Y semiample. Its morphism contracts no curve, hence is finite, so L|_Y is ample. Alternatively, cite Zhu's Theorem 8.2, which makes Y a closed subspace of a proper perfect algebraic space; but then the proof is no longer independent of Zhu as claimed (p. 32).
issues.reason: Keel's Lemma 1.8 is a gluing statement for semiampleness on a proper algebraic space X = X_1 ∪ X_2 with E(L) ⊂ X_1. To obtain ampleness it has to be combined with E(L) = ∅ and Nakai. Applying it requires Y = ∪_{μ<λ} Gr_{≤μ} to be (the perfection of) a proper algebraic space. The induction hypothesis makes each Gr_{≤μ} a projective perfect scheme, but not their union inside the v-sheaf Gr_{≤λ}, whose representability is what is being proved. The union is not a single Gr_{≤μ} in general: for n = 3, λ = (4,2,0), both (3,3,0) and (4,1,1) are maximal below λ and are incomparable. Applying Keel's lemma on the scheme ψ^{-1}(Y) instead does not work, since the exceptional locus there does not lie in one piece. Defence: the missing step is standard and fillable (pinching of perfect schemes along closed subschemes, or gluing sections as above). Theorem 8.3 itself is not in doubt.

issues.locator: p. 37, the sentence introducing Kottwitz' map and Proposition 9.7 ([Zhu14, Proposition 1.21])

issues.correction: Add the hypothesis 'k algebraically closed' (as in [Zhu14, §1.5.2]); then Gal_K is the inertia group. For a general perfect k: Kottwitz's map is κ: LG(k̄) = G(W_{O_K}(k̄)[1/p]) → π1(G)_{I_K}, where I_K ⊂ Gal_K is the inertia subgroup. It induces Gal(k̄/k)-equivariant bijections π0(LG_{k̄}) ≅ π0(Gr_{𝒢,k̄}) ≅ π1(G)_{I_K}. The connected components over k are the Gal(k̄/k)-orbits on π1(G)_{I_K}.
issues.reason: For finite k and an unramified quadratic extension K′/K, take T=Res_{K′/K}G_m with its connected integral model. The geometric components of its affine Grassmannian form ℤ² with Frobenius exchanging the coordinates, whereas full Galois coinvariants give ℤ. Thus BS arXiv v3 p.37 must use inertia coinvariants for geometric components and retain residual Frobenius. Zhu’s published Proposition 1.21 on p.427 has an algebraically closed residue-field standing setting; the broader finite-k assertion does not follow from that setting. The SL_n application has trivial π₁ and is unaffected.

issues.locator: p. 37, Proposition 10.1 (second assertion) and its proof

On a bounded piece X ⊂ Gr_{SL_n} (proper by Corollary 9.6), for a ≪ 0 the map M ↦ p^{-a}M ⊂ W(R)^{ne} sends X into some Gr_{≤λ} for GL_{ne}. The cokernel is Q = W(R)^{ne}/p^{-a}M ≅ p^aW_{O_K}(R)^n/M, killed by a bounded power of p, of constant length −ane. This map is proper and injective on points, hence finite (pass to finite-type models). By definition of det̃ on K(W_{O_K}(R) on R), L|_X is the pullback of the Theorem 8.3 bundle det̃(Q). So L|_X is ample by Theorem 8.3.

issues.printed: After identifying the geometric Grassmannian with factors indexed by the distinct untilts, the description weights each factor’s local cocharacter by that untilt’s multiplicity among the ordered legs.
issues.correction: Sum the combined local cocharacters once over the distinct geometric supports. In a coincident block the local cocharacter already sums the ordered-leg labels. Retain the multiplicity in the product Cartier equation ξ, without applying it again to the local valuation or cocenter degree.
issues.reason: Take G=G_m and two coincident degree-one legs with primitive equation t. Completion for ξ=t² is the same as t-adic completion, and its geometric positive ring is one DVR B⁺. The ordered labels (1,0) give the lattice L=tB⁺, whose local cocharacter and ordinary length length(B⁺/L) are one. The printed extra weight gives two. Alternatively L=ξB⁺=t²B⁺ has ordinary position two and the printed weighting gives four. The sum over ordered labels at the start of p.202 and the product-DVR length identification in VI.3.2 both select the unweighted combined local cocharacter. This does not remove the collision addition of Schubert bounds.

issues.locator: Chapter VI, §VI.10, proof of Proposition VI.10.2, p. 234 (author-hosted 356-page copy, same passage as arXiv v4)
issues.printed: Under rigidity of 𝒞, the source claims that 𝒜 has an inverse. It gives F(X_i)^∨ ≅ F(X_i^∨) ≅ ℋom(X_i, X_i^∨) ≅ ℋom(X_i ⊗ X_i, 1); swapping the factors is said to supply the required involution of 𝒜.
issues.correction: The antipode belongs to the reconstructed algebra ℋ, not to the base category 𝒜: under rigidity of 𝒞 the displayed chain of identifications for F(X_i)^∨, followed by exchanging the two factors, gives an involution of each F(X_i)^∨, and these assemble to the antipode of ℋ.
issues.reason: 𝒜 is the base symmetric monoidal category and is not inverted anywhere. The object under construction is ℋ = colim F(X_i)^∨: the two preceding sentences of the proof give it a commutative multiplication and then call it a Hopf algebra. The inverse that is needed is the antipode of ℋ, induced on each F(X_i)^∨ by the displayed isomorphisms.

issues.locator: Chapter VI, §VI.11, Lemma VI.11.2 and its proof, p. 237 (author-hosted 356-page copy, same text as arXiv v4)
issues.printed: The lemma says that a closed subgroup H of SL₂ over F_ℓ which contains the diagonal torus, and whose irreducible representations are told apart by their highest weights (all in Z≥0), is all of SL₂. The proof reduces to reduced H and then deduces that H is connected from Deligne–Milne, Corollary 2.22, and highest weights.
issues.correction: Retain the subgroup criterion for odd ℓ. At ℓ = 2 the stated hypotheses do not imply H=SL₂: N(T) is a counterexample. The Satake application requires an additional geometric constraint. The proposed replacement compares tensor-power invariants with a coefficient-independent top-cycle count; its precise LP3 representation-theoretic inputs and GS2:correspondences geometric calculation are requested in rank-one-integral-identification and remain an explicit gap. The false subgroup lemma alone does not establish or disprove the integral Satake theorem.
issues.reason: In characteristic two, N(T)=T⋊C₂ is proper in SL₂ and contains T. Its simples are the trivial module and, for n≥1, the two-dimensional induced modules with weights ±n: T is diagonalizable and each nonzero weight orbit is {n,−n}, while a simple supported at weight zero factors through C₂ and is trivial. Thus highest weights 0,1,2,… occur once each, satisfying the lemma. Deligne–Milne Corollary 2.22 on connectedness assumes characteristic zero and cannot justify the printed step. For odd ℓ the sign character of N(T) duplicates highest weight zero; after passing to a reduced Frobenius image the torus and Borels also violate the nonnegative-highest-weight requirement. This verifies the source error, while the proposed geometric repair still has its recorded supplier obligation.

issues.locator: §0.2 pp407–408, setting of Theorem 0.3 (publisher PDF)
issues.printed: The introduction states the Satake equivalence of Theorem 0.3 for a reductive group over O without requiring the residue field k to be algebraically closed.
issues.correction: Assume that k is algebraically closed and G connected reductive, as Section 2 does on p429; equivalently, base change the affine Grassmannian to an algebraic closure of k.
issues.reason: Over a finite k the equivariant perverse sheaves supported at the base point are the continuous Galois representations; this category is not semisimple (Frobenius can act by a unipotent block), and H* forgets the Galois action, so it is not full and cannot be an equivalence onto Rep(Ĝ). The body proves the theorem only over an algebraically closed field. The nodes of this packet carry the hypothesis.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 3.2, p.13, in arXiv:2111.12660v2; citation of [5, Corollary 2.5]
issues.printed: The proof concludes from the flatness theorem for simplices (Banaszczyk–Litvak–Pajor–Szarek, Corollary 2.5) that every translate of the body K = {Σβ_iQ°_i : Σ|β_i| ≤ C_0 n log 2n} contains an integer polynomial. K is a cross-polytope, not a simplex, and the step from the cited statement about simplices to a covering statement for K is not given.
issues.correction: Insert the step: S = conv(Q°_1,…,Q°_n, −(1/n)ΣQ°_i) lies in the unit cross-polytope. For a nonzero integer functional d some |d(Q°_k)| ≥ 1, say d(Q°_k) ≥ 1 (the other sign is symmetric); either some vertex Q°_i has d(Q°_i) ≤ 0, or every d(Q°_i) is positive and the last vertex has the negative value −(1/n)Σ_i d(Q°_i). Either way d varies by at least 1 on S, so the lattice width of S is at least 1. Flt(S) ≤ Cn(1+log n) then gives that every translate of tS with t > Cn(1+log n) meets the integer polynomials, hence so does every translate of tK. Alternatively, BLPS's own Proposition 2.3 with the second part of their Theorem 2.4 (a polytope with 2n vertices) bounds Flt(K) by Cn(1+log n) directly; or, as planned here (GN.4/l1-covering-transference), Banaszczyk's ℓ¹ and sup-norm Gaussian tail inequalities give the covering bound for K directly, with constant 3n√(log(8n)/π).
issues.reason: BLPS Corollary 2.5 bounds Flt(S) for n-simplices S only. A covering bound for the cross-polytope K follows from it through a simplex of lattice width at least 1 inside K, or from the polytope case of BLPS Theorem 2.4; the proof states neither step.

issues.reason: For any odd ℓ, let M=ℤ_ℓ² with pairing diag(1,−1), v=(1,1+ℓ), w=(0,1), and let φ act as +1 on v and −1 on w. issues.locator: Proposition 2.5 and the paragraph after it, physical p.14 (arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The proposition asserts the lattice-point estimate for images R′ = uR of a bounded semialgebraic multiset under triangular unipotent u, with the error measured by projection volumes of R rather than of R′, and says Davenport's proof adapts without significant change.
issues.correction: Davenport's slicing argument applied to R′ produces projection volumes of R′, which can be much larger than those of R (a shear stretches the first-coordinate projection). The estimate as stated holds, but needs a reorganised induction: fibre along the coordinate sheared by the others, so each fibre of uR is a translate of a fibre of R, and count the main term through the superlevel sets of the fibre-length function; the error terms then integrate to projection volumes of R (unipotent-davenport-transfer). issues.locator: Lecture 1, (1.2), p. 1
issues.printed: The source defines condition Φp for G by requiring the maximal pro-p quotient of each finite index subgroup G′ ⊂ G to have finitely many topological generators. It claims equivalence with finite dimensionality of Hom(G, Fp).
issues.correction: “This is equivalent to asking that Hom(G′, 𝔽_p) is finite dimensional for every open G′ ⊂ G” (as the same notes' Exercise 1 states).
issues.reason: Finiteness of Hom(G, 𝔽_p) for G alone is strictly weaker: for p odd, G = (∏_ℕ ℤ/p) ⋊ ℤ/2 with ℤ/2 acting by inversion has abelianisation ℤ/2 (the commutators a^{-2} fill ∏ ℤ/p since 2 is invertible), so Hom(G, 𝔽_p) = 0, while its open subgroup ∏_ℕ ℤ/p of index 2 has infinite Hom to 𝔽_p and is not topologically finitely generated. Exercise 1 on p. 4 of the same notes states the correct equivalence with all open subgroups.
searched: Kisin's Harvard notes page (people.math.harvard.edu/~kisin/notes/), fetched 2026-09-28: a single 4-page PDF, no revision or errata listed.
issues.citation: Mark Kisin, Lectures on deformations of Galois representations (Lecture 1), Lecture notes on the author's Harvard page, 4 pages (Lecture 1: deformations of representations of profinite groups).
issues.reviewReason: Confirmed at Kisin, Lecture 1, (1.2), p. 1: the printed sentence says Hom(G, Fp) for G itself, while Φ_p quantifies over all finite-index subgroups; the counterexample (∏_ℕ ℤ/p) ⋊ ℤ/2 (p odd) is correct, since the commutators a^{−2} generate ∏ℤ/p, so Hom(G, 𝔽_p) = 0 while the index-2 subgroup has infinite Hom to 𝔽_p. Exercise 1 on p. 4 states the correct equivalence.

issues.printed: The source says the converse follows readily from SpC(A) → SpB(A) being surjective when A = F[ϵ], citing [45].
issues.correction: “… using the injectivity of Sp_C(A) → Sp_B(A) for A = 𝔽[ε]”: injectivity on tangent spaces makes the cotangent map surjective, and complete Nakayama then makes B → C surjective.
issues.reason: The converse assumes that Sp_C(A) → Sp_B(A) is injective for all A; surjectivity of this map is neither given nor true for a proper closed immersion (for B = 𝒪⟦x⟧ → C = 𝒪, the tangent map t_C = 0 → t_B = 𝔽 is not surjective). The argument that works uses injectivity at A = 𝔽[ε].

issues.locator: §3.23, p. 17 (the claim on H⁰_{S,T}) and the displayed formula for dim H¹_{S,T} at the top of p. 18
issues.printed: The source takes ρ to be absolutely irreducible and concludes H0(GF,S, ad ρ) = F and hence H0S,T(GF,S, ad0 ρ) = F. It then gives dimF H1S,T(GF,S, ad0 ρ) = #T − Σv|∞ dimF H0(GFv, ad0 ρ) + Σv∈S∖T (dimF L(Dv) − dimF H0(GFv, ad0 ρ)) + dimF H1S,T(GF,S, ad0 ρ(1)) − dimF H0(GF,S, ad0 ρ(1)).
issues.correction: For T ≠ ∅ (the notes assume T contains the places above p), H⁰_{S,T}(G_{F,S}, ad⁰ρ̄) = 0, and the formula reads dim H¹_{S,T} = #T − 1 − Σ_{v|∞} h⁰(G_{F_v}, ad⁰ρ̄) + Σ_{v∈S∖T}(dim L(D_v) − h⁰(G_{F_v}, ad⁰ρ̄)) + h¹_{S,T}(ad⁰ρ̄(1)) − h⁰(G_{F,S}, ad⁰ρ̄(1)).
issues.reason: In Gee's complex C⁰_{S,T} = C⁰(G, ad ρ̄) and the differential sends φ to (∂φ, (φ|_{G_v})_{v∈T}); a scalar φ ∈ H⁰(G, ad ρ̄) = 𝔽 with φ|_{G_v} = 0 in C⁰(G_v, ad ρ̄) = ad ρ̄ is 0, so H⁰_{S,T} = 0 when T ≠ ∅ (as CHT08 Lemma 2.3.4 and ACC+ Proposition 6.2.24 state). With h¹ = χ + h⁰ + h² − h³ and Gee's χ_{S,T} = −1 + #T − …, the constant is #T − 1. The notes' own later counts use the corrected value: Proposition 3.24(3) (dimension at least 1 + Σ_v(dim R_v − n²) − …) and Proposition 5.10 (#T − 1 − [F : ℚ] + r generators) follow from #T − 1 and would be off by one with #T.
searched: arXiv:2202.05818 versions v1 (2022-02-11) and v2 (2022-10-17, the accepted version): v2 read here.

The published version, Essential Number Theory 1 (2022) 73–126 (msp.org/ent/2022/1-1/ent-v1-n1-p06-s.pdf, sha256 3ffa71fd…): the same sentence and the same displayed formula in §3.23, with Proposition 5.10 still counting #T − 1 − [F : ℚ] + r generators.

issues.locator: Chapter II, §1, (1.3)–(1.5), p. 236, Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (GDZ scan)
issues.printed: The source chooses β∈ℤ/2Nℤ subject to β²≡D mod4N, setting 𝔫=(N,(β+√D)/2)=ℤN+ℤ(β+√D)/2. It represents ℂ/𝔞→ℂ/𝔞𝔫⁻¹, whose target lattice is integral, by τ∈𝔥 satisfying Aτ²+Bτ+C=0. It requires A>0 and B²−4AC=D, together with A≡0 modN and B≡β mod2N. Its lattice formulas are 𝔞=ℤA+ℤ(B+√D)/2 and 𝔞𝔫⁻¹=ℤAN⁻¹+ℤ(B+√D)/2, with N_{K/ℚ}(𝔞)=A.
issues.correction: With √D = i√|D| (the branch determined by §3 (3.7) and the change-of-lattice calculation on p.245) the root τ ∈ 𝔥 represents (ℂ/𝔞̄ → ℂ/𝔞̄𝔫̄⁻¹) = c(x), i.e. the pair (𝒜⁻¹, 𝔫̄); x itself is −τ̄ = (B+√D)/(2A). Consistent fixes: read (β+√D)/2, (B+√D)/2 as (−β+√D)/2, (−B+√D)/2 in (1.3), (1.5) (then (3.7) reads τ_i ∈ 𝔞̄_i⁻¹), or keep (1.3)–(1.5) and read τ_{𝒜,𝔫} in §3 as the Heegner point (𝒜⁻¹, 𝔫̄), on which σ_𝒜 acts by 𝒜₁ ↦ 𝒜₁𝒜.
issues.reason: Independent mathematical check: The upper-half-plane root (-B+√D)/(2A) lies in the conjugate lattice. With the displayed plus-sign ideal the represented point is conjugated, so the ideal class and orientation must both be transported.
