issues.locator: The K-book, author-hosted draft of 29 August 2013, paragraph 5.8.2 in the proof of Theorem VI.5.7, PDF p. 499
issues.printed: The source invokes the Künneth formula [223, 6.1.13] to give Hn(T2) ≅ ⊕i+j=n Hi(F×) ⊗ Hj(F×), and says σ swaps the factors.
issues.correction: Integrally H_n(T₂) ≅ ⊕_{i+j=n} H_i(Fˣ) ⊗ H_j(Fˣ) ⊕ ⊕_{i+j=n−1} Tor₁^ℤ(H_i(Fˣ), H_j(Fˣ)). The Tor summand vanishes for n ≤ 2, the degree the proof computes (H₂(T₂)_σ ≅ ∧²Fˣ ⊕ ∧̃²Fˣ); for n = 3 it contains Tor₁^ℤ(Fˣ, Fˣ) ≅ Tor₁^ℤ(μ(F), μ(F)), which is nonzero whenever F has a nontrivial root of unity.
issues.reason: For F = F_5, Fˣ ≅ ℤ/4 has H₀, …, H₃ = ℤ, ℤ/4, 0, ℤ/4. The displayed formula gives H₃(T₂) ≅ (ℤ/4)², while the Künneth theorem for the free bar complexes gives (ℤ/4)² ⊕ Tor₁(ℤ/4, ℤ/4) ≅ (ℤ/4)³. The proof uses only H₂(T₂), and of H₃(T₂) only that the relevant term is 'a quotient Q3 of H3(T2)σ', which the missing summand does not change.

issues.locator: IV.1, paragraph before Theorem IV.1.12, PDF p. 277 (draft p. 269)
issues.printed: The source claims that Brauer lifting takes the trivial and standard representations of GLn(Fq), each of dimension n, to complex representations of dimension n. It gives the associated homomorphisms as 1n, idn : GLn(Fq) →U.
issues.correction: The Brauer lift of the standard representation is an element of R_C(GL_n(F_q)) of virtual dimension n, in general not a representation; ρ_n is obtained from the virtual representation β(id_n) − n through the Atiyah map R_C(G) → [BG, Z × BU], not as B of a homomorphism into U.
issues.reason: For GL_2(F_3) and the natural representation, the Brauer character χ (ι an embedding of F_9^× into C^×) has ⟨χ, χ⟩ = (1/48)Σ|χ(g)|^2 = 2 and no linear constituent (computed by enumerating the 48 elements). A genuine character of degree 2 with ⟨χ, χ⟩ = 2 would be a sum of two distinct linear characters; so χ is a virtual character (a difference of irreducible characters of degrees 4 and 2). The source's own Example IV.5.8 correctly places the Brauer lift in R_C(G).

issues.locator: Example IV.5.8, PDF p. 323 (draft p. 315)
issues.printed: The source begins with a finite field Fq and a homomorphism F×q →C×, claiming these induce RFq(G) →RC(G), which it calls Brauer lifting.
issues.correction: Fix an injective homomorphism \bar F_q^× → C^× (equivalently, compatible embeddings of all F_{q^n}^×); it induces the Brauer lifting R_{F_q}(G) → R_C(G).
issues.reason: The Brauer character evaluates the chosen map on the eigenvalues of group elements, which lie in extensions of F_q: the element (0 −1; 1 0) of GL_2(F_3) has eigenvalues ±i ∈ F_9 \ F_3, on which a homomorphism defined on F_3^× gives no value. Injectivity is needed for the character to be a Brauer character (a non-injective map on μ_{q−1} gives a different class function).

issues.locator: §5.4 'The Brauer lift of k(µl)', p. 12
issues.printed: The source treats k(µl) as having dimension r −1 as a vector space over k.
issues.correction: Dimension r; r is the least integer with l | q^r − 1 (the text says 'l divides rq'); the map k(µ_l) ⊗_k \bar k → \bar k^r is z ⊗ w ↦ (zw, z^q w, …, z^{q^{r−1}} w), and the eigenvalues of z are z, z^q, …, z^{q^{r−1}} (without the 1 listed in the text).

issues.locator: Exercise III.6.11 (PDF p. 252; book p. 244), author-hosted draft of 29 August 2013
issues.printed: The source assigns Ω1F vector space dimension κ when F has transcendence degree κ over its ground field. It further claims that for local F, Moore's Theorem (6.2.4) has an uncountable uniquely divisible summand U in K2(F).
issues.correction: The dimension statement holds in characteristic 0 only; in characteristic p the dimension of Ω¹_F is the p-degree of F. So the argument gives the uncountability of U only for local fields of characteristic 0; for local fields of characteristic p it follows instead from Corollary III.6.3.2 (|K₂(F)| = |F|) and the finiteness of μ(F).
issues.reason: F = 𝔽_q((t)) has uncountable transcendence degree over 𝔽_p but p-basis {t}, so Ω¹_F = F·dt is one-dimensional and Ω²_F = 0: the image of K₂(F) → Ω²_F is zero, not of rank κ. (For a perfect field of characteristic p, Ω¹ = 0.) Also, in characteristic p the image in Ω² is an 𝔽_p-vector space, so it has rank 0 as an abelian group.

issues.locator: §5.6, first two paragraphs (p. 162; PDF p. 24), author copy
issues.printed: The source claims V× = µ(E) × U1, defining µ(E) as the roots of unity in E or V and describing U1 as free over Zp. In equal characteristic, char(E) = p, it gives V = Fq[[π]] alongside E = Fq((π)), citing [55]. It deduces µ(E) = F×q and identifies U1 = W(Fq), claiming its rank over Zp = W(Fp) equals [Fq : Fp].
issues.correction: In characteristic p, U₁ = 1 + πF_q[[π]] is the group of big Witt vectors of F_q, a countably infinite product of copies of ℤ_p, which is torsion-free but not a free ℤ_p-module and not of finite rank; 'free' and 'rank [F_q : F_p]' hold only in characteristic 0 (where U₁ has rank [E : ℚ_p] modulo torsion).
issues.reason: K-book VI.7 (PDF p. 515): 'U1 = 1 + πFq[[π]] is isomorphic to the big Witt vectors of Fq (II.4.3), which is the product of a countably infinite number of copies of Zp', and Exercises VI.7.1–VI.7.2 show that this product is not a free ℤ_p-module; the p-typical W(F_q) of rank f = [F_q : F_p] is the wrong Witt vector group.

issues.locator: Lemma 2.2.3, p. 34 (Annals 158 (2003); arXiv:math/9910186v2, same text in the TeX e-print)
issues.printed: The source names d log πK as a generator of the A-module ω1 (A,M)/W (k). It gives the annihilator as the ideal generated by φ′K(πK)πK and claims p belongs to that ideal.
issues.correction: The annihilator (φ'_K(π_K)π_K) is contained in pA: φ'_K(π_K)π_K = p(π_Kθ'_K(π_K) − e_Kθ_K(π_K)). It equals pA exactly when p ∤ e_K; when p | e_K it is strictly smaller and does not contain p.
issues.reason: From φ_K(x) = x^e + pθ_K(x) and π^e = −pθ_K(π): πφ'_K(π) = eπ^e + pπθ'_K(π) = p(πθ'_K(π) − eθ_K(π)), and the second factor is a unit iff p ∤ e. Example: A = Z_p[π] with π^p = p (φ = x^p − p, θ = −1, e = p): πφ'(π) = pπ^p = p², so the annihilator is (p²), which does not contain p. The proof of Corollary 2.2.5 uses the correct inclusion (it needs p | π_Kφ'_K(π_K) to identify the p-torsion of A/(π_Kφ'_K(π_K)) with A/p·dlog(−p)), so nothing downstream is affected.

issues.printed: The source asserts, for every i under ℓν > wi, an isomorphism H1(E,µ⊗i pν ) with (Z/pν)d ⊕Z/wi ⊕Z/wi−1, setting d = [E : Qp].
issues.correction: For i ≥ 2 and every ν ≥ 1: H^1(E, μ_{p^ν}^{⊗i}) ≅ (ℤ/p^ν)^d ⊕ ℤ/gcd(p^ν, w_i) ⊕ ℤ/gcd(p^ν, w_{i−1}), with w_j = w_j^{(p)}(E); so the printed form holds once p^ν ≥ max(w_i, w_{i−1}). 'ℓν' is a misprint for p^ν, and i = 1 (where w_0 is undefined) and i ≤ 0 are excluded.
issues.reason: E = ℚ_3, i = 7, ν = 1: w_7^{(3)}(ℚ_3) = 1 < 3 and w_6^{(3)}(ℚ_3) = 9, so the printed form gives ℤ/3 ⊕ ℤ/9, of order 27 and not killed by 3. issues.reason: An intersection of ideals contains 0 and is never empty. The Chinese Remainder Theorem needs pairwise comaximality and trivial intersection: V(Ii + Ij) = Vi ∩ Vj = ∅ gives Ii + Ij = R, and ∩ Ii is the nilradical, which is 0 for reduced R. The printed condition I1 + · · · + Ic = R is weaker than pairwise comaximality once c ≥ 3.

issues.correction: GL_n(D)/E_n(D) ≅ D×/[D×, D×] for all n > 1, without exception; hence K₁(D) = GL_n(D)/E_n(D) for all n ≥ 2. The exception n = 2, D = 𝔽_2 concerns the different statement E_n(D) = [GL_n(D), GL_n(D)].
issues.reason: Dieudonné n°6, Théorème 1 (printed p.34), gives the elementary quotient in every rank n>1. His n°5 (printed pp.31–32) places the exception instead in the commutator-subgroup identity. Direct enumeration at n=2 over 𝔽₂ gives GL₂=SL₂=E₂ of order 6 and trivial elementary quotient, while the commutator has order 3. Thus the K-book’s quotient statement survives the exceptional case; its exception and the consequent n≥3 bound concern a different assertion.

issues.locator: Theorem III.2.5 (Bass–Milnor–Serre), part (2), PDF p. 202 (book p. 194), author-hosted draft of 29 August 2013
issues.printed: Part (2) treats F with no embedding into R, termed “totally imaginary”. It asserts SK1(R, I) ≅ Cn, cyclic and finite, with n dividing w1, the order of the roots-of-unity group in R. It gives ordp n as the minimum, taken over prime ideals p containing I in R, of inf{ordp w1, sup{0, [ordp(I)/ordp(p) − 1/(p−1)]}}.
issues.correction: The minimum runs over the primes 𝔭 of R lying over p (BMS (3.3): j_p(q) = min_{𝔭|p}), not over the primes containing I; and case (2) needs R to be the full ring of integers O_F. For R = O_{F,S} with S ≠ ∅ (BMS: A is then not 'totally imaginary', as S_∞ contains a finite prime) SK₁(R, I) = 0 for every I, as in (1).
issues.reason: F = ℚ(i), R = ℤ[i], I = 3R (3 is inert): the primes of R containing I are {(3)}, and ord_{(3)}(2) = 0, so the printed formula divides by zero, or read as +∞ gives ord₂ n = ord₂ w₁ = 2, SK₁(ℤ[i], 3ℤ[i]) ≅ ℤ/4. BMS (3.3) takes the prime (1 + i) over 2, where ord(I) = 0, so j₂ = [0/2 − 1]_{[0,2]} = 0 and r = 1: SK₁(ℤ[i], 3ℤ[i]) = 0. For R = ℤ[i][1/2] BMS Corollary 4.3(b) gives SK₁(R, I) = 0 while the printed (2) gives a nontrivial group for I = 9R.

issues.locator: Proof of Appendix (A.10), printed p.84 (Numdam PDF p.27; Serre author scan PDF p.26)
issues.printed: The proof chooses ā with value a at primes dividing b and 1 elsewhere, obtains tx̄v=ād, and takes c=ad. Its ensuing placewise identifications treat ā as though it were the diagonal idèle of a.
issues.correction: Choose ā with value a⁻¹ at primes dividing b and 1 elsewhere, retain tx̄v=ād, and take c=d. At primes dividing b this gives c=a v_𝔭; elsewhere it gives c=t_𝔭x̄_𝔭v_𝔭. These are precisely the congruence, valuation and local-coset conditions.
issues.reason: With the printed choice, away from primes dividing b the equation says d=t_𝔭x̄_𝔭v_𝔭, so c=a t_𝔭x̄_𝔭v_𝔭, with an unwanted factor a. For F=ℚ, a=2, b=5 and S₀ empty, every selected prime 𝔭₀ other than (2),(5) has ord₂(d)=0 but ord₂(c)=1; the claimed ideal cA=𝔭₀ is impossible. issues.locator: II.8, proof of Proposition 8.2.1 (Nonsingular Curves), PDF p. 154, book p. 146, in the author-hosted draft of 29 August 2013
issues.printed: In the remaining case, the proof takes an arbitrary closed point P of X. Citing Hart [85, Ex. IV.1.3], it asserts affineness of U = X−P and writes U = Spec(R).
issues.correction: The Proposition is stated for every 1-dimensional separated regular noetherian scheme, but the affineness of X − P is justified only by an exercise in Hartshorne's chapter on curves, which works with curves of finite type over an algebraically closed field; likewise the exactness of the bottom row 0 → ℤ → Pic(X) → Pic(R) → 0 is referred to Ex. I.5.12, stated for smooth curves over a field. The conclusion stands with a different argument: by the Cartan isomorphism (Theorem 8.2) and the localisation sequence to the generic point, every rank-zero class is Σ n_y([O] − [O(−y)]) for a divisor Σ n_y y; its determinant is O(Σ n_y y); and a principal divisor has class zero in G₀ (Stacks 0FDS argument). This is the route the author mentions ('Given Theorem 8.2, this does follow from Ex. 6.10') and the one KTheoryLowDegrees:Z.5/curve-rank-determinant-equivalence follows.
issues.reason: The cited results concern curves over a field, while the hypotheses allow any one-dimensional separated regular noetherian scheme (for example regular schemes that are neither affine nor of finite type over a field); no argument is given that X − P is affine, or that n ↦ L(nP) is injective, in that generality. The alternative proof uses only the localisation sequence, the skyscraper formula and the vanishing of principal divisors, all valid for every integral regular noetherian scheme of dimension one (separated or not).

issues.locator: arXiv v3 p. 19, proof of Corollary 5.6
issues.printed: The proof places every obstruction in coherent cohomology of strictly positive degree.

This is a gap in the proof as written, not an exhibited nonzero lifting obstruction or a false Corollary 5.6.

issues.locator: Construction 12.5, pp. 56–57
issues.printed: The construction requires isomorphisms satisfying compatibility.
issues.correction: Add the nullary case: require an isomorphism X_∅ ≅ 1 such that X_{∅⊔T} ≅ X_∅⊗X_T ≅ 1⊗X_T is the unit constraint. Equivalently, index the family by nonempty T and set X_∅ = 1, as in the naive model of Remark 12.6, where an empty tensor product is 1. A property-only fix also works: require X_∅ to be isomorphic to 1. The groupoid of pairs (X_∅ ≅ 1, φ) satisfying the associativity condition is then contractible, and associativity for (∅,∅,T) forces unit compatibility. With either fix, N(C)([0]) ≃ * and N(C)([1]) ≃ N(C).
issues.reason: Freshly read the cited v3 passage; use the extraction correction for E54. Take S∖{s} = ∅. The data are then an object X_∅ with an isomorphism X_∅ ≅ X_∅ ⊗ X_∅ (from T = T′ = ∅), and nothing forces X_∅ ≅ 1. Counterexample: let C be the discrete symmetric monoidal groupoid of the commutative monoid {1, e}, e² = e, with all constraints identities. Both (1, id) and (e, id) satisfy every associativity and commutativity compatibility. So N(C)([0]) has two points, and the Segal condition for n = 0 (X([0]) contractible, which the paper uses on p. 56) fails. Likewise N(C)([1]) = {(1,1), (1,e), (e,e)}, which is not ≃ C. An associativity or commutativity condition on the given isomorphisms cannot repair this: stating unit compatibility needs a map X_∅ → 1, which is extra data. Segal's original version avoids the problem, because there families are functors on subsets that take disjoint unions to sums, and that forces X_∅ to be initial ([Seg74, §2, p. 299]). The case for the defence: the authors explicitly leave the compatibility to the first reading, and they present §12 as conveying meaning, not proofs. In both cases the paper uses, the literal definition already gives the right answer. For Vect(R) under ⊕, X ≅ X ⊕ X forces X = 0, uniquely. For a Picard groupoid, X_∅ is invertible, hence ≅ 1, and the groupoid of pairs (X_∅, φ) is contractible (φ corresponds to u ∈ Aut(1), and v acts by u ↦ vu). So it is an incomplete definition with a standard fix, and no result is affected.

issues.locator: I.5.1.3(2), physical PDF p.55, book p.47, author draft 29 August 2013
issues.printed: The source imposes quasicoherence on F.
issues.correction: Add finite presentation to condition (2). Conditions (3) and (4), which the packet actually uses, remain valid.
issues.reason: Take A=∏_{n∈ℕ} F₂ and I=⊕_{n∈ℕ} F₂, the finite-support ideal. I is not finitely generated: finitely many generators have a common finite support. At a prime corresponding to a principal ultrafilter I_p=A_p=F₂; at any other prime all finite-support idempotents vanish after localization, so I_p=0. Thus the quasi-coherent sheaf I~ has finite free stalks everywhere. If it were finite locally free on Spec A, affine quasi-compactness would make I finite projective, a contradiction. Finitely presented sheaves with free stalks are finite locally free. The reviewed nodes use only (3)/(4), never the invalid (2).

issues.locator: 1999 AWS public author draft, III.5.1 p.48
issues.printed: The singular integral exp* image is asserted to be the local index times p^(−1)Z_p, with no odd-prime qualification.
issues.correction: Add p>2 for the displayed formal-logarithm lattice; at p=2 retain the actual λ_E(E₁(Q₂)) lattice.
issues.reason: The proof uses λ_E(E₁(Q_p))=pZ_p, an odd-prime formal-group logarithm assertion which is not valid for arbitrary elliptic curves at p=2. For E:y²+xy=x³+1, Δ=−433 is a 2-adic unit and a₁=1. In the integral formal parameter, log_E(t)=t+(a₁/2)t²+∑_(n≥3)b_n t^n/n with integral b_n. For t=2u its first two terms vanish modulo 4 and every n≥3 term lies in 4Z₂, since n−v₂(n)≥2. Thus log_E(E₁(Q₂))⊂4Z₂, and log_E(E₂(Q₂))=4Z₂ shows equality, contradicting 2Z₂. The corrected local node and exact p-part bound use odd p.

Since (Q₂/Z₂)² has no GL₂(Z₂)-invariants, the multiplication-by-2 exact sequence injects this H¹ into H¹(GL₂(Z₂),(Q₂/Z₂)²)[2]. Thus the displayed zero is false at 2.

issues.locator: Published Invent. Math. 234 (2023), §3.1.2 pp.205–206, equation (7) and preceding symmetric-power pairing; repeated in §3.1.5 pp.215–216 and Remark 3.3 p.218
issues.printed: The ordinary symmetric power of A² is claimed to be its literal dual tensored with det^(k−2), without inverting a factorial in A.
issues.correction: Require (k−2)! invertible for this symmetric-power self-duality, in particular use rational coefficients. Integrally retain the literal dual, which corresponds to a divided-power lattice; do not replace it by the symmetric-power Tate lattice.
issues.reason: Take p=2,k=4,A=Z₂ and the ordinary quotient Sym² with basis x²,xy,y². Equivariance under diag(3,1) forces B to have antidiagonal entries a,b,c. The unipotent matrix U=[[1,1,1],[0,1,2],[0,0,1]] forces UᵗBU=B, hence a=c=−2b. Its determinant is −4b³, never a unit of Z₂. Thus no such perfect equivariant pairing exists. This invalidates the arbitrary integral identification used in the proof, but not the rational dictionary or a theorem restated using literal duals.

issues.locator: Published Astérisque 295 (2004), 12.8.2 p.223 and its use after 13.4 p.226; compare Ribet §3 pp.190–192
issues.printed: The Ribet attribution is used to assert an open SL₂(Z_p) subgroup in the cyclotomic image at every coefficient place, hence a nontrivial unipotent for the rational Euler-system hypothesis.
issues.correction: Use the cited quaternion-valued theorem with its local splitting condition. It supplies the unipotent argument at split places and the integral package at almost all places. At nonsplit places obtain a separate rational argument; do not infer a unipotent from quaternion openness or Zariski closure.
issues.reason: Ribet p.191 states openness in the reduced-norm group of a quaternion algebra over the inner-twist fixed field. At a division place a nontrivial unipotent would yield a nonzero nilpotent, impossible in a division algebra; taking a power into the finite-index inner-twist kernel does not remove that obstruction. The citation alone therefore leaves the every-place deduction unjustified. No specific modular counterexample or falsity of the all-prime Iwasawa conclusion is claimed.

issues.locator: §2.4.2, condition 2 on the characters χ_{v,i}, p. 37, against the proofs of Lemmas 2.4.7 and 2.4.8, pp. 39–40 (read on the page images)
issues.printed: Condition 2 takes χ̄_{v,i} to be χ_{v,i} reduced modulo λ. Whenever i < j, it excludes both the trivial character and the cyclotomic character as values of χ̄_{v,i}/χ̄_{v,j}.
issues.correction: For i < j the ratio χ̄_{v,j}/χ̄_{v,i} is neither trivial nor the cyclotomic character (equivalently χ̄_{v,i}/χ̄_{v,j} ≠ 1, ε̄^{−1}).
issues.reason: The proof of Lemma 2.4.7 needs H⁰(G, Hom_k(Fil^{i+1}r̄, gr^i r̄)(1)) = 0 and justifies it by χ̄_{v,i}ε/χ̄_{v,j} ≠ 1 for j > i (p. 39); the proof of Lemma 2.4.8 needs H²(G, χ̄_{v,0}^{−1}r̄′) = 0. Both are χ̄_{v,j}/χ̄_{v,i} ≠ ε̄ for i < j, which the printed condition does not give. Counterexample to the printed version: n = 2, F_ṽ = ℚ_l, l > 3, r̄ = ω ⊕ 1 with the ω-line as Fil¹ (χ_{v,1} = ε, χ_{v,0} = 1). Then χ̄_{v,0}/χ̄_{v,1} = ω^{−1} is neither trivial nor cyclotomic, but H²(G_{ℚ_l}, k(ω)) ≅ H⁰(G_{ℚ_l}, k)^∨ ≠ 0; the suitable lifts to B₂(k[ε]/(ε²)) form a space of dimension 1 + 1 + 3 = 5 rather than n(n + 1)/2 + [F_ṽ : ℚ_l]n(n − 1)/2 = 4 (the fibre of Z¹ has dimension (n − 1) + [F_ṽ : ℚ_l](n − 1) + dim H² = 3), so dim_k L_v − dim_k H⁰(ad r̄) = 2 and R^{loc}/𝓘 is not a power series ring in 5 variables. This is the familiar non-smoothness of ordinary weight-two deformations when the sub-character is the cyclotomic character times the quotient; the section is not used by CHT's applications.

issues.locator: arXiv:2202.05818v2, §3.30 and paragraph after Theorem 3.31, pp.19–20
issues.printed: After Theorem 3.31 the notes say that for an inertial Weil–Deligne type τ, which by §3.30 includes the monodromy operator N, there is a reduced p-torsion-free quotient R^□_{ρ̄,χ,τ} of R^□_{ρ̄,χ} through which a ℚ̄_p-point factors if and only if the corresponding lift has type τ.
issues.correction: For the full type retaining N, use the reduced flat closure of exact-type points; the reverse implication is valid only on the appropriate nondegenerate locus, not at all boundary points.
issues.reason: Take p odd and q≡1 mod p, determinant q, ρ_c(φ)=diag(q,1), ρ_c(σ)=(1 c;0 1) for a generator σ of tame inertia, with c=pT over 𝒪⟦T⟧. Arithmetic Frobenius satisfies φσφ⁻¹=σ^q. For c≠0 the type is Steinberg with N≠0; at c=0 it has N=0. A closed quotient containing the dense nonzero-c locus contains c=0 too. Gee §3.30 retains N, so forgetting N cannot resolve the iff as printed. Shotton Definition 3.5 uses the Zariski closure; BLGGT 1.3.4(2) requires points on unique components.

issues.citation: Toby Gee, Modularity lifting theorems, Essential Number Theory 1 (2022), no. 1, 73–126; arXiv:2202.05818v2 (17 October 2022), 45 pages. The arXiv version was read; printed page = PDF page.
issues.reviewReason: Read §3.30 and the paragraph after Theorem 3.31 (pp. 19–20): the inertial WD-type there keeps N, and the quotient is said to have exactly the points of type τ. For q ≡ 1 mod p the lifts ρ_c(φ) = diag(q, 1), ρ_c(t) = (1 c; 0 1) satisfy φtφ⁻¹ = t^q for every c in the maximal ideal and have fixed determinant; the map R^□ → 𝒪⟦c⟧ they define kills every element vanishing at all c ≠ 0, so the point c = 0 (N = 0) lies on the quotient attached to the Steinberg type. Shotton's Definition 3.5 (Zariski closure of the points of type τ) is the correct definition. The hypotheses p odd and q ≡ 1 mod p of the example are not needed for the failure (without the congruence the same family lifts the unramified diag(q̄, 1)). The cheapest repair is to read τ without N: then the equivalence holds by Theorem 3.31(a), and this is how the rings are used in 3.36–3.38; the entry's repair (closure of the points of exact full type) is also valid and defines the unramified and Steinberg-type rings separately.

issues.locator: Proposition 3.5.2 and its proof (the case N = 2, relation (3.21)), arXiv:2108.06998v1 pp. 27–28; the published version (Acta Math. Sin. (Engl. Ser.) 40 (2024), 1599–1644) was not read
issues.printed: The similitude character is η_v^μ ε^{1−N} for an arbitrary μ ∈ ℤ/2. The proposition asserts, for every such μ, that 𝒟^mix is formally smooth over Spf 𝒪⟦x₀, x₁⟧/(x₀x₁) with components 𝒟^unr and 𝒟^ram, and that 𝒟^ram is formally smooth of relative dimension N². The proof (N = 2) takes B = (0, (−1)^{μ+1}(1 + x); q(1 + y), 0) and X = (0, 0; x₀, 0) and deduces (x − y)x₀ = 0 from (3.21).
issues.correction: Assume μ even (equivalently, replace the pair of residual eigenvalues by {(−1)^μ q^{−N}, (−1)^μ q^{−N+2}}). For μ odd, relation (3.21) gives x₀(2 + x + y) = 0, hence x₀ = 0: every lift in 𝒟^mix is unramified, 𝒟^mix = 𝒟^unr, and 𝒟^ram has relative dimension N² − 1.
issues.reason: With B and X as in the proof, B·ᵗX·B^{−1} has the single non-zero entry q(1 + y)x₀/((−1)^{μ+1}(1 + x)) in the lower left corner, so (3.21) is x₀·((1 + y) − (−1)^μ(1 + x)) = 0. For μ even this is the equation of the proof; for μ odd the factor 2 + x + y is a unit (the coefficient characteristic is odd, since it does not divide q² − 1). The residual matrix B̄ gives the eigenvalues q^{−N}, q^{−N+2} for both parities, so the hypothesis of the proposition does not exclude μ odd. The applications are not affected: the source's Theorem 3.6.3 assumes that there are no level-raising places when N is odd, and the main paper raises the level only in even rank, where μ ≡ N is even.

issues.locator: Appendix A, proof of Proposition A.4, printed p. 59 (author PDF; the same in arXiv:2108.12785v4)
issues.printed: To see that the dual W* of the middle term is nuclear, the proof cites Dierolf–Roelcke, Proposition 3.8, for p-adic (nonarchimedean) nuclear Fréchet spaces.
issues.correction: Dierolf–Roelcke prove that nuclearity is a three-space property for real and complex locally convex spaces; the nonarchimedean case needs its own argument. It holds under the packet’s spherical-completeness convention (the lattice argument itself applies whenever nuclearity is characterized by compactoid lattice images) by the lattice proof of LocallyAnalyticDistributions:L0/nuclear-three-space.

issues.locator: Appendix A, proof of Proposition A.4, printed p. 59 (author PDF; the same in arXiv:2108.12785v4)
issues.printed: The proof passes to stereotype duals of 0 → W1 → W → W2 → 0 and asserts an exact sequence 0 → W2* → W* → W1* → Ext¹(W2, K) in LH(C_K); it then applies Proposition A.3 to conclude that W* is Fréchet, and finally compares W with its double dual by the five lemma in LH(C_K).
issues.correction: Hahn–Banach gives vector-space exactness, but the source does not construct the claimed exact stereotype-dual sequence in the left heart or justify its strictness. Only the outer terms are already of compact type; equality of stereotype and strong dual topologies on W is not known at this step. The packet gives a sufficient repair using H1 (strict exactness of the strong-dual sequence) and H2 (continuity of strong biduality), and records both as a gap. These are explicit replacement inputs, not an identification of the source’s unknown stereotype topology with the strong topology.
issues.reason: No derived Hom functor of C_K with values in LH(C_K) carrying the stereotype topology is constructed in the paper, and topological exactness of duals is not a formal consequence of strictness of the original sequence: the known case, a closed subspace of a space of compact type (Schneider–Teitelbaum 1999, Proposition 1.2(i)), is proved through the compact-type structure of the middle term, which is what Proposition A.4 is to establish.

issues.locator: Proposition I.5.6 and its one-line proof, printed p. 20 of the author PDF (page image checked); same passage in Astérisque 330, printed p. 31 (published page image checked)
issues.printed: If φ_1 : ℤ_p → ℤ_p and φ_2 : ℤ_p → L are of class C^r, then φ_2∘φ_1 is of class C^r; the proof refers to the composition of limited expansions in the archimedean case. No restriction on r ≥ 0 is stated.
issues.correction: The statement holds for r = 0 and for r ≥ 1 (the Taylor-composition proof of De Ieso's Proposition 2.12 with F = ℚ_p, after repairing (2.25) as in E14), and for 0 < r < 1 when φ_1 is Lipschitz (v_p(φ_1(x) − φ_1(y)) ≥ v_p(x − y) − c), for example locally analytic or of class C^1. For 0 < r < 1 and φ_1 merely of class C^r it is false. LocallyAnalyticDistributions:L2/cr-composition states the corrected version.
issues.reason: Take r = 1/2 and d(x) = Σ_n a_n(x)p^{⌊2n/3⌋} for x = Σ_n a_n(x)p^n with digits 0 ≤ a_n(x) < p. If v_p(y) ≥ h the digits of x and x + y agree below h, so v_p(d(x + y) − d(x)) ≥ ⌊2h/3⌋, and ⌊2h/3⌋ − h/2 → ∞: d is of class C^{1/2} (with d^{(0)} = d), with values in ℤ_p. But d(p^m) = p^{⌊2m/3⌋} and d(d(p^m)) − d(d(0)) = p^{⌊2⌊2m/3⌋/3⌋}, of valuation at most 4m/9, so inf_{x, y∈p^mℤ_p} v_p(d∘d(x + y) − d∘d(x)) − m/2 ≤ −m/18 → −∞ and d∘d is not of class C^{1/2}. The archimedean analogue fails in the same way: Hölder exponents multiply under composition.

issues.reason: For F = ℚ_p let q(x) = Σ_{n≥0} a_n(x)p^{2n} for the base-p digits of x. The full Lipschitz bound repairs the Taylor-composition argument in cr-composition.

issues.reason: Take A=Q_p, G=1-pT and H=sum_(n>=0)p^n T^n. The leading coefficient -p is multiplicative, H is a nonzero restricted series, and GH=1; G is nonconstant. issues.locator: Proposition 2, (6.6), p.968, and its proof and use, p.969
issues.printed: The Weyl-integral estimate uses an inverse-squared norm normalization but omits its exponential spectral factor.
issues.correction: Replace (6.6) by Weyl(u_φ, χ) ≪_ε r^C|D|^{13/28+ε} for u_φ = φ/‖φ‖. With the a(1) = 1 normalization of (5.7), what Theorem 4 and [12, Thm 5] actually give is Weyl(⟨φ,φ⟩^{−1}φ, χ) ≪_ε r^C cosh²(πr/4)|D|^{13/28+ε}. The two forms agree after changing C, because ‖φ‖² = 2L(1,sym²φ)/cosh(πr) and L(1,sym²φ) = r^{o(1)}; only the upper bound L(1,sym²φ) ≪ r^ε is needed to pass from the second form to the first. In the deduction of Theorem 2, write c(φ)⟨φ,φ⟩^{−1}φ = ⟨f,u_φ⟩u_φ and use ⟨f,u_φ⟩ ≪ r^{−A} in place of c(φ) ≪ |r|^{−A}.
issues.reason: Imported correction from REV-PAPER-DUKE-IMAMOGLU-TOTH-16; this packet uses the corrected statements. The earlier confirmed analysis classifies this as an error because the printed (6.6) is false, not merely unproved. The cited results give an extra factor cosh²(πr/4): Duke 1988, Thm 5 (p.85) has the factor ch(πt/2) with t = r/2, once for each of b(d') and b(d). The failure can be shown directly in the CM case D = −4 = (1)(−4). Here h = 1 and ω_D = 2, so Weyl(⟨φ,φ⟩^{−1}φ, χ) = ⟨φ,φ⟩^{−1}φ(i)/2. With a(1) = 1, ⟨φ,φ⟩ = 2L(1,sym²φ)/cosh(πr) (see item 151), so (6.6) would force |u_φ(i)| ≪ r^{C+ε}e^{−πr/2} for every even φ. Odd forms vanish at i. The local Weyl law at z = i (pre-trace formula) gives Σ_{r_j≤R}|u_j(i)|² + (1/4π)∫_{−R}^{R}|E(i,1/2+it)|²dt ≍ R². By (7.1), E(i,s) = 2ζ(s)L(s,χ_{−4})/ζ(2s), and fourth-moment bounds make the Eisenstein part O(R^{1+ε}). So the even u_j cannot all be exponentially small at i, and (6.6) fails. The paper's own numbers show the same thing. With ⟨φ,φ⟩ = 7.263×10^{−19} and r = 13.78, the unit-vector values are modest: u(i) ≈ 3.76 and u((1+√−3)/2) ≈ 2.44, from the displayed values 4.41046×10⁹ and 2.86296×10⁹. So the printed Weyl values ≈ 10⁹–10^{10} are ‖φ‖^{−1}·O(1), where ‖φ‖^{−1} ≈ 1.17×10⁹. The printed argument for Theorem 2 multiplies the false (6.6) by the true but too weak bound c(φ) ≪ r^{−A}. With both corrected, c(φ)⟨φ,φ⟩^{−1}φ = ⟨f,u_φ⟩u_φ and the proof goes through. Humphries–Nordentoft (arXiv 2211.05890, §9) use the unit-normalized form without comment.

issues.reason: Imported correction from REV-PAPER-DUKE-IMAMOGLU-TOTH-16; this packet uses the corrected statements. By (9.2), −2i∂_zF_m=P_m(z,φ) with φ(y)=−s|m|^{−1/2}(2πy)⁻¹Γ(s)Γ(2s)⁻¹M_{sgn m,s−1/2}(4π|m|y), so i∂_zF_m=−½P_m. I checked (9.2) numerically to 1e-15 at four points, including complex s, and Lemma 7 for both signs and several (t,μ,s). Put the printed Lemma 6 and Lemma 7 together, with μ=sgn m, e(±μ/4)=i, Γ((s+2)/2)Γ(s/2)=(s/2)Γ(s/2)² and the duplication formula. This gives −½Φ_m(2√D/c)=−2^{s−1/2}Γ((s+1)/2)²Γ(s)⁻¹D^{1/4}c^{−1/2}J_{s−1/2}(4π|m|√D/c), which is minus the c-th term of Lemma 5. Quadrature of (9.3) gives the same ratio, −1.0000000, for three (D,c,m,s). To decide which statement is wrong, I computed Lemma 5 directly. I took D=12=(−3)(−4), with classes [1,0,−3] and [−1,0,3], χ=+1 and −1, and γ_Q=[[2,3],[1,2]]. I evaluated F_m from its Fourier expansion at points reduced to the fundamental domain and summed S_m for c≤4000. With C_Q from z to γ_Qz, LHS/RHS=1.0000000000 at (m,s)=(1,4) and 1.00000005 at (2,3.7). Unfolding (a>0, θ from 0 to π, counterclockwise) also shows that the printed Lemma 6 is the statement for the counterclockwise orientation when a>0: forms with a<0 contribute equally, because χ(−Q)=−χ(Q) for d<0 and their orientation is reversed. So Lemma 6 and the Lemma 4 note were carried over from [16] without the sign change that footnote 8 signals. Case for the defence: the paper never states the orientation explicitly. Theorem 4 is unaffected, because its third case is written with (λ/2)∫_{F_A}φdμ, which does not depend on orientation, and the chain Lemma 5 → Proposition 5 → Proposition 6 → Lemma 1 is consistent under the (2.11) orientation. issues.locator: Author copy, Theorem 3.2.7, p.26 (final sentence); compare Theorem 3.1.7, p.21
issues.printed: The mixed Γ₁(N;n) stack is characterized as DM exactly when n is squarefree in the admissible range.

issues.locator: Chapter III, §1, the paragraph after (1.3), p.255; the stack defined on p.254; Invent. Math. 84 (1986), published version (MPIM scan)
issues.printed: The stack used is that of cyclic N-isogenies of generalized elliptic curves whose kernel meets every component of each geometric fibre, cyclic in the Cartier-divisor sense; the source then asserts that at every geometric point the strict henselization of the coarse scheme X is the quotient of the strict henselization of this stack by Aut_k(x)/{±1}, with Aut_k(x) the group of automorphisms of the pair, and derives Proposition (1.4) from it.
issues.correction: For N divisible by p² this is the naive Γ₀(N) stack, which is not Deligne–Mumford at the cusps of residue characteristic p, so it has no étale strict henselization there and the group Aut_k(x) of k-points misses its infinitesimal automorphisms. The statement holds for Česnavičius's refined stack 𝒳₀(N), which is Deligne–Mumford and regular and has the same coarse space; with that stack the argument for Proposition (1.4) goes through (Česnavičius Theorem 6.7 recovers the regularity away from the points with j=0 or 1728 in characteristics dividing N, and Česnavičius §6 reports that Edixhoven 1990 §1.2 computes the completions along the cusps).
issues.reason: On the standard p-gon over 𝔽_p the infinitesimal μ_p of automorphisms fixing the identity component stabilises suitable ample cyclic subgroups of order N whose p-part is non-étale and disconnected, so the automorphism group scheme of that point is not étale (Česnavičius arXiv:1511.07475v2 §1.2, p.2; Conrad 2007 §1.1, p.1). The coarse spaces of the naive and refined stacks coincide (Česnavičius Proposition 6.9), so the coarse scheme X and the conclusion of (1.4) are unaffected.

For p²|N this stack is not Deligne–Mumford at cusps of characteristic p (Conrad 2007 §1.1, p.1; Česnavičius 2017 §1.2, p.2), so the step needs the refined stack, whose coarse space is the same (Česnavičius Proposition 6.9). issues.locator: §2.4, Lemma 2.8: arXiv v3 p. 12; published p. 908.
issues.printed: η²|_{K_v^*} = χ · Norm_{K_v/Q_p}^w
issues.correction: The identity holds on the local units: η²|_{O_{K_v}^*} = χ · Norm_{K_v/Q_p}^w with χ of finite order. It does not hold on all of K_v^*. The final sentence — w even, Hodge–Tate weight w/2 at v — is correct, and is what Lemmas 2.9 and 2.10 use.
issues.reason: Counterexample: K = Q (which has no CM subfield, so every finite place is friendly), v = p, η = χ_cyc^{-1}. Then η is ramified only at p, locally algebraic there, and pure of weight w = 2, since geometric Frobenius at ℓ acts by ℓ. As an idele class character η(p) = 1, because the local Artin image of a uniformizer acts trivially on μ_{p^∞} in either normalisation; so η²(p) = 1 while Norm_{Q_p/Q_p}(p)^w = p², and χ(p) = p^{-2} has infinite order. On units η(u) = u and η² = Norm², so the identity does hold there. The proof cannot give more: local algebraicity is the hypothesis that η_p 'agrees, in a neighbourhood of the identity, with the Q_p-points of an algebraic homomorphism' (p. 12), and the closing step — 'any Q_p-rational character of (Res_{E/Q} G_m)^1 is trivial upon pullback to E_v^*' — is a statement about that algebraic character, hence controls η only on an open subgroup of E_v^*, not on a uniformizer.

issues.locator: Proposition 5.3 and §6: arXiv v3 pp. 26, 29, compared with §§3.1, 3.3, pp. 15–17; published pp. 927, 931–932.
issues.printed: v ∉ S
issues.correction: To apply §3 literally, explicitly restrict to odd residue characteristic and to the §3 good-reduction setup. For the proposition as stated at p=2, replace the whole residue disk by finitely many smaller congruence disks and carry out the argument on each. No counterexample to Proposition 5.3 is asserted.
issues.reason: Friendliness ensures K_v/Q_p is unramified, but does not imply p>2. The quoted estimate for flat sections is |z|<p^(−1/(p−1)). At p=2, points with |z|=1/2 in a residue disk are on its boundary, so that estimate does not justify §6’s assertion that the analytic domain contains the entire residue disk. Subdivision into disks modulo 4 avoids this issue. The original claim that other primes above p must be good for crystallinity at v was incorrect: v∉S already supplies good reduction at v.

issues.locator: §8.3, Lemma 8.2: arXiv v3 p. 42; published p. 951.
issues.correction: Require e to be nonseparating in Y, equivalently [e] ≠ 0 in H_1(Y; Q).
issues.reason: A simple curve bounding a disk away from the branch point is permitted by the paper’s definition. Its q inverse images bound disks, so all q homology classes are zero, contradicting the claimed independence and primitive rank q−1. For a nonseparating curve one can choose the one-face CW decomposition used in the proof; the lifted edge classes are independent and transfer supplies the single relation after primitive projection. The required distinguishing curves can be chosen nonseparating, including curves with q-cycle monodromy; they are not all liftable curves in the paper’s special sense.

issues.locator: §8.3, Lemma 8.3: arXiv v3 p. 42; published p. 951.
issues.printed: rank(Mon(D_e^M) − Id)
issues.correction: Take a nonseparating simple closed curve e in Y−{y} and a positive sufficiently divisible M (for example a positive multiple of the order of Cov(e), and of the relevant stabilizer indices). Then the rank is k−1, where k is the number of cycles of Cov(e).
issues.reason: The lemma is deduced from Lemma 8.2, which needs e nonseparating (finding E13), and it fails without that hypothesis. If e bounds a disk in Y − {y} then Mon(D_e^M) = Id and the rank is 0, while Cov(e) = 1; if e is nonseparating with Cov(e) a q-cycle then k = 1 and the rank is again 0. Two different conjugacy classes give the same rank, so the rank does not determine the class. With e nonseparating the three possible cycle types in Aff(q) — (1^q), (q) and (1, r, …, r) — have k = q, 1 and 1 + (q − 1)/r cycles respectively, all distinct, and the lemma holds. The applications, in the proof of Lemma 8.9, are to nonseparating curves.

issues.locator: End of §8.3: arXiv v3 p. 43; published p. 951.
issues.printed: D_e
issues.correction: Use D_e^{q−1}, or a suitable further positive multiple in the common cover stabilizer. Its lift is D_{e+}^{q−1}D_{e−}; it induces a nontrivial transvection on primitive homology.
issues.reason: For a liftable e the multiplier of Cov(e) generates F_q^×. A dual curve meeting e once has its abelian multiplier changed by this generator under D_e. Conjugation in Aff(q) preserves multipliers, so D_e does not stabilize the cover. The preceding lifting formula instead applies to the (q−1)-st power. If u is the primitive projection of [e+], then the projection of [e−] is −u and the lift acts by x↦x+q⟨u,x⟩u, up to the intersection-sign convention.

issues.locator: Lemma 6.3 and its reduction to Lemma 6.4: arXiv v3 p. 33; published pp. 937–938.
issues.printed: φ : V → V
issues.correction: For the printed proof, require φ to be a semilinear similitude: ω(φx,φy)=c·σ(ω(x,y)) for some c≠0. Alternatively prove a general-position result for the different transported symplectic forms, rather than invoking Lemma 6.4 for one form.
issues.reason: The printed assumptions make φ bijective and Frobenius-semilinear only. Identifying the embedding components V_i via φ need not make their Lagrangians Lagrangian for one common form. Over an unramified extension of degree 8, take φ=Aσ with A=diag(2,1,1,1) and the standard symplectic form pairing e_1,e_3 and e_2,e_4. F=span(e_1+e_2,e_3−e_4) is Lagrangian, but the pairing on A^{-1}F is −1/2. Thus the common-form hypothesis needed for the displayed invocation of Lemma 6.4 is not justified.

issues.locator: Page 448, first sentence of the proof of Theorem 1, and the statement of Theorem 1 (version of record, Invent. math. 107 (1992), read from the scan in the Regensburg repository)
issues.printed: The proof describes numerical equivalence as plainly the coarsest among adequate equivalence relations.
issues.correction: Exclude the trivial relation, under which every cycle is equivalent to zero: numerical equivalence is the coarsest adequate relation other than the trivial one (equivalently, among those with A^0(Spec k) = F). Theorem 1 holds for adequate relations other than the trivial one.
issues.reason: The trivial relation satisfies the conditions for adequacy (pullback, pushforward and intersection are well defined modulo it) and is strictly coarser than numerical equivalence, since it kills [Spec k]. For it every A^j(X) is zero, so M_k is the zero category, which is semisimple abelian, and every A^{dim X}(X × X) is the zero algebra, which is finite-dimensional and semisimple; so a) and b) of Theorem 1 hold and c) fails. The proof of a) => c) uses End(1) = F, which fails exactly for the trivial relation. For any other adequate relation A^0(Spec k) = F and the stated comparison holds (proof in MC.0/numerical-equivalence).

issues.locator: Lemma 1.12(2) and (3), with the proof of (2), p. 7, arXiv v5
issues.printed: Part (2) asserts H^{2n}_Nori(Z) = 1(-n) for a projective variety Z with dimension n. Part (3) asserts H^{2n}_Z(X) = 1(-n) when X is smooth and Z is a closed subvariety that is smooth, irreducible, and of pure codimension n.
issues.correction: In (2) Z must be geometrically irreducible, and in (3) Z must be geometrically connected (for Z smooth, geometrically irreducible); in general the proof of (3) gives H^{2n}_Z(X) = H^0_Nori(Z)(-n). In the proof of (2) the map is the restriction H^{2n}_Nori(P^N) -> H^{2n}_Nori(Z), not the reverse.
issues.reason: Varieties are reduced separated schemes of finite type over Q, not necessarily geometrically irreducible. For Z = {0, infinity} in P^1 (n = 0), or Z = Spec Q(i), H^0(Z(C); Q) = Q^2, so H^0_Nori(Z) is not 1(0). For X = A^1 over Q and Z = V(t^2 + 1), which is smooth and irreducible of codimension 1, H^2_Z(X) realises to H^2_{Z(C)}(C; Q) = Q^2, so it is not 1(-1). The proof of (3) itself starts from the Gysin isomorphism H^0(Z) = H^{2n}_Z(X). Lemma 1.13 applies (3) to the diagonal of W, so it needs W geometrically connected or the replacement of 1(-i) by H^0_Nori(W)(-i); Theorem 1.14 is unaffected.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 1.6, p. 5, arXiv v5
issues.printed: Invoking Definition B.14, the proof calls D^eff_Nori a graded diagram and gives it a multiplication that is commutative, again citing B.14: (X, Y, i) x (X', Y', i') = (X x X', X x Y' union Y x X', i + i').
issues.correction: A product structure in the sense of Definition B.14 (or Remark B.17) must also send a pair (coboundary edge, identity) to an edge (or path). The source defines the product on vertices only, and in general no edge or path of D^eff_Nori has the required ends; the construction needs an enlarged diagram, for instance with excision edges, together with a check that the diagram category is unchanged.
issues.reason: For a coboundary edge (Y, Z, i) -> (X, Y, i + 1) and a vertex (X', Y', j) the product must go from (Y x X', Y x Y' union Z x X', i + j) to (X x X', X x Y' union Y x X', i + j + 1). Coboundary edges into the target start at (X x Y' union Y x X', V); functoriality edges out of (Y x X', ...) go to pairs mapping to Y x X', and X x Y' union Y x X' admits no map to Y x X' restricting to the identity unless Y is a retract of X (it is not for Y two points of X = A^1).

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem 2.6 (page 10), arXiv:1105.0865v5
issues.printed: The proof defines P_{1,2} as the subspace in ∏_{p∈D} T_1(p) ⊗ T_2(p)^∨ cut out by relations from D. It likewise defines A_{1,2}(T) as the subspace in ∏_{p∈D} Hom(T_1(p), T_2(p))^∨ cut out by those diagram relations.
issues.correction: Both are quotients, not subspaces: for finite D, P_{1,2} is the quotient of the sum of the T_1(p) ⊗ T_2(p)^∨ by the span of the elements T_1(f)ω ⊗ γ − ω ⊗ T_2(f)^∨γ, one for each edge f, and A_{1,2} = Hom(T_1|D, T_2|D)^∨ is the quotient of the dual of the product of the Hom(T_1(p), T_2(p)) by the annihilator of the subspace Hom(T_1|D, T_2|D) cut out by the edge conditions, which is the span of the same elements. With 'quotient' the conclusion 'this is the same thing' holds.
issues.reason: Definition 2.4 presents P_{1,2} by generators and relations, which is a quotient; Definition 2.1 takes the dual of the subspace Hom(T_1|F, T_2|F), which is a quotient of the dual of the ambient product. The elements of the product 'satisfying the relations' form neither space.

issues.locator: Proof of Corollary 3.4 (page 13), arXiv:1105.0865v5, against Theorem 1.14 (page 8)
issues.printed: The proof identifies G_1 = G_mot with the motivic fundamental group, saying this holds by definition.

issues.locator: §3, printed p. 183 (PDF p. 7), the published K-Theory 6 (1992) text supplied as Totaro1992
issues.printed: The source takes D to be the normalization of C, calls it a smooth curve, and asserts a finite map D → C. It then defines P(D) as the sole smooth compactification of D.
issues.correction: D is a regular curve and P(D) is the regular proper model of the function field F(C); over an imperfect field F neither need be smooth over F, and residue fields of closed points may be inseparable over F. The argument goes through verbatim with 'regular', because Suslin's reciprocity law (with Kato's norms) is a statement about all places of the function field of one variable, i.e. the closed points of the regular proper model.
issues.reason: Over F = 𝔽_p(s), p odd, the curve y² = x^p − s is regular at the point (y, x^p − s) (its maximal ideal is generated by y, since x^p − s = y²) but not smooth there (both partial derivatives 2y and p x^{p−1} vanish). Normalisations of curves in the cube can therefore be regular without being smooth.

issues.locator: Theorem 10.2, case a + b odd, p. 39, arXiv v1 (p. 36 of the published version, same up to writing ((j+1) mod 2)ρ for ρ^{(j+1) mod 2})

issues.correction: The correction terms must be ρ·Sq^xSq^y with x, y odd and x + y = a + b − 1, summed over j. For a odd and b even, the proof's route (apply β to the even-even relation, using β(τ) = ρ) gives Sq^aSq^b = Σ_j C(b−1−j, a−2j) Sq^{a+b−j}Sq^j + ρ Σ_{j odd} C(b−1−j, a−1−2j) Sq^{a+b−j−1}Sq^j; for a even and b odd the printed Sq^{a+b+j}Sq^{j−1} must read Sq^{a+b−j}Sq^{j−1} (j even).
issues.reason: The printed correction leaves j unbound and is not bidegree-homogeneous: for a = 1, b = 2 it gives Sq^1Sq^2 = Sq^3 + ρSq^2, but ρSq^2 has bidegree (3, 2) while Sq^1Sq^2 has (3, 1), and Lemma 9.5 gives Sq^1Sq^2 = Sq^3 exactly. Weight counting forces x, y odd. For a = 3, b = 2, applying β to Sq^2Sq^2 = τSq^3Sq^1 gives Sq^3Sq^2 = ρSq^3Sq^1, matching the corrected formula (j = 1).

issues.locator: A1.1, generators-and-relations description of differentials, printed p.31 / PDF p.1
issues.printed: The differential-module presentation imposes the product relation and vanishing on base scalars, but omits the sum relation.
issues.correction: Include the additive relation d(x+y)=dx+dy for all x,y∈B. The preceding derivation universal property is the correct specification, and the roadmap should use the existing Kähler differential module with additive derivation.
issues.reason: Leibniz and annihilation of base scalars do not imply additivity. Take A=ℚ, B=ℚ(t), M=B and define δ(f)=f·ord_t(f) for f≠0, δ(0)=0. Valuation additivity gives δ(fg)=fδ(g)+gδ(f), and δ annihilates ℚ, but δ(t+1)=0 whereas δ(t)+δ(1)=t. Thus the displayed relations alone admit a nonadditive map and do not present Kähler differentials.

issues.locator: Proof of Theorem5.8, printed p.21, paragraph immediately following Lemma5.9; own text and page image checked.
issues.printed: The source deduces A[ℓⁿ](K)=A[ℓⁿ](K′) for each n from the coincidence of the fixed subspaces of Vℓ(A).
issues.correction: Keep the equality of rational fixed spaces and their intersections with the integral Tate lattice. Descend the corresponding compatible divisible torsion subsystem; do not infer equality of all finite-level rational torsion points. The integral/divisible descent argument must be supplied.
issues.reason: Equal rational fixed spaces need not give equal invariants modulo ℓⁿ. On Zℓ², a generator with matrix [[1,ℓ],[0,1]] and its ℓ-th power [[1,ℓ²],[0,1]] have the same Qℓ fixed line y=0. Modulo ℓ², (0,1) is fixed by the latter but not the former. A split Tate curve with parameter of valuation ℓ over a strictly henselian DVR of residue characteristic different from ℓ realizes this pattern: adjoining an ℓ-th root of the uniformizer adds ℓ²-torsion without changing the rational fixed line. This is a flaw in the displayed intermediate inference, not a counterexample to the monodromy criterion.

issues.printed: The nonzero-j enumeration lists eight equations. Its rejection argument bounds the number of components of a twisted multiplicative fiber by two and consequently excludes twisted configurations that actually occur.
issues.correction: The twisted case also gives I₂*+E₄+Ĩ₂, I₃*+E₄+Ĩ₁ and IV*+E₄+Ĩ₂. Theorem 10.4 has eleven models, not eight, and §10 has fourteen equations in all. The additional models, with fibres over t=0, 1, ∞, are: y²+txy+t³y=x³+x² [I₂*+E₄+Ĩ₂, Δ=t¹⁰, j=t²]; y²+txy+t³y=x³+tx² [I₃*+E₄+Ĩ₁, Δ=t¹¹, j=t]; y²+txy+t²y=x³+t²x² [IV*+E₄+Ĩ₂, Δ=t⁸(t²+t+1), j=t⁴/(t²+t+1), plus I₁ over t²+t+1=0]. Theorem 10.5 is correct. Proposition 11.1 (p. 33) and the key-reduction proposition of §11 take their elliptic column from Theorem 10.4. The proof of Theorem 15.1 reduces every fibration to I₁*+I₄ or I₂*+III+III. All of these must treat the three configurations; I₃* is never mentioned in §§11–15. On an Enriques surface Y, the multiple fibres would lie over the unstable and the E₄ points, because Ĩ₁ and Ĩ₂ are semistable. Until then the proof of the main theorem has a gap at this point. Whether the configurations occur on a non-exceptional Enriques surface over F₂ with constant Picard scheme is not settled here.
issues.reason: Checked by hand for y²+txy+t³y=x³+x². Δ=t¹⁰. At t=0 (Tate's algorithm): the reduction y²=x³+x² is singular at (0,0), and b₂=t², so the fibre is additive; v(a₆)=∞, v(b₈)=6, v(b₆)=6. The change y↦y+x gives a₂=t, a₄=t³ and P(T)=T³+T²=T²(T+1). Then a_{3,2}=a_{6,4}=0, and a_{2,1}X²+a_{4,3}X+a_{6,5}=X²+X has distinct rational roots. So I₂* with c=4, all seven components defined over F₂, 15 points. At ∞: y²+xy+y=x³+s²x², Δ′=s², node at (1,1) with tangent polynomial T²+T+1, so non-split I₂, 6 points. At t=1: y²+xy+y=x³+x² is smooth ordinary with 4 points (E₄). Total 25, so the trace of Frobenius on NS(J̄) is 10 and Pic_{J/F₂} is constant. Condition (ii) holds: only Ĩ₂ is semistable, and E₄ is ordinary. The other two models are checked the same way: I₃* at t=0 after three steps of the I_n* loop, and IV* at t=0 (Y²+Y distinct roots, c=3). Independent checks (scripts S/tate2.py, brute.py, classify.py, lcheck.py): (1) all 2²¹ equations were enumerated through their 2¹⁸ representatives with a₂=0 (every equation becomes one via x↦x+a₂), with Tate's algorithm at every place; this gives exactly 14 isomorphism classes, taken modulo the 512 coordinate changes of degree ≤(2,1,3) and PGL₂(F₂), that satisfy (i) and (ii); these are the 11 printed and the 3 above, one class per configuration; (2) for every class, the L-function of the generic fibre was computed from naive point counts at all places of degree ≤8; it equals (1−2T)^r with r=8−Σ(m_v−1), which confirms the component counts and the Galois-trivial Mordell–Weil action independently of Tate's algorithm; (3) for all 2¹⁸ normalised equations, Ogg's formula (v(Δ)≥e, δ=0 for I_n, IV, IV*) and Σ deg(v)·v(Δ)=12 hold. The proof's other claims were also reproduced: II*+E₂+E₄, I₃*+E₄+E₄ and IV*+E₄+I₃ are excluded, d₁=1 and 1+t are equivalent in the I₄* case, the second I₁* solution is twisted, and α=1 gives E₂. The error is the unexamined twisted case ('the argument is similar'): the tuples (r_a,i,r_c)=(7,2,2) and (8,2,1) yield these configurations.

issues.locator: Theorem 6.6, pp. 496–497; initial strictly henselian reduction in its proof; notation p. 457
issues.printed: The multiplicity of the torsor fiber is expressed using the original fraction-field period for a DVR that is not explicitly required to be henselian.
issues.correction: Assume the DVR is henselian with algebraically closed residue field, or use the torsor period after strict henselization when describing the geometric fiber multiplicity.
issues.reason: Take R=C[t]_(t−1), E/C with a nonzero two-torsion point P, and the smooth quotient of E×G_m,s by (e,s)↦(e+P,−s), over t=s². E(C(s))=E(C), since a rational map P¹→E extends and is constant. The nonzero translation cocycle therefore has period two over C(t). At t=1 its special fiber is smooth of multiplicity one. Henselization splits s²=t near t=1, and the local torsor period is one. Hence passing to strict henselization need not preserve the original K-period.

issues.locator: §2, the sentence before Lemma 2.2 and Lemma 2.2, p. 191 (Numdam PDF page 8); its uses in the proof of Proposition 4.1, pp. 200 and 202
issues.printed: The source defines δ⁻_{F′} as the Z_p-rank of the Γ_Σ summand with nontrivial action by Gal(F′/F) ≃ Z/2, and cites [Wal] for δ⁻_{F′} ≤ d/2. Lemma 2.2 claims dim R_𝒟/q ≤ δ⁻_{F′} ≤ d/2 whenever q ⊆ R_𝒟 is prime, contains p, and ρ_𝒟 mod q is dihedral with determinant of finite order.
issues.correction: dim R_𝒟/q ≤ δ⁻_{F′} holds, and δ⁻_{F′} ≤ d/2 holds when F′ is totally real (Waldschmidt applied to the minus part of the units of F′, which has rank d). When F′ is CM, δ⁻_{F′} = d, and the bound dim R_𝒟/q ≤ d/2 fails when every place above p splits in F′. Proposition 4.1 therefore needs, when ρ₀ is dihedral, a separate proof (or an assumption) that the dihedral locus of type 𝒟 with finite-order determinant has dimension at most d/2.
issues.reason: Affected: Lemma 2.2, and the three steps of the proof of Proposition 4.1 that use it (hence the proofs of Theorems 5.1 and 5.2), when ρ₀ is induced from a quadratic extension F′/F with a complex place. For F′ CM, the global units of F′ have the same rank d − 1 as those of F, so the minus part of the units is finite; the minus part of ∏_{w|p} 𝒪_{F′,w}^× has ℤ_p-rank d, and class field theory gives δ⁻_{F′} = d > d/2. The lemma's conclusion then fails: if every v | p splits in F′ and ℳ = ∅, Ind_{F′}^F(ψ̃₀ψ⁻), with ψ⁻ the universal character of the free part of the minus quotient of Γ_Σ, is a deformation of type 𝒟 over k[[Γ⁻]] (at each v_i it is Ψ|_{D_w} ⊕ Ψ|_{D_w̄}, nearly ordinary with the χ^{(i)}_1-part as sub). Its determinant has finite order, and its trace ring has dimension d. Such ρ₀ satisfy (2.1): for example ρ̄_{E,p}|_{G_F} for an elliptic curve E with complex multiplication by K, p ≥ 5 split in K, and a totally real F of even degree, linearly disjoint from K(E[p]), over which ρ̄_{E,p} is unramified outside p. The proof of Proposition 4.1 uses the d/2 bound three times: that ρ₁ = ρ^mod mod Q is not dihedral (step one, p. 200); that ρ mod Q₁ is not dihedral because dim Q₁ > 1 + d/2 (step three, p. 200); and that ρ mod Q₂ is not dihedral because dim Q₂ ≥ d/2 + 1 (general case, p. 202). Theorem 5.1 passes to L with ρ₀ = ρ̄^{ss}|_{G_L}, and F′L is CM when F′ is. Not examined: whether Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 fail in these cases, which are partly covered by other lifting theorems when ρ̄|_{F(ζ_p)} is irreducible. When the places above p do not split in F′, the nearly ordinary condition forces Ψ⁻ to have finite order on their decomposition groups, which should cut the dihedral locus down; the paper does not make this argument.

issues.locator: §6.1 after Definition 6.2, printed p. 1757 (PDF p. 50); also Definition 4.5(3), printed p. 1737, and Definition 7.7, printed p. 1761; same in arXiv v4
issues.printed: The definition takes a supremum of character deviations over the entire unit group and associates bounded weights with a strict bound below one.
issues.correction: For boundedness diagnostics take the supremum over a fixed sufficiently small pro-p principal-unit subgroup; keep boundedness itself as affinoid-image boundedness. For quantitative AIP domains use the universal-coordinate annuli of AIP ADIC §2.4.3; do not identify their coordinate δ with this corrected supremum without proof.
issues.reason: For p odd and F = ℚ, the Teichmüller character ω : ℤ_p^× → ℤ_p^× is an L-point of 𝒲, hence a bounded weight, but for a primitive (p−1)-st root of unity ζ, |ω(ζ) − 1| = |ζ − 1| = 1. So the printed |T_ω| = 1, contradicting 'bounded iff |T_κ| < 1'; likewise for any weight nontrivial on the prime-to-p torsion of 𝒪_p^×. Then |δ_κ| = 1 and |p|^{ε_κ} = 1 give ε_κ = 0, contradicting '0 < ε_κ' in Definitions 4.5(3) and 7.7, so the AIP comparison (Theorems 4.8 and 7.14) is stated only over the ordinary locus for such weights. Checked on the page images. This correction alone does not validate the printed analytic radius (E3), nor identify the scalar pro-p norm with all AIP coordinates.

issues.locator: Definition 2.2.1(iv) and Remark 2.2.2, pp. 10–11 (rendered); arXiv v3 only
issues.correction: Define the strict-Iwahori level by the full-level tower quotient by the inverse image of the diagonal torus. A moduli description needs enough ordered symplectic line data to have that stabilizer, not only g pairwise-disjoint order-p subgroups.
issues.reason: For g=1 a single order-p subgroup is one line in F_p². Its stabilizer is a Borel, which contains nontrivial unipotents and is strictly larger than the diagonal torus. Under the source row convention the matrix [1,0;1,1] fixes the first row line and is not diagonal. The displayed block-diagonal stabilizer assertion therefore fails already in genus one. For larger g, pairwise disjointness also does not assert joint independence or isotropy.

issues.correction: The unit ball for the displayed analytic Gauss norm requires integral bounds on the analytic extension to each C_p-disc, equivalently on all scaled coefficients. Pointwise values on Z_p^n alone do not give that lattice.
issues.reason: Take r=1,n=1,B=C_p and an odd prime p. On pZ_p set f(x)=((x/p)^p−x/p)/p and set f=0 on each other residue class. Thus the stated pointwise lattice is larger than the analytic Gauss unit ball.

issues.locator: §8, 'PEL data' and 'PEL Shimura varieties', pp. 87–88 (2017 revision)
issues.printed: The source deduces SV3 from nontriviality of h and simplicity of G^ad. It also asserts that (G, X) meets SV1–4.
issues.correction: SV3 holds only when the projection of h to every ℚ-simple factor of G^ad is nontrivial. For a simple PEL datum of type (A) whose hermitian form is definite at every real place (signature (n, 0) everywhere with n ≥ 2), h(ℂ^×) is central, its projection to the ℚ-simple group G^ad = PU is trivial and G^ad(ℝ) is compact, so SV3 fails and (G, X) is not a Shimura datum (X is a point). Rank n=1 is a torus: its adjoint group is trivial and SV3 is vacuous. This finding concerns the September 2017 author revision, not a verified assertion about the 2005 publication.
issues.reason: For signature (n,0) everywhere, h acts through the centre, so its adjoint projection is trivial although the adjoint group is nontrivial for n≥2. Nontriviality of h itself cannot establish the required nontrivial adjoint projection on every rational simple factor.

issues.locator: Proposition 2.3.4.2, pp.269–271 (May 2008 thesis); definition of LNSch/S₀, p.148
issues.printed: The étaleness equivalence is stated for any base morphism with locally free cotangent sheaf, without a local finite-presentation assumption.
issues.correction: Require S → M_H locally of finite presentation in the converse étaleness criterion. The universal KS isomorphism and dimension formula are unchanged.
issues.reason: Work over a number field E on a nonempty smooth scheme presentation M of the generic moduli space. Set S=M×_E Ebar for an algebraic closure of E. The projection is flat and its relative differentials vanish since Ebar/E is algebraic separable. Base change of the universal KS isomorphism therefore gives the stated KS isomorphism over S, and Ω¹_{S/E} is locally free. The projection is not locally of finite presentation: a fibre at a closed point contains spectra of infinite algebraic field extensions. It is consequently not étale. Locally noetherian S is allowed by the thesis convention. This concerns only the read 2008 thesis, not an assertion about the unread 2013 book.

issues.locator: Proposition 11.2.24, statement, p. 378, author copy courbe.pdf (16 avril 2017); page image checked
issues.printed: The source asserts that completion ϕ-Mod_{E†} −→ ϕ-Mod_ℰ is an equivalence of categories, and therefore applies Dieudonné-Manin classification to ϕ-Mod_{E†}.
issues.correction: Only a filtration descends (Kedlaya [45] Prop. 5.11): every (V, ϕ) ∈ ϕ-Mod_{E†} has a unique filtration by saturated sub-ϕ-modules with isoclinic graded pieces of strictly decreasing Dieudonné–Manin slopes (each a direct sum of E†(λ) when F is algebraically closed). The completion functor is essentially surjective and an equivalence on isoclinic objects, but not fully faithful, and ϕ-modules over E† are not in general direct sums of E†(λ).
issues.reason: Choose c of absolute value greater than one. In the rank-two example F(e₁)=e₁+[c]e₂ and F(e₂)=πe₂, the completed fixed vector uses y=Σ_(k≥0)π^k[c^(q^k)]. This solves y−πF(y)=[c] in the π-adic completion but fails every positive-radius overconvergence bound. Thus completion adds a fixed vector, and an integral endomorphism of determinant π cannot satisfy the claimed invariant descent. The matrix equation for a fixed vector is X=A F(X); applying the source’s argument requires the integral inverse of A.

issues.locator: §3.2, Proposition 3.3 and its proof, pp. 35–36 (Numdam PDF pages 32–33)
issues.printed: Proposition 3.3 assumes that each element of U/U∩F^× acts without fixed points on D^×\G^D(A^f). It claims that M_∞(U) and M⁺_∞(U) are free over Λ′_𝒪, with rank rank_𝒪 eH⁰(X(U⁰_1), 𝒪) times the order of the torsion subgroup of G(U). The proof says it suffices to establish this before applying e.
issues.correction: The argument shows that the Pontryagin dual of eH⁰(X(U_a), K/𝒪) is projective over 𝒪[G(U_a)] and that M_∞(U), M⁺_∞(U) are projective over 𝒪[[G(U)]], hence free over Λ′_𝒪, of rank rank_𝒪(M_∞(U) ⊗_{Λ′_𝒪} 𝒪). The stated rank, and freeness over 𝒪[G(U_a)], need in addition that the ordinary parts have equal 𝒪-rank on the factors of 𝒪[G(U_a)] belonging to the different characters of the prime-to-p torsion of G(U_a).
issues.reason: e is an 𝒪[G(U_a)]-linear idempotent on the free 𝒪[G(U_a)]-module dual to H⁰(X(U_a), K/𝒪), so the dual of the e-part is a direct summand, i.e. projective. 𝒪[G(U_a)] is a product of local rings indexed by the (Galois orbits of) characters of the prime-to-p part of G(U_a), and a projective module is free of the stated rank only if its ranks on these factors agree; the proof's coinvariant computation sees only the trivial character. The components correspond to nearly ordinary forms with different tame characters at p, whose dimensions the argument does not compare. Corollary 3.4 and Lemmas 3.10 and 3.19 use only freeness over Λ′_𝒪, which the argument does give.

issues.locator: II.4.1, p. 17 (arXiv v1); checked on the page image
issues.printed: The source claims that any elliptic curve E over F having bad semi-stable reduction admits some q for which an isomorphism E ≃ Eq exists over F.
issues.correction: This holds iff E has split multiplicative reduction. If the reduction is non-split multiplicative, E is the quadratic twist of E_q by the unramified quadratic character, isomorphic to E_q only over the unramified quadratic extension of F.
issues.reason: E_q has split multiplicative reduction (its reduction y² + xy = x³ has node tangents y = 0 and y = −x, both rational), and the reduction type of the minimal model is an isomorphism invariant. For example 15a1 over Q_3 has non-split multiplicative reduction (a_3 = −1, point count mod 3), so it is isomorphic over Q_3 to no E_q. The conclusion of II.4 (V semistable) survives, since the twist is by an unramified character (PadicHodgeTheory:R06.6/multiplicative-reduction-elliptic-curves (b)).

issues.locator: II.4.3, p. 18 (arXiv v1); checked on the page image
issues.printed: The source names logp(q^(0)/p^{vp(q^(0))}) the ℓ-invariant of V and asserts that this p-adic number is attached canonically to V.
issues.correction: The isomorphism invariant of V is log_p(q)/v_p(q) (with log_p(p) = 0, equal to log_p(q/p^{v_p(q)})/v_p(q)), the Mazur–Tate–Teitelbaum L-invariant; log_p(q/p^{v_p(q)}) itself depends on q, not only on V.
issues.reason: E_q and E_{q²} are isogenous (x ↦ x² on F̄^×), so V_p(E_q) ≅ V_p(E_{q²}), but log_p(q²/p^{2v_p(q)}) = 2 log_p(q/p^{v_p(q)}). In D_st(V) the rescaling y ↦ ay (and hence N(y) ↦ aN(y)) keeps only the ratio of log_p(q) to v_p(q) (PadicHodgeTheory:R06.6/tate-curve-l-invariant).

issues.locator: II.5.1, p. 19 (arXiv v1); checked on the page image
issues.printed: For an abelian variety A, the source asserts Hom_{G_K}(T_pA, Z_p(1)) ≃ H^1_ét(A_K̄, Z_p).
issues.correction: Hom_{Z_p}(T_pA, Z_p) ≃ H^1_ét(A_K̄, Z_p), equivalently Hom_{Z_p}(T_pA, Z_p(1)) ≃ H^1_ét(A_K̄, Z_p(1)).
issues.reason: For an elliptic curve E, Hom_{Z_p}(T_pE, Z_p(1)) ≅ T_pE by the Weil pairing and has determinant Z_p(1), while H^1_ét(E_K̄, Z_p) = Hom(T_pE, Z_p) has determinant Z_p(−1); their Hodge–Tate weights are {0, 1} and {0, −1}. Read literally, Hom_{G_K} (G_K-equivariant maps) would be a finite group.

issues.locator: §8.3, last paragraph, pp. 125–126 (2009 preliminary version); checked on the page image
issues.printed: The source assigns D*st(Vp(Eq)) a classifying parameter cq ∈ Q×p using its earlier account of crystalline classes in H1(GQp, Qp(1)). It claims that computing directly in Bst with contravariant functors yields cq = −λ(q).
issues.correction: c_q = −λ(q)/ord_p(q), an element of Q_p that can be 0 (for q = p when λ(p) = 0).
issues.reason: By Brinon–Conrad's own proof of Proposition 8.3.8 (p. 124) c is intrinsic to D, hence an isomorphism invariant of V_p(E_q). E_q and E_{q²} are isogenous, so V_p(E_q) ≅ V_p(E_{q²}), whereas −λ(q²) = −2λ(q). Directly: with their N = v_0·d/dX (p. 139) the covariant D_st(V_p(E_q)) has N(y) = −ord_p(q)x and Fil^0 = Q_p(y + λ(q)x); in the dual, e_2 = x^*, e_1 = N(e_2) = ord_p(q)y^* and Fil^1 = Q_p(x^* − λ(q)y^*) = Q_p(ce_1 + e_2) with c = −λ(q)/ord_p(q).

issues.locator: Introduction, p. 3 (arXiv v1)
issues.printed: For an Abelian variety A over a local field K, the theorem claims equivalence of crystallinity of Tp (A) and good reduction of A. It credits the “only if” implication to J.-M.Fontaine [Fo-BT] and attributes the “if” implication to a conjecture of J.-M.Fontaine in [Fo-MGF].
issues.correction: Swap "if" and "only if": the "if" part (good reduction ⇒ T_p(A) crystalline) is Fontaine's; the "only if" part (crystalline ⇒ good reduction) was conjectured in [Fo-MGF] and proved there when e < p − 1.
issues.reason: In "T_p(A) is crystalline if A has good reduction" the known direction is good ⇒ crystalline, which is Fontaine's work on p-divisible groups (Brinon–Conrad p. 84 credit Fontaine for linking Grothendieck's criterion to crystallinity), and the next sentence says "The conjecture was proved in [Fo-MGF] if the ramification index of K is less then p − 1", which only makes sense for the converse, the new result of the paper.

issues.locator: §2, p. 9 and p. 12 (arXiv v2); checked on the page images
issues.printed: On p. 9, the source requires a nilpotent endomorphism N of V with ρ(σ)Nρ(σ)^{−1} = N𝔭^{n(σ)}N. It specifies n : W(F̄_𝔭/F_𝔭) → Z as the canonical surjection taking geometric Frobenius … to 1. On p. 12 it requires σN = N𝔭^{n(σ)}Nσ, citing φN = pNφ.
issues.correction: ρ(σ)Nρ(σ)^{−1} = N𝔭^{−n(σ)}N, and σN = N𝔭^{−n(σ)}Nσ since Nφ = pφN.
issues.reason: Fontaine's B_st satisfies Nφ = pφN (on u = log[p̃]: N(φu) = −p = pφ(Nu)), which gives F N F^{−1} = N𝔭^{−1}N for a geometric Frobenius F; this is Deligne's relation and the one forced by Grothendieck's ℓ-adic monodromy theorem. Saito's own Theorem 2 (p. 13: weight w − 2 on ker N, w on coker N; N: Gr_1^W(1) ≅ Gr_{−1}^W) also requires F N F^{−1} = N𝔭^{−1}N. The two printed relations are reversed consistently, so the construction and the theorems are unaffected.

issues.reviewReason: Rejected. Théorème I.3.3(2), p.8, requires that B^{†,pr}_{rig,K} ⊗ D_r has a basis contained in φ(D_r). issues.locator: Remark 3.35, published printed p. 130 / PDF 31; same assertion in arXiv v2 PDF 22.
issues.printed: The source claims there is exactly one homomorphism Q(G) → C_p.
issues.correction: A continuous character integral extends to a localization only when every inverted element has unit image. A pseudomeasure can instead be evaluated by (3-11) once one Dirac difference has nonzero character value. It does not generally extend to all of Q(G).
issues.reason: Take p=3, G=ℤ₃ with generator γ, and R=ℤ₃[[T]] with [γ]=1+T. The continuous nontrivial character χ(x)=4^x gives the convergent evaluation T↦3. The nonzero regular series T−3 maps to zero, so no extension to Q(R) exists: its inverse would force 0=1. This example meets the remark’s nontrivial-character hypothesis. Separately, augmentation T↦0 kills T. The generic obstruction node and the two polynomial test cases isolate the same algebraic failure. Ordered by inclusion of F, these ℓ_F are eventually equal to ℓ at every fixed vector. Hence the net is Cauchy for pointwise convergence, but any weak limit would equal the discontinuous ℓ and could not belong to B*. This concerns completeness for nets, not a claim that every pointwise Cauchy sequence fails. The campaign already rejects unrestricted weak completeness.

Yet (1−3)ζ(−1)=1/6 and (1−27)ζ(−3)=−13/60, whose difference is 23/60 and has 3-adic valuation −1, not at least 1. Thus the blanket congruence, explicitly applied to the Riemann zeta function in the next sentence, is false. Clearing by [2]−[1] multiplies these two values by 2²−1 and 2⁴−1; the difference becomes 15/4, of valuation 1, as expected from the integral smoothed measure. No counterexample to the interpolation theorems or correctly qualified Kummer congruences is claimed. Arithmetic repairs belong to DirichletPadicLFunctions; this finding records the shared source distinction between bounded measures and pseudomeasures.

issues.reason: Take L = ℚ_p(√p), ϖ = √p, M = Λ/(ϖ). The prime (ϖ) has height one, and the length of M at (ϖ) is 1. Pseudo-isomorphism (finite kernel and cokernel) preserves lengths at height-one primes. Λ/(p^n) = Λ/(ϖ^{2n}) has length 2n at (ϖ), Λ/(f^m) with f distinguished has length 0 there, and Λ^r is not torsion. So M is not pseudo-isomorphic to any module of the printed form, and (p^n) cannot equal (ϖ) = Ch_Λ(M). The cited Washington Theorem 13.12 is over ℤ_p⟦T⟧. issues.locator: Lemma 2.4 (TeX label l:size), proof, displays (27) and (28) and the sentences after them, arXiv:2010.00657v3 PDF p. 17 (statement on PDF p. 16). The authors' copy dated 15 February 2022, an earlier text, has the same statement, the same two displays and the same quoted sentence on its PDF pp. 16–17 ((27) on p. 16, the sentence on p. 17); its proof does not write out the step for PIDs, and its sentence after (28) ends ‘in the denominator’.
issues.printed: The proof claims that multiplying by the non-zerodivisor det(A) identifies the numerator space isomorphically with the denominator space.
issues.correction: det(A) is by hypothesis a non-zerodivisor of B, not of the product B′ = ∏ D_i, and the step needs it on B′. It is one whenever no factor D_i is a finite field (so for products of DVRs, and in every use in the paper): B ∩ D_i has finite index in the infinite ring D_i, hence is nonzero, and a vanishing component x_i = 0 would give x·(B ∩ D_i) = 0. With a finite-field factor the step can fail, but the lemma is still true: let K = B ∩ ∏_{D_i finite} D_i, a finite ideal of B. Multiplication by x is injective, hence bijective, on K, so A is bijective on K^m (adjugate), and therefore B^m/AB^m ≅ (B/K)^m/A(B/K)^m and B/xB ≅ (B/K)/x(B/K). The ring B/K is a finite-index subring of the product of the infinite factors, the image of x is a non-zerodivisor of it (if xy ∈ K then xy = xk with k ∈ K, so y = k), and the printed argument applies to B/K.
issues.reason: Take B = {(a, a mod p) : a ∈ Z} inside B′ = Z × F_p, and x = (p, 0). The subring has index p and is isomorphic to Z. For the 1×1 presentation A = (x), x is a non-zerodivisor of B and B/xB has p elements, although x annihilates (0,1) in B′. Here B′/xB′ has p² elements, B′/B has p elements, and xB′ = xB = pZ × 0. Consequently the multiplier map B′/B → xB′/xB is zero and cannot be an isomorphism; the ratios in (27) and (28) are p. The subsequent cancellation of det(A) on the ambient module in the argument for (28) has the same missing hypothesis. Fields are PIDs, so the example satisfies Lemma 2.4 as stated. Its conclusion remains true, as does the general statement after the finite-ideal reduction in the correction. If fields are excluded from the intended PID convention, the ambient non-zerodivisor property is valid but still requires its own argument. The middle ratio in (27) also has an extra cardinality marker inside its denominator; that separate typographical slip has no mathematical effect.

issues.locator: §8.4, proof of Lemma 8.20, p. 37 (arXiv v4); published Lemma 8.20, p. 1775
issues.printed: The proof asserts the existence of a natural injection compatible as n varies.
issues.correction: The map Δ_n(N) → Δ(N) need not be injective. For p odd the lemma holds because the transition maps Δ_{n+1}(N) → Δ_n(N) are injective (η ≡ 1 mod pⁿN and η² ≡ 1 mod p^{n+1} force η ≡ 1 mod p^{n+1}) and the orders are bounded; for p = 2 use Δ_∞(N) := ker(Δ(p^∞N) → 𝒪_p^×), which is finite and suffices for Proposition 8.21(4).
issues.reason: For F=ℚ(√5), ε²=ε+1, U=±ε^ℤ and U⁺=ε^{2ℤ}. Modulo 4, ε has order 6 and −1 is not a power of ε, so U_4=ε^{6ℤ}. Modulo the inert prime 7, ε has order 16 and ε^8=−1, hence U_7⁺=ε^{16ℤ} and U_28=ε^{48ℤ}. Thus Δ_1(4)=ε^{16ℤ}/ε^{96ℤ} → Δ(4)=ε^{2ℤ}/ε^{12ℤ} has order-two kernel generated by ε^48 (η=ε^24∈U_4 has η≡−1 mod7). This counterexample is at an odd inert prime. It does not refute eventual stabilization; the p=2 transition/stabilization issue is an unproved claim here, not a checked numerical counterexample.

issues.printed: The source defines (A ⊗Fp B)+ as the integral closure, inside A ⊗Fp B, of A+ ⊗Fp B +. It calls (A ⊗Fp B, (A ⊗Fp B)+ ) a Huber pair and asserts that some m, n ≥ 1 make both f ($)m /g($0 ) and g($0 )n /f ($) elements of A◦ .
issues.correction: With the topology defined by the ring of definition D_{m,n} = (A° ⊗ B°)[ϖ^m/ϖ', ϖ'^n/ϖ], the plus ring must be taken as the integral closure of the image of (A⁺ ⊗ B⁺)[ϖ^m/ϖ', ϖ'^n/ϖ] (then completed); the charts then are the rational subsets {|ϖ^m| ≤ |ϖ'|, |ϖ'^n| ≤ |ϖ|}, and a pair of maps into (R, R⁺) factors through the (m, n)-chart iff f(ϖ)^m/g(ϖ') and g(ϖ')^n/f(ϖ) lie in R⁺ (the printed 'A◦' should read R⁺, or at least R◦). The lemma itself (existence and perfectoidness of the absolute product) is unaffected.
issues.reason: A ring of integral elements must be open (Berkeley Definition 2.2.12). For A = B = 𝔽_p((t^{1/p^∞})), ϖ = t, ϖ' = s, every open subring contains (t ⊗ 1)^k (t^m ⊗ s^{-1})^j for some k and all j, but this element is not integral over the image of A° ⊗ B°: an integral equation, multiplied by (1 ⊗ s)^{jN}, gives t^{(k+mj)N} ⊗ 1 ∈ (1 ⊗ s^j)(A° ⊗ B°), which fails in A° ⊗_{𝔽_p} (B°/s^j), a free A°-module with basis containing 1. So the integral closure of A⁺ ⊗ B⁺ is not open and the printed pair is not a Huber pair. The 'A◦' is a slip for the target ring R.

issues.reason: Let K be the completion of ℚ̆_p(μ_{p^∞}) (ℚ̆_p the completion of the maximal unramified extension of ℚ_p; residue field 𝔽̄_p) and L = K(p^{1/ℓ}) for a prime ℓ ∤ p(p − 1): a cyclic extension of degree ℓ of perfectoid fields with trivial residue extension. Then L ⊗̂_K L ≅ L^ℓ with ring of integral elements (L°)^ℓ, but L° ⊗_{K°} L° → (L°)^ℓ is injective and not surjective: surjectivity would make K° → L° a Galois extension of rings, so L° would be free of rank ℓ over K°, whereas L°/𝔪_K L° = L°/𝔪_L (the value group of K is dense) is the residue field, of dimension 1. The image contains ϖ(L°)^ℓ (almost purity for perfectoid fields), so it is open, hence complete, and it is not integrally closed (it misses the idempotents of L^ℓ). So (L ⊗̂ L, L° ⊗̂ L°) is not a perfectoid pair and the asserted identification of D⁺ fails; the ring statement is unaffected.

issues.locator: §4, Proposition 4.4 and its proof, pp. 20–21 (arXiv:1709.07343v4)
issues.printed: The source characterizes a perfectoid X as κ-small precisely when it has fewer than κ open affinoids U = Spa(A, A+ ) covering it, each with A of cardinality below κ. It concludes closure of κ-small perfectoid spaces under finite products. The proof asserts that such a cover also forces the cardinality of |X| below κ.
issues.correction: The 'if' direction needs a uniform bound: if X has a cover by fewer than κ open affinoids Spa(A_j, A_j⁺) with sup_j #A_j < κ (automatic for finite covers, for covers indexed by fewer than cf κ sets, and for every cover when κ is regular), then X is κ-small; without the uniform bound only 'every open affinoid ring has cardinality < κ' follows. Likewise fibre products X ×_Z Y are κ-small when X and Y are uniformly κ-small (κ'-small for one κ' < κ), in particular when they are quasicompact, but not in general.
issues.reason: For the specific construction κ = κ(ω₁) in the proof of Lemma 4.1, κ has cofinality ω₁ and exceeds ω₁, hence is singular. Being a supremum of a µ-sequence alone does not show singularity for every possible ordinal µ. With perfectoid fields K_α (α < ω₁), #K_α < κ cofinal in κ (completed perfections of F_p((t^{1/p^∞}))(x_β : β < λ_α) for the Gauss norm), the disjoint union of the perfectoid discs over the K_α is covered by ω₁ < κ affinoids with rings of cardinality < κ but has at least κ points (the classical points of each disc), so it is not κ-small. Similarly X = ⊔_{α<ω₁} Spa(K_α, K_α°), with the K_α ⊇ L transcendental over a perfectoid field L, is κ-small (ℵ₁ points, every open affinoid a finite union of components), but X ×_{Spa L} X is not: Spa(K_α ⊗̂_L K_α) has at least λ_α points, distinguished by |x_β ⊗ 1 − 1 ⊗ x_β|.

issues.locator: Proofs of Theorem 5.3 (p. 28) and Theorem 5.8 (p. 31), first paragraph, arXiv v2
issues.printed: Invoking Lemma 5.2, the proof takes a G-clean open set U_x ⊆ |X|^h around π(x). It then defines Ũ_x = π^{-1}(U_x) and claims that this is open and G-clean around x, with \\overline{\\{x\\}} contained in it.
issues.correction: Ũ_x is G-clean at x only if the stabilizer of π(x) in G equals the stabilizer H_x of x, i.e. π(xg) ≠ π(x) for g ∉ H_x. This holds when π is injective on rank-one points, for instance when |X| is taut; the theorems are recorded with this hypothesis.
issues.reason: A G-clean U_x at π(x) is stable under Stab_G(π(x)) ⊇ H_x; for g ∈ Stab_G(π(x)) ∖ H_x, Ũ_x g = Ũ_x, so Ũ_x ∩ Ũ_x g ≠ ∅. The source's own footnote 7 says it is not clear that π^{-1}(π(x)) is the closure of {x}, so two points of one orbit may have the same image.

issues.reviewReason: Read HJ v2 pp. 28 and 31. U_x ⊆ |X|^h is G-clean at π(x), so π⁻¹(U_x) is stable under Stab_G(π(x)), which can be larger than H_x when π identifies two rank-one points of one orbit; then π⁻¹(U_x) meets its own translates and is not G-clean at x. issues.reviewReason: In characteristic p, BS22 Example 8.3 identifies perfectoidization with the colimit perfection, which need not be ϖ-adically separated. Example: K a perfectoid field of characteristic p, (R, R⁺) = (K⟨T^{1/p^∞}⟩, K°⟨T^{1/p^∞}⟩), S = R/(T) with S⁺ the integral closure of the image of R⁺ (an integral map R⁺ → S⁺). The completion in the correction is needed; maps to perfectoid pairs still factor uniquely.
