At most one ℓ has s_ℓ′ = s (Case 2a), and g has at most three cycles longer than n/4, so some ℓ has s_ℓ′ < s and only cycles of length ≤ n/4 in X_ℓ outside its own cycle; their parts k are ≤ n/4 and the printed argument applies. In Case 3 argue the same way with four parts ℓ ∈ ρ ∩ [n^{1−2α}, n/log n] not divisible by s, which a strengthened E₅ supplies with the same probability bound as Lemma 12.6.

issues.locator: §4.1, the category MF_𝒪, p. 965 (also in arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The source specifies Frob_p^{−1} ⊗ 1-linearity for Φ^i : Fil^i M → M. For M ∈ MF_𝒪, it gives the decompositions Fil^i M = ∏_τ Fil^i M_τ; Φ^i = ∏_τ Φ^i_τ. The component maps are Φ^i_τ : Fil^i M_τ → M_{τ∘Frob_p^{−1}}.
issues.correction: Φ^i_τ : Fil^i M_τ → M_{τ∘Frob_p} (or else make Φ^i Frob_p ⊗ 1-semilinear)
issues.reason: On M_τ = M ⊗_{𝒪_{F_v}⊗𝒪, τ⊗1} 𝒪 the element a ⊗ 1 acts as τ(a). If Φ((a⊗1)m) = (Frob_p^{−1}(a)⊗1)Φ(m) and m ∈ M_τ, then (b⊗1)Φ(m) = τ(Frob_p(b))Φ(m), so Φ(M_τ) ⊂ M_{τ∘Frob_p}; for M = 𝒪_{F_v} ⊗ 𝒪 = ∏_σ 𝒪 the map Frob_p^{−1} ⊗ 1 moves the σ-coordinate to the σ∘Frob_p-coordinate. The components Φ^i_τ are used only to define M(a), where the direction plays no role.

issues.locator: §4.3, proof of Theorem 4.3.3, p. 973 (also in arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The proof deduces H^d(X̃_K̃, 𝒱_λ̃)_𝔪̃[ϖ] = 0 from H^{d−1}(X̃_K̃, 𝒱_λ̃/ϖ) = 0. It also claims that the cokernel of H^d(X̃_K̃, 𝒱_λ̃)_𝔪̃ → H^d(∂X̃_K̃, 𝒱_λ̃)_𝔪̃ embeds in H^{d+1}_c(X̃_K̃, 𝒱_λ̃) = 0.
issues.reason: The result of [CS19] quoted two lines earlier gives vanishing only after localization at 𝔪̃ (H^i(X̃_K̃, 𝒱_λ̃/ϖ)_𝔪̃ = 0 for i < d, H^i_c(X̃_K̃, 𝒱_λ̃/ϖ)_𝔪̃ = 0 for i > d), and every other group in the argument is localized. The localized H^{d+1}_c(X̃_K̃, 𝒱_λ̃)_𝔪̃ vanishes by Nakayama, since its reduction mod ϖ injects into H^{d+1}_c(X̃_K̃, 𝒱_λ̃/ϖ)_𝔪̃ = 0.

issues.locator: §4.3, proof of Lemma 4.3.6, criterion (4.3.7), pp. 974–975 (also in arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The proof gives a sufficient criterion for CTG: a weight μ̃ ∈ (ℤ^{2n}_+)^{Hom(F⁺,E)} that is dominant qualifies if every w ∈ W^P satisfies (4.3.7) Σ_{i=1}^n (μ_{w,τ̃,i} − μ_{w,τ̃c,i}) ≠ Σ_{i=1}^n (μ_{w,τ̃_0,i} − μ_{w,τ̃_0c,i}).
issues.reason: Since λ^∨_{σ,i} = −λ_{σ,n+1−i} (§2.2.1), a w violating CTG (Definition 4.3.5) has λ_{w,σ,i} + λ_{w,σc,n+1−i} = i_0 for all σ and i, hence Σ_i(λ_{w,σ,i} + λ_{w,σc,i}) = n·i_0 for every σ, so the '+' inequality implies CTG. With '−', the dictionary (2.2.2) makes Σ_i(μ_{w,τ̃,i} − μ_{w,τ̃c,i}) the sum of all 2n entries of w(μ̃_τ + ρ_τ) − ρ_τ, i.e. of μ̃_τ, for every w, and the printed criterion is false: for n = 1, [F⁺ : Q] = 2, μ̃_{τ_0} = (1, 1), μ̃_τ = (0, 0) it holds for all w (2 ≠ 0), but for w = 1 one gets μ_{τ̃_0} = 1, μ_{τ̃_0c} = −1, μ_{τ̃} = μ_{τ̃c} = 0, so λ_{w,σ} − λ^∨_{w,σc} = (0) for every σ and μ̃ is not CTG. With '+', raising λ̃_{τ_0,1} by a moves the right-hand side by ±a for each of the finitely many w, so the proof's last sentence goes through and Lemma 4.3.6 stands.

issues.reviewReason: The minus sign in (4.3.7) on ACC 974 gives the total of the unitary row, not the conjugate paired-sum test. For n=1 and two embeddings, unitary rows (1,1) and (0,0) satisfy the printed inequality for every shuffle, but the identity shuffle has paired sums zero at both embeddings and is not CTG. Replacing minus by plus gives the stated sufficient criterion: failure of CTG would force all those sums to equal n times the same integer. The finite-shuffle perturbation argument then works.

issues.locator: §4.4, Proposition 4.4.6(c), pp. 979–980 (also in arXiv v2)
issues.printed: Condition (6) requires a maximal non-Eisenstein ideal 𝔪 ⊂ T^S with decomposed generic ρ̄_𝔪̃. Part (c) asserts, at every place v|v̄ of F, the existence of N̄ ∈ MF_k such that ρ̄_𝔪̃|_{G_{F_v}} ≅ G(N̄) and FL_τ(N̄) = {−λ_{τc,n} + 2n − 1, …, −λ_{τc,1} + n, λ_{τ,1} + (n − 1), …, λ_{τ,n}}.
issues.correction: add the hypothesis A(K, λ, q, m) ≠ 0, i.e. that 𝔪 is in the support of H^q(X_K, 𝒱_λ/ϖ^m)
issues.reason: Conclusion (c) concerns only ρ̄_𝔪̃, and 𝔪 is an arbitrary non-Eisenstein maximal ideal of the abstract Hecke algebra T^S, so ρ̄_𝔪 can be any absolutely irreducible representation unramified outside S with ρ̄_𝔪̃ decomposed generic, including one that is not Fontaine–Laffaille with these weights at v; for such 𝔪, A(K, λ, q, m) = 0, (a) and (b) hold vacuously and (c) fails. The proof reads (c) off a lattice in Ã^{2n}, which needs Ã ≠ 0, and A ≠ 0 forces this because T̃^S → Ã → A/J_0 is a ring map with J_0 nilpotent. Proposition 4.3.4, by contrast, assumes 𝔪 in the support. Corollary 4.4.8 and Theorem 4.5.1 are unaffected: there 𝔪 ⊂ T^S(K, λ) is in the support of the cohomology, and (c) does not depend on q.

issues.reason: For n = 1 the lemma's weight is λ_τ = (−M) for τ ∈ Ĩ_p and λ_τ = (0) for τc ∈ Ĩ_p, and (3)(c) says λ_{w_i} = λ(a_i); then λ(a_i)_τ − λ(a_i)^∨_{τc} = λ(a_i)_τ + λ(a_i)_{τc} = −M + 2a_i for every τ, which is exactly what Definition 4.3.5 forbids, so λ̃_i is not CTG. No other choice helps: for n = 1, part (2) of the lemma (in Proposition 5.4.13, triviality of 𝒱_λ on a finite-index subgroup of 𝒪_F^×) forces λ_τ + λ_{τc} to be independent of τ, and then λ_{w_i} = λ(a_i) is again pure. issues.locator: §5.4, proof of Lemma 5.4.8, the verification that λ̃_i is CTG, p. 1017 (also in arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The proof says it suffices, for every τ ∈ Hom(F^+, E) and w ∈ W^P_v̄, to establish that [w(λ̃_i + ρ) − ρ]_{τ,j} + [w(λ̃_i + ρ) − ρ]_{τ,2n+1−j} = w(λ̃_i + ρ)_{τ,j} + w(λ̃_i + ρ)_{τ,2n+1−j} depends on j over 1 ≤ j ≤ n.
issues.correction: It suffices to show that μ̃_{τ,n+j} − μ̃_{τ,j} (1 ≤ j ≤ n) is not independent of j, for μ̃ = w(λ̃_i + ρ) − ρ; equivalently, that the 2n entries of λ̃_i + ρ cannot be split into two n-element sets, one a translate of the other. The 'look modulo M' argument proves this for n ≥ 2 when applied to differences instead of sums: since 2a_i ≡ M/4 mod M, a difference between the two blocks of λ̃(a_i) + ρ is ≡ ±M/4 up to 2n − 1 modulo M, and these are pairwise distinct; a difference within a block is ≡ 0 up to 2n − 1; and a difference within the first block (of size < nM) never equals one within the second (a nonzero multiple of nM up to 2n − 1). So a translate-split would pair the 2n entries inside one block of n entries, which is impossible. (The multiset I′ should likewise be formed from the entries of λ̃(a_i), which is what I′_1, I′_2, I′_3 list.)
issues.reason: By Definition 4.3.5 and λ^∨_{τ,i} = −λ_{τ,n+1−i}, CTG says that no λ_w satisfies λ_{w,τ,i} + λ_{w,τc,n+1−i} = i_0 for all τ and i, and under (2.2.2) this sum is μ̃_{τ,n+i} − μ̃_{τ,i}. The printed quantity μ̃_{τ,j} + μ̃_{τ,2n+1−j} equals λ_{w,τ̃,n+1−j} − λ_{w,τ̃c,n+1−j}, a different condition, and for n ≥ 3 the multiplicity criterion does not imply CTG: entries 0, 1, 3, 10, 11, 13 (n = 3) have no pair-sum of multiplicity 3, yet split as {0, 1, 3} and {10, 11, 13} = {0, 1, 3} + 10, which makes λ_w pure. (For n = 2 the two conditions coincide.) The lemma's conclusion survives for n ≥ 2 by the repaired argument, and a direct computation for 2 ≤ n ≤ 7 and several p agrees.

issues.locator: §6.5.12, proof of Theorem 6.1.1, choice of E_a, E_b, E_c, p. 1073; the same example in §6.6.10, p. 1083 (also in arXiv v2)
issues.printed: The source requires rational primes under V_0 ∪ V_1 ∪ V_2 to split in E_a · E_b · E_c, and p to be unramified in E_a · E_b · E_c. It proposes any admissible E_a followed by E_b = ℚ(√−p_b), choosing a prime p_b subject to a congruence beginning p_b ≡ 1.
issues.correction: also require p_b ≡ −1 mod l and p_c ≡ −1 mod l for every rational prime l below V_0 ∪ V_1 ∪ V_2 (such l are odd and prime to p, so this is compatible with the other congruences by the Chinese remainder theorem), and, in the Fontaine–Laffaille case, p_b ≠ p
issues.reason: An odd prime l ∤ p_b splits in ℚ(√−p_b) if and only if −p_b is a square mod l. The listed congruences force this only for the primes in the third condition; nothing in the example makes the primes below V_0 ∪ V_1 ∪ V_2 split in E_b or E_c, and they must, for E to be V_0 ∪ V_1 ∪ V_2-split as the proof then asserts. Nothing excludes p_b = p either, which would ramify p in E_b, against the first condition. Fields with the listed properties do exist, so only the example is incomplete.

issues.locator: Theorem 1.4, p. 1241, and its proof in the final paragraph of §4 (after Remark 4.4), p. 1274. The cited result is ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2(4): Ann. of Math. 197 (2023), p. 1030, and arXiv:1812.09999v1, p. 109. The v1 numbering (Definition 6.2.28) is the one Qian cites.; finding scoped to the NSF Springer online-first copy; journal pages are a concordance, not printed in that PDF; physical NSF PDF pages 3 and 36.
issues.printed: Theorem 1.4 (p. 1241) takes an odd prime l. Its proof (p. 1274) asserts that the corresponding properties of r̄ imply every required condition other than decomposed genericity.
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis l > n to Theorem 1.4. This is the second sentence of condition (4) of ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2; the fourth hypothesis of Theorem 1.4 copies only the first sentence. With l > n added, the proof on p. 1274 works as written. For odd primes l < n with l ∤ n, the paper does not prove Theorem 1.4 (the case l | n is already excluded by the enormity hypothesis). Proving it there would need an ordinary automorphy lifting theorem for such l. Neither ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2 nor its subsequent adequate-image version (Miagkov–Thorne, arXiv:2203.04520v2, Theorem 1.3) provides one: both require p > n.
issues.reason:
**How the proof goes.** On p. 1274, Theorem 1.1 is used to make r̄|G_{F'} ι-ordinarily automorphic, and then ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2 is applied at p = l to ρ = r|G_{F'}. The paper says that conditions (3) and (4) of that theorem, apart from decomposed genericity, "follow from the corresponding conditions of r̄".

**The missing condition.** Condition (4) of ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2 reads: "There exists σ ∈ G_F − G_F(ζ_p) such that ρ̄(σ) is a scalar. We have p > n." This is the published text on p. 1030, and it is the same in arXiv v1, p. 109. The fourth hypothesis of Theorem 1.4 reproduces the first sentence and drops the second. Nothing in the hypotheses of Theorem 1.4 implies l > n:
- The enormity hypothesis excludes only l | n. ACC+ notes after Definition 6.2.29 that ad⁰ contains the scalars when p | n.
- Enormity puts no lower bound on l in terms of n. For l ∤ n, large subgroups such as SL_n(F_{l^r}) with r large are enormous.
- The other hypotheses (ordinarity, decomposed genericity, the scalar element) do not involve n.

**The bound is needed in ACC+.** The bound p > n is not a removable formality. It is used in the proof of Theorem 6.1.2 in §6.6: at the Ihara-avoidance places, n pairwise distinct characters trivial modulo the uniformiser are chosen, and §6.2.15 on level-raising deformations assumes p > n.

**What is affected.** For odd primes l < n with l ∤ n, Theorem 1.4 is asserted without proof. The first such case is n = 4, l = 3. No counterexample is known, and the statement may well be true there. So this is a gap in the range of a stated result, not a false statement.

**What is not affected.** With l > n added, the published argument proves the theorem. Theorem 1.1 is also unaffected: there ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2 is applied at the auxiliary prime l′, which Proposition 4.1 (p. 1269) chooses with l′ > 2ln + 5 > n.

**Defence considered.** The introduction (p. 1241) says Theorem 1.4 is obtained by combining Theorem 1.1 with ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2. One could read that as importing the cited theorem's hypotheses implicitly. This reading does not hold up: Theorem 1.4 lists its hypotheses explicitly, copying conditions (1)–(4) of the cited theorem except for this one sentence, and the proof asserts outright that those conditions follow.

**Version history and later use.** arXiv v1 has the same omission, and there Theorem 1.4 says only "Let l be a prime number". The journal version added "odd" but not l > n. One later paper applies Theorem 1.4 as printed under the sole restriction p ∤ 2n (A'Campo, Rigidity of automorphic Galois representations over CM fields, arXiv:2202.14022v4, Corollary 1.0.5), so it inherits the gap for odd p < n.

issues.printed: On p. 24 of arXiv v1, the proof attributes ordinary automorphy of Symm^{n−1} r_{E,l′}|_{G_{F′}} to its choice of l′, then invokes [ACC+18], Theorem 6.1.2, for automorphy of V_{λ′,t} as a G_{F′}-representation. It next invokes Lemma 3.10 (4), citing v_l(t) < 0 for every v_l | l, in discussing V_{λ,t} ⊗ χ_1^{−1}.
issues.correction:
Hypothesis (5) of ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2 needs a regular algebraic cuspidal π that is ι-ordinary at every place above the prime, in the sense of Geraghty's Definition 5.3. An automorphic lift that is only ordinary as a Galois representation is not enough. So "ordinarily automorphic" has to be defined on the automorphic side, as in the published Definition 1.3 (p. 1241), and both applications of Theorem 6.1.2 need that input.

(i) The auxiliary prime l′. Sym^{n−1} r_{E,l′}|G_{F′} is polarizable and ordinary above l′, because E has good ordinary reduction at l′. Geraghty's Lemma 5.9 then gives ι′-ordinary automorphy (published, p. 1273).

(ii) V_{λ,t}, which is not polarizable. Prove ι-ordinarity directly, as in the published Lemma 4.3.
- Write V_{λ′,t} ≅ r_{l′,ι′}(π) with ι′ compatible with ι, so that V_{λ,t} ≅ r_{l,ι}(π).
- At each v | l we have v(t) < 0, and Lemma 3.12 shows that WD(V_{λ′,t}|G_{F′_v}) is a single Jordan block.
- Varma's bound WD(r_{l′,ι′}(π)|G_{F′_v})^{F-ss} ≺ ι′^{−1}rec(π_v|det|^{(1−n)/2}) compares partial sums of block sizes, and the two sides have the same semisimplification. So rec(π_v|det|^{(1−n)/2}) is also one block, and π_v ≅ Sp_n(ψ_v|·|^{(1−n)/2}) is a twist of Steinberg.
- The labelled Hodge–Tate weights are consecutive, so the automorphic weight is parallel. Geraghty's ordinarity conditions for this Steinberg representation then scale linearly in j, and they reduce to the single condition at j = n on val_l(ι^{−1}ψ_v(ϖ_v)^n) = val_l(ι^{−1}φ_{π,v}(ϖ_v)).
- That condition is fixed by the continuous, hence unit-valued, l-adic character r_{l,ι}(φ_π) = det r_{l,ι}(π)·ε^{n(n−1)/2}, whose Hodge–Tate weights are nλ_τ.

So V_{λ,t} ⊗ χ_1^{−1} is ι-ordinarily automorphic, and hypothesis (5) holds in the proof of Theorem 1.4. The Galois-side ordinarity taken from the companion preprint (v1 Lemma 3.10(4)) is then no longer needed, and the published version drops it. The conclusions "ordinarily automorphic" in the published Theorems 1.1 and 1.4 are to be read as ι-ordinary automorphy in the sense of the revised Definition 1.3.
issues.reason:
In arXiv v1, Definition 1.3 (p. 2) calls r̄ ordinarily automorphic when it has an automorphic lift that is "potentially semistable and ordinary with regular Hodge-Tate weights" at every place above l. This is a condition on the Galois side. Under this definition the last sentence of the proof of Theorem 1.1 (p. 24) is correct: Lemma 3.10(4), from the companion preprint, gives Galois ordinarity of V_{λ,t} when v(t) < 0.

The gap is where this Galois-side notion is used in ACC+ Theorem 6.1.2. Hypothesis (5) of that theorem requires π itself to be ι-ordinary in Geraghty's Hecke-theoretic sense. This happens twice:
- On p. 24, for Sym^{n−1} r_{E,l′} ("ordinarily automorphic by our choice of l′").
- On p. 26, for V_{λ,t} ⊗ χ_1^{−1} in the proof of Theorem 1.4, where only conditions (3) and (4) are checked.

Passing from "automorphic and ordinary at l as a Galois representation" to "π is ι-ordinary" is the converse direction of ordinary local–global compatibility. Geraghty's Lemma 5.9 proves it only for polarizable representations. ACC+ Theorem 5.5.1 and Corollary 5.5.2 give only the opposite direction. The Sym^{n−1} case is polarizable, so a citation repairs it. V_{λ,t} is built from a character of H_0 chosen to break self-duality, so it is not known to be polarizable, and it needs a new argument.

The published version identifies exactly this problem in Remark 4.4 (p. 1274), crediting J. Thorne, and supplies Lemma 4.3. I checked Lemma 4.3 against Varma's Definition 1 and Theorem 1 (arXiv:1411.2520):
- A one-block Galois side forces a one-block automorphic side, because (n) is maximal for the order and the semisimplifications agree.
- For a twist of Steinberg with parallel weight, the conditions for 1 ≤ j ≤ n are proportional to j, so only j = n matters.
- The j = n condition says that the normalised central Hecke eigenvalue is an l-adic unit. That follows from r_{l,ι}(φ_π) being a continuous l-adic character.

Small case: n = 2, F′_v = Q_l, λ_τ = 0, the Tate-curve shape. Here r_{l,ι}(φ_π) has Hodge–Tate weight 0, so φ_π has finite order and ψ_v(l)^2 is a unit. Hence π_v = Sp_2(ψ_v|·|^{−1/2}) has a unit U_l-eigenvalue and is ι-ordinary, consistent with the ordinarity of a Tate curve.

The gap therefore affects only proofs. The published version proves Theorems 1.1 and 1.4 in the stronger, automorphic-side sense. Its new restriction to odd l comes from §2 and is unrelated to this point. The phrase "ordinarily automorphic" on its own does not show where the gap is, so the quotation above cites the sentences that invoke Theorem 6.1.2.

A separate bookkeeping remark on Lemma 4.3 (p. 1273), outside this finding: the paper's normalisations are the geometric Artin map and Hodge–Tate weight −1 for the cyclotomic character, as in the proof of Lemma 3.11. With these, a unit-valued l-adic character with labelled Hodge–Tate weights k_τ satisfies val_l(ι^{−1}φ_v(ϖ_v)) = val_l(∏_τ τ(ϖ_v)^{k_τ}). For example, with n = 1, φ = ‖·‖^{−M} and r = ε^{−M}, both sides equal f_v·M. So the exponent −nλ_τ printed there should carry the sign that matches Geraghty's normalisation of the target. Since the same exponent is printed on both sides, the conclusion is unaffected.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 4.3, first paragraph, p. 1273; finding scoped to the NSF Springer online-first copy; journal pages are a concordance, not printed in that PDF; physical NSF PDF pages 35.
issues.printed: The proof invokes Lemma 3.12 to assert that WD(V_{λ′,t}|G_{F′_v}) ≅ WD(r_{l′,ι′}(π)|G_{F′_v}) has maximally nilpotent N, concluding it is Steinberg.
issues.correction:
Under the hypotheses of Lemma 4.3, the only comparison available is V_{λ′,t}^{ss} ≅ r_{l′,ι′}(π). Here ι′ is chosen so that ι′ (through λ′) and ι (through λ) induce the same complex embedding of ℚ(ζ_N). The comparison follows from the equality of Frobenius characteristic polynomials across the compatible system, together with Chebotarev and Brauer–Nesbitt, because r_{l′,ι′}(π) is semisimple.

Replace the sentence by the following argument, which needs no new hypothesis.
1. By Lemma 3.12 (with v(t) < 0), the Frobenius-semisimplified Weil–Deligne representation of V_{λ′,t}|G_{F′_v} is Sp_n(ψ) for a character ψ of W_{F′_v}. Its Weil-group semisimplification is therefore the segment ψ, ψ|·|, …, ψ|·|^{n−1}.
2. The semisimplified Weil–Deligne representation depends only on the semisimplification of the Galois representation. So WD(r_{l′,ι′}(π)|G_{F′_v})^{ss} is the same segment.
3. By Varma's Theorem (1ss), which applies because v ∤ l′, the same holds for ι′^{−1}rec_{F′_v}(π_v|det|_v^{(1−n)/2})^{ss}. Hence the cuspidal support of π_v|det|_v^{(1−n)/2} is a single segment of n characters.
4. Since π is cuspidal, π_v is generic. By Zelevinsky's classification, a generic irreducible representation is an irreducible product δ(Δ_1) × ⋯ × δ(Δ_k) of essentially square-integrable representations whose segments are pairwise unlinked. Splitting one segment into k ≥ 2 pieces always produces two juxtaposed pieces, which are linked. So k = 1.
5. Hence π_v ≅ Sp_n(ψ_v|·|^{(1−n)/2}) is Steinberg, without using Varma's monodromy bound.

Alternatively, at the one place where the lemma is applied, in the proof of Theorem 1.1 (pp. 1272–1273), V_{λ′,t} is irreducible. This is because ρ = V_{λ′,t} ⊗ χ̃_2^{−1} has absolutely irreducible reduction Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′}|G_{F′}. So V_{λ′,t} ≅ r_{l′,ι′}(π), and the printed isomorphism holds there.
issues.reason:
Lemma 4.3 assumes only that V_{λ,t} is automorphic. In the sense of Definition 1.3 this means V_{λ,t} ≅ r_{l,ι}(π). Comparing Frobenius polynomials across the compatible system then gives only V_{λ′,t}^{ss} ≅ r_{l′,ι′}(π).

The representation r_{l′,ι′}(π) is semisimple by construction (p. 1240; Varma, Introduction). But V_{λ′,t} is not known to be semisimple, since semisimplicity of the étale cohomology of the Dwork fibre is not known.

Maximal monodromy does not pass to the semisimplification. A nonzero proper G_{F′}-stable subspace W of V_{λ′,t} is inertia-stable, hence N-stable, so it is some ker N^k. Then N on W ⊕ V_{λ′,t}/W has two Jordan blocks. So the printed claim that WD(r_{l′,ι′}(π)|G_{F′_v}) has maximally nilpotent N is equivalent to V_{λ′,t} being irreducible. Nothing in the statement or proof of the lemma supplies this. With a smaller N on the Galois side, Varma's bound ≺ gives no information, so the printed deduction fails in the generality of the lemma.

Attempts to defend the paper:
- V_{λ,t} ≅ r_{l,ι}(π) does not imply irreducibility of r_{l,ι}(π). The non-polarizable case is exactly the setting of the paper.
- Monodromy density for the family gives irreducibility only for generic t, not for every t with v(t) < 0.
- The gap is filled only at the lemma's application in the proof of Theorem 1.1. There the residual representation of V_{λ′,t} ⊗ χ̃_2^{−1} is stated on p. 1272 to be absolutely irreducible, and Theorem 6.1.2 of ACC+ even gives V_{λ′,t} ≅ r_{ι′}(π′) directly.

The lemma remains true as stated, by the repair above. Its ingredients are:
- Lemma 3.12, which gives the Weil-group semisimplification as a single segment;
- Varma's semisimplified compatibility at v ∤ l′;
- Shalika's genericity of the local components of a cuspidal π;
- Zelevinsky's classification of generic representations, which forces the twisted Steinberg representation.

The remainder of the proof uses only V_{λ,t} ≅ r_{l,ι}(π), the Hodge–Tate weights of Lemma 3.11 and the central character, so it is unchanged. Lemma 4.3 and Theorems 1.1 and 1.4 are therefore unaffected; only the written proof needs repair.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 4.3, second paragraph, p. 1273; finding scoped to the NSF Springer online-first copy; journal pages are a concordance, not printed in that PDF; physical NSF PDF pages 35.
issues.printed: The proof assigns π weight (−λ_τ)_τ, explaining this in Geraghty’s notation by λ_{τ,i} = −λ_τ for every i at fixed τ. It reduces the task to val_l(ι^{−1}(ψ_v(det(α^{(n)}_{ϖ_v})))) = val_l(∏_{τ:F′_v↪Q̄_l} τ(ϖ_v)^{−nλ_τ}).
issues.correction: In the conventions the paper uses, π has weight (λ_τ)_τ, that is, λ_{τ,i} = +λ_τ for all i. Both the identity to be shown and the identity obtained should read val_l(ι^{−1}φ_{π,v}(ϖ_v)) = val_l(∏_{τ:F′_v↪Q̄_l} τ(ϖ_v)^{nλ_τ}), where ψ_v(det α^{(n)}_{ϖ_v}) = ψ_v(ϖ_v)^n = φ_{π,v}(ϖ_v). For general j the condition is val_l(ι^{−1}ψ_v(ϖ_v)^j) = val_l(∏_τ τ(ϖ_v)^{jλ_τ}). Once both signs are corrected, dividing by n and multiplying by j works as before, the argument closes, and Lemma 4.3 holds.
issues.reason:
The page image of p. 1273 matches the quoted text. The paper uses the conventions of Allen et al. [1], Ann. of Math. 197 (2023):
- Art sends uniformizers to geometric Frobenius (p. 906), and HT_τ(ε) = {−1} (p. 907).
- For π of weight λ, HT_τ(r_ι(π)) = {λ_{τ,1}+n−1, …, λ_{τ,n}} ([1, Theorem 6.1.1(5)(b), p. 1029]).
- For the central character, HT_τ(r_ι(ω_π)) = Σ_i λ_{τ,i} and det r_ι(π) = r_ι(ω_π)ε^{n(1−n)/2} ([1, p. 987]).

The paper's Lemma 2.4 (p. 1250) and Definition 1.2 (p. 1240) use the same normalisation. The proof of Lemma 3.11 (pp. 1266–1267) uses it too: there V_{λ,0} ≅ ⊕_i Q̄_l(−M(a_τ)−i) on inertia, with weights {M, …, M+n−1}, and Lemma 3.11(3) gives the ordinary weight λ_{τ,i} = M(a_τ). So consecutive weights {λ_τ, …, λ_τ+n−1} mean λ_{τ,i} = +λ_τ.

The proof itself uses this convention. It computes the weight of r_{l,ι}(φ_π) = det r_{l,ι}(π)·χ_cyc^{n(n−1)/2} as nλ_τ, which requires HT(χ_cyc) = −1; with the opposite sign it would get nλ_τ + n(n−1). By [1, p. 987], weight nλ_τ also forces Σ_i λ_{τ,i} = nλ_τ, not −nλ_τ.

The last step has the wrong sign. Let φ be an algebraic Hecke character and let h_τ be the τ-weight of r_{l,ι}(φ). On F′_v^×, r_{l,ι}(φ)∘Art_v = ι^{−1}φ_v·∏_τ τ(·)^{a_τ}. Near 1 the character φ_v is trivial and ε∘Art_v(u) = N(u), which gives a_τ = −h_τ. The left side takes unit values, so evaluating at ϖ_v gives val_l(ι^{−1}φ_v(ϖ_v)) = val_l(∏_τ τ(ϖ_v)^{+h_τ}). As a check, take φ = ||·||: then r_{l,ι}(φ) = ε, and val_l(q_v^{−1}) = −f_v = val_l(∏_τ τ(ϖ_v)^{−1}), whereas the printed rule gives +f_v.

The target identity has the same wrong sign. Suppose Geraghty labels weights dually, so that "(−λ_τ)" is literally correct in his notation. The target still cannot be right. At j = n the normalised operator is central, so its condition holds either for every π of these Hodge–Tate weights or for none, and ι-ordinary ones exist. Also, [1, Corollary 5.5.2, p. 1028] and Matsumoto (arXiv:2312.01551v3, Lemma 4.34(2), pp. 46–47, from Geraghty's proofs of Lemmas 5.4 and 5.7) apply Geraghty's Definition 5.3 to π of weight λ in the sense of [1] without any change. Matsumoto's criterion requires val_l(ι^{−1}χ_i(ϖ_v)) = e_v^{−1}Σ_τ(λ_{τ,n+1−i}+i−1+(1−n)/2). The constituents of Sp_n(ψ_v|·|^{(1−n)/2}) are ψ_v|·|^s for s = (1−n)/2, …, (n−1)/2, and for parallel weight the criterion reduces to val_l(ι^{−1}ψ_v(ϖ_v)) = val_l(∏_τ τ(ϖ_v)^{λ_τ}).

Both printed identities are false whenever Σ_{τ|v} λ_τ ≠ 0, which happens here: for n = 2, λ_τ = M(a_τ) = (N−3)/2 > 0. The two sign errors cancel, so Lemma 4.3 is unaffected. The passage does not appear in arXiv v1.

issues.reason: There are three slips. First, the paper has no Theorem 5.5.1; in [1] Theorem 5.5.1 is the local–global compatibility theorem for ordinary parts, so “or” should be “of”. Second, the remark restricts V_{λ,t} to G_{F′_v}, so v must be a place of F′; the paper states the same assertion with “any l-adic place of F′” on p. 1243 and in Lemma 4.3 on p. 1273. Third, V_{λ,t} is the λ-adic realisation with λ above l, so it is an l-adic representation. The superseded argument, at the end of the proof of Theorem 1.1 in arXiv:2104.09761v1 (p. 24), deduced ordinary automorphy from V_{λ,t} being automorphic and ordinary at the l-adic places when v(t) < 0 (arXiv:2104.09761v1, Lemma 3.10(4), the main theorem of [14]). The published paper also uses ordinarity of V_{λ′,t} at the l′-adic places (v(t) > 0 there), but only to make V_{λ′,t} automorphic through the lifting theorem; it says nothing about π at the l-adic places. The “local-global compatibility result in this direction” that needs polarizability goes from Galois ordinarity to ι-ordinarity at the same prime, and the paper applies it in that form ([8, Lemma 5.9]) to Sym^{n−1} r_{E,l′} on p. 1273. issues.printed: The remark invokes the main local-global compatibility result, cited as Theorem 5.5.1 or [1], to claim ordinary V_{λ,t} as a G_{F′_v}-representation at every l-adic place v of F. It says this provides a further proof of [14]’s main result.
issues.correction: First fix the misprints: "Theorem 5.5.1 or [1]" should read "of [1]", and "l-adic places v of F" should read "of F′". Then make the deduction only when the residual representation V[λ]_t ≅ χ̄_1 ⊗ r̄|G_{F′} of V_{λ,t} is absolutely irreducible and decomposed generic. Twisting by a character preserves both properties, so this is the same as asking that r̄|G_{F′} be absolutely irreducible and decomposed generic. That holds in the setting of Theorem 1.4, but not in general in Theorem 1.1. Under this condition, cite the single-representation result [1, Corollary 5.5.2], or equivalently [1, Theorem 5.5.1] together with [1, Lemma 6.2.11] after the soluble base change used in that corollary's proof. The conclusion then covers only the global points t produced in the proof, and only on the decomposition groups of F′ at places above l. For those points it gives the conclusion of the main theorem of [14]. It does not give it for every t of negative valuation over every finite extension of an l-adic field containing ζ_N.
issues.reason:
[1, Theorem 5.5.1] is stated on p. 991 and restated on pp. 1026–1027 of the Annals version. It concerns Galois representations valued in ordinary Hecke algebras. It carries the standing hypothesis that F contains an imaginary quadratic field in which l splits, and it assumes [F^+:ℚ] > 1, a non-Eisenstein maximal ideal (by Definition 2.3.6, an absolutely irreducible residual representation) and a decomposed generic residual representation. The version for a single automorphic representation is [1, Corollary 5.5.2] on p. 1028. It requires the residual representation to be decomposed generic and irreducible. That corollary was added at a referee's request and appears first in the June 2022 arXiv revision; it is not in the December 2018 version that the paper cites.

The remark presents its conclusion as a consequence of the proof of Theorem 1.1, where r̄ is only semisimple. For a reducible r̄, or one that is not decomposed generic, the residual representation χ̄_1 ⊗ r̄|G_{F′} fails these hypotheses. A polarized local–global result such as Geraghty's cannot replace them, because V_{λ,t} is deliberately not self-dual. Irreducibility also matters for a second step. Transfer from the auxiliary prime l′ gives only V_{λ,t}^{ss} ≅ r_{l,ι}(π), and ordinarity of the semisimplification does not imply ordinarity of V_{λ,t}, because the order of the characters in the ordinary flag is prescribed. An absolutely irreducible residual representation makes V_{λ,t} irreducible and so closes this step.

Defence: in the setting of Theorem 1.4 the remark is correct. The proof of that theorem on p. 1274 shows that r̄|G_{F′} is absolutely irreducible, using linear disjointness from F^{avoid}, and decomposed generic, using [1, Lemma 7.1.7]. The remark, however, is not restricted to that setting.

The phrase "another way of proving the main result of [14]" overstates what is shown. [14, Theorem 1.1] (arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 2) proves ordinarity for every t of negative valuation over every finite extension of a local field containing ζ_N. The remark covers only the global points given by Moret-Bailly's theorem.

The remark is not used anywhere. [1, Theorem 6.1.2(5)] (p. 1030) needs π to be ι-ordinary, which Lemma 4.3 supplies, and does not need Galois ordinarity of r_ι(π).

issues.locator: Published journal-layout text §7.1, p.1092, purity observation (Artin-up-to-twist definition p.1086 and extremely weak condition p.1085); also author copy pp.189–190,196–197
issues.printed: The source says the assertion also holds when R becomes Artin after a twist.
issues.correction: For extremely weak systems, this implies purity of the good Frobenius eigenvalues. Full purity, including H_{cτ}={w−h:h∈H_τ}, requires the canonical Hodge multisets of the Artin tensor character family (or a very weak realization, which forces those multisets). The roadmap uses this qualified statement.
issues.reason: Take F=ℚ(i), and the standard irreducible two-dimensional rational representation of Gal(LF/F)=S₃, where L is the splitting field of X³−2 over ℚ. Its finite-image family has good roots of unity, determinant Hodge weight zero at every λ, and is Artin up to twist with trivial character. Assign H_τ={−1,1} and H_{cτ}={0,0} at the two embeddings of F. Both sums are zero, so all extremely weak conditions hold. The good roots force w=0, but H_{cτ}≠−H_τ. The Artin-up-to-twist definition compares members only and imposes no H-multiset equality. This does not affect the canonical Artin constructor or the subsequent applications to very weak systems.

issues.locator: Theorem 1.11 and its proof, p.7 of arXiv:2108.07577v2; published RACSAM 117 (2023), article 153, p.7, reference 4 p.15
issues.printed: Theorem 1.11 takes an odd, irreducible and continuous ρ : GalQ → GL2(Kλ), ramified at only finitely many places, de Rham at p, with Hodge-Tate weights {0, k − 1} and k > 1, with absolutely irreducible residual restriction to G_{ℚ(ζ_p)}; for p = 2 it also assumes nonsolvable residual image. It asserts that ρ belongs to a rank 2 system of Galois representations that is almost strictly compatible. The proof cites [Die04, Theorem 1.1].
issues.correction: The cited theorem does not prove the statement. [Die04, Theorem 1.1] (arXiv math/0304433v1) assumes ρ crystalline at an odd prime q with Hodge–Tate weights {0, w}, w odd, and q ≥ 2w + 1. Within the scope planned here, the family construction uses KW II §10.3.2 (potential modularity of lifts of KW types (A), (B), (C) and the Brauer construction) for the lifts of Theorem 1.9(1)–(3). For Theorem 1.9(4), Snowden supplies weight-two lift existence subject to actual local solutions, but embedding lifts of other potentially Barsotti–Tate types in a compatible family requires potential modularity beyond R23.4; that supplier gap is recorded separately. The general de Rham statement needs potential modularity of arbitrary regular de Rham lifts and should cite it, or be restricted to the lifts used.
issues.reason: DP apply Theorem 1.11 in §2 to the minimal crystalline lifts of Theorem 1.9(3), whose weight k ≤ p + 1 can violate q ≥ 2w + 1 (p = 3, k = 4 gives w = 3) or have w = k − 1 even, and to the weight-two lifts of Paso 1, whose crystallinity at the coefficient prime is not guaranteed. Neither class is within [Die04, Theorem 1.1].

issues.locator: Remark 3.1.7, last sentence (arXiv:2201.06120v1, TeX ll. 2131–2132); used in the proof of Theorem 3.4.13
issues.printed: The fpqc descent assertion for Cartier–Witt divisors is presented without its Witt-level effectivity argument.
issues.correction: A proof is needed: for a faithfully flat map R → S the map W(R) → W(S) is not flat in general (W_2(F_p) → W_2(F_p[x]) is not flat: the p-torsion of W_2(F_p[x]) is V(F_p[x]) while p W_2(F_p[x]) = V(F_p[x^p])), so descent of invertible W(R)-modules is not flat descent along W(R) → W(S). A route: morphisms descend because W and W^× are affine schemes; objects descend by induction on the length n of W_n, the kernel of W_{n+1}^× → W_n^× having a finite filtration with quasi-coherent graded pieces on flat R-algebras, whose Čech cohomology for a faithfully flat cover vanishes in positive degrees.
issues.reason: For R = F_p and S = F_p[t], W_2(S) has p-torsion V(S) but pW_2(S) = V(S^p), so its Tor over Z/p² is nonzero. Witt-level effectivity cannot be deduced from flatness of W(R) → W(S). The packet supplies truncated-Witt lifting, quasi-coherent Čech exactness and inverse-limit effectivity as the proof route.

issues.locator: KYcorr introduction p. 1 and Theorem 7 p. 4; original published Theorems 7.35–7.36 (preprint Theorems 7.36–7.37, pp. 81–82)
issues.printed: The original equivalences target all quasi-pro-Kummer-étale Z_p-local systems and all locally perfect complexes on the log diamond generic fibre.

A local system is p-Kummer when pullback along every compatible-chart map from a saturated log diamond with p-divisible characteristic becomes an ordinary quasi-pro-étale local system; use Lemma 1’s equivalent local p-root-chart test. The source explicitly says the remaining results, including smooth proper pushforward, are unaffected.

issues.locator: Definitions 7.1 and 7.14; Proposition 7.16(1), pp. 71, 74, arXiv:2306.00364v1
issues.printed: The underlying-diamond clause in the strict quasi-pro-Kummer-etale criterion is stated using pro-etaleness.
issues.correction: Use quasi-pro-etaleness for the underlying map of arbitrary diamonds. Continue to require pro-etaleness of the perfectoid test pullbacks. The etale and finite-etale clauses are unchanged.
issues.reason: For trivial log structures, the tests in KY Definition 7.14 reduce exactly to Definition 7.1: only strictly totally disconnected perfectoid base changes are required to be pro-etale. The resulting underlying condition is quasi-pro-etale. Scholze, Etale cohomology of diamonds, Definition 10.1, Convention 10.2 and Proposition 10.3, p. 50, distinguish these predicates and explicitly note that the converse from quasi-pro-etale to pro-etale need not hold; they coincide over a strictly totally disconnected target. Thus the missing quasi prefix in Proposition 7.16(1) cannot impose pro-etaleness on an arbitrary underlying diamond map. The corrected packet statement already used quasi-pro-etale; this review brings its typed predicate into agreement.

issues.locator: §3, p. 9 (arXiv v4), definition of H(w)
issues.printed: The source defines H(w)=e^{−w}∫_{−2w}^∞e^{−t}t^{−k}dt and claims convergence when k<1. For w≠0, it likens the holomorphic continuation with respect to k to the continuation of Γ.

issues.correction: Require period one in τ as well as joint holomorphy and the elliptic transformation law before asserting the integer q-Fourier expansion. Without that condition retain only the theta expansion with holomorphic τ-dependent coefficient functions.
issues.reason: The stated elliptic-form definition imposes only the z-lattice law, not τ↦τ+1. For m=1, F(τ,z)=τ·ϑ_{1,0}(τ,z) is jointly holomorphic and has that elliptic law. Since ϑ_{1,0}(τ+1,z)=ϑ_{1,0}(τ,z), F(τ+1,z)−F(τ,z)=ϑ_{1,0}(τ,z), which is nonzero (at τ=i,z=0 its defining Gaussian series has positive real terms, including 1). An expansion with constant coefficients c(n,r) and integer n as in (4.3), converging at every point, is necessarily period one in τ. Genuine neutral-multiplier Jacobi forms already have this period from the T-transformation, so their U_s mapping statements are unaffected.

issues.correction: The unrestricted perfectoid/uniform conclusion cannot include nonreduced divisors. Keep (a) as a sourced conjecture, and require a separate proved reduced/simple-leg hypothesis for any perfectoid assertion.
issues.reason: Over a geometric field take F=O(2) and t=s², where s is a degree-one section with a simple zero. F(-2)=O is globally etale, and t is fibrewise nonzero. Locally the divisor algebra is A/(s²), with nonzero nilpotent s mod s². A uniform Tate algebra is reduced: multiplying a nilpotent by arbitrary powers of a topologically nilpotent unit produces unbounded power-bounded elements. Hence this thickening admits no compatible uniform Banach norm and is not perfectoid.

issues.locator: 6.4, converse paragraph, p. 83 (published IHÉS 83, 1996)
issues.printed: The special-fibre completed local descriptions alone are asserted to imply that (X,Z) is a strict semistable pair, for an arbitrary S-variety.
issues.correction: Keep the forward implication. For a converse require a good generic pair, or add properness and prove the openness/specialization argument. This affects only the unrestricted local criterion, not the projective output of Theorem 6.5.
issues.reason: Take R=Q[[π]], X=Spec R[x,y], H=V(F) with F=(πx−1)²+π²y³, and Z=X_s∪H. Modulo π, F=1, so H misses X_s and the special-fibre local forms all hold. In O_H, π is invertible since 1=π(2x−πx²−πy³). Over Q((π)), F/π²=(x−π⁻¹)²+y³ is a reduced cuspidal curve, singular at (π⁻¹,0); thus H and Z are not SNC. X is a smooth integral S-variety and Z is a proper reduced closed subset containing X_s, so it meets the printed hypotheses.

issues.locator: arXiv1912.03657v4 AppendixA.2 physical/printed81, arbitrary-open section equality and ensuing flabbiness proof; rendered page inspected
issues.printed: The source asserts, for any open U, that Gamma-invariant sections of p-inverse(I) over q-inverse(U) coincide with invariant sections of I over p(q-inverse(U)). It also claims flabbiness for the sheaf descended from an equivariant injective I.

issues.locator: Remark V.3.4.2 (PDF p. 395, book p. 387)
issues.printed: The example uses the doubled affine line while assigning bundle K₀ rank one and coherent G₀ rank two.
issues.correction: The example must be affine n-space with a double origin for n ≥ 2 (the affine plane, as in II.8.2.4 and Ex. II.9.10(d)); for the affine line with double origin K0VB(X) ≅ K0(X) ≅ G0(X) ≅ Z ⊕ Z and Theorem V.3.4's conclusion holds.
issues.reason: For n = 1 the two charts meet in A^1 − 0 = Spec k[t, t^{-1}], which is affine, so X has affine diagonal (Totaro §1: affineness of the diagonal for the doubled affine line, and its failure in dimension at least two); being quasi-compact and regular, X has the resolution property (Stacks 0F8A), hence K0(Vect X) ≅ K0(X) (Stacks 0FDJ) ≅ G0(X) (Stacks 0FDI). Directly: the line bundles L_m glued from O on the two charts by t^m are pairwise non-isomorphic, so Pic(X) ≅ Z, and rank and determinant map K0VB(X) onto Z ⊕ Pic(X) ≅ Z ⊕ Z, so K0VB(X) ≠ Z. The places the remark cites (II.8.2.4, Ex. II.9.10) themselves require n ≥ 2.

issues.locator: §10.5, display (10.7), printed p. 52 (arXiv v2), and (10.8), printed p. 53
issues.printed: The Kummer limit is labelled by an ordinary algebraic tensor product, both for the full multiplicative number-field group and for its p-adic local fields; inverse limits are treated as exact without their derived term.
issues.correction: δ : lim_m F^×/(F^×)^{p^m} ≅ H^1(F, ℤ_p(1)), with the p-adic completion (Rubin's F^× ⊗̂ ℤ_p) in place of F^× ⊗ ℤ_p; likewise for K_n. The limit step holds because lim^1_m μ_{p^m}(F) = 0 (finite groups; Rubin Proposition B.2.3), not because inverse limits are exact.
issues.reason: For a number field F, F^× contains a free abelian group on infinitely many primes, and a p-adic Cauchy sequence such as ∏_{i≤m} ℓ_i^{p^i} involves infinitely many primes, so it is not in the image of F^× ⊗ ℤ_p: the map is not surjective. For K/ℚ_p finite, U^1_K ⊇ ℤ_p and ℤ_p ⊗_ℤ ℤ_p → ℤ_p kills a ⊗ 1 − 1 ⊗ a, which is nonzero for a ∈ ℤ_p ∖ ℚ since ℤ_p ⊗_ℤ ℤ_p embeds in ℚ_p ⊗_ℚ ℚ_p: the map is not injective. Inverse limits of abelian groups are not exact in general; the lim^1 term must be shown to vanish.

issues.locator: Proposition 7.3 proof, author copy printed p. 586
issues.printed: The source argues that both sides commute with filtered colimits.
issues.correction: Use directed unions of finitely generated coefficient submodules and coefficientwise injectivity from the invertible coefficient line. Only H0 on the qcqs model needs the colimit theorem; do not claim colimit commutation for the entire formal-series target.
issues.reason: Let N_j=Z^j with the coordinate inclusions, N=the direct sum of countably many copies of Z. The series whose ith coefficient is the ith basis vector lies in N[[q]] but in no N_j[[q]]. Hence colim_j N_j[[q]]→N[[q]] is not surjective. The source’s conclusion is repaired by the directed-union argument: zero in N is detected already in each N_j because every coefficient map is injective.

issues.locator: Lemma 7.8.3, published p.409, compared with Definition 3.2.1 and §3.1, published pp.201–202

issues.reason: Take F=ℚ(√2), O_F=ℤ[√2], u=7+5√2=(1+√2)³ of norm −1, and ℓ=7. At v=(7,√2−3), F_v=ℚ₇ and u≡1 mod v. The scalar γ=uI₄ belongs to Iw₁(v) and to full integral level at every other finite place. In the faithful rational representation on F⁴ the eigenvalues include u and its conjugate 7−5√2, whose product is −1. Thus γ is not rationally neat and its diagonal adele fails Definition 3.2.1 at every rational prime. Its similitude u² is totally positive, so restricting to G₁(ℚ)⁺ does not remove it. The other 7-adic place has u≡−1, illustrating the missing factor. E15 product closure within one local factor cannot repair this counterexample.

issues.locator: Proposition 10.5 proof, p.101, revised 16 September 2017 author copy
issues.printed: The source asserts the existence of a pro-p subgroup in I whose index is finite.
issues.correction: Absolute local inertia is not virtually pro-p. Either factor the abelian representation through local reciprocity, whose unit-group image is virtually pro-p, or use finite-extension semistable reduction and unipotent inertia. V5 uses the latter with the existing R11.3/R11.5 nodes.

issues.locator: §3.10, p.252, sentence citing [16]; compare the reductive subgroup definition in §4, pp.253–254. Scoped to the public annotated 1983 author scan.

issues.correction: The cited Platonov–Rapinchuk 1979 Theorem 1 proves perfection of the simply connected three-dimensional norm-one group when split at every finite place, not the printed simplicity claim for a full reductive group containing T. The central-adjustment proof must specify the semisimple factor and justify passage back to the marked torus. This review records that remaining proof gap rather than inventing the bridge.
issues.reason: In SU(4,1) over Q for Q(i)/Q with diagonal compact maximal torus, the noncompact ±α block subgroup Hα has derived SU(1,1)≅SL₂ and a positive-dimensional central torus. Its derived rational subgroup is normal, proper and noncentral, even though its semisimple factor is split at every finite place. Thus the literal assertion about this full reductive Hα is false. Independently, the primary 1979 Russian text states perfection in Theorem 1, p.279, and still calls simplicity modulo centre a conjecture on p.282. The central target is abelian, so perfection is the relevant weaker input, but the marked-torus passage is not supplied by citing it.

issues.printed: The source identifies A¹ as the answer to its moduli question when N = 2.
issues.correction: The characteristic-zero coarse ordered level-two curve is the punctured lambda-line A¹ minus {0,1}. It is not a fine moduli scheme of all such families. The Legendre family is smooth only on the punctured line. Restrict the fine comparison in this packet to N >= 3.
issues.reason: The discriminant is 16 lambda²(1-lambda)². The automorphism [-1] fixes E[2]; nontrivial quadratic twists have the same geometric lambda invariant and obstruct the claimed universal property over arbitrary fields.

issues.locator: 5.1.3, printed p.155, published Numdam copy (page image checked)
issues.printed: The assertion covers every real open U ⊂ V(R) and every field extension F of E.
issues.correction: Require U to be nonempty and F/E to be finite in the disjoint Hilbert-specialization assertion. These are precisely the hypotheses of its application in Theorem 5.1.
issues.reason: An empty real open has no specialization. Without finiteness of F the result is false: over E=Q, take the degree-two cover s²=t of V=A¹ minus {0}, U=(1,2), and F=Qbar. A rational specialization either splits or is a nontrivial quadratic field, which cannot be linearly disjoint from Qbar over Q.

Finite F/E and nonempty U give the needed application in Theorem 5.1.

issues.locator: Paragraph explaining Proposition 14.16(b), p.127 in the 2017 author copy; p.356 in the published 2005 version

issues.locator: Theorem 3.11, p.38, relative to the source’s geometrically-reduced definition of algebraic variety on pp.35–36
issues.printed: The source asserts that each projective complex analytic space admits exactly one projective algebraic variety structure.
issues.correction: For analytic spaces with nilpotents use projective algebraic schemes. For the source’s geometrically-reduced varieties restrict the analytic space to be reduced. V2 uses normal reduced compactifications, so its statement is unaffected.
issues.reason: The projective analytic fat point with local ring C[ε]/(ε²) cannot analytify a geometrically-reduced variety. The CA.0 carrier must nevertheless include it for GAGA and general analytification.

issues.locator: Proposition 10.5 proof, p.101, revised 16 September 2017 author copy
issues.printed: The source asserts the existence of a pro-p subgroup in I whose index is finite.
issues.correction: Absolute local inertia is not virtually pro-p. Either factor the abelian representation through local reciprocity, whose unit-group image is virtually pro-p, or use finite-extension semistable reduction and unipotent inertia. V5 uses the latter with the existing R11.3/R11.5 nodes.
issues.reason: For residue characteristic p, tame inertia has quotient ∏_{ℓ≠p} Z_ℓ(1); its infinite pro-ℓ quotients exclude a finite-index pro-p subgroup. Rank-one CM inertia becomes trivial after semistable extension because E⊗Q_ℓ is reduced and (ρ(σ)−1)²=0. The theorem survives; the printed step fails.
searched: The revised SVI author PDF and author xnotes/svi.html index; official-site search for Proposition 10.5 inertia/pro-p errata; older author svi2005.pdf and 2005aX.pdf repeat the sentence. No correction located.
issues.citation: J. S. Milne, Introduction to Shimura varieties, Revised 16 September 2017
issues.reviewReason: Absolute inertia has infinite tame pro-ell quotients for ell≠p, so it has no finite-index pro-p subgroup. Semistable square-zero inertia in a reduced CM algebra supplies the recorded repair.

issues.printed: Gal(Qa/Q)
issues.correction: Use Gal(Qbar/K), after all E-endomorphisms are defined over K. A/K and its endomorphism action need not descend to Q.

issues.locator: §3.10, p.252, sentence citing [16]; compare the reductive subgroup definition in §4, pp.253–254. Scoped to the public annotated 1983 author scan.
issues.printed: The source rules out any normal subgroup of Hα(Q) that is non-central.
issues.correction: The cited Platonov–Rapinchuk 1979 Theorem 1 proves perfection of the simply connected three-dimensional norm-one group when split at every finite place, not the printed simplicity claim for a full reductive group containing T. The central-adjustment proof must specify the semisimple factor and justify passage back to the marked torus. This review records that remaining proof gap rather than inventing the bridge.
issues.reason: In SU(4,1) over Q for Q(i)/Q with diagonal compact maximal torus, the noncompact ±α block subgroup Hα has derived SU(1,1)≅SL₂ and a positive-dimensional central torus. Its derived rational subgroup is normal, proper and noncentral, even though its semisimple factor is split at every finite place. Thus the literal assertion about this full reductive Hα is false. Independently, the primary 1979 Russian text states perfection in Theorem 1, p.279, and still calls simplicity modulo centre a conjecture on p.282. The central target is abelian, so perfection is the relevant weaker input, but the marked-torus passage is not supplied by citing it.

issues.locator: §4, proof of Proposition 4.1, p. 852, and proof of Corollary 4.2 (p ⩾ 5), p. 853
issues.printed: The source invokes Herbrand's Theorem [Was82, Theorem 6.17] to claim that the p-part of the class group for Z[ζp] has zero ω²-eigenspace.
issues.correction: Herbrand's theorem gives the vanishing of the ω^{−1}-eigenspace; Leopoldt's Spiegelungssatz then gives the vanishing of the ω²-eigenspace, which is what the proof uses.
issues.reason: Herbrand's theorem concerns the eigenspaces ω^{1−k} with k even and p ∤ B_k; the ω²-eigenspace is reached from the ω^{−1}-eigenspace by reflection. Schoof's errata note states exactly this. Nothing in this checkpoint depends on it: over ℤ with p = 2 the character group is trivial and the class group of ℤ[1/2] is trivial; the p = 3 cases of R25.4 must use the corrected step.

issues.reviewReason: The text is at p. 852 (proof of Prop. 4.1) and p. 853 (proof of Cor. 4.2, p ≥ 5). Washington Thm 6.17 concerns odd i: A_{ω^i} ≠ 0 ⇒ p | B_{p−i}. One correction to the reason: its last clause ('the p = 3 cases of R25.4 must use the corrected step') is wrong. issues.locator: §6, proof of Theorem 1.1, Case l = 7, p = 3, p. 858 (also arXiv:math/0502356)
issues.printed: The source uses Odlyzko's bounds to claim that every unramified extension of K′ has relative degree strictly below 120/36 < 4.
issues.correction: K′ is cubic over K = Q(ζ3, ζ7 + ζ7^{−1}, 7^{1/3}), which has degree 18, so [K′ : Q] = 54 and the relative degree is smaller than 120/54 < 3.
issues.reason: The root discriminant 3^{25/18}7^{2/3} ≈ 16.83 bounds the absolute degree of an unramified extension of K′ by 119 (Odlyzko's Table 2 gives 17.020 at n = 120); dividing by [K′ : Q] = 54, not 36, gives the relative bound. The argument only needs to exclude degrees 2 and 3, so the weaker printed bound still suffices.

issues.locator: §4, proof of Theorem 4.3, case k(ρ̄) = 14, p. 21 (statement of Theorem 4.3, p. 19), arXiv:math/0412076v1; corrected in the published version (Ann. of Math. 169 (2009), Theorem 5.4, p. 247)
issues.printed: For p = 11, the source claims that the Serre-weight definition expresses ρ̄ as obtained by twisting a level 1 representation of Serre weight 2 with χ, a case it says was already excluded.
issues.correction: True only when ρ̄|I_11 is ω ⊕ ω², a peu ramifiée extension with sub ω² and quotient ω, or ω₂^{13} ⊕ ω₂^{23}. If ρ̄|I_11 is a non-split extension with sub ω and quotient ω², then k(ρ̄) = 14 but no twist of ρ̄ has weight 2 (ρ̄ ⊗ ω^{−1} has weight 22) and the twist-normalised weight is 10; Theorem 4.3 is proved only for p ≠ 11 when k(ρ̄) = 14.
issues.reason: Serre's recipe for a non-split ρ̄|I_p ≅ (ω^a ∗; 0 ω^b), a ∈ [1, p − 1]: k = 1 + a + b + (p − 1)min(a, b) (no extra term unless a = b + 1 très ramifiée). (a, b) = (1, 2) gives 14 at p = 11; ρ̄ ⊗ ω^{j} has (a, b) = (1 + j, 2 + j), and weight 2 needs (a, b) = (1, 0), impossible; j = −1 gives (10, 1), weight 22; j = −2 gives (9, 0), weight 10. Such local representations exist (H¹(ℚ₁₁, ω^{−1}) ≠ 0 and is ramified), so the step fails; the case reduces to level-one weight 10, which KW cannot treat.

issues.locator: Exercise 1.1, second paragraph, p. IV.14, in Kbook.IV.pdf (SHA-256 9f1c1b8c…)
issues.printed: The exercise puts the binary icosahedral group SL₂(F₅) inside O₃(ℝ) and treats it as the polyhedron symmetry group.
issues.correction: Use the binary icosahedral group SL₂(F₅) ⊂ SU(2) = S³, acting freely by left multiplication. Its quotient by the central order-two subgroup is A₅ ⊂ SO(3). The full icosahedral symmetry group A₅ × ℤ/2 ⊂ O₃ has order 120 but is a different group; SL₂(F₅) does not embed in O₃.
issues.reason: SL₂(F₅) is perfect, so an embedding in O₃(ℝ) would land in SO₃(ℝ). By the classification of finite rotation groups, a subgroup of order 120 there is cyclic or dihedral and cannot be perfect. The icosahedral rotation group is A₅ of order 60; its binary cover belongs in SU(2). The full icosahedral symmetry group in O₃ has order 120 and is A₅ × ℤ/2, but not every subgroup of O₃ of order 120 is that group.

issues.reviewReason: Freshly confirmed in the 2021 CLM copy, Lemma 7.1 proof p.30, and the NSF Lemma 1.44 proof pp.39–40. For example, let B be k plus an infinite-dimensional k-vector space V with V squared equal to zero: every geometric fibre of Spec B to Spec k has one underlying point, but V is not a finitely generated ideal and B is not Noetherian or finite type. issues.locator: arXiv1110.3909v3 §2.3,PDF5, paragraph defining the syzygy functor; same assertion in publisher indexed §2.3 HTML, DOI10.1016/j.jalgebra.2013.08.024. Direct publisher request403; publisher PDF not read.

issues.correction: Without further hypotheses use the cokernel of Hom_A(P₀,N)→Hom_A(ΩM,N) from 0→ΩM→P₀→M→0, then dimension shift. Quotienting by every map through every coherent projective module is generally a larger quotient. Additional Ext vanishing against projectives can make the quotients agree; no unrestricted stable-category formula is used here.
issues.reason: Take A=ℤ, M=ℤ/2 and N=ℤ. The finite free resolution is 0→ℤ --2→ ℤ→ℤ/2→0, hence Ext¹_ℤ(ℤ/2,ℤ)=coker(2:ℤ→ℤ)=ℤ/2. Its first syzygy is 2ℤ≅ℤ, which is coherent projective. Every map from that syzygy to ℤ factors through the syzygy itself, so stable Hom is zero. The source defines the stable category of all coherent modules, without a stable-reflexivity restriction in this paragraph. This refutes the unqualified assertion, not the paper’s later restricted approximation theorems.

issues.locator: 2021 author copy Corollary 6.6 proof p.25; later NSF author copy Corollary 1.39 proof p.33

issues.correction: Use generic global generation and the invertible image I of f_*ω^m→C_t*ω^m. Write I=C_t*ω^m(−D) with D effective; nef quotient positivity gives deg I≥0, hence m deg(C_t*ω)≥0. No special-fibre vanishing is needed.
issues.reason: Blow up a smooth constant genus-g≥2 family at one point of a fibre and take the strict transform of the constant section through that point. The special fibre is C∪E with E≅P¹ a rational tail; the section meets E away from the node. On E, ω_f^m(−C_t) has degree −m−1, so H¹(E,O_E(−m−1)) has dimension m. The normalization exact sequence shows the special fibre has nonzero H¹, whereas the smooth generic fibre has zero H¹ for m≥2. Since the fibres have dimension one, cohomology/base change forces nonzero R¹f_* at this fibre. The family is nodal with smooth generic fibre, exactly the stated range. The corollary conclusion remains valid by the corrected image proof.

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed at the first paragraph of Appendix A.1, p.90. issues.locator: 356-page author copy, Remark IV.1.10, p.110
issues.printed: The remark excludes cohomological smoothness of the point atlas for every infinite group, overlooking infinite discrete groups.
issues.correction: For nondiscrete locally profinite H an infinite compact open subgroup gives the distribution obstruction. Discrete H gives an étale, cohomologically smooth point map even when H is infinite.
issues.reason: Take H=π^Z, a closed infinite discrete subgroup of GL_1(E). The pullback of *→[*/H] is H→*, a disjoint union of identity maps, so it is separated étale of local dimension zero; the existing theorem that étale maps are cohomologically smooth applies. Its dualizing sheaf is constant F_ell on every discrete point. The source’s distribution argument obstructs infinite compact profinite neighbourhoods, not infinite discrete sets.

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed at Remark IV.1.10, p.110. The remark says the point of [*/G] is not a cohomologically smooth chart unless G is finite, because the exceptional pullback of Λ along G→* is the sheaf of distributions on G. For a discrete group, finite or not, G→* is a disjoint union of copies of the point, hence étale and cohomologically smooth, and the sheaf of distributions is the constant sheaf. The correct exception is discrete G; for example the subgroup generated by a uniformizer in E^×, which is closed in GL_1(E). The remark's point, that G(E) and its open subgroups do not give smooth charts, is unaffected.

issues.locator: Published Appendix A, Lemma A.5 proof, p.90
issues.printed: The source draws T→X_i×X_i in the diagram and claims that X_i×X_i→X×X is an injective, quasi-compact map.
issues.correction: First use Lemma A.1 and filtered-colimit/finite-product commutation to choose i through which the profinite map T→X×X factors. The monomorphism X_i→X then identifies T×(X×X)X with T×(X_i×X_i)X_i, which is quasicompact by quasi-separatedness of X_i. No quasicompactness of the colimit inclusion is needed.

Compact factorization at some common stage supplies the missing step and avoids the unjustified quasicompact-inclusion assertion. The theorem remains valid.

issues.locator: Chapter II, §II.2.3, proof of Theorem II.2.6: the estimate (II.2.1), p. 65, and the last paragraph of the proof, p. 66 (arXiv v4)
issues.printed: The proof says that taking M sufficiently large bounds the norm of each of its two correction terms by q^(−M−1). Its radius formulas do not match the annulus normalization it specifies.
issues.correction: With the conventions of Proposition II.1.16 (rad = log|[ϖ]|/log|π|, Y_{S,[r,q]} = {|π|^q ≤ |[ϖ]| ≤ |π|^r}) and the normalization ||[ϖ]|| = 1/q, one has |π| = q^{−1/ρ} at radius ρ, so ||π^k||_{B_{R,[r,q]}} = q^{−k/q} for k ≥ 0, not q^{−rk}. The two bounds become q^{−M/q} and q^{(N′−M)/q}, both larger than q^{−M−1}; the printed exponents are those of the reciprocal convention |π| = |[ϖ]|^ρ. The claimed estimate (II.2.1) is itself false as stated, so the proof does not establish global generation as written; the theorem is [KL15, Proposition 6.2.4] and stands, but the quantitative step must be redone (for example following [KL15]). For A = π^N·Id the choice v_i = Σ_j π^{Nj}[ϖ^{Mq^{−j}}]e_i works when (N/r + 1)/(q − 1) ≤ M ≤ (N − q)/(q − 1), i.e. with N made large by twisting and M chosen in a window, not with M large.
issues.reason: Counterexample to (II.2.1): E = 𝔽_q((π)), S = Spa C, A = π^N·Id with N > 0 (so N′ = N, qN > N′), w = π^M e₁ ∈ π^M W_{𝒪_E}(R⁺)⟨([ϖ]/π)^{±1}⟩^m. Every v with (φ − A)v = w is v = c e₁ + h with c = π^M/(1 − π^N) ∈ E and h ∈ ker(φ − π^N) = H⁰(X_C, 𝒪(N))^m. Writing h = Σ h_iπ^i, φ(h) = π^N h gives h_i^q = h_{i−N}; if |h_M| = 1 then |h_{M−kN}| = 1 for all k ≥ 0 and h cannot converge on Y_{C,[1,q]}, so |h_M| ≠ 1 and the π^M-coefficient of v has absolute value ≥ 1. Hence ||v||_{B_{C,[r,q]}} ≥ sup|π|^M = q^{−M/q} > q^{−M−1} for every M ≥ 1 and 1 < r ≤ q. The same computation on φ^{−1}(w₁) = [ϖ]^{(N−1)/q}π^{M−N+1} gives q^{−M/q}, not the printed q^{−(N−1)/q−r(M−N+1)}.

issues.locator: Lemma 3.16, end of proof, p. 17
issues.printed: The proof says that an injection forces h < d because U_λ has Dimension (d,h), whereas V^h has Dimension (h,0).
issues.correction: In the final inequality, use h>d.
issues.reason: The inequality is reversed relative to both the lemma and its own proof. The lemma asserts dim(W) < ht(W), i.e. d < h, and three lines earlier the proof states its goal as 'we need to show that h > d'. Dimension additivity (Proposition 3.2(ii)) applied to the injection U_λ ↪ V^h gives Dim Coker = (h−d, −h), and ht Coker = −h < 0 forces dim Coker > 0 by Proposition 3.2(iii), i.e. h > d.

issues.locator: Corollary 3.21(iv), p. 18
issues.printed: The source claims that a height 0 quotient of a BC whose curvature is ≥ 0 must have curvature 0.
issues.correction: A quotient of height 0 of a BC of curvature ≥ 0 has Harder-Narasimhan slope 0, i.e. is of the form ⊕_x H^0(X,F_x) with each F_x torsion; it has curvature 0 only if in addition the support is {∞}, equivalently if it is a B^+_dR-Module.
issues.reason: The statement is refuted by the paper's own footnote 9 on the same page, which records that for x ≠ ∞ the object U_1/Q_p t_x has ht = 0 but curvature > 0. Take W = U_1/Q_p t_x with x ≠ ∞ and let the quotient be the identity: W is of curvature > 0, hence of curvature ≥ 0, has height 0, and is a quotient of itself, so (iv) would give it curvature 0. But curvature 0 and curvature > 0 are incompatible for W ≠ 0: a nonzero object of curvature 0 is a finite length B^+_dR-module by Proposition 3.17 and so admits a nonzero map to V_1, whereas §3.2.7 computes Hom_BC(U_1/Q_p t_x, V_1) = 0 and End = C_x. The asymmetry with the correct part (ii) is that curvature ≤ 0 already forces support at ∞ (Corollary 3.19(i)), while curvature ≥ 0 does not.

issues.locator: §2.4, Lemma 2.8: arXiv v3 p. 12; published p. 908.
issues.printed: η²|_{K_v^*} = χ · Norm_{K_v/Q_p}^w
issues.correction: The identity holds on the local units: η²|_{O_{K_v}^*} = χ · Norm_{K_v/Q_p}^w with χ of finite order. It does not hold on all of K_v^*. The final sentence — w even, Hodge–Tate weight w/2 at v — is correct, and is what Lemmas 2.9 and 2.10 use.
issues.reason: Counterexample: K = Q (which has no CM subfield, so every finite place is friendly), v = p, η = χ_cyc^{-1}. Then η is ramified only at p, locally algebraic there, and pure of weight w = 2, since geometric Frobenius at ℓ acts by ℓ. As an idele class character η(p) = 1, because the local Artin image of a uniformizer acts trivially on μ_{p^∞} in either normalisation; so η²(p) = 1 while Norm_{Q_p/Q_p}(p)^w = p², and χ(p) = p^{-2} has infinite order. On units η(u) = u and η² = Norm², so the identity does hold there. The proof cannot give more: local algebraicity is the hypothesis that η_p 'agrees, in a neighbourhood of the identity, with the Q_p-points of an algebraic homomorphism' (p. 12), and the closing step — 'any Q_p-rational character of (Res_{E/Q} G_m)^1 is trivial upon pullback to E_v^*' — is a statement about that algebraic character, hence controls η only on an open subgroup of E_v^*, not on a uniformizer.

issues.reviewReason: Rejected. Over an algebraic closure, a subdirect Lie subalgebra of a product of simple sp factors is a product of diagonals. issues.locator: §8.3, Lemma 8.3: arXiv v3 p. 42; published p. 951.
issues.printed: rank(Mon(D_e^M) − Id)
issues.correction: Take a nonseparating simple closed curve e in Y−{y} and a positive sufficiently divisible M (for example a positive multiple of the order of Cov(e), and of the relevant stabilizer indices). Then the rank is k−1, where k is the number of cycles of Cov(e).
issues.reason: The lemma is deduced from Lemma 8.2, which needs e nonseparating (finding E13), and it fails without that hypothesis. Two different conjugacy classes give the same rank, so the rank does not determine the class. With e nonseparating the three possible cycle types in Aff(q) — (1^q), (q) and (1, r, …, r) — have k = q, 1 and 1 + (q − 1)/r cycles respectively, all distinct, and the lemma holds. The applications, in the proof of Lemma 8.9, are to nonseparating curves.

issues.reason: Let F be the algebraic closure of Q_p inside C_p. It is dense and properly contained in C_p. Extend t from C_p minus F to a transcendence basis over F. The automorphism of the rational function field sending t to pt and fixing the other basis elements and F extends to an automorphism σ of its algebraic closure C_p. Thus ν(x)=|x| and ν′(x)=|σ(x)| are distinct complete multiplicative Q_p-algebra norms, with ν′(t)=p^(-1)ν(t). For a_n in F tending to t in ν, the same sequence tends to p^(-1)t in ν′. It is Cauchy for max(ν,ν′) but cannot have a limit for that norm. There is also an actual finite-group counterexample to the parenthesis of Lemme 2.4.1(2): put B=C_p×C_p with N(x,y)=max(ν(x),ν′(y)), let G=C_2 swap factors, and give A=B^G=diagonal C_p its induced norm max(ν,ν′). B is complete and spectral; A is uniform normed, exactly as allowed in §2.4.1, though incomplete. The swap takes (t,0), of norm ν(t), to (0,t), of norm p^(-1)ν(t). The proposed old repair from (2.11) is invalid: that formula determines max_γ N(γb), not N(b), and its proof of individual equality uses G-invariance. The prior extraction also missed the invocation on p.24. For a finite projective algebra over a complete A, its given complete Banach topology agrees with the canonical module topology: choose finite generators, use the continuous surjection A^n→B and open mapping. A-linear isomorphisms are then continuous, so fixed-topology uniqueness applies to p.24 and p.41. This does not repair the general parenthesis on p.22, where A need not be complete.

issues.printed: Theorem 4.1 claims R_an,exp-definability for the period map Φ: (∆*)^n → S_{Γ,G,M} of V, a weight k variation of pure Hodge structures equipped with a polarization on (∆*)^n. Here ∆ denotes the unit disk, as specified in §1.3.
issues.correction: Replace the whole-unit-polydisk assertion by a local assertion after shrinking to (∆*_ρ)^n for a sufficiently small 0<ρ<1, with the Hodge-compatible fixed maximal compact. In §4.1 choose such smaller charts around every point of the compactification and then a finite subcover. Do not justify the several-variable step by calling the remaining punctured annular pieces compact. This correction specifies the necessary domain change; it does not discharge the separate proof gaps recorded below.
issues.reason: with τ(z)=2i+ε exp(−(1+z)/(1−z)), take ε>0 small enough that its image lies in a quotient-injective disk for Γ(3)\H. The trivial integral rank-two local system, its holomorphic weight-one Hodge line and the standard polarization give a PVHS; transversality is automatic in weight one. The fibre at π(2i+ε/e) is EXACTLY {2πin/(2+2πin):n∈Z\{0}} on ∆*. Solving the exponential equation proves equality, not just containment; it is infinite and discrete with accumulation only at the excluded outer boundary. A definable discrete subset of R² is finite. The y>1 strip in the proof covers only |q|<exp(−2π), and Lemma 4.2 explicitly permits shrinking. Confirmed for the literal whole-disk statement. Repaired the original insufficient 'contains' argument and removed the several-variable compact-annulus shortcut. This does not refute Theorem 1.3.

issues.locator: Lemma 4.5 proof, JAMS p.930; author p.15
issues.printed: For each positive integer m and each real c, the source substitutes z_1 = mz_2 + c into f to form f_{m,c}. It asserts that f_{m,c} satisfies the lemma’s hypotheses and that induction on n gives f_{m,c} ≪ 1 throughout Σ_{n−1}.
issues.correction: The induction needs bounds for the substituted functions on their actual domains. Supply a domain-transfer argument, or restate and prove the lemma for every bounded-real-width sector Σ_n^R={|x_i|<R,y_1≥…≥y_n>1}, with constants allowed to depend on R, and verify that stronger curve hypothesis in the application. The substitution z_1=mz_2+c sends Σ_(n−1)^R′ into Σ_n^(mR′+|c|). issues.reason: Independent domain check in Definition 4.4 and the printed induction: x_1=mx_2+c>1 for c≥1 and 0<x_2<1, while for c=0 the original domain requires x_2<1/m. Revised the correction/reason so that the stronger bounded-width input and its application are explicitly requirements, not an independently completed repair. issues.citation: Bakker–Klingler–Tsimerman, "Tame topology of arithmetic quotients and algebraicity of Hodge loci", Journal of the American Mathematical Society (2020)
issues.reviewReason: The published §1.3 expressly chooses the adjoint generic Mumford–Tate group, while §4.2 treats G as acting on the original fibre. The standard representation of SL₂ does not descend to PGL₂ because −I acts nontrivially. Confirmed that a representation/presentation adapter is missing from that transition. However official erratum §1.4 now takes a Q-group inside GL(V_R), addressing the acting-group choice; amended known and the correction to credit that published change. No claim is made that the erratum spells out the comparison with the original adjoint presentation.

issues.locator: §5, JAMS pp.933–934, definition of the target Hodge locus
issues.printed: The locus is described as a union whose members are special subvarieties.
issues.correction: For the exceptional Hodge locus, use proper Mumford–Tate-drop subdata relative to the generic Hodge datum, not the union of every special image including the identity. Supply the correspondence with exceptional Hodge tensors. The proof's stronger assertion that the inverse image of each special subvariety is algebraic is compatible with this correction; Theorem 1.6 is not refuted.
issues.reason: As defined immediately above, a special image may be the image of the identity Hodge morphism. Including it makes the union the whole target, whose pullback is all S, whereas §1.4 defines HL(S,V) using exceptional Hodge tensors. The extraction uses proper special images; the correspondence remains G6. (cc-442dc5) Reclassified to affect nothing: §1.4 defines the Hodge locus through exceptional Hodge tensors, i.e. proper Mumford–Tate-drop special images; including the identity image in §5's description is a slip that the statement of Theorem 1.6 does not use.

issues.locator: Proposition 14, pp.725–727, and Remark 16, p.727, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 709–744 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 814976ee…f40a); also footnote 4, p.712
issues.printed: Proposition 14 claims that nearby CM points of one type, sharing a projection to X(1)×X(1), belong to a Hecke curve of low degree, for both Heegner and anti-Heegner points. Remark 16 says that anti-Heegner CM points lie on no Hecke curves and consequently repel. Footnote 4 says Proposition 14’s stronger repulsion assertion resolves the 2-to-1 ambiguity in [BT13].
issues.correction: Proposition 14 holds for Heegner CM points (CM⁺) only, with Lemma 15 applied with h₀ = 1 (erratum Proposition 2.1). Close anti-Heegner CM points lie on low-degree conjugate Hecke curves instead. The first clause of Remark 16 (Hecke curves contain no anti-Heegner points) is true; its repulsion claim is false.
issues.reason: The real-analytic involution conjugating the second factor preserves distance and swaps Heegner and anti-Heegner CM points; close pairs on a Hecke curve become close anti-Heegner pairs on its conjugate, contradicting the claimed repulsion. The published proof chooses a fixed integral h₀ representing the other normalizer coset and then conjugates small matrices by it. An arbitrary lift modulo p does not preserve those height bounds. In the nontrivial normalizer action, a fixed integral normalizer would induce complex conjugation on the real elliptic torus and have negative determinant, so the SL₂ lift used uniformly by that argument is unjustified. The author erratum restricts the proposition to Heegner points (h₀=1) and replaces the anti-Heegner argument. Its shorthand about nonexistence of a lift should not be read as denying the surjectivity SL₂(Z)→SL₂(F_p).

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 15, pp.726–727, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 709–744 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 814976ee…f40a)
issues.printed: From M′² = −1, the source concludes that M′ equals either t̃ or −t̃. It then writes g = a + b(0 1; −1 0) and asserts that (x,y) belongs to T_m with m = det g = a² + b².
issues.correction: For the order-three lift actually printed, t₀=[[0,1],[-1,−1]], use t̃²+t̃+I=0. A conjugate M′ in the centralizer algebra is t̃ or −I−t̃ (exclude scalar roots using conjugacy when the polynomial splits modulo p). Lifting the small-coefficient identities still shows M_x,M_y normalize the same elliptic torus, and their positive determinant forces them into its centralizer. In the concluding degree calculation use g=aI+bt₀ and m=a²−ab+b². Equivalently one may replace t₀ by −t₀ and use the trace +1 relation and a²+ab+b², but that change of lift must be explicit.
issues.reason: The displayed square relation and Gaussian norm apply only to the order-four lift. The separate order-three matrix on p.725 has trace −1 and determinant 1. Its Cayley–Hamilton relation and direct determinant expansion yield the correction above. Its centralizer is the Eisenstein quadratic algebra, and the same positive-determinant normalizer argument works. The earlier errata correction implicitly changed to the negative lift without saying so. The source proof needs this branch; no counterexample to the Heegner-only conclusion is asserted.

issues.locator: Published Lemma 5 proof, p.718, its upper-bound matrix witness; arXiv v2 Lemma 5 p.9, with the compactification condition on p.8
issues.printed: The source presents γ=[[1−p²,p],[-p,1]] as attaining the trace bound and concludes that this proves the result.
issues.correction: The upper bound for the radius defined using loops nontrivial in the compactification requires a short element of Γ(p) whose image in π₁(X(p)) is nontrivial. The displayed element cannot supply it. Keep the trace lower bound, but supply a different upper-bound witness or a separate geometric argument compatible with that homotopy condition. This review has not supplied that missing argument.
issues.reason: The displayed γ factors exactly as [[1,p],[0,1]]·[[1,0],[-p,1]]. Both factors are peripheral unipotents in Γ(p), killed when cusps are filled: the first is a p-th power of the standard cusp generator and the second a conjugate of its inverse. Therefore their product also maps to the identity in the compactified fundamental group. Although γ is hyperbolic with |tr γ|=p²−2, its geodesic is excluded by the definition immediately above Lemma 5. The published proof itself identifies the kernel with the group generated by these unipotents. Thus the exhibited matrix proves an upper bound for the ordinary nonperipheral systole, not the compactification-nontrivial systole being used. The defect remains after inserting E8’s factor one-half. No counterexample to the eventual asymptotic theorem is asserted; the missing upper-bound argument remains open in this review.

issues.locator: Published proof of Corollary 8, p.720; arXiv v2 pp.10–11
issues.printed: The source claims that ℓ_X(p)(γ) ≤ 2 log p + O(1) ensures γ comes within (log p)/2 of no more than one cusp.
issues.correction: Distinguish the closed-geodesic length ℓ(γ)=2ρ_X(p) from the injectivity radius. Even granting the intended upper bound ρ_X(p)≤2 log p+O(1), the available length bound is 4 log p+O(1). Rework the cusp-avoidance argument to control all cusp neighborhoods visited, with a total O(1) length-comparison error; replacing 2 by 4 alone does not justify the asserted one-cusp claim. This review does not claim to close that geometric step.
issues.reason: The compact definition p.718 sets ρ to half the shortest closed-geodesic length, and the last line of this same proof explicitly uses ℓ(γ)=2ρ_X(p). Its preliminary upper-bound argument therefore provides only ℓ(γ)≤4 log p+O(1), not the quoted estimate. The proof then uses the stronger estimate to reduce its detour and integration to one cusp. Lemma 6’s separation >2 log p−O(1), together with the corrected length bound, does not imply this one-cusp assertion. A bounded-number-of-cusps replacement may repair the strategy but needs a proof controlling visits and detours. The claim confirmed here is the missing justification in this step, not a counterexample to Corollary 8. It is separate from the inadmissible witness in E12.

issues.reason: Put δ=3 log log k/log k. For a primitive character of conductor q∉Q(k), all zeros with |γ|≤T have δ≤β≤1−δ, by reflection in the functional equation. Since q≤k⁴ and log T=O(log k/log log k), the total is O((log k)²), as required. Bennett–Martin–O’Bryant–Rechnitzer, arXiv:1802.00085, p.11 and Proposition 2.5 p.14, explicitly provide the reflection and zero-counting input cited by the paper.

On punctured neighbourhoods those units have constant signs; the negative arc forces even D-orders, making the required sign jump on the positive arc impossible. issues.reason: The printed fixed point is [0:−1:1:0], not the point transcribed in the inherited entry. Factoring f0=u^m h and g0=u^n k at general points of D, with h,k units, the negative-v arc forces m,n even. issues.locator: Theorem A(ii), published p.4, and Theorem 3.16(ii), published p.55, author-hosted journal PDF; corresponding arXiv 1801.00872v3 / Wittenberg-manuscript pp.4,48.
issues.printed: The source specifies dimension d ≥ 1.
issues.correction: For the even-genus equivalence in part (ii), add dim(X) ≥ 2 or X(R) = ∅. A simpler sufficient restriction is dim(X) ≥ 2. In the excluded case dim(X)=1 with X(R) nonempty, Pic descent is always surjective and the equivalence holds precisely when X itself has even genus. This finding does not require restricting part (i).
issues.reason: Use the smooth projective completion E of y²=x³−x over R. The cubic discriminant is 4 (Weierstrass discriminant 64); the point [0:1:0] is real and nonsingular, and E is geometrically integral of genus 1. Coherent H²(E,O_E)=0. Since E(C) is connected, H⁰_G(E(C),Z)=Z, generated by the codimension-zero cycle class [E]; hence the real integral Hodge conjecture for 1-cycles holds. The only reduced geometrically irreducible closed curve in E is E, so no even-genus curve exists. A real point splits Br(R)→Br(E); the low-degree Hochschild–Serre sequence therefore gives Pic(E)≅Pic(E_C)^G and hence the same isomorphism on 2-primary torsion. For the repair, Proposition 3.9 supplies even-genus curves when dim(X)≥2 and X(R)≠∅. If X(R)=∅, Theorems 3.3/3.6 apply without that dimension restriction; for curves this is exactly Lemma 3.7.
