issues.printed: The source invokes genus theory to bound the 2-torsion of the class group of K by O(2^t) times the 2-torsion of the class group of F, yielding O_ε(|Disc(K)|^{1/4+ε}).
issues.correction: A verified sufficient replacement is Klüners–Wang, arXiv:2003.12161v2, Theorem 2.1: h_2(K) ≤ 4^{e-1} h_2(F)², where t counts all ramified places including infinite ones and e = max(t,1), not simply t. Use this in a strong induction on n = [K:Q] rather than with Brauer–Siegel. If m = [F:Q] = n/2 ≥ 3 and the lower-degree case of the theorem gives exponent 1/2 - 1/(2m) + η, then D_F² ≤ D_K and 4^{e-1} ≪_{n,η} D_K^η give exponent 1/2 - 1/n + O(η), which is stronger than the 1/2 - 1/(2n) + ε the theorem needs. For n = 4, quadratic genus theory for F gives D_K^ε directly. This replacement neither proves nor refutes the printed one-factor relative bound, and it reaches the theorem's exponent without the printed D_K^{1/4+ε} claim for this case.
issues.reason: The displayed one-factor estimate has no derivation or precise citation in either preprint, and it is not what genus theory delivers. Genus theory for a quadratic K/F is the ambiguous class number formula, which bounds the Gal(K/F)-invariant classes: |Cl(K)^G| = h_F 2^{t-1} / [E_F : E_F ∩ N K^×] ≤ h_F 2^{t-1}. Passing from those to the 2-torsion costs a second factor: on Cl(K)[2] the map c ↦ c·σ(c) lands in Cl(K)^G and has kernel Cl(K)[2]^G, so the standard route gives only |Cl(K)[2]| ≤ |Cl(K)^G|², and genus theory bounds neither Cl(K)[2]^G nor Cl(K)^G by O(2^t)·h_2(F). That missing step is the whole of the gap, and it is load-bearing here: it is exactly what lets the printed argument finish by applying Brauer–Siegel to F, since h_2(F) ≪_ε |Disc F|^{1/2+ε} ≤ |Disc K|^{1/4+ε}. With the squared estimate that route gives only |Disc K|^{1/2+ε}, which is the trivial bound. Klüners–Wang Theorem 2.1 and its proof give the squared estimate h_2(K) ≤ 4^{e-1}h_2(F)², with Remark 2.2 improving it when the base 2-rank is zero; no statement in the literature gives the one-factor form. A weaker known upper bound is not evidence that the printed bound is false, and none is claimed here: the finding is that the step is asserted without proof or citation, not that it is refuted.

issues.printed: The source fixes a divisor D and takes a semiample Q-Cartier Q-divisor A with A ∼_Q M + Λ. Here M is effective and Cartier, its support contains no curve exceptional for Y → X, and −δD ≤ Λ ≤ δD with δ > 0. For x ∈ F ∩ M having multiplicity k ∈ Z_{>0} in M, it asserts that ε_sa(A; x) tends to k as δ → 0.
issues.correction: Only a lower bound holds. For every rational γ with 0 < γ < k there is δ₀ > 0, depending only on f, D and γ, such that ε_sa(A; x) = ε(A; x) ≥ k − γ for all δ < δ₀ and all such A, M, Λ and x. Equivalently, liminf_{δ→0} ε_sa(A; x) ≥ k, uniformly. This follows by the printed strategy after correcting its intersection estimate as in E9; the strategy provides no upper bound.
issues.reason: Counterexample with Λ = 0. Let k be a field of characteristic p > 0, X = A²_k, and f: Y → X the blow-up of the origin with exceptional curve E = F. Let M be the sum of the strict transforms of the two axes. Then M ∼ −2E, so M is effective, Cartier, globally generated over X (O_Y(−E) = m·O_Y) and has no exceptional component. Let x = E ∩ (strict transform of the y-axis), so mult_x M = 1 = k. Blow up x, with exceptional curve G and strict transform E′. Then E′² = −2, G² = −1, E′·G = 1 and π*M − tG ∼ −2E′ − (2+t)G, which has degree 2 − t on E′ and t on G. Hence ε(M; x) = 2. At t = 2 the ideal (x, y²) pulls back to O(−E′ − 2G) (charts x = ab, y = b, then a = c, b = cd, giving c²d, and a = ef, b = f, giving f²). So π*M − 2G ∼ −2E′ − 4G is globally generated and ε_sa(M; x) = 2. Taking A = M and Λ = 0 (any D), ε_sa(A; x) = 2 for every δ, not converging to k = 1. The proof aims to show that π*A − (k − γ)E is nef; its coefficient estimate must first be repaired as in E9. The consumers need only the lower bound: Proposition 8.15 (p.173) uses the first assertion ε_sa(M; x) ≥ 1, which is correct, and Claim 8.21 (p.178) needs ε_sa > 2 for k = 3. So the paper's results are unaffected. Checked on the page image and by exact arithmetic. Noted by the extraction (diagnostic A, gap-seshadri-limit); verified and proved in the corrected form by this continuation.

issues.locator: Published version, proof of Lemma 4.20, p.122 (final step)
issues.printed: The source concludes from Lemma 2.36 that κ is an isomorphism.
issues.correction: Use the following stronger form of Lemma 2.36: for a proper birational f:Y→X of normal integral Noetherian schemes, let D_X be a Q-Cartier integral Weil divisor and D_Y an integral Weil divisor with f_*D_Y=D_X and D_Y≥floor(f*D_X). Then f_*O_Y(D_Y)=O_X(D_X); D_Y need not be Q-Cartier. Apply this to D_X=ceil(L), D_Y=ceil(π*L+A_Y).
issues.reason: The target divisor in Lemma 4.20 need not be Q-Cartier because Y is only normal. The stronger form is proved by sections as rational functions: if div(g)+D_X≥0, pullback gives div(g)+f*D_X≥0, and integrality gives div(g)+floor(f*D_X)=floor(div(g)+f*D_X)≥0. Thus D_Y≥floor(f*D_X) gives a section upstairs. Conversely push the effective divisor div(g)+D_Y down; normality identifies the resulting sections with O_X(D_X). The ceiling inequality on published p.122 is precisely equivalent to the floor bound, not to the stronger D_Y≥f*D_X. This fills a missing hypothesis adapter, so it affects the proof but supplies no counterexample to the result.

issues.locator: Published proof of Lemma 2.56, p.102, case C≠E meeting E; arXiv v2 p.26 and v3 p.29 (v1 p.21 even prints equality at this step)
issues.printed: γE·C + Λ·π_*C ≥ γE·C − δ|D·π_*C|
issues.correction: Write D=Σ_j d_jD_j with prime D_j and d_j≥0. For each exceptional curve C_i on Y use B_i=Σ_j d_j|D_j·C_i|, so Λ·C_i≥−δB_i. Replace |D·π_*C| by B_i. Choose δ<γ/(1+max_i B_i). This supplies the uniform lower bound in E1.
issues.reason: Coefficient inequalities do not bound intersection numbers by the absolute value of the sum when component intersections cancel. On Y=Bl_0 A² in characteristic p, let E be exceptional and D_x the strict transform of the x=0 axis. Set D=E+D_x, Λ=δE. Then −δD≤Λ≤δD but D·E=−1+1=0 and Λ·E=−δ<0. Take M the sum of the two strict axes and A=M+δE, so A∼_Q−(2−δ)E is relatively ample for rational 0<δ<2; all the lemma hypotheses hold. Blow up a point of E∩M and take C=E′. Thus the displayed inequality itself fails. For the repair, the coefficient condition forces D effective and |λ_j|≤δd_j. The triangle inequality gives the B_i bound. There are finitely many exceptional curves C_i on Y. In the proof case meeting the new exceptional curve, E_new·C≥1, so γE_new·C−δB_i>0 uniformly. The other cases use (k−γ)>0 and nefness of A. Published p.102 and both later preprints were checked; the lower-bound result survives this repair.

issues.correction: Do not use the claimed sheaf/complex isomorphism from v1. Use the revised definition with the direct sum of O_{X⁺}(−S_i⁺) and the revised adjoint-section results. issues.reason: Let I=H⁰(K) and Q=H¹(K) in the old construction. The truncation triangle I→K→Q[−1] gives the exact segment H^{d−2}(RΓ_mRΓ Q)→H^d(RΓ_mRΓ I)→H^d(RΓ_mRΓ K)→H^{d−1}(RΓ_mRΓ Q), with the same twist throughout. This review confirms that proof gap, not a new counterexample to the old image statement. The authors explicitly call v1 Lemma 4.25 incorrect in v2 p.45 and published p.127, and replace the construction. It is already corrected in the published treatment and must not be registered as a new published error.

issues.locator: §4, paragraph after Corollary 15: published p.141; arXiv 2108.13397v3 p.11. Consequent reductions: Lemma 16 p.142, Definition 18 paragraph p.144, Theorem A proof p.146 (published). Both versions directly read.
issues.printed: For affine parabolic X, the source claims all Galois sections of X are cuspidal.
issues.correction: Delete this universal assertion. In the split-boundary cases A¹ and G_m the usual cuspidal description applies, but a nonsplit degree-two boundary must be treated separately. To justify the subsequent use of Lemma 16 and the reduction through Proposition 22, supply a direct argument for t-birationally liftable sections on the remaining parabolic curves, or a separate reduction covering them. Taking the identity map in Definition 18 only proves t-b.l. implies quasi-t-b.l. when X is non-parabolic. This review records the missing argument; it does not claim to supply a complete repair in arbitrary transcendence degree.
issues.reason: Let k=Q and X=P¹_Q minus the degree-two closed point cut out by T²−2. Then X is smooth affine of genus zero and its boundary has degree two, so it is parabolic by the paper’s definition. The point 0 lies in X(Q) and induces a geometric Galois section. There is no rational boundary point, hence no cuspidal section by the definition on published p.129. The section at 0 is also t-b.l.: after extending to Q(t), the local parameter at 0 supplies the usual birational lift. Thus even restricting the printed cuspidality assertion to t-b.l. sections does not fix it. Schmidt, Homotopy Rational Points of Brauer-Severi Varieties, arXiv 1503.08108v1, Theorem A p.2, provides splitting/existence of rational points for the relevant open variety; it does not turn a degree-two boundary into rational cusps. Lemma 16 assumes away the parabolic case, and the start of Theorem A uses Proposition 22 via quasi-t-b.l. The example is geometric and therefore does not contradict Theorem A. The false unnumbered universal assertion is itself a stated result; the downstream issue is a missing reduction, not a demonstrated false main theorem.

issues.locator: Lemma 26 proof: published p.148, reference [19, Theorem 17 (2)]; arXiv 2108.13397v3 p.17, [Sti12, Theorem 17 (2)]. Both versions directly read.
issues.printed: The source says the hypothesis makes the section cuspidal, and subsequently asserts ι_U(s) ∈ P_{U,x} for each U ⊂ X.
issues.correction: First use the hypothesis that each image is geometric or cuspidal. On the hyperbolic X, it determines a unique associated rational point x of the smooth completion, using geometric-section injectivity together with Stix Theorem 17(1) and (3). Compatibility implies that the associated point for every smaller open is the same x. Now restrict to the cofinal family U⊂X with x∉U: only on that family are all images cuspidal at x. Compute both inverse limits over this family to obtain the birational cuspidal section at x. Cite Theorem 17(1) for cusp uniqueness and (3) for disjointness; (2) concerns injectivity of a packet map and is not the uniqueness statement.
issues.reason: If x lies inside X, an open U containing x receives the geometric section at x, not a section in a cuspidal packet indexed by x. Removing x is cofinal among opens, so it does not change the function-field inverse limit. Once x is outside U, disjointness of geometric and cuspidal sections and uniqueness of the associated point force the image to lie in P_{U,x}. The compatibility maps for these packets are the ones already used by the printed inverse-limit argument. Stix, On cuspidal sections of algebraic fundamental groups, Theorem 17 and Remark 18, author PDF p.8, https://www.math.uni-frankfurt.de/~stix/research/preprints/STIXcuspsec20120802homepage.pdf, were directly read. Its injectivity hypothesis holds over finitely generated extensions of Q and their finite extensions: rational points of abelian varieties are finitely generated, hence have no nonzero divisible subgroup; the standard Abel–Jacobi injectivity argument and finite étale neighborhoods give the corresponding geometric-point uniqueness on a hyperbolic curve. The original finding missed the adjacent incorrect theorem-part citation.

issues.locator: Lemma 8 proof: published p.138; arXiv 2108.13397v3 p.9. Both directly read.
issues.printed: The source describes Π_X/k^ab = Π_J/k as a canonical identification.
issues.correction: Use the generalized Albanese torsor P under the semiabelian Jacobian J. The Albanese morphism gives Π_X/k^ab ≃ Π_P/k. The object s=γ(*) supplies a neutralization of this gerbe, giving a chosen-object equivalence Π_P/k ≃ B_k TJ. Identify Π_J/k with B_k TJ using the identity of J. Make the quotient map to B_k TA compatible with these chosen objects before reading it as a homomorphism of Tate modules.
issues.reason: Geometrically, the generalized Albanese map identifies the abelianized fundamental group with TJ; the torsor construction descends that comparison to the banded gerbe Π_P/k. Equality of bands alone does not identify an arbitrary gerbe with the neutral gerbe Π_J/k. Here no extra rational point of X or P is needed: γ maps the preferred object of B_k Zhat(1) to an object of Π_X/k^ab, and any gerbe banded by the commutative group TJ becomes B_k TJ after choosing such an object. Thus the missing choice/descent step is available within the hypotheses. Equivalences preserve isomorphism classes and the finite-image hypothesis; the weight and torus argument can then proceed as written. The following sentence of the source already mentions the images of the preferred object, so this is a small repairable gap in the claimed canonical comparison, not an obstruction to Lemma 8. Added from the later extraction; independently checked here.

issues.locator: Lemma 9 proof: published p.140; arXiv 2108.13397v3 p.10, polynomial lift and finite étale extension paragraph. Both directly read.
issues.printed: The source allows any lift q ∈ R[t] of q̄ and sets R′ = R[t]/(q).
issues.correction: Choose q̄ monic and q a monic lift of the same degree. Write z=f(p) for the closed point of A¹_k occurring here, and use q̄ to present k(z); this avoids confusing it with the original point p of X_k.
issues.reason: For R=Q[u]_(u), q̄=T and q=uT²+T, reduction modulo u is indeed q̄. But T and uT+1 are comaximal, since (uT+1)−uT=1, so R[T]/(q) ≃ R×R[1/u] = R×Q(u), which is not finite over R and has more than one maximal ideal. In contrast, a monic lift of the same degree gives a finite free R-algebra, and separability of q̄ makes its discriminant a unit. It is therefore finite étale; its special fiber is the field k(z), so it is local, and an étale local algebra over a DVR is a DVR. This is exactly the extension needed for the curve through z, whose inverse image has a component through the original p. The intended choice is clear and leaves the lemma unchanged. Added from the later extraction; the polynomial counterexample and the corrected construction were independently checked.

issues.locator: Lemma 5.2(ii), p.956, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 194 (2021), 943–966 (Caltech repository copy of the publisher PDF, SHA-256 77ff3290…790e)
issues.printed: In (ii), the source gives µ(⌊(p−1)/12⌋ − 3/2 + (−3/p) + ½(−1/p)) as a lower bound for supersingular points of X₀(N)(F_{p²}) representing curves over F_{p²} with a_{p²} = 2p or −2p and j different from 0 and 1728. It concludes that under either condition p ≡ 1 mod 12 or the condition p ≥ 31, one such point lies over X(1)(F_{p²})∖{0,1728} and is unramified for π.
issues.correction: The displayed bound is valid, but at p = 47 it equals 0, so the "in particular" does not follow from it. The "in particular" is nevertheless true, and for every p ≥ 13. By the Eichler–Deuring count and the N(t) table in the proof, each of the ⌊(p−1)/12⌋ supersingular j ≠ 0, 1728 has models over F_{p²} with a_{p²} = ±2p and µ points of X_0(N)(F_{p²}) above it. That gives µ⌊(p−1)/12⌋ ≥ µ > µ/6 such points. The displayed bound equals µ(⌊(p−1)/12⌋ − 2δ − ε) in the notation p − 1 = 12m + 4δ + 6ε of the proof, and is weaker than this count.
issues.reason: The deduction needs the lower bound to exceed the number of ramification points, which (i) bounds by µ/6. At p = 47: ⌊46/12⌋ = 3, (−3/47) = −1 and (−1/47) = −1, so the displayed bound is µ(3 − 3/2 − 1 − 1/2) = 0 < µ/6. Every other prime p ≥ 31 passes. The count from the proof's own facts is 3µ at p = 47, so the statement holds and only the deduction from the displayed bound fails. The construction of §5 (p.957) cites Lemma 5.2(ii) and (iii) together, and Rubin's verification (Remark 2.3) covers p = 47, so nothing downstream is affected. The arithmetic is right: at p = 47 the displayed bound is 0, so the "in particular" does not follow from it. This review corrects the reach in place. The entry called this a false stated result, but the "in particular" is true, including at p = 47. The facts in the paper's own proof (p.957) give more than the displayed bound. Write p − 1 = 12m + 4δ + 6ε. The N(t) table gives N(2p) = N(−2p) = m + δ + ε, and the classes with t = ±p and t = 0 occur only for j = 0 and j = 1728. So each of the m = ⌊(p−1)/12⌋ supersingular j-invariants other than 0 and 1728 has models over F_{p²} with a_{p²} = ±2p. Each has µ points of X_0(N)(F_{p²}) above it, by étaleness and Lemma 5.1(i). The true count is therefore µ⌊(p−1)/12⌋. The displayed bound equals µ(m − 2δ − ε), which is valid but weaker. Since there are at most µ/6 ramification points, the "in particular" holds for every p ≥ 13; at p = 47 the count is 3µ. So this is a gap in the deduction, not a false statement, and it reaches nothing. The kind, affects, correction and reason are updated accordingly. I confirmed by hand that 47 is the only prime p ≥ 31 at which the displayed bound fails.

The printed equality holds when every prime factor of f lies above p, and after localizing at height-one primes on components ramified at every 𝔩|f with 𝔩∤p.
issues.reason: z is generated by the elliptic units of the single modulus p^n f (Kato §15.5), whose projection to a character χ carries ∏_{𝔩|f,𝔩∤p}(1 − χ(𝔩)Frob_𝔩^{−1}) (Johnson-Leung–Kings Lemma 7.7); JLK accordingly pair it with H² over O_K[1/pf]. BT's h² is the class-group limit, which Kato (15.6.2) identifies at height one with H² over O_K[1/p]. By purity, 0 → H²(O[1/p]) → H²(O[1/pf]) → ⊕_{𝔩|f,𝔩∤p} Z_p[[G/D_𝔩]] → 0, and since D_𝔩 has Z_p-rank one each term is torsion but not pseudo-null. On the trivial-character component 1 − Frob_𝔩^{−1} is a non-unit even after inverting p, so the printed equality fails whenever f has a prime factor not above p, and footnote 3's "identical" is false for h². Kato p.250 says §15 proves Theorems 12.4, 12.5, 12.6, 14.2 and 14.5 in the CM case, not Conjecture 12.10. Proposition 15.17 (p.265) is an inequality, and p.251 says Rubin's equality is not used. The only equalities in §15 are Rubin's for K itself: Theorem 15.2(2), restated in 15.6. I redid the descent. Put A = O_λ[[G_{p∞f}]]_q, M = H²_q and N = H¹_q/A·z. Lemma 14.15 (pp.243–244) applies to both, because M_(a) = N_(a) = 0 by 15.15. With (15.13.1)–(15.13.2) it gives length(H¹(T~)_p/Z_p) − length(H²(T~)_p) = Σ_{q′} (length N_{q′} − length M_{q′})·[A/(q′+aA)] + length Ker(a|N). An equality of characteristic ideals kills the sum. Ker(a|N) = 0 because A is a UFD, a is prime, H¹_q embeds in its rank-one reflexive hull A, and a does not divide z there. So the correction is right, and the gap is real but small. issues.reason: Counterexample. Let D ⊂ P² over k = F_3 be the projective closure of y² = x²(x − 1). It is geometrically integral (r = 1) with normalization P¹, parametrized by x = t² + 1, y = t(t² + 1), so g_g = 0 and the right side is q + 1 = 4. D(F_3) consists of (0,0), (1,0), (2,1), (2,2) and the point at infinity. The origin is an ordinary node with tangent cone y² + x² = 0. Since −1 is not a square in F_3, its two branches t = ±i are defined only over F_9. The left side is therefore 2 + 4 = 6 > 4. Citing [11] III.5.3 Proposition 2(i), Lemma 7.4 claims Ψ^{[m]}_j has no terms below degree m for j = 1, ..., n. It sets Log^t_j(y) = Σ_{m≥1} ((−1)^m/m) · Ψ^{[m]}_j(y), Exp^t_j(x) = Σ_{m≥1} (1/m!) · ψ^{[m]}_j(x), where ψ^{[m]}_j denotes the degree-m homogeneous component of Ψ^{[m]}_j.
issues.correction: Replace the multiplication-map series by the coefficientwise finite differences Δ_m(t) = Σ_{i=0}^m (−1)^(m−i) binom(m,i)[i](t), for m≥1. Use Log(t) = Σ_{m≥1}(−1)^(m−1)Δ_m(t)/m and Exp(t) = Σ_{m≥1}[Δ_m(t)]_m/m!, where [ ]_m means homogeneous degree m. These formulas have identity linear term, are mutual inverses, and satisfy the claimed denominator bounds. This repair is verified here by formal polynomial interpolation; no claim is made to have directly read Bourbaki III.5.3–5.4.
issues.reason: For the printed definition, [m](t) has linear term mt in every characteristic-zero formal group. Thus Lemma 7.4 fails and the proposed logarithm’s linear terms are (−1)^m t, which do not tend to zero. To verify the repair at all orders, let L and E be the normalized formal logarithm and exponential over K. The degree-d part of [z](t)=E(zL(t)) is polynomial in z of degree at most d. Newton interpolation at z=0 gives [z]=Σ_m binom(z,m)Δ_m coefficientwise. Differentiating at zero gives L=Σ_m(−1)^(m−1)Δ_m/m. The leading z^m coefficient in degree m is E_m(t), so [Δ_m]_m=m!E_m and Δ_m has no terms of degree below m. Since Δ_m is an integral linear combination of integral [i], these identities prove the bounds of Lemmas 7.5–7.6. Exact computation through degree four with L(t)=t+at²+bt³+ct⁴ verifies both identities; the printed exponential’s cubic coefficient is 6a²−4b, whereas E has 2a²−b. The all-order interpolation argument, not that finite check alone, establishes the repair.

issues.printed: Corollary 10.5 asserts that any curve C with genus g ≥ 3 has C^{(2)} with an ample canonical divisor, making C^{(2)} a surface of general type. The proof invokes Lemma 10.4, using the ampleness of θ and the effectivity of every V_ξ.
issues.correction: Under §10.3’s assumptions (smooth projective curve, algebraically closed k, char(k)≠2), C^(2) is of general type for every g≥3. Its canonical divisor is ample for g≥4, and for g=3 when C is nonhyperelliptic. For hyperelliptic g=3 it is nef and big but not ample. In the nonhyperelliptic application in Corollary 1.15 the needed conclusion remains valid.
issues.reason: For a hyperelliptic genus-three curve, the Abel map contracts the pencil E={x+ιx}≅P¹. Hence θ·E=0 and K≡θ has zero intersection with E, contradicting ampleness. To justify the corrected positive statements, π:C×C→C^(2) is finite and π*V is the sum of the two point-fibre divisors, an ample divisor on C×C; thus V is ample. The pullback θ=j*Θ is nef and big because j is generically finite onto its image, and is ample when j is a closed immersion (the nonhyperelliptic case). Now K≡θ+(g−3)V gives all the stated cases. Mere effectivity of V would not justify the original ampleness inference.

No element of O/I_z² has p-th power s, hence no k_m-algebra map k_z = k_m(s^{1/p}) → O/I_z². Reach `the proof` is right: the footnote itself supplies the repair.

issues.correction: For M = Z_ℌ(𝔖)/𝔖, first prove that M_K is anisotropic. A proper K-parabolic would extend over O by properness of its fixed-type parabolic scheme and specialize to a proper k-parabolic, contradicting special-fiber anisotropy. Henselian smooth lifting and this properness argument give the singleton comparison Par(M)(K) = Par(M)(O) = Par(M)(k), where the whole group is counted as a parabolic; this is not a general assertion that reduction of a smooth proper scheme is injective. For the radical torus T = rad(M), lift a finite Galois splitting extension of k to O; its character-lattice description identifies the cocharacters over K, O and k. Hence T_K has no split subtorus. Together these prove generic anisotropy, and Guo Proposition 6 gives M(O) = M(K). Replace the Borel–Tits reference Proposition 6.11 by Corollaire 6.8.

issues.locator: Proof of Proposition 8.4, claim (2), author PDF p. 25 (the published version p. 24)
issues.printed: For claim (2), the proof appeals to Definition 8.1 and concludes from isotropicity that a proper parabolic P ⊂ G exists.
issues.correction: Definition 8.1 gives a proper parabolic over each local ring, not necessarily over the semilocal base. One sufficient repair, explicitly supplied in the later author survey, strengthens the assumption: each simple factor over its own finite étale base contains G_m (and hence has a fiberwise proper parabolic). This is automatic in the quasi-split application of Theorem 9.1. Alternatively retain the original total-isotropy hypothesis and lift radical points separately at each maximal ideal. The earlier extraction proposes this via a Noetherian reduction and nonzerodivisor denominator clearing; its full proposal is preserved in priorExtractionRepair. A precise replacement is the finite-presentation polynomial dilation argument proved in the companion report: spread an identity-preserving affine-space parameterization to R_s with s outside the chosen maximal ideal and inside the others, clear denominators, and dilate again to kill the finitely many relation coefficients annihilated by powers of s. The resulting map A^d_R → G is identically 1 modulo s and has the desired parameterization after inverting s. Lift Laurent-series coordinates at the chosen residue field and evaluate this map; all other residue components are 1. Applying this to both opposite radicals and the corrected Whitehead factorization proves the needed loop-coset surjectivity. This argument allows zero divisors and needs no Noetherian reduction.
issues.reason: Example: let Ō be the semilocal ring of A¹_Q at two closed points with residue fields L₁ (cyclic cubic) and L₂ = Q(i), and R = {f ∈ Ō : f(q₁), f(q₂) ∈ Q}, a one-dimensional Noetherian semilocal domain with residue fields Q, Q. Milnor patching of M₆(Ō) with M₂(D) and M₃(H) gives an Azumaya R-algebra A of degree 6, where D is a cubic division algebra split by L₁ and H = (−1,−1)_Q. Here A is split over Frac R, and A_{R_{m₁}} ≅ M₂(D′), A_{R_{m₂}} ≅ M₃(H′), since the patching over each local ring is unique. So G = SL₁(A), simply connected of type A₅, is totally isotropic. An R-parabolic would have a single type, since Dyn(G) is constant, proper on both closed fibres SL₂(D) and SL₃(H). Their parabolics are the flags of reduced dimensions in {3} and in {2, 4} respectively, so there is none. Theorem 9.1 is unaffected: it applies Proposition 8.4 to quasi-split G, which has a Borel over R. The counterexample disproves the asserted global-parabolic inference, not Proposition 8.4 or Theorem 9.1. A concrete choice is L₁ = Q(ζ₇ + ζ₇⁻¹) and D = (L₁/Q, σ, 2): 2 is inert in this cyclic cubic extension, so its valuation prevents 2 from being a norm and D is division. The companion report spells out the conductor patching and the local matrix decompositions.

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed at three independent points. Definition 8.1 (author p.23) defines total isotropicity pointwise — « for every s ∈ S », with the canonical decomposition over O_{S,s} and each factor containing G_{m,O_{S,s}}, equivalently having a proper parabolic O_{S,s}-subgroup — so it supplies a parabolic over each local ring, while the proof of Proposition 8.4 claim (2) writes « the isotropicity assumption implies that G has a proper parabolic subgroup P ⊂ G (see Definition 8.1) ». issues.locator: Proof of Corollary 9.6, first sentence, author PDF p. 28 (the published version p. 27)
issues.printed: The source asserts that each inner form of SO_n can be written as SO(E), where E is a rank n nondegenerate quadratic space over R.
issues.correction: Every twist of SO_n by an SO_n-torsor is an SO(E) for such an E; these are the only twists the argument uses.
issues.reason: For even n ≥ 4, inner forms also come from central simple algebras with orthogonal involution. Over R = Q (allowed in Theorem 9.1 with O = Q), take H = (−1,−1) and H′ = (−1,3), non-isomorphic quaternion algebras ramified at {2, ∞} and {2, 3}. Then SO(H ⊗ H′, γ ⊗ γ′) ≅ (SL₁(H) × SL₁(H′))/μ₂ is an inner form of split SO₄. It is not an SO(E): for E of trivial discriminant, SO(E) ≅ (SL₁(C) × SL₁(C))/μ₂ with isomorphic factors. For odd n every form is an SO(E), and the proof only twists by H¹(R, SO_n). As a second check, over the real numbers the example has Lie algebra su(2) ⊕ sl₂(R), with one compact and one split simple factor. A four-dimensional real quadratic space gives so(4) (both compact), so(2,2) (both split), or so(3,1) (real simple), never this mixed pair. Thus the Q-example is not SO(E) even without invoking the full classification of algebras with involution. The unrestricted inner-form assertion fails, while pure-inner twisting suffices for the stated corollary.

The unrestricted sentence is false for even n: (−1,−1)_ℚ ramifies at {2, ∞} and (−1,3)_ℚ at {2, 3} — at 3 because −1 is not a square mod 3, at 2 by the unit formula, and split at ∞ because 3 > 0 — so they are non-isomorphic division algebras, and A = H ⊗ H′ with σ = γ ⊗ γ′ is a degree-4 algebra with orthogonal involution of trivial discriminant whose SO(A, σ) ≅ (SL₁(H) × SL₁(H′))/μ₂ is an inner form of split SO₄. issues.locator: Corollary 2.8 and its proof, pp.499–500, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 487–526 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 3425f269…40e2)
issues.printed: For p > 0, the source asserts the existence of nonnegative integers λ and t with 0 < λ ≤ v², together with |disc(NS(X))| = p^t λ |disc(NS(M_H(v)))|. Its proof uses a natural lattice injection Zv ⊕ (v^⊥ ∩ N(X)) ↪ N(X) with torsion cokernel, gives the discriminant of Zv ⊕ v^⊥ as v² disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X)), and infers |disc(N(X))| ≤ v² |disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X))|.
issues.correction: λ need not be an integer. With I = [N(X) : Zv ⊕ (v^⊥ ∩ N(X))], one has |disc NS(X)| = p^t (v²/I²) |disc NS(M_H(v))| with t ≥ 0. So λ = v²/I² is a positive rational number with λ ≤ v², and I divides v² because v is primitive. For p ∤ v², for example v² = 2 and p ≥ 3 as in the applications, λ is still a p-adic unit, which is what the later arguments use.
issues.reason: Take v = (1, 0, −1), the Mukai vector of ideal sheaves of length-two subschemes, so M_H(v) = X^[2]. It satisfies condition (C): it is primitive, of rank 1, v² = 2, and gcd(1, 0, −1) = 1. Then v^⊥ ∩ N(X) = NS(X) ⊕ Z(1, 0, 1) with (1, 0, 1)² = −2, so |disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X))| = 2|disc NS(X)|. The proof's first step gives |disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X))| = p^r |disc NS(M_H(v))|. Hence |disc NS(X)| = ½ p^r |disc NS(M_H(v))|, which is not of the form p^t λ with λ a positive integer when p is odd. The proof passes from the equality disc(Zv ⊕ K) = I² disc N(X) to an integer multiplier without controlling I, here I = 2. The inequality stated for p = 0 is correct. Checked on the page image. Noted by the extraction (items 34–35).

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed, and the counterexample checks out. The statement is verbatim in arXiv:1407.0592v2 (24 August 2014), the latest public version, PDF sha256 37d2b945de77b8a40eb23c401335c91c51553d6c458931928ea05b5b16e6714d and LaTeX e-print sha256 2ee2bcf9f4a9da36a8f3fb39ff77f30fe1182a3f19e65432d6f8ec240452f7d8 as Corollary 2.7 (the §2 numbering of the published version runs one ahead of the preprint's). The printed proof derives |disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X))| = p^r|disc NS(M_H(v))| and then only the inequality |disc N(X)| ≤ v²|disc(v^⊥ ∩ N(X))| from the injection Zv ⊕ (v^⊥ ∩ N(X)) ↪ N(X); writing I for its index, that injection multiplies discriminants by I², so the equality is |disc NS(X)| = p^r (v²/I²)|disc NS(M_H(v))|, exactly the correction. For the Hilbert square, v = (1,0,−1) has v² = 2 and satisfies condition (C) of Definition 2.3 — it is primitive, rk = 1 > 0, v² > 0 and gcd(1, 0, −1) = 1 — and v^⊥ ∩ N(X) = {(r, D, r)} = NS(X) ⊕ ⟨−2⟩ with index exactly 2 in N(X), since (a, D, b) lies in Zv ⊕ v^⊥ if and only if a ≡ b (mod 2). So λ = 2/4 = 1/2, and for odd p no integer λ ≤ 2 can satisfy p^tλ = p^r/2. The corollary as printed is false, so 'a stated result' is right.

issues.locator: Proposition 2.9, p.500, as used in the proof of Theorem 2.10, p.503, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 487–526 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 3425f269…40e2)
issues.printed: Proposition 2.9 takes a positive integer d and a positive definite rank 2 sublattice Λ of Λ_2d. It asserts that some N that is a positive integer and a, b that are nonzero integers ensure a primitive embedding of Λ into Λ_2md whenever positive m satisfies (i) m = 1[N]; (ii) coprimality of m to a and b, with both quadratic residues modulo m. The proof describes the embedding of Λ into Λ_2d as primitive and associates it with (V, W, γ, t).
issues.correction: Assume Λ is a primitive sublattice of Λ_2d. In the proof of Theorem 2.10, choose the lattice Λ containing v, w with v² = 2, v·w = 1 to be primitive. For example, in Λ_2d = ⟨2d⟩ ⊕ U with basis h, e, f, take the span of v = e + f and w = kh + e. It is primitive, since (x, y, z) ↦ (z, y − z) retracts it, and its Gram matrix [[2, 1], [1, 2dk²]] is positive definite.
issues.reason: The proof starts from a primitive embedding Λ ⊂ Λ_2d, which the statement does not provide, and the statement fails for non-primitive Λ. In Λ_2 = ⟨2⟩ ⊕ U, the sublattice Λ generated by 2h and 2(e + f) has Gram matrix diag(8, 8). Take m = 1, which satisfies (i) and (ii) for every N, a, b. A primitive embedding of Λ into Λ_2 would give a 2-dimensional subspace of Λ_2/2Λ_2 = F_2³ on which the half-norm Q(x, y, z) = x² + yz vanishes, since Λ has all half-norms even. The nonzero zeros of Q are (0,0,1), (0,1,0) and (1,1,1), and each pairwise sum has Q = 1, so no such plane exists. Noted by the extraction (items 38–41), which also gave the primitive choice above.

issues.printed: The proof invokes Riemann–Roch to assert surjectivity of H⁰(C, 3L|_C) → 3L|_C/(3L|_C − D(p) − D(q)) for the specified p and q. Its justification is that 3L|_C − D(p) − D(q) has degree 3r − 4 > r = deg(ω_{C/k}), and that evenness of r gives r > 1.

issues.locator: Proposition 3.17, p.517, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 184 (2016), 487–526 (publisher PDF, SHA-256 3425f269…40e2)
issues.printed: The source asserts that suitable positive N and nonzero integers a, b give finiteness of polarized nonsuperspecial K3 surfaces (X, H) over k of degree 2md for positive m satisfying (i) m = 1[N]; (ii) coprimality of m with a and b, both quadratic residues modulo m; (iii) the discriminant of NS(X_k̄) has p-adic valuation at most t_0.
issues.correction: There are only finitely many k-isomorphism classes of nonsuperspecial K3 surfaces X over k admitting a polarization H of such a degree 2md with (i)–(iii). The polarized pairs themselves need not be finite in number.
issues.reason: On a fixed eligible (X, H) of degree 2m_0 d, the line bundles H^{⊗ℓ^j} have degree 2(ℓ^{2j} m_0)d. Choose a prime ℓ with a and b quadratic residues modulo ℓ and prime to N, a and b, and let j run through multiples of the order of ℓ² modulo N. Then m = ℓ^{2j} m_0 satisfies (i) and (ii), and (iii) is unchanged. This gives infinitely many pairwise non-isomorphic polarized pairs on one surface; the paper does not require polarizations to be primitive. The proof bounds NS(X_k̄) and then the surfaces. The only use, the proof of Theorem 1.3 on p.523, reads "there exist only finitely many K3 surfaces over k", so the corrected statement is what is used. Noted by the extraction (items 88–89).

issues.printed: For the B₃ orbit in F₄, the source gives ℜ(s)=ω₁+ω₂+½ω₃+½ω₄.
issues.correction: Delete ω₂: ℜ(s)=ω₁+½ω₃+½ω₄. In the Euclidean coordinates of (6.21), the corrected dominant representative is (5/2,1,1/2,0). This is Weyl-conjugate to (2,−1,3/2,1/2), the parameter at ν=1/2 in the B3 complementary series.
issues.reason: Using the explicit fundamental weights (6.21), the printed parameter is (4,3/2,1,1/2), with squared norm 39/2. Ciubotaru’s primary classification [Ci1], §3.2 table continued on manuscript p.14 and §5 p.37, gives B3 parameters (3/2+ν,−3/2+ν,3/2,1/2), 0≤ν<1, in the SAME coordinates (§2.6 p.10). Their squared norms are 7+2ν²<9, so the printed point is not Weyl-conjugate to any member of this complementary series. The nonzero half-integral value is ν=1/2. Its coordinate vector (2,−1,3/2,1/2) first becomes (2,3/2,1,1/2) by a signed permutation and then (5/2,1,1/2,0) by reflection in (1,−1,−1,−1). This equals ω₁+½ω₃+½ω₄. Independent enumeration gives top adjoint Frobenius weight 16 for the printed point, contradicting the p.34 bound 10. The corrected point has multiplicities n_v(10)=1,n_v(9)=0,n_v(8)=2, as needed there. The coordinate classification statement must therefore be repaired, in addition to the index repair E3; no failure of the intended global theorem is asserted.

issues.locator: §3, published p.493 (PDF p.7), Annals of Mathematics 192 (2020), 487–497; arXiv 1907.13617v1/v2 p.5; HAL hal-02375397v1 PDF p.7 (manuscript p.6).
issues.printed: The source defines the underlying vector space over R by L = 𝓛 ⊗_Q R.
issues.correction: L = 𝓛 ⊗_Z R, the real span of 𝓛 in V_R (equivalently (𝓛 ⊗_Z Q) ⊗_Q R).
issues.reason: The preceding definition makes 𝓛 the kernel of integral polynomial evaluation in the finite free Z-module V_Z. Its rank ℓ = C(d+r,d) − n is positive: the standing assumptions give ℓ ≥ nr ≥ 1. A basis vector of a nonzero finite free Z-module is not divisible by 2, so this Z-module admits no compatible Q-module structure. Thus the displayed tensor product needs Z as its base ring. Extending the integral evaluation matrix to R identifies 𝓛 ⊗_Z R with its real kernel and real span in V_R. This supplies the space used for orthogonality and successive minima.

issues.printed: For a non-real v′ ∈ P(k′), the source says E′_{v′} admits no orderings. Invoking cohomological dimension under field extensions, it concludes cd(E′_{v′}) ⩽ cd(E′) ⩽ dim(E′) + 1 ⩽ dim(Fw) + 1 < r + 1.
issues.correction: Bound E′_{v′} directly: cd₂(E′_{v′}) ⩽ cd₂(k′_{v′}) + td(E′_{v′} | k′_{v′}) ⩽ 2 + (dim(E′) − 1) = dim(E′) + 1, using cd₂(k′_{v′}) ⩽ 2 for a non-real place (a henselian p-adic or algebraically closed field) and Serre's bound cd(K) ⩽ cd(k) + td(K|k). The rest of the chain is unchanged.
issues.reason: The middle inequality cd(E′) ⩽ dim(E′) + 1 is false when E′ is formally real, since a field with an ordering has infinite 2-cohomological dimension. That case occurs here: E′ ⊂ E, a field of representatives for Fw, and k′ may have real places, which is why the second half of the proof treats them. The absence of orderings in E′_{v′}, which the sentence invokes, is exactly what makes the direct bound work.

issues.locator: §1.4.3, p. 13, formulas (4)–(6), in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 12–13 Independent review source locations: v5 PDF pp. 13; v4 PDF pp. 12; v1 PDF pp. 11; published PDF pp. 14.
issues.printed: Given non-degenerate G(F_v)-space pairings ⟨,⟩_{π_v}: π_v ⊗ π_v^∨ → C at each v, the source asserts the existence of C = C(dg, fac_π, fac_{π^∨}, ∏_v⟨,⟩_{π_v}) satisfying ⟨φ, φ^∨⟩_Z = C(…) ∏_v ⟨φ_v, φ_v^∨⟩_{π_v}.

issues.reason: Arbitrary nondegenerate local pairings do not define the asserted product: take the trivial representation of GL1 and multiply the normalized pairing by 2 at every finite place. The claim of existence as stated is false, so change gap/nothing to error/a stated result. This does not disprove the later application with normalized pairings.

issues.locator: §2.3, p. 17, construction of P from hermitian pairs, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at pp. 15–16 Independent review source locations: v5 PDF pp. 14, 17; v4 PDF pp. 15–16; v1 PDF pp. 14; published PDF pp. 15, 18.
issues.printed: The source chooses totally imaginary δ ∈ O prime to p and sets ⟨·,·⟩_i = trace_{𝒦/Q} δ⟨·,·⟩_{V_i}. It defines h_{i,σ} : C → End_R(V_{i,σ}) by h_{i,σ}(z) = diag(z1_{r_{i,σ}}, z̄1_{s_{i,σ}}), and Σ = {σ ∈ Σ_𝒦 : p_σ ∈ Σ_p}. It declares P = (B, ∗, O_B, L, 2π√−1⟨·,·⟩, h) a unitary PEL datum.
issues.correction: δ must also satisfy a sign condition tied to the CM type Σ: Im σ(δ) > 0 for all σ ∈ Σ if ⟨·,·⟩_{V_i} is 𝒦-linear in the first variable (Im σ(δ) < 0 for all σ ∈ Σ if linear in the second). Such δ exist (weak approximation), so the fix is to choose δ after Σ.
issues.reason: A merely imaginary p-unit delta does not guarantee the PEL positivity axiom. With the hermitian form linear in the first variable each nonzero sigma component contributes 2 Im(sigma(delta))*|x|^2. Replacing an allowed delta by -delta reverses positivity without changing the stated hypotheses. Require positive imaginary parts on the chosen CM type (negative for the other linearity convention). Classify as error because the asserted construction is false for permitted choices.

issues.locator: §2.9.4, p. 32, justification of injectivity of (28), arXiv v5 Independent review source locations: v5 PDF pp. 20, 29, 32; v4 PDF pp. 29; published PDF pp. 21, 30, 34.
issues.printed: The source attributes injectivity of these maps to density of S_1 in the special fibre of M^tor_{K,L}.
issues.correction: Supply a level-K_r q-expansion or formal restriction theorem for the stated coefficient rings. For flat noetherian coefficients a possible route is to show every generic component meets the ordinary special fiber and that the space of sections is p-adically separated. The density assertion on the base alone does not establish these facts; general p-adic coefficient rings require a justified base-change argument.
issues.reason: The stated reason gives density on the hyperspecial base, whereas the forms have level K_r on an open quasi-finite cover. That reason alone does not prove injectivity of completion/restriction on this cover: even an etale cover X disjoint_union X[1/p] of a proper base X has a generic-only component invisible in the formal special fiber. This example diagnoses the inference, not the actual Shimura moduli space. A proof needs a separation/density result for the actual cover and the permitted coefficients. Remove the unsupported claim that the report has supplied a full proof for all R; retain the conclusion as unrefuted.

issues.locator: §2.9.6, pp. 33–34, arXiv v5 Independent review source locations: v5 PDF pp. 33–34; v4 PDF pp. 30; published PDF pp. 35; v1 PDF pp. 28.
issues.printed: With R as in Equation (32), the source defines O^+ as the integral closure of Z_(p) inside R. It asserts that Frac(O^+) is a number field supporting a rational model of S_κ(K_r, ψ; R) ⊗ Q.
issues.correction: Choose a number field E0 inside Frac(R) containing the coefficient data and carrying the rational model; take its ring of integers localized at the selected prime above p, with an embedding into R after any needed coefficient extension. Alternatively use the semilocal p-integers where appropriate, but do not identify the two rings or take the integral closure in the whole p-adic R.
issues.reason: R contains Z_p, whose elements algebraic over Q do not lie in one number field. For odd p, each rational prime ell congruent to 1 modulo p has a square root in Z_p by Hensel, giving infinitely many distinct quadratic subfields. Thus the fraction field of the stated integral closure is not a number field. Choose a finite number field of definition instead. Also correct the proposed repair: localization at one prime above p is not generally equivalent to the integral closure of Z_(p), which is semilocal at all primes above p.

issues.locator: Proposition 3.2.5(ii), proof, p. 41, arXiv v5 Independent review source locations: v5 PDF pp. 40–41; published PDF pp. 42–43; moonen04 PDF pp. 23–24.
issues.printed: The proof uses Hida theory to identify V^ord_{κ_p}((G, X); K^p, R) with an R-dual of a module of finite rank over a suitable Iwasawa algebra, placing f in an R module of finite rank. It deduces (ii) from ordinary-locus Zariski density in the integral model of S(G, X), citing [Wed99], if sufficiently many ordinary CM points exist. It then says each ordinary point over a finite field has a lift to the generic fiber, citing [Moo04, Proposition 2.3.12].
issues.correction: Supply a CM restriction/separation argument on each finite Igusa level, including coverage of its frames by the allowed CM pairs and coefficient base change. For torsion-free coefficients, once this coverage is established, reduced special-fiber detection and division by p can be iterated using zero evaluations at characteristic-zero lifts and p-adic separation. For arbitrary p-adic R a valid flat-base-change or devissage argument is still required; the existing report does not establish it.
issues.reason: The cited Moonen Proposition 2.3.12 (arXiv math/0203288, pp.23-24) supplies canonical lift/CM facts for p-divisible groups. It does not itself establish that the maps of CM Igusa towers meet every finite-level frame or a separation theorem for functions with all the stated p-adic coefficient rings. Density on the underlying ordinary locus and finite rank over an Iwasawa algebra do not by themselves supply those steps. The report's claimed complete repair also assumes the needed frame coverage and says general R follows by devissage without justification. Confirm the gap in the presented proof, retain the theorem as unrefuted, and mark the missing steps explicitly.

In rank one the two valuation ranges give X=beta(varpi)chi_wbar(varpi)^-1 q^(-s-1/2) and Y=beta(varpi)^-1 chi_w(varpi)^-1 q^(-s-1/2), hence I=(1-XY)/((1-X)(1-Y)). With beta=1, q=5, s=1/2, and both chi components equal to i, this is 12/13-5i/13, whereas the printed Euler factors give 12/13+5i/13. Such unitary local data occur for a quartic Dirichlet character composed with a CM norm. This confirms the inverse-character mismatch independently of any base-change orientation for beta. Remove the earlier overclaim that equality is possible only when chi|K+ is trivial: special characters can also make the two expressions coincide. Independently checked: v5 PDF pp. 42, 45–47, 49–50; v4 PDF pp. 38, 41–42; v1 PDF pp. 36, 39; published PDF pp. 44, 47, 49, 52–53.

issues.printed: The source defines f_{p,s}(g) = |ν|_p^{sn/2} ⊗_{w∈Σ_p} f_{w,s}(g_w), g = (ν, (g_w)) ∈ G(ℚ_p), in (54). Referring to [Eis15], it asserts f_p ∈ I_p(χ_p, s).
issues.correction: (54) lies in I_p(χ_p, s) only after restriction to U_4(ℚ_p). To lie in I_p(χ_p, s) on all of G(ℚ_p), the factor |ν|_p^{sn/2} must be replaced by ∏_{w∈Σ_p} χ_{w̄}(ν)^n, reading the absolute values of §4.1.2 as the idelic module of 𝒦 (which makes the centre act unitarily). issues.reason: At s=0 take a central element with w-component 1 and conjugate component u, so nu=u. The inducing character requires chi_wbar(u)^n, while (54) gives no such factor. This proves failure on the similitude group independently of the absolute-value convention. For general s, Delta_wbar=nu times transpose(A_w)^-1 supplies the missing product chi_wbar(nu)^n, together with the norm adjustment already described in the correction. On nu=1 the discrepancy disappears. Record reach as the stated membership in I_p, rather than nothing.

issues.reason: The support gives level t for A1,D2 while (66)/(69) give level r>=2t. The actual pointwise statement fails: n=a=2,b=0, partition 1+1, trivial inducing characters in the irreducible normalized principal series Ind_B(1,1), t=1,r=2. issues.reviewReason: The factor D_v is an inverse Euler polynomial. issues.printed: Theorem 6.6.9, attributed to Hida, asserts for every representation π_p of G(ℚ_p) and every r that e_κπ_p^{I_r} ⊂ π_p^{I_r} has dimension ≤ 1. It promises an adaptation of Hida’s proof in §8.3.

issues.reason: Any representation includes a direct sum of two ordinary representations, immediately disproving the stated bound. Even for irreducible admissible representations the weight condition matters: in the split GL2 factor with a=b=1 take kappa_sigma=1,kappa_sigma-c=0, hence kappa_norm exponents (0,1). At p=5 let the unramified normalized inducing characters have values p^-1/2 and 2p^-1/2. Their ratio is not |.|^plus-or-minus-1, so the principal series is irreducible. On its two Iwahori-fixed vectors normalized U_1 has eigenvalues 1,2 and normalized U_2 is 2; both vectors are ordinary. Here kappa_sigma+kappa_sigma-c=1<2. Section 8.3 imposes irreducibility and (166), absent from 6.6.9. The local statement must be restricted; no global weight-one realization is needed for this local counterexample.

issues.reason: A finite algebra over a non-Henselian DVR can acquire a localization that is not finite over that DVR. This is an algebraic obstruction to the stated lattice argument, not an exhibited automorphic counterexample. The complete-coefficient setting adopted later removes this particular obstruction. issues.printed: Part (iii) claims normalized Serre duality gives perfect pairings, equivariant for T^ord_{K_r,κ,R} via Lemma 6.6.7: S^ord_κ(K_r;R)[π] ⊗_R H^{d,ord}_{κ^D}(K_r;R)[π] → R and S^ord_κ(K_r;R)_π ⊗_R H^{d,ord}_{κ^D}(K_r;R)_π → R.
issues.correction: Retain perfectness of the localized pairing under finite direct-factor hypotheses. The saturated eigenlattice pairing is perfect after inverting p; integral perfectness requires absence of the corresponding congruence obstruction. Under the later Gorenstein/freeness hypotheses its image is the congruence ideal described there.
issues.reason: Perfect integral duality of the whole localization does not give perfect duality of saturated eigenspace lattices. In T={(a,b) in O^2:a=b mod varpi^n}, S=T and H=Hom_O(T,O), the first eigenspace lattices are O(varpi^n,0) and O pr_1. Their pairing has image varpi^n O, although evaluation S x H is perfect. This is exactly the congruence obstruction discussed by 6.7.3 and 7.5.2, so the two printed perfectness assertions cannot be justified in the same way. The defect of perfectness is controlled by the congruence module; do not identify every higher-rank pairing image with the congruence ideal without the additional freeness hypotheses.

issues.printed: Theorem 7.1.1 claims a canonical isomorphism T^ord_{K^p,κ_1,R} ⥲ T^ord_{K^p,κ_2,R} for every pair of characters κ_1, κ_2 on T_H.
issues.correction: For any pair of sufficiently regular characters κ_1, κ_2 of T_H (in the range of Hida’s classicality theorem (32)), there is a canonical isomorphism T^ord_{K^p,κ_1,R} ⥲ T^ord_{K^p,κ_2,R}.
issues.reason: These Hecke algebras are defined from classical cusp forms at one fixed weight. On a noncompact connected Shimura curve the weight-zero cusp space is zero: a regular function on its proper compactification is constant, and vanishing at the nonempty boundary makes it zero. In a nonzero ordinary cuspidal family the sufficiently regular weight algebra is nonzero, so unrestricted weight independence cannot hold. The cited control statement (34) explicitly restricts weights by (32). Restricting the assertion to that range is substantive, even if later applications use regular weights.

issues.correction: For the stated right-translation convention use phi(t f)=rho^upsilon(t)^-1 (t phi(f)); transport the inverse if a left-translation convention is chosen. Keep the output Lambda-action explicit. Do not simply restore the older formula while keeping the newer equivalence unchanged.
issues.reason: With right translation (t f)(x)=f(xt), one has t(f rho^upsilon)=rho^upsilon(t)(t f)rho^upsilon. Lambda-linearity of the maps in (2) and the stated formula for the equivalence therefore require phi(t f)=rho^upsilon(t)^-1 t phi(f). The printed formula has no action on the output at all. The correction follows directly from the displayed equivalence, independently of any assertion about existence of a nonzero particular automorphic measure.

issues.correction: Work with joint generalised eigenspaces: ℓ = ⟨φ^{a-ord}_{w,r}, ·⟩_w satisfies ℓ∘(u^GL_{w,i} − a(i,r)) = 0, hence vanishes on every generalised u^GL_{w,i}-eigenspace for eigenvalues ≠ a(i,r); so ℓ ≠ 0 on the joint generalised eigenspace W_{j−1} for (a(1,r), …, a(j−1,r)); u^GL_{w,j} preserves W_{j−1} and u^GL_{w,j} − a(j,r) is not surjective there, so W_j ≠ 0; finally commuting operators on W_n have a common eigenvector.
issues.reason: A nonzero eigenfunctional need not remain nonzero on a true eigenspace: for the Jordan matrix [[a,1],[0,a]], ell(x,y)=y is an eigenfunctional and vanishes on ker(U-a). Hence the displayed induction does not follow merely by restricting (170). The stated conclusion does follow from the joint generalized eigenspace argument: the functional vanishes on every other joint character, the required joint generalized space is nonzero, and commuting operators on it have a common eigenvector.

issues.locator: §9, proof of Lemma 9.0.1, p. 140, in arXiv v5; present in v4 at p. 130 Independent review source locations: v5 PDF pp. 140; v4 PDF pp. 130; published PDF pp. 147–148.
issues.printed: The proof claims ordinarity survives complex conjugation and twists using powers of the similitude character. It invokes Lemma 8.3.6 to say duality interchanges ordinary and anti-ordinary representations, then concludes from essential unitarity that π has both properties.
issues.correction: Prove the precise conjugation compatibility of the normalized Hecke operators, weights, Borel and fixed p-adic embedding, or replace the argument by one that establishes ordinarity directly. Until then retain anti-ordinarity as the standing hypothesis without inferring extra interpolation points from this lemma.
issues.reason: Complex conjugation does not generally preserve the valuation at a fixed p-adic embedding. Concretely, in Q(i) at the prime (2+i) above 5, 2+i has positive valuation and 2-i is a unit. Essential unitarity is an assertion involving complex conjugation and duality, so it does not itself prove the needed valuation invariance. The weight and Borel changes under conjugation must be tracked, especially given E136. This elementary scalar example disproves the general valuation inference, not the specific automorphic lemma under a correctly transported normalization. The original CM-character sketch is not presented as a fully checked global counterexample. The claim is not used to enlarge the proved interpolation range.

issues.reason: The proof imports Proposition 9.1.7, which requires a classical pair in Y_H^class and m>=n, as well as regular-weight control and the local condition (166) at the specialization. Being a classical Hecke character alone does not impose these joint conditions. Corollary 9.2.1 starts by inheriting 9.1.8 hypotheses, and the sentence preceding 9.2.2 may import the archimedean inequalities; those are legitimate defenses and should be preserved. This is a range-of-proof gap, not a counterexample to every possible extension.

issues.reason: S is explicitly away from p, whereas the Euler product contributed by spherical sections runs only over finite places outside S and p. issues.locator: Section 2.9, v5 p.29; published p.30, definition of D_m and V^{cusp}_{n,m}
issues.printed: It defines D_m=S_m-S_m^0 using the reduced structure of a closed subscheme, and sets V^{cusp}_{n,m}(R)=H^0(T_{n,m/R},O_{T_{n,m}}(-D_{n,m})).
issues.correction: Take D_m to be the scheme-theoretic pullback to S_m of the horizontal toroidal boundary divisor, and D_{n,m} its pullback along the etale Igusa cover. Do not reduce the divisor after passage to Z/p^m. Its ideal must impose vanishing modulo p^m, not just modulo p.
issues.reason: For m>1 a boundary chart is A=(Z/p^m)[q] with horizontal boundary ideal (q). Its reduced boundary has ideal (p,q), which contains the nonzero constant p. The ideal (p,q) is also not a Cartier divisor ideal on this thickening. Etale pullback preserves this discrepancy. This is a defect in the stated cusp-module definition; no assertion that the intended, horizontally defined cusp theory is false.

issues.locator: Section 6.7.5, definition of H[pi-flat]_chi, arXiv v5 p.106 and published p.111
issues.printed: H_{kappa-flat,-V}^{d,ord}(K_r-flat,psi^-1,R)[pi-flat]_chi := H_{kappa-flat star chi,-V}^{d,ord}(K_r-flat,psi^-1,R)[pi-flat tensor chi^-1 det].
issues.correction: Transport the finite nebentypus and the tame/p level as well as the weight under twisting. For finite-order chi the new nebentypus is psi^-1 times the restriction of chi^-1 det to I_r^0; choose r and tame level so the twist is trivial on the corresponding pro-unipotent/level subgroup.
issues.reason: Take a finite-order chi nontrivial on determinants of I_r^0 and trivial on I_r, and an ordinary pi-flat vector of nebentypus psi^-1. The twisted vector transforms by psi^-1 chi^-1 det, not psi^-1. Its algebraic weight is unchanged, so changing kappa-flat star chi cannot absorb this finite character. The printed fixed-nebentypus space can therefore lose the entire one-dimensional anti-ordinary component, contradicting the rank-one period assertion of Lemma 6.7.6 even after its E112 typographical repair. Increasing r alone does not make chi trivial on I_r^0 diagonal units. The same issue occurs away from p if chi ramifies outside the fixed tame level.

issues.printed: The proof sets A = R_P, the local ring at P on X, and calls its localization at D by the name A_D.
issues.correction: Take A = R̂_P, the completion of the two-dimensional regular local ring R_P. Write L = Frac(R_P) = F and K = Frac(A) = F_P in the paper’s notation. If v and v̂ are their exceptional-divisor (order) valuations, the natural map identifies L_v with K_v̂. Do not use the erratum’s temporary notation F_P = Frac(R_P) as if it were the paper’s definition.
issues.reason: Gille’s published loop-torsor paper, §2.1 and Theorem 4 (printed pp. 161 and 163), assumes a henselian regular local ring; R_P need not be henselian, whereas R̂_P is. The completion map gives isomorphisms R_P/m^n ≅ R̂_P/m^nR̂_P, hence the same associated graded ring and a dense embedding for the order valuation. Approximating numerator and denominator shows L dense in K for v̂, so their valuation completions coincide. This is the exceptional divisor of the blow-up at P, a valuation of the original function field covered by the hypothesis. The shared parameter/residue field alone is replaced here by this explicit density argument.

issues.printed: On HAL p.14 the source writes T♯(F₁) ⊂ RT♯(F₁), claims density of E♯(F₁) in E♯(F), and gives an inclusion of closures using T(F₁). It asks initially for an isomorphism between T♯_(F₀) and T, then claims projected unboundedness in T♯(F₀). The initial displayed T♯(F₁) is printed without an overbar.
issues.correction: Choose T♯_(F₀) G(F₀)-conjugate to T as an embedded maximal torus. The lifting gives T♯(F₁)^n ⊂ RT♯(F₁). Use density of E♯(F₁) in E♯(F₀), and conclude T♯(F₀)^n ⊂ closure(RT♯(F₁)). The projections of this closure are unbounded in G_i(F₀).
issues.reason: If π:E♯→T♯ and πf = [n], then x^n = πf(x) is R-trivial because E♯ is quasi-trivial; the argument does not make every x R-trivial. Approximate f(x) for x ∈ T♯(F₀) by E♯(F₁)-points to obtain the closure inclusion. Rationality of the maximal-torus variety and openness of the G(F₀)-conjugacy class provide an embedded conjugate torus; an abstract isomorphism alone does not control the factor projections. Each isotropic torus factor has an unbounded cocharacter direction, and taking n-th powers preserves unboundedness.

issues.locator: proof of Corollary 4.7(1), printed p. 19, HAL v5 (26 December 2025). Published main-body passage not collated; confirmation is restricted to the named public manuscript(s).
issues.printed: The source invokes projectivity of Z_k to assert that Z_k(D) = Z_k(k(D)) is nonempty, and deduces that Z_k(k(P)) is nonempty as well.
issues.correction: First replace the normal model by a regular model with strict-normal-crossing special fibre (Lipman's resolution; the reductive model and its flag scheme pull back). Its components are regular curves, and the valuative criterion then gives Z_k(D) = Z_k(k(D)). Corollary 4.6 is applied to the new model.
issues.reason: A component D of the closed fibre of a normal surface need not be regular at P. Properness extends the generic point over the normalization of D, whose points above P may have larger residue fields; it does not give a k(P)-point. For a concrete failure of that implication, D = Spec(R[x,y]/(x²+y²)) is integral with function field C(y) and a real singular point at the origin. The constant projective conic a²+b²+c²=0 has a point over C(y), but no real point at the origin. The local curve occurs as the special fibre of the regular surface x²+y²=t. Resolving the model and its closed-fibre divisor to regular components makes the DVR extension argument valid; local-point hypotheses over all discrete valuations survive the change of model.

issues.correction: Write A_i = O_(X_i,P_i) and m_i for its maximal ideal. Then A_i^h has residue field k(P_i), and the local filtered colimit R = colim A_i^h has residue field colim k(P_i) = O/m. issues.reason: Henselization preserves the residue field of each A_i, but that field can change with i. Blow up a k-rational point and choose a closed point on the exceptional P¹_k with residue field a proper finite extension L/k; continue the chain above it. The initial henselization has residue field k, whereas the final O/m contains L. Thus the asserted equality for every i fails. Filtered colimits of these local maps give the required final equality and henselian local ring; the lemma is preserved.

issues.reason: In the case T = k[[t]], write y = x⁻¹. Then F₁ = Frac(k[[y,t]]) and R̂_p = k((y))[[t]]. Each truncation of c = Σ_{n≥1} tⁿ/y^(n!) lies in F₁ ∩ R̂_p; they form a t-adic Cauchy sequence with limit c in R̂_p. Using those smaller modules repairs the invocation of Theorem 3.13.

issues.locator: Lemma 2.2, second paragraph, p.5 of the published version (arXiv v2 Lemma 2.2, p.6)
issues.printed: The source refers to the index of K_X.
issues.correction: Use the local Cartier index of K_X + S at P, rather than the index of K_X. This is the log index of the localized plt surface pair; it gives the denominator of the different and kills local Weil divisor classes.
issues.reason: Over k = F_7, take X = Spec k[x,y,z]/(xy-z²), S = V(x,z), and P the vertex. The two resolution charts (u,uv²,uv) and (st²,s,st), in coordinates (x,y,z), are crepant and have one exceptional (-2)-curve E. Thus K_X is Cartier. The strict transform S′ meets E once, and f*S=S′+E/2; the snc pullback S′+E/2 proves that (X,S) is plt. Since div(x)=2S and (x,z) needs two generators at P, S is not Cartier. Adjunction gives different P/2. Hence the printed m=1 fails, whereas index(K_X+S)=2 works. More generally, for the plt surface chain with determinant d, the different coefficient is 1-1/d and d annihilates local divisor classes, forcing the log index to equal d. This is the surface adjunction calculation, not a claim about the canonical index. Lemma 4.2 only needs the standard-coefficient different.

issues.correction: Conclude that the divisor is Q-Cartier on a neighbourhood of the special fibre. issues.reason: Let R=Z_p, p>5, and let T be Spec R[x,y,z,w]/(xy-zw) with only its closed special vertex removed. It is integral, flat, normal and excellent. The special fibre is the punctured threefold node, hence smooth, S3, terminal and Q-factorial. The remaining generic vertex Z is closed in T and disjoint from that fibre, so codim(Z∩X,X)≥3. The ruling D=V(x,z) is Cartier on T\Z, restricts to a Cartier divisor on X, and does not contain X. Over K=Frac(R), use the small resolution xt=zs, wt=ys in N×P¹. On its charts z=ux,y=uw and x=vz,w=vy, with v=1/u, the strict transform of D has equations x and z. Since z=ux, its divisor line bundle restricts to O_{P¹}(-1) on the exceptional fibre. There is no exceptional divisor, so any Cartier multiple mD would pull back to that strict-transform multiple and also restrict trivially to the fibre, contradicting degree -m. Thus both stated global conclusions fail. dFH11 Proposition 3.1 explicitly retains a neighbourhood of the Cartier fibre. Under properness the closed complement of the Q-Cartier locus of a fixed D has closed image in Spec R; if it misses the closed point, it must be empty. The projective lifts in Theorem 6.1 have this properness. This example does not refute its other conclusions.

issues.correction: Choose Q-Cartier representatives with 𝒜|_X ≡ A and ℋ|_X ≡ H; clear denominators when constructing sections. For large m choose a primitive section of a divisible multiple of mℋ+𝒜, giving an effective 𝒟 that omits X and has 𝒟|_X ≡ mH+A. issues.reason: Theorem 6.1 defines N¹ as Pic⊗Q modulo numerical equivalence. Its surjectivity supplies rational numerical classes, not specified line bundles or integral representatives of prescribed classes. The proof of (2a), p.31, correctly uses ≡; p.33 uses literal equality. The needed construction can be made numerically: H is nef and big on X, hence its lift is nef and big on the generic fibre; choose m so mℋ+𝒜 is generically big. For a sufficiently divisible multiple L, the nonzero finite torsion-free R-module H⁰(𝒳,L) has a primitive section. The kernel of restriction to X is πH⁰(𝒳,L), so the primitive section does not vanish identically on X. Its divisor restricts with the desired numerical class and is negative on the chosen ray because H.Σ=0 and A.Σ<0. The fixed-resolution hypothesis permits a sufficiently small boundary coefficient. These steps require neither completeness nor H²(X,O_X)=0. They do not by themselves identify the prescribed special flop or prove numerical descent after the perturbed step; those are separate proof obligations. The finding is retained as a local proof gap, not a counterexample to the theorem.

issues.citation: Harpaz–Wittenberg, "The Massey vanishing conjecture for number fields", Duke Mathematical Journal (2023)
issues.reviewReason: Confirmed. Both the statement ('If $2 \leq n \leq 6$, the outer exponent of $\U^1$ is equal to $p$') and the first step of its proof are verbatim in arXiv:1904.06512v2, which the errata records as identical to the author final version it read; I fetched its PDF (sha256 a29ca765863948a7131820c24bf801c3dadf58494b439b11afa5983cec2f89e4) and its LaTeX e-print on 23 September 2026 and read the source at this locator. The definition on p. 13 is that the outer exponent is the smallest e | d such that the powering action of (Z/d)^× on conjugacy classes factors through (Z/e)^×. For p = 2 that action factors through the trivial group (Z/2)^×, so the outer exponent is 1, not 2, and the proof's opening claim that it is divisible by p fails for the same reason: the abelianization having exponent 2 forces nothing, since (Z/2)^× is trivial. So the lemma is false at p = 2 and 'a stated result' is right. The correction is the right one, and the use downstream is unaffected: e enters only through the requirement that L contain the e-th roots of unity, which is vacuous for e ∈ {1, 2}.

issues.locator: He21, published Forum of Mathematics, Pi 9 (2021), e9, §6.3, paragraph invoking [He15, Theorem 2.27]; construction in §5.4.

issues.correction: Supply basic nonemptiness for the constructed a t^γ without assuming that this new alcove is shrunken. A general criterion still requires its own hypotheses to be proved; replacing the citation alone is not a proof.
issues.reason: The cited survey theorem assumes a shrunken alcove. In split adjoint A2 take λ=ω2∨, x=s2s1, y=1. The published construction gives J=∅, J′={s1}, x′=s2, z=s1, γ=λ, y′=1 and a=s1s2. On the negative base alcove u<0, v<0, u+v>−1, w sends (u,v) to (v−1,1−u−v), with positive-root ranges (−2,−1),(1,2),(0,1). The seed a t^γ sends it to (1−u−v,u), whose second coordinate lies in the critical strip (−1,0). Both finite factors have full support. This disproves applicability of the cited theorem, not nonemptiness or the main result. The extraction’s stronger claim that every nonregular γ causes failure is false and is not retained.

issues.printed: The source sets G′ = G × T, V′ = V ⊕ V and X′ = X × {h_T}, claiming (G′, X′) ↪ (G_{V′}, H_{V′}). Restriction of I_{s′_0} to A_T is said to give I_{s′_0} → T, hence I_{s′_0} → T → G^ab. It invokes Corollary 2.1.9 for surjectivity of I_{s′_0} → I_{s_0} and deduces that I_{s′_0} → G^ab factors through I_{s_0}, citing this factorization over Q_ℓ for every ℓ ≠ p.
issues.correction: Replace G′=G×T by H=G×_{G^ab}T. This is a connected reductive central-torus extension of G, with kernel 1×(T∩G^der). The similitude character factors through G^ab, so the two blocks have equal multipliers; h^ab is constant on X, so X×{h_T} factors through H. Once the lifted point and compatible I-group maps have been constructed, use C_H((γ,t))=C_G(γ)×_{G^ab}T: projection is a base change of the surjective morphism T→G^ab, with kernel 1×(T∩G^der). Corollary 2.1.9 then gives surjectivity on I-groups over Q_ℓ for ℓ≠p. The composite through T to G^ab kills that kernel, and this descends faithfully flatly to Q. Surjectivity here means a morphism of algebraic groups, not necessarily surjectivity on rational points. The argument must establish kernel triviality, not infer factorization from surjectivity alone.
issues.reason: The direct-product construction is false as written, not merely an unexplained descent: already for G=GSp_2 and a CM maximal torus T, (1,2·1)∈G×T scales the two blocks of ψ⊕ψ by 1 and 4. Thus it is not a symplectic similitude. Independently of that failed Shimura construction, on the proposed direct-product group the composite G×T→T→G^ab is nontrivial on the kernel 1×T of projection to G, so it cannot descend. The original errata's unconditional claim about I_{s′} is replaced by this group-level obstruction, since the proposed Shimura embedding has already failed. The earlier checkpoint justified centralizer surjectivity by a general central-extension assertion which is false: for GL₂→PGL₂, d=diag(1,−1) and the coordinate swap w satisfy wdw⁻¹=−d, so [w] centralizes [d], but no scalar multiple of w centralizes d. The repaired fibre product has a stronger, direct argument. Since T is commutative, (g,u) commutes with (γ,t) precisely when g commutes with γ. This proves C_H((γ,t))=C_G(γ)×_{G^ab}T as group schemes, giving the asserted surjectivity and kernel without a general semisimple-centralizer claim. Corollary 2.1.9 then gives surjectivity on the I-groups; over Q_ℓ the kernel is killed by T→G^ab, hence over Q as well. Read Lemma 2.2.8, Corollary 2.1.9 and the preceding lifting construction. This repairs the identified local construction/descent; it is not a global certification of Proposition 2.2.2, whose preceding construction has the related E13 defect.

issues.printed: The source takes a flat normal W-scheme S of finite type, a relative Cartier divisor D ⊂ S, and the inclusion j : U = D − S ↪ S. It equips S with the log structure j_*O_U.
issues.correction: U = S − D, and S carries the divisorial log structure O_S ∩ j_*O_U^× → O_S.
issues.reason: D⊂S, so D−S is empty and cannot be the intended open complement on which the abelian scheme lives. For U=S−D, the intended log structure is the multiplicative monoid of regular functions invertible on U. The defect in j_*O_U is not that it is a sheaf of rings (rings also have underlying multiplicative monoids). For S=Spec W[x] and D=(x), j_*O_U contains x^{-1}; a monoid map to O_S agreeing with the identity on U would force the nonunit x to be a unit. Intersecting O_S with j_*O_U^× fixes precisely that problem. Independently checked the p.37 image and A.2–A.3.

issues.printed: The source claims existence and uniqueness of [b_μ].
issues.correction: Require existence of an ordinary class attaining the Hodge average; quasi-split G is a sufficient local hypothesis. The maximal admissible class need not attain that average. Any downstream non-emptiness or density assertion must retain its other hypotheses and separately justify realizability.
issues.reason: Independently checked the local obstruction for the quaternion division algebra D/Q_p. Over L, identify D× with GL₂ with Frobenius σ_D=Int(J)σ, J=[[0,p],[1,0]]. The bijection [b]_G↦[bJ]_GL₂ shifts κ by 1 and both Newton slopes by 1/2: the adjoint Frobenius actions agree and the determinant valuations differ by 1. For μ_m=(m+1,m), an ordinary class would therefore yield two distinct rank-one GL₂ isocrystals of slopes m+3/2 and m+1/2, impossible since rank-one slopes are integral. Admissibility confines the GL₂ slopes to [m+1/2,m+3/2], with sum 2m+2. Distinct slopes would each be integral, but the only integer in that interval is m+1. Thus the sole possible Newton vector is (m+1,m+1), realized by b=p^m J, for which bJ=p^(m+1)1. The G-vector is (m+1/2,m+1/2), strictly below μ_m. Taking m=−1 handles an inverse-Hodge representative (0,−1). Kisin–Zhou v2 Definition 2.2.4 and Remark 2.2.5 explicitly state the same existence restriction. This disproves the universal local assertion as printed, not a fully specified global integral-model example or the entire density corollary.

issues.correction: Replace the asserted equality of Tannakian groups by the subgroup H⊂G_s0 given by the full generated category. Evaluation followed by forgetting Frobenius is Vec_L-valued; F-Isoc(s0) itself remains Q_p-linear. Construct the desired functor by restriction from G_s0 to H and justify the descent of every needed invariant morphism and idempotent; this checkpoint does not complete that descent.
issues.reason: The selected tensors give only H⊂G_s0. This can be strict within the stated Hodge-type setting: take the CM elliptic curve y²=x³−x with CM by Q(i), its torus Shimura datum T=Res_{Q(i)/Q} G_m, and p=5. Its discriminant is a 5-adic unit; direct counting gives #E(F_5)=8 and trace −2, so its two crystalline slopes are 0 and 1. On a geometric component of the zero-dimensional special fibre, the isocrystal is 1⊕L(1), up to the dual convention, where L(1) denotes the rank-one slope-one object. Its full generated Tannakian category, after extension of scalars to L, is Rep_L G_m: the unit has no independent character and all other objects are sums of integral Tate powers. The stabilizer of the CM Hodge tensors is instead T_L≅G_m², of dimension two. Thus the printed equivalence is false, not merely unjustified; kind is changed from gap to error affecting the proof. This does not disprove the final exact faithful tensor-functor statement: restriction along G_m→G_m² can be exact and faithful without being full.

issues.correction: The block-diagonal map into GSp(V⊕V′,ψ⊕ψ′) additionally requires equality of the two similitude characters. Replace the group by the identity component of the subgroup of G′×_{G^ad}G cut out by c′(g′)=c(g). The paired Hodge homomorphism has equal multipliers and factors through this subgroup. Recheck the subsequent lifting and centralizer arguments for this corrected group; the present checkpoint establishes the missing condition, not the full repaired proposition. The related construction in Kisin–Zhou arXiv:2103.09945v2 §4.3.7, p.40, explicitly uses (G₂×_{G^ad,G_m}G)^0. Its Proposition 4.4.10, p.45, checks the projection maps using product projectors, central kernels and Frobenius centralizers. Those results have additional integral-model hypotheses; they are evidence for the repair strategy, not a completed verification of this proposition in its full generality. For the centralizer step, first use a common sufficiently divisible Frobenius power as in §2.1.5 and Corollary 2.1.9, pp.22–24. Its cyclic Zariski closure is a torus, so the relevant centralizers are connected Levi subgroups. The corrected group has central surjective projections; over an algebraic closure the projections identify root groups and carry maximal tori onto maximal tori. Corresponding roots have the same value on compatible Frobenius elements, so the roots taking value 1 agree. The restricted centralizer maps are therefore surjective with the same central kernels. This verifies the geometric centralizer step conditional on the compatible lifted points and I-group morphisms; it does not by itself establish their construction, the rational center embeddings, or the quotient assertions.
issues.reason: The fibre product over the adjoint group does not identify the central multipliers, and taking its identity component does not fix this. Test G′=G=GSp_2=GL_2 with the same Siegel datum and standard representation. The curve a↦(a·1,1) lies in the identity component of the fibre product over PGL_2. At a=2 its block-diagonal action scales ψ′ by 4 and ψ by 1, so it is not a similitude of their direct sum. These data satisfy the accommodating type-C setup (standard two-dimensional representation, with no proper nonzero invariant subspace). Hence the asserted embedding fails even in this basic allowed case. The equality-of-multipliers subgroup removes the obstruction; this is distinct from E5, where equality in all of G^ab is needed for descent. Independently read §2.2.7 pp.26–28 and the p.27 image. E13 avoids reusing E8–E12, which already identify different findings in the newer extraction. The GL₂→PGL₂ counterexample explained under E5 shows why arbitrary semisimple centralizers cannot replace the connected centralizers used in §2.1.5. For the corrected common-multiplier subgroup, each projection is surjective: first lift the adjoint image, then adjust the other component by a scalar to equalize multipliers over an algebraic closure. Taking the identity component preserves surjectivity onto the connected target. The kernels are central, since an element projecting to the identity has trivial image in the other adjoint group. These are statements about algebraic groups, not about surjectivity on Q-points.

issues.reviewReason: Confirmed. Page 27 prints 'let G″ be the connected component of the identity of G′ ×_{G^ad} G' and 'V″ = V ⊕ V′, where V″ is equipped with the symplectic form ψ″ = ψ ⊕ ψ′'. issues.correction: The construction has to be replaced by the one of KPZ26 Lemma 5.1.15, which follows [Ho23] and, in essence, Zink's [Zi99, Theorem 3].
issues.reason: The printed recipe depends on the normal decomposition, even though its diagram commutes. An independent rank-two test: take p>2, R=Z_p[[t]], S=Ŵ(R), M=S², and the universal line generated by e₁+t e₂ modulo I_R. Two normal lifts are l=e₁+[t]e₂ and l′=l+V([t])e₂, both with T=S e₂. In M̃₁ use u=φ(l), v=p e₂. Since φ(V([t]))=p[t], the second lift gives u′=u+[t]v. After base change to B=R/(p,t²), u,v remain a free basis and [t]≠0, so the two inverse comparison maps send the same first basis vector of D̃₁ to different elements. The horizontal map loses their difference because p[t]=0 in Ŵ(B). Thus it cannot determine c. KPZ26 Lemma 5.1.15 supplies a different, functorial map; Remark 5.1.17 explains the resulting failure of Lemma 3.1.12 with the old definition of constant modulo a_R.

issues.printed: The source defines q_loc : M̃^loc_G → M^loc_{G,X} by (f,F) ↦ f⁻¹(F) and claims it is a G-torsor. In diagram (4.2.9), M̃^loc_G → M^loc_G and M̃^loc_G → M^loc_{G,X}, it describes both π_loc and q_loc as G-torsors.
issues.correction: For the natural G-action in the displayed diagram, q_loc is equivariant, not in general an invariant torsor projection. Identify it instead with the action morphism G×M^loc_{G,X}→M^loc_{G,X}. It is smooth of relative dimension dim G: compose the isomorphism (g,m)↦(g,g·m) with projection. This is what the proof uses. An alternative transported G-action can make the underlying projection a torsor; that is not the action asserted in the original diagram.
issues.reason: For the natural change-of-trivialization action, q_loc transforms the image filtration, so its fibers are not G-stable when the target action is nontrivial. Hence it is not a torsor for that action. Independently, (g,m)↦(g,g·m) has inverse (g,n)↦(g,g⁻¹·n), so smoothness follows from the product projection because G is smooth. The theorem only needs equivariance and smoothness, not that both arrows be torsor projections.
