issues.locator: Published version, Publ. Math. IHÉS 128 (2018), 121–218 (Numdam PDF, SHA-256 e2b4a076…); Proof of Lemma 3.1.17, printed p. 169
issues.printed: The proof says it is enough to equip Ŵ(A) ⊗_{Z_p} Q_p with a complete separated topology τ for which p^{−m}φ^m(x) → 0 for every x ∈ W(m_A). It claims that s̃ = s + Σ_{m≥0} Φ^{m+1} ∘ s ∘ Φ₀^{−m−1} − Φ^m ∘ s ∘ Φ₀^{−m} then converges in τ to a Frobenius-invariant element of Hom_W(D,M) ⊗ Q_p.
issues.correction: The ring cW(A)[1/p] is not complete for the topology τ defined there, so establishing p^{−m}φ^m(x) → 0 in τ does not finish the proof. KPZ26 show instead that cW(A)[1/p] is p-adically complete and separated and that p^{−m}φ^m(x) → 0 in the p-adic topology for x ∈ cW(M_A), which does finish it, using Zink's logarithmic coordinates on cW(pN) and [Zi01, Prop. 2.3, 2.4]. Here p-adic topology on the rationalized ring means the topology induced by its integral Ŵ(A) lattice, not the ideal-adic topology for the unit p.
issues.reason: The topology τ is induced by the product of the p-adic ghost-coordinate topologies; it permits coordinatewise limits with unbounded denominators. Explicitly take A=Z_p[ε]/(ε²), p>2, so m_A²⊂pA. In the square-zero ideal εQ_p, the Witt ghost formula is w_i(x)=p^i x_i. Let z_N have Witt coordinates ε/p^i for i≤N and zero thereafter; p^N z_N has integral finite-support coordinates, so z_N∈Ŵ(A)[1/p]. Its ghost coordinates are ε for i≤N and zero afterwards, hence (z_N) is τ-Cauchy. A limit would have all ghost coordinates ε. Multiplying by any fixed p^M would force Witt coordinates p^(M−i)ε for every i, which are not integral for i>M. Thus no limit exists even in W(A)[1/p]. KPZ26 replaces this topology by the lattice p-adic topology and proves the required decay using logarithmic coordinates.

issues.locator: Published version, Publ. Math. IHÉS 128 (2018), 121–218 (Numdam PDF, SHA-256 e2b4a076…); §4.6.21, printed p. 205
issues.printed: Section 4.6.21 takes a Shimura datum (H,Y) with classical H^ad. Citing [20] and [43] 3.4.13, it asserts a central isogeny H̃ → H♯, depending additionally on Y when H has a type D factor, and characterizes abelian type of (H,Y) by H^der being a quotient of H♯.
issues.correction: Restrict the H♯ construction to the conditions in published KPZ26 §7.2.1 (pp.76–77): in each type-D simple factor over its totally real field, all noncompact real places must have the same Hermitian type, always D^R or always D^H. The adjoint Shimura datum being of abelian type supplies these conditions. Do not assert the construction for arbitrary classical adjoint data.
issues.reason: The required quotient is the simply connected cover at a D^R place, but the standard orthogonal quotient at a D^H place. A single central quotient cannot have a trivial kernel after one real base change and a nontrivial kernel after another: a finite central kernel in characteristic zero has constant degree. Thus the real-place compatibility condition is essential to this construction. Published KPZ26 §7.2.1 gives the precise condition and footnote 8 explicitly corrects KP18 §4.6.21. The abelian-type context used immediately afterwards satisfies the extra condition.

issues.printed: The source calls X = Spec k[x, y, x]/(x² + xyz) a normal surface.
issues.correction: X = Spec k[x, y, z]/(x² + xyz), which is not normal: x² + xyz = x(x + yz), so X is the union of two smooth surfaces meeting along x = yz = 0, and its local ring at the origin is not a domain.
issues.reason: In k[x,y,z]/(x(x+yz)), the two factors give nonzero zero divisors even in the local ring at the origin; a normal local ring must be a domain. Both components are graphs isomorphic to A². Since the defining equation has initial term x², the tangent space has dimension 3 and the reduced tangent cone is the plane x=0. In the domain k[[t]], f(f+gh)=0 forces f=0 or f=-gh; with g,h in (t), f has no linear term. The y- and z-axis arcs span exactly that plane. The example works after deleting 'normal'; no claim about the cited P95 chart is needed for this check.

issues.printed: Section 4.2.9 defines W(α) through nonzero action of X_α on a Weyl-module weight space. It identifies this with adjacency of weights and claims (ϖ,β)∈W(α) iff (ϖ,β+α)∈W(−α). Proposition 4.2.10 relies on these claims.

Repair Proposition 4.2.10(2) directly using the RIGHT inclusion of (4.2.7): for g=(1+εt^(⟨λ,α⟩−l)X_α)t^λ and v_β∈V(ϖ), t^⟨μ,ϖ⟩g⁻¹v_β has its X_α-term of exponent ⟨μ,ϖ⟩−⟨λ,β⟩−l. If X_αv_β≠0, integrality gives l≤⟨μ,ϖ⟩−⟨λ,β⟩, hence l≤l_α for ALL dominant weights. Under Proposition 4.2.13's minuscule-set hypothesis, the proof of k_α≥j_α uses only minuscule root strings, for which symmetry holds, and gives k_α=j_α=l_α. Thus its full equality, Remark 4.2.16 and the sign-corrected Corollary 4.2.19 survive, not just k_α=j_α. The printed proof of Proposition 4.2.10(1) outside that hypothesis still needs a valid argument; no counterexample to its numerical statement is claimed.
issues.reason: For GL₂ in characteristic p, in the divided-power basis v_i=F^(i)v_0 of Δ(p,0), wt(v_i)=(p−i,i), E v_i=(p−i+1)v_(i−1), F v_i=(i+1)v_(i+1). Thus E v_1=0 although both adjacent weights occur, while F v_0=v_1≠0, disproving also the pairwise symmetry. The proof's final range assertion fails: input v_p has E v_p=v_(p−1)≠0 but is sent to weight (−1,1−p) in Δ(0,−p)=Δ(p,0)⊗det^(−p), whose raising coefficient is p=0. However the omitted right inclusion yields the stated general bound by the inverse-matrix calculation above, without dualizing Weyl modules. For any S as in Proposition 4.2.13, this gives k_α≤l_α≤j_α; the minuscule argument gives the opposite k_α≥j_α. The earlier report overstated the reach by leaving Proposition 4.2.10(2) and the l_α equalities unestablished. V(ν)* is generally induced rather than Weyl, so Remark 4.2.8(3)'s identification with V(−w₀ν) cannot justify discarding the right inclusion.

issues.locator: Published proof of Lemma 7.2.8, p.79, definition of Bil_Hc(V) and assertion that U_σ is open; arXiv v3 p.82.
issues.printed: The source defines Bil_Hc(V) to comprise every invariant F-bilinear form and claims that its subset U_σ of polarization forms is open.
issues.correction: Work in Alt_Hc(V), the F-linear subspace of invariant alternating forms. Its real extension is the product of the corresponding local alternating-form spaces. Each polarization cone U_σ is nonempty and open in that subspace, and the rational points of Alt_Hc(V), viewed as a Q-vector space, are dense in its real extension. Thus choose Ψ there with all components polarizations and take Tr_(F/Q)Ψ as in the paper. The conclusion of Lemma 7.2.8 is unchanged.
issues.reason: Take F=Q, G=GSp₂≅GL₂ with its usual Shimura datum, Hc=SL₂, and the fundamental Hodge embedding on V=Q²⊗Q² where G acts on the first factor and trivially on the multiplicity factor. With J the standard alternating form, invariant bilinear forms are J⊗A for arbitrary A∈M₂(Q). Such a form is alternating iff A is symmetric; with compatible sign convention the polarization cone is A symmetric positive definite. This is open in Sym₂(R), not in M₂(R): arbitrarily small nonsymmetric perturbations of I leave the cone. In general, h_σ(U(1))⊂Hc_(R,σ) makes b(x,h_σ(i)y) symmetric for invariant alternating b; positive definiteness is open there. Nonemptiness is supplied by the Cartan-involution polarization argument cited in the paper. Deligne 1979 §1.1.10 (p.253) explicitly requires symmetry after applying h(i); §1.1.18(a) (p.256) provides existence, not automatic alternation of every invariant bilinear form.

issues.locator: §2, Lemma 2.1 (statement and proof) and Corollary 2.2, p. 5 (arXiv v1)
issues.printed: Lemma 2.1 bounds the count of monic polynomials p(x) with integer coefficients, degree 2g, and roots of absolute value √q by (2g)^g q^{(1/4)g(g+1)}. The proof places each integer s_k in [−g√q^k, g√q^k]. Corollary 2.2 gives (2g)^g q^{(1/4)g(g+1)} as an upper bound for the count of isogeny classes over F_q of abelian varieties.
issues.correction: s_k is a sum of 2g numbers of absolute value q^{k/2}, so it lies in [−2g q^{k/2}, 2g q^{k/2}], which contains at most 4g q^{k/2} + 1 integers. For polynomials with q^g f(x) = x^{2g} f(q/x) (this includes every Frobenius characteristic polynomial) the bound is (4g+1)^g q^{g(g+1)/4}. For the lemma as literally stated, where f(0) = −q^g can occur (e.g. x² − q), the bound is 2(4g+1)^g q^{g(g+1)/4}. Corollary 2.2 holds with (4g+1)^g q^{g(g+1)/4}.
issues.reason: For g = 1, q = 2 there are six monic integer quadratics whose roots all have absolute value √2 (x² + bx + 2 with |b| ≤ 2, and x² − 2), and elliptic curves over F₂ realize all five traces −2, …, 2, giving five isogeny classes; both counts exceed (2g)^g q^{g(g+1)/4} = 2√2. The proof undercounts twice: |s_k| can be as large as 2g q^{k/2}, and an interval of length L can contain L + 1 integers. The identity q^g f(x) = x^{2g} f(q/x) also fails for x² − q, where x² f(q/x) = −q f(x). Reach: Lemma 2.1 and Corollary 2.2 are false as stated, already for g = 1 and q = 2. The corrected bound differs by a factor e^{O(g)}, so the isogeny-class count p^{(g²/4)(1+o(1))}, Theorem 0.1 and all later results are unaffected.

issues.locator: §3.1.5, display (11) and the sentence after it, together with (13), p. 10 (arXiv v1)
issues.printed: The source asserts #{R-lattices L ⊂ V : length_{Z_ℓ}(R^{⊕n}/L) ≤ δn} ≤ Σ_{a₁+⋯+a_n≤δn} Σ_{length(O_F ē_i/U_i)=a_i} #{R-lattices L ⊂ V : L_i = U_i} ≤ ℓ^{nδ} Σ_{a₁+⋯+a_n≤δn} ∏_{i=1}^n #{R-ideals of colength a_i} … The proof justifies the second bound in (11) by induction using §3.1.4. … (13) ≤ ℓ^{4nδ}.
issues.correction: As a count of lattices, (11) and (13) are false. What §3.1.6 needs is a bound on the number of GL_n(F)-orbits. Apply §3.1.4 along the flag V_{≤1} ⊂ ⋯ ⊂ V_{≤n}. At step i the pairs of unequal eigenvalues between V_{≤i−1} ≅ F^{i−1} and V_{≤i}/V_{≤i−1} ≅ F bound the shear classes by ℓ^{(i−1)δ}. The induction therefore gives ℓ^{n(n−1)δ/2} per graded type, not ℓ^{nδ}. Each isotypic block then has ℓ^{O(n²δ)} orbits (for instance at most ℓ^{4n²δ}), not the linear ℓ^{4nδ}. Explicitly, the corrected ideal bound and stars-and-bars give at most ℓ^{n(n−1)δ/2} ℓ^{nδ}2^{2nδ+n} ≤ ℓ^{4n²δ} orbit representatives for δ≥1; δ=0 gives one orbit. This is not a replacement bound of ℓ^{4nδ} for raw lattices.
issues.reason: For E/F₇ with 6 points (trace 2), ℓ = 3 and A = E^{17}, f = x² − 2x + 7 has discriminant −24, so R = Z₃[x]/(f) is the ring of integers of the ramified field Q₃(√−6), with δ = 1 and R/𝔪 = F₃. Every L with 𝔪R^{17} ⊂ L ⊂ R^{17} is an R-lattice of colength at most 17 = δn. There are more than 3^{73} of them (one per F₃-subspace of F₃^{17}), against ℓ^{4nδ} = 3^{68}, and the largest Schubert cell alone gives 3^{72} with the same graded pieces L_i, against ℓ^{nδ} = 3^{17}. Here R is a discrete valuation ring and there is only one orbit, so what matters is the orbit count, and for it the cited induction gives only the quadratic exponent above. Reach: The linear bound (13) and the first line of the display in §3.1.6 are unproved. Count the pairs λ ≠ μ with order and multiplicity. Each isotypic block then contributes n_i²δ_i to Σ_{λ≠μ} val_ℓ(λ − μ), so the quadratic orbit bound still gives the last line of that display. The bound B(p,g) ≤ p^{O(g²)} of Theorem 0.1 therefore survives, and Theorems 0.2 and 0.3 are untouched.

issues.locator: §3.1.5, sentence before (12), p. 10 (arXiv v1)
issues.printed: The source attributes to Yun [28, §4.12] the inequality #Hilb^j_R ≤ #Hilb^j_{Z_ℓ[[x]]}, explaining it by presenting R as a quotient of Z_ℓ[[x]], the power series ring.
issues.correction: R is local with residue field k_R = F_{ℓ^s}, and it is a quotient of Z_ℓ[[x]] only when s = 1. In general R is a quotient of O₀[[T]], where O₀ = W(k_R) ⊂ R is the unramified coefficient ring and T ↦ θ − ω with ω ∈ O₀ lifting the residue of θ. Count ideals of O₀[[T]], whose residue field has ℓ^s elements, as Yun does after reducing to the residue field. This still gives #Hilb^j_R ≤ ℓ^j·2^j.
issues.reason: Z_ℓ[[x]] is local with residue field F_ℓ, so every nonzero quotient ring of it has residue field F_ℓ; this excludes R whenever f mod ℓ is a power of an irreducible polynomial of degree s > 1. For example, take E/F₃ with 3 points (trace 1) and ℓ = 2: then f = x² − x + 3 ≡ x² + x + 1 mod 2, and R = Z₂[x]/(f) is unramified with residue field F₄. Ideals of R have Z_ℓ-colength divisible by s, and the count over O₀ gives Σ_{λ ⊢ j/s} ℓ^{s(j/s − len λ)} ≤ ℓ^j·p(j/s) ≤ ℓ^j 2^j. Reach: The justification of (12) fails when s > 1, but the bound (12) itself survives, so nothing downstream changes.

issues.locator: §3.1.6, display and (14), p. 11 (arXiv v1)

issues.locator: §3.2.1, first bullet, displayed map, p. 12 (arXiv v1)

issues.reason: The printed assignment is not well defined on the points of the orbit. Take ℓ = 3, f = x² − 4x + 13, R = Z₃[3i], F = Q₃(i), n = 1 and M = O_F = Z₃[i], so that R ⊂ M ⊂ O_F ⊂ R^∨. issues.locator: §3.2.2, (21), case d > 1, p. 14; also the constant C₀ after (28), p. 16 (arXiv v1)
issues.printed: The source invokes strong approximation to claim that the factorwise reduced norm maps give a bijection G(Q)\G(A^fin)/U_{0,d} × ∏_{i=1}^m G_i(Ẑ) → Cl(O_{Q(√p)}) × ∏_{i=1}^m Cl(O_{K_i}) for d > 1. It specifies the alternative targets Cl(U_{0,1}) × ∏ Cl(O_{K_i}) for d = 1 and ∏ Cl(O_{K_i}) for d = 0.
issues.correction: For d > 1 the target should be Cl⁺(O_{Q(√p)}) × ∏_{i=1}^m Cl(O_{K_i}), where Cl⁺ is the narrow class group of Q(√p). Correspondingly, C₀ := max{#Cl(U_{0,1}), #Cl⁺(O_{Q(√p)})}.
issues.reason: For d ≥ 2, strong approximation for SL_d(D₀) identifies the double cosets with Nrd(GL_d(D₀)(Q))\A^×_{K,f}/Ô_K^×, where K = Q(√p). D₀ is ramified at both real places of K, so by the Hasse–Schilling norm theorem Nrd(GL_d(D₀)(Q)) is the group of totally positive elements of K, and the quotient is Cl⁺(O_K), not Cl(O_K). For p = 3, Q(√3) has class number 1, but its fundamental unit 2 + √3 has norm +1, so #Cl⁺ = 2. For A isogenous to B₀^d with d ≥ 2, the left side therefore has two elements, while Cl(O_{Q(√3)}) has one. Reach: Only the constant C₀ changes (#Cl⁺ ≤ 2·#Cl, which depends only on p), so (28), Theorem 0.1 and the later results are unaffected.

issues.locator: §3.2.3, (28), last step, p. 16 (arXiv v1)
issues.correction: Since 8·C(2g,2) = 16g² − 8g, the product equals (2√p)^{(33/2)g²(1+o(1))} = 2^{(33/2)g²(1+o(1))} p^{(33/4)g²(1+o(1))}. With Corollary 2.2 this gives B(p,g) ≤ (2^{33/2} p^{17/2})^{g²(1+o(1))}. That is Theorem 0.1 with exponent 17/2 + (33/2)·log_p 2 + ε in place of 17/2 + ε. After also correcting E5, E9 and E10, the bound obtained by this method is B(p,g) ≤ 2^{34g²}p^{(69/4)g²(1+o(1))}, as Lee states. Lee subsequently improves it to p^{(45/4)g²(1+o(1))}; neither statement is a counterexample to the original stronger bound.
issues.reason: For fixed p the factor 2^{(33/2)g²} equals p^{(33/2)(log_p 2)g²}, and (33/2)·log_p 2 is a positive constant. So it cannot be absorbed into the o(1) of p^{(33/4)g²(1+o(1))}; the power of 2 disappears only as p → ∞. Reach: Theorem 0.1 as stated (for fixed p and every ε > 0, B(p,g) = o(p^{(17/2+ε)g²})) does not follow from the proof; log B(p,g) = O(g² log p) does. issues.printed: The source calls an abelian variety bad when it lacks an isogeny factor meeting the size requirement in the Corollary. For a bad isomorphism class A, it invokes Conjecture 5.2 together with Proposition 5.10 to obtain n_A ≤ exp(0.99g² log g + O(g²)).
issues.correction: The bound is justified only for bad A with no isogeny factor B₀, the simple abelian surface whose Frobenius field is Q(√p). Bad A containing B₀^d need a separate estimate, for example an extension of Conjecture 5.2 and Proposition 5.10 to factors with End⁰(B₀^d) = M_d(D₀). Otherwise Corollary 5.13 must be stated with that restriction. Any restriction must apply to the population being counted, not just to an individual intermediate bound. issues.citation: Lipnowski–Tsimerman, "How large is A_g(F_q)?", Duke Mathematical Journal (2018)
issues.reviewReason: Rejected after independent reconstruction. The limit in the used (1,2),(0,0) case is ∏_{i≥1}(1−ℓ^{−i})² for odd ℓ and one such product for ℓ=2, by Cheong–Huang Theorem 2.10. More generally, use the finitely many irreducible factors of ∏(1−t^{n_j}) modulo ℓ: their primary-module distributions converge with total mass one, and the conditional Haar-lift distribution of the relevant blocks is independent of ambient dimension. Each polynomial determinant is nonzero almost surely in a fixed block, so these lifts yield a probability kernel on finite group tuples. Total-variation convergence survives that kernel. The report gives the lifting argument, which also handles repeated/shared factors and ℓ dividing n_j. Thus omission of this standard reduction does not make Definition 5.16 ill posed. Replacing limit by liminf would not define a probability distribution.

issues.locator: §5.7.3, Lemma 5.19 and its proof, p. 36 (arXiv v1)
issues.printed: Lemma 5.19 asserts that, for any elliptic curve E/F_p, the groups E(F_p) and E(F_{p²}) cannot both be p-groups. Its argument claims that being p-groups simultaneously forces a = 1 together with b = 1.
issues.correction: The lemma holds exactly for odd p. For p ≥ 5 the Hasse interval forces #E(F_p) = p, so a = 1; then b = a² − 2p = 1 − 2p and #E(F_{p²}) = p(p + 2), which is not a power of p. For p = 3, a ∈ {1, 3} gives #E(F₉) ∈ {15, 7}. For p = 2 the lemma is false.
issues.reason: Over F₂, the curve E : y² + xy = x³ + x² + 1 is smooth (its discriminant −557 is odd). It has 2 points over F₂ (trace 1) and 4 + 1 − (1 − 4) = 8 points over F₄, both 2-groups. Its twist y² + xy = x³ + 1 has 4 and 8 points. The step 'a = 1 and b = 1' overlooks that, for p ≤ 3, a p-group in the Hasse intervals can also have order 1, p² or p³. Reach: Lemma 5.19 fails for p = 2. The prime 2 is among those produced in the proof of Lemma 5.11, since it splits in Q(√−7), and the proof of Corollary 5.20 applies the lemma to every E/F_p. So Corollary 5.20 is unproved for p = 2; for odd p the argument stands. Theorems 0.1–0.3 do not use the lemma.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on p. 134 (and the definitions on p. 133). The first half of the proof gives θ_S(G_{S,γ}) ⊆ Hom(S, (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}); the converse step fails. issues.citation: Liu et al., "On the Beilinson–Bloch–Kato conjecture for Rankin–Selberg motives", Inventiones Mathematicae (2022)
issues.reviewReason: Checked on p. 135. The first part is asserted for every abundant tuple and 'proved' by 'obvious from Definition 2.6.5'. Over O_λ/λ^n, A = [[λ,1],[0,λ]] has image {(λx+y, λy)} ⊇ λ²(O_λ/λ^n)² of index |k|², but its coordinate projections are all of O and λO, so the image is not a product of coordinate submodules and no change of basis of S (which preserves the image) makes A diagonal. It is abundant once m₀ + 𝔣(2)r_R ⩾ 2 and is realised whenever θ_S(G_{S,γ}) fills Hom(S, (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) (e.g. [F:F⁺] = 1, where Lemma 2.6.4 holds). When 𝔣(r)r_R = 0 an abundant A is invertible and the claim holds, as the correction says.

issues.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.7.1, published p. 136; arXiv v3 p. 21
issues.printed: The source chooses a positive integer e_α such that the order of (γ′_α)^{ℓ^{e_α}} is coprime to ℓ and h_{(γ′_α)^{ℓ^{e_α}}} has eigenvalue 1. It then replaces γ′_α with (γ′_α)^{ℓ^{d_α e_α}} and claims to obtain the required (γ′₀, γ′₁, ξ′).
issues.correction: Take g ∈ Gal(F̄/F′) whose image (γ′₀, γ′₁, ξ′) mod λ^m lifts (γ₀, γ₁, ξ), and replace g by g^{ℓ^k} for ONE k that kills the ℓ-parts (the kernel of reduction mod λ is an ℓ-group) and is divisible by the d_α and by the order of Frobenius on the residue fields involved; then (γ′₀^{ℓ^k}, γ′₁^{ℓ^k}, ξ′^{ℓ^k}) lies in the image, reduces to (γ₀, γ₁, ξ) and satisfies (a)–(e). For (c) one needs ker(h − 1) free of rank one over O_λ/λ^m, not only '1 is an eigenvalue': this follows since h has order prime to ℓ, so ker(h−1) is the image of the averaging idempotent, a free direct summand lifting the rank-one residual kernel.
issues.reason: Choosing powers independently in the two representations need not give an element in the image of the same Galois element. A common power preserves joint-image membership, the residual triple and the required unit conditions. Re-checked on the page image (2026-09-23): confirmed — checked on the page image of p. 136; the triple obtained by independent ℓ-powers of γ′₀, γ′₁ with ξ′ unchanged need not be in the image of the joint homomorphism. Minor and easily repaired; the lemma is true. The previous record's 'printed' field did not quote the faulty step (corrected below). (GI^m) asks for a single element of the image of Gal(F̄/F′) under the joint map (ρ̄₀₊^{(m)}, ρ̄₁₊^{(m)}, ε̄_ℓ^{(m)}). Powers of the components by different exponents ℓ^{d₀e₀} ≠ ℓ^{d₁e₁}, with ξ′ unchanged, correspond to different Galois elements. Defence: the intended argument is obviously the common power (as in arXiv v1/v2), and conditions (a), (d), (e) are Galois-stable (𝒫 ∈ ℤ[T]; eigenvalue conditions invariant under x ↦ x^{ℓ^k}), so nothing beyond the proof is affected. Independent check: Quote checked on the image of p. 136: 'Replacing γ′_α by (γ′_α)^{ℓ^{d_α e_α}}, we obtain the desired element (γ′₀, γ′₁, ξ′).' (GI^m_{F′,𝒫}) asks for ONE element of the image of Gal(F̄/F′) under the joint map (ρ̄₀₊^{(m)}, ρ̄₁₊^{(m)}, ε̄_ℓ^{(m)}). Powering the two components by different exponents ℓ^{d₀e₀}, ℓ^{d₁e₁} and keeping ξ′ gives a triple that in general comes from no single Galois element. The repair is routine. Take g ∈ Gal(F̄/F′) with image (γ′₀, γ′₁, ξ′) lifting (γ₀, γ₁, ξ). Replace g by g^{ℓ^k} with k divisible by d₀, d₁ and by [O_λ/λ : 𝔽_ℓ], and large enough to kill the ℓ-part: the kernel of 𝒢(O_λ/λ^m) → 𝒢(O_λ/λ) is an ℓ-group, and ℓ^k is odd, so the c-component is preserved. The reduction is unchanged, so (a), (d) and (e), which only depend on it, persist; (b) holds by construction. For (c), h has order prime to ℓ, so ker(h−1) is the image of the averaging idempotent: a free direct summand whose rank is the residual multiplicity 1. The printed phrase '1 is an eigenvalue' does not give (c) by itself. Versions: v1 (Lemma 2.6.1, '(3) implies (2)') says 'after raising sufficiently large ℓ-power, (γ′0, γ′1, ξ′) will satisfy (2a)–(2e)', a common power; v3 is identical to print.

issues.locator: Construction 3.1.8(1) and (2), published pp. 141–142; arXiv v3 p. 24; v1 p. 24
issues.printed: In (1), the source arranges the entries of α in the sequence (α1, . . . , αN), requiring αiαN+1−i = 1, and claims a unique homomorphism. In (2), its chosen sequences for α1 and α2 are respectively (α1,1, . . . , α1,N) and (α2,1, . . . , α2,N), subject to α1,iα2,N+1−i = 1.
issues.correction: Either assume L is an integral domain (then unitarity makes the multisets inverse-stable and the orderings exist), or define φ_α from P_α alone: for N even write P_α(T) = T^{N/2}Q(T + T^{−1}) (for N odd first divide by T − 1, which divides P_α since unitarity forces P_α(1) = 0) and send the i-th elementary symmetric function of x_j + x_j^{−1} in ℤ[X_*(A_{N,v})]^W to the corresponding signed coefficient of Q; similarly in the split case.
issues.reason: In L=F5×F5 use the three roots (1,2),(2,1),(3,3). Componentwise the polynomial is (T−1)(T−2)(T−3), which has the required odd reciprocal identity. No root has square one in L, so no root can occupy the middle of a reciprocal ordering. This does not obstruct the usual field-valued construction. Re-checked on the page image (2026-09-23): revised: the gap is real (the counterexample checks) and occurs also in the split case (2), but every use of Construction 3.1.8 is over ℂ or with an ordered tuple given, so it affects nothing (previous record: 'the proof'). Inert case (previous record, rechecked): L = 𝔽_5 × 𝔽_5, α = {(1,2), (2,1), (3,3)}: both components give (T−1)(T−2)(T−3) = T³ + 4T² + T + 4 over 𝔽_5, which equals (−T)³P(T^{−1}) because 2·3 = 1; but no element squares to 1 (so none can be the middle entry) and (1,2)(2,1) = (2,2) ≠ 1. Split case (new): L = 𝔽_5 × 𝔽_5, α_1 = {(1,2), (2,1)}, α_2 = {(1,1), (3,3)}: P_{α_1} = (T−1)(T−2) and T²P_{α_2}(T^{−1}) = (1−T)(1−3T) = 3(T−1)(T−2) over 𝔽_5, so α is unitary with c = 2; the inverses (1,3), (3,1) of the elements of α_1 do not lie in α_2, so no orders with α_{1,i}α_{2,N+1−i} = 1 exist. Defence: over a field or domain the orderings exist, and when they exist the value of φ_α is independent of the choice (valid orderings give Weyl-conjugate characters). The construction is used only in Construction 3.1.10 with L = ℂ, and Notation B.2.5 starts from an ordered tuple. Independent check: Construction 3.1.8 (pp. 141–142) and Definition 3.1.3 (p. 139) were checked on the images: L is an arbitrary ℤ[‖v‖^{±δ(v)/2}]-ring. Both counterexamples recomputed over 𝔽₅×𝔽₅. Inert case: each component of P_α is (T−1)(T−2)(T−3), and (−T)³P(T^{−1}) = (T−1)(T−2)(T−3), so α is unitary. No element squares to (1,1), and (1,2)(2,1) = (2,2), so no admissible ordering exists. Split case: P_{α₁} = (T−1)(T−2), and T²P_{α₂}(T^{−1}) = (1−T)(1−3T) = 3(T−1)(T−2), so α is unitary with c = 2. But (1,3) and (3,1) are not in α₂, so no ordering with α_{1,i}α_{2,N+1−i} = 1 exists. Over a domain the multisets are inversion-stable and orderings exist. When orderings exist, φ_α is independent of the choice: inverses in a ring are unique, so two orderings differ by a Weyl element. The construction is used only with L = ℂ: Construction 3.1.10, and Definition 6.1.8 via φ_{α(BC(π_v))}. Notation B.2.5 starts from an ordered tuple. The first reading's alternative is also sound over any ring: for N odd, a_i = −a_{N−i} forces P_α(1) = 0 without inverting 2. Versions: same in v1 and v3.

The proof says 'The lemma is trivial if N = 2' and '…is spanned by Tate cycles over κ ([31])'. Re-derived. For N = 2, κ = F_9, {x,y} = x1^σy1 + t x2^σy2, the isotropic points satisfy u^4 = −t. A computer count gives 0 F_9-rational points for each of the six t ∉ F_3 and 4 for t ∈ F_3^×. Frobenius therefore permutes H^0 = L^4 non-trivially, e.g. for L = Q_5 (3-coprime, p+1 invertible). For N = 4, p = 2, κ = F_4, the cubic surface {y,y} = 0 has 45 = 1 + 4·7 + 16 points for the split (Hermitian) form. Random non-degenerate forms give 9, 13, 17, 21, 25, 29 or 33 points, so tr(Frob | H^2(1)) ≠ 7 and the action is not trivial. The cited fact is true only when the Tate classes (F_{p²}-rational linear subspaces) are defined over κ, i.e. for κ-forms that are split. The only use is Lemma 5.6.2(3) (p. 212), whose proof is complete except for (4): the 𝔗-twisted Frobenius defines an F_p^Φ-form of each fibre. So that proof inherits a gap (E9). The needed special case, split forms, is very plausibly true, so Lemma 5.6.2(3) and everything downstream stand. The same mistake at Proof of Lemma 5.6.2(3), published p. 212 (relies on Lemma A.1.4(4), p. 323: Lemma A.1.4(4) asserts that Gal(κ̄/κ) acts trivially on H^{N−2}(DL(𝒱, {,}, N−1)_{κ̄}, L((N−2)/2)) for EVERY pair over κ with 𝒱^⊣ = 0. Admissibility (Definition A.1.1) only provides an 𝔽_{p²}-structure over κ̄, and the claim is false in general. E9's example, re-checked here: κ = 𝔽₉, p = 3, N = 2, {x, y} = x₁^σy₁ + t x₂^σy₂ with t ∉ 𝔽₃. The isotropic points u⁴ = −t are not 𝔽₉-rational, and Frob₉ multiplies u by t² ≠ 1. The 𝔽_{p²}-structure is the fixed space of Φ = 𝔽𝕍⁻¹; here Φ acts on 𝒱 as diag(−1, −t²), not as a scalar. The proof of Lemma 5.6.2(3) invokes exactly this false generality. Construction 5.3.6 only shows that Frobenius preserves Sh(V°, K°_p), i.e. each fibre up to 𝔗; it says nothing about the κ-structure of the fibre. Defence: for the Shimura fibres, Φ^{[κ:𝔽_{p²}]} is the scalar π_{A°}/p^k = τ_∞^c(π_{A₀}/p^k), a root of unity, which acts trivially on ℙ(𝒱_{s°}). So the κ-structure agrees with the 𝔽_{p²}-structure, and Lemma 5.6.2(3) is very plausibly true. The paper does not supply this argument. Lemma 5.6.2(3) is used in Lemma 5.9.3(6) and §6. Independent check: Quotation checked on p. 212: 'Part (3) follows from Lemma A.1.4(4) and Construction 5.3.6.' Construction 5.3.6 (p. 199) says only that Gal(F̄_p/F_p^Φ) acts trivially on Sh(V°, −K°_p) under υ°, and through 𝔗 on T_p. So on the 𝔗-invariant cohomology (Notation 3.5.7) the 𝔗-twisted Frobenius stabilises each link fibre DL_{s°}. Prime-to-p quasi-isogenies identify Dieudonné modules, so this twisted Frobenius acts on V_{s°} ⊗ F̄_p by a σ^f-semilinear bijection that preserves { , }_{s°} up to a scalar. In other words it is the Frobenius of an F_p^Φ-form of a non-degenerate pair. Lemma A.1.4(4), as stated, would then finish the proof. So the proof is complete except for A.1.4(4), which is false in that generality: see E9, whose N = 2 case (F_9) and N = 4 case (F_4: split form 45 points, random non-degenerate forms 9–33 points) I re-ran by computer. What is missing is exactly the check that the forms arising are split, i.e. that the twisted Frobenius is a scalar times a power of the F_{p²}-Frobenius. That holds via η°_𝔭 (Construction 5.6.1) or π_{A°} = i(π_{A0}), and the paper does not give it. So the gap is real and Lemma 5.6.2(3) is very likely true. It is still the same mistake as E9. A.1.4(4) is used only here (grep: its only citation is p. 212). The authors' route is 'A.1.4(4) holds for every κ-form', and restricting A.1.4(4) to split forms (E9's correction) forces precisely the verification this record supplies. Uses of Lemma 5.6.2(3): Lemma 5.9.3(6) (p. 235), Lemma 7.2.5(4) (p. 291), §6.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on pp. 321–323. Lemma A.1.4 is stated for any pair (V, { , }) with V^# = 0 (not only split forms), and the proof opens with 'The lemma is trivial if N = 2'. Over κ = 𝔽₉ (p = 3), {x, y} = x₁³y₁ + t x₂³y₂ with t ∈ 𝔽₉ ∖ 𝔽₃ is non-degenerate (hence admissible by Lang's theorem, Definition A.1.1 being a condition over κ̄); DL(V, { , }, 1) is the set of lines with x₁⁴ + t x₂⁴ = 0, four distinct geometric points, none 𝔽₉-rational because the fourth powers in 𝔽₉^× are {±1} = 𝔽₃^×. So Frobenius permutes H⁰ = L⁴ without fixed points, contradicting (4) (take L = ℚ₅, where p + 1 = 4 is invertible). The added hypothesis (the pair descends to 𝔽_{p²} over κ) restores (4); the downstream check in Lemma 5.6.2(3) is correctly flagged.

issues.correction: For N = 2 define H^prim as reduced H^0, the kernel of the degree (Gysin) map to H^2 of the ambient ℙ^1, and Ω_2 := St = PS(ε_2^TT), of dimension q. Or restrict the cup-product definition to N ⩾ 3 and set Ω_2 := St. Make the same change in Definition 5.6.3: at N = 2 take the kernel of the Gysin map m^{†°}_!: H^0_𝔗(M̄†) → H^2_𝔗(M̄°), which agrees with the printed definition for N ⩾ 3 when p+1 ∈ L^×. Then (5.13) holds at N = 2. At Definition 5.6.3 and Proposition 5.6.4, display (5.13), published p. 213 (same root cause as E10, Appendix C.2 p. 353): Define H^prim as the kernel of the Gysin map m^{†°}_!: H^{N−2}_𝔗(M̄†_𝔭(V°, –), L(i)) → H^N_𝔗(M̄°_𝔭(V°, –), L(i + 1)), equivalently of ∪ξ followed by the trace to the balloon. For N ⩾ 3 (with p + 1 ∈ L^× when N ⩾ 4) this agrees with the printed definition. For N = 2 it is reduced H⁰ (kernel of the total trace), and then (5.13) holds with Ω₂ the q-dimensional Steinberg-type constituent. Alternatively, restrict Definition 5.6.3 and Proposition 5.6.4 to N ⩾ 3.
issues.reason: The Fermat variety is q+1 points. Cup product H0→H2 is zero, so its kernel is all q+1-dimensional H0, containing constants and not the asserted irreducible q-dimensional Tate–Thompson representation. The reduced H0 has dimension q because q+1 is invertible in the coefficients. Re-checked on the page image (2026-09-23): confirmed (locator relabelled: the published label is Proposition C.2.1, not 'Lemma C.2.1'; definition on p. 353). For N = 2, Iso(Λ̄_2) is the set of q+1 isotropic lines of a hermitian plane over κ (dimension 0), so H^N = H^2 = 0 and the printed kernel is all of H^0, a (q+1)-dimensional permutation representation ≅ 𝟏 ⊕ St of U_2(𝔽_q), not irreducible; so the asserted existence of an irreducible Ω_2 ≅ H^prim fails. Independent confirmation from the paper's own formula (C.1): R_2 = −(χ_2((1,1))/2·R_{(1^2)} + χ_2((2))/2·R_{(2)}) = (R_{(2)} − R_{(1^2)})/2 = ((𝟏 + St) − (𝟏 − St))/2 = St, of degree q; likewise C.2.1(2) singles out St (the unique nontrivial constituent of Ind_{P_2}𝟏). With the reduced H^0 (dimension q) everything in C.2.1 holds at N = 2 and the proof of C.2.1(2) works with [pt] − (q+1)^{−1}·1. Case for the defence: for N ⩾ 3 the cup-product kernel is the standard primitive cohomology and is irreducible (Tate–Thompson); N = 2 is a degenerate case the authors presumably had in mind as 'reduced H^0'. But the paper explicitly allows N ⩾ 2 here and in §5.6 (Definition 5.6.3 is the same kernel construction and Proposition 5.6.4 is stated for N ⩾ 2), and N = 2 is used in the main theorems. Independent check: Checked on pp. 352–355: 'Let N ⩾ 2', the kernel definition, and 'unique irreducible representation Ω_N … isomorphic to ι_ℓ^{−1}H^prim'. At N = 2, Iso(Λ̄_2) is the set of q+1 isotropic lines, of dimension 0, so H^2 = 0 and H^prim = H^0. That is the permutation representation Ind_B^{U_2(F_q)} 1 = 1 ⊕ St of dimension q+1, which is reducible, so the asserted irreducible Ω_2 does not exist. From (C.1), with χ_2 = sgn and z = 2 for both partitions, R_2 = (R_{(2)} − R_{(1²)})/2 = ((1 + St) − (1 − St))/2 = St. C.2.1(2) at N = 2 (P_2 = P_2^{(1)} = B) also singles out St. The same degeneration makes (5.13) in Proposition 5.6.4 false at N = 2, where the left side has an extra Map_{K°_𝔭}(…, 1) (E10). Reach: no written downstream argument uses H^prim or Ω_2 at N = 2. Lemma 6.3.2 (p. 275) assumes N ⩾ 4. Proposition 6.3.1 (p. 272) and Corollary 6.3.5 (p. 279) leave N = 2 to the reader. Proposition 5.6.4(1) survives because 1 and St both have Borel-fixed vectors. So the error is confined to the stated definitions/assertions at N = 2. Versions: v1 and v3 have the same 'It is well-known by Tate–Thompson … unique irreducible' sentence. The same mistake at Definition 5.6.3 and Proposition 5.6.4, display (5.13), published p. 213 (same root cause as E10, Appendix C.2 p. 353): §5.6 assumes only N ⩾ 2. For N = 2 each link fibre DL_{s°} is p + 1 points (Theorem 5.3.4(1)), so H² of the link vanishes and the printed kernel is all of H⁰_𝔗(M̄†). Over s₀ it is the (p+1)-dimensional permutation representation of U(Λ°_𝔭)(𝔽_p) ≅ U₂(𝔽_p) on the isotropic lines, which is 1 ⊕ (p-dimensional irreducible) and contains the constants. Appendix C.2 defines Ω_N as 'the unique irreducible representation' isomorphic to the same cup-kernel, which does not exist for N = 2. Proposition C.2.1(2) singles out the Steinberg-type p-dimensional representation. Hence (5.13) is false at N = 2 under either reading: the left side has an extra copy of Map_{K°_𝔭}(…, 𝟏). Downstream, §6.3 (N = 2r even, r = 1 allowed) uses H^{2r−2}_𝔗(M†_N, O_λ)_𝔪 ≃ O_λ[Sh(V°_N, K°_N)]_𝔪 ⊕ H^prim(M†_N, O_λ)_𝔪 (p. 275), which double-counts constants at r = 1 with the printed definition. Defence: for N ⩾ 3 everything is correct; the N = 2 conclusion (1) of Proposition 5.6.4 (π_𝔭 in an unramified principal series) survives; the fix is definitional. Independent check: Page 213 checked: Definition 5.6.3 takes the kernel of ∪(m^{†°*}ι°_!ξ): H^{N−2}_𝔗(M̄†) → H^N_𝔗(M̄†). §5.6 assumes N ⩾ 2 (p. 211). At N = 2, M̄† is 0-dimensional, so H^2 = 0 and the kernel is all of H^0. Over s0 this is the permutation representation of U(Λ°_𝔭)(F_p) ≅ U_2(F_p) on the p+1 isotropic lines, which is 1 ⊕ St. Ω_2 in C.2 is either undefined (the 'unique irreducible' rep isomorphic to a reducible H^prim) or, by C.2.1(1),(2) and (C.1), St. In either case (5.13) is false at N = 2: the left side has an extra Map_{K°_𝔭}(…, 1). The correction is right. For N ⩾ 4 with p+1 ∈ L^×, restriction H^N(ℙ) → H^N(DL) is injective, so ker(ξ∪) = ker(Gysin). For N = 3 both kernels are all of H^1. For N = 2 the Gysin kernel is reduced H^0. The downstream claim in the reason is wrong. H^{2r−2}_𝔗(M̄†_N)_𝔪 ≃ O_λ[Sh]_𝔪 ⊕ H^prim_𝔪 on p. 275 is in Lemma 6.3.2, which assumes N ⩾ 4. Proposition 6.3.1 and Corollary 6.3.5 treat only N ⩾ 4 and leave N = 2 to the reader (pp. 272, 279). So no written argument uses H^prim or (5.13) at N = 2. Conclusion (1) of Proposition 5.6.4 survives, since both 1 and St have Borel-fixed vectors. Reach: a stated result ((5.13) at N = 2), nothing downstream.

ℙ(Y_N) ≅ ℙ^{r−1} has codimension r−1 in the (2r−2)-dimensional Iso(Λ̄_N), so its class lies in H^{2r−2}(r−1) while c_1(O(1)) lies in H^2(1): the subtraction is degree-inconsistent unless r = 2. H^{2r}(Iso) is spanned by h^r, and ∪h kills [ℙ(Y_N)] − c·h^{r−1} iff c = ([ℙ(Y_N)]·h^{r−1})/(h^{2r−2}) = deg ℙ^{r−1}/deg Iso = 1/(q+1). Even for r = 2 the coefficient is 1/(q+1), not 1. The 'well-known' nonvanishing is true: if [ℙ(Y_N)] = h^{r−1}/(q+1) then [ℙ(Y_N)]^2 = 1/(q+1), whereas the self-intersection is c_{r−1}(N_{ℙ(Y_N)/Iso}) = ((−q)^r − 1)/(−(q+1)) ∈ ℤ (from c(N) = (1+h)^r/(1+(q+1)h)). Defence: 'subtracted by c_1(…)' can be read loosely as 'minus the appropriate multiple of the appropriate power of the hyperplane class'; the conclusion Ω^{P^{(r)}} ≠ 0 is unaffected. ℙ(Y_N) ≅ ℙ^{r−1} has codimension r−1 in the (2r−2)-dimensional Fermat hypersurface Iso(Λ̄_N), which has degree q+1. So its class lies in H^{2r−2}(r−1), and subtracting c_1 ∈ H^2(1) is degree-inconsistent for r ≠ 2. Even for r = 2 it is wrong: ([ℙ^1] − h)·h = 1 − (q+1) ≠ 0. The difference is nonzero: [ℙ(Y_N)]² = c_{r−1}(N_{ℙ(Y_N)/Iso}) = ((−q)^r − 1)/(−(q+1)) ∈ ℤ, while (h^{r−1}/(q+1))² = 1/(q+1) ∉ ℤ. By the printed local computation, T^{∘•}∘T^{•∘} acts on the π1-part of the source by c(π1) = p^{r1²+r1}∏_{i=1}^{r1}(α_i+p)(α_i+p^{−1})/α_i (Proposition B.4.3(1)), and T^{•∘}∘T^{∘•} acts on the π1-part of the target by the same scalar (one-dimensional K°- and K•-invariants of the same constituent). Since the Satake parameter of BC(π1)_𝔭 is congruent mod λ to that of Π_{1,𝔭}, intertwining genericity mod λ (which presupposes p invertible mod λ) makes every c(π1) a λ-adic unit; hence both composites have unit determinant on the free O_λ-modules H^i(…)_{𝔪1}, are automorphisms, and T^{•∘} is an O_λ[Γ_F]-isomorphism (also 𝕋^{Σ⁺_min∪Σ⁺_𝔓}-linear).
issues.reason: Freeness of source and target and a rational isomorphism do not imply an integral isomorphism: multiplication by λ on Oλ is a counterexample. P5 and the explicit compositions offer the missing integrality input; the full uniform construction remains to be written. Re-checked on the page image (2026-09-23): confirmed — locator corrected (it is Lemma 8.1.7, not a Proposition) and the correction sharpened to an explicit determinant argument using only the paper's own inputs. Torsion-free O_λ[Γ_F]-modules with isomorphic rationalizations need not be isomorphic: Γ = ℤ acting on O_λ² by (1 1; 0 1) and by (1 λ; 0 1) gives rationally conjugate, integrally non-isomorphic lattices (their reductions mod λ are a nontrivial unipotent and the identity). The integral statement is essential: in (8.7) and its rank-one analogue it transports the fixed exponent m_lat, defined at hyperspecial level, to the level-raised Shimura variety at a prime 𝔭 that depends on m; with only a rational isomorphism the lattice discrepancy could grow with 𝔭 and the final choice 'm > m_per + m_lat + …' would be circular. Case for the defence: every ingredient of the repair (the integral correspondences of Definition 5.8.1, Proposition B.4.3(1), intertwining genericity mod λ) is already in the printed proof; only the passage from 'nonzero' to 'unit' and the determinant argument are missing, so the lemma as stated is true. Independent check: Quotation checked on p. 307. The inference 'torsion-free, and isomorphic after ⊗Q̄_ℓ, hence isomorphic as O_λ[Γ_F]-modules' is invalid in general; the first reading's unipotent example is correct. It is not rescued in this setting. If H^{2r₁}_{𝔪₁} ⊗ Q̄_ℓ were isotypic for one residually absolutely irreducible ρ, every Γ-stable lattice would be ≅ T^{⊕μ} (O_λ[Γ] ↠ End(T) by Burnside and Nakayama, then Morita). But localization at 𝔪₁ only fixes the residual eigensystem, so several π₁ with distinct ρ_{BC(π₁)} lifting ρ̄ can contribute, and lattices in such a sum need not be isomorphic. The repair works, and I checked it. I° = T^{∘•}T^{•∘} ∈ 𝕋°_{𝔭} acts on each π₁-part by a scalar that is, up to a power of p, ∏(p + α_i)(p + α_i^{-1}) = P(−p)/(−(p + 1)). Its value for π₁ is congruent mod λ to its value for Π₁ (Chebotarev), and it is a unit because P_{α(Π_{1,𝔭})}(−p) is invertible mod λ (Definition 3.1.5(2)). The same scalar governs T^{•∘}T^{∘•} on the one-dimensional K•-invariants. Hence both composites have unit determinant on the free modules H^i_{𝔪₁}, and the integral, Γ_F- and Hecke-equivariant T^{•∘} is an isomorphism. The lemma is true; the integral statement is essential for the m_lat bookkeeping in (8.7).

issues.locator: Lemma 2.3.5(b) and its proof, published pp. 127–128; arXiv v3 Lemma 2.3.5, p. 15; arXiv v1/v2 Lemma 2.3.4(b), pp. 14–15
issues.printed: Under (b) dim_{O_λ/λ} R̄ ⩽ min{(ℓ+1)/2, ℓ−3}, semisimplicity of R̄ over (O_λ/λ)[Γ_F], and Hom_{(O_λ/λ)[Γ_F]}(End(R̄), R̄) = 0, the source claims Res_ρ is injective. It views G^i/G^{i+1} as an 𝔽_ℓ[G]-submodule of End(R̄), and thus (G^i/G^{i+1}) ⊗ O_λ/λ as a submodule over (O_λ/λ)[G] inside End(R̄) ⊗ (O_λ/λ) ≃ End(R̄)^d, with d := [O_λ/λ : 𝔽_ℓ].
issues.correction: As (O_λ/λ)[G]-modules, End(R̄) ⊗_{𝔽_ℓ} k ≃ ⊕_{σ ∈ Gal(k/𝔽_ℓ)} End(R̄)^{(σ)} (Frobenius twists), k = O_λ/λ, not End(R̄)^d. Replace the last hypothesis of (b) by Hom_{𝔽_ℓ[Γ_F]}(End(R̄), R̄) = 0, equivalently Hom_{k[Γ_F]}(End(R̄)^{(σ)}, R̄) = 0 for every σ ∈ Gal(k/𝔽_ℓ); then the printed proof goes through. As printed, (b) is correct when k = 𝔽_ℓ.
issues.reason: Counterexample with k = 𝔽₂₅, ℓ = 5, m = 2, O_λ = W(𝔽₂₅). Let ζ generate 𝔽₂₅^× (order 24), H = ⟨h⟩ ≅ ℤ/24 acting on k² by χ₁ ⊕ χ₂, χ₁(h) = ζ⁵, χ₂(h) = ζ⁴, and G := A ⋊ H ⊆ GL₂(O_λ/25) with H = {diag([ζ⁵]^t, [ζ⁴]^t)} (Teichmüller lifts) and A = {1 + 5x·e₁₂ : x ∈ 𝔽₂₅} ≅ 𝔽₂₅, on which h acts by ψ = χ₁χ₂^{−1} (ζ). Realize G as Gal(L/F) with 5 unramified in F (any finite group is a Galois group over some number field; choose the S_n-extension of ℚ split at 5), R = (O_λ/25)². Hypotheses of (b): dim R̄ = 2 ⩽ min{3, 2}; R̄ = χ₁ ⊕ χ₂ is semisimple (A acts trivially, |H| prime to 5); End(R̄) = 1 ⊕ 1 ⊕ ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1}, exponents {0,0,1,23} versus R̄ = {5,4}, so Hom_{k[Γ_F]}(End(R̄), R̄) = 0. But the 𝔽₅-linear map A → R̄, x ↦ (x⁵, 0) is H-equivariant (ψ⁵ = χ₁), so H¹(G, R̄) ≅ Hom_H(A, R̄) ≠ 0; since R̄^G = 0, H¹(G, λR) ≅ H¹(G, R̄) injects into H¹(G, R) = ker Res_ρ. So Res_ρ is not injective. (Here (a) fails: no nontrivial scalar in the image.) Defence: the only verification of (b) in the paper (Lemma 8.1.4 via Lemma 8.1.5(2), for Theorem 1.1.7) proves via Jordan types that ρ̄₀⊗ρ̄₁ is not a subquotient of ad(ρ̄₀⊗ρ̄₁); the same argument applies to every Frobenius twist, so Theorem 1.1.7 is not affected; Theorem 1.1.1 uses (a) (Proposition 2.7.2(1)). But Definition 8.1.1 (L5-1) admits primes satisfying only (b), so Theorems 1.1.5 and 1.1.9 as stated rely on the false lemma when O_λ/λ ≠ 𝔽_ℓ. Independent check: Statement and proof checked on the images of pp. 127–128, including 'End(R̄) ⊗ (O_λ/λ) ≃ End(R̄)^d'. G^i/G^{i+1} is only an 𝔽_ℓ-subspace of End_k(R̄), with k = O_λ/λ. As k[G]-modules, End(R̄) ⊗_{𝔽_ℓ} k ≅ ⊕_{σ∈Gal(k/𝔽_ℓ)} End(R̄)^{(σ)}, which is not End(R̄)^d unless every Frobenius twist is isomorphic to End(R̄). I verified the 𝔽₂₅ counterexample by explicit computation. I built G = ⟨diag([ζ]⁵,[ζ]⁴), 1+5e₁₂⟩ ⊂ GL₂(W₂(𝔽₂₅)) with W₂(𝔽₂₅) = (ℤ/25)[√2]; it has order 600 = |A ⋊ H|. A cocycle computation over 𝔽₅ gives dim_{𝔽₅} Z¹(G,R̄) = 6, R̄^G = 0 and dim B¹ = 4, so dim_{𝔽₅} H¹(G,R̄) = 2 = dim_k Hom_H(A,R̄). As characters of h: End(R̄) = ζ^{0,0,1,23} and R̄ = ζ^{5,4}, so Hom_{k[G]}(End R̄, R̄) = 0. The Frobenius twist is ζ^{0,0,5,19} ∋ ζ⁵ = χ₁. The hypotheses of (b) hold: dim 2 ⩽ min{3, 2}, and R̄ is semisimple. Since R̄^G = 0, H¹(G,λR) ≅ H¹(G,R̄) injects into H¹(G,R) = ker Res_ρ. Realizing G as Gal(L/F) inside an S_n-extension is standard. So Lemma 2.3.5(b) is false whenever O_λ/λ ≠ 𝔽_ℓ is allowed. Reach: (L5-1) (p. 303) accepts assumption (b). Proposition 2.6.6 uses it via 'By Lemma 2.3.5, Res is injective', and so do the proofs of Theorems 8.2.2/8.3.2 (p. 310: 'By (L5-1) and Lemma 2.3.4'). Theorems 1.1.5/1.1.9 are therefore unproved for admissible λ with residue degree > 1 that satisfy only (b). Theorem 1.1.7 is safe: Lemma 8.1.5(2)'s Jordan-type argument works for ad(ρ)^{(σ)}, since twisting keeps the unipotent Jordan type and semisimplicity. Theorem 1.1.1 uses (a) through Proposition 2.7.2(1). Versions: identical in v1/v2 (Lemma 2.3.4) and v3.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on pp. 127–128: the proof identifies End(R̄) ⊗ (O_λ/λ) with End(R̄)^d as (O_λ/λ)[G]-modules, but for a k-representation V, V ⊗_{𝔽_ℓ} k ≅ ⊕_σ V^{(σ)} (Frobenius twists), so the printed hypothesis Hom_{k[Γ_F]}(End(R̄), R̄) = 0 is too weak when k ≠ 𝔽_ℓ. issues.correction: Add a hypothesis ensuring that the O_λ-span of θ_S(G_{S,γ}) contains λ^c Hom(S,(R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) with c independent of m. issues.reason: Consequence of E1: in the example of E1 (F = ℚ(√5, i), ℓ = 3, R = ℤ₃(1), j = 2, S the Kummer class of u = (1+√5)/2 mod 3^m, γ = ρ̄₊^{(m)}(𝔠)) all four hypotheses hold (R_ℚ of rank one; −1 is a nontrivial scalar in the image of Γ_F in GL(R̄) = 𝔽₃^×; γ has order 2; (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} = R̄^{(m)} free of rank one), r_S = 1, m₀ = 0, and G_{S,γ} = {1}, so θ¹_{S,γ}(Ψ) = 0 for every Ψ ∈ G_{S,γ} and no tuple is abundant once m > 𝔣(1)r_R = r_R (r_R = 0 is admissible here since R has rank one). The printed proof is fine except for its appeal to Lemma 2.6.4. Independent check 1: Quotation checked on p. 134 (PDF p. 28): Prop. 2.6.6 asserts an (S,γ)-abundant r_S-tuple exists under: R_ℚ absolutely irreducible; Lemma 2.3.5(a) or (b); order of γ prime to ℓ; (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} free of rank 1. The proof (p. 135) derives this from Lemma 2.6.4. The example of E1 satisfies every hypothesis (see E1 for the §2.1–2.6 conventions): R_ℚ = ℚ₃(1) has rank one; ε̄(Γ_F) = 𝔽₃^× contains the nontrivial scalar −1; γ = ρ̄₊^{(m)}(𝔠) has order 2; h_γ = 1, so (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} = μ_{3^m} is free of rank 1; S = ℤ/3^m·κ(u) has m₀ = 0 and r_S = 1. Recomputed G_{S,γ} = {1}, so θ¹_{S,γ}(Ψ) = 0 for every Ψ ∈ G_{S,γ}. Its image cannot contain λ^{𝔣(1)r_R}Hom(S, R̄^{(m)}) ≠ 0 once m > r_R, and r_R depends only on R (r_R = 0 is admissible here). So the proposition is false for all large m. The proof's only faulty step is the appeal to Lemma 2.6.4. Instances inside the paper's own setting also exist. Take R = R₊|_{Γ_F}. If S lies in the ε-eigenspace and γ acts on (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} ⊂ R̄₊ by −ε, then loc_w(S) = 0 at every γ-associated place and no abundant element exists. If r_S = 2 and S = S₊ ⊕ S₋ meets both eigenspaces, then for every γ one summand is killed by all Ψ ∈ G_{S,γ}, so no γ admits an abundant pair. In the case R_ℚ ≇ R_ℚ^𝔠 the conclusion survives with r_R replaced by the reducibility depth of Ind_F^{F⁺}R (see E1). This item is a direct consequence of E1 and should be recorded as dependent on it (E1's 'affects' already names Prop. 2.6.6) to avoid double counting. Versions: v1/v2 Proposition 2.5.5 (with r_γ, proved from Lemma 2.5.4(2)); v3 is identical to the published text. Independent check 2: Quote checked on the page images: pp. 134–135 (PDF 28–29), 'Then (S, γ)-abundant r_S-tuple exists.' The proof's only nontrivial step is 'It follows from Lemma 2.6.4 …'. In the E1 example (F⁺ = ℚ(√5), F = ℚ(√5,i), ℓ = 3, R = ℤ₃(1), j = 2, μ_Ξ = 1, γ = ρ̄₊^{(m)}(𝔠), S = ⟨κ((1+√5)/2)⟩ mod 3^m), every hypothesis holds. R_ℚ has rank 1, so it is absolutely irreducible. Lemma 2.3.5(a) holds because the image of Γ_F in GL(R̄) = 𝔽₃^× is {±1}, as ζ₃ ∉ F. γ has order 2, prime to 3. (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} = R̄^{(m)} is free of rank 1. S is free of rank 1 over ℤ/3^m, with m₀ = 0. 𝔯_R = 0 here: R̄ is absolutely irreducible, and End(R̄^{(m)}) = O_λ/λ^m. So abundance would require θ_S(Ψ): S → R̄^{(m)} to be surjective. But G_{S,γ} = {1} (recomputed under E1), so θ_S(Ψ) = 0 for every Ψ ∈ G_{S,γ}. No abundant element exists, for every m ≥ 1 (for any bound 𝔯_R, once m > 𝔯_R). The rest of the printed proof (Lemmas 2.3.3–2.3.5, direct summand) is fine; the gap is only the appeal to Lemma 2.6.4. Within §8's own setting the proposition also fails. Suppose R_ℚ ≅ R_ℚ^𝔠 (base change, e.g. Theorem 1.1.1). For S in one 𝔠-eigenspace and γ of the 'wrong' sign, G_{S,γ} = {1}, while all four hypotheses hold by (L3), (L5-1) and Lemma 2.7.1. For S = ⟨s₊,s₋⟩ of rank 2, no abundant pair exists for any γ. An unconditional in-scope instance needs a nonzero H¹_{f,R}(F,R̄^{(m)}), e.g. the rank-one situation of Theorem 1.1.9 for a base-changed pair with △_λ ≠ 0. There H¹_f(F,R_ℚ) is one-dimensional, so its generator lies in a single eigenspace. I have not exhibited such a pair. Versions: v1/v2 Proposition 2.5.5 (with r_γ) relies on Lemma 2.5.4(2); v3 is identical to the published text. Reach to the main theorems: Proposition 2.6.6 is the step in the proofs of Theorem 8.2.2 ('By Proposition 2.6.6 (with m₀ = m_Σ and r_S = 1), we may fix an (S,γ)-abundant element', p. 310) and Theorem 8.3.2 (r_S = 2, p. 317). Here R = R₀⊗R₁, j = 1, and γ is an arbitrary element given by (L5-2). When R_ℚ ≇ R_ℚ^𝔠 the step can be justified with a modified constant. When R_ℚ ≅ R_ℚ^𝔠 it is unjustified, and false for one of the two sign classes of admissible γ. This case includes every instance of Theorem 1.1.1 (base change of Sym^{n₀−1}A₀ ⊗ Sym^{n₁−1}A₁ from F⁺) and base-change pairs in Theorems 1.1.5, 1.1.7 and 1.1.9. In rank one it can fail for every single γ when the Selmer group meets both eigenspaces. So the proofs of Theorems 1.1.1, 1.1.5, 1.1.7 and 1.1.9 have a gap in that case. The gap is repairable for Theorem 1.1.1 (for all but finitely many ℓ, a τ with ρ̄_{A₀}(τ) = −1, ρ̄_{A₁}(τ) = 1, ε̄(τ) = 1 flips the sign without changing (a)–(e)). For base-change pairs at general admissible λ it is not settled by the paper's hypotheses. No main theorem is shown false. Same reach as E1, since the proposition is the channel through which Lemma 2.6.4 enters §8. In 8.2.2 (r_S = 1), the proof fails for a hypothetical Selmer class lying in the 𝔠-eigenspace opposite to the arbitrarily chosen γ. This can happen whenever R_ℚ ≅ R_ℚ^𝔠, which includes all of Theorem 1.1.1. In 8.3.2 (r_S = 2), it fails for every γ when S has one class in each eigenspace, so the single-γ scheme of the paper (𝔭₁ and 𝔭₂ both γ-associated) cannot work. Two γ's of opposite signs are needed. For Theorem 1.1.1 both signs are available when ℓ ≫ 0, so it survives with a modified proof. For 1.1.5 and 1.1.9 at arbitrary admissible λ, and for 1.1.7 via Lemma 8.1.4 (one Frobenius element), the base-change case needs an extra hypothesis or argument supplying a γ of the other sign. For R_ℚ ≇ R_ℚ^𝔠, a version with a bounded loss is plausible but unproved. No main theorem is shown false. Reach: a stated result (Proposition 2.6.6). It is used in the proofs of Theorems 8.2.2 (r_S = 1) and 8.3.2 (r_S = 2).).

issues.locator: §2.7, paragraph before Proposition 2.7.2, published pp. 136–137; arXiv v3 p. 21; arXiv v1 p. 21
issues.printed: For an odd rational prime ℓ unramified in F, the source sets R_α := (Sym^{n_α−1}_{ℤ_ℓ} H¹_ét(A_{αF̄}, ℤ_ℓ))(r_α) for α = 0, 1, regarding it as a ℤ_ℓ[Γ_F]-module. It asserts that R_α has rank n_α in Mod(F, ℤ_ℓ)_fr and carries the canonical polarization Ξ_α: R_α^𝔠 ⥲ R_α^∨(1 − α), of type (1 − α).
issues.correction: Require ℓ ⩾ n_α (sufficient; then all C(n_α−1, a) are ℓ-units), e.g. 'for ℓ > n₁'.
issues.reason: The polarization is induced from the Weil pairing on H¹ (a perfect alternating pairing on a rank-two lattice T); on Sym^k T the induced pairing pairs x^a y^{k−a} with x^{k−a}y^a by ±a!(k−a)! (or ±1/binom(k,a) if normalized), which is not a unit when ℓ ⩽ k = n_α − 1. Then Sym^k T and its dual (a divided-power lattice) are not homothetic Galois lattices when the image is large (e.g. ℓ = 3, n_α ⩾ 4), so no (1−α)-polarization of R_α exists. Defence: only large ℓ are used. Independent check: Text checked on the images of pp. 136–137: 'For a rational prime ℓ (that is odd and unramified in F) … R_α is an object in Mod(F, ℤ_ℓ)_fr of rank n_α with a canonical (1 − α)-polarization'. A_α is defined over F⁺, so R_α^𝔠 ≅ R_α. A (1−α)-polarization therefore amounts to Sym^k H¹ ≅ Γ^k H¹ as Γ_F-lattices, where k = n_α − 1; the twists match via the Weil pairing. Both are lattices in Sym^k V. For non-CM A_α the image of Γ_F is open in GL₂(ℤ_ℓ), so Sym^k V is absolutely irreducible, and an isomorphism would have to be a homothety. With the basis x^a y^{k−a}, the natural map to the divided powers is multiplication by a!(k−a)!. So the lattices are homothetic iff every binomial coefficient C(k,a) is prime to ℓ. That holds for k < ℓ and fails for ℓ ⩽ k ⩽ 2ℓ−2; examples are ℓ = 3 with n₀ = 4 (C(3,1) = 3) or n₁ = 5 (C(4,2) = 6). The first reading's 'ℓ = 3, n_α ⩾ 4' is slightly too broad. For n_α = 6 every C(5,a) is prime to 3, so a polarization exists; the same happens whenever k = dℓ^e − 1. Only large ℓ are used (Proposition 2.7.2, Lemma 8.1.3). Versions: same text in v1 and v3.

Choose g (possible since the image of Γ_F is {det g₀ = det g₁}) with ρ̄_{A_α}(g) diagonal as displayed in bases in which complex conjugation acts by diag(1, −1). Then h_{γ₀} has eigenvalues a^{2ti} (1−r₀ ⩽ i ⩽ r₀) and h_{γ₁} has eigenvalues (ab²)^{2tj} (|j| ⩽ r₁), and (a)–(e) become: 𝒫(−a^{−t}) ≠ 0; (a^{2i}(ab²)^{2j})^t ≠ 1 for (i,j) ≠ (0,0) (as printed); (a^{2i})^t ≠ −1 for 1−r₀ ⩽ i ⩽ r₀; (a(ab²)^{2j})^t ≠ 1 for |j| ⩽ r₁. Such (a, b) exist for ℓ ≫ 0 when 𝒫 ≠ 0, so (3) holds (with E4).
issues.reason: With the diagonal choice, ρ̄⁺_{A₀}(y) = diag(a^t, −1), ρ̄⁺_{A₁}(y) = diag((ab)^t, −b^{−t}), ε̄_ℓ(y) = −a^{−t}; on Sym^{2r₀−1}(r₀) resp. Sym^{2r₁}(r₁) the squares give the eigenvalues above (the printed second bullet matches them). The printed first, third and fourth bullets do not: e.g. r₀ = r₁ = 1, t = 1, 𝒫 = T² − 1: (i) a of order 4 and b⁴ ∉ {±1, ±a} satisfy all printed bullets, but h_{γ₀} has eigenvalue a^{−2} = −1, violating (d); (ii) a ∉ μ₃ ∪ μ₄ ∪ {±1} with b⁴ = a^{−1} satisfies all printed bullets, but h_{γ₁} has eigenvalue (ab²)^{−2} = a^{−1} = −ξ, violating (e). Moreover, fixing ρ̄(g) only up to conjugacy does not determine h_γ: if complex conjugation swaps the two eigenlines of ρ̄_{A₀}(g), then ρ̄⁺_{A₀}(y)² = a^t·I, h_{γ₀} = a^{−t}·I and (c) fails. Defence: the statement is true and the repair is routine; the second bullet (the multiplicity-one condition) is right, and for 𝒫 = T² − 1 the first bullet is harmless. Independent check: The bullets and 'conjugacy class' were checked on the image of p. 137. Put t = [F′:F⁺] and y = g^t𝔠. Then ξ = ε̄_ℓ(y) = −a^{−t}, because ε̄_ℓ(𝔠) = −1. Also h_{γ_α} = ρ̄_α(y²), independent of the polarization matrix B, since y² ∈ Γ_F. Choose ρ̄_{A_α}(g) diagonal in eigenbases where ρ̄_{A_α}(𝔠) = diag(1,−1); this is possible because the image is all of {det g₀ = det g₁ = ξ^{−1}} and is conjugation-stable. Then h_{γ₀} has eigenvalues a^{2ti} for −r₀ ⩽ i ⩽ r₀−1 and h_{γ₁} has eigenvalues (ab²)^{2tj} for |j| ⩽ r₁. My sign convention gives i ↦ −i relative to the first reading's range 1−r₀ ⩽ i ⩽ r₀; every condition (a)–(e) is invariant under inverting the eigenvalues, so this is immaterial. The printed second bullet is right. The first, third and fourth bullets do not match (a), (d), (e): they should read 𝒫(−a^{−t}) ≠ 0, a^{2ti} ≠ −1 and (a(ab²)^{2j})^t ≠ 1. I checked both counterexamples by hand for r₀ = r₁ = t = 1 and 𝒫 = T²−1. (i) a of order 4 with b⁴ ∉ {±1, ±a} satisfies every printed bullet, yet a² = −1 is an eigenvalue of h_{γ₀}, violating (d). (ii) With b⁴ = a^{−1} and a ∉ μ₄ ∪ μ₃, all printed bullets hold, yet (ab²)^{−2} = a^{−1} = −ξ, violating (e). The conjugacy class alone also does not determine h_{γ₀}: if 𝔠 swaps the eigenlines, then ρ̄_{A₀}(y²) = a^t·I and h_{γ₀} is scalar, so (c) fails. The statement survives, with the corrected conditions, for ℓ ≫ 0 when 𝒫 ≠ 0. Versions: same in v1 (Prop. 2.6.3) and v3.

issues.printed: The source interprets (2) as excluding the pair {−‖v‖, −‖v‖−1} from α, and (3) as requiring precisely one occurrence of {‖v‖, ‖v‖−1} in α.
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis ‖v‖² ≠ 1 in L (for (2) it is enough that ‖v‖ ≠ −1 in L).
issues.reason: Let L be a field with char L ≠ 2 and P = P_α unitary. Write P = (T−1)^k R with R(1) ≠ 0. The identity P(T) = (−T)^N P(T^{−1}) gives R(1) = (−1)^{N+k}R(1), so k ≡ N (mod 2); likewise the multiplicity of −1 is even. (3) If ‖v‖ = 1 in L (N even), then 'P(‖v‖) = 0 and P′(‖v‖) invertible' would make 1 a simple root, which is impossible. Yet the pair {1, 1} can appear exactly once: for example ‖v‖ = 7, L = 𝔽_3, N = 2, α = {1, 1}. (2) If ‖v‖ = −1 in L (N odd), then P(−‖v‖) = P(1) = 0 always, so P is never intertwining generic. Yet the pair {1, 1} can be absent: for example N = 1, α = {1}. (1), (4) and the last sentence of the remark are correct. Defence: the remark is an 'easy to see' aside. In every use ‖v‖² ≠ 1 in L: (P2)/(PI2) require ℓ ∤ p(p² − 1) for L = O_E/λ, and Proposition C.2.5 works over ℂ. Independent check: Remark 3.1.6 checked on the image of p. 140. For unitary P with char L ≠ 2, write P = (T∓1)^k R. The functional equation forces the multiplicity of 1 to be ≡ N (mod 2) and the multiplicity of −1 to be even. (3): if ‖v‖ = ±1 in L (N even), the root ‖v‖ always has even multiplicity. So 'P(‖v‖) = 0, P′(‖v‖) invertible' never holds, although the pair can occur exactly once; for example L = 𝔽₃, ‖v‖ = 7, α = {1,1}. (2): if ‖v‖ = −1 in L (N odd), then P(−‖v‖) = P(1) = 0 always, while the pair {1,1} can be absent; for example N = 1, α = {1}. Items (1), (4) and the last sentence are correct, and (2), (3) are correct when ‖v‖² ≠ 1. Uses: the remark is cited only in Proposition C.2.5, over ℂ with q > 1. In §§6–8, (P2)/(PI2) impose ℓ ∤ p(p²−1) with ‖𝔭‖ = p, so the case never arises. Versions: same in v1 and v3.

issues.locator: Construction 3.1.10, published p. 142; arXiv v3 p. 25; v1 p. 25
issues.printed: Under Π ∘ c ≃ Π∨, the source asserts unitarity of the Satake parameter α(Πv) whenever v ∉ Σ+Π.
issues.correction: Assume in addition that the central character ω_Π is trivial on 𝔸_{F^+}^× (true for relevant Π). In general only α(Π_v) = α(Π_v)^{−1} as multisets holds, and at an inert v the product of the entries equals ω_Π(ϖ_v) = ±1.
issues.reason: At an unramified inert v, Π_w ∘ c ≃ Π_w^∨ and c(ϖ_v) = ϖ_v give α(Π_v) = α(Π_v)^{−1} as multisets. Hence (−T)^N P_α(T^{−1}) = (∏α_i)^{−1}P_α(T) with ∏α_i = ω_{Π_w}(ϖ_v). Since ω_Π ∘ c = ω_Π^{−1}, the restriction ω_Π|_{𝔸_{F^+}^×} is quadratic and trivial on norms, so it equals 1 or η_{F/F^+}; in the second case ω(ϖ_v) = −1 and α(Π_v) is not unitary. Explicit counterexample: N = 1, Π = χ a Hecke character of 𝔸_F^×/F^× extending η_{F/F^+} (it exists by Pontryagin duality). Then χ·χ^c = η ∘ Nm = 1, so χ ∘ c = χ^{−1}, but α(χ_v) = {−1} at every inert unramified v, and T + 1 ≠ (−T)(T^{−1} + 1). Defence: the construction is used only for relevant Π. There Definition 1.1.3(3) makes the archimedean central character arg^{Σ(N+1−2i)} = 1, which is incompatible with η_{F/F^+} (the sign character at each real place), so ω_Π|_{𝔸_{F^+}^×} = 1 and the claim holds. Independent check: Construction 3.1.10 checked on the image of p. 142, with Π cuspidal on GL_N(𝔸_F) (p. 138). At an inert unramified v, c(ϖ_v) = ϖ_v and Π∘c ≃ Π^∨ give α = α^{−1} as multisets. Hence (−T)^N P_α(T^{−1}) = (∏α_i)P_α(T), and unitarity (Definition 3.1.3(1)) is equivalent to ω_Π(ϖ_v) = 1. ω_Π restricted to 𝔸_{F⁺}^× is quadratic and trivial on norms, so it is 1 or η_{F/F⁺}. The counterexample works: χ extending η_{F/F⁺} exists by Pontryagin duality and is unramified almost everywhere by continuity. It satisfies χ∘c = χ^{−1}, and α(χ_v) = {−1} is not unitary for N = 1, since that would force α = {1}. For relevant Π (Definition 1.1.3(3)), the archimedean central character is arg^{Σ(N+1−2i)} = 1. This excludes η, which is the sign character at real places, so the claim holds wherever the construction is used. Versions: same in v1 and v3.

issues.printed: The source claims that Hypothesis 3.2.10 makes Q(Π) a strong coefficient field for Π when Π ≃ BC(π) comes from a standard pair (V, π) as in Definition 3.2.7, with V standard indefinite.
issues.correction: Either add the hypothesis that ρ_{Π,ι_ℓ} is irreducible for every ι_ℓ and give the descent argument, or delete the sentence. It is never used: all results take a strong coefficient field E as given, and one exists by [16, Proposition 3.2.5].
issues.reason: Hypothesis 3.2.10 only says something when ρ_{BC(π),ι_ℓ} is irreducible, which the remark does not assume and which is not known in general for relevant Π. Even granting irreducibility, the natural Q(Π)_λ-rational object is the φ_Π-eigenpart M of H^{N−1}_ét(Sh(V,K)_{F̄}, Q(Π)_λ). By the hypothesis, M ⊗ ℚ̄_ℓ ≃ (ρ^c)^{⊕d}, and ρ^c is defined over Q(Π)_λ only if the central simple algebra End_{Γ_F}(M) splits. The remark gives no argument for this. Defence: the claim is plausible (for instance, a Frobenius with an eigenvalue of multiplicity one in Q(Π)_λ would split it), and nothing depends on it.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on pp. 145–146: Remark 3.2.6 asserts that under Hypothesis 3.2.10 ℚ(Π) is a strong coefficient field, with no argument, while Hypothesis 3.2.10 only says something when ρ_{BC(π),ι} is irreducible, which the remark does not assume; even then descending ρ^c to ℚ(Π)_λ needs the relevant endomorphism algebra to split. Unused elsewhere (a strong coefficient field is taken as given).

issues.locator: Proposition 3.2.11 and its proof, published p. 146; reference [37], p. 374; arXiv v3 p. 28; v1 p. 27 (Proposition 3.2.10)
issues.printed: Proposition 3.2.11 declares Hypothesis 3.2.10 valid when N ⩽ 3, or when N > 3 with F+ ≠ Q. Its proof assigns the N ⩾ 3, F+ ≠ Q cases to a future proof in [37]. That entry is an unfinished work by Kisin, Shin and Zhu, provisionally titled as a study of cohomology for certain abelian-type Shimura varieties.
issues.correction: State the cases N ⩾ 3 with F⁺ ≠ ℚ of Proposition 3.2.11 as conditional on [37] (or on Hypothesis 3.2.10). Carry that condition into Theorems 1.1.1, 1.1.5, 1.1.7 and 1.1.9, which all assume F⁺ ≠ ℚ, for every n ⩾ 2 and not only for n ⩾ 3, since N = n₁ ⩾ 3 always occurs; and into Corollaries 8.2.3 and 8.2.5 whenever F⁺ ≠ ℚ. As printed, those corollaries assume only '(c) F⁺ ≠ ℚ if n ⩾ 3'. Their remaining case n = 2, F⁺ = ℚ does not use [37], because Hypothesis 3.2.10 for N = 2, 3 over ℚ comes from [48] and [64], but it has its own gap, E105.
issues.reason: For N > 3 the proposition is proved only by a forward reference to a work that the bibliography lists as 'in preparation' with a temporary title. Nothing in the paper establishes it. It is used as a known input: the proof of Corollary 8.2.3 (p. 314) says 'By Proposition 3.2.11 and (c), Hypothesis 3.2.10 is known in this case'. Remark 1.1.10 (p. 113) explains that the assumption F^+ ≠ ℚ for n ≥ 3 in Theorems 1.1.5 and 1.1.9 is there because Hypothesis 3.2.10 is known for N ≥ 4 only when F^+ ≠ ℚ. Defence: the dependence is stated openly. Whether the later Kisin–Shin–Zhu work establishes exactly Hypothesis 3.2.10 in this generality was not checked here. Independent check: Checked on the image of p. 146 and in the bibliography, p. 374: '[37] Kisin, M., Shin, S.W., Zhu, Y.: Cohomology of certain Shimura varieties of abelian type (temporary title) (in preparation)'. The proof says 'The case for N ⩾ 3 when F⁺ ≠ ℚ will be proved in [37]', so N = 3 with F⁺ ≠ ℚ is deferred too; [64], Rogawski's Picard-surface work, covers only F⁺ = ℚ. Theorems 8.2.2/8.3.2 assume Hypothesis 3.2.10 for n and n+1 and are fine as conditional statements. The unconditional results take the hypothesis from Proposition 3.2.11: Corollary 8.2.3 on p. 314 ('By Proposition 3.2.11 and (c), Hypothesis 3.2.10 is known'), Corollary 8.2.5, and Theorems 1.1.1, 1.1.5, 1.1.7 and 1.1.9. All of these assume F⁺ ≠ ℚ and need N = n₁ ⩾ 3, so each depends on [37] for every n ⩾ 2, including n = 2. The KSZ paper that did appear (arXiv:2110.05381, 'The stable trace formula for Shimura varieties of abelian type') proves only a Frobenius–Hecke trace formula. Its §0.2 says: 'We intend to work out the details in a sequel', and lists LTXZZ among the intended applications. So it does not itself establish Hypothesis 3.2.10.
searched: arXiv:1912.11942 v1 (December 2019), v2 and v3 (August 2021) at the same place: v1 p. 27 (Proposition 3.2.10: '… for N > 3 if [F+ : Q] > 1 … will be proved in [KSZ]'); v3 p. 28 identical to the published text.

issues.locator: Definition 3.3.4, footnote 11, published p. 147; arXiv v3 p. 28 (footnote 11)
issues.printed: The source claims equivalence with requiring [F+q : Qp] to be odd for each prime q of F+ lying above p and inert in F.
issues.correction: Delete the footnote or replace it with a correct criterion. Let M be the Galois closure of F, σ the Frobenius at 𝔭 (for ι_p inducing 𝔭), and H ⊆ Gal(M/ℚ) the subgroup generated by the stabilizers of the CM types of F. Then 𝔭 is very special inert iff σc ∈ H. The footnote's condition is equivalent to something else: that some CM type Φ ∋ τ_∞ satisfies σ²Φ = Φ, i.e. ℚ_p^Φ = ℚ_{p²}, which is condition (P3)/(PI3) of §§6–7.
issues.reason: (i) The footnote's condition does not imply very special. Take F = ℚ(√(−(3+√2))) (minimal polynomial x⁴ + 6x² + 7, Galois group D_4, F^+ = ℚ(√2)) and p = 17. Then 17 = 𝔭𝔮 in F^+, with √2 ≡ 6 at 𝔭. At 𝔭, −3 + √2 ≡ 3 is a non-square mod 17, so 𝔭 is inert in F. At 𝔮, −3 + √2 ≡ 8 = 5², so 𝔮 splits in F. 17 is odd and unramified in F (the polynomial discriminant is 2^{10}·7), and 𝔭 has degree 1, so 𝔭 is special inert. The only prime above 17 that is inert in F is 𝔭, of odd degree 1, so the footnote declares 𝔭 very special. But the CM types of F are primitive with reflex fields of real quadratic subfield ℚ(√7) (√7 = √(−3+√2)·√(−3−√2)), so ⋂_Φ F_Φ = ℚ(√7). Hence F_rflx = F(√7) = M and F^+_rflx = ℚ(√2, √7). Since (7/17) = −1, 𝔭 is inert in F^+_rflx/F^+ and is not very special. (ii) Very special does not imply the footnote's condition. Take F a CM octic field with Gal(M/ℚ) = W(B_4) = (ℤ/2)^4 ⋊ S_4 (a generic F = F^+(√−δ) with F^+ an S_4-quartic). Then H = {(ε, π) : Σε_i even}, which has index 2 and contains c, so 𝔭 is very special iff the number of primes of F^+ above p that are inert in F is even. A Frobenius σ = ((1,1,0,0), (2 3)) (it exists by Chebotarev) gives 𝔭 inert of degree 1, 𝔮 inert of degree 2 and 𝔮′ split of degree 1. There are two inert primes, so 𝔭 is very special, but 𝔮 has even degree. Moreover σ² interchanges τ and τ^c for the embeddings above 𝔮, so no CM type is σ²-stable and (P3) fails. Defence: no proof uses the footnote. Lemma 8.1.4 uses only 'φ_𝔭 ∈ Gal(F̄/F^+_rflx)', which is the definition. In the cases of Remark 1.1.8 (F Galois or containing an imaginary quadratic field) the definition and the footnote both reduce to 'special inert'. The footnote does mislead anyone checking hypothesis (a) of Theorem 1.1.7. Independent check: Footnote 11 and the definitions were checked on the image of p. 147. Let M be the Galois closure of F, σ the Frobenius at 𝔭, and H = ⟨Stab Φ⟩, which is normal. Then Gal(M/F_rflx) = Gal(M/F) ∩ H, so a special inert 𝔭 is very special iff σc ∈ H. The footnote's condition is equivalent to the existence of Φ ∋ τ_∞ with σ²Φ = Φ, i.e. (P3). I checked all of this by machine: I enumerated every σ with σ(τ_∞) = τ_∞^c in D₄ and in W(B₄). There the footnote condition is always equivalent to (P3), while 'very special' differs in both directions. (i) D₄: x⁴+6x²+7 has discriminant 2¹⁰·7. Mod 17 it factors as (x−5)(x+5)(x²−3), H = V₄ ∋ c, and ⋂F_Φ = ℚ(√7). Since (7/17) = −1, the degree-one prime inert in F is not very special, though it meets the footnote. Small slip: for F = ℚ(√(−(3+√2))), the inert prime is the one with √2 ≡ −6 mod 17 (−3−√2 ≡ 3); at √2 ≡ 6, −3−√2 ≡ 8 = 5², which splits. The conclusion is unchanged after relabelling. (ii) Explicit W(B₄) instance: F⁺ = ℚ(α) with α⁴−4α²−α+1 = 0, which is totally real with disc 1957 and group S₄, and F = F⁺(√−(α+4)). Since N(α+4) = 197 is not a square in ℚ(√1957), Gal = W(B₄); Frobenius cycle-type frequencies for p < 20000 match. H is the even-sign subgroup, M^H = ℚ(√197) and F⁺_rflx = F⁺(√197). At p = 43, f ≡ (x−3)(x−11)·(quadratic), and the degree-8 polynomial has type [1,1,2,4]. 𝔭 = (43, α−11) is special inert, since −(α+4) ≡ 28 is a non-square, and it splits in F⁺_rflx because 197 ≡ 5² mod 43. So 𝔭 is very special, but the degree-2 prime above 43 is inert in F: the footnote fails, and no CM type Φ ∋ τ_∞ has ℚ_43^Φ = ℚ_{43²}. No proof cites the footnote. Versions: absent in v1/v2; present in v3 (composite definition), where example (i) still refutes it.
searched: arXiv:1912.11942 v1 (December 2019), v2 and v3 (August 2021) at the same place: v1 and v2 (p. 28) have no footnote. v3 p. 28 has the same footnote attached to the v3 definition (F_rflx generated by F and all F_Φ; 𝔭 very special iff some 𝔭′ | 𝔭 of F^+_rflx has degree one). Example (i) refutes it there too, since in that example the v3 F^+_rflx is also ℚ(√2, √7).

issues.citation: Liu et al., "On the Beilinson–Bloch–Kato conjecture for Rankin–Selberg motives", Inventiones Mathematicae (2022)
issues.reviewReason: Checked on p. 147 (footnote 11 against Definitions 3.3.2 and 3.3.4). Example (i) checks: F = ℚ(√(−3−√2)) is a non-Galois (D₄) CM quartic with F⁺ = ℚ(√2); since (−3−√2)(−3+√2) = 7 and (7/17) = −1, of the two degree-one primes of F⁺ above 17 (√2 ≡ ±6) one is inert in F and the other splits, so the footnote's condition holds and calls the inert one very special. The reflex fields of the CM types meet in their common real quadratic subfield ℚ(√7), so F⁺_rflx = ℚ(√2, √7), and 𝔭 (with ℚ_17 completion) is inert there because (7/17) = −1: not very special. I did not re-check example (ii).

issues.locator: Definition 3.3.2, published p. 147 (and its use in Definition 8.1.1 (L5-2), p. 303, and in the choice of 𝔭 in the proofs of Theorem 8.2.2, p. 310, and Theorem 8.3.2, pp. 318–319); arXiv v3 p. 28
issues.printed: The source defines the reflexive closure Frflx of F by adjoining to F the intersection of all FΦ, indexed by the CM types Φ of F, and taking the resulting subfield of C.
issues.correction: Make the Chebotarev choice in §8 give (PI3). Options: (1) restore the v1–v3 composite, and correct Remarks 1.1.8 and 3.3.3 for non-Galois F. (2) Define F_rflx := F·F̃_{Φ₀}, where F̃_{Φ₀} is the Galois closure of the reflex field of one fixed CM type Φ₀. Then Frob_𝔭 fixing F⁺_rflx gives σ_𝔭 = c·h with h stabilizing Φ₀ and cΦ₀, hence σ_𝔭² does too, which is (PI3). This keeps F_rflx = F when F is Galois or contains an imaginary quadratic field K (take Φ₀ induced from K). (3) Keep the definition, add Frob_𝔭|_M = c to the Chebotarev conditions, and prove compatibility, e.g. M ∩ F⁺^{(m)}F_S ⊆ F_rflx. Options (1) and (2) narrow 'admissible' and 'very special'.
issues.reason: In the proof of Theorem 8.2.2 (p. 310), γ is taken in the image of Gal(F̄/F^+_rflx) by (L5-2), and then 'by the Chebotarev density theorem' a γ-associated place is chosen whose prime 𝔭 is special inert and satisfies (PI1)–(PI7). Condition (PI3) (p. 287) requires a CM type Φ ∋ τ_∞ with ℚ_p^Φ = ℚ_{p²}, i.e. σ_𝔭² ∈ Stab(Φ). The same choice is made on pp. 318–319. Under the published definition, Frob_𝔭 ∈ Gal(F̄/F^+_rflx) only gives σ_𝔭c ∈ H (the group generated by the CM-type stabilizers), and example (ii) of the footnote-11 issue gives such 𝔭 with no σ²-stable CM type. In addition, a γ-associated place is constrained only on F^{(m)}_+ and F_S, so its Frobenius on M must be imposed separately, and the paper does not address whether that is compatible. Under the v1–v3 definition, a lift of γ to Gal(F̄/F^+_rflx) = Gal(F̄/M^+) acts on M as c, so (PI3) is automatic. Defence: if F is Galois or contains an imaginary quadratic field (Remark 1.1.8), every special inert prime satisfies (PI3). For generic data M is linearly disjoint from F^{(m)}_+F_S over F, and Frob_𝔭|_M = c can be imposed. Independent check: Checked on the images of p. 147 (intersection definition), p. 303 ((L5-2) with F′ = F⁺_rflx), p. 287 ((PI3)) and pp. 310, 318–319. There γ is taken in the image of Gal(F̄/F⁺_rflx), and 'by the Chebotarev density theorem' a γ-associated special inert 𝔭 satisfying (PI1)–(PI7) is chosen; then 'remaining data in Sect. 5.1 with ℚ_p^Φ = ℚ_{p²}'. F_rflx enters the paper only through (L5-2), Lemma 8.1.4 and these choices of γ, so its only role is to deliver (PI3)/(PII3). No hypothesis of Theorems 8.2.2/8.3.2 supplies (PI3) otherwise: not the §7.1 setup, not Hypothesis 3.2.10, not (L1)–(L7). The implicit argument makes Frob_𝔭 fix F⁺_rflx, which is compatible with γ because γ comes from Gal(F̄/F⁺_rflx). Under the published intersection this only gives σ_𝔭 ∈ c·(Gal(M/F) ∩ H), which does not imply (PI3). The explicit W(B₄) field of E31 shows this: 𝔭 = (43, α−11) splits in F⁺_rflx = F⁺(√197), yet no CM type satisfies ℚ_43^Φ = ℚ_{43²}. Chebotarev gives such Frobenius classes a positive density inside the set the argument allows. Under v1–v3, F_rflx is the composite of F and all F_Φ, which equals M since only the identity fixes every CM type. There Frob_𝔭 ∈ Gal(F̄/M⁺) gives σ_𝔭 = c, so (PI3) is automatic. Imposing Frob_𝔭|_M = c directly is compatible when M ∩ F⁺^{(m)}F_S ⊆ F_rflx, e.g. for linearly disjoint (generic) data. It is not implied by (L1)–(L7) in general: if M ⊆ F⁺^{(m)}, then γ fixes Frob|_M. So a full repair may require narrowing (L5-2) and 'very special'. Versions: v1–v3 use the composite, and the change appears only in the published version, together with footnote 11.
searched: arXiv:1912.11942 v1 (December 2019), v2 and v3 (August 2021) at the same place: v1, v2 (p. 28) and v3 (p. 28) define F_rflx as 'the subfield of C generated by F and F_Φ for every CM type Φ of F'. With that definition Remark 3.3.3's 'F contains an imaginary quadratic field ⇒ F_rflx = F' is false for non-Galois F, which is presumably why the published version switched to the intersection.

issues.reviewReason: Checked on p. 147 against arXiv v3 Definition 3.3.2: v3 defines F_rflx as generated by F and F_Φ for every CM type Φ (the composite), the published version by F and the intersection of the F_Φ. The proofs of Theorems 8.2.2 and 8.3.2 obtain (PI3) (a CM type Φ with ℚ_p^Φ = ℚ_{p²}) only from Frob_𝔭 fixing F⁺_rflx via (L5-2) and Chebotarev; with the composite this forces σ_𝔭 = c on the Galois closure, with the intersection it does not. So the published proof has a gap at that step. I did not re-derive the W(B₄) example of E31(ii).

issues.locator: Notation 3.4.7, published p. 150; arXiv v3 p. 30
issues.printed: The source says that the quasi-polarization λ induces an OS-bilinear pairing, and that its being perfect is equivalent to λ being p-principal.
issues.correction: 'which is perfect if λ is p-principal, and, when p is locally nilpotent on S, only if'. Or restrict S to schemes on which p is locally nilpotent.
issues.reason: S ranges over Sch_{/ℤ_p^τ}, which includes ℚ_p^τ-schemes. On these, any quasi-isogeny induces an isomorphism on H^dR_1, so the pairing is perfect even when λ is not p-principal (for example, when ker(cλ) has p-power order). The 'if' direction and the characteristic-p uses are correct. Defence: everywhere the notation is applied in §§4–5, p is locally nilpotent or the 'if' direction is what is used.

issues.locator: Lemma 3.4.12 (hypotheses) and proof of (2), published pp. 153, 155; arXiv v3 p. 32; v1 p. 31 (Lemma 3.4.13)
issues.printed: The source assumes F+ lies in Qp through τ: F+ ↪ C ≃ Q̄p, with p denoting the resulting p-adic prime. In proving (2), it writes s = dimκ(ωB∨/κ,τc∞) = dimκ VD(B)τ∞ / pD(B)τc∞.
issues.correction: Add the hypothesis that 𝔭 is inert in F, and read τ as τ̲_∞. For (2), argue directly: Lie_{B,τ_∞} = 𝒟(B)_{τ_∞}/𝚅𝒟(B)_{στ_∞}, so s − r = ℓ(𝒟(B)_{τ_∞}/𝒟(A)_{τ_∞}) − ℓ(𝒟(B)_{στ_∞}/𝒟(A)_{στ_∞}), and στ_∞ = τ_∞^c for 𝔭 inert. This needs no polarization.
issues.reason: As stated, 𝔭 may split in F, and then (2) fails. Take F^+ = ℚ, F imaginary quadratic with p = w_1w_2 split, ϖ = p, E an ordinary elliptic curve over 𝔽̄_p with O_F-action, A = E, B = E/E[w_1], α the quotient map and β: B → E/E[p] ≅ E, so that βα = p. With τ_∞ corresponding to w_1, α_{*,τ_∞} = 0 and α_{*,τ_∞^c} is an isomorphism, so the right side of (2) is 1 − 0 = 1. But B[w^∞] ≅ E[w^∞] for both w, so the Lie ranks agree and the left side is 0. The proof uses σ^{−1}τ_∞^c = τ_∞, i.e. 𝔭 inert. Separately, its first equality s = dim ω_{B^∨,τ_∞^c} needs dim Lie_{B,τ_∞} + dim Lie_{B,τ_∞^c} = rank H^dR_1(B)_{τ_∞^c}, which holds for unitary schemes (a compatible polarization makes B[𝔭^∞] isogenous to its dual) but is not assumed in (2). Parts (1), (3) and (4) are fine; the degree computation in (3)/(4) was checked. Defence: every application (pp. 168, 170, 197, 202, 206, 210) has 𝔭 special inert and unitary A, B, and S ∈ Sch_{/𝔽_{p²}} points to the inert case. Independent check: Lemma 3.4.12 checked on the images of pp. 153–155. The hypotheses only require F⁺_𝔭 = ℚ_p, not that 𝔭 is inert in F. Split counterexample: F⁺ = ℚ, p = w₁w₂, A = E ordinary with O_F-action, B = E/E[w₁], β∘α = [p]. On Dieudonné modules α_{*,τ_∞} ≡ 0 and α_{*,τ_∞^c} is an isomorphism, so the right side of (2) is 1. But B[w^∞] ≅ E[w^∞] for both w, so the Lie ranks agree and the left side is 0. The proof's step 'ω_{B^∨,τ_∞^c} = V𝒟(B)_{τ_∞}/p𝒟(B)_{τ_∞^c}' uses στ_∞^c = τ_∞; by Notation 3.4.10(3) this holds only for 𝔭 inert. I checked the first reading's polarization-free argument: s − r = ℓ(𝒟(B)_τ/𝒟(A)_τ) − ℓ(𝒟(B)_{στ}/𝒟(A)_{στ}), and ℓ(𝒟(B)_τ/𝒟(A)_τ) = dim ker α_{*,τ} because p𝒟(B)_τ ⊆ 𝒟(A)_τ. With στ = τ^c this gives (2). In the split case στ = τ, which gives 0, consistent with the counterexample. All six uses (pp. 168, 170, 197, 202, 206, 210) sit in §§4–5, where 𝔭 is special inert (§4.1). Versions: same in v1 (Lemma 3.4.13) and v3.

issues.reason: By Remark 3.4.6 the τ-part of the Hodge filtration ω_{A^∨,τ} ⊆ H₁^dR(A)_τ has rank N − r_τ. For A₀ (rank 1, signature Φ ∋ τ∞) r_{τ∞} = 1, so ω_{A₀^∨,τ∞} = 0 and the printed condition α(0) ⊆ ω_{A^∨,τ∞} is vacuous: the printed set is all of Hom_F(H₁^dR(A₀/C), H₁^dR(A/C)), not a line. For A (signature NΦ − τ∞ + τ∞^c) ω_{A^∨,τ∞} has rank 1, so Hom(H₁^dR(A₀)_{τ∞}, ω_{A^∨,τ∞}) is a line; it is the (1,−1)-part of the weight-0 Hodge structure V_x ⊗_{τ∞} C = Hom(H^{−1,0}(A₀)_{τ∞}, H^{−1,0}(A)_{τ∞} ⊕ H^{0,−1}(A)_{τ∞}), which is the negative line for the signature (N−1,1). Reading the condition at τ∞^c instead (ω_{A₀^∨,τ∞^c} = H₁^dR(A₀)_{τ∞^c} of rank 1, ω_{A^∨,τ∞^c} of rank N−1) gives a hyperplane, so no reading of the printed formula yields a line.
